title: Police searching for missing 15-year-old Boston girl
text:
Boston police are seeking the public’s help in locating a 15-year-old girl, who has not been seen for three weeks.

Briyana Jacques, a resident of the city’s Dorchester neighborhood, was last spotted leaving her Rosedale Street home for school on the morning of Tuesday, May 19. She was wearing a black zip-up jacket and gray sweatpants at the time. Authorities received a report of a missing person on Saturday, May 23.

“Jacques is described as a Black female, approximately 5 feet 5 inches tall, weighing approximately 120 pounds, with a slender build and medium brown skin,” police said, adding that she has brown hair “with some red coloring, worn in lengthy box braids.”

Since she was reported missing, the teenager has had limited contact with family and friends, authorities noted.

Boston police ask that anyone with information related to her whereabouts call 911 or B-3 detectives at 617-343-2309.

title: Family remembers woman killed in Mattapan carjacking crash as a ‘beautiful soul’
text:
Relatives are remembering 32-year-old Mabinty Janneh for her “beautiful soul” as newly available footage shows the Dorchester woman trying in vain to run from the carjacking suspect who allegedly struck and killed her in Mattapan Saturday.

“Her life was tragically taken far too soon, leaving our family heartbroken and struggling to come to terms with this unimaginable loss,” Janneh’s relatives wrote in a GoFundMe to help cover her funeral expenses.

Prosecutors allege Ibraim Matos, 37, of Hyde Park, was driving a stolen car when he jumped the curb and sped down the sidewalk along Blue Hill Avenue in Mattapan Saturday afternoon.

Surveillance footage obtained by Boston 25 News appears to show Matos carjacking a woman outside a Mattapan car wash before getting behind the wheel and driving the wrong way down Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square. In additional video published by WCVB, Janneh and other pedestrians can be seen running for cover as the SUV hurtles down the sidewalk.

Prosecutors say Janneh was struck and dragged “several hundred feet.” She was ultimately pronounced dead at the scene.

Matos has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder, carjacking, leaving the scene of personal injury, leaving the scene of personal injury and death, and motor vehicle homicide by reckless operation. He was held without bail Monday and ordered to undergo an evaluation at Bridgewater State Hospital ahead of his next court date July 10.

In the meantime, Janneh’s relatives say they are “committed to seeking justice for Mabinty and ensuring that her life is honored and remembered,” according to the GoFundMe.

“She deserved so much more, and we will continue to fight for her voice to be heard,” the family added.

The GoFundMe had raised just shy of $4,500 as of Tuesday afternoon.

“Mabinty was a beautiful soul whose kindness, love, and hardworking spirit touched everyone who had the privilege of knowing her,” her family wrote. “She was a devoted family member, a loyal friend, and someone who always put others before herself.”

title: Lakeville man, 19, killed in Dorchester shooting
text:
A 19-year-old Lakeville man was fatally shot Monday night in Dorchester, authorities said.

Officers responded shortly after 7:30 p.m. to reports of a person shot near 115 Milton Ave., the Boston Police Department said in a community alert.

Officers found the victim, identified as Jalen J. Tavares, at 6 Seldon St., suffering from a gunshot wound, the department said.

Emergency medical personnel pronounced Tavares dead at the scene, police said.

No arrests have been made, and investigators have not identified a suspect, a BPD spokesperson told Boston.com.

The department’s Homicide Unit is investigating the shooting. Police are asking anyone with information to contact the unit at 617-343-4470.

As of Tuesday afternoon, there have been no updates in the investigation, the BPD spokesperson said.

title: Man convicted after breaking into the wrong Boston apartment and murdering resident
text:
A Boston man was convicted of first-degree murder in the 2015 killing of a Dorchester man after prosecutors said he and two accomplices mistakenly entered the victim’s apartment while looking for someone else.

A Suffolk Superior Court jury on Thursday found Victor Arrington, 40, guilty of first-degree murder, home invasion, armed assault with intent to murder, unlawful possession of a firearm, and two counts of kidnapping, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden announced. Arrington is scheduled to be sentenced on Tuesday.

Under Massachusetts law, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The verdict came after Arrington’s first trial ended in a mistrial in May 2024 when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.

Prosecutors said Arrington and two other men planned to assault and rob a man who lived on Harvard Street in Dorchester on March 31, 2015. Instead, they forced their way into the apartment of Richard Long, 37, an ironworker and member of Iron Workers Local 7 who had no connection to the intended target.

According to prosecutors, the intruders bound Long and his fiancée with electrical cords. “Realizing that they had entered the wrong home, the men decided to kill Long and his fiancée to cover their tracks,” Hayden said.

Prosecutors said the men stabbed Long with a knife, shot him in the head, shot Long’s fiancée in the head, and poured bleach on their bodies before setting fire to the kitchen and fleeing. Long died at the scene. His fiancée regained consciousness and rescued the couple’s infant son from the apartment before escaping to a neighbor’s home for help.

Arrington was arrested in July 2016. A second defendant, James Boyd, 33, is charged with home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, and two counts of kidnapping. He is expected to change his plea on July 1, according to the district attorney’s office.

A third alleged accomplice was identified during the investigation but was never charged because he was killed in an unrelated homicide in April 2015, Hayden’s office said.

The retrial was also notable for prosecutors’ use of location information stored in the Frequent Location History feature on Arrington’s iPhone. Following an extensive evidentiary hearing, the court allowed prosecutors to present the digital evidence to jurors over the defense’s objection, according to the district attorney’s office.

“This team effort helped secure a just verdict in an extraordinarily harrowing case, notable not only for its shocking violence against completely innocent victims but also for the precedent it set in the use of advanced digital evidence,” Hayden said. “But most important of all is the opportunity for Richard Long’s family and loved ones to see someone held accountable for this terrible crime.”

title: Suspect flees after crowd throws drinks at lone BPD officer, prompting renewed staffing worries
text:
A suspect fled a Boston police officer who was attempting to arrest him Sunday night after crowds surrounding the officer threw alcoholic beverages and other items at him, according to a report. The incident prompted Boston’s largest police union to renew calls for higher staffing levels.

A bystander captured part of the incident on video, which was then viewed thousands of times on social media. It shows an officer chasing and struggling with another man, attempting unsuccessfully to place him in handcuffs. Beverages and cups are seen hitting the officer before the suspect flees.

The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association responded multiple times on social media, saying the altercation was life-threatening for the officer and calling for more staffing.

“The disrespect is disgraceful. This officer’s lucky to be alive. And, understaffing didn’t help him. Sending cops from one understaffed station to another is an absolute joke. Fewer cops means less safety,” the union said.

In a follow-up post, the union said the incident showed “Boston at its worst.”

An incident report written by the officer involved gives more context. He responded to the intersection of Old Road and Ellington Street in Dorchester just before 9:30 p.m. Sunday for reports of a disturbance with loud music. The officer found traffic “gridlocked” in the area. Between 100 and 150 people were there blocking the roads, along with “low riders, cars, mopeds, and dirt bikes.” The crowd was playing loud music and drinking alcohol, according to the police report.

The officer turned on his lights and sirens, parking his cruiser at the corner of the intersection. As he attempted to disperse the crowd, he saw a dirt bike with no rear license plate being driven by a man. The officer approached the bike, placed his hands on the handlebars, and told the man to get off the vehicle so that he could verify its registration status, according to the report.

The man allegedly refused to get off the dirt bike, telling the officer that it was registered and to look at the back of the bike. The officer believed this was an attempt to have him let go of the bike and allow the man to “make good on his escape.” The man then tried to drive away, but the bike toppled over. It brought the officer to the ground as well, which apparently caused his body camera to fall off his outer vest, according to the report.

The officer and the man continued to struggle, falling multiple times. The gathered crowd threw “various items,” including alcoholic beverages, at the officer. This intervention allowed the man to escape, the officer wrote. More police responded and later cleared the intersection.

“It should never be acceptable to assault a police officer or first responder. Anyone involved in this assault should be arrested and prosecuted and if convicted, a state sentence is warranted. As a city, we can’t allow this ongoing disrespect and violence against any police officer,” Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn said in a statement.

Staffing concerns driven by resignations and retirements have been an ongoing concern for police leaders and elected officials. Eleven Boston City Council members sponsored a hearing order in April about the topic. There was only one resignation in 2018, compared to 36 in 2022, according to the hearing order. Voluntary retirements rose from 17 in 2018 to 127 in 2022.

City law requires the Boston Police Department to maintain a minimum staffing level of 2,500 patrolmen at any given time. But only about 2,100 are available for duty at the moment, Lisa O’Brien, a BPD bureau chief, said at a hearing on the police overtime and staffing issues in May.

With the additional retirements and resignations, mandatory overtime has also been on the rise. Mayor Michelle Wu called public safety overtime spending a “significant long-term challenge” when she filed her initial budget proposal for fiscal year 2027. That proposal saw the lowest year-over-year spending increase since fiscal year 2010.

“New classes and management initiatives” are causing the number of overtime hours to “move in the right direction,” and the administration says it will continue working to make overtime spending “more predictable and manageable.”

Councilors held their hearing in May, but some expressed frustration that Police Commissioner Michael Cox did not attend in person to answer all their questions. They are working to schedule another hearing on the two intertwined topics.

“Being expected to come back for a hearing that will probably last an hour, an hour-and-a-half, and not showing the respect to the body who funds his salary and all of the good work the police do, I think is insulting,” Councilor Erin Murphy said.

title: Officers shot at during Dorchester traffic stop, police say, prompting outcry from union
text:
Two Boston police officers narrowly escaped injury Wednesday night after a man allegedly opened fire on them during a subject stop in Dorchester, police said.

Officers responded to a report of “an officer in trouble” near the intersection of Devon Street and Laredo Street around 9:10 p.m., the Boston Police Department said in a statement.

Police said the officers were conducting a stop when they questioned a man, who then fled on foot and allegedly fired a gun in their direction. Authorities later found ballistic damage to the windshield of a Boston police cruiser, according to the department.

The suspect, identified by police as 20-year-old Rasiel Joel Carbuccia, of Jamaica Plain, allegedly ran down Devon Street toward Normandy Street, cutting through backyards as officers pursued him.

Authorities said Carbuccia was taken into custody near 8 Stanwood St. after allegedly attempting to flee again by climbing fences and ignoring officers’ commands.

The two officers were taken to local hospitals for evaluation, but did not suffer any physical injuries, police said.

In a statement, Police Commissioner Michael Cox praised the officers for their “immense bravery and professionalism” and said he was grateful they were able to return home safely.

“This incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers our officers face every day to protect this community,” Cox said. “To anyone who chooses to commit crime and attempts to inflict harm on our officers: we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will hold you fully accountable under the law.”

The shooting also drew a response from the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, which called on elected officials to condemn the attack.

“When criminals start shooting at police officers, everyone should be outraged and concerned,” the police union wrote on X. “Police officers have a right to go home safe[ly] to their families. They deserve to be protected.”

“Normalizing violence against our police officers puts everyone in peril,” the post concludes.

Carbuccia is charged with two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carrying a firearm without a license, carrying a loaded firearm without a license, possessing ammunition without an FID card, discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a building, possessing a large capacity firearm, possessing a covert or undetectable firearm, possessing a large capacity feeding device, and trespassing, court records show.

Police also said a records check showed Carbuccia was wanted on an active Roxbury District Court warrant charging assault with a dangerous weapon.

Investigators recovered what police described as a ghost gun with no serial number, as well as a projectile along the suspect’s flight path. The firearm contained one spent shell casing lodged in the chamber and a large-capacity magazine loaded with 16 live rounds, according to police.

Carbuccia pleaded not guilty at his arraignment Thursday morning. He was ordered held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing scheduled for July 28, court records show.

Attorney information for Carbuccia was not immediately available Thursday evening.

title: Wu, Army Corps of Engineers release $10B plan to prevent $41B in future flood damage
text:
Add Boston.com on Google (opens in a new tab)

Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.

Boston residents could eventually see new flood walls, berms, floodgates, and other coastal defenses stretching across 16 miles of the city’s shoreline under a plan released Monday that aims to protect neighborhoods from rising seas and increasingly severe coastal storms.

The draft plan from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) outlines more than 20 projects to close areas along Boston’s 47-mile coastline that are prone to flooding, with the baseline infrastructure expected to cost about $10 billion, Mayor Michelle Wu’s office said in a press release.

The draft report also details proposed infrastructure options for Boston’s coastal flooding protection, which include floodwalls, floodgates, and berms, Wu’s office said.

Advertisement:

“Boston leads with bold action to protect our communities and our future,” Wu said in the release. “The future of our city depends on the steps we take now to build resilient communities. With more frequent flooding in vulnerable areas during extreme weather events, the Coastal Storm Risk Management Feasibility Study is critical to understanding how to protect inland neighborhoods most at risk and unlocking resources to take action.”

The study, expected to be completed in 2028, would prevent an estimated $41 billion in flood damage by securing 65 percent of construction costs for coastal resilience projects from the federal government, according to Wu’s office.

Advertisement:

About 40 percent of Boston residents live in areas vulnerable to coastal flooding, according to USACE. Without additional protections, officials estimate roughly 20,000 buildings could face severe flooding as sea levels rise and storms become more intense, Wu’s office noted. The plan focuses on the city’s shoreline in East Boston, Charlestown, Dorchester, downtown, the North End, and South Boston.

The draft is open for public comment through Sept. 18 before the study is finalized.

“Today marks a major milestone in our shared mission of community resilience,” Deputy Commander of the New England District of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers David MacPhail said in a statement. “The reality is that doing nothing is not a viable option. Without action, the costs to public safety and economic vitality from coastal flooding will only be compounded.”

title: Family identifies woman, 18, found dead in home owned by Ayanna Pressley’s husband
text:
Family members have identified the young woman found dead Saturday inside a Mattapan rental home owned by Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley’s husband, describing the teenager as a “beautiful spirit” who died as the result of domestic violence.

Yoseliani Marte, 18, was “deeply loved by her family, friends, and everyone whose life she touched,” her mother wrote in a GoFundMe to help cover the cost of her burial.

Authorities have not publicly identified the person found shot inside 25 Malta St. shortly before 2 p.m. Saturday, nor have they announced any related arrests. In fact, the Boston Police Department has said little about the circumstances of Marte’s death, though an incident report notes that she died of a single gunshot wound.

Marte’s mother, Elenie Ocasio, says her daughter was killed in an act of domestic violence that “has taken a beautiful young life far too soon,” according to the GoFundMe. She also told Boston 25 News she knows who may be responsible.

“This coward killed my baby. He put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house, and left her to die,” she told the news outlet.

It was not immediately clear whether Marte lived at the Malta Street home. While Pressley’s husband, Conan Harris, is the property’s listed owner, the couple does not live there. Pressley’s office told The Boston Globe Saturday she “extends her deepest condolences to the impacted family.”

Writing on the GoFundMe page, Ocasio described her daughter’s death as an “unimaginable loss.”

“No words can truly express the pain of losing someone so young, with so many dreams, hopes, and milestones still ahead of her,” she said. “Her kindness, beautiful spirit, and bright future will never be forgotten.”

Shea Butter Smoothies in Dorchester identified Marte as one of its employees and praised her as a “brilliant and motivated young lady” who “brought joy and positivity to our workplace.”

“Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many,” the shop wrote on Facebook. “She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

For now, Ocasio told Boston 25 she’s focused on getting justice for Marte.

“My daughter didn’t deserve this,” she said. “My daughter did not deserve this, and it’s all going to come out to light. Everything’s gonna come out.”

title: Transit advocates call the Orange Line extension proposal 'not very serious.' Two Boston councilors say it's overdue.
text:
Two Boston city councilors recently proposed extending the Orange Line as an alternative to the divisive center-running bus lane planned for Blue Hill Avenue, igniting a debate over whether the city should pursue immediate bus improvements or a decades-long rail expansion.

“We should have the community decide, and what we’ve heard from community members is that they do not want the center-running bus lane down Blue Hill Ave.,” Councilor Brian Worrell said of the proposal he made alongside his colleague, Miniard Culpepper. “So if they don’t want the center-running bus lane, let’s provide them with multiple different options.”

Blue Hill Avenue runs through Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan — neighborhoods with some of Boston’s largest Black populations. Situated between the Orange and Red lines, the corridor is home to some of the city’s busiest bus routes, but lacks rapid rail service.

In 2024, the city, MBTA, and federal government committed roughly $44 million, in addition to a $80 million federal grant, to redesign the part of Blue Hill Avenue between River Street in Mattapan and Warren Street on the border of Dorchester and Roxbury.

The project would include the center-running bus lane, with construction scheduled to begin in 2027, per the MBTA’s Blue Hill Avenue Transportation Action Plan.

The center-running bus lane stirred controversy, with many arguing it would worsen traffic and eliminate parking for local businesses. On June 24 of this year, Worrell and Culpepper proposed their alternative: extending the Orange Line from Ruggles station to Mattapan Square.

The councilors argue the city should study bringing rapid transit to the corridor rather than committing to the dedicated bus lane. Transit advocates, however, say the rail proposal lacks details and could delay improvements that bus riders need now.

Unreliable buses, frequent crashes on Blue Hill Avenue point to need for improvements

As detailed in the MBTA’s Blue Hill Avenue Transportation Action Plan, the corridor between River and Warren streets serves 10 highly utilized bus routes. Riders make about 20,000 bus trips along Blue Hill Avenue each week and collectively lose 3,056 hours sitting in traffic.

The corridor also sees a crash requiring EMS response every three days, on average, according to the MBTA.

For Jackie Jones, of Dorchester, unreliable bus service has become part of her daily routine. Jones, a Boston Public Schools bus driver, relies on the Route 31 bus from Mattapan to Morton Street to get to work by 5 a.m. Recently, she said buses have been arriving as much as 30 minutes later than expected, causing her to be late for work.

She said she regularly reports the delays to the MBTA, but has grown frustrated by the response.

“‘Sorry’ ain’t cutting it,” Jones told Boston.com. “I can’t keep telling my boss that I’m late for work, and I told them, ‘If I get fired, who’s gonna pay my bills?’”

Not everyone is sold on a center-running bus lane

While few disagree that Blue Hill Avenue needs improvements, residents remain divided over the city’s proposed solutions.

While shorter-term investments have already been completed, the center-running bus lane intended to expedite service and improve safety is meant to be the centerpiece of the 2024 redesign.

Opponents argue the bus lane would reduce traffic lanes, eliminate street parking, and hurt small businesses that rely on customers arriving by car.

In June, residents opposing the plan asked the Trump administration to rescind the $80 million federal grant, with more than 2,150 people signing a petition calling for the center-running bus lane to be scrapped.

Jones said she worries narrowing the roadway could create safety issues, particularly as scooters and other vehicles share the corridor. Instead, she said she’d rather see buses become more reliable without redesigning the street.

Culpepper, who lives near Blue Hill Avenue on Seaver Street, echoed those concerns.

“It’s highly congested with the two lanes at Blue Hill Avenue,” he said. “Can you imagine what it’s going to be like if it’s cut down to one lane?”

Not everyone sees the project that way.

Natalie DeLaCruz, who commutes from Jackson Square to Mattapan, said her trip often requires taking the Orange Line and then transferring to a Route 29 or 31 bus. The commute can take more than an hour, and the buses are frequently overcrowded, she said.

“I know the people that live in Mattapan have different opinions,” she said, “but for me, I think it would make the traffic less congested and maybe make that hour [commute] a little bit shorter.”

A new proposal shifts the debate

Rather than redesign Blue Hill Avenue around buses, Culpepper and Worrell want to bring rapid rail service back to the corridor.

The councilors’ proposal would branch the Orange Line at Ruggles, with new underground rail stops at Nubian Square, MLK Boulevard (and Warren Street), Grove Hall, the Franklin Park Zoo, Harvard Street-Blue Hill Avenue, Morton Street-Blue Hill Avenue, Walk Hill Street-Blue Hill Avenue, and Mattapan Square.

Culpepper and Worrell said the proposal grew out of residents’ opposition to the center-running bus lane.

“We knew that the community was strongly opposed to the center-running bus lane,” Culpepper said. “It’s been years that we’ve been fighting that, so we wanted to present an alternative that the community could get behind.”

The expanded Orange Line proposal remains in its early stages.

Following a June 24 meeting with interim MassDOT Secretary and MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng, Culpepper said Eng agreed to have the proposal reviewed through the MBTA’s process for evaluating potential rail expansions.

Culpepper said Eng also emphasized that underground rail offers the fastest and most reliable service because it avoids conflicts with vehicle traffic and pedestrians.

“The underground rail is the most efficient. That’s what we want,” Culpepper added. “We want what every other community has, and there’s no reason why we can’t have that.”

Mayor Michelle Wu’s office, however, is striking a more cautious tone, as indicated by a statement sent to Boston.com shortly after the councilors unveiled their proposal.

“The City is always looking to expand public transit access for our residents in partnership with the MBTA. However, digging new miles of subway tunnel under City streets would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment,” a city spokesperson said.

“Today, Boston has an opportunity to deliver more immediate improvements and beautification of the Blue Hill Ave corridor with nearly $150 million secured in state and federal funds,” the spokesperson continued. “As we continue to work with community members to incorporate feedback into the proposed project design, we are focused on ensuring improvements to speed up commutes, expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor, and boost quality of life for families in our neighborhoods.”

Transit advocates say bus improvements shouldn’t wait

While the Orange Line extension would take 15 to 20 years, the bus project is a more “near-term improvement,” said Cole Lewis, Bus and Mobility Hubs program manager for TransitMatters, a pro-public transit organization.

“We want people who use transportation in Dorchester, in Mattapan, in Roxbury to have quality and dignified access to transportation, and they shouldn’t be deprived of that just because they’re not served by rail at the moment,” he said. “They should be able to depend on when their bus will arrive … The amount of time that someone’s stuck in traffic [or] delayed on a bus should not be measured in hours.”

Lewis and the organization’s executive director, Caitlin Allen-Connelly, questioned whether the councilors’ project is ready to move beyond an idea.

“We don’t see it as a very serious transit proposal,” Lewis said. “They had the map, but it didn’t have things like operations considerations, funding considerations, any sort of timeline, and so we didn’t see it as something that was immediately actionable.”

Culpepper said the councilors have not yet developed a cost estimate for the proposed extension.

Allen-Connelly acknowledged that there have been previous discussions about extending the Orange Line to Roslindale, but that proposal differs because it could make use of existing rail infrastructure. Building an entirely new subway beneath Blue Hill Avenue, she said, would require significantly more time and investment.

Instead, Lewis said, the city should focus on making bus service faster and more reliable for the thousands of riders who already depend on it in the corridor. During rush hour, he noted, bus passengers make up more than half of the people traveling along Blue Hill Avenue.

“Only cars are being prioritized, and a lot of those cars are people coming from the suburbs or just passing through,” he said. “What we want to see is an investment in bus riders and a prioritization of bus riders that are making up such a huge amount of people who use the corridor.”

Councilors say the issue is more than just about transportation

Worrell and Culpepper announced the Orange Line proposal as a “long-promised-but-never-delivered transit expansion.”

“The first subway was here in Boston in 1897 and for it not to be in Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury in 2026 is completely mind-blowing and just shows the lack of seriousness when it comes to this corridor from our executives,” Worrell said.

Culpepper pointed to history, explaining that the Orange Line served the neighborhoods beginning in the early 1900s until it was demolished in a Southwest Corridor project in the 1980s.

“When we lost that, we lost any semblance of rail transportation for our community,” he said.

On social media, the councilors highlighted a 40-year history of “broken transit promises.”

In an Instagram post, Culpepper outlined four broken or partially delivered transit “promises.”

Some of these included the planned Green Line branch that was ultimately swapped for a Silver Line bus route and the delayed Fairmount Line stations. Officials were legally mandated to add Fairmount Line stations after a massive highway project in the 1990s generated air pollution and increased traffic. Three of the four “promised” stations opened in 2012, but the stop on Blue Hill Avenue wasn’t installed until 2019.

“When you look at the different rail investments around Boston and not in the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, that’s what you call a disparate impact,” Culpepper said.

He pointed to projects outside the corridor, including the Red Line’s Northwest Extension in 1981, the 2014 opening of the Orange Line’s Assembly Square Station, and the Green Line Extension completed in 2022.

Culpepper emphasized that many of these projects surrounding Blue Hill Avenue serve predominantly white populations.

Allen-Connelly, however, said the councilors’ focus on past issues, while “understandable,” is ultimately a “distraction” from providing corridor residents with the immediate transit improvements they need.

“I think a scenario where you’re improving people’s lives today is a better path forward than focusing on an option that’s not really realistic and is more a distraction to the conversation than is actually adding value to people’s lives and putting forward a plan,” she said.

What happens next?

According to city officials, the transit project that includes the center-running bus lane remains in the design phase, while the MBTA notes construction is set to begin next year. Wu’s office declined to comment further on its progress.

On the project’s website, city officials have specified the redesign “does not have to include center-running bus lanes.”

“The City does have an opinion on the benefits of bus priority and center-running lanes,” the page notes. “The City will only spend public money on a project with public support.”

Nearly three weeks since the Orange Line extension proposal, the city still appears to be focused on making more immediate improvements.

“It’s important to be honest that a proposal to dig new miles of subway tunnel under City streets would take years of evaluation and billions of dollars of federal investment to make it real,” Wu’s office said in a statement to Boston.com in mid-June, adding that the city can “deliver more immediate improvements and beautification” with current state and federal funding.

Even as they advocate for the Orange Line expansion, Culpepper and Worrell said the city should move forward with certain immediate, short-term solutions.

Culpepper suggested that short-term funding could be directed toward beautification investments, pedestrian safety, and ADA compliance.

“There are things that can begin now that they have the money for,” he said.

Worrell said the city could be focusing on implementing signal prioritization, fixing street lights, and improving crosswalks. He also recommended implementing an express bus stop at the highest ridership sites.

“There’s a whole host of recommendations that can be sought out prior to locking us into a bus-only future,” he said.

title: Boston teen dies while swimming at Milford quarry
text:
An outing with friends turned deadly when 17-year-old Yanick Rodrigues went swimming in the Shadowbrook Quarries in Milford, authorities and family said.

The Worcester County District Attorney’s Office identified the teen on Monday, after family shared the teen’s experience in an online obituary.

Rodrigues left Cape Verde in 2016 and moved to Dorchester. He was currently a senior at Madison Park High School in Roxbury.

“Everyone knew him as the kid who could do it all — a smooth soccer player with a bright smile and a strong drive to build a career as an automotive technician,” the obituary says.

Rodrigues and a group of friends went to Shadowbrook Quarries on Saturday for a swim.

After he entered the water, his friends realized he was in trouble and called for help.

The obituary says that more than 50 emergency personnel came to the quarry, including firefighters, police officers, and specialized dive teams. The crews worked through the evening and into the next morning. Dive teams ultimately located Rodrigues’s body 50 feet below the surface.

The Worcester County District Attorney’s Office is investigating the incident.

The death comes only a week after Milford police rescued an 18-year-old who had fallen from a ledge onto jagged rocks about 12 feet below at the quarries.

Police officers found the young woman conscious but bleeding from several areas while lying among broken bottles and leaves. The woman was transported to a local hospital for treatement.

“While we’re thankful this incident did not have an even more tragic outcome, it serves as an important reminder that the Quarries are not a safe place for recreation,” Milford Chief of Police Robert Tusino said in a statement, regarding the initial incident. “We continue to strongly discourage anyone from entering the property or swimming in the quarries.”

Tusino added that the steep rock faces, unstable terrain, and limited access for emergency responders create an “extremely dangerous environment where a single misstep can have life-altering consequences.”

title: Online and phone lottery games are now live in Mass. Here’s what to know.
text:
The Massachusetts State Lottery officially entered the digital age Monday, launching online games that allow players 21 and older to try their luck and shoot for the jackpot directly from their phones, computers, or tablets.

The long-awaited virtual platform, aptly dubbed Mass Lottery Online, features familiar favorites like Mega Millions and Powerball, as well as two new daily numbers games and several “eInstant” games that function similar to a slot machine.

Lottery officials have also teased additional games expected to launch later this year, including virtual horse racing. But certain games remain available only for purchase at retail locations, including Keno, a Bay State favorite.

“In creating Mass Lottery Online, we took a similar approach that gives our players new play experiences with the same standards they have grown to expect, wherever in Massachusetts they find themselves to be,” said Mark William Bracken, executive director of the Massachusetts Lottery.

He emphasized the Lottery’s commitment to its retail partners, adding, “While our mission has expanded, our retail sales operation will continue to serve as an essential source of unrestricted local aid for cities and towns.”

How can you sign up for Mass Lottery Online?

Players must be 21 or older and physically located in Massachusetts to gamble through the online platform or make a deposit into their account, Lottery officials explained in a press release. A Mass Lottery Player Account is required and can be set up via masslottery.com or through the mobile app.

According to the press release, Mass Lottery Player account holders will undergo identity verification at registration, or a one-time re-verification if they held an account prior to the launch of Mass Lottery Online. The process includes checking a player’s Social Security number, full legal name, birthday, and residential address.

To help prevent underage access to registered accounts, Mass Lottery Online will require multi-factor authentication for all players logging in for the first time each day, or from a new device. Players will only be able to sign in on one device at any given time, according to the press release.

Mass Lottery Online will also require players to add a payment method to get started, officials said. While credit cards won’t be allowed, online banking, bank transfers, debit cards, PayPal, and Apple Pay all qualify.

What happens if you win the online lottery?

Any prizes under $601 that are won online will immediately be deposited into the player’s account, Lottery officials said. Prizes between $601 and $49,999 will go through an online claims process and typically be deposited within 24 to 48 hours, while prizes greater than $50,000 will need to be claimed at the Mass Lottery headquarters in Dorchester.

Players may not claim prizes through a trust, according to a news release.

Are there any checks and balances?

Lottery officials touted several features designed to avoid problem gambling, including session timers and an option to set personalized deposit and play limits. Players can also adjust their personal limits, but stricter limits kick in immediately, while increases take 48 hours.

Online players could also opt for a cool-off period that prevents them from being able to make a deposit, place a bet, or receive direct marketing communications from the Lottery for a set period of time, according to the press release.

Additionally, officials said, Mass Lottery Online provides players the ability to directly opt-in to PlayBreak, a voluntary tool that helps problem gamblers take a hiatus from internet gaming websites.

“The Massachusetts Gaming Commission is excited to partner with the Massachusetts State Lottery to offer the PlayBreak voluntary self-exclusion program to support iLottery patrons who may need a break from the platform,” Jordan Maynard, Massachusetts Gaming Commission chair, said in a statement. “PlayBreak is an important tool to help players manage their gambling and add a level of friction when it is needed.”

The Massachusetts Problem Gambling Helpline number, 800-327-5050, is displayed in multiple locations across Mass Lottery Online.

“The Lottery is committed to player wellness and responsible play, and we want our players to have tools and resources readily available for them to ensure that online game play remains an enjoyable experience,” Bracken added.

Where do the profits go?

Profits generated from online lottery sales will be funneled back into Massachusetts to fund a grant program supporting early childhood education and care, Lottery officials said.

“The launch of our online platform marks an exciting new chapter for the Lottery as we continue to evolve and meet the needs of today’s players,” said state Treasurer Deborah Goldberg, who chairs the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.

She added: “Online lottery will allow us to compete on a more level playing field in the state’s gaming marketplace, and sales will help make childcare more affordable for families across Massachusetts.”

title: Have Mass. farms seen an increase in sales due to cyclospora fears? It’s a mixed bag.
text:
At Hutchins Farm in Concord, the lettuce is flying off the farm stand.

“Normally for the farm stand on an average day we’re picking 200 heads of lettuce to feed the farm stand, and now I’m like, oh, that’s not enough,” said Liza Bemis, a fifth-generation co-owner of the organic farm, which has been growing fruits and vegetables since 1973. “We have to be picking almost close to 300 heads of lettuce a day to feed the farm stand.”

A few miles away in Lexington, Lauren Wilson is fielding a different but related demand. Her phone is ringing more than usual, although her lettuce sales haven’t increased. The concern on her customers’ minds? Cyclospora.

“We have seen an incredible number of people calling about it and an incredible number of people coming in just to make sure that it is still our own lettuce,” Wilson, also a fifth-generation farmer, at Wilson Farm, said. “I would say people are nervous about both California and Mexico right now,” she added.

As a national cyclospora outbreak rattles shoppers, Massachusetts farms are seeing mixed effects: Some are selling more lettuce, others are fielding anxious questions, and some haven’t noticed much change at all.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has logged more than 1,947 confirmed domestic cyclosporiasis cases since May 1, with a multistate cluster tied to iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico hitting Midwestern states hardest.

Massachusetts, however, has not been part of that outbreak. State health officials say the 18 cases reported here so far this year fall within the normal seasonal range.

For some Massachusetts farms, the gap between the national narrative and the local case count is translating directly into foot traffic.

At Kimballs Fruit Farm in Pepperell, which sells at eight farmers markets around the Boston area, co-owner David Wadleigh said the farm has seen “an increase in sales across the board” over the past few weeks, not just in lettuce, but in corn, zucchini, cucumbers and green beans. Markets that once sold out by the end of the day are now selling out early, he said, and the farm has had to add staff at its busier stops.

“The numbers are almost double what they were last month,” Wadleigh said, though he cautioned that June-to-July sales typically climb in New England regardless of outside factors. What stood out to him isn’t customers name-checking the outbreak — in fact, he said almost no one at the markets has mentioned it directly — but rather how much more product the farm has had to load onto its trucks to stock farmers markets.

“The last couple of weeks, we’ve been surprised,” he said. “People are definitely coming out more to the farmers markets.”

At Allandale Farm in Brookline, the surplus of harvest this time of year makes the cause of any bump hard to pin down. A spokesperson for Allandale Farm said in a statement to Boston.com that it’s difficult to know whether stronger demand is coming from cyclospora anxiety or simply from the arrival of corn, tomatoes, and other peak-summer crops.

Some especially worried customers have started buying only Allandale-grown produce, the farm said, and while questions about the outbreak came in heavily early on, it has tapered off as more coverage frames the outbreak as a large-scale agriculture problem rather than a risk tied to small local farms.

“We’re hoping that more folks use this as an opportunity to think about where their food comes from. We are all connected to each other, in a myriad of ways, especially in our food system. Shopping with local farms and politically supporting federal public health regulations are two very important ways we all can take care of each other,” the farm said in a statement.

Bemis has noticed something similar: an uptick in new faces and more frequent visits from regulars, on top of the lettuce surge. What’s struck her most, she said, is how differently customers are reacting compared with the E. coli-tainted spinach scare nearly two decades ago, when she said shoppers avoided an entire category of greens out of fear of the contamination.

“I’ve been happily surprised at their understanding that our lettuce is not the problem,” Bemis said. “That universally lettuce is not an issue. It has to do with supply chain stuff.”

She said customers have been asking more pointed questions about food safety and where, exactly, their produce travels before reaching the stand — something she said she’s glad to walk them through.

Not every farm is seeing a shift at all, though. At the Urban Farming Institute, a nonprofit that runs farms across Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury, CEO Amber Valbrun said cyclospora rarely comes up with customers. The organization has welcomed dozens of first-time visitors in recent weeks — 30 one Friday, more than 40 the next — but Valbrun attributed the increase to word of mouth rather than cyclospora concerns.

“We actually don’t hear much about it at our farm, which is a good sign,” Valbrun said. “From what we have heard, it’s positive for us — that folks feel comfortable and excited to be able to come to our farm stand and feel that sense of security with what they’re purchasing.”

Back in Concord, Bemis said she’s glad the scare has pointed people toward a shorter, more visible supply chain. But she’s careful not to frame the outbreak as good news.

“This is a terrible thing that is happening, but I’m happy that people are finding us — that’s a silver lining for us,” she said. “But overall, it’s pretty awful. The whole problem is from consolidation in the food system, and that’s an awful thing.”

title: Lawsuit against Suffolk DA, BPD aims to force release of footage of fatal police shooting in Roxbury
text:
A legal nonprofit organization sued the Boston Police Department and Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office on Tuesday, alleging the agencies unlawfully withheld footage from the fatal police shooting of Stephenson King despite months of public calls for transparency.

Lawyers for Civil Rights filed the lawsuit in Suffolk Superior Court after both agencies denied public records requests seeking body-camera and dashboard-camera footage from the March 11 shooting that left King, 39, of Dorchester, dead.

The nonprofit argues the agencies improperly relied on the state’s investigatory exemption to the public records law and is asking the court to order the release of the videos, along with attorney’s fees and other relief.

“Few records implicate a greater public interest than footage of a police officer taking a life,” LCR senior attorney Victoria Miranda said in a press release. “The public has a right to see what happened. Every day that BPD and the DA’s Office refuse to release the footage is another day the community is denied the transparency and accountability the law demands.”

Boston police officer Nicholas O’Malley fatally shot King after he and other officers responded to a reported carjacking and located a vehicle matching the description in Roxbury, authorities said.

O’Malley has since been charged with manslaughter in connection with the shooting and has pleaded not guilty.

After finding the vehicle, O’Malley and another officer confronted King, who partially opened his window but did not stop the car, prosecutors wrote in a document filed in court. King then allegedly attempted to flee and struck a cruiser behind him in the process. O’Malley subsequently fired three shots at King through the driver’s window.

The shooting sparked months of public calls for the release of police video. Two Boston city councilors urged the department to make the footage public, the City Council later unanimously voted to request broader access to body-camera footage involving Boston police officers over the last year and several months, and King’s family publicly demanded the videos be released.

According to the lawsuit’s complaint, LCR submitted public records requests to the Boston Police Department and the DA’s office on June 12, seeking all officer body-camera footage of the shooting and dashboard-camera footage from police cruisers at the scene.

Twelve days later, BPD denied the request for body-camera footage, saying the records are part of an active death investigation and criminal prosecution. The department also said it had no “responsive” dashboard-camera recordings, according to an email, filed with the complaint, purportedly from a BPD administrator.

“The Department is denying your request at this time because the records are part of a death investigation,” the administrator wrote in the email. “The records requested are now evidence in a criminal case that has not yet been adjudicated. The release of these records at this time may prematurely disclose details of the case prior to trial and may influence potential witnesses.”

The DA’s office likewise denied the request on June 26, saying the records fall within the “investigatory exemption” because releasing them could influence the ongoing prosecution and witness testimony.

“It is this Office’s position that production of the records related to this case is not in the public interest, as it could jeopardize an active and ongoing investigation,” the DA’s office wrote in an email to LCR.

LCR argues neither justification is sufficient under the state’s public record laws.

“To the extent a witness’s account materially changes after viewing an objective recording of the events, that discrepancy bears on the witness’s credibility and the weight of the testimony — not on the public’s right to access records of extraordinary importance,” the complaint states.

BPD did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday evening.

A spokesperson for the DA’s office declined to comment and instead pointed to a July 23 protective order approved by Suffolk Superior Court Judge Joshua Wall that limits public dissemination of two body-camera videos before O’Malley’s trial.

In the motion requesting the order, prosecutors argued public release of the videos before trial could generate extensive publicity and expose potential jurors to commentary about the shooting.

“[Releasing the footage] will prompt members of the public to give their opinions — some as self-styled experts — on whether O’Malley’s shooting of Stephenson King Jr. was a justified use of force, a cold-blooded killing, or something in between,” prosecutors wrote. “Release of the video before trial would therefore expose the jury pool not just to footage of the homicide itself, but to a barrage of inadmissible commentary about it.”

Following the news of the filing, former Suffolk County DA and former U.S. Attorney Rachael Rollins, who is challenging District Attorney Kevin Hayden for her old job, pledged to adopt a policy requiring critical incident footage to be released within 30 days if elected.

“Transparency, trust, and accountability are not just campaign slogans; they are the building blocks of a fair justice system,” Rollins said in a statement. “For too long, the delay in releasing vital footage has created a vacuum filled by uncertainty and grief. My administration will treat the public as partners in safety.”

title: 12-year-old seriously injured after train surfing Red Line, Transit Police says
text:
A 12-year-old boy sustained serious injuries early Tuesday morning after falling while attempting to “train surf” on a Red Line car, MBTA Transit Police said.

The boy got onto a train at the JFK/UMass station in Dorchester shortly before 1 a.m. and afterwards fell from the car onto the ground, Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan said in a statement.

The boy suffered a “serious but non-life-threatening head injury,” according to Sullivan.

The incident remains under investigation, authorities said.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with this child, and it is our sincere hope he makes a full recovery,” Sullivan said.

Train surfing is not a new phenomenon, and authorities have long warned of dangers regarding the activity.

Back in 2014, a man was issued a summons for train surfing on a Worcester-bound commuter train, and a teenager faced charges after allegedly “surfing” the Orange Line.

More recently, in 2023, a video of a man standing on top of a train went viral, earning him the nickname “the Red Line surfer.” Later that year, the MBTA Transit Police began investigating two people who were captured on video attempting stunts while riding on top of a Red Line train.

“This incident underscores the inherent extreme danger of ‘Train Surfing,’” Sullivan said. “It could literally cost you your life.”

title: Why this state senate race is seen as a major test of Wu's sway in Boston
text:
As primary day approaches, an election in Boston is set to become a referendum on Mayor Michelle Wu’s political power. Wu has taken a prominent role in recent municipal elections, helping boost allies on the City Council. Now, she is attempting to wield her influence to shape the power dynamics on Beacon Hill.

That dynamic is on full display in the Democratic primary for the First Suffolk district, where incumbent state Sen. Nick Collins is running against the Wu-backed political newcomer Latoya Gayle and former city of Boston youth worker Juwan Skeens. Collins and Gayle hold a wide fundraising lead on Skeens, who lost to Collins in 2024.

The district includes South Boston, Chinatown, Dorchester, the South End, Bay Village, and parts of Mattapan, Roxbury and the Back Bay.

Here’s what to know about the race, and why it is seen as a proxy war between Wu and Collins.

Tax proposal tensions

To many observers, Wu’s interest in unseating Collins can be traced back to 2024. That year, Wu introduced a proposal to temporarily shift the city’s property tax burden onto commercial real estate in order to give homeowners relief.

Boston is heavily reliant on property taxes. When office vacancy rates increased during the pandemic, commercial property values fell and residential real estate values rose. Warning that homeowners were set to see a spike in their property taxes to make up the difference, Wu sought the authority to temporarily increase property taxes on commercial real estate.

Versions of the plan made it through the City Council and the House of Representatives twice before stalling in the Senate. As the plan died in late 2024, Collins used procedural moves to block votes on the measure and blamed Wu for stoking a “campaign of fear and manipulation.”

Collins explained his rationale in an opinion piece in The Boston Globe. Updated valuation data showed that the “sky was not falling,” Collins wrote, adding that Wu’s plan risked “cratering the Boston economy.”

About a year later, riding high after a dominant reelection campaign, Wu renewed her push for a similar proposal. The mayor called out Collins directly, leading to more heated rhetoric. Wu’s plan was once again rejected in the Senate.

The current race

Wu has a strong group of allies in the House, but has faced a more hostile landscape in the Senate. She is working to shake up that chamber through two key endorsements this year. Sen. Will Brownsberger, who joined Collins in opposing Wu’s tax plan, is facing a challenge from Wu’s former aide Daniel Lander. Wu is campaigning on behalf of Lander, arguing that he will better champion affordable housing while forging a stronger partnership between the city and the State House.

Wu’s other major Senate endorsement is for Gayle, who is running against Collins as a progressive. Gayle is a seasoned community activist who currently works for a nonprofit, Neighborhood Villages, which advocates for child care policy reform. She is running because she believes Collins is too conservative on issues like rent stabilization, the Globe reported. On Gayle’s website, one of the first priorities listed is her support for Wu’s property tax shift proposal.

In announcing her endorsement of Gayle, Wu denounced the Senate for “blocking solutions” that come from City Hall. Earlier this month, Wu used an interview with NBC10 Boston to again call out Collins directly.

“Senator Collins and I just see things very differently when it comes to policy and also the role of government,” she said. “I don’t think it’s acceptable to have incumbents who see their job as outsourcing decision making to the real estate industry or other interests, and that’s not how our democratically-elected government should work.”

Collins, meanwhile, is touting his work supporting “the largest tax relief package in state history” in 2024 and securing hundreds of millions in state aid for the city of Boston.

Collins remains the frontrunner in the race, with endorsements from Gov. Maura Healey and a slew of labor unions. The editorial staff of the Boston Herald recently endorsed Collins, praising him for seeing the “big picture” in the fight over Wu’s tax plan.

Last month, he introduced and helped pass a property tax proposal that “triples the property tax exemption for seniors, triples the personal property tax exemption for small businesses, and authorizes the use of surplus funds for direct homeowner rebates.” Collins appealed to Wu directly in a letter, asking her to put aside “personal differences” and publicly support the legislation.

Wu declined to hop on board, saying that Collins was “disconnected from the facts” and that it would be irresponsible for the city to use reserve funds in the way Collins suggested, per WBUR.

Collins, Gayle, and Skeens met last week for an hourlong candidate forum, where they were asked what the proper relationship should be between someone representing the First Suffolk district and City Hall. Gayle said that collaboration was paramount.

“This work has to be high impact and low ego. It’s not about how you feel, it’s about what your constituents need and you should do everything possible to work with everybody who’s in positions to get that done,” Gayle said.

Collins spoke about the importance of being “an advocate for the people” as a whole, instead of one person in particular.

“Sometimes it’s in lockstep, and sometimes it’s with a debate,” he said.

WBUR reporter Eve Zuckoff, who moderated the forum, followed up by asking Gayle to name an area where she disagrees with Wu. Gayle declined to name any specific areas of disagreements, saying she was aligned with the mayor and had not had the chance to work with her yet.

When asked to name an issue where he did agree with Wu, Collins spoke about affordable housing legislation, efforts to expand liquor licenses in the city, and a Boston program that allows students to visit museums and other cultural institutions for free.

“Sometimes you have debates, and you have differences on issues that are based on data, and that’s what we’ve had in the past,” Collins said. “Not many, but we know the big one.”

title: Third West Nile virus case in Mass. this year found in Boston
text:
A Boston resident has tested positive for West Nile virus, the third such case among Massachusetts residents this year, according to public health officials.

The Boston resident was identified as a man in his 60s.

Positive mosquito test samples have been found in multiple Boston neighborhoods this summer. The first was found in Jamaica Plain in early July, before other positive samples were found in areas like Dorchester, Mattapan, South Boston, Allston, Charlestown, East Boston, Roslindale, and West Roxbury, according to the Boston Public Health Commission.

The first human case of West Nile virus in Massachusetts this year was confirmed last week. It was found in a man in his 90s, who was exposed somewhere in Middlesex County. Officials announced the second human case of the year on Monday, saying that a man in his 60s in Middlesex County was exposed.

After the second case was detected, officials elevated West Nile virus risk levels to “high” in Boston, Brookline, Cambridge, Everett, Newton, Somerville, and Watertown.

The state maintains an online map that shows current West Nile virus risk levels for every Massachusetts city and town. The current epicenter is Boston and the surrounding communities, but risk levels are “moderate” throughout Middlesex, Norfolk, Bristol, and Plymouth counties.

About 80% of people infected with West Nile virus do not have any symptoms. Some people will develop a fever, headache, body aches, nausea, vomiting, a rash, or swollen lymph glands. Less than 1% of infected people develop severe illnesses like encephalitis or meningitis, according to state health officials.

Symptoms usually develop two to six days after someone is bitten by an infected mosquito. Symptoms can take longer to show up in immunocompromised people.

Most of the time, people with mild symptoms recover on their own. But people who are older than 50 or immunocompromised are at a higher risk of developing severe illness.

“West Nile Virus can result in very serious illness and may pose serious danger to older and more vulnerable members of our communities,” Bisola Ojikutu, Boston’s commissioner of public health, said in a statement. “BPHC will continue to closely monitor this situation with our partners at the Massachusetts Department of Public Health.”

Those who are at a greater risk of severe illness should adjust their outdoor activity schedules in order to avoid peak mosquito hours that last from dusk until dawn.

West Nile virus is most commonly transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, and officials say residents should work to remove areas of standing water around their homes. Roof gutters, birdbaths, unclean swimming pools, recycling bins, and unused flowerpots are some of the places where mosquitoes can breed.

Residents should also utilize EPA-approved insect repellents and permethrin products. Covering up exposed skin with high socks and long sleeves is also beneficial.

Last week, Massachusetts officials confirmed that they had found the first positive samples of Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) virus of the year. The samples were collected on Aug. 17 in Kingston.

EEE is also generally spread to humans through mosquito bites. It is a rare disease, but considered serious and can be fatal.

Twelve human cases of EEE were detected in Massachusetts in 2019, resulting in six deaths. Five cases were detected in 2020, killing one person. Most recently, an outbreak in 2024 led to four human cases and one death.

title: A new report reveals the slowest MBTA bus route in Boston — and it averages 6 mph
text:
The SL4, a Silver Line that travels between South and Nubian Stations, won the not-so-esteemed honor of slowest MBTA bus route, according to a new report.

Transit Matters, a Mass. transportation advocacy nonprofit, found the route traveled at an average speed of 6.09 mph in October 2025 — a trend of Boston’s slowest routes getting even slower.

The third annual report analyzed publicly available bus data to reveal the top 10 slowest and top 10 most bunched bus routes. Each report has used the previous October as a sample for a “faithful” year-over-year comparison, according to the report.

The top 10 slowest bus routes in Boston recorded an average speed of 6.42 mph, which is a drop from 6.83 mph two years ago, according to the report.

However, it’s not all bleak.

The report found that the MBTA’s top 10 most bunched routes — routes with the highest percentage of buses arriving together as opposed to evenly spaced apart — are improving. The average bunch rate for the top 10 routes is 13.9 percent, which is down nearly two points from last year, the report found.

“Traffic-slowed and blocked buses impact the daily lives of riders by introducing uncertainty into their schedules and costing them time with loved ones,” the report says.

Seven of the slowest routes from last year’s list found their way back onto this year’s list, while eight of the most bunched routes repeated, according to the report. Many of these routes travel through Black and brown communities and low-income neighborhoods, the report says.

“Poor bus service is not just an issue of inefficiency; it is an issue of opportunity, mobility, and quality of life for these communities,” according to the report. “Inefficient service is felt every day by riders who may have to wait fifteen minutes longer in the extreme heat or cold.”

The report comes at a time when the city plans to expand bus lanes and transit signal priority, along with the addition of bus-mounted enforcement cameras to fine vehicles stopped in bus lanes. However, the report says several bus infrastructure projects have slowed.

Some of the potential solutions suggested by the report are continuing the city’s progress on projects, such as ones along Hyde Park Avenue and Blue Hill Avenue, as well as reinstating bus lanes on N. Washington Street and Boylston Sreet after they were removed.

Slowest bus routes

The SL4, which takes the crown for slowest route of the year, saw a decline in speed of nearly 0.8 mph over the last three years, according to the report.

The 1 bus, which travels between Roxbury and Harvard, earned runner-up with an average speed of 6.2 mph. The 93 bus, 47 bus, and CT3 bus all round up the top five slowest routes in the city.

Other buses included in the report’s list are the 92, 66, SL5, 19, and 10.

Seven of the top 10 slowest buses service Roxbury — a community with a median household income of about $46,000 and nearly 39% without access to a car, the report says.

The 116 bus, which travels from Revere to East Boston, shot up from an unranked position last year to the No. 2 spot. The report says the rise in bunching might be due to the 117 bus dissolving into the 116, which led to an increase in frequency.
