A weekly dispatch with all the best relationship content and commentary – plus exclusive content for fans of Love Letters, Dinner With Cupid, weddings, therapy talk, and more.

Enter Email

EDUCATE As November’s election nears, the BPL’s Dorchester branch is hosting a civic-minded panel discussion. Led by Andrés Ballesteros, community director of White Snake Projects, the panel will feature Occidental College Assistant Professor Ainsley LeSure and Boston-based activists Eric Kennedy and Madison Foley. The event will also feature a performance from Naomi Westwater, a local folk-rock and poetry artist. Sept. 4, 6:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. Free. 690 Adams St., Dorchester. bpl.bibliocommons.com

JAM OUT At the Christian Science Plaza, the summer vibes are far from over with a free concert on the lawn, featuring folk artist Farayi Malek; the Robbie Pate Group, who will play R&B and soul covers; and Albino Mbie, who will play Afro-pop originals. Then cool off with a new world view with free admission to the Mapparium, the iconic, stained glass domed structure — representing the globe circa 1935 — where sound, vibration, and light bounce and reflect in extraordinary ways. Sept. 6, 5 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. Free. Christian Science Plaza, 210 Massachusetts Ave. christianscience.com

ARTIST’S POINT This coming weekend, Christopher Columbus Park hosts over 50 artists at the annual Boston Arts Festival. The festival, which has been hosted since 2003, will feature two days of music — including performances from local artists like Fly By Brass Band, blindspot, and the 94s. Plus, there will be numerous vendors, including paintings by Joseph Mushipi, clothing by Sherry Divedi, and ceramics by Lori Gardinier. Sept. 7 and 8, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Free. Christopher Columbus Park, 100 Atlantic Ave. thebostonartsfestival.com

NOT A ROOK-IE MISTAKE Try a twist on chess with a free meetup in Harvard Square. The Creative Chess Club invites like-minded gamers to take on a non-traditional variant — from Magic: The Gathering hybrid, Eternal Kings, to eight-player Party Chess. The group encourages new members (and novices) and meets every other Saturday. Check their website or join their Discord for up-to-date locations and times. Sept. 7, 11:30 a.m.-2 p.m., the Richard A. and Susan F. Smith Campus Center, 1350 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge. bostonscreativechessclub.com

VOCAL CHORD ACADEMY The Boston Lyric Opera and Boston Conservatory at Berklee join forces for an opera masterclass featuring Lawrence Brownlee. Brownlee, who will star in the titular role in Mozart’s “Mitridate” at the BLO later this month, will coach five singers through technique, and offer performance and acting tips. Members of the public are welcome to sit in on the lesson and get a glimpse behind the scenes of the world of opera. Sept. 8, 3 p.m. Free. Seully Hall, 8 Fenway. bostonconservatory.berklee.edu

ON-THE-HOUSE ARTS In honor of Labor Day, the Institute of Contemporary Art will offer free admission all day long. Visitors can catch the Firelei Báez exhibition and Hew Locke’s The Procession (located at the ICA’s Watershed) on their final day at the museum. Advance tickets are required. Sept. 2, 10 a.m to 5 p.m. Free. Institute of Contemporary Art, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. icaboston.org

Emily Wyrwa can be reached at emily.wyrwa@globe.com. Follow her @emilywyrwa.

title: ‘I’ve always wanted to paint a roller rink.’ Rollerama brings art and free fun to Kendall Square.
text:
Through Sept. 29, the pop-up skating rink offers free fun to the public Wednesday through Friday from 2 p.m. until 8 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday from 11 a.m. until 8 p.m. Picnic tables and food and drink vendors are scattered around the rink, ringed by bright orange barriers. While both entry and skate rentals are free, organizers recommend reserving a time and booking rentals in advance.

Created by MIT’s real estate group alongside design consultants Isenberg Projects, Rollerama sits in the newly coined Kendall Common, a 10-acre site formerly home to the US Department of Transportation Volpe Center. MIT built a new facility for the DOT offsite and has been in an eight-year process of developing the acreage into a multi-use retail, parks, and business space. When the project is completed, the site of Rollerama, at the corner of Broadway and Third Street, will be called Third Street Park.

“Even though it’s a temporary installation, we thought it could help people do something fun together, and start to give people a sense of what the Kendall Common build out will be like,” said Sarah Gallop, director of government and community relations at MIT.

At the Thursday DJ night, in late August, strangers found themselves dancing together as Mr. Big Stuff moved through the speakers. The disco nights are hosted by Spin the Bottle, a group of local DJs including Thursday hosts, stealth.mode, and DJ Rad Joy. One man stopped to show another how to break with their skates, and legs flew up ever so often as a wipeout was marked by the sounds of clacking skates.

As skaters rode around the winding stripes on the rink, the setting sun peaked through the trees in dancing bursts of light around them.

Grullon, the muralist, is an independent artist who describes her style as Supergraphic, a distinctive ‘70s design style that uses bold colors, lines, and size. At Rollerama, she hired eight other people to help paint the rink’s design; a large oval of blue and white striped lines, sometimes moving straight, wavy, or following the natural curve of the rink.

“I wanted to create a pattern and shapes that show movement,” Grullon said. “When you go to the roller rink, you’ll see some people, they’ll literally follow the lines.”

David Nichol of Jamaica Plain brought his kids, Ari, 12, and Liora, 9, to Rollerama after they spent the day with him at work across the street for a bring your kid to work day. The children linked hands on either side of their dad, following the lines for at least an hour.

Liora said she liked the mural’s cool design.

“It’s flat and round and perfect and symmetrical,” she said. “And it’s blue.”

Grullon said she seeks to evoke a sense of nostalgia throughout all her work, as well as incorporate movement, harmony, and a sense of the familiar.

Friends Vandan Jakharia, 24, and Shreya Ramesh, 25, heard about the rink through Instagram and came for the first time Thursday. They sat on the orange barrier for a break and talked about the years it had been since they last skated.

“It brings back nostalgia from childhood,” said Jakharia, who then pointed to a group of faded scars on his legs earned roller blading a decade earlier.

Meanwhile Dayvon Webb, 9, made new scars skating with his brother, Dante, 10, and grandmother, Tracey Sullivan, 62. It was their third time at Rollerama, after hearing about it from Sullivan’s sister who lives around the corner.

“I got hurt three times,” said Dayvon.

“I never got hurt,” said Dante, cutting off his younger brother.

“This is great,” said Sullivan. “This is nowhere else,” she added, referring to it being free to all.

When she began painting her own murals, Gullon, 37, reached out to numerous roller rinks because their typically ‘70s aesthetic lends itself to her painting style.

She said even friends and fans online would mention that she should paint a roller rink; some would send her old rink photos that reminded them of her art.

“I’m like, ‘That is very cool, and I’ve seen that before, and it’s great. I want to do something like that. No one’s hiring me,’” she recalled.

Grullon has since done murals in various areas of Boston, but was denied the roller rink fantasy until Isenberg Projects, a previous client, reached out to her about Rollerama.

Now, the space has become a corner of liveliness on a property that was physically closed off from the community before they acquired it, says Kathryn Brown, director of real estate at MIT’s Investment Management Company.

“It’s just so nice to see people in the neighborhood who’ve walked around this site for so many years, to be able to walk into it and enjoy it,” she said. “And it’s really just been a great activity for the community for this summer.”

Rollerama also hosts Drift and Drag nights on Saturdays, as well as Wednesday night and Sunday afternoon concerts.

Grullon frequents the rink herself now, and enjoys hearing from people who say it has brightened up a previously depressing lot.

“it’s really amazing what murals can do to transform spaces, bring the community together, and make it, you know, colorful,” she said.

title: The beautiful rainbow of Nantasket Beach
text:
“This is beautiful, " said Badrizamn Zaman Khan of Quincy. “Every weekend, I’m going to come in here with my kids, my family, and some of my guests.”

No one ever bothers them there.

“It’s nice,” he said. “Everyone here is equal. Everyone is the same here. No different.”

As refreshing as the water is on a hot summer day, so is the attitude of a half dozen people interviewed on its fine grain sand.

A rainbow of different folks from all over, blanket to blanket, relaxing in harmony.

Imagine a world like that.

“I do call it a United Nations place,” said Mabasa Masunungure of Zimbabwe. ”Because if we are to take 20 random people, there’s a very high chance that those people would be from different backgrounds.”

Masunungure is a Suffolk University graduate who lives in Waltham with his family and works as a night auditor.

The first time he visited Nantasket Beach, he went alone.

“I was just passing through and I noticed there’s mixed people. I really loved that. I really enjoyed the people, the place, and the environment.”

Then he came back with his wife, daughter, and mom, and they had a ball.

“You feel so welcome. No restrictions, no whatsoever. It’s actually beautiful.”

Israa Abbraa, of Syrian descent, loves to visit with friends. She hears Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese, and French Creole spoken there.

“It’s very nice. It’s beautiful how everyone gets along. It’s peaceful. It’s very diverse.”

The best part is “the nature and the vibes. "

Jalen Williams is a hip-hop therapist from Quincy.

He uses the music as a catalyst for change, development, and growth. He’s not a beach person but he comes for inspiration.

“From what I’ve seen, it seems like there’s a lot of different cultures,” said Williams. “It’s peaceful. It’s pretty chill. Relaxing.”

He improvised a spiritual rap: “I’m pushing hope, faith, and mindfulness. Yeah. Love. Yeah, of course. Because God is love, and that’s where it all comes from.”

Rob McCormack, originally from Dorchester, parked his Harley Davidson and sat on the seawall. He has a Santa Claus beard and American flags on his motorcycle. He’s been coming to the same spot for years.

He believes the diverse crowd livens up the scene.

“They’re beautiful,” he said. “You got all different colors, all different creeds. I think the majority of the people get along. That’s what we’re supposed to do: get along.”

“We don’t have any major problems. I haven’t seen a fight in two years. There’s no bums on the street, and there’s no needles and stuff all over the place. Well, we’re doing good here, my friend. "

Elie St. Brice Sr., a district social worker for the SLIFE (Students with Limited or Interrupted Formal Education) program at the Boston Public Schools, spends the day with his wife, Mallory; son, Elie Jr., 16; and daughter, Eliama, 8.

They also made new friends.

“As a Haitian American, we are all part of the human race, and it’s important to focus on love, unity, and peace. These values shouldn’t be divided into separate categories; they are intertwined and universal. As humans, we all have the capacity to love, and that should be our common ground.”

“At Nantasket Beach, it’s about shedding the layers and fears that we all carry. Everyone there shares a sense of camaraderie, brought together by the oneness and the salty scent of the ocean. It creates a mindful state, a feeling of unity, and that’s a beautiful place to be,” St. Brice Sr. said.

“One of the most powerful things we can do is let go of our preconceived fears. When we do, we start to see each other for who we truly are. It’s about reaching one, teaching one, and finding ways to help each other move forward. Together, we can change the dynamics, build, and grow as a community.”

title: Healey, Warren, and Wu join picketing workers in Labor Day actions across Boston
text:
Locally, UNITE-HERE Local 26 — representing nearly 900 hotel workers — had their contract expire on Aug. 31 and are now marching outside the Boston Park Plaza, Hilton Boston Logan Airport, Hampton Inn Boston Seaport, and Fairmont Copley Plaza hotels, with strikes also authorized in Providence and New Haven. Union officials say the strike will continue until late Tuesday.

The breakfast is a flagship event of the labor council, where elected officials join labor leaders in solidarity, picking alongside them. Several teachers unions and the firefighters union joined the event, alongside the council, an umbrella organization that represents 100,000 workers in the area.

Though the event typically takes place inside the Hilton, this year’s stood out as it took place at a park opposite the hotel, to the backdrop of chanting workers.

“Breakfasts taste good outside right?” said Mayor Michelle Wu of Boston.

“We are here outdoors because we stand on the threshold of a historic moment in Boston’s labor movement, where three-quarters of the unionized hotels may potentially walk the picket line later today,” she said.

Three other actions are taking place across the city including among resident assistants at Boston University, medical interns and residents at Mass General Brigham, and among SEIU janitors in downtown Boston.

Last March, BU’s Residential Life workers voted to unionize, forming an organization of nearly 300 resident assistants, graduate resident assistants, and graduate hall assistants. But after 15 negotiation sessions, they have yet to agree on a contract with no clear end in sight.

Among health care workers, union leaders say 2,500 residents and fellow physicians in training are demanding higher compensation, adequate access to health care, and safe training conditions for staff.

In her remarks to attendants, Wu also pointed to health care workers at Carney Hospital in Dorchester whose jobs were recently cut as Steward Health Care, the private-equity backed conglomerate, deals with bankruptcy filings.

“These workers cared for our communities and are now suffering the consequences . . . Workers shouldn’t be stuck footing the bill for disastrous decisions made by a profit company machine,” she said, while calling on Steward to pay workers severance and PTO.

US Senators Elizabeth Warren, Ed Markey, and Representative Ayanna Pressley took to the stage at the event, alongside Governor Maura Healey and Attorney General Andrea Campbell.

“Workers are the backbone of our economy, and all workers deserve to be fairly paid,” Healey said, as drivers honked in solidarity from their cars.

“I ask all the employers involved to come to the table and get a deal done for our workers, for our economy.”

Nearby the streets were awash with the red shirts of the striking workers, with cheers and the echoes of makeshift drums. Even as labor officials had trouble with the audio equipment on stage, speakers made do, temporarily relying on a bullhorn.

The hotel workers strike comes on the heels of a hospitality industry changed by a pandemic. While average hotel room occupancy rates remain below 2019 levels, average revenue per available room is expected to reach a record high, thanks in part to higher room rates and guest spending, according to the Associated Press.

Workers, however, cite the impact of staffing shortages and the ripple effect this has had on women of color specifically, who comprise much of the workforce.

“We’re always underhanded, we’re never getting ahead [of the orders],” said Gary Stillwell , a chef at the Fairmont Copley Plaza, adding that the hotel tends to hire entry-level staff to save money, many of whom find it difficult to keep up with the workload.

Stillwell said his kitchen has been understaffed since the pandemic: in some instances where they once had three line cooks, he said, now there’s only one.

Aissata Seck , a 34-year old worker at the Hilton Park Plaza, who said she’s been working at the hotel since she was a teenager, was marching Monday because she is struggling to make ends meet under her current salary.

“I cannot afford to lose my apartment because my mom lives with me,” she said.

Seck lives in Quincy and has taken to driving for Uber to supplement her income.

A spokesperson for Hilton said it is making every effort to maintain a cooperative and productive relationship with the unions.

“We remain committed to negotiating in good faith to reach fair and reasonable agreements that are beneficial to both our valued Team Members and to our hotels,” the spokesperson said.

Elected officials at the breakfast also brought up the upcoming presidential election, encouraging union members to vote blue come November.

Chants of “When we fight, we win,” an oft-used labor slogan that has recently been repurposed by the Harris campaign, followed most speeches.

“The unions of America are going to make sure that everyone gets the protections which they need, and that Kamala Harris is the next president of the United States of America,” Markey said, to cheers.

title: After the closing of Carney Hospital, residents wonder who is to blame
text:
These aren’t the words of an idle bystander. Walczak co-founded the Codman Square Community Health Center decades ago. And he served as president of Carney Hospital for just over a year during the early days of its ownership by Steward Health Care.

The closing of the Carney is a done deal, of course. It suffered from constant benign neglect during its decade as a Steward Health Care hospital, and now stands as a poignant symbol of the power and promise of a community health center for patients in need — a promise callously broken by the for-profit chain.

The damage done by Steward in this state has been well-documented in the months since this weird health care/real estate giant filed for bankruptcy. Four of its former Massachusetts hospitals are in the process of being sold, while two — Carney and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer — closed for lack of acceptable bidders.

The reckoning with the mess of Steward’s collapse has barely begun. The Globe reported Tuesday that not one but two federal investigations into Steward’s financial dealings are underway. One is looking at the company’s alleged foreign corruption, while a second, based in Boston is said to be taking apart the company’s lavish spending and executive compensation, particularly during the years in which it was tanking financially.

No doubt, those investigators will have plenty to keep them busy. But in Dorchester, where the Carney had operated in some form since the 1800s, the results of these shenanigans will be felt on a personal level.

Consider that Carney Hospital’s emergency room had 31,000 visits last year. That is an awful lot of people who will now have to look elsewhere for urgent care.

Walczak has singled out Secretary of Health and Human Services Kate Walsh and Department of Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein as the officials who didn’t do enough to preserve Carney Hospital’s most important service to the city and especially to Dorchester

He noted that when Quincy Hospital closed in 2014, the attorney general’s office insisted that its emergency room continue to operate. (Ironically, it was Carney Hospital that operated it, after Quincy Hospital closed.)

“Why couldn’t something like that have been done here?” Walczak asked.

In a telephone interview, Goldstein diplomatically but firmly insisted that state officials are not to blame for this messy situation.

“I think we’ve been doing the best we can with a very volatile situation,” Goldstein said. “This has changed every day through the past nine months, sometimes multiple times a day.”

As for why another entity couldn’t run the Carney’s emergency room, Goldstein noted that Quincy and Carney were both Steward-owned hospitals, making it relatively simple for the operating license of one to be transferred to the other.

Goldstein said the lack of a buyer for Carney Hospital left the state with no good options for preserving its services. He speculated that Steward’s legacy of disinvestment made Carney a less attractive purchase than the other hospitals being unloaded.

“There’s parts of the physical plant that have been neglected for 10 years since Steward took over,” Goldstein said. “That makes it challenging to take over — not impossible, but challenging. So business people were making some business decisions about where they want to invest and how much they have to invest.”

Business people making business decisions. In a sense, that sums up the Steward scandal in a nutshell.

One group of business people decided to treat community health care as an afterthought, while they allowed an entire health care ecosystem to collapse. Another group of business people picked through the wreckage and decided saving Carney was more trouble than it was worth.

Meanwhile, the people entrusted with protecting communities from these predators watched it all happen, over a period of years.

It’s not much comfort to think they did their best.

title: Man recalls victim of Dorchester barbershop shooting; neighbors shaken by ‘execution-style’ attack
text:
Meanwhile, the grandfather of the second man shot said his grandson, 20, was shot in the leg, chest, and side of the head as he fled the Exclusive Barber Shop on Washington Street shortly before 1 p.m. on Monday.

A day earlier, Renier Thompson said he had warned his grandson’s mother “don’t let the streets take your son.”

“You’ve got to get your son away from these people,” Thompson recalled saying. “Get him out of that crowd.”

His grandson was best friends with the victim, whom he said was a rap artist. His grandson had appeared in some of his friend’s music videos.

Police haven’t released the name of the person who was killed. No arrests have been made. Investigators said the shooting was not random.

On Tuesday, neighbors recalled a chaotic scene as shots broke out.

“I was just sitting on my back porch when all of a sudden, I heard ‘pop! pop! pop! pop!’” said Javier Nieves, 50.

He said he saw four people sprinting out of the barbershop, including the gunman, who was wearing all black.

Nieves said the owner later told him a male suspect entered the shop while the man who was killed was getting a haircut. The owner said the suspect asked him how many customers were inside, and he said two, according to Nieves.

The suspect left and returned a short time later, opening fire inside the shop, Nieves said.

“The kid probably thought about it, came out, went back in and actually did the shooting [with] no remorse, no nothing,” Nieves said.

Nieves and his wife, Denise Nieves, said the young man who was killed recorded music and had attended TechBoston Academy.

Denise Nieves said some of the victim’s former teachers had written on social media that “he had great potential, a basketball opportunity. He was great in school. He was a good student.”

A chilling video clip of the immediate aftermath of the slaying circulated online Tuesday, showing the slain victim laying limp in a barber’s chair, a pool of blood on the ground beneath his head.

“I cried the minute I saw that video,” Denise Nieves said. “There’s just been so many [shootings] that just like, as a mom, you can’t help but to cry.”

She said people in the neighborhood are “just trying to raise our kids and this area is just so tough.”

“This whole situation is heartbreaking,” she said. “This one hurt just a little bit more because of his age and the way that it happened.”

On Aug. 24, a man was fatally shot nearby at 159 Washington St.

On Tuesday afternoon, the barbershop remained closed. A couple of police vehicles were parked in the vicinity, including one in front of the shop. A few police officers patrolled on foot, checking in on local businesses.

Maria Medina, whose family owns Island Style Jamaican restaurant at Washington and Erie streets, said she is concerned for her family’s safety.

“This is where we work, we spend time here and are worried because too many things happen,” Medina said in Spanish. “There is too much shooting, too much death, a lot of violence, a lot of everything.”

Nasir Ahmed, a cashier at SKB Food Mart near the barbershop, said he was working when the shooting happened.

“In the [last] week, two people have been shot dead,” he said. “We are losing customers. They’re afraid to come.”

Javier Nieves said his son also patronizes the barbershop and that it was “scary to know that something like that can happen.”

“That’s crazy, where somebody could just walk right inside of a barbershop and kill somebody execution-style,” he said.

Correspondent Sabrina Lam contributed to this report.

title: Mass. lawmakers announce deal to add 225 new liquor licenses for Boston
text:
The deal they filed Tuesday would add 195 new restricted licenses for 13 ZIP codes in Boston — with five distributed per year, per ZIP code, over three years. Of the five licenses, three would be for all alcohol sales, and two would be for sales of beer and wine, according to lawmakers.

A dozen other new permits would be unrestricted licenses, meaning they can be used anywhere in Boston and sold for a profit. Moran called those permits “pocket licenses” because it allows the city to parcel them out for specific projects.

The bill would also set aside 15 licenses for nonprofits, small theaters, and outdoor spaces for all alcohol sales, while three others would go to Oak Square in Brighton, which Moran represents and doesn’t have a single sit-down restaurant with a full liquor license, he said.

The decision to root the vast majority of new permits in specific neighborhoods — and require they remain in the ZIP codes to which they were allotted — is crucial to create new economic opportunities in neighborhoods starving for them, said state Representative Chris Worrell, a Dorchester Democrat and lead sponsor of the legislation in the House.

“I see more tourist dollars. Instead of stopping at Newbury [Street], at the Seaport, at Back Bay, I see them coming to Roxbury, Mattapan, and Hyde Park and being amongst the locals,” Worrell said.

The bill has been eyed as a boon for communities of color and small business owners, who have not always had the luxury of affording a liquor license, which can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.

License holders in the new batch of permits would also be required to sell food.

“People want more restaurants, they want more options for food,” said Moran, a Brighton Democrat. “This bill was about underserved areas.”

Senator Liz Miranda said the bill would go far in closing the racial wealth gap across the city, particularly in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park. She said Blue Hill Avenue was once a “cultural mecca” with Black-owned restaurants and nightlife, but that the cost of purchasing a liquor license on the secondary made it difficult, if impossible, for many to launch a business.

“[A cost of] $500,000 to $700,000 to a million dollars is inaccessible to most people. It’s not just neighborhood folks. It literally shatters dreams,” said Miranda, a Roxbury Democrat. “This is more than just about liquor licenses.”

House and Senate leaders both said they hope to send the bill to Governor Maura Healey by the end of the week. Both chambers have informal sessions scheduled for Thursday.

Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement that each of the new licenses “represents new life and economic prosperity for an entrepreneur, a business, a neighborhood, and families throughout our city.”

The bill was one of several still locked up in closed-door negotiations when lawmakers wrapped up formal sessions on the morning of Aug. 1.

The Senate had passed its version just days prior, proposing to give Boston 264 new liquor licenses — more than the 250 number proposed in a home rule petition from the Boston City Council. The bill also sought to bring discounted licenses to 13 ZIP codes from Mattapan to the South End, with the aim of increasing access for owners of restaurants and bars in neighborhoods of color, who are often priced out of buying their own permits.

The House passed its own version in May, seeking to add 205 permits, mostly in underserved neighborhoods across the city.

The Legislature has long limited the number of liquor licenses that can be issued in most cities and towns, including Boston. The city hit its cap of roughly 1,200 permits two decades ago, and acquiring one usually requires buying one from another restaurant or bar that has closed. The asking price to pour wine, beer, and cocktails can top $600,000.

The soaring costs have concentrated many licenses in well-to-do neighborhoods, such as the Back Bay and the Seaport.

The agreement’s emergence on the day of the state primary continues the slow drip of major legislation to emerge during what is typically a quiet period on Beacon Hill. In the weeks since ending formal sessions, lawmakers have passed agreements to expand access to midwives and improve maternal health care in Massachusetts, and increase oversight of long-term care in the state.

Legislative leaders have said they’re also prepared to call lawmakers back to the State House for another formal session to pass a multibillion-dollar economic development bill that collapsed on the final, chaotic day of formal sessions this week.

Lawmakers have yet to announce a deal on that legislation, however, leaving it unclear when they could return for a formal vote. To pass a bill that authorizes borrowing, such as the economic development bill, lawmakers are constitutionally required to take a roll-call vote, which occurs in formal sessions.

Other legislation, such as the bill to expand liquor licenses, can typically pass in an informal session as long as there isn’t opposition.

Niki Griswold, Diti Kohli, and Shirley Leung of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: In apparent upset, challenger Evan MacKay in Cambridge declares victory over state Representative Marjorie Decker
text:
Meanwhile, Decker did not explicitly concede the race, nor did she call MacKay, but seemed to come close as she gave an emotional speech about her time in the Legislature.

“There’s a lot of tears to be had. I’m not shedding any tears,” Decker told supporters at her election night party at the Fresh Pond Beer Garden. “I’ve had 25 incredible years of doing what I love.”

Her campaign, however, said MacKay’s celebration was premature.

“Declaring victory is irresponsible,” said Democratic consultant Jason Cincotti, who works on Decker’s campaign. “It’s reckless and it’s incorrect. We are waiting for all the votes to be counted.”

As of little after 1 a.m., Associated Press results showed MacKay leading Decker 50.3 percent to 49.7 percent, with 99 percent of votes counted.

Decker avoided a reporter’s questions Tuesday night, instead making a quick exit to her car.

A loss for Decker would represent a notable upset in a state where few incumbents ever face a serious primary challenge, let alone meet defeat at the ballot box.

Decker, chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Public Health, has faced little substantive competition before MacKay decided to challenge her. She has never faced an opponent in the general election, and her last primary challenge was six years ago, in 2018.

In a speech, MacKay thanked volunteers for helping surmount what they said they were told were “impossible odds.”

“This is a wake-up call to the political establishment,” MacKay said. “We’ve shown that our movement is mighty.”

Every two years, all 160 House districts and 40 Senate districts are up for reelection, and this year, like most cycles, just a sliver of voters this year had the chance to cast ballots in a contested primary election.

Many state representatives and senators spent this campaign season unopposed, gliding their way to the November ballot. Some will face Republican opponents, but others will notch victory without even that challenge.

It’s a familiar pattern — only 25 Democratic House candidates have beaten an incumbent in a primary between 2002 and 2022.

Still, there were still a few other contested races around the state.

In Somerville, voters handed incumbent state Representative Erika Uyterhoeven, a democratic socialist, victory over challenger Kathleen Hornby, a progressive who previously worked as a State House staffer for Decker.

MacKay made inaction and the lack of transparency on Beacon Hill central to their campaign. Fellow elected officials rallied to Decker, including some of the state’s top Democrats such as Governor Maura Healey, US Senator Ed Markey, and US Representatives Katherine Clark and Ayanna Pressley, who sent out text messages on behalf of Decker to voters in the days leading up to the election

Before unofficial results were released, Decker supporters ate pizza and sipped beer at her event. But the mood quickly turned somber as word of precinct tallies trickled in.

Attendees hugged and cried. Decker walked around the beer garden and hugged every attendee who came.

“I’m not going away, trust me,” Decker said in her speech. “I don’t know how to go away.”

Other incumbents facing challengers Tuesday included Democratic state Representatives Francisco Paulino of Methuen, Bud Williams of Springfield, David Linsky of Natick, Jack Lewis of Framingham, Thomas Stanley of Waltham, Rady Mom of Lowell, Joseph McGonagle of Everett, Paul Donato of Medford, Rita Mendes of Brockton, and Boston’s Russell Holmes and Jay Livingstone. Republican state Representatives Susan Gifford of Wareham and Paul Frost of Auburn also faced challenges on the GOP ballot.

On the Senate side, state Senators Mark Montigny of New Bedford, Adam Gomez of Springfield, and Nick Collins of Boston, all Democrats, faced primary challenges.

Despite the lack of competition, surrogates and supporters were still hard at work Tuesday.

State Representative Aaron Michlewitz, the powerful House chair of Ways and Means — who had no primary challenger of his own — turned out to promote some of his House colleagues. Photos posted to Instagram showed him handing out flyers with the Massachusetts Building Trades Union for Decker, standing out with signs for Donato, and calling voters for McGonagle from a camping chair in Everett.

Bonde Fine Wine Shop in Harvard Square put out a sign that said “They Say Vote For Marjorie Decker,” and Chrissy Lynch, president of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, posted a selfie with Decker while promoting the candidate at the polls.

Collins, the incumbent Democrat running in Boston, showed up at Florian Hall in Dorchester to speak with voters headed to the ballot box.

As of Tuesday morning, the state had already exceeded the turnout percentage in 2016, with 9.8 percent voter turnout as of 7 a.m. A total of 497,428 ballots had been cast at that time, most of those by mail.

Secretary of State William F. Galvin said his office expects about 15 percent turnout — which would exceed turnout in the last two comparable state primaries in 2016 and 2012. (2020 was an anomaly, given the COVID pandemic.)

Leslie Morgan, a high school English teacher, said she came to the Friends Center to vote for Decker, as she had for several election cycles.

She said she likes Decker’s policies on gun control and the environment, and while she appreciated MacKay’s progressive politics, she wanted a representative with the experience of multiple terms under her belt.

“Sometimes I’m comfortable with what I already know,” Morgan said. She added, however, that she was dissatisfied with the current political calendar setup, which puts primary day right after Labor Day.

”I almost forgot about it, as a matter of fact, so thank God I was talking to a friend of mine who reminded me,” she said. “I think it means that fewer people will come out and vote.”

Owen Andrews, 67, stood outside the Baldwin School in Cambridge holding a sign for MacKay.

He said his choice was a way to express his discontent with leadership at the State House, which he said has “no accountability” and his excitement to challenge an incumbent — a choice he rarely gets to make.

“As a Democrat, I find that unacceptable,” said Andrews, a retired poet and educator. “I don’t know what is going on in the way the [Democratic] party runs things that nobody feels safe challenging an incumbent. That suggests to me some decadence, and I’d like to see that change. I’d like there to be choices every year. Then it’s a democracy. Right now it’s something else.”

At Somerville’s Albert F. Argenziano School, Katharine Lange, 27, said she was glad to have a choice for state representative in Somerville, because it helps reinforce to elected officials that they can always lose their seats if they don’t get things done.

Other districts don’t have that luxury, she said, and there are consequences.

”The legislative session was quite disappointing. At the end they left a lot of stuff on the table,” she said.

In the end, though, she decided to stick with Uyterhoeven as well, noting that she had only been at the job for one term.

”She seems to be as progressive as I think Somerville is,” Lange said. “She’s done a good job so far.”

Globe correspondent Izzy Bryers contributed to this report.

title: Match High valedictorian is headed to Brown, taking her passion for learning with her
text:
“I would always have my homework done on the bus ride home from school, just because I didn’t want to wait until I got home,” Kasongo said. “And then I would ask the teacher for more homework because it was fun for me.”

“She’s someone who really likes to be in school, even when she’s home,” said her mother, Germaine Kasongo, 40, adding that Marie often falls asleep at night while reading a book.

It’s that drive that made her the valedictorian at Match, where she also co-founded a student group called Mosaic that works to build a welcoming and inclusive school environment. The experience helped the formerly introverted teen develop more confidence in her leadership skills, a teacher said.

“She realized the power of her voice,” said Ishrat Chowdhury, her chemistry teacher at Match. “She realized the need to create more community at our school, and she no longer needed an adult to be the leader of that group. . . . This is the first time where it was really her voice and her leadership abilities.”

When she wasn’t busy excelling academically or working to change her school’s climate, Marie Kasongo was often at home, helping her single mother care for her younger siblings, ages 15, 13, and 8, two of whom have autism. She also has a 22-year-old brother.

She said her siblings are mostly pretty self-sufficient, so her job is mostly making sure they shower and brush their teeth on schedule and finish their homework, but sometimes she has to put on her mom hat and do things like monitor their screen time.

“If I notice, like, ‘OK, you haven’t touched your homework,’ I’ll tell them, ‘Yeah, time to switch it off,’” she said. “Sometimes it does feel like I’m a parent, but it also just feels like I’m an older sister. I want to be someone that they can talk to, someone they can come to.”

She often takes on a similar role with classmates, “holding everyone accountable to seeing through their commitments,” according to the school’s principal, Joseph Gallagher.

As the school’s cheer captain last year, she tutored other girls who needed help to maintain their athletic eligibility, Gallagher said, and once he overheard her “give some of our ninth graders some much-needed tough love about what it means to be seen as a leader amongst your peers.”

“I think her words inevitably had more of an impact than anything that the coach or I could have said,” Gallagher said.

The Kasongos immigrated to the United States when Marie was 5, and her two youngest siblings were born here. She has only hazy memories of life in Africa, mostly of the loving extended family they left behind and the food, like her beloved fufu, a sort of starchy dough made from root vegetables, and the fresh fruit, which had a different flavor than the fruit available here.

She spoke only French when her family arrived in Boston, where she was placed in a kindergarten class for children learning English. Not only did she quickly master the language, she also began developing the study habits she’s taking with her to Providence.

“I think where I started to really fall in love with school and enjoy learning was actually from learning English, because I would read a lot of books,” she said. “That’s how I learned English.”

Over time, her love of learning grew into a love of sharing what she’d learned.

Once, when Marie Kasongo was in middle school, her mother was approached by a classmate’s mother who wanted to give her a hug and thank her, because Marie had spent her lunch period each day tutoring the woman’s daughter, enabling her to pass a difficult class. She hadn’t told her mother she was helping.

“She doesn’t work only for herself,” Germaine Kasongo said. “She has a big heart.”

The desire to help others extends to her career plans, which were set at an early age.

“I’ve always wanted to be a doctor,” she said. “It’s something pretty personal to me. You can see videos . . . where I’m like 8 years old saying I’m going to be a doctor and cure the world.”

A decade later, she has refined her vision and sees a future in developing biomedical devices. She believes that the open curriculum at Brown, the university she has dreamed of attending since she started high school, will enable her to delve into some of her many interests and prepare her for that future.

“Hopefully, I can work at a biomedical company and spend all day working in a lab making devices that . . . help people,” she said. “That’s the dream, like just a mad scientist in a lab 24 hours a day.”

title: When the market speaks, it does not demand health care equity
text:
Explaining the state’s initial decision to accept the closing of Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kate Walsh said in July, “The market has spoken.”

While the bluntness of that statement was shocking, the principle behind it is not. Whether they are for profit or technically nonprofit, hospitals are businesses. Like any business, they need customers — for hospitals, that means patients — and the revenue they generate for a healthy bottom line. Steward Health Care decided that five hospitals it operated met that criteria. Steward has reached deals with other operators to run four of those hospitals. The state seeks to take control of another one — St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton.

Without a rescuer, the two hospitals that did not make the cut will disappear. When the market speaks — and people listen to it — that’s what happens.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

All kinds of businesses disappear. Convenience stores and hardware stores. Bakeries and coffee shops. Banks, supermarkets, drug stores — and hospitals.

Economies of scale — defined as the advantages that can happen when a business increases in size — are part of the big cultural shift that has occurred, one that moves away from local businesses and toward large operations that are supposed to provide more efficient service and savings for consumers.

There’s no more Jordan Marsh or Filene’s and no Bank of Boston. John Hancock Financial Services is owned by Toronto-based Manulife. Large hospital networks like Mass General Brigham and Beth Israel Lahey Health dominate the health care landscape. When the market spoke, it said bigger is better, the strong will survive, and the weak will not.

The collapse of the for-profit hospital network operated by Steward , driven by the extraordinary greed of its CEO, Ralph de la Torre, is an exceptionally ugly part of that big economic picture. Meanwhile, the state’s initial acquiescence to the closing of Carney Hospital in Dorchester as a result of that collapse represents an acceptance of a common outcome: Businesses that don’t survive are often the ones located in low-income areas, which means the poorest and most marginalized suffer the most.

“As a business model, it’s just not succeeding,” said Larry DiCara, a former Boston city councilor and longtime political observer who grew up in the Carney neighborhood. “The constituency for the hospital is now people on the margins of society. As a business, it’s just not lined up to succeed.”

If Carney Hospital closes, leaving what social justice advocates call a health care desert, it won’t be the only potential desert in the Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan communities it serves.

As the Globe recently reported, after the fourth Walgreens shut down, there’s a growing drug store desert in the predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods of Roxbury and Mattapan. That happens when a chain like Walgreens comes in, and through economies of scale, squeezes out small, independent pharmacies by offering more variety and lower prices. However, if Walgreens or another large chain decides it’s not making enough money in a specific location, it feels free to shut it down, leaving behind people who no longer have a place nearby to pick up prescriptions.

People in those communities must also fight for food access. According to a city report issued in 2021, when it comes to availability of food through supermarkets and convenience stores, sections of Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, and Hyde Park are more than a half-mile from a grocery store — a distance that can be a barrier for elderly people or those with disabilities, and for those relying on public transportation.

Last April, it took a judge’s decision to put the Edgar P. Benjamin Healthcare Center, a Mission Hill nursing and rehabilitation home that has prioritized care for Black patients, into receivership to give it a chance to survive. A new administrator took over in May, after the previous administrator was ousted amid allegations of financial mismanagement. Whether it’s a winning business model is still unknown.

In Massachusetts, political leaders talk a lot about “health equity.” In January, the Healey administration announced what it said was a new approach to reducing health disparities across the state through “community-based interventions.” That was the same month that the Steward Health Care crisis began to publicly unfold, and when the Healey administration began to wrestle with the fallout.

In July, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu also announced a new health equity agenda aimed at improving life expectancy and reducing racial health disparities across the city of Boston

But when the market speaks, it does not demand equity. Unless political leaders intervene to make that happen, communities like the one served by Carney Hospital pay the price.

Joan Vennochi is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at joan.vennochi@globe.com. Follow her @joan_vennochi.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
CHARLY BLISS The power-pop foursome’s third album, “Forever,” faces life-altering upheavals with big hooks, storming riffs, and the sweet-and-sour-candy-coated voice of lead singer Eva Hendricks. Sept. 6, 7 p.m. Royale. 617-338-7699, royaleboston.com

Sept. 6 and 7, 7:30 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

49 WINCHESTER “Playing country music’s how I make my livin’/ And the bills ain’t gonna pay their self,” sings Isaac Gibson on the entirely autobiographical road song “Travelin’ Band,” from 49 Winchester’s fine new record, “Leavin’ This Holler.” Judging by the upward trajectory the band’s been on lately, the livin’s presumably getting a little better. Royale, 279 Tremont St. 888-929-7849. www.axs.com

BOY GOLDEN Winnipegger Liam Duncan, who performs as Boy Golden, brings his idiosyncratic folk ’n’ country to town in support of new album “For Eden,” which is chock full of songs that are singular and oddball, sometimes exuding his self-described “wide-eyed optimism” and at other turns prone to rip your heart out. Sept. 10, 7 p.m. $15. Red Room at Café 939, 939 Boylston St. 857-337-6206. www.berklee.edu/cafe939

JEFFREY FOUCAULT WITH ERIK KOSKINEN These sympatico singer-songwriters have been pairing up quite a bit recently, a double bill that’s entirely to our benefit. Koskinen will open the show with a set of his own music, then lend his formidable guitar talents to helping Foucault celebrate his new record, “The Universal Fire.” Sept. 12, 5:30 p.m., 7:30 p.m. $35. Fruitlands Museum, 110 Prospect Hill Road, Harvard. 978-228-5193. www.thetrustees.org/fruitlandsconcerts

STUART MUNRO

IVANNA CUESTA QUARTET The 2024-25 Dot Jazz Series kicks off with a concert by the dynamic Dominican drummer, synthesist, and composer’s band — featuring saxophonist Rick DiMuzio, pianist Jose Soto, and bassist Max Ridley — performing pieces from her debut album, “Letter to the Earth,” inspired by her love of nature and concern for our planet. Sept. 7, 7:30 p.m. $15-$20. Peabody Hall, Parish of All Saints, 209 Ashmont St., Dorchester. mandorlamusic.net

ANTHONY GOMES The Canadian blues rocker’s gritty vocals and galvanic guitar have been slaying international audiences since the late ‘90s. The Music Room, 541 Main St., West Yarmouth. musicroomcapecod.com

DOMINIQUE EADE TRIO Arthur’s House of Jazz presents an evening of American Songbook and jazz standards featuring superb singer Eade, who marries the cool tone of June Christy and the vocal virtuosity of Sarah Vaughan. With primo pianist Tim Ray and ubiquitous bassist John Lockwood. Sept. 12, 7:30 p.m. $20. The Sahara Club, 88 Oak St., Methuen. arthurshouseofjazz.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

Sept. 7 and 8. Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bostonpops.org

JUVENTAS NEW MUSIC ENSEMBLE Juventas kicks off its 20th year with a free concert of new music in a historic building, featuring the trio of clarinetist Celine Ferro, horn player Anne Howarth, and pianist Julia Scott Carey performing pieces by Oliver Caplan, Valerie Coleman, Stacy Garrop, and more. Sept. 8. 3 p.m. Longfellow House-Washington’s Headquarters National Historic Site, Cambridge.www.juventasmusic.org

A.Z. MADONNA

THE HOMBRES When a construction crew clashes with a yoga studio, both groups discover that when they get past the machismo, they find new strength in male friendships. Gloucester Stage Company and Teatro Chelsea, at Gloucester Stage Sept. 6-26, Chelsea Theatre Works Black Box Sept. 27-29. https://gloucesterstage.com/hombres/

ROMEO AND JULIET Award-winning director Diane Paulus reunites with choreographer Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui (“Jagged Little Pill”) for a movement-driven retelling of William Shakespeare’s tale of star-crossed lovers. Rudy Pankow (Netflix’s “Outer Banks”) and Emilia Suárez (Hulu’s “Up Here”) play the title roles while Terrence Mann (“Pippin”) plays the Friar. Through Oct. 6. American Repertory Theater, Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. https://americanrepertorytheater.org/shows-events/romeo-and-juliet/

THE HOUND OF THE BASKERVILLES Three women, led by award-winning Boston favorite Aimee Doherty, take on all the roles in the comic retelling of Arthur Conan Doyle’s mystery. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. Sept. 12-Oct. 6. www.centralsquaretheater.org/shows/the-hound-of-the-baskervilles

TERRY BYRNE

ARROWFEST DANCE SHOWCASE As part of the celebratory opening of its venue, Arrow Street Arts presents a one-night-only mini-festival bringing together five Boston-area dance companies. On the docket are performances by Anubhava Dance Company, Human Movement Project, Jean Appolon Expressions, Public Displays of Motion, and Unyted Stylz. Sept. 8, $20.Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. www.arrowstarts.org

CASSIE WANG The choreographer’s new ensemble work “SKY, UNOBSTRUCTED” blends contemporary dance, spoken text, and projection to explore themes of longing, ephemerality, presence, and absence. The collaboration between Arrow Street Arts and Midday Movement Series began in Mexico and was further developed remotely before reuniting the artists for this performance in Boston.

Sept. 9, $10. Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. www.arrowstarts.org

VIOLET NOX: IN THE HEART OF THE SUN In this immersive dance/theater/music performance, Miami dance artist Wisty Heart join the Boston-based electronic music trio Violet Nox. Called a “journey through the awakening, destruction, and resurrection of the human heart,” the new work promises a fusion of movement, sound, symbols, and light, using the sun as a metaphor for desire. Sept. 12, $20-$40. Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. www.arrowstarts.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

ON CHRISTOPHER STREET: TRANSGENDER PORTRAITS BY MARK SELIGER Last chance: Seliger, a renowned celebrity portrait photographer for magazines like Vanity Fair and GQ, ran a personal side project from 2013 to 2016, taking street portraits of people on Christopher Street in Manhattan’s West Village. A historic epicenter of the American gay rights movement, the neighborhood remains a hub of gay life in America. (The Stonewall Inn, a bar that was the site of a 1969 protest against police raids, considered by many to be the foundation of the modern LGBTQ+ movement, is at 53 Christopher.) Seliger’s street portraits evolved into a larger documentary project about contemporary LGBTQ+ culture. This show includes 32 of those portraits, as well as a film and responses and exhibitions from the local LGBTQ+ community. Through Sept. 8. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.gardnermuseum.org

AMERICANS IN PARIS: ARTISTS WORKING IN POSTWAR FRANCE, 1946-1962 This exhibition sketches a nascent movement of American artists in Europe at the foundation of late American Modernism: Ellsworth Kelly, Kenneth Noland, Jack Youngerman, to name but a few. With 135 works by approximately 70 artists, the show both looks back and projects forward to the moment’s lasting influence with works by such notables as Beauford Delaney, Carmen Herrera, and Joan Mitchell. Through Jan. 5. Addison Gallery of American Art at Phillips Academy, 3 Chapel Ave., Andover. 978-749-4015, www.addisongallery.org

ABSTRACT FLASH: UNSEEN ANDREW WYETH Last chance: Wyeth, a giant of American realism who died in 2009, went against the grain of mid-20th-century American art, dominated by the Abstract Expresssionists and their many descendants. But while his work could be crisply representational (if almost unfailingly dour and bleak), the loose, naturalistic brushwork of his watercolors revealed an interest in the medium’s more wayward tendencies. Did he ever paint abstractly? That’s a question even this show — predicated on that very notion — doesn’t answer clearly. But the intimations, hints, and teases of the loose washes of color present here surely tantalize, if not resolve. Through Sept. 8. Farnsworth Museum of American Art, 16 Museum St., Rockland, Maine. 207-596-6457, www.farnsworthmuseum.org

MURRAY WHYTE

THE ART OF PAPER: CLAIRE VAN VLIET AND THE JANUS PRESS In 1955, Van Vliet, a handmade paper and book artist, founded the Janus Press, which specializes in collaborations between artists and writers. This show spotlights the attention to social issues and delight in the natural world evident in her own collaborations: sculptural books, pigmented paper pulp paintings, and more, made with poets such as Rita Dove and Denise Levertov. Sept. 9-Dec. 30. Boston Athenaeum, 10½ Beacon St. www.bostonathenaeum.org/whats-on/exhibitions/van-vliet/

CATE McQUAID

CARMEN LYNCH When one of the comedian’s friends gave birth, she brought the placenta home to eat, which puzzled Lynch. “Apparently it has a lot of vitamins,” she says. “I was like, you know what else has vitamins? Vitamins. Vitamins have a lot of vitamins.”Sept. 6, 8 p.m. $30. Off Cabot Comedy and Events, 9 Wallis St., Beverly. www.offcabot.org

NEIL HAMBURGER In the 30 years since he first popped up, Hamburger has moved beyond parody and become his own twisted little universe. KATIE BOYLE Moving to New York City from Ireland, Boyle has experienced a few culture shocks over the past several years. “For example, as a foreigner, I really hate tipping,” she says. “But as a bartender, I really hate foreigners.”Sept. 6-7, 8 p.m. $25. The Comedy Scene, 200 Patriot Place, Foxborough. www.thecomedyscene.club

Old State House, 206 Washington St. revolutionaryspaces.org

ARUSHI JACOB

title: Steward CEO Ralph de la Torre refuses to comply with subpoena for federal hearing
text:
“De la Torre is as cowardly as he is cruel,” Markey said in a statement issued with fellow Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren. “He owes the public and Congress answers for his appalling greed — and de la Torre must be held in contempt if he fails to appear before the Committee.”

An attorney for de la Torre sent a letter to Committee chairman Bernie Sanders of Vermont on Wednesday arguing that de la Torre is prohibited by Steward from discussing the company’s bankruptcy “because those matters had already been delegated exclusively to an independent sub-committee of Steward’s board of managers.”

The attorney, Alexander J. Merton, added that if de la Torre were to testify next week, it could disrupt the proceedings and be used by the lawmakers to “turn the hearing into a pseudo-criminal proceeding in which they use the time, not to gather facts, but to convict Dr. de la Torre in the eyes of public opinion.”

The letter concludes by asking the committee to “reschedule its hearing for a more appropriate date after the conclusion of Steward’s bankruptcy proceedings.”

De la Torre was subpoenaed in July, after he did not honor several requests to appear voluntarily. It was the first time in more than four decades the committee opted to compel a witness to testify.

Failure to comply with a subpoena “without adequate excuse” can result in a contempt charge, according to Cornell University’s Legal Information Institute. Both the committee and the full Senate would likely have to vote to send the charge to the Department of Justice.

Sanders made clear Wednesday that he did not believe de la Torre’s reasons were adequate, promising the committee would ”move forward aggressively to compel Dr. de la Torre to testify to the gross mismanagement of Steward Health Care.”

“We will not accept this postponement,” Sanders said in a statement. “Congress will hold Dr. de la Torre accountable for his greed and for the damage he has caused to hospitals and patients throughout America.”

As the sides girded for a potential legal showdown in Washington, the company and its creditors were haggling in a Houston courtroom over how to unwind a financial crisis that has left major parts of the Massachusetts health system in limbo for months.

Judge Christopher Lopez ruled Boston Medical Center can buy St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center and Good Samaritan Medical Center, while Lifespan Health System can acquire St. Anne’s Hospital and Morton Hospital, and Lawrence General Hospital can buy Holy Family Hospital.

Two other Steward hospitals in the state — Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer and Carney Hospital in Dorchester — closed last weekend after neither received qualified bids for a takeover.

The proceeds of the sales are largely tied to the hospitals’ underlying real estate, which Steward sold in an unorthodox move that left the institutions on the hook for millions of dollars in annual rent payments that would ultimately compound the system’s financial stress.

The sales would mark an unceremonious exit from the state’s health care market for de la Torre, an ambitious cardiac surgeon who led efforts to convert a chain of struggling Catholic hospitals into for-profit businesses. That launched the company that would become Steward, which expanded nationally, then moved to Texas before its collapse.

The transactions could face some further hurdles. The hospitals must change hands by Sept. 30 or the buyers can terminate the sales. But the deals are still subject to state and federal regulatory reviews in processes that typically take months.

Governor Maura Healey’s administration — which helped midwife the hospital sales — will be pushing for rapid approvals by regulators.

Meanwhile, the judge said he would withhold about $17 million from the sales proceeds to determine at a later date how much, if any, should go to a group of Steward’s secured lenders that strenuously objected to how they were allocated. The purchase deals assigned the bulk of the hospitals’ value to their real estate.

Judge Lopez, at a hearing in US Bankruptcy Court in Houston where Steward filed for bankruptcy on May 6, also green-lighted another $42 million in funding from Massachusetts to keep the hospitals solvent until new owners can take over operations. The money must be released by Friday for the hospitals to meet their payrolls.

That outlay will raise the state’s total bridge funding commitment to $72 million. The hospitals’ dire financial condition was underscored in a Labor Day court filing in which Steward said it had effectively run out of bankruptcy financing from private lenders.

Other issues remain to be worked out. The hospitals’ buyers, for instance, are in discussions with the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Boston — which sold the hospitals to Steward in 2010 — about whether to retain their names and religious artifacts.

“This is the best deal that’s on the table, and that’s saying a lot,” the judge said, citing the Healey administration’s role.

The state’s financial support is only beginning. While terms of the sales deals were disclosed last week, the administration negotiated separate agreements to back each of the buyers with additional money — some from the federal government or other hospitals — to support the transition over the next three years. Those packages haven’t been made public, but are expected to total as much as $700 million.

In the deals approved Wednesday, the lion’s share of the proceeds will be allocated to Apollo Global Management, an investment firm that holds the mortgages on Massachusetts properties owned jointly by Medical Properties Trust and Macquarie Infrastructure Partners.

Boston Medical Center, the state’s largest safety-net hospital, is paying $140 million for St. Elizabeth’s in Brighton and Good Samaritan in Brockton. All but $9.5 million of the sale will be going to Apollo, though the number could change depending on the resolution of the state’s effort to take the St. Elizabeth’s real estate by eminent domain.

Similarly, all but $8.2 million of the $175 million that Providence-based Lifespan is paying for St. Anne’s in Fall River and Morton in Taunton is being allocated to the real estate. And Lawrence General’s entire $28 million purchase price for Holy Family, which has campuses in Haverhill and Methuen, is being assigned to mortgage holder Apollo.

Jackie Kucinich of the Globe staff contributed to this report.
