While terms of the sales deals were disclosed last week, the administration negotiated separate agreements to back each of the buyers with additional money — some of it collected from the federal government or other hospitals — to support the transition over the next three years. Those packages haven’t been made public, but are expected to total as much as $700 million.

In the deals approved Wednesday, the lion’s share of the proceeds will be allocated to Apollo Global Mangement, an investment firm that holds the mortgages on Massachusetts hospital land and buildings owned jointly by Medical Properties Trust and Macquarie Infrastructure Partners. The landlords are turning the properties over to Apollo because the mortgages they owe exceeds the value of the sales proceeds.

Boston Medical Center, the state’s largest safety-net hospital, is paying $140 million for St. Elizabeth’s in Brighton and Good Samaritan in Brockton. All but $9.5 million of the sale will be going to Apollo.

Similarly, all but $8.2 million of the $175 million that Providence-based Lifespan is paying for St. Anne’s in Fall River and Morton in Taunton is being allocated to the real estate. And, Lawrence General’s entire $28 million purchase price for Holy Family, which has campuses in Haverhill and Methuen, is begin assigned to mortgage holder Apollo.

Objecting to the allocations of the proceeds, Michael Price, a lawyer representing a consortium of private credit firms that gave Steward about $575 million in secured loans during the bankruptcy process, said the allocation of the proceeds created “a zero-dollar economic situation” for his clients, “eviscerating the rights of the secured creditors” in the bankruptcy.

“No one can be surprised that we’re standing here in opposition,” Price said, noting that Steward still owes about $40 million in paid time off to hospital workers who aren’t secured creditors. “We’d like for employees to be paid but... we can’t subordinate our claims to junior claims.”

But noting that the hospitals are operating at a loss, Candace Arthur, a lawyer for Steward, said the lenders aren’t required to consent to the sales deals if the debtor has conducted a robust sales process and there is a compelling business reason for the transactions.

“These sales for the Massachusetts hospitals are the debtor’s only option available after a thorough search” for buyers, Arthur said. “And the transaction terms reflect hard-fought negotiations, compromises, and settlements... The marketing process has spoken.”

This story has been updated to correct the total value of the hospital sales.

title: Dolan upsets 25-year incumbent, Civil emerges from four-way race in Governor’s Council primaries
text:
In a crowded race for an open Second District seat, Tamisha Civil, a probation officer from Stoughton and daughter of Haitian immigrants, topped three other Democratic opponents in her bid to become the first woman of color to ever serve on the council. Civil, 43, will face Republican Francis T. Crimmins, a retired judge and former municipal official, in November’s general election.

The races stood out on a Democratic ballot with little competition elsewhere. The council has proven a hotbed for political activity, drawing anywhere from two to seven competitive Democratic primaries for its eight seats every year since 2012. This year, three primaries, including one for the Second District’s open seat, drew multiple candidates — the most since 2018.

Every seat on the current council is held by a Democrat.

The rematch between Dolan, of Concord, and Devaney, of Watertown, was the most heated.

They have attacked each other’s records and have accused each other of lying, including two years ago, when Devaney had prevailed by fewer than 1,700 votes among the 119,000 cast. Dolan then vowed to challenge her again, and this time ran with a swell of support from other Democratic leaders, including US Representatives Katherine Clark, Ayanna Pressley, Lori Trahan, and Seth Moulton, and four sitting members of the Governor’s Council.

Dolan, 61, this time launched her campaign nearly a year ahead of the November election, offering her campaign a long runway against Devaney, who had previously beaten back 11 primary challengers since first taking office in 1999.

“When I started running 2 ½ years ago [in the first challenge], I had people say that no one would care and no one would pay attention. I knew that wasn’t true. But I had no idea it would get this much attention,” Dolan said of the race.

“It’s definitely a new era for the Governor’s Council with new people and new perspectives,” she said.

Devaney, 85, said Wednesday that her push for changes on the council, including continuing to livestream its meetings and hearings, didn’t make her “popular” with her fellow councilors, some of whom she clashed with publicly and repeatedly over other issues. Current Councilors Eileen R. Duff, Paul M. DePalo, Joseph C. Ferreira, and Terrence W. Kennedy all backed Dolan.

“I’m going out proud,” Devaney said after a council meeting at the State House. “I try to have openness, and that’s what I’ve done. So no good deed goes unpunished. But you know what? I made it better, and that’s what I’m going out thinking: My reforms made this council better than when I came in.”

In the Fourth District, which includes parts of Boston and the South Shore, Iannella captured nearly 57 percent of the vote on Tuesday, fending off Stacey Borden, a Dorchester Democrat and the founder of New Beginnings Reentry Services, and Quincy Democrat Ron Iacobucci, executive director of the city’s Workforce Development Department.

Borden, too, was vying to become the first woman of color on the council, which has roots in the Colonial era, and the first person of color on the panel in more than three decades.

Iannella said voters “rewarded me for the work I’ve done.” By the end of his current term, he will have served 38 of the last 40 years on the council.

“As long as my health continues to be great, I’ll keep running,” Iannella, 71, said. “I’m a lawyer, and people will ask, ‘You gonna retire?’ What am I going to do? You know, how often can you play golf? So I’m not the retired-type person.”

Civil emerged from a four-way primary for the vacant seat in the Second District, which stretches southwest of Boston from Milton to Attleboro. The Stoughton Democrat has said she was motivated to run by the experience of her cousin, James Lucien, who spent nearly 27 years in prison before his murder conviction was tossed in 2021 because the trial was marred by police misconduct and perjury.

She won 39 percent of the vote, outdistancing fellow Democrats Sean Murphy and Muriel Kramer, who each won 22 percent, and David Reservitz, who won 17 percent, according to the AP.

“A lot of people are fed up with the injustices [in the judicial system] and they want someone with my experience who can bring transparency and bring integrity to the council,” Civil said Wednesday. “For 244 years, not having a woman of color on the council speaks volumes as to what we need to do in order to make sure the injustices that are happening are changed.”

Civil will face Crimmins, who served for 18 years as a judge, including at the district and appellate court levels. He later served as Stoughton’s town manager for two years before working as Avon’s town administrator.

The matchup is one of four on the November ballot. There’s also a three-way race for an open seat in the North Shore-anchored Fifth District between former Methuen city councilor Eunice Zeigler, a Democrat and daughter of Haitian immigrants; Republican Anne Manning-Martin; and Jody Elliott, an independent candidate.

In the Seventh District, DePalo faces a Republican challenger in Andrew Couture, a Fitchburg city councilor, while Ferreira, the incumbent in the First District, faces a challenge from Wareham’s Krysten Condon, an independent candidate.

title: Steward CEO Ralph de la Torre could be charged with contempt of Congress. What now?
text:
But Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who chairs the committee, said he would refuse to delay the hearing until after the company’s bankruptcy proceedings had concluded, setting the stage for the legal showdown.

“If Congress has a legitimate legislative purpose to subpoena someone and ask them to testify, then they have to show up and testify,” said Jeremy R. Paul, a professor at the Northeastern University School of Law.

“If the person called to testify is concerned about potential criminal exposure, they can take the Fifth Amendment and not [answer questions],” Paul continued. “But that’s something that they have to actually assert. They can’t just not show up.”

But if de la Torre does, in fact, turn out to be a no-show, charging him with contempt of Congress would be a multistep process, lawmakers and legal experts said. The procedure depends on whether lawmakers decide to pursue a criminal or civil charge — or both — which the committee is still weighing, Senator Ed Markey said in a press conference Thursday in Boston.

“Ralph de le Torre has shown contempt for our health care system, and now the United States Senate must bring contempt charges against Ralph de la Torre,” Markey said in the press conference, next to a sign with the question, “Where is Ralph de la Torre?”

Senator Elizabeth Warren, meanwhile, took the threat a step further. “If Mr. de la Torre continues to resist, federal marshals can arrest him and bring him before the committee,” she said. “If Mr. de la Torre wants to try to weasel out of responsibility, he will have to do that in public — that is what the subpoena demands.”

In the case of a criminal charge, first, both the committee and the full Senate would likely need to hold votes in order to issue de la Torre a criminal contempt citation, according to a report from the Congressional Research Service.

According to the report, the “President of the Senate,” who is currently Vice President Kamala Harris, would then certify this with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. The office would then choose whether to convene a grand jury to potentially indict de la Torre over the alleged misdemeanor. If a grand jury chose to indict him, that would launch a standard criminal trial.

But while a criminal conviction can carry a fine of up to $100,000 and up to a year in prison, it ultimately can’t force de la Torre to talk, said Stan M. Brand, an attorney who represented former Trump White House official Peter Navarro in his own contempt of Congress case.

“What they get out of that is the satisfaction of convicting him of contempt, but they don’t necessarily get his testimony,” said Brand.

And there are no guarantees that federal prosecutors would pick up the case, said Stephen A. Saltzburg, a law professor at George Washington University. Saltzburg pointed to the recent example of Mark Meadows, another former White House official in the Trump administration who, unlike Navarro and fellow aide Steve Bannon, avoided a contempt charge by negotiating with federal prosecutors.

“There’s a lot of discretion there,” said Saltzburg. “I think if somebody stonewalls . . . it’s more likely to produce a criminal charge.”

Lawmakers could also pursue a “civil enforcement” of the subpoena. For this to happen, the Senate would have to greenlight a lawsuit against de la Torre with the US District Court for the District of Columbia, according to the Congressional Research Service. This would likely be a quicker undertaking than the criminal route, Brand said, and, if successful, would compel de la Torre to testify, per the research service.

“Unlike criminal contempt, in a civil enforcement, sanctions (imprisonment and/or a fine) can be imposed until the subpoenaed party agrees to comply thereby creating an incentive for compliance; namely, the termination of punishment,” the Congressional Research Service said in a report.

But the possibility of a legal action may be just as much a bargaining chip as a legitimate threat, experts said.

“[De la Torre’s] lawyer could be playing for time — maybe he tries to negotiate with the committee, reduce the scope of what he has to testify to,” said Brand. “The bluster that occurs in public sometimes belies what’s going on behind the scenes.”

During the press conference Thursday, lawmakers repeatedly referenced a Globe Spotlight report published this week that detailed de la Torre’s immense personal profit from Steward even as the company failed vulnerable patients, laid off staff, and stiffed vendors. De la Torre, per the report, used Steward’s coffers to finance his personal travel and a large donation to his children’s Dallas private school, and pushed Steward to sign contracts with outside companies in which de la Torre also held an ownership stake.

De la Torre has been the face of the public collapse of the for-profit hospital system he founded in 2010, which is now wading its way through bankruptcy proceedings. A judge agreed Wednesday to sales of six of its Massachusetts hospitals, but two of its other facilities in the Bay State — Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer — closed last weekend after no takeover bids were deemed qualified.

According to Markey, he and Senator Sanders are currently working with their Republican colleagues to determine if they want to pursue a civil or criminal contempt charge and to quickly organize a vote on the citation, adding that they would determine a pathway over the course of the next week.

“We will have a hearing, regardless, next week, with an empty chair, where he would have sat,” Markey said.

But no matter lawmakers’ path forward, if the matter does end up going to the courts, it’s unlikely to be settled quickly, especially given the potential for appeals, said Brand.

“Maybe [de la Torre] thinks he can run out the clock to the end of the year when there’s a new Congress, and then who knows what happens?” said Brand.

title: Federal prosecutors detail how reputed street gang members allegedly perpetrated a mail theft scheme in Boston suburbs
text:
In an affidavit filed Aug. 27, ATF Special Agent E. Austin Wozniak wrote that the men allegedly perpetrated the fraud between July 2023 and February 2024. Their alleged behavior is called “card cracking,” he wrote.

“Card cracking schemes are fueled by checks that are stolen from U.S. Postal Service (’USPS’) collection boxes,” Wozniak wrote. “The ink from stolen checks [is] chemically washed and rewritten to various recruited bank account holders. These washed checks are deposited into checking accounts for cash withdrawal or laundering through money transfers and other means, such as the purchase of postal money orders.”

Once the parcels are purloined, Wozniak said, “offenders wash stolen checks with chemicals that erase handwritten ink, leaving the check otherwise intact. This process allows for the blank check to be rewritten to any intended payee in any amount.”

Straw account holders are typically recruited through social media and word of mouth and get compensated with a cut of the ill-gotten cash, according to the affidavit.

“Account holders essentially allow for a card cracking suspect to take control of their bank account,” Wozniak wrote. “Stolen, washed checks are deposited into account holders’ bank accounts via ATM deposits or mobile deposits, the account balance is monitored, and cash is withdrawn at ATM machines as soon as it is made available by the bank.”

He wrote that during the summer of 2023, Wellesley police and surrounding law enforcement agencies started receiving numerous check fraud reports pertaining to checks placed in the mail in June and July of last year.

There were 21 such incidents during that time period reported in Wellesley, Brookline, West Roxbury, Newton, Needham, Sherborn, Brockton, and Braintree, the affidavit said.

“Wellesley Police had detectives assigned to this long running investigation, and we are obviously very pleased at the results with these charges,” said Wellesley Police Chief Scott Whittemore in a statement. “Our officers and detectives have invested a great deal of time and effort investigating this case, as well as the many other mail theft cases that have occurred.”

The fraudulent check cashing “unfortunately continues however,” Whittemore said.

He said Wellesley and other communities “continue to experience theft from blue mailboxes. These thefts, usually by suspects with keys, occur during the overnight and early morning hours. We’ve noted the thefts are prevalent after hours on the weekends as well. I would continue to stress that citizens avoid using blue mailboxes, and instead go inside the Post Office to mail letters. I would strongly suggest never mailing a letter after the posted collection times, or in a case where the letter would potentially sit overnight in a mailbox.”

And the stolen cash fuels devastating violence, according to agent Wozniak.

“I learned that some Mission Hill members and associates use the proceeds from the target offenses to purchase weapons, which facilitates violent crime within the gang,” he wrote in the affidavit, adding that the gangsters also allegedly “sell stolen checks to further profit from their mail theft.”

Such theft has been a longstanding issue in Massachusetts.

In January, Needham police warned residents of mailbox “phishing” and urged them to bring outgoing mail into a post office instead of trusting public boxes. Thieves had allegedly been using keys to open mailboxes at mail drop-off locations and stealing mail inside, police said at the time.

In late 2022, Needham, along with other neighboring communities, was targeted for mail thefts by people looking to steal checks, authorities said. In December 2022, cops in Dedham said they had received “multiple reports of mailbox fishing,” and in September 2022, two members of the Newton Police Department took part in a sting operation that resulted in the arrest of an alleged mailbox thief. In August of that year, after receiving multiple reports of checks being stolen from mailboxes and altered (for amounts totaling more than $250,000), police in Mattapoisett arrested two 18-year-olds from Dorchester who were allegedly seen mailbox fishing.

Then, last November, police arrested two men and recovered more than 1,000 pieces of mail allegedly stolen in Wellesley after thieves crashed a vehicle in Brookline.

Some thieves have been even more brazen, robbing letter carriers at gunpoint.

In late December, Boston police responded to a radio call reporting an armed robbery at Talbot and Welles avenues, police said in a statement. Officers located a postal worker who said his mail key was stolen at gunpoint, the statement said.

Another robbery of a mail carrier by a gun-toting assailant was reported in December 2022 in Melrose.

title: Boston Public Schools welcomes back students for first day
text:
“I’m too tired for this,” Landen complained around 7:15, five minutes after the scheduled pickup. Minutes ticked by, and eventually, the Buckmans could see the bus drive by in the distance, skipping Landen altogether. The Buckmans rushed to a neighbor’s house, asking for a ride to school, where Landen arrived 20 minutes late.

“That was an epic fail,” Buckman said. “Hopefully they pick him up tomorrow.”

BPS students in grades 1-12 returned to school Thursday, with promises of more reliable bus transportation in a district that has been plagued for years by late buses. This year, district leaders announced the new bus tracking app and announced they were fully staffed with both bus drivers and bus monitors for for the first time in recent memory, with more than 700 of each. But despite such progress, stories still abounded of families such as the Buckmans who were left waiting for buses that came hours late or never showed up at all.

The district did not share data on the day’s on-time bus arrival rate by press time. In 2023, 61 percent were on time for the first day, far from the 95 percent on-time rate the district is required to hit under a state improvement plan. Last year’s on-time arrival rate was an improvement over the district’s most recent five-year average of 51 percent.

It’s unclear if skipped stops such as the Buckmans were rare occurrences or a systemic issue Thursday morning.

In the West End, Stefano Spina faced the same trouble getting his 7-year-old daughter, Miriam, to the first day of second grade at the Warren-Prescott School in Charlestown. The family waited for 30 minutes at the bus stop, located on a bustling Cambridge Street, before calling an Uber to get her to school. (He heard from another parent that the bus eventually showed up two hours late.) Last year, Miriam was often late to school because of a late or no-show bus, and the new year did not begin promising.

“We hoped things would get better,” Spina said. “Unfortunately, today, on the very first day of school for my daughter Miriam, the bus never showed up.”

At the Joseph Lee K-8 School in Dorchester, the first bus pulled into the school at 7:10 a.m., 20 minutes before the school day started, but most came after 7:30 a.m., after the school day was underway.

Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper, at the Lee to greet students for the first day, acknowledged students would be tardy because of bus delays and encouraged parents to be patient as bus drivers navigated construction, additional traffic, and new routes at the beginning of the school year.

“The more we’re in communication with the parents, the quicker we can solve the issue,” Skipper said.

Still, as students arrived at the Lee, excitement came with them. One girl sashayed confidently up the sidewalk donning a tiara to mark her birthday, while a classmate sported a Spider-Man themed outfit. Others moved at a slower pace, sleep still in their eyes. Little ones with toothy grins appeared eager to assert their independence, letting go of their parents’ hands before reaching the school entrance.

Wu, Skipper, and campus educators greeted students with high-fives, fist bumps, or hugs, handing them orange pencils as they filed in the front doors, and wishing them luck on their first day.

“If you can’t tell, we love the first day of school,” Wu said.

The district had 50,603 students registered as of Aug. 27, although the official Oct. 1 enrollment tends to be lower.

The district transports 22,000 students daily on its 632 buses, although it will not have a full ridership until next week, when its youngest learners return to school. The district already has been responsible for busing some students, including private school and charter school students, some of which returned to school in August.

BPS will have to improve bus transportation if it is to meet a two-year-old state mandate to have 95 percent of buses arrive on time. By the end of the the last school year, the district was nearing 90 percent of buses arriving on time. For 2023, the district reported that there were no uncovered bus routes on the first day. However, that data didn’t count buses that don’t show up at all to pick up students at certain stops.

In previous years, BPS was hit by a national driver shortage, prompting the district to consolidate bus routes and step up recruiting and training of drivers. The district also struck a new contract with the bus drivers union in 2022 that barred drivers from skipping work — leaving students stranded — then retroactively classifying their no-show as “personal time off.” That contract expired June 30 but has been extended for a few additional months.

title: Buy you a drink? Boston may score 225 liquor licenses
text:
Massachusetts is on the verge of enacting a landmark overhaul of its liquor laws, which will significantly reshape Boston’s cultural and economic landscape. The legislation, which introduces 225 additional liquor licenses in the city, goes beyond a mere regulatory update — it is a powerful advancement in equity, with substantial implications for social justice, economic opportunity, and cultural enrichment.

Spearheaded by Senator Liz Miranda of Roxbury and Representative Christopher Worrell of Dorchester, the bill would expand access to liquor licenses and stimulate growth in Boston’s dynamic hospitality sector. It would create a limited number of new, nontransferable liquor licenses for specific ZIP codes in Boston. This legislation would increase opportunities for business owners and aspiring restaurateurs to contribute to the economic and cultural vitality of neighborhoods that have historically faced disinvestment and gentrification.

Without these new licenses, often the only path to obtaining a liquor license is to purchase one from a current license holder, with a reported price tag of up to $600,000. For many entrepreneurs of color, this is an insurmountable hurdle to launching their hospitality ventures.

For Boston’s Black communities, this legislation is particularly significant. Historically, systemic barriers and high costs have prevented Black entrepreneurs from entering and thriving in the city’s hospitality sector. Alcohol sales are twice as profitable as food sales, and 80 percent of restaurant concepts are not profitable without alcohol sales. However, according to the Boston Black Hospitality Coalition, less than 2 percent of Boston liquor licenses are held by operators who identify as Black — even though 22 percent of Boston residents are Black.

The anticipated increase in Black-owned restaurants and bars promises to enrich Boston’s cultural fabric, notably in Dorchester, East Boston, Hyde Park, Mattapan, and Roxbury. This influx of new businesses is expected to create job opportunities within the community, driving economic growth and fostering a renewed sense of ownership and pride. Moreover, the potential for increased investment in Black neighborhoods could catalyze broader economic revitalization and enhance social cohesion.

The bill would also contribute to the creation of “third spaces” — vital community hubs where people can gather, connect, affirm, and sustain their cultural heritage. By enabling more diverse ownership of hospitality venues, the new licenses would support the cultivation of these vibrant social and cultural gathering points, particularly in neighborhoods, like Nubian Square, that are undergoing development but lacking destinations for community connection.

Boston’s cultural landscape is set to benefit considerably from this paradigm shift. These new licenses would help nurture vibrant community ecosystems where creativity and innovation can thrive. A more varied array of liquor licenses would lead to a dynamic hospitality scene that reflects the city’s diverse population. New establishments will bring fresh perspectives, excitement, and creative energy to Boston’s neighborhoods, enhancing the city’s reputation as a cultural hub.

The reform also addresses the pressing issue of retention and attraction of talent in the city and across Massachusetts by supporting the growth of Black-owned businesses and generating new job opportunities. Small, diverse businesses are more likely to contribute to the local economy by hiring workers in the neighborhood. This promotes both economic development and strengthens Boston’s competitive edge in an evolving job market.

We applaud the Legislature for coming to an agreement and look forward to the bill being sent to and signed by Governor Maura Healey. This overdue reform will reflect the city’s diverse and dynamic communities.

Nicole Obi is president and CEO of the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts. Imari Paris Jeffries is president and CEO of Embrace Boston.

title: Netflix’s ‘Love Is Blind’ is casting a new season in New England. Here’s how you can audition.
text:
Locals looking for love have a chance to shoot their shots on Netflix’s hit reality series, “Love Is Blind.”

For the uninitiated, the experimental dating show pairs potential mates in separate pods that allow for smooth talking, but prevent them from seeing each other. If sparks fly, couples must get engaged before they can meet face-to-face, with subsequent episodes following their journeys down the aisle.

While “Love Is Blind” season 7 — which sets up its love shack in Washington, D.C. — debuts on Netflix on Oct. 2, producers are already casting for the next across New England. According to Donna Driscoll, executive vice president of casting and talent at Kinetic Content, the audition process for the New England season is “in full swing,” with her team “actively going through every single application” from the region.

“There’s been such a great response and we’ve received so much support from communities all around New England,” Driscoll told the Globe in a recent Zoom interview.

“Love Is Blind” is no stranger to New England’s charms. Season six, which tapped singles in North Carolina, featured Dorchester native and former Patriots cheerleader Amber Desiree “AD” Smith as a contestant. Driscoll, whose team features many New Hampshire natives, is excited to cast in New England, praising locals for their “uniqueness and authenticity,” which she claims are key to being “successful in the experiment.”

“I am always curious and wide open about what I’m looking for in each city that we go to because I feel like each city offers something very very different,” Driscoll explained. “But for New England, I think the main thing that I don’t have to worry about is finding people who are authentic.”

“I feel like there’s going to be a lot of strong characters here,” she added.

According to Driscoll, hopeful candidates should fill out an application on libcasting.com and, to be safe, should have everything submitted over the next three months or so. Driscoll noted that it’s important to be thoughtful with your answers, as they “absolutely read every single application.”

“In that same application, there’s a 15-second video submission that I highly recommend you take the time to really talk about why you need ‘Love Is Blind,’ why you want to find love in such an unorthodox way,” Driscoll said, adding that they are looking for “somebody who is serious, mature, authentic, has the ability to be vulnerable, and excites us.”

If an applicant fits the bill, the next step is a phone interview, which can take up to an hour. Should all go well, the candidate will then move on to a one-on-one chat with a casting producer from the show.

“After that, we’ll make the decision of whether or not we’re going to move that forward to present our partners at Netflix,” Driscoll said.

Although no details are available yet as to when the “Love Is Blind” New England season will film and air, Driscoll shared that there are plans to have an open casting call “within the coming weeks” where candidates can audition over Zoom (Kinetic Content will share details on its Instagram page when available). Driscoll encourages applicants to also do the virtual casting call, which will give them the chance to let their personalities shine.

Driscoll believes the show’s popularity is because it showcases “authentic people” who are “not afraid to be themselves” and come from diverse backgrounds.

All occupational backgrounds need apply — just as long as they aren’t doing it for the ‘gram.

“I think the major thing to distinguish is that we aren’t looking for influencers,” Driscoll said. “We’re casting very real people who are functioning in their everyday life and have everything going for them. They just are missing that one puzzle piece, which is finding the love of their life.”

Matt Juul can be reached at matthew.juul@globe.com.

title: With cash running dry, regulators pressed to green-light Steward hospital sales by end of September
text:
But the deals still are subject to review by the state Department of Public Health, the state Health Policy Commission, the US Department of Justice, and the Federal Trade Commission in a compressed timetable dictated in large part by the hospitals’ precarious finances.

Some of those agencies are already familiar with the high-profile Steward health care crisis. Whether that will enable them to act more swiftly than they typically do remains to be seen.

“Time is of the essence,” said Paul Hattis, senior fellow at the Lown Institute, a health care think tank in Needham. “Money is running low. Given the stakes, I don’t think there’ll be an extensive government review process. Nobody wants to risk these deals falling by the wayside.”

Two factors are putting pressure on regulators to quickly stamp their approval on the Steward hospital sales. Under the terms of the deals outlined in bankruptcy court filings late last week, either Steward or the nonprofit buyers can back out if the deals don’t close by Sept. 30.

Just as important, a separate court filing last Monday made it clear that Steward, which filed for bankruptcy in May, has exhausted its own financing and is relying on monthly payments from the state of Massachusetts — totaling $72 million to date — to meet its payrolls and keep the doors open to patients until the hospitals change hands.

“Without the September funding [from Massachusetts],” the debtors have insufficient liquidity to continue funding the losses of these hospitals,” Steward’s bankruptcy lawyers wrote in the filing.

If the deals aren’t consummated by the end of the month, the Healey administration would be pressed to provide a third tranche of bridge financing to keep the six hospitals afloat or risk a scenario in which Steward liquidates its holdings and shutters the hospitals.

Such a scenario isn’t far-fetched. Two other Steward hospitals, Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, closed Aug. 31 after failing to attract bids that Steward deemed qualified. The shutdowns idled 1,400 workers and disrupted care in low-income Boston neighborhoods and rural north central Massachusetts.

Federal inquiries into mergers and acquisitions, which focus on antitrust concerns such as competition and market concentration, typically take between six months and a year — and sometimes run longer. The state Health Policy Commission, which examines issues ranging from health care cost and quality to access and equity, can take up to nine months if it decides to launch a full “cost and market impact review.”

One agency seems ready to act quickly. The state DPH, which issues hospital licenses sought through “determination of need” applications, evaluates operators’ suitability along with the physical standards of the hospitals. The department has been monitoring the Steward hospitals for months, and an administration spokesperson said the approval process “should not alter the timeline for sales and transfer of ownership.”

For the Healey administration, the meter is running. The bridge financing is only one part of the state’s financial commitment to the surviving hospitals, which will immediately need to offset financial losses and make substantial repairs and upgrades after years of neglect.

In addition to the $72 million, Healey administration officials have said it would spend $417 million over the next three years to support five of the hospitals being purchased by Boston Medical Center, Lifespan Health System, and Lawrence General Hospital. Some of those dollars will come from federal reimbursements to the state Medicaid program, called MassHealth, and from assessments on other hospitals.

The administration didn’t specify whether the state funds would be used for transition costs, operating expenses, renovations, or making up financial shortfalls. And it didn’t disclose its financial backing for the largest Steward hospital, St. Elizabeth’s. In addition to that support, the administration may be on the hook for a big payout to a Wall Street investment firm that controls the hospital’s Brighton Center property.

State officials have begun steps to seize the St. Elizabeth’s land by eminent domain to turn over hospital operations to BMC. But the firm, Apollo Global Management, has rejected the state’s financial offer as inadequate and indicated it will challenge the valuation in court.

As the financial collapse of Steward became public early this year, state officials and lawmakers promised reforms and held legislative hearings on measures to restrict for-profit health care in Massachusetts. Attorney General Campbell said she’d carefully review Steward’s deal, unveiled in March, to sell its doctors’ group to a unit of United Healthcare, pledging to use “every tool available” to scrutinize the for-profit giant.

Eight months later, bills to place limits on private equity ownership of health care assets in the state have failed to pass the Legislature. United backed away from the buyout of Steward’s doctors group, Stewardship Health, after the bankruptcy filing. But a new deal to sell the group to private equity firm Kinderhook Industries, announced last month, has quickly passed muster with the attorney general’s office.

Rushing regulatory reviews of acquisitions can lead to problems down the road. But in the case of Stewardship, as with the hospitals, getting Massachusetts health care assets out of the hands of Steward has become a top priority for state officials, including the attorney general.

“Working with our state partners, our office has reviewed the hospital and Stewardship sales, and supports the implementation of these agreements to protect public health,” a spokesperson for the attorney general said Thursday. “No further review is contemplated.”

The state’s Health Policy Commission, called the HPC, will review the sale of St. Elizabeth’s and Good Samaritan to BMC, the sale of the Holy Family hospitals to Lawrence General, and the sale of St. Anne’s and Morton to Providence-based Lifespan, a HPC spokesperson said.

HPC officials have yet to receive formal “notices of material change,” the HPC said. Once it does, the agency “will conduct its reviews as expeditiously as possible to support a smooth and orderly transition to new hospital operators, minimizing further disruption.” The commission has begun a review of the Stewardship sale to a Kinderhook affiliate, but it has yet to receive all requested information, the spokesperson said.

How federal agencies will approach their reviews of Steward’s hospital sales in Massachusetts remains unclear. Representatives of the Justice Department, which is investigating Steward’s financial dealing, declined to comment. A spokeswoman for the Federal Trade Commission said the agency doesn’t discuss pending mergers or acquisitions.

title: Brockton man indicted, two other Mass. residents to plead guilty to health care fraud
text:
A Brockton man has been indicted and two other Massachusetts residents and a New York woman have agreed to plead guilty to participating in a conspiracy to defraud multiple health insurance companies out of more than $1 million, officials said Monday.

Henry Ezeonyido, 36, of Brockton, was charged with conspiracy to commit health care fraud and six counts of health care fraud, the US attorney’s office for Massachusetts said in a statement.

Brendon Ashe, 40, of Dorchester, and Darline Cobbler, 40, of Randolph, have agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud. Ariel Lambert, 34, of Brooklyn, N.Y., who also participated in the conspiracy, agreed to plead guilty to the same charge.

All four were first charged in a criminal complaint unsealed July 11, officials said.

From October 2019 to February 2022, Ezeonyido allegedly submitted fraudulent health insurance claims under the names of all four suspects and others for medical expenses that they had allegedly already paid for out-of-pocket while they were travelling internationally, according to the statement.

The allegedly bogus claims included reports of traumatic injuries including stabbings, gunshot wounds, and hit-and-run crashes, which allegedly required hospitalization, the statement said.

Ezeonyido allegedly stole more than $1 million from insurers by submitting fraudulent medical records showing the care received, fake bank records showing payments to international treatment facilities, and false police reports describing the events, officials said.

Ashe, Cobbler, Lambert, and several others allegedly paid Ezeonyido and his co-conspirators a small portion of the stolen money, officials said.

Kiera McDonald can be reached at kiera.mcdonald@globe.com.

title: With nearly monthlong shutdown underway, Red Line riders turn to shuttles
text:
Our reporters are at Braintree, Quincy Center, and Ashmont stations to document how the commute plays out.

Follow live updates.

While speaking on GBH News’ Boston Public Radio Monday, the T’s General Manager Phil Eng said commuters have been “waiting far too long for this work to be done.”

“All the years of disinvestment has led to where the only real, reasonable way to tackle this in the timeframe is to do it in the diversion,” said Eng during the “Ask the MBTA GM” segment with hosts Jim Braude and Margery Eagan. He acknowledged “how impactful” this particular shutdown is for riders and said the Braintree branch will be speed restriction-free soon.

The agency intends to get Red Line trains on the branch “back to even greater speeds,” or traveling beyond the current maximum of 40 miles per hour to 50, on parts of the tracks where possible, Eng said.

Marcel Bell, who lives in North Quincy, said he relies on the MBTA daily to get where he needs to be as he stood on the platform with his headphones on and waited for the train. Bell, 58, said he is disabled and takes the Red Line to the city to attend his weekly medical appointments and therapy sessions.

The Red Line, he said, seems to have the “most problems” and the ongoing closure has been “really inconvenient” for him. Bell took the shuttle all weekend.

The closure has added “at least a good hour” to his normal commute, and Bell said he had to wake up a couple of hours early Monday morning in order to catch the shuttle on time. ”I value my sleep,” he said.

“I rely on public transportation every day. Seven days a week,” he said. If Bell misses some of his medical appointments in the city, it could take him up to six months to get another on the calendar. ”I rely on the T,” he repeated.

Still, he’s resigned to the fact that the shutdown will last until the end of the month. “What can you do about it? All you have to do is deal with it,” Bell said. “I’ve just accepted it.”

“It’s a pain in the neck and that’s being kind,” said Bob Cousy, 80, a retired salesman, talking about the shutdowns, and the MBTA in general.

Cousy has been waiting at Quincy Center 40 minutes for his bus to Hingham to pick up a prescription from his doctor.

“It’s ridiculous how much money they spent on transportation and it never runs right,” said Cousy. “Bring back the horse and wagon, it will be more reliable.”

Typically by now, the morning commute would’ve died down, but due to all the bus delays, the Quincy Center station still has a continuous flow people waiting for shuttle buses.

Sighs are growing louder, foot tapping is speeding up, and some people are pacing back and forth. MBTA workers make the announcement: more buses are coming but there are delays. Many heads shake in frustration.

Commuters Corey Boudreau and Keith Smith make small talk while walking to the platform at Braintree. Boudreau is a pharmacy tech who lives in Weymouth and Smith is a producer who lives in Kingston.

Depending on when they get to the station, they use both the red line and commuter rail frequently to get to work. When asked if previous closures have affected their commute, Smith quickly said, “Oh yes.”

”The buses are a pain in the butt, but they do the best they can,” he said. He’s hopeful the repairs can shorten his hour-long commute to Harvard station. ”If they can cut that down, that’d be great.”

Boudreau was optimistic and also not that bothered by the latest shutdown .”If it does its job a little quicker, that’d be nice,” said Boudreau.

Smith did, however, have a bone to pick with the new red line cars, where he says the seats are uncomfortable, the slick plastic leaves people sliding around, and the fold down seats are a pinch hazard. ”You’ll put the seat down and it’ll catch their leg,” he said.

Dany Jeanphillipe, 15, a sophomore at GOALS, an alternative high school in Quincy, sits alone at the bus stop at the Quincy Center station, listening to music on his phone. He normally takes the Red Line, but not today.

Jeanphillipe’s school starts at 9 a.m. Today he’s taking a bus to Quincy Center then waiting for the 210 bus to get dropped off near his school. ”I miss going places without taking multiple buses,” said Jeanphillipe.

Jeanphillipe said he’s not too worried about being tardy since the teachers said if you’re late because of the train closing it’s understandable.

At Ashmont, the platform to take the Red Line train inbound was becoming regularly packed with passengers, with many heading into the city for work during rush hour.

At least a few commuters waiting to catch the train said they were feeling stressed about how the shutdown, only a few days in, is affecting the length of their commute. One rider, Yong Lei, who took the shuttle bus from North Quincy, said he would normally already be in downtown Boston, where he manages a kiosk exchange. ”If the train is working,” he quickly added.

Lei, 28, said this was his first time taking the shuttle and it took “longer than expected,” adding that there was “a lot of traffic” on the way to the station. He guessed that the diversion would add “a little bit over 30 minutes” to his commute — at least on Monday morning — and said he was feeling “not great” about that.

He originally thought the shutdown ended on Sept. 26, but when he was informed by a reporter that it was scheduled to end three days later, on Sept. 29, he let out a deflated chuckle. ”It’s ridiculous,” Lei said.

“They keep fixing it. It never gets fixed.” And he isn’t confident it will be fixed this time either. ”Maybe it will be for three months. Then head back to slow zone again,” he said. “I’m pretty sure.”

Wearing a New England Patriots hoodie, Tom Gilmore, 60, sat on a bench before boarding an inbound Red Line train. Unlike other passengers who arrived at Ashmont station via a Yankee Line shuttle, Gilmore took the trolley.

The closure hasn’t posed any trouble to his normal commute, said Gilmore, who lives in Lower Mills. The trolley is only about a mile away from where he normally boards, so it wasn’t an added hassle, he added. “No trouble,” he said.

Sometimes the subway trains can run “pretty slow,” Gilmore said, so he is hopeful that they will be travel faster after the track repairs are completed. ”I would like that,” he said before heading into the Red Line train that had just pulled in.

Madison Leuchte, 20, a day care teacher at Kids & Company in Canton said the Red Line closing for the month has affected a lot of her upcoming plans. Leuchte has driving school Thursdays and Fridays and the shut down down impacts how she’s going to get there. “All the shuttle buses are full,” said Leuchte.

Leuchte has a concert on Sept. 25 and worries how she will make it. “I don’t want to pay an expensive Uber to TD garden but I can’t rely on these buses,” said Leuchte.

A main concern for riders this morning is the consistency of the shuttle and regular buses. Aeronx Essel, 29, kept checking the time on his phone as he waited for the 220 bus. Essel needs to get out of the house at 5:30 a.m. as he travels from his house in North Quincy to Quincy Center Station, then he waits for a bus for his work at Bruegger’s Bagels in Hingham.

“I have to wake up an hour-and-a-half earlier,” said Essel. He said he’s been waiting 45 minutes and still hasn’t seen the 220 bus that was supposed to arrive at 7:14 a.m. and 7:30 a.m. “I start work at 8 a.m., I’m going to be late and that’s every day now,” said Essel.

When the the 220 bus finally arrives, commuters run and line up. “There needs to be more than one or two buses for everyone here,” said Leuchte.

At the Ashmont station, passengers pour down the steps after arriving via shuttles. From here, they’ll take the Red Line into Boston, where service is running quicker than usual during the closure on Monday morning.

The trains, which are arriving about every about five to eight minutes, did not appear too packed once riders boarded, with enough room for riders to stand and sit comfortably. On an average day at the Ashmont station, wait times are normally about 10 to 15 minutes, said a transit ambassador on the platform, who did not give their name. ”This will be the service for the rest of the day,” he said.

The train operator waited to depart from the station until the wait time for the next arriving train had ticked down to about seven minutes. Despite another train coming soon, that did not stop one woman from jamming a stroller into the train door and narrowly getting caught herself. (She was able to board safely.)

People run to the commuter rail platform just after 8 a.m. as the bell rang signaling the arrival of the commuter rail. Meanwhile, a line of three empty shuttles waits on call.

Alexis Raab, 29, and Bryan Meade, 22, wait for the commuter rail at Braintree into downtown for a date at the Boston Common. Raab, who takes the red line to work in Cambridge, said this closure is a big change from previous ones. Raab complained that this latest shuttle route only makes a few stops besides dropping passengers at Ashmont, and there is no shuttle to or from JFK/UMass.

”It seems like they had a plan [for past closures] that was albiet slow, but stopped at every station,” she said.

This shutdown isn’t the first rodeo for most riders at the Ashmont station, and 28-year-old Michael Costello is one of many daily commuters who have had to deal with disrupted MBTA service before.

”It’s happened a few times over the past couple of years,” said Costello, who took the Yankee Line shuttle from Wollaston station on Monday. But Costello, who lives in Quincy, said while the nearly monthlong closure is “annoying,” he said he recognizes that “they gotta do what they gotta do,” referring to the agency making track repairs to rid the branch of slow zones.

So far, it’s been a “smooth” process, said Costello, adding that the first couple of days he was confused about whether he could take the shuttle from JFK/UMass station (riders cannot).

Overall, he said, the shutdowns have been handled better over the past year, noting that “it took so long to get to work” during prior diversions. This go around, his commute is only “a little bit delayed,” he said, estimating that having to take the shuttle probably added another 15 or so minutes to his travel time.

As to whether he thinks the trains will run faster after repairs — and possibly up to 50 miles per hours on some parts of the branch — he’s playing the waiting game. ”I’ll believe it when I see it,” Costello said with a laugh.

Sabrina Garvin, 27, of Weymouth, is trying out the commuter rail for her journey to work at Harvard Square. She took the shuttle bus on Friday, but that added an extra 30 minutes to her commute.

She said that last time they closed the red line from JFK to Kendall/MIT, there was a day her commute to work took three hours. The way home took more than two hours.

”It’s been almost a year of people commenting that they could walk faster,” she said.

During this latest shutdown, the Ashmont station is serving as the hub of action for riders who will have their commute impacted over the next few weeks. Riders can take shuttle busses to the Red Line stop, then continue on their commute on the subway to downtown Boston.

Passengers, a mix of commuters dressed in business suits, chatty high school students, and young families disembarked from and boarded Yankee Line shuttles at the relatively quiet station, where employees stationed at platforms and by fare machines yelled out directions and answered questions.

Only a few days into the MBTA’s biggest diversion since last year, one employee, who did not give his name, said he understands that the disrupted commute can be “annoying” for passengers, but echoed MBTA General Manager Phil Eng’s message that, by the end of the shutdown, they expect trains on the branch to run smoother, faster, and perform better overall.

So far, the closure has been running well and without issues, he said. “Things have been good,” he added.

At the Braintree station, commuters lined up for shuttle busses. Dan Linik, 31, of Quincy sat on the commuter rail platform with an energy drink in hand. Linik usually gets on at the Quincy Adams station but said it’s easier to get on at Braintree with the closure.

“It’s inconvenient to have to go out of my way to go different routes and not being able to get on the train at any times,” said Linik, who gets off at South Station for work. “I have to look at the commuter rail schedule and go at certain times.”

Until Sept. 29, service on the Red Line will be suspended between JFK/UMass and Braintree stations. Shuttle buses will be available and will make stops at the Braintree, Quincy Adams, Quincy Center, Wollaston, North Quincy, and Ashmont stations. There will be no shuttle bus service to or from JFK/UMass station.

Riders are encouraged to take the commuter rail on the Kingston, Middleborough, or Greenbush lines for fare-free service between Braintree, Quincy Center, JFK/UMass, and South Station. On the weekend of Sept. 14-15, service will be suspended between South Station and Braintree. Shuttle bus service will be provided.

Service will be increased on the Ashmont branch. Shuttles will be available between Ashmont and Braintree.

Read more about what to expect and upcoming shutdowns.

title: The bus ride to nowhere
text:
It turned out to be short-lived. Not only did her youngest son’s morning bus never show up — he’s a fifth grader at the Murphy K-8 School in Dorchester, she said — but the afternoon bus was more than two hours late. The school is about three miles from their home.

“They had told me his school releases at 3:10 p.m. and the time BPS had quoted me was 3:55 p.m. that he would be home,” Chatfield said. This year, the district is using Zūm, an app that allows families to track their students’ buses by providing bus information on a live map. “And I watched the bus wander all throughout Dorchester, come into South Boston, go back to Dorchester, go back to South Boston, go back to Dorchester.” Her son was dropped off home at 5:36 p.m., she said.

Sadly, late buses have become a first-day-of-school tradition in Boston. For some parents, the day is marked by extreme frustration and disruption because of the seemingly intractable dysfunction of the district’s bus system. It begs the question: Why can’t the BPS figure out the perennial challenges it has to bus more than 20,000 students? Has the city become so inured to the district’s transportation struggles that they barely make news?

Multiple posts on social media provided a look into the problems some families went through with school buses on Thursday. And the data show it: According to the district, only 34 percent of buses were on time getting student to school in the morning of the first day. The rest were late: 62 percent arrived within 15 minutes of start time and 80 percent within 30 minutes. Last year, the first-day-of-school on-time arrival rate was 61 percent. As for the afternoon buses, 57 percent were on time on Thursday.

“These delays that happen in the first days of school were largely expected due to drivers and bus monitors navigating new routes and greeting new faces for the first time, and the implementation of the new Zūm technology that the majority of our bus drivers, families, and school-based staff were using in real-world conditions for the first time,” BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper said in a statement. “We saw a significant day-over-day improvement in OTP [on-time performance] on Friday, which put us on track with our first day of school last year.”

Lest we forget, the city’s school system signed an improvement plan with state education authorities two years ago that, among other goals, states that BPS buses ought to achieve a districtwide on-time arrival rate of 95 percent or better each month. My Globe colleague James Vaznis reported last week that, in the past school year, “the highest monthly average BPS achieved was 90 percent in March.”

Chatfield’s son, while on the lost bus that afternoon last week, was texting her that the driver didn’t seem to know where he was going, she said. There were apparently four students on the bus the whole time, she said. “At one point, I considered calling the police to ask them to pull the bus over so that I could get my child off of it because I was scared,” Chatfield said.

Chatfield said her husband, Patrick, called the district to raise alarm bells about his son’s bus but could not get anyone on the phone. Her husband said on social media that he understands how bad the traffic has gotten in Boston but having drivers seemingly unaware of where they’re going is unacceptable and frightening. (On Sunday, the Chatfields received an email from Dan Rosengard, the executive director of transportation for the district, apologizing for the challenges the family went through.)

Chatfield reached out to District 2 City Councilor Ed Flynn, who told me in an interview that he and his office heard complaints from 12 to 15 families about school transportation issues on Thursday. It prompted him to send a letter to Skipper on Friday. “A parent mentioned they drove their child from Hyde Park to a school in the South End because their bus did not arrive,” he wrote. Flynn is also filing a motion to hold a City Council hearing to discuss what happened with school buses the first week of school.

“I would like to hear directly from BPS professionals on what happened,” Flynn said. “I don’t necessarily want to place the blame. I just want to figure out how we don’t make this mistake all of the time. ... I wouldn’t say they’re not concerned with the students. I just think they were overwhelmed. The [transportation] plan was poorly implemented.”

To be sure, the district did make a much-needed move toward transparency by signing a three-year contract with Zūm, the app that allows families to track their students’ buses. This has provided families with peace of mind regarding the whereabouts of their children — or, as in the case of the Chatfield family, anxiety when things go wrong, giving a rare view into how dysfunctional the system can get.

As for accountability, or lack thereof, Chatfield said the bus driver who dropped off her son more than two hours late on Thursday refused to tell her his name. Friday and Monday mornings bus pickups went smoothly, she said. But she’s still apprehensive about the afternoon route (the family made plans to pick up their son from school on Friday).

Meanwhile, Mayor Michelle Wu, when announcing the rollout of the new bus tracking app last month, said in a press release: “We have heard from parents and caregivers that there has to be more information and better communication when it comes to transportation.” But transparency without accountability is virtually meaningless. “I don’t want you to come to my school and hand my kid a pencil,” Chatfield said about Wu’s first-day-of-school photo op. Indeed, parents want answers and won’t be afraid to hold officials responsible for their actions.

title: ‘God really did draft the best two boys’: Gaudreau brothers’ widows, BC chaplain honor pair at somber funeral service
text:
”They were doing this tennis match,” Penna recalled. “’I love you,’ ‘No, I love you.’ They must have said it to each other 19 times. That was the conversation.

“I saw in those two brothers a love that I do not have with my own brother. They had an intensity to their love that was unbelievable.”

Penna said Boston College “terribly misses these young men because when they were on our campus, they lit up our campus, not only on the ice, but on the campus, in the classroom. They were wonderful.”

Penna asked those inside the church to look around at how many people made the trip to pay their respects, calling it a source of comfort for parents Guy and Jane.

“By the overwhelming presence and overwhelming number of people here today, they’re sending a message to you loud and clear that John and Matthew’s lives mattered, that they were noticed on this earth, they were loved on this earth and they were valued on this earth,” Penna said.

“This robust crowd wants you to know that they’re here to tell you, all of you, that they love you, too, and they have your back and they’re here to support you in our loss.”

Both widows of the brothers gave eulogies.

Meredith Gaudreau spoke of the bond her husband Johnny had with two teammates in particular. Sean Monahan played with Johnny in Calgary and signed with Columbus this offseason and was to be reunited this year. Kevin Hayes was teammates with Johnny at BC, and is a member of the Penguins organization.

“You’ve both known John longer than I have, which means you helped shape him into the man I fell in love with,” said Meredith, who revealed she was pregnant with the couple’s third child. “He looked up to you both on and off the ice. You are his brothers, which means you’re my brothers too.

“Thank you for being there with me when you’re experiencing such a great loss as well.”

Kevin and his brother Jimmy, who also played at BC, often hosted Johnny and Matt at their family’s home in Dorchester. Jimmy died unexpectedly in August of 2021.

“Kevin, you and your family were a big part of John’s upbringing into this crazy NHL life,” Meredith said. “He looked up to you and loved being around your brother and sisters. I think summers spent with the Hayeses reminded him of his own family, so I know that this is something he cherished. The friendship and bond you have created despite any distance is so strong and admirable.

“You’ve been through so much, and you were never not there for John no matter what. You are a great, great person to your core, and John loved you so much.”

Madeline Gaudreau began dating Matthew when both were in high school, and the two continued their relationship when he left for BC.

“Matty was so excited to play alongside his brother, something he never took for granted,” Madeline said. “The bond that Matt and John shared is something that unless you knew them personally, even the most perfect words, pictures or videos cannot adequately describe it. They were attached at the hip. They slept in the same room up until college, and neither of them ever wanted that to change.

“John took care of Matty, and Matty would take care of John. To know both of them was to truly love them. It was impossible not to fall in love with them.

“Meredith said it best. ‘You do not hear one name without the other.’ They were so extremely proud of each other, and it brings me comfort knowing they are still together forever as they always were.”

She closed her speech by urging people to not drink and drive. The brothers were killed by a man who had allegedly been drinking.

“Call a ride. Please do not put another family through this torture. The loss of Matty and John will leave a hole in the family, his close friends, the community, for eternity. However, their legacy will live on through the lives of everyone they touched — their kids, their wives, their parents, their siblings.

“God really did draft the best two boys. Linemates forever. I love you so much, Matthew Ryan.”

A GoFundMe for Madeline to support her and their baby due in December, has surpassed $645,000, with donations from nearly 9,000 people pouring in, many from NHL players and their families.

“He didn’t make the millions that Johnny did and doesn’t have the pension from the Players’ Association,” said Michael Myers of the ECHL’s Worcester Railers, for whom Matthew played two seasons. “It’s important that the hockey community recognizes that and embraces that to help Matthew’s family.”

Hockey East, in which BC plays, was scheduled to hold its annual media day Monday before it was canceled for the funeral.

“Johnny and Matty Gaudreau were pillars of the hockey community and the Hockey East family continues to mourn their loss,” commissioner Steve Metcalf said in a statement. “Our thoughts remain with their family, friends, loved ones, and those who were touched by these two exceptional individuals during this difficult time.”

A private viewing for the family was held Sunday.

According to police, the brothers were riding on County Route 551 — a two-lane highway in a rural area — in Oldmans Township, N.J., at 8:19 p.m. on Aug. 29 when they were hit. According to a criminal complaint obtained by the Associated Press, the driver, Sean M. Higgins, told a responding officer he had five or six beers before the crash and admitted to consuming alcohol while driving. He failed a field sobriety test, the complaint said.

Johnny Gaudreau was an on-ice wizard who scored goals the way no one else did, but always humble

title: Alan Shawn Feinstein, R.I. philanthropist who battled world hunger and encouraged kids to be kind, dies at 93
text:
A former author of children’s books and teacher at schools in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, Mr. Feinstein, beginning in the 1970s, amassed millions through his subscription newsletters, including “Alan Shawn Feinstein’s International Insider’s Report.”

Mr. Feinstein’s wealth was also collected through sales of direct-mail collectibles featured in his publications – such as presidential autographs, coins, and stamps – with a money-back guarantee, as reported in a 2004 profile in The Providence Journal.

After he was made aware of food scarcity in Providence in the early 1980s, Mr. Feinstein began donating money to food pantries and other public service programs, and by 1986, his $1 million gift launched the World Hunger Program at Brown University to help combat the issue on a global scale, backed by a matching $1.5 million from the Ivy League institution.

“So many people go to bed hungry in this country, about 10 percent if not more, and that’s a disgrace for the richest country in the world,” Mr. Feinstein told the Globe in March 1998. “There is no shame in hunger; there is shame in knowing about hunger and doing nothing about it.”

The Feinstein Foundation launched in 1991, working under the mission to inspire children to “do good deeds and be kind whenever possible.”

More than 600,000 kids have since participated in the Feinstein Leadership school program, earning the title of “Feinstein Jr. Scholars” – a designation that gives them complimentary access to attractions throughout southern New England – as they pledge to “do good deeds to make our world a better place,” the foundation’s website states.

Tax filings for 2023 valued the foundation at just shy of $30 million and indicated the organization served 265 schools that year.

In her statement, Leila Feinstein recalled how important the Jr. Scholars were to her father.

“Knowing that Feinstein Jr. Scholars were doing good deeds every day brought my dad tremendous joy and comfort,” she said. “It gave him peace in his final moments knowing our work will continue even though he is no longer with us.”

Born in Dorchester, Mass. on June 25, 1931, Mr. Feinstein was a graduate of Boston University and Boston Teachers’ College, and once taught at schools in Mansfield and Newton, Mass. as well as in Bristol, R.I., according to his death notice. He was married to Dr. Pratarnporn “Pat” (Chiemwichit) Feinstein for 61 years. The couple had three children and five grandchildren.

A funeral service for friends and family will be held on Sept. 21 in Providence and also streamed online, followed by a private burial, the obituary said.

In a post on X, formerly known as Twitter, Governor Dan McKee described Mr. Feinstein as not only a philanthropist, but as“a change agent who invested in the lives and futures of Rhode Island’s children.”

“We will always remember him, not just for his impact on education but for his kind and full heart,” McKee said.

US Senator Jack Reed said Mr. Feinstein’s “memory will live on through the countless lives he touched and improved,” pointing to not only the foundation’s work but also his efforts “to feed millions around the world through initiatives with leading universities across our region.”

“Above all, Alan urged us all to be kind and compassionate toward one another,” the senator said in a statement. “He knew that good deeds reverberate throughout our neighborhoods and that every one of us can make a difference.”

Speaking to the Globe in 1992, a year after his foundation launched, Mr. Feinstein reflected on the difference he himself hoped to make someday.

“Hopefully when I go,” he said, “there will be a few less hungry people in the world and a few more compassionate ones.”

title: A former Boston cop opens a new investigation into some of the city’s darkest years
text:
Now a criminologist, Joyce has produced a groundbreaking study of Boston’s street gangs and gang culture, “It Started With the Hats: The Life Experiences of Boston’s Founding Street Gang Members,” the heart of which are his in-depth interviews with 30 original gangbangers: one-on-one.

“The book’s credibility is that it’s based on their words, the men who lived it,” Joyce says of the “OGs” who participated — some of whom he arrested decades ago. They came from a cross section of gangs that mostly take the name of their street or housing project, like Castlegate, the Corbet Crew, the Humboldt Boys, or the Franklin Hill Crew.

The interviews confirmed a suspicion Joyce had way back at the start of his policing career: that outrunning and arresting gang members wasn’t enough to combat gang violence. “Even when the violence was out of control, we’d talk in the unit about how these kids, many were talented. Real smart. Or athletic. And we’d wonder about their potential if different pathways were offered. The pull of the street was just so strong.”

His book, which will appeal to policy makers, youth workers, and public safety officials confronting gun violence, also offers the first deeply reported origin story of the Boston street gangs that terrorized neighborhoods and killed at a record-setting pace. The broad outlines of that history are known — how crack cocaine first arrived in the mid-1980s via gangs encroaching from Detroit and New York City, setting the stage for homegrown armed gangs to pursue for themselves the profits from trafficking in cocaine. The Corbet Crew, the city’s first and most powerful gang, was dominant until its charismatic kingpin, Tony Johnson, a star athlete who’d gone to college, was gunned down in June 1988 next to his Dorchester home. Mayhem followed as street gangs scrambled to solidify and prevail.

“By the fall of 1989, Boston was in the midst of its most violent time,” Joyce writes. “Gang violence was a driving force behind over 100 people being shot or killed in a forty-day period” in an area covering only about 1.7 square miles. The next year Boston experienced a record number of homicides — 152.

Joyce expands on this history with both new information and the personal and at times heart-wrenching perspectives of former gang members who were at war. “Nobody seen that coming,” an ex-Corbet Crew member told Joyce about the killing of Tony Johnson, the gang leader who’d seemed invincible. “Then things turned up heavy,” he said. “People wanted revenge.” Said another Corbet Crew member about Johnson’s death: “Turned the city upside down. He kept the peace in a lot of neighborhoods. Once he passed away, all bets were off.” Joyce writes that the impact of Johnson’s death “cannot be overstated.”

Joyce, who joined the police force in 1983 and retired in 2014 as a superintendent, was part of Boston’s first tactical response to the emerging gang crisis, the Citywide Anti-Crime Unit, formed in 1988. He then played a key role implementing Operation Ceasefire, the innovative and nationally acclaimed partnership of Boston police, religious and community leaders, and Harvard criminologists that achieved a dramatic drop in homicides in the 1990s. Not your typical cop, Joyce has moved from the street to the classroom, earning first a master’s degree at Boston University and then, in 2017, a PhD in criminology and justice policy at Northeastern University. He now chairs the criminal justice and criminology department at Salve Regina University.

In his studies, Joyce knew he wanted to dig deeper into gang culture. He found plenty of research on the front end — when teens joined a gang. But he saw little that had been done examining a gang member’s later life, whether he “desisted” or “persisted.” “The final phase of gang membership — the long-term changes that occur over time when gang membership comes to an end — has been understudied,” he writes. To help recruit participants for his interviews, he reached out to two former youth workers and a Boston police detective who knew many ex-gangbangers. He nicknamed them his Boston Street Gang Advisory Group, and together they enlisted 30 Black and Latino men between the ages of 35 and 54. Joyce spent three years conducting interviews, one-on-one, at locations of their choosing — their workplace, a community center in Roxbury, an office at Northeastern, or a restaurant. He promised to use pseudonyms to protect their privacy and, possibly, to prevent retaliation.

He knew they’d be doing something that went against their street code — talking to cops about the gang. “Getting the subjects to open up and share with me their life experiences was difficult due to my past profession as a police officer,” he writes. But in time he won their trust; some he interviewed helped him recruit new subjects. Joyce compiled more than 1,300 pages of transcripts.

Joyce painstakingly asked his subjects to recall the emergence of street gang culture in Boston and the role they played. Their responses are raw, blunt, and often emotional. “They did not hold back,” Joyce says.

There’s Reggie, who joined a Jamaica Plain street gang at age 14 and told Joyce about the impact of crack. “It made everybody instantly rich,” he said. His family was broke, and suddenly he had $465 after selling “a package.” “It was like so much money.” He could now buy pizza, or whatever. “Like for us, that was a big thing, eating. It was like we’re able to eat.”

Reggie became an enforcer, and guns were easy to obtain. “I came across MAC-10s, TEC-9s, shotguns, .38 revolvers, all different kinds of guns.”

Then there’s Edward, an enforcer for a gang in Dorchester, who “changed best friends three times because they kept getting killed.” He told Joyce about an emotional deadness that set in from killing and seeing others killed. “I’m numb to murder,” he said. “When people used to get murdered, I’d be like, ‘Damn, that’s [expletive] up,’” then switch topics in an instant: “‘Who do you think the Celtics are going to draft this year?’”

From those who have “desisted,” Joyce learned that willpower alone, while essential, was not enough. The gang was family, the camaraderie and friendships deeply embedded. Leaving that life, he found, required “human agency” in combination with some other turning point, something that helped them resist the pull to return to the gang and the quick money from selling drugs. For one ex-gangbanger, that meant leaving Boston for a stretch. For others, it was parenthood, education, religion, a mentor, or work.

Tony, who bore scars from being shot and stabbed 17 times in 12 years, told Joyce: “Being in the gang, selling drugs, doing shootings, getting shot. Other kids went to school, graduated from college; I went to jail. I had choices, and I made the bad choice.” After prison, Tony was determined to move on. For him the key was steady work, despite “temptations all the time to get back in the streets.” He learned to cook. “I’m a chef,” he told Joyce. “I love to cook, and I like working with people.” It’s not been easy, though. Tony ran afoul of the law several times, but he had been crime-free for six years when Joyce interviewed him.

Joyce hopes the “set of rich and thick narratives” will prove useful to officials here and elsewhere in devising comprehensive approaches to teen and gun violence, a responsibility he says must involve “multiagency partnerships and a balance of public safety and public health services.” In Boston, he noted, Police Commissioner Michael Cox, whom he’s known for years, was a young cop during the city’s worst years of gang violence. Cox, he says, “gets it; he knows it.”

For the book’s jacket, Joyce turned to a Boston graffiti artist, or “tagger,“ named Alvin “Acoma” Colon, who was barely a teenager in the early 1990s when he “was tagging everything but a canvas.” Colon and his tagger friends, guided by a teacher at the Martin Luther King Middle School, were eventually steered to practice their art on approved walls; they became known as the “Young Graffiti Masters.” Colon, now an airbrush artist and sculptor, told me he worked out the cover design on a blank wall in Norwood, using the tone and spray-paint style of ’80s graffiti to portray Boston’s street gang lifestyle. His colorful mural depicts a housing project, a cemetery, bejeweled gangbangers, and the fists of one gangbanger breaking free of the bonds of handcuffs.

To help Colon get a feel for the book, Joyce gave the artist the manuscript. “Oh, man,” Colon said, exhaling deeply, recalling his reaction to reading oral histories about a violent time when he was just a Roxbury kid trying to survive. “Tears came down my eyes.”

title: On the 50th anniversary of Boston busing, what have we learned?
text:
Why? Because Boston’s school desegregation and busing crisis was the single most important event in Boston in the past 75 years. Aspects of the desegregation orders of Judge W. Arthur Garrity Jr. from the 1970s are still present and the legacy of desegregation and busing is still with us as our schools face today’s challenges.

This includes the student assignment plans where parents apply for three choices out of 10 to 12 schools for their child, who isn’t likely to attend their nearest neighborhood school. And the goal of hiring 25 percent Black and 10 percent Latino and Asian teachers and administrators has still not been met.

As a community organizer back then in Dorchester, Boston’s largest neighborhood, I got to see the racial tensions up close. For a year or more after busing began, the only place in all of Dorchester that both our white and Black students felt safe going to a meeting at night was at the then-Grover Cleveland School in Fields Corner. Buses carrying Black schoolchildren were frequently showered with rocks. Racial epithets were yelled by adults and teens. Fights were started again and again at certain high schools.

A Haitian man was attacked by a mob in South Boston and saved by an off-duty police officer who fired his gun into the air. A white truck driver was pulled out of his truck in the South End and beaten and died days later. Black community leader Ted Landsmark was attacked by protesters who were outside City Hall demonstrating against busing. One wielded an American flag on a flagstaff at him like it was a spear.

Listening to white community members of Dorchester back then, I heard their anger over their court-ordered inability to send their kids to their neighborhood schools.
