Watertown has been a city for decades. Now, it’s acting like one.

title: How a six-year ‘situationship’ built love to last a lifetime
text:
“The difference is that Sam and I were genuine friends. I don’t think people understand that’s part of a situationship,” Winston says. “Because before it was the ‘situationship,’ it was called ‘friends with benefits.’ And I emphasize the friend part.”

Their friendship began when Samantha (who goes by Sam) was 27 and living in Revere. She swiped right and messaged Winston: “Do you even lift, bro?” (Three of his four Tinder photos were shirtless gym selfies.)

“I was not a ‘message first’ kind of gal,” she says, “but I was just in it that day for whatever reason.” The message, she explains, was at least partly “a test of whether he had a good sense of humor.”

They met that evening at the former Living Room in the North End. There were fruity drinks, flirty vibes, and a friendly kiss before they left for their respective homes.

At the time, Winston, then 27, lived in Miami and would start an MPH-PhD in Kinesiology program at Oregon State University that fall. She was a spa director in the North End and loved the excitement of being single and young — afterwork dinner and dates with endless possibilities. They agreed to keep things casual, reuniting during his visits with family in Dorchester. The relationship was label-less, the terms were transparent, but above all, their dynamic was consistent.

Sam described him at the time as: “this cute guy I see once a month.”

They texted near-daily, though, swapping career, life, and even romantic advice, the conversations growing deeper and topics more intimate as time went by. They dated other people and promised to be honest if something became more serious. Each sent the eyes emoji when the other let the text chain go dry.

“I didn’t have many people to talk to the way I used to talk to her. I never had an opportunity to process and be like, what does this mean to me?” says Winston of this time. “Then I realized that when you don’t do that and reflect, it’s hard to appreciate the things that you have.”

Sam was the first to sense a change — she had caught feelings; she wanted more. She bravely broached the topic in 2019 and was met with a gentle rebuff, a reality check on geography and time. A few months later, Winston texted Sam: To be honest, I love you, too, but this won’t work.

“We had very serious feelings for each other, but there wasn’t much to do about it because of the circumstances,” she says. “It was this common understanding, but neither of us wanted to give up on it. So we lived in this limbo of not wanting to stop talking but not wanting to move forward either.”

Just before Christmas 2021, Sam told Winston she couldn’t speak to him anymore. She wanted a full romantic relationship — not a situational one. With heartbreak on both sides, Winston understood her decision.

“It was very respectful, but I was so devastated,” she remembers.

That March, Winston texted — he was moving back for a postdoctoral fellowship at Merrimack College in North Andover. When Sam told him she had a new boyfriend, he was prepared.

“That’s OK,” he told her. “I can wait it out.”

Their friendship resumed after Sam ended the other relationship that summer. She would head to Merrimack’s campus when her schedule allowed; their conversations were now held in real time, over taco salads and two extra-long-twin beds pushed together to make one.

”My life started getting better, just having someone to talk to, someone who cares about you and thinks about you,” says Winston. “It was just me and her — and if it wasn’t for her, I don’t know if I would have made it through my post-doc or been able to muster up the ability to just do the stuff I needed to do.”

By February 2023, Winston was spending nearly every night at Sam’s East Boston apartment, waking up at 5 a.m. to get back to North Andover. (”He’s an early riser, anyway,” says Sam.)

In June 2023, Sam and Winston bought a home in West Roxbury. The decision came after he accepted a role at Northeastern University, where he is currently an assistant professor with the Bouvé College of Health Sciences.

“At this point in my life, I got what the expectation was — I knew, black and white, what she wanted from me,” he says. He proposed the following February.

“Winston will say that the big lifelong commitment was buying this house together, and obviously that’s a huge deal, but I’ve always been vocal about the fact that marriage meant something to me,” says Sam. “If we hadn’t gotten married, I don’t think it would really matter too much to me, but I did still want it.”

Sam and Winston wed at Dearly Studio in Somerville on Sept. 7 with 20 of their family members and friends.

The couple, now both 34, had initially planned for a large wedding, but changed lanes after joyfully discovering their family of two would become three. Their first child is due on Christmas Eve.

“Even when we were not [romantically] together, we had talked about kids and families and our own family dynamics,” says Sam. “That’s one of the things that was attractive to me about him — he always talked about wanting to have kids … and we were so often on the same page about what our approach to parenting would be.”

Dearly’s owner Jusmine Martin and Sam are best friends who met as freshmen at Emerson College. Sam’s father, Samuel Frandino, a professional carpenter, had built the micro-chapel’s altar where the pair wed with Jusmine as officiant.

The party continued at Tony and Elaine’s, Sam’s favorite North End restaurant, where guests cheered the newlyweds. They dined on plates of chicken parmesan and meatballs, and cut into quirky vintage-inspired cookies and cream cake from Buttercream Boston. Frosting was piped into the words “double trouble” — the couple’s “catch phrase” for themselves.

Sam asked that the restaurant keep out their signature checkerboard tablecloths and red tea lights for the family-style meal. She said the classic and “cozy” atmosphere felt familiar to her Italian-American upbringing: “I automatically just felt at home there.”

During the ceremony, Winston recited what he called “Wedding Vows: The Trilogy” in sequential order, a three-part declaration of gratitude and commitment to his wife and family:

“I’m sorry for all the bullshit in the past. Truly. You are teaching me what freedom is and I can never repay you for this. So I’ll give you everything else. I always have and always will always love you. It was already written.”

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s new wedding column.

title: Remembering Jack Connors, Ethel Kennedy, Seiji Ozawa and others we lost in 2024
text:
Boston mayors come and go, each leaving their stamp on the city. But one figure outside of City Hall wielded wide influence for more than half a century: Jack Connors.

The history books will note that the legendary advertising-CEO-turned-philanthropist never held public office, but he didn’t need to. He built a constellation of relationships that reshaped business, health care, education, politics, and philanthropy.

When Connors died in July at 82 after a battle with cancer, it marked the passing of an era. He was a construct of his time, a rare blend of corporate savvy and civic passion, coming along when Boston needed a champion.

He was, at times, everywhere at once: running advertising agency Hill Holliday; chairing the board of the state’s biggest hospital system, Partners HealthCare (now Mass General Brigham); serving as trustee of his alma mater, Boston College; and raising millions of dollars for his beloved Camp Harbor View, which assists struggling city kids and their families.

Connors was as generous with his time as he was with his own money, giving away nearly $100 million of the fortune he made in the business world.

Perhaps his greatest contribution has been left unsaid: Connors helped Boston get back its swagger. It’s not often you hear Bostonians lament how great New York City or Silicon Valley is.

There will never be another Jack Connors — nor does Boston need one anymore. That’s part of his legacy: leaving behind a place confident to stand on its own and fulfill its destiny of being that enviable city on a hill. – Shirley Leung

Long before Pedro Martinez and David Ortiz became icons at Fenway Park, there was Luis Tiant.

During an era when Latino players were gaining a foothold in the Major Leagues, Tiant captivated Red Sox fans with his twirling delivery, Fu Manchu mustache, and charisma.

The righthander from Cuba joined the team as a free agent in 1971 and went on to win 122 games over eight seasons. What “El Tiante” lacked in physical stature, he made up for with determination to work deep into games.

“Tiant was a fierce competitor,” said Hall of Fame catcher Johnny Bench, whose Cincinnati Reds beat Tiant and the Red Sox in an epic seven-game World Series in 1975. “He never backed down.”

After a 19-year career and 229 wins, Tiant returned to Boston to work for the Sox. His titles changed from time to time but he was essentially a resident sage, always available to counsel players — especially fellow pitchers from Latin American countries.

“He was Mr. Tiant, our friend,” Martinez said. “There was respect.”

From the fans, there was love. Tiant was a regular at Fenway, posing for photos and signing autographs. Sunburnt New Englanders would gather around his golf cart during spring training in Florida as he patiently signed baseball cards and teased them with jokes.

Tiant was 83 when he passed away in October after a series of illnesses. Fenway won’t be quite the same next season. – Peter Abraham

Few can forget that iconic photo of Ethel Kennedy, in a black veil and pregnant with her 11th child, at the funeral of her husband, Robert F. Kennedy, just days after he was killed by an assassin while running for president in 1968.

More anguish lay ahead. Two of her sons would die, one of a drug overdose, another in a skiing accident.

But Ethel Kennedy, who died October 10 at the age of 96, was more than the sum of her suffering. She was also known as athletic and funny, charming and loyal. She started what is now the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights nonprofit organization, championing her husband’s causes. She marched with labor leader Cesar Chavez, sat with Native Americans at Alcatraz, and visited unjustly convicted prisoners in Mexico.

She had deep ties to the Cape, spending much of her later years at the Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port. She enjoyed sailing and golfing, and was an avid supporter of the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum.

She encouraged her children to look beyond their privileged lives. At her memorial service in Washington, D.C., her youngest daughter, Rory, recounted a day in 1984 when she was a teenager, sitting next to her brother Douglas, watching TV coverage of anti-apartheid protests and arrests at the South African Embassy. So moved by the cause, they turned to each other and said, “Let’s get arrested.” When they told their mother of this plan, her response was unflinching: “Great, I’ll drive.”

At the service, Rory said her mother influenced so many inside and outside the family because she “loved people.”

“She believed in people, in everyone’s innate potential,” she said. – Patricia Wen

“We’re in the ‘yes’ business.” “Don’t tell me no; show me how.” “It can be done.”

Larry Lucchino — who served as the president and CEO of the Red Sox from 2002 to 2015 and was chairman of both the Jimmy Fund and the Triple-A WooSox when he died in April — often spoke in aphorisms. His favored phrases revealed an idealist’s unrelenting belief in possibility married to a pragmatist’s attention to the minutiae necessary to give form to blueprints.

By the 1990s, Lucchino’s visionary ambition, meticulousness, and doggedness had established him as a legendary baseball executive. Unconstrained by industry convention, he transformed the ballpark experience as the mastermind behind the construction of Oriole Park at Camden Yards in Baltimore.

After Lucchino helped form the Red Sox ownership group led by John Henry and Tom Werner and became the team’s CEO and president in 2002, he took on a different responsibility: The transformation of a team and ballpark that increasingly seemed trapped by their pasts. Conversations about replacing Fenway were scrapped in favor of stunning renovations, most notably the iconic “Monster seats” above the park’s famed left-field wall.

Generations of on-field despair and an 86-year title drought were vanquished through boldness and pugnaciousness embodied by Lucchino’s characterization of the New York Yankees as “the evil empire.” The championship of 2004 ushered in a new era where titles became regular occurrences.

Those championships as well as five ballparks — also including Petco Park in San Diego, JetBlue Park at Fenway South in Fort Myers, Florida, and Polar Park in Worcester — stand as monuments to Lucchino’s ability to turn sandcastles into sandstone. – Alex Speier

When influential Boston music critic Michael Steinberg first saw Seiji Ozawa conduct in the 1960s, he described “an incredible current of energy” that emanated from the Japanese conductor’s body “all the way to the point of the stick, and into the air beyond. It was a beautiful thing to watch.”

During his lengthy career, which included a 29-season tenure as music director of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Ozawa channeled that energy into classical music in Boston and beyond.

Preferring turtlenecks to tuxedos and wearing his hair long and shaggy, Ozawa was a distinctly approachable and relatable foil to the European elder statesmen of the podium when he arrived on the scene. Like his mentor Leonard Bernstein, he became an inescapable presence not only in the relatively small classical music cultural sphere, but among the general public.

Ozawa recorded extensively with the BSO, and excelled in leading performances of monumental works for orchestra and chorus, such as Mahler’s Symphony of a Thousand, Schoenberg’s Gurre-Lieder, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. For the opening ceremony of the 1998 Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan, he conducted the fourth movement of that Beethoven work with a live orchestra and chorus while also leading simulcast vocal ensembles (including the Tanglewood Festival Chorus) on five different continents.

Even after he stepped down at the BSO, his ties to the city persisted. He was a regular presence at Fenway Park and in Foxborough, and when traveling abroad, he often visited the local American embassy to catch a Boston sports broadcast.

“‘Seiji,’ not ‘maestro,’” wrote music critic Andrew Pincus in The Berkshire Eagle after the conductor’s death in February. “That’s what musicians, fans, backers, critics, even strangers called him.” – A.Z. Madonna

The odds may have seemed stacked against Gloria Fox’s success in life. She bounced around foster homes as a girl in the 1940s, then became a single mother raising two sons in a Boston housing project.

But when she began volunteering as a community organizer in Roxbury, local leaders spotted her passion for social justice and knack for leadership. Soon she was running antipoverty programs, and helping teens apply for summer jobs or families obtain fuel assistance. “I just became the woman that got busy,” she said in a 2009 interview.

Then, in her early 40s, she heard the pivotal words: “OK kid, it’s time.”

This came from two of Roxbury’s political elite: Mel King, the first Black candidate to reach a Boston mayoral general election, and former state lawmaker Doris Bunte.

Fox would run for — and eventually win in 1985 — the legislative seat representing Roxbury and parts of Dorchester, a position she held for more than 30 years. Fox, who died in November at the age of 82, would become the longest-serving woman in the Massachusetts State House when she announced her retirement in 2016.

Roxbury today is full of vivid reminders of her influence, from the Reggie Lewis Track & Athletic Center, which she helped open, to Malcolm X Boulevard, which she pushed to rename from New Dudley Street. And what is absent is also related to her: She and other leaders in the 1970s stopped a controversial extension of Interstate 95 that would have run through the neighborhood, uprooting housing and businesses.

Sometimes called the “Queen of Roxbury,” she was known to speak up forcefully for affordable housing, improved health care, foster care reform, and other causes she held dear. Upon news of her death, state Senator Lydia Edwards told the Globe: “She never apologized for doing the right thing.” – Patricia Wen

A chef, a reinventor, a mensch. That was Jasper White, who died in May after a career that shined new light on American — and specifically New England — cuisine.

It’s funny that it took a Jersey boy to bring national attention to Boston’s restaurant scene, but that’s what White did — with longtime friend and collaborator Lydia Shire at Seasons in the Bostonian Hotel, then with Restaurant Jasper, opened in 1983. Chef-owners were a rarity at the time, and French tradition still dominated local menus. White’s influences were as likely to be Chinese or Portuguese. Rather than relying on heavy sauces, he focused on local, seasonal ingredients and more modern preparations. Located on the waterfront, Jasper’s also paid particular attention to seafood, from oysters to the pan-roasted lobster that became a favorite of luminaries such as Julia Child.

White influenced home cooks, authoring volumes such as Jasper White’s Cooking From New England. As a progenitor of New American cuisine, he helped change the course of fine dining in this country.

And then he turned the game on its head, launching Jasper White’s Summer Shack in Cambridge in 2000. A tribute to seafood shacks, it was casual, fun, and accessible in a way upscale restaurants were not. Soon there were multiple locations. This trajectory — from fine dining to relaxed, replicable concepts — was one countless other chefs would follow. As usual, White was ahead of the curve. – Devra First

title: 10 new restaurants to try in the new year
text:
In 2020, husband-wife team Aaron and Shanna Chambers opened Salem restaurant Settler, where the menu takes its cues from Mediterranean cuisine and New England farmers and fishermen. Bernadette, their follow-up, focuses on France while continuing to make use of ingredients from the North Shore and beyond. The menu is like a capsule wardrobe for your stomach, stocked with really good versions of staples you want to return to again and again: endive salad, mussels, Parisian gnocchi with mushrooms, roast chicken. Come for l’apéro, the tradition of pre-dinner drinks and snacks; stay for desserts like mille-feuille with quince and brown butter cream.

65 Washington St., Salem, 978-224-2976, www.bernadettesalem.com. Appetizers $8-$28, entrees $28-$48.

Desnuda Cocina & Bar

Japan-inspired listening lounges are gaining ground here, and this latest spot from Mazí Food Group (Gigi, Ilona, Kava Neo-Taverna) gets in on the action with a downstairs sound bar. Come hang out and listen to vinyl after eating ceviche, pork belly bao buns and tacos, miso eggplant, and grilled steak with chimichurri sauce. Chef Jesus Preciado’s menu draws from Asia and Latin America (including his native Colombia). On the cocktail list, find drinks like Beet the Heat (made with spicy pisco and beet syrup) and Amarillo Passion (in which tequila meets yuzu liqueur, passion fruit syrup, and the aji amarillo chile).

647 Tremont St., South End, Boston, 617-286-2333, www.desnudacocina.com. Smaller plates $6-$18, larger plates $18-$32.

Kaia

The latest from Xenia Greek Hospitality, which brought us Bar Vlaha, Krasi, and more. This time, culinary director Brendan Pelley and team whisk diners to the Aegean (with a South End mind-set) via dishes like sea bream crudo with fermented squash broth; barley toasts with beets, pears, and vegan feta; black truffle spanakopita; and grilled whole fish. The wine list is devoted solely to selections from the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean islands.

370 Harrison Ave., South End, Boston, 617-514-0700, www.kaiasouthend.com. Dishes $16-$44.

Masons Steakhouse

Here’s what happens when a group of powerhouse South Shore culinary pros (including Jimmy Liang of JP Fuji Group and Kevin Long of Tosca) join forces. This swank Quincy steakhouse is located in a former Masonic temple and serves up lobster bisque, oysters Rockefeller, pappardelle bolognese, salmon with spiced cauliflower — and, of course, beautiful steaks. The also-beautiful, creative desserts are from pastry chef and Masons co-owner Robert Gonzalez, who is behind Quincy’s Niveaux Pâtisserie. In a landscape (increasingly) stocked with steakhouses, it is nice to see a new one open with local ownership.

1170 Hancock St., Quincy, 617-689-8818, www.masonssteakhouse.com. Appetizers $14-$32, entrees $29-$45, steaks $52-$160, sides $6-$14, desserts $12-$19.

McGonagle’s Pub

If you appreciate the Dubliner, bringing excellent fish and chips and Irish hospitality to downtown Boston, you will likely feel the same about McGonagle’s in Dorchester. Pigs in a blanket made with sausage from Adams Village Butcher Shop, smoky seafood chowder with Irish soda bread, shepherd’s pie, bangers and mash, and other pub favorites are here, along with wood-fired pizza, brunch (yes, full Irish breakfast), and festive cocktails. Or just drop in for live music and a proper pint of Guinness.

367 Neponset Ave., Dorchester, 617-514-4689, www.mcgonagles.com. Appetizers $8-$16, pizza $18-$19, entrees $18-$34.

Mikiya Wagyu Shabu House

If you’re starving, cold, and enjoy wagyu beef, Mikiya is calling you. This Chinatown restaurant serves all-you-can-eat wagyu hot pot at a variety of price points; you have 90 minutes to cook a variety of cuts in the broths of your choosing, while eating specialty dishes such as sweet shrimp sashimi and wagyu bone marrow, plus fruit and ice cream for dessert. Mikiya is a project from Chubby Group, whose Kevin Liu is also behind Matsunori Handroll Bar.

Wagyu sets $45-$98 (less with annual membership; free or half-price for kids).

Russ & Mimi’s

Named for the parents of owner Kelly Walsh (Sweet Cheeks, Tiger Mama), this Roslindale market offers wine (it’s in the former Solera space), olive oil, hot sauce, and other must-haves. But it’s the food that has the neighborhood most excited. Start the morning with egg wraps, overnight oats, cheesy grits, and cumin-spiced black beans with fried egg, salsa, and avocado; then segue into the “Cubano, veggie grinder, muffuletta, charred broccoli Caesar” part of the day. Chef Stephen Marcaurelle (the Nautilus Pier 4, Tres Gatos) helped design the menu.

16 Birch St., Roslindale, 617-833-6950, www.russandmimis.com. Dishes $8-$16.

Soul on Shawmut

Roxbury-raised chef Aadam Abdul-Musawwir began serving prepared meals and pop-up dinners as Aadam’s Halal Meals. Now, he and two siblings have opened Soul on Shawmut to feed their community. Lightly updated soul food classics are on the menu, along with Buffalo chicken egg rolls, grilled cheese burgers, and more. Fried chicken with Old Bay honey, smoked mac and cheese, slow-cooked collard greens with sauteed cabbage, sweet potato cheesecake, and hibiscus watermelon juice sounds pretty unbeatable for dinner tonight.

722A Shawmut Ave., Roxbury, 617-238-7525, www.soulonshawmut.com. Sandwiches $10-$18, fried chicken $7-$18, sides $5, desserts $3-$6.

Standard Italian

Where others fail, there is Italian food, everyone’s favorite. Standard Italian, in the Eastern Standard complex looming over Fenway, replaces the former All That Fish + Oyster, and it’s a smart move. Lasagna bolognese, porchetta, and espresso martinis could just get us all through the winter. Culinary director Brian Rae is in his element, having previously worked at Coppa, Faccia a Faccia, and Rialto.

771 Beacon St., Fenway, Boston, 857-305-3095, www.standarditalian.com. Appetizers $5-$20, entrees $28-$42, desserts $9-$12.

Zurito

It’s named for the small glass of beer that often accompanies pintxos, the Basque take on tapas, of which this Beacon Hill restaurant serves up plenty: Gildas, skewers of anchovies, peppers, and olives; griddled shrimp with garlic and chile oil; mini croissants stuffed with jamon iberico; squid ink risotto. Cocktails such as the sherry-based Perfect Bamboo and fizzy glasses of tzakolina are perfect accompaniments. Zurito, located in the longtime Bin 26 space, is run by chef Jamie Bissonnette, Babak Bina, and Andy Cartin of BCB3 Hospitality, also behind Somaek, Temple Records, and Sushi @ Temple Records.

26 Charles St., Beacon Hill, Boston, 857-305-3177, www.zuritoboston.com. Pintxos $4.50-$12, raciones $9-$19, platos especiales $17-$125.

title: Remembering MLK’s 1965 March on Boston
text:
On Monday, Boston, along with the rest of the country, celebrates King, whose historic demonstrations against legally sanctioned segregation in the South often overshadow the civil rights leader’s strong connection to the city. Yet, King’s time in Boston, particularly during the April 23, 1965, march, highlights his commitment to combatting what was commonly called “de facto” segregation in the North.

That day, King visited tenement housing in Roxbury, which he described as a “deplorable outrage,” according to Globe reporting from the time. He tried and failed to have an audience with the Boston School Committee, chaired at the time by Louise Day Hicks, a staunch opponent of school desegregation efforts whom King likened to a modern-day “pharaoh.” He successfully met with Massachusetts Governor John Volpe and Boston Mayor John Collins, urging them to act against northern “de facto” segregation, which he had described in an address to the Massachusetts Legislature the day before as “a new form of slavery covered up with certain niceties.”

When Glynnette Byron (now Scott), first laid eyes on King from the Common’s bandstand, she recalled being “happy, amazed, elated.”

“I was so glad ... our father wanted to take us with him; I think he knew how important that moment was going to be in our lives,” she said.

The Byron sisters grew up in Boston at the tail end of the Great Migration, a period when a massive number of Black people migrated from the Jim Crow South to northern industrial cities. Although most northern states lacked the formally legal kind of segregation practiced in the South, racist attitudes and policies such as redlining, which limited where racial minorities could rent or buy homes, still relegated Black people to the status of second-class citizens.

In the 1960s, the majority of Black Bostonians lived within a few overcrowded neighborhoods poorly serviced by the city, with their children attending overcrowded and underfunded schools. The threat of racially motivated harassment or violence, though diminished compared with the South, was still ever-present.

“We didn’t go to Charlestown, we didn’t go to South Boston,” Beverly Byron said. “Even in the ‘60s, my mother was teaching in South Boston, and it was awful. The little kids were calling her the N-word when she’d drive down the street.”

Marchers who attended the April 1965 demonstration and modern scholars look back on the event with a mixture of pride, joy, and apprehension, from the perspective of a 21st-century Boston and United States, where racially based inequities are still alive and well.

Ed Forry, an Irish Catholic raised in Dorchester and founder of the Dorchester Reporter newspaper, grew up on the other side of that racial divide. Forry was a 21-year-old English student at Boston College when he attended King’s march as a member of the Catholic Interracial Council of Boston, a group that advocated for civil rights through the lens of Catholic social teaching.

He called King’s speech on the Common “a rallying call for all of us who listened.”

“I’m proud I chose that day to bear witness to Martin Luther King’s message,” he said.

Jeanne Theoharis, a professor of political science at Brooklyn College of the City University of New York, described King’s march through Boston as “a site of contradiction.” A Globe article published the day of the march claims that while, “Dr. King was ever solemn and unsmiling in Selma and Montgomery,” up north “he could laugh as he walked the Boston streets.”

Theoharis clarified the historical record: “The day he gets to Boston, there are so many death threats, so he’s not free. Let’s start there.”

Theoharis said the rosy depiction of the march in newspaper columns from that day — juxtaposing King’s warm welcome from Bostonians with the harsh reprisals civil rights demonstrators often faced down South — played into a convenient narrative white Northerners enjoyed telling themselves about race relations in the region at that time.

“Many white Bostonians are very opposed to the idea that Boston is systematically segregated, and they’re very angry at King for trying to shine a light on that,” Theoharis said. “There’s this kind of self-congratulatory sense of ‘King is here,’ and at the same time, this real rejection of what he’s actually saying.”

Glynnette Scott recalled feeling an immense sense of hope growing up during that period. Both she and her sister agreed that as they grew older, especially in the aftermath of King’s assassination, that optimism began to fade.

Reflecting on her lifetime spent witnessing the evolution of American race relations, Glynnette offered her perspective.

“I get a sense now that they’re heading back in the wrong direction. … There’s some talk about Black history not being taught. There’s a push against some of the history that’s part of America being taught. So that’s why I feel things are changing,” she said.

Correction: Because of a reporting error, Glynnette Scott’s last name was omitted in a previous version of this story.

title: In wake of Steward collapse, new state law takes aim at private equity in health care
text:
“The Massachusetts bill has a lot of weaknesses but it’s a big step forward over what we had in the past and what other states have done,“ said Eileen Appelbaum, co-director for the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank. ”And it’s a message to other states — hey, you can regulate.”

It does this in part by targeting one of the primary ways that Steward’s owners extracted money from the system — a major contributing factor in its collapse last year in Massachusetts — by prohibiting hospitals from selling their primary campus to outside investors.

The Massachusetts law also accomplishes what many states have tried and so far failed to do — establish ongoing financial monitoring and oversight of investors in a health care provider.

Under the law, investors with as little as 10 percent equity will be required to participate in the state’s annual health care oversight hearings and file ownership and governance information with state watchdog agencies, including notice when they buy or sell stakes in a system. State watchdogs could go so far as to require audited financial statements from equity investors.

David Seltz, executive director for the state’s Health Policy Commission, said that before, researchers had to resort to searching Google and listening to investor podcasts to understand the scale of private equity investment in Massachusetts health care. The law is a tremendous first step to “pull back the veil” on ownership and the effects of those relationships, he said.

While the law will help regulators understand who is profiting from the state’s critical health care infrastructure, it will not stop that profiteering entirely. Mary Bugbee, a researcher with the nonprofit watchdog Private Equity Stakeholder Project, said true reform would be legislation to fully curb the profit-driven decision-making that has contributed to health systems failures in the first place.

“There’s an avoidance of actually going after the business practices themselves that we know really have only an extractive role in health care,” Bugbee said.

But it will curb one business practice that the Globe Spotlight Team found played a major role in Steward’s troubles: the sale and leaseback of hospital buildings themselves.

Much of those sales have involved companies known as real estate investment trusts, or REITs, which hold portfolios of properties and make money by leasing them out. Steward sold its Massachusetts real estate to one such company — Birmingham, Ala.-based Medical Properties Trust — for nearly $1.3 billion. The sum was nine times what Steward itself had initially paid, and Steward’s owners profited handsomely from the sale. But the deal tied the hospitals to long-term leases, which saddled the international health system with onerous rent payments that contributed to its bankruptcy, and ultimately led to the closure last summer of Dorchester’s Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer.

Such deals would be prohibited, in most cases, under the new law.

A spokesperson for Medical Properties Trust did not return messages seeking comment on the new Massachusetts law.

Zirui Song, an associate professor of health care policy and medicine at Harvard Medical School in Boston, said the new law does not touch many of the other tools private equity firms use to draw money out of the companies the own, such as loading up hospital systems with debt while they draw out payments for their investors and themselves. But in many ways, he said, the state had to do this step first to uncover who owns what in the health care industry.

“We can certainly go further. That is undoubtably true,” he said. “But ... I think of it as a substantial meaningful step in the right direction.”

State Senator Cindy Friedman of Arlington had supported a stronger version from the Senate, which would have required private equity firms to post a bond with the state when filing notice of a transaction. But she, too, hailed the measure as a good start. She said she plans to file a bill in the new legislative session that would further restrict private equity ownership in health care, including the bond requirement.

“This was a compromise; it took the first step,” Friedman said. “Now we have to keep going.”

It’s far more than other states have done.

In September, California Governor Gavin Newson vetoed a proposal that would have required private equity groups and hedge funds to receive approval from the state’s attorney general for certain investments in health care facilities and provider groups. Similar efforts in Minnesota, Oregon, and Connecticut also failed.

Connecticut state Senator Dr. Saud Anwar stressed the need for federal, state, and local protections from what he said was “the greed of private equity and entities like REITs more interested in profit than of the well-being of the patient.”

In his work as a physician, Anwar said, he has seen the harm private equity control can bring, such as delayed results for important medical tests including a CT or MRI scan.

“I have yet to see any good example come out of it,” he said. “This activity is nothing short of being criminal. It is centered on financial benefits for some people whose greed sees no boundaries, and it’s a situation that does not help the patient’s well-being.”

Other states are grappling with the teetering of private-equity owned health systems. Prospect Medical Group, once backed by private equity group Leonard Green, owns three hospitals in Connecticut and two in Rhode Island, and filed for bankruptcy earlier this month.

Rhode Island Senator Lou DiPalma said his state has robust oversight of hospital conversions, but in light of the Massachusetts bill, particularly the restrictions on real estate investment trusts, he said perhaps they could go further.

Louisiana state Representative Michael Echols, whose district is near Steward’s Glenwood Regional Medical Center, also intends to file legislation there to hold executives of equity investors such as REITs civilly liable if a health care facility was not appropriately operated for 36 months in a row.

“It’s just like a big cartel with a shield,” Echols said. “I just want to take away the shield so the cartel can’t win.”

title: ‘They’re everywhere’: Boston losing fight against spread of used drug needles
text:
While long a problem, the proliferation of discarded needles has reached crisis levels since city officials abruptly ended a popular program last June that paid drug users to collect them. The number of 311 service requests for needle pickups surged nearly 50 percent in the final six months of last year, compared with the same period in 2023. Needle-pickup requests last year reached the highest level since the program’s inception in December of 2020 — with an average of 1,125 requests a month during the second half of last year, according to a review of 311 requests.

City crews and community groups that run needle exchange programs are scrambling to contain the problem, which has been exacerbated by a surging homeless population and persistently high rates of illicit drug use. The needles have become so widespread that they have become a major public health concern, as accidental stabbings can result in the spread of blood-borne infections such as HIV and hepatitis C.

Two years ago, a 9-year-old boy from Roxbury was rushed by ambulance to the hospital after he was pricked by a dirty needle while practicing with his Pop Warner football team. Increasingly, tourists have to navigate around the discarded syringes, with their distinctive orange caps, as they walk Boston’s Freedom Trail.

“We’re talking about thousands and thousands of syringes in places where children play and people congregate,” said Mario Chaparro, program director of low-threshold housing at Elliot Community Human Services, a nonprofit that provides mental health and housing services. “It’s only a matter of time before someone gets stuck.”

Street outreach groups trace the worsening problem to the end of a needle-for-cash program that, in just a few years, took 5 million dirty needles off Boston’s streets.

The program, known as the Community Syringe Redemption Program, gave drug users an incentive to collect their own needles by offering them 20 cents per syringe, with a limit of $10 a day per person. It wasn’t much, but it was enough of an incentive for people struggling with addiction and others to collect 25,000 to 35,000 used needles per week and hand-deliver them to one of the program’s vans, which parked early each weekday morning outside of areas of Boston with high concentrations of drug users.

Some months, the program was responsible for collecting nearly 80 percent of the total volume of used needles removed from Boston’s city streets.

But the program’s impact extended far beyond needle collection. The outreach workers in the mobile vans would offer people overdose-reversal drugs and would connect them with treatment programs and housing services to help them overcome addiction. And for many, the $10 in cash from collecting needles was enough for a meal and a “sense of pride” that they were contributing to the city’s safety, said Allie Hunter, cofounder of the company, Addiction Response Resources, that ran the program.

“People felt like they were part of something bigger than themselves, and that was a beautiful thing,” Hunter said.

Gobbi credits the needle-collection program with possibly saving his life.

He encountered the van nearly two years ago while he was homeless and using heroin near a troubled area known as Mass. and Cass, long the epicenter of the city’s homeless and opioid crises. He started bringing in more than 100 needles a day that he picked up from area parks and streets. Then one of the outreach workers told him about a nearby clinic that provides methadone treatment, which helped alleviate the agonizing pangs of withdrawal he felt every time he stopped taking heroin.

“If it wasn’t for that van, I swear to God that I’d either be dead or in prison,” said Gobbi, who is now sober and this month moved into an apartment of his own in Dorchester.

But the federal pandemic relief funds that covered the program’s roughly $1.2 million annual cost dried up last year, and the Boston Public Health Commission decided to focus on other initiatives.

In a statement, the health commission said it continues to maintain a mobile sharps team that last year responded to 10,736 requests through 311 to remove needles. The city fulfills 99.9% of all requests with a median response time of 28 minutes. The outreach team also proactively checks schools and parks for discarded needles, the commission said.

City and public health commission officials also said they have decided to try a different model of syringe removal — one focused on ending open-air drug use and expanding workforce opportunities for people who have struggled with addiction. The city last June expanded a contract with the Newmarket Business Improvement District, which hires former drug users to pick up 300 to 350 needles in city parks and squares with high concentrations of illicit drug use.

“The city is committed to ending outdoor substance use and drug dealing on city streets,” said Kellie Young, director of the city’s coordinated response team. “We will quickly respond to any 311 calls for needles, but we know that outdoor drug use undermines quality of life in our neighborhoods and we are committed to ending it in Boston.”

Yet city and nonprofit outreach teams have not kept pace with the volume of needles being discarded on city streets.

For most of the past four years, the city has collected more discarded needles than it has given out through various programs that dispose of used syringes and provide access to sterile ones. But that changed dramatically late last year. In December, city programs took in 132,463 used needles, while giving out nearly 190,000. That’s a sharp change from last April, when the city took in 250,931 needles and gave out 97,754, according to a city dashboard.

“There are a lot of folks out in the community using drugs — and they don’t have as much incentive now to pick up,” said Katie Weixler, deputy director of prevention at Victory Programs, a Boston nonprofit that offers a range of support services for people who are homeless and struggling with substance use disorders.

On a cold and windy weekday morning, it did not take long for a duo of street outreach workers with Victory Programs to spot a slew of dirty needles near its drop-in center along Massachusetts Avenue. They were scattered on busy sidewalks, behind fences, and under bushes, the needles glistening in the sun. In their backpacks, the workers carried dozens of clean needles and other harm-reduction supplies that they offered to people on the streets.

At one point, the two outreach workers — Dinay Von Johnson and Azzy-Mae Ní Mháille — stopped to scrutinize a forlorn patch of dirt-and-gravel along Melnea Cass Boulevard that was littered with hundreds of bright-orange syringe caps. Yet amid the refuse, the pair couldn’t find a single discarded needle — an encouraging sign, they said, that people who had injected drugs at the site had picked up their needles.

“People sometimes think that people out here don’t care, but they do,” Von Johnson said. “They just need options.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
PORRIDGE RADIO “Clouds in the Sky They Will Always Be There for Me,” the final album from this Brighton rock outfit, manages to be both pensive and grand, with leader Dana Margolis’s live-wire poetry accompanied by churning, abstractly hooky music that underscores the tumult she’s describing. Jan. 26, 7 p.m. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

DHRUV This London singer-songwriter’s soulful balladry is given extra emotional heft by his smooth, supple voice. Jan. 30, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

CHUCK PROPHET Prophet is touring behind his latest album, “Wake the Dead,” which was the result of his cumbia obsession (an obsession that turned therapeutic in getting him through his recovery from lymphoma). He’ll be accompanied by a band, dubbed Cumbia Shoes, that combines members of his Mission Express and cumbia outfit ¿Qiensave?. Jan. 28, 7:30 p.m. $25-$45. City Winery, 80 Beverly St. 617-933-8047. www.citywinery.com/boston

MATT POND PA Matt Pond changed the name of his self-referential collaboration to The Natural Lines in 2022, but now he’s left that name behind to return to Matt Pond PA. Well, not entirely behind: The name of Matt Pond PA’s about-to-be-released record is “The Ballad of the Natural Lines.” You can hear some of it this Wednesday. Jan. 29, 8 p.m. $20. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. therockwell.org

OLE 60 They describe themselves as “not your father’s country band,” and proceed to pull together strands of what might well have been your father’s music in outlaw-leaning country and Southern rock. How these youngsters have secured a date in a room the size of Royale without having released a full-length record is an interest-piquing question. Jan. 30, 8 p.m. $45. Royale, 279 Tremont St. 888-929-7849. www.axs.com

STUART MUNRO

NEAL & THE VIPERS Biting blues guitarist Neal Vitullo and his high-voltage group are among New England’s premier American roots music bands, and have shared stages with the likes of B.B. King, Bonnie Raitt, and The Fabulous Thunderbirds, among many others. Jan 25. 8 p.m. $15-$20. Chan’s Fine Oriental Dining, 267 Main St., Woonsocket R.I. chanseggrollsjazz.com

THE ZAHILI ZAMORA QUARTET Arts Wayland presents the exciting Cuban pianist and composer’s group — Panamanian saxophonist Samuel Batista, Dominican percussionist Francis P, and Dominican bassist Abner Cabrera — in a set of originals slated for her upcoming album, as well as standards with an Afro-Cuban accent. Jan. 26, 3 p.m. $20. First Parish in Wayland, 225 Boston Post Road, Wayland. artswayland.com

ELAN MEHLER SEXTET The acclaimed pianist is often likened to fellow keyboardists Bill Evans, Keith Jarrett, and Brad Mehldau, but has certainly carved out his own identity within that realm. His powerhouse band for this gig comprises saxophonists George Garzone and Loren Stillman, guitarist Ben Monder, bassist Tony Scherr, and drummer Francisco Mela. Jan. 30, 7:30 p.m. $25-$35. Regattabar. regattabarjazz.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO and music director Andris Nelsons wrap up the Beethoven symphonic marathon this weekend with the trim, lighthearted Symphony No. 8 and the evergreen Symphony No. 9, featuring soloists Sara Jakubiak (replacing Amanda Majeski, who withdrew for health reasons), Tamara Mumford, Pavel Černoch, and Andrè Schuen with the Tanglewood Festival Chorus (Jan. 24 and 25). Next week, the orchestra unveils one of the season’s banner events: concert performances of Korngold’s “Die tote Stadt,” with Christine Goerke and Brandon Jovanovich in lead roles (Jan. 30 and Feb. 1). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

JAMIE BARTON, MATTHEW LIPMAN, TAMAR SANIKIDZE Mezzo-soprano and Metropolitan Opera leading-role regular Barton teams up with violist Lipman and pianist Sanikidze for a unique recital program featuring songs and sonatas by Brahms and Clara Schumann, ending with the Boston premiere of Joel Thompson’s new piece “On Mars.” Jan. 25, 8 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-482-2595, www.celebrityseries.org

BOSTON YOUTH SYMPHONY ORCHESTRAS Under the direction of Federico Cortese, BYSO routinely punches above its weight with regard to repertoire, and the annual opera in concert is a reliable highlight. The young players tackle Verdi’s “Don Carlo,” a sweeping epic of love and duty amid the terrors of the Spanish Inquisition, in a production stage-directed by Joshua Major with tenor Bruce Sledge in the title role. Jan. 26, 3 p.m., Sanders Theatre, Harvard University, Cambridge. 617-353-3348, www.bysoweb.org

A.Z. MADONNA

AIN’T NO MO’ Broadway doesn’t always have the last word on the merits of a new play. And a good thing, too. Otherwise, Boston theatergoers might not have a chance to see a wildly inventive work like Jordan E. Cooper’s “Ain’t No Mo’.” But they do, and they should. Under the sure-handed direction of Dawn M. Simmons, with a topnotch cast of six, “Ain’t No Mo’” delivers a combination of knockabout comedy, stiletto-sharp satire, and scalding fury — the kind of abrupt transitions where your laugh dies in your throat. Through Feb. 8. Coproduction by SpeakEasy Stage Company and Front Porch Arts Collective. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, www.bostontheatrescene.com

HAUNTED The premiere of a horror comedy, written and directed by Tara Moses, that focuses on Indigenous siblings Ash (Bradley Lewis) and Aaron (Chingwe Padraig Sullivan). Dead for two decades, they’ve been haunting the families who have attempted to move into their house. Now, they’re hoping for admission to the Spirit World while they’re wondering, according to press materials, “if they’ll ever be free from the shackles of racist stereotypes.” To relax, the siblings dance to the songs of Britney Spears and Mariah Carey. Jan. 24-Feb. 15. Company One Theatre in partnership with the Boston Public Library. At Rabb Hall, Boston Public Library. Tickets are “pay what you want,” at 617-292-7110 or www.companyone.org

THE PIANO LESSON In August Wilson’s Pulitzer-winning drama, two siblings are locked in a fierce contest of wills over what to do with the family’s antique piano, on which an ancestor had carved the faces of family members. Boy Willie (Omar Robinson) wants to use the money to purchase the land where their ancestors were enslaved. But Berniece (Jade Guerra), who sees the piano as a deeply meaningful part of the family’s history, wants to keep it. Directed by Christoper V. Edwards. Jan. 23-Feb. 13. Actors’ Shakespeare Project, in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall. Tickets at 617-241-2200 or ActorsShakespeareProject.org/Piano-Lesson

DON AUCOIN

BOSTON CONSERVATORY COMMERCIAL DANCE BFA CONCERT Well respected nationally for its stellar dance training, Boston Conservatory at Berklee showcases the program’s inaugural class of graduates in commercial dance, embracing styles ranging from hip-hop and K-pop to jazz and heels. In addition, the concert highlights students in cirque/circus arts — the school is the first institution in the country to offer a minor in the discipline. Jan. 30-31. $11.50-$26.50. Berklee Performance Center. www.etix.com/ticket/e/1048147

MYLES KERCHER This one-night-only event is not just a dance performance, but also a fund-raiser to support the Ipswich dancer/choreographer’s training opportunities overseas plus a dance party afterward, complete with refreshments. Kercher and guest artists present two of his original works, a new duet and the solo “face.” Jan. 25. $12. MAGMA, Gloucester. https://magma.center/event/dance-performance-myles-kercher/

THE LOOK OF LOVE This wildly popular new work by the Mark Morris Dance Group marks the company’s first Boston appearance in six years. Featuring a live band and vocals from Broadway star Marcy Harriell, the evening-length work is set to chart-topping hits by award-winning composer-songwriter Burt Bacharach. Presented by Global Arts Live. Jan. 23-26. $58-$95. Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre. www.globalartslive.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

FUTURE FOSSILS Just opened: A hindsight view of our current moment from the far-flung future, this exhibition brings together a stellar roster of artists — Ai Weiwei, Nari Ward, Rachel Whiteread, Sanford Biggers — to imagine what might remain of the fractured world we now live in when all we know is gone. Through April 13. MassArt Museum, 621 Huntington Ave.. 617-879-7333, maam.massart.edu

SAINTS, SINNERS, LOVERS, FOOLS: 300 YEARS OF FLEMISH MASTERWORKS A showcase for the collection of the Antwerp-based Phoebus Foundation, this traveling exhibition brings together marquee Netherlandish old masters from the 15th to 17th century, including Peter Paul Rubens, Anthony van Dyck, Hans Memling, Jan Brueghel, and Michaelina Wautier, augmented by a wunderkammer crafted from PEM’s own collection of antiquity. Through May 4. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500, PEM.org

STEVE LOCKE: THE FIRE NEXT TIME Locke is likely best-known to Boston audiences as the artist who proposed — and had approved — a memorial to victims of the slave trade embedded in the cobblestones outside Faneuil Hall only to withdraw it amid a firestorm of public complaint, most notably from the local chapter of the NAACP. But Locke’s work has always drawn on the history of American injustice, whether racial or otherwise, and “the fire next time,” which takes its title from James Baldwin’s book, published in 1963 at the peak of the civil rights movement, is no exception. This exhibition amalgamates recent works, including paintings, drawings, and sculpture, that deal with such subjects as police brutality, mass murder, and the wrongfully accused. Through Nov. 8. Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, 1040 Mass MoCA Way, North Adams. 413-662-2111, www.massmoca.org

MURRAY WHYTE

TRASLUZ/TRANSLUCENT For centuries, the genre of landscape painting in Western society relied on a binary algorithm of human versus nature. That’s changing. Here, contemporary painters Juan José Barboza-Gubo and Michael Zachary offer metaphysical visions of landscape — porous, engulfing, and shot with light — as if to reposition humanity within the wild rather than apart from it. Yet still, there is a veil obscuring mystery. The exhibition is organized by Sarah Montross, chief curator at the deCordova Sculpture Park and Museum. Through March 7. Faye G., Jo, and James Stone Gallery, Boston University Art Galleries, 855 Commonwealth Ave. www.bu.edu/cfa/featured-work/trasluz-translucent/

CATE McQUAID

MEN IN COMEDY PRESENTS… ALL BANKSYS: A BAD ART AUCTION Part of this night organized by the Men In Comedy collective will be an all-femme stand-up show with Brieana Woodward, Kristina Feliciano, Katy Coughlin, Maddie Kelly, Parvo the Wise, Mel Moscoso, and Laith, and part bad art auction, in honor of the Museum of Bad Art housed by the Dorchester Brewing Company. The top three winners will get gift cards to Mighty Squirrel Taproom and Kitchen. This family-friendly game, hosted by the G&G Trivia group, is inclusive and fun for everyone.
