title: UMass Memorial Health considering stand-alone emergency room in Nashoba Valley to replace shuttered Steward hospital
text:
The region in north Central Massachusetts has been without a dedicated health care facility since Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer closed in August last year.

The proposal is still in its early stages, officials said.

“While there is significant work to be done before this plan becomes a reality, we remain committed to supporting and protecting the health care needs of residents throughout Central Massachusetts,” UMass Memorial Health said.

It’s not clear where the new facility will be located. A spokesperson for UMass Memorial Health said that plans to use the empty Nashoba Valley hospital “did not work out” and that the hospital group is now exploring other site options.

Once a location is secured, the emergency room won’t be expected to open for another year-and-a-half, the spokesperson said.

Advocates are encouraged that UMass Memorial Health, which operates five hospitals in Central Massachusetts, is looking to fill the void created by the closing of Nashoba.

“They have the capacity to operate across the region,” said Steve Adams, president of the Community Foundation of North Central Massachusetts, in an interview. “They’re not a community hospital that has to struggle with financials; they’re a much more stable position.”

“Now, I know all hospitals are in financial challenges, including theirs, and I’ve heard them talk about that,” he continued. “But if someone can do it, UMass Memorial is the one that can.”

In August, Steward closedNashoba and Carney Hospital in Dorchester, the company’s only hospitals in Massachusetts that did not receive qualified bids during a sale process.

The closures elicited fierce opposition from community members.

For residents of Ayer and the surrounding communities, the loss of Nashoba Valley has caused the average travel time for emergency care to more than double. The two nearest hospitals, UMass Memorial HealthAlliance-Clinton Hospital in Leominster and Emerson Hospital in Concord, are both roughly a half-hour away. And that’s not accounting for traffic or the time it takes for an ambulance to respond.

By comparison, ambulance trips to Nashoba usually took less than 10 minutes, officials have said.

The closure has also strained ambulance services and emergency rooms in the area, with officials saying they are not equipped to deal with the higher demand.

In a statement Wednesday, Governor Maura Healey said she was “grateful to UMass Memorial Health for stepping up to ensure continued health care access in Central Massachusetts.“

Healey said she was aware of the “significant strain” that the Nashoba Valley closure had caused on local communities. She credited the Nashoba Valley Working Group, which convened in October in an effort to “preserve access to high-quality care and services in the region.”

State Representative Margaret Scarsdale, who chairs the working group’s emergency health care subcommittee, described Wednesday’s announcement as “a community victory.”

“We are thrilled to have UMass Memorial as the new operator, and very eager to work with them,” Scarsdale said in an interview. “This isn’t the final step. Of course, there’s more work to be done, and I know we are eager to partner with them to make sure that we are restoring these essential services that this area desperately needs.”

But some advocates have characterized the plan as a disappointing half-measure.

“I appreciate UMass Memorial proposing an ER facility in the Nashoba Valley,” said state Senator Jamie Eldridge in an interview. “However, I remain saddened that we don’t have a full hospital coming back to the region. And I continue to be frustrated that the Healey-Driscoll administration did not do more to provide funding to allow [Nashoba] the same opportunity that allowed other hospitals to remain open.”

Eldridge, a Democrat whose district includes Ayer, said he will continue to push to restore full medical services to the region.

A union leader pointed out that the plan will do little to alleviate the strain on nearby hospitals in the near term.

“Suggesting that they will find land, plan and develop a new [emergency department], recruit staff and get required approvals in a rapid time frame is not possible,” said David Schildmeier, a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Nurses Association, in a statement. “Building a new stand alone ED outside of Nashoba is unlikely to bring any relief for a period of two years — the community does not have that luxury.”

Schildmeier said the ideal solution would be resuming operations at the Nashoba Valley Medical Center site. First responders have been “working diligently” to keep that option on the table, he added.

title: I considered Boston my only home. Then I visited Ireland.
text:
For me, I knew the idea of living anywhere outside Boston would be a hard sell. As a lifelong Massachusetts resident, my sense of home is firmly rooted in the Hub. I was born and raised in Dorchester, and I wear my neighborhood pride on my back: The words “Dot Rat” are tattooed in Old English letters across my shoulder blades.

To cover as much ground as possible, we plotted out an ambitious plan to visit Dublin, then drive to the port town of Kinsale, and then get a taste of the countryside in the Irish Midlands — all in a span of three days.

Comparing the sizes of Ireland and New England, we figured it would be roughly like driving from Logan Airport to Stamford, Connecticut, back up to Marlborough, Massachusetts, and then back to Boston again. An easy jaunt, right?

“Are you crazy? What are you two thinking?” my mother asked when I told her we might add some additional stops on our trip.

After arriving at Dublin Airport, we picked up our rental car. Driving in Europe — which I had worried about — turned out to be easier than I expected. I just recited the opening lyrics to Beyonce’s “Irreplaceable” over and over in my head — “To the left, to the left” — and reminded myself to stay out of the right lane.

The minute we walked through the door of our hotel in Dublin, I heard my name being called from across the lobby. We received warm greetings from my father’s cousins Teresa and Danny, as well as Danny’s wife, Carmel — members of my extended family whom I’d never met. It felt like a homecoming.

Chatting over pints of Guinness, they talked about how my grandmother grew up in a modest homestead with more than a dozen siblings in a tiny village in Northern Ireland. They reminisced about my father, aunt, and uncles, and how they came over for a big family reunion years ago. I felt I was talking with relatives I’d known my whole life.

Later, Cody and I walked around the city and watched the ducks and swans at St. Stephen’s Green. We checked out vintage clothing stores — something we like to do back home — all the while, marveling at how clean Dublin’s sidewalks were. The architecture and atmosphere reminded me of Boston.

The next morning, we headed to Kinsale, a quaint town on the southern coast of Ireland about 175 miles away from Dublin.

As we strolled around that evening, I couldn’t believe how quiet it was. It was like a thick blanket of silence was draped over this little port city and its colorful buildings. The place looked so cute, we wondered out loud if the crime rate was zero.

“I think we’re the most dangerous people here,” Cody whispered.

“By far,” I replied.

The next morning we were back on the road, driving three hours north to a bookstore in County Kildare, where I had a book-signing event.

The store was packed. The fact that my book, which is about a legendary Irish-American wrestler who started a detox center in Acton, drew so much interest spoke to the pride Ireland has in its diaspora. Everyone was so friendly and engaging that I felt like I was at my own neighborhood bookstore.

At the end of the event, the staff bid us goodbye, told us to come back soon, and gave us a thoughtful parting gift: a notebook with a leather cover that was handcrafted by a saddlery down the street.

As we waited for our flight to Scotland the next morning, neither of us was quite ready to leave. We both agreed: Ireland definitely passed the vibe check.

Which got me thinking: What makes somewhere feel like home? A familiar place that puts you at ease. You feel safe. There’s shared history. A sense of belonging. These things are why Boston will always be home.

But as I reflected on my whirlwind trip, I saw that Ireland checked those boxes, too. Walking the streets, I felt as comfortable as I do sauntering past triple-deckers on Dorchester Avenue. The people — relatives and total strangers — were so welcoming they made me feel I was part of Ireland’s history, even though I grew up 3,000 miles away.

Back home, I sent text messages to my relatives over there, letting them know we wanted to come back. I was surprised to find myself missing and yearning for a place I had only visited once. A return trip is surely in order, and who knows what the future holds?

Because for this Dot Rat, the concept of home is beginning to expand.

title: During a nine-hour City Council hearing, Boston residents voice opposition to White Stadium plan
text:
Just five voiced support for the project.

“Boston students deserve a renovated White Stadium – they deserve a public White Stadium, not a private sports and entertainment complex built to enable private profits,” said Jean McGuire, resident of Roxbury and longtime civil rights advocate. “It’s clear that this entire process is being driven by the needs of private investments, not the needs of Boston students. The process has been launched, the state reviews having been conducted, and community members’ concerns about public access and transportation impacts are being ignored, all in a mad rush to next March for White Stadium in order to be a soccer team’s desired opening day.”

In addition to committee chair Julia Mejia, the other councilors there for the duration were District 6 Councilor Ben Weber, whose district abuts Franklin Park, and At-Large Councilor Erin Murphy and District 2 Councilor Ed Flynn. Both Flynn and Murphy have voiced their support for at least pausing the demolition in the interests of the council getting, in part, a better handle on the project’s costs.

In response to a question, Dion Irish, the city’s chief operating officer, upped the city’s share of the project from the $91 million that had emerged last month to “roughly $100 million.”

The soccer team’s share remains unknown, except that it will exceed the city’s share, which elevates the total cost above $200 million.

The meeting was split into two parts, with the morning and early afternoon devoted to discussions of finances and facilities, including the Madison Park high school renovation, and the latter session devoted to community engagement.

Mejia, a councilor at-large, said she would file a resolution for councilors to be polled on their support or lack of support for both White Stadium and Madison Park at the next City Council meeting on Jan. 29.

Diana Fernandez Bibeau, the deputy chief of urban design for the city, pushed back on the notion that the community was not part of the process.

“Our work without a doubt has been impacted by the community feedback that we’ve received today,” said Fernandez Bibeau. “I certainly understand that there is reservation of a particular type of partnership being able to sort of deliver on this project, but we have responded, and we have tried to sort of meet the community where they are in terms of where they are, in terms of where those concerns are, and try to address them every step of the way.

“I also want you to know that it’s hard to do this right, that it’s the reason why no other mayor has taken on the renovation of White Stadium, why no other administrations have taken on the hard work to go ahead and make an improvement at White Stadium and deliver on this promise for historically disinvested communities.”

Also on hand for portions of the meeting were District 7 Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson, whose district encompasses Franklin Park and District 4 Councilor Brian Worrell, whose district also abuts the park. Also in attendance for portions of the meeting were Councilors John Fitzgerald, Enrique Pepén, Sharon Durkan, and Henry Santana.

Anderson expressed concern with the degree of engagement from the city with citizens.

“The administration should have told the community what planning and engagement would look like,” said Anderson. “We have not done enough to engage the community.”

Weber said he has heard both support and opposition for the plan from his constituents. He found it “disturbing” to hear that there has not been a community process. As for opponents like the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, who have filed a lawsuit that will go to trial in March, he said, “I hear a lot of rhetoric, I don’t hear much about solutions.”

“Some of the rhetoric around the opposition is not tied to the facts, and I wish that it was more tied to the facts, I think we could have a more constructive conversation,” Weber said.

Stevan Kirschbaum, a former BPS bus driver, described the White Stadium plan as “appalling and criminal.”

“We should be chaining ourselves to those trees – this is a criminal rush to judgment.”

Ann Walsh, a Dorchester resident, expressed the belief that the presence of the women’s professional team would be an inspiration to BPS student-athletes.

“My expectation is that a professional women’s soccer team is going to be a good commercial partner like the Red Sox are and offer mentorship and internships.”

title: Boston school leaders to present enrollment forecast, closure plans through 2030
text:
“We need to ensure as quickly as possible that every student has access to this high quality experience,” Skipper said. “And unfortunately, we know that’s not the case right now. And so that’s the reason we feel a sense of urgency, as I’m sure you do.”

The city leaders already are seeking to close Excel High School in South Boston, Dever Elementary School in Dorchester, and the Mary Lyon Pilot High School in Allston/Brighton, and merge Winthrop and Clap Elementary Schools.

But critics of the planned closures, including Langston Peace, a world history teacher at Excel, said students and staff had little say in the schools’ fates. “This is not a community proposal,” he said.

Those who have worked to build the Excel community won’t benefit from those efforts, he said.

“We face closure. The people of Excel are disappointed, discouraged. Many of us are just demoralized,” Peace said. “Physically, mentally, and financially, we’ve been investing in Excel High for decades. And we are not going to see the return on our investment that we hoped for.”

The School Committee is expected to vote on the proposed closures and merger in March. The meeting will be remote-only, as will all meetings, including annual budget hearings, before April 16.

Wednesday’s meeting was the first since Skipper and Mayor Michelle Wu presented their plans to close three schools and merge two others at the end of the next school year.

District administrators estimate the building closures and mergers will save about $10 million to $20 million, according to Del Stanislaus, the district’s chief of capital planning, in a memo to the School Committee released Wednesday.

The district will also provide individualized support to multilingual learners, to find schools that meet their needs, and work with students with individualized education plans for special education purposes to make sure they receive the services they need, according to Stanislaus.

While the district has closed and merged dozens of schools since 2011, the vast majority were converted into another school, or are slated to be. That means the physical capacity of the district remains much higher than enrollment, which has fallen by more than 8,000 students in that time. At the same time, costs to run the system have only grown.

Projecting enrollment can be difficult and has proved to be problematic for the district, which has routinely overestimated its future enrollment. The pandemic accelerated enrollment losses in Boston and across the country, then an increase in immigration in the last few years has stabilized the district’s population. Enrollment increased this year for the first time in a decade.

And the trend in coming years is highly uncertain, particularly as birth rates across the country and the impact of immigration crackdowns by the Trump administration take effect, administrators and committee members said Wednesday.

District administrators conducted surveys and community meetings to learn what students, families, and staff wanted, and determined which schools should close based on a number of factors, including the building’s condition, and whether it is underutilized.

During the board’s discussion, committee member Brandon Cardet-Hernandez called on district administrators to provide more transparency around which schools could be closed over the next five years.

The proposed closures wouldn’t take effect until June 2026 -- and that time is critical for district to prepare other buildings for the relocated students and staff. Skipper said that if the district announced all of the potential school closures immediately, it would have a detrimental effect on those communities and the students who remain in those buildings.

“Students don’t choose that school,” Skipper said. “So you get a very slow drain down of a school, and staff leave.”

While some have said the district has yet to go far enough, the recently proposed closures have already provoked some pushback, including a protest at the Dever and a petition to save the school.

Cheryl Buckman, a parent of a sixth-grader at the school, said her family was devastated to learn the building would be closed. The Dever, she said, is “a family-driven community.”

“The Dever has been blossoming on its own with the help of educated staff and parents,” she said. “This is a major blow to the staff and educators that teach our children.”

Another Dever parent, Edzna Vazquez, urged the School Committee to not close the school, where there is “ a community of people” helping kids, the teachers, the staff, she said in Spanish through an interpreter.

“It is critical that this school is not closed,” Vazquez said.

title: ‘A life and death matter’: Shelters, volunteers work to reach Boston’s homeless as Mass. faces cold snap
text:
Advocates say that mission is especially crucial now, as a blast of Arctic air chills Massachusetts. On Wednesday, temperatures are expected to climb no higher than 21 degrees, according to the National Weather Service.

Boston has warned residents to be on the lookout for unhoused individuals who may be at risk, according to a cold weather advisory issued Monday.

“If you see an individual experiencing homelessness and individuals out in the cold who appear immobile, disoriented, or underdressed for the cold, please call 911,” the advisory said. “If residents are aware of anyone staying in a vehicle or a place not intended for living during these extreme cold temperatures, they are encouraged to call 911 as well.”

Because of the dangerous temperatures, the Southampton Street Shelter and Woods Mullen Shelter will offer admission to individuals who otherwise would be barred, such as those prone to violence, city officials said.

Sheila Dillon, director of the Mayor’s Office of Housing, said the city works closely with nonprofits to ensure that enough shelter space is available. But she reiterated that residents should be proactive for anyone that appears disoriented, improperly dressed, or who seems to be struggling.

“It really is [about] creating a community and having the public help us identify any issues,” she said. “Because while the street outreach teams are fabulous … we need to make sure that our responses are swift.”

Leaders serving the homeless say the extreme cold has left homeless residents more at risk.

“We’ve moved from the nights being tolerable to the nights being life threatening,” said Lyndia Downie, president of Pine Street Inn, at a Tuesday press conference. “Of course, we’re nervous, because one thing could tip this for people [between life and death].”

Pine Street Inn, which operates shelters in the South End, Dorchester, and Jamaica Plain, houses approximately 660 people every night — around 100 more than the number of beds available, Downie said. Those who don’t have beds sleep on mats and cots set up in the lobby and dining room areas.

But there are still upward of 50 people in the city who are either unable or unwilling to go to a shelter, staff say. Most of them suffer from substance abuse or mental illness, making them especially vulnerable.

That’s where the outreach teams come in.

Roving vans of volunteers, from Pine Street and other organizations, visit as many people in the streets as possible every night. If staff can’t convince them to go to a shelter, they make sure they’re safe and not at imminent risk, Downie said.

“Sometimes, they ask them to sit in the van and keep the heat on so they can defrost a tiny bit, keep them safe,” she said. “We’re taking out blankets and hot soup, sandwiches, additional clothing for people if they want it.”

Pine Street volunteers have been trained to evaluate hypothermia and frostbite. Over the past few weeks, staff have made several emergency calls — though typically only as a last resort.

Severe cold also means that homeless individuals with underlying health conditions are at risk.

“People who are already sick, the cold can make them much sicker,” Downie said. “If you’ve got circulation issues or heart issues or breathing issues, all of those things could [worsen].”

The Capuchin staff operate their outreach service three days a week, all year long. But they say that winter is the most dangerous time for the folks they know as “rough sleepers” — or people who sleep outside year round.

“The reality is, there are people out here that are going to end up dying on the street,” Fesefeldt said.

The St. Francis House in downtown Boston acts as as refuge for those sleeping in overnight shelters, many of which close their doors during the day. The day shelter is usually open from 6:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. but has recently extended its hours to 5 a.m. to 5 p.m., giving those on the street more time to get a hot drink and a warm meal.

“What we’re really trying to do is capture those folks early in the morning that might have stayed outside [overnight] and be able to get them inside as early as possible,” said Karen LaFrazia, St. Francis’ president and chief executive.

“With this extreme cold ... coming inside is a life and death matter,” she added.

But there’s only so much the shelter can do, since many individuals have other places to be — especially if they plan to sleep at overnight shelters that assign their beds on a first come, first serve basis.

“As much as we try to protect them, the reality is that often they need to get out into the weather early to make sure they get a bed,” said Angel Marte, St. Francis’ manager for community, engagement, and safety.

LaFrazia said St. Francis House doesn’t necessarily see an uptick in people seeking shelter during the winter months, but they do notice people who stop by tend to stay for longer during times of extreme cold.

“That makes it challenging, because there’s limited capacity,” she said. “The space doesn’t get bigger as the days get colder. … [But] at this point, we’re able to manage and make sure that everybody who is seeking shelter is able to come in and get their needs met.”

Overall, though, the organization has seen a notable rise in people needing their services, which is not unique to Boston.

“I don’t think there is a city or town in Massachusetts that has not seen a significant increase in the numbers of people who are becoming homeless,” she said.

Boston’s most recent annual homeless census, conducted in January 2024, found that the rate of homelessness in the city had increased by 12.9 percent from 2023. That trend has continued through the start of 2025, LaFrazia said.

Advocates have attributed the recent surge in homelessness to the influx of undocumented migrants, many of whom have experienced living on the street, as well as the region’s protracted housing crisis.

Back in Harvard Square, Fesefeldt broke out the sandwiches and hot chocolate, steaming in the cold January air.

“Mostly it’s spiritual care,” he said, of his mission. “It’s bringing back to people on the streets a little bit of dignity to their day that they don’t get anywhere else.”

title: Josh Kraft wants to be mayor. Where does he stand on the issues facing Boston?
text:
For about a year, Kraft, who is also chair of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, a civil rights organization based in Roxbury, has been running something of a shadow campaign, where he shows up at events, often in communities of color, and then posts about it on social media. According to the Boston Herald, last week he also showed up at a Dorchester neighborhood meeting on the hot-button topic of bike lanes.

On its own, the anti-bike crowd is not big enough to defeat an incumbent mayor who is also the first woman, person of color, and mother to win election to that office in Boston. But put that constituency together with other Boston voters who are turned off by Wu’s often stubborn style of governing and there is a potential anti-Wu coalition for someone with a lot of money and charisma to theoretically harness. Kraft definitely has money, but his charisma quotient is known only to those who frequent the local charity circuit, and his political beliefs remain a mystery. The family connection to President Trump — Robert Kraft contributed $1 million to Trump’s 2017 inauguration — hardly seems like a plus in Boston.

Josh Kraft is running as a Democrat, and last fall he said he was supporting the Democratic ticket for president. However, as I previously reported, in past years he has also contributed to a small group of very conservative Republican lawmakers. They include Representative Bob Latta of Ohio, who supported a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage; Representative Mike Bost of Illinois, who voted against a bill to protect marriage equality; Representative Buddy Carter of Georgia, who sponsored the Sanctity of Human Life Act, which protects life from conception with no exceptions; and Representative Glenn Grothman of Wisconsin, who in a speech on the House floor last July attacked government programs such as subsidized child care for taking “the purpose out of the man’s life because now you have a basket of goodies for the mom.”

Asked about those contributions, a spokesperson said at the time, “Josh is Jewish, is pro-Israel and has family and friends there. And that is why he has supported policy makers who are pro-Israel.” The spokesperson also noted that Kraft supports LGBTQ+ rights and abortion rights.

Whether Kraft’s past contributions matter in a Boston mayoral election remains to be seen. These are strange political times. After all, Massachusetts, including Boston, tilted rightward last November.

As tracked by the Dorchester Reporter, Trump increased his 2024 showing in Boston to 20.2 percent of the vote, up from 15.4 percent in 2020 and 13.7 percent in 2016. Now that Trump is in office, resistance will likely stiffen to actions he takes, for example, regarding immigration.

Yet Massachusetts is not immune to the anti-immigrant fever that is breaking out across the country. Governor Maura Healey, who as attorney general battled Trump immigration policies, is now pushing policies that limit shelter stays and could ultimately restrict shelter resources to residents. And Representative Stephen Lynch, whose district includes parts of Boston, recently voted in favor of The Laken Riley Act, which requires Immigration and Customs Enforcement to issue detainers and take custody of undocumented immigrants charged with theft and other crimes.

Wu, meanwhile, faces critics on several fronts. Property taxes are up. There’s the lingering problem of drug use and homelessness that is centered at the South End encampment known as Mass. and Cass but has also shifted to other neighborhoods. North End restaurant owners are still angry at Wu over on-street dining prohibitions in that neighborhood.

After her plan to move the John D. O’Bryant School of Math & Science from Roxbury to West Roxbury was met with stiff resistance, Wu dropped it, along with efforts to upgrade the facility. She recently released plans to close some Boston schools, a necessary but thankless mission.

Wu also faces community resistance to her plan to demolish White Stadium in Franklin Park and replace it with a stadium for a professional women’s soccer team that would be shared with Boston Public Schools. (Globe CEO Linda Henry has a small, noncontrolling ownership stake in the team.)

Out of that, can Kraft cobble together a coalition of the disgruntled? Perhaps. But first, he has to pick a side on those issues and more. Then he has to build and run a winning campaign by November.

That puts him and the Patriots on the same tight timetable.

title: I always leaned on my sister when she was alive. After Oct. 7th, I needed her more than ever.
text:
My sister Dena was the boss of me. She was my teacher, mentor, mother, best friend, nurse — my ballast. When our mother died a week after my 12th birthday, it was my sister who took over.

Then Dena was diagnosed with leukemia at age 29. There was no doubt that I would be her match for a bone marrow transplant: if not by genetic design, then by sheer will. Despite the bone marrow and platelets and late-night singing by her bedside, she did not make it. When she died two years later, it was hard to believe I could continue on without her.

What sustained me was a single memory. We’d always shared a bedroom until my sister realized there was such a thing as privacy — and she needed it. Just the same, every night from our separate bedrooms she’d coach me through the harmony of “Blowin’ in the Wind” (the Peter, Paul and Mary version). She claimed I was tone-deaf but continued to drill it into me anyway until I got it right. If I couldn’t have Dena, at least I had that song in my head as a sort of security blanket to get me through the grief.

Forty years later, I hit another wall. I’m a trauma therapist and I had deployed to an evacuee site in Israel after the October 7th massacre. I was stationed in the port city of Eilat. A city of 68,000 people had absorbed about 60,000 more — all evacuees, many of whom had lost more than everything.

The Israeli government was virtually absent in the first weeks following the attack. The immediate civilian response was provided by community organizations, NGOs, and volunteer groups. I was summoned to provide support to those teams, which were awe-inspiring.

After a lifetime tethered to tending the raw wounds of seemingly intractable trauma, I was no stranger to burnout and secondary traumatic stress. As heroic as the front-line support teams were, nerves were frayed. The national mood of shock, grief, and helplessness evolved into the desire for some power through revenge. My clinical approach contradicts revenge as a military strategy, but that wasn’t something you could say out loud — everyone was too raw.

One night, after a long day of work, I, too, reached something of a breaking point. I was tired and lonely. Flipping through my Facebook posts, I came across the Solidarity Project, a musical collaboration between Israeli and Palestinian singers. In their music video, they sang “Think of Others,” an adaptation of a poem by renowned Palestinian writer Mahmoud Darwish.

Their courage to transcend the bloodcurdling hate to come together moved me. And it wasn’t just the words that were uplifting:

As you wage your wars with guns, think of all the other ones

Those who still believe in peace and love

My sister Dena and I had launched from the womb into the civil rights struggle. In 1964, rather than attend a traditional summer camp, we went with our parents to a retreat for social workers and their families in Pine Hill, New Hampshire, where the grown-ups figured out how to fight the War on Poverty and we sang “Down by the Riverside” around the campfire.

Dena had become a social worker and labor organizer before her early death. And me, well, here I was trying my best, not abandoned because in a world tone-deaf to peace, memories of finding the harmony with my sister echoed in the refrain of that song I’d just discovered: If only I could be, a candle in the dark, I wish I were a candle in the dark.

And so, the morning after that dark night, I ventured out again. Despite missiles falling all around, my sister propelled me forward. I would find the harmony and make it through.

Lisa Fliegel is a clinical consultant to the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute in Dorchester, and a former member of Kibbutz Ketura, 20 miles from Eilat, Israel. Send comments to magazine@globe.com.

title: State receivership was supposed to save Dever Elementary, but now Boston wants to close it. What went wrong?
text:
“There’s so little success in this field,” said Paul Reville, a former Massachusetts education secretary who pushed for a 2010 law that enabled state takeovers of individual schools. “It’s not just an uneven record here but all across the country.”

Reville said part of the problem are the receivership laws themselves, including those in Massachusetts, because they often don’t provide for additional resources to state education departments, stretching their oversight capacity thin.

Overall, Massachusetts’s record with takeovers has largely been disappointing, plagued by low MCAS scores. In one significant move, the state this summer plans to end its decade-long takeover of Holyoke schools.

And in two other districts in receivership, Southbridge and Lawrence, where early turnaround results were promising, the state’s endgame remains unclear.

Dever was among four schools that were declared chronically underperforming in 2013, clearing the way for state takeovers of just the individual schools and not the entire district. The others were a Dorchester school now called UP Academy Holland, Parker Elementary School in New Bedford, and Morgan Full Service Community School in Holyoke, which came one year before the Western Massachusetts school district went into receivership.

Since then test scores have been up and down, and the schools continue to struggle, according to state data. And now, Massachusetts education officials appear to be ending the effort.

The state returned Parker to New Bedford in January, deeming it a successful turnaround. But New Bedford plans to convert the Parker into an early childhood center next fall as part of its own reorganization of facilities.

The Morgan Full Service Community School will return to local control this summer when the state releases the entire Holyoke district from receivership.

And if the Boston School Committee approves Dever’s closing, only UP Academy Holland will remain in receivership.

In a statement, BPS said the recommendation to close Dever “was made independent of the school’s state receivership status.”

It “is part of a broader effort to right-size Boston Public Schools,” said Sujata Wycoff, a district spokesperson.

But dissatisfaction with state receivership of the Dever and UP Academy Holland, which ran into trouble early on by suspending many students, including those in kindergarten, runs deep in Boston.

“Experience has shown us that state takeovers don’t work,” said Erik Berg, president of the Boston Teachers Union. “They don’t help students, they don’t help communities, and they don’t help schools.”

In the case of Dever, Berg criticized the decisions by state officials to replace scores of teachers and dismantle a popular dual-language program that allowed students who are native speakers of English or Spanish to become fluent in the other.

More than half of Dever’s 450 students are English learners, while 90 percent of all students, most of whom are Black or Latino, live in low-income households.

In an ironic twist, the state is now working with BPS to add dual-language programs to more schools to improve outcomes for English learners.

The state initially tapped Blueprint Schools Network, a local nonprofit that never ran a school before, as Dever’s receiver, but within two years the school was skidding off track: It had burned through five principals and was beset by student discipline problems, low test scores, and teacher turnover.

Blueprint and the state defended the turnaround efforts, expressing confidence it would lead to sustaining improvement.

But one year later, the state and Blueprint parted ways. Dever then cycled through two other receivers before the state in 2020 brought in the current receiver, School & Main Institute, a local nonprofit, which also was running New Bedford’s Parker School.

Under School & Main’s leadership, Dever has made strides, increasing staff retention significantly, integrating students with disabilities into mainstream classrooms, and boosting family engagement, among other accomplishments, according to a state review. The state has paid the nonprofit about $1.5 million.

But MCAS scores have risen and fallen repeatedly. On the spring 2024 MCAS exams, just 10 percent of Dever students in Grades 3-6 met or exceeded grade-level expectations in English, and 16 percent in math, well below state averages for both.

School & Main president Chantel Devaughn said a turnaround can be tough, noting that other factors — such as poverty and, more recently, the pandemic — can create obstacles that schools cannot fully address on their own.

She called the recommendation to close the Dever disappointing, adding that progress had been steady and significant while also emphasizing the proposal was based on Dever’s building conditions and other facility needs. (BPS has indicated an adjacent school, Ruth Batson Academy, which will be completely renovated, might use the space.)

“It’s not some indication that the work that we have been doing under receivership is a failure,” she said.

The state’s acting education commissioner, Russell Johnston, told families in a letter this month that he supported the Dever closure, noting “the urgent importance” of enabling BPS to move forward with its long-term facilities plan. The state has been pressuring BPS to address deteriorating facilities under a three-year district improvement plan, which Wu agreed to in 2022 to avoid a state takeover of BPS.

Families, however, are pushing to keep Dever open, even if it means relocating the school to another building and keeping it under state oversight. They believe the school is providing rigorous academics and a supportive environment. They hope the Boston School Committee will be persuaded.

“I feel proud I found this school,” Edzna Vázquez, whose son is a third grader and daughter is a fifth grader, said in Spanish through an interpreter. “It was almost like destiny was guiding me to the right place.”

Vázquez enrolled her children at Dever about three years ago shortly after arriving from Mexico. Her children didn’t know English but are now fluent. She said the teachers do a good job keeping her son, who loves to talk, focused on learning and has seen substantial growth in her daughter, who has disabilities and is now earning high grades.

“Before she used to feel very scared or anxious about math ... but now she adores math. It’s her favorite class,” Vázquez said, adding that her daughter’s biggest worry is getting into college.

“She tells me things like, ‘If they close the Dever, does that mean I’m not going to university anymore?‘”

title: White Stadium’s rebirth is coming soon, and that’s good news
text:
“All three of these communities are ones who have been long ignored and underserved,” Wu told me recently. “I felt a lot of pressure to make sure to get this right, because these communities have faced disappointment so many times already.”

The White Stadium project is a partnership between the city and a professional women’s soccer team, BOS Nation, slated to begin play in 2026.

From the outset, the project has drawn controversy, including a lawsuit from the nonprofit Emerald Necklace Conservancy, and ongoing complaints from a related advocacy group, the Franklin Park Defenders, which includes neighborhood stalwarts Jean McGuire and Louis Elisa.

Just this week, opponents of the project spearheaded a nine-hour City Council hearing to give full voice to their dissent.

That the city’s share of the project has ballooned in cost - from an early estimate of $50 million to roughly double that - has not helped quiet the criticism.

But I think the critics are wrong. Building a new White Stadium is one of Wu’s boldest ideas, and one that could eventually help shape her legacy.

Unlike some people who have just recently found their passion for Franklin Park - like the Emerald Necklace people - I have been a public advocate of renovating White Stadium for well over a decade. As many people will tell you, the facility—which opened in the 1940s—has been a dump for a whole lot longer than that.

Everyone agrees, or claims to agree, that White Stadium absolutely should be renovated. They just don’t like the price tag. Or the plan. Or the traffic professional soccer will bring. Or the idea that this whole project hinges on the support of a well-heeled group of soccer investors who will have dibs on the facility for 40 days a year. (Globe CEO Linda Henry is a minority investor in the soccer team.)

Forgive me, but I’ve spent years listening to people talk about how much they care about Franklin Park, while never getting behind any proposal to actually improve it. Obviously, renovating White Stadium is just one piece of bringing Franklin Park to its full potential. But it is an important piece, and letting this moment slip away is a terrible idea.

Wu told me she has become a bit obsessed with Franklin Park and its legendary designer, Frederick Law Olmsted, over the two years this project has been germinating. It’s led her to think a lot about what the park can and should be.

“He was basically the first person to say that parks should be for real people, not just, you know, manicured fancy bushes in shapes that you’re not supposed to touch,” she said. “The idea that you could feel a sense of connection to people whose name you might not know, but who you felt were part of your same community because you were in these same spaces.”

One frequent complaint has been that the soccer team will displace the high school football teams who use the stadium for much of their season. But that’s a trade-off for having a facility that can be used for things it cannot accommodate now - soccer, track and field, after-school programs. I love high school football, but why is it the only activity that counts?

Fixing White Stadium is an idea that comes around roughly once a decade. But the naysayers have always won, as Wu points out.

“As you’ve seen over the years, there are many reasons not to do something, and each time this has been promised in the past has fallen apart, either for funding or crumbling political will or voices from outside the city who don’t use the park or stadium, who were listened to,” she said.

The project is a great opportunity to reject the politics of “no”. Which, in this case, is exactly what should happen.

title: Man who was 17 when he killed teenager in Dorchester robbery in 1995 granted parole
text:
A man who was 17 when he shot and killed a teenager during a Dorchester robbery in 1995 has been granted parole, records show.

The state Parole Board voted 4-2 to grant release to Anthony Robinson, who was convicted in 1997 of first-degree murder in the shooting death of Barrington Nevins, according to a Jan. 22 ruling from the agency.

First-degree murder normally carries a sentence of life without the possibility of parole, but Robinson became eligible for parole after a 2013 court ruling struck down such sentences for defendants who were minors when they committed their crimes, records show.

On Nov. 24, 1995, Robinson and two others approached Nevins, 17, and several of Nevins’s friends as they stood on a sidewalk, the ruling said.

Robinson had a rifle and a co-assailant was carrying a handgun, officials said. They demanded that Nevins and his friends give up their leather jackets.

“Although the victims surrendered their jackets and pocket money, Mr. Robinson nonetheless shot Mr. Nevins in the chest, killing him,” the ruling said.

The ruling said Robinson began to “invest in rehabilitation” before the 2013 ruling from the state Supreme Judicial Court gave him a chance at freedom, completing a number of programs.

“Mr. Robinson was forthcoming at his hearing and presented as motivated for continued treatment in the community,” the ruling said. “The Board viewed behavioral challenges in the context of his age and untreated mental health issues. As he was afforded treatment, he responded well in addressing his needs.”

He also has a “strong support system” to help him reenter the community, according to the ruling, which said the board considered supporting testimony from a psychologist, another mental health professional, Robinson’s former attorney, and his pastor.

“The Board concludes that Anthony Robinson has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society,” the board ruled.

Assistant Suffolk District Attorney Montez Haywood testified in opposition to granting Robinson parole, officials said.

Robinson will be released to a halfway house after three months in a lower security facility, according to the ruling.

He’ll have to abide by a nightly curfew, submit to electronic monitoring and drug and alcohol testing, have no contact with Nevins’s family, and engage in “counseling for trauma, with a trauma-informed treatment plan,” among other conditions, the ruling said.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: Resolution to halt White Stadium renovation fails in City Council
text:
A letter from Wu to the council after the vote acknowledged there is work to do.

“We will continue to engage community members, including those with serious doubts, to work together, share information, and make this ambitious renovation the best possible project for our students and for Franklin Park,” wrote Wu. “I thank the Council for your engagement on this exciting and important renovation. We will keep you updated as construction advances.”

As part of the project, the city has signed a lease agreement with Boston Unity Soccer Partners to allow a professional women’s soccer team to use the facility

Two of the three city councilors whose districts either encompass Franklin Park, District 7’s Tania Fernandes Anderson, or abut it, District 4’s Brian Worrell, voted for the resolution. Also voting for it was Julia Mejia, who introduced it, Ed Flynn, Erin Murphy and City Council president Ruthzee Louijeune.

“This was a tough call,” said Louijeune after the vote. “There’s been so much disinformation, so much distrust in government, it’s time for us to deliberate more on the increasing costs, get commitments written down.” She urged the city to hold “big community meetings” and say more about ensuring supplier diversity and helping the brown and Black community that lives near the park and is most immediately affected by the project.

Mejia said that supporting the resolution was not a vote to oppose the renovation.

“It means making sure that we, as this body, are doing everything in our power to make sure that we are operating with all the facts, that we have all the plans and all the financial details before moving forward,” Mejia said.

Councilor Ben Weber, whose District 6 abuts the park, spoke against the resolution and in favor of the ongoing renovation.

“Politics has been too often about division and White Stadium certainly has highlighted that,” said Weber, who went on to say that claims of lack of engagement with the community were off-base. “There’s been a lot of process. I hope at some point we can get to a place where people feel they are OK with a community process where they don’t agree with the outcome. I don’t know if that’ll ever happen – in all of human history. I don’t know if that’s ever happened."

Also voting with Weber were councilors Gabriela Coletta Zapata, John Fitzgerald, Enrique Pepin, Henry Santana, and Sharon Durkan.

“This is about giving our BPS kids the opportunities they deserve,” said Durkan after the vote. “After 150 community meetings and more public input than any BPS sports project has ever had, we have a plan that keeps the same land use while finally upgrading White Stadium. For the first time, our students will have real, guaranteed access to a top-tier athletic facility. But instead of focusing on that, some of our colleagues are playing politics. Our kids can’t afford more delays – let’s get this done.”

The council has 13 members, but District 9 Councilor Liz Breadon, who is recovering from knee surgery, was not present.

Last week’s 9-hour two-part committee hearing chaired by Mejia centered mostly on White Stadium, with opponents getting the most air time.

At least via email, proponents of White Stadium let councilors know how they wanted them to vote, plus a change.org petition supporting the project had gathered 385 signatures by Wednesday night.

David Shapiro, CEO of YMCA of Greater Boston, sent a two-page letter to councilors urging them to not delay and instead “disrupt a cycle of false starts and inaction.

“At this point, it is time to move forward with a balanced generational investment and transformation of a public jewel in lockstep with a creative, accountable plan to ensure the majority of benefits go to Boston’s residents with BPS students at the center,” wrote Shapiro.

Stadium proponent and park neighbor Dot Fennell lauded the project as a “rare” redevelopment opportunity that “will have a lasting positive impact on education, public health, social capital, climate readiness, and economic development for decades to come. These benefits will extend far beyond the limited number of BPS high school students who currently use the stadium.”

Rickie Thompson, president of the Franklin Park Coalition, which supports the project, expressed relief that the resolution did not pass.

“I’m glad to see there’s support for this project to move forward,” said Thompson. “Hopefully we can all come together for the benefit of the BPS students, the park users, and the surrounding community.”

Part of that community that does not want this project to proceed is gathering at White Stadium at 11 Thursday morning in a “protest to save Franklin Park & protect the trees.”

The Emerald Necklace Conservancy is holding a public meeting to receive feedback from the community on its alternative design proposal. The meeting will be held at 6 p.m on Feb. 6 at the Lena Park Community Center in Dorchester.

On a perhaps more consequential front, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy-led plaintiffs pursuing a lawsuit to delay or stop the stadium project have added to their list of formal charges against the city and others.

The new concerns stem from the lease and stadium usage agreement signed by the team and city late last year.

One primary charge claims that besides altering the intent of open space parkland in the park, the project has stepped outside of its purview of building only on the parcel of land where the stadium sits by converting usage of roads in the park into shuttle and supply routes to the stadium.

The trial is scheduled for March 18.

Bids for the city’s assorted construction contracts for its share of the stadium’s rebuild are due Feb. 7, according to the city’s website.

Linda Henry, CEO of Boston Globe Media Partners, has a minority, non-controlling stake in the women’s professional soccer team.

title: Does Josh Kraft have a chance against Mayor Wu? 4 writers react.
text:
Meaning, it could happen. But he’s definitely the underdog, and if I had to place a bet right now, my money is on incumbent Michelle Wu coasting to a second term.

Of course, Kraft does have strengths most challengers lack — money and name recognition.

And there are plenty of Wu-haters ready to vote for any opponent with a pulse — though not nearly as many as Twitter and the comments sections might lead you to believe.

But Wu has the advantage of incumbency. She can also boast of Boston’s exceptionally low crime on her watch. And her base of white progressives shows no sign of abandoning her.

In my view, to win Kraft would have to do three things, all at once:

First, in 2024 20 percent of the city’s electorate backed Trump. For those Republican-leaning voters, there’s often no point in voting in municipal elections, since the two finalists are almost always both Democrats. Kraft will need to motivate those voters to show up and vote for him. The trick is, he can’t court them too explicitly without alienating the rest of the city.

Second, Kraft needs to peel away Black voters. He has spent a lot of time wooing the Black community, but it’s an open question whether his philanthropic record will translate into votes.

Third, “the business community” whose complaints about Wu we keep hearing about will need to show that it’s not all bark. I don’t necessarily mean downtown businesses so much as local businesses in the neighborhoods. When every bodega and dry cleaner in the city has a Kraft sign in the window, I’ll believe he’s got a shot.

To be clear, all three are possible. But making all three happen in the same election would be a political feat.

By Joan Vennochi

During nine hours of testimony at a recent Boston City Council hearing about Mayor Michelle Wu’s grandiose renovation plan for White Stadium, several dozen residents spoke out against it. Only five residents expressed support.

In that well of citizen discontent is an opening for Josh Kraft, the philanthropist son of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. The grumbling about Wu is about more than one project. It’s about what critics see as a top-down style of governing, whether the issue is bike lanes or the stadium renovation plan, which calls for a partnership with a professional women’s soccer team and at least $100 million in taxpayer money.

“I understand that in politics, you make decisions,” Jacquetta Van Zandt, a political analyst and host of the Politics and Prosecco podcast, told me. But Wu, she said, took office “with the idea that she would be collaborative with the community. That has not happened.” Van Zandt, who lives in Roxbury, contends that Wu’s approach makes her especially vulnerable in communities of color.

The city’s website on the stadium project lists 13 public meetings and another 15 commission meetings where it was discussed. But in politics, perception is reality. And with Wu’s critics, the perception is that rather than first asking residents what they want, she comes to them with her vision of what she wants – and won’t budge.

Because of what developers contend is her refusal to mingle with their crowd, her ban on outdoor dining in the North End, and a proposal, which ultimately failed, to raise commercial property taxes, Wu also has detractors in the business community.

Out of such discontent, a smart, savvy challenger who knows Boston well could cobble together a credible challenge to Wu. But is Kraft that person? He is a political neophyte, who is known to few voters. He’s a rich white guy, who comes from a family that may not be super popular in Boston right now. Can he beat an incumbent mayor who has a serious political operation? Under the best case scenario – maybe?

By Carine Hajjar

Unseating an incumbent isn’t a common occurrence in Boston mayoral politics. But lately, politics have been anything but conventional. Yes, Josh Kraft’s bid to unseat Mayor Wu is going to be an uphill battle, but don’t write it off in a city struggling with progressive policies.

Who can forget the death, violence, and addiction that the city allowed to fester at Mass. and Cass in the name of “harm reduction” until enough public outcry led to a crackdown? And what about Wu’s message that “we want immigrants to know that it is safe for everyone, to be able to feel comfortable reaching out for emergency services, to report a crime,” as the state continued to conceal alleged rapes and assaults in shelters?

Kraft is likely to run to the right of her, but still as a Democrat in a city where an R next to your name will kill any and all chances. His ties to both the business and nonprofit worlds might be a boon if his campaign focuses on affordability and the revival of Boston’s business, while underlining the social causes that matter to the city.

That won’t make his path to victory easy, but it’s not impossible. The country is in new political territory. Voters in blue cities like Portland, Los Angeles, and San Francisco have started to reject certain progressive policies, and a correction might be due in Boston. Will Kraft be able to capitalize on the vibe shift?

By Marcela García

Anne Chatfield, whose three sons attend Boston Public Schools, has become increasingly disillusioned with the state of the district. And she lays the blame squarely at the feet of Mayor Michelle Wu.

I first connected with Chatfield at the beginning of the school year, when she was dealing with repeated issues of late and no-show buses for her fifth grader at the Murphy K-8 School in Dorchester. While the timeliness of buses has reportedly improved somewhat, the frustrations haven’t disappeared. Last week, Chatfield texted me about yet another no-show bus — this time on the coldest morning of the year. With temperatures below freezing, she had no choice but to drive her son to school herself for the second consecutive day. “I couldn’t let him be outside,” she said.

Her frustrations go beyond the buses. “I’m so happy there is someone running against [the mayor] this fall,” she said, referring to mayoral challenger Josh Kraft. Chatfield said she has lost confidence in Wu’s ability to manage Boston Public Schools effectively and believes many families with children in her South Boston neighborhood feel similarly.

Although Chatfield admitted she doesn’t yet know much about Kraft’s stances on education or transportation, she said she’s “very excited about having a viable alternative and perhaps someone who’s going to bring something different to the table.”

That’s an obvious lane for Kraft to seize. He has plenty of time to articulate his positions and vision for BPS; after all, his campaign hasn’t officially launched. Whether his policies will resonate with disillusioned voters like Chatfield remains to be seen, but one thing is certain: Parents like her are tired of waiting for solutions and are ready to listen to someone new who promises to deliver.

Curated by Jim Dao

FROM THE RIGHT: Why Trump is correct that there is no Constitutional right to birthright citizenship, by Edward J. Erler in National Review from 2015. (Yes, Trump was talking about ending birthright citizenship even before he was president.)

FROM THE LEFT: Why Trump is wrong, because birthright citizenship is clearly guaranteed by the 14th Amendment and “a century’s worth of Supreme Court case law.” Thomas Wolf of the Brennan Center.

FROM THE CENTER: Why it’s complicated, by Jim Gerahty who offers a comprehensive, deeply researched, and very balanced review of the issue in National Review. “It is likely that the courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court, will look skeptically upon the argument that the president can redefine who is and who is not a U.S. citizen through executive order,” he writes.
