title: Free events this week: Latin rhythms, ancient games, and a trip to Oz
text:
Boston, it’s officially spring. The equinox has come and gone, symbolizing a time of rebirth and growth. For those who spent the past three months spending on things to keep them warm, you may want to take this era of renewal as a time to save your cash while still having a good time. Thankfully, there are plenty of no-cost events to greet spring with this week, March 24-30.

INFECTIOUS LAUGHS If you need a laugh right about now, Boston’s many free comedy shows have you covered. Monday night, The Turing Tavern will host their weekly Laughaholics comedy night. While over in Dorchester, another group of funny folks will take the stage at The Dot Tavern this Thursday for their weekly laugh-out-loud comedy night hosted by Comedy Near Me. March 24 and 27, 7:30 and 8 p.m. Locations vary. theturingtavern.com,dorchestertavern.com

BRING THE HEAT Boston’s Latin presence stretches far and wide, with plenty of opportunities to immerse yourself in rich cultures that can feel both enriching and a lot like home. At the Grove Hall Branch of the Boston Public Library, participants can learn about the many styles of Latin dance with instructor Jose Zamora Orellana. From merengue to salsa, the hands-on session will lead participants — newbies and aficionados alike — through the steps with accompanying music. March 24, 3-4:30 p.m. 41 Geneva Ave. bpl.bibliocommons.com

TWINKLE TOES Unlike adults, children don’t have their weekly pilates or cycling class to let off some steam from their stress-filled lives. Thankfully, CambridgeSide is inviting families to drop by for a half-hour-long movement session with Little Beats Dance Academy, a Newton-based school committed to using dance to nurture development and encourage creative thinking in young minds. Wednesday’s event will be curated for children ages 0-5 years old, but all ages are welcome to attend. March 26, 4 p.m. 100 CambridgeSide Place, Cambridge. cambridgeside.com

A ‘WICKED’ GOOD TIME If you still have the iconic “Defying Gravity” riff in your head you’re not alone. The “Wicked” earworm persists, especially after Cynthia Erivo’s powerful rendition at the Oscars last month. At Trident Booksellers & Café, fans of the blockbuster film can re-immerse themselves in the world of Oz, while those who haven’t seen the film can skip out on the movie theater fee most of us paid last winter. March 27, 6:30 p.m. 338 Newbury St. tridentbookscafe.com

OLD GAMES, NEW PLAYERS The Harvard Museum of Science and Culture’s upcoming ArtsThursdays night will allow attendees to explore a thousands-year-old pastime: board games. The intense competition sparked by strategy and luck traces back to 3000 BCE, when ancient Egyptian societies played the game Senet — a game requiring calculated moves and defensive maneuvers as players attempt to move their pieces off the board. Event attendees can learn to play Senet, as well as other games favored by ancient societies, including al-qirkat and the Royal Game of Ur. For a more low-stakes evening, guests can also make personalized medallions and visit the museum’s Ancient Near East exhibition. March 27, 5-9 p.m. 6 Divinity Ave., Cambridge. hmsc.harvard.edu

MOVING TOWARD WELLNESS The Human Movement Project, a Boston-based dance community, is inviting locals to prioritize their physical wellness through the art of dance. Instructor and Human Movement Project founder Kim Holman will be leading a contemporary dance class for dancers of all skill levels and backgrounds, encouraging participants to use fluid movements as a form of expression. Those who preregister for the class will receive a code to attend the organization’s showcase — featuring the work of local choreographers and dancers — at the same location later that night for free. March 30, 1 p.m. 98 Business St., 1B. humancmvmtproject.com

SWEET TREATS The reward of a “little treat” transcends basic wants — it’s a need. With Boston’s many cafés, restaurants, and bakeries, there’s plenty to choose from. Over at picturesque 75 on Chestnut on Beacon Hill, customers can get their dessert half-off with their Sweet Tooth Tuesday special. The menu features the likes of chocolate chip cookies and blood orange cheesecake parfaits. Tuesdays, 5-11 p.m. 75 Chestnut St. 75chestnut.com

Marianna Orozco can be reached at marianna.orozco@globe.com.

title: In a Dorchester skating rink, a lesson in ballet choreography from a pair of former dancers
text:
A pair of retired professional dancers brought their ballet — and some valuable lessons — into a Boston neighborhood Sunday.

Families, arts organizations, and locals gathered in Chez Vous Roller Skating Rink in Dorchester for the opportunity to learn choreography from Renee Robinson and Amos Machanic Jr., who formerly performed with the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater.

The two dancers spent the weekend leading community workshops in the city’s neighborhoods of Hyde Park, Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester. At their free public events, Robinson and Machanic taught the choreography for iconic late dancer and choreographer Alvin Ailey’s “Revelations,” his best known ballet.

Accompanied by percussionist Roderick Jackson, Robinson and Machanic patiently took an enthusiastic crowd of children, teens, adults, and seniors through the three soulful acts of “Revelations,” set to passionate spirituals that the performers could sing along to.

As they demonstrated the evocative movements, Robinson and Machanic also shared historical facts about Ailey’s inspirations for “Revelations,” rooted in his experiences growing up in Black churches in Texas. When the afternoon drew to a close, Machanic awarded T-shirts and prizes to participants who could recall some of these facts.

The dance theater and Boston arts nonprofit Celebrity Series have been in partnership for nearly 60 years, but this year is the first to see more than one community educational event, according to Shaumba-Yandje Dibinga, founder of OrigiNation Cultural Arts Center in Boston and program manager for the “Revelations” event.

“We normally do one, but we did four this year,” Dibinga said. “Renee and Amos are legends. They led three back-to-back workshops yesterday and their energy never changed, they’re spectacular.”

The addition of three community events meant that around a thousand people in total were able to attend, Dibinga said.

Machanic said that hosting more events meant fulfilling the vision of Ailey himself, who believed “dance came from the people and that it should always be delivered back to the people.”

Courtney Boston, the event’s emcee, emphasized the importance of hosting these workshops in predominantly Black neighborhoods of greater Boston.

“We didn’t want to have these events in Seaport or anywhere that our people might not have access to,” Boston said. “We’re right here in our neighborhoods and our backyards.”

Boston was pleased by the event’s inclusivity of people from all walks of life, including those with dance backgrounds and those without.

“It was awesome. There’s people being centered in Black culture today, using music and dance and arts to bring people together,” she said. “I’m not a dancer, but they had me moving.”

title: A crack in the Ivy wall as Columbia caves to Trump
text:
The recent reports of Columbia University’s capitulation to the Trump administration’s demands in order to secure federal funding should worry everyone who values academic integrity (“Columbia yields to Trump’s demands,” Page A1, March 22). This decision raises questions about the role of elite institutions in the safeguarding of principles of higher education. The Ivies, with their immense resources, alumni networks, and powerful platform, have a responsibility to lead in this moment. Instead of individual acquiescence, these institutions should issue a joint statement reaffirming their unwavering commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion and their unyielding protection of freedom of speech.

If the Ivy League schools fail to stand firm, they risk eroding foundations of academic inquiry, research, and open discourse. Their collective voice would reach far beyond their campuses and would offer cover to smaller, more vulnerable colleges and universities. History will judge the Ivies by their courage to defend the principles of intellectual freedom. A coordinated, inspiring message from these institutions would not only protect their own integrity but also send a powerful signal to the nation that the pursuit of knowledge and the values of inclusion are not negotiable.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

If the Ivies don’t stand strong, who will?

Darcy Daniels

Sharon

When the history of President Trump’s pursuit of authoritarianism is written, his bullying of Columbia University and the school’s eventual capitulation will figure prominently on the timeline. Where that timeline leads will depend on how vigorously the rest of the country resists Trump’s future assaults on free speech, the rule of law, and democracy.

Carl Nagy-Koechlin

Dorchester

Shame on Columbia University for caving in to Donald Trump’s effort to control the school’s free speech policies. Private colleges and universities establish endowment funds, a major purpose of which is to provide economic stability for activities that are jeopardized by costly or debilitating financial fluctuations. Columbia’s $14.8 billion endowment yielded an 11.5 percent return in fiscal 2024. That $1.7 billion return on investment dwarfs the $400 million Trump has already cut ($5 billion in federal grants and contracts could be at risk over time).

It’s hard to imagine a better time to turn to those reserves than when constitutionally protected speech and intellectual integrity are under direct assault by a would-be dictator.

Steven Swanger

Sudbury

The Globe is using the word “crackdown” in headlines (“As Trump broadens crackdown, focus expands to legal immigrants and tourists,” BostonGlobe.com) and stories, such as the front-page article about Columbia University, to describe the Trump regime’s attacks on people or groups that are in its way.

Journalists typically use the word “crackdown” to describe intensified enforcement of measures to fight crime. That is not what is happening here. The Globe owes its readers a more fitting description of Donald Trump’s tools of repression.

William Ira Bennett

Somerville

Donald Trump has become an extortionist, unfettered by the aggressive transactional approach that served him well, apparently, in the world of business. Transactions include quid pro quos. Extortion, however, is considered a criminal offense in a court of law, though maybe not when it involves our president.

I am truly terrified.

Lee Leffingwell

Hingham

The Trump administration is clearly waging war against American universities. It has forced Columbia University to buckle by pulling $400 million in federal aid because of the university’s alleged failure to prevent antisemitic harassment. In the face of that loss, the university has agreed to nearly all of the administration’s terms, including expanding the “intellectual diversity” of its faculty. This is not to say that antisemitic harassment is acceptable, but there is grave danger in the precedent being set in terms of federal power to get its way on any and all issues that arise.

However, Columbia could have survived the loss of federal funds, and not acquiesced to federal pressure, by shedding a majority of its roughly 5,000 administrators, essentially enough for many students to have their own administrator.

Harvard’s administrative staff swelled by more than 40 percent since 2004, according to The Harvard Crimson, with no significant increase in the student body. In my unsuccessful campaign for Harvard’s Board of Overseers last year, I made this one of my issues.

If the majority of Harvard’s administrative positions were eliminated, it too would not be so dependent on federal support. This administrative bloat is pervasive at colleges and universities throughout the nation. Hillsdale College, a private liberal arts college in Hillsdale, Mich., that does not accept federal funds, is a notable exception.

Harvey A. Silverglate

Cambridge

title: Black gun ownership is on the rise. These Boston instructors are at the forefront.
text:
Howard owns 617 Defense, a company that offers firearms training throughout Greater Boston. He’s also president of the Massachusetts chapter of the National African American Gun Association, an organization that boasts 45,000 members nationwide, nearly half of them women. And he’s one of several local Black entrepreneurs serving a growing market niche: Black people who feel the need to arm themselves.

Greater Boston is famously safe compared with other US metro areas. But not quite safe enough for Howard — or his students. He warns the students that 911 is not enough, that it generally takes 10 or 15 minutes for the police to arrive.

“You are your own first responder,” Howard said. “No one’s going to save you. You’re going to save yourself.”

Despite a high level of gun violence in many Black communities, Black people are much less likely than white people to own guns. A 2024 study from Pew Research found guns in only 34 percent of Black US households compared with 49 percent of white households.

The ownership gap might be due in part to a history of racist efforts to keep Black people disarmed. After the Civil War, for instance, many Southern states made gun ownership illegal for Black people. And even where it was legal, Black people often faced unjust discrimination and were not allowed to obtain gun permits. When Martin Luther King Jr.’s home was bombed in 1956, he requested a gun permit to defend his family. But authorities in Montgomery, Ala., refused.

But there’s evidence that more Black households are arming up. After the 2020 murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer, the National Shooting Sports Foundation reported a spike in gun purchases by Black people. The organization’s latest survey finds that African Americans comprise 32 percent of people who’ve taken up shooting in the past five years, the biggest increase of any demographic group.

Howard said he’s seen rising attendance at his classes, which he began teaching three years ago. He said he believes the root cause is declining trust in government.

“People are taking control of their own lives and doing what they have to do for protecting themselves and their family members,” Howard said. “They’re making their decisions, instead of waiting on the government to help them out.”

Howard is a vocal opponent of laws limiting gun ownership that were enacted in Massachusetts last year. He keeps a loaded pistol on his hip and said law-abiding people of every race should always be ready to defend themselves.

You’ll hear the same sentiment from Howard’s friend and business competitor Antonio Miles, a Black New Hampshire resident who runs the training companyUrban Shooting Experience. A former car salesman who grew up in Roxbury, he first took up arms out of concern for his family.

“My ‘why’ is my three daughters,” Miles said. “I wanted to be able to defend my family by any means necessary.”

He also sees himself as a role model.

“I wanted to bridge a gap on people who look like me teaching about firearms,” Miles said.

Both Miles and Howard offer gun classes to men and women of all races, but they primarily cater to gun-curious African Americans.

It all makes perfect sense to Nicholas Johnson, a Black man who teaches law at Fordham University in New York.

“I grew up in Black gun culture,” Johnson said. “I grew up in rural West Virginia; everybody had guns.” But as a young faculty member, he felt a chill in the air whenever he discussed the Second Amendment.

“If you were a good liberal and had a good social conscience you were supposed to be anti-gun,” Johnson said. “And I wasn’t.”

Years later, Johnson co-authored what he believes to be the first academic textbook devoted to US firearms law. He’s also written “Negroes and the Gun,” a book about how Black people have a long history of relying on personal firearms for defense against racist mobs and criminals.

Meanwhile, Johnson said, there has historically been “tremendous bias in enforcement” of gun laws in the United States. For instance, in 2018 the US Sentencing Commission found Black people were far more likely than white people to be convicted of illegal gun possession.

“We end up with gun control policy that operates in a kind of perverse intersection of the interests of white liberals and white conservatives,” Johnson said. Conservatives dislike gun laws, Johnson said, but don’t mind them being used to lock up Black men; liberals want fewer Black people in prison but are happy to see brisk enforcement of the gun laws.

But instructors like Howard and Miles might help break the cycle by ensuring that Black gun owners know the rules. Both teach a two-hour basic firearms safety course certified by the National Rifle Association. It’s just the first step in getting a Massachusetts firearms license. Each person must also get a “license to carry” issued by their city police department.

One of Howard’s students, sixty-something and retired, already owns several guns and is now interested in making it legal. Others are first-timers.

“When I was in my early 20s, I was grazed by a gun,” said Jermaine McNeill, 46, of Dorchester, a housing inspector and podcaster. “I had friends of mine who were shot with guns. So I just had a fear of them.”

McNeill had a change of heart after he interviewed Howard for his podcast.

These days he’s convinced that gun ownership makes sense, and not just for himself.

“My daughter is 15 years old,” he said, “and I told her, whether you like it or not, when you get older, you’re gonna learn how to shoot.”

Also in attendance were attorney Rochelle Jones, 34, of Randolph and her 32-year-old schoolteacher brother Marcus Jones of Weymouth. Both are interested in personal protection, but Rochelle Jones said gun ownership is frowned upon by left-leaning people like herself.

“I’m not thinking too much of the stigma,” she said, adding, “It’s there, sure.”

Marcus Jones said he wants to dispel the stereotype of Black men as trigger-happy killers.

“I know going forward that I can be a model to show people that we are responsible about this,” he said, “and it’s not just always the negative stuff you see in the news.”

The training is over in two hours, and not a shot is fired. For that, they’ll have to sign up for the two-day basic handgun course, featuring a trip to a gun range. Howard also teaches rifle, shotgun, and even a course called “Stop The Bleed” that teaches lifesaving measures for people who’ve taken a bullet.

“All the Black instructors I know say some of their students, they had friends who got shot,” Howard said. “They didn’t know how to save their life.”

But for Howard, all his courses are about saving lives. He said crime-ridden Black communities will become a lot safer when a lot more of their law-abiding residents have guns and know how to use them.

“To the average person who lives in the suburbs, it doesn’t seem right to them,” Howard said. “But have them trade places.”

title: Four brothers, vast power, and now a shot at politics
text:
“Mer-cee bo-coop!” he concluded, gamely, for a nice applause.

And then the real campaigning began. Kraft smoothly wound through the narrow gaps between the tables, greeting each of the hundred or so attendees individually, shaking every hand, and dropping to one knee for extended conversations with seated guests, like a man about to propose.

Campaigning for government office is personal, intimate, tactile. But, no one in Kraft’s famous family has opened themselves to scrutiny in quite the way a political campaign demands.

Josh, 57, the third of the four sons of billionaire businessman and New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and his late wife, Myra, is the first in his family to run for office.

But Boston politics is one arena that has confounded the Krafts in the past. In a failed attempt to win support for a South Boston football stadium in the late 1990s, for instance, they showed a knack for stepping on rakes and angering the community.

If Josh Kraft can solve that puzzle and become mayor, the amount of local influence concentrated under one family name would be unprecedented.

So unprecedented that it’s fair to ask: Is that too much power for one family?

“When I’m mayor of Boston,” Josh Kraft said, in answer to that question, “my number one priority is going to be the people of Boston.”

It speaks to their incredible influence in Boston that many of those close to the brothers personally or in business declined to talk for this profile of Josh Kraft and his three brothers — even other wealthy and powerful people who are fans of the family. One went to comic lengths to elude an interview. “Totally off the record?” this Kraft associate said. “They’re wonderful people.”

It is not just the Patriots that make the Krafts so influential. Robert Kraft bought the team for about $172 million in 1994, then the highest price ever for an NFL franchise. League revenue has since exploded; what Kraft paid for the team now buys about a three-year contract with a good veteran quarterback. With a current estimated worth of $7.4 billion, the Patriots are the sixth most valuable sports team in the world, according to Forbes.

The eldest Kraft brother, Jonathan, 61, is president of the holding company for the family’s many businesses, employers of 9,500 people in industries such as paper and packaging, sports and entertainment, construction and real estate development, and venture capital investment. He represents the Patriots in NFL league matters and shares the title with his father as investor/operator of the New England Revolution soccer team.

He is also chairman of the board of Massachusetts General Hospital, a top position at one of the state’s most important institutions.

Daniel, 59, the next eldest, is president & CEO of International Forest Products, one of the paper companies that built the family’s wealth, and which has quietly grown into a massive enterprise — the fifth largest exporter in the United States, according to the Journal of Commerce.

Josh’s campaign résumé is built on decades of community work that affected thousands of children. He was hired by a South Boston nonprofit shortly after college to do outreach to prevent kids from dropping out of school. In 1993, he was brought in to build up and run the Chelsea Boys & Girls Club, and then in 2008 became CEO of Boys & Girls Club of Boston, a job he held for 12 years. Until recently he was president of the New England Patriots Foundation.

David, 53, and the youngest, worked for the family business until leaving around 2012, according to news articles of the time. He maintains a minimal public profile, though in a short interview with the Globe, David spoke highly of his brother’s qualifications for mayor.

A fifth brother, Joseph, born between Josh and David, died as an infant shortly after his birth.

Josh Kraft, who is divorced with adult daughters, would say little about his kids for the sake of their privacy. It’s a sharp contrast with his likely opponent, Mayor Michelle Wu, who this month brought along her infant daughter, Mira, when Wu testified before Congress, and whose family story has long been an intimate part of her identity as a candidate.

But few things are more destructive to privacy than a political campaign: Voters want to know a candidate’s origin story, which begins with how they were brought up, and with whom.

To understand how the Krafts grew into a powerhouse, you have to go back 50 years, to Chestnut Hill. Before Josh, the closest anyone in the family came to seeking public office was when Robert Kraft, then in his late 20s, was chairman of the Newton Democratic City Committee. He considered running for Congress in 1970 against incumbent Democrat Philip J. Philbin. But Kraft, who had young kids by then, passed on the race, in part due to the loss of privacy that comes with a run for high office.

He excelled in business. His father-in-law owned a paper company, Rand-Whitney, that Robert Kraft ultimately took over and grew; he also founded International Forest Products, in 1972. It would be another couple decades before he bought the Patriots, a move that launched the family into an era of fame and enormous wealth the sons have enjoyed as adults.

Before that, they were more of a prototypical breed of Boston affluence, a family known for their gaggle of boys who loved sports and excelled in the finest schools, each taking on the type of distinct roles that often mark large clans.

Jonathan and Daniel Kraft declined to be interviewed for this story, either about their childhood or their family now.

As an adult, Jonathan is familiar to Patriots fans for his conspicuous seat next to his father in the owners’ box during games. He is known as acerbic, a keeper of grudges who does not suffer fools easily, and has bawled out reporters on occasion for writing things he didn’t like.

People who know him well praise his intellect, discipline, meticulous preparation, and charitable instincts, which tend toward the realm of health care. “Jonathan is the smartest, most driven person I’ve ever met in my life,” said a powerful friend of the family who knows them personally.

He is most like his father from a business standpoint. “Jonathan worships his father,” said another family friend, who knows them through business. “Worship is not too strong a word for the relationship.”

Married with grown children, Jonathan can speak extemporaneously on a wide array of topics, from finance to rock music; in an interview with a podcast dedicated to the Australian rock band AC/DC, Jonathan named all five band members and recounted a good bit of their history off the top of his head.

From an early age, he gravitated to the world of business. As kids, “I remember playing Monopoly with Jonathan and he’d always crush me,” Josh Kraft recalls. “I had to mortgage everything.”

Jonathan went to high school at Belmont Hill, a private boys-only prep school, where he was president of the student council his senior year. The boy he beat in the election, Robert Ricciardelli, recalls finishing second to Kraft.

“I was well liked and I was running on being a likable person,” Ricciardelli told the Globe recently. “Jonathan was determined to do stuff.

“He was 10 years ahead of everyone else. I think this is because he grew up watching his father do deals in business. He knew the politics of it, understanding what people want.”

Ricciardelli became Kraft’s vice president. The major achievement of their administration was a new school rule exempting seniors who maintained high grades from taking their final exams.

“That was Jonathan’s big push,” Ricciardelli said. “The argument was, if you keep your grades up, you don’t have to take your final exam,” as an incentive to avoid the “senior slump,” when kids already accepted to college tend to slough off.

Ricciardelli, who also knew Daniel and Josh as kids, said that from the outside, the Kraft boys seemed a cohesive bunch.

“The dynamic I saw was that they had no conflict,” he said. “Maybe that’s because Jonathan was expected to be the heir apparent and Danny never had a problem with that. Josh wasn’t interested in [running the business] and went his own way. They each had their own lanes.”

Daniel Kraft, also married and with grown children, followed his big brother to Belmont Hill, and then went to Tufts University, where he played lacrosse, which remains one of his passions. He has promoted the sport in Israel with such zeal that the country’s top players train at the Daniel Kraft Family National Lacrosse Center. He is known as an easy-going person who gives off normal-guy vibes.

“Jonathan is a little intense; Danny is the guy you want to hang out and have a beer with,” said a friend who got to know them as adults.

Dan Kraft was part of a group of business, labor, and government leaders who worked to find the money to dredge Boston Harbor and open the port to greater commercial shipping, said Tom Glynn, former head of the Massachusetts Port Authority. In 2016, the group put Dan’s affable persona to use, when it invited then-US Secretary of Transportation Anthony Foxx to Boston for a briefing on the dredging project, looking to earn some federal grants. As the local team had hoped, Dan Kraft and Secretary Foxx hit it off personally.

“That was fortunate,” Glynn said. “And we got $42 million.”

Foxx, now co-director of Harvard Kennedy School’s Center for Public Leadership, recalls the briefing and meeting Dan Kraft for the first time. The pair got along well and talked sports, as mutual fanatics.

“Somebody like Dan clearly had a great head start in life and sometimes people who do are not relatable,” Foxx said. “But he’s not that way. He’s easy to talk to and has a grip on regular-people stuff.”

If Jonathan and Dan are their father’s kids, attuned to the world of business, Josh and younger brother David are their mother’s, say people who know the family well. Myra Kraft, who died of cancer at 68 in 2011, treated philanthropy as an occupation. “She got up every day wanting to give her money away,” said one friend.

Like most of his brothers, David Kraft was schooled at Belmont Hill, where he was on the varsity wrestling team. He went to Columbia College in New York, as his father did, and then Harvard Business School. A Globe article in the early 2000s said that David worked in media and technology for Kraft Group investments.

But later articles reported that David Kraft left the family business around 2012, apparently after an undisclosed dispute with his father. His public persona largely disappeared. David Kraft, it appeared, was done with life in the Boston spotlight. “He tries to live as anonymously as a person can with the Kraft family name,” said a family friend.

Josh Kraft would say little about David. They stay in touch and “have a good relationship,” he said. Campaign finance reports show that David Kraft in February donated $1,000, the maximum allowed, to his brother’s campaign.

In a short telephone call with the Globe, David wholeheartedly backed Josh’s run for mayor. “He’s been dealing with Boston city politics for many years in his position with the Boys & Girls Club,” he said. “He knows Boston well. He has unique gifts and is a genuinely altruistic person.”

As far back as high school, Josh took a different path from his brothers. He was the only one not to attend Belmont Hill, and instead went to The Rivers School, a private prep school in Weston. It simply felt like a better fit. “I do a lot by feel and intuition,” he said. He went to Williams College, and then spent a year as an intern teacher at a private school. He liked helping kids. “I wanted to keep doing that but I wanted to do it in a different venue,” he said, which led him to community work.

One of the people Josh Kraft helped in his work, Abens Maurice, temporarily moved back to Boston from California when he learned Kraft was running for mayor, to help with the campaign. They first met around 1990, when Maurice was 12 and living in South Boston. Kraft helped him navigate school, relationships, conflicts, racism — Kraft’s influence on his life is almost too great to measure, he said.

“Josh has been my counselor, my big brother, my dad — whatever you want to call him, he’s my man,” said Maurice, now 47.

Josh Kraft, who moved to Boston from Newton in 2023, said he wouldn’t be running without what he learned from Bostonians along the way, and from his brothers. Yet when he announced his campaign, asking the voters to grant him the vast powers of mayor, he pleaded for people not to prejudge him by his influential family name.

Why?

“I read some of the comments — ‘Oh, rich kid … What does he know?’ ” Kraft explained.

He repeated the “rich kid” dig several times, as if it was a slur, seeking to refute it.

“I know I’ve been in a room with a kid breaking down … about seeing his parents shot in front of him. I’ve had experiences like that many times. I think I understand.”

Focus on what he’s done, Kraft asks, not what he came from.

“I guess I was pleading with people: Take the time, ask around about me. Hear about me. Because you’ll hear it.”

title: The Globe took a close look at the Kraft family. Here are five key takeaways.
text:
Send questions or suggestions to the Starting Point team at startingpoint@globe.com. If you’d like the newsletter sent to your inbox, sign up here.

Josh Kraft, the longtime nonprofit leader and son of New England Patriots owner Robert, is the first member of his family to seek elected office. If he succeeds in unseating Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, it would concentrate a huge amount of local power in the hands of a single family.

Yet that family remains something of a black box. Josh’s three brothers, billionaire father, and their associates are private and tight-lipped. So my colleague Mark Arsenault decided to spend a few weeks reporting on the family. He interviewed Josh, watched him campaign, and spoke to people in the Krafts’ orbit.

Here are five takeaways from Mark’s story.

People who know the Krafts say that Josh, Robert’s third-born son, philosophically resembles his philanthropic mother, Myra, who died of cancer in 2011. “She got up every day wanting to give her money away,” one friend told Mark.

Josh, 57, spent a year teaching after graduating from Williams College, which cultivated an interest in helping children. He later worked to prevent kids from dropping out of school at a South Boston nonprofit, led the Boys & Girls Club of Boston, and helmed his family’s charitable foundation. “He has unique gifts and is a genuinely altruistic person,” said Josh’s brother David, 53, who left the family business more than a decade ago and has donated to Josh’s mayoral campaign.

Their older brothers, by contrast, gravitated to the family business. Jonathan, 61, is president of the Kraft Group holding company and sits next to his father at Patriots games. Daniel, 59, runs a subsidiary paper company that is now the country’s fifth-largest exporter.

Chief among them are deep pockets and a moneyed network. Robert Kraft’s net worth is nearly $12 billion (although state campaign finance laws regarding immediate family members prevent him from donating to or leading any super PAC supporting his son’s campaign, according to my colleague Shirley Leung). The family’s businesses employ nearly 10,000 people. And Josh’s eldest brother, Jonathan, is chairman of the board of Massachusetts General Hospital, a leading state institution.

Those connections already seem to be helping. A Globe analysis found that Josh’s campaign raised 2.5 times as much money last month as Wu’s did. But most of that came from donors outside Boston, including the owner of the Los Angeles Chargers.

The Kraft family is largely new to electoral politics. It came closest when Robert chaired the Newton Democratic City Committee in his 20s. That inexperience has sometimes been a hindrance. In the 1990s, Robert failed to convince residents — or then-Mayor Tom Menino — to build a 69,000-seat football stadium in South Boston.

Robert also has a decades-long friendship with President Trump, which seems unlikely to endear Josh to most Bostonians. The elder Kraft said last year that the friendship ended after the Jan. 6 Capitol attack. But Trump recently named Robert’s second wife, Dana Blumberg, to the board of the Kennedy Center in Washington.

Josh has also had to rebut suggestions that he’s merely a wealthy dilettante. “I read some of the comments — ‘Oh, rich kid … What does he know?‘” Josh told Mark. He says he advises voters to “take the time, ask around about me. Hear about me.”

He may be a neophyte, but he appears to have a knack for pressing the flesh. Mark describes how Josh navigated the room during a recent campaign stop in Dorchester, shaking hands with each attendee and kneeling for longer conversations with seated guests.

His work has also inspired loyalty. Abens Maurice met Josh more than three decades ago as a 12-year-old Black kid growing up in South Boston. Josh helped him deal with school, relationships, and racism. “Josh has been my counselor, my big brother, my dad,” Maurice, now 47, said. When he heard Josh was running, he moved back to Boston from California to help.

Josh is divorced and won’t talk much about his adult daughters. His elder brothers also declined Mark’s interview requests. They may have inherited an instinct to dodge the public eye. Ensuring his family’s privacy was one reason Robert passed on running for Congress in 1970.

Josh has made a different choice. Yet despite his famous last name, he remains politically unknown to many Boston voters. Trying to fix that could strain his family’s inclination to stay behind the scenes. As Mark writes, “Few things are more destructive to privacy than a political campaign.”

Read more: Mark’s story is full of other fascinating details, like the awkwardness of campaigning in a different language and the lengths to which some Kraft associates went to avoid talking with a reporter. I recommend his full piece.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
POPPY: THEY’RE ALL AROUND US “Negative Spaces,” the latest album from this enigmatic singer, has an unpredictability that tracks with its themes of paranoia and despair; harder tracks like the threashy “the center’s falling out” and the walloping “they’re all around us” act as heavy, bellowing counterweights to gentler offerings like the blown-out electropop cut “crystallized” and the gauzy “hey there.” April 4, 7 p.m. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

J BALVIN: BACK TO THE RAYO TOUR The reggaeton mogul’s latest album, “Rayo,” is a boisterous celebration of the genre he’s helped define for the last decade. April 4, 8 p.m. Agganis Arena. 800-745-3000, ticketmaster.com

KYLIE MINOGUE: TENSION TOUR Somehow it’s been nearly 14 years since this Australian pop supernova last stopped by Boston while touring the globe; her live shows are full of spectacle and pomp, as well as undeniable hits like the ebullient early-‘00s smash “Love at First Sight” and the kinetic 2023 dancefloor come-on “Padam Padam.” April 9, 7:30 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

BELLA WHITE This rising Canadian singer-songwriter plays unvarnished country music, mostly on the forlorn side of things, and she has a voice that’s perfectly suited to making you feel as sad as her songs. She arrives on what she’s calling her “Red Rhododendron Tour” to perform in trio mode on Friday.April 4, 8 p.m. $29. Brighton Music Hall, 158 Brighton Ave.www.livenation.com

THE WAR AND TREATY “Plus One,” the latest album from married couple Michael and Tanya Trotter, who perform as the War and Treaty, is an 18-song mess, sometimes glorious, sometimes frustrating. The frustrating: the obvious attempts to land something on country radio; the glorious: when they put that aside for their distinctive, smoking-hot country-soul mélange. But while the new record is uneven, they are a force to behold live. April 6, 7:30 p.m. $29.50 The Sinclair, 52 Church St., Cambridge. 888-929-7849. www.axs.com

JIM KWESKIN AND COMPANY For his latest collaboration, “Doing Things Right,” this jug band giant got together with a bunch of folks, dubbed “the Berlin Hall Saturday Night Revue,” to capture the spirit of what was once known as “skiffling,” or catching gigs as you found them, which required giving the customers what they wanted to hear, from western swing to blues, jazz to pop, hokum to polka. They’ll celebrate the album this Tuesday. April 8, 8 p.m. $40. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 617-492-7679. www.passim.org

STUART MUNRO

NATALIE DIETRICH QUARTET The skillful Swiss vibraphonist returns to her old Boston-area malleting grounds for a concert of grooving jazz, featuring longtime collaborators flutist Hiro Honshuku, electric bassist Oscar Stagnaro — who literally wrote the book on Latin jazz bass — and drummer Mark Walker. April 6, 4 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

NICK MOSS BAND Acclaimed, hard-working Chicago native Moss is a blistering guitarist and gutsy singer-songwriter, whose smoking band features New Jersey’s own harmonica whiz, singer, and showman Dennis Gruenling, for a double-shot of gritty urban blues. April 6, 7:30 p.m. $22. Bull Run Restaurant, 215 Great Road, Route 2A, Shirley. bullrunrestaurant.com

YULIA MUSAYELYAN QUARTET Mandorla Music’s Dot Jazz Series presents the accomplished Russian flutist and composer — whose credits encompass both jazz and classical music — with a jazz group featuring ace local improvisers Maxim Lubarsky (piano), Fernando Huergo (bass), and Gen Yoshimura (drums). April 10, 7:30 p.m. $10-$15. Peabody Hall, Parish of All Saints, 209 Ashmont St.mandorlamusic.net

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA This week, Dima Slobodeniouk conducts a program of music composed in the shadow of wartime, including Adolphus Hailstork’s “Lachrymosa: 1919,” Stravinsky’s Symphony in Three Movements, and Elgar’s Violin Concerto, the latter with Frank Peter Zimmermann. Next week, music director Andris Nelsons and the orchestra prepare for May’s Shostakovich Festival Leipzig with plenty of Shostakovich at home, starting with Symphonies Nos. 6 and 11 (April 10) and No. 11 again with the Cello Concerto No. 1 featuring Yo-Yo Ma (April 11). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA BLO ends its mainstage season by taking a spin on Rodgers and Hammerstein’s musical “Carousel,” in a stage production by company artistic associate Anne Bogart starring Jamie Barton as Nettie Fowler, Brandie Sutton as Julie Jordan, and Edward Nelson as Billy Bigelow. Fun fact: This 80th anniversary production takes place in the same theater where it first premiered. Emerson Colonial Theatre. April 4-13. 617-542-6772, www.blo.org

LES ARTS FLORISSANT Care for some “Spring” to help you spring into spring? The storied early music ensemble and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte team up to celebrate the 300th anniversary of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” with plenty of additional music from the Italian Baroque on the program as well. Presented by Boston Early Music Festival. April 4, 8 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-661-1812, www.bemf.org

BOSTON SYMPHONY CHAMBER PLAYERS The big-ticket item on the program is Shostakovich’s Piano Quintet in G with elder statesman of the keyboard Gilbert Kalish, but it’s just as worth buying a ticket for the opportunity to hear Sofia Gubaidulina’s Sonata for double bass and piano, featuring retiring BSO principal bassist Edwin Barker; it might be the first major performance of Gubaidulina’s music in town since her death last month at age 93. April 6, 3 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

A.Z. MADONNA

HER PORTMANTEAU In terms of concept, scope, and execution, Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play cycle about three generations of a Nigerian-American family has proven to be one of the most exciting things to happen in Boston theater in a long time. Directed by Tasia A. Jones, “Her Portmanteau,” the fourth installment of Udofia’s series, is a work of fiery intensity about the tense reunion and fraught reconnection of a mother and her two adult daughters. Featuring flat-out wonderful performances by Patrice Jean-Baptiste as matriarch Abasiama Ufot; Lorraine Victoria Kanyike as Adiaha Ufot, who was raised in the United States; and Jade A. Guerra as Iniabasi Ekpeyong, who was raised in Nigeria. Through April 20. Coproduction by Central Square Theater and Front Porch Arts Collective. At Central Square Theater, Cambridge. Tickets at 617-576-9278 x 1, CentralSquareTheater.org

THE GREAT REVEAL The premiere of a play by David Valdes about the complications surrounding a gender-reveal party held by newlywed, seven-months pregnant Lexi (Paige Clark) and her husband, Christopher (Arthur Gomez), who is anxious about what fatherhood will look like. Lexi’s brother, Linus (Jupiter Lê), is a trans man in a relationship with Dosia (Antonia Turilli), and when Lexi asks Dosia to bake a cake for the celebration, it puts Linus between his sister and Dosia, who views the gender-reveal party as an event that “goes against everything they stand for.” Co-directed by Bridget Kathleen O’Leary and Charlotte Snow. Presented by Lyric Stage Company of Boston. April 4-27. Tickets at lyricstage.com and 617-585-5678.

DON AUCOIN

RIVERDANCE 30 — THE NEW GENERATION The world-renowned fusion of Irish and international dance and music celebrates three decades this season with a touring production featuring a full cast of performers who were not even born when the cultural phenomenon began. In addition, this time around the show is sporting some new choreography, costumes, lighting, and set design. April 8-13. $41.15-$203. Boch Center Wang Theatre. www.bochcenter.org

DANZA ORGÁNICA Founded in 2014 to shine the light on area BIPOC artists, the company presents “We Create Festival 2025: The Movements that Freed(s) Us.” Over the past decade plus, the multidisciplinary arts festival has featured hundreds of artists across a range of disciplines, from dance and music to circus arts and mixed media, so the upcoming show should be a lively and diverse showcase. April 4-5. $15-$25. Hibernian Hall, Roxbury. www.danzaorganica.org/calendar.php

LOKMA (PT3) Mira Göksel, an interdisciplinary movement artist from Izmir, Turkey, and a Dance Lab Residency artist at Boston Center for the Arts, shares the third part of her multidisciplinary exploration of Turkish and Islamic traditions for observing and honoring life’s significant milestones. This open rehearsal focuses on rites and rituals around death, burial, and mourning. April 4. Free with registration. Martin Hall, Boston Center for the Arts. https://bostonarts.my.salesforce-sites.com/ticket/#/instances/a0FPk000004jI9lMAE

COMPLEXIONS CONTEMPORARY BALLET If you missed the outstanding New York company’s Boston show in the fall, you might want to plan ahead for this one-night-only in Portland, Maine. Led by former Alvin Ailey stars Dwight Rhoden and Desmond Richardson and celebrating its landmark 30th anniversary, the troupe is known for its athletic and virtuosic approach to contemporary ballet. The Portland engagement features the 2019 consciousness-raising “Woke,” set to music by Kendrick Lamar, Logic, Drake, and others, alongside a mix of repertoire favorites. April 11. $20-$65. Merrill Auditorium, Portland, Maine. https://portlandovations.org/calendar/

KAREN CAMPBELL

DEEP WATERS: FOUR ARTISTS AND THE SEA Contemporary artists John Akomfrah and Ayana V. Jackson bridge a couple of centuries and cultures in this presentation pairing them with renowned historical painters J.M.W. Turner and John Singleton Copley, centered on their shared fascinations with the sea from very different points of view. Through Nov. 9. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

SARAH CWYNAR Using film, video, photography, and installation, Cwynar creates dizzying cascades of overlapping images that capture — and critique — the contemporary reality of an image-saturated consumer culture in hyperdrive. Art imitates life: Her work is as disorienting as it is seductive, a dark mirror to the smartphone-and-social media world that dominates contemporary society. Her show at the ICA features a brand-new two-part photo installation in collaboration with — how else to put it? — the whims of search-engine algorithms. Through Aug. 3. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

FUTURE FOSSILS A hindsight view of our current moment from the far-flung future, this exhibition brings together a stellar roster of artists — Ai Weiwei, Nari Ward, Rachel Whiteread, Sanford Biggers — to imagine what might remain of the fractured world we now live in when all we know is gone. Through April 13. MassArt Art Museum, 621 Huntington Ave. 617-879-7333, maam.massart.edu

MURRAY WHYTE

GATHER 2025 Textiles in art have been having a moment, so it’s the perfect time for Gather 2025, spotlighting the vibrant local fiber art community. It opens on April 5 with a symposium at Arts Collaborative Medford, “Common Cause in Fiber Art: Connection and Care” (registration required). In addition, close to 100 events take place all over the Greater Boston area in a spirit of education, community building, advocacy, and art. They include banner-making, weaving, and lacemaking workshops, exhibitions, and panel discussions about art, textiles, and social justice. Through May 3.www.gatherfibersymposium.com

CATE McQUAID

TROY HAWKE: THE GREETERS GUILD Milo McCabe, a.k.a. Troy Hawke, is known for his social media videos in which he delights absolute strangers with encouraging words. He’s also a regular on the UK comedy festival circuit, and making a few stops in the US before he records a new comedy special in Los Angeles on April 15. April 4, 7 p.m. $35-$40. Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. 617-718-2191, www.artsatthearmory.org

KELLY MACFARLAND: HOT GNOME One of Boston’s most reliable sources for laughs, MacFarland is self-producing a new one-hour comedy special called “Hot Gnome.” The set list will be a selection of some of her best stuff over the years, and also a bit of a love letter to her parents. A release date is yet to be determined, but if you go, you can look for yourself in the audience later. With Carolyn Plummer. April 4, 8 p.m. $34-$41.50. The Cabot, 286 Cabot St., Beverly. 978-927-3100, www.thecabot.org

GREG FITZSIMMONS “You can’t just be whatever type of doctor you feel like being,” says the Boston University grad and Emmy-winning writer. “Depending on your grades, you’re qualified to be certain types. Like, you don’t just graduate and go, ‘I think I’m gonna work on brains.’ And then they look at your report card and they’re like, ‘Nah. We got you down for feet.‘”April 4 at 7 p.m. and April 5 at 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. $33. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

PANCAKES & PLAY WITH THE EASTER BUNNY Easter is on April 20 this year, but the festivities come early at Peachy Girl Parties. Cravings Cart RI will provide a mini pancake bar with treats for families. Visitors will also have the chance to make their own Easter-themed slime. Starting at 10 a.m., the Easter Bunny will be available for pictures and a 30-minute dance party. The event is sponsored by ABA Centers of Rhode Island, which seeks to improve care for children with autism. April 5, 9:30 a.m.- 11:30 a.m. Tickets are $46.65. Peachy Girl Parties, 2 Olney St., Seekonk. eventbrite.com

KIDS CON NEW ENGLAND Kids Con celebrates its 10th anniversary on Sunday with a day of comic book fun. Attendees can practice their arts and crafting skills, enjoy musical performances and magic shows, go for a scavenger hunt, and dress to impress in a cosplay contest. Families will have the opportunity to meet over 100 authors, artists, and creators, as well as characters from Pokémon, Bluey, Star Wars, and more. April 6, 10 a.m.-4 p.m. Free admission for children under 5; tickets are $16. Sheraton Castle, 11 Tara Boulevard, Nashua, N.H. kidsconne.square.site

BEYOND THE SPECTRUM KIDS This Museum of Fine Arts program is designed for youth on the autism spectrum and their families to enjoy art and create their own. Beyond the Spectrum occurs on select Saturdays with new educational material and activities for each event. This weekend, families can tour the historical rooms on display throughout the museum, including realistic depictions of homes in Peabody and Dorchester. As a closing activity, attendees can celebrate the spring season and decorate their own bird houses to take home. April 5, 10:30 a.m.-noon. Tickets are $11 for nonmembers, $9 for members. MFA Boston, 465 Huntington Ave.mfa.org

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Community benefit or conflict? A neighborhood fund and a Boston city councilor’s role in it.
text:
In an interview, Fernandes Anderson said the District 7 Community Fund is an independent nonprofit and that a group of her constituents came up with the idea. She said she connected them to a law clinic at Harvard University to get it set up last year and has no affiliation with it.

Its goals are to fund scholarships and beautification projects in the district, according to one of its backers, and its only expense to date is a fee paid to a fiscal sponsor that accepted and held money on behalf of the fund as it was being set up.

Fernandes Anderson said the fund was set up in such a way “to separate or remove councilors or the city from” the process in which money and other benefits negotiated as part of development approvals are distributed to neighborhood stakeholders.

“This way the community takes full control of that process,” she said. “This is not a foreign concept.”

A developer for a separate project, on Elmwood Street in Roxbury, said he understood Fernandes Anderson was encouraging donations to a community fund as a way to move business along, though Fernandes Anderson disputes this account.

In February 2023, one year before the District 7 Community Fund Inc. officially launched, Triple W Development proposed paying $200,000 to an entity with a similar name, the “District 7 Boston Fund Inc.,” according to documents at the city planning department. Triple W principal Scott Webster said his company was looking for community support for the project. “We went to Tania and she said that was the procedure,” he said.

Webster said he did not recall the conversation verbatim with Fernandes Anderson, but the crux of her response to him was that she could support the project, “but you’ll have to do these things.” One of the “things,” Webster said, was to contribute to an entity called the District 7 Boston Fund.

“We wanted to put our best foot forward,” he said.

There is no record in Massachusetts corporation filings of a legal entity with that exact name, and Triple W did not make a contribution as a community benefits agreement was never signed, according to the city’s planning department.

Lou DiNatale, a veteran Massachusetts pollster, said there is potential for an “appearance problem” with the District 7 fund because it could be viewed Fernandes Anderson’s supporters conceived it to support her initiatives or preferences. DiNatale said it would be understandable that developers believe contributing to such a fund would give them an advantage in the review process.

“This is a good idea for the neighborhood which is now going to come under question because of her indictment,” he said.

But, Katherine Levine Einstein, a Boston University political science professor whose specialties include urban politics and policy, said there is sometimes a very fine line between a politician aiding her community and pressuring a developer for payments or other concessions.

“Funds like the one you’re describing feel to me perilously close to crossing that line, particularly depending on how they’re being disbursed,” she said.

Boston has a history of controversy over the spoils of big development projects. Perhaps the most notable example unfolded around the buildout of the Seaport more than two decades ago, when then-mayor Thomas M. Menino engineered a deal with leaders from South Boston for that neighborhood to reap the majority of the public proceeds from the waterfront boom. However, questions about oversight dogged the South Boston Betterment Fund for many years and some stakeholders complained their neighborhoods were boxed out.

There are different types of funds set up to disburse community benefits from construction projects in Boston, with developers, private nonprofits, politicians, and city development authorities often all involved in the deal-making.

For instance, in recent months, community benefits from a trio of South End projects were distributed via the city’s planning department to local nonprofits that help first-generation high school students get into and stay in college, and to a group that represents a local park, among others.

There is also the East Boston Housing Stabilization Trust Fund, which receives funds from the redevelopment of Suffolk Downs to help mitigate housing displacement. That fund was established by City Hall, and its members include three elected officials as well as others nominated by the district councilor and selected by the mayor.

In the case of the District 7 Fund, one of its directors, community activist Louis Elisa, said Fernandes Anderson has no say in how the board distributes its money.

Currently, Elisa said the fund has less than $155,000 in its coffers, all from philanthropy; no developer has yet to make a payment to the fund, including the team behind the Alexandra Hotel project.

“I don’t consider it a shakedown to ask someone to contribute to the community,” Elisa said.

Still, there is a clear overlap between Fernandes Anderson’s political life and the fund. All the officers and directors of the fund have either donated money to her campaign or served on her advisory council for the district, which is anchored in Roxbury and includes parts of Dorchester and the South End.

Documents released in response to a public records request to the city’s planning department suggest Fernandes Anderson had a hand in setting up the fund. In a 2022 email to city planners, an attorney for the Alexandra developer references a contribution to be administered by the District 7 Fund, which he notes was “being created with assistance from Councilor Anderson.”

As for the Elmwood development by Triple W, Fernandes Anderson disputed Webster’s recollection of his interaction with her. She said the Elmwood developers conveyed to her that they wanted to do something for the community as part of the process, but she was clear she could not make any recommendations about which groups should receive community benefits or how much. She said she suggested the developers speak with those behind the creation of the fund.

However, Fernandes Anderson said the developers included the fund in a memorandum of understanding, a document that typically outlines a non-binding agreement between parties, without her knowledge.

After it was included in the memo, she said she decided she had to remain neutral, neither supporting or opposing the Elmwood project.

“I definitely wanted to remain neutral,” she recalled thinking.

The Boston planning department also has records of an agreement in 2022, two years before the fund officially launched, involving the planned revival of the Alexandra Hotel on Massachusetts Avenue. At that time, developers agreed to pay the fund $660,000.

No payment has yet to be made, however, because it’s contingent on the issuance of building permits, which the developers have yet to receive.

In December, Fernandes Anderson was arrested on federal wire fraud and theft charges for allegedly pocketing a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff. The charges are not related to any development activity before the city.

Now in her second term, the 46-year-old Fernandes Anderson was the first Muslim and first formerly undocumented immigrant to be elected to the council in 2021.

Councilors do not vote on individual projects; that is the purview of other agencies such as the Boston Planning & Development Agency Board. However, community support and political buy-in can make the development process go more smoothly for a project. Councilors often speak in favor of or in opposition to a project and the BPDA board takes such input into consideration.

City Councilor at Large Erin Murphy, who has clashed with Fernandes Anderson on the council, called the fund “definitely out of the norm.”

”What is this group going to actually do?” Murphy asked.

But, City Councilor Liz Breadon, who represents Allston-Brighton, said such a fund focused on the needs of a council district is “not a bad idea if it’s done right.”

“The main thing is transparency and knowing what the money is being used for, that it’s not being siphoned off to preferred partners,” she said.

Jeremiah Manion of Globe staff contributed.

title: Alleged drunk driver in fatal South Boston crash held on $100,000 bail
text:
Romero wore a blue hooded sweatshirt as he stood in the dock listening to a Spanish translation of the proceedings on earphones.

He occasionally shut his eyes as Assistant District Attorney Lynn Feigenbaum recited a brief statement of facts.

Around 9:20 a.m. on Jan. 12, Romero was driving on Southampton Street toward Dorchester Avenue, Feigenbaum said.

He approached that intersection traveling “at a high rate of speed” and “veered across the double yellow [line] into the wrong side of the road,” Feigenbaum said.

At that time, Noah Greany was “walking home from Dunkin’ Donuts across Southampton Street and was fatally struck by Mr. Romero,” Feigenbaum said. “After striking Mr. Greany, the car driven by Mr. Romero crashed into the Small Victories restaurant located at 400 Dorchester Avenue.”

Greany was taken to Boston Medical Center, where he was later pronounced dead.

Romero and his passenger were both taken to Tufts Medical Center.

“Mr. Romero was interviewed at the hospital, where he stated that while he was heading to work, he felt the car was giving gas on its own,” Feigenbaum said. “He was asked if he had been drinking any alcohol or had any drugs, and he stated no, [shaking] his head in the negative.”

She said security video showed the vehicle initially heading toward Andrew Square at a proper rate of speed and in the correct lane.

But then the car “appears to accelerate through the intersection towards Andrew Square ... The motor vehicle strikes Mr. Greany with the front passenger side corner, throwing him into the intersection.”

Romero’s blood was drawn at the hospital with an alcohol level calculated at between .091 and .096, Feigenbaum said. The legal limit is .08.

Feigenbaum said Romero has no previous convictions but was charged in 2019 with negligent use of a motor vehicle. That case was continued without a finding.

Romero’s lawyer, Virgen M. Palermo, requested that bail be set at a couple of thousand dollars, saying that $100,000 is “too much” for her client. She said Romero has worked the same job at a seafood facility in South Boston for decades and lives with his romantic partner and their six children, two from her prior relationships.

The couple has 5-year-old twins, and Romero was dropping his partner off at her restaurant job at the time of the crash, according to Palermo, who said her client voluntarily turned himself in to authorities.

“They were ... in the car talking about Chuck E. Cheese for the birthday for the twins when all of this stuff happens,” Palermo said. “It appears that the car is going fine ... and then all of a sudden it doesn’t, and that I think is consistent with something wrong” with the vehicle itself.

Palermo said Romero bought the used car for $2,500 and repeatedly brought it back to the seller for repairs.

She said he indicated that the night before the crash, he drank about five beers and perhaps a glass of wine while he was cooking with his partner.

“So there are two questions here that need to be examined,” Palermo said. “One is whether, what is the rate of metabolism of alcohol that he’s drinking the night before, and it still shows up in the blood in his system, the question is to what extent that was affecting ... his ability to drive carefully.”

And, she said, “what is the condition of this car that he is in?”

Greany’s mother, Marie Lambalot Greany, said shortly after her son’s death that he “had so much left to give this world.”

Greany grew up in Mattapoisett with his parents and younger sister, Grace. He went to high school at Tabor Academy in Marion. A high academic achiever, Greany set his mind to attending Northeastern University.

He excelled there, receiving a bachelor’s degree in cellular and molecular biology in 2021, followed by a master’s degree in bioinformatics enterprise in 2022. He worked at the time of his death at Hayden Consulting Group, a Boston-based health care consulting firm.

“He was doing what he loved, researching and trying to make the world better,” his mother said. ”We had this family saying that with his brains and everything about him, he was meant to do great things in this world.“

At the time of the crash, Greany had left his girlfriend’s home and was walking a few blocks to his apartment, where he planned to watch soccer with some friends, his mother said. He stopped at a coffee shop and was talking with a childhood friend about an upcoming soccer game, she said.

When he didn’t return home, his friends became concerned. After they saw a social media post about a car crash in Andrew Square, they checked his location app. His phone was in the same spot as the crash, his mother said.

“He didn’t suffer,” his mother said. ”That’s all we could have hoped for."

She recalled that when her sometimes distracted son went to Northeastern, she and her husband worried about him crossing the Green Line tracks that run by the campus.

“You know, smart kids with no common sense? My husband and I, our nightmare was that he was going to cross those train tracks and not look. But he survived his years at Northeastern,” she said. ”It was just some freak accident on a Sunday that he died that way. Our worst nightmare. Crossing the street in Boston. In a crosswalk. Like we taught him."

Material from prior Globe stories was used in this report.

title: ‘It’s very disheartening.’ Violent assaults leave educators reeling in Massachusetts schools
text:
“It was pretty traumatic,” said Jones, who has taught for eight years in Boston Public Schools. “Not once did I feel unsafe until this year.”

Educators have for generations been entrusted to keep their students safe, but over the last four years Massachusetts educators, including some who have been injured by students, have repeatedly raised concerns about their own safety. Many students have been struggling to readjust to in-person learning after the pandemic shut down school buildings or dealing with other mental health challenges.

Last month, a nurse at Community Academy of Science and Health in Dorchester suffered a concussion and a pinched nerve after she was allegedly attacked by a student, according to a police report and the nurse’s attorney.

Student brawls at Revere High School last fall, which injured at least one administrator and a teacher, prompted educators to pack a City Council meeting and demand better safety measures. Brockton educators made a similar push the previous school year as ongoing student fights at the high school injured multiple staffers.

Elsewhere, a student at a Lynn charter school allegedly stabbed a teacher several times last April with the intent to murder, according to an indictment; a Lowell High School staffer was injured during a student fight last spring; and a teacher at Mel King Academy in the South End was rushed to a hospital in January 2024 after a student allegedly punched her in the head and then hit her in the head with a chair.

“Nobody should expect to go to work and be hurt,” said Donna Grady, president of the Franklin Education Association. “It’s very disheartening.”

Grady, a kindergarten teacher, said she has seen an increase in chair throwing, scratching, and yelling and swearing at adults, even among her school’s youngest learners. Some educators with broken fingers or bites delay treatment so they can finish the school day, she said.

Bringing attention to the safety concerns has been awkward for many educators, like Grady and Jones, who are careful not to blame students. They note that violence is a sign that students need more support — staffing, counseling, and other interventions — to tend to their needs and educators need more resources to better serve them and also measures to keep them and other students safe.

Educators also sometimes receive injuries when caring for students with disabilities as they attempt to calm them down or restrain them.

Efforts are underway in Massachusetts to create safer school environments, including an ongoing initiative by the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education that is designed to prevent incidents from escalating into injuries, such as identifying problem areas and creating action plans to address them.

The Massachusetts Teachers Association, the state’s largest educators union, also has created a Safe Schools for All task force, which Grady co-chairs, to examine ways to improve the mental well-being of staff and students. The MTA plans to lobby state policy makers for more funding to reduce class sizes and provide more behavioral support for students.

A report last year by the American Psychological Association raised concerns that an increase in violent episodes in schools is causing more educators to resign or retire.

The report found 56 percent of educators who took part in a survey after pandemic restrictions were lifted said they had experienced physical violence from a student, and 26 percent said they had encountered similar behavior from a parent, both of which were up notably from before the pandemic.

Injuries to educators, which frequently cause them to miss school to recover physically and emotionally, can carry financial costs to districts as educators file for workers’ compensation to help pay for medical expenses and time off.

A handful of districts contacted by the Globe, including BPS, declined to provide data on the number of employees injured by students who filed workers’ compensation for this story.

In Brockton, the district reported a sharp rise in student-involved accident reports in the wake of the pandemic that resulted in employees filing workers comp claims. The district recorded 105 such claims during the last school year as student-related violence at Brockton High made national headlines, more than twice the number of claims filed during the 2018-19 school year.

Nationwide, workers’ compensation claims spiked following the pandemic shutdown, according to data from Gallagher Bassett, a claims and risk management services firm, which tracks national trends on workers’ compensation claims filed by educators.

During the 2022-23 school year, assault claims filed by educators following incidents with students, which were culled from approximately 2,000 urban, suburban, and rural districts nationwide, reached a high of 1,426, slightly above pre-pandemic levels. Claims dropped dramatically the following year to 868, an unusually low number that could indicate student behavior is improving or could represent a temporary dip.

Greg McKenna, national practice leader for the public sector at Gallagher Bassett, said it is hard to know, based on one year’s worth of data, what the drop in claims truly means. The drop, he said, could reflect the attention educators have drawn to the issue and steps local districts took to address student mental health issues, or it could be temporary.

“I would never say these kinds of incidents are eradicated,” he said. “They are not. … Until we get to a frequency and severity of zero, it’s something that should be worked on pretty heavily.”

Worker’s compensation is just one way to measure educator injuries. School workers also can use personal or sick time, while others don’t seek medical treatment.

At the Donahue School in Holyoke, Kendra Kwasnik, an elementary school adjustment counselor, tapped workers comp after sustaining multiple injuries in November while tending to a student whose behavior was escalating. She was holding a door open, and the student either kicked or pushed it hard from behind, slamming into her.

Medical tests, covered by workers compensation, later revealed torn connective tissue in her shoulder, two herniated discs in her neck, and a fractured right arm caused by its dislocation from her shoulder.

She had to navigate months of red tape with the insurance company and the district as she prepared for surgery, which will put her out of work for several weeks this spring.

“I definitely have had moments when I have broken down crying,” she said.

Kwasnik, who was trained in de-escalation strategies, said districts and the state need more comprehensive behavioral support plans, staffing and other resources for students, noting that students often don’t mean to intentionally hurt others.

Brandon Stratford, an education researcher with the research center Child Trends, who studies school employee wellness, said many teachers need more resources.

“Putting in place programs and skills for the adults at a universal level where we’re creating the sense of belonging around students, is your foundation for school safety,” he said.

In Boston, Sujata Wycoff, a BPS spokesperson, declined to comment on Jones’s case, noting it was a personnel matter. But she added any incident resulting in injury is thoroughly investigated.

“Based on the outcome of the investigation, we work with all involved parties to ensure an appropriate response,” she said in a statement.

Jones, who’s out on medical leave, is still negotiating her return to the classroom, including a safety plan, but is running into problems. The district wants to transfer her to another school, which she opposes, because she filed a police report, she said.

Jones wants to return to Tobin because “I love my students dearly and see bigger and brighter things for them.”

But she added, “the response from the district where they have been trying to demonize me has been overwhelming. ... This has upended every facet of my life.”

Globe staff writer Christopher Huffaker contributed to this report.

title: ‘The flood gates are open’: In the wake of Fernandes Anderson’s bombshell plea agreement, what happens now?
text:
“It is a sad day for Roxbury and the residents of District 7,” said Ahmed, a 43-year-old father of five and track coach who has previously run for state representative.

Abdikarim, a 39-year-old nonprofit executive and father of six who has run for the council in the past, referred to Fernandes Anderson stepping down as “the decision she’s made.”

“I can only concentrate on what I bring to the table,” said Abdikarim.

Afonso’s campaign, meanwhile, confirmed Wednesday afternoon that he was also running for District 7.

On Tuesday, court filings showed Fernandes Anderson will plead guilty to two counts for allegedly arranging to receive a kickback from a City Council staff member: one count of wire fraud and one of theft from a program receiving federal funds. Four other wire fraud counts will be dropped by prosecutors as part of the deal.

Prosecutors will recommend that she be sentenced to one year and a day in prison, followed by 36 months of supervised release, and be ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution.

US District Judge Indira Talwani, who is presiding over the case, is not required to accept that sentence and the plea agreement does not say what punishment Fernandes Anderson’s defense lawyer will recommend. As part of the deal, Fernandes Anderson waived her right to appeal.

Fernandes Anderson was arrested in December on federal wire fraud and theft charges for allegedly pocketing a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff. But in a statement of facts filed in court Tuesday she also admitted to filing fraudulent federal income tax returns for three years; however, she has not been charged with tax offenses.

Prosecutors alleged Fernandes Anderson willfully omitted about $11,000 in income she earned from a Massachusetts-based corporation from her 2021 tax return, as well as not reporting campaign funds she used for personal enrichment on her 2022 and 2023 tax returns and the $7,000 kickback that she received from her staffer on her 2023 tax return.

A federal indictment alleges Fernandes Anderson, 46, hired her relative in December 2022, then gave her a $13,000 bonus months later with a caveat: She had to funnel more than half of it back to the councilor.

Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a political consultant who lives in the district, said on Wednesday that Fernandes Anderson did the right thing in resigning. Ferriabough Bolling hoped that Fernandes Anderson will not receive prison time. Constituents, she said, feel good about Fernandes Anderson apologizing.

“Everybody can make a mistake and this is a big one because many people in the community felt let down,” said Ferriabough Bolling, whose late husband, Bruce, was a councilor who represented the district.

Still, Ferriabough Bolling said the District 7 constituents are resilient and she anticipated whoever runs for the seat will be deeply scrutinized.

“There’s a whole bunch of people talking about it now,” she said. “The floodgates are open.”

But for now, Afonso, Ahmed, and Abdikarim seem to be three declared candidates vying to succeed Fernandes Anderson. Ahmed had more than $33,000 cash-on-hand in his campaign coffers at the end of March, according to state records, while Abdikarim’s campaign had more than $14,000, and Afonso had more than $24,000.

Ahmed, who is a cofounder of Boston United Track and Cross Country Club, has worked with Boston youth for decades. He moved to Boston from Somalia at age 12. He was a track star at Boston English high school, where he won the national championship in the 800 meters and set numerous state and New England records. He ran at the University of Arkansas and also professionally under a Nike sponsorship deal.

Wednesday, Ahmed said providing quality constituent services would be his priority on the council.

“Roxbury has been my America. Roxbury has been my home from the moment I came to the United States until today,” he said.

Abdikarim was resettled, along with his family, from Somalia by Catholic Charities when he was 9 years old. Housing continues to be among the most pressing issues for district residents, he said. It’s an issue he has firsthand experience with, he said, having lived in four different public housing developments in Boston.

He was the oldest of 10 siblings, and it was difficult to find a home large enough to accommodate the size of his family, he said. He started working at 13, he said, to help provide for his family.

“I don’t think anyone understands the housing issue more than me,” he said.

Afonso, meanwhile, is a 36-year-old Cabo Verdean American who is originally from Dorchester’s Four Corners neighborhood. He works for the state’s Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, where, according to his campaign website, “he is focused on bringing down the cost of housing and bringing together stakeholders on the state’s five-year housing plan.”

Afonso’s site states that he is running to “help lower costs, close the wealth gap and provide opportunities in District 7 so that we all can thrive.”

At the City Hall Plaza Civic Pavilion on Wednesday, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said she has not looked over the plea agreement Fernandes Anderson signed, and has not been briefed on whether the councilor reached out to the mayor’s office before announcing she intends to resign.
