Wu, who previously called for Fernandes Anderson to resign when the federal indictment became public, on Wednesday called the situation “incredibly unfortunate.”

“It seems that there has been a resolution,” Wu said, when asked by reporters about the issue at an unrelated event Wednesday. “We will be working to support [Fernandes Anderson’s] district, and make sure that services and city programs can still be available for residents.”

When Fernandes Anderson officially resigns, it will trigger the city’s process to schedule and hold a special election to fill her seat, if it is more than 180 days before the next regular municipal election, according to the city charter. Her seat would remain vacant until the special preliminary, then general elections determine her successor.

When asked about how Fernandes Anderson’s open seat would leave her district’s residents unrepresented during the budget process, Wu replied that that advocacy will have to come from her administration, at-large councilors, and the council president.

At Wednesday’s meeting, Council President Ruthzee Louijeune removed Fernandes Anderson from all the council committees that she sits on.

Fernandes Anderson attended Wednesday’s regular City Council meeting, but refused to speak with most reporters or answer questions about the plea agreement and her case.

In a statement responding to Globe questions Wednesday, she said she attended Wednesday’s meeting because, “It is important to me to put my constituents first, focus on accountability, do the right thing, resign but, with a sound transition plan that ensures stability for my District.”

She wrote that she does not know what comes next for her work-wise, but “the timeline for an exit plan has to be decided by the District 7 Advisory Council and my Constituents.”

”My focus in this moment is to do everything I can in collaboration with the District 7 Advisory Council to create a proper transition,” she said in her statement.

title: Emmy award-winning actress Ayo Edebiri visits Boston Latin School
text:
Emmy award-winning actress and former Boston Latin School student Ayo Edebiri returned to her alma matter Thursday for the first time since graduating and shared with the mayor and students how her time at the campus shaped her career.

“There’s a rigor that I have and level of care that I have that would not be possible if I hadn’t gone to this school,” she said. “It really shapes you and molds you.”

Edebiri gave praise to the performing arts, staff productions, and community she joined at the school, which sparked her early talents in comedy and theater.

Away from the stage, she said her willingness to commit extra time to her craft was inclined from her teachers committing extra time for her after class.

On the screen, Edebiri has held lead roles in several acclaimed movies and shows, including “The Bear,” “Big Mouth,” and most recently musical horror “Opus.” She has also worked as a writer and producer on countless sets.

Originally from Dorchester and the daughter of a Nigerian father and a Barbadian mother, Edebiri became interested in comedy through her eighth-grade drama class, which prompted her to join the improv club at Boston Latin School, where she graduated in 2013.

She graduated in 2017 from New York University, where she intended to get an education degree but instead switched to dramatic writing after more than two years. In college, she juggled several jobs, including as a baby sitter, a barista, and a liaison in the campus call center.

She started her career in comedy as an intern at Upright Citizens Brigade, a Chicago-founded comedy institution and training center. Edebiri also dedicated time to stand-up, and eventually worked in production for “Broad City” on Comedy Central.

“It really impacts the kids’ whole motivations for education,” said ninth-grade student Yuki Jiang. “She is a really good, effective public leader for us.”

Seeing Edebiri up close helped students set goals and believe in their futures, Jiang said.

Students rushed onto the podium and peppered Edebiri with questions about her transition from education to the entertainment industry.

The middle and high school students talked with Edebiri about her college experience, her biggest challenges stepping into the entertainment industry, and the influences Boston Latin’s performing arts played in her success.

At the school, which held a celebration rally for the actress, Mayor Michelle Wu issued a proclamation announcing April 10 “Ayo Edebiri Day.”

Wu said Edebiri’s return to the campus to connect with students brings a familiarity to Massachusetts that’s pivotal for their goal setting and personal development.

“It means so much that while you’re supposed to be at home relaxing with your family, you chose to come here,” she told Edebiri. “There’s a lot of need and hope for communities to stand and be an example of what is still possible.”

Auzzy Byrdsell can be reached at austin.byrdsell@globe.com.

title: Why are cops are addicted to confidential informants? The Globe investigates Snitch City
text:
Amazon Music | Apple Podcasts | iHeartRadio | Pocket Casts | Spotify

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the April 10 episode of the “Say More” podcast.

Jazmin Aguilera: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Jazmin Aguilera. In the US, there’s no one frontline of the war on drugs. That’s because the so-called war is just about everywhere between addiction disorders and overdoses. It’s pretty obvious the way drugs are hurting American communities, but the war itself is also hurting us.

The Boston Globe Spotlight team has a new five-part investigative podcast series called “Snitch City.” The podcast looks at police use of confidential informants in New Bedford, Massachusetts, and the ways this whole informant system prays on vulnerable people and seems to invite police corruption.

“Snitch City” (trailer clip): The CI system is based on blind trust and can have deadly consequences. It is shadowy. Things had just gotten to the point of no control. It is underground, the corruption level is just off the hook. It really was.

Aguilera: I’m in the Globe studio catching up with two Spotlight reporters who have been working on this story. Dugan Arnett, who hosts the podcast, and his reporting partne Andrew Ryan.

So let’s start off at the very beginning here. Can you describe to me, Dugan, what a confidential informant is and how they’re used to make arrests?

Arnett: The simplest way to put it is, I get pulled over. I’ve got a small amount of drugs on me. An officer says, “Hey, we can make this case go away, but we need something in return, and what we need is information, so who’d you get the drugs from? Who’s selling drugs, et cetera.”

I’m now in this pact, no contract. There’s no real rules of engagement. And I’m now working for the police to get them information in order to save myself.

Ryan: Often the people who are involved in these cases are folks who are struggling with addiction, vulnerable populations.

There will be a confidential informant who provides information, and then we’ll do essentially a series of undercover buys for the police.

And all of this stuff happens outside of the view of lawyers or the courts. It’s just as Dugan said, a pact between essentially a police officer and their informant or the person that they caught with drugs or a gun or something like that.

Aguilera: So let’s talk about New Bedford, Massachusetts. Dugan, your reporting starts there. What brought you to New Bedford?

Arnett: So this was about 2022, I think. I was in the office one day, got an email, the subject line of which was just, “I need help!”

It was a little hard to follow. It was an email from a woman who was sort of explaining that “I got involved with a New Bedford detective who then started investigating my fiancé for heroin trafficking and from there, sort of everything went off the rails.”

And so it was one of those things where I just happened to have a couple of minutes free. I was waiting for an edit, or something like that, and ended up calling this woman and she lays this story out and it’s even wilder than the email.

It sounds so farfetched that it was one of those things where you’re sort of like, this is a lovely, wild, ridiculous story. But you have some doubts about whether it’s true.

And then she starts providing some documents and she starts providing some screenshots from her phone. And as she does that, this wild story comes together and you realize that this is an actual thing that happened. Then that story was published a few months later.

From there, the floodgates opened. It was just tips from New Bedford about how New Bedford Police had been abusing informants, manipulating the informant system.

And it was sort of, for lack of a better term, off to the races.

Aguilera: So you both reported a lot of shady police behavior, especially with informants in New Bedford. There’s police sleeping with informants, coaching informants, misusing informants and search warrants, and putting their safety at risk.

Dugan, can you talk to me about one of these cases that you think really illustrates the problem?

Arnett: Yeah, so the podcast starts with a story that, again, seemed pretty farfetched the first time I heard it. It involves an officer named George Santos, who one night under the cover of darkness boards this fishing boat in the port of New Bedford.

This boat is filled with some fishermen who are getting ready to leave the next morning on a fishing trip. The officer shows up. A gun on his hip, dressed in black, off duty, bloodshot eyes, according to one member of the crew. And he starts demanding drugs.

So the fishermen are asking why this guy is on the boat. And his response is, “A confidential informant told me that you have drugs on this boat and that’s why I’m here.”

That phrase for police is like a hall pass. They can do just about anything they want, simply by citing a confidential informant. “I have a confidential informant who told me X, Y, Z, so now I can search your car, your boat.”

Ryan: So in the example with this boat and with Officer Santos, I think it’s a symptom of basically a police officer being emboldened by the secrecy of this system. When officers are even supposedly operating within the guidelines of their department, we found examples of pretty egregious misconduct of attributing false information or falsely attributing information to a confidential informant to get a warrant. We found officers who have acknowledged coaching informants, telling them to miss court, telling them to buy drugs for themselves, for their own personal use, and to lie in court.

And on the flip side, we found example after example of police officers who have been found to have lied in court, who still get this blind trust to be able to say, “I have this confidential informant who’s telling me all this, so just believe me and trust me and let me go search someone’s car, or someone’s boat or someone’s phone.”

Aguilera: So Andrew, what is it about the informant system that makes it so ripe for corruption?

Ryan: I think what makes it so ripe for corruption is the fact that there’s no checks and balances.

These things are all done within the police department, and there’s no outside oversight. Police say they do their own internal audits. They won’t provide them to us or anyone else. Many of the large departments won’t provide basic information about how many informants they have, how much money they’re paying the informants, how many informants have been accused of misconduct, how many officers have been accused of misconduct with informants.

So it is the ultimate black box.

Aguilera: Wow. So it seems like once these informants sign into this role, they’re basically screwed. This whole system is such a black box. There’s no one that can help them once they’re in it. So if things go sideways with the police, they can’t complain to their friends because then they might be implicated in their informing.They can’t go to the police, obviously.

So are CIs basically always the loser in this arrangement?

Arnett: It’s hard to say that there aren’t arrangements that work the way they should, which is a sort of agreed upon quid pro quo. You do this for me, this one case, we’ll make your case go away. That’s the end of it.

But what I think happens much more frequently is that informants begin to feel stuck because they thought they were signing on for one thing, and then the calls keep coming from police. The police want more information. They’re afraid to say no because they could go to jail. They’re worried that their cases could come back, that the police could out them. And then they’re just in this horrible catch-22.

So there’s one former confidential informant that we talked to. He’s in the podcast in episode two. His pseudonym that we used is Daniel. He thought he was going to help the police seize one gun, and then that became more and more and more and more and more.

Hearing the way he sort of felt trapped over the course of months, this became a months-long thing where he is afraid to tell them no.

He’s afraid of being outed and so he’s living like this double life where every so often he gets a call from police and it feels like he’s got to look around and feel and decide, who am I going to essentially set up.

His story is uniquely disturbing, as you’ll hear if you listen to the podcast. It’s like you get on a hamster wheel and then you just can’t get off. And I think that’s the case, not just for Daniel, but other informants, who we spoke to as well, describe it the very same way.

Aguilera: More of my conversation on the Boston Globe’s Snitch City investigation after a short break.

So, Andrew, you’ve done a lot of data reporting on the use of informants. Broadly, what have you learned?

Ryan: What we’ve learned is in Massachusetts, nearly nine out of 10 drug raids are based on the word of a confidential informant. And we learned this by literally going page by page through 2,000 search warrants from courts across the Commonwealth.

We got that number because we wanted to put it in context. We wanted to see how widespread informant use was in these cases. What we found was that New Bedford not only matched that state average, but it exceeded it.

In New Bedford, 99 percent of warrants were based on confidential informants. There are certain places where there are other kinds of drug cases, things with drug dogs, especially at Logan Airport, but by and large, confidential informants are the lifeblood of drug raids in the Commonwealth, and quite frankly, across the nation.

Arnett: Hopefully, this isn’t too far. There’s no drug war in New Bedford or Massachusetts without confidential informants. I think that’s fair to say.

Ryan: Yep.

Aguilera: So, Dugan, in the very opening of “Snitch City,” you say that police departments are addicted to using confidential informants in the war on drugs. That’s a particularly strong word.

Tell me why the CI system is used so much, especially when it comes to drug busts.

Arnett: Because it’s easy, I think. It’s easy for a drug cop to say, ‘Hey, I have a confidential informant who told me this.’

When you think about the other ways that police sort of go about investigations, take undercover work, these are lengthy operations, they’re dangerous, they’re time consuming, they’re costly.

It’s much easier to pull over a kid who’s got some drugs and essentially put them to work for you. You do that 10 times, you have 10 people working for you. You’ve got your own little sort of pyramid scheme.

Aguilera: So using the informants, the ease of it, the lack of transparency, lack of accountability, the fact that it’s used nine out 10 times, do you think it’s crowding out other, maybe more ethical ways of combating drug trafficking?

Ryan: These are hard cases to make. Another method is undercover work.

One of the people that we interviewed down in Florida is a lawyer who helped write confidential informant law down there that was passed. He doesn’t call them informants.

What’s the word he uses?

Arnett: Civilian operatives.

He was a great quote. One of my favorites was like, “We don’t trust civilians to direct traffic at a football game, yet we’re going to send them into some of the most dangerous places in any given city alone without protection to do the work of police.”

Aguilera: Right. Your show does a great job of outlining the ways that this system can be problematic, but are there ways that it does actually work?

Ryan: It certainly is a successful way to get a search warrant approved, that the record shows undoubtedly. A search warrant is issued, and then police have to file it back to the court and file what’s called a return and a return lists exactly what was taken.

We spent a lot of time looking at returns. And sometimes they got stuff, other times not so much, sometimes nothing at all. But what gets lost is it’s not like there’s any public keeping of a scorecard for an informant. All informants are referred to as reliable, which is important for legal reasons, but by and large, there’s not a whole lot of measure of that reliability.

And you know, we’ve done our best to try to trace individual informants in their different cases. And sometimes they’re right, sometimes they’re wrong, but it doesn’t mean that they don’t get used in the next one.

Arnett: One of the most interesting conversations I had in this whole process was with a one-time informant in New Bedford. He was essentially a mid-level drug dealer.

What he says he did was he would, in exchange for being able to deal drugs with impunity and not be hassled by the police, he would set up lower level dealers. So he would essentially drop off drugs, let his police handler know this is where the drugs are gonna be, and within hours police would be there, raiding the house.

Now the problem with that is that. In any normal definition of the war on drugs, you clearly wanna be going up the food chain. You want to be flipping a dealer for a supplier. But this was like the opposite way.

What this guy was describing is essentially allowing the drug war or allowing drug dealing to keep going. What the police are getting out of this is that they’re making sizable, significant busts that look good on paper that allow them to hold press conferences and put out press releases saying, “Hey, look at what we’re doing.”

When in actuality, nothing is really happening.

Aguilera: I’m struck here. You say so yourself in the podcast that the informants broke the law. It’s not like they’re innocent people completely.

And there are some people you name in your stories, who say that the informants are not credible sources, and yet the police themselves say that they’re reliable. They have to legally.

How do you square that?

Arnett: It’s a great irony, and Andrew and I have talked about this quite a bit.

Ryan: As we mentioned, we read a ton of search warrants in New Bedford, in particular. A lot of these warrants look like cut and paste jobs. They just fill in the names and some specifics.

One of the lines that was in warrant after warrant is always “I know this person is credible or reliable because they acknowledge to me that they’re involved in criminal activity.”

It’s basically saying, “I know they’re trustworthy because they’re criminals, and so therefore I can trust their word in this search warrant.”

Aguilera: And yet they turn around and look at this reporting and say, you can’t trust those people.

Correct?

Ryan: Correct.

Arnett: Correct. Some of the same criminals that they’re blaming us for relying upon, are the same ones that they would rely upon to obtain the search warrants that allow them to do their jobs.

Ryan: Just because of television, police shows, you see search warrants all the time. But a search warrant’s a big deal.

It allows law enforcement to set aside part of the Bill of Rights. The right against unwanted search and seizure is a big deal in this country, or it should be.

Aguilera: Yeah, you gotta bug a judge to sign a document for that. It’s not easy.

Ryan: Or a clerk magistrate.

Aguilera: Or a clerk magistrate.

There are other cases that have happened over the years, where nonviolent drug offenders or first time offenders, the kind of people who aren’t usually in the system, get coerced into becoming informants.

There’s a case like Rachel Hoffman in Florida, who was arrested for possession of marijuana and ecstasy back in 2008, and while she was trying to do a controlled buy-with-a-wire, she was discovered and ultimately killed.

If something like that, a beautiful college student with practically no priors, not somebody who’s in this drug world, can get caught up like this, if something this obvious doesn’t stop or reform the system, will anything?

Arnett: That’s a great question.

Ryan: We drove down the road where her body was found outside Tallahassee. I think there’s change anytime you have things that trigger laws to be named after people.

In Florida, they passed something called Rachel’s Law, which isn’t perfect, but it put some protections in place. It included that police have to keep in mind the safety of the informant. The informant can access a lawyer if requested.

In California, it was Chad’s Law, which sets up some kind of age restrictions around the use of informants.

But there have been tragedies here in Massachusetts. In February of 1988, there was a drug raid at an apartment in Dorchester that was based on a confidential informant that ended up not existing, and a police officer was killed.

I mean, Boston was also home to Whitey Bulger, who served as an informant for the FBI. And obviously we now know that he was playing both sides and lots of people were hurt and killed because of that.

Aguilera: And yet, despite those cases, we don’t have laws here in Massachusetts, at all, protecting informants.

Arnett: No.

You think about the case at University of Massachusetts Amherst where there was a college student who was caught with some drugs and was recruited to become an informant. The university didn’t tell his parents, it was kept hush hush. And he ended up dying of an overdose while working as an informant.

The university did stop the use of students as informants, but there was no triggering of any sort of larger look at the informant system in Massachusetts, who they were using as informants, that sort of thing.

Aguilera: So you say at the beginning of your podcast that no one in the system wants the information to get out.

Certainly not the police, but also the informants themselves. Andrew, how do you report on a policing system that is by its very nature a secret?

Ryan: That’s a great question. We try to use all the different tools that we have as reporters. We file a lot of records requests, and quite frankly, a lot of those get ignored, particularly here in Boston.

We work our own sources. We dig through court records. We talk to people on the street.

It often feels like you’re building a little bit of a brick wall and you take a piece from here, a piece from there, but it’s never one thing. Often it’s a series of things, and sometimes you’ll get some breakthrough person who has firsthand knowledge of something or some document that kind of lays some things out.

But it ends up being this kind of tedious process of slowly building the foundation.

Aguilera: Dugan, I had this thought while I was listening to an episode. One of the people featured in your reporting is a man you called Daniel, who was himself a confidential informant. He’s now in jail for unrelated crimes, but he’s extremely scared that his identity as a CI will get out and he’ll be hurt or killed in jail.

He literally calls you crying for help at one point.

“Snitch City” (clip): Daniel: “I’m so stressed out, Dugan. Man. I mean, you’re the only number I can call. I’m so stressed out.” Dugan: “Can you tell me what’s going on?” Daniel: “Hello?” Dugan: “Can you hear me? Daniel: “Can you hear me, Dougie?”

Aguilera: I know you used a voice actor to portray him, but I guess there are enough details about him that somebody who really wants to know about this community and try to figure it out could probably get pretty far doing that.

Do you worry about your responsibility in protecting him?

Arnett: Yeah, that’s a really good question. We had lots and lots and lots of conversations about how to protect him in every way possible, while maintaining the broad strokes of the story. These conversations, a lot of times, went up until publication.

We asked, “Are there certain details that we can take out, that we can vague up, that we can leave out?” All of this was in an effort to make it as difficult as possible for anyone who doesn’t already know his story, which there are some that do, to sort of limit that.

Aguilera: What would you say to somebody if you were trying to convince them to talk to you, who was scared about how vulnerable it would make them?

Arnett: Well, there were a lot of conversations like that in this story. The nature of it is so sensitive and there’s risks involved on all sides.

The pitch usually was, “Here’s why we think that your story is important.”

And with Daniel, there was a lot of stuff in documents that sort of laid out that story, but by hearing from him and from some other informants who will appear later in the podcast, the hope was that this humanizes these people.

It’s one thing to hear the word confidential informant and brush that off. Hearing how this system has impacted and affected people, on a daily basis in their current lives, is something that hopefully makes people, listeners, readers, and lawmakers think a little bit harder about this system and what it’s doing and if it’s doing it the right way.

Aguilera: Since all of this reporting has come to light, have you had any response from the Police Department of New Bedford or City of New Bedford?

Ryan: Dugan began digging into this story in 2022. He first requested an interview with the New Bedford Police Chief regarding their use of confidential informants on August 10th, 2022, which is 974 days ago [number updated to reflect publication date].

As we reported this story, and then prepared to publish, we requested interviews with the mayor, police chief, and several police officers. We sent them emails, we knocked on the doors of their homes. Dugan and I showed up in the mayor’s office in New Bedford when they didn’t respond, saying, ‘We’d like to see the mayor now, please.’ And they said he was there, but he wouldn’t see us.

And they released a series of short statements leading up to publication. Then after we published, they posted. It was a series of point by point rebuttals on the city’s website.

Now we’ve gone through that because we take all these things really seriously. I mean, accuracy is our main thing, and what we found was that much of what they said was already included in our reporting or wrong.

They claimed that they had given us a document, which they hadn’t given us. They’ve subsequently given it to us, and it backed up our reporting.

So they have not engaged with us directly, despite us trying to sit down to talk to them about this issue again, going back 974 days.

They have put word out on their own, and that’s fine, but we would still love to sit down with the mayor and talk to the mayor about this. We would love to sit down with the police chief and talk to the police chief about this. We’d love to sit down with all the police officers that we called, and that we emailed and talked to them about this system because it matters.

Aguilera: And last question, I’m going to start with you Andrew, and then go to you Dugan, but the same question. Do you have any hope that this reporting will lead to some changes in the police use of informants in Massachusetts?

Ryan: I hope so, but I’m not optimistic.

Aguilera: What about you Dugan?

Arnett: I’d say the same. Again, so many things had to sort of go right in order to pierce this veil of secrecy in New Bedford. In New Bedford, I think if you listen to the podcast or read the series, it’s sort of a poster child for informant abuse and how easy it is to manipulate that system.

It’s just hard for me to imagine, especially based on what the city has said in response to the coverage that they’ll take this seriously in any real way and give it an honest look.

Ryan: One thing I would add, is that we do have more coming. We have more stories that we’re pushing towards publication, not just about New Bedford, but about places across the state. So there’s definitely more that we’re gonna report about this.

But, also, I understand the use of confidential informants and I understand why they can be such an important tool. What I don’t understand is anything that operates entirely contained by one agency, shrouded in complete secrecy.

I think there’s a way that you can be transparent and you can be fair, and you can put checks and balances and controls in the system. And still protect people who provide information.

Aguilera: Dugan Arnett and Andrew Ryan are investigative reporters for the Globe Spotlight Team.

Listen to more “Say More” episodes at globe.com/saymore and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: ‘I’m very appalled’: In wake of her guilty plea, constituents express disgust, sadness at Tania Fernandes Anderson
text:
As the District 7 councilor, Fernandes Anderson represents some of the most historically diverse neighborhoods in Boston, including Roxbury, Dorchester, part of the South End, and the Fenway. Thomas-Jones felt Fernandes Anderson, as her council representative, was doing good work to improve her Roxbury neighborhood.

Now, Fernandes Anderson no longer has her support.

Thomas-Jones is far from the only resident in Fernandes Anderson’s district who is grappling with a range of emotions in the wake of the news the councilor agreed to plead guilty to two of the six federal corruption charges against her.

In a series of interviews in Fernandes Anderson’s district last week, residents and business owners expressed deep sadness, cynicism, and disappointment at the news, which was still reverberating throughout the district.

“You’re here to serve the people, not serve your purpose,” Thomas-Jones said. “To get a kickback from somebody? No, that’s not how we do things, and it’s a bad representation of the Black community. ... I’m very appalled at her behavior.”

Fernandes Anderson announced on April 8 she plans to step down, but has not officially done so, saying she is working on a transition plan to ensure stability for her constituents. Vacating her seat would leave the district without a designated elected advocate during budget season. Though some in the district said a vacant seat is preferable to Fernandes Anderson continuing to receive a taxpayer-funded salary after pleading guilty to federal crimes.

According to the city charter, if a district councilor formally resigns from their position more than 180 days before the next municipal election, a special election will be held. This year, that deadline is May 8.

Marijke Simmons, a 56-year-old born and raised Bostonian and District 7 resident, said she also had been cautious to believe the allegations against Fernandes Anderson when they were announced in December, arguing that everyone has the right to due process. But now that Fernandes Anderson has agreed to plead guilty, Simmons’ mind is made up.

“I don’t like thieves, period. That’s what it comes down to. ... [I’m] very disappointed,” Simmons said.

Simmons had felt hopeful when Fernandes Anderson ran for office, and voted for her, believing she could make a difference. Now, that trust is gone, she said.

“She hit financial trouble, and she said, ‘Oh, let me steal from the people who need me,’ ” Simmons said. “When you tell me who you are, I believe you. You told me you were guilty, you told me you were sorry. OK, go away and let somebody else do a better job.”

For Sandra Younge, Fernandes Anderson’s corruption case only confirmed the deep cynicism she has toward local elected officials.

Younge, a 65-year-old retiree who previously worked as a special education assistant in Boston Public Schools, grew up in Roxbury and now lives in Dorchester. She remembers being glad Fernandes Anderson was running for office and was pleased when she won.

But as she watched the developments in Fernandes Anderson’s case play out in recent months, she said she had a familiar feeling.

“My first reaction was, ‘Here we go again,’ ” Younge said. “Who do we trust? You know, she’s supposed to look out for the community, and she’s doing nothing but ripping us off.”

“She’s not the first, not gonna be the last, and whoever dropped the dime on her [is] probably doing the same damn thing, it’s just that they didn’t get caught,” she continued.

Longtime Mattapan resident Danny Hardaway expressed sympathy. As a Muslim man who owns a business in Fernandes Anderson’s district in Nubian Square, Hardaway said he was incredibly proud of her when she was elected.

Signing the plea deal is “probably the best thing for her at this point in time,” Hardaway said. But “She represents the community … and a lot of our people, constituents, I should say, looked up to her as a leader, and to see one of the leaders go through this, it’s a sad day.”

TiElla Grimes — a 38-year-old small business owner, lifelong Boston resident, and current District 7 constituent — said she feels Fernandes Anderson’s plea agreement and pledge to resign are the first steps toward redemption.

“It’s unfortunate, it was wrong. However, it’s a system of politics that has always done that: Some people get caught, some people don’t,” Grimes said. “If you can take accountability for where you went wrong, I feel like that is a start in being able to repair some of the harm that you’ve done.”

title: ‘I remember, I reclaim, I restore, I reimagine’
text:
All of her work is reparative, but the art most of all.

“We were disconnected by a continent and moved,” she said of Black Americans. “That middle passage didn’t stop our DNA. It did not stop our relocation of culture. I’m always trying to put the parts back together, to re-member them.”

As the federal government targets Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiatives and cultural organizations such as the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, she is clear-eyed.

“This is another cycle for me,” Frazier said. “It’s an ongoing struggle since 1492.”

Where to find her: www.lmerchiefrazier.org

Age: When asked her age, Frazier said “We don’t do that.”

“It’s not because I’m ashamed of my age. It’s because you get put in these categories where people don’t see you anymore,” she said. “Excuse me. Probably I can work circles around certain people who are young.”

Originally from: Jacksonville, Fla.

Lives in: Dorchester

Making a living: “I work as a matter of life subsistence and to feed my art,” she said.

Studio: Frazier has been a resident artist with Northeastern University’s African American Master Artists-in-Residency Program for more than two decades. Her quilts hang on the walls in her large space in AAMARP’s Jamaica Plain studio building. She describes the overhead lights as “minimal,” and keeps her big sewing machines at home. Her living room and dining room, she said, “are a one-person sweatshop.”

How she started: “My grandfather was a tailor in the hills of West Virginia,” the artist said. “My mom followed in his footsteps.”

“She just was a genius,” Frazier said. “She could master woodwork, anything that came in front of her. She was like her dad. That’s the legacy I represent.”

What she makes: Quilts in Frazier’s studio depict people like 19th-century abolitionist, suffragist, and public speaker Frances Ellen Watkins Harper and Ethiopian activist Lale Labuko; they relate stories of racial violence, oppression, and the struggle for civil rights. Shimmering layers of nylon let light pass through and suggest the porousness of time — a technique she developed after learning holography.

“I remember, I reclaim, I restore, I reimagine,” Frazier said. “That’s my life work.”

How she works: “Check me out at two o’clock, three o’clock in the morning,” she said. “I have ancestors and some kind of angels visiting me in my sleep, and I get up and do something.”

Question for artists: “Are you firm in your stance as a human being?” she asked. “Then everything else will flow.”

title: Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune moves to bypass special election process if Fernandes Anderson resigns
text:
But Louijeune and her council colleague Liz Breadon on Monday announced they plan to file a home rule petition to cancel that process, after hearing concerns about turnout and public awareness from elected officials and community leaders in Fernandes Anderson’s district.

The home rule petition would also allow the winner of the race for Fernandes Anderson’s seat in the November election to assume the role as soon as officials certify the election results rather than waiting until the start of the new year, according to a press release from the two councilors.

The councilors also noted that the state’s Supreme Judicial Court has previously ruled that the council does not have the power to remove a councilor from office unless they have been sentenced for a crime, which has not happened yet in Fernandes Anderson’s case.

If Fernandes Anderson does resign, and the council and Beacon Hill approve Louijeune and Breadon’s proposal, that would leave Fernandes Anderson’s seat vacant until November.

“It is our collective responsibility to ensure that every voice in our community is acknowledged and represented,” Louijeune said in a statement Monday. “Given the accelerated timeline, the risk of excluding residents from the process is significant. With the general election approaching later this year, it would be inequitable to ask the public to participate in such a hastened process that will leave voices out.”

Breadon said in a statement that she’s heard from residents in Fernandes Anderson’s district who worry about whether a special election would be in “the best interests of public awareness, civic engagement, or the effective administration of our municipal elections.” She called forgoing the special election “the responsible course of action.”

As the District 7 councilor, Fernandes Anderson represents some of the most historically diverse neighborhoods in Boston, including Roxbury, Dorchester, part of the South End, and the Fenway.

Councilor Erin Murphy pointed to the past marginalization of those neighborhoods as a reason for the city to hold a special election to replace Fernandes Anderson as soon as possible.

But Louijeune and Breadon emphasized that Secretary of State William F. Galvin also opposes a special election in the city in such a tight timeframe. Galvin took the city’s elections department under state oversight earlier this year after reports of a variety of problems during last November’s election, including widespread ballot shortages and communication failures.

In a phone interview with the Globe Monday, Galvin called the idea of holding a special election for Fernandes Anderson’s seat “particularly ridiculous,” arguing it would compromise the efforts to fix the issues the city’s elections department experienced last year. He also said a special election this summer would likely come after the council votes on the budget for the next fiscal year, and the body does not historically meet much in July or August.

“The representation gained is, I think, very limited,” Galvin said. “The cost in terms of potential lost opportunity to correct the bigger problem is greater, and obviously the cost in terms of confusion is greater. ... There’s no good reason to do it, it’s a bad idea.”

Several District 7 residents, community advocates, and other elected officials, including state Senator Liz Miranda and state Representatives Chynah Tyler, John Moran, and Christopher Worrell, also said they support bypassing a special election.

Emma Pettit, a spokesperson for Wu’s office, said in a statement the city’s elections department is ready to hold a special election, but the mayor will review any legislation the council passes, and has directed more staff to help District 7 constituents maintain access to services.

The last time the city held a special election was during the summer of 2023, when Sharon Durkan won the race to replace former Councilor Kenzie Bok after Mayor Michelle Wu appointed Bok to lead the Boston Housing Authority.

Fernandes Anderson did not immediately return the Globe’s request for comment.

At least five candidates so far have filed paperwork with the state to run to replace Fernandes Anderson on the council — Said Abdikarim, Said Ahmed, Mavrick Afonso, Tchad Cort, and Samuel Hurtado.

Federal authorities arrested Fernandes Anderson in December on federal wire fraud and theft charges. Prosecutors allege she paid a staff member, who was also a relative, a $13,000 bonus and later pocketed $7,000 of it as a kickback. Fernandes Anderson initially pled not guilty to the charges.

Last week, she announced she signed a plea agreement and will plead guilty to two of the six federal corruption charges against her, and intends to resign. Fernandes Anderson will appear in federal court for her plea hearing on May 5.

title: A legacy of love: New sports center honors Boston Marathon bombing victim Martin Richard
text:
But it is also a family’s way of honoring the spirit of 8-year-old Martin, who was killed by a terrorist’s bomb at the finish line of the 2013 Boston Marathon, becoming a face of one of Boston’s greatest tragedies. Bill Richard says this project connects him to Martin’s tenacious but kind spirit.

“It makes our family feel that we continue to fight for him and build a legacy for him,” Richard said. “This type of work keeps me going.”

The Fieldhouse+ is a project that has been years in the making. The parcel is leased from the Boston Public Schools. The project ran into some community opposition, partly because it is in a neighborhood soon to be transformed by new development that is making some residents anxious.

Years of design changes, many of them suggested by the neighborhood youth the program will eventually serve, made the project more elaborate — and more expensive. But with $43 million already raised, and strong support from political and philanthropic leaders, it’s time to begin construction.

“We have a pathway we see to the goal of $70 million,” said Bob Scannell, the longtime head of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester, which will manage the facility. “And that’s why we’re ready to go in.”

After Martin’s death, the Richard family quickly turned to philanthropy, selflessly turning their loss into a catalyst for helping others. To date, the Martin Richard Foundation has donated $10 million to worthy causes across the region. It fielded a team of runners in the Marathon for a decade, until Bill and Denise Richard decided to wind down that effort a couple of years ago.

But the family’s lives will be forever linked to the Marathon.

It’s jarring to think that Martin Richard — forever frozen in memory as a joyous and peace-loving child — would be 20 now.

Martin’s older brother, Henry, now 23, will be running the Marathon for the fourth time Monday.

The Richard family was deeply scarred, literally, by that bombing. Both Martin’s mother, Denise, and his sister, Jane, then just 7, suffered serious permanent injuries in the bombing. Denise lost vision in one eye, while Jane lost one of her legs.

But to call this family resilient would be a huge understatement.

Henry is graduating soon from Pace University in New York City and hoping to settle, at least for a while, in New York. The bombing — and its huge public significance — gave him a prominence he never asked for.

“Henry appreciates being recognized (in Boston).” Bill said. “But I think he also appreciates disappearing in New York City and trying to figure out what the start of his future is going to look like.”

Jane is 19 and a freshman at Skidmore College in upstate New York. She’s interested in theater and writing, and hosts a weekly show on the campus radio station called “Jane Says.”

“Moving away is a big step, and it’s always a bit of a roll of the dice,” Bill said, sounding like many an anxious college parent. “But she’s having a great first year.”

And Martin is memorialized in many places. There is Martin Richard Park in the Seaport, of course. And there’s also a statue of him at Bridgewater State College, the alma mater of both of his parents. It’s been there five years, and over time Bill has noticed a change when he and Denise visit campus.

Incoming students now have to be told who Martin is. Preschoolers in 2013, they only vaguely know the story of the Boston Marathon bombing.

April is a fraught time, always, for the Richard family. They are showered with kindness from friends and strangers, but also deluged with memories. It is the month that forever redefined their lives.

But Marathon Day has also become the day they get to celebrate the resilience of Martin’s siblings, cheering Henry as he makes the turn onto Boylston Street.

“They could have been frightened, or they could have been just triggered,” Richard said. “Knowing that he’s out there and coming down Boylston Street and running by the spot where you know, his life turned upside down, it just you know, it reinforced the idea that maybe we did a few things right as parents.

“It takes your breath away. So as much as I would rather maybe be elsewhere, as long as he does it, we’re going to be there watching him.”

title: Veo Robert is staging pop-up dinners to test the area’s appetite for the dishes of his native Laos
text:
“It’s hard not to get choked up when I see that I’m putting the food out there that I might not have been proud of, like 10-15 years ago, and people are enjoying it,” Robert says. “And I don’t have to keep asking them: Is this too spicy? Is this too funky?” Another plus: “I get to cook with some of my chef friends.”

On hand to help Robert are some of the region’s Asian culinary standouts who are also doing their own pop-ups: Laurence Louie of Rubato in Quincy, Ashley Lujares of Mango Tao Yum and a Food Network Chopped champion, Peter Nguyen of Lê Madeline in Quincy, and Thanaphon “Song” Authaiphan of Merai and nearby Mahaniyom, both in Brookline. The friendships have been nurtured over Robert’s years working at Radius, Myers+Chang, Menton, Bar Mezzana, Shore Leave, and other restaurants.

“We have found our tribe,” says Lujares, who worked with Robert at Myers+Chang and specializes in Filipino dishes. “We’re all Asian Americans and in the industry. [A pop-up] is our way to cook our food and help each other out. And, also, time to hang out again in a happy setting and having fun.”

Pop-ups have become increasingly prevalent since the pandemic. A Yelp June 2024 study found pop-ups were up a whopping 155 percent between May 2023 and April 2024 from the previous year. The study said pop-ups have “continued to see the most significant growth as restaurateurs debuted new temporary concepts with limited menus to test diners’ interest.”

Pop-ups are comparable to the tech practice of studying the “minimum viable product” to determine what people want to get their hands on before a larger investment is made, says Trish Fontanilla, a Boston community and experience consultant and self-described “lover of all foods” who attended the Rubato event. “If you do the data correctly, you can [quickly] find out what works,” she says.

Robert says the impetus for his pop-up is to bring attention to Lao food and culture. He’s been cooking other people’s food since he was 14. He got his start in his aunt’s restaurant, the Thai Star in Providence, after his family emigrated from Laos following his dad’s death. The fact that Robert’s Laotian family began a Thai restaurant, rather than cooking culturally closer to home, is not uncommon among the Asian diaspora.

While 12 percent of all US restaurants serve Asian food, seven out of 10 focus on Japanese, Chinese, or Thai cuisines, according to a May 2023 Pew Research Center report. The Pew Center says those groups constitute only 33 percent of the entire US Asian population of more than 24 million. Laotians, meanwhile, represent just under 5 percent of the total US Asian population in 2023, per USA Facts. (The largest Laotian communities in New England are in Middlesex County and Providence, according to US Census data.)

Robert’s journey away from fine dining coincided with the 2020 COVID outbreak that led to restrictions on restaurant service. He was nearing 40 years old and evaluating his life. His wife — Carla Cornejo, who is a restaurant consultant and cofounder of Prepshift with Irene Li of Mei Mei — urged Robert to revisit his native country.

Last December, Robert went to his parents’ hometown of Luang Prabang in Northern Laos. He also learned, in conversations with his mom, to fully embrace the value of Lao hospitality. “We have a word for it: ‘liang.’ It literally means to feed or to nurture, but it’s so much more than that,’ he says. “It’s an obligation to make guests feel welcome and at home.”

That hospitality ethos shone at the Rubato event, says Fontanilla. She applauds Robert for talking to guests, welcoming feedback about his food, and for his social media posts. “These days, getting back to the simplicity in food is a differentiator” in dining, Fontanilla says. “If people don’t like the food, it doesn’t matter how velvety your chairs are; nothing else will save it.”

Lujares believes the pop-up approach has served Robert well. “I’ve known Veo for a very long time, but I’ve seen a change in him and even in his food,” she says. “He’s happier as a person right now.

“I know he was nervous cooking his food. Being an Asian-American, you have to find Asian identity and your American identity. He struggled with that. I think that’s why we all relate. I told him: ‘I didn’t know you cooked like this. You did a good job, bro!’”

Robert hopes to find a permanent home for his concept. But, he says, “If Phaeng & Phiu does not end up in a brick-and-mortar restaurant, but I get you beginning to talk more about Lao food in Boston, that would make me really, really happy.”

Check the Phaeng & Phiu Instagram account for information about pop-ups: www.instagram.com/phaengandphiu. Tickets to the pop-up at Comfort Kitchen can be purchased here, at www.opentable.com/r/comfort-kitchen-boston.

title: The politics of representation and belonging in Roxbury
text:
The district includes iconic Black strongholds like Roxbury but also parts of Dorchester, the South End, and the Fenway. Of the roughly 78,000 people who live there, about 25,000 are Black, 20,000 Hispanic, and another 20,000 white, according to Census Reporter, an independent US Census Bureau data visualization platform.

The area’s council seat is opening up because the incumbent, Tania Fernandes Anderson, has pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges and has said she will resign.

According to paperwork filed with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance, there are now at least six candidates seeking to take her place: Said Abdikarim and Said Ahmed, both Somali immigrants who came to the United States as children and declared their intentions to challenge Fernandes Anderson last year; Hurtado; Mavrick Afonso, a Cabo Verdean American who works for Governor Maura Healey’s administration on housing policy; Tchad Cort, a Black woman born and raised in Roxbury who works for the Boston Public Schools transportation department, according to her website; and Miniard Culpepper, a well-known Roxbury pastor who ran for state Senate in 2022.

Hurtado, who works now as the business manager for the city’s supplier diversity department, told me he’s not running as a Latino candidate but rather as someone who wants to represent everybody. In the early 2000s he created South Boston en Acción, a nonprofit to help public housing residents advocate for tenant rights and education access.

First as Janey’s chief of staff when she was the District Seven councilor and then as a senior adviser when she was interim mayor, Hurtado got to know city government. As highlights of his time there, Hurtado mentioned constituent services, working on the cannabis ordinance that Janey authored, and securing funding for the Malcolm X Park, which, Hurtado said, “was the first park that included goals to utilize minority women subcontractors.” (Janey contributed $500 to Hurtado’s campaign, one of the first individuals to do so, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment for this column.)

“This race will be a huge statement if I can build a coalition that’s truly representative of all parts of this district — new voices, people who haven’t been heard, who don’t feel hopeful about change,” Hurtado said.

Still, it took years for Black leaders in Boston to acquire the political power that they have, and the onus will be on Hurtado to prove that his election would be a new chapter in that history — not a retreat from it.

Not that any of the candidates starts off a clear favorite. As wide and multiethnic as the field of contenders is, Jacquetta Van Zandt, a political strategist and host of the “Politics and Prosecco” online show, is not impressed. “There are really no formidable candidates who have had enough of a history in politics to really bring about change,” Van Zandt, who is a homeowner in the district, told me. “A lot of times these community advocates think that they can come with the same kind of piss and vinegar that they bring to the streets and bring that into City Hall, and I think that’s what we’re seeing now.”

Van Zandt said this district is “very mistrustful” because it’s “often the first sought out for votes but the last to get resources.” That’s the reason why the district has some of the lowest voter turnout rates in Boston municipal elections. She said she’s afraid the race will turn into ”just a bunch of community activists screaming and shouting and trying to out community each other, instead of actually talking about governing and what that looks like and what could help this district.”

Hurtado’s candidacy challenges the notion that political representation in District Seven must come only from within the Black community, even as he insists he isn’t running as a Latino candidate. The question is whether he can convince voters to give him a chance.

Correction: An earlier version of this column mischaracterized Samuel Hurtado’s two roles working for former mayor Kim Janey. Hurtado was Janey’s chief of staff when she was the District Seven councilor and senior adviser when Janey was interim mayor.

title: Top Spots to Live in Boston and Cambridge 2025
text:
Median home price: $658,331

Increase since 2019: 42.2%

Pat Tierney moved to Hyde Park for the space. After growing up in densely packed South Boston, she was delighted to find a home in Boston that had a sizable lawn and even horses grazing across the street. In the half-century since she arrived, the horses have gone, but the appeal of the neighborhood’s tree-shaded lots remains, says Tierney, an agent with Insight Realty Group.

“You have bigger yards here” compared with some other parts of Boston, she says. “It’s a more suburban, country feel.”

There’s plenty more to love about Hyde Park as well. Two commuter rail lines and proximity to the Red Line make it easy to get into the heart of the city for work or entertainment, while restaurants, shops, Roundhead Brewing Co., and the thriving Menino Arts Center all make it easy to stay in the neighborhood. An indoor sports complex hosts soccer games and pickleball matches, a well-regarded golf course welcomes the public, and the nearby Neponset River offers opportunities for canoeing and kayaking.

Hyde Park’s housing stock includes many single-family, detached homes — some updated, some in need of a little TLC — and a smaller number of condos, mostly located in renovated houses. The area is also home to Boston’s first LGBTQ, affordable senior housing complex, The Pryde.

Word seems to be getting out about the appeal of the once-overlooked neighborhood. Sales were up last year over 2023, and Tierney sees a wide range of buyers, from city employees and teachers to young professionals, drawn to a rare, relatively affordable area. “Everyone is coming in,” she says.

Median home price: $741,710

Increase since 2019: 37.5%

Roslindale has everything that makes for a vibrant neighborhood: thriving local businesses and eateries, cultural diversity, and plenty of outdoors spaces where the community can connect. Yet it remains something of a hidden gem, with less buzz than some other areas, and condos and some single-family homes still available at comparatively accessible prices by Boston standards.

Median home price: $712,483

Increase since 2019: 27.4%

Boston’s largest neighborhood, culturally rich Dorchester has shaken off much of its past reputation as an unsafe place. Today it offers a diversity of people, places, and price points that make it a dynamic and compelling place to live (and eat — the City of Boston lists more than 200 restaurants in the neighborhood).

Median home price: $993,400

Increase since 2019: 28.6%

Aileen Gorman, 43, has never considered moving out of Charlestown. She grew up in the waterfront Boston neighborhood, made her First Communion and attended school there. When it came time to start her own family, she wanted to raise her children in the walkable, welcoming community she says is unfailingly supportive of its residents, old and new.

“Family and community and a sense of pride are very much part of the makeup of Charlestown,” says Gorman, who volunteers with several local organizations. “We all just take care of each other.”

Boston’s oldest neighborhood, Charlestown is tucked into the corner of Interstate 93 and Route 1. The area’s deep history is evident in ways both big (the 221-foot-tall Bunker Hill Monument) and small (cobblestones and gas street lamps), but the community has not remained stagnant. Once an enclave of working class, Irish-American families, new residents have been renovating traditional red-brick row houses and helping attract a mix of independent businesses and restaurants. Today, the market is dominated by condos and a few single-family homes with prices north of $1 million, though smaller units — and even the occasional houseboat — can be found for less.

Even as Charlestown changes, Gorman says, she has every intention of sticking around for whatever comes next.

“There’s no replicating what we have here,” she says. “Why leave?”

Median home price: $764,463

Increase since 2019: 28.5%

West Roxbury combines the tree-lined streets, grassy lawns, and community vibe of the suburbs with the urban energy and walkable stores and restaurants of the city. That makes it hard to beat. Housing options include single-family homes and condos in renovated houses and newer developments, many with price tags lower than $800,000 (some even come in under $500,000, though they tend to move fast).

Median home price: $801,556

Increase since 2019: 22.7%

Even as home prices have increased in JP, the neighborhood has so far managed to hang on to its bohemian reputation with its annual Porchfest music event, strong arts community, and significant LGBTQ population. It is also home to iconic green spaces, including Jamaica Pond and the Arnold Arboretum, Frederick Law Olmsted’s iconic 281-acre preserve.

Median home price: $1,400,786

Increase since 2019: 70.1%

Even Boston locals would be forgiven for not knowing the exact boundaries of Cambridge’s Riverside neighborhood. The diminutive, densely packed district along the Charles River largely comprises parts of what are otherwise known as Harvard Square and Central Square, as well as a web of smaller residential roads.

Whatever you call it, however, there is no confusion that it is one of the most in-demand areas in Cambridge, with median home prices soaring more than 70 percent over the past five years. Real estate agent Charles Cherney, of Compass, recalls a single-family home recently listed for nearly $1.9 million that quickly garnered multiple offers.

“There are a handful of residential streets and a few lucky people who call this neighborhood home,” Cherney says.

The appeal of the area has a lot to do with the proximity to Harvard Square, Harvard University, and the businesses and restaurants along Massachusetts Avenue, Cherney says. It is also an attractive spot for families, with several well-kept parks and playgrounds scattered throughout, as well as one of the city’s most highly-rated elementary schools, the Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. School.

The future of the neighborhood is less clear. A recent city vote will allow four-story homes to be built on residential properties without special permits or variances, with six stories permitted on some lots, as long as they include affordable housing. Whether this density increase will change the popularity of Riverside — or simply create more of it to love — remains to be seen.

“It will be fascinating to see how it plays out,” Cherney says.

Median single-family price: $1,862,594

Increase since 2019: 52.2%

Downtown Boston conjures images of office buildings and parking garages, it’s true. But the business-oriented district has been popular with home buyers drawn to the neighborhood’s central location and the stunning views and luxury amenities offered by the high end condos that generally dominate the market.

Median single-family price: $1,523,781

Increase since 2019: 46.9%

The appeals of Cambridgeport are numerous: elegant houses, the waterfront beauty of Magazine Beach Park, and easy access to the food, culture, and shopping of both Boston and Cambridge. Would-be residents will have to be patient and willing to pay. There are rarely many listings in the neighborhood and they come with hefty price tags. But what around here doesn’t?

West of Boston

North of Boston

South of Boston

Methodology: To arrive at this annual list, we relied on the finite — but meaningful — wisdom of supply and demand: Significantly increasing prices in these communities are a signal that many buyers are eager to call them home. We analyzed median home prices from 2019 and 2024 to find the biggest five-year increases across three price tiers for each region. In the Boston suburbs, we looked at single-family data from The Warren Group, excluding communities with fewer than 50 sales in 2024. For Boston and Cambridge neighborhoods, we used median home price data — including both single-family and condo sales — from Redfin. Three journalists with real estate expertise collaborated to select our “May We Suggest” entries, our admittedly subjective picks of communities to consider.

title: The Globe investigated a Zionist group that claims credit for Trump’s efforts to deport students. Here are 5 takeaways.
text:
Send questions or suggestions to the Starting Point team at startingpoint@globe.com. If you’d like the newsletter sent to your inbox, sign up here.

You’ve probably heard that the Trump administration has revoked the visas of hundreds of international students studying in the US, including scores in New England. Immigration agents have also detained and sought to deport several, including a Tufts PhD student and a Columbia student arrested this week in Vermont.

What you may not have heard is that the administration seems to have had help.

A handful of pro-Israel groups are publicly taking credit for some of the government’s recent arrests. One such group is Betar, a century-old Zionist organization whose mantra is “Jews Fight Back.” In recent months, Betar’s US branch has compiled a list of allegedly pro-Palestinian students it believes the administration should deport.

My colleagues on the Globe’s Spotlight team have just published an investigation into Betar’s work. Here are five takeaways.

Betar isn’t new to this. Last fall, it criticized prosecutors in Newton for charging a supporter of Israel who shot a pro-Palestinian man at a rally there, urging businesses to boycott the city. Yet Betar’s influence was limited. The Newton boycott fizzled, and local officials considered the group “very fringe.”

President Trump’s inauguration, however, seems to have given it new reach. An attorney for Rümeysa Öztürk, the Tufts PhD student detained last month, said that Betar and groups like it were once seen as “gadflies.” Now, he and other lawyers for targeted students believe the administration is “more than willing to act on the information” Betar provides.

That information came in the form of a list of dozens of allegedly pro-Palestinian students that Betar says it gave to the Trump administration. According to the group, the students’ offenses include pro-Hamas advocacy, as well as jaywalking and a noise complaint.

So far, the administration has targeted at least seven of the people Betar listed, including Öztürk and Mohsen Mahdawi, the Columbia student immigration officials arrested in Vermont this week.

While Betar wouldn’t give the Globe a copy of its list, my colleagues found a version briefly posted on the group’s website. It featured the names, photos, and descriptions of 77 people.

Some of Betar’s entries, however, appear to be completely wrong. In one case, the group listed the name and photo of a woman wearing a hijab, identifying her as a Nigerian Harvard student who spoke at a pro-Hamas rally. Contacted by the Globe, the woman said she’s never visited the US, attended Harvard, or been to a pro-Hamas rally, calling Betar’s claims “completely false.”

Betar made similar mistakes in describing at least two other students it listed, my colleagues found. “Go to hell,” a Betar spokesperson said in response to their questions. “Who are you to judge us?”

The administration isn’t trumpeting any associations with Betar so far, telling the Globe that State Department staff make decisions about visas. Ross Glick, a former Betar employee who spoke to the Globe, wouldn’t say who in the administration received Betar’s list.

But the group does seem to be well connected. A public relations executive named Ronn Torossian, who founded Betar US last spring, has organized fund-raisers for Mayor Eric Adams of New York and done work for the foundation of Eric Trump, the president’s middle son.

Glick also claims to have made inroads with lawmakers. He has said he met with Senator John Fetterman, a pro-Israel Pennsylvania Democrat, and with aides to two Senate Republicans, Ted Cruz and James Lankford. In statements to the Globe, Fetterman denied “any involvement” with Betar, while Lankford’s aides said they have no evidence that anyone from the group met with the senator or his staff. Cruz’s office didn’t respond to requests for comment.

So far, Betar seems unbothered by those disavowals. Its website says it hopes to establish 25 chapters in the US this year, and it has raised tens of thousands of dollars on GoFundMe.

Betar isn’t alone in highlighting the Trump administration’s supposed ideological foes. Canary Mission, another pro-Israel group, has also compiled names of allegedly anti-Israel students. Turning Point USA, a right-wing campus group, publicly lists professors it claims “discriminate against conservative students and advance leftist propaganda in the classroom.”

Betar isn’t done, either. This week, the group predicted that immigration officials would soon target students at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. As Glick, the former Betar employee, told the Globe, “We want to help our government.”

Read more:

Explore my colleagues’ full story here.

ICE has also used a little-known government database to terminate foreign students’ legal status in the US, sometimes without giving a reason.
