title: Man shot and killed in Dorchester
text:
A man was shot in Dorchester late Saturday night near the intersection of Blue Hill Avenue and Georgia Street.

Officers from District B-2 (Roxbury) responded to a call, and at the scene found an adult male with a gunshot wound. Boston EMS transferred the victim to Boston Medical Center where he was pronounced dead, according to the police report.

The police said this is an active investigation with the Boston Police Department Homicide Unit.

Sunday morning, the intersection showed no visible signs of the shooting that had occurred hours before. On the cloudy Sunday, the neighborhood buzzed with normal activity—residents strolled down the sidewalks, parishioners made their way to church and cars passed through the intersection. There were no police cruisers, no yellow tape and no indication that a man had been killed there last night.

Most residents seemed unaware that a fatal shooting had even occurred.

While Dorchester, particularly the Meeting House Hill neighborhood, has experienced moments of violence, overall fatal shootings in Boston have declined sharply in recent years.

In 2024, Dorchester accounted for seven homicides of Boston’s 37 total homicides, a historic low for the city. Despite a fatal shooting occurring in the neighborhood in January 2025 — the city’s second homicide of the year — the broader trend shows a steep decline in gun violence.

From 2023 to 2024, shootings have dropped sharply in Boston’s neighborhoods of Dorchester, Roxbury and Mattapan — areas that have long experienced the most gun violence. In 2023, Dorchester recorded 61 shooting victims, Roxbury had 31, and Mattapan 19. In 2024, those numbers have fallen to 23 in Dorchester, 14 in Roxbury, and just four in Mattapan.

This is a developing story.

Rachel Umansky-Castro can be reached at rachel.umanskycastro@globe.com.

title: Prom for teachers? Mass. educators of color celebrate event fostering community.
text:
“When people are going through their everyday work schedule, it can become very easy to feel somewhat isolated,” said Ashley Dodson, a history teacher at Boston Green Academy. “Events like this really help us to come together and remember we’re all living the same shared struggle.”

Founded in 2018, The Teachers’ Lounge provides educators with training and professional resources. That includes mentorship programs for young teachers, networking opportunities, and other events — such as their very own high school dance.

Organizers say the importance of providing a space for community is crucial for educators, given ongoing threats to public education. That’s especially true, they say, for educators of color, who make up about 15 percent of educators in the state. That’s far below the proportion of students of color in Massachusetts classrooms, who make up nearly half of the public school population in the state.

Educators of color see turnover rates higher than the national average, with studies often citing poor conditions and feeling unsupported in the workplace. Lagging salaries have also contributed to high levels of turnover, particularly at schools serving students of color.

That’s something that The Teacher’s Lounge and its programming work to address, organizers said.

“We didn’t just want it to be just a party,” said Titciana Barros, the organization’s director of community and culture. “That’s not what we’re about. We’re about retention and revitalizing our educators of color.”

Barros said their priority is making sure that educators of color stay in the profession. Students of color perform better, she noted, when they are taught by an educator of the same race or ethnicity.

Events like the Educators Prom are simply a way to make sure that those teachers are “recharged” — even if that means drinks and a dance floor.

“When I think about the work day to day, it’s really easy to fall into the cycles that are rooted in survival mode,” said Evelyn Jean-Louis, a former Cambridge middle-school principal. “Just trying to make it through the day, just trying to get through the lesson plan, just trying to start over so you have tomorrow. What this event does to foster community is emphasize that it’s not a sprint, and it’s honestly not really a marathon.”

Instead, it’s like “passing a baton,” said Jean-Louis, who is now the organization’s director of learning and development. Educators of color starting their career can find community with veterans who have come before them, so they don’t have to “learn these really hard lessons on their own” in a system that too often leaves them feeling adrift.

Enthusiasm for the organization is growing. Last year, more than 1,800 educators participated in Teachers’ Lounge programming — an increase of nearly one thousand people from the previous season.

Kettlynn Prophete, an assistant principal at the Academy of the Pacific Rim in Hyde Park, said the strong sense of identity and community fostered by the organization goes a long way in helping educators connect with their students — especially students of color.

“To me, being here is getting things done,” Prophete said. “Being in the community is getting things done for the betterment of our respective communities. But [also] with each other as people. ... if I am modeling and being transparent about how I make decisions with teachers, then teachers are being transparent and modeling and with kids, and they’re being much more gracious with kids.”

Attendees said that, because teaching can often be a thankless job, Saturday’s prom was an opportunity to find camaraderie with fellow professionals in an atmosphere far more relaxed than a conference or a faculty meeting.

“As educators, you don’t necessarily hear ‘Great job, we appreciate you,’” said Malcolm Andrews Jr., an instructional coach in Boston Public Schools. “That’s probably the last thing [you hear].”

Getting hundreds of educators with similar lived experiences coming together in a shared space is a “sacred” experience, Andrews added.

“Having that community that understands what you’re going through, that has similar values, that understands the commitment we make every single day when we go into the school and how we show up for the students, I think it’s really important,” said Antonelli Mejia, principal of the Sarah Greenwood School in Dorchester.

Prophete said that teachers want to be “acknowledged and valued.” That doesn’t only mean fair pay, she added, but also means smaller gestures and acknowledgements — for example, taking a night to celebrate educators.

“If we can take a moment and have fun like this, imagine what we can open ourselves to when kids are also excited about things like prom, or maybe a birthday party,” Prophete said. “It continues to bring us more and more together, and see each other for our humanity.”

title: ‘Practically impossible’: As the White House pushes women to have more babies, the women who want them can’t afford it
text:
“It took me handing over the day care bills to my parents for them to understand,” Nguyen said. “They would just be like, ‘Oh, well, you can just have another one. It all works out. You can’t really just plan for them.’ And I‘m like, ‘No. Look at these numbers.’”

The Trump administration has made it clear it wants women to have more children, with aides reportedly evaluating policy recommendations aimed at incentivizing higher fertility rates, from a $5,000 “baby bonus” when a woman gives birth to a “National Medal of Motherhood” for mothers with six or more kids. There are plenty of women in Massachusetts who would love to welcome the babies the White House covets — if only they could afford it.

The Globe spoke with more than 20 women who harbor an interest in starting or expanding their families but feel they’ve been priced out of parenthood by the region’s sky-high cost of living — a stark financial reality they believe the "pronatalist" policy recommendations flooding the White House are ill-equipped to handle.

“I would love to have a small baseball team of children,” said Tierney Elison, 38, a Winthrop mom of two and a midwife who thinks she wouldn’t be able to afford the third child she and her husband envisioned. “I love being pregnant. I love giving birth. I love the newborn stage. I love watching the kids grow. But it is such a slog trying to make all of this work.”

“No amount of baby fever can overcome economic anxiety right now,” she added.

While parenthood, here and elsewhere, has long been a notoriously expensive endeavor, it has now become something of a microcosm of the region’s affordability problems. The median-priced single-family home in Greater Boston is inching toward $1 million. Child care prices here are among the highest in the country. The expense of fertility treatments sometimes crucial to conceiving a child and health care costs over the course of a child’s life can be crushing.

Some people have unplanned pregnancies or embark on parenthood regardless of money. But for women in Massachusetts who would otherwise be on relatively strong financial footing, the decision to add a child into their budget can feel like taking on a line item that is increasingly reserved for the well-to-do — and the bar just keeps on rising.

“It feels like I‘m doing something financially indulgent,” said Mariah Maines, 38, a Quincy mother of two who works as a financial adviser. She and her husband make good money — about $300,000 between them — and yet feel like their plan to have a third child will put them in the position of living “paycheck to paycheck.”

“If I was a financial adviser to myself, I would say, ‘Don’t have this third child,’” she added. “But I‘m still doing it, despite the facts.”

Those facts might help explain why the fertility rate in Massachusetts is one of the lowest in the country — and falling. “Fertility overall kind of fell off during the Great Recession, around 2008, and then people were kind of waiting for it to rebound,” said Susan Strate, senior program manager at the UMass Donahue Institute. “But it never did.”

According to a Pew Research Center survey from last year, 36 percent of women ages 18-49 who said they were unlikely to have children reported that their inability to afford it was a major reason. (Other reasons included just not wanting to, a desire to focus on other things, and concerns about the state of the world.) A recent report from the City of Boston Office of Early Childhood said, “The high cost of formal child care is likely one of the factors behind why families are moving out of Boston or have fewer children or no children.”

That was the case for Tania Del Rio, a 39-year-old living with her husband and two children, 9 and 5, in East Boston. The cost of child care played a big part in her family planning: She and her husband spaced out their kids in age more than they would have liked to avoid an overlap in day care costs, which clocked in between $1,200 and $2,000 a month. By the time her youngest was in public school, she felt it was “not time to have kids anymore,” though she would have loved to have another.

“What you hear in conversations is, ‘OK, when you have kids, save up for college,’” Del Rio said. “No one ever tells you, really, that you should save up for child care.”

It’s a daunting prospect before there’s even a sonogram to fawn over. Linnea Mayfield, 30, is getting married this summer and would love to have three children, just as her parents had done in Estonia, where she grew up.

But unlike that Baltic country, which has a generous paid leave policy for new parents, the United States offers no such assurances on a federal level. Massachusetts’ 12-week paid family medical leave policy isn’t enough for the Dorchester resident to feel comfortable taking the plunge into motherhood, she said, but she also doesn’t feel she would be able to afford additional unpaid time off from her $70,000-a-year job in the tourism industry.

“It’s a huge decision to make in the first place, and then to add this additional financial pressure that, maybe this isn’t even possible, is just very limiting,” she said.

“It just seems like such a cool adventure, too, like an experience I don’t want to miss, but I might, because I can’t afford it,” she added.

In some cases, that reality leads families to other corners of the country. Massachusetts has long had a problem with domestic outmigration — more people moving out of the state than into it — and the City of Boston report found that from 2017 to 2022, the city’s population of 3- to 5-year-olds declined at a higher rate than those ages birth to 2. That suggests “families with young children are moving out of Boston,” the report said.

And yet for many women, it feels like there’s no other option. Sydney Baughman, 38, and her husband had their first two children in Somerville before moving to New Hampshire in 2022 to get a bigger place. When they felt the pull toward a third child, they knew they needed a more drastic change to afford it, especially if Baughman wanted to continue to take time off work. So last year, they packed up and moved to a five-bedroom house in the Atlanta area with a backyard and a playroom — luxuries that would have been out of the question in New England’s housing market.

“I feel like they’re getting the sort of life that I‘d hoped to be able to provide for my kids with the money we’re making that we weren’t getting in the Massachusetts area,” Baughman said.

title: Josh Kraft is focused on persuading Black voters in Boston’s mayoral race. Is it working?
text:
“This couldn’t be a more appropriate place for our campaign to call home,” Kraft said in March at the opening of his campaign HQ. “This campaign is about making sure that every voice in Boston is heard and valued.”

A first-time candidate up against a savvy incumbent, Kraft believes his narrow path to victory runs directly through Roxbury and other communities of color, swaths of the city where, Kraft contends, voters feel ignored and let down by Wu.

Wu’s campaign rejects that claim and the idea that she doesn’t engage with communities of color. The campaign points to the coffee hours she hosts in every neighborhood, her “Commute with me” series where she joins residents on their way to work, and the numerous community events, listening sessions, and ribbon-cuttings she attends in her official capacity as mayor. Wu also speaks fluent Spanish, and regularly does Spanish-language interviews with the media.

Kraft’s strategy, nonetheless, reflects the campaign’s view that the political newcomer can make inroads among voters of color. Kraft in recent weeks has appeared on at least four radio shows with Black hosts that focus on the Black community, and has frequently sat in pews for Sunday services and joined iftars in neighborhoods such as Dorchester and Mattapan. His team has recruited people specifically to lead outreach among Haitian and Cape Verdean residents. Last month, the Kraft campaign hosted an event in Mattapan featuring a couple dozen of the city’s Haitian residents endorsing his candidacy.

Since he launched his challenge to Wu in February, Kraft has argued that she “doesn’t listen” to residents, and has neglected Black neighborhoods and other communities. And as Kraft’s campaign sees it, the connections he developed through his nonprofit work, largely in communities of color, give him an opportunity to capitalize on what they view as Wu’s vulnerability in Boston’s diverse neighborhoods.

More than two dozen interviews with Black Boston voters, including some civic leaders and political strategists, indicate Kraft will find at least some willingness to hear his message in these communities, but he has a lot more work to do before November.

Like any voting bloc, Boston’s Black community is incredibly diverse and not at all a monolith. Some prominent Black leaders, a portion of whom supported Wu in 2021, confirmed they are disillusioned with her leadership. Other Black voters said they still strongly support the mayor, particularly in light of the national political climate. Several others said they could possibly be open to voting for a challenger to Wu, but don’t know enough about Kraft’s policy positions to decide yet. A couple hadn’t even heard of him.

The interviews indicate the dissatisfaction and frustration that Kraft seeks to capitalize on is real. Several of Wu’s policy initiatives have angered some very vocal and influential leaders in Black neighborhoods, including her plan to move the most diverse exam school from Roxbury to a mostly white neighborhood. Wu later reversed course, abandoning the move, in response to the intense community uproar.

“I feel like she’s kind of failed Black people,” said Priscilla Flint, executive director of the Marcus Anthony Hall Educational Institute, which serves city youth. “[Wu] doesn’t listen, and then she makes decisions,” without first soliciting community input, she said. Flint voted for Wu in 2021, but said she’s been disappointed in Wu’s leadership and, at this point, doesn’t plan to back her again. Flint’s organization has also received support from Kraft’s philanthropic work in the past.

Other prominent civic leaders said the mayor’s decision to block the creation of an elected School Committee was a turning point. During her first mayoral campaign, Wu said she supported a hybrid, partially elected School Committee, but as mayor she vetoed a bill to switch to an elected board, saying the change could bring instability and compromise the district’s ability to address its significant challenges.

Many voters who spoke with the Globe also said Wu has been too hasty installing bike lanes and took issue with her administration’s redesign of Blue Hill Avenue, with a center-running bus lane. Some also voiced opposition to her controversial plan to redevelop Franklin Park’s White Stadium for Boston Public Schools students, in partnership with a new, professional women’s soccer team.

“[In] conversations that I’m having with many, many people in the Black community, a lot of it comes down to, ‘[Wu] doesn’t show up for us unless she needs something, or she only shows up when it can benefit her,’ ” said Jacquetta Van Zandt, a senior adviser to the Kraft campaign and host of the show “Politics and Prosecco.” “She has made decisions and choices that have conveniently left out Black voices.”

Wu’s campaign did not directly comment on the Kraft team’s accusations, but in a statement emphasized her nearly 15 years in city government, the many Black leaders she appointed to key positions in her Cabinet, and various programs she’s implemented that benefit Black Bostonians.

It hasn’t been enough for some.

Louis Elisa, president of the Garrison Trotter Neighborhood Association, said he’s particularly disappointed in the stalled progress on plans to overhaul the city’s only vocational high school, Madison Park Technical Vocational High School, and what he sees as minimal improvements to BPS. Elisa was also a plaintiff in a lawsuit that aimed to block Wu’s White Stadium plan, which a judge ultimately rejected.

He said he did not vote for Wu in 2021, but was pleased that she, both as a city councilor and as a mayoral candidate, showed interest in addressing some issues he deeply cares about, like Madison Park.

But “there are so many things she said she was going to do that didn’t happen,” Elisa said. “I started off very much in support of her administration doing good things, and she basically squandered that trust and that support by doing things that are totally unrelated to the needs of the community in which I live.”

Other Black voters defended the mayor’s record.

Denise Williams, a 53-year-old former certified nursing assistant who lives in Roxbury, said she proudly supports Wu and appreciates how frequently she attends community events. As a mother, she said Wu feels more relatable to her than Kraft, the third son of billionaire Patriots’ owner Robert Kraft.

“I just pray that she wins,” Williams said. “I don’t like for somebody to say, ‘Well, I have Black friends’ ... No, you have to really be in it to understand what we go through on a daily basis.”

Jasen Lambright, a cybersecurity expert and Dorchester resident, said he voted for Wu in 2021 and will likely do so again. As a father of three kids in BPS, he said he still sees room for improvement. But he praised her work on public safety, including progress she made tackling homelessness and the opioid crisis in the Mass. and Cass area.

“I used to drive by there all the time to drop my kids off [at a youth program] . . . and I can say it looks markedly different,” Lambright said.

He was also impressed by Wu’s recent testimony before Congress, in which she defended Boston and its policies on how and when local law enforcement cooperates with federal immigration authorities.

“That was phenomenal, I agreed with everything she said,” Lambright said. “What I like about Mayor Wu is I feel like she gets the overall picture. . . . I haven’t heard why [Kraft] would do a better job.”

Antoinette Johnson, a 47-year-old Dorchester resident and morning show host on the Black-owned radio station Spark FM, also said Kraft hasn’t articulated how his leadership would be different than Wu’s.

“Instead of him saying, ‘This is what I’m doing, this is what I’m doing,’ it seems like he’s kind of harping on what she’s not doing,” Johnson said. She does, however, believe Kraft’s efforts to reach Black voters are working. “He’s made himself available in a lot of spaces that we probably wouldn’t think that Josh Kraft would be in.”

Kraft recently joined Johnson and her cohosts on their Spark FM show, and left a good impression, she said. While Johnson said she’s supported Wu for years and approves of the job she’s done in her first term, she sees Kraft as a strong contender.

“In speaking to people in my community, it’s probably split down the middle. There’s a lot of people who are very, very excited about Mayor Wu running again. . . . There are some other people who [think], ‘Maybe there could be some change if we give Josh Kraft a chance.’ ”

“It’s gonna be a tough race,” Johnson continued, “but I think it’s gonna be a good race, and I think that both of them have the opportunity to prove themselves.”

title: Meet Katie Draisen, the young private chef who fuels a Celtics star
text:
Draisen moved throughout the kitchen in her striped apron, recalling how her client, who the Globe agreed to keep anonymous, encouraged her to start a TikTok page that chronicles the meals she prepares to fuel a champion.

“It’s really cool what TikTok can do,” Draisen said. “I was surprised it had success early on because I know it can be a not very rewarding process for a long time. But I also thought I’m lucky to have this niche thing that I do.”

Besides teaching her how to cook, working long hours as a prep cook on a farm in Martha’s Vineyard and other back-of-house jobs taught her how to think on her feet. When she launched her meal prep business in 2023, those long hours paid off.

After a client recommended her services to the Celtics player, Draisen completed a trial run last summer and officially became the family’s chef in the fall. Now she tailors a new menu to her client’s daily needs, evident in the day’s lunch packed with leafy greens high in nitrates to improve cardiovascular health.

She says her experiences are responsible for teaching her an important lesson: “Don’t serve something you wouldn’t eat.”

At the time of this interview, it’s hours away from the tipoff of Game 5 between the Boston Celtics and Orlando Magic (which the Celtics won, big time), and Draisen is sticking to the routine that’s yielded positive results.

Before each game, Draisen prepares a beet juice packed with nutrients proven to increase blood flow to the muscles, promoting recovery and as an efficient way to absorb necessary nutrients without actually eating fiber. Draisen calls the smoothie “nature’s pre-workout because there are a lot of sugars in it” to provide energy.

Pregame staples include simple carbs such as pasta or rice, but post-game meals usually consist of starchy vegetables and salmon, rich in Omega-3s and the nine essential amino acids crucial for tissue repair and nutrient absorption.

“Making sure that these are consistently in the diet, you will see a bigger difference than when eating it occasionally. So that’s why we do repetition.”

Consistency is possible through working closely with the team’s nutritionist to meet her client’s daily macro requirements. An athlete’s diet becomes even more important during the playoffs.

“On a game day, we’re focusing on carbs that are easy to digest, leafy greens that are very cooked through, so they’re not too fibrous, and lean protein,” Draisen says.

A favorite dish among the whole family is miso salmon. Draisen sears the skin of a salmon filet and cooks it under the broiler in a sweet lime miso sauce. While the meal’s base remains the same, the sides are substituted to meet everyone’s tastes and needs. Some will have their salmon served with a noodle stir fry, while others may opt for Japanese sweet potatoes.

Draisen credits her ability to balance nutrition and flavor for her success. Instead of following the basic formula of having starch, vegetables, and protein on the plate, Draisen looks for ways to reinvent staples. For example, she’ll make a flavorful pilaf instead of boiling brown rice.

An athlete’s needs are non-negotiable, so if he has to eat chicken breast for the protein, Draisen asks herself, “What marinade can I make for this?” The answer: marinating the chicken in a coconut turmeric sauce to deliver an equally beneficial and rich dish.

Inspiration comes from scrolling through food videos from accounts like Wishbone Kitchen and flipping through recipe books, taking note of the different proteins and cuisines. As a Massachusetts native, she’s also inspired by Via Cannuccia in Dorchester and other local favorites.

Unique to this role is the direct impact her cooking has on her client’s success. By following a strict schedule of feeding her client specific foods at set times, Draisen has been able to help him achieve his lowest body fat percentage since he came to the team.

When she and her client share the same goal, Draisen says she’s more motivated. With this specific family, her fulfillment comes from the direct effect she has on their quality of life in Boston.

“I honestly feel like I am living my dream,” she said. “This was a goal I talked to so many people about, and the fact that it is happening, I really can’t believe it.”

title: Woman says Boston hotel guard accused her of being a man in women’s bathroom: ‘My worst nightmare coming true’
text:
“I look more masculine and oftentimes that elicits a reaction if I’m in a designated women’s space,” Baker said in an interview Wednesday. “I’ve gotten used to the comments.”

But shortly after Baker entered a stall, someone banged on the door and told her to come out. After she pulled her shorts up and stepped out, a security guard accused her of being a man in the women’s restroom and demanded to see her ID, Baker said.

“He was aggressive right off the bat, telling me to get out and accusing me of being a man,” she said.

Although Baker showed the guard her ID and she and Victor repeatedly told him she is a woman, the couple was escorted out of the hotel, she said. As they left the restroom, Baker said, a couple of other women made comments, calling Baker “a creep” and telling the guard to “get him out of here.”

The confrontation left Baker and Victor shaken and crying as they waited outside the hotel for an Uber.

“As much as the comments don’t bother me and as confident as I am ... it honestly just felt like my worst nightmare coming true,” Baker said.

A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office said they’ve received two complaints and were processing them, and a spokesperson for the state commission against discrimination said they could neither confirm nor deny the existence of a complaint.

On Monday, Victor posted a Google review of the Liberty Hotel that presented her account of what happened, according to Baker. That review, as well as numerous other 1-star reviews that were posted in the aftermath of Saturday’s incident, appear to have been removed from Google.

In her review, Victor asked others to boycott the hotel and reach out to the mayor’s office, according to published reports.

“No guests stepped in. No staff de-escalated the situation. No compassion was shown,” Victor wrote, according to the reports. “This was not just unprofessional — it was traumatizing, discriminatory, and dehumanizing. My partner and I are devastated.”

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the hotel said in a statement that the security guard had been suspended and that all hotel staff would undergo “mandatory retraining ... on inclusive practices and guest interaction protocols, with a particular focus on creating a safe and welcoming space for LGBTQ+ individuals.”

“The Liberty Hotel is and always will be an ally of the LGBTQ+ community and a place where everyone is welcome and celebrated,” the statement said. “We will continue to educate and train our team to ensure that everyone feels safe and accepted within our four walls and guests who do not show tolerance and acceptance towards others will be removed.”

In an earlier statement, however, a hotel spokesperson said that multiple women had alerted hotel security that two people were sharing a bathroom stall, according to published reports.

“The bathroom was cleared out as two adults in one stall are not permitted,” the spokesperson said, according to the reports. “After leaving the bathroom, a member of the couple from the stall put their hands on our security team and it was then that they were removed from the premises. The Liberty Hotel has a zero-tolerance policy for any physical altercations on our property.”

Baker denied that account and said she and Victor never entered the stall together. She said Victor spoke with a manager at the hotel on Tuesday, demanding an apology and asking them to retract the earlier statement.

When the hotel issued its new statement Tuesday, which said the security officer had “immediately” been suspended, there was something missing, Baker said.

“Nowhere in there was an apology,” she said. “There is no apology in that statement.”

Still, she said, “it was better than what they put out initially.”

Baker said she and Victor have been encouraged by an outpouring of supportive messages they’ve received in the past few days.

“We’ve been absolutely inundated with love and support from countless people and I can’t begin to describe how appreciative I am,” she said. “That’s been overwhelming in the best way and really uplifting.”

“We’re just trying to heal a little bit,” she added. “It’s still hard to wrap my head around that this incident even took place.”

title: Americans’ trust in medicine is declining. But doctors can still turn it around.
text:
Indignant, Harding sensed that her providers saw her as a stereotype — an elderly Black woman they wrongly assumed was poor and neglectful of her health — and so they did not look deeply into her complaints. Fed up, two years ago she wrote letters to each of her doctors, firing them. They had lost her trust.

By any measure, such scenarios are a huge loss for patients and doctors — and data suggest that a growing number of Americans experience them.

Dr. Andrew W. Bazemore likens trust to a new drug or device. “It’s one of the most powerful tools of medicine, frankly, and if you don’t have it, no number of drugs, devices, or other interventions are going to achieve much,” says Bazemore, a primary care doctor in Virginia who is senior vice president of research and policy for the American Board of Family Medicine.

Research backs up his assertion. When patients trust their health care provider, they experience fewer symptoms, a higher quality of life, and more satisfaction with treatment, according to a review of 47 studies published in 2017.

But now, Bazemore says, trust in medicine is “under siege.”

A strained medical system often fails to provide attentive care — as doctors burn out, patients struggle to get appointments , and costs keep rising. Social media influencers are peddling useless or dangerous remedies, and the anti-vaccine movement is gaining traction, even amid a measles outbreak that has already led to more than 880 confirmed cases in the United States this year. Meanwhile, the nation’s secretary of health and human services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has been sowing doubts and spreading falsehoods about vaccines.

Trust in doctors, in state and local public health officials, and in key federal health agencies declined by roughly 10 percentage points from 2023 to 2025, according to KFF, the health policy research and news organization.

Changes in federal leadership are making people less trustful of recommendations from agencies that once were guiding lights for doctors and patients alike. According to a March poll by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the de Beaumont Foundation, 44 percent of respondents said their trust was eroding.

Notably, though, the KFF poll found that, even as trust declines overall, doctors remain by far the most trusted. Some 85 percent of respondents said they have a great deal or a fair amount of trust in their doctors, down from 93 percent in 2023.

A trusted doctor‘s advice, given in the privacy of the exam room, may be the sturdiest bulwark against misinformation. But that relationship can also be precarious.

Dr. Andrea Reilly, a primary care doctor in Boston, remembers the exact moment she lost the trust of a patient’s family.

Reilly described the troubling encounter in an essay, “The Fragility of Trust in Medicine,” in Harvard Medicine magazine. At the end of a long, complex visit with a teen patient and her mother, amid calls from the reception desk saying two patients were waiting, Reilly told the mother that her daughter was due for vaccines.

When the mother balked, saying she wanted to do her own research, Reilly blurted out, “Don’t you trust me?”

“As soon as the words left my lips,” Reilly wrote, “I knew I had said too much.”

Three days later the mother called the office to say the family would be seeking care elsewhere.

Reilly wishes she had handled the exchange differently. But in an interview, she admits that the mother‘s suspicions about her professional credibility had hurt her feelings. “We’re trying to get it right,” she says. “I really want to help you — I don’t have another agenda.”

Reilly says she appreciates it when patients bring her their research so she can go over it with them. But some just drop off a stack of studies, expecting it to overrule her years of training and experience. “It’s an insult in some ways,” she says.

Today, credentials, smarts, and good intentions are often not enough. A more complex and open-minded relationship must be nurtured.

“Trust is built in the context of human relationships,” says Dr. Katherine Gergen Barnett, a family medicine doctor at Boston Medical Center. It can be fostered by asking open-ended questions, staying curious about the reasons behind the patient’s beliefs, and “recognizing that a patient knows their body better than anybody else in the world,” says Gergen Barnett, who is a vice chair of primary care innovation and transformation at BMC and a Boston University associate professor. Clinicians, she says, need to give back to patients “that power to be in charge of their health.”

At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, Gergen Barnett cared for an immunocompromised patient and her elderly mother — exactly the profile of patients most likely to die from COVID. But they didn’t want the vaccine, worried that it had been derived from human embryos.

“It took multiple visits where I sat with them, I talked to them, I heard their concerns, I told them my concerns. And they prayed on it,” Gergen Barnett recalls. The patients ultimately decided to get vaccinated, telling her they appreciated her willingness to listen.

Gergen Barnett is a white doctor who works with the diverse population at BMC — about 70 percent of patients there identify as people of color, a group that research shows is more likely to distrust doctors and hospitals. In Massachusetts, trust levels among commercially insured Black, Asian, and Hispanic people consistently fall several points below those of white people, according to surveys by the Massachusetts Health Quality Partners, a nonprofit that tracks patient experiences. There’s good reason for that distrust, from a legacy of historical abuses to current-day mistreatment, says Molly Totman, MHQP‘s senior director of quality initiatives.

Dr. Oni Blackstock, a primary care doctor who led New York City’s effort to end the HIV epidemic, recalls that in the early days of AIDS, some patients believed the virus was created by the government to kill Black and gay people. She sees many parallels with the response to COVID-19 vaccines. One of her HIV patients resisted vaccination for COVID even after two family members had died of the disease. He was unnerved by how quickly the vaccine had been developed. “It makes me think about Tuskegee and whether they’re testing this on us,” he told her.

The Tuskegee study is the notorious federal experiment carried out from 1932 to 1972, in which doctors withheld lifesaving treatment from a group of Black men with syphilis so they could observe the disease’s progress. “A lot of young people don’t know about Tuskegee,” says Blackstock, who now runs the consulting firm Health Justice, “but they do know how they’re treated by the health care system and by society at large.”

People such as Cheryl Harding, who felt dismissed and unseen.

Or the Rev. Irene Monroe, a well-known Boston theologian, activist, and podcaster, who recalls with still-raw outrage how a doctor once expressed surprise at her sophisticated vocabulary.

Or any Black person who gets lower levels of pain medication or waits longer for test results than their white peers.

The question, Blackstock says, is not whether Black people have enough trust, but whether the institutions and providers they encounter are trustworthy. As doctors, she says, “It’s really incumbent on us to build that trust.”

Sylvie Leotin, a Black woman and immigrant from France, isn’t sure whether race was a factor in a medical ordeal she experienced in 2017. But it certainly destroyed her trust.

Leotin, who now lives in California, was undergoing an MRI-guided core biopsy to detect breast cancer, which she was told would be minimally invasive. Instead, for an hour she lay face down in the MRI machine, while the doctor working underneath her jabbed her many times with a “biopsy gun,” trying and failing to extract cells from the targeted area. He never asked how she was holding up, or even talked to her. Speechless with pain and confusion, all she could do was wait “for the torture to end.”

In her view, the doctor had completely forgotten that she was a human being.

Leotin was told that she didn’t have cancer. But months later it was discovered she did, and then only because she insisted on surgery. Her friends urged her to sue. Instead, she resolved to take action to help other people avoid what she’d gone through.

The fundamental problem, Leotin says, is that doctors don’t always understand what it’s like to be a patient with a serious illness. With a grant from the Genentech Innovation Fund, she interviewed dozens of patients from marginalized communities and developed a workshop for clinicians at Emory University, intended to help them see health care through those patients’ eyes.

“If you’re making assumptions about what patients experience, you can do things that are harmful without realizing it. This is the root of mistrust,” Leotin says. And repeated violations of trust cause both physical and mental harm, as well as increased costs from extra testing and delayed diagnosis.

Another project that draws from patients’ experiences is underway in Boston. With a grant from the National Institutes of Health, the nonprofit Everyday Boston has teamed up with Boston Medical Center and several community groups in a project to address medical distrust among people of color.

Called Storytelling to Build Medical Trust, the project has held community roundtables eliciting the experiences and beliefs that can destroy trust. Patients have spoken about the lack of access, transparency, and understanding — the sense of being “stereotyped and exploited,” says Cara Solomon, founder and creative director of Everyday Boston, a group that uses storytelling to challenge stereotypes and bridge divisions. (Harding is a strategic adviser to the group.)

“It’s been a humbling and a horrifying experience to hear these stories,” Solomon says. “When things go wrong, you can almost guarantee that there was a lack of humanity.” The foundation of a solution, Solomon says, is the “deceptively simple and incredibly powerful” notion of treating people as humans and listening to them.

In a pilot that will be expanded in the fall, students from the state’s four medical schools got together with community members to hear their stories. One session was held in Springfield with nine students from the UMass Chan Medical School and nine community members. Ellie Parker, a medical student who helped organize the session, says a classmate told her afterward that it helped him learn how to ask better questions.

“We do so many exercises as medical students in taking a medical history,” Parker says. “But of course, so much of your interaction with people is just people skills.”

Hearing people’s stories lies at the heart of good medicine, says Dr. Jay M. Baruch, a professor of emergency medicine at Brown University. Years ago, as a medical student, Baruch took a year off to study writing and work on a novel. When he returned to medicine, he found that his approach had changed because he was better attuned to patients’ narratives.

“Medicine and the patient encounter is essentially a creative act, and we can’t care for patients without caring for their stories,” Baruch says. “Trust begins at the level of entering this story together and lowering our guard, each of us being vulnerable.”

This can happen even in the rushed high-pressure conditions of the emergency room where Baruch works — provided doctors are curious and pay close attention. Early in his career, Baruch recalls, a woman came to the ER with a raft of worrisome complaints. But she seemed strangely content amid the hubbub. Doctors kept her overnight to run tests, and when everything came back normal, Baruch apologetically told her they couldn’t detect the problem and asked if he could call someone to pick her up.

“Whatever you do,” the woman replied, “don’t call my husband.”

Baruch realized she’d come to the hospital to escape domestic violence. “It was like she opened up this door for me that I should have been curious about 12 hours before,” he says.

Baruch says clinicians can form a kind of “rapid trust” in the ER. Even though trust often needs to be nurtured over many conversations, sometimes it can indeed happen fast.

Leotin, the woman who underwent painful breast biopsies, says a new oncologist “gained my trust in less than one minute” because he greeted her first with an apology for all she’d been through. That showed he had read her medical records, acknowledged what happened to her, and empathized.

And Harding, the woman who fired her doctors, needed only an hour on Zoom to trust the new doctor she found — Gergen Barnett. “She listened to me,” Harding recalls about that first meeting. “She asked me questions about me, Cheryl, the person. . . . She trusted me and what I was saying about what I felt about my care.”

Gergen Barnett discovered that Harding had severe iron-deficiency anemia, a condition her previous doctors had somehow missed. A series of iron infusions renewed her energy. Although Harding has multiple health issues — and will turn 79 on May 18 — she says her life has improved despite some limitations. She’s been living in her home of 50 years, even though it’s still sometimes difficult to climb the stairs. She has the energy to work with Everyday Boston, and travel the world.

“I just came back from Japan last year,” Harding says. She brought her youngest granddaughter, Aria J. Harding. “We spent 10 days there. It was amazing.”

Felice J. Freyer is a health care journalist and frequent contributor to the Globe Magazine. Send comments to magazine@globe.com.

title: At Dorchester Catholic school, joy, excitement as new pope is elected
text:
“[The next pope] needs to be a leader, holy, and dedicated to God,” Gidel said after casting his ballot.

In the third-grade classroom, students filled out a worksheet about their knowledge of the century-old ritual. Their teacher, Bridget Crane, asked the class questions such as who votes for the pope, why the church sometimes needs a new pope, and what the pope’s job is.

On a poster hung on a classroom wall, students wrote characteristics they want in the next pope, including “kind,” “respectful,” and “awesome.”

“[The next pope should be] loving, careful, fair, and patient,” said Walter Koellner, one of the third-graders. He said he was most excited for when he and his classmates would get to hold their own conclave.

In first grade, each student wrote a paragraph about what they would choose as their name if they were elected pope and what they would focus on.

Gianna Pena, a first-grader, said her name as pope would be Pope Gianna, and she would focus on helping the sick and poor. Adah Alves, who was sitting next to her, said she would go to church every day and help her family.

Another classmate, Wynter Cohen, said her name would be Pope Sun because “the sun is God.”

“The pope should be really nice, really kind, and have patience,” she said.

The fourth-graders’ list of personality traits that the next pope should have included “wise,” “selfless,” “love for everyone,” and “embodiment of the Holy Spirit.”

“It’s so exciting for them,” said Anne Gallagher, principal of the Columbia Campus of the academy. “We care about our faith and integrate it as much as possible in our classroom and community.”

The fourth-graders kept their chosen characteristics in mind as their teacher, Lauryn Hall, ran the class conclave. She started with a full stack of index cards for students to write their votes on, but her supply quickly dwindled as rounds concluded without a clear winner, which would have required a two-thirds majority, or nine votes.

Hall reminded students to pray over their choice before they placed it in a basket she was bringing around the room. Once all the index cards were collected, Hall read each one aloud before asking the class whether the results would be signaled by black or white smoke.

“We learned that when the pope isn’t picked, black smoke comes out, but when they are picked, white smoke comes out,” said Gabriel Akinola, one of the students.

At around 12:15 p.m. Thursday, white smoke finally billowed out of the Sistine Chapel. Almost an hour and a half later, Prevost, who will be known as Leo XIV and is the first US pope to hold the position in history, stepped out onto the balcony, eliciting cheers from students who watched live in their classrooms.

Nasim Amado, a first-grader, said he “felt excellent” about the new pope as he danced in excitement. Ruth Simola, a fourth-grader, said she’s “very happy that he’s American.”

title: Last meals for the Daily Table, as Dorchester-based nonprofit grocer is set to close
text:
A decade ago, Doug Rauch had a novel idea. The longtime president of Trader Joe’s had spent over 30 years in the grocery industry, but had always been bothered by a sobering statistic: 40 percent of the items on supermarket shelves eventually go to waste. Rauch also knew another fact: That 40 percent of families who qualified for food banks didn’t use them because they were too ashamed. The two facts, taken together, didn’t make sense.

So in 2015, after attending the Advanced Leadership Initiative at Harvard,Rauch opened a new nonprofit grocery store in Dorchester that aimed to solve both problems. The Daily Table worked with a network of growers, manufacturers, and other suppliers to source high-quality food and sell it at a price that people on federal food assistance could afford. The stores were bright and open to all, and in time, the concept expanded to several locations in Greater Boston, eventually serving over 3 million customers and providing them over $16 million in savings.

But on Friday, Rauch and his board announced that due to ongoing financial pressure, the stores were suspending operations. All four Daily Table locations will close within the week. Rauch called the decision devastating, and said it stemmed from a cascading set of factors.

“The decision is entirely economic,” he said. “There is no shortage of people who want to work for us and suppliers who want to work with us. It’s a shortage of funds, and we ran out of funds.”

Problems started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when sales dropped 40 percent, Rauch said. They didn’t layoff staff at the time, he continued, because “we felt that part of our mission was to provide affordable nutrition and good jobs and uplift our community.” The stores were eventually able to bounce back and saw record sales, but then faced another challenge as food prices skyrocketed.

“Food inflation really clobbered us,” he said.

Rauch said a typical grocery store would pass along rising prices to consumers, but that didn’t match The Daily Table’s ethos. The combined pullback of USDA programs that subsidized their work and the slowdown of food-focused philanthropy efforts made the math even harder. The final straw, Rauch said, was the IRS’s delay in paying out a $1.4 million tax credit designed to pay back companies that kept their employees on payroll during the pandemic.

Rauch said he’s been waiting over two years for the funds, and he and his board has been using their own money in the interim to keep the stores afloat.

“If we had [those funds] right now, we probably woudn’t be having this conversation,” he said.

In a letter to customers Friday, The Daily Table’s board noted that the “heartbreaking” decision weighed heavily on them, knowing that “this comes at a time when other food access resources and organizations are at risk.” They steered customers to other local food resources in the Greater Boston area.

The stores will remain open and sell off their merchandise in the coming days. The Dorchester, Roxbury, and Salem stores will close at the end of the day on Sunday, while the Cambridge store may remain open through Monday.

“While I personally, and my team and staff are really devastated and sad to have to be ceasing this operation and closing down the business, the amount of support gratitude and love that our communities and customers have shown our suppliers, vendors and funders is truly humbling and overwhelming,” Rauch said. “I have a feeling of immense gratitude for ten years and am deeply grateful.”
