title: Driver of Boston school bus that killed 5-year-old tried to flee scene after crash, according to police radio calls
text:
But, more than two hours of recordings of Boston police radio calls that were reviewed by the Globe Friday revealed officers had been advised about the bus shortly before the deadly crash in Hyde Park.

Around 2:20 p.m., a police dispatcher told a cruiser that a caller from Goodale Road in Mattapan witnessed a school bus hitting two parked cars, according to police radio calls reviewed by the Globe.

Children were on board the bus at the time, the dispatcher said.

The dispatcher gave the identification number of the bus — 015 — and said it “took off” on Walk Hill Street toward the nearby cemetery, the recording said.

Shortly after the crash involving Lens in Hyde Park, a dispatcher contacted the same cruiser.

“Operation center to Charlie 435 on Wellington Hill: Sir, I’m just advising you, it’s a completely different incident, but that same school bus just ran over a child in Hyde Park,” the dispatcher said.

“I have that ma’am,” the officer replied.

Video of the crash scene aired by WCVB-TV showed a yellow school bus with B015 painted in large black type on its roof.

Police spokesman Sergeant Detective John Boyle declined to comment on the recordings, including whether investigators confirmed it was the same bus in both incidents.

The recordings also reveal police had taped off an area of Wellington Hill as a crime scene shortly after the crash.

According to police radio calls, the Hyde Park crash occurred at 107 Washington St., although the bus was stopped at an address about 100 feet away.

A department member told a colleague shortly after the crash that the bus driver who struck Lens tried to leave the scene, but was stopped by another vehicle, according to the police recordings.

“It’s bus number B015. The driver did try to take off,” the police department member said in the recording. Another vehicle blocked the bus in, she said.

There were nearby residents on the street when the crash occurred and many rushed to aid the boy. He was found lying on the ground, people at the scene told the Globe, before responding Boston police, firefighters, and EMS took him to a local hospital where he was later pronounced dead, officials have said.

None of the other children on the bus were injured, according to authorities, but were taken to the hospital as a precaution.

Now 10 days since Lens’s death, investigators have said little about the crash. They have not identified the driver or said whether that person is currently working or has been placed on leave. No one has been charged in connection with the death, according to James Borghesani, a spokesperson for Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden.

On Friday, investigators declined to answer questions about the crash, which is being investigated by the Suffolk district attorney’s office and Boston Police’s Homicide Unit, Borghesani said.

The homicide unit investigates death cases, and its personnel include the police department’s accident reconstruction team, according to Borghesani.

Representatives for Mayor Michelle Wu and schools Superintendent Mary Skipper did not respond to questions Friday about the police radio recordings. The company that operates the buses for BPS, Transdev, and Emmanuel Marcellus, the president of union for Boston bus drivers, also did not respond to requests for comment.

Members of Lens’s family could not be reached for comment Friday.

But they previously said the boy was with his 11-year-old cousin when they were dropped off by a substitute bus driver, according to WCVB-TV. The pair got off on Washington Street, rather than at their regular stop nearby on Glenwood Avenue.

Lens attempted to walk across the street in front of the bus on his way home, according to his family’s account published by WCVB. Boston police have not confirmed those details, the station reported.

City Councilor Erin Murphy said if the facts recorded in the police radio calls were true, “we definitely need answers and a full investigation.”

She said any school bus driver carrying children should stop if they strike a a parked car.

The incident comes as BPS is trying to improve the efficiency of its beleaguered bus system, which for years has been challenged by late arrivals, changing start times for schools, and tensions with the city’s bus drivers union.

Based in Illinois, Transdev was the only bidder for the city’s bus contract in 2023. The city’s schools use roughly 600 buses each day to transport more than 20,000 students to hundreds of public and private schools, as well as specialized programs.

City Councilor Ed Flynn said he was unfamiliar with the police transmissions, but said the city must ensure its school bus fleet is safe for students.

“Bus safety needs to be a number one priority. Transportation to and from school is a serious responsibility,” Flynn said. “We must ensure we do everything we can to prove the safest buses for our children, and ensure that every driver is in full compliance, as well.”

In a GoFundMe page, Lens’s family said he was a sweet boy who, at age 3, talked of becoming a pilot, and then wanted to become a police officer at 5. Portraits of Lens shared on the site showed him dressed in a button-down shirt, gray vest, and pink tie, and of him grinning widely for the camera.

“Lens’ smile lit up every room he was in and his energy was unmatched,” his family said on the site. “Lens was so funny and witty that he would make all of us laugh out loud with a joke or comment and then [we’d] look at him wondering how did he come up with it.”

His death has left his family with unbearable mental, emotional, and financial hardships, according to the fund-raiser posting.

“Lens loved running around outside and playing with his siblings and cousins. He loved watching planes fly, and seeing fast cars. Lens was a beautiful, curious, and intelligent boy taken from us too soon,” the posting said.

Neighborhood residents are planning a community safety meeting at 6:15 p.m. Tuesday at Moynihan Park.

title: ‘It’s beautiful to see’: Black Bostonians react to the pope’s Creole ancestry
text:
On Friday, Chambers was among Black Bostonians to react with warmth and pride to the revelation that the new pope is a descendant of Creole people of color.

Chambers, who is a parishioner at St. Katharine Drexel in Dorchester, said the pope appears to be a man of humility and worldliness, someone who cares about justice and someone who wants people to care about one another. He was elated when he heard about the pope’s lineage, saying it was “a matter of pride.”

“It’s going to be a matter of healing pride because there‘s been some tough times, politically,” he said. “We’re living in tough times.”

Multiple outlets, including The New York Times, reported this week that the maternal grandparents of Leo XIV were described as people of color in historical documents.

The grandparents, Joseph Martinez and Louise Baquié, lived in New Orleans and eventually moved to Chicago in the early 20th century and had a daughter: Mildred Martinez, the pope’s mother, according to the Times.

In Boston, the genealogical discovery of Leo XIV, which is the name the new pope chose, was broadly welcomed.

M. Shawn Copeland, a professor emerita at Boston College’s department of theology, said, “Such a discovery ought not to be surprising to anyone in the Americas.”

“Nearly all of us are racially and culturally mixed; sadly, we either do not know our interwoven roots or sometimes choose to ignore and forget them,” she said.

Copeland said as “an African American, a practicing Roman Catholic, and a professional theologian, this discovery of the pope’s background strikes a chord of joy and pride.”

“Yet what is most important is that Leo XIV already has extended himself to all human persons, especially those whom our society marginalizes and demeans,” she said. “The pope forcefully reminded the world of God’s unconditional love for all of us, for humanity, and he assured us that ‘evil will not prevail.’”

State Senator Lydia Edwards, a Black Democrat from East Boston and practicing Catholic, said Black Catholics in the US are often overlooked and considered by some within the American Black community to be “an anomaly.”

“He couldn’t be more American than to have come from that particular ancestry in the United States,” said Edwards.

About 6 percent of Black adults in the US are Catholic, the Pew Research Center reported in 2022. Among adult American Catholics, only 4 percent are Black.

Edwards noted that the pope’s family did not identify as Black while he was growing up and that the pope would not have the same lived experience as someone who identified as Black.

But still, for her, Leo XIV is technically the first “African American pope.”

“It’s beautiful to see and I wish him well,” Edwards said.

She added, “He is probably related to some people in Louisiana who are Black. That’s a big deal that you are related to pope.”

Boston resident Lorna DesRoses, a multicultural ministry consultant at the Archdiocese of Boston, said the pope’s roots speak to the history of the US, and the hardships faced by people of color.

DesRoses learned of the pontiff’s lineage through social media, where she said it spread quickly through local Black Catholic and Haitian threads. (The National Catholic Reporter this week reported that a grandfather of the pope, Joseph Martinez, was born in Haiti.) She said there was a time when it was not unusual for someone with Creole roots to move north and not acknowledge their roots, especially if they were white-passing.

“It’s a complicated history,” she said.

Creoles, also known as “Creole people of color,” have a history almost as old as Louisiana, the Times reported this week. While the word Creole can refer to people of European descent who were born in the Americas, it commonly describes mixed-race people of color, according to that newspaper.

DesRoses, who is of Haitian descent, called the pope’s heritage “a blessing for the church.”

“This is historic,” she said. “It’s a historic moment in the life of the church, in the life of this country.”

Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, who is the first Haitian American to lead the city’s legislative body, said the pope’s heritage is “deeply meaningful for lots of different communities.”

“There’s a lot to be proud of here,” she said.

The news comes at a particularly painful time for Haitians living in Greater Boston, as bloody civil strife and unrest continues in Haiti, said Louijeune, who is not Catholic but whose father is.

Given so much ongoing suffering there, the pope’s connection to the island nation “is pretty uplifting,” she said.

Material from Globe wire services was used in this report.

title: ‘Devastating’ closure of Daily Table leaves affordable fresh food ‘desert’ in Greater Boston neighborhoods
text:
Daily Table, a nonprofit local grocery chain that offered shoppers fresh food they could more easily afford, announced Friday that it is closing its doors after a decade in business. Residents of Cambridge, Boston, Roxbury, and Salem are already beginning to feel its loss.

Molly Warner, a Dorchester-based dietician and owner of Hand in Hand Nutrition, said she was saddened to hear that Daily Table is ceasing operations.

“In a season when Boston residents are under financial and political stress, the loss of a community gem like Daily Table will not go unnoticed, especially for our most vulnerable residents,” Warner said.

Daily Table’s board of directors said the closure was “heartbreaking” and “not an easy decision” in a letter to customers on Friday. “We are proud to have served over 3 million customers, returning over $16 million in savings to the community while removing the barriers to healthy food.”

The grocery chain cited a number of reasons for its closure, including challenges brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic, “historically high levels of food price increases,” and a lack of sufficient funding to stay afloat.

Jonathan Berk, resident of downtown Salem, said the closure will be tough to bear considering the rising cost of living.

“Everything seems like it’s continuing to rise every day. For folks that are living on tight budgets, not being able to stretch their grocery dollars every week is just gonna cut down on how much food they’re able to provide for their families,” Berk said. “It’s gonna have a major impact on folks’ ability to just put food on their table.”

Berk said Daily Table’s closure is also a great loss for members of the downtown Salem community as there are no other options for fresh produce within walking distance.

“This store served a much larger purpose than just lower costs, it also served a fresh food desert out here,” Berk said. “[Daily Table] was really the only place in downtown or near downtown where you could get fresh bananas or fresh fruits and veggies for that day.”

V. Saragoni, a resident of Salem, shared similar worries.

“I think about many friends and neighbors who may or may not drive or have access to a car,” Saragoni said. “Many folks will have to ride share to the grocery store, which will only add further financial strain to those shopping.”

Teddy Beamer, a former resident of Cambridge, said he shopped at Daily Table’s Central Square location a handful of times as a college student on a budget.

“The only other options for groceries in my neighborhood were H Mart and Whole Foods, which are more expensive. And Target, which can be cheaper but has a limited selection of produce,” Beamer said.

Along with the combination of affordability and quality, Beamer said no other store in his neighborhood had the same genuine sense of community.

“I think that there should be more programs that bring healthy and affordable food to people that need it,” Beamer said. “It’s a shame that [Daily Table] is closing, it had a really strong community feeling to it.”

Daily Table’s four locations will be selling their remaining inventory over the next several days and all items will be deeply discounted until operations close.

Sabrina Lam can be reached at sabrina.lam@globe.com.

title: Their children have died, their motherhood remains
text:
These mothers walk, grieve, celebrate, and uplift each other during the yearly walk through Dorchester on a day that is tremendously difficult for those who have lost a child.

Chaplain Clementina Chéry cofounded the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute after her son Louis David Brown was killed while heading to a Teens Against Gang Violence meeting. Louis was supposed to call his mother when he got to the meeting, but the call never came. He was struck by crossfire.

The day Louis died, changed Chéry forever.

“I say, the day Louis died, is the day I woke up,” Chéry said. “Why are we OK when this happens to Black and brown children?”

A year after Louis’s death, Chéry cofounded the Peace Institute to honor her son and help other families deal with the trauma and grief associated with the killing of a loved one.

“Many times, what we tend to do, is we want to shame mothers for grieving. No. Grief is just how much we loved the person who is no longer here,” she said.

In 1996, Chéry and a small group did the first peace walk on Mother’s Day, connecting mothers who had lost a child. This year will be the 29th walk.

Even in death, Chéry is grateful to Louis and her two other children for being her best teacher.

“Louis wasn’t my son, he is my son,” she said.

Chéry still does not know who killed her son.

The Louis D. Brown Peace Institute has been serving the Boston community for over 30 years. The group has recently gotten plans approved to open a three-story center in Dorchester.

LaToya Minus was making Thanksgiving dinner in 2021, waiting for her daughter Dejah Nichole Jenkins-Minus to arrive. The family dinner never took place. Instead, she received the news that her daughter was found dead, allegedly the victim of domestic violence.

Leaving Minus without her eldest daughter thrust her into becoming the mother to Dejah’s 2-month-old daughter, Dai’Lani, who reminds her of Dejah more and more every day.

Minus says chasing Dai’Lani around keeps her going but it’s the inevitable conversation about Dejah that weighs heavily on her.

“I feel like the worst is yet to come,” she said. “I still have to explain to the 3-year-old what happened to her mother.”

Minus said a trial in her daughter’s death is set to begin in July. Last year, the Boston City Council declared May 13 as “Maé Day” in memory of Dejah. Minus affectionately called her “Maé” because, she said, Dejah acted like a little old lady.

Kianna Battle lost more than her son on July 14, 2023. She lost her best friend, her everything, when Kamari Aaron Perry, 16, was hit by a car while on a scooter.

Perry wanted to be a basketball player. Battle says Kamari still receives college basketball recruiting letters.

“My son was so giving of himself to his peers. I’ve been trying to follow in his footsteps and give back myself,” Battle said. “I’m just trying to turn my pain into purpose.”

Battle recently organized a basketball tournament in memory of Kamari called Mari’s World Heart of Hope, where she was able to give away a $5,000 scholarship.

This will be Battle’s second year participating in the Peace Walk. She says the walk does bring sad memories but also serves as a way to uplift each other.

“We’re all a part of a club we don’t want to be a part of,” she said. “But it’s uplifting because we’re there for each other, we uplift each other, we hold each other when we hold this walk and we come together as one.”

It was Friday during Lent and like many Catholics, the Couho family had to refrain from eating red meat. But on this particular Friday in 2014, it was the baby of the family’s birthday. Joel Santiago Leon Couho was turning 19 and he was sick of eating fish every Friday. After promising his mother, Beatriz Couho, he would go to church if she made him steak, the family delighted in eating their food and poking fun at Beatriz for breaking the rules.

It was a perfect day. Three days later, the family would be rocked by the sudden death of Joel who was hit by a lone bullet that came into his car and struck him in the neck.

Couho had brought Joel from Mexico when he was 2 months old. He was with her throughout the entire journey to the United States and just like that he was gone.

“I learn to live, I learn how to live with this, and it took me 10 years to put myself together, and start to do things for people,” she said. “Some days I’m down, some days I’m up, but I learned to live and that new process in my life.”

Beatriz Couho works on an initiative of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute called “Pan con Café,” where she works with Spanish speakers dealing with the death of loved ones due to homicide, overdose, and suicide.

title: A grieving mother’s tale of reconciliation
text:
The organizer of this walk for nearly three decades has been Chaplain Clementina Chéry, mother of Louis. In 1993, Louis was a 15-year-old straight-A student at West Roxbury High School. In the most deadly of ironies, a bullet to the back of his head ended his promising life right before Christmas as he was on his way to a gathering of Teens against Gang Violence.

While the killing was still under investigation, Chéry didn’t stop to mourn. The next year she formed the peace institute and became what she has described as a “wedding planner for funerals” — helping suffering neighbors deal with reporters’ loaded questions, plan a meaningful service, and figure out how to go on. In the 30 years since, the institute has become the most important support system in Boston for families of the victims of violence. Today, it’s become a national anti-violence model and is halfway toward the $25 million needed to build a proposed center for healing, just blocks from where Louis was killed.

Three years after Louis’s murder, police arrested a suspect. Charles Bogues was, by his own account, in the neighborhood to do a drug deal armed with a .45-caliber handgun. At some point, he acknowledges, he fired it during a shootout. When his lawyer told him that police had proof he was responsible, Bogues assumed it was true. He later told me that his father, a Boston police officer, said to him, “if you think you did it, do the right thing and plead guilty.” So, based on that advice and his attorney’s dubious representation, he did. What Bogues says his lawyer didn’t tell him was much more consequential than what he did.

But given the chaos of that night, how could police know he fired the deadly shot? From the outset, Chéry was skeptical about the police narrative. The day of the plea, Chéry says she turned to her then-husband, Louis’s father, and said: “God said he didn’t do it. People will think I’m really crazy, but he didn’t kill Louis.” Evidence is emerging that her instincts might have been right.

In 2012, after about 16 years in prison, Bogues was granted parole after Chéry and prosecutors declined to oppose it. Not long after, he appeared onstage with Chéry at the Mother’s Day walk. Together, they joined me for an interview on GBH 2 later to discuss their budding relationship. I asked Chéry why she sought to connect first with Bogues’s mother, Doris, then with Bogues himself. She replied: “It could’ve been my son on the other end of that gun. … No winners here.” Bogues, who more than once told me he hoped his own son would grow up to be like Louis, said he’d asked the chaplain for forgiveness.

In late 2021, Chéry, who relentlessly continued to fight to reform a system she argues revictimizes and retraumatizes survivors, suggested that I watch a nearly hour-long video titled “I didn’t kill Louis Brown.” In it, Bogues convincingly contends that he did not receive effective legal representation and that if all the facts had come out, there would have been more than reasonable doubt that he was guilty.

He maintains that the police and prosecutors were guilty of misconduct for a host of reasons. First, they failed to tell the grand jury there were at least two guns involved — that is, there was more than one .45-caliber shell casing with a unique marking at the scene. They did not ask their own witness about a photo lineup in which she picked out someone other than Bogues. And they failed to call an eyewitness who identified the shooter as someone who looked very different than Bogues.

These are not simply the assertions of a man seeking exoneration; they were also confirmed through rigorous investigation by a team of Northeastern law students.

“I just want to know who killed my son,” Chéry said when I called her after watching the video. Why, she wondered, was Bogues the only one from the multi-person shootout who had been arrested?

Every attempt to reopen the case has failed. Most recently, in 2022, the office of the Suffolk County district attorney wrote Chéry saying it was not persuaded that Bogues’s plea was “either unreliable or unjust.”

If history is prologue, when Chéry, a force of nature, takes the stage on Sunday in Dorchester, she’ll make a deep connection to people like her who have suffered unimaginable loss, while giving a special shout-out to people with a loved one whose killing remains unsolved. Most will think she is not in that group. She would disagree.

While the legal system remains resolute in saying justice was done, the people most intimately involved make a compelling case that it was not. Here’s hoping the mother of Louis D. Brown and the son of Doris Bogues finally get the fair hearing they deserve.

title: Is Boston the safest city in America? Not for everyone, says Josh Kraft.
text:
Last month, Andrew Owens stopped by the Roxbury headquarters of Josh Kraft’s mayoral campaign to sign up as a volunteer. A few days later, Owens, 38, died from gunshot wounds, incurred around 11 p.m. in Nubian Square, according to Boston police.

The April 19 shooting of Owens and a second victim, who suffered non-life-threatening injuries, drew scant attention — just a brief police report and the listing of Owens’s name in the running tally of homicides reported by Universal Hub, the community news and information site managed by Adam Gaffin. There was no official mayoral response to that loss of life.

Kraft shared the story of the shooting during a recent meeting with the Globe editorial board when he was asked about Mayor Michelle Wu’s description of Boston as the safest big city in America, a framing that is largely attributed to last year’s homicide count. In 2024, there were 24 killings, down from 36 the year before, and the lowest number of homicides in the city since 1957. While it’s “awesome” that the homicide rate is down, Kraft said, “a lot of people feel a lot of fear.”

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

No mayor can prevent every act of gun violence, and Wu has said that any life lost is one life too many. But celebrating the historically low homicide statistics of last year leaves her open for criticism should they start heading in the opposite direction. So far in 2025, there have been eight homicides, according to Universal Hub. At this time last year, there were four.

As GBH’s Adam Reilly reported last October, whether Boston is the safest city in America depends on how you analyze the numbers and on which cities are used as comparison points. If people feel less safe, that may also be due to reports that some crime is spreading to areas such as Downtown Crossing and the South End, a scenario that is linked to the breakup of encampments at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard. That spillover effect from Mass. and Cass — what has long been the epicenter of the city’s opioid and homelessness crisis — is something Kraft is pledging to address.

I asked the Wu administration for response to the uptick in homicides, as well as to Kraft’s contention that two youth outreach programs have been disbanded on Wu’s watch. I also asked the administration what the city’s plans are for the upcoming summer months, when gun violence has increased in past years. A spokesperson told me they are working on a response.

Whatever the statistics, for some Boston neighborhoods, violent crime is still a reality. Of the eight homicides so far in 2025, two were in Mattapan, two were in Roxbury, two were in Charlestown, one was in Dorchester, and one was in Allston.

Police are still investigating the April 19 shooting that killed Owens. Through the Kraft campaign, I connected with two people who knew him.

According to Garrick Thames, executive director of Lives Are Meant to Be Changed, a nonprofit that helps people break the cycle of addiction, unemployment, and recidivism, Owens was about to get custody of a daughter. To help make that happen, he had been attending a weekly father’s group meeting, Thames told me in an interview. Owens was known as “Goofy” because of his friendly, outgoing personality, and that’s why he thought he would be a good fit on a campaign.

He said he referred him to the Kraft campaign because he knows Josh Kraft through his work with the Boys & Girls Club, where Kraft worked for three decades.

At Kraft campaign headquarters, Owens met with Dana Jackson, a Kraft supporter who also knows the candidate through his community work. In an interview, Jackson said he talked with Owens about joining other volunteers on April 30 to gather signatures needed to put Kraft’s name on the ballot. Both Thames and Jackson said Owens was excited to be part of that effort. But he never got the opportunity. A door that was opening for him closed when he was fatally shot in Nubian Square. Thames and Jackson both contend that Owens was caught in crossfire and was not a gang member.

When it comes to dealing with gun violence, “we still got work to do,” Thames said. The city could “absolutely” be doing more, he said, especially with more outreach programs to young people. Jackson said that while programs “are not the end-all, be-all, if we’re going to talk about the city being the safest city, how do we explain taking them away?”

Thames told me that Kraft attended Owens’s funeral and memorial service — something Kraft did not mention at the Globe meeting but which a Kraft campaign spokesperson confirmed afterward.

It may not fit the narrative, but not everyone here is safe. In the safest city in America, Owens wasn’t.

Joan Vennochi is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at joan.vennochi@globe.com. Follow her @joan_vennochi.

title: Boston school bus driver that fatally struck 5-year-old has been placed on leave
text:
But some residents Tuesday voiced frustration about the limited amount of information released in the case.

“There’s a death of a child, and I haven’t heard anything after that,” said Marie Kelley, 65, in an interview. “Somebody’s got to answer [for] this.”

The Globe, on Friday, reported the same bus involved in the Hyde Park crash also struck two parked cars in Wellington Hill in Mattapan before fleeing that scene, according to recordings of Boston police radio calls reviewed by the Globe.

After the deadly crash in Hyde Park, police reported the driver tried to take off, but was blocked by another vehicle.

Wu, speaking to reporters Tuesday after an unrelated event in Roxbury, declined to comment further and directed questions to police.

“I’ll defer to Boston police on the investigation and how that is unfolding. It is not completed yet, but I know they’re in the process of working through a lot of the pieces of that, including trying to make sure they get to the bottom of what exactly happened with the driver,” Wu said.

Since the crash, few other details have been released. Boston police did not immediately respond to questions Tuesday, and a spokesperson for Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden declined comment.

City Councilor Enrique J. Pepén, in an interview Tuesday afternoon, said he was concerned about the limited information authorities have released about this case.

“I think that it is concerning, just because I know that the community is looking for answers,” he said. “They’re looking for an explanation as to what happened.”

Community members have been asking how this crash could have been prevented, or steps that could be taken to make streets safer, he said. The involvement of a BPS bus driver in the crash also raises concerns about driver training, he said.

“It’s a conversation that I think that we need to have with the Boston Public Schools, especially the transportation department, to ensure that those bus drivers are just getting the proper training,” he said. “We don’t want this to happen anywhere in the city.”

In Hyde Park Tuesday, a handwritten note displayed on a chain link fence near the crash scene had a message from the Joseph family: They asked for privacy, and praised people for their support.

Nearby, a pile of stuffed animals were placed at the foot of a utility pole, next to a bouquet of flowers.

“Thank you all for all the toys, flowers and condolences,” the note read, asking people to refrain from leaving more objects. “Please respect the family and keep them in your prayers.”

Kelley, the Hyde Park resident, said she knows the Joseph family, who she sees outside tending their garden often. “They’re good neighbors. They’re nice, awesome,” Kelley said.

For Kelley, the limited information authorities have released about the crash has been frustrating. Given what happened, residents should know more about what caused the crash, and whether anyone should be held responsible, she said.

And finding out two weeks after the crash that the driver had been placed on leave wasn’t sufficient, she said.

“I don’t think that’s good enough for a child being killed, do you?” Kelley said.

Not all agree that the investigation is moving too slowly. Marcia Kimm-Jackson, who leads the West Fairmount Hill Community Group, expressed faith in investigators and city leaders.

“I think [residents] understand that the Boston police are doing their job, and I know the city of Boston is equally concerned,” she said.

Kimm-Jackson organized a community meeting Tuesday night at the Boston Police Academy building, where about a dozen Hyde Park residents gathered for part of the meeting to share their concerns with city officials and police on issues like traffic and road safety.

Several attendees called for traffic safety improvements and raised concerns about school bus driver training.

Some, including Robert Deveer Jr., 36, said he’s seen Boston school buses drive through stop lights and travel at unsafe speeds through residential neighborhoods. He asked for more signage, and a greater police presence.

Since the crash, Deveer said there is a lot of anger about what happened in the neighborhood. He said there needs to be far greater transparency in the investigation.

“Somebody should be held accountable, and there needs to be transparency,” Deveer said in an interview. “Right now, there is no accountability.”

Anthony Richardson, a 53-year-old resident of the neighborhood, said he believed investigators were being careful to “dot the i’s and cross the t’s” in their work before saying anything publicly.

But the crash raises questions about how prepared Boston’s school bus drivers are to operate their vehicles, he said.

“I wonder about the training for the drivers who transport those kids,” Richardson said.

title: In Roxbury court, weighty issues of religious freedom and due process clash
text:
Worried the witness would choose not testifying over removing the niqab, the Suffolk district attorney filed an emergency petition with the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court asking that she be allowed to wear it on the stand. Otherwise, Fiandaca’s ruling would be “tantamount to a dismissal” of the case, prosecutors argued.

The request exposed a deep tension between the constitutional rights of religious expression and a defendant’s right to confront an accuser. Both are ingrained principles of the Constitution, and there are rarely easy ways to balance them.

Last Thursday, the woman, whom the Globe is not naming as she says she is a victim of domestic violence, returned to the courthouse as word trickled in that a ruling from a single justice of the high court was imminent.

Minutes ticked by as the sun beamed into the quiet, stuffy courtroom. The defendant sat quietly. He wore a black suit and tie, and only spoke to his attorney next to him.

The ruling landed shortly before noon: Justice Serge Georges Jr. sided with the prosecution and the woman would be allowed to testify.

“The right to confrontation is not absolute,” Georges wrote. He said other courts have “recognized limited and exceptional circumstances in which a defendant’s rights under the Sixth Amendment” to confront his accuser may “appropriately yield to competing constitutional interests.”

Fiandaca acknowledged the ruling and proceeded with the trial. It was the woman’s turn to take the stand.

She entered from the rear of the courtroom. A black covering shrouded the top half of her body with a slit around her eyes. She spoke so quietly that a juror raised a hand, indicating they couldn’t hear. She calmly testified for about one hour, describing the alleged assault by her ex-boyfriend, whom she dated for more than a year until about May 2022.

She testified that about one month after she broke up with him, a noise awoke her around 4:30 a.m. She said she found him downstairs in her Dorchester townhouse, acting belligerent and mumbling incoherently, seemingly drunk.

She urged him to leave but he grabbed her by both arms, hard, she said.

“I could feel his nails digging into my arm,” the woman testified. She clutched her biceps where she said he grabbed her.

The struggle continued as they made their way out the front door, she said. The woman’s boyfriend — now husband — was woken up by the noise. He tried to get between them, she said. Amid the fracas, the ex-boyfriend grabbed her near the neck and punched her in the face, she testified.

“I felt like I was being choked,” she said. “I just felt the hand hitting my mouth.”

An attorney for the defendant, Andrew Lloyd, argued to jurors that the woman’s testimony contradicted evidence that police observed at the scene. Officers, for instance, found no sign of a break-in, he told jurors during his closing arguments.

Lloyd also noted the defendant had been found stabbed and bleeding badly after the confrontation with the woman’s boyfriend. The woman had told police she thought he had arrived at the home already bleeding.

“It’s simply not possible that [he] had arrived with those injuries,” Lloyd argued.

After just over an hour, the six-person jury found the defendant not guilty. He bowed his head.

The woman left the courtroom immediately after the verdict was announced, walking quickly to her car. She was upset, she said, and needed to process it.

Prosecutors did not address the verdict, but in a court filing said the woman had the religious right to testify with her niqab all along. Preventing her from doing so would have dissuaded other victims of assault from wanting to testify.

“This would no doubt embolden those who would commit violence against such persons to do so with impunity,” they argued.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
RAUW ALEJANDRO “Cosa Nuestra,” the latest full-length from this San Juan-born dynamo, threads salsa, tropicália, and old-school reggaeton through its dancefloor-ready mix of modern música urbana’s heavy beats and insistent hooks. May 17, 8 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

LOS AMIGOS INVISIBLES The long-running Venezuelan funk act throws a Sunday-night rager. May 18, 7 p.m. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

SWIRLIES The locally grown shoegaze pioneers play an all-ages show—and given their chosen genre’s recent revival, it’s a perfect opportunity for fuzz aficionados of all generations to come together in the name of blissing out. May 22, 6 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

THE WOLFF SISTERS They describe themselves as a “gritty and raw folk-rock outfit,” and that description fits this Boston-area sister act to a T. And with a musician father and poet mother, you could say that both words and music run in the family. May 17, 7 p.m. $25. The Burren, 247 Elm St, Somerville. 617-776-6896. www.burren.com

MARK SCHATZ AND BRYAN MCDOWELL The weekly Bluegrass Tuesdays event brings a duo with plenty of bluegrass pedigree to Cambridge this week. Both have lent their talents to a multitude of players, including, to name just a handful, Bela Fleck, Tony Rice, Jerry Douglas, Sierra Hull and Alison Brown. May 20, 7 p.m. No cover. Lily P’s, 50 Binney St., Cambridge. www.bluegrasstuesdays.com

PEPPINO D’AGOSTINO Sicilian by birth but American by residence for the past forty years, in that time Peppino D’Agostino has made his mark in the world of fingerstyle guitar, incorporating a gamut of influences and styles to produce what he calls“minestrone music.” May 21, 8 p.m. $30. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 617-492-7679. www.passim.org

STUART MUNRO

DUKE ROBILLARD BAND New England’s own jump-blues guitar maestro helped found the legendary Roomful of Blues and has played with everyone from Big Joe Turner to Tom Waits. And no less an eminence than B.B. King once called him “one of the great players.” May 17, 8 p.m. Tickets: $33-36. Spire Center, 25 1/2 Court St. Plymouth. spirecenter.org

CONTEMPORARY JAZZ ORCHESTRA EAST Saxophonist and bandleader Christopher Pitts – who’s collaborated with such orchestral jazz avatars as Dizzy Gillespie and Thad Jones – debuts his 16-piece CJO East big band, exciting equal to its original San Francisco iteration, featuring an extraordinary lineup of internationally renowned jazz musicians. May 20, 7;30 p.m. Free. Newton City Hall/War Memorial, 1000 Commonwealth Ave., Newton. jazznation.com/contemporary-jazz-orchestra

MARK ZALESKI’S MIXTAPE SESSIONS The accomplished alto and soprano saxophonist interprets 1990s popular music – top 40 to metal to punk – from a jazz perspective with a distinguished cast: trumpeter Jason Palmer, tenor saxophonist Jon Bean, guitarist Caio Afiune, pianist Peter Vazquez, bassist Matt Dwonszyk, and drummer Jonathan Barber. May 22, 8:30 p.m. Tickets: $18-$34. The Mad Monkfish, 524 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. themadmonkfish.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

MUSIC FOR VIOLS AND FRIENDS Early stringed instrument specialists Olav Chris Henriksen and Carol Lewis are the longstanding Duo Maresienne; they perform an evening of virtuoso pieces from the early Italian baroque period with countertenor and cornetto player Michael Collver. May 16, 8 p.m. Lindsay Chapel, First Church in Cambridge. www.duomaresienne.com

SARASA CHAMBER MUSIC ENSEMBLE Sarasa takes inspiration from three literary figures – Soviet/Russian poet Anna Akhmatova, Japanese author Yukio Mishima, and French poet Charles Baudelaire – in “The Muse,” its final program of the season, which includes pieces by Florence Price, Philip Glass, and Emilie Mayer. May 17, 7 p.m., Friends Meeting House, Cambridge; May 18, 3:30 p.m., Follen Community Church, Lexington

BOSTON PUBLIC QUARTET The Public Quartet and flutist DeShaun Gordon-King offers two performances of “Source Code: Music She Wrote”, featuring music of five women composers including Gabriela Lena Frank, Eleanor Alberga, and Boston’s own Amy Beach. May 18, 3 p.m., First Parish of Milton; May 22, 7:30 p.m. Strand Theatre, Dorchester. www.bostonpublicquartet.com

A.Z. MADONNA

JAJA’S AFRICAN HAIR BRAIDING Directed by Summer L. Williams, with a 10-member cast skillfully navigating rapid-fire crosscurrents of conversation and conflict, this vibrantly alive production offers a showcase of ensemble acting at its finest. Jocelyn Bioh’s play takes place in a Harlem salon on a scorching summer day in 2019. Most of the characters are immigrants — meaning that, for them, the past is often commingled with an increasingly uneasy present — and their individual narratives are strands within a larger story. Through May 31. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, SpeakEasyStage.com

LEARNING HOW TO READ BY MOONLIGHT Natsu Onoda Power directs the premiere of Gaven D. Trinidad’s drama about the struggles of an undocumented Filipino family in 2017-2018 as they try to stay afloat in a hostile political environment shaped by two presidents: Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines and Donald J. Trump in America. We see the story through the eyes of a six-year-old boy who is learning English from an imaginary friend. Coproduction by Company One Theatre and CHUANG Stage features original songs composed by Trinidad. At Plaza Theatre, Boston Center for the Arts, from May 16 – 25. Then at Pao Arts Center, Boston, from May 29 – June 1. Then at the Umbrella Arts Center, Concord, from June 5-8. www.companyone.org

DON AUCOIN

DAVID DORFMAN DANCE Nearing its 40th year, the company is known for lively, engaging dance theater that tackles socially relevant themes in a personal, humanistic way. The Bessie Award-winning Dorfman’s 2024 “truce songs,” which Global Arts Live presents at the ICA/Boston, is an evening length work about healing and peace with text by the choreographer and an original score by Lizzy de Lise and Sam Crawford. May 16-17, $63. Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET SCHOOL NEXT GENERATION This one-night-only performance provides a glimpse of aspiring stars of tomorrow while highlighting the possibilities of the artform moving forward. Featuring dancers of Boston Ballet II (BBII), Graduate Program dancers, and students of Boston Ballet School’s Professional Division at Walnut Hill School for the Arts, the program includes classical excerpts as well as the premieres of Jorma Elo’s “Five Etudes” and Adrienne Canterna’s “Hold Me Tight,” plus works by Paul Craig and Helen Pickett. May 21, $25 and up. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

(JUST) 33 In this Boston Dancemakers Residency Showcase, Nailah Randall-Bellinger / RootsUprising presents a multimedia dance narrative celebrating the life and inspirational music of the late performing artist Donny Edward Hathaway. Using Hathaway’s music and archival documentation, including recorded interviews and photographs, the choreographic work explores the intersection of artistic expression and mental health. May 22-24, $25. (Free video access May 26-30.) Boston Center for the Arts’s Martin Rehearsal Hall. https://bostonarts.org/

CONTINUUM DANCE PROJECT The company presents its immersive dance-theater work “Not Eye, Us,” which explores diversity and the power of perspective. The work aims to create an interactive journey that plays off Michael Alfano’s sculpture “Cubed,” which allows the manipulation of nine moveable pieces, each hued with a different skin tone. May 22, $0-$20. Brookline High School Tappan Street Gym, Brookline. https://continuumdance.org/

KAREN CAMPBELL

EDVARD MUNCH: TECHNICALLY SPEAKING I know, I know: “The Scream,” right? There’s no getting around the cultural oversaturation of Munch’s most famous work, but recent efforts have done much to broaden our understanding of Norway‘s most-loved artist beyond his all-time smash hit. In the summer of 2023, “Edvard Munch: Trembling Earth,” the Clark Art Institute‘s voluminous presentation of the artist’s deep affinities with — and anxieties for — the natural world opened a universe of difference for all but the most devoted Munch fan. “Technically Speaking,” at Harvard, takes a different tack, exploring the artist’s material genius and almost manic enthusiasm for media across painting, drawing, and every manner of printing. With it, a view of an artist too long seen as one-note broadens further. Through July 27. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400,harvardartmuseums.org

HUGH HAYDEN: HOME WORK Hayden‘s first solo exhibition in New England brings with it a decade‘s worth of work centered on his prickly vision of the American Dream – a school desk studded with thorns, un-sittable chairs sprouting thickets of branches, and, in a holistic metaphor of unattainability, cookie-cutter tract homes so tangled with overgrowth that entering is an impossibility. Hayden‘t work, which ranges from the sculptural to the architectural, portrays that dream as “seductive but difficult to inhabit,” a bald truth in this era of housing inaffordability that seems to grows worse by the day. Through June 1. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434,www.brandeis.edu/rose

SOVEREIGN MEMORY: PHOTOGRAPHY, REMEMBRANCE, AND DISPLACED HISTORIES Photography and modernity go hand in hand — the upheavals of a world remade first by colonialism and then industrialization ran right into the new technology, able to capture it firsthand. This exhibition seizes on the medium’s ability to record, but also deceive and reshape collective memory — and, finally, through these artists’ various pieces, be stitched together into something resembling whole. Through June 1. The Davis Museum at Wellesley College, 106 Central St., Wellesley. 781-283-2051,www1.wellesley.edu/davismuseum

MURRAY WHYTE

FRANK POOR The artist grew up in the small town of Woodstock, Georgia. He goes back to the South often to photograph the spaces – details of houses, churches, barns. Back home in his Rhode Island studio, Poor sculpturally builds out from an image of a door, window, or wall, crafting works that mix two dimensions and three dimensions. The vivid visuals of the photos play against the physicality of the spare structures that support them. They pose a question: “what’s real here?” As with a lot of art, the answer is both … and neither. Through June 7. Krakow Witkin Gallery, 10 Newbury St. 617-863-0952, (cq)www.krakowwitkingallery.com

CATE McQUAID

EUGENE MIRMAN SPECIAL RECORDING It has been ten years since Mirman’s last special, “Vegan On His Way To the Complain Store,” came out on Netflix. The Boston comic, who voices Gene on “Bob’s Burgers,” is recording his new hour with two shows Friday, tentatively slated for a fall release through his Pretty Good Friends. Early show is sold out. DANAE HAYS: THE FIRST TIME TOUR She was a social media star first, creating country-flavored characters and singing funny country songs on TikTok and IG during the pandemic, but her rise in live comedy has been lightning quick. Hays’s first time doing stand-up was February of 2024, and now she’s touring theaters, and made her Grand Ole Opry debut in March. May 16, 8 p.m. $49-$74. AAPI COMEDY FESTIVAL The second edition of the AAPI Festival kicks off at the Rozzi Square Theater to celebrate Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month with four shows over three days.
