title: Wu and Kraft face off in first candidate forum of this year’s Boston mayoral race
text:
They addressed a range of policy issues, from fixing persistent problems in Boston Public Schools, to making housing more affordable, to mitigating the effects of climate change and traffic congestion in the city.

For DaRosa and Alex, the forum was a key opportunity to introduce themselves and their visions for the city to voters. For Wu and Kraft, it was a chance to restate their pitches to voters, tout their individual accomplishments, and land swings in real-time.

Wu and Kraft engaged in tense back-and-forth exchanges. Wu on several occasions directly criticizing pillars of Kraft’s platform, rebutting criticisms he‘s fired her way in recent weeks, and reiterating her characterization of Kraft as an outsider with no experience in elected office.

While answering a question about how each candidate would maintain the city’s fiscal health in the face of possible reductions in federal funding, Wu defended her administration’s proposed budget for the upcoming fiscal year, while also taking aim at Kraft, who has previously criticized Wu for her management of the city’s finances.

“We are preparing for the un-plannable while at the same time not jumping ahead [and] buying into the fact that we need to slash and cut,” Wu said. “It’s not just billionaires at the federal level who said we need to cut everything in the name of efficiency, there are people on the stage right now who said, ‘Let’s take a 2 percent cut across the board to city services.’ That, when you tell the truth, translates into firing police officers, teachers, etc, mass layoffs.”

In his rebuttal, Kraft argued the consequences of trimming the budget wouldn’t be as drastic as Wu claimed.

“The city administration said there wasn’t a penny to cut from [the budget], I just find that hard to believe, but I also think it’s disrespectful to so many citizens in Boston, that are making hard fiscal decisions that impact their families every day,” Kraft said.

Wu, in return, highlighted Kraft’s background as she disagreed.

“It’s easy to stand on the sidelines if you’re new to the city, new to any city, policy making, to say, ‘Just cut, cut, cut,’ and not have to say from where,” she retorted.

Wu and Kraft also diverged when asked whether their administrations would prioritize reducing residents’ dependence on cars. Kraft answered no, saying he would like to invest in alternative transportation options like improving the MBTA in the long term, but his immediate priority would be fixing roads and sidewalks, and potholes.

“There‘s a lot of folks in this city, I hear from them every day, they need their car. They have to get their child to day care, they have to get to work,” Kraft said.

Wu answered with a firm “yes,” while highlighting progress her administration has made on improving public transportation. But she also fired back at Kraft, who has been especially vocal in his criticism of Wu’s push to install bike lanes across the city. She highlighted a recent interview with Politico Massachusetts, in which Kraft was asked whether he has a plan to reduce traffic congestion, other than pausing construction of bike lanes. He didn’t have an answer, saying his team has been more focused on bike lanes.

“That’s not a plan, that’s not even a concept of a plan,” Wu said.

The two also went head to head on how to tackle homelessness and the opioid crisis that has been centered at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, as well as whether Wu’s increased affordability requirements for new housing developments is an effective way to address the city’s housing affordability crisis.

Meanwhile, DaRosa and Alex highlighted their personal stories in their pitches to voters. DaRosa emphasized his upbringing in Boston and experience in the public school system, as well as his years of grass-roots activism and time as a Pop Warner football coach. When Wintersmith asked the candidates whether they support ending Boston’s engagement with a controversial police gang database known as the BRIC, DaRosa gave an emphatic, “Yes,” revealing that he was at one point included on that list.

Alex, a 24-year-old Dorchester resident, shared his story as a formerly undocumented minor who experienced homelessness, but ended up attending and graduating from New York University. He advocates for a broad range of detailed policies, from congestion pricing, to rent control, and increased enforcement for traffic violations.

The night ended with a round of rapid-fire and then light-hearted questions, including the candidates’ favorite cultural events in the city, favorite coffee shops, and what ward they reside in.

Wu and DaRosa had ready answers, while Alex hesitantly guessed ward 3.

Kraft answered, “I’m embarrassed to say, I don’t know.”

title: School bus tragedy has prompted many questions, not enough answers
text:
But for days and days, no answers were forthcoming. Just official, maddening silence.

Finally, a few answers have begun to emerge. The driver of the bus, Jean Charles, was placed on leave after the incident. Charles resigned Wednesday, ahead of a termination hearing. Turns out, he had been driving school buses without a required state certification for months.

We know a few other things now. Charles was a substitute driver that day who had never driven the route before. As the Globe reported last week, he hit two parked cars in Mattapan just minutes before the fatal accident.

Under established policy, Charles was supposed to report those prior accidents to a safety monitor, who then would have decided whether he should continue to drive that day or be replaced.

None of that happened.

Perhaps because Charles was unfamiliar with the route he was driving, he missed a turn and dropped Lens and his 11-year-old cousin across the street from their normal bus stop. Apparently, they were crossing the street — a street they normally would not have needed to cross — when Lens was struck by the bus.

Charles, the driver, attempted to leave the scene. But he was stopped by another driver, whose vehicle blocked him in.

Even in a city whose problems related to schools and buses have been unsurpassed, this is a remarkable tragedy.

Boston’s school bus system is operated by an outside contractor, Transdev, which is based in France. It operates school bus systems across the country, and was awarded the contract to operate Boston’s buses in 2023. They hire and manage the drivers, and oversee issues such as certification.

Transdev notified Charles that his state certification had lapsed, but allowed him to continue to drive. That was a mistake.

The accident is under investigation by the Suffolk district attorney’s office, which hasn’t really said anything beyond, “We’re working on it.”

That’s standard practice during a criminal investigation. But the thousands of families who depend on the Boston Public Schools every day to get their children home safely deserve more answers than they have been given so far.

Specifically, the public needs to know how the city works with the bus operator to make sure safe practices are being followed — every day, on every bus. Who makes sure drivers are properly licensed and certified? Is BPS notified when a driver isn’t? And what kind of monitoring system allows a driver to hit parked cars — with children on board — and keep on driving?

For whatever reasons, transportation is on the list of issues the BPS never seems to be able to get right. Whether the issue is driver absenteeism, or on-time performance, or simply the staggering cost of transporting kids across the city, the next crisis is seemingly never far away.

But the recent revelations make this tragedy even more shocking than it appeared initially. By all appearances, this driver should probably have been yanked off this bus before it ever got to Hyde Park. Before he ever had a chance to somehow end the life of a child in his care.

Regardless of the outcome of the criminal investigation, Wu and her appointed school committee are going to have to face some hard questions about what they are doing to keep the city’s children safe.

Because here’s the one thing we already know: Whatever they’re doing fell tragically short one day last month, and a life may have been lost because of it.

title: Reinstatement of Pete Rose, others has this Hall of Fame voter wondering why worry about ‘character,’ and other thoughts
text:
On Tuesday of this past week, commissioner Rob Manfred, at the request of President Trump, made a mockery of the office, reinstating known gambling violators Pete Rose, Shoeless Joe Jackson, and 15 others deceased individuals. Buffered with soft semantics (“permanent ineligibility” ends when you die), Manfred’s message to uniformed baseball personnel seems to be: Don’t worry too much about that rule you were always told was so sacred. It may not happen until after your death, but if you gamble on baseball you will eventually be reinstated by MLB. The commissioner will leave it up to others to decide if you are Hall of Fame worthy.

So there you go.

Pete Rose, baseball’s all-time hit king, who died last September, is free at last. A couple of years from now, Rose’s name likely will come up before a committee of 16 voters (Hall of Fame players, longtime executives, and veteran historian/media members), and if he gets 12 of their votes, his family will see him enshrined in Cooperstown in the summer of 2028. After that, prepare for everybody else. Barry Bonds. Roger Clemens. Alex Rodriguez. Manny Ramirez. Mark McGwire. Sammy Sosa. Jose Altuve. Carlos Beltran. Omar Vizquel.

Open the gates. These were all great players. Fans want them in. So let’s put ‘em all in. O.J. Simpson is in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Why should baseball have any “character” consideration? Gambling on baseball no longer takes you out of the running.

For decades, the Baseball Writers’ Association of America has been charged with vetting Cooperstown candidates. A lot of Hall of Famers seemed happy with the system, and I remember late Hall of Famer Tom Seaver telling scribes, “Keep sending us class acts.”

In this spirit, many players with HOF numbers have been denied tickets to Cooperstown because of things such as failed steroid tests, the Mitchell Report, whisper campaigns, drug trafficking, domestic violence charges, sexual offense charges, trash can banging, and electronic sign-cheating. Unlike Clemens, Bonds, and Co., Rose never made it to the writers’ ballot because he was on the “permanently ineligible” list.

A Hall of Fame voter for more than 35 years, I find myself asking, “If Pete’s OK to be considered now [Rose also was a convicted felon for tax evasion and faced uncontested allegations of statutory rape] why should anybody be denied because of off-field issues? Manfred’s willing to reinstate Rose and Jackson after they committed the No. 1 sin against baseball. So why should writers continue to weigh a ballplayer’s ‘character’ or off-field foibles? Why not just go by the numbers?”

It’s easy.

I can count. Clemens won seven Cy Young Awards and 354 games. He’s a Hall of Famer. Bonds hit 762 home runs. Hall of Famer. Sosa hit 60 or more homers in three seasons. Manny was the game’s best righthanded slugger since Jimmie Foxx. These are all Hall of Famers, just like Pete and his 4,256 hits.

Dorchester-born Mark Mulvoy, managing editor of “Sports Illustrated” when it was a powerhouse magazine that exposed much of Rose’s gambling, says, “Sandy Koufax had a home near me in Florida for years. I can tell you a whole lot of Koufax-era players will never go to Cooperstown if Rose gets in. I’ve probably gone to my last baseball game.”

Swell. But who else still cares? Mulvoy is 83 and players from the age of Koufax are dying every month. DraftKings and FanDuel have taken over the sports world. Pretty soon there’ll be very few voices that care about a silly thing such as gambling on baseball.

Partnerships with legal gambling operations are lucrative for MLB and a big part of its future. No punishment is forever. Let anybody in who has Hall of Fame numbers. Nothing else matters anymore.

Right, Rob?

My favorite comes from Charley Steiner, who was the Yankees’ radio broadcaster in 2003. Steiner recalls sitting alone with Grady Little an hour before the Red Sox and Yankees played Game 7 of the 2003 ALCS at Yankee Stadium (the game when Grady went too long with Pedro and got fired for it). “Grady said, ‘We’re [expletive] tonight. And then on the morning of the parade, I am going to go from one talk-radio station to the next, and tell them they’re a bunch of freaking geniuses, and then I’m going to retire.’ ”

title: At funeral, 5-year-old boy killed in Boston school bus crash remembered as ‘definition of life’ for family
text:
In an at-times heartrending service, family, loved ones, and friends bid goodbye to Lens inside the church’s packed worship space.

His uncle, Ricardo Joseph, speaking in Haitian Creole, called Lens the “definition of life” for his family. Lens, Joseph said, “was a grown man who lived in the body of a 5-year-old boy.”

“We are thankful to have had the chance to live with Lens for 5 years, which has been more valuable than 50 years,” said Joseph, a transcript of whose remarks were also provided in English. “It always takes a long time for nature to produce a person like Lens.”

The funeral Saturday came as Boston police and the Suffolk district attorney’s office continued investigating the crash that killed Lens, who was struck and killed April 28 by a Boston Public Schools bus after he had been dropped off from school with his 11-year-old cousin on Washington Street in Hyde Park.

Law enforcement authorities have not released any updates from the investigation since the tragedy occurred.

This past week, officials with the city and Boston Public Schools said the driver, Jean Charles, resigned just before a scheduled termination hearing, and said he was driving with an expired credential required to work as a bus driver. The revelations came after the Globe reported Charles was in another accident in Mattapan and Boston police were told he struck two cars just minutes before the deadly crash, according to police radio recordings.

City and school officials, who have said Charles struck one car in Mattapan, said Charles didn’t report the Mattapan crash as he was supposed to and continued on his bus route.

Charles had been employed for two years by Transdev Transportation, a French company that employs and oversees Boston’s school bus drivers. Transdev told Charles to renew his school bus certificate, but he did not.

City and school officials learned that Charles’s credential had expired after the Hyde Park crash, they said. Transdev has not commented on the crash or about Charles. Before the city and schools released information about Charles, some community members raised concerns that there has not been enough transparency in the investigation.

Inside the church Saturday, speakers during the nearly two-hour service addressed well-wishers in a mix of Haitian Creole and English, reading passages from the Bible and singing songs.

Lens was born in 2019 in Arcahaie, Haiti, and moved to the US in 2023 with several family members, including his father, uncle, and grandmother, and settled in Hyde Park, according to his obituary.

Lens, who would have turned 6 on Aug. 8, was his parents’ only son and left behind many family members, including his mother and two sisters, aunts and uncles, and cousins.

People wept openly at the funeral. A woman cried out in grief, and was comforted by several people, including a member of the city’s community support team. Some people held their heads in their hands as neighbors patted their shoulders or rubbed the backs of their necks.

Among those paying their respects were city leaders, including Mayor Michelle Wu, City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, and City Councilor Enrique J. Pepén, who represents the district including Hyde Park.

Television screens inside the worship space displayed family photos of Lens as people spoke.

They were of Lens grinning wide for the camera, cheek-to-cheek with loved ones for candid photos; him proudly holding up a drawing of a house done in school; kissing a loved one; holding up a sign that read “policeman” — the job he dreamed of doing when he grew into a man.

When his teachers greeted him every morning at school, he’d jokingly reply, “My name is policeman!”

People were visibly moved when Lens’s teachers gave his school certificate to his family. His father stood and gave the educators a hug. His teachers said what made Lens special was his heart — he made friends easily and “lifted people up just by being himself.”

Pastor Joel Piton, in remarks that smoothly switched between Haitian Creole and English, spoke in his sermon of the deep grief that arises from a child’s death. But it also reflects the fact that people are all mortal, he argued.

“A life that is brief is a reminder that all of us can be recalled at any time,” Piton said. “Since we have no guarantee of how long God chooses to give us life, therefore, we must maximize the opportunity God gave us.”

He admonished the crowd: “We cannot forget him.”

The most common photo of Lens displayed at the funeral was perhaps him at his most dapper: in a grey pinstripe vest, pink tie and handkerchief, and a striped button-down shirt. In the image, Lens is posed, turned to the camera, his hands folded on his leg, his face serious, with one eyebrow raised as if studying someone.

But Lens was still a little boy. Spider-Man’s image, in a heroic pose — arms out, legs bent, as if jumping into action, graced Lens’s casket, which was also painted in the superhero’s signature red and blue colors.

At the end of the service, loved ones dressed in white and black gathered around the casket to escort it from the church. But even in that moment of grief, the superhero’s colors could still be seen, glimpsed in bright flashes, through the crowd.

title: ‘We must hold space for joy.’ In Boston, Haitian Flag Day brings optimism amid Trump immigration threats
text:
It’s a day, several people said, about freedom. It is a word imbued with special meaning for Haitians, who proudly talk about how their country was the first Black-led republic in the world after it won independence from European colonialism and slavery.

“The idea of freedom is important to us and always has been,” said Edwing Guilloteau, one of the chaperones with the Pathfinder drum corps, a Seventh-day Adventist youth group that led the way in the parade, beating out a clean, jaunty march. “Ever since Haiti began, we’ve been fighting to be recognized as free people.”

Speakers and attendees alike spoke with a mix of uncertainty and optimism — about their home country and their adopted one, where the current Trump administration is seeking to deport increasing numbers of immigrants and has targeted Haitians.

Many of those who fled Haiti did so because of severe political turmoil and widespread violence that has flourished since a 2010 earthquake, which devastated and destabilized the country. It’s never fully recovered; violent gangs continue to have significant sway, and its president was assassinated in 2021.

But the Haitian people persist, said Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, who’s Haitian American.

“We must hold space for joy,” she told a crowd, saying they’ll work for a better Haiti that they can one day return to. “We are here, we are strong, and we are getting even stronger.”

And then she referred to President Trump’s harsh immigration rhetoric, which has at times has at times specifically targeted Haitians.

“No matter what this administration says about our people, we know who we are,” she said.

In August, the federal government plans to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, a program that has allowed hundreds of thousands of Haitians to live and work in the United States. The program lets people remain here when it would be unsafe to return to their home country due to armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary circumstances.

Standing on a ridge in Harambee Park on Sunday, 38-year-old Joseph Wilson noted the uncertainty facing the Haitian diaspora.

The Dorchester resident is here legally under TPS for now, but it’s unclear what the future might bring for him and his six-month-old child.

“The news isn’t very good,” he said, adding that he arrived in 2021. “We don’t know what’s going to happen. ICE is everywhere.”

He gestured around the park at people chowing down and chatting. “But today’s very calm.”

Greater Boston is home to more than 50,000 Haitian-born residents, according to a Boston Indicators report based on 2021 data. Large populations live in Mattapan and Brockton.

In recent years, the region has become a top destination for Haitian migrants fleeing extreme violence and poverty, who make their way north, often living for years in other countries like Brazil and Chile before continuing to the United States.

Tamisha Civil, the marshal of Sunday’s parade, said there needs to be more services available in the U.S. But locally, many people are on their side.

“Our parents came here seeking the American dream for the next generation,” she said, addressing the many young people in the crowd. “You are all the next generation.”

title: Charlene Roberts-Hayden, pioneering Black woman in computer programming, dies at 86
text:
Away from her hush-hush work, though, Ms. Roberts-Hayden was inspirational. As a person of strong Catholic faith, and a Black woman in a workforce made up mostly of white men, she set an example for family and friends about how to excel while facing challenges.

“She made a lot less than her white male counterparts, but she never showed that it bothered her,” her daughter Karen McAdams of Wellesley recalled. “She just kept going and succeeding.”

Ms. Roberts-Hayden, who also was a longtime soprano in the Archdiocese of Boston Black Catholic Choir, died May 11 in hospice care at her home in the Falls at Cordingly Dam senior living center in Newton. She was 86 and her health had been declining.

“She was a tremendous role model,” said her daughter Dr. Deborah Hayden, a physician who lives in Attleboro.

Ms. Roberts-Hayden was proficient at a high level with the Ada computer programming language, which has been used in areas such as air traffic control, space technology, and military systems.

Her family said she had worked for GTE Government Services, a defense contractor in areas such as electronics and intelligence services.

In 1996, she was among those honored by the Special Interest Group on Ada, a professional organization that promotes understanding and use of the computer language.

“Charlene distinguished herself in a variety of visible roles during the introductory years of Ada, including being an early Ada-for-design pioneer,” the Special Interest Group on Ada said in a 1996 statement.

She served as the organization’s vice chair for meetings and conferences for more than seven years, and also had been its “first users committee chair who really represented real users,” the group said.

Part of her work involved traveling to Europe, which “was something she really enjoyed and something that probably would not have been possible for her without that career,” Karen said.

Ms. Roberts-Hayden “was in a field where very few Black women were working,” her son said, adding that “in many ways, she was a trailblazer, and an unknown one.”

Part of the legacy Ms. Roberts-Hayden left to her children was “her faith in God,” Deborah said. “It was unwavering, and she passed that on to me, and it’s gotten me through my life.”

Ms. Roberts-Hayden’s marriage to Robert C. Hayden, an author of books about Black history, ended in divorce while their children were growing up.

“She was our primary caregiver before, during, and after,” Kevin said.

“She was a woman of deep faith — she was a Catholic through and through,” he added. “My dad instilled our work ethic and she instilled our faith and spiritual beliefs. I believe her prayers and her faith literally saved my life, probably more than once.”

When her children were growing up, Ms. Roberts-Hayden made sure they had a strong religious foundation. When they turned 18, she left to them the decision about the faith path they would follow.

Childhood, though, was a time of devotion. During Lent, for example, the family went to church daily.

“I can remember being an altar boy at 7 a.m. Mass every single day during Lent,” Kevin said, “and then she’d take me to school.”

Born on Sept. 24, 1938, Charlene Roberts grew up in Medford, the second of three siblings.

Her mother, Doris Ringles Roberts, was an elocution coach who worked with theater students.

“My grandmother also was a woman of great faith, so that definitely was passed down,” Karen said.

Deborah said Doris Roberts “was a tremendous role model for me also, and a very strong woman, which she passed on to my mom — between taking on racism and being in service to people.”

Ms. Roberts-Hayden’s father, Charles Roberts, was a maintenance supervisor for the Medford Public Schools, and kept a desk by the boiler in a public school basement.

When she needed a break from the racism she faced among classmates, she would go down there to share lunch with her father at his desk, Karen said.

In 1960, Ms. Roberts-Hayden graduated from Boston University with a bachelor’s degree in mathematics. She and Robert Hayden married after her junior year, when Robert had just graduated from BU. He died in 2022.

Outside of her programming work, she tutored students in mathematics at the middle school, high school, and college levels, and was an adjunct professor at area colleges.

After retiring, she worked in the Boston Archdiocese’s office of Black Catholic ministries and volunteered extensively, including with women jailed at the Massachusetts Correctional Institute at Framingham. An expert card player, she taught them to play bridge.

Because of her work success, Ms. Roberts-Hayden was able to design and build a summer house in Oak Bluffs, on Martha’s Vineyard, in 1991.

She gardened extensively outside the home, which has become a retreat for three generations of her family, and she took up tennis with as much determination as she brought to computer programming.

“Anything that my mom decided to do, she put every ounce of who she was into it,” Kevin said. “If she did something, she did it 110 percent. That’s just how she was.”

Karen said their mother “had this amazing can-do attitude. She was very steadfast in her confidence in herself. There was really nothing she felt couldn’t be done if we as a family put our minds together. One of our good family friends described her as a warrior recently, and I think that’s a perfect word for her.”

In addition to her two daughters and son, Ms. Roberts-Hayden leaves five grandchildren.

A funeral Mass will be held at 10 a.m. Monday in St. Katharine Drexel Church in Dorchester.

The Archdiocese of Boston Black Catholic Choir will sing at Monday’s funeral Mass.

“Charlene was an incredible woman — a lovely human being, a very caring, hard-working, faithful, dedicated, solid person,” said Meyer Chambers, the choir’s director.

“Once she became a member of the choir, she never stopped,” he recalled. “She loved singing, she loved the camaraderie, she loved going to rehearsals.”

Even as age made singing more challenging, “she still sang with us,” Chambers said.

“When somebody finds joy in being around you, that’s infectious, it gets into every fiber of your being and makes you want to be better, and Charlene did that for people by her nature, by her personality,” he said, adding that she brought warmth to every encounter.

“I never ended a conversation with Charlene without her telling me how much she loved me,” he said.

title: Jury finds R.I. man guilty of daytime shooting of taxi driver in Back Bay
text:
A 40-year-old Rhode Island man found guilty for the 2019 shooting death of a cab driver in the Back Bay is due back in Suffolk Superior Court on Friday for a sentencing hearing, prosecutors said.

Phillip Foy of Pawtucket is facing a mandatory sentence of life in prison after a jury on Monday convicted him of first-degree murder, according to the Suffolk district attorney’s office.

Luckinson Oruma had driven cab number 192 for nearly 10 years — 10 hours a day, six days a week. The same white cab put the Dorchester man’s five children through college.

The 60-year-old Nigerian immigrant’s fatal encounter with Foy unfolded on a sunny morning on Huntington Avenue on June 4, 2019, the Globe previously reported.

Just before 11 a.m., Oruma idled in front of the Colonnade Hotel. A tall, thin man who had spent time in jail on a cocaine charge, appeared at his cab window demanding a ride to Mansfield, 35 miles outside the city.

When Oruma refused the fare, Foy dragged him from his cab and shot him nine times, continuing to fire even after Oruma fell, prosecutors said.

Foy drove away in the cab, parked on Ring Road, and tossed the murder weapon. He took off his shoes, and sat in front of a Starbucks, according to law enforcement authorities.

When police arrived, Foy grabbed a pedestrian and tried to shield himself. After his arrest, Foy confessed to shooting Oruma but said he did so in self defense, prosecutors said.

“The shooting death of Luckinson Oruma was shattering not just for his family and friends, but for anyone who goes to work each day expecting, as they should, to be in a safe environment,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement.

Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com. Follow her @talanez.

title: Man sentenced to 17 to 24-years for shooting and killing man on Dorchester porch
text:
After pleading guilty to manslaughter midway through his trial, a Mattapan man will spend at least 17 years in jail for fatally shooting a man on a porch in Dorchester in 2020, prosecutors said.

Yaliek Allah-Barnes, 42, was sentenced Monday to 17 to 24 years in prison for shooting and killing Derek Fitzpatrick, 49 of Dorchester, the Suffolk district attorney’s office said in a statement.

Testimony had begun in the trial on May 2, and Allah-Barnes changed his plea to guilty on May 5, the statement said.

Allah-Barnes drove by Fitzpatrick as he was parking his car on Bernard Street. shortly after 12:00 p.m. on May 18, 2020, prosecutors said.

He then turned onto an adjacent street and parked. Allah-Barnes then walked up to the front porch of 45 Bernard St. and fired multiple shots at Fitzpatrick, prosecutors said.

He then returned to his car and drove away.

Boston police detectives arrested Allah-Barnes on May 21, 2020, prosecutors said.

In court on Monday, several of Fitzpatrick’s family members delivered victim impact statements. His aunt said that the family often met for Bible study at the Bernard Street home. Fitzpatrick’s father said he was proud of his son and that he was “quite a community worker,” and that “he was taking senior citizens to church, picking them up Sundays.”

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said the statements were a touching remembrance and a testament to how deeply Fitzpatrick is missed by his loved ones.

“I thank Mr. Fitzpatrick’s family for sharing their special memories and I thank the investigators, prosecutors and victim witness advocates who worked to secure a measure of justice for his tragic death,” Hayden said.

Adam Sennott can be reached at adam.sennott@globe.com.

title: ‘Marie Antoinette,’ ‘private jet’: Michelle Wu, Josh Kraft trade barbs as Boston mayor’s race gets off to a fiery start
text:
That first day offered an apt preview to the lines of attack that have dominated the race so far. Wu argues Kraft — the third son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft — is a carpetbagger with no government experience trying to buy City Hall with daddy’s money. Kraft counters that Wu has plastered the city with ill-conceived bike lanes and ignored residents’ concerns about projects such as the White Stadium renovation.

Copy, paste, tweet.

Those familiar critiques emerged again Thursday evening at the first mayoral forum of this year’s race at Suffolk University’s Modern Theater in downtown Boston, where Wu and Kraft each took the opportunity to land several blows in person, largely ignoring the two lesser-known candidates on stage.

Only rarely glancing her challengers’ way, Wu wasted no time, launching a thinly veiled snub about Kraft’s wealthy background in her opening statement: “This is a city that cannot be bought.”

That theme continued throughout the evening. Wu compared Kraft’s calls for budget cuts in the middle of its fiscal year to “billionaires at the federal level” wreaking havoc on the federal government by slashing spending.

“The city administration said there wasn’t a penny to cut from [the budget]. I just find that hard to believe,” Kraft said.

“It’s easy to stand on the sidelines if you’re new to the city — new to any city policymaking — to say, ‘Just cut, cut, cut,’ and not have to say from where,” Wu retorted.

Kraft, for his part, criticized Wu’s approach to mitigating the opioid crisis and persistent homelessness centered at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, slammed what he described as her hasty rollout of bike lanes across the city, and blamed the affordability requirements she has imposed on new development for exacerbating the city’s housing crisis.

When Kraft sought to hedge his answer to a rapid-fire “yes or no” question from the moderator, Wu directly called out his wavering by dubbing him “Mr. Halfsies.” (Kraft offered a good natured handshake to the mayor in response).

To be sure, Kraft and Wu diverge on serious policy matters: what to do with the beleaguered Boston Public Schools, whether and where to change streets to accommodate bikes and buses, how to solve the city’s housing crisis. The two Democrats often make their differences known on those major topics, as they did Thursday.

But they have also sparred over matters less mission-critical. Kraft has swiped at Wu over everything from the incomplete Copley Square renovations (“soul-less”) to the location of her campaign kickoff at Cyclorama in Boston’s South End (“an exclusive private venue”) to the $10,000 the city spent to fly Wu and her team to a Congressional hearing in Washington, D.C. “Marie Antoinette would be proud,” Kraft snarked on X.

On several occasions, social media-savvy Wu has engaged with his attacks. After being compared to the famously out-of-touch French queen, the mayor quickly shot back: “Don’t have a private jet to transport everyone.”

All that, and it’s only May. The campaign is only going to intensify before the election this fall.

It’s a contrast from 2021, when despite a crowded field, the mayor’s race stayed relatively civil until the final months. Wu and her major opponents — now Attorney General Andrea Campbell, then-Acting Boston Mayor Kim Janey, and former city councilor Annissa Essaibi George — had been known as “sisters in service” during their days on the Boston City Council, and the tone of the campaign was milder, particularly in the beginning. Days after they earned the top spots in the preliminary election, setting them up for a head-to-head contest, Wu and Essaibi George met over oatmeal at McKenna’s restaurant in Dorchester.

Political experts said elections involving incumbents can get uglier than open-seat races. That’s because reelection campaigns offer a referendum on a sitting politician. Challengers have to persuade voters not only to hire them, but to fire the person who‘s doing the job currently. That means criticism, and lots of it.

Four years ago, the leading candidates were all colleagues, and their collegiality came across even at competitive events such as forums, said Katie Prisco-Buxbaum, who was Campbell’s campaign manager.

“People were focused on running their own race, telling their own story,” she said. This year, because Wu is an incumbent and the field of serious contenders appears smaller, she said, the dynamic is much more “responsive ... she did this; he said that.”

The candidates acknowledge that dynamic, too. Don’t hold your breath for a Wu-Kraft oatmeal summit.

In a recent interview, Wu pointed to notable outside funding in the race — Jim Davis, the billionaire owner and chairperson of New Balance, donated a whopping $1 million to a super PAC backing Kraft — and said there has been an “unprecedented early start to negative campaigning.”

Why is the tone different this time? Wu’s answer included a critique of her opponent.

“Last time, it was an accomplished field of candidates of color, people who had served the city for many years … and there was a sense of mutual respect across the entire field, of people who had put in the work and were making the case with different visions for the city,” Wu said. “This time, I’m running against someone who has not even voted for the office he’s running for before, has not even voted for City Council before, recently moved into a luxury condo that his father’s company purchased for him.”

“So it is a different race,” she continued. (An LLC that lists its address as Gillette Stadium purchased Kraft’s North End condo in 2023.)

Kraft’s campaign argued that his rhetoric offers “a serious contrast” to the mayor, who they allege is “out of touch with working Bostonians.”

”What may be seen as name calling is actually Josh holding the Mayor responsible for her own lack of leadership and many management failures," said Eileen O’Connor, a Kraft campaign spokesperson, in a statement to the Globe.

Criticism plays an important role in any political contest; substantive engagement is “a very good starting place for an election,” said Kathleen Hall Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center at the University of Pennsylvania.

“Unless you attack, you can’t differentiate. If you can’t differentiate, you don’t have a basis for voting,” she said.

But there could be risks for both candidates in a race that has so far been “swing, counter swing, swing, counter swing — back and forth and back and forth,” said Cam Charbonnier, a political consultant who ran a rival mayoral campaign in 2021 and is not involved in the race this year.

Kraft, he said, “is swinging way too often at her. It’s like the boy who cried wolf.”

For Wu, Charbonnier warned, responding too much to Kraft’s attacks can have the unintended consequence of elevating his candidacy.

“If I was advising the Kraft campaign, my advice would be: Focus your attacks,” Charbonnier added. “If I was advising the Wu campaign, my advice would be: Pretend he does not exist.”

title: Here’s what the data show about fatal school bus crashes
text:
Emily Stein, executive director of the advocacy and awareness group Safe Roads Alliance, said her group largely has the same messages for all drivers — don’t speed or drive distracted — but they’re even more important for bus drivers.

“The responsibility is multiplied because of all the kids in the back,” Stein said. “You are in charge of the lives of every child on this bus, but you’re also modeling behavior, because the kids are going to watch.”

These data come from the state’s Department of Transportation IMPACT dashboard, based on reports from police agencies. Crashes from 2022 forward may be added, updated, or deleted due to corrections or new information. The Department of Transportation cautions that the dashboard may include errors or be missing crashes. Still, it is the most comprehensive source available on Massachusetts crashes.

The measure in the data for school buses only checks whether a school bus was involved, meaning the buses’ involvement could be relatively minor.

Here’s what the data show on school bus crashes:

Except for the depths of the pandemic when many schools were closed, Massachusetts has more than 1,500 crashes involving school buses per year, and at least 15,000 in the past decade. About one-fifth resulted in injuries, and there were 19 total fatal crashes from 2015 to 2024. The database’s most recent fatal crashes involving school buses were in 2023.

For the most part, the frequency of school bus crashes is related to population, with Massachusetts’ three biggest cities being three of the five most frequent sites over the past decade. But New Bedford, a smaller city, had the most crashes, nearly 900, and Boston, the largest city, ranked fifth with 442.

Lowell, Worcester, and Springfield each had more than 600 bus crashes.

Stein emphasized the role of road design in many crashes — although the biggest factor in Lens’s death seems to have been the driver.

“Instead of looking at one particular aspect of [road safety], you have to look at the whole system,” Stein said. “What could the driver have done differently? What was the road design infrastructure? Could it have been changed to make it safer?”

For large vehicles like school buses, it is also important to ensure there are mirrors and cameras to prevent blind spots, Stein added, including on the exterior front.

“If there was a camera on the bus, would the driver have seen him?” she asked, referring to Lens.

Only a small minority of bus-involved crashes also involve pedestrians, according to the state data, ranging from 11 such crashes in 2021 to 28 in 2017. Most years, Boston reports one or two crashes involving both a pedestrian and a school bus.

Pedestrian-involved crashes are very dangerous: more than 80 percent result in injuries. Over the past decade, five resulted in deaths.

Stein touted a recently-passed law that allows school bus cameras to record vehicles that don’t stop for buses with their stop arms extended, which is dangerous for children getting on and off the bus.

In Boston specifically, school bus-involved crashes are less common than early in the century, when there were sometimes more than 100 each year, but 2024 had the most such crashes since 2008, 67.

Overall, the city had seven fatalities in bus-involved crashes from 2002 to 2024.

The state database does not include information on which school district is responsible for the buses, meaning the above chart does not reflect annual Boston Public Schools-related crashes. Boston school buses, for example, often pass through Brookline transporting students between Allston/Brighton and other parts of the city, and private schools and visiting athletic teams from other districts bus students within Boston.

Over the past decade, Boston’s school bus crashes are concentrated in Dorchester, Roxbury, and the center of the city, unsurprisingly given that more school buses cross those areas ferrying students around the city. Fewer were reported in outlying areas like Hyde Park and East Boston.

Prior to April’s Hyde Park crash, the last fatal bus crash in Boston was in Mattapan in 2021.

title: Former Transit Police sergeant on trial for alleged coverup of beating of homeless man
text:
“Rather than covering up for Officer Bartlett, David Finnerty did his job,” Patrick Garrity told jurors. He “alerted higher-ups and blew the whistle on Officer Bartlett.”

If not for Finnerty, according to Garrity, the truth of what happened may not have become known.

However, prosecutors allege Finnerty falsified reports minutes before a deputy superintendent showed up unexpectedly at the police station. Mundele said Finnerty only revealed there had been “a bad use of force” when the higher ranking officer asked him how the shift had been.

Prior to that, Finnerty “did not stop Bartlett from filing a false police report” and arresting Watson on “trumped up charges,” Mundele said. “He let Anthony Watson sit in jail.”

Watson was held for seven hours before he was ordered released.

Finnerty, 49, of Rutland, who was the duty shift supervisor at the time of the 2018 assault, is charged with filing false reports and aiding and abetting. He is accused of “including false and misleading statements” and omitting relevant information to obstruct an investigation into the assault.

His indictment on the federal charges in August 2023 came 10 months after Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden dropped similar charges just as Finnerty was poised to stand trial. Hayden said at the time his office had discovered new evidence that exonerated Finnerty, who had already been fired.

On Tuesday, Mundele told jurors an FBI digital analysis of documents recovered from a police computer showed that Bartlett revised his report of the incident several times, allegedly at Finnerty’s direction, to include a claim that he “perceived a threat to my immediate safety” while trying to arrest Watson.

Prosecutors showed jurors video clips of Watson, who was 31 and homeless at the time, being escorted off a train at the Ashmont Station by Bartlett after 1:30 a.m. on July 27, 2018.

Watson, who is expected to testify at the trial, previously told the Globe that he had fallen asleep on the train and was awakened at the last stop of the night by Bartlett.

The video shows Bartlett grab Watson by the arm as he walks him along the platform, then strike him three times in the leg with a baton as Watson falls to the ground. Bartlett then pulls Watson to his feet and is seen on another video clip escorting him out of the station and walking away.

Watson called 911 to report the attack, but when Boston police arrived Bartlett returned to the scene and claimed he had been searching for him. He arrested Watson on a false charge of assault, according to prosecutors.

Another video clip played for jurors showed a chaotic scene at Transit Police headquarters as Bartlett grabbed Watson by the neck while he was being booked. Watson repeatedly shouted that the officer had beaten him at the train station and begged other officers to review surveillance video showing the assault.

Transit Police Officer Paul Clooney, who was working the night of the incident, testified Tuesday that he reviewed surveillance video from the station and immediately alerted Finnerty that he should look at it.

“From what I could see in the video, it appeared there might be a use of force issue,” Clooney said.

In his opening remarks, Mundele told jurors that you didn’t need to be a police officer to know Bartlett hit Watson with a baton three times “for no reason.”

That was one point the defense agreed on.

“Our client realized there was no justification for what Bartlett did on camera and off camera,” Garrity told jurors. “The evidence will show you the arrest of Watson was unjustified, that the use of force was excessive and that it needed to be reported.”

The government’s witness list includes Bartlett, who will testify under a grant of immunity from federal prosecution. He pleaded guilty to state charges related to the assault on Watson and was sentenced to probation. He was placed on leave immediately after the incident, then retired from the force.

In 2021, Watson filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the MBTA, Finnerty, Bartlett, and another officer, alleging they lied to absolve Bartlett by claiming Watson was the aggressor during their 2018 encounter. That case was settled last year for $50,000, according to a spokesperson for the T.

title: Alex Alex’s quixotic candidacy for Boston mayor
text:
As expected, Wu was polished, sharp, and unsparing in her critiques of Kraft: “This is a city that cannot be bought,” she said in her opening remarks. Meanwhile, Kraft came across as overly cautious, vague, and out of his depth, calling for a “pause” on bike lanes and generic “new sources of income” for the city. He may have the money to run for mayor, but judging by his debate performance, he forgot to buy an actual plan.

Then there was Alex — no tailored suit, no entourage, no name recognition. The formerly undocumented immigrant only decided to run for office last month and won’t even make the ballot; the deadline to submit the required 3,000 certified signatures from registered Boston voters is May 20. As of Monday morning, he’d only collected around 150.

And yet, Alex, for all his inexperience and rough edges, seems clear-eyed about the odds. “I don’t really have the delusion that I’m gonna win the race for mayor, but I know that my ideas are gonna get out there. I know that people are gonna see there’s value in them,” he told me over the weekend at a coffee shop in Roslindale, where he’d biked from his place in Uphams Corner.

So why run at all?

Before I get to that, it’s worth learning who Alex is, including the story behind his undeniably odd name. He was born Alex Palacios Santos in Oaxaca, Mexico, to a single mother who left for the United States when he was just 8 months old. When Alex was 3, his aunt brought him illegally through the US-Mexico border to reunite with his mother in Boston.

“My mother was abusive my whole life,” Alex said. “There were a few weeks where I couldn’t leave my room.”

Despite the instability at home, Alex stood out academically. After attending two public elementary schools in Boston, he landed at Excel Academy, a charter school in East Boston, for fifth grade. Around that time, he was connected to Steppingstone, an education nonprofit that helped him transfer to Milton Academy on financial aid. Through Steppingstone, Alex also secured pro bono legal assistance and eventually obtained permanent resident status.

At 16, he left home and has been estranged from his mom ever since, he said.

Sorting his legal status “helped him feel settled, because there was so much that’s unsettled in his life,” said Josh Fischel, a former Steppingstone program associate who met Alex about 15 years ago and remains a mentor today. “He denies this, but I have a strong memory of him always carrying a dictionary around. Not because he needed to translate stuff. He just wanted to know what bigger words meant.”

Fischel, now an English teacher in Acton-Boxborough, was surprised when Alex told him he’s running for mayor. “Did I try and talk him out of it? Sure.” Fischel was worried that Alex would come across like “a bit of a crank” at the debate. “But he sounded more prepared than the billionaire’s son.” Alex, Fischel told me, “was not born to stay in his lane. If he’s interested in doing something, he’s just going to do it, damn the consequences.”

Alex attended college at New York University and majored in critical systems studies, an academic field perhaps fitting for someone who’s interested in dismantling inefficiencies and spotlighting structural injustice from the ground up. Big, ambitious goals for any public servant, let alone a 24-year-old long shot candidate.

“I’ve faced so many issues that people my age and people older than me would not have faced,” Alex said. “I’m also trying to gain experience.” He said he’s applied to multiple jobs at City Hall with no luck, including a youth outreach coordinator position and a climate innovation analyst role, “looking at the city’s infrastructure and making sure that it’s more responsive to the realities of ecological collapse,” he said.

At the forum, Alex shined when he shared his perspective as a struggling young person in Boston, a story that contradicted the rosy picture Wu painted of the city. “What Mayor Wu was saying was a picture of Boston that was just not true for me” in terms of successes and opportunities. “I work in retail, like a lot of people my age, because that’s just the only jobs you can find,” Alex said. When I asked him about the biggest issue the city faces he was quick to say housing, or lack thereof. It’s hardly a novel answer, but it’s not an inaccurate one either.

Where Alex starts to lose the room is when the conversation veers into lofty rhetoric and sweeping, sometimes implausible ideas, like his belief in the need for a new Constitution (as noted on his Instagram page). “He’s so smart and agile and personable,” Fischel told me. But “I want people to learn about him more slowly on increasingly bigger stages instead of the very biggest first.”

As for his last name, Alex said he changed it when he became a US citizen in 2023. He’d thought deeply about how neither of his last names reflected any part of him, but he also didn’t feel it was right to appropriate an Indigenous name without the connection. “People don’t see me as Black. People don’t really see me as Native. They just see me as a question mark,” Alex said. So, he doubled down on the one thing he could claim fully: himself.

Gimmicky? Maybe. But also revealing — it’s a symbol of someone who’s still in search of an identity, political or not. After our interview and before starting his work shift at a fast-casual Mediterranean restaurant, Alex biked to Franklin Park Zoo to clean up garbage, something Fischel told me Alex does regularly. (A politician picking up Boston’s trash? Who does that remind you of?)

Sure, he’s not going to be your next mayor. But in a race filled with polish, money, and manufactured messaging and barbs, maybe we needed someone like Alex Alex to make us look twice.

title: Boston worries it won’t be able to cover rent hikes for Section 8 recipients as federal funding dries up
text:
In the short term, the BHA is expected to be in a budget shortfall this year due to a lack of federal funding for expensive housing assistance programs and is seeking to cut costs. Longer term, the Trump administration is proposingmassive cuts to the program that stand to fundamentally alter Boston’s housing ecosystem and could displace thousands of low-income families.

“We’re sending this letter because we are concerned about the short-term deficit we may be looking at in a few months, and because we’re worried about the long-term outlook for Section 8,” said BHA administrator Kenzie Bok. “If we’re in a budget crisis at level funding, what in the world does it look like, and how many people suffer, under massive federal cuts?”

Section 8, which provides rental vouchers to lower-income families, seniors, and people with disabilities, is the nation’s largest housing assistance program. In Boston, the housing authority distributes 18,000 vouchers, and the waitlist can stretch longer than a decade.

The federal government allocates vouchers to municipalities and other distributing agencies, who in turn distribute them to tenants to rent market-rate apartments. Voucher holders pay no more than 30 percent of their income in monthly rent, with the local housing authority covering the rest of the cost with federal funds.

Acceptable rents are set through a formula set by the Department of Housing and Urban Development, with limitations on how much landlords can raise the rent in a year based on the local housing market. Those rates are often less than what landlords would make renting to market-rate tenants, and so many seek to raise rents when HUD allows.

“You’re losing money on the units you’re doing Section 8, at least compared to market rate,” said Ed Kelly, a landlord with apartments in Boston and on the South Shore who rents some units in Dorchester to voucher holders. “Doing the program is a lot of work with all of the extra inspections the government requires. You kind of have to raise the rents to make it work.”

Kelly said he would hold off on raising rents this year on the Section 8 units because the money he makes on the market-rate apartments is enough to sustain his business but said that other Section 8 landlords may not be able to do the same.

Rising rents are ultimately responsible for BHA’s budget deficit, Bok said.

When market rents rise, so do Section 8 rents, but the federal government has in recent years kept funding for the program at roughly the same level. That’s a reason why it is fairly common for the BHA and other housing authorities to end fiscal years in shortfall. Typically, they will try to cut some costs to make up as much of the gap as possible, and at the end of the year, HUD will draw on other untapped funds to fill the rest.

Bok is concerned that extra funding will not be available this year, and HUD has directed BHA to come up with ways to cover the anticipated shortfall.

But the bigger concern, Bok said, is a scenario in which the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to the program become reality.

In its budget plan filed earlier this month, the administration called for slashing housing assistance spending by roughly 43 percent and replacing federal programs like Section 8 with block grants for states to distribute aid themselves.

Those cuts would be “catastrophic” for tenants and the broader housing ecosystem in Boston, said Michael Kane, a longtime local housing advocate who is also the co-chair of the national Leaders and Organizers for Tenant Empowerment Network, cutting a program that many already consider underfunded.

“Millions of people would be displaced,” Kane said. “People would be homeless. It would be utter chaos.”

Under the proposed cuts, the BHA would have to cancel vouchers for some 7,900 families, including nearly 11,000 children.

Cuts would also make it harder to finance affordable housing projects, which sometimes have their own allotment of Section 8 vouchers that effectively guarantee a portion of the rent will be paid, making it easier to take out loans to finance construction.

The BHA has some 4,000 of these “project-based vouchers,” which support roughly $600 million of debt in real estate portfolios across the city. The federal cuts could impact those projects and buildings, too.

Still, the biggest impact would be human, said Kelly, the landlord.

While he agrees that Section 8 has its flaws — Kelly said he has had problematic tenants who have abused the program — he has seen many more families who lived in his apartments with a voucher use it to steady their lives. One single mother he rented to, he said, recently bought a home for herself and her children.

“Some people just need help,” Kelly said. “To take this program away or to cut it like they’re talking about would be putting people on the street.”

title: Uncle of George Floyd speaks at State House rally five years after nephew’s murder
text:
Nearly five years after George Floyd’s murder by a white Minneapolis police officer, his uncle stood outside the Massachusetts State House for a rally Wednesday and spoke of hope that police brutality against Black and brown people will decrease.

But for Selwyn Jones, his hope is tempered by a sense that progress comes in small steps instead of bold leaps. Even after nationwide protests following his nephew’s killing, and federal and state legislation banning chokeholds and no-knock warrants, police misconduct continues to be too high, Jones said.

“How do we fix this? We fix this by fighting,” said Jones, who spoke with more than a dozen people who had been wrongfully convicted or were related to people who had been fatally shot by police.

“How many George Floyds were there before my nephew?” Jones said during the anniversary event. “Someone decided they would be judge, jury, and executioner.”

Floyd was fatally asphyxiated on May 25, 2020, when Minneapolis police Officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck and back for nine minutes while Floyd, who had been suspected of passing a counterfeit $20 bill, repeatedly cried, “I can’t breathe.” Those words became a rallying slogan for the Black Lives Matter movement.

According to Mapping Police Violence, a study that used US Justice Department data, nearly three times as many Black people since 2013 were killed by police than whites. This year, the Trump administration announced it would end an effort seeking federal oversight of police departments in Minneapolis and Louisville, Ky., which had been found to violate the civil rights of Black people.

Despite federal retrenchment, Jones said Floyd’s death has made a difference in bringing attention to police brutality.

“I’ve got hope,” he said. ”Every day you wake up, hope is invented.”

In honor of his nephew, Jones co-founded Justice 929, a nonprofit group that works on a broad range of civil rights issues, including wrongful convictions, police brutality, and gun violence.

“We can slow some of these things down,” Jones said, referring to police violence, particularly against Black and brown people. “But it’s hard to teach old dogs new tricks. The new generation has to step up.”

Other speakers included the mother and two sisters of Burrell Ramsey-White, a 26-year-old Black man from Dorchester who was fatally shot by Boston police in the South End in 2012. Ramsey-White was shot while fleeing on foot after a traffic stop, allegedly after pointing a gun at an officer.

His mother, Carla Sheffield, said yesterday that the gun he had been suspected of carrying did not have his fingerprints.

“My life hasn’t been the same,” Sheffield said. “A big part of my life was stolen, and for what? They weren’t looking for the truth.”

Nikia Ramsey, Ramsey-White’s sister, created the group Better Opportunities as a way to honor her brother and help young people from urban neighborhoods by focusing on social responsibility and life improvement.

“We are not here for pity. We are here for policy,” Ramsey said outside the state Capitol. “We will never stop fighting in their name.”

Jennifer Root Bannon, whose brother Juston Root died after being shot 31 times by six police officers following a car chase from Boston to Brookline in 2020, excoriated the Norfolk County District Attorney’s investigation into his death, which cleared the officers.

Root was believed to be armed, but initially had shown a paintball gun near Massachusetts Mental Health Center by Brigham and Women’s Hospital. His family said Root had suffered from mental illness.

“They will never get truth and transparency as long as law enforcement is investigating themselves,” Root Bannon said. “That needs to change.”

Several people who had been wrongfully convicted told chilling stories of spending decades behind bars. One of them, 74-year-old Hank Houghton of West Brookfield, said he was freed in 2021 after being imprisoned for 44 years for a rape he did not commit.

DNA evidence finally exonerated him, Houghton said, but he lost all his family members while incarcerated, including his 12-year-old daughter, who was killed by a drunk driver. The experience was harrowing, scarring, and mistaken, he said.

Instead of the Department of Correction, Houghton said, “it should be called the Massachusetts penal colony because ‘correction’ has nothing to do with it.”

Brian MacQuarrie can be reached at brian.macquarrie@globe.com.

title: With this big, ugly bill, the rich get richer and everybody else pays
text:
Even after people at the bottom of the ladder get hosed, those tax cuts (plus big boosts in funding for defense and so-called border security) are projected to swell the national debt by trillions over the next decade. That debt is an abomination when Democrats are in charge, but it’s no big deal when Republicans are in power.

Hey, it’s all for a noble cause: Remaking the country into a GOP utopia, where the rich get more handouts, and the poor have only themselves to blame.

To sell this money grab, Republicans are using a tactic that has worked ever since Saint Reagan walked among us: Portraying aid recipients as lazy layabouts who cheat the system and sponge off hard-working Americans. These lesser souls should sing for their supper, by golly. Would it kill these fraudsters to do a little work once in a while?

“If you don’t want to work, you’re the one that decided you don’t want health care,” said Florida Senator Rick Scott.

You tell ‘em, senator! Scott and his fellow-travelers deplore those who abuse the system. Never mind that most Medicare fraud happens on the provider side. Or that Scott himself once headed a hospital chain found responsible for the largest Medicare and Medicaid fraud case this country had ever seen.

States like ours have pretty good systems to catch all kinds of fraud, which, as the Globe’s Jason Laughlin reported, made up way less than 1 percent of Massachusetts’ $20 billion budget for Medicaid, known here as MassHealth, in 2024.

Be that as it may, Republicans want to introduce Medicaid work requirements that will finally get the freeloaders off their butts. Let’s take a closer look at these miscreants, shall we? Of the 2 million people who get MassHealth to cover their medical care, 76 percent are in families that are already working full time or part time, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (Nationally, only 54 percent of employers provide health insurance). About a quarter of all recipients here are children, and 30 percent have disabilities or are over 65.

Republicans are using a problem that barely exists to kick millions out of the system, and proposing a so-called solution that doesn’t work anyway. In states that have tried them, Medicaid work requirements haven’t led to higher employment. Instead, imposing yet more demands on recipients to prove their eligibility tangles them up in red tape, leading to way lower enrollments in the programs to which they are entitled. Which is what the GOP really wants.

In addition to the work requirements, the giant bill being debated in Washington means Massachusetts would lose billions more in Medicaid funding in coming years — as punishment for using state money to provide health insurance to immigrants, including undocumented ones.

The thing is, the medical needs of those kicked off MassHealth won’t go away. They’ll just get worse, more deadly, and more expensive for everyone. They’ll get dealt with in emergency rooms already at their breaking points. And they’ll put the squeeze on struggling health centers, hospitals, and, ultimately, state budgets.

“These are cuts that are going to impact the entire program, and have a ripple effect across the Massachusetts economy,” said Kate Symmonds, senior health law attorney at the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute. “It will reduce revenues for community health centers, hospitals, and medical providers, and it will destabilize our health industry.”

Guy Fish, CEO of Codman Square Health Center, has a good idea how much it will cost if Republicans get their way on Medicaid. His Dorchester health center serves about 26,000 patients each year, almost all of them below federal poverty guidelines and about half of them on MassHealth, which makes up some 40 percent of the center’s revenues, Fish said.

Fish said his MassHealth patients are often working multiple part-time jobs with no benefits, and that even then, some have to be convinced to apply for the program.

“The narrative couldn’t be more wrong,” he said. “These are hard-working people, some who don’t know how to access the system.”

Kicking them off MassHealth won’t make them any healthier.

“They will still have medical needs, and if they can’t see us, where are they going to go,” he said. “The state will have to pick that up, or they are not going to be seen, so they are going to be sicker and end up in emergency rooms. You pay more later for not paying for coverage now.”

If Codman loses funding from MassHealth, that will mean staff cuts. Unemployment ripples out into families, and to local businesses, because fewer people have money to spend. The whole community will be worse off.

“There is a whole domino effect that happens here,” Fish said. “And the tragedy is it is not just in Massachusetts or blue states, but in red states too. There are community health centers in every single state … including deep red ones.”

Those states will be left holding the bag, pulling money from education and transportation and law enforcement to make up the shortfalls.

Ah yes, but by then, the billionaires’ pockets will be even fatter.

Downright evil.

title: In potential sea change, Mass. Senate votes to give local officials, not Legislature, power to set liquor license caps
text:
Senate leaders questioned why the Legislature remains involved in approving most liquor licenses, which Senator Michael Rodrigues, the chamber’s budget chair, likened to a “routine rubber stamping.”

“I don’t even remember us saying ‘no,’ ” said Rodrigues, a Westport Democrat. “To eliminate that level of bureaucracy, I think is helpful.”

Senator Jacob Oliveira, a Ludlow Democrat who sponsored the proposal to hand that power to municipalities, said it would allow them to avoid the “lag time” they often face on Beacon Hill. The Democrat-led Legislature routinely blows past deadlines and has often left a litany of bills undone until late in its two-year session, meaning proposals, both big or small, can languish for months.

“We all know that the legislative process can be cumbersome,” Oliveira said. “We want to make sure that we empower our 351 cities and towns, as well as provide some flexibility to our businesses.”

The proposal, however, faced immediate resistance in the House, where Democratic leaders say they see no reason to change a model giving lawmakers a say in policy that can affect their neighborhoods.

“In our community, liquor licenses can be great or they can be problematic, and for me to give my community’s voice away would be political recklessness on my behalf,” said House majority leader Michael Moran, a Democrat from Brighton who last year negotiated a bill that gave Boston hundreds of additional liquor licenses. The final version included language specifically steering several licenses to Oak Square in Brighton, a detail that was not in the original proposal.

“My residents, the people that I represent, deserve a voice in that process,” he said Thursday, “and I have no intention of giving up their voice.”

The Senate embraced the measure just days after it became a touchpoint in simmering tension between House and Senate Democrats. A House chair last week blocked Oliveira from testifying remotely on the proposal, citing a House rule barring committee members from participating remotely in a hearing. (Moran criticized senators for not regularly attending hearings, saying the House is a “stickler” for appearing in person.)

Still, the move drew a public rebuke from Senate President Karen E. Spilka, and underscored the long-running friction between the Democratic leaders of the two chambers, particularly as they hash out different takes on the very rules governing how the Legislature operates.

“I’m glad to see that my voice is being heard now” on this bill, Oliveira said Wednesday.

Under the proposal, local officials would have to create a plan, approved by the mayor and city council or select board, that lays out a process for granting licenses.

Oliveira said the state would retain some role in the liquor license process through the Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission. The agency would still have to approve new retail license applications after they’re cleared at the local level, a responsibility the ABCC currently has.

The liquor licensing approval process has roots in the post-Prohibition 1930s when it was built largely to restrict the flow of alcohol after the 21st Amendment made booze legal again. The Yankees who ran the Legislature did not trust the Irish who ruled Boston, the Globe has reported, and Beacon Hill capped the number of licenses available in communities across the state.

That squeeze has been felt particularly in Boston, where even an effort in 2014 to expand the number of licenses did not remake the system as many hoped, instead applying a first-come, first-served approach that benefited veteran operators.

The Legislature last year approved dozens of bills authorizing additional licenses, including one to add 225 over three years in Boston, making it one of the most sweeping efforts ever to reshape the city’s licensing scheme.

That new law was billed as potential boon particularly for communities of color and small business owners, who have not always had the luxury of affording a liquor license. Because of caps on new issuances, many licenses had to be bought on the secondary market, and a full unrestricted license can sell for $600,000.

Shifting the power over license caps, however, has been a years-long debate on Beacon Hill and a contentious one among Boston officials.

Governor Maura Healey said last year that she would pursue a measure allowing local officials to set their own limits as part of a wider bill, but quickly backtracked, including after Moran, the House majority leader, said he had concerns about giving too much power over liquor licenses to the mayor of a city, particularly one as large as Boston.

“The current mayor [Michelle Wu] lives in Roslindale. The previous mayor [Martin J. Walsh] lived in Dorchester, and the previous mayor to that [Tom Menino] lived in Hyde Park,” Moran told the Globe on Thursday. “None of them wake up every morning and go to bed every night in my neighborhood.”

Emma Pettit, a Wu spokesperson, welcomed the Senate proposal shifting the power over liquor license limits to local officials.

“The mayor supports all efforts to increase local authority over matters impacting their own communities,” Pettit said in a statement.

Other House leaders said they’ve yet to review the Senate proposal, but questioned whether towns and cities are facing roadblocks in the State House over extra licenses.

“We don’t have issues in the city of Lawrence,” said Representative Frank Moran, the chamber’s second assistant majority leader. (He is not related to Representative Michael Moran from Brighton.)

Healey’s office last year said that despite shelving the idea of local control in her own municipal-focused legislation, she still supported the concept but needed more time to get the “language right.” She didn’t include the measure in a similar package of municipal reforms that she filed again in January, to the chagrin of local leaders.

Dave Koffman, legislative director for the Massachusetts Municipal Association, said town and cities back the Senate measure as a way to “right-size” a process on liquor license proposals that often aren’t controversial.

“Local communities know what their local downtowns need best,” he said.

title: Son of taxi driver shot to death in Back Bay tells killer: ‘I’m not here to celebrate your punishment’
text:
Luckinson Oruma was behind the wheel of a white cab in the Back Bay ″doing what he always did, working hard to provide for his family" when he was shot to death on a sunny morning in 2019, his son told his father’s killer in Suffolk Superior Court on Friday.

“He put five of us through college ... all while driving a cab,” Will Oruma said to the Rhode Island man who gunned his father down in front of the Colonnade Hotel.

Will Oruma and several of his relatives were in court to see Phillip Foy of Pawtucket receive a mandatory life sentence for killing his father.

Foy, 40, is not eligible for parole.

A Suffolk County jury had convicted Foy of first-degree murder on Monday.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office provided a recording of Oruma’s tearful, six-minute statement outlining the impact of the tragic loss of of his father, a 60-year-old Nigerian immigrant.

“On June 4, 2019, my life and my family’s life changed forever,” Will Oruma said.

His father had come to the United States in 1981 and “worked tirelessly to build a better life,” he said.

Luckinson Oruma had driven the same white cab, number 192 for nearly 10 years — 10 hours a day, six days a week.

He raised his family in Dorchester, providing “not just a comfortable home” but love and devotion, finding time, despite his long hours, to make dinner for the family every single weekend, Will Oruma said.

Luckinson Oruma’s fatal encounter with Foy unfolded on a sunny morning on Huntington Avenue.

Just before 11 a.m., Oruma idled in front of the hotel. Foy appeared at his cab window demanding a ride to Mansfield, 35 miles outside the city.

When Oruma refused the fare, Foy dragged him from his cab and shot him nine times, continuing to fire even after Oruma fell, witnesses told authorities.

Foy drove away in the cab and was arrested a short time later.

“It’s been nearly six years, life has changed,” Will Oruma said in court.

His mother, he said, still struggles to live life without her husband.

“I’m married now; I have a child,” Will Oruma said.

“I’m not here to celebrate your punishment,” he told Foy. “I’m here to let you know I truly feel sorry for you and for your family.”

“I have no desire for vengeance,” Oruma continued.

Instead, Oruma wished Foy self reflection and inner peace.

“I hope you are able to reflect for the rest of your life and truly understand the magnitude of what you have done, and I hope you find some peace and forgiveness within yourself,” Oruma said.

In a statement after the verdict was read on Monday, Hayden said Foy intruded upon Oruma while he was in what should have been a safe space.

“The shooting death of Luckinson Oruma was shattering not just for his family and friends, but for anyone who goes to work each day expecting, as they should, to be in a safe environment,” Hayden said. “This defendant turned Mr. Oruma’s environment into something tragically different, and I’m very grateful that the jury held him accountable for his devastating actions.”

Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com. Follow her @talanez.

title: After George Floyd’s murder, Boston groups pledged $1 billion toward equity causes. Where did it go?
text:
But five years later, it’s difficult to discern what all that money bought. Anecdotally, those in Greater Boston on both the giving and receiving end agree the energy for social change has waned. People moved on — and took their money with them.

“That’s part of the problem that we see in philanthropy over time,” said Shanique Rodriguez, executive director of the Massachusetts Voter Table, a nonprofit coalition of more than 40 advocacy groups. “It’s whatever is popular, whatever is urgent, whatever fire is happening right now that we see philanthropy put its energy behind.”

In just four months, the Trump administration has rattled the landscape for such initiatives. The White House has targeted diversity, equity, and inclusion — and anyone who supports those initiatives. The chilling effect has hit donors and nonprofits alike, with some rescinding dollars and others scrubbing their programs of DEI-related language, while a select few approach the threat head-on.

Some nonprofit leaders worry philanthropic support for equity is dwindling at a crucial moment: The Trump administration is cutting all manner of federal funds, groups committed to racial justice face retaliation, and Republicans are floating laws that could strip “terrorist supporting organizations” of tax-exempt status.

The apparent retreat is a turnaround from the proclamations made in the wake of Floyd’s murder, when powerful Boston-based brands, foundations, and universities promised to do better, and funded different causes. The Globe reviewed 25 pledges from roughly 20 local institutions made in the year after Floyd’s death. Of those, 60 percent were grants. A select few promised pro bono services or workplace initiatives in lieu of money. Roughly one in 10 were made as investments — meaning the result also ended up benefiting the donor’s bottom line.

Bain Capital promised $100 million over a decade to nonprofits. The University of Massachusetts Boston launched the George Floyd Honorary Scholarship Fund, which has grown to just under $175,000. So far, the university has awarded $11,500 in scholarships.
