title: Henderson school faces accountability. Where is Wu?
text:
In an email sent on May 28 around 7 p.m., the school principal, Dr. Lori Wiggins, told parents that there was a “a physical altercation” between two ninth graders in the 8th grade hallway during a class transition. Savara Willis, a Henderson parent, told me in an interview that her daughter, who is 14 and a ninth-grader, was assaulted by another student. According to Willis, she met with BPS officials on May 30 to discuss what could be done to protect her daughter.

On June 6, Willis wrote an email to BPS officials, including Superintendent Mary Skipper, saying she was still awaiting a promised safety plan. On June 10 - the same day as the playground ribbon-cutting -the Henderson assistant principal emailed a draft safety plan to Willis but said he wanted to meet with the two students involved in the incident before it was finalized. By that point, however, Willis said her daughter was so traumatized, she was not attending school.

Asked for a response, Boston school officials said in a statement, “School leadership stands ready to implement the plan upon the student’s return to school.” They don’t get it. As Willis told me, “I don’t trust them at all. I’m taking my daughter out of that school.”

This is the latest chapter in the sad unravelling of the Henderson, which describes itself as a fully inclusive K-12 school — meaning that it offers a specially trained staff and what is supposed to be a nurturing environment to a mix of general and special education students. But, as my colleague Marcela García has written, things began to slide at the school after Patricia Lampron, a beloved principal, was attacked in November 2021 by a 16-year-old student. Lampron suffered permanent injuries, and the Boston City Council just recently approved a home rule petition that would increase disability pension benefits for her. According to several parents of current and former Henderson students who spoke to me, the Henderson community also has not recovered from the trauma.

According to these parents, what happened on May 28, is part of a larger pattern of fights and bullying, which they contend is being ignored and not fully reported by school officials. School officials deny that, and say that overall there is a decrease in student “incidents” and more accountability for students. At Tuesday night’s School Committee meeting, two people from the Henderson community tried to get their side of the story out during the two minutes they were given to speak.

In a statement she read on Zoom, Carol Gracia said that her daughter, a 10th-grader and longtime Henderson student, would be switching to Charlestown High School. “It is so sad that the vision and mission of this school is gone,” said Gracia, who also said her family was “well aware of the violence” that occurs at the Henderson.

In her statement, Caroline Cain, a past chair of the BPS Special Education Parent Advisory Council and parent of a former Henderson student, told School Committee attendees, “The school has gone from a shining star, and internationally recognized inclusion program, to a school where staff and students are leaving in droves because the district has not provided the necessary leadership, oversight, and accountability.” Cain’s full, written statement, which she shared with me, also said she had shared concerns of parents and staff who are afraid to speak out with BPS administrators, along with “videos of repeated violence at the school this year, incidents that are frightening and dangerous for staff and faculty.”

In their statement, BPS officials also said they are committed to fostering “a safe and welcoming culture for all” and have “worked diligently throughout the school year to address concerns raised by families.” The BPS statement said the administration communicates about all incidents that cause disruptions. But the parents who talked to me said that happens only when the administration is pressured to do so.

Running a school like the Henderson is challenging. But challenging is no excuse for what seems to be a lack of empathy and a plan to restore community trust.

Ultimately, that’s on Wu. She is demanding accountability from ICE about its tactics in Boston. What about accountability for the true cost of her White Stadium renovation plan,for the City Hall scandal that has drawn in Segun Idowu, a top member of her cabinet, and for the circumstances surrounding the death of the little boy who was hit and killed by his own school bus?

I went first to Wu’s office for comment on the Henderson, but ended up getting it from BPS. In this case, Wu showed up at the Henderson for the good stuff, while handing off the bad stuff to others.

title: A new theater festival wants audiences to ‘love deeper’ in dark times
text:
“Our work aims to change the world,” Bennett said. “Hopefully, when you leave, you’ll feel moved towards creating a more beautiful world in your immediate community.”

Each work presented by the festival was developed through one of TTO’s artist residency programs, which provide resources to queer and trans artists of color who reflect the organization’s larger mission: to create art that “transcends artistic boundaries, celebrates cultural abundance, and dismantles oppression,” as the festival’s mission statement puts it.

“There are many ways to push against oppressive systems, and I want my work to help people consider their actions and values, and how they want to show up in this world,” said Victoria Lynn Awkward, whose dance piece featured in the festival, “In the Space Between," was developed during TTO’s 22-month Emergent Artist Residency. Set to an original composition of piano, flute, and percussion, “In the Space Between” uses aerial movement, audible breathwork, and flowing fabrics to create a dance piece inspired by iconic Black feminist Audre Lorde’s writings on power and eroticism.

The sensuous nature of the piece is designed to “build empathy,” Awkward said. “Empathy is what’s needed to bridge divides, and to be able to care for people with different cultures and backgrounds, as well as yourself.”

As an organization, the Theater Offensive has been creating and cultivating cutting-edge art by LGBTQ+ makers since 1989, when it was born out of a gay men’s guerrilla theater troupe. At the time, founder Abe Rybeck imagined a button- and boundary-pushing company that could amplify queer voices and themes through a cross-disciplinary approach of art, activism, education, and community building.

Over the years, and among other initiatives, TTO went on to produce innovative fringe theater festivals, establish its national award-winning program True Colors: Out Youth Theater, and create accessible opportunities for all Bostonians to experience queer art. For instance, TTO developed a signature approach to programming, dubbed Out in Your Neighborhood, that took productions out of downtown theaters and into community centers, schools, and streets in areas of town, such as Roxbury and Dorchester, that are historically underserved by major arts organizations.

More recently, TTO has evolved to explicitly focus on art by and for queer and trans people of color, who face unique challenges accessing financial backing and other forms of support for their work and are most vulnerable in what the organization calls an ongoing “battle against authoritarianism, homophobia, transphobia, and racism” in the Trump era. Artists are looking to the past to process this dangerous present, said Bennett, who noted that ancestral connections are a common thread in the festival’s performances.

“I live in Harlem, where my great-grandmother moved in the early 1900s and my grandmother and mother were raised,” said Awkward. “I feel very connected to that lineage, and to the hope and joy they had throughout all the challenges they faced.” She added that the prevalence of textiles in her work is inspired by the legacy of Black quilting, including lore that quilts were used to mark safe houses and provide direction on the Underground Railroad. “For me, textiles are beautiful and eye-catching — but also deeply entwined with my ancestry and lineage.”

Another festival piece, “The Messenger,” is a coming-of-age play with music about a burgeoning young oracle who takes a spiritual journey with her elders, learning from their wisdom so that she can serve her nation. Playwright and TTO resident artist Cheyenne Wyzzard-Jones said they were inspired by their lineage, including their Wampanoag background, as well as “conversations with my community of Black diaspora folk, Native American family, elders, [and] medicine workers.”

There’s also “Theater of Union," a three-fold artistic exercise developed by Annalise “River” Guidry. It is composed of “Remembrance," a community-building performance on the festival’s opening night that “explores and honors our many ancestries,” Guidry said, as well as a workshop that explores “grief as a pathway toward collective liberation.” Both the performance and workshop are additionally preceded by a “table talk” that expands on the artist’s intentions.

Guidry wants to impart to their audience the notion of “love ethic,” Black author and social critic bell hooks’s framework for considering love as a series of actions and choices, not just a feeling. “Lovelessness pervades in our society,” Guidry said, pointing to racist, anti-queer, and otherwise oppressive “systems of domination” that keep Americans divided and at odds.

The Queer [Re]Public Festival, then, aims to establish a more perfect union. “The current culture and systems we are functioning under are not sustainable,” Guidry said. “I believe in love to transform and save us.”

title: New trial ordered for former Boston police officer convicted of driving drunk
text:
A new trial has been ordered for a former Boston police officer convicted of driving drunk and causing a New Year’s Day crash in 2018 that left two people with serious injuries, according to court records.

A three-judge panel of the Massachusetts Appeals Court concluded that Domenic E. Columbo’s constitutional rights were violated when the trial judge dismissed a juror who had called in sick by voice mail during deliberations.

“Juror service is at its apex in deliberations and cannot be terminated by a juror merely calling in sick through a voicemail message,” the panel ruled. ”The process used to discharge a deliberating juror requires reversal."

The trial judge should have held a hearing before deciding to dismiss the juror, the panel ruled.

A spokesman for Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden said Friday the office will make a decision on whether to retry Columbo after it reviews the ruling. (Columbo’s trial was handled by the Essex District Attorney’s office due to conflict of interest concerns)

Columbo’s attorney, John T. Diamond III, did not return a request for comment.

Columbo was convicted of one count of operating under the influence of alcohol causing serious bodily injury and two counts of assault and battery by means of a dangerous weapon, records show.

He was sentenced by Superior Court Judge Peter B. Kruppto serve two-and-a-half years in the House of Correction in 2022.

It wasn’t immediately clear from court records if Columbo has served that sentence.

While granting Columbo a new trial, the appeals panel judges rejected the defense’s claim that there was not enough evidence to convict him of any crime.

“Ample evidence enabled jurors to conclude that alcohol diminished the defendant’s ability to operate his vehicle safely,” they wrote. “He consumed alcohol in the hours preceding the crash, he approached an intersection at high speed, he drove at a speed that exceeded the speed limit, he failed to yield to a vehicle passing through an intersection, he failed to apply the brakes before the crash, he smelled of alcohol, and his blood alcohol content exceeded the legal limit.”

According to court records, Columbo purchased a 30 pack of beer and began drinking with other officers at the Youth Violence Strike Force’s office around 11:45 p.m. on New Year’s Eve.

Around 3 a.m. on New Year’s Day, he got into his Ford F-150 and within 20 minutes crashed into another vehicle in Dorchester after driving into an intersection at 65 miles per hour, according to court records.

The driver was injured and a passenger sustained catastrophic injuries and had to learn to walk, talk, and read again, according to court records.

Columbo had a blood alcohol level of .11 and .12 during post-crash testing, which is above the legal limit of .08, records show.

Columbo was placed on the decertificationlist by the state’s police oversight agency in 2023, records show.

John R. Ellement can be reached at john.ellement@globe.com. Follow him @JREbosglobe.

title: At Embrace Ideas Festival, Black Bostonians discussed politics, art, business
text:
Margaret Breeden, daughter of Boston civil rights leader Rev. James Breeden, who protested educational inequalities in the 1960s, was one of the attendees. Breeden said she attended the event to learn more about how she could get involved in racial justice efforts in Boston.

“My parents really ingrained social justice in me every day at the kitchen table, so I came here to figure out what I could do to help,” she said.

In the first panel of the day, State Senator Liz Miranda and Segun Idowu, chief of economic opportunity and inclusion for the City of Boston, discussed how they were using government policy to uplift Black Bostonians in light of the new presidential administration. Miranda represents the 2nd Suffolk district, which includes parts of Roxbury, Mattapan, Dorchester and Northeastern University or “the Blackest district in the Commonwealth” in her words. Idowu, a member of Mayor Michelle Wu’s cabinet, led a grant program that helped Boston businesses recover from the pandemic.

Idowu said Trump’s tariffs and executive orders would impact the “five pillars” of Massachusetts’ and the city of Boston’s economy — medical institutions, educational institutions, life science research, tourism and climate technology.

Idowu also said Trump’s tariffs were impacting community projects in the city like the P3 project, a plan to build affordable housing and a research lab on the site of a vacant lot in Roxbury.

Miranda was critical of the Trump administration’s rollback of diversity, equity and inclusion policies. She said Trump’s actions would hurt sectors like medical research.

“It’s not just symbolic, it’s sidelining brilliant people,” Miranda said.

Miranda also said that even when DEI policies were not under attack, Massachusetts’ government was not representative.

“I’m one of four Black women in the entire Legislature of 200 people … we’re not even represented in the bluest state in the country,” Miranda said.

Miranda encouraged attendees to boycott companies that rolled back DEI efforts and to contact their alma maters if the institutions were abandoning programs to foster diversity.

The politicians also told the audience policy wins they’re proud of. Miranda said that she’s proud of a bill she passed last year that addresses the higher morbidity rate that Black mothers face compared to white mothers.

“Six years ago when I first started talking about this issue, everyone told me ‘there’s no problem here,’ here in the public health Mecca of the world,” Miranda said sarcastically.

Idowu said that he felt proud that people of color have started businesses in almost every neighborhood in the city and no longer feel limited to Mattapan, Dorchester and Roxbury.

“The whole city belongs to us … we can go to establishments in other neighborhoods now and not feel policed,” Idowu said.

Priscilla Douglas, an executive coach and author who recently stepped down from the board of the Boston Public Library, attended the Embrace Ideas Festival. She is a lifelong resident of the city who went to Northeastern University and worked at the Roxbury YMCA and the Urban League growing up, but said the festival was eye-opening.

“Listening to the policy panel, I had no idea that 17 percent of Boston residents live in poverty,” Douglas said.

At the last panel of the day, Jeneé Osterheldt, deputy managing editor for culture, talent and development at The Boston Globe, interviewed entrepreneur Morgan DeBaun about her new self-help book and her career. DeBaun is the founder and CEO of Blavity Inc., a digital media company geared to Black millennials.

DeBaun said she had the idea to start a company focused on Black people when she was working for Intuit in Silicon Valley because she didn’t see anyone building technology with Black users as the primary customer they were targeting. DeBaun, who is originally from Missouri, said the murder of Ferguson teenager Mike Brown at the hands of the police in 2014 also led to her wanting to work with Black people.

“I was sitting in a cubicle in San Francisco after Mike Brown and the people around me were asking ‘what’s for lunch,’ they just were not seeing what I was seeing,” DeBaun said.

In the audience, Laurie Nicolas resonated with DeBaun’s experiences of working in predominantly white offices. Nicolas works in the healthcare space but started her own nonprofit called Pink Sunday which focuses on physical fitness for women. Nicolas learned about the Embrace festival after the inauguration of the Embrace statue in Boston Commons in 2023. She said she appreciated the diversity of the speakers at the festival.

“I want to focus on cultivating spaces where people feel included, not just people who look like me, but all kinds of diversity and I learned a lot from this event,” Nicolas.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: BAMS Festival expands through new events and continued ‘Momentum’
text:
Toki Wright, BAMS Festival’s community partnerships and programs manager, said the festival’s organizers have always wanted to create an event like Essence Festival of Culture in New Orleans or South by Southwest in Austin, Texas, allowing them to bring together small businesses, creators, curators, and promoters from the area and spotlight their work.

“BAMS Fest has never been about self-aggrandizement,” Wright said. “It’s never been about ‘look at me, look at us.’ It’s always about highlighting what’s happening in the arts and culture sector, highlighting small businesses, highlighting community development.”

The series launches this Wednesday in Cambridge at The Sinclair with a local musician showcase called “Authenticity: A Boston Lover’s Dream," which will feature acts like Western Massachusetts soul singer Kimaya Diggs and Boston R&B artist Aric. B.

Other live music events in the series focus on DJs and producers; Thursday’s “She’s in the Mix” gathering at The Record Company aims the spotlight at women DJs and producers through live DJ sets, mini music workshops, and panel discussions, while “The Stew: Beat Showcase” at High Street Place will test music producers’ skills on Sunday with a live beat-making contest.

Two parties also help Momentum ramp up for Saturday’s festival: the karaoke and game-filled “S.O.U.L.STICE: Play Playe Edition” on Thursday at the Emerson College UnCommon Stage, and Friday’s “Make ’Em Sweat: Kickoff Party” at the Boston nonprofit Artists For Humanity.

On Friday, the Museum of Fine Arts will show the film “May the Lord Watch” in collaboration with the Roxbury International Film Festival. The documentary follows North Carolina rap group Little Brother through their successes in the industry, eventual breakup, and subsequent reunion in 2019. Afterward, journalist Dart Adams will lead a discussion with the hip-hop group.

The screening tees up Little Brother to take the stage at BAMS Festival the following day at Franklin Park. R&B artist Lalah Hathaway and genre-blending singer-songwriter Durand Bernarr also lead this year’s lineup as headliners, with Boston performers such as Kasia Lavon and Cole Rodriguez rounding out the afternoon.

Folks looking to explore Momentum’s non-music offerings can check out a fashion designer showcase on Thursday called “Bogosplit: Runway Heat,” where a variety of local designers will share their work at the Liberty Hotel. On Sunday, poets like Jessica Care Moore and Boston’s own Tim Hall display the power of poetry at JustBook-ish in Dorchester for the “Wordspeak Lounge” event.

Momentum ends at Boston City Hall on Monday with “BAMS Fest Day,” which includes a screening of the documentary “BAMS Festival: A Local Anomaly” and will be officiated by Mayor Michelle Wu. The film chronicles the festival’s creation by founder Catherine T. Morris, as well as the events leading up to last year’s edition of the event.

Wright said Momentum has allowed BAMS to further diversify their events and support artists, vendors, and programming in a way that previously wasn’t possible due to factors like time constraints.

“We want to highlight this city,” he said. “Specifically, we want to highlight these creators of color, and say, ‘You are valid and important and you will survive, and there’s an ecosystem here that will help you with your survival.’”

Because Momentum takes place during Pride Month, and roughly a week after Juneteenth, Wright said he hopes BAMS Festival and its accompanying events will continuously demonstrate intersectionality and showcase how Black and brown people aren’t monoliths.

“For us, it’s about saying, ‘We’re not one thing. We’re not one identity. We’re multiple identities’,” he said. “We’re also loving people. We are also embracing people. We are also innovators and creators. And we create safe spaces, and we create an environment where this is the possibility for us.”

Wright’s past experience has taught him that hosting a festival is like creating a city within a city. He said that with BAMS Festival, organizers are trying to create safe spaces for people to feel loved, be themselves, and have productive conversations about complex topics such as race and queerness.

“This is bigger than just the show,” Wright said. “This is really building a world that we want to live in.”

title: As questions linger, family and school grieve for Boston 5-year-old killed in April bus crash
text:
That afternoon, Edmond was waiting for the bus when her adult daughter spotted police rushing around outside, but a neighbor’s home obstructed their view. The two women rushed out their door. In a moment, horror dawned on Edmond as she viewed the scene.

The school bus stopped a few doors down. Her granddaughter, on the sidewalk, screaming hysterically. The body, the size of a child, on the street. And no Lens.

Terror gripped Edmond like a vise, and she screamed at the police officer blocking her way.

Let me see my grandson!

There have been few answers in the nearly two months since Lens was struck and killed by his Boston Public Schools bus April 28, seconds after being dropped off at the wrong stop on the wrong side of the street with his 11-year-old cousin.

The driver has not been charged in connection with his death, while the Suffolk district attorney’s office and Boston police continue their investigation, and they have released no updates since the crash occurred.

Nearly a month following the crash, and after the Globe reported that the bus driver struck two other vehicles in Mattapan just minutes before the fatal crash, and tried to flee the Hyde Park scene, Mayor Michelle Wu and BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper announced an independent investigation of Transdev, the French contractor that provides bus drivers to the city’s public schools. They also have not provided updates on their investigation, which is being led by a former federal prosecutor.

City and school officials have said the bus driver, Jean Charles, had been pulled from the road for retraining after a series of collisions while behind the wheel. Charles, who worked for Transdev as a BPS bus driver starting in May 2023, resigned last month, just ahead of a scheduled termination hearing. At the time of the crash, he had an expired state certification required to drive a school bus.

Lens was a bright, gregarious child with a sunshiny disposition; his life was cut short, leaving an ache — and anger — in the hearts of his family, his school, and community.

For Esaie Joseph, Lens’s father, the lack of answers is maddening: How could this happen? Where is the accountability? How will this be prevented from ever happening again?

There is no backpack by the door, his Spider-Man toys no longer littered across the living room. Lens is not there to ask how he can help or sweetly nudge his grandmother to make spaghetti for dinner.

“We still talk about him; we’re never going to stop talking about him,” Joseph said in an exclusive interview with the Globe. “But every time it happens, we all get emotional, and we all start to cry.”

Lens was born in Haiti in August 2019. Four years later, Lens came to the US, where he lived in Hyde Park with several generations of his family, including his father, uncle, older cousin, and grandmother. His mother also lives in the region and was active in Lens’s life.

He was an old soul, prioritizing chores over play, responsibility over goofing around. At his funeral, his uncle, Ricardo Joseph, described Lens as a grown man who lived in the body of a 5-year-old.

“He was a great worker who always had something to do,” the boy’s uncle said. “If he wasn’t playing, he was cleaning; if he wasn’t cleaning, he was doing homework.”

Sophonia Lucien-Fontin, who has known the family for several years, and whose husband grew up with Lens’s dad and uncle in Haiti, said Lens was like the “2.0” version of his father.

Lens looked up to his dad, who she described as responsible, hard-working, and funny, and Lens took after him, she said. “He’s exactly like his father,” she said.

Lens also idolized superheroes, and Spider-Man was his favorite. The comic book hero fights crime and has a mantra, “With great power comes great responsibility,” and that message appeared to resonate with Lens.

Spider-Man doesn’t look for someone to reward him for doing good, Lucien-Fontin said. “That’s exactly what was going on with Lens.”

For his kindergarten graduation at the end of the school year, Lens picked out a dazzling suit — a dark, handsome “Spider-Man blue,” Lucien-Fontin said.

Instead, he was buried in that suit, his body laid to rest in a casket decorated with images of Spider-Man.

He took the superhero’s example of doing good to heart. Lens thought police officers do that work every day, and wanted to become one when he grew up, Lucien-Fontin said.

He wanted to serve his country, his uncle said. Such dreams will never be realized.

At the time of the bus crash, Esaie Joseph, Lens’s father, was driving a commercial truck through North Carolina.

He had been away from home for several days at that point, and the time away from family had been taking its toll. Lens last spoke to his father the Friday before the crash, in a video call.

“He called me and said, ‘You’ve been out for too long. You have to find a way to come back home,’ “ said Joseph, who said he feels tremendous guilt for not being at home when the crash occurred.

He compared his son’s life to a force of nature, maybe a crack of lightning. A flash of light, brilliant but brief. Or an object in the heavens.

“He’s a star that just went away,” Joseph said of his son. “I just thought his mission was over on Earth, because it was like lightning that just struck, and disappeared.”

At UP Academy Dorchester, where Lens was a kindergartner, the boy stood out as a helper, according to his teacher, Christina Vick. He’d offer to pass out assignments or guide classmates through a tough math problem.

When students lined up in the cafeteria at dismissal so they could board their buses, Lens loved to be the “line leader,” a role he cherished, assisting the educators by guiding his peers from one destination to the other, the example of how to walk down the hall orderly.

The day he died, there was much to celebrate in his classroom. Lens had just made a breakthrough in his reading, Vick said.

Haitian Creole is spoken in the Joseph home, while Lens spoke English in school, according to Vick. He excelled at arithmetic, but struggled with reading English words.

Vick recalled the challenge Lens faced:A word starting with “c”? Maybe it means “cat.”

But on that late April day, Lens, for the first time, started sounding out the words. He listened to each syllable, how one by one they blended together, the sounds turning into meaning.

As his mind opened itself to reading, his smile grew wide, Vick, who is a nine-year educator, recalled.

“When I see a student thriving, I know I did my job,” Vick said. “And he was thriving.”

While Lens’s father and uncle were at work, his grandmother, Edmond, the matriarch of the family, would care for the boy. Lens, in turn, wanted to help her.

Edmond, who has a strong voice, expressive hands, and bright, clear eyes, is on her feet all day running the large household. At times, she would take a moment to sit on the living room couch, a few steps from the family kitchen.

If Lens saw this, he’d grow concerned. Like clockwork, the questions would start. Grandma, he’d say, do you have a headache? Do you want some water?

When Edmond said she was OK, Lens would stay with her. “He would give me a hug, and say, ‘You’re just tired,’ “ Edmond said in Haitian Creole through an interpreter, a smile growing upon her lips.

The highlight of her day was in the afternoon, when he and his 11-year-old cousin returned home from school. The bus stop was just outside their home, and by the time she made her way downstairs, Lens would come bounding off the vehicle’s steps, his toothy grin and bubbling laugh rolling over her as they came together in a great hug.

How was your day? Edmond would always ask, and Lens would rattle off every detail: The math problem he solved brilliantly. How he helped his teacher by getting kids lined up for lunch. The funny joke his friend shared.

Edmond would listen intently, barely able to get a word in, as the child chatted away, fits of laughter throughout his tales.

“He was my son,” the matriarch said. “He was my hero.”

But the afternoon of April 28 changed everything.

Nathaniel Thomas, who lives in the same neighborhood as Lens’s family, was off-duty from his job as a Massachusetts Environmental Police officer.

As he drove, he spotted a stopped school bus on Washington Street, and saw a girl, Lens’s 11-year-old cousin, standing on the sidewalk less than a block away, screaming. A child’s body lay in the street.

Thomas stopped his car, and ran to the child on the roadway, a little boy whose injuries clearly indicated he had been struck by a large vehicle. Thomas remained with the boy for several minutes, trying to help him as best as he could. The girl continued screaming.

That’s my cousin! she yelled through tears.

A yellow bus was stopped about 100 feet away. Between sobs, the young girl pointed to the vehicle, yelling that the vehicle had struck her cousin.

Neighbors rushed up, some on their phones calling for help. He left the boy in their care, and ran toward the bus, up the vehicle’s steps, and confronted the driver — later named by officials as Charles — still behind the wheel.

Thomas identified himself as a police officer. Stay here, Thomas ordered. Give me your license.

The driver, who Thomas said appeared to be in his 30s or 40s, slender, clean-shaven, wearing a dark hat, waved his hand back at the children: “I have these kids,” the driver said. “I have to leave.”

Thomas said the driver appeared in shock and he told the driver he wasn’t going anywhere. The driver handed over his identification, which Thomas then gave to the first Boston police officer on the scene.

Emergency crews arrived.

Nearby, Edmond watched as the paramedics rushed to load Lens into an ambulance bound for Boston Children’s Hospital. She pushed up against an officer, pleading to be allowed to pass.

No, you’re not going to be able to see him. We cannot let you see him, the officer told Edmond.

She was taken by authorities to Boston Children’s Hospital with Lens’s other family members, but she wasn’t allowed to be near him, as surgeons fought to save his life.

Now, the sight of a school bus in the neighborhood has become a body blow.

“I don’t know how I’m going to go through life without him,” Edmond said on a recent afternoon, tears rolling down her cheeks. “I’m just going through this pain over and over again.”

She paused, wiping the tears from her eyes, as she gazed out the window. “Oh God, let me see him again, one last time,” she said.

The family wants accountability, Esaie Joseph said. He can’t understand how the bus driver, with all the training that is required, could strike a child he had just dropped off.

The family has not heard directly from Transdev since the crash, Joseph said. And despite their requests, they still haven’t seen footage from the cameras mounted to the bus.

Joseph said the family wants to work with state legislators to strengthen laws on school bus safety and driver training. There should be monitors on all school buses so children are able to board and exit the vehicles safely, he said. Right now, the buses aren’t safe, he said.

“They could give more training to the drivers and educate them better in terms of safety,” Joseph said.

For now, the family is also focused on healing. Their attention is on Lens’s cousin, the girl with him at the time of the crash.

She doesn’t talk much about what happened. But she remains affected by the tragedy.

“Sometimes she would, out of nowhere, she will just say his name,” Joseph said.

Lens’s classmates miss him, too. They struggle with the notion Lens won’t come back.

“They talk about him every single day, and they have so many questions,” Vick said. “I don’t have the answers. It’s just hard.”

For the remainder of the school year, Lens’s classroom cubby remained decorated by self-portraits and scenes of the classroom drawn by students, a Spider-Man poster signed by everyone in the class is also on display.

On the last day of school last Wednesday, when students cleaned up their stuff to take home, Vick collected the poster and artwork.

She thinks she’ll put it back in the fall, so Lens isn’t forgotten.

title: Boston City Councilor Fernandes Anderson invites constituents to attend her final city council meeting
text:
As Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson nears her final day in office after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges, she is inviting her constituents to attend her final council meeting to “celebrate all we’ve built together.”

In an email to District 7 constituents Monday, Fernandes Anderson invited the public to attend Wednesday’s meeting “as the sun sets on my time in the Council Chamber.”

“Let’s celebrate all we’ve built together, and look ahead to the bright paths still to come,” she said in the email.

Federal authorities arrested Fernandes Anderson in December on charges of orchestrating a kickback scheme while in office.

She was accused of hiring a relative in December 2022 and giving them a $13,000 bonus months later, with the caveat that Fernandes Anderson receive $7,000 in cash. Last year, she made $114,557 in salary on the City Council, according to city payroll data.

Fernandes Anderson initially pleaded not guilty to the charges but in April agreed to plead guilty to two of the six corruption charges against her.

In exchange, prosecutors agreed to drop the other four charges, recommending she pay $13,000 in restitution and serve one year and a day in prison, followed by three years of supervised release.

She is scheduled to be sentenced in federal court on July 29.

After prosecutors announced the charges, Mayor Michelle Wu and five city councilors called for her resignation.

Under state law, the council does not have the authority to remove a sitting councilor unless they have been sentenced for a felony conviction, but Fernandes Anderson announced June 12 that she had submitted her letter of resignation and that her last day in office would be July 4.

Fernandes Anderson represents Roxbury, Dorchester, part of the South End, and the Fenway. In 2021, she became the first Muslim and formerly undocumented immigrant to be elected to the council.

In her email to constituents Monday, Fernandes Anderson said she would be “grateful to share this closing chapter with you.”

“This isn’t goodbye, it’s a moment to honor the work we’ve done together, the voices we’ve lifted, and the community we’ve loved forward,” she said.

Fernandes Anderson did not return messages seeking further comment Tuesday.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
JESSIE REYEZ: PAID IN MEMORIES TOUR Hailing from Toronto, this singer-songwriter boasts a lithe soprano and an innate skill for penning lacerating lyrics. June 28 and 29, 7 p.m. doors. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

PIGS PIGS PIGS PIGS PIGS PIGS PIGS “Death Hilarious,” the latest album from this English metal outfit, is sludgy and pummeling, with vocalist Matthew Baty’s guttural wail slicing through the chaos. June 29, 7 p.m. doors. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

JULIE DOIRON Since the early ’90s, this New Brunswick-born vocalist and guitarist has been one of indie rock’s top-tier songwriters, first with the beloved shoegaze act Eric’s Trip and then on her own. Her 2021 full-length “I Thought of You” — her most recent solo album — is hooky and lively, with her warm alto framed in guitar fuzz and sparkle. July 1, 7 p.m. doors. Middle East Upstairs, Cambridge. 617-864-3278. mideastoffers.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

MAYA DE VITRY The Nashville-based singer-songwriter with the resonating, soulful voice is in duo mode this time through, playing with longtime collaborator Joel Timmons (whose recent debut solo album, “Psychedelic Surf Country,” she produced). Expect songs from across her burgeoning catalog, along with a few of his and perhaps a detour into a cover or two as well.June 28, 7 p.m. $25. Firehouse Center for the Arts, 1 Market Square, Newburyport. 978-452-7336. www.firehouse.org

NEW ENGLAND AMERICANA FESTIVAL The Bellforge Arts Center and the New England Americana Association are hosting this daylong, two-stage festival of local and regional acts. Among those scheduled to perform are Jimmy Ryan and Wooden Leg, FauxMenco, Comanchero, Molly Pinto Madigan, and Kier Byrnes & The Kettle Burners. June 28, 1 p.m. (rain date June 29). Free. Bellforge Arts Center, 45 Hospital Road, Medfield. www.bellforge.org

THE DESLONDES They’ve been based in New Orleans since their beginnings, but through four albums (including their latest, “Roll It Out”) the Deslondes have roamed the length and breadth of the roots-music landscape, pulling in country, folk, blues, soul, and good old rock ’n’ roll along the way. Call ’em a 3rd Ward version of the Band. July 1, 8 p.m. $25. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. www.therockwell.org

STUART MUNRO

CURTIS SALGADO The powerhouse performer is known for his soulful voice, hot harmonica, and insightful songwriting. The winner of 11 Blues Music Awards, including B.B. King Entertainer of The Year, he co-led the Robert Cray Band, fronted Roomful of Blues, and taught John Belushi to play the blues harp, among many other accomplishments. June 28, 7 p.m. $41.29. The Fallout Shelter, 61 Endicott St., Norwood. extendedplaysessions.com

THE ART OF CUBAN PIANO Piquant pianists Anibal Cruz and Zahili Zamora join forces with flute virtuoso Melvin Lam and singer-songwriter Barbara Zamora for a soul-satisfying evening of Afro-Latin rhythm and melody. July 1, 8 p.m. $20. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

KRISTALIS SOTOMAYOR Y LAS NENAS DEL SWING The young flutist and singer, recipient of a Latin Grammy Cultural Foundation Scholarship, fronts a nonet of improvisers comprising vocals, violin, piano, bass, and a battery of three hand percussionists. July 3, 6 to 8:30 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St.www.longlivebeerworks.com/boston

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

MASSOPERA MassOpera and creative partner Horizon Ensemble mount Handel’s Baroque gem “Alcina,” a story of love, lust, and several mistaken identities featuring some of the most exhilarating arias in the repertoire. Hannah Shanefield stage directs the production, starring Kayla Kovacs as Alcina and Naré Kim as Morgana. June 27-29. Arlington High School, Arlington. www.massopera.org

ROCKPORT CHAMBER MUSIC FESTIVAL This Friday, the Grammy-winning ensemble Imani Winds performs with Pulitzer Prize finalist composer Andy Akiho on steel pan drum, with music by Villa-Lobos and Fazil Say in addition to several of Akiho’s pieces (June 27). Saturday, pianist Jonathan Biss offers up a sunset program of two late Schubert sonatas (June 28). Shalin Liu Performance Center, Rockport. 978-546-7391, www.rockportmusic.org

TO THE PEOPLE LIKE US White Snake Projects presents its first-ever collaboratively crafted community opera, a new piece of music theater from composer Jorge Sosa and a crew of teenage librettists from 826 Boston’s Youth Literary Advisory Board. The plot concerns issues of gentrification and its impact on climate in the city. June 28, 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Strand Theatre, Dorchester. www.whitesnakeprojects.org

A.Z. MADONNA

THE GLASS MENAGERIE The elements of direction, design, and performance merge in Doug Lockwood’s rigorously thought-through, beautifully executed staging of this autobiographical work by Tennessee Williams. Among other things, “The Glass Menagerie” is a portrait of the artist at the moment when he chooses his art over everything else. Lockwood and his excellent cast (De’Lon Grant, Adrianne Krstansky, Liza Giangrande, and Patrick O’Konis) make clear the difficulty, the cost, and, ultimately, the necessity of that choice. Through June 28. Gloucester Stage Company. 978-281-4433,

https://gloucesterstage.com/

LITTLE SHOP OF HORRORS Yes, it’s basically a depiction of a botanical Armageddon. And yes, our recent experience with a global pandemic has given end-of-the-world scenarios an unsettling currency. Those sci-fi tales no longer seem quite so “fi,” do they? But the point of “Little Shop of Horrors’’ is to give you a good time, and on that score, Ilana Ransom Toeplitz’s high-spirited production largely delivers, especially when Jared Troilo is onstage, playing a sadistic dentist and a host of other characters. This musical revels in over-the-top camp and is loaded with good songs by Alan Menken (music) and Howard Ashman (lyrics). Featuring Stephen Markarian as Seymour, a nebbishy employee at a flower shop who makes the mistake of feeding a bloodthirsty plant just what it wants, and Kayla Shimizu as Audrey, the fellow employee with whom Seymour is hopelessly in love. Through June 29. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. 781-279-2200, www.greaterbostonstage.org

THE VICTIM The premiere of a play by Lawrence Goodman built on three interconnected monologues. One is by a Holocaust survivor (Annette Miller) looking for ways to heal as she is flooded with horrific memories; one is by a top New York physician (played by Stephanie Clayman) whose racial diversity training has taken a dreadfully wrong turn; and one is by a home health aide (Yvette King) forced to deal with racism in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic. Directed by Daniel Gidron. Through July 20. Shakespeare & Company, Elayne P. Bernstein Theatre, Lenox. 413-637-3353, shakespeare.org

DON AUCOIN

LAURA SANCHEZ The dancer-choreographer’s new one-woman flamenco monologue, “Welcome to Holland!?,” explores the vicissitudes of motherhood and caregiving. The 75-minute theatrical work fuses dance, poetry, and humor to challenge stereotypes of non-traditional families, trauma, disability, and belonging. June 28-29. $35. The Center for Arts at the Armory, Somerville. https://artsatthearmory.org

JACOB’S PILLOW DANCE FESTIVAL The renowned summer festival in the Berkshires gets fully underway this week with a host of performances, from the powerful Michelle Dorrance/Ephrat Asherie collaboration “The Center Will Not Hold” (through June 29) to Los to Angeles-based BODYTRAFFIC (July 2-6) to a range of performances outdoors on the Henry J. Leir stage, such as Almanac Dance Circus Theatre (July 2) and West African dance by the visionary mother-son duo Marie Basse-Wiles and Omari Wiles (June 27). Ticket prices start at $40. Becket. www.jacobspillow.org/festival/ticketed-performances

REVOLVE DANCE PROJECT The Providence company brings together professional composers, choreographers, dancers, and musicians from Rhode Island and beyond to create an entirely new show over the space of a few weeks. The upcoming concert “Sound in Form” features six world premieres plus a restaging of last year’s “Runner’s High” and an extended version of Lauren Lovette’s “Bones.” June 29. $25-$100. The Strand Ballroom and Theatre, Providence. www.revolvedanceproject.com

VICTORIA L. AWKWARD The premiere of the choreographer’s new “In the Space Between” anchors The Theater Offensive’s inaugural QUEER [RE]PUBLIC FESTIVAL. The four-day festival celebrates the artistry of queer and trans people of color as an expansion of its commitment to radical art and community-building. Awkward’s new work, a choreographic ritual for seven dancers incorporating aerial dance and personal storytelling, takes inspiration from Audre Lorde’s vision of the erotic as power. June 26-29. Free to $25. Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. https://thetheateroffensive.org/

KAREN CAMPBELL

MING FAY: EDGE OF THE GARDEN Fay, who died earlier this year, was best known for his fanciful, outsize papier-mâché sculptures of botanical forms — past works include a pepper, a walnut, a pear, a maple twirler — that he gathered together into fantastical hothouses conjured by his vivid imagination. An associated exhibition at the Pao Arts Center in Chinatown will put Fay’s work in league with the photographer Mel Taing and artist Yu-Wen Wu in an exploration of Boston‘s Chinatown gardens. June 26-Sept. 21. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org

MAKING HISTORY: 200 YEARS OF AMERICAN ART With nearly 100 works from the collection of the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, this exhibition offers a retrofit of the standard American art-historical tale with a broader, more inclusive story of the country’s diverse cohort of creative giants who shaped — and continue to shape, and expand — the very notion of American creativity. Featuring such artists as Edward Hopper, Winslow Homer, Gilbert Stuart, Barkley Hendricks, Georgia O’Keeffe, Horace Pippin, Thomas Hart Benton, Mary Cassatt, and Stuart Davis, among many others. Through Sept. 21. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500, www.pem.org

VAN GOGH: THE ROULIN FAMILY PORTRAITS Vincent van Gogh met few successes in his short, unhappy life, but between 1888 and 1889, he was as content as he’d ever been. In the French town of Arles, he found peace in the friendship of local postman Joseph Roulin and his family. A collaboration with the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the show brings together some 20 portraits made in that moment, and a glimpse of a famously tortured artist breifly calmed. ThroughSept. 7. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

BOSTON PUBLIC ART TRIENNIAL: Artist Gabriel Sosa is hosting open hours for his Ñ Press project at Maverick Landing Community Services in East Boston. Sosa, who works frequently in text, has created a print studio for the triennial, open to the public, where he helps transform community projects like zines, posters, pamphlets, and artist books into “vessels of connection, activism, and education.” June 28 (and every Saturday), noon-6 p.m. at Maverick Landing Community Services, 31 Liverpool St. www.thetriennial.org/events/

MURRAY WHYTE

CANTASTIC! Korean artist Eunseok Han makes jewelry and sculptures out of recycled aluminum cans. She sorts them by color and cuts them into tiny shapes, which she bends and folds, then joins them together in flowing, fanning forms with brilliant, shifting hues. Centering her practice around sustainability, she crafts works that reflect and celebrate nature, depicting feathers, fish, plants, weather and water currents, and endangered animals. Through July 25. Mobilia Gallery, 348 Huron Ave., Cambridge. 617-876-2109,www.mobilia-gallery.com

CATE McQUAID

STEVE SWEENEY “I’ve got two self-help books that I wrote myself,” says Sweeney, who plays Giggles with Mitch Stinson and Johnny Pizzi. “’The Power of Negative Thinking’ and the big one, ‘You Are a Mistake.’ I am a demotivational speaker.”June 27-28, 8:30 p.m. $33.85. Giggles Comedy Club, 517 Broadway (Route 1), Saugus. 978-395-9060, www.princerestaurant.com/giggles-events

RAFI GONZALES The Boston comic thinks people can be too judgmental. “If we see a homeless guy go into the liquor store at 9 a.m. to get a bottle of vodka we go, holy crap, that guy’s an alcoholic,” he says. “But if Trisha goes to brunch at 9 a.m. and has 10 mimosas in an hour, people are like, holy crap, Trisha’s a morning person.” June 28, 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. $40.46.Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

WEAPONS OF MASS DYSFUNCTION Host Caroline Moore has apparently given the comics on this late-night show a directive to “get weird with it,” which shouldn’t be tough for Andrew Mayer, Will Pottorff, Brieana Woodward, and other possible special guests.June 28, 11:30 p.m. $10. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

CAMBRIDGE CITY DANCE PARTY Boogie down at the annual Cambridge City Dance Party. A block party kicks off at 5 p.m. on Temple Street, followed by the big dance party at 6 p.m. in front of City Hall, featuring several local DJs on decks. The festivities are set to span from Massachusetts Avenue to Prospect Street. June 27, 4-11 p.m. Free admission. Cambridge City Hall, 795 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge. cambridgema.gov

NORTH SHORE PRIDE PARADE AND FESTIVAL Watch the parade proceed from Shetland Park to Salem Common in celebration of Pride Month. A festival will take place after the parade at 1 p.m., featuring tunes, fun, and more from DJ Ms. Jackie the Mixtress and host Madam Zapple. Food vendors like Clyde’s Cupcakes, Atomic Coffee Roasters, and Matilda Empanadas will also be on hand offering treats, while the 21+ crowd can head over to Bit Bar following the festival for the North Shore Pride After Party. June 28, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. Free admission. Salem Common, N. Washington Square, Salem. northshorepride.org

INDEPENDENCE DAY CELEBRATION Celebrate Independence Day a little early at Canton’s Irish Cultural Centre. Families can enjoy face painting, a performance at 7 p.m. from Classic Trax classic rock band, and the fireworks display at 9 p.m. Refreshments will be available for purchase from the Irish Cultural Centre Pub. June 29, 6:30-9:30 p.m. Free admission. Irish Cultural Centre, 200 New Boston Drive, Canton. cantonma.myrec.com

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Illuminus’s ‘On the Rox’ sessions build toward October festival
text:
Illuminus, a Boston artists group, is best known for the nighttime light festivals it has staged in the city for more than a decade, with dazzling lights and images projected on buildings, attracting massive crowds.

These days, however, founder Jeff Grantz and his team are trying something very different — picking one neighborhood to draw local talent and inspiration for a wholly original and new kind of public exhibition.

It’s so new, in fact, that it’s hard yet to even say what it will be this year, which is part of the point. Illuminus organizers say it will be large and immersive and it will take place in October in Roxbury, this year’s designated neighborhood. But the form and content will evolve with the help of Roxbury artists and community members themselves.

Illuminus chose artists — dancers, poets, rappers, and more — who would work with community members at monthly public sessions through the spring and summer to conceive and create an exhibition organic to the community.
