title: These local teens love transit so much they made a hyperrealistic MBTA bus simulator on Roblox
text:
Players can also imitate transit police, roaming around in Fords to nab speeding buses, direct traffic, and ticket parked cars. Officers can’t make arrests and don’t carry weapons, Benmokrane added; the game, much to his relief, has yet to devolve into an MBTA-themed spinoff of “Grand Theft Auto.”

Benmokrane, now a political science major at Boston University, said he and his team began piecing together the “Boston Bus Simulator” in 2022. Work progressed in fits and starts until this year, when a concerted months-long push put the game online in late June. Twin passions drove the effort: an obsession with public transit, and a love for Roblox.

“I grew up on that stuff, and I kind of just loved it when I was a little kid,” said Benmokrane. (And the passion has proven lucrative: he says the game has brought in a few grand.)

The digitally disengaged may know little about Roblox, let alone its scale.

The platform and its accompanying game-creation tool, run by a San Mateo, Calif., corporation of the same name, allow users to develop, play, and monetize their own video games.

Potential themes and styles are vast.

There are, a Roblox spokesperson said, more than 6 million active games (called “experiences”) on Roblox today — among them a funeral simulator, Wordle copycats, and “Get Fat And Roll Race,” in which players must “Eat food to gain weight and roll faster” down a hill.

Roblox games attracted, on average, almost 112 million active users every day between April and June of this year, the company announced in July.

Almost 36 percent of Roblox‘s daily active users are under the age of 13 as of June 30, according to company data shared with The Boston Globe. The platform’s most successful game developers are, on average, around 25, a Roblox spokesperson said.

More than 463,000 Roblox users had visited Benmokrane’s MBTA simulator as of Aug. 13, according to the Roblox website.

“I’m surprised it’s done so well, honestly!” he told the Globe.

Pretend operators shuttle passengers through parts of Medford, Malden, Revere, Everett, Chelsea, and Boston. They earn in-game cash making stops and completing routes.

The in-game buses — three-dimensional renditions of actual vehicles — bear a remarkable resemblance to the real things. They were stylized with attention to minute real-world details even daily riders could be forgiven for never noticing: the stickers in the windshield; the size and shape of the bike rack fastened to the bus’s face, and so on.

Players can accelerate, brake, turn, and shift gears with their keyboards. Other keys control hazards, doors, signals, interior and exterior lights, and the bus’s “kneeling” (when it tilts to approach a curb).

Drivers can also program real destinations into the bus’s displays. The Ro-buses, true to form, lumber and wobble as they move.

Those less inclined to drive can wait for and board buses at stops. Buses can’t trample and kill Roblox pedestrians, according to Benmokrane (but, strangely, police vehicles can).

Benmokrane, aside from managing the game’s marketing and overseeing its operation, is the simulator’s less domineering and disruptive Robert Moses, the 20th-century “master builder” who reshaped New York’s transportation landscape.

“I’ve done all the roads in the games,” he said. “That’s pretty much all I do.”

With Google Maps open on a separate monitor as a guide, Benmokrane re-creates the bus paths manually, piecing together roads, curbs, signs, and lane-striping with quick and deliberate mouse clicks and drags. He tries to keep everything to scale by converting feet to “studs,” a Roblox unit of length.

Held up by doubts or dated satellite imagery, Benmokrane says he will visit a street in person and take photographs.

“He is a master at making roads,” said Jarek Alexander, Benmokrane’s colleague and friend. He went on, “It’s just so beautiful how he does it.”

Alexander, a 20-year-old Dorchester resident, is an assistant conductor for Keolis, the Commuter Rail operator. He moonlights as the simulator’s “quality control” guy.

“I just make sure everything’s realistic,” he said.

Managing the game and guiding its expansion has become, at least for Benmokrane, a job unto itself.

“Honestly, the management is a lot. I have Discord on my phone. I’m always checking it,” he said, referencing the messaging app that serves as the community’s nervous system. “My girlfriend and my friends, they get mad at me.”

He estimates he spends at least two hours a day tending to the game; he’ll spend around six hours in front of his monitors if he’s developing.

But the effort isn’t fruitless. Satisfaction aside, Benmokrane suspects he’s made at least $4,000 from the game since its release in late June, largely from users purchasing decals for buses, police cars, and in-game character designs.

“It’s enough that I’m probably going to quit my job” as a server at a Japanese restaurant, he said.

Benmokrane sharpened his Roblox skills by reproducing the Worcester Regional Transit Authority’s bus system; users have visited the game more than 284,000 times since its release in 2020.

Other Roblox re-creations of MBTA bus services predated Benmokrane’s latest project. Rail enthusiasts can also try their hand at a “semi-realistic simulation” of the Blue Line or an “ultra-realistic” model of the Commuter Rail’s Providence/Stoughton line.

Transportation games are plentiful and well-played on Roblox, according to the company.

“In general, driving, flying, busing and other transit experiences are popular on the platform,” a Roblox spokesperson wrote to the Globe.

“Stepford County Railway,” a train simulator, has garnered more than 107 million visits since its release. Bus simulators abound — re-creations of Vermont school buses, London’s bus system, and Hong Kong’s network, to name only a few.

The MBTA, for its part, is aware of Benmokrane’s game.

“It’s great to see the public embracing their creativity and engaging with transit in a new and fun way,” the agency wrote in a statement.

Kenneth Dumas, the cartographer who modernized the MBTA’s rapid transit map in the mid-1990s and helped rework it in the 2010s, drew up a route diagram for the game’s website.

Benmokrane hopes to work for the T one day, not just simulate its services.

“There was an internship that I really wanted to do [at the MBTA],” he said, “but I had to focus on the game.”

title: Independent investigation to be released on BPS bus contractor involved in crash that killed student
text:
An attorney’s investigative report on the Boston Public Schools bus contractor involved in an April crash that killed a kindergartner in Hyde Park will be discussed at a City Council hearing Aug. 28, City Councilor Henry Santana told the Globe Wednesday in a statement.

It’s unclear whether the report will be released publicly prior to the hearing.

The probe, announced nearly three months ago by Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper, was to review safety policies and performance of Transdev, the French company contracted with BPS to provide transportation services since 2013, according to a May statement from Wu and Skipper.

The attorney’s investigation was announced following the April 28 bus crash that killed Lens Joseph, a 5-year-old student enrolled at UP Academy in Dorchester. Joseph was struck and killed by his school bus after he was dropped off near his Hyde Park home.

The investigation, led by former federal prosecutor Natashia Tidwell, was expected to review existing safety policies and performance, including the bus driver collective bargaining agreement, according to Wu and Skipper’s statement from May.

Representatives of BPS did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday afternoon.

Santana, who serves as chair of the City Council’s Education Committee, told the Globe Wednesday a previously planned hearing for Thursday to discuss BPS school bus driver safety was canceled in favor of the session next week, when Tidwell’s report will be available.

Tidwell, Transdev, and BPS Transportation officials will participate in the hearing, Santana said.

Tidwell also was expected to make recommendations on strengthening bus safety measures, the May statement from Wu and Skipper said.

The Joseph family in July filed a lawsuit against Transdev and the bus driver, who was identified by city and school officials as Jean Charles.

“We are eager to read the report and learn about the fruits of the investigation,” said Matthew Fogelman, one of the attorneys representing the family. “The family really hasn’t been provided with a lot of information.”

Thursday’s canceled hearing was expected to review the hiring, training, and compliance certification of BPS bus drivers. City Councilor Erin Murphy, one of the measure’s backers, opposed canceling the hearing that focused on the safety of BPS students.

“We have to look closely at the hiring, training, and compliance certifications [of bus drivers] to make sure all 22,000 students who ride the bus are being driven by certified safe drivers,” Murphy said.

Charles has not been charged in connection with the crash. The Suffolk District Attorney’s office and Boston police are conducting a separate investigation of the crash, and have not announced any updates.

The Globe reported that minutes before the deadly crash, Charles struck two other vehicles in Mattapan, then tried to flee the scene after Lens was struck.

Charles also had been driving for months with an expired state credential required to operate a school bus, according to city and school district officials.

In the year prior to the Hyde Park crash, Charles was involved in four “minor incidents” with other vehicles — hitting a parked car, a rear tire, a bumper, and a side mirror, Wu and Skipper said in May.

Under the current contract with Transdev, signed in 2023, BPS pays the company roughly $18 million a year to hire, train, and manage the district’s roughly 750 school bus drivers and maintain the district-owned school bus fleet, according to the statement and Transdev’s contract with the district.

title: Despite promise, some co-op grocers struggle to catch on
text:
“We are running against name recognition and habitual practices,” said Darian Leta, co-president of Dorchester Food Co-op’s board.

Disappointing sales numbers have been a problem for the co-op since it opened in October 2023, she said. Since sales fell short of expectations, the $2 million to $3 million from fund-raising and grants obtained over ten years of advocacy and planning are being poured into operating costs.

Another venture, the Charles River Food Co-op, has spent years planning for a co-op in Newton, Waltham, or Watertown to replace the shuttered Russo’s Market.

Having amassed almost 1,000 members, organizers were initially hopeful that they could open quickly, said Treasurer Kathryn Loup. But finding a suitable space has proved difficult, Loup said, and they’ll need to raise at least $7 million to get up and running — and to get the word out.

“You feel like, ‘Wow, we have all these members,’” she said, “But the amount of money you need is just a lot. It’s gonna take some time.”

JQ Hannah, executive director of the Food Co-op Initiative, which helps launch food co-ops across the country, said it’s not unusual for new co-ops to take a few years to reach profitability, and rely on grants and donations until they do.

“I can point to numerous food co-ops startups that didn’t perform quite as hoped at first … who had the time and opportunity to course-correct and figure out their business model a little more precisely and get to profitability because of different forms of outside support that may not be available to Dorchester right now,” Hannah said.

It’s a tricky time for independent grocery stores as costs continue to rise. Dorchester-based nonprofit grocery store Daily Table, which had four locations, closed in May citing inflation and rollback of government programs that had helped fund their work.

“I like to think that Daily Table, when it closed, it didn’t fail as much as its success just couldn’t continue,” said Doug Rauch, Daily Table’s founder and a former president of Trader Joe’s. “We ran out of funds.”

Attracting customers without a marketing budget is a challenge for any small, independent grocer, Rauch said, and the solution is to “get your customers to be your ambassadors” by offering something specific that addresses their needs, whether that’s significantly lower prices, innovative local products, or a unique store experience.

Labor is Dorchester Food Co-op’s biggest cost, Leta said. Rent is significant too, although it’s lower than market-rate because it’s in an affordable housing community.

Since the store opened, Dorchester Food Co-op has made lots of improvements: They’ve introduced bulk discounts — 5 percent for non-members and 10 percent for members — and expanded catering services. They’ve reduced the prices of popular items to draw in more customers, Leta said, and they could lower prices even further if more people shopped at the store.

Leta said the co-op generates $10,000 to $13,000 in sales each week. To cover operating costs, that figure would need to at least triple, she said. She estimates they’d need $500,000 to survive long enough to reach next summer’s grant application period. But relying on future grants is far from a safe bet.

Leta said the board has notified member-owners in newsletters over the past several months that the co-op was not reaching its goals. The letter was a “challenge” to people to “shop their values.”

When you spend $300 on groceries at a mega chain, she said, “you’re giving money to a space that doesn’t necessarily give back to your community.”

And, Leta notes, when big grocery chains’ egg shelves were bare and what little was available high-priced, the locally-sourced Dorchester Food Co-op had plenty.

“We posted, ‘hey, we have eggs for $7,’ and we were sold out by the end of that night,” she said. “People just need to remember that we’re there.”

title: After this month’s raise, the future of the attorney work stoppage remains unclear. For answers, some are looking to Maine.
text:
But two years later, he said, there is still a shortage. “It hasn’t solved all our problems,” he said.

Maine offers a case study, lawyers say, as Massachusetts confronts a work stoppage by private attorneys that has thrown its courts into turmoil. Earlier this month Beacon Hill boosted their pay — a far more modest raise of $10, with an additional $10 next year to bring the total base level pay to $85 — but it hasn’t ended the impasse.

As a result, dozens of criminal cases are being dismissed each week because defendants lacking the means to pay have no access to a lawyer, a right guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment of the US Constitution. A resolution doesn’t appear imminent.

“I don’t see this ending anytime soon,” said Elyse Hershon, a lawyer in Suffolk County who’s been one of the most vocal court-appointed attorneys in the stoppage. “They didn’t solve the problem.”

Maine and Massachusetts are two of only three states that rely on private attorneys, known as bar advocates, to represent such a high percentage of indigent defendants, according to the Sixth Amendment Center.

In Massachusetts, bar advocates have historically represented 80 percent of cases, with staff lawyers from the state’s public defender agency covering the remainder.

In Maine, all cases were handled by private lawyers. Now, it’s building a public defender agency, with the goal of staff lawyers handling half of cases and private lawyers the rest. Massachusetts is considering a similar ratio.

But as Maine has shown, hiring public defenders can be slow and difficult. Currently, about 20 to 30 percent of cases are covered by public defenders. The state has now hired 32 public defenders, the governor’s office said.

“Despite having significantly more money, the number of rostered attorneys has not increased to required levels,” Governor Janet Mills’ office said in a statement.

Massachusetts has more law school graduates, but legal analysts said it’s likely to struggle as well. The state aims to hire more than 300 public defenders. The Committee for Public Counsel Services, which runs the indigent defense system, said it is working on a recruiting plan.

The bill passed by the Massachusetts Legislature this month to address the labor action allocates $40 million to double the number of staff public defenders.

Aditi Goel, head of the Boston-based Sixth Amendment Center, which charts indigent representation nationwide, said Massachusetts should learn from Maine’s experience.

That means identifying the core reason why private lawyers weren’t willing to work in the first place, and why they still haven’t returned, Goel said.

“The reality is increasing the rate without understanding why there is a problem might just involve throwing more money at a problem without solving it,” she said.

The leaders of the work stoppage say the raise from $65 an hour to $85 over two years is not nearly enough to get them to begin taking cases again. They had sought a $60-an-hour increase over two years.

Another similarity between Massachusetts and Maine: Because private attorneys are independent contractors, there’s no binding bargaining process that will bring about a resolution, the way it would in a union negotiation. Rather, the question is whether the raise will persuade enough lawyers to take cases.

Some attorneys have returned. A review of attorney shift logs shows some have signed up to take cases in August in Boston courts, compared with none in June.

In Suffolk Superior Court last week, Assistant District Attorney Alexander Jones told a judge he had “good news” — he’d found a defense attorney for a man accused in a violent kidnapping in Revere. That meant the man’s case would not be eligible for release and eventual dismissal because of the stoppage, as prosecutors had feared.

“I can take him off the list” for release, Judge Christopher Belezos said, holding up a Post-It note, before moving on to another case.

Still, the number of people accused of crimes who continue to go unrepresented is increasing, now reaching over 3,900, including more than 100 who are being held in jail.

District courts in Suffolk and Middlesex remain under an emergency procedure established by the state Supreme Judicial Court known as the Lavallee protocol, through which judges are tasked with holding hearings for defendants without lawyers; those who have been held for more than seven days without a lawyer are being released, and cases that have languished for more than 45 days are being dismissed.

On some Tuesdays, when hearings are held in Boston, as many as 100 cases have been dismissed. The cases are largely misdemeanors such as drug possession and shoplifting, but some involve allegations of violence. Last week, a man accused in a machete attack in a school parking lot had his case dismissed.

The cases dismissed under the protocol can be refiled, and the Suffolk DA’s office says it’s working on doing so for many cases. But if a case is dismissed, any conditions of release vanish, including GPS monitoring and orders to stay away from alleged victims.

In total, the state trial court last week provided a conservative count of 500 dismissed cases, including 178 in Boston and 322 in other courts, largely in Middlesex.

Some of the dismissals are cropping up in daily court business outside the Tuesday Lavallee hearings, a mark of the broad impacts the stoppage is having on the system.

In Dorchester District Court, it’s become commonplace for First Justice Jonathan Tynes to dismiss cases without prejudice over prosecutors’ objections. Over the past week, he’s thrown out a case involving gun charges and several that included crimes of violence, according to court records. Among those were allegations of assault and battery of someone over 60, assault and battery against a family member, and strangulation.

“We’ll do it on a case-by-case basis,” Tynes said from the bench at the start of one recent day’s court proceedings. By the end of the day, he’d dismissed charges against one man and released another.

On a different day in Lowell District Court, First Justice John Coffey gazed down on a man accused of assault and battery on a family member and violating an abuse prevention order. The man’s two cases had lingered for more than 45 days, and he didn’t have an attorney in either one.

“You’re entitled at this point to have these matters dismissed,” Coffey said. But, he noted, prosecutors could refile them, so the charges would show up twice on his record.

“I’d like them dismissed, your honor,” said the man, Ramon Ruiz.

Coffey nodded. “These matters now stand dismissed.”

title: Bike thefts spike every summer in Greater Boston. Check out the hotspots.
text:
Reno Sarge, 29, knows the high cost of bike theft well.

His Himiway D3 Cruiser, which cost around $1,000, was stolen in Back Bay this Juneteenth. Sarge was enjoying his day off and stopped by his office at the John Hancock Tower to pick up something. He usually parked in a garage but decided to lock the bike at a rack at 140 Clarendon Street with a cable lock because he knew he wouldn’t be in the office long.

“That was a big mistake,” Sarge said, “When I got back, it was gone.”

Last year, there were 628 reported bike thefts in Boston, according to police data. This number is in line with the number of bike thefts annually in the city, save for 2020, when the number of stolen bikes reached 1,006.

The number of bikes reported stolen totaled 57 this July, 59 in July 2024, and 68 in July 2023.

Bike thefts aren’t just a problem in Boston. Last year, Cambridge reported 500 thefts and Somerville reported 160, according to police data from the two cities.

Most of the Boston bike thefts occurred in Back Bay, downtown Boston, Dorchester, Fenway, Jamaica Plain, and the South End, according to a Globe analysis of Boston Police Department reports from January 2023 to July 2025. According to the department, location data in the reports can sometimes correspond to the police station where the victim reported the theft, even if it occurred in another neighborhood.

A review of the Boston Police Department’s crime incident reports since 2015 revealed which intersections were the biggest targets for bike thieves over the last decade — and the worst places to park your bike. The top spot for bike thefts was an intersection between the Downtown Crossing and Park Street MBTA stations, where 67 bikes were stolen within a 160-foot radius. A collection of intersections in Back Bay, such as one near the Boston Public Library and in Fenway, were also among the top ten spots for theft.

Worth Smith, who runs NEMO, a service similar to AAA for bike repairs, thinks bike theft is underreported.

Before NEMO, Smith worked at the electric scooter company Superpedestrian and was planning to start a business selling bike insurance with a GPS tracker to help people recover their bikes when they were stolen. He conducted 25 interviews with people whose bikes had been stolen and found that most victims felt dejected about being able to recover their bikes.

“A lot of people wouldn’t even report theft to the police because they feel hopeless about it,” Smith said.

Most people also underestimated the risk of theft until it happened to them. Smith said that the people he interviewed also didn’t report theft because they were reluctant to tell people that they had used cheap locks.

“There’s a lot of victim-blaming when it comes to bike theft,” Smith said, “and most people aren’t willing to pay for bike insurance or better locks until their bike gets stolen.”

Sergeant Robert “Bob” Reardon Jr. of the Cambridge Police Department urged people to report their stolen bikes.

“Pictures, serial numbers or anything that can help differentiate your bike from others can help us do our jobs,” Reardon said. “We really want the public to report and help us make a record of these thefts.”

Free, public bike registries such as Bike Index allow bicycle and e-scooter owners to register their vehicle’s serial number along with photos and contact information in case of theft. Before buying a used bike, you can check if it’s been reported stolen by looking up the serial number on Bike Index and other online registries. City-run registries such as Somerville’s WRAP antitheft program are also used by police to more easily identify a bike and return it to its owner.

Sarge, the bike rider whose bike was stolen on Juneteenth, reported the theft to the police that night. He heard from the police a week and a half later. They said they looked at the building’s security footage, but he hasn’t heard anything since.

“Bike theft is kind of low priority for them,” Sarge said.

title: Fear not — Boston’s beaches are safe for swimming
text:
First, don’t be fooled by appearances. Algae, foam, and silt do not necessarily equal bacteria. Sometimes the ocean can be gross to look at but still safe to swim in.

Second, combined sewer overflows are not the primary cause of contamination on most coastal beaches. More often, significant rainfall causes waste from streets, lawns, and pipes to flow into the ocean. Waiting at least 24 hours after a heavy rain lets bacteria break down naturally, and the tides flush out the area.

Let’s keep legislating and funding infrastructure projects to eliminate combined sewer outflows, contaminated stormwater, and runoff. However, leading with fear erodes people’s trust in these reliable urban natural resources.

Massachusetts has the third-safest beaches in the country, and South Boston is proudly home to some of the cleanest urban beaches nationwide — safe to swim in practically every day of the year.

Chris Mancini

Executive director

Save the Harbor/Save the Bay

Boston

Your article about bacterial levels forcing closures at the state’s beaches implies that combined sewer overflows containing sewage and stormwater are causing beaches to close in Boston. But state water quality testing shows that at least in Boston Harbor, that is not the case.

Boston beaches are actually among the cleanest urban beaches in the country. This is thanks in part to the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority having built a massive underground tank in Dorchester that stores stormwater runoff for later treatment at MWRA’s Deer Island plant.

While combined sewage systems still exist in the MWRA system, the fecal bacteria counts downstream of active combined sewage outfalls are actually lower than upstream — and often low enough for safe swimming.

The Wastewater Advisory Committee to the MWRA supports reducing the amount of pollution entering all our water bodies, but the evidence shows that stormwater appears to be the source of most of the problem. Addressing the cleanliness of stormwater, or allowing it to seep into the ground where it falls, would make a greater impact on the number of beach closures.

Kannan Vembu

Chair

Wastewater Advisory Committee to the MWRA

Natick

title: Boston’s ‘For the Culture Week’ to celebrate HBCUs, R group New Edition
text:
The city of Boston is hosting a weeklong celebration of Boston-based R&B group New Edition, and the legacy of Historically Black Colleges and Universities, known as HBCUs.

“The City is proud to celebrate the historic impact of New Edition while bringing the spirit of HBCUs to the region. We look forward to welcoming residents, families and visitors from across the country for a week of celebration, pride, and community,” said Mayor Michelle Wu in a press release.

The multi-day festivities, which the city has dubbed “For the Culture Week,” comes at a time when city councilors are pushing to bring an HBCU Satellite Campus to Boston. A satellite campus is a site associated with a main campus, but is in a different location, while offering a similar curriculum for students. On Tuesday, Councilor Brian Worrell and the City Council Committee on Education will hold a hearing to explore the possibility.

The United States has more than 100 HBCUs, the majority based in the South where Jim Crow laws prohibited Black Americans from attending almost all of the region’s universities. HBCUs were established to provide opportunities for Black Americans, and are credited with expanding the Black middle class.

Boston is home to more than 24 colleges and universities — but that number does not include a single HBCU or an HBCU satellite campus. According to the order for the hearing, sponsors of the measure believe having an HBCU in Boston would “create a magnet for Black students to attend and later settle in the area.”

City councilors cite a need for an HBCU presence, pointing to persistent educational inequalities. Fifty years after Boston was ordered to desegregate its public schools, the legacy of busing leaves the district scarred, as academic outcomes continue to show racial disparities. For example, Black students go to college at a lower rate than their white peers.

“[It] would also send a message that the city, once marred by the busing battles of the 1970s, has moved forward to a new era,” reads the order for the hearing.

As the city considers drawing an HBCU presence, Culture Week will host events celebrating the schools. On Thursday, The Mix, a restaurant in Dorchester, will have a “Hella Black Trivia,” where attendees will be tested on their knowledge of HBCUs. The next day, The Mix will welcome the Harvard Black Graduate Alliance and local professionals for a mixer featuring food, music, games, and networking.

A highlight of Culture Week is the football game between Johnson C. Smith University and Morehouse College — both HBCUs — at Harvard Stadium, set for Saturday at 4 p.m. Tickets are priced at $30 each.

Ahead of the game, Wu, representatives from the two schools, and the City of Boston Marching Band will host a pep rally at City Hall on Friday at 4 p.m. For those who cannot make the game in person, The Mix will put on a game day watch party, followed by an afterparty.

“When the game ends, the real turn-up begins! 🎶💃🏽 Rock with us late into the night,” The Mix wrote on Instagram.

Other events of the week include parties, music performances, and sports games. Sunday’s Boston Red Sox v. Pittsburgh Pirates game, which starts at 1:35 p.m., will recognize HBCU alumni.

In addition to HBCUs, festivities will celebrate the music and arts scene. On Sunday at 5 p.m., Boston will host the 25th Annual Boston Gospel Fest, New England’s largest Gospel music celebration, at Leader Bank Pavilion. John P. Kee, who was inducted into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame in 2005, will be the headliner.

Culture Week will pay tribute to New Edition, which formed in Roxbury in 1978. The city is set to rename Dearborn Street to “New Edition Way,” and throw a community block party at Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club on Saturday. Wu will also declare that day — August 30 — to be “New Edition Day.”

The Grammy-nominated group is known for hits, like “Candy Girl,” “Cool It Now,” and “Mr. Telephone Man” that garnered attention not just in Boston but also across the country. New Edition gained popularity in the 1980s, and topped the Billboard R&B chart throughout that decade.

“Boston is where it all began for us. This honor means the world to me,” said Bobby Brown,a member of New Edition, in a statement.

“From the Roxbury streets to the Harvard Stadium stands, we are showing the world what it looks like when a city comes together for culture and for one another,” City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, who is also pushing for HBCU presence in Boston, said in a statement.

Previous coverage from The Globe was used in this report.

Jessica Ma can be reached at jessica.ma@globe.com.

title: Police seek public’s help in identifying suspects in Dorchester shooting
text:
Police are asking for the public’s help to identify suspects in an Aug. 22 shooting in Dorchester that started as an attempted carjacking.

Police on Monday issued a community alert and released photos of several people on scooters who were allegedly involved in the incident, which happened around 6 p.m. in the area of Old Colony Terrace and Savin Hill Avenue.

There, officers found a male victim lying in the middle of the street next to a pickup truck. He had been shot in the abdomen; his wounds did not appear to be life-threatening, police said.

Police said one suspect was described as wearing a white full-face mask, dark clothing, and white and red footwear. Police said that person’s right forearm and wrist area may be injured.

A second suspect was described as wearing a black full-face mask with a gray hooded top with black lettering across the mid-back, police said.

Police did not provide any details about the other individuals in the photographs.

Anyone with information that could help the investigation is urged to contact detectives at 617-343-4335. Information, photos, or videos can also be provided anonymously through the CrimeStoppers Tip Line webpage or by calling 1-800-494-TIPS or by texting “TIP” to CRIME (27463).

Emily Sweeney can be reached at emily.sweeney@globe.com. Follow her @emilysweeney and on Instagram @emilysweeney22.

title: COVID-era babies enter kindergarten, bringing hope the pandemic learning losses will end with them
text:
At 1, Asa started attending a child care center, and now, at 5, “he’s caught up, if not ahead.” Still, Schneider worries. While Asa learned to socialize with other kids, he still prefers adult company.

“We wonder how much isolation so early in life has impacted his sense of self,” she said.

In coming weeks, Asa and about 60,000 other children born around the 2020 COVID shutdown in Massachusetts are starting kindergarten, marking a shift from those whose childhoods were shaped by lockdowns to those with no memory of them. Across the country, more than 3.6 million children entered the world at the height of the pandemic and are expected to enroll in schools this fall.

Research shows many were developmentally affected by spending their first year in a narrowed social world, and pediatricians and others report seeing higher rates of disorders like ADHD, especially among children kept out of child care longer than Asa.

But children like Asa may signal a long-awaited return to normalcy for public schools after years of trying to help older students recover from pandemic setbacks. Many who were in school when campuses shut down will graduate without ever catching up, and toddlers from that period also started school with delays. But this year’s kindergartners could finally reverse the trend.

Roslindale parents Alissa and Dave Guertin are optimistic about their son Jake, born in February 2020.

“It could have affected him in ways we don’t know, but seemingly, he dodged a lot of the harmful effects of lack of socialization, and had some really nice nesting time with both of his parents,” Dave Guertin said.

Jake was even able to attend child care with few modifications at six months, Alissa Guertin said.

“He was young enough that he didn’t know anything different and he was young enough he didn’t have to wear a mask,” she said.

Jake did get COVID at a young age. Ultimately, though, he has thrived. Like many Massachusetts children, he attended pre-kindergarten last year, and his parents are looking forward to the next step.

That seems to be a typical story, said Lauren Cook, CEO of Ellis Early Learning.

“I wouldn’t say there should be any fear on the part of kindergarten teachers welcoming pandemic babies,” Cook said. “In my experience, pandemic toddlers had it way harder.”

Cook noted that while Massachusetts public schools stayed shut much longer, early child care centers like hers reopened in July 2020, giving many pandemic babies social and academic stimulation. Ellis Early Learning serves both subsidized and full-pay families, she said, and enrollment continued across the board.

“Even though it was a modified group setting, it was a group setting,” she said. Those children “were in some ways better off than those who were isolated at home.”

While many children may have overcome pandemic learning hurdles, research suggests COVID babies from low-income families were harmed developmentally, at least early on.

Larisa Kuehn, a nurse with the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Center, analyzed data on about 50,000 babies in the national Nurse-Family Partnership, which pairs low-income first time mothers with nurses for regular home visits.

She compared babies born after the pandemic began to those born less than a year, one year, or more than two years before the pandemic, using standard developmental and social-emotional assessments, adjusted for demographics and health risks. Babies born during or just before the pandemic were more likely to show social-emotional delays and, by 18 months, more communication problems.

“Kindergarten teachers and kids will need extra support,” Kuehn said. “It would be really important that we give additional funding to education systems to deal with a new generation of kids.”

Greg Campbell, a pediatrician who serves mostly migrant families at a community health center in Springfield, cautioned that some English learners are still showing pandemic effects. Some of his patients, for example, never enrolled in Head Start because of the pandemic.

“When the parents are not native speakers of English . . . you are now entering kindergarten with much less exposure to English,” Campbell said. “That’s the particular challenge that some of the patients I’m seeing now have.”

That was the case for some of his patients last year, and it “showed up as them being inattentive or acting out.” Parents asked for ADHD evaluations, but Campbell discovered the problem was different: their children didn’t understand what was going on in English language classrooms and got bored.

Kindergarten teachers and school administrators need to be prepared for heightened language needs for some groups, Campbell said, or the pandemic will continue to exacerbate gaps between English learners and their peers.

Chloe Campbell, a pediatrician in Salem (no relation to Greg Campbell), said she is seeing elevated rates of mental health issues, particularly ADHD, among her very diverse patient pool.

“The isolation was profound,” she said. “Even when we were easing out of the pandemic, if you were a fearful family . . . those kids might not see other people for years. This is super critical for children that were 12 months, 18 months, 2 years.”

Campbell said kindergarten teachers will have to be patient with children, particularly those who didn’t go to preschool at all.

“If they were never exposed to other children, the kids are going to be a little shell-shocked,” she said. “But kids are resilient. I have to say that.”

Dorchester mother Laura Rosa’s son Josiah certainly has been resilient. He was born premature in November 2019, so his family was already taking health precautions before COVID arrived.

In COVID isolation, Josiah thrived, benefiting from extra time with his two older sisters. He went to Head Start when he was 12 months and loved it. It took some time for him to get used to loud public places, but today, he’s “doing pretty well,” Rosa said.

Like many parents, Rosa feels her older children, her daughters entering grades 9 and 12, were much more negatively affected by the pandemic. Josiah, however, will be thrilled to be back to the classroom, Rosa predicts, playing kitchen with his best friend or learning to read and tie his shoes.

“He won’t say he wants to go to school, but I know he does,” Rosa joked. “Once he’s there, he’s going to have all the stories.”

The Great Divide team explores educational inequality in Boston and statewide. Sign up to receive our newsletter, and send ideas and tips to thegreatdivide@globe.com.

title: ‘Their pain is our pain.’ Louis D. Brown Peace Institute in Boston mourns Minneapolis Catholic school shooting victims.
text:
The Louis D. Brown Peace Institute in Boston issued a statement Wednesday evening saying it was “shattered” by the mass shooting during a Catholic school Mass in Minneapolis that killed two elementary school children.

“Our hearts are shattered by today’s murders in a place of sanctity and sanctuary. Spoken words are inadequate on a day such as this. Rather, we speak through our hearts to the victims, their families who love them, and the community that nurtured them,” the institute said in a statement.

Seventeen people, including 14 children, were injured in the morning shooting at Church of the Annunciation, where students from the parish school were attending Mass to mark the opening of a new school year.

The two children who died were ages 8 and 10 and the 14 students injured ranged in age from 6 to 15, the Associated Press reported.

The Louis D. Brown Peace Institute is named for the 15-year-old killed in the crossfire of a shooting in Dorchester in 1993.

Its mission is to promote non-violence and to provide resources for the survivors of homicide victims.

“We mourn with those who have suffered such unimaginable loss from this act. Their pain is our pain, their tears are our tears, and we pray devoutly that someday healing may come,” the institute said.

Camille Bugayong can be reached at camille.bugayong@globe.com.

title: Nine ways to celebrate Labor Day weekend, including fireworks over the harbor tonight
text:
From fireworks to parades, a wicked witch to medieval kings and queens, it’s time to jam all the fantastical summer vibes into one last epic weekend. Let’s do this.

FIREWORKS

Here’s your chance to send off summer with a bang. Boston Harbor Now and Meet Boston fire off their 13th Annual “Illuminate the Harbor Fireworks Celebration” Aug. 28 at 8:30 p.m. According to their Instagram, live music kicks off the night at 7 at Piers Park in East Boston and Christopher Columbus Park in the North End. Public viewing along the Boston Harborwalk in East Boston, Charlestown, North End, and Seaport. Free. bostonharbornow.org/fireworks

CAMPFIRE SONGS

Say you saw ’em when.

Once upon a time, Josh Ritter, Lori McKenna and Mary Gauthier were new kids on the block shooting their shot at Passim’s Campfire Fest. Now in its 27th year, Passim’s semi-annual Campfire Fest brings some 60 up-and-comers from around New England for four days of peace, love, and nonstop music Aug. 29-Sept. 1.

Passim managing director Matt Smith told me previously he came up with the idea on Labor Day Weekend 1998 “as a way to experiment with new artists.” Named after the idea of folks “sitting around a campfire … something informal and inclusive,” the fest remains a chance to hear a full slate of new artists in one extended weekend.

Students free, $15 day pass, $30 weekend. Performances begin 6 p.m Aug. 29. Lineup and details passim.org. 47 Palmer St., Cambridge.

A WICKED GOOD TIME

You might’ve passed Gregory Maguire on the street and not recognized him. He has described himself as “just a Boston schlub.” But I’m going to guess you do know the Tufts and Simmons alum’s 1995 novel “Wicked.” Apparently it turned into a Broadway play and then a movie or something?

Catch “Wicked” — that wicked popular movie with a wicked Massachusetts connection — when it screens for free at the Frog Pond Aug. 29 as part of the city’s Park’s Movie Nights. Come dressed “in your most wicked attire or as your favorite character” for a costume contest, trivia, “surprise guest appearances” and more, according to billing. Pre-show party at 6 p.m., movie at dusk. Free popcorn while supplies last. 38 Beacon St. boston.gov

MARCH INTO SEPTEMBER

Marlborough marches into fall with a Labor Day festival and parade. Soak up the last of the summer vibes at its fest on Main Street Aug. 31 from noon to 5 p.m. Expect food trucks, live music, local vendors, kids activities, bounce-house, and more, according to its website.

Then march into September at its Labor Day parade, stepping off at noon Sept. 1 from the intersection of Pleasant and Lincoln streets, and concluding at the American Legion. Expect “bands, floats, performers, community groups, and surprises,” according to the event’s Facebook page. marlboroughlaborday.org

FREE HARBOR CONCERT AND ART

Kick off the long weekend early by basking in free art and music by the sea. The Institute of Contemporary Art offers free museum admission Aug. 28 for entry between 5 and 8:40 p.m. Advance tickets are recommended and will be available online that day starting at 10 a.m. It’s the last call to visit “Chiharu Shiota: Home Less Home,” partially inspired by stories of the immigrant experience that Shiota crowdsourced locally, at the ICA’s Watershed, closing Sept. 1. Meanwhile, catch a free outdoor concert from 6 to 8:30 p.m. with “Harborwalk Sounds” featuring music from Berklee students. This week: pop singer-songwriter Ness DeJean.

Then on Aug. 29, bring your crew and get down with the free Vinyl Night from 5 to 9 p.m. Expect “highly curated, vinyl-only DJ sets,” according to billing. 25 Harbor Shore Drive, Boston. icaboston.org

LAST BITES

Burgers: The Official Meal of Summer. Don’t let the season end without one last juicy bite. For its annual Best of the Best awards, The Globe Magazine rounded up the area’s seven best burgers. Must-stops include:

Bred, where, critics note, “the stars of the show … are not the buns (though they are excellent) but the thick, juicy, smoked patties in the middle … Consider the Maui, topped with pineapple, a fat slice of ham, fried onions, spicy pepper jack, plantains, and barbecue sauce.” #SummerInOneBite. 2255 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester. bredgourmet.com

At Little Donkey in Cambridge, the patties are “burger brilliance. Griddled dry-aged beef … American cheese, buffalo pickles, and fried jalapeno chips, served on a potato roll slathered with onion-y mayo … high-low restaurant cooking at its best.” 505 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. littledonkeycambridge.com

Best veggie burger goes to … Veggie Galaxy, where the Galaxy Smashburger, “is a standout: hearty and delicious, served on plush, slightly sweet buns slathered with a vegan mayo sauce.” 450 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. veggiegalaxy.com

LAST LICKS

Ice Cream: The Official Dessert or Anytime Meal of Summer. Globe Magazine rounded up the area’s top 11 in their “Best of the Best” series. Picks include:

Toscanini’s, where the colorful ice creams look like an artist’s paint palette, and are tasty on your palate. Perhaps a scoop of B3 (brown butter, brown sugar, and brownies), goat cheese brownie, guava, mango sticky rice, or mocha rose water. Flavors change often, and vary at locations, so check its website. 899 Main St. and 159 First St., Cambridge. tosci.com

At Honeycomb Creamery, “owners strive to source every possible ingredient … from local farms, and you can taste it in exceptional, ripe flavors,” Globe critics noted. Perhaps a cone of black sesame and raspberry, peanut butter fudge crunch, sweet corn and blackberry jam, or vegan watermelon hibiscus chamoy. Again, small-batch flavors rotate frequently. Check its site if you’re craving something specific. 1702 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. honeycombcreamery.com

New City Microcreamery also offers creative flavors (and cones). Think Cake Batter, Baklava (honey and cinnamon ice cream with swirls of walnut filling and gooey filo dough pieces); Dubai Chocolate (spiced caramel ice cream with chunks of chocolate pistachio candy bar, candied pistachios, and chocolate swirl). The spot is “a surprisingly great choice for vegans … The sprinkles are vegan, too.” Perhaps a scoop of “Vegan Mounds” (its dairy-free take on a Mounds bar) or a vegan peanut butter Oreo. Ditto on the flavor warning. 403 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. 28 Main St., Hudson. 534 Boston Post Road, Sudbury. newcitymicrocreamery.com

SWAN SONG

You’ve eyed tourists on ‘em all summer while secretly wanting to hop on yourself. Now’s your last chance. Swan Boats: they’re for locals, too. Last day of the season is Sept. 1. 4 Charles St., Boston. swanboats.com

TIME OF RENAISSANCE

’Tis renaissance season, m’lords and m’ladies! Embrace thy medieval vibes and the change of season at that annual New England autumn staple, King Richard’s Faire. The largest Renaissance festival in New England opens for its 44th season Aug. 30 at its new location, “the historic Edaville property, just down the road in Carver,” per a fest announcement.

Don thy costume, munch on turkey legs, watch knights joust and party like it’s 1399. Carver residents: you get in free on opening day with ID, according to his majesty’s Facebook page. Open weekends through Oct. 19, including on Labor Day proper. 5 Carver St. kingrichardsfaire.net
