title: ‘It’s where our heart is.’ New Edition to be honored in Roxbury.
text:
Bell and the five other members of New Edition, which formed in 1978 in Roxbury, will be honored with a street renaming ceremony and block party on Saturday, which Mayor Michelle Wu will also declare “New Edition Day” in Boston.

The event is part of “For the Culture Week,” which also celebrates Historically Black Colleges and Universities, or HBCUs. The multiday festivities come at a time when city councilors are exploring bringing an HBCU to Boston via a satellite campus.

Boston is home to more than 24 colleges and universities — but that number does not include a single HBCU or an HBCU satellite campus. As the city considers drawing an HBCU presence, For the Culture Week will host events celebrating the schools.

On Thursday, The Mix, a restaurant in Dorchester, will have a “Hella Black Trivia,” where attendees will be tested on their knowledge of HBCU culture and traditions. The next day, The Mix will welcome the Harvard Black Graduate Alliance and local professionals for a mixer featuring food, music, games, and networking.

For New Edition Day on Saturday, the city is set to rename Dearborn Street to “New Edition Way” at 10 a.m. A community block party will kick off an hour later at Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club, which used to be the Orchard Park Community Center, where the band members first met each other. As residents of the Orchard Gardens Housing Project, the six boys, Ronnie DeVoe, Bobby Brown, Ricky Bell, Michael Bivins, Ralph Tresvant, and Johnny Gill, used to gather and play basketball and music, leading to them forming the group.

“It’s the place that New Edition really met each other on the basketball courts, on opposing teams,” said DeVoe. “And for the Boys & Girls Club to be able to come in there and establish some type of partnership with the community. It’s just a full circle situation.”

The event was originally scheduled for September 2024, but was postponed because of scheduling conflicts, according to Dion Irish, Wu’s chief of operations, who helped plan the event.

The block party will include a backpack giveaway for back to school, free food, and activities for the community.

Additionally, a mural honoring the group will be announced by Wu at the block party. The mural was originally scheduled to be painted on the Boys & Girls Club last year, but will now be painted on the Strand Theatre because of its significance to the group.

”That’s actually where the talent shows were held back in those days, where [New Edition] actually ... became first runner-up and led to them getting a recording contract,” Irish said.

While the group has found success outside of the confines of their hometown, they are still dedicated to giving back to the city that raised them and allowed them to grow, the band members said.

Additionally, New Edition, along with the New Commonwealth Fund, an organization that works to address systemic racism through community investment and development, will be making a $25,000 donation to Orchard Gardens Resident Association to benefit youth and senior programs.

“It’s intentional what we’re looking to do,” said DeVoe. “To a certain extent, the world is our home because we’re entertainers, but the foundation was made in Boston, and we want to make sure that we’re pouring back into our city in a number of different ways.”

The event itself will not only showcase the success of New Edition, but also the potential that everyone in Boston has to do something great.

“One of the things we’re hoping to come out of this is just to make sure that the members of the community, the kids in Boston, realize the potential that they have,” Irish said. “So it’s just making it full circle to show the talent and capability of youths in the city of Boston.”

Along with New Edition Day, another highlight of For the Culture Week is the football game between Johnson C. Smith University, located in Charlotte, N.C., and Morehouse College, located in Atlanta — both HBCUs — at Harvard Stadium, set for 4 p.m. Saturday. Tickets are priced at $30 each.

Ahead of the game, Wu and representatives from the two schools will host a pep rally at City Hall at 4 p.m. Friday. For those who cannot make the game in person, The Mix will also put on a game-day watch party, followed by an afterparty.

Other events of the week include parties, music performances, and sports games. Sunday’s Boston Red Sox v. Pittsburgh Pirates game, which starts at 1:35 p.m., will recognize HBCU alumni.

In addition to HBCUs, festivities will celebrate the music and arts scene. On Sunday at 5 p.m., Boston will host the 25th Annual Boston Gospel Fest, New England’s largest Gospel music celebration, at Leader Bank Pavilion. John P. Kee, who was inducted into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame in 2005, will be the headliner.

For the group members, the street renaming and the block party are not only an honor as a group, but also as community members. When they first started rehearsing in basements and recording albums, they never expected to have a physical dedication to them on the streets they called home.

“It’s like when we first started, that was probably one of the furthest things from our minds or in our plans to one day have a street named after New Edition. But to leave a mark in history as a part of your legacy, something that your children’s children and years beyond us and our families can continue to see. [We are] beyond excited,” Bell said.

Now they have the opportunity to return to their hometown and give back to their neighborhood, in partnership with the city, to donate money and resources for the youth and elderly, is an honor for the group.

“It’s just the stuff that dreams are made of,” DeVoe said.

title: Independent probe of Transdev says BPS bus contractor failed to track safety, accident, driver records
text:
The findings of the investigation also come just a week before more than 20,000 Boston students will be transported on BPS buses for the first day of school.

Wu and Skipper, during a press conference Thursday in Roxbury, said the city and BPS will adopt all of the report’s recommendations, and will implement them as soon as possible.

“The City of Boston will do everything in our power to make sure that every child is safe in our city, and that every Boston family is confident that their children will be safe at school, and on the way to and from school,” Wu said. “We will do everything we can to make sure this never happens again.”

Lauren Skiver, Transdev’s chief operating officer, told city councilors during a City Council hearing Thursday that the company is steadfast in ensuring safety on school buses.

“I feel confident that an accident won’t happen again like this, and I feel that the commitment of the entire Transdev team . . . are in place and will remain in place,” Skiver said.

Former federal prosecutor Natashia Tidwell, who conducted the probe, also faulted both Transdev and BPS administrators for not implementing “any meaningful and sustained” auditing and oversight measures.

That’s despite warnings about Transdev’s poor data collection practices that were identified by the state’s education agency in 2019, an internal 2020 safety audit, and a 2023 report by the state inspector general’s office, Tidwell said in her report.

Tidwell recommended numerous changes to improve Transdev’s school bus services in Boston, including having Transdev streamline drivers’ records; expand training for drivers; and use training and accident data to measure progress toward safety goals. BPS also should increase the cadence of performance audits and unannounced on-site checks at the district’s bus yards, and add more staff to oversee Transdev, according to the report.

But even if all the measures were to be put in place, Tidwell warned, they would not prevent another fatal crash.

“The improvement opportunities identified in this report do not explain why tragic events like the April 28 incident happen,” Tidwell said in her report. “Sadly, the related recommendations, even if wholly adopted and perfectly implemented, cannot prevent recurrence.”

In a statement, Transdev said it was committed “to continue making safety our top priority” as it transports students in Boston every day.

Anger over the safety and oversight failures was on display during the City Council hearing later in the day, when several councilors expressed outright distrust of Transdev, and a few asked what it would take to cancel the company’s contract.

“We have to learn from this, and honestly find a different way to transport our kids around,” Councilor Benjamin Weber told Transdev officials during the session. “I don’t really have a lot of trust in Transdev at this point.”

Emmanuel Marcellus, president of the Boston School Bus Drivers union, United Steelworkers-Local 8751, declined comment Thursday. He said he needed to read the full report.

Matthew Fogelman, an attorney representing the Joseph family, said they appreciated the report and the work that went into it.

“Some very troubling deficiencies were identified,” Fogelman said. “We hope that changes can be implemented to prevent any future tragedies.”

According to Tidwell’s report, a 2020 internal safety audit BPS requested of Transdev’s operations put both the district and the contractor on notice that Transdev struggled to maintain “up to date” driver qualification files; store driver training files in a readily accessible manner; ensure accurate, complete, and timely reporting of accidents; and consistently staff key safety positions, according to Tidwell’s report.

BPS officials, who held monthly meetings with Transdev regarding school busing issues, did not regularly inspect records of accident reports involving BPS school buses or bus driver training files until after the deadly Hyde Park crash, according to the report.

“Transdev has not conducted, and BPS has not commissioned a similarly comprehensive review since [2020],” Tidwell said. “Nevertheless, the Investigators found that many of the issues identified in the 2020 Audit continue to exist today, as evidenced by Transdev’s deficient record keeping systems and inability to show a measurable impact of its training and coaching on safety outcomes.”

BPS, in the current contract, changed its approach to overseeing Transdev from a “trust but verify” method to one that focused “‘more on outputs than inputs,’ with increased reliance on Transdev’s industry experience,” the report said.

“While the investigators are not advocating for a return to what some might have viewed as micromanagement of Transdev’s operations, the investigation revealed BPS has not fully leveraged its contractual right to audit and inspect Transdev’s operations and related data,” the report said.

Skipper said administrators are “committed to learn from the report and decisively implement the recommendations so that we ensure our transportation is as safe as possible while we await the district attorney’s investigation conclusions from the April 28 incident,” said Skipper on Thursday.

A Globe review in May found at least 15 personal injury claims against Transdev, and its drivers, since it began operating BPS school buses in 2013. Since that review, the family of Lens Joseph in July sued Transdev and the bus driver, Jean Charles, for negligence after the Hyde Park kindergartner was struck and killed near his home by a BPS bus driver in April.

And in June, the family of an 8-year-old boy sued Transdev for injuries caused when another BPS bus driver lost control of his vehicle and struck the boy outside a school in Jamaica Plain in December.

Wu on Thursday said the investigation into the crash by the Suffolk district attorney’s office and Boston police remains ongoing. However, Wu said the driver, identified by city and school officials as Jean Charles, should not have been operating a bus.

Charles has not been charged in connection with the crash. He was an employee of Transdev. He resigned from the company in mid-May, shortly before a scheduled termination hearing, city and school district leaders have said.

During Thursday’s City Council hearing, BPS and Transdev officials said they are taking additional steps to shore up safety and oversight of bus drivers in wake of the April crash. The session was attended by Lens’s father, Esaie Joseph, as well as Lens’s cousin.

The sides have daily meetings to review performance data, including accidents; training has been stepped up; and drivers must provide physical copies of credentials before they can operate a bus this year. BPS will also receive an updated roster of all drivers and their credentials, school and company officials told councilors.

“There have been two very significant failures; we own that we will continue to own that,” said Daniel Rosengard, the head of BPS’s transportation department, referring to the crashes in December and April. “And we’re going to continue doing everything we can to ensure every student’s safety.”

City Councilor Erin Murphy, a former school teacher, said the city is ultimately accountable for failures of its school bus system.

“We contract out the bus drivers to Transdev, it in no way means we aren’t responsible. We are always responsible,” Murphy said.

title: Frazzled already? Escape back-to-school stress at these 9 restaurants
text:
Hi, friends. Have your kids gone back to school yet? Mine don’t start until next week, so we’ve escaped to the beach for a last gasp of summer, even though I’m spending a lot of time ordering school supplies and trying to help my newly minted 9th-grader switch electives.

Your calendar probably looks like a Tetris game right now. I just imported my younger one’s third-grade soccer schedule, and I’m already frightened. One thing keeping me quasi-calm: building in some time to go out with my husband, even if it won’t happen until late October or so.

In my other life, I’m a food reporter, and I wanted to suggest some new spots I’m incredibly excited about. I hope you can carve out a date night (or a friend night, or a solo night) for yourself amid the madness, too.

But first, an important note from my colleagues: Sign up for the Globe’s K-12 education newsletter, The Great Divide, a digest that examines the public education system in Massachusetts and beyond. It’s an important read, now more than ever, and you’ll get it weekly. It’s free.

Get Starting Point

A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday.

Enter Email

And now, here are my recommendations. Deep breaths!

Bernadette

A friend celebrated her birthday at this French-inflected Salem spot last weekend. The verdict: “run; don’t walk.” Aaron and Shanna Chambers also run Settler nearby; Aaron, who’s British, previously worked with star chef Daniel Boulud in New York City, for Tony Maws at Craigie on Main in Cambridge, and at Le Manoir aux Quat’Saisons, a two-star Michelin destination in England. Get the heirloom tomato salad (while you can), steak tartare, and fruits de mer with lemon saffron spaghetti. They take reservations if you can plan ahead, or pop in for a perch at the 12-seat bar, which serves their full dinner menu. It’s just a lovely refuge amid the traditional Salem fall frenzy. 65 Washington St., Salem, www.bernadettesalem.com

Bubble Bath Back Bay

Picture it: Somehow your friends’ calendars all align, and you can slip away to the Back Bay for drinks. This is the place to do it: Tiffani Faison’s sleek cocktail bar high atop the citizenM hotel serves over-the-top mixed drinks, champagne, and fancy party food that you didn’t have to make yourself: miniature lobster sandwiches, steak tartare, smoked salmon. The vibe: festive, escapist, no 7 a.m. carpool wakeup. 408 Newbury St., Boston, www.bubblebathboston.com

Capri

A dreamy fireplaced patio, a prime South End address, and a comforting Italian menu: Bolognese, cioppino, garlic bread. This is the newest spot from the team behind the stylish, satisfying Prima in Charlestown, and here, there’s an added perk for those of us driving into the city from the ‘burbs: free parking in the lot next door. 500 Harrison Ave., Boston, www.capriboston.com

Darling

If you’re feeling adventurous, head to this new dim sum and drinks lair in Central Square, with small plates from Mark O’Leary (JM Curley, O Ya, Shojo) and cocktails from Brian Callahan (Coquette, Tiger Mama). Libations are grouped by sensation — fresh and cooling; gentle and vibrant — while the menu is thrillingly unpredictable, ranging from the retro (shrimp toast) to the unusual (a filet o’ fish-inspired bao with tartar sauce). It’s a worthy update for the beloved former Mary Chung space and very babysitter-worthy. 464 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, www.darlingcambridge.com

Eva’s Little Kitchen

A shoutout to this lovable new West Concord café with a Bedford sibling, run by mom-of-three Eva Badra. It’s perfect for a workday pick-me-up when you really deserve a treat: sweet and savory danish; focaccia pizza; and a range of Middle Eastern specialties like homemade falafel and a signature labneh box, with za’atar flatbread, mint, veggies, and jammy eggs. 110 Commonwealth Ave., Concord, www.evaslittlekitchen.com

Lou’s

An old-fashioned supper club in Harvard Square, with music, live entertainment, and excellent food courtesy of Jason Bond, who ran Cambridge date-night spot Bondir for years. The menu blends familiarity with friskiness: steak frites and roast chicken, but also seldom-seen grilled tilefish and gnocchi with walnut pesto. 13 Brattle St., Cambridge, www.wearelous.com

Nine Winters Bakery

Sometimes, you just need to treat yourself, and this Bow Market spinoff in West Cambridge is a cozy, succulent place to do so, with Korean-influenced sweets and savories: gochujang brownies, peanut butter chili crisp, and Gochujang Bolognese washed down with milk punch or chai. Exhale (for a minute). 292 Concord Ave., Cambridge, www.ninewinters.com

Nine

At long last, a special occasion replacement for No. 9 Park, featuring a gin bar and caviar service, with cuisine from former No. 9 chef Andrew Simonich. It’s a definite splurge: Save the $180 chef’s tasting menu for when you have something to celebrate (last daycare payment; finally paring down to one sport instead of three). 9 Park St. Place, Boston, www.ninerg.com

The Nightly

The talented Jeff Fournier (51 Lincoln, New Hampshire’s Thompson House Eatery) returns to town at this test kitchen above The Daily Market in Dorchester. Stop in for a full dinner menu — no reservations — Thursday through Sunday. It’s the ideal impromptu stop for better-than-bar-food delights: French onion dip and homemade potato chips, citrus yuzu chicken wings, cheese and charcuterie, and Aperol spritzes. 110 Savin Hill Ave., Boston, www.thenightlyboston.com

Kara Baskin can be reached at kara.baskin@globe.com. Follow her @kcbaskin.

title: The Celtics sale has closed. Now for the big question: Where to build a new arena?
text:
Sure, a new arena would be a hefty investment, likely $1 billion or more. But it might be worth it, especially if Boston gets an WNBA team that could fill a decent block of nights alongside the Celtics.

Currently, the Celtics share TD Garden with the Bruins, and rent from Garden owner Delaware North. That’s been the model since the 1970s, when Delaware North bought the old Garden and built a new one in 1995.

But these days, sports facility experts, say team owners often like to build their own arena and then develop the real estate around it. Think restaurants, hotels, offices, and apartments. It’s about making money beyond game nights and TV rights, and it’s what Delaware North has already done with its Hub on Causeway project that opened alongside the Garden in 2019.

“This is another stream of revenue for them to realize instead of letting other real estate investors and developers have success off the back of these venues,” said David Demarest, who runs the national sports and entertainment practice for real estate advisory firm JLL, which counts several pro sports teams, including the Red Sox, among its clients. (Red Sox principal owner John Henry also owns The Boston Globe.)

So after paying an eye-popping $6.1 billion for the Celtics, the Chisholm ownership group has to be exploring ways to maximize a return on their investment. They’re also likely looking around the NBA at arenas that are, frankly, newer and shinier than the Garden, which turns 30 in September.

“The time when something like a Boston Garden, you played in a facility like that until it was about to fall down, those years are over,” Demarest said. “The life cycles of these venues have become shorter and shorter.”

There’s also something to be said for playing in a place designed for basketball.

The experience is more intense and intimate, said Bill Hanway, executive vice president and global sports leader at design and engineering firm AECOM, compared with a hockey arena designed around a sheet of ice that’s three times the size of a basketball court. And that’s increasingly important as teams have to convince fans to leave the comfort of their homes and big-screen TVs.

“Major sports teams, stadiums, and arenas are trying to create something that is unique and special, and draws people to come and be there in person,“ said Hanway, whose firm has designed or built over 20 NBA arenas, including renovating TD Garden. ”Celtics fans are already very, very committed and loud, but if you think about taking that type of fan commitment and putting it into a space that is even tighter with the fans directly on top, that can be an incredible change."

So how much land would a new arena need? Eight acres just for the arena but more like 20 to 30 acres if a team wants to build retail development around it, Hanway said. Ideally, it’s in or near the urban core of the region. In this city, transit access is a must.

Of course, TD Garden checks all these boxes, and has been a good home for the Celtics for a long time. The team’s lease expires in 2036, and you can bet Delaware North — and the influential Jacobs family behind it —will do all it can to keep the team there.

One thing’s for sure, it can take years to plan any major development around here. So it’s not too soon to start thinking about where a new arena might go and if it makes financial sense.

“2026 seems the right timing to get a better understanding,” said Rob Hale, CEO of Quincy-based Granite Telecommunications and a minority owner who sits on the managing board of the Celtics.

Real estate brokers and developers have already started to make their own short list of sites. So here they are, in no particular order:

The Kraft family already wants to build a soccer stadium on a slice of waterfront land near Encore Boston Harbor casino across the Mystic from Charlestown. As Everett Mayor Carlo DeMaria will remind you, there’s plenty of room for another sports venue next door, with close to 100 acres of former industrial land that’s waiting to be cleaned up and redeveloped.

One downside: Weak public transit. DeMaria says he has been pushing for better rail connections, but it’s not happening fast enough. There have been plans for creating a commuter rail stop by Encore, extending the Silver Line, and creating a pedestrian bridge to connect Everett to Somerville’s Assembly Orange Line station. But for thousands of fans coming on winter weeknights, Everett might feel like a bridge too far.

A decade ago, when Boston was making its bid to host the 2024 Summer Olympics, this industrial patch south of downtown gained fame as a potential site for a stadium to host opening and closing ceremonies and other major events. Olympic supporters touted the 24-acre parcel off I-93 as an area that could be redeveloped after the Games into a new neighborhood of Boston.

But the Olympics never came, and the MBTA needed a rail yard close to South Station, and that’s what became of Widett Circle. But build a deck — similar to New York City’s Hudson Yards over Long Island Railroad train yards — and you might be able to have it all: a sports arena, a new Red Line stop along nearby Dorchester Ave., and a whole new neighborhood. And it turns out the new Celtics ownership group includes someone who knows a lot about complex construction projects: Bruce Beal Jr., the president of Related Companies, which developed Hudson Yards.

This long-dreamed-of project can still feel like a blank canvas, but the straightening of the I-90 Allston interchange is expected to unlock dozens of acres around a new train-and-bus hub known as West Station. The megaproject, dubbed Allston’s Big Dig for its transformative nature, has the potential to create a whole new neighborhood between Harvard and Boston University. And maybe that neighborhood could include a basketball arena.

Perhaps the most desirable site, but one fraught with political peril, is a 31-acre parcel in South Boston along Fort Point Channel that has long served as Gillette’s “World Shaving Headquarters.” It’s right by the Financial District, near I-93, and close to the Red Line’s Broadway station. And just think of the views of downtown on TV broadcasts.

But Procter & Gamble, which owns Gillette, is already getting lots of input from the neighborhood as it launches community discussions about the redevelopment. And South Boston has chased off other stadium ideas before, from the Patriots going into what’s now the Seaport to a soccer stadium on Columbia Point. A basketball arena in Fort Point could prove a battle royale.

Speaking of Columbia Point, what about Dorchester Bay City?

Construction has yet to begin on the massive city-approved project which would put office, housing, retail, and research and development on a 36-acre site that encompasses the old Bayside Expo Center. It sits just off the Southeast Expressway, walkable to both the Red Line and commuter rail at JFK/UMass station. Could the mini-city include a Celtics arena?

As long as the broader project can still honor community commitments like affordable housing, co-developer Dick Galvin said he’d be “open to a conversation with anyone.”

And then there’s Suffolk Downs.

Plans have been carefully crafted for the 161-acre former horsetrack that straddles Revere and East Boston to become 10,000 units of housing. But high interest rates and high cost of materials have slowed construction, while a glut of office and lab space has stalled other parts of the project. The site, being developed by Tom O’Brien’s HYM Investment Group, is big enough that it could fairly easily include a sports arena and related uses, which could help jumpstart other development there.

But it’s on the far northern edge of Boston, and transportation is tough. Yes, the site has two Blue Line stops, but highway access is difficult and Route 1A would need an overhaul.

The Celtics spent the offseason being taken over by new owners andshaking up their roster. Will a change of venue be next?

Shirley Leung is a Business columnist and host of the Globe Opinion podcast “Say More with Shirley Leung.” Find the podcast on Apple, Spotify, and globe.com/saymore. Follow her on Threads @shirley02186

title: Boston officials balk at Trump National Guard talk
text:
“It creates the possibility of bad situations” in which some local kid, perhaps, loses their head and tries to fight back, she said. “Then all bets are off.”

A survey on Saturday of city politicians in deep-blue Boston hardly reveals a surprise: They broadly oppose Trump’s idea to send National Guard troops into Boston in an effort, according to the Republican president, to help fight crime. It’s one of the few topics that unify Boston’s progressive mayor, her challenger, the even-more-progressive wing of the Boston City Council that needles her from the left, and some of the council’s relatively more conservative members.

For example, Councilor Ed Flynn, a centrist critic of Wu who represents South Boston and Chinatown, said in a statement that he has great respect for the Guard and appreciation for the role they played in mobilizing resources quickly and efficiently during the pandemic, but “it is not necessary to activate the National Guard for law enforcement support in Boston.”

Trump continues to float the prospect of using the Guard, which is typically called up by state governors to help in the cases of national disasters or specific unrest, to augment local, state, and federal law enforcement in multiple cities Trump has deemed to be suffering from severe street violence. He took control of the police force in Washington and sent the Guard into Los Angeles, and threatened to do the same in other cities, such as Chicago and Boston.

Supporters have cheered this hard-line stance and unusual use of the Guard, saying it’s necessary after years of what Trump characterizes as soft-on-crime policies in Democrat-led big cities that, in some cases, are objectively struggling with violent crime.

“Boston has more than its fair share of crime, and President Trump’s offer to provide National Guard assistance should serve as a wake-up call to Governor Healey and Mayor Wu: If they don’t protect our residents, the president may step in for them,” Amy Carnevale, the chair of the Massachusetts Republican Party, said Saturday.

But critics say this is a page out of a classic authoritarian playbook, and is merely meant to use a show of force to punish and intimidate those who don’t support the president.

“Trump is fighting to make himself and his friends richer and more powerful at the expense of the rest of us,” said Sharon Durkan, a progressive councilor who represents the Back Bay and Beacon Hill. “He has ballooned the debt, handed tax cuts to billionaires, gutted health care, and now he’s using the National Guard to stoke fear and destabilize our democracy.”

Boston officials argue that this city is “the safest major city in America,” as Mayor Michelle Wu repeatedly contends; in reality, that’s a difficult claim to parse, but there’s no doubt that it does have generally low and declining crime rates.

Wu and other Democrats in Massachusetts have repeatedly drawn the ire of the Trump administration. She has been called down to D.C. to testify about Boston’s policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, and the administration has targeted the Boston area with multiple major immigration-enforcement efforts in the past few months. Trump is eyeing another concerted effort here, Politico reported last week, based on administration sources.

“Unlike the Trump administration, Boston follows the law — city, state and federal. We are the safest major city in the country because all of our community members know that they are part of how we keep the entire community safe," Wu said in a statement. “Boston will never back down from being a beacon of freedom and a home for everyone. Stop attacking cities to hide your administration’s failures.”

Other city councilors said similarly. Councilor Brian Worrell, whose district includes Mattapan and parts of Dorchester, said such a move would only “further fear and division in our communities.” And Councilor Enrique Pepén of Hyde Park called it “nothing more than a political ploy by the Trump administration.”

Joshua Kraft, who’s running against Wu in this year’s election, also rejected Trump’s ideas about using the Guard. He’s criticized Wu for her approach to crime, but said Boston can handle whatever public-safety issues it has by itself.

“Bringing the National Guard into American cities has nothing to do with public safety and is all about Donald Trump exerting power on cities that stand behind their immigrant communities,” Kraft said in a statement.

On Saturday, several people going about their business in Boston said they were worried.

Mary Walsh, 64, was walking down a residential block in Allston to help her daughter move into a new home. She called it a “shame” that Trump is in office — and added, “We have to deal with it.”

“He’s so into theatrics that I really try not to give anything he says much attention,” she said. “Personally, I just roll my eyes, and I’m like, ‘Here we go again.’”

title: Double Up Food Bucks savings program expands to Roxbury market
text:
Her dollars may stretch further thanks to the Boston Double Up Food Bucks program, which provides a discount on fruits and vegetables to low-income residents at some grocery stores.

Chance, a Roxbury native who now lives in Dorchester, celebrated the expansion of the Double Up Food Bucks program last month to Nubian Markets, a locally owned grocery store in Roxbury that celebrates the African diaspora.

With the addition of Nubian Markets, Boston now has six “Double Up” locations, with other stores located in Dorchester and East Boston.

Introduced in 2018, the Double Up program is funded by the city and the USDA Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program, according to Mayor Michelle Wu’s office.

Each day, people who use SNAP benefits can get up to $20 in discounts at participating stores to purchase fresh fruits and vegetables. Customers can get double the amount of produce for half the cost, but cannot exceed the daily $20 discount limit.

Wu, who attended the program’s expansion at Nubian Market, said the goal is to provide access to fresh food at an affordable price for Boston families.

“[We can] now add to the list of local grocery stores where residents can use these Double Up Food Bucks and get more value,” Wu said in an interview. “This is making sure everybody has the full range of options available, no matter your income level [or] where you live in the city.”

The Double Up program does not require any additional sign-ups; users simply pay with their EBT card and let the cashier know they would like to receive the Double Up discount.

Chance, along with her friend Gwendolyn Mitchell, shared their frustrations with food costs in Boston.

“The prices have gotten out of control,” Mitchell said. “But you do the best you can with what you have, you have to just calculate.”

A recent Globe report comparing the cost of breakfast staples at five different grocery stores showed that ten items cost between $38 and $50.

In Mitchell’s experience, three bags of groceries at a chain store can cost her up to $200, which isn’t enough for her large household in Roxbury.

Mitchell has a habit of letting extended family and friends stay with her. She said it’s in her nature to “take everyone in.” But her budget for groceries has to remain in the $100 range.

“What I could get before for $150 is now $300, it’s insane,” Mitchell said. “It’s not an option at all.”

Boston has 143,000 residents receiving SNAP benefits, and since the program’s founding, $850,000 in discounts have been applied through the Double Up program, according to Emily Sinsky, Double Up Food Bucks program manager.

Since 2021, the program has been funded by a federal grant of $500,000 from the US Department of Agriculture through the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program, as well as a $500,000 match from the city.

Wu noted that the program benefits local retailers, making it so residents can shop at neighborhood stores with more flexibility.

“Our communities are beautiful and diverse and reflect so many cultures, and it’s in stores like this where the owners are from and are connected to the community ... there’s the ability to provide a specific kind of product or to connect with a cultural need,” Wu said.

Yusuf Yassin, co-owner of Nubian Markets, sees many of the same Roxbury residents come through the door every day.

The produce and food, which aims to “give a platform to the amazing foods and flavors of the African diaspora,” serves as a community staple for its cultural offerings.

“It’s spaces like this where people are seen in the fullness of who they are and have every resource to be able to take care of their families,” Wu said.

Now, residents can make a one-stop shop for cultural groceries and fresh produce.

“With food costs going up, every little bit helps. People come here and shop a small amount, but with the program, they would definitely be motivated to grab more items, and particularly fresh produce,” Yassin said.

Levi Caldwell, who is from the Caribbean but now lives in Roxbury, said that he comes to Nubian Markets because they sell a particular type of fish he ate growing up.

Now, he can shop at Nubian Markets for produce too, rather than going to chain grocery stores.

“This is amazing, I’ll definitely be back for more,” Caldwell said.

Emmanuel Moore, from Dorchester, is diabetic and said he has trouble staying healthy on a budget of $50 a week for groceries.

Moore prioritizes eating food that is good for him, but some weeks, it isn’t feasible.

He’s only been to Nubian Markets a few times, but with the program, he plans on making it his new favorite store.

“I think this is great to have a market like this that is so easy and convenient for people like us [EBT users],” Moore said.

title: Saving lives, one swim lesson at a time
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

At the Thomas M. Menino YMCA in Hyde Park last Thursday, 10 preschoolers clad in colorful bathing suits and toting foam noodles practiced a skill that could one day save their life: They went for a swim.

The students, whose teacher had shepherded them down the street from New Beginnings Academy, were there as part of an eight-week course subsidized by a city program called Swim Safe Boston. It’s an effort to keep kids safe in pools and reduce accidental drownings. During the half-hour lesson, two instructors wearing blue YMCA shirts waded in the shallow end and took kids out from the wall, keeping them above water as they learned to glide, paddle, and kick.

Swim Safe Boston started awarding grants to support free swim lessons a few years ago. This summer, those grants helped the Menino Y teach 210 kids, according to Jessica Colón, its executive director. Over the program’s lifetime, the city says, it has helped more than 10,600 get lessons — many of whom might not otherwise have had the chance.

“For most of the kiddos that we get signed up, it’s their first actual swim lesson,” Colón said. “Some of them, it’s their first time in a pool.”

Nationwide, drowning is the leading cause of death among children under 4 and the No. 2 cause for those aged 5 to 14, according to the CDC. In Massachusetts, nine children and 48 adults drowned in 2022, the last year for which complete data is available. This year, children have drowned in a backyard pool in Brockton, at a Framingham beach, and in multiple ponds in the state — tragic accidents that might have been avoided.

For reasons that go back decades, Bostonians of color are at particular risk. During segregation, nonwhite residents were effectively blocked from accessing public pools and beaches. “There’s been instances of intentional gatekeeping,” said José Massó, the city official who oversees Swim Safe Boston. As a result, successive generations have missed out on what Massó called “a life skill that everybody should have.”

For other families, money is the bigger problem. City-subsidized lessons — to the tune of about $900,000 in grants so far, according to Massó — help. Other Swim Safe grantees include the Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston and Dorchester and various nonprofit and cultural organizations. Boston Centers for Youth and Families facilities also offer free lessons.

Most drownings in Massachusetts happen during the summer, when families flock to pools, lakes, and beaches. And while program signups spike during the warmer months, Swim Safe Boston supports lessons year round; it plans to open new grant applications later this month. It’s impossible to know how many drownings the program has prevented, but annual enrollment keeps rising. The program has also supported adult swim lessons, certified lifeguards, and prioritized pool maintenance.

Communities of color aren’t the only ones at elevated risk. In July, Massachusetts launched a water safety public-awareness campaign for children with autism, whose affinity for water and tendency to wander make them more vulnerable than their neurotypical peers. In January, a 6-year-old girl with autism bolted toward a Norton pond and drowned; an 8-year-old boy did the same in Clinton in June. So far, the program has distributed 10,000 brochures to family resource centers, autism support centers, and special education offices around the state.

For the preschoolers at the Menino Y last week, the goals varied. Sanai, 6, didn’t want to worry about accidentally falling into a pool. One of her classmates enjoys hot tubbing with an auntie and talked about learning to float on her back in a bigger body of water. And Zanne, 5, had been swimming in Florida and described watching someone perform a cartwheel in a pool — though doing one herself still seemed a little too scary.

The kids’ example may also have ripple effects. Rosetta Thompson, who has taught at New Beginnings for 17 years and sat on the pool deck behind her students on Thursday, had a confession to make: “I’m embarrassed. I can’t swim.” But now she’s thinking about learning through the Y’s adult swim program. “It’s something I should be able to do,” she said. “They have inspired me.”
