title: A house divided: Has much-heralded food incubator CommonWealth Kitchen lost its way?
text:
Instead of feeling like one of CommonWealth Kitchen’s success stories, Lecorps felt undermined at every turn. CWK had promised business support and training, but she hadn’t received any coaching in years. Now, it seemed the kitchen was trying to poach one of her employees and she was being forced to compete against the nonprofit for a lucrative contract. The incubator was celebrated for its mission to empower minority small business owners, but from where Lecorps sat, the reality was something else entirely.

“If they really stuck to their mission, CommonWealth Kitchen would be an amazing place,” Lecorps said. “People who are donating millions of dollars a year really don’t know what’s going on in there.”

CommonWealth Kitchen today feels like a house divided.

There is a bloc of entrepreneurs happy to sing its praises, while others — current and former business members, as well as former employees — describe a worthy organization riven by mismanagement, infighting, and constant tension. Businesses are leaving in frustration, dozens of employees have quit or were fired, and leadership has been a revolving door since nearly the entire board quit four years ago in a power struggle with longtime executive director Jen Faigel.

Indeed, many of the complaints center around Faigel and her hard-charging style.

Faigel came from the real estate world and has spent a decade building CWK into a fund-raising and publicity powerhouse. She says its mission of empowering, supporting, and connecting small businesses is her North Star. Yet she acknowledges CWK can, in some ways, feel like a “cult of personality.”

She says the nonprofit has struggled in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. And the abrupt departure of several staff members last year — which coincided with the sudden death of her father — has unsettled some members. It was, she said, a “down period.”

”I’m the first to admit that,” she said. “We have grown in an absurd way, in an intense way. And as a nonprofit, to have that kind of growth is very hard to sustain in the best of circumstances. And we are not in the best of circumstances.”

What became CommonWealth Kitchen opened as CropCircle Kitchen in 2009 out of a redeveloped brewery in Jamaica Plain. When CropCircle’s leadership team departed in 2014, Faigel, who had overseen the brewery project for the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Development Corporation, stepped in as interim director and has led it since.

Faigel reshaped CropCircle’s shared kitchen concept into a mission-driven organization that created opportunities for minority, women, and immigrant food entrepreneurs. It was a mission that resonated, as did Faigel’s valiant efforts to help her members weather the pandemic.

CWK has been showered with praise and money, winning millions in grants from the likes of the Barr Foundation, The Boston Foundation, and charitable arms of financial institutions. In 2022, CWK bought and renovated its building — a former hot dog factory in Grove Hall — for $11 million, $8 million of which came from state and city loans and grants.

CWK charges its members rent for kitchen and storage space and use of its manufacturing facilities. CWK also has in-house staff who make its own products — falafel, sauces — that it sells to local universities and hospitals, relationships that are designed to benefit its small-business members down the line.

Over the last decade, CWK’s annual revenue has grown ten-fold, to $6.6 million in 2024, most of which came from grants and donations. And its portfolio today is expansive: CWK entrepreneurs serve food to MIT students and in Boston Public Schools and pitch products to Sodexo and Whole Foods. Its alumni own local cafes and sell products nationally in stores.

Faigel has a big vision. She talks about the organization as a way to disrupt the “procuriarchy” of commercial food, giving historically underestimated entrepreneurs a chance to break in. But that work, she said, has gotten more challenging for CWK and its members alike.

“Pre-COVID, you could make a living as a food truck being downtown. You can’t do it anymore. You could make a living at a farmers’ market. You can’t do that anymore,” she said. “Our work has gotten enormously harder and enormously more complicated.”

Many nonprofits have challenges, particularly when earnest ideals clash with financial realities. CWK is no exception. Its 40-plus business owners share space but compete for valuable contracts. And food businesses in particular right now face rising costs and a pullback in consumer spending that makes already modest margins even tighter.

But many business owners such as Lecorps became so disillusioned they elected to leave. These entrepreneurs, as well as some current and former workers, describe a persistent plague of microaggressions, undercutting the very values the nonprofit seemed to stand for. And while entrepreneurs hustled to build their businesses, they were also expected to sell a story about the broader enterprise and pose for pictures with oversized checks. And some say that part had increasingly come to feel more exploitive than congratulatory.

Moreover, the political culture feels like it’s turned against them.

Five years after COVID and George Floyd, the corporate, philanthropic, and government support for Black- and brown-owned businesses that fueled CWK’s rise is fading. The very notion of DEI feels under attack, and many people worry that speaking out about CWK’s problems could undermine a mission they treasure.

But this moment is also why many feel CWK simply needs to do better.

Lecorps is far from alone in viewing her time at CWK as “stuck in misery.”

In October of 2024, Felipe Ramirez, who runs Lalu’s Chicken out of CWK, sent a companywide email questioning CWK’s promise to be an “equitable incubator.” Why, he asked, did he only learn of city and state minority-vendor programs from someone outside the organization? In 18 months at the kitchen, he saw constant staff turnover and several rounds of confusing corporate reorganizations. Billing for kitchen time was a mess, and at least 20 businesses had left, he said, all citing Faigel’s leadership as the cause.

CommonWealth Kitchen, he wrote, “has failed to be a place that nourishes ‘young’ businesses to prepare them for scaling to be sustainable and viable. ... How long do you think we will have to wait for the kind of support you so proudly brag about?”

Frustrations were mounting throughout the building.

Linh Vu was among a cohort of entrepreneurs who arrived in June 2024 and hoped to develop a business plan for her baked energy bites, L’s Goodies Snacks. Two months in, CWK’s small business coaches abruptly left and were not replaced. She kept paying her monthly fees, but says she never heard from Faigel.

Eventually, she and most of her cohort members pushed to get their $700 deposits back. Vu quit the program and moved to Food Revolution, an incubator in Stoneham. Nearly her entire class of startups moved on.

“I wasn’t happy with the experience,” Vu said. “I felt like that experience delayed my progress.”

For Lecorps, pride in her accomplishments was marred by internal conflicts. She said Gourmet Kreyol was routinely overcharged for rented kitchen time — no small sum at $16,000 a month. And in 2023, after securing the migrant contracts herself, Lecorps learned CWK had bid against her for the work.

CommonWealth Kitchen shouldn’t be competing against its own members, she remembers thinking. Hadn’t it promised to support her?

Lecorps knew her migrant work made for a good news story, and she participated in some media coverage about her efforts. But over time, she kept getting congratulatory text messages for being in news stories from outlets she hadn’t talked to. Without her knowledge, Lecorps said, CWK had been pitching her success story while simultaneously trying to underbid her for the business.

It got to the point that in October 2024, Lecorps hired an attorney and sent a cease-and-desist letter demanding CWK stop using Gourmet Kreyol’s name in press reports. That, she said, prompted increased hostility from Faigel.

(In response, Faigel said Lecorps had signed a standard photo release as part of her contract with CWK and received “substantial benefits” during her time there, including discounted rent. Kitchen charges had risen because the volume of meals had soared. As for going after the same contracts, Faigel said, CWK was simply responding to a need.

“We weren’t trying to compete with her,” Faigel said. “We just saw opportunity for our folks.”)

Regardless, things got so bad Lecorps thought about quitting the business entirely. But she’d been saving up, and then won a $200,000 storefront grant from the city of Boston. In December 2024, she left CWK to run her own restaurant in Mattapan that opened this May.

“I was in a dark place for a long time,” she said. “CommonWealth Kitchen is the place where dreams go to die.”

These concerns crystallized in an anonymous organization-wide email that arrived on May 1. May Day is typically associated with workers’ rights. But the email, addressed to Faigel, was clearly a call for help and enumerated the many ways the writer felt CWK’s mission had shifted. Faigel had failed to create a diverse leadership team that reflected the community it intended to serve, the author wrote. And the small-business members were feeling stuck.

“The people you built CWK for are being tokenized, under-supported, and quietly pushed to the margins while the organization profits off their stories,” read the email from the person, who used the moniker, ”The People of CommonWealth." “They’re turned into poster children for progress, paraded like trophies of impact, while behind the scenes, many of them are unsupported, underdeveloped, or worse discarded.”

Faigel responded in an email by pledging to take the accusations “extremely seriously,” but also calling on its anonymous author to come forward.

So far, no one has. And some entrepreneurs at CWK push back on the email’s message.

“From day one, we found a supportive environment — never once did we experience discrimination or hardship," Tarun Bhalla, whose sauce company Meal Mantra has been at CWK for eight years, wrote in an email to the Globe. “CWK gave us the tools, space, and encouragement to turn our dream into reality.”

But with others, the message clearly resonated. In the weeks since, more than two dozen people with ties to CWK have told the Globe they believe the heralded organization has lost its way.

Even if the email was anonymous and aggressive, it held “undertones of truth,” said Kamaal Jarrett, who launched his Caribbean sauce business, Hillside Harvest, out of CWK and has been operating independently for about two years. He watched its values change.

“The place that I left,” Jarrett said, “was not the same place that I joined.”

The root of CWK’s troubles, according to those who spoke to the Globe, lies with high staff turnover caused in part by ever-shifting agendas. They say Faigel often asks staff to pivot midstream to respond to new opportunities or grants. That could mean quickly shifting from organizing holiday gift boxes to mapping out a new university partnership to overseeing falafel production for a local hospital.

But more than a dozen former employees say they felt under-supported, undermined, and often overwhelmed. While the organization’s mission is to uplift people of color, many female and minority employees say they learned they were being paid less than white counterparts, after a salary list was circulated among the staff.

Faigel admits the organization’s priorities frequently pivot but says that’s the nature of the work, and she measures success by the impact it creates. And while she said she couldn’t comment on some HR issues, she acknowledged that her leadership means sometimes grappling with her own blindspots.

“I’m a white leader running an organization that is doing racial equity, racial justice work,” she said. “I recognize the importance of and the nuance and complexity of that role, and I’m the first person to always say part of being in my job is understanding privilege.”

Several former employees said they believed in the mission of CWK but were shocked to learn member businesses collectively owed hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt to CWK for kitchen hours and storage fees. Several recounted learning some longtime members didn’t have a basic understanding of their cost of goods — a key element in manufacturing.

That was Sherie Theriault’s experience. She ran a salsa business out of CWK from 2011 through 2018 and accrued $40,000 in debt for kitchen use and packaging fees. She said she received no real coaching on how to grow and felt trapped.

“I dug into a hole I couldn’t get out of, no matter much how much salsa I sold,” Theriault recalled. “Not one person sat down with me and looked at the cost of goods and told me how to scale this.”

Eventually, Faigel and CWK wrote off Theriault’s debt, and she became a small business coach to help others avoid the same fate. In the years since, she’s been hired back to CWK twice as a consultant and said she sees the same vicious cycle playing out. The businesses they tout, she said, aren’t as healthy as they could be.

“If you looked at their real financials,” she said, “they’re not success stories.”

Some former employees, too, described feeling burned.

Misha Thomas was recruited from Roxbury’s Haley House in 2022 and was excited to join CWK. But Thomas quickly became concerned with how Faigel interacted with staff, saying she pitted workers against each other and made insensitive comments about race and identity.

Thomas said that after experiencing snide remarks, condescending statements, and public shaming by Faigel, Thomas took those concerns to a board member, only to later walk in on Faigel complaining to a colleague that Thomas, who is Afro-Indigenous, was “playing the race card.” (Faigel said she had no recollection of that conversation and Thomas had not communicated any concerns directly to her.)

Eventually, Thomas left CommonWealth Kitchen.

“I remember being really uncomfortable with her style of leadership,” Thomas said. “It was totally different from what I experienced at a healthy nonprofit.”

Lee Ann Song felt similarly.

Inspired by CWK’s mission, Song took a job there as director of development after graduating from Harvard and then Tufts with a master’s in innovation. She found CWK’s finances confounding and said Faigel routinely overpromised and underdelivered on grant applications. Song said she was so stressed about her mental health that she took a six-month leave, only to learn later Faigel had disclosed her medical issues to a colleague, which she felt was a serious violation of her privacy.

“I felt [Faigel] had control over me and she could badmouth me to the entire fund-raising world,” Song said.

In June, Song was terminated. At least two-dozen other staffers quit or were fired in 2023 and 2024, according to one employee who kept a running tally. Another former employee’s spouse said they’d leave them if they didn’t find another job. The turnover continues: CWK’s chief program officer recently departed after just nine months in the role.

Mary Doucette, who was hired as a consultant at CWK in 2023, described an atmosphere where Faigel would routinely badmouth employees and created a culture that had people fearful and doubting themselves.

“The language, and the verbiage, was so caustic,” she said. “Rather than it just being a business conversation, it was really personal attacks on people.”

In 2021, the board of directors intervened, telling Faigel they wanted new leadership because of mismanagement, communication issues, and culture concerns.

Faigel said she was surprised at the turn, having received a raise and positive performance review just months earlier. She pushed back, prompting five of the six outside board members to leave en masse. Disruptions continued last year when the new chair stepped down after being fired from her law firm.

For most of the past year, the board was down to just four members, one of whom is Faigel. Small-business consultant Jae Gustavo thought he would be a fifth.

Gustavo said Faigel recruited him last fall, and he began working with members while awaiting final approval. After first seeing the email from Ramirez, and then the anonymous May Day missive, Gustavo said he reached out to staffers and members about their concerns.

Two days after the May letter, he emailed his presumed colleagues on the board a plan to navigate the crisis. A response came two weeks later, from board chair Sheldon Lloyd. Gustavo was no longer invited to join.

In retrospect, Gustavo said, the concerns in that email rang true.

“People don’t trust the organization to do what it needs to do to fix itself,” he said.

Faigel said Gustavo was among a slate of candidates under consideration and there were some outstanding questions about whether his work as a business consultant for CWK members might pose a conflict of interest. Three new board members were added to the organization’s website late last month.

And Lloyd, the board chairman, defended Faigel, noting “more than one hundred businesses employing more than 5,000 people were launched with the help of this organization.

“Like many young, rapidly growing organizations, we have had our challenges,” he wrote. “The food services industry overall was hit particularly hard by COVID and post-COVID labor turnover. We are always looking to improve and enhance how we do things.”

Faigel, too, said she has taken steps to improve the climate at CWK: hosting town hall meetings for members and listening to concerns as they arise. She’s rebuilt the board and is hiring a new chief operating officer. The complaints in the May Day email? “Old news,” she said. CWK is moving forward, and has a lot to be proud of.

“There’s an absurd amount of good stuff this organization has done right, even in the worst times,” Faigel continued. “The impact this organization has had and will continue to have is real.”

Still, the anonymous email and the sentiment it reflects are rippling through CWK’s community. Some members pushed back and criticized its writer for calling for transparency while staying anonymous.

“[D]o not speak for all Black entrepreneurs or for all members of this kitchen without their consent,” wrote Jermaine Tulloch, who co-owns Family Affair Catering. “Our community is not a monolith.”

Others questioned the timing of the email, noting staff turnover has mostly stabilized and infighting doesn’t feel productive given the mounting economic challenges food startups face.

“Right now it seems like they have a pretty good crew that is trying their hardest to do what is needed and balance it all,” said Alys Myers, who runs Supply Bulk Foods. “It does seem like a huge endeavor.”

But these complaints have been building for years, and some former CWK members and staff say they resonated for a reason: People feel tokenized and trapped. Lecorps certainly did.

When she thinks back on her time at CommonWealth Kitchen, she realizes how the nonprofit benefits from keeping startups under its roof. They give Faigel a steady base of paying tenants, products to sell, and feel-good stories to share with donors.

But at some point, she said, the goal is to leave. Entrepreneurs like her want to be out on their own and she wishes CWK did more to help make that happen.

“I didn’t leave CommonWealth Kitchen confidently. I left CommonWealth Kitchen because I was having a mental breakdown,” she said. “And I was lucky I was able to.”

title: Meet the four candidates vying for Boston mayor
text:
You can check early voting locations here, and check your Election Day polling place here.

Age: 80

Neighborhood: East Boston

Key Issues: Ending the Boston Trust Act, closing methadone clinics, no affordable housing or other benefits for undocumented immigrants

Favorite place in Boston: The Dunkin’ Donuts on One Harbor St. in the Seaport

Favorite Boston food: Legal Seafoods

Robert Cappucci, 80, is a perennial political candidate and lifelong resident of East Boston. He’s run for office at least 13 times, between many unsuccessful bids for Boston mayor, Boston City Council, the Massachusetts House, and Congress. Cappucci successfully won election to the Boston School Committee in 1987, and was reelected to the position in 1989. His time in the post was cut short when then-Mayor Ray Flynn moved to transition the city’s elected school committee to a body with only mayoral appointees in 1991. He has not held elected office since.

Cappucci was born in a Cambridge hospital and raised in East Boston in a family comprising his parents and five children, he told the Globe. Cappucci’s father, Enrico Cappucci, represented East Boston in the Massachusetts House from 1937 to 1948. He graduated from Boston State College, which was absorbed into UMass Boston, with a degree in political science in 1968. He then enlisted in the Navy, served on active duty for two years, and was in the reserves for several more years, according to the National Personnel Records Center.

Cappucci spent roughly 10 years employed with the East Boston Community Development Corporation, working on housing and development issues, he said. He also worked as a Boston police officer for 13 years. In that time he earned a master’s degree in criminal justice from Anna Maria College. Cappucci retired in 2010 from the force, after a lifetime of being a “workaholic,” he told the Globe.

Cappucci is running as a Democrat, and said he is more concerned with economic and job issues over social issues. But Cappucci espouses conservative positions on many topics that he said are key priorities for him. He emphasized that as mayor he would end all so-called sanctuary city policies — a politicized term that immigration critics, most often on the right, frequently use to refer to municipalities that limit local officials’ cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts. He opposes Boston’s local ordinance known as the Trust Act, which only allows local officials to comply with federal immigration authorities’ requests to detain people for possible deportation if the person is also wanted for a serious crime.

He told the Globe he would move to close all methadone clinics, where people struggling with opioid addiction receive treatment and assistance reducing withdrawal symptoms. He also opposes Mayor Michelle Wu’s project to redevelop Franklin Park’s White Stadium for Boston Public Schools students in partnership with a professional women’s soccer team. He said he would move to ensure that no undocumented immigrants are able to access affordable housing programs or other social benefits, and would not allow any new homeless shelters in the city.

“I have a platform that I think reflects the voters, and so the voters will decide, you know, do they want to keep the status quo,” Cappucci told the Globe. “I believe there are people out there, hopefully the majority, will give me an opportunity.”

He emphasized that he supports “law and order,” “peace through justice,” and assistance for veterans, seniors, and people with disabilities. Cappucci describes himself as a “lifelong bachelor” and practicing Catholic. He lives alone.

Age: 48

Neighborhood: Hyde Park

Key Issues: Boston Public Schools, public safety, and the economy/displacement

Favorite place in Boston: On the field at Clifford Park, coaching football

Favorite Boston food: Clam chowder

Whether it’s gun violence in the city’s Cape Verdean community or needles strewn on athletic fields located near Mass. and Cass, Domingos DaRosa is known for his outspokenness — a reputation earned by not pulling punches when it comes to criticizing the city’s powers-that-be, including the mayor’s City Hall administration and Boston police.

The 48-year-old Hyde Park community activist has made his name in city political circles as a thorn-in-the-side of those in power. Now, for the fourth time, he is seeking public office.

His previous three attempts — all campaigns for an at-large City Council post — were unsuccessful. This time around, he’s running for the top job in municipal government: the mayoralty.

And while City Hall observers characterize his current campaign as a long-shot bid for the fifth-floor City Hall corner office, DaRosa projects optimism.

“Folks are tired of the same old politics,” he said.

His candidacy, he said, stands in contrast with those of front-runners Michelle Wu, the incumbent, and Josh Kraft, a nonprofit leader who has publicly jousted with the mayor for months. He gives voters another option: a product of Boston Public Schools, a renter, and someone who has been a victim of the city’s gun violence.

“I’m a survivor of Boston,” he told the Globe recently over the phone.

DaRosa said humanity is missing from city politics. People don’t treat each other well and the city is being sold to “the highest bidder,” he said.

“We talk a good game, but we don’t deliver,” he said.

For too many Bostonians, the city is becoming unlivable, thanks to the rampaging housing and cost-of-living crises, he said.

Failure to fix quality-of-life problems, such as mold, at public housing units over the years, has led to systemic and pricey overhauls of such developments, he said. Government should do a better job when it comes to maintaining such properties, he said.

DaRosa said the city should simply be building more public housing. He said he would favor capping rental increases year-to-year.

“We’ve lost so many of our neighbors because of the policies that are coming out of this administration,” said DaRosa. “We can’t continue to allow those families to be displaced because of those policies. It’s not an equitable city for all communities.”

Central to his campaign is the notion that Boston is simply not working for too many people.

Boston Public Schools, he said, is a failing system. Too many students in the district won’t be able to get into prestigious local colleges because their schooling is lacking, he said.

He said he understands the plight of immigrants because he is one. He was 10 months old when he came to the US from Cape Verde. At the time, he said, he was undocumented. It’s important for the city to educate immigrants on their rights and what the law entails, including what is and is not covered under a city ordinance that spells out how and when police officers should interact with federal immigration authorities.

Regarding White Stadium, he is against the city’s current plan, saying the structure should have never been demolished. He said he favors the plan put forward by the Franklin Park Defenders. The $64 million alternative proposal calls for a roughly 5,000-seat facility, compared to the 11,000-seat stadium of the current project. It would have fewer amenities — such as no professional-grade media and medical rooms or a beer garden.

Public safety is another major issued for DaRosa, who works in property maintenance. DaRosa has experienced street violence firsthand: a bullet grazed his leg outside his mother’s house in Dorchester in 2018. Two other men, including DaRosa’s brother, were shot in the incident.

While homicides are at historically low levels in the city, DaRosa said that even one murder is too many.

Mass. and Cass, the epicenter of the city’s homelessness and opioid epidemics near Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, also continues to be top of mind for DaRosa. In recent years, DaRosa has objected to the preponderance of dirty needles at Roxbury’s Clifford Park, located down the street from Mass. and Cass.

The conditions were so bad at one point Boston Bengals Pop Warner football program, which used the field for practice, merged with another team so that they could move their practice location.

Open drug-dealing and use on the streets of Boston, as well as quality of life issues on Mass. and Cass including public lewd acts, continue to be a problem, he said.

Additionally, not enough city jobs are going toward city residents, said DaRosa. He noted the income gap between Black and white households locally remains stubbornly large. And while the city has laws on the books requiring construction sites to meet certain diversity and residency quotas, projects have historically failed to meet such standards, he said.

Age: 58

Neighborhood: North End

Key issues: Housing, schools, Mass. and Cass

Favorite place in Boston: Rose Kennedy Greenway, particularly where the mural is, near South Station

Favorite Boston food: Pino’s Pizza in Brighton, because the college kids in the area breathe so much culture into our city

Josh Kraft is best known for two things: his decades as a nonprofit leader in the city, and his privileged background as the third son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft. Josh Kraft has never had an operational role in the family business, though he did for years lead the family’s philanthropic efforts as head of the New England Patriots Foundation. A graduate of Williams College and the Harvard Graduate School of Education, Kraft worked for more than three decades at the Boys and Girls Club of Boston, including 12 years as its leader. His interest in nonprofit work started young; loved ones say he followed closely in the footsteps of his mother, Myra Kraft, who was beloved for her philanthropy work.

Kraft, 58, grew up in the nearby suburbs in Chestnut Hill and has lived most of his life just outside city limits. He moved in October 2023 to Boston, where he now lives on the waterfront in the North End with his partner, Michelle Perez Vichot. He has two grown daughters from a past marriage.

Kraft is a political newcomer; this is his first run for office. He’s involved himself in past races, however, as a political donor to Democrats — including Michelle Wu in 2021 — as well as Republicans, donations that his staff said were motivated by his support for Israel. Kraft is registered as a Democrat, though over the years he has voted in some GOP primaries.

As a candidate, Kraft has fought to define himself as his own person, distinguishing himself from his father, who has at times been a close friend and supporter of President Trump. The younger Kraft says he has never supported or voted for Trump and believes the president is unfit for office. Still, Kraft has benefited from his wealthy background and his family’s connections; he has put millions of dollars into his own campaign and received donations from associates of his father’s, including NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell.

Kraft has focused his campaign largely on housing, which polling shows is the top issue for most Boston voters.

“I’m running for mayor because Boston has become the most expensive city in America to raise a family,” Kraft said in a recent ad. “As mayor, I’ll listen — not lecture.”

Kraft says as mayor he would prioritize building more homes; he has blamed some Wu administration policies for blocking or delaying construction. He and Wu are split on a number of policies, including the idea of a real estate transfer tax, which would impose a small fee on high-dollar real estate sales to support housing efforts. Wu supports it, Kraft opposes it. They’re also divided on the issue of rent control, which Wu has championed as a signature issue for years. Kraft has proposed an alternate, opt-in form of the policy that would offer landlords tax breaks if they agree to cap annual rent increases. Wu has rejected that plan as “fake rent control.”

One of the candidates’ sharpest divides is over White Stadium, a decades-old facility that Wu is rebuilding into a home for BPS athletes as well as a professional women’s soccer team. Kraft argues the city should not be pouring tens of millions of taxpayer dollars into a project that will also benefit private interests. He has called Wu’s handling of the renovation a “catastrophic failure,” particularly because the mayor has not shared a recent cost estimate for the pricey project.

On immigration, Kraft, like Wu, supports the Boston Trust Act. Kraft has also called for the city to provide more support for individuals returning from incarceration. On transportation, Kraft has said he would immediately pause the construction of city bike lanes, and called for an audit of existing ones. His plan for Boston Public Schools would add more seats in coveted exam schools, change the district’s leadership structure, and transition from a fully appointed School Committee to a partially elected body.

Age: 40

Neighborhood: Roslindale

Key Issues: Community safety, housing affordability, education and youth opportunities

Favorite place in Boston: Franklin Park

Favorite Boston food: Roxbury Russet apples

Michelle Wu is the mayor of Boston and a groundbreaking politician in the city’s history, as the first woman, person of color, and mother to be elected to City Hall’s top job. Wu has served as the city’s chief executive since she won the open mayoral race in 2021, after then-Mayor Martin J. Walsh left the role to serve as former president Joe Biden’s secretary of labor.

Wu, 40, was born in Chicago to Taiwanese immigrant parents, and is the oldest of four children. She attended Harvard College and worked as a consultant before moving back to Illinois to care for her two young sisters and her mother, who was struggling with mental illness. Wu often credits her experience opening and running a tea shop in Chicago — specifically, having to navigate the cumbersome city permitting process — as her inspiration for getting involved in local government. Wu later moved back to Boston with her mother and youngest sister to attend Harvard Law School, where she met her longtime mentor, US Senator Elizabeth Warren.

She worked in then-Mayor Thomas M. Menino’s administration, then on Warren’s first Senate campaign in 2012, before winning election to the Boston City Council as an at-large member in 2013. During her eight years on the council, she earned a reputation as an effective, policy-oriented workhorse and spearheaded several notable policy changes, including implementing a parental leave policy for municipal employees, and regulations on short term rentals such as Airbnbs.

As a first-time mayoral candidate in 2021, Wu ran an unapologetically progressive campaign, championing rent control, free public transit, and a municipal “Green New Deal,” among other issues. Now that she’s an incumbent running for a second term, some say she has evolved, focusing on a more pragmatic version of her earlier vision. Whereas she once supported reducing funding for BPD, Wu this year accepted the endorsement of the city’s largest police union, and touts the city’s low violent crime rates as one of her top accomplishments from her first four years as mayor.

In making her case for reelection, Wu also points to her expansion of pre-K and child-care seats, guaranteeing paid summer jobs for Boston Public Schools students, and efforts to increase the city’s affordable housing stock and promote home ownership opportunities for low-income families. Wu often says her goal is to “make Boston a home for everyone,” emphasizing her personal stake in the city’s future as a Boston Public Schools parent. Wu lives in Roslindale with her husband, Conor Pewarski, their three children — 10-year-old Blaise, 8-year-old Cass, and 7-month-old Mira — and Wu’s mother.

She’s also faced criticism and controversy over her administration’s implementation of bike lanes across the city, and her plan to redevelop Franklin Park’s White Stadium for Boston Public Schools students in partnership with a new professional women’s soccer team.

In recent months, she’s gained national attention over her fierce defense of the city’s diverse communities and immigrant-friendly public safety policies in the face of the Trump administration’s mass deportation efforts. From Capitol Hill, to City Hall plaza, and the set of “The Daily Show,” Wu has defied pressure and threats from the Trump administration to roll back the city’s ordinance that limit local officials’ cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts.

The resulting spotlight has earned her a reputation of being an example of successful Democratic leadership in the resistance to Trump’s White House.

“At a time when this federal administration is already causing so much fear and harm in our communities, these threats are serious and consequential, but our same communities have told me loud and clear that silence in the face of oppression is not an option,” Wu proclaimed at an August press conference.

“The Trump administration seeks to divide, isolate, and intimidate cities and make Americans fearful of one another,” she continued. “But Boston is proof of something far more powerful than lies and intimidation; that safety and community come from loving your neighbor as yourself.”

title: ‘Where dreams go to die’: inside the reckoning at CommonWealth Kitchen
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

For the past decade, the Dorchester-based food incubator CommonWealth Kitchen has been celebrated for its work helping culinary entrepreneurs pursue their dreams. The nonprofit centers its work around uplifting small business owners of diverse backgrounds, focusing particularly on BIPOC-, women-, and immigrant-led companies.

The small business owners at CWK work hard, and they have great stories to tell. I know, because I’ve written about many of them over the past several years: Participants in its small business mentorship program, startups supplying food to local colleges and serving those in need during the pandemic, and the trials of a new restaurant trying to make it in Fields Corner.

Today, CWK’s small businesses serve food to MIT students and Boston Public Schools, own local cafes, and sell products nationally in stores. Over the past 10 years, CWK has been showered with both praise and money, winning millions in grants from the likes of the Barr Foundation and The Boston Foundation. Its annual revenue has grown tenfold, to $6.6 million in 2024.

But a few months ago, an email landed in my inbox from a source. It was an anonymous note that had been sent to the staff, and it singled out CommonWealth’s hard-charging executive director, Jen Faigel, saying her leadership left members feeling “exploited, ignored, and stuck” and “quietly pushed to the margins while the organization profits off their stories.”

I was intrigued, to say the least.

The note arrived on May Day, a holiday typically associated with workers’ rights. But the email was clearly also a call for help. The person, using the moniker, ”The People of CommonWealth,” wrote that the small business owners who had come to CWK for opportunities were instead “turned into poster children for progress, paraded like trophies of impact, while behind the scenes, many of them are unsupported, underdeveloped, or worse discarded.”

This would be an interesting story in and of itself. But what got me even more intrigued was that the anonymous missive had arrived at a particularly fraught moment. Five years after COVID and the killing of George Floyd, the corporate, philanthropic, and government support for Black- and brown-owned businesses that had fueled CWK’s rise seemed to be fading. Indeed, the very notion of DEI felt under attack. And yet in this instance, the critique of DEI efforts seemed to be coming from inside the house.

And so, I set out to learn more. And as I began talking to the many people within CWK’s orbit — entrepreneurs and the many employees and board members who’d cycled through the organization — it became increasingly clear that frustrations had long been brewing within CWK’s walls. Many described a worthy organization riven by mismanagement, infighting, and constant tension.

More than a dozen former employees told me that they felt under-supported, undermined, and often overwhelmed. Perhaps more importantly, while outwardly celebrating diversity, the organization seemed to operate internally by a different set of rules. Business members told me they felt financially beholden to CWK, and noted how the nonprofit benefits from keeping startups under its roof. They give Faigel a steady base of paying tenants, products to sell, and feel-good stories to share with donors. There’s little incentive, they say, to actually help them go out on their own.

Meanwhile, many also told me they experienced a persistent plague of microaggressions, undercutting the very values the nonprofit seemed to stand for. While entrepreneurs hustled to build their businesses, they were also expected to sell a story about the broader enterprise, and pose for pictures with oversized checks. And some say that part had increasingly come to feel transactional and exploitive.

As one longtime business member told me: “There’s a big difference between doing actual good work and telling everyone you’re doing good work.”

Over the course of some two dozen interviews, I’ve come to learn that CWK has been a house divided ever since that May Day missive hit inboxes. Since I’ve started my reporting, many business owners have come out in support of Faigel, and say CWK is a supportive place, and one that they critically need to survive the current political climate.

But for other business owners, including restaurant-owner Nathalie Lecorps, CWK is something else entirely: “CommonWealth Kitchen,” she told me, “is the place where dreams go to die.”

And so for them, this moment is something larger: A reckoning of a reckoning.

It’s also why many now feel CWK simply needs to do better.

Read my full report on the turmoil at CommonWealth Kitchen.

title: At Suffolk sheriff’s office, employees say a troubled history is repeating itself
text:
This time, it’s Steven W. Tompkins who is accused of wrongdoing, pleading not guilty to two charges of extortion and announcing he would step away while the federal case is ongoing.

Both Rouse and Tompkins were known more for their political pedigrees than for relevant work experience. Rouse was a popular state representative from Dorchester at the time; Tompkins, whose background was in public relations, was a constant presence at Democratic political events.

Some current and former employees and advocates say the office has regressed under Tompkins and harks back to the early 2000s, when the department under Rouse routinely made news for all the wrong reasons. The progress made by Rouse’s successor, Andrea J. Cabral, a career prosecutor who had a mandate to clean house, they say, has been wiped away.

“Rouse seemed like a decent man, but he had no idea what he was doing,” said retired corrections Captain Mickey Walsh, whose tenure at the sheriff’s office began in the late 1990s. “Andrea [Cabral] righted the ship. And then Steve [Tompkins] came in and boom — he got promoted, he got that title.

“Absolute power corrupts,” Walsh added. “It immediately went to his head, and he showed it every day.”

Walsh is among eight former and current Tompkins subordinates interviewed by the Globe; each was strongly critical of his tenure as sheriff. Six spoke on the condition of anonymity over fear of retribution. All painted a picture of an image-obsessed politician with no prior law enforcement experience and little interest in corrections, though his primary responsibilities are to oversee the Nashua Street jail and the South Bay House of Correction.

They said under Tompkins, patronage flourished, with some longtime employees referring to new hires with obscure job titles by the acronym FOS — Friends of the Sheriff. Strict screening of job applicants fell by the wayside, while chronic understaffing forced officers to work double shifts, they said. Reports of violence in the jails have also ticked up in recent years, according to an advocacy group that tracks the issue. Tompkins’s presence at the jail in particular was sporadic at best, and employees said there is a culture in which they feel they are expected to contribute to his campaign.

“It was a boys club,” said one former employee who spoke with the Globe. “It was very much, if you were on his side, you were going to be taken care of. And if not, you were on your own.”

In response to questions from the Globe, Tompkins’s attorney, Martin G. Weinberg, brushed off those characterizations as the laments of a few disgruntled former staffers.

“Over his 12-year tenure as sheriff, the department has had up to a thousand employees,” Weinberg said in a prepared statement. “It is not surprising that one or two of them would make random statements critical of the sheriff, who is widely respected within the department and has been elected three times by the voters of Suffolk County.”

Tompkins stands accused of pressuring the cofounder of the cannabis company Ascend Wellness Holdings to sell him stock before the venture went public, using as leverage a partnership with the sheriff’s office that was central to winning its state license. Then, after the value of his shares tanked, Tompkins demanded to be repaid his full $50,000 stake, according to the indictment.

The sheriff has pleaded not guilty, and Weinberg reiterated he plans to “meet the federal prosecutors’ accusation in a future trial before a jury of the sheriff’s peers and not in the media.”

Under Tompkins, inmate complaints about assaults by officers and access to health care are higher than in state-run facilities, according to data collected by Prisoners’ Legal Services of Massachusetts. Reports of violence in particular have shot up; in 2024, the number of such incidents was double what it had been averaging in recent years.

“It rings some alarm bells for us,” said Dave Rini, the advocacy group’s executive director. “Any time you see a lot of complaints about brutality it means something is wrong with the management of a facility. Because in a well-run facility, staff don’t assault prisoners and prisoners also don’t assault staff.”

A spokesperson for the Suffolk County Sheriff’s Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Echoes of 2002

In 2002, a blue-ribbon state commission — convened in the wake of Globe exposés and federal indictments — rapped Rouse for faulty leadership and absenteeism. The Stern Commission’s report came amid a host of other allegations during Rouse’s tenure: guards having sex with women behind bars, officers brutally beating inmates, and runaway political patronage.

Rouse, a Democrat, was appointed by Republican Governor William Weld in what was widely seen as an attempt to woo crossover support for Weld’s unsuccessful campaign for the US Senate. Rouse had no background in corrections, and the Stern report found he showed little interest in the field after becoming sheriff in 1996.

Rouse kept his offices at the Suffolk courthouse rather than at either of the sheriff’s jails, keeping him distant from their operations, the report said. A year earlier, the Globe had tailed Rouse for six work days and found he was in his office for just 14 hours.

Under Rouse, the department was buffeted by allegations of physical abuse and sexual exploitation. Eight guards were indicted on federal charges they beat inmates who were awaiting trial. Between 1999 and 2001, eight employees were fired or suspended for alleged sexual misconduct at the department.

Rouse was never accused of or charged with a crime.

In a brief telephone interview last week, Rouse took issue with the Stern report — which was commissioned at his request — as well as the findings of the Spotlight Team that prompted it. He and most of his leadership team resigned around the time the report came out.

“I took a very difficult job that was requested of me by the governor and we accomplished it,” Rouse said. “I did quite a bit to improve it. I took it over at a very difficult time.”

He declined to respond to the commission’s assertion there was a fundamental “failure of leadership” during his tenure. Rouse also disputed the Spotlight Team’s findings he spent little time at the office, and while he accepted political donations from employees, he stressed that he never solicited them.

“I know a hatchet job when I hear one,” Rouse said. “You’re going to write what you’re going to write. It’s the Globe. See you later. Take care. Goodbye.”

Cabral, the prosecutor who was installed as sheriff after Rouse’s departure, mostly hewed to the Stern Commission’s blueprint, and several former correctional officials said conditions improved during her decade at the helm. One former department employee told the Globe that when he began working for Cabral, he was given a copy of the Stern report for insight about past problems to ensure the department “would never go there again.”

A return to form

Instead, under Tompkins, some of the practices that had drawn the commission’s ire resurfaced, the employees interviewed by the Globe said.

Among them: a return to taking campaign contributions from employees and a seeming disinterest at the top in the actual operations of the office’s two correctional facilities.

“He cares about it when it’s convenient for him,” meaning when it’s politically beneficial, Arthur Bacon, a former Suffolk sheriff’s correction officer, said of Tompkins, whom he unsuccessfully sued for wrongful termination.

“He’s very transactional, just like [President] Trump,” said Bacon, who alleged in court documents that he was fired after he reported finding $5,000 in cash on an inmate during a search. In his suit, Bacon alleged that he reported the cash against Tompkins’s wishes.

In court documents, the sheriff’s department said Bacon was fired because he failed to notice a detainee attempting to hang himself. As for the incident with the cash, the sheriff’s office said Bacon improperly abandoned his post. Bacon disputes that explanation.

Like Rouse, Tompkins owed his appointment to a governor, and had no background in corrections other than serving as a Cabral aide for external affairs. When Patrick named him sheriff in 2013, Massachusetts Republican leaders called the selection a patronage pick. Patrick more or less conceded the point.

“It’s a political job, so the folks that are criticizing it as a political hire, tell them: They’re right,” Patrick said at the time.

Patrick didn’t return a message from the Globe for this story.

Three years into the job, Tompkins made a particularly notable patronage hire that got him into trouble with the State Ethics Commission. He paid a $12,300 fine after admitting he created a job specifically for his niece and had her help him with child care and other personal responsibilities.

While Tompkins, unlike Rouse, has offices at both the House of Correction and the Nashua Street Jail, his presence at either has been spotty, the eight former and current employees interviewed said. (The Globe has requested records showing the use of his office swipe card, but has yet to receive them.)

Several former and current employees noted he rarely walked through the Nashua Street Jail.

“We barely saw him,” said one former employee. “There was this running joke that he’s only coming in if he’s going to get his picture taken; he’s only coming if he’s going to be in the newspaper. He was not someone that was doing a 9-to-5 in the office every day.”

A history of patronage

The Stern Commission rapped Rouse for rewarding political allies and supporters with jobs and promotions, a practice that stoked cynicism among employees.

“Many staff owe their employment to political sponsors and believe that assignments and promises are tied to political support for the sheriff,” read the report.

When Cabral took over, she pledged to not accept political contributions from her employees, a promise that records show she appears to have honored.

But Tompkins, who has publicly said he considers Cabral a close friend, made no such promise. And since 2023, one of every two donations Tompkins has received came from a current or former employee or their family members. The Stern report dinged Rouse for almost identical numbers.

Tompkins “was closely monitoring who was donating, who was holding signs,” said one former employee who spoke with the Globe. “If you were part of what he called his team, you were golden. You walked on water.”

Common Cause, a nonprofit that focuses on the role of money in politics, criticized Tompkins and other Massachusetts sheriffs in a 2021 report for taking significant donations from vendors that do business with their offices. Tompkins, it noted, received $7,100 from the company that has come under fire for the quality of the health care it provides at Suffolk’s jails.

While elected officials are allowed to accept contributions from employees they oversee, they are forbidden from soliciting them directly. And experts say taking them at a large scale creates a perception that employees are expected to donate.

The office of sheriff in Massachusetts, unlike in some states, tends to be an obscure one, since law enforcement duties are primarily handled by police departments, while the sheriff is essentially an elected jail warden.

The office is a vestige of county government, which in Massachusetts is largely comprised of a collection of obscure, down-ballot offices.

Last week, Tompkins agreed to take leave from his office at the request of Governor Maura Healey and Attorney General Andrea Campbell. But the sheriff described it as a medical leave and gave no indication would resign.

After his indictment, Tompkins designated Mark Lawhorne as the “special sheriff” who will fill his seat on an interim basis. That authority under state law belongs to him alone.

Lawhorne, who was hired in September 2023 as director of the sheriff’s reentry/reintegration division, has a resume similar to the man who gave him the job. Like Tompkins, Lawhorne has a background in communications and came to corrections through public relations. Until recently, he also co-hosted a music podcast.

Lawhorne, who will be managing an office with a $130 million budget, owes the Internal Revenue Service more than $25,000 in unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest, according to a tax lien filed in March 2019 with the Middlesex Registry of Deeds.

He’s also been sued repeatedly in small claims court for unpaid credit bills and other debts, records show. As recently as three weeks ago, a credit card company sued Lawhorne in Malden District Court for an unpaid debt of $1,200.

Lawhorne did not return messages seeking comment for this story.

Jeremiah Manion, Matt Stout, and Sean Cotter of Globe staff contributed to this report.

A federal judge ruled the Trump administration unlawfully cut nearly $3 billion of Harvard’s research funding.

Josh Kraft parted ways with his top advisers, in a major campaign staff shakeup just days before the Boston mayoral primary.

Nursing homes in Massachusetts are being flipped in deals that put quick profit ahead of long-term success.

The last US jobs report was a shocker. Will the next one, set for release on Friday, deliver another jolt?

After the July report, the labor market suddenly seemed weaker than previously thought, as employers hit the brakes on hiring. Employment gains for the previous two months were revised sharply lower, and the jobless rate ticked up to 4.2 percent.

Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, assessed the data and other indicators and concluded that the US was on “the precipice of recession.”

In Zandi’s view, Massachusetts and 20 other states are already in or at high risk of a contraction.

President Trump reacted to the July employment numbers by firing the head of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. He suggested the report had been rigged to make him look bad.

More likely, his policies are starting to stunt economic growth.

Tariffs are cutting into corporate profits and forcing businesses to delay hiring and other investments until their impact becomes clearer. Restrictive immigration policies are shrinking the workforce.

With fewer workers, it is harder for the economy to expand.

The local angle: The Massachusetts economy grew at an annual rate of 2.6 percent in the second quarter, according to MassBenchmarks, an economics journal produced by the Donahue Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

“We weren’t in a recession as of July,” said Alan Clayton-Matthews, senior contributing editor at MassBenchmarks. “Is one coming? That’s a different matter.”

Recessions are marked by a significant decline in economic activity — including employment, industrial output, and personal income and spending — that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months.

It’s true that the state’s labor market has lagged behind many parts of the country for some time. That reflects our dependence on immigration for population and workforce growth.

But broader data on wages and spending show the economy continued to expand from April through June.

Up next: We’ll get a fresh snapshot of the US job market on Friday, when the August employment report is released. (State numbers will follow in two weeks.)

The consensus among forecasters is that employers added 75,000 jobs last month, little changed from 73,000 in July.

Barring another big revision, that would bring the average gain over the past four months to 45,000, compared with an average increase of 123,000 in the first four months of the year.

The unemployment rate is expected to tick up to 4.3 percent.

Zandi, the Moody’s Analytics economist, says we will probably dodge a national recession thanks to economic momentum in big states such as Florida and Texas, as well states that are holding their own, including California and New York.

But that’s little consolation to struggling states such as Massachusetts and others in the same boat, including the rest of New England, except Vermont, and the Mid-Atlantic states, except Pennsylvania.

“The striking thing (at least to me) is the regional diversity of the economically troubled states,” Zandi said in an email. “The economic struggles are evident from coast-to-coast. If there is a common denominator among the troubled states it is their older populations and weaker demographics.”

Why it matters: The labor market isn’t as strong as the current 4.2 percent jobless rate suggests.

The supply of workers is declining as people leave the workforce — many due to deportations or the fear of being deported. That holds down unemployment because those people aren’t counted anymore.

At the same time, hiring demand has cooled. On Wednesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said the number of unemployed people in July exceeded US job openings for the first time in four years.

“I believe that any decline in labor supply is only masking weakening demand in the labor market. Whether or not supply is down, weakening demand is not good,” Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said in a speech late last month.

A closer look: Waller highlighted other data that “support the idea that labor demand may be on the edge of a sharp decline.”

Raises for people switching to new jobs are lower than for workers staying in the same job, the opposite of what usually happens in a strong labor market.

Teen joblessness has risen significantly in 2025, back to levels seen in the mid-2010s, pointing to reduced demand for entry-level workers.

Waller, a Trump appointee, was one of two governors who voted against holding interest rates steady at the Fed’s most recent meeting in July. He argues the central bank should be cutting rates now to prop up the job market.

Final thought: A recession isn’t inevitable — or even probable.

Forecasters surveyed by Bloomberg put recession odds over the next year at 30 percent.

But the outlook for Massachusetts is dimmer.

Employers will struggle as more workers retire and immigration restrictions curb population growth. Professional business and technical services, biotech, and tech — key engines of the local economy — are in a downturn. And the high cost of doing business will limit the state’s ability to attract and retain jobs.

“There is a real threat of a recession,” Clayton-Matthews of MassBenchmarks said.

Friday’s job report could signal just how big that threat is.

“Obviously we have a lot of work to do.”

— Bill Belichick, following a 48-14 drubbing in his debut as football coach at the University of North Carolina.

Copycat: After ousting Susan Monarez, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. pitched ideas to overhaul the agency that mirrored hers.

Ill wind: Projects blocked. Work stopped. Funds canceled. What’s left of offshore power?

Tariff appeal: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to rule quickly on whether the president has the power to impose sweeping import taxes.

Food fight: CommonWealth Kitchen, the much-praised food startup hub in Dorchester, has been hit by toxic workplace allegations.

Another hit: State Treasurer Deborah Goldberg plans to appeal a judge’s decision to reinstate Shannon O’Brien as head of the Cannabis Control Commission, a move that could prolong the fight over the foundering regulatory agency.

Supply boost: Enbridge launched a $300 million expansion of its Algonquin natural gas pipeline in Massachusetts and Rhode Island, with Eversource as its first customer.

1,135

— The number of billionaires in the US in 2024, according to data from Altrata, a wealth intelligence firm. Their collective wealth: about $5.7 trillion.

You may have heard that Amtrak has upped its game with new high-speed trains along the Northeast Corridor, the heavily traveled route connecting Boston with New York and Washington, D.C.

Development of the NextGen Acela took 10 years and $2.35 billion to complete. Was it worth it? Yes, says Globe travel writer Christopher Muther, even if he experienced delays on his virgin voyage.

“The NextGen Acela is a beautiful train. Sleek, chock-a-block with thoughtful details, and a huge improvement over the 25-year-old previous generation that was decidedly showing its age,“ Muther writes.

Among the improvements: large panoramic windows, a quieter ride, a dedicated USB port and power outlet for each seat, and fast 5G Wi-Fi.

One thing the new Acela is not: faster. At least for now. Its top speed is 160 miles per hour, 10 mph faster than the old Acela. But Muther explains that the new train can’t always cruise at max speed because of the 100-year-old tracks, congestion, tunnels, and outdated signals.

Does anyone here remember the Metroliner? (Nostalgia is a big part of being a railfan.) That was the “high-speed” service — eventually around 120 mph — on the Northeast Corridor from 1969 to 2000, when Acela entered the station.

title: A.R.T. and ProBlak team up to lead creative workshops for upcoming mural
text:
Earlier this summer, the American Repertory Theater announced that it had commissioned a 200-foot mural by Roxbury artist Rob “ProBlak” Gibbs to adorn its new campus in Allston. And now, both Gibbs and the A.R.T. want your input.

The collaborative initiative plans to tap locals for inspiration and ideas for the upcoming artwork. The idea is a community-inspired mural, created with the help of the Bostonians the new creative space will serve, said Dayron J. Miles, the A.R.T.’s associate artistic director.

“We didn’t want to just put another mural up,” Miles said. “We wanted the art that enveloped our building to emanate from stories that reflected our community.”

Before the mural’s installation — which is scheduled for this spring, according to Miles — the A.R.T. and Gibbs will partner with local artists to host conversation-driven creative workshops across the city throughout September. At each, attendees will be encouraged to share their personal stories as Bostonians and their ideas for Boston’s future. These lived narratives and hopeful visions, in turn, will help shape the mural’s final outcome.

The A.R.T. enters its 2025-26 theater season this fall with its Allston relocation on the horizon. Its new home base, the David E. and Stacey L. Goel Center for Creativity & Performance, began construction last summer; once complete, the 70,000-square-foot building will expand the organization’s performance, teaching, and public spaces. Gibbs’s mural, which is set to be completed between late spring and early fall of 2026, according to Miles, will be featured on the Goel’s north-facing exterior wall.

The mural workshops kick off Sept. 6 in Cambridge with additional sessions in Malden, East Boston, Allston-Brighton, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Back Bay. Artists and non-artists are invited to participate.

Gibbs — one of the founders of Artists for Humanity, a nonprofit that supports young creators in Boston — will co-lead each workshop session alongside a fellow local artist.

“Art is typically categorized as two- or three-dimensional — for me, there is a fourth dimension: the shared story. That is what makes the mural or theatrical experience live on, long after it’s created,” Gibbs said in a statement issued by the A.R.T.

The community engagement efforts emulate the Goel’s intended function to “not just be a culture palace for artists and theater makers, but rather be a place where the community could come and investigate their own creativity,” said Miles.

“The mural [will be] another line of respect that can be shown to the community, since the art of storytelling is not from one person [or] one narrative. It’s all of our stories combined,” Gibbs told the Globe in an interview. “I want to show how much we’ve got in common.”

During each two-hour session, Gibbs and the local artist will facilitate conversation between attendees, using the session to stimulate ideas for the city’s future, and, in turn, the future mural. Each guest artist brings their own method for ideation to the experience, whether that be hands-on activities or conversation prompts. (All supplies will be provided.)

Muralist Gina Latham — who co-leads the Cambridge Public Library session on Sept. 6 from 2-4 p.m. — says the opportunity allows her to “flex [her] creative muscles.” She believes community engagement is “the most important piece of the puzzle.”

Interdisciplinary artist Phoebe Warner will co-lead the series’ final workshop at the Harvard Ed Portal in Allston. They said their involvement in the session is especially meaningful to them, as Allston-Brighton is where they first found a home in Boston’s arts scene.

“I’m really hoping that I can honor the community that accepted me and brought me in. That’s my hood, in a way,” Warner said. “I am really grateful and excited that I get to [lead] that space.”

To attend a workshop, find details and locations at americanrepertorytheater.org.

This story has been updated to correct a reporting error in Dayron J. Miles’s comments about the Goel Center’s purpose.

Isabella Bernstein can be reached at isabella.bernstein@globe.com.

title: Trial for police officer, city employee who allegedly ran illegal nightclub in Jamaica Plain slated for January
text:
A Boston police officer and a city employee are set to go on trial in January for allegedly running an “illegal after-hours nightclub” in a Jamaica Plain basement in 2021, prosecutors said in court filings.

Richard McDermott, a suspended Boston police officer, and Luigi D’Addieco, a suspended campus police officer for the Boston Public Health Commission, were indicted last year after a shooting at the nightclub in 2021 brought the illegal operation to light, prosecutors said.

McDermott faces charges that include witness intimidation, maintaining a gambling nuisance, and seeking a criminal record check under false pretenses.

D’Addieco is charged with withholding evidence from a criminal proceeding and maintaining a gambling nuisance.

Prosecutors allege that both men sold alcohol without a license at the club on Centre Street, and that they misled investigating officers.

After the 2021 shooting, in which Evan Velez, 38, of Dorchester, allegedly shot a bouncer multiple times in a dispute with the club’s promoter, arriving officers recognized McDermott, who was armed with a gun and was “one of the last people to leave,” prosecutors said.

McDermott allegedly told officers that he “had no idea what was going on” and that he was only visiting his brother-in-law’s party, prosecutors said.

“Contrary to that misleading statement, video surveillance captured McDermott looking out of the front door of the club, having had to step over the blood and broken glass before Boston Police responded,” prosecutors wrote.

D’Addieco, meanwhile, allegedly parked outside the club after the shooting, which occurred at 4:30 a.m., according to security video reviewed by prosecutors.

The two men allegedly had multiple telephone conversations with each other on the night of the shooting, prosecutors said.

Later, in interviews with detectives, McDermott and D’Addieco made false statements to detectives about their involvement in the club, prosecutors said.

Additionally, McDermott allegedly used a police database to “illegally search information on the shooting and witnesses without authorization,” prosecutors said.

Originally, McDermott and D’Addieco rented the basement to run a heating, ventilation, and air conditioning company, according to court records.

During the pandemic, they redesigned the space to accommodate a nightclub with hookahs, a DJ, and bottle service, prosecutors said. Patrons paid more than $100 for full bottles of liquor.

Both men have been free on personal recognizance since pleading not guilty last year in Suffolk County Superior Court, records show.

D’Addieco’s attorney, Francis Sacco, declined to comment Friday. McDermott’s attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.

Last year, Sacco said his client is “looking forward to his day in court.”

Material from prior Globe stories was used in this report.

title: Ex-City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson scheduled for Friday sentencing on federal corruption charges
text:
She urged US District Judge Indira Talwani not to send her to prison for the sake of her children, “to spare them the pain of separating from me.”

The judge denied that request, insisting that some prison time was necessary because of the seriousness of the offense.

“There’s no question you knew it was wrong,” Talwani said as she announced the sentence. “And it’s serious. Everyone gives tax dollars to the government assuming it’s going to be used properly . . . and not just going into someone’s pocket.”

She ordered Fernandes Anderson to self-report to an as-yet-to-be designated federal prison on Oct. 17. She also ordered her to pay $13,000 in restitution.

Talwani rejected the government’s request to sentence Fernandes Anderson to one year and a day in prison, citing nationwide court data showing the average sentence for hundreds of other first time offenders convicted of similar offenses was one month in prison.

The 46-year-old Democrat, who came to the United States from her native Cape Verde at age 10, made history in 2021 as the first Muslim elected to the Boston City Council. She represented District Seven, which covers neighborhoods including Roxbury, Dorchester, the South End, and Fenway. She attended her final council meeting in June, and officially resigned in July.

Fernandes Anderson was arrested in December by the FBI at her home in Dorchester. In May, she pleaded guilty to two of six federal wire fraud and theft charges she faced for taking the $7,000 kickback. As part of a plea agreement, the government agreed to drop four additional charges and recommend she serve a year and a day in prison.

According to an indictment, Fernandes Anderson hired her relative, then gave her a $13,000 bonus with a caveat: She had to funnel more than half of it back to the councilor.

“This is not just a one-off incident,” Assistant US Attorney John T. Mulcahy told the judge Friday, arguing that a one-year prison term was warranted. “It was not an accident. It was not a mistake.”

Prosecutors said Fernandes Anderson arranged the kickback when she was struggling financially, missing rent and car payments, and facing bank overdraft fees and a $5,000 fine from the state Ethics Commission for previously hiring relatives to her council staff.

Mulcahy also told the judge that records show Fernandes Anderson used her campaign account for personal purposes, including purchases of clothing, jewelry, and toys, then falsified campaign finance reports.

“The public needs to know that their public officials are honest, they’re ethical, and they’re transparent,” Mulcahy said. “The conduct this defendant engaged in is conduct that erodes the public trust.”

Fernandes Anderson’s actions were “an aberration that will not be repeated,” her assistant federal public defender Scott Lauer wrote in a sentencing memo, describing how she had overcome poverty and a difficult childhood to serve on the council as “a voice for a marginalized community.”

During Friday’s hearing, which was packed with Fernandes Anderson supporters, Lauer urged the judge to sentence his client to probation and community service. He noted she has been convicted of a felony and has lost her job and her reputation.

“I’m not here to tell you she did no wrong,” Lauer said. “She is imperfect. She let down all of those who placed their trust in her.”

Lauer said federal sentencing guidelines, which are advisory, suggest Fernandes Anderson should not be required to spend any time in prison, or, at most no more than six months.

He said she was seeking the opportunity to stay in the community “to repair the harm she has caused.”

More than 90 people, including three city councilors and three state lawmakers, wrote letters to the judge describing Fernandes Anderson’s commitment to her constituents and asking her to exercise leniency when imposing a sentence.

Among the submissions were City Councilors Julia Mejia, Liz Breadon, and Brian Worrell, two state representatives, Christopher Worrell and Russell Holmes, and state Senator Liz Miranda.

Talwani, the judge, said the letters spoke to the work Fernandes Anderson had done as a councilor and attested to her compassion, support, and work in the community. However, she said, “the burning question” is why she committed theft and fraud.

“I don’t take issue with very good things she’s doing in her life,” Talwani said. But she said it wasn’t clear that Fernandes Anderson has accepted responsibility for her actions.

“Is the problem in her view that she got caught or is the problem in her view that there was something wrong?” Talwani said.

Fernandes Anderson acknowledged in court in May that prosecutors had accurately described her admitted crimes.

Prosecutors said that if the case had gone to trial they were prepared to prove she arranged for her relative to receive a bonus “nearly twice as large as total bonuses to other staff combined,” based on their agreement that she would kick $7,000 of it back to the councilor.

After the city deposited the bonus into the relative’s account, the relative withdrew the money in three increments and arranged to meet Fernandes Anderson.

At around 4 p.m. on a Friday in June 2023, the pair met in a bathroom at City Hall, where Fernandes Anderson took the $7,000 cash from the staffer and stuffed it in her pocket. Fernandes Anderson received a one-word text from her relative saying, “Bathroom,” and replied, “Ready,” before meeting to collect the cash.

On Friday, as she stood before the judge, Fernandes Anderson said she was reluctant to speak “because I didn’t want to say the wrong thing” or create the impression that she believed she was a victim.

“I take full responsibility,” she said. “There is no excuse and I know this.”

title: Markey demands RFK Jr.’s resignation following combative senate testimony
text:
Walensky, who served as CDC director under President Biden from 2021 to 2023 and previously led the infectious diseases division at Massachusetts General Hospital, reflected on her time at the CDC, saying she had often warned about the nation’s fragile public-health infrastructure and lack of preparedness for future pandemics.

“I reminisce about those days when lack of support for public health was our biggest challenge,” she said.

She stressed that most Americans continue to embrace vaccines.

“In today’s divided America, there’s one consensus that remains: 92 percent of parents still vaccinate their children,” she said. “Surely we can all agree we don’t want our children to die.”

At Thursday’s Senate hearing, Kennedy defended his decision to reorganize the agencies he oversees. “We are the sickest country in the world. That’s why we have to fire people at CDC. They did not do their job. This was their job to keep us healthy.”

Markey reiterated that he had opposed Kennedy’s nomination from the start, calling him “unqualified” and “dangerous” during confirmation hearings in January.

He accused Kennedy of repeatedly misleading the public and lawmakers — from misrepresenting the COVID-19 death toll to questioning the safety of vaccines, overstating access to the new COVID boosters, and denying that the Trump administration made cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. Markey said Kennedy’s record showed a consistent pattern of lies.

“The only truth we came away with is how dangerous Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is to the health of our nation, in our communities.” Markey said referring to the Senate hearing.

The senator underscored vaccines’ role in extending American life expectancy over the past century and warned that rolling back vaccine requirements would undo those gains.

He pointed to Florida’s move to eliminate school vaccination requirements as a public-health “calamity,” saying outbreaks there could easily endanger families traveling not just from Massachusetts, but around the world.

“The price of admission to Disney World shouldn’t be a case of measles or COVID,” he said.

To hold Kennedy accountable, Markey announced the launch of an “RFK Jr. attacks tracker” to monitor his actions at HHS. Later on Friday, he issued a letter to CVS and Walgreens pressing them for information on booster availability nationwide.

In June, Kennedy removed all 17 members of an influential committee that advises the CDC on vaccine policy and replaced them with a smaller group that includes vaccine skeptics. The shakeup has delayed critical guidance on booster eligibility and has kept many pharmacies, hospitals and doctors’ offices from offering the shots. Last month, the FDA also restricted COVID vaccines to adults 65 and older or individuals with high-risk medical conditions.

Markey and Walensky praised Governor Maura Healey for requiring Massachusetts insurers to cover state-recommended vaccines regardless of shifting federal guidance. Under a Healey administration order, insurers must cover updated vaccine doses for everyone 6 months or older. That order allowed many people across Massachusetts to secure vaccination appointments at pharmacies starting Friday.

Walensky described the dismantling of vaccine infrastructure as incremental but deliberate. She argued that these changes have eroded long-standing protections, particularly programs such as the Vaccines for Children initiative, which provides free immunizations to underinsured and uninsured children.

“Unless action is taken and fast, you may be lulled into thinking vaccines are here, when vaccinations themselves may no longer be within reach,” she said.
