title: ‘People either think I’m crazy, or they’re intrigued.’ Meet the travelers tackling JetBlue’s 25-airport challenge.
text:
Fillinger took the airline up on the challenge. As he stepped off his final 25 For 25 flight at Logan, he was understandably excited that he had won the points and the status, but he seemed equally, if not more, excited about how his strategy (and computer programming skills) helped him complete JetBlue’s challenge in less than a month. He didn’t find a secret loophole, but he did hit 25 cities in 25 days with points and just $2,000.

And this is where the story really begins.

When JetBlue announced the promotion in June, there was little fanfare, and then it seemed to fade away. But by July, Fillinger noticed rumblings on online forums — especially Reddit and Discord — and people were suddenly talking about it.

“And then it just snowballed,” he said.

Now, people are sharing 25 For 25 itineraries and spreadsheets. They’re offering advice on transportation to airports, which airports to avoid, flight deals that make completing the challenge less expensive, and even which airports are better for overnight sleeping. But what’s most remarkable in these online communities is that people are encouraging and helping one another. In some cases, they’re meeting up in person so they don’t have to make the trips alone.

“It’s like a throwback to 2010,” said one participant. “Before the Internet was all politics and bickering.”

These communities formed because of the JetBlue promotion, but the genuine human engagement is something JetBlue couldn’t have planned (nor anticipated). Even the reporter of this story didn’t learn about the JetBlue promotion until he started combing the Reddit message boards.

For Fillinger of Waltham, the timing of 25 For 25 was ideal during a less-than-perfect period of his life. He was laid off from his job in the telecom industry, as part of a wave of tech layoffs in Boston. He was informed of the layoff in June, not long before the challenge was announced. His last day was Aug. 1, and on Aug. 4, he began flying in earnest. He completed the challenge on Aug. 27. Two days later, the 350,000 points were added to his account, and his Mosiac 1 status was official.

He was the seventh person to complete the challenge.

What makes 25 For 25 a genuine challenge is that JetBlue operates as a hub-and-spoke airline. That means most flights originate and return to JetBlue’s hubs in Boston, New York, and Fort Lauderdale, making it impossible to fly direct from Los Angeles to Las Vegas or Cleveland to Detroit. That’s where the spreadsheets and complicated itineraries come into play. It’s a lot of back-and-forth with constant returns to hubs.

“The interesting thing that we learned through this process is that JetBlue’s route model is not designed to do this,” said Kyle MacDonald of Dorchester, who is taking the challenge with his husband, Andrew Parlato. “You’re constantly flying back to Boston or JFK. I think [JetBlue] is doing it because it’s actually quite complicated. Had we known how challenging this would be when we first started, I don’t know if we would’ve booked the first ticket.”

ChatGPT is ineffective at planning itineraries. Ask the AI program to create a schedule, and it will spit out routes that don’t exist or airports where JetBlue doesn’t travel. That’s where Fillinger’s tech background proved helpful. He designed an itinerary through a program he created and then shared it with others who took the challenge.

Adrianne Parent of Framingham said she learned of the challenge in mid-August while looking at Reddit, and the self-described aviation nerd decided she needed to jump in. Friends and family members have gifted her JetBlue points to help her make her travels less expensive

“When I first went on Reddit, it seemed like it was just a scattered amount of people talking about it,” she said. “But there were a couple of days in August where, in the course of 36 hours, it really ramped up and everybody was getting excited and sharing their itineraries and advice. It makes me wish that the airline gave everybody a pin or something they could wear, so we could acknowledge each other like, ‘Oh, you’re crazy, too.’”

Even without the pins, people taking the flights are finding each other. The online forums are filled with participants reaching out for travel companions for the legs of their flights. There are lots of “I’m based in Boston, does anyone want to do the challenge with me?” They’re also finding each other randomly on flights.

“I started to make friends throughout this entire journey,” said Shaun Ganly of Norwood. “As the journey went on, it really became apparent that this was a close-knit group of people who were just very friendly and all trying to figure out ‘How do I get to this goal?’ ”

Like Fillinger, Ganly had recently lost his job, and the JetBlue promotion offered an excuse to travel around the country. Ganly didn’t take the challenge to simply tick off boxes. He used it for a genuine vacation. In Detroit, he went to the Henry Ford Museum. He flew to San Diego to see his favorite team, the New York Mets, play.

“It’s weird,” Ganly said. “I’m excited, and there’s also part of me that’s a little sad that the adventure is over. ”I was able to see things that I’d never see otherwise. I’m 44 years old, and I had never been to Philadelphia. This gave me an excuse to finally go."

While Ganly was discovering Philadelphia, Parlato and MacDonald were learning the hidden joys of Tampa.

“We had a great time in Tampa,” Parlato said. “I feel like we’ll go back, and I never thought I would say that about Tampa before this trip.”

Even the point-obsessed travelers who entered the challenge simply to rack up more miles and status have found themselves pulled into the tight community of 25 For 25 participants.

“I met someone on a flight a couple of days ago,” said Jonathan Beer of Los Angeles. “And I moved seats on a flight I have in a couple of days to sit next to someone I met in the Reddit group. That’s never happened to me on any other airline, or Reddit group, or Facebook group, or Twitter group, or what have you. It’s nice to know you’re not doing this all by yourself, and that there are a lot of us out there.”

title: Following scandal, the field to succeed Fernandes Anderson on city council is narrowed to two
text:
Ahmed, who moved to the US from Somalia as a youth, said he was deeply humbled by the support.

“There is much more work ahead: tackling our housing crisis, ensuring quality schools, making our neighborhoods safe, and addressing Mass. and Cass head-on,” he said in a statement. “I will be out in the community every day, listening and working with residents to move District 7 forward.”

Culpepper, meanwhile, on Wednesday said the three biggest issues facing the district were housing, cost-of-living, and Mass. and Cass, which has become shorthand for the epicenter of the city’s dual opioid and homeless crises. He told the Globe that Tuesday’s result represented confidence in his leadership from would-be constituents.

“It’s a vote of approval for all that I’ve been doing,” he said during a brief phone interview.

The next three top vote getters — Mavrick Afonso, Samuel Hurtado, and Said Abdirahman Abdikarim —each collected about 14 percent of the votes cast, unofficial results show.

All told, 7,349 votes, including 39 write-in ballots, were cast.

Ahmed, who is originally from Somalia, was a track star in high school and later ran professionally under a Nike sponsorship deal.

He has worked with Boston youth for decades as the founder of Boston United Track and Cross Country Club, and previously ran unsuccessfully for state representative.

Culpepper is a Dorchester native and has worked at the Pleasant Hill church for more than 20 years, according to the church’s website.

He has been a longtime housing advocate, exposed racial discrimination in the Boston Housing Authority, and worked for the US Department of Housing and Urban Development, his campaign website says. He ran unsuccessfully for a state Senate seat in 2022.

Eleven candidates were vying for a two-year spot on the city’s legislative body representing District 7, which is anchored in Roxbury and includes parts of Dorchester and the South End.

It was an open seat after the July resignation of Fernandes Anderson, who was sentenced last week to one month in prison for taking a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff.

It was quite a tumble for the 46-year-old lawmaker. In 2021, she made history as the first Muslim and first formerly undocumented immigrant to be elected to the council.

District 7 is among the most diverse of the city council areas in Boston, with many residents feeling the squeeze of the city’s housing and cost-of-living crises, and a handful of the council hopefuls from the district debated housing, reparations, and ethics reform at a forum last month.

The majority of residents in Roxbury, where the district is rooted, are people of color: 41 percent Black and 30 percent Latino, according to city statistics. The neighborhood’s median household income is $42,000, well below the citywide median of $94,000.

The race has seen controversy in recent days. Ahmed allegedly harassed a Healey administration official at a mosque and during early voting over the weekend, according to police reports.

Deeqo Jibril, the Director of Small Business Development under the state’s Executive Office of Economic Development, filed a police report Saturday alleging that Ahmed had “continually harassed” her and other voters while she participated in early voting at the Shelburne Community Center in Roxbury.

One of Ahmed’s opponents also complained of his behavior to the Boston Elections Commission and the Secretary of State.

Ahmed was “harassing any Somali voters who was [sic] not voting for” him according to Jabril’s report, which was obtained by the Globe. He was also allegedly acting as a translator for Somali voters. Eventually, election officials removed him from the voting location, Jibril said.

Whoever succeeds in the general election will look to bring stability to a post that has had scandal swirling around it for months. Indeed, for a city council engulfed in controversy in recent years, Fernandes Anderson’s indictment represented a legal nadir.

She was the first Boston councilor to be indicted by the federal government since Chuck Turner in 2008, who at the time represented District 7, as well. He was convicted in 2010 of attempted extortion and three counts of providing false statements to FBI agents for accepting $1,000 in cash in exchange for helping a nightclub owner win a liquor license.

Fernandes Anderson had succeeded Kim Janey in representing District 7. Janey became acting mayor when Martin J. Walsh was tapped to become US labor secretary. Janey then ran for a full term as mayor and lost.

Samantha J. Gross, Niki Griswold and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed.

title: After a bruising defeat in the preliminary election, what’s next for Josh Kraft?
text:
When he spoke to supporters and media Tuesday night, the nonprofit leader and son of the New England Patriots owner pledged to keep campaigning.

“I believe in life, there’s always a path. It’s just hard work and sweat equity,” Kraft said. “Keep working, grinding. Sweat equity. Never quit.”

He was less clear, though, about what that fight would look like in the short term. What did he have planned? “We’re gonna figure it out tomorrow,” Kraft said late Tuesday.

But after Kraft made no appearances on Wednesday, a spokesperson for his campaign did not respond to repeated Globe queries. The only word from him was a tweet Wednesday night about the shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk that Kraft called “unimaginable and horrific.”

For some political experts, Kraft’s road ahead is limited.

“Insurmountable” was how longtime consultant Joyce Ferriabough Bolling summed up Kraft’s disadvantage.

He does not seem to have a chance of winning, she predicted, but does have the chance to reset the tone of the race. His attacks on Wu — particularly as she has won plaudits for defying President Trump’s immigration crackdown — have done him no favors with the electorate, she said.

“I definitely don’t think that he will beat her, but he has an opportunity to . . . be in the race in a more dignified way than he started out,” Ferriabough Bolling said.

As the lopsided preliminary results suggest, what Kraft has done to date isn’t working. In the last six months, he’s criss-crossed the city, attacked Wu on numerous fronts, and blanketed the airwaves with television ads that tout his experience as a nonprofit leader. Yet polling shows that Kraft’s vote share and his favorability have declined from February, when he launched his bid.

Kraft’s campaign has poured $5.6 million into the campaign so far — about $260 for every vote he received, based on a Globe analysis of monthly reports from January to August. Wu has spent just under $1.2 million this year, roughly $17 for every vote cast for her.

“The message is simply not going through. It’s not connecting with the public,” said Vincent Raynauld, an Emerson College communications professor who specializes in political messaging.

If he wants to close the gap, Kraft should undertake “a complete rethink of the campaign,” Raynauld said. “This is not going to be a minor adjustment.”

In particular, Raynauld said, Kraft needs to address “the elephant in the room”: his last name. His father’s ties to Trump, as well as his privileged background, have proven to be political liabilities; Kraft needs to address the issue head-on and put some distance between himself and his father, Raynauld said.

Scott Ferson, a political consultant who worked on an unsuccessful mayoral campaign in 2021 but is not involved in this year’s race, said Kraft “should take a few days of reflection.“

“He needs to reassess and sort of say, ‘Can I add value to the conversation, and what might that be?’ ” Ferson said. Kraft’s promise Tuesday night to recommit to the race struck an odd note, he added.

“It’s sort of like the captain of the Titanic saying, ‘No, I’m gonna look for another iceberg,’ ” Ferson said. “ ‘I want to double down on the iceberg.’ ”

Meanwhile, for Wu, the preliminary improved markedly on her results in the 2021 final election, when she defeated former city councilor Annissa Essaibi George by 28 percentage points.

In that race, Wu won an impressive 19 of the city’s 22 wards, claiming victory everywhere but in South Boston and parts of Dorchester.

This week, Wu won all 22 wards.

Recent political history offers few examples of victories as lopsided as Wu’s latest triumph. Eight years ago, when former mayor Martin J. Walsh cruised to reelection against former city councilor Tito Jackson, he won 63 percent to Jackson’s 29 percent, a margin of 34 percentage points. In 2001, former mayor Thomas Menino beat former city councilor Peggy Davis-Mullen with a margin of more than 50 percentage points.

Wu took a victory lap Wednesday during a press conference on City Hall Plaza.

“We saw resoundingly yesterday that in Boston, wins can’t be bought,” Wu said, repeating her criticism of the millions Kraft has poured into the race. “They are built day by day, by showing up and getting results for our community members.”

Some of the supporters standing by her side put a sharper point on it.

“I would not want to wake up this morning and be Josh Kraft’s campaign manager,” said state Representative Mike Moran, a Brighton Democrat. “I wouldn’t want to be his consultant.”

Indeed, the road ahead seems challenging for Kraft, political experts said.

“It’s incredibly unlikely,” said Doug Rubin, a longtime political consultant who worked for one of Wu’s rivals in the 2021 race.

“The biggest challenge to Josh Kraft is that people really love Mayor Wu and clearly have indicated they think that she’s doing a good job and that she deserves reelection,” he said. “Until he’s able to offer a compelling vision that’s different from hers and more popular than what she’s doing, I just don’t think that there’s much of a chance there.”

Rubin said Tuesday’s margin marks a significant victory for Wu, and at this point, he doesn’t see any indication the political landscape of the race will change before November.

“You just don’t normally see that kind of spread between an incumbent and what should be a serious challenger,” he said. “It’s very likely that the mayor is going to get reelected with a historic margin, and that it’s going to give her a mandate to continue to lead the city the way she’s been doing it.”

title: Springing into the fall housing market
text:
“We’re noticing more days on market. We’re noticing a closer list-to-sale price. We’re noticing price reductions across the state,” said Sarah Gustafson, president of MAR. “But at the end of the day, there’s still not enough housing for the people that need it, and that’s something to just be mindful of.”

Earlier this year, Ziegler suspected buyers and sellers were waiting for the other shoe to drop. “Headlines swirled around rates, around recession, and things were slow to start as a result,” she said. Dana Bull, a real estate adviser with Compass in Marblehead, said she noticed more canceled contracts than usual in the spring.

Will the upcoming fall market see a flurry of activity, then? While inventory has ticked up in early September, according to Ziegler, a sea change is unlikely.

“We have some people coming over from the spring. They’ve taken a couple of breaks and stepped away from [the market] to go on vacation,” said Bull. “I think they’re going to really get back into it in the fall, but I don’t see any major shifts.”

Though there likely won’t be a dramatic shake-up, there are still ways buyers and sellers can remain competitive. For buyers, that’s putting the hunt for a forever home aside, and instead reconsidering a starter home. “Metro West is still moving fast, but smaller homes farther inbound are facing more headwinds and so present more opportunity, if you can make them work for now,” Ziegler said.

Those opportunities are very location-dependent, echoed Bull. “If you’re trying to buy in Andover, good luck … you’re gonna hit a lot of competition with that, right? But, say you wanted to buy a condo in Dorchester right now? I’d be like, ‘Let’s go. You’ll get your pick of the litter.’”

In April, MAR noted the monthly supply of inventory remained flat for single-family homes, but increased 13 percent from 2024 for condominium units. Then in June, the median sales price for single-family homes jumped 3.6 percent from the previous year to $725,000, but was down 1 percent to $579,000 for condos.

“Inventory has been steadily increasing with single-families, a little bit more so with condos,” Gustafson said. “So there’s no reason that we wouldn’t anticipate that to continue into the fall, based upon what we’ve seen historically.”

According to The Warren Group, which tracks Massachusetts banking and real estate data, the condo market had four months of inventory in May for the first time since 2011. “Though the number of sales was down, an increase in inventory helped hold prices down,” said Cassidy Norton, associate publisher and media relations director for The Warren Group.

Aside from condos and town homes, properties that need a little TLC could be the ticket to homeownership. Tariffs and their potential impact on supply chains and renovation costs are something to keep in mind, Ziegler noted.

“Properties that are move-in ready, especially recently renovated, are going to command a premium price as buyers get selective despite low inventory,” she said. By avoiding those properties altogether, you might have a better shot at finding a deal.

For sellers, this fall marks a time to have honest conversations with their agents about their priorities, whether that’s selling quickly or nabbing a high sales price. If sellers aren’t pricing aggressively, there may be more work to be done.

“With fewer ‘highly motivated’ buyers, sellers are needing to consider more intensive listing preparation, such as repairs or longer periods for showings,” Ziegler said.

The bottom line is that Massachusetts is still experiencing a housing shortage, Gustafson said. For the past several months, the state has seen just over 2.2 “months of supply,” which is the inventory of homes for sale at the end of a given month divided by the average monthly pending sales from the last 12 months, according to MAR.

“So even though things may be staying on the market a little bit longer and maybe prices aren’t going up as quickly … there comes a point where the prices are only rising at the rate that the people can support it, and we’re still in a critical housing shortage,” Gustafson said.

title: Meet 5 standout leaders from the 2025 ALX100 list — and find out what they would bring to a dinner party
text:
As a middle-schooler, she participated in summer programs at the University of Massachusetts Boston and eventually received a full ride to Northeastern University — she was the first in her family to attend a four-year college.

Today, the civil engineer works as an assistant project superintendent at Suffolk Construction, one of the relatively few women of color in her field. On the day we talk, she’s waiting on a shipment of windows for a new building on Cape Cod.

In January, Sanchez closed on a home in Brockton. Though she admits she still struggles with imposter syndrome, Sanchez says her next goal on the horizon is slowing down and reflecting on all she’s accomplished so far.

“Mi orgullo es saber que vine a este país con el sueño americano de mi madre y que pude lograrlo,” she says in Spanish. I’m proud to know that I came to this country with my mother’s American dream and I was able to achieve it.

What she would bring to a dinner party: Her famous chocolate chip cookies — a recipe she honed during 2020.

By the time she was 4, it was clear to Marcela del Carmen’s family that she was going to be a doctor. Like her grandfather, she was going to enter the medical field and discover for herself the thing that seemed to make him light up inside.

“He would turn into like a teddy bear anytime that he ran into a patient or a patient’s family. I’d never seen anything like it in my life,” she recalls.

“This connection to patients and this deep love for what he did was almost intoxicating. And I remember thinking: Whatever he does, I want to do.”

She moved to the United States from Nicaragua at age 10 and never wavered from her path. Trained at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (like her grandfather), today, Dr. del Carmen is a professor of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology at Harvard Medical School.

In 2021, Del Carmen became the first woman and first person of Latino heritage to be named president of Massachusetts General Hospital and, despite her busy schedule leading one of the country’s most prestigious teaching hospitals, she intentionally looks for ways to open the door to women and people of color in the field.

“That is probably my biggest responsibility now,” she says.

What she would bring to a dinner party: Flor de Caña rum, a Nicaraguan tradition.

Yvonne Castañeda has lived many lives: personal trainer, yoga instructor, and then life coach — all before turning 44 and deciding to go back to school for social work.

The daughter of Mexican and Cuban immigrants, Castañeda knew she wanted to help others but wasn’t sure of her calling or purpose. That’s when a friend suggested psychotherapy and her trajectory shifted yet again. After earning her master’s at Boston College, in 2022 she founded her private practice, SoulFuerza Therapy, providing trauma-informed psychotherapy to individuals, couples, and families, in English and Spanish. Today, she is the director of community-based initiatives and a part-time faculty member at BC.

“I couldn’t have planned it,” she says. “There was no way for me to know at 20 that being a therapist is what I want to do.”

That same year, she published her book, Pork Belly Tacos with a Side of Anxiety, a deeply personal memoir exploring her life and struggles with anxiety, addiction, and an eating disorder. It was the kind of book she wanted to be able to give to others to help them feel less alone. It’s also a nod to her personal therapeutic style with clients: not rushing to make them better, but allowing them to show up as their full selves, thus making space for healing.

What she would bring to a dinner party: Pork belly tacos, of course.

It all started on a golf course.

After his family moved from Venezuela to Philadelphia when he was 4, Carlos Febres-Mazzei would go on to eventually land a job as a caddy. That sparked a love for the game, which motivated him to study urban planning and landscape architecture at the University of Maryland. He started his career designing courses, and if you’ve golfed at resorts in the Caribbean or Central America, he might have had an influence on them.

Realizing he could have more sway if he were on the financial side of things, Febres-Mazzei then went to Babson College to complete his MBA. From there, he entered commercial real estate, leading to construction projects in the Seaport and Cambridge, as well as other locations across the country. In 2012, the Boston Business Journal named him on its “40 under 40” list.

Febres-Mazzei is now the managing principal at QuakerLane, an enterprise he started in 2018 to help investors raise capital for big developments. “It’s a great opportunity to show the world what [people of color] can do,” he says. “And that means being great partners, but also being great citizens and participants in our community and our economy.”

When he’s not serving on nonprofit boards, he’s in a group chat cheering on other local Latino entrepreneurs — and he’s recently entered the hospitality business, too. He loves fine dining and now co-owns a French restaurant in the mountains of Colorado called Betula Aspen.

What he would bring to a dinner party: Venezuelan arepas and a mushroom truffle risotto from his restaurant.

Food is sacred, the land is sacred — and so are those who care for it.

That is what Michael Del Río’s grandfather preached. As a queer Afro-Latino, Del Río, who uses they/them pronouns, found power in learning about the connection between personal health, food justice, and Indigenous land rights while growing up in the Dominican Republic.

After attending the University of Rhode Island, they spent a couple of years in Ethiopia with the Peace Corps. Del Río returned to the United States in 2020 and started hatching plans. Ideally they could work at the nexus of food production and food justice but with an educational bent...if only such a place existed.

That’s when Del Río discovered The Farm School in Athol — 130 acres filled with goats, chickens, cows, and pigs, as well as dozens of varieties of fruits and vegetables. Every year an estimated 1,500 students visit to learn about the production of milk and cheese and the essentials of running a farm. Del Río teaches many of these students while also working the land, which ultimately provides food for local senior citizens, with surplus produce going to the Dorchester Food Co-op.

Del Río hopes that through this work, more youth will be inspired to follow a similar path. “I know the need is still huge in our state,” they say. “If anything, I would love for more projects like [our school] to be a reality for more students...where they’re able to develop a relationship to the land and see where their food is coming from.”

What they would bring to a dinner party: A fresh watermelon from the farm and Ethiopian food.

Because of a reporting error, a previous version of this story misidentified Michael Del Río’s country of birth. He is from the Dominican Republic. It also incorrectly identified who brought Jhadley Thahychy Sanchez to the United States, and the location of her childhood home, which is Santo Domingo. The Globe regrets the error.

title: UMass Boston security incident deemed ‘all clear’ by police, university says
text:
UMass Boston chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco said in a letter to the university community that the campus had “experienced reports of shots being fired in a residence hall and other locations” but police found no evidence of gunfire anywhere on campus, and no injuries were reported.

“We know how unsettling this incident was, especially for those on campus who experienced the large public safety response and campus-wide sweep, as well as for all of your families, friends, and loved ones,” Suárez-Orozco wrote.

The university alerted students about 3:40 p.m. of a “police incident” on campus and urged people to avoid the area. Another alert about 20 minutes later reported a “public safety threat” near a residence hall, and at about 5:11 p.m., the university said police had declared there was “no ongoing threat to the community.”

Boston police also responded to the university but did not confirm any reports of gunshots, according to Sergeant Detective John Boyle, a Boston police spokesman.

The incident came a week after the UMass Lowell campus went into lockdown when a suspected gunman was seen outside a dorm, but was later determined to be a boy carrying an airsoft replica gun.

Students at UMass Boston were seen running from buildings and toward police as fear spread that an active shooter might be on campus.

Bella Biondi, 21, a senior majoring in entrepreneurship, watched from the balcony of her apartment across the street from campus. Biondi said she saw “cop car after cop car pulling up” and moved closer to find out what was happening.

She said she saw students running, with some saying “shots fired.” Some referenced the seventh floor of the East Residence Hall, while others said the 10th floor, Biondi said.

After the “all clear” came, Biondi said she heard murmurs of a “false alarm.”

“You can’t just say, ‘false alarm,’” Biondi said, adding that it left her feeling uneasy.

State Police reported that they checked the 10th floor of Residence Hall East as well as the 12th floor and found no sign of an active shooter, according to the recordings on Broadcastify.

Olivia Burke, 18, a freshman from Scituate who lives in the East Residence Hall, said she was in her dorm when an alarm — not a fire alarm, but something quieter — went off. She went to her friend’s dorm in the West Residence Hall, where they looked outside and saw police and SWAT officers going into the East Hall.

“They told us to stay in the dorm and not to open the door unless it was police officers and to not talk,” Burke said.

After about 10 minutes, they were evacuated with their hands up and were patted down by officers, she said.

“It was very crazy,” Burke said. “This whole day has become really unfortunately frightening.”

Students arriving at the campus for afternoon classes and activities were also confused and concerned by the scene.

Kobe Hoang, 25, a senior majoring in business analytics and information systems, commutes from Leominster. He got an alert on his phone as he was riding a bus to the campus. When Hoang got off the bus, he said he saw about 15 students running toward police officers.

“I don’t know the full extent of what’s going on, I don’t know if anyone is armed or if someone got hurt,” he said.

Kevin Rodrigues, 19, a sophomore, said he was in a lecture hall with a couple hundred other students waiting for their class to begin when they heard people shouting outside.

“The whole lecture hall ... just went quiet to look back, and then panic just erupted everywhere and everybody ran,” Rodrigues said. “There were some people that stayed behind to help others that were physically unable to help themselves, which I was really happy to see.”

Police were searching both the UMass Boston campus and nearby Boston College High School, according to broadcast transmissions.

Pat Sullivan, 17, a student at BC High, said he and other students were held in rooms as the campus went into a lockdown. He said they watched out windows as police, fire trucks, and ambulances passed by.

“We saw crowds [of] people move into the intersection of Morrissey Boulevard, so we had assumed that they evacuated the area, but it was like a very tense scenario there,” he said. “There was just not a lot of info going around, so everyone was sort of worrying.”

BC High did not immediately return messages seeking further information Thursday.

The incident is under investigation by police, UMass Boston officials said on social media. Classes and activities on campus were canceled Thursday night.

Mike Bello and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: After firing their brother, are the Demoulas sisters prepping Market Basket for a sale?
text:
📢 Sign up now for the inaugural Trendlines webinar, where Globe reporter Dana Gerber and I will break down President Trump’s pressure campaign on higher education. Tune in on Sept. 30 at noon.

Times have changed. That’s why there’s been no uprising at Market Basket this time around.

Harvard said it received notice that the federal government will begin restoring research grants the administration had previously revoked.

Inflation edged up in August and initial jobless claims hit a nearly four-year high last week, bolstering the case for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates.

Arthur T. Demoulas is gone, forced out as CEO of Market Basket by his three sisters. What will the supermarket company look like without him?

A lot like it does now, the company says. Same low prices, same friendly people behind the deli counter and cash registers.

But don’t be surprised if Market Basket gets more aggressive, adding stores at a faster clip and in a wider geographic swath. Moreover, it’s a reasonable bet that 10 years from now, maybe sooner, the Tewksbury company will be controlled not by the Demoulas family, but by a private equity firm or another grocery operator.

Artie T., as Demoulas is widely known, “missed an opportunity to expand throughout the Northeast,” said Burt Flickinger III, managing director of Strategic Resource Group, a retail consulting firm. “This company can double its market share and triple its market value in seven years.”

Demoulas did run the company cautiously, in part to conserve cash to pay off the $1.6 billion in debt that he and his sisters took on when they bought out a rival faction of the family. It was a strategy that largely worked for Market Basket.

But the sisters appear to have been convinced it’s time for a new approach that will pay off in the future. Artie T. was fired as CEO late Tuesday by a board they installed and told to wrest operational control from their autocratic sibling.

“The board’s actions are a farcical cover up for a coup,” Justine Griffin, a spokesperson for Demoulas, said in a statement. She declined to say whether Demoulas, who has contested the ouster, would sue the company to get his job back.

On Wednesday, board chair Jay Hachigian tried to calm fears that Demoulas’ departure signaled changes ahead at the 90-store chain revered by customers and many employees.

Market Basket will not alter “its operations, profit-sharing, bonuses, or culture, and will continue to offer the best groceries at the lowest prices anywhere in New England — well into the future,” he said in a statement.

If that’s the plan, you might be wondering why his sisters — Frances, Glorianne, and Caren — went to war with their brother, his children, and loyal senior executives.

The stated reason: Artie T. didn’t fully comply with the board’s demands to provide more detailed information on finances and store openings, and pinky swear that he wouldn’t put one of his kids in charge down the road.

In May, the directors put the obstinate CEO on paid leave, saying they suspected he was organizing an employee uprising to protect his job — similar to the events of 2014 when Demoulas was temporarily pushed out by cousin Arthur S. Demoulas.

An investigation by outside lawyers doesn’t appear to have turned up any evidence of a plot. A spokesperson for the board declined to comment on the investigation’s findings.

Then there is the unstated reason: the sisters’ frustration with their brother’s cautious approach to expansion. A faster-growing company could increase profits — and payouts to shareholders. Market Basket has opened about two stores a year since 2014.

The sisters together own roughly 60 percent of Market Basket — 20 percent each — while Artie T. holds 28 percent. The four siblings each received dividends of about $200 million last year, or about 10 percent of revenue. Not bad for a business their grandparents started more than a century ago in a Lowell storefront.

But the sisters will need capital if they want to expand quickly. They’ve got several options, including borrowing money or bringing in a deep-pocketed private equity partner.

Flickinger estimates the company’s market value is between $8 billion and $10 billion. He thinks it would be worth as much as $30 billion after adding another roughly 60 stores. He sees no reason why Market Basket couldn’t line up financing for new locations.

Eventually, however, a sale seems likely. Why?

Supermarkets are rapidly consolidating. From Whole Foods to BI-LO/Harveys to FreshDirect, local and regional chains are being bought up by national players and private equity. Market Basket is caught in the middle, neither a small local operator nor a giant national one.

Perhaps the biggest indicator of the sisters’ intentions is the very firing squad they assembled to terminate their brother.

Hachigian is a lawyer who specializes in mergers and acquisitions. Steven Collins is a private equity executive who has bought and sold numerous retail companies. And Michael Keyes, the third remaining board member, is a real estate executive. Market Basket owns most of the real estate where its stores are located, a valuable asset to potential buyers.

A sale would need Artie T.’s approval. Or maybe the sisters will buy him out. He’s 70 — how long does he want the family feud to continue?

The directors are trained deal-makers. They should start with the CEO they just canned.

“I think the economy is weakening. Whether it’s on the way to recession or just weakening, I don’t know.”

— JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon, after the Labor Department reported that employers added 911,000 fewer jobs than previously estimated from April 2024 to March 2025.

Greasing the skids: Governor Maura Healey unveiled regulatory reforms that aim to speed up environmental reviews while ensuring that new housing developments meet state climate and environmental standards.

Slimming down: Danish pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, maker of Wegovy, said it would cut 9,000 jobs amid heightened competition for weight-loss drugs

Stymied: The Trump administration appealed a Tuesday night ruling blocking the president from firing Fed Governor Lisa Cook as he seeks more control over the traditionally independent board.

Fresh start: Lawrence General Hospital, along with Holy Family Hospital campuses in Haverhill and Methuen — which it acquired from bankrupt Steward Health Care — are being rebranded as Merrimack Health.

— The net worth of Larry Ellison, the 81-year-old cofounder of Oracle, on Wednesday, when hebriefly surpassed Elon Musk as the world’s richest person, according to Bloomberg, until Musk climbed back to the top spot by a mere $1 billion.

Two Boston restaurants — whose renowned chefs the Globe has lauded — received an important nod this week from The New York Times.

La Padrona in the Back Bay and McGonagle’s in Dorchester were named to the Times’ annual 50 best restaurants list.

Globe food correspondent Kara Baskin explains.

Globe critic Devra First awarded star chef Jody Adams’ La Padrona four stars in her review, praising its extensive bread program, “ethereal” Tagliatelle Emilia-Romagna, and “perfect” lobster and uni risotto. The restaurant sits high atop the Raffles luxury hotel and condos.

McGonagle’s is an Irish pub whose executive chef, Aidan McGee, has worked at Michelin-star restaurants in Europe, and helped to modernize Boston’s Irish food scene with another pub, The Dubliner, across from City Hall.

The new pub makes the list “thanks to McGee’s reimagining of what Irish food can be,” including Irish cheese croquettes with black truffle mayonnaise, and a “spice bag” with cumin-spiked fried chicken, Kara writes.

McGonagle’s arrival is good news for Dorchester, which kissed the Blarney Stone goodbye last summer.

title: Hasbro’s move to Boston was years in the making. Here’s how it went down.
text:
Both moves reaffirm the value of big-city locations for employers, after their draw came into question during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Quest for Hasbro turned out to be worthy of an adventure cooked up by Wizards of the Coast, Hasbro’s West Coast business, for a Dungeons & Dragons module. It started back in 2018, with a different adventuring party: Governor Charlie Baker’s administration.

Baker’s then-economic development secretary, Jay Ash, had learned Hasbro might be looking to leave while running point on another relocation effort for Baker: moving the Pawtucket Red Sox, now the WooSox, to Worcester.

Ash says he reached out to Hasbro to start a conversation. A junior community relations person told him, thanks, we’ll be in touch if the need arises. Ash never heard back.

Rumors that Hasbro chief executive Brian Goldner wanted a more modern, urban headquarters persisted. After Ash left state government at the end of 2018 to oversee the Massachusetts Competitive Partnership (a group of high-powered CEOs), the state agency he had led continued its overtures to Hasbro in 2019, without much luck.

Pitches flowed in to the Baker administration, from Worcester, Attleboro, Seekonk. At one point, Reebok’s former campus in Canton (now home to insurer Point32Health) was brought up. Still, no dice.

Goldner was tight with then-Rhode Island governor Gina Raimondo, and a big booster of the state through the Partnership for Rhode Island (the Mass. Competitive Partnership’s counterpart). You didn’t need a Ouija board to know the smart money was on Providence, not Massachusetts.

Headquarters talk then took a back seat to other issues. The pandemic hit in 2020. Goldner died after a long fight with prostate cancer in 2021. Chris Cocks ascended to the Hasbro CEO throne in 2022, elevated from his job running Wizards of the Coast; he then had to contend with a proxy fight with an activist shareholder eager to see Wizards spun off. Cocks won, the Wizards stayed. In 2023, Cocks reached a deal to sell off Hasbro’s film and TV business, eOne, to Lionsgate.

Fast forward to April 2024. Governor Maura Healey’s economic development secretary, Yvonne Hao, was having dinner with business leaders at Zuma, a swanky Japanese restaurant in the Four Seasons on Dalton Street. Cocks was among them. They struck up a conversation. Cocks mentioned that Hasbro was considering a move to help attract more talent, Hao recalls, and she was happy to offer a solution: Come here.

The next day, at 6 a.m., Hao emailed Cocks saying the Healey administration would love to talk more about a potential relocation, and cited all the consumer brands already in Boston’s orbit, such as Converse, Wayfair, New Balance, Whoop, and now Lego.

Cocks responded right away. This time, there was considerable interest. Cocks mentioned Hasbro’s Massachusetts roots in his note to Hao, and the Springfield-born Milton Bradley business in particular. “It would be great to figure out a permanent home for us in Boston and to be a creative center for the toys and games industry in the city,” Cocks wrote. “We are just kicking off the process so the timing of our meeting is propitious.”

Cocks connected Hao with Tarrant Sibley, Hasbro’s chief legal officer, to continue the conversation. Sibley also struck a positive tone, asking for a meeting to discuss “what Massachusetts might be able to do to facilitate a move to the greater Boston area.” That led to a meeting on Beacon Hill in July of last year: State officials discussed the Economic Development Incentive Program, which offers tax credits to companies that add jobs here. (Next week, a state council will take up offering $14 million in EDIP credits for Hasbro, the biggest such award since 2020.)

To keep the conversation going, in August, Hao emailed Sibley and other Hasbro executives a photo of playing Scrabble in the office with lieutenant Ashley Stolba while waiting to see if the Legislature would pass a major economic development bill. (That ended up happening in November.)

Meanwhile, the rumors swirled around Boston about where Hasbro might land. What about the Burnham Building, in the heart of Downtown Crossing, which was about to be vacated by ad agency Arnold for GE’s former Fort Point headquarters? Great transit access there. Or maybe the former Boston Globe building in Dorchester, now called Southline? Plenty of parking there. (No, BU’s “Jenga Building” was not considered.)

Eventually, the chatter turned to 400 Summer St., a new WS Development building in the Seaport that Roche-subsidiary Foundation Medicine had leased. With the decline in the lab market, Foundation no longer needed all that room and offered a significant chunk up for sublease, presumably at a big discount. It became hard for other office landlords in town to compete on price. By sometime in the spring of 2025, the word on the street was that Hasbro had signed a letter of intent with Foundation.

But still no word from Pawtucket. Maybe things died down because summer was starting. Maybe the tariff craziness under the Trump administration prompted caution about any big decisions.

Finally, on Monday, the day before Mayor Michelle Wu would dominate the preliminary elections in Boston, Hasbro announced it would move its Pawtucket operations to 265,000 square feet across seven floors at 400 Summer, by the end of 2026. Hasbro currently expects workers to come in three days a week, and no changes are expected to that. The company made a point in the press release to highlight its Wizards office in Renton, Wash., where 500 people work, as its other main hub.

It’s notable that Rhode Island’s T.F. Green Airport has no direct flights to Seattle, while Boston’s Logan Airport offers nonstops there from Delta, JetBlue, and Alaska Airlines. A spokeswoman said the convenience for “colleagues and partners flying in to visit” is just one of many reasons Hasbro picked the Seaport location, a short drive from Logan.

Many questions remain for Pawtucket. The hardscrabble city has lost its hospital, baseball team, and now its one big publicly traded company. (Hasbro owns its site and says it wants the place to “be a meaningful space for the community” after it leaves.)

But the Hasbro news represents a victory for the Healey and Wu administrations — and for Boston. Hasbro becomes the latest big New England company to move here, after GE in 2016, Alexion in 2018, and Lego’s North American headquarters more recently. (GE is now gone, but its spun-out energy businesses remain, under GE Vernova, in Cambridge.)

Hao, who left state government this year, says Hasbro’s decision underscores the strengths of our underrated consumer sector. To Ash, it represents the promise of innovation converging across numerous industries, coming together in the same place. To Segun Idowu, Wu’s economic development chief, it highlights how Boston’s vibrancy is a draw of its own.

Maybe a case can be made that Boston is turning into Toy Town, with two of the world’s biggest players here.

More importantly, the Hasbro move confirms that dynamic cities such as Boston will continue to draw major employers, as they did pre-COVID, even amid the wide acceptance of hybrid and remote options. Employers are still hunting for talent. That means setting up shop in places where people — particularly young people — want to work and live. And maybe play a little Scrabble, too.

title: Sheriff Tompkins was once set up for a lifetime of easy reelections. A lot changed in the past five years.
text:
On the very same day that purchase closed, one of his top aides announced she was running against him — a stiff challenge that prompted Tompkins to put up tens of thousands of dollars of his own money to fight off.

Soon, the value of his stake in the weed company was in free fall. And that’s when Tompkins doubled down on what prosecutors say was already an illegal deal and demanded that the owner of the cannabis company refund his $50,000 investment.

Now, Tompkins faces charges that could put the longtime jailer behind bars himself. Last month, a federal grand jury indicted the sheriff on two counts of extortion for allegedly using the power of his office to strong-arm the cannabis company.

Tompkins, 68, has pleaded not guilty and taken medical leave from his post. His attorney, Martin G. Weinberg, said Tompkins will defend himself “in a future trial before a jury of the sheriff’s peers and not in the media.”

An early stumble

Tompkins first came into the sheriff’s office in 2013 when he was appointed to replace his boss, who had accepted a position in then-Governor Deval Patrick’s Cabinet. But the ink was hardly dry on his commission when a number of store owners in Roxbury complained he had flashed his new badge at them and pressured them to take down signs supporting his opponent in the upcoming election.

The State Ethics Commission fined him $2,500, and Tompkins said he’d “learned from the experience” and wouldn’t slip again. But Tompkins found himself in the commission’s crosshairs a second time after he created a taxpayer-funded job for a niece a few years later, and had her and other employees do errands and other personal business for him.

Globe interviews with eight former and current subordinates, as well as public records, paint a picture of a sheriff who was more interested in the trappings of the office than in the running of it, and who spent heavily on travel and other perks.

Those employees said Tompkins is seldom if ever seen at the Nashua Street jail, which along with the House of Correction is one of the two main facilities the sheriff oversees. Over the past five months — the full span of available records — Tompkins never swiped his access card at the jail, according to records the sheriff’s department provided in response to a Globe request.

While employees describe Tompkins as an absentee boss, he has been a longtime fixture at Democratic Party events, and his resume is heavy on politics and light on law enforcement; in fact, when Patrick appointed him sheriff, he said that was what drew him to Tompkins.

“It’s a political job, so the folks that are criticizing it as a political hire, tell them: They’re right,” Patrick said at the time.

But unlike many Boston pols, Tompkins wasn’t born here. He was raised in Harlem by a single parent on public assistance, he has said, describing his youth as “hard-knock.”

Tompkins came north to Boston College, where he was a classmate of Cabral, who would hire him when she became sheriff in 2002. After graduation, Tompkins worked a variety of jobs, including at AT&T’s cable division and the Federal Emergency Management Agency and a stint as director of marketing and public affairs for the Dimock Community Health Center in Roxbury.

He became more politically active, landing a position with the local branch of the NAACP and serving on various boards: the Sportsmen’s tennis club, the youth-focused nonprofit City Year, the fiscal watchdog known as the Boston Finance Commission, and more.

Affable and chatty, with a wide smile, Tompkins became a regular at Boston political events. He would sometimes show up at rival rallies, giving the impression he supported both camps.

In 2013, while attending an event for US Representative Stephen Lynch’s Senate bid, the newly minted sheriff parroted the tagline from the candidate’s ad: “We are all Stephen Lynch.”

Tompkins had also appeared at an event for Lynch’s rival, then US Representative Edward Markey, prompting both campaigns to tout his support. When asked, the sheriff hedged his bets.

“I wasn’t with either candidate,” Tompkins told the Dorchester Reporter.

In 2016, Tompkins made an unsuccessful bid to be chairman of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, a campaign he had to pause briefly because of the sudden death of his wife.

The sheriff’s Facebook page is a who’s who of Democratic politics. There’s a picture of Senator Elizabeth Warren speaking at a 2014 Tompkins campaign event with future Mayor Michelle Wu looking on. A 2017 image shows Tompkins in a top hat with Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and Middlesex Sheriff Peter J. Koutoujian. There’s Tompkins with Mayor Martin J. Walsh at Fenway Park in 2018, and more recent shots with Governor Charlie Baker and his successor, Maura Healey.

In 2018, Boston Magazine named Tompkins No. 76 on its list of the 100 most influential Bostonians, saying the sheriff had “quietly become one of the most popular elected officials in Boston.”

In short, in the world of Boston politics, everybody knew Steve. And many like him — though many are loath to talk about him in the wake of his indictment.

A couple of exceptions: state Senator Lydia Edwards, an East Boston Democrat, who considers Tompkins a friend. She described him as “funny, loyal, good guy.”

“I’m withholding all judgment,” she said of his current predicament. “I don’t dance on my friend’s grave.”

Michael Curry, former president of the Boston branch of the NAACP, recalled seeing Tompkins work the room this year at the Reggie Lewis Center during the Brothers IV Breakfast, a community event intended to foster fellowship. Tompkins tried to connect with every young person in the room, he said.

Curry described Tompkins as “always available, a people person who leads with humor.”

Former state treasurer Steve Grossman, whom Tompkins has supported in past political campaigns, described the sheriff as “popular, well liked, and well regarded.”

Like Edwards, Grossman said Tompkins was owed due process.

“You can understand why people are grieving over this,” he said. “And why people across the political spectrum are not rushing to judgment. People don’t want the charges to be true.”

‘Comfort and complacency’

For some erstwhile Tompkins supporters, the sheriff lost his luster well before his indictment.

Paul Parara, better known as the Notorious VOG, a local radio host who interviews politicians for a primarily Black and brown audience, noted that early in his tenure as sheriff, Tompkins talked forcefully about rehabilitating inmates. Indeed, at the sheriff’s office, Tompkins helped create a vocational training program for inmates about to be released.

But Parara doesn’t believe those efforts have amounted to much, and he recently called on Tompkins to resign.

“Tompkins once spoke of reform and rehabilitation,” he said. “But today he represents the comfort and complacency of the system.”

But Curry had a different take, recalling how Tompkins had helped steer the NAACP’s messaging on policing, community violence, education, and the economy. He described the sheriff as “super knowledgeable . . . always committed to community and social justice issues.”

Curry has had Tompkins in to speak to his students at New England Law | Boston, where Curry is a lecturer, and said the sheriff focused on reentry rather than incarceration, and posed societal questions: “How do we understand what are the conditions that made young people and people in general commit crimes?”

It was Tompkins’s reentry program that is at the heart of his current legal troubles. Ascend Wellness Holdings, a cannabis firm, struck a partnership with the sheriff’s office to hire former inmates as part of its licensing process. Prosecutors allege Tompkins used the deal as leverage to buy a stake in the firm.

But it appears Ascend was unable to hire any of the former inmates the sheriff steered its way, according to a sheriff’s department spokesman and email correspondence obtained by the Globe through a public-records request. Ascend did not respond to messages from the Globe.

Parara isn’t the only observer who accuses Tompkins of doing little to help those in his care.

Janhavi Madabushi, director of the Massachusetts Bail Fund, which lobbies for less restrictive conditions for the accused, tends to be broadly critical of sheriffs. But he singled out Tompkins in particular, saying he “co-opts progressive language and buzzwords” to make it seem like he’s an advocate for the downtrodden when his main interest is “political power.”

In 2021, Tompkins proposed a portion of an unused Suffolk County detention center be repurposed to house people who struggle with homelessness, drug addiction, and mental health problems in the drug-plagued neighborhood known as Mass. and Cass. Some other public officials criticized the idea as inhumane, and though it was the subject of intense discussions, it never got off the ground.

On the other hand, Tompkins was an early critic among law enforcement officials of the war on drugs. In a 2016 panel discussion, he called the effort a “flaming joke,” complaining that kingpins tended to skirt arrest, and saying it had mostly resulted in young men of color spending years behind bars.

Despite those progressive views, Tompkins wasn’t ready to legalize marijuana. When Massachusetts was preparing to vote on the question in 2016, Tompkins led a group of Massachusetts sheriffs in denouncing the idea.

“As a Commonwealth, we need not take actions that could increase availability to, and use of drugs among, young people,” Tompkins said at the time. “If this referendum were to pass, Massachusetts would surely see an increase in the amount of marijuana use and addiction.”

Four years later, Tompkins was angling to get into the pot business.

Milking the office

According to prosecutors, sometime in 2020, Tompkins told Frank Perullo of Ascend — the businessman and lobbyist he is now accused of extorting — that “he wanted to get in on the stock so [he] could make some cannabis money.”

Perullo allowed him to invest in Ascend in November 2020, when the company was still privately held; Ascend went public in May 2021, and initially its stock rose. Tompkins’s $50,000 stake came from a retirement account, according to the indictment.

Records show Tompkins made another significant investment a few months after Ascend went public, adding to his debt. On Jan. 5, 2022, he bought a property in Roxbury for $550,000, putting 25 percent down. Weeks earlier, he had refinanced the debt on his primary home, in Hyde Park, taking out a much bigger loan on it.

The same day Tompkins closed on the Roxbury property, Sandy Zamor-Calixte, the sheriff’s chief of external affairs, announced she was running against him. Zamor-Calixte, who declined to comment for this article, eventually received 41 percent of the vote.

In the face of that challenge, Tompkins ended up loaning his campaign a total of $67,500 in personal funds — a bit more than the value of his holdings in Ascend. It took him nearly two years to raise the money to pay himself back.

Throughout the campaign, his stake in Ascend was losing value. Tompkins demanded to be made whole, according to the indictment.

By the end of 2022, Perullo had returned nearly all of Tompkins’s $50,000 investment. His shares were worth less than $17,000 at that point.

Over Tompkins’s tenure, meanwhile, state credit card records for the office suggest a growing department spending habit on restaurants, conferences, and junkets.

During the last fiscal year, the Sheriff’s Department spent more than $133,000 using the card, a tally that covered trips for multiple employees to visit Austin, Texas; New Orleans; Baltimore; Washington, D.C.; the Bahamas; and Martha’s Vineyard.

Last year’s spending on the office credit card — which typically is used for travel, meals, and miscellaneous items — was more than five times the amount billed to it a decade earlier, when Tompkins was still new to the job. Records provided to the Globe thus far are incomplete, but show that Tompkins traveled frequently on the card.

On Aug. 8, Tompkins was on one of the trips billed to the card. He was arrested by FBI agents in Hollywood, Fla., while attending the annual conference of the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives, or NOBLE. Tompkins was a regular at the group’s annual meetings, records show, and two NOBLE leaders say he was instrumental in establishing its current state chapter.

Renée Hall, NOBLE president, said Tompkins currently does not hold any leadership positions there. She said she had no “personal thoughts” about Tompkins’s arrest and indictment.

“If he is found to be on the other side of the law, then he should, like anyone else, be held accountable,” she said. “Until that happens, we support him as a member.”

Jeremiah Manion and Matt Stout of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Jeff Rogers, creative consultant who cofounded Hella Black Trivia, dies at 43
text:
From its beginnings in Roxbury, Hella Black Trivia grew rapidly in popularity as gatherings expanded at cafés, restaurants, and universities. “It’s really about opening people’s minds to what Black trivia could be,” he told WBUR-FM in 2020.

Mr. Rogers, whose sharp knowledge of arcane facts and details about past Black experiences often reached beyond the grasp of those who were historians by trade, died Sept. 7 after collapsing at a friend’s home. He was 43, lived in Dorchester, and tests to determine the cause are pending, his family said.

“What’s remarkable about his work was that he was finding intriguing and innovative ways to make Black history relevant,” said Noelle N. Trent, president and chief executive of the Museum of African American History, Boston and Nantucket, which partnered with Mr. Rogers in June for a Hella Black Trivia event.

“This is a loss that I think will be felt across the community,” Trent said, “and that says he left a mark that was meaningful.”

Friends recalled that as a trivia night host, Mr. Rogers showed how disparate facts were linked to each other, illuminating connections audiences had never considered. He did so, they said, in ways that were entertaining and never condescending.

“He created an energy,” Trent said. “With Jeff, you saw his passion to educate. He was about telling people all the things that they should know.”

Mr. Rogers always had “hard to find information” at his fingertips, said Rufus J. Faulk, a friend since middle school who co-owns The Mix restaurant in Dorchester.

“It was like, ‘How do you even come up with this?’ He was a Rolodex of information,” said Faulk, who formerly worked in the mayoral administrations of Martin Walsh and Michelle Wu.

The lessons Mr. Rogers taught went beyond the joys of trivia to fostering a sense of belonging in the Black community, friends said.

“It was profound the way he would see the world and see our history as a very affirming thing,” said state Senator Liz Miranda, a Boston Democrat.

Hella Black Trivia “was not just about knowing Black history,” Miranda said. “It’s about community, it’s about joy, it’s about the act of remembering.”

Hosting trivia nights, Mr. Rogers “was not just smart. He was a level above,” Miranda said. “He was incredibly witty, innovative, kind, brilliant. I swear he was gifted.”

And he was always ready to share what he had learned.

Audiences crave both knowledge and the feeling of belonging, Mr. Rogers told writer Jacquinn Sinclair for WBUR’s 2020 report.

“People have a thirst for trivia,” he said. “They have a thirst for community.”

As a friend and a consultant, Mr. Rogers helped others begin or improve their own careers, said Sheena Collier, founder and chief executive of The Collier Connection consulting firm and of Boston While Black, a membership community that connects Black professionals.

“He was someone who gave so much of himself,” Collier said. “He really took care of his people. The breadth and depth of the ways he’s impacted people have been overwhelming.”

On his LinkedIn profile, where Mr. Rogers discussed his approach to being an executive coach and a diversity, equity, and inclusion facilitator, he stressed the importance and necessity of unity.

“I love bringing people together to solve problems,” Mr. Rogers wrote. “I understand that solving problems is about uniting people. I know that that’s what leadership is.”

Jeffrey Mark Rogers was born in Dorchester on Nov. 4, 1981.

The third of four siblings, he was a son of Paul K. Rogers, who retired as a phone company manager, and Kathleen Arsenault Rogers, who has worked in medical research and health care.

The nickname “The Professor” that Mr. Rogers used when hosting Hella Black Trivia dated back to his youth.

“As a kid, he was very, very, very precocious. He was always advanced in learning,” said his younger brother, Dwayne, of Tampa.

That didn’t make school an easy place for Mr. Rogers.

If teachers and adults wanted to debate a point with him, “you needed to have facts, you needed to have understanding, you had to have reasoning to back up what you were saying,” Dwayne recalled. “As you can imagine, he drove many teachers wild.”

Though he would later teach college graduate students, Mr. Rogers left high school and earned a general equivalency diploma.

“It took him a while to find his way because of his questioning of authority,” Dwayne said. Then Mr. Rogers followed the path of his curiosity and growing knowledge into the consulting field.

“It had been right there in front of him all the time,” Dwayne said.

Naeemah Smith was Mr. Rogers’s partner of 16 years. She and her son, Sahmir Russell, survive him, as do Jaiyere and Chief Jasaad Rogers, Mr. Rogers’s sons from his marriage to Kimesha Janey, which ended in divorce.

In addition to his parents, who live in Dorchester, and his brother Dwayne, Mr. Rogers leaves another brother, Paul D. Rogers of Quincy, and a sister, Jill Clark of Riverview, Fla.

A viewing will be held from 2 to 4 p.m. Monday in the Floyd A. Williams Funeral Home in Dorchester. A celebration of life will begin at 6 p.m. Monday in the Venezia waterfront restaurant in Boston.

Bringing the same patience and careful listening to his family and friends as he did to his consulting clients, Mr. Rogers would “help you clear up the fog in your own head,” Dwayne said.

“The main thing about him was that he had an open ear,” Dwayne said. “If you had a question, he could sit down and act like a therapist.”

Mr. Rogers centered conversations so they were “about you, and it would always come down to you making a decision about yourself,” his brother said. “When things were chaotic, his favorite thing was to come in, calm things down, and leave things better than he found them.”

Though Mr. Rogers will long be remembered for his consulting work and by the countless people who attended Hella Black Trivia, “he really flourished as a father,” Miranda said.

Dwayne said that because his brother “took so long to find his own way, because he took the road less traveled, he was able to take those lessons and hand them to his sons.”

“The number one thing about his legacy,” Miranda said, “will be the sons that he raised — that they are compassionate, brilliant, service-minded, innovative young men.”

title: Recount being sought in Boston City Council District 7 race after Mavrick Afonso finishes 20 votes shy of 2nd place
text:
District 7 candidate Mavrick Afonso is formally requesting a recount of last week’s preliminary election in the crowded race to succeed federally convicted Tania Fernandes Anderson on the Boston City Council, Afonso’s campaign announced Monday.

Afonso, who works for the state’s Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, came in third in last week’s preliminary election with just 20 fewer votes than the second place finisher, according to the city’s unofficial election results.

Former track and field star and current coach Said Ahmed earned 1,155 votes last week, while attorney and senior pastor the Rev. Miniard Culpepper claimed 1,102 votes, according to the city’s unofficial tally. The two were set to advance to November’s general election, a result Afonso — who got 1,082 votes in the preliminary — is now seeking to contest given the tight margin between him and Culpepper.

“With so much at stake for District 7, voters deserve certainty that every ballot was counted correctly,” Afonso said in a statement Monday. “This isn’t about politics, it’s about protecting the integrity of our democracy. The fact that other candidates and community leaders are united proves that fairness matters more than campaign lines.”

Several other candidates who ran for the District 7 spot, the only open seat on last week’s preliminary election ballot, support Afonso’s recount request, his campaign said.

Fellow District 7 candidates Said Abdikarim, Samuel Hurtado, and Wawa Bell are helping Afonso collect the necessary signatures for his recount petition, which his campaign will file with the Boston Election Department Monday, according to the Afonso campaign.

“This race is far too close to leave to chance,” Abdikarim said in a statement shared by the Afonso campaign.

“A transparent recount will allow us to respect the voter’s voices, and allow the District to move onto November,” Hurtado added in a statement.

Culpepper fully supports a recount in light of how close Tuesday’s results were, he told The Boston Globe in a statement Monday. But he said he remains confident the recount will be consistent with the city’s unofficial tally, and that his campaign will move on to November.

“Every voter deserves the assurance that their voice was heard and their ballot counted,” Culpepper wrote in the statement. “What matters most is protecting trust in this process.”

Ahmed, in a statement Monday evening, also said he respects Afonso’s right to request a recount, but is confident he will retain his first place spot.

The District 7 position had the most crowded field of candidates out of all the races on last Tuesday’s ballot, with 11 people vying for the seat. The district includes some of the city’s most diverse and historically disenfranchised neighborhoods, including Roxbury, and parts of Dorchester and the South End.

Fernandes Anderson, who previously made history as the first Muslim and formerly undocumented person to be elected to the council, decided not to run for reelection after agreeing to plead guilty to federal corruption charges earlier this year.

Correction: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated the number of votes Afonso received in Tuesday’s preliminary election. He got 1,082 votes, according to the city’s unofficial results. The Globe regrets the error.

title: Two juveniles face gun charges after police investigate gathering in Dorchester
text:
Police arrested two juveniles and recovered two loaded handguns after questioning a group of people gathered in the courtyard of a Dorchester housing development Sunday, officials said.

The arrests took place around 6:50 p.m. Sunday in the Franklin Field housing development, a Boston Housing Authority property, police wrote on social media.

“On directed patrol in the area due to recent gun violence, officers observed a group of six to eight individuals gathered abnormally in the courtyard along Westview Way,” police said. “Several members of the group wore multiple layers of clothing and face coverings, drawing officers’ attention.”

When officers walked toward the group, a 14-year-old boy stepped away and “displayed nervous behavior, including avoiding eye contact, wide-eyed stares, and fidgeting,” police wrote.

“Fearing he might be armed,” the officers conducted a pat frisk and found a Glock handgun “loaded with one round in the chamber and four rounds in the magazine,” police wrote.

As police took the teenager into custody, a 16-year-old boy ran from the group “into a nearby building, where he was located attempting to hide,” police wrote.

Officers retraced the teenager’s route and located a 9mm handgun hidden under a bush, police said. The pistol had one round in the chamber and nine rounds in the magazine.

Each teenager was charged with carrying a loaded firearm without a license, unlawful possession of ammunition, and carrying a firearm without a license.

They are expected to be arraigned Monday, police said.

title: These are the Mass. residents on Forbes list of 400 richest people in the US
text:
Here’s a quick rundown:

Abigail Johnson, 63, was 27th on this year’s list, with a net worth of $35 billion. That’s up three spots from her 2024 position, when Forbes pegged her net worth at $31.3 billion.

In March of 2024, Bloomberg reported that Johnson, chief executive officer of FMR, the parent company of Fidelity Investments, had reduced the company’s reliance on old-fashioned mutual funds and embraced low-cost index funds popularized by US rival Vanguard Group.

Edward Johnson IV, 60, the brother of Abigail Johnson, was 76th on the list with a net worth of $14.2 billion.

That’s down from his 2024 ranking of 70th, when Forbes estimated his net worth at $12.6 billion.

Edward Johnson “is the president of Pembroke Real Estate, which is owned by Fidelity’s parent company FMR,” according to his profile on the Forbes list.

It’s no days off for Kraft, the 84-year-old New England Patriots owner who landed at 78th on this year’s list, with a net worth of $13.8 billion.

Kraft last year came in 81st, with a net worth estimated at $11.8 billion.

And his team defeated the Dolphins in Miami on Sunday, a rarity in the post-Tom Brady era.

Elizabeth Johnson, 62, sibling to Abigail and Ed Johnson, landed at 99 on this year’s list, with a net worth of $12.3 billion.

Last year, Elizabeth Johnson came in at 91 with a net worth of $10.6 billion.

“In 2013, [Elizabeth] Johnson founded Louisburg Farm, a stable of show jumping horses based in Wellington, Florida,” says Forbes says in her profile entry.

Hale, 59, came in at 246 this year, with a net worth of $6 billion.

Last year, Hale was 225th on the list with a net worth of $5.8 billion.

The telecom executive ran the Boston Marathon in April 2024 and sent an email to more than 70 local charities, announcing that he and his wife, Karen, would be donating a collective $26.2 million to them, including $9 million to the Fieldhouse Plus project in Dorchester being developed by the Martin Richard Foundation and the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester.

Hale also sits on the managing board of the Boston Celtics.

Boston Globe and Boston Red Sox owner John Henry, 75, finished at 264 this year, with a net worth estimated at $5.7 billion.

Last year, Henry was 216th on the list with a net worth of $6 billion.

Forbes lists Henry as a Florida resident, but he’s very much a part of the Boston community. During his ownership, the Red Sox have won four World Series titles.

Henry’s Fenway Sports Group also owns the Liverpool Football Club in the UK and the Pittsburgh Penguins in the National Hockey League.

New Balance chairman Jim Davis, 82, and his family landed at 295 on the list this year, with an estimated net worth of $5.2 billion.

Last year, Davis and family sat at 198th on the list, with a net worth of $6.5 billion.

“He got his start working for his father’s restaurants as a ‘lumper’ carrying trays,” according to the Forbes profile.

These days, the executive deals in lump sums.

“He and his family own an estimated 95% of the [New Balance] company, which is private,” the profile states.

Ragon, 76, founder of the software company InterSystems, was 352nd on the list this year with a net worth of $4.2 billion.

“Ragon retains full ownership of the company, which generates around $1 billion in annual sales,” says his Forbes profile.

The profile also notes that Ragon and his wife, Susan, “announced a $200 million gift to endow the Ragon Institute of Massachusetts General Hospital, MIT and Harvard in 2019.”

Trefler, 69, was tied for 352nd this year, with a net worth of $4.2 billion.

“The son of a holocaust survivor, Alan Trefler worked at his father’s small antique restoration company as a teen, before starting Pegasystems in 1983,” says his Forbes profile.

The software company, based in Waltham, “generated $1.5 billion in 2024 sales and employs over 5,000 people,” the profile says.

Hostetter, 88, a former cable TV magnate, finished 382nd on the list this year, with a net worth of $3.9 billion.

Last year, he was 347th with a net worth of $3.8 billion.

“His family’s Barr Foundation has donated more than $1.7 billion to support the arts and education and to fight climate change,” says his Forbes profile.
