title: Former BC High School student takes stand at trial for priest accused of rape
text:
A judge is presiding over the bench trial, meaning there is no jury. The judge will decide the case on their own.

Assistant District Attorney Laura Montgomery said White’s accuser was “the perfect victim” as a gay student at an all-boys Catholic school.

“The defendant was in a position of trust and authority,” she said in an opening statement. “[White’s accuser] was a vulnerable victim. He believed the attention that the defendant was showing him was positive.”

In his opening statement, White’s lawyer, Douglas S. Brooks, disputed the credibility of White’s accuser and said her version of events was unreliable and inconsistent.

“There’s no testimony or documents corroborating what she now says,” Brooks said. “Her inconsistencies go to the very core of her allegations and the very core of the crime charged here itself.”

She first disclosed her allegations in a 2020 Instagram post and then sent a letter to high school officials the following year, Brooks said.

She testified that she did not report the alleged assaults to school authorities, her parents, or her friends before 2020, because White told her “not to tell anybody,” and because she did not think at the time that she had been abused.

“I didn’t think I would need to tell anybody,” she said. “I didn’t think anything that had been done to me was wrong.”

The USA East Province of Jesuits removed White, 63, of Weston, from public ministry and placed him under supervision after it learned of the allegations last year.

The student began taking White’s scripture class in 2008, and White soon took an interest, she testified. He put his hand on the teenager’s back and asked about the teenager’s parents and home life, she said.

White began inviting the student to a classroom after school, where he allegedly assaulted the student multiple times before he left the school in February 2009.

Brooks disputed that the meetings between White and his accuser ever took place, saying that White was a cross-country coach in the fall of 2008 and would have been busy at the track after school.

Brooks also said the room opposite the one where the assaults allegedly took place was a “very active” faculty lounge that would have been bustling after class let out.

“This is a very, very busy area,” Brooks said. “This alleged sex happened in a busy and crowded area where there was absolutely no privacy.”

“The evidence will compel a finding of not guilty,” he added.

In a statement last year, BC High President Grace Cotter Regan said the school was not made aware of any allegation of abuse while White was teaching there.

“BC High is committed to providing a safe and secure environment for our students, faculty, and staff and ensuring their spiritual, mental, and physical well-being,” she said.

In 2002, during the Globe’s Spotlight Team investigation into child sexual abuse in the Catholic Church, White wrote an opinion piece in The Globe in praise of clerical celibacy that expressed “horror at the sin of priests preying upon children.”

“Celibates urge us to trust that God’s promise of love and grace makes us rich enough and wanting for nothing more,” White wrote in the essay, published March 6, 2002. “Celibates stake everything on God, convinced that God is worth a life.”

title: In Randolph, residents who had sought refuge from Boston’s housing woes face high prices, evictions
text:
Long a haven for residents pushed out of Boston’s increasingly competitive housing market, Randolph has one of the largest Black populations in the state and a large number of renters. Thirty percent of the population rents, mostly from a few large apartment complexes. The average rent hovers around $2,600 a month, roughly 30 percent above the national average and higher than in nearby Brockton, Holbrook, and Weymouth.

Among all Massachusetts municipalities with more than 2,500 renters, Randolph had 41.5 eviction filings per 1,000 renter households in the first half of 2025, according to a recent report by the affordable housing nonprofit Massachusetts Housing Partnership.

“Rents just keep going up,” said Cheryl Lloyd, a Randolph resident who said she has to live apart from her two children because she cannot afford an apartment big enough for all of them. “It’s getting to the point, I told my daughter for high school we might have to go to Rhode Island. But their prices are going up, too.”

Randolph Town Manager Brian Howard argues the town’s high eviction rate is primarily a math problem: high rents and a large tenant population with limited incomes. Today, 57 percent of Randolph renters are cost-burdened, meaning they pay more than 30 percent of their income on housing costs.

“When you are living paycheck to paycheck, when you can’t save for an emergency, all it takes is for one significant issue to occur,” Howard said.

In a state where housing costs have seemingly gone up everywhere, evictions across Massachusetts have increased since the tail end of the pandemic, to a recent high of 3,600 court filings in March 2025, from about 2,600 per month before the pandemic, according to the Massachusetts Housing Partnership.

But there’s a particular dynamic at work in Randolph. More than 40 percent of Randolph residents are Black or African-American, and 60 percent are people of color. Nearly one-third were born outside of the United States.

“Growing up, everybody on my street came from Mattapan, Roxbury, Dorchester, or were immigrants,” said Howard, who was born and raised in Randolph. “That still tends to be the situation today.”

But one noticeable change is that the apartments are mostly owned by large corporate landlords, several of whom are located out of state. There are roughly 2,275 apartment units in the town, not including homes, duplexes, or condos that are rented, according to town data.

“That is a significant difference from Randolph 30 years ago, where the owners of [those] properties actually lived here,” Howard said. “They were far more willing to try to work with folks.”

As apartment properties have changed hands in the ever-heated housing markets, rent prices have increased. At Rosemont Square, one of Randolph’s largest housing complexes, which accepts Section 8 vouchers, a one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 735-square-foot apartment was listed for $2,160 as of early September. At Highland House, another large complex that also takes vouchers, a 435-square-foot studio was listed for $1,975.

Lauren Honigman, a staff attorney with Greater Boston Legal Services who sometimes represents tenants in Randolph, sees a more explicit racial component.

“Every case that I’ve had from Randolph, the tenants have had terrible housing conditions, almost across the board,” Honigman said. “And the tenants that I’ve had have been primarily Black renters. I don’t think that that’s an accident. It’s a racially concentrated, economically strained community.”

The town has tried to help stave off some evictions by using more than $2 million in federal COVID dollars, bolstered by private donations and some state funds, to pay the rent, utilities, or food during emergencies of some residents. But the fund has since dwindled to $115,000.

As a small, suburban town, Randolph doesn’t have access to nonprofit resources and some federal funding, such as housing grants, that larger, more urban areas receive.

Town officials also want the state to make Randolph eligible for a program that provides residents in struggling communities aid for child care and transportation, which could free up more of their income for rent.

“When I think of those thousands of dollars residents could use to go into housing that go into child care instead, it’s frustrating,” Howard said.

Howard and other Randolph officials regularly hear from tenants complaining of poor housing conditions, rising rents, unresponsive landlords, and eviction threats. But without additional resources, and unable to adopt rent control, Howard argued the town can only do so much.

Paul Foos, an organizer with ​​Randolph Tenants United, views these explanations as excuses. He says the town has not done enough to enforce housing codes to improve conditions for renters.

“The places are in terrible condition, and the municipal government lets them get away with it,” he said. “They give puny fines that don’t make a dent for these large companies.” When asked to intervene in evictions, Foos said, the town government will deflect responsibility. At housing court, Foos said, he has seen evicted tenants directed to a homeless shelter in Brockton.

Cheryl Lloyd, the Randolph mother of two, said town leaders have supported too many market-rate housing units, rather than requiring more affordable housing.

She pointed to The Meridian, a new building where an 819-square-foot one-bedroom, one-bathroom was listed for $2,370, plus fees, as of early September. She can’t afford any of the city’s major apartment buildings and instead rents a room in a house for herself while her two kids live nearby with her parents.

“Town leaders are not looking at how the town is actually changing and how they could be moving with it. It’s breaking families apart. I work. I do all these responsible things. And I still can’t afford to live with my kids.”

“Rent caps should be reintroduced in Massachusetts,” Lloyd continued. “If people can’t afford [rent], why do you keep pushing it up?”

Howard noted that a recently approved 100-unit building will have 25 percent of the units reserved for affordable housing.

Back at housing court in Canton, Patrick Okeke was facing eviction from Highland House, the Randolph apartment complex he’s lived in for more than 20 years.

In the hallway outside the courtroom, a lawyer representing Highland House told Okeke he owed hundreds of dollars in additional fees for late rent. If he did not pay, Okeke would need to leave, the lawyer said.

Okeke argued that Highland House was paid when he received support from the state’s Residential Assistance for Families in Transition program, which provides emergency housing assistance. Since then, he’s paid his rent within the month. The fees, he said, “don’t make sense.”

A few hours later, Okeke relented, agreeing to pay the $500 in two weeks. The alternative — eviction — was too dire.

Another renter, Kelly Walker, didn’t want to negotiate with a lawyer for Woodview at Randolph, another large apartment complex, without having a lawyer of his own. According to documents reviewed by the Globe, Woodview has charged Walker legal fees on several occasions in the past year, totaling more than $2,000. Walker said he was told he had to cover legal costs associated with previous attempts to evict him.

Walker is in trade school in the hopes of a better income, but his partner passed away, leaving him as the sole caretaker of their son. His monthly rent is $1,835. The additional fees, he said, were just too much. And he doesn’t understand why he has to pay for his landlord’s attorney.

Exasperated, Walker spotted a lawyer with Greater Boston Legal Services and roped her in for a discussion with the Woodview lawyer. By the next day, Walker agreed to move by the end of September and pay the fees in installments.

The management of Woodview at Randolph did not respond to a request for comment, and the management at Highland House declined to comment.

After the ordeal in housing court, Walker said he felt exhausted, and just wanted out. He plans to go to a homeless shelter, while his son will live with one of his grandmothers in Taunton or Dorchester.

“I’ve been calling around, I would go to any shelter that would take me and my son,” he said. “They say there’s no space.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: What it’s like to be a foster child in Massachusetts
text:
It’s a big commitment (volunteers must pledge at least 18 months and meet with their child multiple times). But there’s lots more that busy families can do to support foster kids, and little things add up to make a big difference.

How do kids end up in the foster care system?

There may be allegations of abuse or neglect, investigated [by the Department of Children and Families]. For those that are substantiated, the kids are likely then removed from their home, but they do go through a court process. At that time, it’s determined whether or not that child is safe to be in their home. If not, that child is taken into the custody of the Department of Children and Families and then placed into a foster home.

We have kids who may have a myriad of different challenges. … If they have a difficult time placing a child, the youth may end up in a group home. For me, I ended up in a foster home, and I also did independent living. Essentially, you’re placed in a home and it’s monitored. Somebody comes by who works directly for DCF or is contracted through DCF. They check on you in the home. You have a curfew. You have an allowance that’s provided to buy groceries.

What do you want other people to understand about that foster child experience?

It’s very traumatic. If we just look through the lens of a kid who has to return to school: This is something that’s difficult for most children. But for kids who are in foster care, often they’re lacking the emotional security that children who come from stable homes have.

While most kids are thinking about: What am I am going to wear on the first day of school or if I have all the right school supplies, reconnecting with friends who I haven’t seen throughout the summer, children experiencing foster care are also coping with navigating new social workers, different foster home or group home placements, adjusting to new families. They have court dates.

It’s a lot of work for them to go through, mentally and emotionally, while still trying to focus on school. What I would want readers to imagine is if their child didn’t know where they would be staying once they left school that day, or had to live in a group home and had no parental support; if they didn’t have a quiet place to do their homework or anyone who cared enough to even help them to get it done.

Frequent moves — which I experienced, too, and placements — force kids to have to switch schools. There’s a lot of disruption in your friendships, and it’s difficult to do well academically. It’s hard to be involved in extracurricular activities, which oftentimes can be a really positive outlet for kids, both socially and emotionally.

For readers, we may not think about the stigmatization for foster children, and the natural questions that they have to face from their peers. I remember having to navigate this. It’s natural to talk about your home and your family. Those are really awkward, difficult, and sometimes triggering conversations for young people. Even for me as a parent now, sometimes I look at my own son and it makes me reflect on exactly what I did go through then. It wasn’t normal. That was my norm, but it wasn’t normal.

Are there any statistics about how often a foster child is moved from place to place?

I don’t have the statistics surrounding that particular information, but I have the broader statistics, and you can infer from that. Less than 50 percent of children who’ve been in foster care graduate from high school. [In 2023, the four-year graduation rate for foster children was 58.3 percent.] Only 3 to 4 percent will earn a four-year college degree. That’s why I feel very fortunate to have two master’s degrees, because I know that I have beat odds. Seventy percent will likely experience homelessness before age 26; 70 percent of foster youth have been arrested at least once by the age of 26. Seven out of 10 girls are pregnant by the age of 21. That speaks volumes to the effects of the totality of the experience of being in foster care.

What are some actionable things that readers can do, even if they don’t become a foster parent?

I think that you can also develop awareness within your own communities. If that’s too much, you can start with your own children. Speak with them about inclusion and kindness. We don’t have a choice of who we’re born to or the conditions that were born into us.

You can also support foster families. You can donate school supplies, you can advocate for better education, you can get involved legislatively and advocate for policy reforms that directly support the well-being of children and youth in the foster care system. It could be advocating around domestic violence. It could be advocating around poverty.

Tell me about your Youth Advisory Board forum.

These are transitional-age youth, kids between the ages of 14 and 22 years old. They’re nearing the age when they’re going to lose access to services from the Department of Children and Families.

Transitional age youth face enormous amounts of challenges. They have all of the developmental challenges that every adolescent has, but the odds are stacked so high against them in comparison to their peers.

Our goal with the Youth Advisory Board is to do whatever we can to prevent those outcomes. [We] aim to center, amplify, and uplift the voices of these young people with lived experience. Our goal is to help prepare them for their futures and provide them with essential life skills like financial literacy, job search readiness, self-care, and self-love.

We do a whole component, which is really critical, on civic engagement. We’ve partnered with the Youth and Family Rights Clinic from Boston College, who helped us develop the civic engagement curriculum. We really try to teach our young people about advocacy, the importance and the power in their voice and their stories. And importantly: How do you lift others up as well? How do you become change agents, not just for yourself, but for others who may be in similar circumstances?

Every year, the youth are tasked with developing a capstone project. There are five youths and five topics. [One topic] is awareness of young adults experiencing homelessness, because 70 percent of our youth will have experienced homelessness. Another is fostering a better environment for youth in residential programs.

It’s Nov. 1 at the Cambridge Library. We invite a number of stakeholders. Educating your children around the effects [of foster care] is one way that you can actually get them engaged; young people can come and learn.

How else do we raise awareness about foster care?

Developing awareness within our communities really starts at home. … Even if you can’t attend, even if you can’t become a CASA, you can take an hour and learn about the challenges that our foster children are facing.

Once you’re more aware, then you know you can also talk to your children. You can ask them if there are any children in their classroom in foster care. Speak with them about inclusion and kindness. Everyone’s born into different situations. We do that around lots of issues, right? But we don’t often mention foster children.

Tap into a few different organizations that support foster families and see: What if there’s anything that you can do to support those families? Can you donate school supplies or advocate for better educational support in their communities?

This isn’t just your job. This is your past. What do you want for these kids, if you could fix just one thing?

There are so many things, right? But when I look back over my life, I realize how fortunate I am. I had someone advocating for me to go to really good schools. I was fortunate to be able to get into an all-girls private boarding school. … I had educational opportunities, which also gave me exposure to a different way of life, outside of where I came from.

Before the age of 15, I lived in at least 7 different foster homes, but I did have the very good fortune of living with one foster parent from age 5 to 11, the only person I ever called “mom,” Bertha Crumble. She was someone who believed in me, who showed me the power of a trusted adult, and she really did set me on the trajectory of success. She gave me the foundation through education, which set me on the path to eventually be able to earn two master’s degrees, which isn’t a big deal. But for me, given the statistics surrounding children who have grown up in foster care, it is a big deal. I became a licensed school principal and a licensed independent clinical social worker.

I’m very keenly aware of the challenges that children in foster care face. It’s also why I care so deeply about the work of Boston CASA, and why I believe so strongly and it is so personal.

One person truly can make a difference in somebody’s life. My foster mother only had me from 5 until 11. I had endured physical abuse, sexual abuse. I had faced domestic violence. I had attempts of suicide because I couldn’t see the value of my life.

It’s having that one person who believes in you. My message is that you can change a child’s story, and it doesn’t always take a whole lot. If we all just did one piece — what is the analogy? — you throw the pebble in the water, and it makes many ripples.

Here’s how to get involved in supporting foster youth:

Volunteer: Attend an info session, give financially, or in-kind support for holiday gifts or extracurricular opportunities for foster children and youth at Boston CASA.

Advocate: Visit Citizens for Juvenile Justice and Children’s Advocacy Center of Suffolk County.

Watch: “Possible Selves: Overcoming the Odds in Foster Care“ and “The Day I Picked My Parents.”

Foster a child: Learn more at DCF.

Raise awareness: Visit the 440k Project and attend YAB’s forum on Saturday, Nov. 1, at 10 a.m. at the Cambridge Main Library, 449 Broadway.

Interview was edited and condensed for clarity.

title: Ex-MBTA Transit Police sergeant sentenced to probation for falsifying report on homeless man’s beating
text:
A former MBTA Transit Police sergeant on Monday was sentenced to probation and community service for helping a fellow officer falsify a report and cover up an unprovoked beating of a homeless man, federal prosecutors said.

David S. Finnerty, 49, of Rutland, went to trial in May in federal court in Boston. After an eight-day trial, a jury convicted him of one count of aiding and abetting the filing of a false police report. Finnerty was acquitted of a second count of filing a false report.

The case had been closely watched in political and law enforcement circles because the federal charges were brought against Finnerty in August 2023 after Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden dropped similar charges 10 months earlier.

At trial, prosecutors said Finnerty was the duty shift supervisor on July 27, 2018, when Transit Officer Dorston Bartlett beat a homeless man with a steel, expandable police baton after pulling him off a Red Line train at Ashmont station around 1:30 a.m.

The victim, 31-year-old Anthony Watson, was arrested by Bartlett on false charges of assault, then begged officers at the police station to review surveillance video that would prove he was beaten by the officer, according to prosecutors.

After watching the video, Finnerty said he did not see enough to determine excessive force.

Jurors also watched video snippets during the trial.

On Monday, US District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV sentenced Finnerty to two years’ probation, ordered that he complete 150 hours of community service, and pay a $500 fine.

Prosecutors sought a prison sentence of two years.

“By falsifying a police report to cover up an unconstitutional assault, Mr. Finnerty betrayed his badge, the victim he was sworn to protect, and the public’s trust,” Leah B. Foley, US Attorney for Massachusetts, said in a statement.

“Instead of protecting a vulnerable man who had been abused, he tried to shield the officer who assaulted him,” Foley said. “Our justice system depends on officers who follow the law, not those who violate it. Mr. Finnerty’s conviction affirms a simple truth: no one is above the law, and those who abuse their power will be held accountable.”

When Finnerty, who previously served in the US Coast Guard and worked as a transit officer for 16 years, reviewed Bartlett’s police report, Finnerty encouraged Bartlett to add more details, or “falsehoods to justify the assault,” Foley’s statement said.

“As law enforcement officers, we must be held to the highest of ethical standards, and Sergeant Finnerty blatantly ignored those standards when he shirked his sworn duty and tried to cover up an unprovoked beating of a homeless man by one of his fellow officers,” Ted E. Docks, FBI’s special agent in charge of the Boston division. “What he did was a gross betrayal of trust.”

Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com. Follow her @talanez.

title: Community activist Monica Cannon-Grant pleads guilty in federal fraud case
text:
Prosecutors agreed to recommend a sentence at the low end of sentencing guidelines, which is about 18 months in prison. The defense is not required to make any specific recommendation, and may seek probation.

US District Judge Angel Kelley scheduled sentencing for Jan. 29.

“Are you pleading guilty because you are in fact guilty and for no other reason?” Kelley asked.

“Yes your honor,” Cannon-Grant said. She, and her lawyers, declined to comment after the hearing.

Cannon-Grant, who ran the now-defunct nonprofit Violence in Boston Inc., was indicted along with her husband, Clark Grant, in 2022 on charges that they raised more than $1 million for their charity and received nearly $60,000 in pandemic relief funds to provide meals for people in need, but instead spent much of the money on themselves.

In March 2023, Clark Grant was killed in a motorcycle crash in Easton.

The initial indictment charged Cannon-Grant and her husband with three separate schemes: defrauding people who donated money to their nonprofit; illegally collecting an estimated $100,000 in pandemic unemployment benefits; and lying on a mortgage application.

Additional fraud charges were brought in 2023, alleging that Cannon-Grant and Clark Grant received nearly $60,000 in pandemic relief funds to provide hot meals to struggling people but instead used the money to pay a car loan, auto insurance, and other personal expenses.

They were also accused of concealing their income to fraudulently obtain $12,600 in rental assistance funds from Boston’s Office of Housing Stability in 2021, around the same time they were buying a new home in Taunton.

In court Monday, Assistant US Attorney Adam Deitch said if the case had gone to trial, prosecutors were prepared to prove that Cannon-Grant and her husband falsely claimed that they drew no salaries from their nonprofit, while she took hefty weekly paychecks and they routinely spent donations and grants on themselves.

In one instance, Deitch said, Cannon-Grant’s nonprofit was awarded a $6,000 grant from the Suffolk district attorney’s office in 2019 after she claimed it was to take a group of at-risk young men to a retreat in Philadelphia.

The trip was meant “to give these young men exposure to communities outside of the violence riddled neighborhoods that they navigate daily” and focus on community-building activities and coping skills, according to her grant proposal.

“None of the funds were used to take young men from Roxbury on a trip to Philadelphia,” Deitch said. Instead, prosecutors allege, Cannon-Grant and her husband used the grant money to take a vacation to Maryland, on dining at Bubba Gump Shrimp Co., Shake Shack, and other restaurants, and paying for car rentals, groceries, Walmart purchases, and visits to a Boston nail salon.

While Cannon-Grant reported to the IRS and the state attorney general’s charity division that she received no salary, prosecutors said that in October 2020, she started paying herself $2,788 a week.

She admittedly filed false tax returns for 2017 and 2018, and failed to file tax returns for 2019 and 2020.

Cannon-Grant acknowledged Monday that she had committed the crimes detailed by the prosecution.

After the hearing, Cannon-Grant hugged her mother, who was seated in the spectator section, and thanked a group of about 10 friends and relatives who showed up to support her.,

The judge rejected a request last week by Cannon-Grant’s lawyers to let her appear remotely for the change of plea hearing, ruling she must be physically present in the courtroom.

In a motion filed Thursday, Cannon-Grant’s lawyers asked to submit a sealed filing detailing their reasons for seeking a virtual hearing.

The motion “contains highly sensitive and personal information, including mental health information and information related to minors, that is not appropriate for public disclosure at this stage,” wrote George Vien and Emma Notis-McConarty, who represent Cannon-Grant.

Prosecutors opposed the motion, saying the documents should not be sealed “because there is a legal presumption of public access to judicial proceedings and records, and because there is a strong public interest in this case.”

Kelley allowed the defense to file its motion under seal but rejected claims that her presence should be waived.

“Although difficult circumstances, Ms. Cannon-Grant’s offered justifications cannot waive the requirement, nor overcome related policy interests that underscore the importance of her in-person presence,” Kelley wrote Thursday in an entry on the court docket.

Cannon-Grant rose to prominence in 2020 after organizing a march in Franklin Park that drew thousands to protest the killing of George Floyd and other Black people at the hands of police. She formed a collaboration with a Dorchester restaurant to distribute more than 1,000 free meals a day to people struggling during the pandemic.

For her efforts, the mother of six was honored as a Bostonian of the Year by the Boston Globe Magazine and hailed as the city’s “best social justice advocate” by Boston Magazine.

She started her nonprofit in 2017, operating out of her Roxbury home, but by 2020, it had moved to a sprawling headquarters in Hyde Park. Donations poured in, with the group receiving more than $50,000 in April 2020 alone, prosecutors allege.

title: Boston Health Care for the Homeless workers protest cuts and layoffs
text:
Over a dozen speakers, including staff members, supporters, and politicians, spoke at the protest, listing the union’s demands for the new contract, including “humane treatment during layoffs and people to have the option to return.”

“We need leadership that fights for us and for our mission and our patients, like we and our patients do every day,” said Claudia Lopez, a unionized employee at BHCHP, who read the demands at the event.

David Reyes, 61, has worked for the program for 17 years, and his job is one of the casualties of the cuts. His last day, he said, will be Oct. 10. Reyes benefited from sobriety programs himself over 20 years ago, and then went back to school to learn about addiction recovery before joining BHCHP to provide the care he knows is crucial in helping people overcome addiction.

Reyes’s personal journey allows him to connect deeply with patients he meets every day.

Andre Groomes, 43, of Dorchester, is a certified recovery coach who “wears a lot of hats” at his job, he said. Like Reyes, Groomes was laid off and has not received any information about severance or support, he said.

“I’m definitely one of the people who worked here, that’s definitely for the people. I’m not here to win an award,” Groomes said. “There [are] a lot of people that I have special relationships with that I bonded with, and just seeing them today, it really, really made me emotional. I started crying. And because I really love what I do.”

Stacey Arroyo, 41, and her husband, Fernando Arroyo, 50, worked with Groomes for many years and said they have built up a strong bond of trust during that time. Groomes would visit jails to speak with inmates and start them on the road to recovery early on.

“I met [Groomes] in jail years ago, and I never broke ties,” Fernando said.

Stacey and Fernando are three and four years sober, respectively, and they credit much of their recovery to BHCHP staff.

“Whenever I needed them, I called, they never went to voicemail, never not answering anytime I needed,” Fernando said.

When he heard that Groomes was being let go, Fernando “started bawling,” he said.

“This is our second home,” Stacey said, tearing up. “What are we supposed to do now?”

The program’s leadership declined an interview request about the causes and impacts of the cuts but released a statement.

“We fully respect the rights of our unionized colleagues to express their concerns, and we remain committed to bargaining with our union in good faith to reach agreement on an initial collective bargaining agreement.

BHCHP is confronting one of the most difficult financial periods in our 40-year history. For the first time, we have had to make the painful decision to eliminate some positions. These decisions were made only after a thorough review and with deep appreciation for the dedication and service of the affected staff,” they said.

title: Boston nonprofit leader arrested on drug charges, US Attorney’s office says
text:
The leader of a Boston nonprofit that provides reentry support services was arrested Tuesday on charges of distributing crack cocaine, according to the Massachusetts US Attorney’s office.

Javan Tooley, 36, of Dorchester and Brockton, was ordered held until a hearing on Friday in US District Court in Boston, prosecutors said in a statement.

Tooley is the CEO and founder of Adapt & Evolve LLC, a legal advocacy firm that helps clients clear their records and navigate the justice system, according to its website.

He was indicted on Sept. 18 by a federal grand jury on charges of distributing more than 28 grams or more of cocaine, the US Attorney’s office said.

According to the indictment, on Sept. 10, Tooley sold about 100 grams of crack cocaine from his car in Fields Corner, a a short distance from his nonprofit in Dorchester, while a young child, about six or seven, was in the back seat.

He was in a hurry because he was late to drop off a child — “I have to bring her to class,” he told the buyer, according to court records.

On Tuesday, Tooley arrived to make a sale near Roxbury District Court to a cooperating witness, and police arrested him. Officers seized roughly 160 grams of crack cocaine, the statement said.

Tooley has a long history of drug convictions, according to US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office.

In 2010, he was convicted for a hand-to-hand sale of crack cocaine to an undercover officer, for which he was sentenced to five years in prison and five years of supervised release, according to Foley’s office. However, he violated the release terms at least five times, ultimately serving an additional 22 months.

He allegedly also has a history of targeting women — many struggling with substance abuse — whom he controlled through violence and access to drugs to perform commercial sex and sell drugs, the statement said. He “created a climate of fear” by claiming connections to law enforcement and other influential figures through his nonprofit and coordinated drug transactions using the nonprofit’s phone, the statement said.

Because of his prior conviction, Tooley faces a minimum of 10 years and up to life in prison and a fine of $8 million, if convicted of the new charges.

Adapt & Evolve LLC did not respond to the Globe’s request for comment Wednesday evening.

Rita Chandler can be reached at rita.chandler@globe.com.

title: Boston School Committee expected to hear recommended changes to exam school admission policy tonight
text:
If the changes are approved by the School Committee, they would be the most significant changes in the admission policy for Boston Latin School, Boston Latin Academy, and the John D. O’Bryant School of Math and Science in the past five years. The School Committee is expected to vote on the recommended changes to the exam schools’ admission policy during its Nov. 5 meeting.

Skipper said families were seeking “clarity, simplicity, and stability” in the admissions policy that would be left alone for a number of years.

“We are preserving the goals that we have had, while still making appropriate tweaks to it [regarding] students with the highest scores... being blocked out,” said Michael O’Neill, the board’s vice chairman Thursday.

Administrators have said the proposed changes would result in marginally more seats going to white and non-low-income students. But critics like Rosann Tung argue the district can’t risk losing progress in making the exam schools open to more of Boston’s students.

“I’m alarmed that BPS proposes widening the opportunity gap,” said Tung, who served on an earlier task force that developed the current policy, which was enacted in 2021.

“Eliminating bonus points would privilege private-sending schools. The vast majority of BPS schools had no hope of their students getting invited until the [2021] policy change,” Tung told officials.

Before the pandemic, the city’s exam school application process was based only on a student’s grades and an entrance exam score, but that process was criticized for failing to draw in a diverse applicant pool for the exam schools. The School Committee in July 2021 approved a complex system that was intended to improve the odds of students from disadvantaged backgrounds to enroll in those schools.

The goal, proponents said at the time, was to help prevent disadvantaged students from competing with applicants whose families had the means to pay for tutors and educational consultants.

State data show increases in the proportion of Black, Latino, and multi-race students enrolled in the city’s three exam schools from the 2021 to 2022 school year compared to the past year.

The system approved in 2021 divided up applicants into socioeconomic tiers that grouped students based on factors such as poverty level, households with single parents, educational attainment of adults, and households where English was not the primary language. Students would still be judged on an entrance exam score, but it carries less weight under the updated policy.

Students would receive up to 100 points in a composite score based on academic grades and the entrance exam. Applicants could also receive 10 additional points for attending a high-poverty school. Alternatively, students living in some public housing, who are homeless, or in the care of the state’s Department of Children and Families, could receive up to 15 additional points.

In January 2024, the policy was tweaked by the School Committee so the number of school-based points was determined by where an applicant lived in the city, regardless of whether they lived in a low-income household.

The change was made so students from affluent areas wouldn’t need perfect or near-perfect scores to enter their first choice exam school, Skipper said at the time.

But critics of the current policy argue it makes it harder for more affluent students to attend the city’s exam schools. A federal lawsuit filed in July alleges the policy discriminates against white children.

The suit was filed by the Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence, which sued the district in 2020 over a temporarily discontinued policy that awarded seats based on grades and ZIP code. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case last year, as one justice said the policy was no longer in use.

The district would also work to increase the enrollment of students with disabilities and English language learners at the exam schools, she said.

If the changes are approved, administrators are seeking to leave them in place for three years in order to gather enough data to help guide any future potential changes, according to Skipper. “You need to have reliable data,” she said.

Board member Brandon Cardet-Hernandez raised concerns about approving a policy that wouldn’t change for a set time: “I think that’s really good for policy makers, but not great for constituents,” he said.

During the meeting Thursday, Mike Heichman of Dorchester said even with the current policy, white and Asian students “remain disproportionately well represented” at the exam schools.

“We must move away from elitism, which... fails many children,” Heichman told the School Committee.

Among the supporters of the recommended changes was Anna Dore, a parent of a BPS second grader who believed the current policy was too confusing for families.

“I’d like to see an adjustment to the point system. It has been confusing to parents as it is tweaked each year and feels arbitrary to BPS students who don’t receive points,” Dore said.

Emma Yashar, a parent of a second grader and fourth grader who also backed the changes, said what’s being proposed seems like “a balanced approach.”

“It’s a reasonable resolution to the chaos and confusion of the past few years,” Yashar said.

But Jeri Robinson,the board’s chairperson, argued that the attention on the city’s exam schools drew focus away from Boston’s earlier grades, as well as the city’s other high schools.

“My issue is, we’ve got 32 high schools. Why aren’t we putting the pressure there to make sure those seats are equally competitive?” Robinson asked her colleagues.

Globe correspondent Camille Bugayong and Christopher Huffaker of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Financial margins at Massachusetts hospitals tightening, or in the red
text:
Total margins also fell to 0.6 percent, down from 2.2 percent in 2023. Only 39 percent of acute hospitals ended the year in the black, adding to the concerns over the sustainability of some hospital operations across the state.

The situation flared on Beacon Hill when lawmakers last week rushed a $234 million hospital and community health center aid package to Governor Maura Healey just ahead of the end of the hospital fiscal year. It is the second infusion of state funds into the health care system in just over a year, following a $417 million aid package in 2024 focused primarily on hospitals formerly operated by the now-defunct Steward Health Care.

CHIA’s latest report highlights a stark divide among hospitals.

At the bottom of the financial spectrum was Steward’s Carney Hospital in Dorchester, which reported $23.7 million in losses, a -39.9 percent operating margin, the lowest in the state. Steward shuttered Carney and Nashoba Valley Medical Center last fall as its bankruptcy case unfolded. Other former Steward hospitals, which were bought by new operators, also posted deep deficits, including:

Saint Elizabeth’s Medical Center: -$68.4 million

Holy Family Hospital: -$44.1 million

Good Samaritan Medical Center: -$29.5 million

Saint Anne’s Hospital: -$5.3 million

These figures reflect not only the ongoing aftershocks of the Steward Health Care collapse but also the inability of other facilities to maintain positive operating performance.

Even beyond Steward, major losses were recorded at:

Anna Jaques Hospital: -$30.7 million

MetroWest Medical Center: -$22.4 million

Lowell General Hospital: -$22.5 million

Melrose-Wakefield Healthcare: -$15.5 million

Baystate Franklin Medical Center: -$15.1 million

Meanwhile, a handful of hospitals managed to post healthy margins, such as:

Massachusetts General Hospital: $528.6 million

Brigham and Women’s Hospital: $400.9 million

Lahey Hospital & Medical Center: $147.2 million

Berkshire Medical Center: $143.7 million (9.6 percent operating margin, highest in the state)

These more stable institutions often benefit from higher private-payer mixes, better reimbursement rates, and stronger capital positions, while struggling hospitals frequently serve higher shares of Medicaid or uninsured patients.

The aid bill Healey signed this week sets aside $122 million in targeted hospital relief, prioritizing facilities with negative margins, low “relative prices,” and large Medicaid patient loads. It also allocates $77 million to the Health Safety Net Trust Fund, which helps cover the cost of care for uninsured and underinsured patients.

Lawmakers characterized the aid as essential to stave off defaults and keep doors open.

“Many of our hospitals are at — very close to ... defaulting on their bond covenants, and they need this cash infused now,” Senate Ways and Means Chair Michael Rodrigues said during last week’s debate on the bill.

The 2024 unraveling of Steward Health Care, the state’s largest for-profit hospital system, led to layoffs, closures, and hundreds of millions in emergency state spending commitments. But CHIA’s data makes clear that financial distress is not limited to Steward legacy sites.

“This year’s report shows continued volatility in the system, albeit widely varied across hospitals,” said CHIA executive director Lauren Peters.

At the system level, 17 of 23 hospital health systems posted positive total margins, buoyed largely by non-operating gains, including $2.6 billion in unrealized investment income. However, only six systems reported positive operating margins.

Aggregate operating revenues for acute hospitals rose $2.8 billion (6.5 percent) over the previous year. However, expenses rose by $2.9 billion (6.8 percent) — continuing a pattern of costs outpacing revenues. Revenue growth for the hospital’s fiscal year 2024 was significantly lower than the year prior, when aggregate operating revenues across all hospitals increased by $3.6 billion.

Temporary labor costs dropped sharply by $500 million — 37 percent — though workforce spending overall at acute hospitals increased by $500 million. The spending, representing salary, benefits, and temporary labor, makes up 41.5 percent of the total expenses in the hospital’s fiscal year 2024.

In April, then-Secretary of Health and Human Services Kate Walsh warned that hospital closures, like that of Carney and Nashoba Valley, could happen again.

“I think we all have to think differently about what hospitals are and what they’ll be in the future ... I love hospitals. I hate to see them close. The sad fact is, across our country, there are 1,300 critical access hospitals — there’s one in Massachusetts, in Athol — and a third of those hospitals were projected to close. The small community hospital is, it’s just really threatened,” she said.

Talking with lawmakers about providing health care access in Dorchester after Carney’s closure, Walsh added, “This is not the last conversation like this we’ll have in the next couple of years.”

Other officials have also recently expressed concern about hospital finances, pointing to unsustainable cost inflation and federal healthcare funding cuts.

Senate minority leader Bruce Tarr last week called the state’s repeated inability to contain costs a “vexing problem,” while many others are pointing to cuts authorized under the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill that they say will create coverage and health care system funding nightmares.

“With more than half of all hospitals operating in the red and three-quarters of hospital health systems reporting losses, the cost pressures that local providers were facing in FY24 took an undeniable toll,” said Daniel McHale, senior vice president for health care finance and policy at the Massachusetts Health & Hospital Association.

He called the newly approved state aid “critical for patient care” and said the “basic stability of our system should remain front-and-center in every health care policy conversation.”

title: Fallow Kin plans highly anticipated debut; Boston Public Market throws a bash
text:
Coming soon: Cambridge’s long-awaited Fallow Kin (853 Main St.), from the team behind Huron Village’s cozy-chic Talulla, will open in the coming few weeks pending inspections, say owners Conor Dennehy and Danielle Ayer.

“The word Fallow refers to a piece of land that is left untouched in order to restore itself to optimum fertility under natural conditions — representing our mission of renewal, sustainability, and having a strong connection with the Earth,” Ayer told the Globe when announcing the venue, which takes over the onetime Craigie on Main space.

The menu is organized by breads, pasta, vegetables, meat, and seafood, sourced from a long list of local vendors. Look for duck fat brioche; chilled corn soup; bass crudo; cider-braised halibut; and beef tartare with nasturtium, chile mayo, and onion.

Food trucks: Culinary incubator CommonWealth Kitchen launches Park’d, a food truck park in Roxbury and Dorchester coinciding with Franklin Park Zoo’s Boston Lights exhibit. Visit (enter the park at Blue Hill Avenue) Friday through Sunday from 6 until 10 p.m. beginning Sept. 27. Sample dishes from a rotating lineup of CommonWealth businesses including Artees Food, Bosstown Hot Dogs, El Rey de Chimis, Extreme Flavor, and Lalu’s Chicken. The park is open through October.

title: Titan Casket chief executive wraps up a third season of shows featuring celebrity interviews — in caskets
text:
“We thought, why not have people lying in caskets being interviewed?” Ginsberg said. “It’s certainly different. It certainly gets people’s attention.”

Aside from what’s happening in their careers, guests of the Titan-sponsored show are asked about their thoughts on death, including how they want to be remembered in a “You-logy.” Each episode gets tens of thousands of views; the one with Gunn, timed for the release of his “Superman” movie, racked up 116,000 so far.

Ginsberg said season three went so well, the producers are making plans for a fourth. Titan remains a small company — even after a cameo in a Taylor Swift video in 2022 — with 21 employees globally and a corporate office in Methuen. Still, Titan bills itself as the country’s largest direct-to-consumer casket company, with a logistics network that can ship to any funeral home within two days.

The marketing often takes quirky turns — like that time Ginsberg dressed up as a stuffed casket called Mort (the company mascot) in a mascot race at a Worcester Red Sox game in August.

“Our goal is to normalize conversations around death and dying,” Ginsberg said. “We’re having fun. And we’re just getting started.”

Could Wayfair chief executive Niraj Shah be in line for a $1 billion payout over the next decade?

Sure looks that way — if Wayfair stock can hit some pretty high milestones.

Shares in the home furnishings seller have nearly doubled so far this year, rising around 90 percent into the $85-dollar range as Shah’s leadership team brings the Boston ecommerce company back to profitability. But the stock is still a far cry from the $300-plus range in which it traded in 2020 and 2021. Investors saw Wayfair as a smart pandemic-era bet when everyone was stuck at home, ordering items on their phones or computers.

The board this month approved a payout plan for Shah that would deliver tranches of restricted stock if Wayfair shares rise to certain levels. For example, Shah would get 1 million shares if the price exceeds $176 within the next six years.

Shah would collect the ultimate prize of up to 5 million shares if the stock rises to $679 within 10 years. The value of the potential payout is impossible to know today, though it could easily clear $1 billion.

Shah and Steve Conine, cofounders and cochairs of the board, already rely heavily on the stock’s performance for their compensation.

Conine addressed Shah’s massive potential payout in a Sept. 19 email to staff, as well as why he isn’t receiving something similar. Conine stepped back from the chief technology officer role in 2015, and has generally tried to make way for a new generation of company leaders, making him far less involved in the day-to-day operations.

He also noted that the award indicates the board wants Shah to stick around for the next decade. (The two college friends are both in their 50s.) The reward for Shah, he said, won’t affect employee compensation, and is intended to emphasize long-term accountability over short-term rewards.

Eastern Bank chair Bob Rivers did not hold back about his concerns for Boston’s postpandemic future during a panel discussion organized by State House News Service last week.

His message: It’s not the time to celebrate recent gains, such as the increase in downtown foot traffic and the stabilization of office vacancy rates. Instead, it’s time to worry about what the still-high office tower vacancies will mean for the city’s finances and the downtown’s vibrancy.

“Folks, we’ve got to stop whistling through the graveyard,” Rivers said. “The trends are moving in the right direction, but they’re moving very slowly.”

Rivers said one of the most important solutions is building more housing. The Healey and Wu administrations have provided subsidies to help with office-residential conversions and other housing construction, but they aren’t big enough.

Rivers said many of Eastern’s multifamily developer clients can’t make the numbers work. Some permitting barriers, including Boston’s affordable housing requirement, may need to be loosened, he said.

And most office towers aren’t suitable for conversion. Rivers argued for tearing down obsolete office buildings and replacing them with new multifamily housing.

“Make no mistake,” Rivers said. “We are approaching a crisis here. And we’ve got to think about it that way.”

When Matt DeMichele-Rigoni opened Boston’s first Chick-fil-A shop in early 2022, his business became a magnet for hungry fans of chicken sandwiches and waffle fries, as well as the delivery drivers who serve them.

Now, there will be a break in all that traffic along Boylston Street: DeMichele-Rigoni closed down the shop for two months for renovations. But he’s still taking orders: He opened a backup location to support deliveries at a CloudKitchens commissary in Roxbury, where he employs around 30 people.

DeMichele-Rigoni has worked with Georgia-based Chick-fil-A for his entire career. He started as a teen at a Chick-fil-A in New Hampshire, and after graduating college at Southern New Hampshire University, he entered the chain’s leadership development program. Eventually, he became a franchisee.

DeMichele-Rigoni said the renovations and the new Roxbury location are aimed at better handling his shop’s popularity and responding to concerns about scooter traffic and double-parking. After the shop reopens, many deliveries will be handled out of Roxbury; the renovations to the Back Bay location will include a new door for delivery drivers and a retractable canopy for the streetside patio. (A separate operator is opening a Chick-fil-A at Logan Airport later this year.)

DeMichele-Rigoni hopes he has hit on the right recipe to reduce traffic complaints — and speed up delivery orders at the same time.

It’s been more than a year since ad mogul-turned-philanthropist Jack Connors died, but the flow of accolades hasn’t abated.

The latest came last Thursday at an event held by the Irish Cultural Centre of Greater Boston at the Venezia restaurant in Dorchester, where the ICC gave out its third annual Brian J. Donnelly Award for Leadership in Public Service. This year, the ICC granted the Donnelly award posthumously, to Connors.

Formerly head of ad agency Hill Holliday and chair of Partners HealthCare, the predecessor of Mass General Brigham, Connors devoted much of his life in recent years to Camp Harbor View, a summer camp for Boston kids that he founded. He died from cancer in July 2024.

ICC board chair Martina Curtin talked about Connors’s devotion to Boston’s civic and philanthropic life, and recalled how proud he was of his Irish roots. New England Council president Jim Brett, a previous Donnelly award winner, gave remarks praising Connors and Brian Donnelly, the former congressman who died in 2023.

PR honcho George Regan recalled how he needed to audition for Connors before he could be hired onto then-mayor Kevin White’s press staff. Then, when Regan thought about striking out on his own, Connors tried to recruit him to Hill Holliday, he said, but eventually offered to invest $25,000 in Regan’s then-new PR firm, launched in 1984.

For 18 months, Regan said, the two would meet weekly over a breakfast of Diet Cokes and English muffins, to go over the “nuts and bolts of business leadership.” While Connors joked about how he would never see his money again, he also wanted to protect that investment.

“I’m not ashamed to say,” Regan told the crowd, “that he saved me more than once from my own demise.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
PIXEL GRIP The Chicago trio’s latest album, “Percepticide: The Death of Reality,” vibrates with rage underneath the synthy gloom of cuts like the grinding “STAMINA” and the snappish “Work or Shut Up.” Oct. 5, 7 p.m. Sonia, Cambridge. 617-864-3278, mideastoffers.com

ADDISON RAE This social-media star turned Charli XCX associate released her first album, “Addison,” this summer; it’s a ruthlessly self-aware collection of abstracted pop, with songs like the glassy “Summer Forever” and the pumping “Aquamarine” placing her breathy coo amid spun-candy electronics. Oct. 5, 8 p.m. Roadrunner Boston. roadrunnerboston.com

AMINÉ “13 Months of Sunhine,” the latest album from this Portland, Ore., MC, scatters knottily diaristic verses over a full-spectrum shuffling of styles, including modern alt-funk (“Cool About It”), roller-rink soul (“New Flower!,” which features of-the-moment R&B singer Leon Thomas), and fractured house (“Familiar”). Oct. 8, 8 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

SONS OF THE EAST Situated in their Australian homeland, they’re sons of the east and boys from down under in these parts, but the anthemic indie folk purveyed by this trio has a hooky, anthemic charm wherever it’s played.Oct. 3, 7 p.m. $30. Royale, 279 Tremont St. 888-929-7849. royaleboston.com

THE CACTUS BLOSSOMS On their latest album, “Every Time I Think of You,” Minnesota brothers Jack Torrey and Page Burkum continue to make mood music that’s rooted in but not beholden to the vintage. At its heart, as ever, are their spectacular sibling harmonies. Opener Jenna Nicholls’s music is more overtly rooted in the vintage, and worth a live listen.Oct. 4, 7 p.m. $21. Red Room at Café 939, 939 Boylston St. 857-337-6206. college.berklee.edu/events/cafe-939

EVA AYLLÓN Living legend status often comes with an honorific title; in Eva Allyon’s case, a half-century-plus of performing and promoting Afro-Peruvian folk music has earned her the moniker “the queen of Landó.” Oct. 8, 7 p.m. $79 and up. Berklee Performance Center, 136 Massachusetts Ave. 857-337-6206. berklee.edu/BPC/full-calendar-of-events-at-the-bpc

STUART MUNRO

REVOLUTIONARY SNAKE ENSEMBLE Boston’s own combustible New Orleans-inspired brass band, led by saxophonist Ken Field, brings funky beats and incendiary improvisations, boldly breaching the booty/brain barrier. This gig celebrates the release of their fifth album, “Serpentine,” recorded live last year during their 35th anniversary concert at this very venue. Oct. 4, 7:30 p.m. $24.33-$35.97. Regattabar, 1 Bennett St., Cambridge. regattabarjazz.com

FIFTH SEASON QUARTET Versatile pianist and accordionist Plamen Karadonev’s band blends jazz with Balkan beats and Eastern European melodies. With vibrant vocalist Elena Koleva and the buoyant rhythm team of bassist Greg Loughman and drummer Austin McMahon. Oct. 5, 3 p.m. $20. First Parish in Wayland, 225 Boston Post Road, Wayland. artswayland.com

CEDRIC BURNSIDE The gruff blues shouter and gritty guitarist, grandson of blues legend RL Burnside, is the current doyen of the Mississippi hill country blues, whose hypnotic, gutsy grooves keep tradition trenchant. Oct. 8, 7:30 p.m. $20.15-$72.70. Jimmy’s Jazz & Blues Club, 135 Congress St. Portsmouth, N.H. jimmysoncongress.com; Oct. 10, 8 p.m. $31-$33. Narrows Center for the Arts, 16 Anawan St., Fall River. narrowscenter.org

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO and music director Andris Nelsons hail the 125th anniversary of the orchestra’s Symphony Hall home with a program of music composed during the hall’s construction; Debussy’s “Nocturnes” and Mahler’s Symphony No. 4. (Oct. 3 and 4). Next week, the party continues with Beethoven’s “Missa solemnis,” which the BSO performed during its very first concert in the hall in October 1900 (Oct. 9-11), and a solo organ recital by James McVinnie (Oct. 10). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Handel’s epic and cathartic oratorio “Saul” unites the H+H Orchestra and Chorus, a cast of soloists headed by bass-baritone Neal Davies in the title role, the organization’s youth choruses, and several CitySing participants, on the Symphony Hall stage under the baton of artistic director Jonathan Cohen. Oct. 3, 7:30 p.m.; Oct. 5, 3 p.m. Symphony Hall. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

SPHINX VIRTUOSI The outstanding chamber ensemble and cello soloist Sterling Elliot offer a lineup of music from throughout the Americas, including pieces by Jessie Montgomery, Alberto Ginastera, José White Lafitte, and Quenton Blache. Advance tickets are sold out, but a waitlist is available. Oct. 5, 1:30 p.m. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. 617-278-5156, www.gardnermuseum.org

A.Z. MADONNA

OUR TOWN In a world incessantly driven by the quest for Big — in politics, business, media, sports, entertainment, virtually every corner of contemporary existence — Thornton Wilder’s “Our Town” stubbornly insists on the importance and power of Small. Director Courtney O’Connor doesn’t try to make “Our Town” anything it’s not, maintaining an unhurried pace in Acts One and Two, taking care to avoid sentimentality — and mindful of the gut-punch that awaits the audience in Act Three. Even then, what makes “Our Town” cut deep is its matter-of-factness about questions of mortality and eternity. A cast loaded with blue-chip Boston actors, led by Will McGarrahan as the Stage Manager, hits all the right notes. Through Oct. 19. Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, www.lyricstage.com

PRIMARY TRUST While it’s tempting to call Eboni Booth’s play a home run, it’s more like a well-executed bunt in the clutch: subtle, built on craft and patience, deceptively small in the doing but with stakes and scope that can’t be measured by size, and an impact that lingers. David J. Castillo is extraordinary as Kenneth, a lonely guy in his late 30s who was orphaned at a young age and now is uncertain how, and whether, he could expand the narrow boundaries of his world. Helmed by Dawn M. Simmons in a promising debut as SpeakEasy Stage Company’s artistic director, “Primary Trust” is a work created and performed in a spirit of affirmation — something we could all use these days. Through Oct. 11. Presented by SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, speakeasystage.com

THE HILLS OF CALIFORNIA A shattering drama of guilt, recrimination, and blasted dreams that is also bursting with life and laced with rowdy humor: Yep, “The Hills of California” is a Jez Butterworth play, all right. Directed with a combination of focus and flair by Loretta Greco, this Huntington production stands as proof positive that the play deserves a place alongside such other Butterworth masterworks as “Jerusalem” and “The Ferryman.” Greco’s cast of 15 meshes together beautifully, led by Allison Jean White, who plays two crucial roles brilliantly: a mother in the mid-1950s convinced she can make her daughters a singing-siblings act on the level of the Andrews Sisters, and in the mid-1970s as the daughter who paid the steepest price for that delusion. Through Oct. 12. The Huntington in association with Berkeley Repertory Theatre. At Huntington Theatre. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

MACBETH Omar Robinson and Brooke Hardman, who traded barbs as the sharp-witted Benedick and Beatrice in Actors’ Shakespeare Project’s 2018 production of “Much Ado About Nothing,” are reunited in the Scottish play as a couple whose relationship is even more … let’s say complicated. (Robinson won an Elliot Norton Award this year from the Boston Theater Critics Association for his performance in ASP’s first-rate production of August Wilson’s “The Piano Lesson.”) Immersed in the paranoid atmosphere of the Cold War, this “Macbeth” is directed by Christopher V. Edwards and features Jesse Hinson as Banquo and Dennis Trainor Jr. as Duncan. Oct. 2-26. Actors’ Shakespeare Project. At Mosesian Center for the Arts, Watertown. 617-241-2200, actorsshakespeareproject.org

DON AUCOIN

URBANITY DANCE The company’s annual Fall Dance Crawl takes on AI with “dear chat, make it human.” Bringing together more than 50 Boston-based movers, musicians, storytellers, and poets of all ages spread over sites around historic South End, this new roving community event explores the impact of artificial intelligence on our urgent need for human connection. Oct. 3-5. Free but tickets must be reserved. www.urbanitydance.org/events

NEENA PRASAD The acclaimed Indian classical dancer opens her upcoming monthlong tour with a performance at the Dance Complex, offering area audiences a rare opportunity to see one of the foremost performers of Mohiniyattam. The dance form from the southwest Indian state of Kerala is known for its lyrical grace and wavelike footwork, and Prasad is known for honoring the tradition while enhancing the form’s vocabulary. She brings with her four musicians with whom she has collaborated for decades. Oct. 4. $22-$75. Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org

SYREN MODERN DANCE The 22-year-old New York-based company returns to the Museum of Science with the premiere of “At the Table: Humanity at the Dawn of AI.” Created during a residency at the museum exploring artificial intelligence, neural networks, machine learning, and consciousness through the lens of dance, the work invites viewers to engage with AI not just with caution but also curiosity. Oct. 3. $10. Museum of Science. www.mos.org/events/subspace/table-humanity-dawn-ai

TWIST & SHOUT OrigiNation Cultural Arts Center’s annual performance fund-raiser showcases the young artists of the organization’s Professional Dance Division. The evening begins with a reception and auction, and along the way it celebrates community leaders who have helped elevate the arts. But the fireworks begin at 8 p.m. with the performance, featuring modern and contemporary dance plus spoken word. Oct. 4. $75-$100. Strand Theatre. www.originationinc.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

COUNTER HISTORY: CONTEMPORARY ART FROM THE COLLECTION “How do we remember the past, and how does it inform the present?” is the central query posed by this exhibition of more than 140 works, and it’s hard to imagine a more fraught or timely frame for the current moment. In a regressive time for American culture, the show feels like a flashing beacon in the gathering dark, with artists including Andy Warhol, Mark Bradford, Jeffrey Gibson, Dana Chandler Jr., and Steve Locke here to “stand against official narratives” to “set the record straight.” Hold that thought tight. Ongoing. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

HEW LOCKE: PASSAGES Boston audiences will remember Locke from “The Procession,” an enormous still life parade of figures at the ICA’s Watershed last summer, mirroring the mass of diverse humanity that’s crisscrossed the globe since the advent of colonialism almost four centuries ago. This exhibition promises to both strengthen and clarify that movement, and its frequent injustices, as a lifelong theme for the Guyanese-British artist, as it draws on a quarter century of his work, right up to now. Oct. 2-Jan. 11. Yale Center for British Art, 1080 Chapel St., New Haven. 877-274-8278, britishart.yale.edu

BERENICE ABBOTT’S MODERN LENS Last chance: As a young assistant to Man Ray, who defined the vanguard of modern photography in the early part of the 20th century, Abbott could hardly have guessed that her own photography practice would eventually come to rival that of her master. It did, and then some; and this exhibition, of more than 400 pictures spanning the whole of her career from the 1920s through her death in 1991, exemplifies why. Through Oct. 5. Clark Art Institute, 225 South St., Williamstown. 413-458-2303, www.clarkart.edu

BOSTON PUBLIC ART TRIENNIAL At Faneuil Hall, Triennial artists New Red Order will stage “The Urge 2 Merge,” a one-night only performance/symposium/music and film festival centered on the Triennial work “Material Monument to Thomas Morton (Playing Indian),” the scandalous founder of the 17th-century Utopian colony Merrymount, which, with its egalitarian view merging Anglicism, paganism, and Native American spirituality, became a thriving countercultural colonial hub of diverse people and ideas whose success for a time threatened the straight-laced Puritan Plymouth Colony itself. Oct. 4, 6-11:59 p.m., Faneuil Hall, 4 South Market St. Free; registration required. www.thetriennial.org/events/new-red-order-presents-the-urge-2-merge

MURRAY WHYTE

FEDA EID: MADE IN USA The artist investigates her own identity as an Arab and Muslim American, along with histories of orientalist art, imperialism, and colonialism. She stages photos using thrift-store finds and poses alone and with other marginalized people, exploring the complexities of their culture and their souls. Her work is shown in conjunction with historical images from the Levant region, from collection of the estate of Tufts Arabic scholar Mohammed B. Alwan. Through Oct. 26. Abakus Projects,450 Harrison Ave.www.abakusprojects.com

CATE McQUAID

BOBCAT GOLDTHWAIT The comedian/actor/director got his start in rooms like the Comedy Studio that took chances on offbeat stand-up like his.
