title: South Boston restaurant, rooftop bar to close months after opening, citing neighborhood opposition
text:
“With these restrictions to limit and regulate the vibrant atmosphere that we were trying to create, it is in our best interest to halt service at the Essex Rooftop and Essex Dining Room at the Cambria Hotel at this time,” Jenkins said in a statement.

The restaurant opened in March, with the rooftop bar debuting two months later. The restaurant served ceviche, pasta, and steak, with sip martinis and oysters on the rooftop.

Jenkins also owns 1928 Beacon Hill, a restaurant and cocktail bar on Mount Vernon Street. (A man, naked and armed with a knife, allegedly broke into the restaurant last week before being shot by police. He survived his injuries).

The Essex had previously applied for a license to play recorded music and televisions on the rooftop. At a hearing of the Boston Entertainment Board in April, an attorney for the restaurant said both would be kept at “a very low volume” to “curate an atmosphere and ambiance of an elevated, chic rooftop,” adding that there were no plans for live entertainment or DJs at the rooftop.

The application drew nearly 200 signatures in opposition, including several neighbors, officials said at the time, according to a recording of the hearing.

“These residents don’t feel its appropriate,” said Conor Newman of the city’s office of neighborhood services. “They wanted to make the distinction that they feel their neighborhood is separate and different from the Seaport, which has more entertainment options.”

Resident Marcy Jackson agreed, saying the stretch of West Broadway in South Boston is too densely populated for the sort of nightlife the Essex would bring.

“This is a residential neighborhood,” Jackson said at the hearing. “It started as a residential neighborhood, and the Cambria came after the fact.”

Residents also expressed their negative experiences with the previous operator of the rooftop, who they said allowed a disruptive atmosphere and were unresponsive to community concerns.

“From our experience last time, it was so loud that the dishes in our house rattled, we couldn’t open our windows, we couldn’t possibly sit on a deck,” neighbor David Green said at the hearing. “When it wasn’t the actual dance band and pounding, it was a continual ambient sound, like elevator music nonstop.”

The Essex replaced the former Six/West Rooftop at the Cambria, which closed in 2023.

The entertainment board, which took the application under advisement at the hearing, did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday.

Jenkins, a former art preservationist from Barrington, R.I., has run 1928 Beacon Hill since it opened last year. Her fiancé, Aaron Sells, is a well-known local businessman — though Jenkins said through a spokesperson Wednesday that he had “absolutely nothing to do with” 1928, Essex, or any of her other business ventures.

Former business partners of Sells disputed that claim in a 2022 court case, accusing Sells of fraudulently diverting their funds from another restaurant venture in Seaport to help finance 1928 Beacon Hill. Sells has denied the allegations, both in court and in a recent Boston Magazine profile. One case against him was dismissed after Sells’ bankruptcy, while another was settled out of court in August, court records show.

Sells does have one connection to Essex Rooftop: his nephew, Avery M. Sells, is director of operations for the company that runs 1928 and Essex, a spokesperson confirmed.

This story has been updated. Material from previous Globe coverage was used.

title: Boston tourists turned away as government shutdown affects the area
text:
Roper’s story was all too familiar on Wednesday as visitors showed up at Boston-area historical sites and attractions only to find closed signs because Congress deadlocked and missed the deadline for funding the government late on Tuesday night.

The government’s shutdown comes during the ongoing tourist season as foliage starts to change colors around Boston and the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution nears.

Governor Maura Healey laid blame on Trump and Republicans for the shutdown.

“People need to know that this dysfunction in Washington affects them and all of us,” the first-term Democrat said in a statement. “In Massachusetts, we are focused on doing everything we can to mitigate these impacts and continue delivering for people. But we need Donald Trump and the Republicans to get the government back to work.”

The governor’s office warned that an extended shutdown could impact benefits and other programs, including assistance for home energy projects. Also, more than 30 Head Start programs would be “interrupted” and hospitals would not receive federal reimbursements, according to Healey aides.

The shutdown was triggered at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. Along the historic Freedom Trail, Bunker Hill Monument and the USS Constitution Museum, as well as parts of Faneuil Hall, were closed while 13 sites remained operational as of Wednesday afternoon. It’s unclear what could happen in the days to come as the shutdown continues, but Boston Globe reporters who visited several federally-run facilities and parks could already see the fallout.

Roper came to visit the area on Tuesday and planned to leave Wednesday. But it was the JFK museum that drew her to Boston. Roper, a lifelong Democrat who became an Independent after she campaigned for Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. last year, said she is frustrated with party politics that lead to this shutdown.

“It’s crazy that we’re played like this,” she said. “I’m tired of paying [my representatives] money to not do their job.”

Security guards standing outside the John F. Kennedy library were turning visitors away and recommending other tourist attractions around Boston.

Christine and Simon Jones were visiting New England from Southern California and had planned to visit the presidential library.

“I try to find the silver lining and assume that, you know, it wasn’t meant to be today,” Christine said. “But I felt very connected to this one in particular.”

Simon Jones, 57, said he was frustrated but not surprised by the shutdown.

“I mean, we clearly don’t have a functioning government right now,” he said. “It’s expected that they can’t seem to get anything right at this point.”

At the Navy shipyard in Charlestown, visitors to the USS Constitution were met with a sign reading “Ship is closed.”

Anthony Johnson, 57, who was visiting Boston from Arkansas, was surprised to see the ship closed but said he still planned to tour the museum, which remained open.

“I guess it’s just part of the process, living in a democracy, that there’s inconveniences sometimes to work out the differences both parties have, and hopefully they’ll come to an agreement and it’ll open back up before long,” Johnson said.

Kathy Hollin, 65, and Peggy Chandler, 67, from Indiana, came to the ship as part of a bus tour and were disappointed for themselves but more frustrated with the overall shutdown.

“What I found out is the military are not getting paid for this shutdown, but people in [political] office are,” Hollin said.

During a government shutdown, all active-duty personnel, as well as National Guard who are currently deployed, must carry out their assigned duties with their pay delayed until the shutdown is over. Civilian personnel whose work the Defense Department considers essential, or “excepted,” will also continue to work, while other civilians are furloughed for the duration of the shutdown.

Staff at the Visitor Center of the ship declined to comment.

The Bunker Hill Memorial, a tall concrete monument in Charlestown, also was affected. While visitors could still walk around the monument and enjoy the park, the visitor center and the inside of the monument was closed.

Visitors are typically able to climb 294 steps to the top and enjoy a 360-degree view of the city. However, since the monument is a National Historical Park, it, too, was closed.

In Boston’s bustling Faneuil Hall marketplace, just furloughed National Park employees were seen leaving the hall carrying clear plastic bags full of their belongings, including wide-brimmed park ranger hats.

The shutdown closed the great hall and museum, while retail on the first floor stayed open.

Lynell Cannell, 78, visiting from Rockford, Ill., said she came to Boston for the express purpose of visiting federally funded historical sites in the city.

“I’m very disappointed because we pay a lot of money to go, and you’re looking forward to doing things here,” she said, adding, “It’s not like you come from Illinois every day.”

Though they lived closer to Boston, Michelle Murphy, 58, and her husband, 56-year-old Brian Murphy, of Hartford, were similarly disappointed.

The Murphys have a son who manages a restaurant in Yellowstone National Park, a federally funded park also vulnerable during government shutdowns.

“They should separate this part of the government out of all of their other spending,” Brian Murphy said. “It’s for us, the people, for these places to be open for us, not be a pawn in their debating.”

Cannell said her trip isn’t ruined but said it was bad timing that it coincided with the government shutdown.

“I’m 78,” she said. “How many more times am I going to be back here?”

Matt Stout of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: It’s an exciting moment for Boston sports. Here’s where the major teams stand.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

No matter which Greater Boston team they support, many local sports fans are living through an exciting and expectant moment.

The Red Sox, who won their first Wild Card series matchup against the Yankees last night 3-1, have made it fun to be a fan again. Under a new head coach, The Patriots are showing signs of life. The Celtics are recalibrating as their star forward heals. The Bruins are taking steps to bounce back. And the Revolution, New England’s pro soccer team, has, well, few places to go but up.

Here’s an update on each team, with help from my Globe colleagues who cover them.

Maybe it’s the walk-up songs or the thrill of a classic rivalry. Maybe it’s skill at reading opposing pitchers or the healing power of chanting “Yankees suck!” Either way, last night’s come-from-behind win underscored this season’s theme: turnabout.

The Sox started off the season lackluster, losing more than they won and catching flak for trading away Rafael Devers. But as my colleague Tim Healey chronicled this week, they caught fire in July, jumpstarting a 10-game winning streak that earned a third-place finish in the AL East and reaching the postseason for the first time in four years. The Globe’s Julian Benbow has crunched the numbers behind that streak, including the team’s hardest hitter (rookie Roman Anthony) and hardest hit (outfielder Jarren Duran).

The Sox-Yanks playoff series continues tonight.

New England’s first season with coach Mike Vrabel at the helm was always going to be seen as a test of his leadership. Though far from over, the early results look promising.

As my colleague Chad Finn wrote after the Patriots thumped the Panthers 42-13 on Sunday, the team’s first few games have showcased dynamics that suggest it “might just have something satisfying happening.” They include new offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels’ creativity and wide receiver Stefon Diggs’ knack for finding an opening.

The Pats will face the undefeated Buffalo Bills Sunday.

Jayson Tatum’s season-ending ruptured Achilles’ tendon during the playoffs was a dispiriting punctuation mark to a disappointing run for the former champions. And since then, Boston has lost standbys like Jrue Holiday and Al Horford.

Yet as the Globe’s Gary Washburn notes, the coming season offers opportunities for others. They include Jaylen Brown, who may have to step up in Tatum’s absence; Anfernee Simons and other newcomers; and new owner Bill Chisholm, who aims “to win championships and raise banners.”

Tatum is still recovering, but he’s been working out and won’t rule out returning this season. The preseason starts next Wednesday.

After failing to make the playoffs for the first time in nearly a decade, the team hopes to reestablish itself this season with leading players like Charlie McAvoy and David Pastrnak, my colleague Conor Ryan writes. Joining them are returning franchise pillar Zdeno Chara, winger Tanner Jeannot, and Hampus Lindholm, who’s back after breaking his kneecap.

Boston has won half its preseason games so far; the regular season starts next Wednesday.

OK, excited and hopeful might not be the words to describe Greater Boston’s Major League Soccer fans after the Revolution fired coach Caleb Porter last month and missed the postseason for a second straight year. Some fans want sporting director Curt Onalfo fired, too.

But defeat can bring renewal. As my colleague Frank Dell’Apa notes, Porter improved things, proven coaches who could replace him are on the market, and a couple good strikers could solidify the club’s serviceable roster. “I’m very optimistic,” Onalfo recently said. “When it turns, it turns.”

More sports news: Napheesa Collier of the Minnesota Lynx criticized WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert, accusing her of failing to resolve officiating and player compensation issues.

title: Erewhon hinted its trendy smoothies and organic groceries might be coming to Boston — or that’s what fans thought
text:
Erewhon, the trendy, Los Angeles-based whole foods grocer, is coming to Boston. Just maybe not the way its fans expected.

The company, best known for its pricey organic smoothies and its celebrity clientele, appeared to suggest in a cryptic Instagram post Tuesday that it was expanding to Boston, as well as more than a dozen other cities outside its Southern California domain.

The initial caption, according to People, read simply, “The Taste of Erewhon in Your City. Coming soon.” For fans of the luxe chain, which has been promoted by celebrities and influencers ranging from Sabrina Carpenter to Kendall Jenner, it seemed to be a sign that Massachusetts would be getting its own branch of the health food retailer in the near future.

But the excitement died down when the company quietly edited the post’s caption, which now reads “A Taste of Erewhon Shipping to Your City.”

“Shipping” being the operative word.

Instead of a physical, brick-and-mortar location in Boston, the suggested “taste of Erewhon” (pronounced error-uh-wan) appears to refer to a limited-edition $100 “smoothie kit” that went on sale Friday, according to a follow-up post.

The kit, which includes ingredients for the Erewhon’s Strawberry Glaze Skin Smoothie promoted by Hailey Bieber, offers customers the opportunity to “recreate our signature smoothie from the comfort of your own home, in any city, nationwide.”

But even with the promotion, fans of chain weren’t thrilled with the apparent bait-and-switch.

“Erewhon, can you get it together?” said Danielle DaSilva, a Boston-area wellness influencer, in a video posted to TikTok. “I don’t want to order stuff online. I want to get stoned and wander around an Erewhon and spend $150 on one cucumber, and then I want to get a $50 Haley Bieber smoothie.”

“I don’t care if it’s overpriced,” she continued. “What’s it gonna be? Because that Instagram caption, y’all really switched up on us. Everybody was so excited in Boston, every girl I know re-posted that on their story. And now it’s looking like you guys aren’t even physically coming to Boston.”

Erewhon did not return a request for comment Friday.

An Erewhon expansion to Boston would actually be a return to its roots: the company originated in 1966 as a basement stall selling natural foods at 303 Newbury St. (where Le Rosier Bakery now stands) before relocating to Los Angeles in 1969.

And how about this local trivia: Erewhon’s founders, a married Japanese-American couple from Brookline, eventually sold the company and returned to Massachusetts to found the Kushi Wellness Institute in Becket.

Erewhon is making a return to the East Coast, albeit in limited form; there’s a stall inside a luxury fitness club in New York City, Eater reported in June. Membership at the club is eye-poppingly exclusive — a $36,000 initiation fee, with $7,000 in annual dues — but customers in the Brooklyn area will be able to order their Erewhon smoothies for delivery, per the report.

That doesn’t mean the California company isn’t looking at New York — or, potentially, Boston — for a full-fledged location. Erewhon executive Kabir Jain said Monday that the company had plans to build five new stores over the next three years outside the Los Angeles area, including “further east across the country,” according to trade publication Grocery Dive.

Erewhon, with its frequent celebrity sightings and A-list endorsements, has become a byword for everything healthy and fashionable in Los Angeles. Its colorful smoothies, curated produce shelves, and organic juices have become sensations on social media. Dorchester native Ayo Edebiri, describing her rise to fame as a star of TV’s “The Bear,” told Elle Magazine last year that she used to go to Erewhon to spot random Hollywood actors.

“Now I’m the random actor!” she added.

Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.

title: Boston police warn of law enforcement imposter scam
text:
Boston police on Friday warned residents of a scam involving a caller pretending to be a police sergeant seeking money for uncovered court costs.

“The Boston Police Department reminds community members that we will never call and request money, banking information, or electronic transfers as part of any investigation or court matter,” the department said in a statement Friday.

Police were notified of the scam after a Dorchester resident received a call on Sept. 30 from the phone number 617-634-5528.

The caller claimed to be a Boston police sergeant, who claimed that the resident owed money “for a court related matter earlier,” the statement said.

The scammer said for them to make payments through Zelle, an app that allows money to be transferred via a mobile phone number or email address.

The caller provided several phone numbers for the money transfer, and the resident made two payments, police said.

Police advise residents to protect themselves from money scams by never sharing personal information to suspicious callers, and to verify the legitimacy of a caller through an official number, the statement said.

Residents should report suspicious activity to Boston police, either by calling or visiting a district station. In an emergency, dial 911.

Information can be provided anonymously through the department’s tip line at 1-800-494-TIPS (8477), texting the word “TIP” to CRIME (27463), or by visiting the Boston Police CrimeStoppers Website, the statement said.

Adam Sennott can be reached at adam.sennott@globe.com.

title: From trash heap to carbon sink: the rise of urban ‘food forests’ in Boston
text:
The roots of the organization began at a trash-filled lot around the corner from Kriegman’s apartment in 2014 in Egleston Square, not far from the Franklin Park Zoo. With his neighbors joining in with shovels and spades, the crew spent hours digging up beer bottles, even a car that was half-buried in the soil. Within months, a small food forest filled with budding flowers and edible shrubs had sprouted.

Food forests differ from traditional community gardens by design and intent. While community gardens typically feature raised beds with caretakers seeding flowering annual plants, food forests center around perennial and indigenous fruit-bearing plants, mimicking the ecosystems of untamed woodlands in lots that range from 10 by 10 feet to the size of a city block.

When BFFC opened the Egleston Community Orchard, the city owned the land. That meant that at any point, the city could decide to develop it. So in 2015, Kriegman formally established BFFC as a community land trust that can acquire and hold land to ensure it remains permanently accessible for community use.

“We realized all our good work could be lost if we didn’t actually own the land,” Kriegman said.

From Mattapan to the North End, the nonprofit has now opened 13 food forests, with a goal of opening 30 by 2030 — a target shared by the city as part of its 2030 Climate Action Plan. The idea is simple: More trees and plants provide shade in areas lacking green space and suck carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas that drives global warming, from the atmosphere.

The carbon reductions from small patches of land may be small, but every tree or shrub makes a difference.

“Boston has ambitious climate goals, and the only way to achieve them is with robust efforts from diverse stakeholders,” said Elizabeth Jameson, director of climate policy and planning for Boston’s environment department.

The mayor’s housing office’s Grassroots Open Space Development Program and the Boston Planning and Development Agency provide city-owned parcels at reduced prices. The land the city distributes for grassroots initiatives is typically undesirable — due to size, location, or inaccessibility — for real estate or commercial development.

When a community identifies a site it wants transformed into a food forest, BFFC helps residents prepare a proposal. If approved — after a years-long process of community meetings — the city transfers the parcel into the group’s land trust, ensuring permanent community ownership.

Kriegman’s hope is that since food forests are now officially part of the city’s climate plan, the approval process will quicken, arguing that 30 food forests in a city of almost 700,000 people could be transformative.

That’s because urban food forests can enhance biodiversity, offset pollution by filtering out pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, and mitigate the urban heat island effect — the double whammy of heat trapped by asphalt and concrete. Vegetation and soils in food forests combat that heat. Trees and shrubs provide shade, plants release moisture, and soil naturally absorbs and stores heat more gradually.

A 2025 study by researchers in Taiwan examined a rooftop farm and other sites over three years and found lots with food forests were cooler on average by 2.2 degrees Celsius, about 4 degrees Fahrenheit, than surrounding areas.

The cooling effect of a small green space doesn’t extend far beyond the site itself — up to 100 meters — but expanding the number of food forests across a city could ease heat stress in neighborhoods that lack green spaces.

In Boston’s historically Black communities, there is a 20 percent disparity in accessible parklands and a 40 percent disparity in tree coverage compared with predominantly white neighborhoods, according to Boston’s Heat Resilience Plan. That means Black communities feel, on average, 7.5 degrees Fahrenheit warmer during heat waves.

Beyond mitigating heat stress and pollution, food forests also provide fresh produce and a gathering hub.

More than 525 fruit trees and shrubs, with apples and cherries alongside lesser-known fruits such as pawpaws and serviceberries, can be found in Boston’s food forests. It’s all free with one caveat: take only what you need. Communities use the parks for picnics, birthday parties, movie nights, and yoga classes.

Neighborhood residents, called community stewardship teams, care for the land and collectively govern it through BFFC’s community land trust. Stewardship team leaders — 73 percent are women and 47 percent are people of color — ensure that community voices shape the coalition’s direction.

Every response is decided collectively — whether the problem is drought or an infestation of pests — a process that fosters trust-building and balances urgency with consensus.

That can be a challenge, too, said Kriegman. “Most people understand individual ownership, so it’s a constant challenge trying to educate people on what it means to own land together.”

The movement is growing despite headwinds from Washington. In May, the Environmental Protection Agency terminated $60 million for its Environmental Justice for New England Program. BFFC had been approved for a $250,000 grant, and it is unclear whether the organization will receive the money.

Still, momentum is not slowing. The nonprofit coalition has opened two food forests this year, and in August, it broke ground on a third site in Dorchester. It plans to open two or three new food forests in 2026.

“We’re moving faster than the city can keep up with because community demand and interest continue to grow,” Kriegman said.

title: Why five feet of building space can doom construction
text:
When a building is defined as a “high-rise,” that triggers the need for better, more expensive, fire safety systems than a smaller building. State requirements include an automatic sprinkler system, a power generator, emergency communications systems, and pressurized staircases. These rules, although they add significant costs to building, are important to ensure occupants remain safe in case of emergency.

The question is the threshold at which the high-rise requirements kick in. By making the threshold needlessly low, Massachusetts is creating unnecessary hindrances to building housing. That should change.

The International Building Code, a model code commonly used in the United States, sets the high-rise threshold as 75 feet above ground, measured at the floor of the highest story. Typically, this translates to seven stories, with the high-rise requirements kicking in at eight.

Massachusetts’s building code, however, differs in some ways from the International Building Code. Massachusetts defines a high-rise as a building that’s 70 feet above ground, measured at the roof. Typically, this translates to six stories, with the high-rise requirements kicking in at seven.

That means one less story in which to build units that can be sold or rented — translating to less housing and less money to pay for the building. Sometimes, the difference between six and seven stories can be the difference between making a project work — or not.

Colin Booth, a principal at Stack + Co., an architectural and construction management firm, said the limit is why Boston-area buildings are often either 69 feet and 10 inches — or more than 100 feet, where the additional floors can cover the extra building costs.

Two Boston projects Booth is working on illustrate the impact. One project, at 2 Bowdoin Street in Dorchester, is slated to have seven stories, 22 apartments, and ground-floor restaurant or commercial space. Booth said an original design proposal was for a six-story building, but the finances didn’t work. He redesigned it using cross-laminated timber, a newer engineered wood product that allows for a shorter floor-to-ceiling height. That let the project proceed with seven stories, but still remain under the 70-foot high-rise limit.

However, not all projects can be redesigned. Even as the Dorchester project advances, Booth is drafting multiple feasibility studies for another Boston housing project, at 745 Hyde Park Avenue. There, he has yet to find a design that pencils out. Because of the site’s topography, a seventh story won’t fit even using cross-laminated timber. If it could be built up to 75 feet, a seventh story would be an option, and the project would be viable. “It does make it easier if you have more options on the table to make a project work,” Booth said.

The Massachusetts threshold stems from a state law stating that a building that rises 70 feet above ground level needs automatic sprinkler systems. That law passed in 1973, 27 years before the first International Building Code was published.

House and Senate journals from 1973 don’t record any discussion about the reason for the 70-foot limit.

John Nunnari, executive director of AIA Massachusetts, the state chapter of the American Institute of Architects, said the law’s origin appears to be that firefighters’ ladders in the 1970s could only extend to 70 feet.

But ladders today can extend more than 100 feet. And Brockton Fire Chief Brian Nardelli, second vice president of the Fire Chiefs Association of Massachusetts, said ladder height matters less now because firefighters tend to operate by using the building’s own systems, hooking hoses into a standpipe system. The difference between 70 feet and 75 feet is “splitting hairs,” Nardelli said.

The state fire marshal’s office declined to comment, referring questions to the Board of Building Regulations and Standards. A board spokesperson said neither the state statute setting the limit nor the first edition of the building code, which became effective in 1975, provide any context as to why the heights differ between the Massachusetts Building Code and the International Building Code.

Steve Smith, executive director of the New York-based Center for Building in North America, said he’s not aware of any other state building code with a high-rise threshold below 75 feet. While some cities may impose lower limits, that is changing — the Santa Monica, Calif., City Council voted in September to raise that city’s 55-foot high-rise limit to 75 feet.

The limit may have made sense in 1973. The question is why the Legislature or Board of Building Regulations and Standards haven’t bothered updating it since then. Boston architect Sam Naylor submitted a proposal to the board requesting that the state change its building code to conform with the International Building Code on this issue, and Naylor said he expects the board to hold a hearing on his proposal in November.

With the state in a housing crisis, updating the high-rise threshold in Massachusetts’s building code so it’s in line with the International Building Code seems like basic common sense.

text:
Later in the afternoon, she learned that her father, Asaf Schlezinger, was one of the roughly 360 people killed by the heavily armed Hamas-led militants who ambushed the festival. The militants also took more than 40 festival-goers as hostages.

“People came to dance or to work, like my father, and they never came back home,” said Schlezinger, 30.

Schlezinger will spend the anniversary of his death at an exhibit run by survivors of the Nova festival attacks, which opened on Sept. 26 in the former F.W. Webb building on Dorchester Avenue in South Boston. Part of her job at the exhibit, which includes videos from the festival and from survivors, is not that different from her father’s — to comfort visitors in a space they call the “healing room,” dedicated to visitors’ reorientation after the heaviness of the exhibit.

On Saturday afternoon, Schlezinger was overwhelmed by memories of the overall attack on Oct. 7, in which some 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed and 251 people were taken hostage in the deadliest attack on the Jewish people since the Holocaust. The ensuing retaliatory war conducted by Israel in pursuit of Hamas has killed more than 67,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry does not differentiate between civilians and militants in its toll but has said women and children make up around half the dead.

Israel and Hamas have signaled support for the new US plan to end the war in Gaza and release all remaining hostages there. Yet, much remained unsolved Monday as Israel and Hamas conducted indirect talks in Egypt.

Two years after the attacks, many affected by the conflict describe Oct. 7 as a day suspended in time. Feelings of helplessness, fear, and grief are impossible to shake.

Sammy S. Nabulsi, a Palestinian American attorney living in Dorchester, said the time since the Oct. 7 attacks has felt like a “two-year bad day,” in which anxiety hangs over him constantly.

“It’s very prevalent and pervasive and always there,” he said. “It’s a horror show.”

Near the start of the war, Nabulsi spent 27 days working to get his friends, Abood Okal and Wafaa Abuzayda, and their son, out of Gaza. It was the scariest and most stressful time of his life. Then, the relief he felt when the family made it to the United States quickly dissipated when people started reaching out to him about their own friends and family stuck in Gaza, asking for help.

“It’s kind of perpetually haunting,” he said. “There’s just a ton of people that are just trying to stay alive.”

Rabbi Marc Baker, the CEO of Combined Jewish Philanthropies of Greater Boston, said the trauma of Oct. 7 is still very alive for him, partially because of the Israeli hostages in Gaza.

“In many ways, it feels like it is still Oct. 7, 2023,” the Brookline resident said. “We’re not even in post-trauma yet. And so there’s a way in which we haven’t even been able to begin the grieving process.”

Baker’s daughter was traveling in Israel when the attacks began, and he remembers early conversations with her as she talked to Israeli friends who were directly affected by the attacks.

“I think the sense of living through history, and not just history, but terrible history, was powerful and scary,” Baker said.

The anniversary of the attack comes as public sentiment about the ensuing war is shifting after livestreams of violence and deaths have been seen across the world. Images of the ongoing food crisis in Gaza have also spread across media outlets, television screens, and social media.

Just last month, a team of independent experts commissioned by the United Nations’ Human Rights Council concluded that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, which the UN defines as “acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group” — a conclusion Israel vehemently denies.

Israel and its defenders argue they are in a war with the terrorist group Hamas, not Palestinian civilians.

Michael Maria, 51, a Palestinian American from Roslindale, has watched livestreamed videos of the Israel-Hamas war over the past two years and called the images “unimaginable” and “unconscionable.”

Maria’s family is Palestinian Christian, and they are originally from Bethlehem. His father immigrated to the United States in the 1950s, and his mother followed in 1970 after experiencing bombings and Israeli occupation in the West Bank during the 1967 war.

Maria said a silver lining to the Israel-Hamas war has been watching public attitudes shift since his childhood in Burlington.

“Back in the day, my parents would hide their identity. They wouldn’t share the fact that they’re Palestinian. They would make up that they came from,” he said. “Today, people use the word ‘Palestine’ regularly.”

Eli Gerzon, an organizer with anti-Zionist advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace, said that not a day goes by in which they don’t think about the loss of life in Gaza.

“We cannot think about all of the people that Israel is killing every single day and feel the compassion and the grief that they each deserve,” said Gerzon, who uses they and them pronouns.

But their work as an organizer gives some hope. Since last year’s anniversary, Gerzon said, condemnation of Israel’s actions has become more mainstream.

“There were groups that had a slightly different approach to what kind of language they wanted to use and how they wanted to define things … and now you just see full-throated, unapologetic support for Palestine and condemnation of Israel,” Gerzon said.

The mood was somber and quiet at the Nova Exhibition on Saturday, especially in candlelit rooms with names and faces of the dead. Schlezinger said she has coped with the life-changing loss by talking about her dad and what he meant to her and the Nova music festival survivors. She finds “bright spots” where she is reminded of him, recalling how she felt when she met a woman named Inbar, whom her dad treated at the music festival.

“I feel like he led her there to give us meaning,” she said.

Schlezinger said she misses everything about her dad. But day-to-day, she mostly wants to see his beer belly again, and lie her head in the nook of his shoulder.

Correspondent Nathan Metcalf contributed to this report. Material from The Associated Press was also included.

title: Developer Tom O’Brien will draw up new plans for Carney Hospital site, closed after Steward Health Care bankruptcy
text:
The property owners of the former Carney Hospital site in Dorchester have tapped prominent local developer Tom O’Brien to lay out a plan for the site’s future.

O’Brien’s firm, HYM Investment Group, will co-manage the planning process, the developer confirmed in a Tuesday statement. Carney, one of several hospitals operated by Steward Health Care, closed its doors last year after having served the community since the Civil War era.

“We recognize the important role the Carney Hospital has played in the Dorchester community, and we see the future of this site as an opportunity to create something that is once again meaningful for the neighborhood,” O’Brien said in the statement.

Founded in 1863, Carney Hospital was part of the Caritas Christi system, a chain of Catholic hospitals operated by the Archdiocese of Boston, before being acquired by Steward in 2010. Serving a diverse population of patients, the hospital’s closure only worsened what some advocates have called a “health care desert” in low-income areas of Boston.

HYM will work with My City at Peace, a local community advocacy group, to devise a framework for the property.

“Together, HYM and MyCAP welcome conversations with all who care about the site’s future and look forward to presenting a plan that includes a health care component and reflects the needs of Dorchester,” O’Brien said.

MyCAP, cofounded by the Rev. Jeffrey Brown, could not immediately be reached for comment on Tuesday. Property owners Apollo Global Management declined to comment.

HYM, which O’Brien founded, has undertaken several high-profile development projects in recent years, including the mixed-use Boston Landing campus in Allston/Brighton and the former Suffolk Downs race track in East Boston and Revere.

It has also partnered with MyCAP for P3Roxbury, a $1.5 billion development on Tremont Street which envisions 466 housing units, most of them classed as affordable, and approximately 700,000 square feet of life sciences space.

Earlier this year, O’Brien, the city’s top planner under former mayor Thomas M. Menino and one of its best-known developers, weighed a bid to run against incumbent Mayor Michelle Wu. He ultimately reversed course and decided against challenging Wu, who went on to soundly defeat her opponent, Josh Kraft, in the September preliminary election.

O’Brien’s involvement in the Carney redevelopment was previously covered by the Dorchester Reporter.

The 12.7-acre site is owned by Apollo, the private equity giant that acquired the land and hospital buildings from Steward’s landlords, Medical Properties Trust and Macquarie Infrastructure Partners. The complex real estate structure contributed to Steward’s financial spiral, as the for-profit health care firm buckled under millions of dollars in rent payments.

Carney was one of two Massachusetts hospitals to shutter as part of Steward’s bankruptcy proceedings, along with Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer. Though Steward managed to sell off six of its eight hospitals in the state, including St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton (now operated by Boston Medical Center), it said there were no qualified bids to keep Carney or Nashoba Valley running.

The site is zoned for multifamily residential use, which limits what developments might replace the Carney complex. Wu has said she is opposed to rezoning the site for nonhealth care related purposes.

A report issued by the Carney Working Group in April also recommended the site continue to provide some sort of health care service.

Any new health care service would need to ensure “a path to long-term financial sustainability,” the report said, potentially through specialty services with higher revenue margins.

Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.

title: Boston city councilors propose publicly-owned grocery stores to make healthy food more accessible
text:
Councilor Liz Breadon, one of the two authors of the proposal, told her colleagues that city-owned grocery stores could help make healthy food more accessible to lower-income residents. She emphasized that many Bostonians are struggling to afford grocery prices rising due to tariffs and inflation, or as a result of federal funding cuts to SNAP, the country’s food stamp program.

“In this moment, the Greater Boston Food Bank is flagging up the fact that an increasing number of our residents in the city of Boston are food-insecure,” Breadon said. “Developing alternative modes of food access is vital at this point.”

City-owned grocery stores could be set up “to prioritize community benefit over profit, enabling lower prices, better food access, and stronger local sourcing,” the councilors wrote in the hearing order.

Breadon and Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune filed the hearing order to discuss the matter, and on Wednesday the council sent it to committee for potential further consideration.

Louijeune said on Wednesday that she hopes the council explores not just the feasibility of setting up city-owned grocery stores, but looks at all options for increasing food access and bolstering the city’s existing food infrastructure.

She emphasized the need to better support nonprofits and cooperatives already making healthy food accessible to Boston residents, pointing to the closure earlier this year of Daily Table, a nonprofit local grocery store chain, and the recent financial struggles of the Dorchester Food Co-op.

“We have a number of others — the closure of Freight Farms, the closure of Boston Organics, and we have the Dorchester Food Co-op, which is in need of assistance and in need of help," Louijeune said. “So I want this hearing to be about how we support our nonprofit grocers, how we’re supporting more urban farming, and looking at what’s been working in [other] places.”

Louijeune pointed to Atlanta as an example of a city that has recently opened a city-supported grocery store through a public-private partnership, and Madison, Wis., which last year signed a lease with a grocery store to fill a city-owned property.

The hearing order mentions “other municipalities across that country [that] have piloted or proposed publicly-owned or supported grocery stores as a means to stabilize access to affordable, nutritious, and culturally appropriate food, particularly in communities where private chains have withdrawn or declined to invest.”

Louijeune said before Wednesday’s meeting that the pursuit of the idea for Boston is not inspired by Mamdani’s platform in New York City’s mayoral race.

Mamdani has proposed setting up a network of publicly owned grocery stores across New York City on city-owned property, which would be able to sell produce to residents at wholesale prices, thanks to not having the burden of paying rent or property taxes.

“It had nothing to do with what’s happening elsewhere,” she told the Globe, saying the hearing order was in part inspired by a call she and several councilors took with the Boston Food Access Council last week. “It has everything to do with pocketbook issues for our residents here in the city of Boston, and our residents who are facing food insecurity.”

Louijeune did not directly answer whether she’s heard from Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration about whether it supports the idea of city-owned grocery stores. But she said the city’s office of food justice is doing great work to reduce food deserts in the city and make healthy food more affordable, and she looks “forward to having more discussions” on the issue.

Wu, speaking at an unrelated event Wednesday, said she knows Boston families are increasingly struggling to put food on the table, but did not indicate clear support for city-owned grocery stores.

“We have not turned to government-run grocery stores as an effective and efficient way to address food insecurity,” Wu told reporters. “We have instead put resources towards [other] programs,” like offering additional discounts on fresh food or providing financial support for local grocers.

title: Wu condemns attacks on police at pro-Palestinian protest on Boston Common
text:
Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said Wednesday that his department’s role is to keep the peace.

“For protests and or for protesters, we’re there to keep the peace,” he told a Globe reporter.

“Certainly protesting is your right, and we can do it peacefully, and we will,” he said. “We’re there to keep the peace so people can do that. But the fact is, we won’t tolerate violence.”

Police on Wednesday said officers were trying to rush to an emergency in another area of the city at 6:46 p.m. when protesters blocked Tremont Street near Winter Street.

“Many protesters, wearing facial coverings and gloves, interlocked arms, chanted over amplified bullhorns, and refused to clear the roadway,” police said.

The protest drew between 200 and 300 people, police said.

Four officers were injured, police said. One officer suffered a broken nose when he was allegedly punched in the face by a protester, a second was pepper-sprayed in the face, a third injured a finger, and a fourth injured their back carrying a protester to a police vehicle, police said in a report.

One protester, identified as Roder Atwood, 21, of Somerville, allegedly punched the officer, breaking his nose. At his arraignment in Boston Municipal Court Wednesday, Atwood pleaded not guilty to assault and battery on a police officer and several other charges.

The courtroom was filled with supporters of Atwood and the 12 other people who were taken into custody.

Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Olivia R. Izzi requested Atwood be held on $10,000 bail, saying the officer he allegedly struck will need reconstructive surgery.

Atwood’s lawyer, Peter A. O’Karma, asked Judge James M. Stanton to set bail at $500. He said Atwood is a senior at Tufts University studying cognitive science who has no prior convictions.

O’Karma said bail is meant to ensure Atwood shows up for trial, not punish him for the charges against him.

But Stanton was not convinced and set bail at $10,000, drawing a collective gasp from Atwood’s supporters, 15 of whom were wearing keffiyehs, a symbol of Palestinian support.

Stanton also ordered him to stay out of downtown Boston.

A handful of other protesters were also arraigned, and Izzi asked that they be released on personal recognizance. But Stanton required that they pay either $500 or $1,000 cash, depending on their criminal history.

Prahlad Iyengar, 25, of Boston, Laith Hintzman, 19, of Boston, and Benjamin Andre Choucroun, 20, of Medford, were ordered to pay $500 bail.

Owen Woodcock, 26, of Boston, and Amun Prophet, 25, of Allston, were ordered to pay $1,000 bail, with Stanton noting they had prior charges for disorderly conduct.

Each person was handcuffed from behind by court officers. Prophet rolled his eyes as Stanton set his bail.

More defendants will be arraigned Thursday.

“These defendants were not in court today because they were protesting,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden said in a statement Thursday. “They were in court because they committed crimes.”

“If you assault police and commit other offenses you’re going to be arrested and prosecuted, period,” he added. “Peaceful protests happen all the time in this city. We support everyone’s right to protest. But these individuals chose against protesting peacefully and they are now facing the consequences of those choices.”

Earlier Wednesday, Governor Maura Healey offered strong support for police who confronted the Boston protesters and for officers who faced “street takeovers” in multiple communities this past weekend.

“I believe in free speech. I believe in the right to protest. We’ve been doing it for 250 years here in Massachusetts,” she said while attending an annual Massachusetts Law Enforcement Memorial ceremony at the State House.

“What I do not accept are attacks on police officers, men and women, who are simply there on the scene to try to ensure the exercise of a peaceful right to protest and to keep the public safe,” she said. “My commitment is to stand with the men and women who do the difficult and dangerous work out there every single day.”

In the report, police detailed the confrontation with protesters.

“When officers attempted to move the group to the sidewalk to allow emergency vehicles to pass, protesters surrounded police cruisers, kicked vehicle doors, and resisted dispersal efforts,” police wrote. “Several officers were assaulted during this period, including one struck in the face. Protesters also ignited smoke devices and flares, further endangering officers and bystanders.”

More officers were called in “as violence escalated,” to engage “in crowd control to restore order and effect lawful arrests,” police said.

Police reported “equipment being forcibly removed or damaged, including body-worn cameras, radios, bicycles, and other duty gear.”

“Despite these challenges, officers made numerous arrests of individuals engaged in unlawful assembly, violent resistance, and the obstruction of emergency response efforts,” police wrote.

Speaking at the same event as Healey, Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, said “there’s way too much violence going around when it comes to attacking police officers.”

Pointing to the “street takeover” in the South End over the weekend, in which a police car was set on fire, Calderone said, “There has to be repercussions for these actions” and applauded Healey for her strong stance against takeover participants.

The other seven people charged with resisting arrest, disorderly conduct, and disturbing police were identified as Osama El Khatib, 26, of Watertown; Atlanta Carrig-Braun, 20, of Boston; Haley Macintyre, 24, of Dorchester; Madeline Weikel, 27, of Watertown; Jacob Pettigrew, 22, of Malden; Styx Hatch, 19, of Boston; Gabrielle Smith, 28, of Cambridge.

title: ‘I’m very happy if it’s real’: Locals react with relief and skepticism to Israel-Hamas cease-fire deal
text:
Davis Galper is among many Greater Boston residents grappling with a swirl of emotions this week at the idea that the violence and horror of the war in Gaza could soon come to an end. Israel and Hamas agreed to pause fighting in Gaza and release hostages and Palestinian prisoners, but many of the details of the deal were not immediately announced.

“It all feels rather surreal,” said Rabbi Keith Stern, 71, the senior rabbi at Temple Beth Avodah in Newton. “I’ve been burned too many times to allow myself an unrestrained sense of joy.”

If the peace deal doesn’t go through, Davis Galper said, her family has “no choice” but to continue fighting for the release of all hostages, living and dead.

“Nothing’s going to give us these two years back and nothing’s going to give us Omer back alive,” she said.

Sammy S. Nabulsi, a Palestinian American lawyer based in Dorchester, said he was overjoyed at videos of people celebrating in Gaza. But concerns about the details of the cease-fire agreement and what it means for Palestinians occupied his mind.

“I’m very happy if it’s real,” he said. “I gotta see it to believe it, so I’m in a little bit of a purgatory when it comes to my emotions.”

Uncertainty remains about some of the thornier aspects of the plan advanced by President Trump, such as whether and how Hamas will disarm, and who will govern Gaza.

Some Greater Boston residents were also mourning friends and family they lost in the conflict, as well as deaths of those who’ve they’ve learned about through community gatherings, places of worship, on social media, and in the news. Some questioned whether peace would last if a deal goes through considering the history of conflict in the region.

Stern, the Temple Beth Avodah rabbi, said his early morning conversations Wednesday with friends in Israel were full of tears both of joy at the news and sorrow about the Israeli and Palestinian lives lost.

“When one does the calculus on it all, it is just breathtakingly sad,” he said. “This war has completely ripped apart the soul of the Jewish people throughout the world, and specifically in Israel.”

Karameh Kuemmerle, 55, whose family is from Nablus in the West Bank, said a cease-fire is a “much-desired outcome” that she hopes will be permanent.

Kuemmerle cofounded the group Doctors Against Genocide, a coalition of medical professionals advocating for humanitarian support in Gaza, and said she is in daily contact with physicians and medical students in Gaza. Her first concerns are about the introduction of humanitarian aid into Gaza.

“I’m relieved, but I can’t be happy because I realize the loss,” said Kuemmerle, a pediatric neurologist in Boston.

In the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel that launched the war, Hamas-led militants abducted 251 people and killed around 1,200, mostly civilians. Most of the hostages have been released in cease-fires or other deals.

Gaza’s Health Ministry said the Palestinian death toll has exceeded 67,000 people. The ministry, which doesn’t differentiate between civilians and combatants but says around half of the deaths were women and children, is part of the Hamas-run government. The United Nations and many independent experts consider its figures to be the most reliable estimate of wartime casualties.

As part of the cease-fire deal, Hamas has agreed to release the remaining 48 hostages, around 20 of them believed to be alive, in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners.

Rabbi Marc Baker, CEO and president of Combined Jewish Philanthropies of Greater Boston, a group dedicated to strengthening Jewish life, said the hostages’ return means the Jewish community can begin to repair itself.

“The idea of them finally coming home feels like we can finally begin to actually properly grieve and begin to move forward,” he said.

If the hostages are released, Baker said, their return will be fraught and emotional, especially for Boston Jews with direct connections.

“We’re going to have to navigate all of those emotions together as a community, with our Israeli brothers and sisters,” he said.

Fatima Razzaq, 36, operations director of the Boston Palestine Film Festival, said that while a peace deal is the immediate goal, she doesn’t believe it will last without “the Palestinian people gaining their freedom, sovereignty, and self-determination.”

Razzaq, whose parents immigrated to the United States from Palestine, said the celebrations of Palestinians in Gaza that she’s seeing on social media are a sign that people there share hope that the fighting will end.

“If anyone would be skeptical, it would be the Palestinian people on the ground,” she said.

Sadaf Tokhi of the Globe staff contributed to this report. Material from the Associated Press was used.

title: Food banks suffer from policy changes, anticipate increased stress from government shutdown
text:
“[SNAP] is not enough because I have my grandkids,” Brown said. “They’re hungry. We don’t have time to fight over the piece of chicken.”

Even on cold or rainy days, the line at the pantry snakes down the sidewalk. Brown and other patrons hope for meat, bread, milk, and fresh produce . But recently, as the number of peopleseeking food assistance has increased, the bags have been lighter.

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 limited eligibility and benefits of SNAP, a program many low-income families and individuals rely on for groceries. Earlier this year, Trump cut 94 million pounds of food aid, leaving food banks scrambling to scrape together enough for their increasing numbers of patrons.

These problems, which many food bank workers in Greater Boston described as an impending crisis as the holiday season approaches, are expected to be exacerbated by the government shutdown, which, on Oct. 18, entered its 18th day.

“We’ve seen a 30 percent increase in the distributions that we’ve handed out over the past three months,” said Jonathan Tetrault, vice president for basic needs at Catholic Charities Boston, a nonprofit organization that provides community support, including food services, child care, and healthy families programs.

“So what that tells us is, not only are more people needing support, but the people that have been coming to us are needing to come more frequently.”

MaryAnn Laughlin, a volunteer at the Yawkey Center food pantry, said that recently, it has sometimes had to start closing earlier. Having to turn away the hungry is her least favorite part of the job, she said.

“There’s not enough food because sometimes...as you could see, the bag is not that full,” said Laughlin. Bags are still packed with a variety of foods, including dried beans, rice, and canned fruits and vegetables, but they often include fewer fresh products and less meat, which volunteers and employees have said have been more difficult to get.

Catherine D’Amato, Greater Boston Food Bank president and CEO, said the USDA cuts in March meant that the food bank needed to raise more money “to keep providing the healthy food that our 600 food pantry partners rely on to serve their community.”

“Our donors and the food acquisition team at GBFB rose to the occasion and we never had to change the amount of food going to our food pantry partners,” she said in a statement to the Globe.

She also said any government shutdown will only exacerbate the already growing problem of hunger and emphasized that while exact numbers are not yet available, prior shutdowns have shown that the need for additional assistance is clear.

“What we’ve experienced in previous shutdowns is that when federal workers don’t get paid, many of them turn to the food pantry system to keep food on the table, some of them will likely be visiting a pantry for the first time,” she said.

Jennifer Lemmerman, the chief policy officer at Project Bread, a nonprofit group that helps connect people in Boston with food sources and advocates for food security policies, said that she is worried about the Massachusetts hunger crisis being exacerbated by the government shutdown.

During the last government shutdown in 2019, which lasted 35 days, Lemmerman said thousands of government employees who were furloughed or working without pay experienced food insecurity for the first time. Now, she predicts the same will happen.

“We’re in a crisis in Massachusetts. Food insecurity rates right now are the same as they were at the height of COVID,” she said. However, with the government shut down, the government programs that were implemented during COVID to help with food insecurity are not available, causing further stress to a system already burdened by heightened food insecurity rates.

David Waters, CEO of Community Servings, a nonprofit organization based in Jamaica Plain that provides meals to people experiencing critical and chronic illnesses, said he is worried about the looming impact the cuts will have on the organization, which relies heavily on federal funding.

Waters said Community Servings has already felt the effects of increased food insecurity in the Boston community, with the wait list for its program growing longer and longer.

“Community Servings in February had a waiting list of about 100 people. Yeah, that’s close to 300 people now, and some of them could be waiting six months,” he said. “And, if you’re dealing with a critical illness and you’re food insecure, you can’t wait six months.”

Eric Lindsey, a director and food pantry manager with Omega Men in Action, a nonprofit organization that helps families in need in Greater Boston, said he has seen an influx in families visiting the monthly food bank, and anticipates that number will keep growing.

“Two years ago, when I took over the position, we were probably looking at, like, on average, 30 to 40 families a month. And [now] we’re at like 90 to 100, so we [have] definitely more than double, close to triple, the amount of families we’re seeing,” he said.

Brown, the Yawkey Center food pantry patron, was able to take some fresh fruit and vegetables, including tomatoes and apples, and add them to her bag. It’s a luxury that the Yawkey food pantry can sometimes give people when they have fresh food.

Brown said she is grateful for the food that she can get at the pantry, even with less being offered at times.

“I can survive. But there’s certain things, you know, there’s certain things that you need,” she said. ”You [can’t] to go to sleep [when] your stomach is growling."

Correction: Due to incorrect information given to the Globe, an earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the percentage of food the Greater Boston Food Bank gave to the Catholic Charities Greater Boston/Yawkey Center food pantry.

title: Gold is having its best year since 1979. Here’s why the price might keep hitting new highs.
text:
👀 In case you missed the Trendlines webinar, the full discussion on President Trump’s pressure campaign on higher education is now up on YouTube.

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts has offered buyouts to hundreds of employees amid soaring health care costs and steep losses.

Here’s why Boston’s biotech supremacy is at risk.

The Trump administration said it isn’t planning to impose tariffs on generic drugs from foreign countries.

In April, our financial adviser did something new: He put my wife and me in gold.

I’d always dismissed gold as a fringe asset — something for investors who are 1) obsessed with inflation; 2) don’t trust paper money; 3) are convinced the world is about to fall apart, or 4) all of the above.

But I’m quite pleased our adviser made the move. It’s turned out to be the best year for the yellow metal since 1979.

The price of gold on the spot market closed Thursday at $3997 a ounce after ending Wednesday above $4,000 for the first time. It has gained 51.5 percent this year and nearly 150 percent since 2022.

Gold has outshined bitcoin, another don’t-trust-the-government asset, US stocks, and play-it-safe funds that mix stocks and bonds.

After such an extended run-up, it’s fair to ask whether the Great Gold Rush is nearing an end. The general consensus is no.

Goldman Sachs just raised its gold forecast to $4,900 an ounce for the end of next year. That would mark a gain of more than 21 percent from Wednesday’s record close of $4,042.

“Even when adjusted for inflation, gold is at an all-time high,” Jack Ablin, chief investment strategist at Cresset Capital Management, said in an interview. “But it’s still not too late” to add gold to your portfolio.

No investment is a sure thing, but here are three reasons many experts think gold is a prudent play right now.

Insurance: Plenty of investors speculate in gold by betting on short-term price swings.

But the metal is mostly used as a hedge against inflation, a drop in the value of the US dollar, and financial or political turmoil. Right now, investors are anxious about all three.

As the impact of tariffs kicks in, forecasters see inflation remaining elevated at about 3 percent, one percentage point above the Federal Reserve’s target.

The dollar is on track for its worst year in five decades. Morgan Stanley blames the decline in part on slowing US economic growth, falling interest rates, and foreign investors reducing their exposure to the greenback.

Tensions are running high over the federal shutdown, mounting government debt, and the Trump administration’s threats to Fed independence.

For these reasons, investors are starting to view gold as safer than the dollar, according to Ken Griffin, the billionaire hedge fund manager.

“People are looking for ways to effectively de-dollarize, or de-risk their portfolios,” Griffin told a Bloomberg conference this week.

Silver is also on a run, mostly for the same reasons.

Diversification: Gold can add balance to a conventional portfolio heavy in stocks and bonds.

The metal often appreciates when equities fall or when fixed-income returns wane. Because gold is priced in US dollars, it often rises in value when the dollar weakens, since it takes more dollars to buy the same ounce of gold.

A weaker dollar also makes gold cheaper for buyers using stronger currencies, increasing global demand and driving prices up.

My adviser, Alex Burke of Financial Solutions Associates in Dedham, bought shares in April of an exchange traded fund that invests in gold. The price has appreciated 28 percent since.

The ETF is a small slice of our IRA — about 6 percent. Burke recommends being judicious.

“Don’t put all your eggs into one golden basket, use it as a small part of a well-diversified portfolio,” he said in an email. “Even if you are entering at the top, if you limit the allocation to a small part of a portfolio you will limit your potential losses, but still have plenty of upside if gold soars.”

Market trends: Gold prices have been on an upward slope since the Great Recession as central banks sought to diversify their reserves beyond the dollar and protect against financial shocks.

The buying accelerated after Western countries froze Russia’s foreign currency reserves as punishment for its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. That triggered a flight to safety and concerns among some emerging market governments that their dollar holdings might not be so safe.

Analysts expect central banks to continue buying gold to reduce their exposure to the US. Falling interest rates, federal deficits, and fears of an AI stock bust will increase the metal’s appeal to investors.

Final thought: Gold supply increases only about 2 percent a year, so even a modest rise in demand can send prices sharply higher.

In June, JPMorgan Chase analysts forecast that gold would top $4,000 by the third quarter of 2026. It was off by almost a year.

Of course, financial markets reverse course all the time. Gold’s surge could lose steam due to an unexpected rise in interest rates, an easing of geopolitical tensions, or a rebound by the US dollar.

Gold isn’t always effective as a hedge.

Still, a modest allocation makes sense — not because gold is going to beat stocks or bonds over every stretch, but because its appeal as an inflation hedge and diversification tool, combined with strong demand, make it a reasonable insurance policy in tumultuous times.
