title: Police pursue a moose, and a driver’s attempt to squeeze past a bus backfires
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police log books (a.k.a. blotters) in our communities.

At 8 p.m. Oct. 9, a 39-year-old man from Boston attempted a bold move while driving when he tried to squeeze by an MBTA bus in Andrew Square. It didn’t go as he had planned. In fact, if he were trying to save himself some time, it backfired in a very big way, as his car hit the side of the bus and became wedged between it and the curb. MBTA Transit Police determined he was impaired, took him into custody, and had his vehicle towed. Thankfully, no injuries were reported, and police shared a video of the debacle on social media along with this timeless bit of advice: “Don’t Drink & Drive!!!!”

A moose got a police escort in Keene, N.H., on Oct. 5. Police said the animal “made its way through downtown” and video footage shared on social media showed cruisers following behind the animal as it galloped down the street. Police reported that they guided the moose out of downtown safely and away from residential neighborhoods.

At 2:41 p.m. Sept. 14, Medway police got a call from a resident of Fisher Street who reported that his Boston Globe mailbox had been “thrown from its post.” Police responded and lent a hand with “getting the box back together.” According to the log entry, the caller was satisfied by the police response and didn’t want to take further action.

At 8:53 p.m. Oct. 3, Norwood police got a call from someone walking a dog and heard yelling in the area of Hampden Drive. According to the log entry, the caller “thought it was possibly a Halloween decoration but was not sure.” Police checked the area and didn’t see or hear anything suspicious. They spoke to a man, however, who said he had also heard something, but he, too, thought it sounded like one of those audible Halloween decorations.

A harrowing event took place recently in Dorchester — not the neighborhood in Boston, but the tiny New Hampshire town with a population of 339. It started around 4:07 p.m. on Oct. 10, when New Hampshire State Police and the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department were informed that a 2-year-old child there was missing. When they got the call, the child had not been seen for over 45 minutes, and first responders quickly swung into action. Conservation officers, state troopers, and firefighters from Canaan, Rumney, and Grafton responded along with area search and rescue teams to look for the toddler. All told, over 90 volunteers showed up to help. Several K-9 teams searched along drainage areas and in thickly wooded spots near the the toddler’s home, and drones and a state police helicopter were used to search a large swamp from the air. Almost four hours later, at about 7:52 p.m., the mission ended happily when the child was located safe and sound (albeit a little chilly). WMUR reported that when Jeremy Corson and his dog Freya from New England K9 Search and Rescue found the toddler, she said: “I’m cold, I think I’m ready for a bath.”

Emily Sweeney can be reached at emily.sweeney@globe.com. Follow her @emilysweeney and on Instagram @emilysweeney22.

title: Boston elections: District 7 council candidates go head to head in Roxbury debate
text:
The two candidates presented very different pitches as to what kind of leadership they would offer the district based on their backgrounds.

Ahmed painted himself as a “young, energized fighter,” saying his approach to elected office would be rooted in his lived experience as a Somali refugee and former professional athlete, along with his years of working with youth in Boston Public Schools and as a coach and cofounder of the Boston United Track and Cross Country Club.

Culpepper, a Dorchester native, emphasized his decades-long track record as a grass-roots community advocate, including his nearly 30 years as an attorney in the US Department of Housing and Urban Development, as well as his tenure as a well-known senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church.

The two also offered different policy strategies to address the range of challenges in the district.

When asked how they would spur investment in Roxbury’s economy and support local businesses, Ahmed focused on pushing developers to include affordable commercial space in new developments, and increasing education and awareness for how to apply and qualify for Community Development Block Grants.

Culpepper said he would seek to get the district designated as an “empowerment zone,” a federal program that offers tax incentives and grants to spur economic development in particular areas, and that he’ll also work closely with the mayor’s Office of Economic Opportunity and Inclusion to funnel more funding to the district.

On housing, Ahmed emphasized his support for rent control, while Culpepper outlined his “gentrification neutralization plan,” which would aim to increase homeownership options for people with Section 8 vouchers or residents of public housing developments.

The two also committed to being “independent” representatives, but Ahmed indicated he would be inclined to “be aligned” with the mayor and work in partnership with her, while Culpepper offered a specific example of an issue on which he and the mayor do not agree. He would fight her administration’s effort to put a bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.

The debate turned tense on a few occasions when Ahmed opted to question and request a fact-check on Culpepper’s record. Ahmed also emphasized the age difference between himself and Culpepper, referring to himself as a “young, go-getter.”

Culpepper brushed off the attacks, and later told the Globe he is “confident” in his decades of experience advocating for Roxbury residents, which he said “speaks for itself.” After the event, Ahmed said he felt it was appropriate to question Culpepper’s background working on housing issues, particularly when residents are still suffering from rising housing costs and facing being pushed out of their neighborhoods.

Toward the end of the debate, the moderators asked how each candidate will demonstrate “integrity, transparency, and ethical leadership” considering recent scandals that have plagued the district. Both candidates painted themselves as role models poised to earn the trust of their constituents.

“When folks look at Miniard Culpepper, they look at someone that has fought for the community all of his life, someone that grew up in the community and fought when it came to housing,” Culpepper said. “They look at somebody they can trust, someone that cares and someone that will fight for them.”

“This neighborhood took me in, this neighborhood gave me home, access, and opportunity,” Ahmed said. “We need someone that’s a go-getter ... and I will be there fighting for you day and night.

The District 7 position is the only open seat on the November ballot, after Fernandes Anderson stepped down from the role earlier this year after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges for taking a $7,000 kickback while in office. Fernandes Anderson was ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution, and sentenced to one month in prison.

She is set to self-report to an as-yet-to-be designated federal prison on Friday.

Ahmed has also faced some controversy and accusations of misconduct during his District 7 campaign.

Another District 7 candidate previously accused Ahmed of harassment, as did a Healey administration official, who filed two police reports about Ahmed’s alleged behavior during early voting in the lead-up to the preliminary election in September. A municipal court judge later terminated the harassment prevention order the official had requested against Ahmed.

Several longtime civic leaders also criticized Ahmed last week over a recent Instagram post, which they said misleadingly and incorrectly implied they are supporting and have endorsed his political campaign.

Ahmed later deleted the post from his Instagram and told the Globe he did not intend it to be misleading, or imply that all the men pictured in the post had endorsed him.

District 7 voters will choose between Ahmed and Culpepper in November, after the two advanced from a crowded field of 11 candidates in the September preliminary election, with Ahmed receiving 1,170 votes and Culpepper winning 1,112, according to the city’s official election results.

Mavrick Afonso, who came in third place by a tight margin, had formally requested a recount in the race last month, but it did not ultimately change the outcome of which finalists will compete to fill the District 7 seat in November.

District 7 comprises some of the city’s most diverse and historically disenfranchised neighborhoods, including Roxbury, and parts of Dorchester, Fenway, and the South End.

Both Ahmed and Culpepper have previously run for office. Ahmed ran a failed campaign for the State House last year, and Culpepper unsuccessfully ran for a state Senate seat in 2022.

title: ‘Trump wants to be a tyrant’: Thousands attend ‘No Kings’ demonstrations around Boston
text:
By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Saturday’s rally concluded after a performance by the Boston-based rock band The Sheila Divine.

Attendees began heading off the Common, still waving flags and holding up signs.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Several members of the state’s Washington delegation took the stage and fired up the crowd with more chants and calls to resist the Trump administration.

Senator Elizabeth Warren called Trump “a bully” and “weak.”

“When we don’t bow down to kings or bullies, they start to lose their power,” she told the crowd. “The American people do not bow down.”

Senator Ed Markey and Representatives Katherine Clark, Ayanna Pressley, and Seth Moulton also spoke to the demonstrators from the stage.

“I want him to hear this down in Washington, DC, that freedom is knocking on Donald Trump’s door,” Moulton told the crowd. “Ding Dong, Donny! Freedom is here.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As demonstrators began heading towards the exits, vendors at tables piled with “No King’s” merchandise struggled to make their final sales. Others wove through the thinning crowd with stickers and flyers, handing out protest paraphernalia to anyone willing to take one.

“I think it’s a good message,” said John Leonard, 68, as he passed out laminated stickers that read “President Chump” in bold block letters. “I even sent some to my friends to put up around Mar-a-Lago.”

Leonard said the crowd was just what he expected — peaceful and joyful. He was glad to see both older and younger protesters in attendance, and said the turnout represented “all kinds of people.”

“People may be depressed, but the solution is getting out and being counted,” said Leonard, who lives in Hingham. “People have to stand up right away. We can’t hesitate.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As the demonstration neared the three-hour mark, there was no sign of waning energy from the crowd. Dozens of protesters climbed the Soldiers and Sailors Monument to lead chants. Cheers grew louder and views of the stage were hard to find.

“Our democracy is melting away,” said Trish McClean, 75, of Dorchester. “It’s heartbreaking and very frightful.”

McClean said that the Trump administration has no respect for the US Constitution, and she worries that people will lose their health insurance.

Saturday’s sizable crowd made her more hopeful than she’s been in some time, but she said the rally still doesn’t feel like an adequate response to the world’s atrocities. “I can’t believe there’s not more people here, and that this isn’t happening every day. ... We can all make a difference.”

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

Among the eye-grabbing costumes and outfits were many people dressed up as frogs.

Barb Brunelle, a 65-year-old retired math teacher, said the inflatable full-body frog suit she wore was a symbol of solidarity with protestors from around the country, including those in Portland, Oregon. She said a viral social media post of a person in a frog costume hexing an ICE official inspired her attire.

She said she ordered the $60 inflatable suit on Amazon last Saturday, and by the next day, she said, they weren’t available until after Halloween. She said she hopes the costume brings a bit of levity to a “dark” time.

“If we can bring some joy to all the insanity that’s happening, even for a few minutes, why not?” she said.

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

For Corrine Jones, a 31-year-old mom of four, protesting President Trump was a family affair. She had all four of her children, from ages one to 10, in tow during the “No Kings” protest in Concord on Saturday.

“I think it’s really important that my kids don’t get used to the insanity of the last nine or 10 months,” she said. “I want them to realize that everything that’s going on now is abnormal.”

She said she’s also disappointed in how Democrats are responding to the Trump administration.

“I’m really worried about the fact that both parties seem to serve the same masters,” Jones said. “They’re both really bought out by corporate interests. It feels like the Democrats can’t launch an effective and credible resistance because they’re paying homage to the same billionaires that the Republicans are.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As the Common continued to fill with people, families dotted the crowd. Some parents hoisted toddlers onto their shoulders, and others followed teenagers weaving toward the stage.

“They were the people who introduced me to protesting and marching, so I wanted them to come with me,” said Amina Castro Jacobs, 19, who suggested the family attend Saturday’s demonstration together. “And we hate Trump.”

The family, active in Boston’s immigrant community, said they’re deeply worried about the future of their neighbors. But protesting together, said Jenny Jacobs, Amina’s mother, serves as a way for parents to pass down important political values while learning from young people.

“Our child’s generation has created a new energy,” said Jacobs, 50, who lives in Jamaica Plain. “There’s a lot of things to be angry and frustrated and depressed about right now, but following their lead has been really hopeful.”

By Amanda Gokee, Globe Staff

Protesters gathered in front of New Hampshire’s State House on Saturday afternoon for a “No Kings” rally.

Speakers addressed people on the State House lawn, with the crowd extending along the surrounding streets, where they were met with the honking horns of passing cars and live protest music.

“I came here specifically because I wanted to stand up for my state in my capital,” said Pebbles Sillars, 61, who donned a handmade outfit representing a “wolf in sheep’s clothing.” She wore an actual sheep’s skin on her back and a hand-felted wolf’s head over her face.

She said the outfit is meant to represent President Trump, who she sees as a wolf in sheep’s clothing.

“I think that a lot of people were misled by Trump and his promises,” she said.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Some who came out to the Common were dressed in costumes ranging from unicorns and dinosaurs to lobsters and frogs.

Many stopped to take pictures with Richard Saunders, 69, of Newton, who was dressed as Pope Leo XIV. Saunders said he bought the costume after friends remarked on his close resemblance to the pontiff.

Saunders, who was raised Catholic, carried a sign quoting the sonnet inscribed on the Statue of Liberty pedestal that symbolizes the country as a beacon of hope for immigrants.

“This is what made America great,” he said.

He said the country was built “on the backs of immigrants, like my Irish ancestors who came over during the potato famine.”

“People are losing sight of that,” he said.

He said he felt inspired by the large turnout in Boston on Saturday.

“It gives me so much strength,” he said. “When you get cynical for the future, come to something like this if you want to get your faith restored in humanity.”

By Steven Porter, Globe Staff

Among the throngs of protestors who descended on Market Square, many bobbed about in colorful costumes, including one man who wore an inflatable suit depicting President Trump as a giant baby.

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell touted the approximately 40 lawsuits she’s filed against President Trump.“They will keep coming, and we will keep fighting,” Campbell said. “And if they want to come for Massachusetts, I say: Bring it on.”

The crowd cheered.

Campbell ran through the lawsuits over funding cuts, attempts to end birthright citizenship, and more.

“We are here to send a message: In America, we have no kings, we have the people,” she said.

As they did with Mayor Michelle Wu, a small group of hard-left protesters in the front row, waving Palestinian flags and ones with the Soviet hammer and sickle, attempted to yell over her.’

“You’re not going to out-noise us,” Campbell told them. And then she added: “We’re with you.”

By Carlos Munoz, Globe Staff

From the steps of the State House, Providence Mayor Brett Smiley spoke to the need for people to be around “like-minded people” to know they are not alone in their frustration, and to send a message “this is not the direction we want our government to be going in.”

He estimated more than 2,000 people in attendance at the city’s “No Kings” rally.

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

As hundreds of people pressed toward the stage, others spread out across the southeast corner of Boston Common, chatting with friends and clapping along to a live rendition of Yankee Doodle.

“We thought it would be fun to bring a little humor,” said Elizabeth Barry, 50, who came dressed as a calico cat after her first-choice raccoon costume didn’t arrive in time. “I think it’s really important to make this feel safe.”

Inspired by demonstrators who wore inflatable animals at protests in Portland, Ore., Barry said the costumes are meant to make rallies feel more welcoming for people who might otherwise be nervous to attend. The unicorn beside her nodded in agreement, adding that the pair is meeting President Trump’s absurd decisions with their own showing of absurdity.

“Fascists hate when you laugh at them,” said Rosy, Barry’s friend, who lives in Somerville. “This is a way of saying we’re out here protesting and we’re wearing funny costumes because they’re ridiculous and we can be, too.”

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Ingrid Geis, 65, said she was surrounded by fellow demonstrators on their way to the protest in Boston as she boarded a train in her hometown of Winchester on Saturday morning.

She said she has participated in local protests regularly, where a few hundred people attended, but she wanted to join thousands of others at the big protest on the Common.

“I wanted to see thousands of people, I wanted to be with the thousands,” she said.

Geis said she is the daughter of German immigrants who came to the US after World War II. She said she sees parallels between the authoritarian uprising her parents witnessed in Germany in the 1930s, and what is happening in the US today.

“People ask me what were average Germans doing during that time, and I say, ‘What you’re doing now. They were listening to the news and saying it’s awful, and then they’re just leading their normal lives, not doing anything about it.’ That’s why I’m here today,” she said.

Geis carried a sign that read, “A king is only a king if you bow.”

She said she is “embarrassed” by the institutions in media and academia that she said have capitulated to the Trump administration, noting her alma mater, Columbia University, among them.

“I can’t believe how quickly they bowed,” she said. “If you bow, bad changes can happen.”

The other side of her sign read, “Democracy is not a spectator sport.”

“You’ve got to get out here and make your voice heard,” she said.

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

A stage with a huge American flag as a backdrop and an LED screen above. A riser 50 feet in front of the stage for TV cameras to capture what’s on it. A sound team, under a canopy, keeping tabs on the full rig of speakers on the sides and base of the stage.

The “No Kings” rally on the Common diverted from some of the ad-hoc nature of many of the protests that have raged here in recent years. It was a festival atmosphere that included various sing-alongs, as well as an appearance from Mayor Michelle Wu.

This one began with a brass band pumping out a jaunty tune.

One of the members began a rap verse that quickly churned through references to “free Palestine,” rent control, white supremacy, and capitalism.

Later, the lead singer of the 2000s band Dispatch sang a few songs, including their main hit, “The General.”

As is common with progressive protests, organizers wearing orange vests identified themselves as the “safety team.” There was a sizable police presence around the Common, with dozens of officers in yellow vests, but they stood at ease, chatting as they looked around the area.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

Jaden Leegeary, a Canadian visiting the country, who attended the “No Kings” protest wearing a MAGA hat, called the protesters “clueless.”

Leegeary said that when he arrived and began confronting demonstrators, several organizers reacted by asking him to move to a less crowded area. “I said, this is America. I’m gonna use my free speech right here,” he said.

He said he came “to call these people’s hypocrisy,” arguing that Trump is not a fascist.

By Steven Porter, Globe Staff

Retired public school teacher Jayne G. Winsor gathered with demonstrators Saturday in this town of fewer than 10,000 residents to publicly express disapproval with the nation’s trajectory under President Trump.

“It’s time for all of us to be loud and clear, get the message across not only to everyone in our country but the world that the direction that our country is being led in right now is not the direction we want it to go,” she said, holding a protest sign in one hand and the leash of her miniature golden doodle, Acadia, in the other.Her dog wore a sign that said, “I bark at kings.”

Winsor said the list of issues that have her unhappy with the Trump administration is long: there is the immigration crackdown, the deployment of military forces on domestic soil, and the shift in federal health care policy. One topic of particular worry is the dismantling of the US Department of Education, she said.

“I’m concerned for kids who have any kind of challenges. I’m concerned for all kids. I’m concerned for staff. I’m concerned for educators,” she said. “I’m concerned about free thought.”

Winsor said she is a registered Democrat and never misses an election, but she’s feeling more like an independent lately as she’s “rather disappointed” in many elected Democrats.

“I don’t think they’re doing enough,” she said.

“Every day it’s something new. The Democrats need to be out there having press conferences, making their voices heard,” she said. “I really don’t get where many of them are.”

By Lylah Alphonse, Globe Staff

Protesters gathered in the town common in Middlebury, Vermont, for the “No Kings” rally organized by the pro-democracy group Indivisible Middlebury.

They chanted “USA! USA!” and sang along as a small band played “This Land Is Our Land.” At noon, cowbells started clanging and the crowd cheered.

Little kids colored in pictures of butterflies and the Liberty Bell, which were hung on a line with colorful clips. A couple wore matching rubber chicken heads and carried signs calling President Trump a “motherclucker.” People in their 50s and 60s, some wearing daisies in their hair, others dressed in Colonial-era costumes, carried a Revolutionary flag, upside-down American flags, and signs that read “Let Freedom Ring.” A golden retriever with a small “No Kings” sign around his neck drew a cluster of college students.

Elizabeth Melican, a freshman at Middlebury College, stood with friends, holding a handmaid sign adorned with a monarch butterfly that read “the only orange monarch we want. No kings in the USA.”

This wasn’t her first protest — she’s from Manhattan and has participated in walkouts in support of Roe V. Wade and gun control — but came to the” No Kings” protest because Trump’s policies are “impacting our education and our ability to protect people.”

“It’s important that we stand up for that as young people,” she said.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

Sue Doherty joined the “No Kings” protest with members of the grassroots group Quincy4Palestine, carrying a red sign that read “End Zionism. Arms Embargo Now. Free Gaza.”

Doherty, 65, a retired educator, said she wished the “No Kings” movement centered pro-Palestinian causes more directly.

“I think they leave it out,” she said. “People are still afraid of the issue. There’s still this kind of fear that it’s antisemitic to stand up for Palestinians.”

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Mayor Michelle Wu told a roaring crowd, “Boston doesn’t back down,” during a “No Kings” protest at Boston Common.

“What scares them about Boston is that we are the America they say is impossible,” Wu said.

She said America is a nation of immigrants and laws, and “both make us stronger.” She continued that Trump mistakes “cruelty for greatness.”

Trump, she said, is “counting on us going quiet.” She said Boston will “stand with LA and Portland,” where Trump has tried to send in the National Guard.

When she took the stage, Wu was greeted by cheers, but someone in the front row, amplified by a bullhorn, began chanting criticism of her from the political left. The man was shouted down, but loud arguing continued as she spoke, even as a couple of police officers walked over to stand nearby.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

“Donald Trump wants to be a tyrant,” said Claire Fitzmaurice, 64, of Quincy, who arrived at the “No Kings” protest in hand-sewn colonial attire beside her friend Mimi Balsamo, 78.

Fitzmaurice’s sign read “Same Shite, Different Century,” while Balsamo’s read, “Democracy Needs Your Courage.”

Fitzmaurice said their outfits were meant to symbolize how Trump’s politics represent a return to an era of tyranny.

“It’s not just women’s rights,” she said. “Donald Trump wants to be a tyrant, and we’ve beaten tyrants before. The Massachusetts Constitution is against tyrants, and so are we.”

Both women are members of Quincy’s United First Parish Church, where John Adams once worshiped and where he and Abigail Adams are now buried.

“This church has been standing up for social justice since the beginning of the American Revolution,” Balsamo said.

By Nick Stoico, Globe Staff

Protesters continued pouring into the Common as the crowd grew and the event began.

Sue Donaldson, 76, a retired doctor from Northampton, was dressed in a dinosaur costume and carried a sign that read, “Don’t let democracy go extinct.”

Donaldson said the Trump administration does not adhere to the rule of law, and she criticized the White House for its attacks on science and attempts to slash billions in medical research.

“I don’t want to be in a fascist country,” she said.

She said she has participated in numerous demonstrations since Trump was elected to a second term. She said protesting, “Is about all we can do at this point.”

“I keep hoping that some Republican members of Congress will grow a spine,” Donaldson said. “They see how unpopular all of this is, and maybe they’ll be more scared of us than they are of Trump.”

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Betsy Ross met George Washington by the parking kiosk.

“Someone told me there was a George here — this is great!” said Betsy, real name Eileen Ryan, of Watertown.

Dave Beyna, 57, of Norton, had dressed as Washington in a deep blue costume and trademark gray curls. Ryan, 65, was in a light blue dress and a straw hat, and her husband, Guy Holt, 66, was in a tri-cornered hat.

“We’re trying to take back the flag,” Ryan said, waving a star-spangled sign. “We’re real patriots.”

Beyna said he’s gone to protests around the country in his apparel. He wants to remind people, he said, that Washington could have sought to become king — but had no interest.

“He basically said, ‘This is not what we did this for,’” Beyna said.

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

By noon, crowds had gathered around ‘The Embrace,’ a bronze sculpture honoring Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King’s legacy in Boston. It was a scene of gray and white hair, hugs, and laughter as old friends reunited beneath the towering arms.

“I’m here because liberty is in peril,” said Rob Means, 74, pausing to puff on a cigar. “Donald Trump and all of his supporters have to do a rethink, or we’re in trouble.”

As John Lennon’s Imagine played from speakers behind the memorial, Means watched demonstrators dance and clap. The turnout, he said, was “heartwarming,” a reminder that people still care about what’s happening in the country.

“I got my skull cracked in Washington Square back in the ’60s, so I’ve done this a few times,” said Means, who lives in Melrose. “I’m not going to stop now.”

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

Katrina Brown stood beneath a red, white and blue banner stretching over six feet across and emblazoned with the words “No Kings Since 1776” above an image of George Washington brandishing a pistol.

“We don’t have any kings, and he wants to be a king,” said Brown, 59, of Quincy.

Brown called the “No Kings” protests an act of patriotism.

“How much like democracy and patriotism can you be to go to a protest to try to help your government change properly?” she said. “That’s part of what America is about — saying what we want as a public, saying what we want, and having our voice heard.”

By Alyssa Vega, Leanne Burden Seidel, and Kenneth Singletary, Globe Staff

READ MORE

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

“I think just the horror of what I see going on,” said Bill Valentine, 81, of Dorchester, describing what drove him to write daily “resistance poetry,” as he sat amid Quincy “No Kings” demonstrators holding a sign reading: “Resist the Felon.”

Over the past year, he said, he has written and posted a new poem every day, publishing his 209th this morning.

The first two stanzas of Resistance Poem #209 read:

“Nestled, as I am, in the cradle of liberty, warmed by the mohair mantle of justice,

I feel as if I am a wanderer on the barren, lowest point of Death Valley where sailing rocks fly at me on their own accord.”

Valentine said his writing is fueled by what he witnesses in his classroom.

“I teach ESL to immigrant adults, and they are so threatened and so devastated,” he said. “They’re afraid to come to class. ICE is just frightful.”

A poet for about 40 years, Valentine said he began writing politically this year as “one way of resisting what is going on in our country.”

By Lila Hempel-Edgers, Globe Correspondent

An hour before the ‘No King’s’ rally was set to begin, clusters of demonstrators streamed through Back Bay toward Boston Common carrying handmade signs and small American flags. On the Orange Line, Northeastern University student Jason Seestadt leaned against the train wall, a pin of a crossed-out golden crown fastened to his jacket.

“I don’t agree with the current administration’s policies at all,” said Seestadt, 23, who was on his way to meet his grandparents at the protest.

Originally from Minnesota, Seestadt said he and his grandparents planned to spend their weekend making their opposition to President Trump’s agenda known.

“They’re trying to take greater control of democratic states and cities, and I don’t think that’s appropriate for any president to do,” he said. “It’s the defining traits of the beginning of fascism.”

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

A crowd in the thousands converged in the northwest corner of the Boston Common ahead of a planned “No Kings” rally at noon.

People waved American flags and a wide array of signs on poster boards with ire focused on President Trump, immigration agents, and tech moguls.

“Impeach Trump!” read one sign. “Prevent truth decay,” said another.

Ahead of noon, a speaker from the full stage that had been assembled urged a“completely violence-free event.”

The crowd cheered.

“If someone’s here to agitate, walk away, don’t take the bait,” the crowd chanted at the behest of the speaker.Shortly before noon, there were no obvious counter protesters.

By Nathan Metcalf, Globe Correspondent

“I am representing grandmothers,” said Denise Grant of Rockland, who stood outside Quincy City Hall on Saturday in a pink-and-white unicorn costume. “I’m a 59-year-old grandmother who is coming out to exercise her constitutional right to call out this lawless administration,” Grant said. “I’m doing this for the future generations. I’m speaking up for them.”

Grant, who calls herself the “democracy unicorn,” said she wanted to challenge portrayals of protesters as violent rioters.

“From what I’m hearing as far as Republicans and MAGA on the news, they’re categorizing these protests as violent, and that it’s a bunch of anti-democratic, America-hating people,” she said. “And I just want to show them that no. We’re out here for fun, for peace, for love, for joy.”

Grant said she chose to commute to the Quincy “No Kings” protest because “the Founding Father John Quincy Adams is buried here,” she said, referring to the United First Parish Church just yards away from City Hall.

“This is just a highly historical, patriotic site. So I thought, ‘what an excellent spot,’” she said.

By Tonya Alanez, Globe Staff

Turnout is expected to exceed 100,000 at Saturday’s No Kings demonstration at Boston Common, one of more than 100 events planned across the state during the national day of action to protest President Trump’s authoritarian policies and defend democracy, according to organizers.

No Kings rallies are scheduled in all 50 states, marking the third nationwide protest against Trump this year.

READ MORE

By the Associates Press

Big crowds of protesters are expected Saturday in thousands of places around the US in opposition to what some are characterizing as increasingly authoritarian practices by President Trump.

Some conservative politicians have condemned the protests as “Hate America” rallies, while others say that it represents a “patriotic” fight for First Amendment rights.

Here’s what to expect.

By Boston.com

“No Kings” protests will be taking place across the United States this Saturday, Oct. 18— and if you’re in the Greater Boston area, there’s likely one happening near you. Cities and towns throughout the region will be hosting protests in support of democracy, with Boston’s rally on the Common expected to feature Mayor Michelle Wu as the headlining speaker.

The demonstrations come after the nationwide “No Kings” protests held June 14, when Bostonians gathered to counter President Trump’s military procession on the same day.

Many local organizers have not revealed their exact locations yet, but those who RSVP through the official event link can receive more information.

Here’s where the protests are taking place around Greater Boston.

By Laura Crimaldi, Sean Cotter, and Sadaf Tokhi, Globe Staff

With another round of No Kings Day of Action protests, many protesters throughout the Greater Boston area are determined to continue nonviolent activism in the face of threats from the White House.

They are well aware of President Trump’s embrace of military intervention to suppress demonstrations in Chicago and Portland, Ore., and want to avoid what happened on Oct. 7 when a pro-Palestinian rally at Boston Common turned violent.

Four Boston police officers were injured, including one who suffered a broken nose, and 13 demonstrators were arrested. The Suffolk district attorney’s office charged 13 pro-Palestinian protesters with violating the “prohibition of the promotion of anarchy.”

READ MORE

By the Associated Press

The last “No Kings” protest took place on June 14 in thousands of cities and towns across the country, in large part to protest a military parade in Washington that marked the Army’s 250th anniversary and coincided with Trump’s birthday. “No Kings” organizers at the time called the parade “coronation” that was symbolic of what they characterized as Trump’s growing authoritarian overreach.

Confrontations were isolated and the protests were largely peaceful.

Police in Los Angeles, where protests over federal immigration enforcement raids erupted the week prior and sparked demonstrations across the country, used tear gas and crowd-control munitions to clear out protesters after the formal event ended. Officers in Portland also fired tear gas and projectiles to disperse a crowd that protested in front of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building well into the evening.

One protester was killed during the Salt Lake City march in June. A safety volunteer shot at a person allegedly pointing a rifle at demonstrators, but inadvertently struck and killed protester Arthur Folasa Ah Loo, a beloved fashion designer.

title: Charles Stuart is a bad chapter in the book of Ray Flynn’s life
text:
After winning office in 1983 by defeating Mel King, the first Black mayoral candidate to make it to the final election round, Flynn worked hard to unify Boston. He confronted the racial conflict that tore neighborhoods apart during court-ordered school desegregation and took on difficult issues, including the desegregation of public housing. With humble roots — his father worked as a longshoreman and his mother was a cleaning lady — Flynn also found common ground between working-class voters and progressive activists.

“That was Flynn’s success,” Gillis told me. He had “organizers and working-class neighborhood leaders … all working together despite and in spite of difference.”

With today’s Democratic Party struggling to bridge a yawning gap between the working class and the elite, surely there’s a lesson in Flynn’s success on that score. But only if people can get past the Charles Stuart debacle, and some won’t be able to.

When Stuart, a white man, killed his pregnant wife in October 1989, he said a Black man did it. Flynn accepted Stuart’s story, and the police manhunt that was launched in the aftermath turned every young Black man into a potential suspect. That was wrong. In 2023, Mayor Michelle Wu formally apologized to two men falsely linked to the murder, and the city recently paid $150,000 total to them.

Since his book launch last spring, Gillis has spoken at many events, including one that I participated in last June as a co-panelist in Roslindale and one I attended on Sunday at the Dorchester home of Joyce Linehan, a well-known convener of political guests, who also worked for former mayor Marty Walsh. The Gillis answer to the Stuart question is basically that mistakes were made, but they shouldn’t define Flynn’s entire legacy. “What defined Ray Flynn was uniting Boston racially against all odds,” he told me after Sunday’s event.

Flynn, who is 86, has attended some of Gillis’s book events, including the book launch. He was supposed to be at Sunday’s event, but missed it because of health issues.

As a reader, I wish the book had more detail about what it was like to be in the room where tough policy decisions were made, including those involving the Stuart case. If it reads like an academic journal, that’s because it began as research for a doctoral dissertation and continued in that vein.

Even so, it does raise important questions about the role of government when it comes to sharing the benefit of wealth and, by doing that, easing racial tensions. In the book, Gillis concludes that Flynn “is a progressive — a term he never used to describe himself — having steered Boston’s economy toward greater fairness and opportunity for poor and working-class citizens while embracing the city’s racial, ethnic, and cultural diversity.” He sees Flynn as a bridge to Wu, and even to Zohran Mamdani, the progressive candidate and Democratic nominee for mayor of New York City, who calls Wu his role model.

The leap from Flynn to Mamdani may be one too far. But overall, I think Gillis is right.

Flynn is accountable for everything that happened between 1984 and 1993, his years as mayor. That includes his mishandling of the Stuart case. But it also includes moving the city in a positive direction during difficult times and building a foundation for progressive change by putting the issues of economic inequality and social justice front and center.

“We’re better on race than we were,” Gillis said in an interview after the Sunday event. “There’s more racial equality and more class inequality.”

If everyone who believed Stuart back in 1989 raised their hand, there would be a lot of raised hands. And yes, they would be white. But people learn and grow. Today, Boston is not at war with itself. There is still racial inequity and much work to be done. But today, Stuart’s story would be subject to much more scrutiny from everyone, and especially from the mayor.

Now, what does it take to change the economic inequities that still break down along racial lines?

Three decades after Flynn left office, that’s the question a progressive mayor must answer.

title: Sister Mary Veronica Park, a cherished corner of South Boston, saved with the help of neighbors
text:
“You’re not always talking to your neighbors anymore,” Langdon said recently by telephone. “We’re kind of an unusual part of the population these days, where we don’t just drive into our house and then never come out again until we go to work.”

The Archdiocese of Boston had owned the property, then a vacant lot near St. Augustine Church, since 1955. The church and a neighborhood committee collaborated to turn it into a so-called “vest pocket park,” the first of its kind in a non-urban renewal area of the city in 1968, the Globe reported.

It was named for Mary Greene, “a South Boston girl,” who joined the Catholic religious order of nuns in 1939 and died in 1960, the Globe reported.

Over the decades, residents came to care for the small park they looked after with pride.

“While the archdiocese owned the land, they had almost never done anything with the park,” said resident Vicky Shen.

When the archdiocese listed the property for sale in 2023, surprised residents formed the “Save Sister Mary Veronica Park Committee,” said Shen, the committee’s spokesperson.

Last month, the city formally acquired the 4,675-square-foot park from the archdiocese for just over $200,000, saving the park from any future development.

It was a neighborhood committee in the late 1960s that turned the lot into a park, Shen said, and the newest generation of neighbors ultimately saved it.

Every other week, one neighbor uses their own leaf blower to move leaves and debris away, Shen said. Another neighbor wheels the park’s trash cans to the curb every Wednesday for pickup.

The park has five benches around its perimeter and is surrounded by tall trees with Dorchester Avenue is just a few blocks away.

South Boston has the second-lowest tree cover in the city, making every foot of green space “precious,” said Donna Brown, president of the South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation.

“It has touched newcomers to South Boston as well as long-term residents because it is a rare open space in a really dense part of the neighborhood, and that’s why it means so much to people,” Brown said.

Brown said people walk their dogs in the park, kids ride their bikes, and neighbors talk. That’s why it was essential to save.

“It was really just neighbors talking to neighbors and then trying to figure out what we could do as citizens to get visibility and try to do something to prevent the sale of it to a developer,” Shen said.

At a public hearing on July 28, the Boston Parks and Recreation Commission voted to approve the purchase of the park, the city said in a statement.

The property was placed under a Conservation Restriction held by the South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation, which ensures the space will not be converted to another use, Brown said.

“It was really inspiring and made you realize that a neighborhood and a community matter,” Shen said. “It was saved because people who live in the community came together to try to fight for something important to us.”

title: Massachusetts says most consumers on the ACA exchange would pay hundreds more next year if subsidies expire
text:
With extension of the subsidies at the heart of the stalemate behind the government shutdown, specifics on the size of the premium increases could add new pressure on Congress.

The subsidies were introduced in an expansion of the ACA in 2021. Democratic leaders want to make the subsidies permanent, but Republicans have declined to consider that until Congress authorizes new funding to reopen the government. The expanded tax credits doubled participation in the ACA exchanges over the past four years, and while their expiration wouldn’t end all of federal subsidies for health insurance, it would reduce support back to 2021 levels.

The 2021 legislation made subsidies more generous and extended them to a larger number of people. In Massachusetts, some 337,000 people benefited from the federal subsidies that made health insurance more affordable through the connector.

Losing the subsidies could play a role in increasing the number of uninsured people in Massachusetts by roughly 300,000 over the next decade, officials have said.

On average, the loss of the expanded subsidies will trigger double-digit increases in for people in most eligible income brackets, according to the connector. Those averages, though, obscure a wide range of increases that vary depending on location, family size, and type of coverage. Almost 20,000 Massachusetts residents would no longer get any subsidized insurance at all, said Alex Sheff, senior director of policy and government relations at Health Care For All, a Boston-based health advocacy organization.

“There are particular groups that are going to see these really astronomical cost increases,” Sheff said.

Judith O’Gara, a part-time editor at community newspapers, and her husband, a self-employed computer animator and mural artist, were notified this week that their monthly premium would increase by $435. A cheaper plan would likely offer higher copays or premiums and would still be $200 more. It’s less than she feared, but still a burden. She hopes, but isn’t certain, that she could get insurance through her employer if she works more hours. If not, she must make difficult choices.

“It’s not great to be presented with rising costs and $200 to $400 a month at the same time the cost of food was rising, the cost of oil is rising, the cost of electricity is rising,” O’Gara, 56, of Millis, said.

The premium notifications in Massachusetts may give some exchange customers sticker shock, said Matthew Fiedler, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a centrist Washington policy think tank. They may decide they can’t afford to renew their insurance, and stick with that decision even if the subsidies are saved.

“We are getting to the point where the fact that the subsidies have not been extended will have actual consequences for who has health insurance and who doesn’t,” Fiedler said.

Lidia Pruente, of Dorchester, recalled first receiving her notice from the connector this week.

“My first reaction was definitely dread, but I think things might not be as bad as I currently feared,” said the 35-year-old.

Her premiums would increase by $70 a month in 2026, she said. The increase comes as she also faces higher costs for compression leggings and shorts and bandages she needs to manage swelling in her legs and abdomen caused by lymphoedema, a chronic condition that causes fluid to build up in parts of her body, she said.

“$70 plus a ton more in durable medical equipment, that would be a challenge,” said Pruente. “It’s very stressful to know this is what health insurance costs.”

But for some, the rate increase looks to be manageable. Sara Hamlen, a Boston resident who works in catering, was notified that her premium would increase by just $12 a month.

The 61-year-old said the subsidized insurance is a lifesaver as she manages a year of bills with seasonal employment.

“I’m just treading water,” she said.

The White House did not reply to a request for comment Wednesday.

The notifications drive home the point that, “nobody is coming out ahead as a result of the Republican cuts,” said Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren in an interview Tuesday. “The only question is how much higher people’s insurance premiums will be.”

Insurance through ACA exchanges nationwide is expected to increase by a median of 18 percent next year, KFF, a health policy analysis foundation, reported. That is in part driven by the expected end of the expanded subsidies, but also increases in medical costs and prices in general due to the Trump administration’s tariffs.

Massachusetts began sending out notifications of premium increases last week, and will continue notifying customers through the end of the month, according to the Connector. The state is one of 19 that, along with the District of Columbia, run independent ACA insurance exchanges, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The other independent exchanges are expected to send similar notifications, Fiedler said.

Nationally, about 70 percent of people insured through the exchanges use a federal marketplace operated by CMS, said Fiedler. They may have to wait until that agency posts rates for 2026 on its website before Nov. 1, when the open enrollment period for insurance begins, CMS said in a statement Wednesday.

Until now, the government shutdown has been driven by estimates of the cost of the expiring subsidies. The information released now by Massachusetts is among the first to put a number to premium increases, said Fiedler, of the Brookings Institution.

“It hasn’t necessarily been individuals being told, ‘here’s what’s happening to your premiums next year,’” he said. “The conversation is about to change.”

title: To dine beneath Whitey Bulger’s gaze
text:
So it isn’t hard to understand the shock waves triggered when the owners of a Dorchester restaurant, embarking on a revamp of the place, decided to adorn its walls with oversize photographs of the two notorious killers.

“The first thing patrons see when they walk into Savin Bar and Kitchen is a poster-sized mugshot of the late notorious South Boston gangster, James ‘Whitey’ Bulger,” reporter Shelley Murphy wrote in a recent Page 1 story in the Globe. “A mugshot of his partner in crime, Stephen ‘the Rifleman’ Flemmi, hangs on another brick wall of the Dorchester restaurant.”

The owners of Savin Bar — which is located on the same block where Eddie Connors’s tavern, Bulldogs, once stood — were encouraged by celebrity TV chef Gordon Ramsay to play up the neighborhood’s link to the infamous serial killers. When Kenneth Osherow and Driscoll DoCanto opened the eatery in 2011, they promised to make it a place “where people feel comfortable going a few times a week.” Now, apparently, they have other priorities.

“We’re not hanging those images to celebrate them, but to recognize a chapter in the gritty story of our neighborhood,” Osherow told Murphy. “We’re acknowledging the history of this very spot.” In a letter to the Globe, he reiterated that claim: “The images displayed are mug shots, reminders of accountability, not admiration,” he wrote. “By acknowledging this past, we honor Boston’s resilience and evolution.”

But serving brunch and cocktails beneath poster-sized portraits of murderers, elegantly matted and framed, is not how you acknowledge history; it’s how you romanticize evil.

If the proprietors of Savin Bar had truly wished to meaningfully convey the neighborhood’s history, the framed photographs would be of Connors or Davis or some of the others whose lives were destroyed by Bulger and Flemmi. True remembrance centers the victims of murder, not the perpetrators.

Perhaps Ramsay and his production team believed that turning mobsters into wall décor was an appropriate way to showcase Boston’s “gritty” past. Maybe it never occurred to them or to Savin Bar’s owners that what might come across as edgy and stylish on a chef’s TV reality show would feel like desecration to neighborhood residents.

But many of those residents have been vocal in their outrage.

“How can you go into a restaurant that says it’s a community restaurant,” Donna Blythe-McColgan, whose family has lived in the neighborhood for generations, said in a WBZ interview, “with photos of the very people who murdered and maimed many of the people in this community?”

To be fair, Savin Bar’s obtuseness isn’t unique. It’s merely a local variant of a larger cultural sickness — the glamorization of evil. From Hollywood movies that portray mass killers as sympathetic, to T-shirts and mugs emblazoned with the faces of communist butchers, to Mafia-themed party decorations, depravity is treated as charisma.

This perversity has become ubiquitous. Think of Rolling Stone’s cover photo of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, which rendered the Boston Marathon terrorist as a brooding rock star. Think of Manhattan’s KGB Bar, a watering hole named for the Soviet Union’s grim security network of secret police and torture sites that features Soviet propaganda posters and a hammer-and-sickle flag. Think of President Trump’s 2024 campaign promise to restore the names of Confederate generals to the Army bases from which Congress had ordered them removed.

The same moral blindness runs through it all. Making images of evil fashionable doesn’t sanitize what they stand for. Defending monuments to slavery and those who fought to preserve it on the grounds that they are emblems of “heritage” is equally dishonest and dishonorable. And hanging framed mugshots of Whitey Bulger and his partner in a Dorchester restaurant is a homage to murderers, no matter how piously the owners deny it.

Particularly feeble is Osherow’s excuse that because the images featured on Savin Bar’s walls are mugshots, they serve as “reminders of accountability, not admiration.” The power of a mugshot depends entirely on context. Some police photos have indeed become icons of esteem — think of Rosa Parks’s mugshot, taken during the Montgomery bus boycott, or that of Martin Luther King Jr., arrested in Birmingham in 1963. Other mugshots have been turned into symbols of defiance or martyrdom. A mugshot isn’t inherently a rebuke; it can just as easily become a banner.

In a restaurant, wall hangings are meant to set the mood. Guests read the space before they eat or drink anything. When the first thing they see is the framed face of a gangster, elegantly lit against a brick wall, the message isn’t accountability — it’s atmosphere. No dining room displays mugshots to emphasize shame. They do it to signal edge, swagger, attitude. If you doubt that, ask yourself why no one proposes lining a dining room with mugshots of drunk drivers, wife beaters, or child abusers.

There are ways to confront a painful past with dignity and truth.

In Europe, the Stolpersteine Project marks the doorways of Holocaust victims with small brass plaques — “stumble stones” — embedded in the pavement, each engraved with a name and fate. Passers-by are reminded that real people once lived there until they were destroyed by the Nazis.

In Montgomery, Ala., the National Memorial for Peace and Justice pays tribute to the thousands of Black Americans lynched to death; each victim is honored by a rust-colored steel column hanging in a quiet, somber space. There are no statues of the killers, no nostalgic murals of Southern heritage — only the unflinching recognition of what was done and to whom.

In Boston, the 9/11 Memorial at Logan Airport honors the passengers and crew of the two flights that took off from Boston on that awful morning, only to be hijacked by terrorists and crashed into the World Trade Center. The memorial is a glass cube, inscribed with the names of the victims, and accessed by two walkways that mirror the flights’ paths.

That is how history should be remembered: with humility for the dead, not glamor for their tormentors.

Boston has never lacked for grit. What it needs, always, is moral sense. Those Dorchester residents who have spoken out against the mugshot motif understand that difference. They know there’s nothing trendy about hanging killers’ portraits on a restaurant wall. That isn’t history; it’s a cynical attempt to refashion one of Boston’s darkest chapters as ironic interior design.

Bulger and Flemmi weren’t colorful rogues or local celebrities. They were cruel, violent men who left a trail of corpses and broken lives. To turn them into décor is to strip that truth of all its gravity.

Boston once trembled before Whitey Bulger. It shouldn’t now dine beneath his gaze.

To subscribe to Arguable, Jeff Jacoby’s weekly newsletter, visit globe.com/arguable.
