title: Boston Arts Academy Foundation honors New Edition’s Johnny Gill, NKOTB’s Donnie Wahlberg
text:
“Can You Stand the Rain” sounded a little different in Fenway Thursday night, with a member of New Edition joined on stage by Boston high school students.

The performance was a part of the Boston Arts Academy Foundation Honors, the foundation’s annual awards ceremony and fundraiser at MGM Music Hall. Johnny Gill, a member of the Roxbury R&B and pop group, was the music honoree this year, according to a statement from the public arts school and its foundation.

“The power of this night lies in what our students show us — that art is not just a subject, it’s a lifeline,” BAAF President and CEO Denella Clark said in the statement. “Tonight’s performances remind us that when we invest in arts education, we invest in Boston’s future leaders, creators, and changemakers.”

Michael Bivins, New Edition member and Roxbury native, introduced Gill to the stage, officials said.

Gill performed the song alongside seven students from the academy who are from Hyde Park, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, according to the statement.

The event raises money to support the academy’s “robust academic and arts curriculum, bridging the gap between public funding amounts and the total cost of delivering a world-class arts education to more than 500 students,” according to the statement.

Actor and New Kids on the Block member Donnie Wahlberg received the foundation’s lifetime achievement award, officials said.

Wahlberg, now starring in the new CBS police drama Boston Blue, was not in attendance, but recorded a video for the event.

“This is why we go to school and why we put all the effort into these endeavors…so when the opportunity comes, you can make the most of it,” the Dorchester native said on the video. His brothers Paul and Bob Wahlberg were in attendance to accept it on his behalf, according to the statement.

Other honorees included internationally recognized tap dancer Dianne Walker, designer for fashion David Josef, and former actress Eliza Dushku, officials said.

The fundraiser also included performances from dancer Leah Pires, salsa musician Sebastian “SBM” Medina, and Gospel singer Jason Price — three Boston Arts Academy alumni, according to the statement.

Breanne Kovatch can be reached at breanne.kovatch@globe.com. Follow her @breannekovatch.

title: The crisis in food aid is being felt far and wide, from needy families to small grocers and local farms
text:
“It’s going to be devastating,” Otero said. “How are we going to get through bills? How are we going to get through Thanksgiving?”

In Massachusetts, more than 1 million people are at risk of losing their benefits next month if the federal government shutdown continues and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program runs out of money — an unprecedented lapse in benefits that advocates say the already strained network of food pantries can’t come close to compensating.

The US Department of Agriculture has posted a notice on its website saying federal food aid will not go out Nov. 1.

With food insecurity increasing to COVID-era levels and resources declining, the loss of SNAP benefits could press low-income families already reeling from rising costs related to inflation and tariffs to a breaking point.

Advocates have been pushing the state to dip into its “Rainy Day” fund, which has a balance of some $8 billion, to make up the difference in SNAP benefits until the shutdown ends, but the Legislature has traditionally been reluctant to tap into this fund. Both Governor Maura Healey and Massachusetts House Speaker Ronald Mariano said the state can’t replace the roughly $212 million in federal SNAP funds received by Massachusetts residents every month. Instead, the United Way is launching a fund for private donations to help SNAP recipients across the Commonwealth, the governor announced Friday.

“Donald Trump is the first president in US history to cut off SNAP benefits to people in America,” Healey said recently.

A few states, including Virginia and Hawaii, have committed to providing state funds to residents who rely on SNAP, and Vermont is also set to do so. In New Hampshire, officials announced a plan to provide mobile food pantries open to SNAP recipients with $2 million in public funding.

In Roxbury, the 46-year-old Otero said her family will rely more on rice and beans, pancakes with protein powder, and McDonald’s $6 meal deals: a double cheeseburger, four chicken nuggets, small fries, and small drink, which Otero sometimes splits with one of her children.

“I’m low-key terrified,” she said. “I’m heartbroken, not just for myself but for little ones [whose] families may be experiencing way worse than I am economically.”

The Department of Agriculture, which oversees the nation’s largest antihunger program, distributing $8 billion a month to about 42 million Americans, has a contingency fund that advocacy groups say could cover much of the shortfall. But on Friday the agency said it couldn’t tap into that money, as it must be used for emergencies such as hurricanes and other disasters, according to a memo first obtained by Axios.

The USDA didn’t respond to questions from the Globe but sent a statement referencing the partisan fight over extending health insurance subsidies that led to the shutdown, including an inaccurate claim that undocumented immigrants are entitled to them.

“We are approaching an inflection point for Senate Democrats. Continue to hold out for healthcare for illegals or reopen the government so mothers, babies, and the most vulnerable among us can receive timely WIC [Women, Infants & Children Nutrition Program] and SNAP allotments.”

In Massachusetts, 665,000 households rely on SNAP benefits, at an average of $323 a month, and more than one in three households have reported not having enough to eat, according to a recent study by the Greater Boston Food Bank.

“One in six Massachusetts residents simply just cannot be the consequences of a political football,” said Victoria Negus, senior economic justice advocate at the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute.

The need has been growing, even with SNAP in full effect, as resources shrink.

The Trump administration has cut food aid by 94 million pounds, according to ProPublica, and with the government shut down, food insecurity programs implemented during COVID aren’t available either. Furloughed government workers, and those working without pay, could soon also find themselves in greater need.

If Congress doesn’t approve a budget to keep federal agencies running, the USDA can’t issue new benefits beyond those that are already funded. On Friday, the USDA instructed states to notify SNAP recipients that November benefit allotments have been suspended. When federal funding is available, the agency said, it will notify state agencies to immediately resume issuing benefits.

For the state’s four food banks to make up for missing federal benefits, they would have to provide up to 56 million additional meals next month, according to a letter sent to Healey and the state Legislature by local antihunger organizations. That would be four times what is currently distributed each month — “an impossible outcome,” they wrote.

Other federal food assistance programs, including WIC, which provides food aid to pregnant women, new moms, and young children, and school lunch and breakfast programs, are also at risk if the shutdown continues.

The nonprofit Food For Free has seen a rising need from almost all the food pantries, schools, and other groups it works with in Eastern Massachusetts, said Alex Gladwell, associate director of programs and partnerships. Boxes of food that previously took up to two hours to distribute are now gone in 15 minutes, she said.

“We’re being hit from all fronts,” Gladwell said, noting the cuts to government programs alongside shrinking private grants and donations.

On a recent morning at the East End House in Cambridge, more than a dozen people were lined up in the rain before Dominic Carter arrived with a delivery from Food For Free.

“You see a line like that? Before it even opens,” Carter said. “It will probably be wrapped around the corner soon.”

SNAP also accounts for 20 percent of grocery sales in the state, according to the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute, and the loss of that spending would have a significant impact on the small grocers that fill a big need in low-income communities.

“We need every penny … to continue to serve the community,” said Michael Valente, general manager at the Dorchester Food Co-op.

Customers are already starting to pull back on buying produce in anticipation of SNAP funds coming to an end, said Keisha Oneal, the co-op’s grocery store manager. And with Thanksgiving approaching, it’s the worst time for people to worry about feeding their families.

“People are nervous,” Oneal said. “They’re not buying in the quantity they used to.”

Even before the potential SNAP cutoff, Renée Dingman has been trying to eat all her meals at Mount Holyoke College, where she goes to school, so that she can focus on feeding her 13-year-old son. If the cuts go into effect, she may skip meals to make sure he can eat.

“It makes me wonder, am I going to fight for food, or am I going to fight for my apartment?” Dingham said. “Because that’s how I became homeless five years ago. I chose to feed my son over paying my rent, and I don’t want to have to make that decision again.”

In addition to families going hungry and grocery stores losing revenue, farmers who sell food to SNAP recipients will also lose customers. Liz O’Gilvie, who leads the Springfield Food Policy Council and the urban farm Gardening the Community, said 90 percent of the people who shop at its store rely on SNAP.

“Everyone gets nervous about the state’s Rainy Day fund: ‘Let’s save it, what if we need it?’” she said. “Well, I think a tsunami is coming. I think some people are looking outside and maybe seeing clouds, and I can see the big waves offshore that are going to hit us and slam people in ways that will be very hard to recover from.”

November is also when new eligibility rules start kicking in for SNAP recipients, a result of the so-called Big Beautiful Bill that passed this summer, which also included the largest cuts to SNAP funding in history. More than 150,000 Massachusetts residents are at risk of losing some or all of their food stamp benefits due to expanded work requirements and termination of benefits for immigrants here legally who fled persecution, many of whom are on a track to get a green card.

All told, the threats to the SNAP program are “horrifically short sighted” for residents and for the economy, said Negus of the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute: “There are massive human cost implications.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: A tiny device is identifying invisible health hazards in Boston schools
text:
Boston Public Schools went a step further, installing the sensors and partnering with researchers at Boston University to analyze the results. With new support from a city grant, the district is developing an action plan to guide how the data is used in schools to bring in cleaner air.

“They’ve set a model for how it should be done going forward,” said Joseph Allen, director of the Healthy Buildings program at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Indoor air is less regulated than outdoor air, even though most people spend the vast majority of their time indoors, and the concentration of some pollutants can also be several times higher than outdoors.

Contaminants such as vehicle exhaust and wildfire smoke — made increasingly common in New England by fires in Canada and the West that are exacerbated by climate change — can seep into buildings. Pollutants can also originate inside, such as dust and volatile organic compounds emitted by cleaning products. Aging infrastructure is especially vulnerable. In Boston Public Schools, the oldest public school system in the country, a quarter of the buildings are over a century old. About a third have central HVAC systems.

The sensors give the district the ability to pinpoint air quality issues and, more importantly, fix them. They have helped spur actions to improve ventilation systems, curb activities that worsen indoor air, and support policies that reduce pollution.

Research backs up Boston’s approach. Allen, the Harvard professor, contributed to a report on how school buildings impact student success that reviewed more than 200 studies. He said researchers have found a clear relationship between better indoor air and lower rates of viral transmission. Indoor air is also associated with better reading and math test scores. And there are studies linking high pollution to anxiety and depression.

“We’re talking about fundamental human physiology here,” he said.

A study in Connecticut found that addressing air quality problems reduced absenteeism in a school district by more than 50 percent. Another paper observed a drop in student attention in poorly ventilated classrooms that was roughly equivalent to the effect of skipping breakfast. The Boston sensors also measure temperature, and a study in New York found that for every 1 degree Fahrenheit increase in exam room temperatures, average student test scores fell by 0.2 percent.

Boston Public Schools got to work installing the sensors in 2021 after receiving about $7 million in federal COVID relief funds for the program. More than 4,000 devices were placed in classrooms, main offices, and nurses’ offices, and on rooftops. Every classroom in the district, which encompasses more than 100 schools, is outfitted with a sensor.

The sensors measure six parameters: temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, fine particulate matter, and coarse particulate matter. Parents can track the measurements in individual classrooms through a real-time dashboard online.

Katherine Walsh, who leads the program for BPS, said the district has staff monitoring the data and identifying opportunities to respond. The data has guided decisions on school closures during heat waves, prompted repairs of faulty HVAC components that were raising carbon monoxide levels in classrooms, and supported enforcement of policies to eliminate vehicle idling near schools, among other interventions.

“It’s one of the best investments Boston Public Schools has ever made,” Walsh said. “It has just paid for itself already over and over again.”

There are limits, however, to what can be done to fix problems identified by the data. Classrooms that are too hot or too cold have drawn particular attention. During a brutal heat wave at the start of the 2023 school year, a handful of classrooms recorded temperatures that exceeded 90 degrees. The district said schools without air conditioning were making sure to have ample fans on hand and were opening windows in the mornings and evenings to let in cooler air.

Walsh said other districts have reached out for advice on establishing their own programs, and some have gone on to follow Boston Public Schools’ example, including Denver Public Schools and Montgomery County Public Schools in Maryland.

The data from the sensors are also sent to Patricia Fabian, an environmental health associate professor at Boston University. She works with a team of interdisciplinary researchers, including data scientists, statisticians, and building science specialists, to make sense of the measurements. Right now, they’re developing an algorithm to detect air pollution events in real time and plan to eventually connect the sensor data to student outcomes.

During school breaks, the researchers go into schools and do field experiments, such as measuring ventilation rates by using dry ice and incense to raise carbon dioxide and fine particulate matter concentrations.

“Billions of data points are generated every year,” Fabian said. “There’s a lot of work that needs to be done.”

The sensor network project recently received a boost from the City of Boston, which awarded it nearly $200,000 through its Community Clean Air Grant program to develop an air pollution action plan. Tori Hass-Mitchell, the city’s air quality project manager, said the initiative had the potential to reach “the greatest number of people of any of the projects.”

Lindsey Burghardt, the chief science officer at Harvard’s Center on the Developing Child, acknowledged that it can be difficult to believe indoor air can have far-reaching impacts. She has studied how polluted indoor air negatively affects children’s development, including their brains, lungs, and immune systems.

She compared sitting in a classroom with high carbon dioxide levels to feeling drowsy on a long car ride. That sleepiness, she said, is partly due to CO2 building up inside the car. Just as rolling down a window to improve ventilation can boost your alertness and ability to drive safely, better classroom air can improve students’ learning, she said.

“We all know how we feel when we’re inside a hot, stuffy, or poorly-ventilated room without a lot of windows or without fresh air,” she said.

A study from Fabian’s team using data from the 2022-23 school year found the highest concentrations of carbon dioxide in classrooms exceeded 5,000 parts per million. Studies have shown that concentrations of 1,000 parts per million can impair decision-making.

Principal Harry Gilliam of the Richard J. Murphy K-8 School in Dorchester said parents had questions when the sensors first went in: Why is it wired into the wall? What do the lights mean? Now, he said, the sensors are no more or less notable than the light switches.

Coming from a family of HVAC engineers, Gilliam said he was excited to have the sensors. They give him peace of mind, especially for his students with special health needs.

“It means another level of protection inside the building, identifying some of the things that we can’t see and we can’t smell,” he said.

title: Biden’s message: ‘Get up, America’
text:
He did that and more. Having recently completed a round of radiation therapy for an aggressive form of prostate cancer, Biden looked frail and sounded raspy. But for those willing to listen, his message was loud and clear.

Democracy, Biden said, “depends on respect for institutions. It depends on a presidency with limited power. It depends on a functioning Congress. It depends on an autonomous judiciary. It depends on a free and independent press.” He did not mention Trump by name. But anyone who is paying attention knows that each of those pillars of democracy is under assault with Trump in the White House.

Acknowledging how tempting it is to check out from the bad news, Biden urged Americans to do the opposite. “It’s time to fight like hell, to fight like Teddy would fight,” he said. “Get up, America, get up, get up, get up now.”

He’s absolutely right about that.

Biden, who was honored as part of the institute’s 10th anniversary celebration, was introduced by Victoria Reggie Kennedy, the widow of Ted Kennedy, who served as ambassador to Austria during the Biden administration. She described Biden as a “remarkable human being” who championed labor, cancer research, and health care reform, among other causes, and displayed “the values and decency that you want your children to emulate.” Biden, she said, “has never seen his opponents as enemies. He has always understood that you can vote for the other candidate and still be a good American. Teddy was like that, too.”

But for all the praise directed at him Sunday night, Biden has been kicked around so much since he left office, it is hard to see the body of his accomplishments for the deep scars left by his detractors.

Trump has never stopped bashing him and has made it his mission to punish Biden allies. Biden has also been slammed for everything from his failure to secure the border to not being able to achieve a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas and not stopping Russia from invading Ukraine.

But the worst hurt is that his own party wants him on the sidelines and has not stopped blaming him for the 2024 loss to Trump.

For example, on a tour promoting her book, “107 Days,” former vice president Kamala Harris has expressed concerns that she didn’t ask Biden to pull out of the White House race sooner than he did. In the book, Harris, who lost to Trump, said Biden’s decision to run shouldn’t have “been left to an individual’s ego, an individual’s ambition.”

Are top Massachusetts Democrats keeping their distance from Biden? Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, state Treasurer Deborah Goldberg, Secretary of State Bill Galvin, and House Ways and Means Chairman Aaron Michlewitz attended the Sunday night event.

But Governor Maura Healey and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu were not there. Neither were Senators Ed Markey or Elizabeth Warren.

According to Bruce Percelay, chair of the institute’s board of directors, the event raised $3 million.

During his remarks, former Boston mayor Marty Walsh, who served as Biden’s secretary of labor and was also honored by the institute, said that Biden’s legacy “is going to be incredible.”

In a follow-up interview, Walsh described Biden as “a bridge-builder” who was “closing the division we had seen in the previous two administrations.” He cited the infrastructure bill as among Biden’s key accomplishments, as well as Biden’s focus on bringing back manufacturing jobs.

Walsh also said it’s time for Democrats to stop the blame game. Of fellow Democrats who continue to criticize Biden, he said, “I think it’s completely wrong. I don’t agree with that. Joe Biden gave his complete adult life to public service. As Democrats, we should all look in the mirror and reflect and see where does our party need to go for the next decade.”

Added Walsh: “We need to work collectively together on a path forward. Winning the midterms is not turning the party around.”

Turning the party around means looking forward, not backward, Walsh said. Can Democrats put aside the bitterness of loss and do that?

In urging Americans to fight back, Biden brought up a familiar story about his father telling him, “Joey, get up. You get knocked down, get up, Joey. Get up. That’s my message for you tonight. We have to get up.”

In that moment, it seemed as much a message to himself as to the rest of the country.

A previous version included a statement about invitations to the event that could not be fully verified.

title: Mass. residents with family in Caribbean watching Hurricane Melissa closely. ‘It’s dangerous when it’s close.’
text:
His church has close connections to Jamaica, having made several missions to the island, delivering food and other basic supplies over the years.

Stephenson, who came to the United States from the island more than 50 years ago, is receiving updates from the Saint Catherine Parish community in Jamaica.

“Right now, they don’t know the full extent of the damage other than what they are seeing,” he said. “It’s devastating though — homes are being washed away, areas are flooded, thousands of people are in shelters, without electricity. Many of them are feeling trapped.”

As Hurricane Melissa made landfall on the island shortly after 1 p.m. Tuesday, the Caribbean diaspora in Massachusetts watched and waited for word from their loved ones.

The large and powerful storm also threatened parts of Haiti and Cuba, forecasters said Tuesday evening.

Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, the daughter of Haitian immigrants, said in a phone interview Tuesday that her family, both in Boston and in Haiti, was “praying for Jamaica.”

“Jamaica really lies squarely in the storm,” she said. “We’re just hoping that it can move quickly and do the least amount of harm.”

Noting Boston’s large Caribbean community, Louijeune said lots of people “are concerned for their loved ones back home.”

Gertrude Delsoin, a Haitian immigrant who lives in Dorchester, said she has a cousin living in Okap, the second largest city in Haiti, who is “scared to die.”

”They have wind, they have water coming inside the house," she said.

Delsoin said she and other Haitian friends are nervously checking on relatives as the hurricane approaches the island.

“Everybody is scared, they are waiting to see what happened to the people they know,” she said.

Stephenson said he is rallying his church community to help after the hurricane passes.

“Jamaicans are resilient, they will come through it, they’re gonna find a way,” he said. “It’s gonna be long, it’s gonna be hard, but you can expect Jamaica, with whatever support they receive, to bounce back. That’s the kind of people they are.”

Other Jamaicans in Massachusetts were trying not to worry too much.

“Jamaicans don’t really take things serious until it actually happens,” said Skylar Campbell, 24, of Brockton.

“That’s kind of how they are down there,” his father, Ernie Campbell, 51, added. “They’re kind of used to it.”

Ernie Campbell is the owner of Jamaica Mi Hungry, a restaurant in Boston, where Skylar works as well. Ernie Campbell said he came to the United States from Jamaica in 2002 but still has a house there. His mother and nephews live in that home, and he said before the storm, he sent them money for provisions.

“The house is pretty safe,” he said. “It’s been through a couple of hurricanes already.”

Skylar Campbell said that for a lot of his younger cousins, this will be their first major storm and they don’t know what to expect. But for the adults, it’s just another day, another storm.

The Campbells have family in Negril, which is more than 100 miles outside of the capital, Kingston. Their relatives were boarding up windows and housing neighbors whose homes may not have as strong a foundation.

“People just buckle down and wait for the storm to end,” Ernie Campbell said. “It’s dangerous when it’s close.”

He recalled living through many storms growing up, even Hurricane Gilbert in 1988, the last direct hurricane hit in Jamaica.

“I was on the porch, and didn’t know how serious it is until I see my neighbor’s house go up in the air,” Ernie Campbell said.

Still, he said times have changed, and depending on where tourists are staying, most hotels have protocols and accommodations in place to ensure everyone’s safety.

“They’re probably scared because they’re not used to it,” Ernie Campbell said. “There’s just more panic because they would prefer to be home than experience [the storm].”

title: At the BPL, ‘Revolution!’ lives up to its exclamation mark
text:
To emphasize the provisional, unfinished nature of revolution as idea they’ve hung “Revolution!” in what would seem to be a provisional, unfinished fashion. The McKim Exhibition Hall is a grand space. There is nothing grand about the show’s presentation. The backings for the works on display are made of plywood — yup, good old buy-it-at-Home-Depot plywood. And bare metal scaffolding supports those backings. A revolution is (among many other things) a kind of worksite, and “Revolution!” looks like one. Nor should we forget that un-fancy and un-fussy are in no way un-American.

There are nearly 120 items in “Revolution!,” all from the BPL’s holdings. Some are as unexpected as their presentation. The show’s first section, “Making History,” includes paintings of George Washington and Benjamin Franklin and Paul Revere’s famous engraving of the Boston Massacre. So far, so conventional. But it also includes Bob Tomolillo’s 2020 “reboot” of Revere’s engraving and Larry Rivers’s 1970 reimagining of the massacre. There are photographs of Bicentennial reenactments. The one of a guy on horseback dressed up as Paul Revere in front of a Somerville liquor store is a hoot.

Far different are photographs of a Union regiment of Black troops from the Civil War and the remains of dead Union soldiers being collected on the Cold Harbor battlefield. The images speak to the continuation of an American revolution, if not the American Revolution, and the making of revolutionary history extending well beyond 1783.

The next section, “An Age of Revolution,” goes abroad. It includes a portrait of the Marquis de Lafayette, an evocation of the Paris Commune, and two renderings of Toussaint L’Ouverture. One of them, Jacob Lawrence’s splendidly dynamic screen print of a sword-wielding L’Ouverture on horseback — a great artist paying tribute to a storied leader — may be the single most extraordinary image in the show.

“Talking About a Revolution” is the section that covers the most ground, since there are multiple revolutions being talked about. Its contents can be very traditional, with 19th-century portrait busts of Harriet Tubman, the abolitionist Wendell Phillips, and the abolitionist and suffragist Lucy Stone. Its contents can be very untraditional, with a photograph of a 1977 Gay Pride parade on Commonwealth Avenue and one of Malcolm X debating on WBZ radio in 1964. An 1856 William L. Champney lithograph of the Boston Massacre highlights the presence of Crispus Attucks. Note the date. Here’s the American Revolution being enlisted in the service of a subsequent American revolution.

“Free to All” attends to learning and education. This includes the library paying justified tribute to itself. What, after all, is more revolutionary than the idea of knowledge made freely available to all citizens (non-citizens, too)? The BPL, as both idea and actuality, is Boston at its best. The crisis over court-ordered desegregation showed a very different side of the city, and that’s noted here, too.

“All Together Now” focuses on protest of various sorts: picket lines, strikes, demonstrations by Indigenous people, rallies against the Vietnam War. “Revolution!,” it must be said, is starting to feel a bit diffuse, even scattershot, though the show’s presentational vigor and moral force remain undimmed. Happily, Michael Thorpe’s George Washington quilt, in the final section, “Another World Is Possible,” ties things together. It’s inspired by the Washington painting in the first section, Emmanuel Leutze’s “Washington at Dorchester Heights.” Depending on where a visitor stands it can be seen in juxtaposition with the quilt. Here the past really is prologue, artistic no less than political.

“Revolution!” is the latest observance of the semiquincentennial, that hifalutin’ word for “250th.” The Massachusetts Historical Society has “1775: Rebels, Rights & Revolutions” (note the plural) through Dec. 19. “Transformed by Revolution” is at the Concord Museum through Feb. 22. Ken Burns’s 12-hour “The Revolutionary War” starts airing on PBS Nov. 16. “Forging Independence/Building a Nation,” opens at the New Bedford Whaling Museum on Dec. 1. The Museum of Fine Arts unveils a reinstallation of the 18th-century galleries in its Art of the Americas Wing on June 19. The reinstallation is the centerpiece of a two-day “America at 250” celebration. Less than a month later comes July 4, 2026. The beat goes on. For now, so does the republic.

REVOLUTION! 250 Years of Art + Activism in Boston

At Boston Public Library, McKim Exhibition Hall, 700 Boylston St., through April 21. 617-536-5400, www.bpl.org/revolution-exhibition

title: SNAP benefit cuts are looming. Here are some of the food pantries serving the Boston area.
text:
With food benefits set to run out Saturday for some 1.1 million Massachusetts residents, many Boston-area residents will likely turn to food pantries and soup kitchens for assistance.

“There might be a lot of people who are looking for emergency food assistance who haven’t before,” a spokesperson for the Greater Boston Food Bank said in a phone interview Wednesday.

In a statement, the organization emphasized there was “no way” food pantries alone can provide enough food to replace what people stand to lose in SNAP cuts. To cover the gap, food banks in Massachusetts would have to provide “up to 56 million more meals in November alone.”

Nevertheless, food bank officials said they will do “everything we can” to provide meals for people “in this time of great need,” the statement said.
