That one was removed nine years ago, generating a $50,000 hospital bill that her health insurance provider initially declined to pay but eventually did — something Bassett fears could happen again.

“You save for a rainy day,” she said, “but that rainy day always seems to come.”

***

Buying a house, long a signifier of middle-class status, is considered the most dependable way to build wealth. But in Greater Boston, doing so requires a household income of $229,000, according to the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. That’s more than twice the income needed 10 years ago.

Richardson Andre has been thinking about buying a house since he dropped out of college in 2009 and got his real estate license to help pay his sister’s hospital bills. To achieve that goal, he’s had to hustle, working two jobs for more than a decade “to try to realize the American dream.” He sold houses — about 15 in total around Boston — while working in home improvement and as a security guard.

Each time he drove past beautiful homes in Brookline, Newton, and Canton, he thought: It will be my turn one day.

That day has still not arrived.

More than anything, Andre, 41, wants to leave a legacy for his 10-year-old daughter and is working on a construction management degree at Benjamin Franklin Cummings Institute of Technology and a business degree from the University of Phoenix. But being a renter isn’t helping, especially considering that costs for lower-priced rentals have risen faster than for higher-cost units over the past five years, according to the rental platform Apartment List.

No one in Andre’s immediate family has ever owned a home, including his parents, who raised four children working in food service and clothing manufacturing in Roxbury. A few other relatives owned homes but lost them due to predatory lending practices that left them unable to afford their mortgages, Andre said — an experience that helped compel him to get his real estate license.

“In my family, everybody’s in survival mode: We work, we live, and we die,” he said. “The world is changing. If you’re in survival mode, you’re never going to make it.”

Financial assistance is out there for first-time home buyers, but affordable homes are hard to come by — especially since government subsidies were directed more toward rentals following the housing market crash in 2008.

Over the past decade in Boston, 90 percent of affordable housing production — funded by the government as well as by developers — has been for rentals, according to the Massachusetts Affordable Homeownership Alliance, although that ratio has narrowed as the city increases its commitment to homeownership.

Between 2022 and 2024, 811 income-restricted homes were completed or under construction in Boston – a historic high but not nearly enough to meet demand.

“We’re working on chipping away at a historical, structural gap,” said Hillary Pizer, director of organizing and policy at the alliance. “We need more affordable home-ownership opportunities to stabilize our families and communities.”

***

Higher education historically has also been a reliable doorway to the middle class.

But tuition costs have soared over the past two decades as has student debt, which doubled during that time. The earnings boost provided by a college education has also declined, leaving many wondering if the expense of a degree is worth it.

That calculus is likely to get more difficult. Artificial intelligence is increasingly taking on simple coding tasks and junior-level customer service duties, potentially eliminating half of all entry-level white-collar jobs on the crucial bottom rung of the career ladder. The unemployment rate for 20- to 24-year-olds with a bachelor’s degree hit 9.3 percent in August, the highest rate in more than four years.

For those who can afford it, having a four-year degree remains a proven way to climb the economic ladder. It still leads to higher incomes, greater wealth accumulation, and an increased likelihood of being a homeowner.

Ortiz, the city employee living in the Seaport District, is on the brink of getting her degree. But as a single mother with three daughters, she faces significant challenges.

Single mothers have a 28 percent poverty rate, according to the Center for American Progress. Meanwhile, the share of children raised by single mothers has doubled over the past few decades, and research shows those children are more likely to drop out of school and get caught up in the criminal justice system.

“Any household that lacks two earners is going to be in financial trouble,” said Katherine Newman, a sociology and public policy professor at the University of California Berkeley who has written about middle-class economic insecurity. “For most families, a middle-class standard of living is very hard to achieve without more than one income.”

Ortiz is used to dealing with adversity. Her whole life has been an uphill battle. Between work, school, and her children — and efforts to adopt her two nephews, whose mother is in prison — she worries about money constantly. Her 10-year-old daughter has a heart defect and will need surgery soon.

Prayer helps keep her anxiety at bay.

More than anything, she wants to provide a home where her children feel safe and loved — something she never had. She is trying to save money to buy a house, maybe even some land. But she knows how daunting it will be. She’d love to work with troubled children again but also knows the nonprofit world doesn’t pay what she needs.

So for now, she has resigned herself, like so many others in this economy, to focus on what’s realistic rather than on her dreams. And even then, she isn’t sure how she’ll get there — or how far she can go.

Photos by Erin Clark.

title: It’s ridiculously hard to open a restaurant in Boston
text:
At first glance, District 7 Café in Roxbury looks tiny: a takeout coffeehouse with no tables. Then a bookshelf in the corner, a secret door, rolls to the left, revealing a speakeasy with a newly stocked bar. Hundreds of pennies encased in the bar top — some shining bright, some burnt black — form the name “Roxbury” and its ZIP code, 02119. Above windows looking out on Warren Road, italic letters spell a translation of the neighborhood’s 1800s Latin motto: “In this rocky borough, by God’s right, we are confident.”

It’s late September, and District 7 Café, which just got its liquor license, is rolling out its first boozy Sunday brunch. “Home of the $7 mimosa,” the owner, Royal Smith, declares as he serves waffles with chicken. He sits to chat with customers at one of the six tables. Jazz is playing: Herbie Hancock, John Coltrane. Abstract art by a local painter lines one wall: sunny yellows, earthy greens.

It’s a success story — but it’s a fragile one, because serving his restaurant’s first mimosa has taken Smith a lot longer than he’d hoped.

District 7 Café is among the dozens of Boston restaurants now serving alcohol thanks to a new state law that finally put liquor licenses within reach of entrepreneurs in more parts of the city. But uptake has been slow in the neighborhoods where it was most eagerly anticipated: Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, the heart of Black Boston.

Restaurateurs like Smith who’ve gotten the first new licenses think they know why: The biggest problem now isn’t liquor regulation. It’s that the city makes it too hard to open a new restaurant at all.

For too long, aspiring restaurateurs in Boston faced an unjust barrier: Massachusetts’ antiquated liquor laws created an artificial scarcity of liquor licenses in the city. Restaurateurs usually had to buy one for $500,000 or more from an existing business — and that didn’t include the cost of a lawyer to negotiate the purchase and navigate the licensing system. The law tended to hold back entrepreneurs of color especially, because liquor licenses in the city cost 100 times more than in the suburbs, where town halls usually had plenty of licenses available.

Finally in August 2024, the Legislature passed a law creating 225 new Boston liquor licenses, 195 of them nontransferable and earmarked for neighborhoods outside downtown, Back Bay, and the Seaport. This year, the city and state have approved about 50 new neighborhood licenses.

This should be a boost to neighborhood prosperity. The restaurant industry has razor-thin margins and a high rate of startup failure. A liquor license helps bring more customers and more profits and supports a business model built on sit-down visits, conviviality, and community — not just takeout.

“Anywhere that has a bar, it enhances people’s dining experience, because it brings a socialization aspect to that restaurant, where people congregate,” says Marcia Satchell, owner of Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant in Mattapan. She just added liquor at the six-table eatery on Blue Hill Avenue, painted in floor-to-ceiling deep blues that evoke Caribbean sky and sea.

But Blue Mountain is the only Mattapan restaurant that’s applied for a new neighborhood liquor license so far. East Boston and Jamaica Plain restaurants have made the most use of the new law.

So what’s going on?

Although the new liquor licenses have opened up new opportunities, restaurateurs of color often have fewer resources to tap when they deal with the city’s slow, confusing process for opening a new business.

When Royal Smith signed the lease for District 7 Café in January 2024, the Legislature hadn’t yet approved the neighborhood liquor license bill. He was betting that lawmakers soon would, and they did.

But Smith — who’s also a cofounder of the Boston Black Hospitality Coalition — thought he’d be able to open his restaurant in 12 months. Instead, it took 18.

Smith says he spent months bouncing between City Hall and the Boston Inspectional Services Department at 1010 Massachusetts Ave. “You’re going back and forth: It’s A to B, come back to A, then go to C, come back to A, to go to D.” From January to June 2025, he says, he waited for a plans examiner to sign off on his café. During the long wait, says the café’s general manager, Carolyn Rigueur, she came close to looking for a different job.

“The Roxburys, Dorchesters, Mattapans cannot just sit idle and pay rent and insurance and labor for areas that aren’t being used,” Smith says. “The communities don’t have the deeper pockets like the bigger, established restaurant groups.” Bigger businesses often hire representatives to deal with the city’s red tape — but owner-operators like Smith have to figure it out themselves.

In 2022, the Institute for Justice, a think tank, found that out of 20 cities around the country, Boston is the hardest place to open a restaurant. The report counted 92 required regulatory steps to start a restaurant here, compared with 52 in New York City and 43 in New Orleans. “In Boston, the cost, delays, and complexity created by the regulatory process for small businesses make it difficult — or sometimes even impossible — for entrepreneurs to start their ventures,” the report said.

The process hasn’t gotten much better since. “It takes absolutely forever to open a restaurant in Boston,” says Nick Korn, a longtime bartender turned hospitality consultant and advocate for restaurateurs.

If regulation “were a for-profit business or product, or if there were something like a restaurant liaison or small restaurant advisory board,” says Korn, they’d be “identifying pain points and motivations and optimizing for the user.”

Mayor Michelle Wu has hired senior advisors to focus only on permitting reform, says Segun Idowu, Wu’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion. An August press release from Wu points to new online systems for requesting inspections and paying for permits. Next steps include new technology. “The departments’ systems don’t talk to one another,” Idowu notes; a new platform should fix that. “We’re looking forward in 2026 to a lot more of these reforms being rolled out,” Idowu says.

Maya Mukhopadhaya opened Jadu, a Jamaica Plain coffeehouse and wine bar, in December 2024, adding the wine thanks to acquiring a neighborhood liquor license in June 2025.

In her six months seeking city permits — related to health, plumbing, and fire codes — she got contradictory instructions about which permits had to come first.

“If you ask five different people in the City of Boston what the order [is], you’ll get five different answers,” she says. “How can we expect the poor unsuspecting souls going through the process to know?”

Most city workers whom Mukhopadhaya talked to were “pleasant people who wanted to help out and not be a roadblock,” she says. But not all.

She discovered that the city’s health department and plumbing division have different rules. The health department’s website says restaurants must install either a commercial dishwasher or a three-bay sink. She chose the commercial dishwasher. Then, she says, a plumbing inspector told her no, she needed a three-bay sink; it took three plumbing inspections and her call for help to the health department to get the dishwasher approved.

“Very begrudgingly, the plumbing inspector came and signed off on our final [inspection],” she recalls. “But as a parting shot, the person — who was I think a little upset at me — said, ‘Who opens a coffee shop next to a Dunkin’ Donuts? I hope your wine bar does better.’”

City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, who advocated for the neighborhood liquor license law, agrees the city needs to make inspections and permitting more coordinated and efficient. Sometimes “it takes pressure to move things along,” she says.

“The margins in the food industry are very, very thin,” she says. “These liquor licenses, that can help,” but “we do need more systemic reform to make it easier to speed up the process.”

While the city struggles to issue restaurant permits quickly, it’s doing better at opening the liquor license process to smaller restaurants. Until a year ago, says Korn, the hospitality consultant, nearly all restaurant owners who wanted a Boston liquor license hired lawyers. That’s no longer necessary. “The city’s done a really great job of reaching out to these small-business owners, trying to support everybody, doing more outreach than they ever had before,” he says.

Still, Boston restaurateurs have plenty of ideas that could make it easier to open new bars and restaurants:

Boston is so into giving residents every chance to express an opinion about neighborhood change — liquor licenses, new housing — that the process can become a choke point, even when there’s no opposition.

In Jamaica Plain, Jadu had to hold three “abutters meetings” with three neighborhood groups to get its liquor license. “So this four-to-five-block radius around Jadu got flyers from me three separate times about the same thing,” says Mukhopadhaya. “I asked the groups, ‘Hey, can’t we consolidate this? I feel like I’m harassing my neighbors, putting stuff on their doors.’ And it was sort of a ‘Sorry, no can do.’”

She had to go to each house three times with tape and flyers, take photos of each flyer on each door, and upload the photos to a Google Drive to send to City Hall.

In the end, she says, “There was a lot of overlap in who was in those meetings, so it just kind of felt I was meeting the same people three times about the same thing. And they weren’t anti having us in the neighborhood or anything. It was just an extremely arduous process.”

Boston’s Licensing Board and Massachusetts’ Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission use the same application form. But they don’t process applications at the same time, and they often ask different questions about them. So approval can take several months.

“It is quite common that the city will provide edits and requests and ultimately approve an application,” says Korn, “only to have the ABCC come back in a few months with some additional edits or requests.”

Last November, the Legislature passed a law that makes it easier for legal immigrants to qualify for liquor licenses as owners, partners, or managers. The little-known change could help restaurants in Mattapan and other neighborhoods popular with immigrants.

Restaurant owners praise City Hall’s technical assistance program, which connects small businesses to consultants for help with websites, staff training, and more. “I can’t really say enough about the City of Boston in terms of making sure that small businesses are supported,” says Satchell.

Mattapan has a shortage of rentable storefronts for would-be restaurants. “Residents in Greater Mattapan have consistently asked for sit-down, family-style restaurants,” says Fatima Ali-Salaam, chair of the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Council. “A lot of landlords, because it’s easier to do, may want a convenience store.”

​Too many neighborhood storefronts aren’t zoned for restaurants or don’t have a hood-and-exhaust system for a full kitchen, Korn says. He thinks the city should rezone to allow more restaurants and work with community development and nonprofit Main Streets organizations to identify vacant spaces and help get them move-in ready for restaurants.

Boston neighborhoods also need developers to build new restaurant spaces. For years, says Korn, “new buildings were built expecting a bank or a day care or a dentist’s office, not a restaurant.” One reason: Developers knew getting a liquor license was not financially possible for startups in certain parts of town.

Market forces may eventually address that problem, but Korn thinks the city can help it happen faster. He says City Hall could encourage developers and existing landlords to accept a percentage of a restaurant’s revenue as rent instead of a flat monthly rate, to invest in the tenant and the neighborhood’s long-term success. “Occupied street-level retail spaces, especially ones like restaurant spaces that extend beyond sunset, create foot traffic and more vibrant, more safe commercial districts and neighborhoods,” he says.

Of course, raising startup money can still be harder for entrepreneurs in neighborhoods that have suffered from decades of disinvestment. Louijeune, the City Council president, says she wants to help restaurateurs get access to funds for development of new food concepts. She’s hoping to see community development financial institutions accept liquor licenses as soft collateral for loan underwriting.

Meanwhile, District 7 Café’s Smith is working on a road map to the city’s permitting process, so that it’s easier for future startups than it was for his. A growing neighborhood restaurant scene fits the times we’re in, Smith says. After COVID, he says, “community is where it’s at.” And amid cost-of-living concerns, he says, people want “cheaper eats and food while things skyrocket everywhere else.”

title: It’s affordability, stupid: A conversation about the disappearing middle class in Massachusetts
text:
Amazon Music | Apple Podcasts | iHeartRadio | Pocket Casts | Spotify | YouTube

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 13 episode of the “Say More” podcast.

Shirley Leung: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Shirley Leung.

Zohran Mamdani is the new mayor of New York, and his election last week has got me thinking. Even though we talk about affordability a lot, I’m not sure we talk about it enough.

Between housing costs, childcare, and grocery prices, people are so stressed out right now, especially here in Massachusetts. The Boston Globe has been working for months on a project called “SQUEEZED” about the shrinking middle class.

Here’s how Kris Hooks, the editor-in-chief of the Globe’s Money, Power, and Inequality team described it.

Kris Hooks: The middle class is shrinking constantly and in part because either side of the middle class is growing. You got more people in the upper class, you got more people in the lower class, and everyone in the middle feels squeezed on either side.

Leung: Over the last couple weeks, I’ve been talking to the Globe team who worked on this project, Kris and some of the reporters.

I can’t say the project surprised me. It’s not a secret that times are tough for people, but the intensity of the struggle took me aback. It’s rough out here in Massachusetts.

Right now I’m in the studio with one of the reporters, Mara Kardas-Nelson, who is part of the Money, Power, and Inequality team at the Globe.

Hi, Mara.

Mara Kardas-Nelson: Hi. Thanks for having me.

Leung: So one of the first things I want to do is establish definitions here. When I was talking to Kris, it seemed like there was no one definition of the middle class. So how are you defining the middle class in terms of this project?

Kardas-Nelson: For this project, we’ve defined it as someone who makes double to two thirds the median income.

In Massachusetts, that’s anywhere from $66,000 to $200,000, so a huge range. And of course that varies a lot by geography, right? If you’re in Greater Boston being middle class and making $66,000, you’re going to have a really hard time making it. You’re going to need to be on the kind of upper end of that spectrum.

Whereas in other parts of the state, having a lower income can still put you in that middle class category.

Leung: $200,000. I mean, that sounds like a good amount of money.

Kardas-Nelson: It does. There’s a study that shows that in order to buy a house in Greater Boston, you need to make an annual income of around $250,000.

Leung: Oh, wow.

Kardas-Nelson: So even that’s above the middle class, right, that we’re talking about.

Just to be able to get what we think of as “classic middle class things” like a house, a car, stable daycare, things like that, we’re pushing the upper end of that middle class, that spectrum.

Leung: I guess it makes sense to me because the average cost of a house is like a million dollars in Greater Boston.

Kardas-Nelson: Exactly.

Leung: So, if you just want to live in Massachusetts, you need at least $250,000 just to have a roof over your head, it sounds like.

Kardas-Nelson: Exactly.

Leung: So more than a number, it’s a concept, it’s an idea. It’s the dream, right? Everyone wants to achieve being in the middle class.

Is that what your series tried to dissect?

Kardas-Nelson: Yeah, so we looked a lot at what people expect when they think they’re going to be in the middle class. It’s things like — as we spoke about — having a house, having a car, having stable childcare, and being able to have a child. These are things we kind of traditionally associate with the middle class, and a lot of the people that we spoke to are not able to do the bare minimum of those things.

So I’m thinking of someone named Sasha White, who’s a music teacher in Dorchester. She makes $98,000 a year for a single person. Sounds like an okay salary, right? And she said that the thought of having kids is not even something she allows herself to think about because it feels so out of reach with her salary.

She’s dealing not only with the day-to-day cost of living, but also with over a hundred thousand dollars in student debt that she said she can’t even think about because she’s so overwhelmed by day-to-day costs. When I spent the day with her, she had planned out what she was going to eat for breakfast, lunch, and dinner down to the cent. She knew how much her dinner was going cost so that she could parse it out between two days.

So these are things that we often associate with people who are maybe on kind of the lower end of the spectrum, who are hustling a little bit harder.

And for someone who has this “good job,” she still feels...

Leung: Almost six figures.

Kardas-Nelson: She’s making almost six figures, and she’s working two jobs, so she has a normal job, another job on top of that, and side hustles just to make ends meet.

So we’re talking about numbers here, right? We’re talking about figures. We’re talking about how much money people make, but we’re also talking about a feeling, right? The fact that even people who make these “good incomes,” and certainly what would be considered a good income in other parts of the country, are really feeling this constant squeeze.

Leung: So when we talked to Kris, he talked a lot about why the middle class feels squeezed in Massachusetts.

It’s because there’s this gap, this widening gap, between cost, huge run up in costs, and also wages. Wages have not kept up with costs. Here’s what Kris had to say about that.

Kris Hooks: Home prices have been quadrupling over the past 20 years, childcare expenses are among the highest in the nation, the cost of getting a public degree has tripled since 1999. All of these things you factor in, and then think about wages essentially being stagnant.

Kardas-Nelson: There’s this really astounding fact that I think kind of brings us home, which is that since 2006, the state’s richest 5 percent have seen their income soar, earning 34 times more than the bottom 20 percent.

So when we all live in one state together, and we live in close proximity, when you have so many rich people, that really pushes up the cost of living for everyone else. That’s part of why we see housing costs rising. That’s why we see daycare costs rise.

At the same time that some people are getting really wealthy, we still have around the same percent of poor people. So those poor people are still kind of stuck at the bottom and not really able to get out, and they’re dealing with these higher and higher prices. One thing that Kris talked a lot about was this thing called the Massachusetts Miracle, which kind of explains why we have so many high income earners in Massachusetts.

Hooks: Coming out of the industrial age, Massachusetts politicians understood that they had to pivot somehow. Mills were closing. Factories were closing. “How do we figure out a way to have our middle class survive?”

Then comes the Massachusetts Miracle. They start to invest in the big businesses that we see now: healthcare, tech, science, all of the stuff that Massachusetts, and Boston specifically, is known for. And one of the outcomes of that, is people coming here to make more, and those essentially drive up prices for everyone else.

Leung: One thing that really got to me while talking to Kris, was about the generational dynamic here. Parents who are working class, who could afford to live here, their kids, who are in the middle class, can’t buy a house, they can’t live the same lifestyle.

Hooks: This is some data that came out some years ago from Raj Chetty at Harvard University. Generations now are essentially never seeming to outearn their parents or even getting close to it. For the people born after 1984, only half have outearned their parents, based on that study. So it’s pretty startling.

Leung: This is actually a perfect segue into one of my favorite parts of the series. It really is about how the “American Dream” has stopped for the next generation. There’s one example that our colleague Katie Johnston featured.

She describes this family. One generation could buy a home, but not the next. I want to play some tape of her describing it.

Katie Johnston: It started with Mary Greenaway. She came to the United States from a Caribbean island, and opened a daycare in her basement of this two-family home she and her husband had been able to buy in Mattapan. They bought this on his salary, working for Raytheon on the assembly line. She was working in medical billing at the time, so they bought a home, which is kind of unfathomable in this day and age.

So then they got a divorce and she was able to buy a triple decker in Dorchester on her own, where she moved her business and raised her daughters. Then her daughter, her oldest daughter, lived on the second floor of that triple decker, opened her own childcare business, and then her daughter, so Mary’s granddaughter, worked for both of them, doing childcare,

So Mary’s still doing it, but her daughter closed her business during COVID when things got really hard. She now works in real estate and the granddaughter went and got a degree in graphic design and she got a job for a nonprofit that advocates for childcare workers.

So she’s still in the industry, but the younger generations realized that they weren’t able to support themselves in the way Mary was able to on a childcare workers’ salary, so they moved in other directions.

Kardas-Nelson: Right, it is pretty amazing that within one or two generations you’re seeing someone who is definitely hustling and trying to make ends work, but she’s able to buy first a home with her husband and then by herself. Then her granddaughter is completely unable to do that, right? This is a really, really fast change. So we’re not talking over multiple, hundreds of years. We’re talking about within one or two generations, people are feeling like what was attainable for their mom or their grandma is no longer attainable at all.

And what really struck me about this with Katie’s reporting and all the reporting that we did, was just about how young people are feeling about this.

There’s this incredible instability that young people feel today. And I pulled out a couple quotes from the people that I talked to because I just thought they said it best.

So this one is from Nacaira, this is Mary Greenaway’s granddaughter, the childcare provider. She recently spent a year trying to find a job, and she told me this about her prolonged job search.

She said, “I’ve been ignored, I’ve been scammed. I’ve been to interviews that led nowhere, and they didn’t say anything. There’s just so many things that make me uneasy. I have a stable job, but the only thing I’m thinking of in the future is, ‘What is my plan B if this doesn’t work out?’”

I talked to another 20-something woman who works as a legal assistant, and she said nothing’s guaranteed as much as it was before. And another woman who works in the mayor’s office of housing, she makes $70,000 a year and has three children. She used the word “terrifying” to describe her finances and said her job could go away in the blink of an eye. They all just had such profound worries about stability and just this uneasiness.

Leung: A lot of people were probably listening to this and nodding their heads, thinking, “This is how I feel.”

Kardas-Nelson: Yeah, absolutely. I think what was really surprising in doing this project was this sense that people had of both how common this was — this sense of, “I know that it’s not just me. I know that I’m working as hard as I can and yet I’m still not getting to where I think I need to go,” — but also a lot of shame, right?

So it both feels very collective and very individual at the same time. One of the people that we spoke to is this woman named Jess Cunningham, who’s a social worker and she works mostly with younger people, people in their late teens, early twenties. She said that a lot of the depression and anxiety that she’s seen among her clients, she attributes to financial stressors.

This is both everyday financial stressors, like not being able to make ends meet, but also this sense of, “I’ll never be able to get ahead no matter how hard I work, no matter how hard I try.”

Leung: Mara, as you know, part of the project was people in the newsroom walking downtown, grabbing what we call man and women on the street interviews, asking them about their thoughts in the middle class, so I want to play some of the tape.

"We’re just living paycheck to paycheck. The idea that we’re going be able to afford our dream house, we’re going to be able to raise a child and have a family is impossible because it takes a full-time job to support one person. Now, to be middle class means that you’re sort of working yourself to the bone just to be able to survive."

"They left Boston because they could not afford to rent an apartment and they couldn’t afford to buy a house. Two of my three children had to leave Boston for that reason, yes."

"My understanding is you are able to pay your bills, live your life, and you are getting by with no issues, that’s considered middle class. Your paycheck is gone by the end of the month, or before the end of the month, so saving has gone. Trying to accumulate savings, I just don’t see it happening."

"But I just think the bar is getting farther and farther. The rich just continue to get richer. I don’t know what the middle class is. I really don’t. It’s lost to me."

Leung: I love that last one about, “I don’t know what the middle class is anymore.” You could hear a little anger in their voices.

And we saw that play out in the election a few weeks ago. Given what happened with the election in New York and other parts of the country, how do you see affordability being embraced by politicians going into the midterms?

Kardas-Nelson: Yeah. I think people are really upset about this.

It’s really interesting seeing political analyses in the wake of Mamdani’s election, people saying, “Oh my gosh, affordability is the new thing.” No, it’s not. This is something that everyone’s talking about all day, every day. It’s something I talk about in my personal life. It comes up in our reporting.

This is not new. It may just be new to the kind of political class, but this is very much on the tips of everyone’s tongue. I think what’s really interesting about Mamdani is that Trump ran on affordability. One of his lines while he was running was “Make America Affordable Again,” right?

This was really important to him. He focused a lot though on things like grocery prices.

What Mamdani is doing is focusing on the much bigger drivers of both cost and inequality. So he’s focusing on housing and daycare, and he’s talked about how he’s going to do that. It’s going to be a huge hurdle. We’ll see whether he’s able to do it, but he’s able to really focus on the big things that matter. I think it’s smart politically, whether you’re a Republican or Democrat, to really look at where people are at and people are really angry and they want very specific, very real change.

Leung: So one of the things that Mamdani also talked about was passing a Millionaire’s Tax in New York City. In Massachusetts, we do have the Millionaire’s Tax, which was passed by ballot petition in 2022. It’s basically a 4 percent surtax on people making incomes of a million dollars or more. So is that the solution? It took almost a decade for Massachusetts to pass that and all that money.

Kardas-Nelson: So it’s exciting that we have the Millionaire’s Tax here. It does potentially pave the way for other states, including New York and for Mamdani. But there is this sense of, “Okay, we have this on the books, and yet we’re still feeling squeezed.” This is in our daycare costs, our housing costs.

So why is that? It feels like, “Okay, we’ve done the thing, we’ve taxed the rich, right? We’ve done the thing that’s been promised. Why are we still feeling like things are so out of reach?”

Leung: So the way the law is written is that this money can only go to education and transportation.

And you think about, let’s say just transportation or just the MBTA, it’s been underfunded by billions of dollars for decades. So it’s gonna take some time for the Millionaire’s Tax to really make a dent. I do say that having the Millionaire’s Tax gives the T a little more cushion.

They can spend a little bit more to upgrade service, and I think they are doing that. I think you are seeing the T improve a lot. But you’re right, it hasn’t lowered the cost of housing in Massachusetts for a lot of people. It hasn’t lowered the cost of childcare.

And maybe someday the way the millionaires tax should work is that there’s this dedicated stream to go to education and transportation. That would free up money in the budget that was supposed to go to education and transportation, so perhaps it can go to housing now. Perhaps it can go to other buckets that will make the middle class feel more financially secure here.

I want to end on how this whole series began, and this is from Kris Hooks, the editor of the project, and his own experience growing up poor in Sacramento, California. Now that he’s an adult, actually a new father, he’s squarely in the middle class now in Boston, but it’s not a comfortable feeling.

Hooks: I have, actually on my phone and it was created a long, long time ago, a list of houses and apartments that we lived in from the time that I was born to the time that I graduated high school. It was 18 years, and there’s 21 places on that list.

Hooks: Living on a single parent income, sometimes there were evictions, sometimes it was a matter of trying to get out of a place that didn’t make sense for my mom financially, in terms of getting to and from work.

Financially, maybe I made it. When you look at how much my wife and I make a year, technically we’re middle class, so we made it to that.

We made it out of what I grew up in, but I don’t own a home. I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to own a home in Boston. We would love to put down roots here. We would love to have our kid live here for the rest of her life. I don’t know what that looks like. The things that we were not necessarily promised, but, you know, winked at, “Hey, if you do this, you’ll have this.”

It doesn’t quite feel that way.

Leung: So Mara, what do you want people to take away from this reporting project?

Kardas-Nelson: I think the thing that’s really remarkable about this is how many people are feeling the same across a variety of backgrounds, jobs, industries, and locations across Greater Boston. There’s a real commonality here.

I hope that our readers feel that they’re not alone in this struggle. That this is something that people across Greater Boston are facing and also that people really want change on this. I think that the Mamdani win, and also the wins across the elections two weeks ago, really show that affordability is the issue of the day and that people are demanding change.

Listen to more “Say More” episodes at globe.com/saymore and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Man who oversaw safety of Boston’s school buses charged with accepting more than $870,000 in bribes and kickbacks
text:
Authorities said Muller’s employer, identified in court documents as the “Transportation Company,” had a contract with Boston’s public schools to manage the operations and maintenance of the school district’s fleet of more than 700 school buses.

The district has contracted with Transdev to provide transportation services since 2013. In September, an independent investigation revealed failures by the bus contractor and the school system in overseeing and managing school bus operations following an April crash that killed a Hyde Park kindergartner.

Between 2010 and 2021, when he left the company, Muller allegedly solicited and accepted more than $870,000 in bribes and kickbacks from five vendors, including Colantuoni, prosecutors said.

Muller held the same job duties for a company that operated the school system’s bus fleet before the school district’s contract with Transdev, according to the indictment.

“Today’s arrests are shining a light on an alleged bribery and kickback scheme spearheaded by the manager of a company entrusted by Boston Public Schools to maintain its fleet of vehicles used to transport the city’s most precious cargo, its children,” Ted E. Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, said in a statement.

“These two men stand accused of padding their income with ease, turning a tidy profit at the expense of taxpayers,” he said. “Add in the allegations of extortion and obstruction of justice and you’ve practically got a playbook of the varied ways to violate the public’s trust.”

A Boston Public Schools spokesperson said the district contacted law enforcement after learning of the allegations in 2022 and “ensured Muller’s firing.”

“The new bus contract, signed in 2023, requires greater transparency and stronger oversight of payments for maintenance and facilities related work,” the school district said in a statement. “BPS will continue to fully cooperate with law enforcement to ensure individuals who have betrayed the public trust are held fully accountable.”

Lawyers for Muller and Colantuoni could not be reached for comment.

Prosecutors said Colantuoni was president and half-owner of a small construction and landscaping company in Norwood that did HVAC, plumbing, and electrical work in buildings at the bus yard.

Authorities allege that Colantuoni’s company bought about $85,000 in building materials from a lumber company for Muller’s vacation home in Pascoag, R.I. Meanwhile, his company’s revenues from Transdev “increased dramatically,” prosecutors said.

“Muller allegedly tried to conceal his business relationship with Colantuoni by telling the lumber company that Colantuoni was his uncle,” prosecutors said. “Colantuoni allegedly tried to keep Muller’s address off the lumber company’s invoices, at one point telling the lumber company to use a false address in Falmouth.”

Colantuoni also made false and misleading statements to a grand jury about the purchase of the building materials for Muller’s vacation home, prosecutors said.

Muller also allegedly conspired to have a second vendor, whose company power-washed Boston’s school buses and the engines, inflate their invoices by claiming to have washed more engines than they actually had, prosecutors said. Muller then allegedly told the company to pay him part of their total revenues as a kickback, prosecutors said.

A third vendor allegedly conspired with Muller to invoice the transportation company more than $189,000 for work clearing snow from bus roofs that was never done, and paid Muller most of the money, prosecutors said.

Muller also demanded that a fourth vendor pay him a 5 percent kickback on their revenues with the transportation company, prosecutors alleged. Some of those alleged payments were made to a landscaping company Muller owned in exchange for fake invoices from the landscaping company, prosecutors said.

The transportation company’s contract with the school district said Muller’s job was to “ensure that BPS’s fleet is safe, well-maintained and ready for service on a daily basis,” according to prosecutors.

Muller is charged with five counts of soliciting and accepting bribes as an agent of BPS, five counts of conspiring to commit bribery, five counts of conspiring to commit honest services mail fraud, and four counts of extortion, prosecutors said.

Colantuoni is charged with one count of paying bribes to Muller as an agent of BPS, one count of conspiring to commit bribery, one count of conspiring to commit honest services mail fraud, and one count of obstruction of justice, officials said.

Muller will make his initial appearance in federal court in Boston on Friday afternoon.

Colantuoni was arrested in Florida on Friday morning and is expected to make his initial appearance in federal court in Tampa. He will appear in Boston at a later date, prosecutors said.

Transdev, a French company, has about 1,000 employees assigned to Boston Public Schools, officials have said. A representative for the company could not be reached for comment Friday.

According to prosecutors, Muller left his role overseeing safety for the district’s buses in 2021. That was years before the April crash in Hyde Park that killed Lens Joseph, a student at UP Academy Dorchester. The driver hit the 5-year-old just after dropping him off.

No one has been charged in the crash, which remains under investigation.

In August, an independent investigator faulted Transdev for failing to keep proper track of bus accidents, or ensuring that bus drivers had the proper credentials or completed the required training. The same investigation criticized school administrators for not regularly following through and inspecting accident and training records until the fatal crash.

John Hilliard and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Coalition of Boston churches, community leaders rally to fight food insecurity, pass out over 350 turkeys
text:
Savina Martin was distraught over the pause of SNAP benefits during the government shutdown. So she made some calls to fellow community organizers with an idea, create the “Food on the Table” coalition.

The group had crowdsourced more than 350 turkey donations and servings of side dishes to hand out on Saturday at a Dorchester church.

“The inception of the coalition was just watching the cruel and unjust situation that’s been unfolding,” said Martin, who also serves as a co-chair of the Massachusetts Poor People’s Campaign. “We shall not go hungry as a community.”

During the longest government shutdown in American history, food aid through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, was in limbo for low-income and disabled people. Funding for the program has now been restored and benefits are again being distributed, but the importance of serving one’s community was made clear, Martin said.

Edith Sorrell, 74, gathered Thanksgiving side dishes while her sister-in-law stood in line for a frozen turkey on Saturday.

Sorrell used to receive SNAP benefits, but since her monthly amount was cut from more than $200 to about $44 in September, she said she no longer goes to the trouble of applying.

“It’s just not easy. We all got to stick together and do what we gotta do,” Sorrell said.

Saturday’s event at the Grace Church of All Nations in Dorchester was part food distribution, part community education. Speakers touched on recent violence in their community, including the killing of 18-year-old G’Kiyah Lewis, who was shot to death.

“There are many mothers in Boston [who] will not have their child sitting at a Thanksgiving dinner,” said Danielle Williams, executive director of Prophetic Resistance Boston, a faith-based advocacy group, speaking to the crowd. “You are here for a purpose, and that purpose isn’t just turkeys.”

The combination of food and discussion was intentional, said Rev. Kevin Peterson, a community minister and public theologian at Grace Church.

“During the civil rights movement, there were teach-ins about justice, about fairness and inequality,” Peterson said. “We decided to mold the teaching aspect of our Black history with the historical effort from the Black church to feed the poor.”

Peterson said Black churches have historically worked to address food insecurity in their communities, something which he feels is even more important because of cuts to safety net programs such as SNAP.

“The SNAP benefit cuts by the federal government created a great deal of anxiety and fear, and in fact desperation that we feel on the ground,” Peterson said. “This event today does not happen in a vacuum.”

The food distributed on Saturday was mostly procured by the Massachusetts Poor People’s Coalition, organizers said.

For Marie Perre, 42, the food will go a long way, since her SNAP benefits were paused earlier this month. Her friends and family have been angry and stressed since the government shutdown started, she said.

“They don’t expect the world’s going to be like that,” she said, with a Thanksgiving pie in hand.

Initially, the coalition planned for 150 turkeys, hoping that would be enough to feed everyone, the event co-organizer Williams said. It became apparent that would not come close to feeding the crowd. But then another 200-plus turkeys came through, and she said she thanked God.

Still, within an hour and a half on Saturday morning, all the turkeys were distributed, leaving some people without. Williams offered to drive two guests to another Thanksgiving distribution event that day.

“I think the turkey shows what society is missing. It’s symbolic,” Williams said.

Katie Muchnick can be reached at katie.muchnick@globe.com.

title: ‘None of our children should die in the streets.’ Mattapan leaders call for action after shooting death of 18-year-old woman.
text:
Community leaders on Saturday, called for action after the shooting death of 18-year-old G’Kiyah Lewis and a recent string of gun violence in Mattapan, including a double shooting Friday night that wounded two people.

Late Saturday morning, community members gathered at the Grace Church of All Nations on Elm Hill Avenue in Dorchester for a press conference that also served as a Thanksgiving food distribution event. Faith leaders, including Rev. Kevin Peterson, urged residents to come forward with any information about Lewis’s killing and demanded police action.

“None of our children should die in the streets,” said Peterson, a community minister and public theologian at Grace Church of All Nations. “No blood should be in the streets of our community.”

Lewis, of Malden, was one of three people found shot on Hiawatha Road in Mattapan on Oct. 11, police said. The other two victims, who were male, suffered non-life-threatening injuries.

“Three weeks later, we haven’t heard anything from the police. It’s an embarrassment,” Peterson said. “We in our community have a responsibility to protect our community. We’re the first line of defense.”

Peterson also condemned Friday night’s shooting on Standard Street in Mattapan, which sent two people to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, according to police. A building and vehicle were also damaged in the incident. No arrests have been made as of Saturday afternoon, according to Boston Police Officer Michael Torigian.

“We’re calling particularly Mayor Wu and Commissioner Cox to employ all the energies of the city of Boston today to arrest [the murderer or murderers of Lewis],” Peterson said.

Lewis’s mother, Rehema Grayson, told the Globe that Lewis had been with her boyfriend and other friends the night she was shot.

“They were at the wrong place at the wrong time,” Grayson said.

Lewis was bubbly and giggling, Grayson said. She loved bubble tea and feeding her friends when they were in need. “She was a caring heart.”

“She’s an angel,” Grayson said. “She’s my daughter - say her name.”

Grayson said she hopes to someday start a nonprofit in Lewis’s name. But for now, she wants justice and accountability.

After Lewis was shot, Grayson spent days at the hospital with her daughter, and said she is thankful that Lewis “gave me time with her.”

“She showed me how strong she was,” Grayson said. “Now I’m going to show her how strong I am.”

At the Saturday event, Peterson also urged the “Black community in Boston to refrain from all violence.”

“Now, let me say this. I don’t want to racialize anything but it is racial. If a white woman had been murdered in Mattapan last night, the murderers of that white woman would have been found within 48 hours,” Peterson said.

Material from a previous Globe story was used in this report.

Katie Muchnick can be reached at katie.muchnick@globe.com. Sarah Mesdjian can be reached at sarah.mesdjian@globe.com. Follow her on X @sarahs_journal.

title: For Bostonians of color, wealth is often beyond reach: ‘There’s more survival thinking than investment thinking’
text:
Cox shared her experience with a group of people in Roxbury this summer as part of a series of conversations about wealth at a time when poor and middle-class Bostonians are struggling as wages stagnate and the cost of living soars. Over the course of 26 small-group discussions in Dorchester, Mattapan, Roxbury, the South End, South Boston, Downtown Crossing, East Boston, and Cambridge, 153 community members shared stories of financial hardship and of gentrification and displacement, and a hunger for the financial freedom to spend more time with loved ones. The conversations were led by moderators trained by the RealTalk Network, a Greater Boston nonprofit coalition that holds conversations in underserved communities, in partnership with MIT’s Department of Urban Studies and Planning, and held in collaboration with the Globe.

As one participant in Roxbury put it: “When you are wealthy … you have access to a different schedule than everyone else.”

Running through many conversations was an overwhelming frustration with not having the financial literacy to build enough wealth to live a comfortable life.

A middle-age Latino woman in East Boston said she had inherited a “culture of debt” from her family because of their reliance on credit cards.

In Dorchester, an older Black woman recalled that when she was growing up, she didn’t learn how to write a check or open a bank account.

“Money is funny with Black folks,” a woman in Roxbury said. “I think within our community, money is kind of, like, evil.”

Many participants in the conversations — which were recorded and analyzed for common themes — didn’t want to be identified, as the details they shared were personal, often about their own finances. But some agreed to speak to the Globe afterward in more detail.

Cox, a lifelong Bostonian, owns a house in Uphams Corner. She’s a visiting nurse, an occasional substitute teacher, and CPR instructor, and she recently opened a thrift shop as part of her nonprofit,DAC Enterprises, that supports women and families.

Financially, she said, she’s surviving. But she will always regret not getting more advice — or trying to go in with family members to do something with the Codman Square lot — before she relented to the nonstop calls from developers who wanted to buy it. And she’s determined to help others learn from her mistakes.

“Why is it so difficult for us as Black folks to pool our funds to build our own community institutions?” she asked at a small-group discussion in Roxbury in early August.

Sometimes, Cox said, people don’t want to talk about money because they don’t want others to know what they have — or don’t have. “You get a leg up, and that’s your own little world,” she said. You get “protective of your little nest and afraid somebody’s going to ask you for it.”

A number of people brought up their families’ reluctance to discuss money, saying it was considered impolite, or even taboo.

Makai, who attended a conversation held at a Boston agency for at-risk youth, said he recently learned the budgeting rule about using 50 percent of your income on needs, 30 percent on wants, and 20 percent on savings.

“I never knew that was a thing that existed,” he said. “I just thought, you know, as long as you get your basic necessities, everything else is whatever ... you have left over.”

People who don’t have much money to begin with may not have the time, training, networks, or family resources to establish traditional pathways to financial stability, said Stefanie DeLuca, director of the Poverty and Inequality Research Lab at Johns Hopkins University and coauthor of a new study examining credit access by race and class. Paying bills late can lead to lower credit scores, for instance, which can inhibit access to loans that could be used to buy a car or take a class that could improve income potential.

“Based on 20 years of field work, I’ve observed that there’s more survival thinking than investment thinking going on among low-income families,” DeLuca said, especially for people who don’t have stable employment, live in high-crime neighborhoods, and have family members who rely on them. “It’s like a daily game of whack-a-mole to stay afloat.”

And parents pass their habits down to their children whether they intend to or not, said Ron Bell, a civic engagement organizer in Boston who helped facilitate the community conversations.

“If you see your father or your mother or your family members are going to the check cashers to cash their check, that’s what you think is normal.”

Jose, an Afro-Latino man who attended a conversation in Roxbury, said that many people in his community didn’t know they needed to have “proof of your existence as an adult.”

“If you don’t have tenant history, if you don’t have references, if you don’t have some of these things that you built along the way in this country, they don’t know who you are,” he said. “You can’t even get in the door without some type of proof of your ability to be a citizen.”

A number of immigrants and children of immigrants who took part in the conversations, four of which were held in Spanish, expressed frustration with their inability to build a better life for themselves here. Francisco, in East Boston, had hoped that the “American Dream” would allow him to establish well-being, if not wealth. But neither has come to pass.

“After so many years working, I began to think that the American Dream wasn’t meant to be experienced personally, but rather to be experienced by others, in my case, by my children,” he said in Spanish. “I think I had the wrong idea of the American Dream.”

Some people of color simply don’t trust the government or financial institutions, said Carole Montgomery, who lives on the Roxbury/Dorchester line, and that can inhibit their ability to grow their money.

“African Americans, we have a fear of actually putting our money in the bank. You still have folks who will keep their money in their house,” she said.

Montgomery, who is in her 60s, worked in commercial property management and is partially retired, owns a three-family home, and is doing OK financially. But she lost her husband five years ago and still doesn’t have a will of her own — and worries about not having her affairs in order. She also worries about a recent $600 a month increase to her mortgage payment after her property taxes and insurance both went up.

People from disadvantaged neighborhoods who break out of poverty are sometimes pulled back by the “undertow” of deep need in their community, DeLuca said, whether it’s because they are asked for financial help or they feel an obligation to offer it.

During research for her book “Coming of Age in the Other America,” about poor Black teens in Baltimore, DeLuca was told by a woman that people who found success were often clawed back down by less fortunate members of their community: “It’s kind of like crabs in a bucket.”

Bad credit can also pull people down, and the average credit score for Black individuals is about 100 points lower than it is for white people, said Nathan Hendren, an MIT economics professor who coauthored the credit study with DeLuca.

This isn’t necessarily a result of poverty or bad choices as an adult, he said. Behaviors learned in childhood can lead to low credit scores early in life. By the age of 25, nearly 70 percent of Black borrowers have late payments of more than 90 days on their credit report, research shows, twice as many as whites and more than four times as many as Asians. People with a history of late payments are given lower credit scores because they indicate a likelihood of falling delinquent in the future, Hendren said. And low scores are difficult to undo — and generate higher interest rates that make things cost more.

“It is so hard to claw your way back out,” Hendren said.

Being poor is also traumatic, said Wilbur Brown, director of the Roxbury nonprofit Transitional Remedies Solutions, which helps people recover from addiction, sexual assault, and other forms of trauma. One woman at a Dorchester conversation said that when her paycheck was deposited in her bank account just a few hours late, the experience scared “the hell out of me.”

People are hungry to escape this reality, even if it means spending beyond their means, Brown said.

“If you don’t have a lot of money, you tend to spend it on things that will help you present yourself in a way that you’re probably not, like expensive clothes or jewelry,” said Brown, 70, following his participation in a group conversation in Roxbury.

For people without much money, wealth can be a dirty word, especially when it comes to well-off buyers purchasing property in low-income neighborhoods and upending well-established community support networks.

In East Boston, Sarah, a paraprofessional for the Revere public schools, and her husband, an HVAC technician in Cambridge, have been living in a three-bedroom apartment with their three sons since 2008, when the rent was $1,875 a month. Now it’s more than twice that.

They’ve been trying to buy a home for years, but they make too much to qualify for many first-time homeownership programs, and the $700,000 loan they were approved for isn’t enough to buy a home in Boston, where they are enmeshed in the community — bringing in their neighbors’ mail, riding the T, and sending their youngest sons to vocational school.

“When you’re in that middle class, you’re stuck, and there’s nowhere to go,” said Sarah, who came to the United States from Vietnam when she was a baby.

“It becomes a vicious cycle,” said Jamie, who attended the same session in East Boston. “If you are in this income bracket where you can’t afford to live in the city where there are social services like the train, like access to Boston public schools … then you move to the suburbs where you have less services available to you, then it’s harder to live that way.”

In Roxbury, “the incredible shrinking neighborhood,” as 40-year resident Laura Younger put it, properties close to the border of the South End or Jamaica Plain tend to be described as part of those more well-to-do communities. Roxbury, she said, is often portrayed as a less-desirable area filled with crime and poverty, ignoring the many middle-class residents who live there.

“It’s just what happens when you don’t have a stable, influential, wealthy community,” she said.

And this erosion has an impact, said Younger, 75. Residents feel devalued, unity fades, and the rich history of the community’s struggles and achievements gets lost as more outsiders move in.

“I think there’s no question that wealth is used to quash people, quash ideas in community,” she said during a group conversation in early August. “It’s almost as if when you talk about, ‘How do we make Roxbury wealthier,’ it’s almost like people want to laugh. It’s like, OK, well, the way is when the new people come in, they’ll be wealthy, and you won’t be here.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Boston proposes three new school closures, reconfigurations for three more
text:
Administrators will formally present the School Committee on Wednesday night with the plan to close Lee Academy, a PreK-3 school with 195 students; Another Course to College, which enrolls 253; and Community Academy of Science and Health with 398 students, officials said Monday afternoon.

The proposal also would reconfigure three other schools. The district would add sixth grade to the William E. Russell School, which serves children in grades PreK-5. It would eliminate Grades 7 and 8 from the Tobin Elementary School, converting that building into a PreK-6 school. And the Henderson K-12 Inclusion School would be converted into a PreK-8 program, according to Monday’s presentation.

“I just want to be clear that when it comes to closures, merges, and reconfigurations, these aren’t just seats,” Skipper told reporters on Monday. “These are children, these are staff, these are families, these are communities,”

If the School Committee approves the proposed closures and reconfigurations, the district would reap one-time savings of $20 million, which would be reinvested in the city’s schools, according to a BPS spokesperson Monday.

Both Wu and Skipper said the focus of the plan was to serve students better, not to save money.

“We’re not just about trying to close or reduce seats to save dollars,” Wu told reporters Monday. “This is truly about delivering the highest quality student experience for all of our students, and having all of the resources aligned to do so.”

Boston had more than 53,000 students in 2019. Enrollment dropped dramatically during the pandemic, to less than 48,000 by 2023. New immigrant students in the city helped level off the enrollment decline last year, but BPS’s headcount dropped even further this school year, to around 46,800, according to district data.

Today’s district is far smaller than the BPS of the last century; as late as 2003, there were nearly 62,000 students enrolled in BPS. That’s a decline roughly the size of Lowell’s entire school system, according to state data.

As part of a state improvement agreement brokered in 2022 to avoid a takeover of the city’s public schools, the district was required to create a long-term facilities plan.

BPS operates 109 schools, down from 114 in the 2023-24 school year. A previous round of closures announced last year is expected to drop that total to 104 by the 2026-27 school year.

The closures and reconfigurations announced Monday would not be implemented until the 2027-28 school year.

The plan immediately drew fire from Erik Berg, president of the Boston Teachers Union. The union has called on BPS to modernize its buildings as part of any facilities restructuring.

No school should be closed unless the district can guarantee “a clearly better” option, Berg said in a statement.

“That means providing students with a modern, safe school building, expanded academic programming, and meaningful improvements in opportunities for students,” Berg said. “Anything less risks destabilizing school communities and undermining student success.”

Jeri Robinson, chairperson of the School Committee, declined to comment on Monday.

Monday’s announcement came shortly after some BPS administrators met with city councilors to discuss the upcoming fiscal 2027 budget, which is expected to be more than $1.7 billion.

During that hearing, Councilor Liz Breadon pressed officials on the details of the district’s long-term facilities plan, including funding, execution dates, and priorities. Given the leadership turnover at BPS — seven superintendents since 2013 — plus the pandemic, the district needs to spell out its plans, she argued.

“We’ve been talking about the long-term facilities plan for years at this point,” Breadon said. “When might we expect to see it?”

In response, David Bloom, the district’s chief financial officer, pointed to a document released by the district nearly two years ago.

By making the closure announcements after the hearing, city councilors were denied the chance to ask questions, Gregory Maynard, executive director of the Boston Policy Institute, said.

“The council could have shed a light on it,” Maynard said. “The council plays a role in asking questions, and educating the public.”

As with previous closure announcements, Monday’s plan was also not well received by families of students.

Suleika Soto, a member of the Boston Education Justice Alliance who has two daughters enrolled at TechBoston Academy, said the district has not demonstrated how the money saved from closures and reconfigurations will be reinvested to benefit students.

Advocates with BuildBPS and the Green New Deal Stakeholders Coalition are hosting a Thursday night session to discuss BPS school closures over Zoom, she said.

“There is no transparency,” Soto said of the district. “It’s just really frustrating that they continue to do the same thing, they continue to not include the families.”

In March, nearly 20 community groups demanded that BPS collaborate more closely with families and advocates on the closure plans.

Cheryl Buckman, a parent of a student at Dever Elementary School in Dorchester, was one of the organizers of the protests. Buckman warned any closures or changes to schools will disrupt students, teachers, and families.

“BPS must prioritize equity, protect all student well-being, and ensure meaningful community input before any decision is made,” Buckman said.

Skipper on Monday said years of family surveys, focus groups, and input on what families want for their children informed the decisions.

In the case of the closures announced last year, many of those students are being moved to their first choice for a new school, according to Skipper.

“We have to look at the whole system, and we have to look at how to best set up the system so that we’re able to create a high quality seat for every student,” Skipper said, “not just the ones that are in schools right now, but the ones that are to come.”

title: Share your thoughts on this story: We asked 150 Bostonians about wealth and financial security
text:
Over the summer, more than 150 Boston area residents sat down for a series of small-group community conversations to answer a question: What does wealth mean to you?

During the course of the discussions in Dorchester, Mattapan, Roxbury, the South End, East Boston, Cambridge, and other communities, people shared stories of financial hardship and missed opportunities for wealth building, the impacts of gentrification and displacement, and how the thing they often yearn for most is the financial freedom to spend more time with their families and friends.

title: After 16 years, Nadine Dowling walked herself down the aisle to Brian Kavanagh as ‘At Last’ played
text:
They’d been on two dates and had agreed to be exclusive, when the dating site notified Nadine Dowling that Brian was ”recently active" on Match.com’s platform.

“I called him up the next day,” Nadine remembers. “I’m driving, tears streaming down my face. And I said, ‘You told me you didn’t want to meet with anybody else and you really wanted to see how this would work, and now I find out you’re looking at other women and you’re communicating,’ and he’s going, ‘No, no, no. I didn’t do that.’”

Brian was baffled, reassuring Nadine of his commitment to their budding relationship, but Nadine didn’t believe him. (They’ve since deduced the site triggered “activity” when he opened an email related to his subscription.)

After a live agent joined the line, he spent about 45 minutes attempting to cancel his subscription.

“They said, ‘That’s the way it is.’ And I said, ”That’s not good enough! I want to cancel. ... Just cut me loose! I know, I just paid for this month’s membership. Keep the money. I don’t care,’” Brian remembers. The account was eventually closed, as was Nadine’s, who was relieved to find out that a misunderstanding was simply that.

Match.com had suggested the Boston-area residents, both divorced, to each other based on their shared geography and interests. Nadine’s profile photo featured her in her doctoral robes; at the time, she was a director of a college in Woburn — the photo was from a commencement celebration at Harvard — and Brian had initially dismissed her as a romantic prospect. He was an EMT and emergency room tech at Carney Hospital in Dorchester after a decades-long career in information systems, all while attending night school to earn his nursing degree.

“What would she see in me?” he remembers thinking.

But Nadine, then 62 and living in Hull, received a notification that someone in Scituate had viewed her profile and wondered why — given their proximity — he didn’t reach out.

The then-57-year-old’s profile earnestly outlined what Brian offered and hoped to find: “fun-loving, dedicated, hardworking man here in search of a soulmate and lifelong partner.” (The couple has kept a printout of his profile that they shared with the Globe.)

His bio appealed to Nadine, plus, “he liked to dance,” she says. So she reached out to him.

“Maybe because we live so close, what if we met for coffee?” she proposed.

He replied: “How about we go for dinner?”

They met for corned beef and cabbage at Stars On Hingham Harbor on St. Patrick’s Day. Brian wore a navy pinstripe suit and gave Nadine a green-dyed carnation. They talked about their careers, upbringings, and shared passions for helping people.

Brian was instantly smitten: “I thought she was beautiful.”

For Nadine, surprise sparks arrived in the form of crushing disappointment after she thought he had ghosted her before their second date. Once they figured out the miscommunication, they met for dinner at 99 in Hingham, where they agreed to be exclusive.

“It was his compassion, his empathy,” says Nadine. “He was just a really nice man, and there aren’t that many of them out there.”

They survived the “recently active” debacle, too, and continued to date. One night, Brian prepared (overcooked) roast beef — Nadine is a butcher’s daughter. But after dinner, they had their first dance when Etta James’s “At Last” came on the radio in the living room.

That May, Nadine was in Chicago for a conference, and Brian called.

“I’m thinking about saying something to you,” he told her. “It begins with an L and ends with an E. ... Can you guess what that means?”

“Lettuce,” she replied, just moments before she tripped off a curb and fractured her ankle, ending up at a Chicago hospital.

“She checked herself out [of the hospital],” says Brian. “She says, I have a train to catch.’” (“I have a very high tolerance for pain,” she explains.)

Brian provided advice over the phone for Nadine’s 24-hour journey back home; she took most of it. She drank wine for the pain and kept her foot propped up with ice and pillows. When she arrived, Brian brought her to the hospital.

“I was used to taking care of everything myself,” she explains. ”It was very sweet of him to be concerned, but also step up and go, ‘All right, this is the way it’s going to be,’ because that’s usually [me]. It was comforting.”

“Lettuce” became “love” three weeks later.

That fall, Brian moved into Nadine’s Hull home as a favor. She had taken a role as interim president of Daniel Webster College in Nashua, N.H. He cared for her five dogs and two cats while she temporarily moved closer to campus during the work week. After a while, they leaned into an easy domesticity; he began to help maintain things around the house, “cutting the grass, raking the leaves ... doing the house cleaning.”

When he worked a late shift, she waited up.

“That made me feel very loved,” says Brian, “[someone] who stayed up waiting for me to walk through the door safe and sound.”

Marriage was something they had “talked about off and on for years, but neither one of us seemed ready at the same time,” explains Nadine. They fell into step after receiving troubling news related to Brian’s health last year. (It’s “under control,” they assure.)

“I thought, ‘my God, I could lose him,’” Nadine remembers. ”’Life’s too short ... I have no children, my parents are deceased, I’m an only child. Brian, in effect, is my whole world. Even if we have all the legal safeguards of hospital proxies, it just made sense for us to legalize the relationship we’ve had for so long.”

Just before Thanksgiving 2024, she proposed: “So, do you want to get married or not?”

“And [he] said, ‘OK,’” she says with a laugh. “It was very romantic.”

Nadine Dowling, now 78, and Brian Kavanah, 74, were married on Sept. 14 at The Parrot in Hull.

They chose the date based on their favorite “Singo” (singing bingo) caller/DJ’s availability.

“He’s a hot ticket,” explains Nadine. ”He’ll be dancing on a chair, and you’re talking about a bunch of geriatric people here, and they’re like, ‘OK, I’ll have another drink.’"

The majority of their 62 guests were “quite elderly,” and they wanted people on the dance floor. Nadine’s favorite song is “Europa” by Gato Barbieri — “I think it’s very sexy.” But when she walked herself down the aisle, the song that played was “At Last.“

Every guest received one of the 63 “comfort hearts” that Brian hand-carved from two 4-foot planks of African mahogany.

While the wedding occupied the Parrot’s indoor space, the outdoor bar remained open to patrons. As the couple exited the restaurant, three young men congratulated the newlyweds. And before the couple could walk away, the trio had a small request: “I want to have my picture taken with the bride!”

Nadine smiles. “So we did.”

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s new weddings column.
