title: It’s arguably the world’s worst conflict, but few Americans know much about it. Massachusetts’ Sudanese community hopes to change that.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

When paramilitary forces finally breached the city last month, they quickly got to work. Fighters gunned down civilians or ran them over with trucks. They raided homes, raping women and torturing men. They held doctors for ransom. They dug what appear to be mass graves.

Those details — drawn from eyewitnesses, videos, satellite imagery, and other reports — are the latest horrifying twist in a long-running war that has killed or displaced more civilians than any other active conflict on Earth. But this massacre didn’t happen in Gaza or Ukraine, the two hotspots that get the most attention in the US. It happened in Sudan, a northeast African country that has been wracked by civil war for more than two years.

“It’s definitely falling beneath the radar given the scale of the humanitarian crisis,” said Mai Hassan, an MIT professor who has studied the conflict. Today’s newsletter explains why — and how the war’s reverberations are being felt as far away as Massachusetts.

Most of the Sudan war’s victims have brown skin, which may explain some of the international apathy. But that was also true two decades ago when activists and celebrities focused attention on a devastating civil war and humanitarian crisis in the country’s Darfur region. Thousands attended a 2006 “Save Darfur” rally in Washington, D.C., that featured George Clooney, Elie Wiesel, and then-Senator Barack Obama.

So what changed? The intervening years have made the origins of the current fighting all the more complex. “Each conflict is nestled into each other,” Hassan said.

Some of the underlying tensions — religious and ethnic — predate the country’s 1956 independence. But where Darfur was a story of rebel groups fighting Sudan’s government, today’s warring factions used to be on the same side. Together they overthrew the country’s long-serving president in a 2019 coup, then pushed aside its civilian leaders in 2021. But disagreements soon split the country’s military, called the Sudanese Armed Forces, from the Rapid Support Forces, the paramilitaries accused of murdering civilians in the city of El Fasher last month. They’ve been fighting ever since.

The different reactions also have a lot to do with how America’s international priorities have shifted.

Obama pledged to make Darfur a “Day One” priority. But after his Sudan policy failed to safeguard legitimate elections, didn’t help the country become a democracy, and stoked dissent within his administration, his successors took the hint. The first Trump administration showed little interest in Sudan. The Biden administration, wary of foreign entanglements with little strategic value for the US, focused on bolstering Ukraine against Russia and Taiwan against China.

“The pendulum has swung, I think, from over-engagement to under-engagement,” said Alex de Waal, a Sudan expert at Tufts University.

De Waal credits President Trump’s current secretary of state, Marco Rubio, with trying to fix that; this month, Sudan’s military rejected a US-crafted ceasefire proposal. But other Trump initiatives have worsened the crisis. Elon Musk’s shuttering of USAID cut off funds that helped feed Sudanese civilians. “I don’t know how many thousand children starved to death because of Elon Musk’s chainsaw,” de Waal said. So far, famine and fighting have killed as many as 400,000 people.

Even as many Americans look elsewhere, that suffering is palpable for Massachusetts’ tightly knit Sudanese community, many of whom live in Greater Boston. “Everybody is affected by this war,” said Osama Abdelgadir, the former president of MA Sudanese, a community group.

Abdelgadir, a retired Framingham State University geography professor who arrived in Worcester from Sudan in 1996, recently visited a Dorchester family who lost a brother in the fighting. Others have lost friends or former neighbors. Members of Abdelgadir’s own extended family, who he keeps tabs on using WhatsApp, are among the more than 12 million people who have fled their homes or the country. For those left behind, “They’re in fear,” he said. “Anytime there could be an attack.”

If too little attention has worsened Sudan’s suffering, more may help. MA Sudanese is helping plan a rally in Copley Square on Sunday to raise awareness.

How might the conflict ultimately end? Nearby countries including Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates have vested interests in Sudan and are backing different sides. But all three are US allies, and de Waal thinks Trump’s involvement could seal a compromise to end the fighting — something a president desperate for a Nobel Prize might try.

For now, though, civilians remain stuck between two factions with little interest in their wellbeing. “Ninety percent of the Sudanese in Sudan and outside of Sudan, they don’t take any side,” Abdulgadir said. “Both of them are worse than each other.”

title: South Boston developer, state senator’s brother, faces pile of lawsuits over stalled Dorchester Ave. project
text:
Now, at least 11 of those investors have sued Collins in state and federal court, claiming he owes them about $143 million in all. Some have already won judgments, while others remain in line to get repaid.

Their filings allege a series of unmet promises, unpaid debt, and a similar pattern: Collins or his companies would borrow money, then default on the loan. He would settle lawsuits, then default on the settlements. He would offer investors to convert their loans to stakes in his companies, then shift those assets to a new company.

Through his attorneys, Collins disputes all of this. The court filings are just accusations, he said, nothing has been proven. Collins has repaid $34.6 million of the $52 million he borrowed, said Collins’s attorney Mark W. Corner, noting that many of the lawsuits seek to recover “substantial accumulated interest which was among the selling points for investment in the project.” Some lenders are “barred from seeking money damages,” he said, because they previously agreed to convert their loans to an ownership stake.

“The total amount of outstanding obligations to which you repeatedly refer to is based on allegations — nothing more," Corner said. “There is a significant difference between one party making an unverified allegation in a court pleading, and a final determination being reached.”

Both Collins twins stress that Nick Collins had nothing to do with his brother’s real estate business.

“Senator Collins comes from a large immediate family that he loves,” a spokesperson said in an email. “He maintains a separate professional life from all of them in line with the state’s conflict of interest laws.”

Over the last several years, Andrew Collins has amassed a portfolio of dozens of residential properties in South Boston, and had borrowed against many of them. The crown jewel of his real estate holdings, and the focal point of the lawsuits, has been a collection of low-rise warehouses and a self-storage property along the South Boston block where Dorchester and Old Colony avenues split.

It sits in the heart of a corridor that the city in 2016 highlighted for a wave of new development along the stretch of land between the Broadway and Andrew MBTA stations. A city plan envisioned up to 16 million square feet of new development in the area — “a 21st century mixed-use district” less than 2 miles from downtown. Developers moved fast to revamp the vestige of old Southie into a blend of housing and retail, offices and modern industrial buildings.

City officials approved 6.7 million square feet of projects along the corridor between 2016 and 2024, according to a Globe analysis. Nearly a dozen housing projects rose up, but amid the real estate market turbulence of the past few years, several developments remain unbuilt.

Collins spent years cobbling together parcels at 376-384, 400, 404, and 408-410 Dorchester Ave., 135 Old Colony Ave., and 30 D St. — 3.2 acres in all.

The development potential for such a large site is substantial; across the street, National Development has approvals to build a four-building life-science and residential complex with buildings as high as 15 stories. While Collins pitched investors on the site’s potential for hundreds of thousands of square feet of development for lab space or housing, he never formally proposed a project to the city.

“Together these parcels comprise a prime city block of land and are more valuable in the aggregate,” Corner wrote in an email. “It has drawn highly sophisticated investors locally and nationally.”

Another Collins attorney, Raymond P. Ausrotas, said in an email that the project had “been delayed by market and economic conditions.”

One investor was Cottonwood Group, a real estate private equity firm that built and opened a $900 million mixed-use project in the Seaport, and this summer acquired much of the unsold St. Regis condos on Seaport Boulevard. In 2022, Cottonwood put $130 million into Collins’s project, though it later exited the development team after being repaid.

“Cottonwood provided $130 million in senior financing in 2022 and the loan was successfully repaid in due course shortly after maturity in 2023,” said Jeffrey Horowitz, the firm’s chief financial officer, in a statement.

Another investor is Extell Development Co., the New York firm behind some of the ultra-tall residential towers in Manhattan called Billionaires’ Row. In 2023, along with some partners, Extell bought into the project.

Now, Extell said, it owns the whole thing, along with other property it acquired next door, and plans to push ahead with a 7 -acre development.

“Andrew Collins does not maintain any financial interest or have any business involvement with the current development team,” said a statement from Extell, contractor JT Magen & Co., and The HYM Investment Group, a Boston-based developer acting as adviser on the project. “We look forward to collaborating with the City of Boston to advance a plan that will create much-needed housing on this underutilized parcel as soon as possible.”

Collins disputed that, contending in numerous statements that he still has a stake in the property.

“Mr. Collins and his entities own the Dot Avenue property,” Corner wrote in an email to the Globe.

A Suffolk Superior Court judge in September ordered the properties sold — along with two South Boston residential properties — to pay off different investors, a pair of California entrepreneurs who have a judgment of more than $8.6 million against Collins.

“Properties shall be sold one at a time until the judgment is satisfied,” Judge Jackie A. Cowin ordered.

Cowin rejected a claim from another LLC that Collins no longer owns an interest in the property. An appeal is pending regarding whether Collins still retains interest in the properties.

Collins, who holds a bachelor’s degree in business from Babson College, came across as “very believable” and “very trustworthy,” said another investor, who is attached to Sapphire Property Ventures, which is now suing Collins for $69 million.

“He seemed very open and friendly and came across as a nice guy,” albeit “a little bit over his head with such a big project,” said the investor, who spoke with the Globe on condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation.

That investor said Collins did not refer to his twin brother when courting backers, but his family name — on top of a promised 40 percent return — naturally added to the investment’s appeal.

In one instance, a brochure circulated to potential investors cited Andrew Collins’s connections. The pitch deck from Touchstone Capital Partners, which was obtained by the Globe, sought $8 million for two residential projects in the city and emphasized Collins’s “strong ties and longtime relationships with local officials.”

Ausrotas, an attorney representing Andrew Collins, said Nick “was not remotely included in the pitch deck prepared five years ago.”

“Most people would understand that a state senator is not a local official,” Ausrotas said in an email.

Nick Collins acknowledged that he had been familiar with Andrew Collins’s plans to develop along Dorchester Avenue, but stepped back after learning of them.

“Once Senator Collins became aware of his brother’s interest in acquiring property in the area, he recused himself from any matters involving those properties,” according to an emailed statement.

In a letter to the Globe, an attorney representing Nick Collins said that financial statements required of state lawmakers make clear he has no financial interest in any of his brother’s real estate dealings and that it would be “inappropriate to mention Senator Collins in connection with any family member’s business activities.”

Nick Collins’s roots in South Boston run deep. He grew up in the neighborhood, himself the son of a former state representative, and has represented it on Beacon Hill since 2011, first as a state representative and since 2018 in the Senate — which makes him the host of the annual St. Patrick’s Day political breakfast. He’s known as a proponent of business community interests, and has at times weighed in on development issues in South Boston.

He and Andrew Collins attended Boston Latin School together and Andrew served as his brother’s campaign treasurer from 2015 to 2017. In a deposition last year, a lawyer for two investors suing Andrew Collins homed in on the relationship.

“Have you used your relationship with your brother to solicit loans or investments?” the lawyer asked, according to transcripts.

“That question is absurd and offensive,” Collins replied. “And the answer is no.”

That hasn’t stopped at least one of Andrew Collins’s critics from coming at the brothers.

Fliers appeared around South Boston last year that read, “Andrew Collins stole my money, call Senator Nick Collins,” according to filings in Boston Municipal Court.

They were traced, court filings show, to Joshua Thompson, a 38-year-old Boston fire lieutenant who invested money with Andrew Collins and encouraged family and friends to do the same.

Thompson was arrested in August on numerous counts, including weapons charges and trafficking of methamphetamine. When police went to serve a restraining order filed against him by his wife, they discovered a stockpile of “assault style” rifles, guns, ammunition and body armor inside his Milton home, according to court records. The military veteran was released on bail and is receiving residential treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder. He has been on unpaid leave since his arrest, a Boston Fire Department spokesperson confirmed.

“Mr. Thompson denies any wrongdoing and looks forward to the opportunity to clear his name,” Thompson’s attorneys, Daniel F. Conley and Edmund P. Daley, said in an email.

Thompson “was an early investor in the Dorchester Avenue assemblage” and “has been paid in full,” said Corner, the lawyer representing Andrew Collins.

Thompson’s father, Peter, is also among the investors suing Collins, seeking $4.3 million. He alleges Collins drafted documents he knew were fraudulent as part of an ongoing scheme through which he “induced others to provide him with funds based on false repayment and security pledges.”

The two California investors, Divas Pant and Dhiraj Bora, obtained the $8.6 million judgment against Collins in September after filing their third lawsuit in an effort to collect on a loan repayment due in 2021. They said Collins pledged to repay them with his interest in a limited liability corporation, then “ignored that pledge” and merged that LLC into another.

“Put simply, Collins does not believe that the rules apply to him,” the lawsuit filed in Suffolk Superior Court alleges.

Pant and Bora are among a number of investors battling to locate and seize Collins’s assets.

Multiple South Boston properties owned by Collins or LLCs he controlled have already been sold at auction or are facing potential foreclosure, according to bankruptcy filings and property records. His attorney earlier this month said he expects “a transaction” on Dorchester Ave. within the next 60 days, but did not elaborate further.

There are so many lawsuits, and so much in dispute, it can be hard to know how much Andrew Collins even owes. During that September 2024 deposition with David Russcol, a lawyer representing Pant and Bora, Collins was vague about how much debt he and his myriad LLCs have amassed.

“Are you aware that there are four judgments against you for more than $10 million?” Russcol asked.

“I don’t know the total,” Collins responded.

“What debts do you currently recall?” Russcol asked. “You can’t give any estimate of that?”

“If I’m going to answer truthfully,” Collins said, “I don’t know or recall, so why would I give an estimate?”

Sean Cotter of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: In the Epstein emails, a parable of intellectual clubbiness, proximity to power, and money
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Larry Summers has long been paid to exercise judgment. As the president of Harvard, he shepherded the world’s most prestigious university. As President Bill Clinton’s Treasury secretary and President Barack Obama’s National Economic Council director, he counseled the world’s most powerful men. As an adviser to leading think tanks and as a TV and newspaper pundit, Summers sat in judgment of prominent people and their decisions.

So when newly released emails showed that Summers maintained a chummy correspondence with Jeffrey Epstein for years after the latter pleaded guilty to sex crimes, the fallout was swift. Summers said he would step back from public commitments and resigned from several of his positions.

Summers wasn’t the only powerful academic to keep in touch with Epstein. So did others — including Summers’ wife, Elisa New, an emeritus Harvard literature professor who specializes in analyzing poetry. How did a couple paid for their discernment make what Summers now calls “a major error” of judgment? What emerges from the Epstein emails is a parable about intellectual clubbiness, proximity to power, and the pressure to fund-raise.

Epstein’s crimes can make it easy to forget that he was also a wealthy financier who donated millions to hospitals, universities, and nonprofits. Even at well-endowed institutions like Harvard, academics often rely on philanthropy. The emails suggest New was no exception, showing her soliciting support from Epstein for Poetry in America, an educational initiative she directs.

In 2014, New emailed Epstein after hearing that he wanted to contribute. “Hallelujah and thank you a million times,” she wrote. (The Globe reported yesterday that a 2020 Harvard review of Epstein’s giving didn’t mention that gift to New. Harvard says it will investigate Summers and New’s links to Epstein, while New says she regrets taking Epstein’s money and maintaining contact with him.) In 2015, New sent Epstein a copy of a letter about “my needs in the coming year” and signed off with a personal touch: “It really means a lot to me, all financial help aside, Jeffrey, that you are rooting for me and thinking about me.”

Some of New’s fund-raising emails read like flattery. But others suggest she and Summers took a genuine intellectual interest in the sex offender, who cultivated a scholarly air by cozying up to academics, holding seminars on Harvard’s campus, and professing a fascination with science.

The emails show the brainy couple corresponding casually with Epstein about geopolitics, math, and literature. In 2016, Summers referenced President Trump’s “proximity” to Russia’s Vladimir Putin and “mindless response” to Cuban leader Fidel Castro’s death. Elsewhere, the men traded ideas about mathematical probability.

One of New’s emails asks, “When are we reading Whitman together.” She recommended that Epstein read Willa Cather’s “My Ántonia,” which New called the story of “a man whose life is stamped forever by his impression of a young girl.” New also discussed “Lolita,” Vladimir Nabokov’s novel about an older man who sexually abuses a 12-year-old girl. (Epstein’s private jet was nicknamed the “Lolita Express.”)

Epstein’s purported knowledge of other elites may have had its own allure. Summers occasionally ran gossip by Epstein. “How plausible is idea that trump is real cocaine user?” he wrote in 2016.

In some cases, access seems to have gone both ways. In the same thread, Epstein asked Summers whether someone at Harvard could show a friend around campus. (Summers said yes.)

It’s impossible to know how Summers and New really felt about Epstein, but they may simply have seen him as a friend. In one email, New lumped Epstein in with her “friends and supporters.” Summers made off-color jokes and, despite his marriage to New, sought Epstein’s advice about wooing a woman Summers described as a mentee. (Epstein responded sympathetically, calling himself Summers’ “wing man.”)

There’s no evidence that Summers or New participated in Epstein’s crimes. For some, though, the correspondence will raise questions about their judgment in other areas. But that’s a judgment you’ll have to make for yourself.

title: After 16 years, Nadine Dowling walked herself down the aisle to Brian Kavanah as ‘At Last’ played
text:
They’d been on two dates and had agreed to be exclusive, when the dating site notified Nadine Dowling that Brian was ”recently active" on Match.com’s platform.

“I called him up the next day,” Nadine remembers. “I’m driving, tears streaming down my face. And I said, ‘You told me you didn’t want to meet with anybody else and you really wanted to see how this would work, and now I find out you’re looking at other women and you’re communicating,’ and he’s going, ‘No, no, no. I didn’t do that.’”

Brian was baffled, reassuring Nadine of his commitment to their budding relationship, but Nadine didn’t believe him. (They’ve since deduced the site triggered “activity” when he opened an email related to his subscription.)

After a live agent joined the line, he spent about 45 minutes attempting to cancel his subscription.

“They said, ‘That’s the way it is.’ And I said, ”That’s not good enough! I want to cancel. ... Just cut me loose! I know, I just paid for this month’s membership. Keep the money. I don’t care,’” Brian remembers. The account was eventually closed, as was Nadine’s, who was relieved to find out that a misunderstanding was simply that.

Match.com had suggested the Boston-area residents, both divorced, to each other based on their shared geography and interests. Nadine’s profile photo featured her in her doctoral robes; at the time, she was a director of a college in Woburn — the photo was from a commencement celebration at Harvard — and Brian had initially dismissed her as a romantic prospect. He was an EMT and emergency room tech at Carney Hospital in Dorchester after a decades-long career in information systems, all while attending night school to earn his nursing degree.

“What would she see in me?” he remembers thinking.

But Nadine, then 62 and living in Hull, received a notification that someone in Scituate had viewed her profile and wondered why — given their proximity — he didn’t reach out.

The then-57-year-old’s profile earnestly outlined what Brian offered and hoped to find: “fun-loving, dedicated, hardworking man here in search of a soulmate and lifelong partner.” (The couple has kept a printout of his profile that they shared with the Globe.)

His bio appealed to Nadine, plus, “he liked to dance,” she says. So she reached out to him.

“Maybe because we live so close, what if we met for coffee?” she proposed.

He replied: “How about we go for dinner?”

They met for corned beef and cabbage at Stars On Hingham Harbor on St. Patrick’s Day. Brian wore a navy pinstripe suit and gave Nadine a green-dyed carnation. They talked about their careers, upbringings, and shared passions for helping people.

Brian was instantly smitten: “I thought she was beautiful.”

For Nadine, surprise sparks arrived in the form of crushing disappointment after she thought he had ghosted her before their second date. Once they figured out the miscommunication, they met for dinner at 99 in Hingham, where they agreed to be exclusive.

“It was his compassion, his empathy,” says Nadine. “He was just a really nice man, and there aren’t that many of them out there.”

They survived the “recently active” debacle, too, and continued to date. One night, Brian prepared (overcooked) roast beef — Nadine is a butcher’s daughter. But after dinner, they had their first dance when Etta James’s “At Last” came on the radio in the living room.

That May, Nadine was in Chicago for a conference, and Brian called.

“I’m thinking about saying something to you,” he told her. “It begins with an L and ends with an E. ... Can you guess what that means?”

“Lettuce,” she replied, just moments before she tripped off a curb and fractured her ankle, ending up at a Chicago hospital.

“She checked herself out [of the hospital],” says Brian. “She says, I have a train to catch.’” (“I have a very high tolerance for pain,” she explains.)

Brian provided advice over the phone for Nadine’s 24-hour journey back home; she took most of it. She drank wine for the pain and kept her foot propped up with ice and pillows. When she arrived, Brian brought her to the hospital.

“I was used to taking care of everything myself,” she explains. ”It was very sweet of him to be concerned, but also step up and go, ‘All right, this is the way it’s going to be,’ because that’s usually [me]. It was comforting.”

“Lettuce” became “love” three weeks later.

That fall, Brian moved into Nadine’s Hull home as a favor. She had taken a role as interim president of Daniel Webster College in Nashua, N.H. He cared for her five dogs and two cats while she temporarily moved closer to campus during the work week. After a while, they leaned into an easy domesticity; he began to help maintain things around the house, “cutting the grass, raking the leaves ... doing the house cleaning.”

When he worked a late shift, she waited up.

“That made me feel very loved,” says Brian, “[someone] who stayed up waiting for me to walk through the door safe and sound.”

Marriage was something they had “talked about off and on for years, but neither one of us seemed ready at the same time,” explains Nadine. They fell into step after receiving troubling news related to Brian’s health last year. (It’s “under control,” they assure.)

“I thought, ‘my God, I could lose him,’” Nadine remembers. ”’Life’s too short ... I have no children, my parents are deceased, I’m an only child. Brian, in effect, is my whole world. Even if we have all the legal safeguards of hospital proxies, it just made sense for us to legalize the relationship we’ve had for so long.”

Just before Thanksgiving 2024, she proposed: “So, do you want to get married or not?”

“And [he] said, ‘OK,’” she says with a laugh. “It was very romantic.”

Nadine Dowling, now 78, and Brian Kavanah, 74, were married on Sept. 14 at The Parrot in Hull.

They chose the date based on their favorite “Singo” (singing bingo) caller/DJ’s availability.

“He’s a hot ticket,” explains Nadine. ”He’ll be dancing on a chair, and you’re talking about a bunch of geriatric people here, and they’re like, ‘OK, I’ll have another drink.’"

The majority of their 62 guests were “quite elderly,” and they wanted people on the dance floor. Nadine’s favorite song is “Europa” by Gato Barbieri — “I think it’s very sexy.” But when she walked herself down the aisle, the song that played was “At Last.“

Every guest received one of the 63 “comfort hearts” that Brian hand-carved from two 4-foot planks of African mahogany.

While the wedding occupied the Parrot’s indoor space, the outdoor bar remained open to patrons. As the couple exited the restaurant, three young men congratulated the newlyweds. And before the couple could walk away, the trio had a small request: “I want to have my picture taken with the bride!”

Nadine smiles. “So we did.”

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s new weddings column.

This story has been updated to correct a spelling error in the groom’s last name.

title: Boston weighs city-owned grocery stores to combat food insecurity
text:
“We need to explore all the options to try and figure out how we are able to deliver better food access that’s affordable, easily accessible, and culturally appropriate for our residents,” Councilor Liz Breadon, one of three co-sponsors of the proposal, said at a hearing Thursday.

The hearing was planned before the government shutdown, which lasted a record 43 days and sent many families dependent on SNAP benefits into crisis.

Supporters of city-owned grocery stores have pitched the idea as a way to lower food costs, given that the store wouldn’t have to factor rent or overhead costs into their prices.

Publicly owned stores can “be structured to prioritize community benefit over profit, enabling lower prices, better food access, and stronger local sourcing,” the councilors wrote in the hearing order.

Councilors discussed different models of city investment into grocery stores and nonprofit partners.

Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune pointed to the New Jersey Food Desert Relief Act, which provides tax credits for the development and initial operating of supermarkets that open in food deserts, as a possible model. She expressed interest in expanding support for nonprofit food partners, mentioning the closure earlier this year of the Daily Table, and asked about the possibility of a feasibility study for a city-owned grocery store.

Councilor Ben Weber also highlighted Atlanta’s recent opening of a city-supported grocery store through a public-private partnership.

“During the government shutdown, there were a lot of folks that were eager to fill in gaps,” Weber said. “The city has limited resources, so to tap into that might make the feasibility issue easier to digest.”

City-owned grocery stores have recently attracted more attention. Mayor-elect Zohran Mamdani has proposed setting up a network of publicly owned grocery stores across New York City on city-owned property.

In October, Louijeune said that the hearing on city-owned stores in Boston is not related to Mamdani’s platform.

Running a public grocery store is no easy feat, however.

There are several difficulties for setting up such a store, said Jack Kenslea, political director for the United Food and Commercial Workers Union. Warehousing, cold storage, and transportation are challenges that become much easier to address for large chains, rather than one or two city-owned stores.

The most successful stores, Kenslea said, are owned by the city but operated privately. This strategy allows grocery stores to access preexisting networks to solve operational problems, while cutting rent costs on city-owned land.

Another consideration is the optimal size of the store. Urban stores often see smaller carts — because customers travel on public transit or by foot to shop — which makes the volume of sales smaller, Kenslea said. But smaller stores mean less options and could limit the possibility of a loading dock to receive shipments.

Community advocates who spoke at the hearing stressed the thin margins of grocery stores, which make it hard for local shops to stay open in competition with large chains.

Darian Leta is board president of the Dorchester Food Co-Op, a community-owned store that earlier this year warned of financial troubles and implored members to shop. While Leta said the store is not going to close immediately thanks to donations and grants, operating it is “still a constant struggle.”

“We are just not getting the shoppers,” she said.

Leta encouraged people to shop at community-owned stores rather than larger grocers, saying that co-ops aren’t incentivized to build stores in high-income areas and increase profit.

Continuous investment is required to improve access in a food desert, said Maxwell Chezem, assistant executive director at Maverick Landing Community Services.

“The total volume of sales is so much smaller for an urban grocer, as opposed to the Market Basket that’s right across the river,” Chezem said. “Essentially gentrification of the neighborhood would be necessary for it to be profitable to run a grocery store in the spaces where there currently aren’t grocery stores.”

Louijeune said she expected more hearings on the topic to follow, featuring managers of city-owned grocery stores in other cities.

To fully address food insecurity, “political courage” is required from all levels of government, Councilor Enrique J. Pepén said.

“Our health care is at risk, our SNAP benefits obviously are at risk, our housing is at risk, our transportation grants are at risk,” he said. “But when you look at the agenda, it’s kind of all connected.”

title: ‘You’re not alone’: Families of homicide victims find strength in community
text:
The ceremony marked the start of Survivors of Homicide Victims Awareness Month, an annual nationwide effort to educate the public, appeal to policymakers and empower grieving families. It lasts from Nov. 20 to Dec. 20. Advocates said it’s held around the holidays because this can be an especially difficult time for families.

“There’s an empty seat at our table,” said Clementina Chéry, president and CEO of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, which is named after her son who was 15 when he was shot and killed outside the Fields Corner MBTA station. Chéry founded the Dorchester organization in the wake of her son’s death.

“Instead of leading with my anger, I lead with my love, my faith, my hope … in making sure my child’s name is not a number,” she said.

Dozens of people attended the ceremony, where speakers endorsed proposed legislation that would create a statewide system to address unsolved homicides and increase access to bereavement leave, among other changes.

In the audience, Christine Coppin wiped away tears with a crumpled tissue. Her son was shot to death in Dorchester five years ago, but suddenly she was reliving the pain like it was yesterday.

From a few seats away, Anne Murphy noticed her neighbor’s distress and understood immediately. She slid closer and placed an arm around Coppin’s shoulders. They stayed like that for several minutes.

In an interview after the event, Coppin said the interaction brought her some unexpected peace. She said she’s still haunted by memories of her son’s death. Watching her granddaughter grow up without a father, she keeps reliving the loss.

“I’m just trying to move through it,” she said.

Even with time and distance, the grief is always there, Murphy added. Her son was killed in a 2002 stabbing in Wareham.

“Be patient with yourself,” she told Coppin, wrapping her in a hug. “Hang in there.”

Spurred to action after losing her son, Murphy now leads the Southeastern Massachusetts Chapter of Parents of Murdered Children, which supports families in her region. She said that even though Massachusetts has a low homicide rate compared to other states, these families can’t be forgotten.

“When you go through that and look at the landscape, you know things have to change,” she said. “Because as survivors, we don’t always get listened to.”

Turning pain into power means making their voices heard, said Lisa Randolph, whose brother died in a 1991 shooting in Roxbury. She placed a framed photo of him on the podium before beginning her speech.

“I would keep my grief in the shadows so that no one would know what I was going through,” she said. But that changed over time with healing and community support.

“Now, when the word beats me down, I stand my ground,” she said.

State Representative Chris Worrell said homicide survivors play an important role in anti-violence activism, calling them “the front-line workers of peace.”

“Their strength doesn’t always appear in headlines. Their leadership isn’t always seen from a podium, but it’s seen in community centers, in classrooms, in circles of grieving families,” he said. “They are holding communities together. They are interrupting the cycles of retaliation.”

The state must continue doing more to support them, said Liam Lowney, executive director of the Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance, whose sister was a victim of gun violence.

“You’re not alone,” he told the audience. “We are all in a club that we didn’t choose to be in,” he said, but it’s a powerful community.

title: Emails have ended many careers. Will Larry Summers’ be one of them?
text:
US employers added a surprisingly solid 119,000 jobs in September, the government said, issuing a key economic report that had been delayed for seven weeks by the federal government shutdown.

Market Basket and Wegmans stand out for their quality and prices, according to a new report.

These are the airlines most likely to experience Thanksgiving delays.

Larry Summers, one of the most influential American economists of the past 40 years, never let a good controversy slow him down.

His stature survived battles over Clinton-era financial deregulation, a tumultuous presidency at Harvard University, and, more recently, his public attacks on the school’s leadership for what he called an excessive focus on diversity. Armed with exceptional brilliance and arrogance, he rarely hesitates to make his opinions known.

But the revelation last week that Summers stayed in touch with Jeffrey Epstein long after the disgraced financier’s 2008 guilty plea for soliciting a minor — and right up to his 2019 arrest on charges of sex trafficking minors — is an imbroglio from which Summers may not easily recover.

Summers had previously acknowledged his friendship with Epstein, calling it a lapse in judgment. But some 20,000 pages of documents released by Congress last week included emails in which the married Harvard professor asked Epstein for romantic advice concerning a younger economist he had mentored.

The two also discussed Epstein’s potential donations to “Poetry in America,” the TV series created by Summers’ wife, Elisa New, along with politics and Harvard-related projects. Epstein died in custody in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

Summers has not been accused of wrongdoing. But on Monday, he said he would step back from his public commitments. On Wednesday, he said he wouldimmediately stop teaching at Harvard, where, at 28, he became one of the youngest tenured professors in the school’s history. He has since given up roles at OpenAI, the Yale Budget Lab, and several other organizations.

“I am deeply ashamed of my actions and recognize the pain they have caused,” Summers said in a statement. He pledged to “rebuild trust and repair relationships with the people closest to me.”

Why it matters: Summers has had an outsize influence on economic debates, especially within the Democratic Party.

His early research reshaped mainstream thinking about unemployment, taxation, inequality, and long-run growth, helping define the economic framework Democrats relied on for decades. While in government, he played pivotal roles in guiding the country through financial crises.

Leaving academia: After more than a decade at Harvard, Summers entered public service in the early 1990s as chief economist at the World Bank before moving to the Clinton Treasury Department.

As deputy secretary, he worked with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan to calm markets during the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis. The effort landed the three men on the cover of Time as “The Committee to Save the World” — and cemented his reputation as a policy heavy hitter.

Summers later became Treasury secretary before returning to Harvard, where he served as president from 2001 to 2006.

Crimson cross fire: His tenure was contentious.

Summers pushed the university to modernize, emphasizing science, engineering, and improved undergraduate teaching, and advocated expanding access for lower-income students.

But he was dogged by two controversies: Harvard’s costly settlement tied to conflict-of-interest violations by economist Andrei Shleifer, a close associate, and Summers’ suggestion that women lacked the same “intrinsic aptitude” for science as men. A faculty vote of no confidence preceded his 2006 resignation.

Another D.C. stint: In 2009, he was became President Obama’s director of the National Economic Council, where he was instrumental in developing the federal response to yet another crisis: the Great Recession that followed the housing market meltdown.

Admirers credited him with preventing a total financial collapse, while critics, especially on the left, argued the stimulus he supported was too small. Summers has long defended his position, saying Congress would not have approved a bigger package.

Policy guru: After returning to Harvard once again, he revived the concept of “secular stagnation” to explain the sluggish post–Great Recession recovery, influencing debates over government spending, interest rates, and the limits of monetary policy.

He argued that advanced economies were suffering from chronically slow growth due to aging populations, inequality, and a surfeit of savings. He urged governments to pour money into public projects and programs, a notable pivot for the longtime Democratic centrist.

But many on the left remained skeptical. Progressives believed his Clinton-era deregulatory decisions contributed to the 2008 financial crisis.

His polarizing record resurfaced in 2013, when he withdrew from consideration for Federal Reserve chair amid opposition from progressive senators including Massachusetts’ Elizabeth Warren.

Inflation warning: Summers alienated the left again in 2021 when he became the most prominent critic of President Joe Biden’s pandemic stimulus, warning it would fuel inflation.

When prices later surged, his credibility with centrists and financial markets rose, and resentment among liberals hardened.

Final thought: Summers, who will turn 71 at the end of the month, has never been afraid to speak his mind.

He will likely keep a low profile for some time to come. But it would be unfortunate if his expertise were silenced for good.

“There’s been a lot of talk about an AI bubble. From our vantage point, we see something very different.”

— Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after the AI chip maker released blockbuster quarterly earnings that soothed some concerns about overpriced tech stocks.

Name game: Organizers of a ballot initiative that would establish rent control statewide in Massachusetts said they have gathered enough signatures to take a major step toward putting the measure before voters in 2026. Business-backed measures to trim the state’s income tax and to increase the frequency of taxpayer refunds also moved forward.

Falling out: Andrew Collins, the twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, has been sued by at least 11 investors over his stalled South Boston real estate project along Dorchester Avenue. The lawsuits claim he owes them about $143 million.

Bargain hunting: The Framingham-based owner of discount chains TJ Maxx and Marshalls posted sales last quarter above estimates and raised its outlook. The results suggest that shoppers are becoming more price conscious as the economy shows signs of stress.

Scrooged: The Retailers Association of Massachusetts says its small business members expect holiday sales to rise 1.7 percent this year, down from 4 percent last year and less than half the National Retail Federation’s nationwide forecast. The group cited the state’s higher costs and the continued shift of holiday shopping to online sellers.

Cause/effect: The US trade deficit fell by nearly 24 percent in August as tariffs pushed imports lower. Imports of goods are services fell 5 percent, while exports rose 0.1 percent.

Off the air: An exodus of on-air talent is depleting the ranks of local broadcasters. Former staffers say cost reductions are making it difficult to do the job in a way that makes the long hours and high stress worthwhile.

— The price fetched this week by Gustav Klimt’s “Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer,” making it the second most expensive artwork sold at auction, and the most expensive work of modern art sold at auction.

The tech bros were there, including Elon Musk and Palantir’s Alex Karp. So were Wall Street masters of the universe Bill Ackman and Stephen Schwarzman. Even Portuguese footballer Cristiano Ronaldo attended.

But there weren’t many guests with deep Massachusetts ties at President Trump’s Tuesday dinner for Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (a.k.a. MBS) — a reminder of the state’s political leanings and its limited presence in the AI and crypto sectors that have clustered around the president.

Michael Dell, who Dell Technologies acquired Hopkinton-based EMC, attended. So did Jeremy Allaire, cofounder of Circle Internet Financial, which last year announced it was moving from Boston to New York. And two General Electric honchos were among the diners: Scott Strazik, CEO of Cambridge-based GE Vernova, and Larry Culp, who was Boston-based GE’s last CEO before he broke the company into pieces. Culp now runs GE Aerospace, which has a jet-engine plant in Lynn.
