title: A Boston veteran’s 57-year journey to find peace
text:
Amazon Music | Apple Podcasts | iHeartRadio | Pocket Casts | Spotify | YouTube

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the November 20 episode of the “Say More” podcast.

Jim Dao: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Jim Dao, the editor of Globe Opinion.

When it comes to veterans, no one at the Globe has written more than one man. My guest today is columnist Kevin Cullen, who joins me in the studio. Like Kevin, I’ve spent a fair bit of time talking to and writing about veterans.

I’ve often found their stories to be heartbreaking, full of loss and trauma, but I’ve also often found them to be tales of resilience and renewal. Either way, the personal stories are essential to the American story because they reveal the lasting price of war. Kevin has captured all of these things in the scores, maybe hundreds of columns he has written about veterans, and now he has a new story that blew me away about one veteran and his decades long quest to find peace.

Welcome, Kevin.

Kevin Cullen: Thanks for having me, Jim.

Dao: So you’ve said that this story is one of the best you’ve ever written. Tell me about Ed Kochanowski and Paul Grasso.

Cullen: Well, Ed grew up in South Boston. He was literally conceived in the ruins of World War II. Ed’s parents met in a refugee camp in Eastern Europe. I don’t know if it was Poland or somewhere in that area, and they immigrated to Boston.

Ed was conceived in that refugee camp, but Ed told me that as a young man or as a teenager he noticed how damaged his parents were. They eventually drifted apart and split up. When he was 16 years old, he got permission from them to join the Marine Corps.

Dao: And this is during Vietnam?

Cullen: This was during the Vietnam War. He would’ve been in Vietnam when this fellow named Paul Grasso showed up.

Paul grew up kind of as the crow flies, maybe two miles across Dorchester Bay and Quincy, which is a city that borders Boston. Paul would’ve grown up in a completely different environment than Ed. If Ed was this kid longing for some sort of sense of normalcy and belonging, Paul grew up as the baby in this loving big Italian family in Quincy.

The one thing that really struck me when I talked to his brother Ray and his wife Susan, is that Paul was like a jock. He was like a really popular, great athlete, great baseball player, great football player. But he was the one of those jocks that didn’t look down or didn’t think he was the big man on campus. And he was very friendly. In fact, Ray got a letter while in the middle of this reporting process before I wrote anything, and it was from a woman who was a classmate of Paul’s and she said she just wanted to let him know, “I never forgot him. I always think about him because he was our classmate and he was very kind.” That’s the way she described it.

That story to me, it just made me think that I know kids like that. I know athletes and popular kids that were always kind to the least popular kids. It made me think quite a bit of Paul as a person. In September of 1967, Paul got a tryout with the New York Yankees. It was up in Vermont where I live now. And Ray, his brother, told me there were 600 kids, various baseball players from all over New England invited and only 60 of them made the cut. Paul was one of them.

So his family, like, “Wow.” This is an Italian family. They’re thinking he’s going to join a team of Joe DiMaggio, Yogi Berra, and Phil Rizzuto, all these great Italian players. They’re all getting excited. And then Paul just drops a bomb on them and says, “By the way, I just enlisted in the Marine Corps.”

Dao: Can you talk about that decision a little bit? I think we’ve both met veterans who look like they were young men who seemed to be going places in business or school and then they decide to enlist or sign up instead. What motivated him do you think?

Cullen: I think it was — and this is one of the things I tried to capture in the story — Boston and the working class, cities like where I grew up in Malden and just north of Boston, very similar to Quincy.

In the rich suburbs of Boston, there were kids desperately trying to get deferments, kids that probably didn’t even want to go to college were going to go on the eight year plan.

You know, “I’m gonna stay in college as long as I can to avoid the draft.”

Dao: Yeah, and people will forget that the draft existed then. It ended after Vietnam, but it was very much a huge issue back in the 1960s.

Cullen: Sure, and that’s why it’s kind of one of those defining characteristics that we see in our culture today.

You could trace back to them when poor kids, and kids that didn’t go to college, either got drafted or kids like Ed and Paul, they signed up. They went on their own volition.

Ed just went on his own. He described a very poignant scene of his buddies from D Street getting all the local girls. They lined up and they all kissed him. And then he said he just got on the train at South Station to go down to Parris Island holding a vodka bottle out the window.

So these guys meet and they just happen to be assigned to the same unit, and they would’ve gravitated to each other because they had accents like mine.

Their youth would’ve been similar except Paul had this incredibly warm family that was all there and his sisters fussed over him, and Ed was alone. I remember the other thing Ed told me when I did the interviews with him, he said that Paul was always talking about his family and, “I didn’t have any stories to share with him in that, but he said he was going to fix me up with his sister, one of his sisters.”

And then, obviously, we get to that fatal day in the river near Kon Tum.

Dao: That’s kind of one of the amazing things about the military is it brings people of very different backgrounds or family experiences together.

They were both from Boston, but from different kinds of families. The military puts them together and they become friends. But then it has a tragic turn. Tell us about that.

Cullen: This is in May of 1968 and they’re forwarding a river and as Ed explained to me, these marines were going about waist deep and they’re going across the river.

And when they would get to the river bank, the marine that would climb the river bank would then turn and help the marine in back of him. Paul was in front, directly in front of Ed, and so all of a sudden, while he’s in the river just about to get to the bank, the strap to his mortar pack just snapped. Broke.

And Ed grabbed it with one arm, maybe two. He had his M-16 rifle and had to keep that out of the water. And so he’s trying to hold the mortar pack with one arm, and then Paul mounts the riverbank and looks back to help Ed and sees that Ed’s really struggling. So Ed holds out his M-16.

So then Paul latches onto it and starts pulling him up the bank. And just as Ed’s getting to the top of the bank, a shot runs up. Ed fell backwards into the water fall. Paul fell, gravely wounded, on the riverbank. When Ed came out of the water, he told me he thought they were under fire, and then it dawned on him that it was his rifle that went off somehow.

He said in his movements to save the mortars from going into the water and keep his rifle above the water, he hit the safety. He assumes that’s what happened because he thought he had the safety on.

And so he gets up there and finds their sergeant kneeling by Paul, and the sergeant was telling Paul, “You’re gonna make it. You’re gonna make it. Don’t worry about it.” He said that Paul was joking, “Yeah, I’ll be okay, blah, blah.”

Ed told me he died within five minutes on that riverbank.

Dao: Tell us a little bit about how that affected Ed.

Cullen: We talked quite a bit about this. Ed said that obviously he was just wracked with guilt, and they sent him to a doctor in the Vietnamese Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). They took his gun away. They took his grenades.

So he’s saying, “I’m not a soldier. I’m not a marine anymore.”

The doctor felt bad for him. He goes, “Hey kid, I can send you home right now.” And Ed said, “No, no, no. I gotta go back to my unit. I gotta go back.”

So he did go back, but he said that as soon as he walked in the room, nobody said anything. Nobody talked.

He felt eyes were on him. He felt that these guys didn’t trust him anymore because he shot and killed one of their brothers. Ed said it was more than just these guys. He said that the officers said, “We gotta move on. It’s terrible what happened to Paul.”

The officers are worried about cohesion, they’re worried about keeping these guys in a fighting frame of mind, so you just got on with it.

No one talked about it, as if it didn’t happen.

Ed said, “People didn’t talk about it, that’s fine, but I knew that they were looking at me, and they were judging me and they didn’t trust me anymore.”

Then within weeks of that happening, I think it was about a month after Paul was shot. Ed got blown up. The next thing he knew he woke up in the Naval Hospital in Philadelphia. There’s no room at the Soldiers’ Home in Chelsea. That’s how bad it was back then. That’s how many wounded there were.

So then, while he was recovering from his wound. He was informed that his unit got whacked back in Vietnam and he said four or five guys got killed. Some of these would’ve been the guys that were there when Paul was shot.

Ed had bad survivor’s guilt to begin with, and this just made it worse — that he’s in a hospital in Philadelphia and all his buddies just got killed in Vietnam. So he got released from the hospital, and there was no follow-up treatment for a guy like this.

You’ve got to remember, 50 thousand plus guys got killed over there, and there were no services for him. So he came back to Boston, he came back to Southie. While Southie would’ve respected them, the greater Boston area, particularly in Harvard and MIT, there were anti-war protests. Soldiers and marines and airmen and sailors were treated with open contempt.

Yeah, while Southie would’ve respected these guys, the wider community would’ve not. That was very difficult for Ed to deal with.

Dao: So Ed managed to avoid Paul’s family on a couple of occasions, and then he actually ran into Paul’s brother, which is an amazing moment. Tell us about both of those things.

Cullen: Well, Ed, when he came back from Vietnam, he guessed correctly that the first Memorial Day after Paul’s death — which would’ve been May of 1969 because Paul was killed in May of 1968 — he guessed correctly that the family would visit Paul’s grave on Memorial Day at the Mount Wollaston Cemetery in Quincy. He went there with the intention of approaching them and telling them what happened.

But he said that he just lingered in the distance, and Ray Grasso told me that his mother Carmela noticed some fellow in the distance and described him as a young man with haunted eyes. Carmela Grasso actually called out, but Ed told me he just walked away. He just couldn’t bring himself, in that moment, to approach them.

And then some years later, at a memorial to Paul in Quincy, Ed attended the ceremony and the Grassos were there. Again, he said he was going to meet them and tell them what happened and introduce himself and beg for their forgiveness and all that, but he just couldn’t bring himself to do it.

So 57 years after that fatal day on the riverbank, Ray Grasso walked into Chuck Ayers auto body shop in North Quincy because his daughter Amy had borrowed his van and got it dented and she felt terrible. She said Tim, her husband, would pay for it and suggested that Ray bring the van to Chuck Ayers place because he had worked for her before and did very good work.

Ray just handed his registration to the fellow behind the counter to get a quote for the damage. The fellow behind the counter was Ed. Ed looked at the registration, the name, he looked at Ray and said, “Did you have a brother who was killed in Vietnam?” And Ray was taken aback and said, “Yes,” and Ed said, “We need to step outside.”

When they stepped outside of the auto body shop, Ed said, “It was me.”

They fell into an embrace. They hugged each other and at some point, Ray pulled away and said, “We never blamed you. Never.” Ed was able to quickly fill in some of those blanks and both of them separately — when I talked to Ed and Ray separately about this — they said that in that moment, they felt like a huge weight was lifted off them. In that moment, finally the Grassos knew what happened to Paul, how he died, and he died helping Ed.

Ed was able to unburden himself and explain to them what happened that day and that it was an accident and that he felt horrible all these years for it. And that’s, to me, when the story gets good because up until this point it was a pretty sad story.

The bottom line is the Grassos have embraced Ed and have become that family, that close-knit, loving family that Ed always desired but didn’t get when he was growing up in South Boston because his family, parents were victims of war themselves. They were walking wounded. They suffered so grievously during World War II that they couldn’t stay together.

Ed was, you could argue, an orphan of war. Now, in this moment, this incredibly powerful redemptive moment that shows what love and forgiveness and empathy can mean, Ed had that family and it was the Grassos.

Dao: You had a nice way of describing the different situations of the two families. In Ed’s case, he was scarred by the knowledge of what had happened in Vietnam. In Ray’s case, to some degree, the family was scarred by what they didn’t know about.

Cullen: One of the greatest books I read about war was Tim O’Brien’s “The Things They Carried.” I made a direct reference that Ray and Ed were sort of the prisoners of the things they carried. In Ed’s case, it was knowing what happened that day and in Ray’s case, it was not knowing what happened that day. This is where the story comes full circle.

I remember Susan Grasso, Ray’s wife, who as far as I’m concerned, makes the best chicken salad in the world.

She told me that Ed coming into their life has just closed this circle of grief that this family had, that they love him and respect him. I think as much as Ed was able to be born again in a spiritual way, I think it’s this final embrace of this family that has really healed him.

I didn’t put this in the story because it’s more just me and Ed and Ray talking and trading messages about the Red Sox and Patriots and stuff. But Ed made some reference about how he knows that he’s going to be reunited with Paul one day. I think that the story is about so many different human emotions, but I think at the end of it, the most powerful emotion throughout this story is love

Dao: Kevin, what has motivated you to write so much about veterans?

Cullen: You know, to be honest, Jim, I don’t think it was until I started having conversations with you and Anna about doing this podcast that I didn’t really kind of sit back and think, “Why do I write about veterans so much?”

It really made me think about my dad. He grew up in Malden. His dad was like a Department of Public Works (DPW) worker. He had to be the only white kid in Malden, nicknamed after Duke Ellington. His nickname was Duke because he was a jazz nut. But he went off to war and it wasn’t until he died, he died at 65 and was a firefighter. And, the guys that I met at the wake and the funeral — some of them served in the military with him, in the Navy — they described my father as this happy-go-lucky guy who just loved jazz and just loved music and was always singing, always dancing.

Then he came back from the war — he was in the Pacific for three years — and he was a different man. He was a different person. My dad was an alcoholic. He had a drinking problem as long as I could remember, and he was out of the house quite a bit.

The other firefighters would cover for him. You get thrown out of the house, well you sleep in the firehouse. You shower at the firehouse. You eat at the firehouse, and you go on. I don’t know when it dawned on me, but I kind of never judged my dad. I wasn’t angry at him that he was this person that struggled with alcohol and I think somewhere, by his osmosis or whatever you want to call it, I kind of figured out that my dad suffered really badly during the war.

Like I said, he never spoke about it. I tried to engage him, particularly in my twenties when I was a newspaper reporter by this time. Several times I tried to bring up the war, something to shoot the shit, whatever, talk about, and he just wouldn’t go there.

And it wasn’t unusual for his generation. Those guys, World War II guys, weren’t big talkers about that stuff in general. But it was only after he died that I learned from other people who served with him that he was a Navy flyer, not a pilot. I think his title was like “radio man,” but he also dropped the bombs and hit and manned the machine gun in the plane.

Those planes flew off aircraft carriers in the Pacific, and what they did is before the marines would land, these navy planes would fly over islands in the Pacific that the Japanese controlled. And so, they went straight for the beaches from a pretty low altitude and bomb them. So my dad, I’m presuming, would’ve seen the faces of people he killed.

I think, like I said, by the time I was in my teens, I kind of understood even if I didn’t have a name for it. I didn’t know it was post-traumatic stress. My dad eventually found some kind of sobriety and he ended up on lithium for his depression. The last five or six years, he had a pretty good five or six years. He was very involved in Club 24, which is a program, a 12-step program in Malden that gets people sober.

I recently met the chief probation officer up in Lowell District Court. The probate is a woman who was an addict years ago, and now she’s the chief probation officer. She told me she got sober at Club 24, and that made me just really admire my dad. But I think I write about veterans because of my dad.

Dao: What, after all your experience writing about veterans, learning about their stories, do you think you would say to your dad today?

Cullen: I would love to have just talked to him about what he went through, and that, “Give me a better understanding.” But I don’t think I ever told my dad that cliché, “Thank you for your service.”

I don’t think I ever told him that I was proud of him, that he was part of the Greatest Generation, and at great cost to him and to our family. He went and helped save the world from fascism and I never told him. Maybe I write about veterans because I can tell them what I never got to tell my dad. I admire what they did.

At the same time, Jim, I’m so angry at our government, at that we don’t take care of these people. We love veterans on Veterans Day. We love those who served and died on Memorial Day and you know what, for those 363 other days, we don’t give a shit about these people.

It shows the amount of services that are needed. Trying to get services from the VA should not be as hard as it is. I guess you could say back in World War II, we had the excuse of ignorance. We didn’t provide services for people like my dad. You were just told to get on with it, raise a family, get a job, do the things that, “Oh, by the way, we’ll give you a VA loan so you can buy a house and we’ll give you healthcare for the rest of your life, blah, blah, blah.”

Yeah sure, healthcare for the rest of your life. To this day, we have 20 something veterans killing themselves every day in this country.

That’s an indictment of this country. We don’t have the defense of ignorance anymore. We know what’s going on with folks who serve and the challenges that they face getting back into civilian life, particularly combat veterans.

But not just combat veterans, because as far as I’m concerned, the military hasn’t done nearly enough to confront the scourge of sexual assault.

Every once in a while, I’ll hear from a reader who just says, “Oh, you’re like a pro-military fascist,” or something crazy like that. I said, “Nah, I’m not. I love our vets, but I know the foibles and problems of our military.” A lot of it just comes down to bad people who are not held accountable and often by commanders who don’t want any of that on their watch.

And it happens in all institutions that protect themselves. They protect themselves at the expense of individuals who are harmed by those institutions because institutions care about — and I’ve seen it my whole life as a reporter, whether it was the church, the FBI, protecting Whitey Bulger and letting him kill people or the military, certain facets of the military — they don’t care about their service people. They care about their own reputation. They care about their unit integrity, and they care about the next promotion.

Dao: How have you found the response to your stories? Because I can talk from my experience that it almost felt like for a lot of readers it was like you were exploring a foreign country.

Because so few Americans today actually have a direct link to the military or to veterans. How have you found it?

Cullen: We always talk about the 1 percent. We describe it as the people that are rich and the others who aren’t. But the other 1 percent is those who have served, so 99 percent of the country hasn’t.

The Vietnam War tore this country apart, and one of the lessons that came out of that is we decided to get rid of the draft, which was wildly unfair because if you are rich enough, connected enough, had bone spurs, you could avoid military service. We sent poor kids, mostly, went off and fought these wars. And, not just poor kids, because it always angered me that Harvard — I wrote about this — Harvard wouldn’t let Reserve Officers Training Corps (ROTC) on the campus, sort of this hangover from the 1970s. And then you’d walk into Memorial Hall and just see the names of all these Harvard guys who went off to war.

All the wars, including Vietnam, their names are right there. They died serving this country and they honored Harvard with their service and Harvard, because of some silly, I don’t know what I would call it, some whole anti-war movement there that they wouldn’t allow the ROTC.

It was so patronizing. “Harvard kids, we can’t let them be recruited to the military and become killers.” What a bunch of nonsense. The tradition of Harvard is written on those walls.

Dao: Looking back on all your writings on the subject, what do you think has surprised you most about veterans and their place in America?

Cullen: One thing, and Ed and Ray did comment on this, we talked about it after the story appeared because the comments, they were really very warm and generous comments and Ed and Ray and Susan and the whole Grasso family took a lot of comfort from that. I talked to Ray and more traded messages — Ray, me, and Ed — that the culture has come a long way.

You could be angry about Vietnam, a war that shouldn’t have been fought, but be angry at the politicians who did it. Don’t be angry at the teenagers we sent over to fight it. And I do take some comfort, I think the country has come through that by and large, but again, I wish that we as a culture embraced and loved and supported our veterans more than we do, and I think we have a long way to go to improve that.

Dao: Kevin Cullen is a columnist at the Boston Globe, and he specialized in veteran stories, among many other things. We’ll link to his latest piece in the show notes. Thanks so much for joining me, Kevin.

Cullen: Thanks for having me, Jim. I really enjoyed it.

Listen to more “Say More” episodes at globe.com/saymore and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: ‘Does Globe Santa still exist?’
text:
“It was the best gift of the year,” said DuCharme, now 76. “We all wanted that gift. We were thinking, ‘Why did he get that?’“

The Gardikis kids were among the early beneficiaries of the 70-year-old Globe Santa program, which was just two years old at the time. Its mission was — and still is — to make holidays brighter for poor children by making sure they got gifts of toys.

“Seriously, I don’t know if we would have gotten anything if it wasn’t for Globe Santa,” DuCharme said. “For many years, prior to the older kids growing up and getting jobs and contributing to the household finances, we relied on Globe Santa to provide gifts for me and my siblings.”

There were years when their father only worked sporadically and “lots of times there wasn’t food,” DuCharme said, speaking from her home in Tennessee, where she’s lived for 24 years (and retains her Boston accent). She said her mother would get government-issued surplus food boxes with powdered milk, peanut butter, rice, butter, and eggs, lugging them up to their third-floor apartment.

Still, lots of times there was nothing to eat.

They were so poor that her parents would make candles from slabs of paraffin wax and melted crayons, and dispatch the kids on Christmas Eve to go out and sell them door to door. “We told people: ‘We’re not going to have a Christmas, will you buy a candle?’ We didn’t get rich, I can tell you that!”

She shared another “good story” from childhood. “We used to have ‘cocoa parties.’ Mom would put a blanket over the table and we had Saltines and yukky Hershey’s cocoa. Years later my sister Irene told me: ‘You know why she did that? Because we didn’t have supper! To make it a game!’”

But Christmas was always joyful, thanks to Globe Santa. “You don’t forget something like that,” she said. Year after year, she vowed she’d donate to the charity “for their blessings to our family.” But she never did. And she always felt guilty.

“It wasn’t that I couldn’t do it,” she said. “I’ve been blessed. I’ve got the most beautiful house down here. My husband saved and saved and now I am able to help so many people.”

But she decided this would be the year, assuming the charity was still there. She searched online.

“I put in: ‘Does Globe Santa still exist?’ and was shocked to see that it does. Usually, nothing good lasts forever, you know what I’m saying?”

And so she made a donation, and emailed Globe Santa with the 1958 photo. “Sorry it took me so long,” she wrote. “I am so blessed to be in a position to help this year and I’m sure with the current state of the economy that many will be asking for help. I hope to continue to do this on an annual basis. … Congratulations and I pray you have many more years of helping people.”

For 70 years Globe Santa, a program of the Boston Globe Foundation, has provided gifts to children in need at holiday time. Please consider giving by phone, mail, or online at globesanta.org.

title: Is your bus route one of the slowest in Boston? A new study shows the worst performers.
text:
Is your bus route one of the slowest in Boston? A new study shows the worst performers.

The T’s slowest buses only got slower last year, according to a study published this fall by research and advocacy group TransitMatters.

The MBTA’s 10 slowest bus routes clocked an average speed of 6.52 miles per hour in October 2024, a slight decline from 6.83 miles per hour the year prior.

The slowest high-ridership bus in New York City, by contrast, registered an average speed of 5.25 miles per hour, according to city research and advocacy groups.

Bunching — when buses on the same route travel closer together than their schedules dictate — also worsened. Bunching can undermine bus reliability and the broader efficiency of a bus system, experts warn. The percentage of bunched buses among the worst-performing routes increased from 14.1 percent to 15.8 percent between October 2023 and October 2024, the most recently analyzed time frame in the study.

The causes are manifold, says TransitMatters: worsening road congestion, rule-flouting cars, and inadequate bus infrastructure. So too are the consequences, namely, slow and sporadic bus service for some of the city’s least-privileged communities.

“MBTA bus riders are disproportionately people of color, low-income, and transit-dependent, making improvements to bus service a critical equity issue,” the report noted.

The T wrote in a statement to the Globe that “improving the speed and reliability of our bus service is one of our top priorities.”

Insulating buses from frequent and dense thickets of traffic is, transit advocates stress, among the most effective and intuitive ways to speed them up. Dedicated bus lanes, they say, do the job.

The T and Boston have publicly committed to expanding bus lanes throughout the city. Over 45 miles of dark red bus-only lanes wind through Roxbury, downtown Boston, and other nearby municipalities, the T says. Other lanes are in the works, while others have been removed.

Often in Boston, a bus lane is little more than a paint job. The city’s drivers habitually slip through or stop in them.

The T plans to begin spotting and punishing these scofflaws with bus-mounted enforcement cameras next year.

Reconfiguring traffic signals to reduce wait times at intersections could also help, advocates and experts note. The T says it has activated “transit signal priority,” as the adjustment is known, at 118 locations.

The T itself could do more to improve bus performance, TransitMatters said, namely by better managing vehicle intervals. TransitMatters observed, for instance, that the 22 bus route experiences severe bunching, despite traveling through dedicated bus lanes along Columbus Avenue. The group noted that “much of this route’s bunching can be attributed to poor operations.”

Route 1, coincidentally, claimed the top spot (for the second year running), clocking an average speed of 6.03 miles per hour. One of the T’s most popular routes, Route 1, travels from Harvard’s campus along Mass. Ave. until it hooks toward its southern terminus at Nubian in Roxbury.

The CT3 line links the Longwood medical district to Andrew Station in South Boston, cutting through Roxbury. The average CT3 bus traveled 6.42 miles per hour.

Despite being categorized as “bus rapid transit,” the SL4 and SL5 buses connecting downtown, the South End, and Roxbury are among the T’s slowest. They registered an average speed of 6.49 miles per hour, according to the study, 6 percent slower than in 2023.

Route 19, which connects Kenmore to Fields Corner in Dorchester, making stops throughout Roxbury in between, also clocked an average speed of 6.49 miles per hour.

The 66 bus, another very popular route, links Nubian to Cambridge through a more roundabout route that passes through Brookline and Allston. The 66 bus averaged 6.57 miles per hour last year.

The 45 bus, which connects Ruggles, near Northeastern University, to the northeastern edge of Franklin Park, services much of Roxbury. It registered an average speed of 6.62 miles per hour last October.

Route 91 links Sullivan Square, just east of Somerville, to Central Square in Cambridge. The 91 bus averaged 6.63 miles per hour.

The 23 bus, one of the T’s most used lines, links Ashmont to Ruggles, passing through the hearts of Dorchester and Roxbury. Buses traveling the route averaged 6.63 miles per hour last October. The 23 bus is one of three routes that are free to ride until early 2026.

The 10 bus, which loops from Back Bay to City Point in South Boston, registered an average speed of 6.65 miles per hour.

Route 28 buses, some of the T’s most popular, clocked average speeds of 6.7 miles per hour. The 28 bus connects the heart of Roxbury to Mattapan, and spends much of its route trudging up and down Blue Hill Avenue. The 28 bus is one of the three routes that are free to ride until early 2026.

Many of the T’s slowest bus routes also experienced the most bunching, according to TransitMatters. The research group defined the “bunching rate” as the share of buses where the time interval between vehicles (the headway) was less than 25 percent of the scheduled interval.

Route 23 had the highest bunching rate of 19.3 percent.

Route 111, which connects downtown Boston to Chelsea, had a bunching rate of 18.9 percent, a 14 percent increase from the year prior.

Route 1 had a bunching rate of 17.6 percent, a minuscule improvement from 2023.

The 39 bus, a popular route that connects Back Bay Station to Forest Hills, had a bunching rate of 15.9 percent.

The 32 bus, which runs a roughly straight path between Hyde Park and Forest Hills, had a bunching rate of 15 percent.

The SL4 and SL5 had a bunching rate of 14.7 percent.

The 22 bus, which also connects Ashmont to Ruggles, had a bunching rate of 14.6 percent.

Route 66 had a bunching rate of 14.4 percent.

The 28 bus had a bunching rate of 14.2 percent.

Route 57, which connects Watertown to Kenmore, had a bunching rate of 13.2 percent.

Jaime Moore-Carrillo can be reached at jaime.moore-carrillo@globe.com.

title: Dorchester couple charged for death of their 5-week-old daughter who was exposed to drugs
text:
In court papers, Suffolk prosecutors alleged that Reed learned she was pregnant in September 2024 and delivered the baby, identified as G.R.W., in her Dorchester apartment on Dec. 5, 2024. She gave birth two months early, according to prosecutors.

On Jan. 9, Reed called 911 reporting the child wasn’t breathing. She was rushed to Boston Medical Center and later pronounced dead, prosecutors said.

She weighed 2.5 pounds at the time.

“During the five weeks of her life, G.R.W. failed to gain or maintain weight and was severely malnourished,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Laura C. Drohan wrote in court papers. “Despite knowing that their baby was born at least two months premature and observing the newborn was unable to gain or maintain weight, the defendants never sought any medical care for the infant as her health continued to significantly deteriorate.”

The baby’s cause of death was acute intoxication from the combined effects of fentanyl and cocaine in a premature infant with malnourishment and sepsis, according to the autopsy by the state medical examiner’s office.

Prosecutors alleged Reed and Winn “used illegal substances in the infant’s presence, resulting in her exposure to these substances.”

Reed’s court-appointed defense attorney, Paul J. Davenport, said she has struggled with fentanyl addiction. But she’s spent the past six months in a residential treatment program and “largely turned her life around,” Davenport said. He asked for a lower bail, saying her progress could be lost if she’s forced to leave the program for jail.

“It would just seem tragic, in my humble opinion, to derail this sobriety that she’s managed to achieve,” he said.

Winn’s court-appointed attorney, Christopher M. Kenney, said Winn has been cooperating with law enforcement throughout the investigation. He was arrested Monday after showing up to court, handcuffed and taken into custody after sitting through Reed’s arraignment in the public area of the courtroom.

“He’s maintaining his innocence. He’s cooperated with police up until now,” Kenney said. “He showed up on his own two feet.”

Kenney said Winn has other children he wants to have contact with while the case proceeds.

But Suffolk First Assistant Clerk Magistrate Edward J. Curley ordered both Reed and Winn to stay away from anyone under 16.

In a statement, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden said the child died from “sheer neglect.”

“It’s difficult to conceive of something more tragic than a child being born and then ignored to the extent it leads to death by malnourishment and sheer neglect,” he said in the statement. “The allegation that the parents were using dangerous drugs in the newborn’s presence only adds to the terrible aspects of this crime.”

title: UMass Boston student charged in fraud scheme targeting R.I. seniors
text:
PROVIDENCE — A UMass Boston student was arrested after he allegedly took part in a fraud scam targeting Rhode Island seniors, according to federal prosecutors.

Samyag Uday Doshi, 25, a citizen of India residing in Dorchester on a student visa, was arrested on Nov. 17 and charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud. He appeared before US District Court Magistrate Judge Amy E. Moses in Providence that day.

“It is alleged that he participated in a scheme that caused a Rhode Island resident to turn over $54,000 in cash, with an attempted loss amount totaling more than $385,000,” the Rhode Island US attorney’s office said in a press release.

According to a criminal complaint filed in court, police in Newport, R.I., received a call earlier this month regarding an elderly resident “who may be the victim of an elder abuse financial fraud scam.”

“The individual received a voicemail on his cellular phone regarding a phony purchase and was instructed to call a telephone number provided to him to address the issue,” prosecutors said. “When he called the number, scammers falsely told him that he was speaking with a federal official and was under investigation for a myriad of charges, including money laundering. The scammers represented that they could assist the individual through the investigation.”

For about three weeks, the alleged scammers instructed the man to make multiple cash withdrawals “of tens of thousands of dollars and to then mail the funds out of state or provide the funds to ‘couriers,’ whom he met in person in Rhode Island,” according to officials.

“The individual also made multiple inquiries about purchasing hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of gold bars,” prosecutors said. “These inquiries are believed to have been directed by members of the conspiracy.”

On Nov. 17, the scammers tried to arrange for the man to deliver an additional $45,000 in cash, and the victim contacted police, officials said. Prosecutors allege authorities observed the delivery as it was made to Doshi, who was arrested at the meeting spot.

Moses ordered Doshi detained, noting there was serious risk he could flee if released, filings show. Moses also cited that Doshi lacked stable employment and strong ties to the community, and noted the evidence against him is strong.

In a motion filed on Nov. 21, Kevin J. Fitzgerald, an attorney representing Doshi, requested Doshi be released on pre-trial conditions, writing that Doshi has a longtime family friend in the Boston area who has offered to support Doshi in finding a new residence.

Doshi’s family is also looking to travel to the United States to help support him as the case moves forward, Fitzgerald wrote.

Doshi has been in the United States for nearly two years while studying at UMass Boston, and had been living with five roommates, who “were fairly shocked when they heard he had been arrested,” Fitzgerald wrote.

“Mr. Doshi is charged with a serious felony offense,” Fitzgerald wrote. “While the evidence has been deemed strong, there is no question that his part in the charged conspiracy is as a cog in the machine rather than the control panel.”

Responses to the motion are due by Dec. 5.

title: House fire in Dorchester displaces five residents and two cats, officials say
text:
Five residents were displaced after a fire broke out in a triple-decker in Dorchester on Monday night, officials said.

At approximately 11:45 p.m., firefighters responded to 11 Annapolis St., where a fire had started on the second floor, according to social media posts by the Boston Fire Department.

The one-alarm fire was under control in approximately 30 minutes, according to a department spokesperson.

One resident was transported ⁦⁦by Boston EMS, officials said.

The Red Cross was assisting the residents who were displaced, officials said. Two cats were also displaced.

The cause of the fire is under investigation, officials said.
