title: Thankful as always, but this year was different
text:
This year it’s easier than ever. What is unusual is that, when I sit down to think about the year in food, my first response is one of anger. For the first time, SNAP funds were held hostage from those who need them, the bulk of whom are children, senior citizens, and people with disabilities. After 43 days, the government shutdown ended and the benefits were issued. But not before the country learned that those now in power will treat hunger not as an urgent problem to be alleviated but as a weapon, the suffering of the citizens who elected them a convenience, for they can use it as a bargaining chip.

I’m angry that a country that can afford whatever it wants chooses not to afford this. Those responsible can fight over who gets to borrow Melania Trump’s hideous jacket, emblazoned with the message “I really don’t care, do u?” For the rest of us, the answer is yes, always yes. We really do care, very much.

So, gratitude: I could not be more grateful for the community that stepped up to care for neighbors, to make sure that friends and strangers had access to food. Allandale Farm set up a free weekly farmers’ market for November in Jamaica Plain, giving away produce and bread donated by Iggy’s. Watertown restaurant Ritcey East, known for its comfort food, offered real comfort: free prepared meals, plus a food drive. Roslindale butcher shop and Italian grocery Tony’s Market “adopted” families, providing them with meat, eggs, and prepared foods.

In Newton, Blacker’s Bakeshop leaned into the Jewish mitzvah of maakhal revi’im, feeding the hungry, through its Community Table initiative; they gave away loaves of challah, which community members could also sponsor, alongside Inna’s Kitchen’s donated soups. East Boston’s EBO & Co. Grocery set up a “take what you need” stand outside the shop, offering everything from diapers and formula to oatmeal and mac ’n’ cheese; neighbors contributed money and groceries to keep supplies stocked. In Taunton, Kinfolks BBQ offered $6 dinners, first-come-first-served free meals, and free Thanksgiving dinners.

These are just a few of the examples we heard — on top of the increased, tireless efforts of food banks, food pantries, soup kitchens, and their volunteers and donors longtime and new.

So, to the powerful few who have long perverted “welfare” into a word of shame and scorn rather than compassion and concern: no thanks to you. Everyone else, hell yeah: You make me proud to be a human.

Beyond that, I was thankful for so many smaller things that make life brighter every day:

Like tacos! The local supply of good ones continues to grow, at places such as Esquite in Revere, Pátzcuaro Taqueria & Bar in Newton, Plazita Mexico Tacos in Watertown and Wakefield, and Taqueria El Amigo in Waltham. This year’s big news was a second Taqueria Jalisco in East Boston, with a branch in Orient Heights joining the well-loved Day Square branch. The place is wonderfully festive, and the birria tacos are as good as ever.

I’m always grateful for the Boston area’s strong Asian food scene, from pho in Dorchester to dim sum in Malden to Chinatown’s vibrant assortment of restaurants and bakeries. It was nice to see that recognized by the Michelin Guide, in its first pass through this area. Michelin gave one star to 311 Omakase, serving chef’s tasting menus focused on sushi and sashimi in the South End. The recognition reached from the high end to the more affordable, from the traditional to the innovative — designating Jahunger, Mahaniyom, Pagu, and Sumiao Hunan Kitchen as Bib Gourmand restaurants and recommending Nightshade Noodle Bar, Somaek, Wa Shin, and Zhi Wei Cafe. Mahaniyom also won an award for its cocktails.

In addition to 311 and Wa Shin, I’m grateful for omakase restaurants with unique local flavor that surprise and delight — places like Akame Nigiri and Sake in Lexington, Sushi Sang Lee in Gloucester, and Washoku Renaissance in Charlestown.

I was also glad to see Korean cuisine expand in interesting, thoughtful, and delicious ways ­— at places like Damgeuda in Haverhill, where husband-wife chefs Walter Gorrell and Yu Gin Kim continually re-create their tiny menu of hand-hewn, seasonal gems; Nine Winters Bakery in Cambridge, where Marissa Ferola crafts Korean-American baked goods (gochujang-citrus sticky buns, peanut butter chile crisp cookies) and more (milk bread finger sandwiches, galbi pot au feu); and Somaek, Jamie Bissonnette’s ode to the cuisine he married into, falling in love with the flavors while cooking alongside his mother-in-law, Soon Han, who is consulting chef at the restaurant.

In these days of Instagram and influencers, I sometimes feel that emphasis is placed on how a restaurant looks over how its food tastes. So when Jody Adams’s new Italian restaurant, La Padrona, opened — equal parts style and substance — I was thrilled to ascend its glamorous staircase and quaff fancy martinis and slurp down handmade noodles and tiramisu. Time to do that again soon.

Boston’s Italian food always shines. I was thankful for Little Sage, chef Tony Susi’s new-again restaurant, on its own strengths (those delicate, pillowy gnocchi!) but also because it’s wonderful to have a North End restaurant ready to recommend when people ask, “Where should I eat in the North End?”

Dorchester got the Irish pub it deserves with McGonagle’s, serving perfectly pulled pints of Guinness alongside gorgeous fish and chips and more. The place is named for owner Oran McGonagle, also behind the Dubliner and others; executive chef Aidan McGee worked in London at places such as gastropub the Truscott Arms and the Michelin-starred Dinner by Heston Blumenthal before bringing his excellent pub fare to Boston.

And Jamaica Plain got the cafe/wine bar of my dreams in Jadu, a winning little hangout that brings us chai, savory oatmeal, and brothy beans by day, fancy snacks and glasses of nice wine by night.

One of the best meals I experienced this year was not in Boston at all but on the Cape, at the extremely charming Lune in Dennis Port. I met up with great friends; sat at the counter and watched the chefs do their thing; ate mind-blowing foie gras tarte topped with glowing green chartreuse gelee, confit halibut with fava bean ragout, and house-made sourdough bread with cultured butter; and felt fortunate, fortunate, fortunate.

Perhaps the best part of the year was revisiting places that endure, excel, and enrich our lives — from Slade’s, sometimes called “the Black Cheers,” open since 1928, to Brookline tapas legend Taberna de Haro, now stewarded by new ownership and as wonderful as ever, to — yep — the Ground Round, that nostalgic favorite, reincarnated in Shrewsbury. In Harvard Square, Harvest marked its 50th anniversary this year. Fifty! I’m thankful for everything that makes the food scene wonderful and new, and also for the restaurants the community respects and supports for the long haul.

title: Women’s Lunch Place expands services for homeless women
text:
“I just really want to move forward now, and I’m almost there,” said Debbie, who asked to be identified by only her first name to protect her privacy.

The housing program through Women’s Lunch Place is a short-term solution for women like Debbie experiencing homelessness in the Boston area. Unlike some other shelters, it’s designed so each woman can have their own room, and they’re paired with an advocate, or social worker, who helps them find permanent housing. The Globe is not naming the specific location of the shelter because some of the women living there have been victims of domestic violence.

So far, 13 women have moved from the Women’s Lunch Place shelter to permanent housing. The wraparound services — including meals, access to a kitchen, laundry machines, and a social worker — give women experiencing homelessness more stability than they’re used to in typical nighttime shelters, said CEO Jennifer Hanlon Wigon.

Many women experience homelessness as a result of physical or sexual assault, Hanlon Wigon said. Between 22 and 57 percent of all homeless women report that domestic violence was the immediate cause of their homelessness, according to the National Network to End Domestic Violence.

“Having safe gendered spaces is a real key to their ability to turn off that fight or flight aspect of their trauma,” Hanlon Wigon said.

Women’s Lunch Place opened its pilot housing program in response to a spike in homelessness last winter, she said. The number of people experiencing homelessness in Greater Boston peaked in 2024 at over 20,000 people, and fell to around 19,600 in 2025, according to a report from Boston Indicators, the research arm of the Boston Foundation. Women in Greater Boston experience homelessness at slightly higher rates than men — 30 per 10,000 women compared to 27 per 10,000 men — in contrast to the national trend, the report said.

Women’s Lunch Place increased the shelter capacity by 50 beds for women experiencing homelessness in Greater Boston. Now, thanks to a new grant from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, the pilot program will be expanded to 65 beds.

“The first night that we were up to capacity, the shelter system had a bed for every woman,” Hanlon Wigon said.

In addition to adding 15 beds, the $760,000-plus grant will extend the shelter program from November through April.

Because of Massachusetts’ unique right-to-shelter law — which means state officials have to provide housing to families with children and pregnant women — shelters in Greater Boston are often overburdened. At overnight shelters, women may have to carry all their belongings if they can’t get a locker, and sleeping arrangements are in flux.

Marcia Fabiola Davis, 65, remembers her time living in other shelters. When she stayed in a safe house in Florida after escaping domestic violence, local restaurants would send leftovers when they closed, but she couldn’t always keep her young daughter awake until 11 p.m. to eat.

When her daughter, now married, asked Davis how the food was at Women’s Lunch Place recently, she said, “Not the same as the safe house in Florida.”

“That makes me more calm,” Davis remembers her daughter saying.

Davis has lived in the Women’s Lunch Place shelter program since November. Originally from Brazil, Davis moved to the US to take care of her sister in Florida, who has liver problems, and eventually became a citizen in 2018.

While in Florida, Davis worked at a grocery store on-and-off — a job she loved despite having to pause work to navigate multiple health crises — before eventually following her daughter to Boston.

“This year, in May, [my daughter] married, and it’s time that I go,” Davis said, insisting to her daughter that she should have her own private life.

Davis said she had been working on housing applications since 2023. Earlier this year, she stayed in the Missionaries of Charity shelter in Dorchester, where she had an early curfew and shared bedrooms. Now, she loves having her own key and access to laundry.

“The mission is nice, too, but in here, it’s five stars,” Davis said.

Through the daytime programs at Women’s Lunch Place, Davis takes crochet and English classes. After she finds an apartment, she plans to go back to school and finish the political science degree she started in Brazil.

Finding permanent housing has gotten more difficult as affordable housing grows scarce in Greater Boston, said Doris Romero, senior director of housing and advocacy at Women’s Lunch Place. She leads a group of 11 advocates who help guests fill out apartment applications and address barriers to housing. Last year, advocates held 11,830 meetings with 1,275 guests, including visitors to the Women’s Lunch Place daytime program and the shelter.

Jackeline Dixon, 59, moved from a shelter to her own apartment in May. In her own place, she’s able to rest when her sciatica flares or cook whenever she wants.

“When you’re homeless, it’s a different kind of stress,” she said.

Dixon, who lost her housing after a fire in her apartment complex in 2023, credits the staff at Women’s Lunch Place with helping her fill out applications every day.

Staff at Women’s Lunch Place said they still hear from women who have since moved to permanent housing because of the community at the shelter. Debbie G. promises to come back and help volunteer in whatever way she can.

“You know Cheers? The place where everybody knows your name?” Debbie said. “That’s what the Lunch Place is. Everybody knows your name.”

title: Demand for bilingual education outpacing Boston schools efforts to keep up
text:
Soto, who considered taking them to a psychologist at first, was relieved when a Spanish-speaking teacher’s aide stepped in for language support and the kids started doing better.

Now Soto, 33, is doing the same for other children, by working as a parent mentor at her kids’ school four days a week for $19 an hour.

The parent mentors are one of many strategies Boston Public Schools is using to address a serious shortage. One-third of the district’s 47,000 students primarily speak a language other than English, but the schools don’t have nearly enough bilingual teachers to offer them support in their native tongue.

Research shows English language learners do best when they receive at least some instruction in two languages.

In Boston, the district has only 13 such programs, mostly in elementary schools, and they have long waiting lists. Last year, only 7 percent of English learners — or about 1,200 students— were enrolled in dual-language programs. For the most part, other English language learners are simply integrated into regular classrooms.

The result has been lower test scores for English learners. Almost three-quarters of English learners and former students who were English learners failed to meet or exceed MCAS scores for math and science in 2024. And over the past four years, more than 15 percent dropped out, twice the dropout rate of other students, according to state education data.

“Most of these kids are being dumped into general education classrooms and are pulled out for 45 to 90 minutes a day to take English as a second language classes,” said Rosann Tung, an education researcher who resigned from a BPS task force on English learning after criticizing the district’s approach.

Tung and seven other task force members left in protest in late 2023 after the district announced it could not keep up with an influx of new English learners and would not guarantee instruction in their native language. Instead, the district doubled down on an “inclusive education plan,” integrating English learners into general education classrooms.

“We are implementing inclusive classrooms, so multilingual learners and students with disabilities can learn close to home, in the same room as their peers,” said Mayor Michelle Wu at the first ever State of the Schools address this fall.

Wu did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

In Boston, where students hailed from 139 different countries, the district last year promised to add 1,060 students to bilingual classrooms by the 2032-2033 school year, while hiring 40 new bilingual teachers over almost a decade. After this story was published, BPS said in an email that it had increased its hiring plan to 54 teachers and that it “currently offers over 2,500 seats” to students wanting dual language bilingual programs.

Four out of 10 new teachers hired this year were fluent in a second language, BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper said in an interview.

“We’ve had more bilingual programming approved by the state and operationalized in the last couple of years — and will continue to do that — than we have had in decades,” she said.

For the upcoming school year, the city invested $123 million, nearly 8 percent of its total school budget, in multilingual programs.

Of that funding, $4 million will go toward adding or expanding multilingual programs in seven elementary schools and two secondary schools.

The district is also in the process of planning a new bilingual program taught in Cape Verdean creole.

The growth of those multilanguage programs won’t come close to keeping up with the growing need, as half of pre-K and kindergarten students entering the district don’t speak English as their first language. Only five new bilingual teachers will be added for the next school year districtwide, according to the district’s budget.

St. Stephen’s parent mentors are filling in the gaps where they can.

Since 2017, the youth program at the church in the South End has been training mothers who hail from Haiti, Mexico, Morocco, Somalia, Ecuador, Paraguay, and other countries to work in kindergarten classrooms. The moms help with academic development and provide social, emotional, and language support by stepping in when a child can’t communicate.

Backed by BPS, the program also aims for some of the bilingual parent mentors to eventually become professionals, with 40 percent of all participants going on to work for the district.

“We are building a pipeline for bilingual people who come from the same communities as our students to enter education,” said Ari Branz, director of organizing at the St. Stephen’s youth program.

Kayra Amador, a Dominican parent mentor who provides support at the William Monroe Trotter Elementary school in Dorchester, said she is striving to become a lead teacher so she can have a positive impact on children’s lives.

“The kids who don’t speak English are always more isolated and lonely,” Amador said. “When I am there in the class with them, I feel like I can help them.“

A grant provided by the City of Boston pays for Amador and 19 other parent mentors to enroll at Urban College, where they take courses required to become certified lead teachers. After that, they can choose to pursue an associate’s degree in education.

These programs are all part of BPS efforts to recover from state law zigzagging on bilingual education.

A 2002 ballot campaign led by a conservative Silicon Valley millionaire eliminated bilingual instruction in schools in Massachusetts until it was lifted in 2017.

The 15-year-ban has left a hole in the state’s teaching workforce, Branz said.

“There is a whole generation of students who graduated without learning a second language,” said Branz, who previously worked with the Boston Teachers Union. “Those are the people who are now entering the workforce as teachers.”

Since 2017, the number of districts statewide offering dual language programs grew from 15 to 25, across 62 individual schools, according to the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.

Experts said initiatives like the mentorship program at St. Stephen’s will help, but not enough to address the shortage.

“The parent mentorship program is a very positive step,” said John Mudd, a former member of the School Committee’s task force on English language learners. “But in no way can it substitute for broader reform in the education of multilingual learners.”

Meanwhile, mothers who participate in the St. Stephen’s mentorship program continue to do their part.

Every Friday, they gather at the church to talk about what they have experienced Monday through Thursday in the classroom and to receive training from educators. About 40 parents participate in the program this year.

In a crowded meeting room adjacent to the church, they sit at round tables and scribble in notebooks, as a team from the nonprofit Boston Partners in Education offers a presentation on the best ways to provide support.

”When one of our mentors shows up, [teachers] are relieved to finally have someone to help them communicate," said Rafaela Polanco, director of parent organizing and engagement at the church. “So at least for 2½ hours, four days a week, we are helping to bridge that gap.“

(This story was updated on Dec. 3, 2025)

title: Bostonians ‘can do a lot’ this Giving Tuesday, aid groups and religious charities say
text:
“It was like watching the sunrise,” Brown, 25, said about moving into her apartment on Nov. 1.

Giving Tuesday — a national day of philanthropy held on the first Tuesday after Thanksgiving — has leaders of Boston-area nonprofits hopeful for the donations they need this year to help people in the community, such as Brown.

Amid cuts to critical federal funding, the high cost of living, and rising fear among immigrants facing possible deportation, nonprofits have carried a heavy burden. Staff, such as the social workers who worked for months to help Brown find a home, have witnessed the upheaval first-hand.

”We’re seeing a surge in demand for our services just as federal resources are being cut,” said Catholic Charities Boston CEO Kelley Tuthill.

Boston-area nonprofits said support on Giving Tuesday doesn’t have to come in the form of money.

People who themselves may need extra help paying bills often give in other ways, such as volunteering, they said.

No matter what form it takes, giving to others has psychological benefits, experts said.

“People call it warm glow giving, you get a hit of joy from giving to other people or helping others,” said Paige Amormino, a post-doctoral researcher at Pennsylvania State University who studies moral psychology.

Catholic Charities Boston started their Giving Tuesday campaign earlier than ever this year, toward the beginning of November, Tuthill said.

The decision came after months of rising demand for emergency aid and shelter spots, such as the one Brown and her daughter were able to access earlier this year.

When donors write a check on Giving Tuesday or later this holiday season, they will be helping the approximately 100,000 people across Eastern Massachusetts that the nonprofit serves, Tuthill said.

“I think right now, many people are feeling powerless,” Tuthill said. “They feel like they don’t agree with some of the things happening right now in our country. They think, what can I do? And I say to them, ‘You can do a lot.’”

Brown said her worst moment living unhoused came early one morning when her family’s makeshift sleeping area in a storage unit was almost discovered by a staff member doing a walk-through.

“I had to jump up real quick and deconstruct our set-up,” said Brown, who knew that living in a storage facility could get her in trouble with police. “That was a really scary point, almost getting caught, and thankfully, I managed to make it look like we were just there super early going through stuff.”

Now, Brown said, she feels like she can persevere through anything to take care of her kids, ages four and three months.

“Even when you feel like nothing is going right, any effort you give is your best,” she said.

In East Boston, some people who fear possible encounters with federal immigration agents have been too afraid to go to the drug store alone, said Neenah Estrella-Luna, who helps run Mutual Aid Eastie. The group gives emergency aid to residents in the form of grocery store gift cards and toiletries. In many cases, cash is the most dignified form of aid, Estrella-Luna said.

“We don’t judge what people need; we let them decide what they need,” she said.

People who give monthly are the top factor keeping Mutual Aid Eastie’s work “sustainable,” Estrella-Luna said, including those who can give only $5.

Donors benefit from the group’s resources too, Estrella-Luna said, even if simply by knowing that a safety net will be there to catch them if they lose their job or get sick.

“It’s not charity, I think that’s a really key piece of it,” Estrella-Luna said.

While many on Giving Tuesday may feel more accustomed to writing a check for their favorite cause, plugging in to a hyper-local network could come with unique psychological benefits, Amormino said.

“There’s this bigger theme of reciprocity ‐ you’re helping me right now, and it might take a couple months or even years for me to get back on my feet and be able to help you ‐ but there’s a motivation to give back once you’re able to," Amormino said.

In Boston, some are worried about funding changes the Department of Housing and Urban Development proposed in November that could push 170,000 formerly homeless people back onto the street nationwide, said Philip Mangano, founder and president of the American Round Table to Abolish Homelessness.

“When a Bostonian sees a wrong, they want to right it. When they see an evil, they want to end it,” said Mangano, whose group is based downtown.

Mangano’s group solicits donations on Giving Tuesday, he said. The inflow of cash helps his advocacy work preventing and ending homelessness, which increased by 53 percent last year in the state, he said.

In Somerville, a group of low-income residents cook food and get a steady stream of donations from farmers markets, which volunteers place inside free sidewalk refrigerators for anyone who needs them, said Crystal Huff, who has helped manage three fridges across Union Square, Tufts, and East Somerville since 2020.

Lately, there are almost always people waiting at the fridge to see if there will be a food delivery, Huff said. She said she hopes that Giving Tuesday raises awareness for the fridges and that people know anyone can get food from them.

When Huff was on a late-night cooking kick that resulted in an enormous batch of cardamom-ginger applesauce, there were people waiting outside by the fridge when she brought a surprise delivery at 2 a.m.

“It’s hard to see how much food insecurity there is in Somerville, and it’s hard to be part of a household that’s experiencing food insecurity, but the community fridges give me hope that we can help each other get through this,” Huff said.

title: It’s Giving Tuesday. What makes people give?
text:
Globe Santa hears all these reasons (except, happily, the one about feeling guilty saying “no”.) When donors write to Globe Santa, they typically express empathy for struggling families, and gratitude for their own good fortune in life. As one donor wrote in an email this year: “I’m so very fortunate and so many are not. It’s the least I/we can do.”

But many people donate to Globe Santa for a reason that’s unique to this charity, one that would never show up on any survey. They want to give because they themselves were Globe Santa recipients as kids. And they remember how much that big box landing on their doorstep transformed a potentially dismal time of year into something indelible.

“My sister and I were Globe Santa recipients, back in 1964,” Stephen Factor of Hyde Park emailed Globe Santa this year. “I never, ever forgot about Globe Santa.”

Factor was born in 1956, the same year the Globe Santa program started. His father was “not a stable man mentally,” he said in an interview, and after his parents divorced, Factor moved with his mother and sister to the Franklin Field housing developments in Dorchester. “It was tough, mostly for my mother,” he said. “She would always fly off the handle. I got the brunt of that.”

His memories of those years are hazy. He vaguely recalls the family was on welfare and that his mother had no money for presents. But he distinctly remembers that Globe Santa brought gifts to his sister and himself.

“One thing I’ll never forget is what it was like to feel like as a kid; I’m very, very sensitive to kids’ needs,” he said. “Kids want things, too. They watch TV. They dream. And then they go back to school [after Christmas] and they hear ‘I got this’ and kids are showing everyone their new laptop. And then there’s this poor kid who didn’t get anything.”

His philosophy is that “life is about doing the best you can and taking some time to help others whenever you can. Donating to Globe Santa is one of the things I do that puts a smile on my face this time of year, and hopefully others do too. “

Mary Ann Sperandio, 75, a retired school teacher living in Franklin, was also a Globe Santa recipient.

She grew up in housing developments in Jamaica Plain with her mother, sister and brother. Her father was out of the picture, she said in an interview. “My mother left my father when I was three because he’d beaten her up nonstop for seven years.”

She describes a childhood spent in cheerless surroundings. They had no car. No telephone. When she was seven years old, she saw her first gun. (“It was domestic abuse outside our window. The man was waving a gun because his wife had left.”) She acquired the knack of getting herself to school without being beaten up by gangs.

At Christmastime, her mother tried to compensate for their meager means by filling red mesh stockings with oranges and candy bars, and hanging them from the doorknobs. But young Mary Ann saw right through this ploy.

“I knew it was from her because Santa doesn’t give out oranges,” she remembers thinking. “Why would he give me an orange and a candy bar?” Also, she knew from watching TV that Santa came down the chimney and put presents under a tree.

“Does Santa just go to rich people’s houses?” she’d ask her mother. “Is it because we’re poor?” Her mother told her it was because they didn’t have a chimney.

But Globe Santa came to their house, with the intervention of a social worker. “I knew the presents were coming from the Boston Globe, but I didn’t care,” she said. “I knew Globe Santa was a charitable foundation for poor kids. I knew that at a very young age. But I was just happy to get the big box.”

Among the gifts Globe Santa delivered to her home was a jewelry-making kit with “little tiny plastic beads in different shapes that fit one into the other.” She coveted it, as she did the metal roller skates Globe Santa brought “that you put under your shoes with a key to tighten them. Zipped all through the projects on them.” They also got paper dolls and games like Checkers, Pick-Up Sticks, and Jacks.

“Every year we waited for that box,” she said. “It made such an impression.”

The deprivation of her childhood years left a deep impression. “It made me who I am today,” she said. “I really feel for the underdog.”

Happily, as the years went on, her family’s situation improved greatly. Sperandio taught school, mainly 7th grade, for more than 30 years. As for her mother, “The first half of my mother’s life was hell, and the second half was absolutely wonderful,” Sperandio said. “She was surrounded by family. She saw her grandchildren grow up.” And she became an artist, a passion she’d long wanted to indulge.

When Sperandio donated to Globe Santa this year, it was in memory of her beloved mother, Mary Boyajian, who died at the age of 96.” Sperandio sent a note accompanying her donation, saying: “When that package arrived each Xmas, it brought such joy to us. Thank you!”

Linda Matchan can be reached at linda.matchan@globe.com

For 70 years Globe Santa, a program of the Boston Globe Foundation, has provided gifts to children in need at holiday time. Please consider giving by phone, mail, or online at globesanta.org.

title: Homicide victims’ families honored at annual breakfast
text:
More than three years since her daughter was killed in a Dorchester triple shooting, Deniquaa Ellison is doing everything she can to prevent the case from going cold.

A young mom, business owner and singer, Quaaneiruh Goodwyn, 24, was helping her friends film a music video when gunfire broke out. No arrests have been made in the October 2022 shooting.

At a breakfast Thursday morning in Dorchester to honor the families of local homicide victims, Ellison said she wants to keep her daughter’s memory alive — in hopes of someday getting justice.

Despite the statistics placing Boston among the safest major cities, the roomful of grieving families was a stark reminder that the problem hasn’t gone away. Dozens of people attended the ceremony, where speakers commended a range of local programs and services aimed at reducing gun violence and supporting victims.

“There shouldn’t be this many people,” Ellison said. “It’s still happening. Where is the prevention?”

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office organizes the annual gathering to recognize the unimaginable grief experienced by homicide survivors and highlight their ongoing efforts to promote peace. It takes place during Survivors of Homicide Victims Awareness Month, a nationwide initiative to educate the public and appeal to policymakers and grieving families.

Hayden said the message remains as important as ever amid the city’s relative peace.

“When you truly believe that one homicide is one too many, when you say that because you mean it, when you say that because you’ve experienced it, the numbers just don’t seem to matter,” he told the crowd.

Nonetheless, he said in an interview after the event, “We should be proud of where we are.”

Ellison wore a pin featuring her daughter’s name and photo. As organizers read off the names of homicide victims, Ellison filmed the ceremony on her phone. After hearing her daughter’s name, she ended the recording, bowed her head, and wiped away tears.

Denella James Clark, whose only brother was shot and killed in 1989, said that even decades later, the pain still sometimes feels fresh.

“It never goes away,” she said, recalling how her father fell to his knees upon hearing the news. “I often wonder what my life would be like if my brother was still here.”

The shooting took place not far from her family’s Mattapan house. Clark said her mother never moved — just in case her son’s killer ever decided to come apologize.

“Well, that apology never came. But we as a family forgave in our own hearts,” she said. “Carrying that pain is just too much to bear.”

Clark, the CEO of the Boston Arts Academy Foundation, said she pursued a career in the nonprofit sector because she wanted to do something positive for her community. She’s working on a campaign to raise money for the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, which supports families and communities impacted by violence. The organization is planning to build a new headquarters in Dorchester.

The ceremony concluded with a song by Janet Connors, whose son, Joel Turner, was stabbed to death in 2001.

“We did not come here alone; we carried our ancestors in our bones,” she sang, her voice filling the banquet hall. “We did not come here alone; we carried beloveds in our souls.

“We carried each other in our hearts.”

Lea Skene can be reached at lea.skene@globe.com. Follow her on X @lea_skene.

title: Boston College football team already has turned the page to 2026 season
text:
That meeting signified the beginning of an action-packed week for the Eagles. On Monday, former wide receiver Kenyatta Watson became the first general manager in program history.

The next day, director of athletics Blake James confirmed that O’Brien will return. On Wednesday, the Eagles welcomed 23 recruits.

“Signing Day is always a very exciting time,” O’Brien said in a BC Athletics video. “It’s the beginning of a new chapter.”

Watson has made stops at Florida State (director of player relations) and Georgia Tech (director of scouting), and was most recently Auburn’s assistant general manager of recruiting.

He’s part of a growing trend of former players returning to their alma maters as GM. Watson will support roster management, player recruitment and development, and general program oversight.

“Appreciate all the love and support!” Watson wrote on X. “I hope my journey has been motivating to some! Never give up and ALWAYS BELIEVE IN YOU!!!! Thank y’all.”

James said in a statement that the season “did not meet the standards” of the athletic department, but that he believes O’Brien is “the right man” to lead the program.

He also noted that BC plans to adjust its revenue-sharing plan.

“While our athletics program participated in revenue sharing this past year, effective immediately, it will increase its commitment to the maximum permissible level, putting it in line with our Autonomy Four conference peers,” James wrote.

James added that philanthropic support will be critical, and he’s grateful for the ongoing involvement of the alumni. The school, he announced, has received a $50 million challenge to match on a 1-1 basis over the next 5-7 years new endowment gifts for athletics scholarships and operational costs — be they travel, nutrition, medical care, or others.

The Eagles hope the 2026 recruiting class will join the 2025 class in shaping the trajectory of the program.

It features 10 offensive players, 12 defensive, and one specialist. It includes players from as far away as Germany and as close as Boston.

“I believe we’re on the right track with this group,” O’Brien said.

Here’s a closer look by the numbers:

Five offensive linemen: On paper, offensive line is the strongest group. The Eagles managed to land highly recruited prospect Marcelino Antunes, a 6-foot-8-inch, 300-pounder from Dorchester and Catholic Memorial.

They also signed Marek Jin, a 6-3, 290-pound standout from Phillips Exeter, who is the No. 3 offensive interior lineman in the nation and a four-star recruit on ESPN. Dean Ruksnaitis (Paxton/Williston Northampton), Bruno Werner (Chemnitz, Germany/NFL Academy), and Lawrence Iyalekhue (Yonkers, N.Y./Roosevelt) round out the group.

“They’re going to bring this position back to what it is, O-line U,” O’Brien said.

Four players from Massachusetts: In addition to Antunes and Ruksnaitis, defensive tackle Mac Fitzgerald (Boston/Catholic Memorial) and defensive end Dominic Funke (Needham/Xaverian) are part of the class. Fitzgerald’s father, Craig, is the Eagles’ director of football performance, and Funke’s brother, Jack, is currently on the BC roster.

Three defensive ends: Without Donovan Ezeiruaku this season, BC struggled to get to the quarterback. This group has a chance to change that. Along with Funke, Demetrius Thompson (247Sports four-star from Missouri) and Mason Leak (No. 1 player in Connecticut via 247Sports) form a promising trio.

Two quarterbacks: With Dylan Lonergan in the transfer portal and Grayson James out of eligibility, this will be a new era at quarterback for BC. Shaker Reisig gained experience this year, and BC will likely look to the portal for an additional option. Incoming freshmen Anthony Coellner (6-2, 195 pounds) and Femi Babalola (6-4, 220 pounds) will join them.

Coellner, Carmel High’s all-time leading passer, is 247Sports’s No. 2 quarterback in Indiana. Babalola is a top 25 QB nationally, per ESPN, and also a track star.

“Both guys chose us over some really stiff competition, which says a lot about Boston College and where we’re headed,” O’Brien said.

One five-star kicker: The Eagles secured one of the top kicking prospects in the country in Jonathan Hewitt. Hewitt, who hails from Eaton, Ohio, is Rivals’ No. 8-ranked in the nation. He hit a 57-yard field goal in a game as a sophomore and is a two-time first-team All-Ohio selection.

title: Haiti is playing a World Cup game at Gillette. Some Boston locals are thrilled.
text:
FIFA on Saturday detailed the day, time, and place of every group-stage match-up for next year’s World Cup.

The announcement capped off an exciting two days of news for Greater Boston’s soccer fanatics. FIFA on Friday bundled competing nations into 12 groups of four, finalizing which countries will compete to advance to the elimination rounds (a few World Cup slots have yet to be filled). Some fans filed into local pubs to watch the procession live.

The World Cup will unfold across three countries over the course of about a month next summer.

Seven games will be played in Boston, one of 16 cities hosting matches. (To be precise, teams will play at Gillette Stadium — rechristened “Boston Stadium” — in Foxborough.)

Besides Haiti, Ghana, England, Scotland, Morocco, Norway, France, and either Iraq, Bolivia, or Suriname will compete in group-stage games at Gillette. The venue will also host two knockout games.

For soccer’s heavyweights — the likes of Spain, Brazil, Germany, and others — the World Cup is a quadrennial chance for the world’s elite players to showcase their brilliance and jostle for the sport’s ultimate prize. It’s also a source of immense national pride for the World Cup’s infrequent attendees, for soccer-obsessed countries rarely associated with the highest echelons of the game.

Two such countries — Haiti and Cape Verde — have sizable and vibrant diasporas in the Bay State. Haiti has participated in the World Cup only once before, in 1974. Next year’s World Cup will be Cape Verde’s first.

“We have been dreaming of being in this World Cup for a long, long, long time,” said Hudson Julsaint, who said he’d immigrated to Boston from Haiti in 2023. “It’s a really, really big deal for Haitian people.”

Manny Coleta, a Cape Verdean immigrant who watched the group unveiling at a Dorchester bar Friday, says he still hasn’t fully grasped the fact that his home country will be competing among the world’s best.

“It hasn’t sunk in yet,” he said. “Maybe after I watch the first game I’ll actually believe it.”

Cape Verde, grouped together with Uruguay, Saudi Arabia, and world number one Spain, will play its group-stage games in Atlanta, Miami, and Houston.

“It doesn’t really matter whether we play here, Canada, or Mexico,” he said, a scarf with Cape Verdean colors draped over his shoulders. “I’m going to catch at least one game live.”

For many, the pride and exaltation of a World Cup appearance offer an uplift that extends well beyond the realms of the sport.

Such is the case for many Haitians, Guillaume, the Hyde Park restaurant owner, said.

“We have been through so much,” she said — vicious gang wars and cataclysmic health crises at home, and demonization in the places they’ve sought refuge.

Julsaint hopes the World Cup will help other nations form a richer, more human picture of his home.

“It’s a good opportunity to make people know better about our culture,” he said. “They’re gonna say, ‘Where is this country?’ or, if they know it, ‘Let me try to learn what they have.’”

Many Haitians, Guillaume and Julsaint observe, have, over the years, developed a fondness for other national teams.

“The Haitians love the Brazilians,” Guillaume said. Julsaint says he’s followed Argentina since childhood, and will be rooting for the defending world champions — as well as Haiti — next year.

Other Bostonians born and raised in the States are also overcome with anticipation.

“I’m rooting for the US,” said Steve Cherenfant, a Massachusetts native. “I don’t think they’ll go that far, but it’s the opportunity to prove the doubters wrong.”

Cherenfant, sporting a black, sheen-finished US Soccer jacket and a scarf printed with the gold World Cup trophy, sat with friends at The Phoenix Landing, a Cambridge bar and popular gathering spot for soccer junkies.

The US national team will face off against Paraguay, Australia, and either Turkey, Romania, Kosovo, or Slovakia in the group stage. The Americans will play their first (and perhaps only) matches of the competition in Los Angeles and Seattle.

The United States finished third in the 1930 World Cup — the inaugural tournament, hosted in Uruguay — but hasn’t advanced past the quarterfinals since.

Whether he’ll attend a match depends on ticket prices, said Cherenfant, though he plans to be part of the moment in some way.

“If you want to meet people who are supporters, come to a bar for a big game,” he said. “You’ll find somebody, make connections, and you can be friends for a long time.”

title: ‘Ella McCay’: Emma Mackey and James L. Brooks on finding America’s ‘heartland’ while filming in Rhode Island
text:
Complicating matters more, her estranged father (Woody Harrelson), who cheated on her mother, wants to weasel his way back into her life, while a mistake involving Ella and her overbearing husband (Jack Lowden) also hangs over her head, threatening to derail her career. Thankfully, Ella has her aunt Helen (Jamie Lee Curtis) as her rock through stormy professional and personal weather.

“A little of it is autobiographical,” Brooks said of the film’s story, noting how Harrelson’s character is partly inspired by Brooks’s father, who abandoned his family before Brooks was born. “I had a dad like that, and I had two women, my mom and older sister, who got us through when it was tough to get us through.”

Hopping back into the director’s chair for the first time in 15 years, Brooks wanted to take viewers to an era when we “weren’t divisive,” according to the 85-year-old mastermind behind hits like “The Mary Tyler Moore Show,” “The Simpsons,” “Terms of Endearment,” and more, seeing the 2008 political landscape as a time before “we lost our way about being together as a people.”

“To me, the most powerful thing the picture says is in the first 30 seconds: we still liked each other,” said Brooks, referencing the film’s opening narration by Julie Kavner, with the voice of Marge Simpson appearing as Ella’s feisty secretary.

Explaining that, in his view, there was nothing to get out of naming the film’s setting outright as any particular state, Brooks just wanted to showcase the “heartland” of America — which he found in Rhode Island.

“I’d never been there before ... I spent time in Los Angeles, in New York, and then I go to Rhode Island, I say, ‘Oh, I’m in America,’” said Brooks. “That’s it. That’s what it’s like in America, you know.”

“It was very good to live there,” he added, noting how he spent time on his porch on Saturdays, getting to know the folks who walked by. “It helps the spirit of your life.”

The warm welcome extended to the halls of the State House in Providence, according to Mackey, where several scenes were filmed. Brooks called it the “perfect location,” noting the lucky timing of the production, as the State House was “vacant during a month of our shooting.”

Other notable locations featured in the film include Blithewold Manor in Bristol, which stood in as the governor’s mansion, according to production notes, and the fictional Helen’s 445 Tavern, the bar run by Ella’s aunt. Despite the New England pub decor like a noticeable Narragansett Lager sign, the tavern was a work of fiction, built specifically for the film. However, the space on Broadway now serves as home to Sawyer’s, a market, café, and wine bar.

While finding filming locations for “Ella McCay” seemed like easy enough lifts, casting the right person to play the main role was a bit more difficult, according to Brooks.

The Oscar and Emmy winner wanted to channel the fast-paced, “screwball comedy energy” of films that Katharine Hepburn and Audrey Hepburn would star in, but “combine that with enough real-life crap that we all have to go through to make it real and to make it relatable.” After an exhaustive search for an actress, Brooks admitted he was a bit worn down. That was, until Mackey auditioned, where she impressed him with her take on a monologue scene.

“I almost didn’t believe my eyes, because I was beaten down a little from looking [for the right actress]‚” said Brooks, who also praised Mackey’s ability to play the character’s younger self in flashback scenes. “People think we did something with technology or something. It’s all acting.”

Mackey, who’s perhaps best known for her four seasons of work as teen troublemaker Maeve Wiley on “Sex Education” and will soon reteam with “Barbie” director Greta Gerwig in next year’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” calls landing the role of Ella “a big step” and cherishes the feeling she got while making a comedy icon like Brooks laugh during her audition.

“To be championed by someone like that, and to be able to make him laugh ... like, I love this feeling. I want to do this again all the time,” said Mackey. “It was quite addicting.”

The actress praised Brooks for his continued enthusiasm for the craft and for being so open to collaboration.

“I feel like we were really each other’s buddies,” said Mackey.

“He’s still so proactive and so buoyant and so curious and has such incredible experience that I had everything to learn,” she added. “But I really felt like we were learning from each other, and that we both were in this thing together.”

“Ella McCay” has plenty of laughs to go around, with Dorchester native and “The Bear” star Ayo Edebiri making a brief appearance as the love interest of Ella’s brother Casey (Spike Fearn). Brooks noted that Edebiri “was one of the first ones cast” and hailed the actress for her improv comedy talents.

“She’s a dream and she trusts her impulses, and her impulses are great,” said Brooks.

Curtis also showcases her comedic skills as Ella’s aunt, with their relationship serving as the heart of the film. The veteran actress proved to be just as caring and supportive off set when Mackey briefly fell ill during shooting.

“When she found out, 15 minutes later, there was a basket on my front door with hair things for me, broth and graham crackers and a book, and I cried,” explained Mackey. “That’s so wonderful, when you’re far away from your family and you’re on your own ... to have someone like that who’s able to bring you a bit of comfort and reassurance in a moment, is so lovely.”

For Brooks, even after all these years, he still loves working with actors and enjoys seeing the magic of a scene come together. But he’s not resting on his laurels and knows just how hard it is to get a movie made, especially now.

“There’s no high horse here,” said Brooks. “It’s always a struggle. It’s always human beings coming together and trying to make it work. ... Everybody sweats and gets dirty and tries to do the damn job.”

Mackey said making “Ella McCay” was “really a labor of love” for Brooks, praising him for fighting to get it made and seeing his vision through with the same passion that Ella brings in the film.

“[Ella is] someone who works consistently, achieves her goals with some struggle, but keeps going,” said Mackey. “That’s all we can do, is keep going.”

title: Hellenic College could sell 25 acres to bolster its bottom line
text:
A small religious college on the border of Jamaica Plain and Brookline is moving toward selling a portion of its campus as conservation land.

The board of directors of the Hellenic College Holy Cross Greek Orthodox School of Theology on Tuesday voted to explore the sale of up to 25 acres of its campus overlooking Jamaica Pond to The Lyme Timber Co., a New Hampshire real estate investment management company that owns 1.3 million acres of forestland across the country.

The property under consideration is mostly a wooded area called Hellenic Hill. Lyme Timber would pay up to $30 million, or $1.2 million per acre, for the property, college president Demetrios S. Katos said in a recent letter to faculty, staff, and students. That money would then be invested into the college’s endowment, generating up to $1.2 million per year as “a stable recurring revenue for scholarships, faculty support, facility upgrades, and operational sustainability,” Katos said.

The potential sale follows financial challenges at the Greek Orthodox school. Its state accrediting agency placed the college on a two-year probation from 2019 to 2021.

“This proposal is the result of years of deliberate study and exploration of all feasible options, including sales to developers, joint ventures, and leases,” Katos wrote. “Conservation emerged as the optimal choice, offering alignment with our values, improvement to the student experience, and a strengthening of HCHC.”

Lyme Timber declined to comment prior to the vote.

If the board ultimately agrees to a deal, the goal is to eventually sell the property to local conservation organization The Trustees of Reservations, which would partner with the Emerald Necklace Conservancy to steward the land. The groups would “create the vision and plan for the property,” Katos said, and the Trustees would eventually steward the land as part of a broader collection of protected property around Jamaica Pond.

That process would incorporate feedback from both outside partners and community members, Katos said. It would, meanwhile, be “contingent upon raising the necessary funds to make this a reality” and “may take up to five years.”

In a joint statement, the Trustees and Emerald Necklace Conservancy said Lyme Timber and Hellenic College are actively outlining the “several steps needed to acquire the property for conservation with private philanthropic support.” Lyme Timber and the Trustees have previously partnered on land conservation in Massachusetts, most recently with 2,000 acres of forest in Pelham and Belchertown.

“This wooded drumlin that overlooks Jamaica Pond has long been on the City of Boston’s Lands of Interest list for preservation,” the groups said. “This potential acquisition would forever protect an important part of the historic Emerald Necklace.”

Hellenic is the latest example of small colleges and universities in Greater Boston leveraging their real estate to financially support school operations. In 2023, Simmons University in Boston’s Fenway neighborhood signed a 99-year ground lease with Swedish development giant Skanska for a chunk of its campus, while the board and building authority of the University of Massachusetts in 2019 agreed to a $235 million ground lease for the former Bayside Expo Center site in Dorchester.

Katos said Hellenic had considered developing the forested area but chose conservation instead after considering the myriad “zoning, regulatory, and community hurdles that would take years to address and may have never been resolved.” Preserving the property will instead protect Hellenic’s core campus and operations as an Orthodox Christian college, seminary, and graduate school of theology.

He stressed that Tuesday’s vote is nonbinding, and the board hasn’t yet reached a final decision.

“If realized, it would serve as the cornerstone of a transformational plan that aims to fortify our institution’s future,” Katos said. “We remain focused on outcomes that honor our heritage and secure our legacy.”

Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

title: Out of prison, Tania Fernandes Anderson is still speaking her mind
text:
“Enough of this safe politics of this pretty diplomacy thing in Boston,” she said. “It is extremely depraved.”

Fernandes Anderson spoke in the heart of the council district she once represented about three weeks after completing a monthlong sentence at FCI Danbury in Connecticut, a low-security facility with more than 1,200 inmates, according to federal records.

In May, she pleaded guilty to two of six federal wire fraud and theft charges she faced for taking a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff.

According to an indictment, Fernandes Anderson hired her relative, then gave her a $13,000 bonus with a caveat: She had to funnel more than half of it back to the councilor.

Prosecutors said Fernandes Anderson arranged the kickback when she was struggling financially, missing rent and car payments, and facing bank overdraft fees and a $5,000 fine from the state Ethics Commission for previously hiring relatives to her council staff.

Fernandes Anderson, a 46-year-old Democrat who came to the US From Cape Verde at age 10, was once a rising star in city politics. She made political history in 2021 on multiple fronts. She was the first Muslim, the first formerly undocumented immigrant, and the first African immigrant to serve on the city’s legislative body. On the council, she represented District Seven, which covers neighborhoods including Roxbury, Dorchester, the South End, and Fenway.

Her political rise came with a compelling backstory, punctuated by stints of homelessness, an eviction as a teenager, racism at school, and immigration complications.

But her political career came crashing down last year when the FBI arrested her at her Dorchester home.

She attended her final council meeting in June, and officially resigned in July of this year.

On Monday night, she spoke at an event hosted by New Beginnings Reentry Services at the Bruce C. Bolling Municipal Building. Among the crowd were local luminaries including former Boston mayoral candidate Josh Kraft, City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, and Fernandes Anderson’s elected successor, the Rev. Miniard Culpepper.

Known for calling out racism on the City Council floor during the days as a lawmaker, Fernandes Anderson on Monday railed against the perpetuation of “intentional, systemic oppression.”

“We think about how do we defend ourselves?” she said. “We never think of the offensive plan, and we’re never ready. We’re always chasing the carrot.”

She also described her political style.

“To every battle, you need a barbarian and you need a diplomat,” she said. “And I’m no diplomat.”

She continued, “I just don’t fit in that stage, in that place where we still believe in politics and we still say ‘We should lobby the politicians’ or ‘We should go to Mayor [Michelle] Wu and tell her to move money.’ Well, there isn’t enough money, when you do the math.”

She lamented that too many people in Boston are beholden to a “government that holds the purse.” She described the city as a place “where no one dares to speak, where pretty politics take place.”

“No one will open their mouth and say ‘This is [expletive]. This is not working,’” she said.

The crowd applauded.

“If you have a contract with the city, you’re not going to say anything, if you work for the city, you’re not going to say anything,” she said. “If you are cousin, wife, son, whatever of somebody that works for the city you’re not going to say anything.”

Black people, said Fernandes Anderson, need to organize.

“We’ve just been so inundated by our stressors, by our headaches, by our problems, that we can’t organize. And then we wonder why they won’t listen,” she said.

Fernandes Anderson featured on a panel that included others who were formerly locked up, including Sean K. Ellis, who served 22 years in prison before his murder conviction was overturned because of police and prosecutorial misconduct.

The discussion was emceed by Rickey “FuQuan” McGee, who was released in October from prison after prosecutors declared he did not receive a fair trial for a 1997 murder.

During the discussion, Fernandes Anderson appeared to allude to her recent legal troubles.

“I’m very grateful for my journey,” she said. “There ain’t no shame in this game,” meaning there’s no shame in taking accountability.

She added, “It’s a book some day.”

Shelley Murphy of the Globe staff contributed.

title: Mike Vrabel’s little motivations, what the Patriots did on the bye, and other beat writer notes
text:
Still, Vrabel has managed to incorporate various milestones to motivate his players.

“He’s always creating these little goals and ways to keep us ready, prepared, and motivated to go out there and play football,” cornerback Carlton Davis said. “I appreciate him for that because I’ve been in this league for eight years. I know how it can get, especially when you have a long season.”

Heading into the Week 10 matchup in Tampa, Vrabel framed the game as an opportunity to win the NFC South because the Patriots already had beaten the other three teams in the division. When the Patriots hung on for a 28-23 victory over the Buccaneers, Vrabel greeted his players on their way into the locker room by yelling, “NFC South champs! NFC South champs!”

Two weeks later, with the Patriots sitting at 9-2 heading to Cincinnati, Vrabel emphasized the importance of becoming the first team in the league to 10 wins.

“We’re kind of a week-to-week team, as far as goals,” Davis said. “He’s always finding creative ways to motivate us and keep us going. It’s a long season. Sometimes it can be mundane when it’s week after week and we’re doing the same thing. He finds ways to keep it interesting and keep us excited about playing football.”

Now, in Week 15, Vrabel doesn’t have to get creative.

The Patriots can clinch the AFC East title with a win over the Bills on Sunday, which would snap Buffalo’s five-year streak as division champion.

“We’re just trying to play for the championship that we have available this week,” Vrabel said. “I think it’s a great testament to our players that have put us in this position to be able to do that.”

2. Let’s take a look at where things stand in the race for the AFC’s No. 1 seed and first-round bye.

The Broncos and Patriots are both 11-2, but Denver has a better winning percentage within the conference and among common opponents. The teams don’t have any more common opponents remaining, so the Broncos have clinched that crucial tiebreaker.

The Patriots close the season with the Bills, Ravens, Dolphins, and Jets, while the Broncos close with the Packers, Jaguars, Chiefs, and Chargers.

3. The Patriots took full advantage of their bye week, using the time off to recharge.

Tight end Hunter Henry went to New York with his wife, Parker. Punter Bryce Baringer ventured up to Vermont with his wife, Bella. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins and his wife, Jayda, traveled to California. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore flew to Florida to train at the House of Athlete facility. Kicker Andy Borregales went home to Florida, where he spent time with family and watched the NHL’s Panthers take on the Predators.

Multiple Patriots went to TD Garden to support the Celtics. Baringer, long snapper Julian Ashby, and special teams captain Brenden Schooler were in the building for Celtics-Knicks last Tuesday, while rookie Efton Chism and offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels attended Celtics-Lakers last Friday.

Wide receiver DeMario Douglas, meanwhile, stayed busy in the community. He met with students at the Lower Mills campus of Saint John Paul II Catholic Academy, participated in a flag football event with Big Brothers Big Sisters of Eastern Massachusetts, and attended a holiday party at Gillette Stadium for the nonprofit Friends of Children.

Wide receiver Stefon Diggs, too, stayed busy, celebrating his 32nd birthday in Miami with his girlfriend, Cardi B. Diggs also launched his own furniture collection, called Si Vis Pacem, which he unveiled this past week at Design Miami.

“I know these guys got some rest, much-needed rest, but we’ve got to crank this thing back up,” said Vrabel, whose Titans teams were 6-0 when coming off of their bye.

The 2021 Patriots — who started the year 9-4, before collapsing after the bye week to finish 10-7 and then lose in the wild-card round — are a cautionary tale.

4. The offensive line’s weekly Thursday night dinners have taken a bit of a hiatus because of “Thursday Night Football” (Nov. 13), Thanksgiving (Nov. 27), and the bye week (Dec. 4). But the unit is expected to resume this week and next.

5. In other food news, apparently even Vrabel has tried Ann Michael Maye’s viral apple cinnamon oatmeal crumble bars, calling them “delicious.”

6. Twelve days after fan voting opened, quarterback Drake Maye is still the league’s top vote-getter for the Pro Bowl. Maye sits first with 64,576 votes, followed by Seahawks wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba (55,486), 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey (54,611), Packers edge rusher Micah Parsons (54,058), and Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (51,359).

Fan voting remains open until Dec. 15 and will comprise one-third of the final tally. Coaches and players will weigh in later this season.

In addition to Maye, other deserving Patriots include return specialist Marcus Jones and cornerback Christian Gonzalez.

7. One stat that makes this 11-2 Patriots team so stunning is the fact that they rank second in the league in most snaps by rookies. The other teams that rank in the top four? The 3-10 Browns, 3-10 Jets, and 2-11 Titans. The fact that the Patriots are getting major contributions from their rookie class — and winning — is impressive.

title: The Boston Music Awards swapped its reggae/ska category for one honoring Afro/Caribbean artists. Here’s why it matters.
text:
Which is why when he attends the Boston Music Awards this Wednesday at Big Night Live and hears his name announced as a nominee in the Afro/Caribbean artist category, the moment will feel like its own sort of victory.

“Now, Afrobeats music is a worldwide phenomenon and people are speaking our various languages word for word,” says Echezona, whose most recent album, “Ényì,” includes lyrics in both English and Igbo, one of the most widely-spoken languages in Nigeria. (The album’s title is the Igbo word for “friend.”)

The Afro/Caribbean artist category is one of five additions to this year’s awards ceremony, which honors standout artists and industry professionals from the Greater Boston music community every December. In the last decade, the BMAs have mushroomed to include over a dozen new categories, namely ones that recognize behind-the-scenes industry personnel: managers, talent buyers, journalists, live audio engineers, and lighting technicians, to name a few.

Other new titles for 2025 include honors for local festivals, radio DJs, graphic designers, and music-focused nonprofits (titled the Margaret Stewart Lindsay Music Non-Profit of the Year award). The inclusion of the new Afro/Caribbean category is unique, as it replaces the previous Reggae/Ska category.

Echezona calls the switch “historic,” noting that “I am now among folks who have broken the door down for people in the city to have to say, ‘We need to make room and recognize this whole other music lane taking shape.’”

The shift not only recognizes the growing global influence of genres like Afrobeats, but also refines the category to include acts that are more closely culturally associated with Afro-Caribbean music. That distinction is especially important for category nominees like Roots Alley Collective, a Caribbean group who strive to bring traditional music to communities throughout the diaspora.

Drummer Shaquan Gabriel was born and raised in St. Lucia, and moved to Massachusetts as a teenager, while keyboardist RJ Walters and bassist Christoff Glaude are the first-generation children of immigrants from Barbados and St. Vincent, respectively. Gabriel says that Roots Alley Collective’s shows are a key link to traditional music for folks of Caribbean descent who “were born here [in the US] but don’t really get to have that full effect of being raised in the Caribbean.”

Gabriel also says that the boost in visibility from the BMAs nomination helps the group’s goal of bridging a “generation gap” between Caribbean performers in the region. In Gabriel’s experience, Roots Alley Collective — whose members are in their late 20s and early-to-mid 30s — is the youngest Caribbean music act in the Northeast. Most groups are in their 40s and older, he notes.

“We have to get our generation to support and learn about what we’re doing,” Gabriel says. “We’re trying to really craft that same kind of model that the older guys had — the community coming out to see shows, and buying the records and the vinyls.”

“I think [the nomination] gets everybody more involved in what we’re doing,” Gabriel adds, “and that makes it 10 times more important to us.”

GIG GUIDE

At Roadrunner on Friday, PVRIS celebrate the 10th anniversary of their debut album, “White Noise.” In the decade since the electrifying Lowell group broke into the mainstream, PVRIS have whittled down to just frontwoman Lynn Gunn, who released the EP “F.I.L.T.H” last fall.

The local takeover of Roadrunner continues on Saturday, when Converge launch Saddest Day, a one-day festival curated by the Salem-born metalcore band. Performers on deck for the inaugural event include LA’s Touche Amore, Soul Glo of Philadelphia, and Boston’s The Hope Conspiracy, among others.

Atlanta rapper and lyrical gymnast JID promotes his August album, “God Does Like Ugly,” at MGM Music Hall at Fenway on Friday, followed by an appearance from Haitian-raised singer-songwriter Medjy, who imports his R&B twist on Afropop at the venue on Saturday.

Pittsburgh’s Ghost Hounds, who split their rock between the blues and country, howl at the House of Blues across the street on Friday. Boston country favorites Dalton & the Sheriffs open the show, which will be their last before an indefinite hiatus.

On Friday, mgk — the Cleveland artist formerly known as Machine Gun Kelly — revs his eccentric hybrid of hip-hop and pop-punk at TD Garden. The arena hosts its final concert of the year on Sunday, welcoming KISS 108’s annual Jingle Ball extravaganza. Ed Sheeran and Laufey lead the bill, which otherwise feels a little lacking in star power.

Likewise,Whiskey Myers provide the 2025 finale for the Orpheum on Saturday. The Texas country-rock band, which is currently on a special acoustic tour, released their seventh studio album, “Whomp Whack Thunder,” in September.

Some standout holiday shows this week include indie folk duo Milk Carton Kids at the Cabot in Beverly on Saturday, and gospel great CeCe Winans at the Boch Center Wang Theatre on Wednesday.

Finally, don’t let KiNG MALA slip under the radar at Somerville’s Warehouse XI on Friday. In May, the alt-pop singer released her debut LP, “And You Who Drowned in the Grief of a Golden Thing,” one of the Globe’s favorite albums of the year.

NOW SPINNING

Juliana Hatfield, “Lightning Might Strike.” Juliana Hatfield has established quite the album release pattern in the last decade or so, alternating between original LPs and covers albums to flesh out her already-prolific oeuvre. Right on cue, after last year’s “Juliana Hatfield Sings ELO” comes “Lightning Might Strike,” another collection of scrappy alt-rock, crafted during a year of upheaval and loss for the Massachusetts artist.

Senseless Optimism, “graveyard flowers.” Senseless Optimism — a.k.a. Lowell-born singer-songwriter Brittany Tsewole — entered the Massachusetts scene a few years ago as a soul-pop savant. But her latest effort, the EP “graveyard flowers,” sees Tsewole gunning for the more mainstream-friendly world of bedroom-pop. The sped-up version of her toe-tapping single “War & Peace” seems poised for a viral TikTok moment any day now.

BONUS TRACK

If you didn’t get your kicks at Patti Smith’s 50th anniversary show for “Horses” last month at the Orpheum — or perhaps you just can’t get enough of the “godmother of punk” — Smith will be back in town on Wednesday promoting her newest memoir, “Bread of Angels.” Brookline Booksmith has coordinated a stop on Smith’s book tour at the Chevalier Theatre in Medford.

title: Dalton the Sheriffs, one of Boston’s leading country acts, are pressing pause
text:
“Failure and success can be measured in different ways,” said Scully, sitting in the back room at McGonagle’s Pub in Dorchester, where he’d performed solo the day before. “The community we built — total success. Trying to tour nationwide and crack that — not a success.”

Over three albums, several live releases, and a slew of singles, Scully’s band grew from regulars at the Bell in Hand to headliners at Leader Bank Pavilion and MGM Music Hall at Fenway. They’ve opened for Jason Aldean, Sam Hunt, Thomas Rhett, and other Nashville stars, and they stepped in as a last-minute replacement for TLC at this year’s Boston Calling.

But they haven’t been able to gain enough traction outside of their hometown.

“We’re a rock band, but we tell pretty ‘country’ stories,” said Scully, a burly, bearded father of three teenagers in a crisp new Notre Dame cap. “I think we sound like what a country band that was born and raised in Boston would sound like.”

The rest of the current version of the band — Jay Tagg and Joe Pantaleo on guitars, Dennis Walsh on bass, and Dan Vassallo on drums — have day jobs and other music projects to focus on. Tagg owns Matt’s Music Center, a guitar shop in Weymouth, where Pantaleo works.

Scully, meanwhile, plans to regroup by performing his solo shows, which are a mix of Dalton songs and covers. Working closely with his wife, Kate, he calls himself a full-time “barroom hustler.”

Last year the band released a cover version of Zach Bryan’s “Oklahoma Smokeshow,” and they’ve covered Eric Church’s “Springsteen,” the Wallflowers’s “One Headlight,” and many more. Scully said he grew up with grandparents who loved “the whole Irish cable-knit sweater” folk scene of the 1960s.

“I could play three hours of Clancy Brothers music at the drop of a hat,” he said. “That was my entry into country music.”

Some of his current bandmates joined the group after attending shows as fans. Walsh said he and Tagg convinced each other to sign on together about a half-dozen years ago.

“Make no mistake — Dalton has put the five of us on stages that we only dreamed of,” Walsh said. (There is no actual “Dalton” — the band’s name comes from Patrick Swayze’s bouncer character in 1989’s “Road House.”)

“It’s weird to have to count how many times we played House of Blues or the Pavilion, places we never thought we’d play once,” he continued. “Walking on the field at Fenway doing the [National] Anthem. So many pinching moments.”

On a phone call, Walsh explained that the band members had been anticipating changes. The younger guys are starting families; Scully’s oldest son is about to head to college.

“We knew coming out of this year that something drastic had to change, and it hadn’t yet,” Walsh said. “Basically, we’ve been running as fast as we can since 2020.”

For Scully, the fact that he felt compelled to put the band on hold doesn’t necessarily mean it’s the end.

“There’s no animosity. I know we have the right guys,” he said. If the right deal came along, “the band’s ready.”

“At the end of the day, you really have to be lucky with certain things rolling your way at the right moment,” Scully said. “We’ve been lucky with the relationships and the community we built, the people we got to make music with. And that’s pretty remarkable.”

DALTON & THE SHERIFFS

title: Lawsuit attempts to block alleged sale of R.I.’s ‘Conjuring’ house to ‘Ghost Hunters’ star
text:
The civil complaint alleges Hawes was aware of Nuñez’s “various mental health issues” at the time she signed the agreement, and it alleges he and Demay “are taking advantage of Nuñez’s lack of legal capacity for their own personal and financial gain.”

“After conducting a reasonable investigation, the Plaintiff has reason to believe that the Property has been (or will soon be) sold to Defendant Hawes for approximately $1.3 million, which is well below its fair market value,” the lawsuit states. “The Plaintiff brings this action to protect Nuñez’s interests by voiding the [agreement] as well as any resulting Purchase and Sale Agreement for the Property because Nuñez lacked the capacity to enter into the [agreement] when she signed it.”

Greenhalgh’s attorneys filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order earlier this month, asking the court to restrain Hawes and Demay from closing on the sale of the property.

An order was granted at a court hearing earlier this month. Hawes also agreed not to close on the sale of property at least until a Jan. 7 hearing, according to court filings.

In a text message prior to the hearing, Hawes wrote, “While claims have been made, they are not supported by facts.”

“The documentation will make that clear as the legal process moves forward,” Hawes wrote.

Hawes’ attorney has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, which will be addressed at the Jan. 7 hearing.

Demay, of Middleborough, Mass., could not be reached for comment, and Nuñez did not return requests for comment. Attorneys for Greenhalgh did not respond to an inquiry from the Globe.

The lawsuit also names Hawes’s real estate attorney, Jonathan Lynch, and the firm that employs him, Percy Law Group, as defendants. Lynch did not return a message seeking comment.

The lawsuit is the latest in a series of controversies that have shrouded the historic home — made famous by “The Conjuring” horror movie franchise — over the past year and a half.

Last year, Nuñez faced allegations of harassment from Hawes, and accusations from former employees who say she owes them money; she allegedly fired one after claiming a spirit told her he was stealing from the business.

In November 2024, the Burrillville Town Council opted not to renew the house’s business license after Nuñez — who bought the 1677 Round Top Road property for about $1.5 million in 2022 — was arrested and charged by local police with allegedly driving a Lexus SUV while intoxicated and leading officers on a chase through town.

The home was headed to foreclosure auction in October of this year, but the event was abruptly canceled after Needham Bank sold the underlying mortgage to YouTuber Elton Castee, through his Summit & Stone LLC, a corporation formed in Rhode Island in September.

Castee, who touts more than 4 million subscribers on his “TFIL” (Traveling to every country in A-Z order) channel on YouTube, along with comedian Matt Rife, purchased the former Connecticut home of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren earlier this year, with its vast collection of allegedly haunted objects. (Castee’s LLC was named as an “interested party” in the lawsuit. Castee declined to comment when reached by email.)

At the urging of Andrea Perron — whose family was supposedly haunted in the 1970s at the Burrillville home where the Warrens were called in to investigate — Hawes launched a GoFundMe to try to raise money to purchase it at auction.

Hawes has said his effort is not about making a profit, and the goal is to raise as much money as possible to keep costs down for visitors, and to keep the house in the hands of people who want to preserve it, not exploit it.

The GoFundMe has continued despite the sale of the mortgage; Hawes said in an interview in November, “It doesn’t change our path.”

As of last week, Hawes has raised $321,850 of his 500,000 goal.

The lawsuit alleges Nuñez was “previously a successful attorney and businesswoman,” having founded WonderGroup LLC, a real estate development firm in Boston, in 2003.

But since January 2024, she has “been experiencing serious mental health issues that have impaired her judgment and rendered her incapable of understanding the nature and consequences of her actions,” according to the lawsuit. Her sister and employees held multiple interventions, but Nuñez declined their attempts, the filing states.

Nuñez has since been committed to at least three hospitals for psychiatric care in Rhode Island and Massachusetts, , according to the lawsuit, but “upon information and belief, Nuñez is presently experiencing and/or operating under various delusions, including but not limited to, that she owns the Property outright and that she is ‘The Savior of Humanity,’” the lawsuit alleges.

Nuñez recently made an “outlandish” allegation that her sister, Greenhalgh, and Greenhalgh’s husband “are engaged in criminal activity that has absolutely no basis in reality,” the lawsuit states.

When asked by the Globe in November to comment on the sale of the house’s mortgage to Castee, Nuñez responded, “I have the Rightful Entitlement to the Vast [John Arnold] Estate as the underlying Leasehold,” along with several insults and expletives.
