title: Another Trump target? The college essay.
text:
“Homelessness,” she wrote, “taught me resilience.”

Kouame’s essay, which recounts how she learned to thrive as a low-income student of color “surrounded by classmates whose lives felt worlds apart from mine,” is about overcoming adversity.

That’s a theme the White House has identified as a problem in its campaign against diversity, equity, and inclusion. Over the past year, the federal government has flagged “cues” such as personal essays, along with narratives about “overcoming obstacles” and “diversity statements,” as being potentially unlawful: a stand-in for talking about race.

More than two years have passed since the Supreme Court ended race-conscious affirmative action, and the Trump administration has since demanded colleges submit data proving they don’t consider race in admissions. It has also expanded what it sees as “discriminatory admissions processes” to include considering a student’s sexual orientation, gender identity, ethnicity, nationality, political views, and religious associations.

For Kouame, not writing about her identity felt “impossible,” she said in a Zoom interview, “because the things that I’ve gone through in life make me who I am now.”

Other students are weighing the pros and cons, said Ethan Sawyer, founder of College Essay Guy, which offers one-on-one coaching and free online resources through the admissions process. He added the key is “to step back and take stock” of what colleges are actually looking for. Essentially: “How will you be a valuable, contributing member of the community?”

Navigating the college admissions landscape has never been easy, but for the class of 2030 it’s particularly fraught. Plenty of advisers can be hired for a fee: Private consulting is a $3 billion industry, with parents paying tens and even hundreds of thousands of dollars to give their kids an edge. Community organizations, college-prep programs, and high schools are also on hand to assist students.

There’s no question it’s an uneven playing field, though this year there is one equalizer in the college admissions game: No one really knows what’s coming next.

In 2024, one year post-affirmative action, Black first-year student enrollment plunged at many prestigious colleges, and this fall Harvard enrolled fewer Black and Latino freshmen. Meanwhile, the Crimson reported that Harvard banned alumni interviewers from commenting on an applicant’s race, ethnicity, or national origin in their written evaluations.

College consultant Sara Harberson, in a blog post on her website, warned of a future where students are reduced to test scores and transcripts and admissions staff are replaced by AI.

For now, it’s still a human process with human workarounds. Many colleges and universities encourage applicants to submit video introductions using platforms such as Glimpse. It’s a way for students to talk “more authentically and off the cuff,” said Rachel Rubin, the Brookline-based founder of Spark Admissions, noting that, in some cases, video can convey information about race and ethnicity.

Essay questions nudging students to describe their “lived experience” or their “community” proliferated after the Supreme Court ruling and became known as the Chief Justice Roberts Loophole‚ said Jayson Weingarten, a senior admissions consultant with the Manhattan-based Ivy Coach.

“A lot of students might read [a community prompt] and think, Oh, I’m in the band, I’m the editor of the paper, and I’m going to write about an activity,” he said, but other students “read between the lines of what admissions officers are asking — and they’re going to talk about their race, culture, ethnicity, heritage, socioeconomic status, anything like that.“

Weingarten said that after the flurry of executive orders and other memos targeting DEI earlier this year, “there was widespread speculation that many of America’s top universities would be desperate to avoid the crosshairs of the Trump administration” and abandon such prompts. However, most elite institutions have preserved them, he noted.

“It’s a quiet signal, but it’s an unmistakable act of resistance,” said Weingarten.

Sara Barber-Just, an English teacher and chair of the department at Amherst-Pelham Regional High School, said many of her students are answering a Common App question touching on identity. Their topics range from the strengths of being autistic to the musical influences of their Puerto Rican grandparents to accessing gender-affirming care as a transgender person.

“They write really beautiful essays about the experience of being human,” she said. “No president can stop adolescents from writing about their identity.”

And federal policies can’t stop adults from helping them. This spring the tutoring nonprofit 826 Boston rejected $250,000 in funding rather than comply with President Trump’s demands to eliminate DEI programming.

“By not accepting the money, we are able to continue to support students about anything that they want to write about, particularly their identities or historical oppression,” said 826 Boston executive director Corey Yarbrough, who hopes students will see “their perspectives matter, and someone out there cares and will listen.”

Some schools have added prompts to get at themes of viewpoint diversity.

Harvard and Columbia asked students to recall a time they disagreed with someone, and how they handled it. Kouame wrote about going to Ivory Coast in West Africa, where her family is originally from, and meeting a woman selling skin-bleaching cream.

“You’re not trying to change somebody’s point of view,” she said. “You’re just trying to inform them about what you think.”

Kouame worked on her college essays with Thrive Scholars, which assists high-achieving students from under-resourced communities. The Boston-based nonprofit Steppingstone also provided essay and college-prep support and helped her get into the prekindergarten-12 Buckingham Browne & Nichols School, a private school in Cambridge. When she started there, her family lived in Dorchester (they later moved to Belmont). She commuted to Cambridge, doing her homework on the bus ride in and contemplating outer space on her ride home on the T.

“The blur of city lights outside the window reminded me of distant constellations,” she wrote in her college essay, “and in that moving train car, my fascination with space was born.”

She submitted her college applications through QuestBridge, which has a full four-year “Match Scholarship” with various partners.

Other seniors are still finishing their applications before regular-decision deadlines in January.

Ella Daillie, a senior at Northampton High School with Iraqi and Yemeni heritage, marked herself as “white” and “Middle Eastern” on the Common App, which has an optional race and ethnicity question for research purposes.

She had a harder time deciding whether to mention her leadership in her school’s Students for Justice in Palestine club, following campus crackdowns on pro-Palestinian protests. Daillie, who is Jewish, ultimately decided it was too important to omit from her applications to schools such as the University of Wisconsin and Grinnell College in Iowa.

“Like one of my friends says: ‘I don’t want to go somewhere that doesn’t want me there,’ ” she said. “I want to go to a school that wants me for who I am.”

title: Our Dorchester school has thrived in receivership. Don’t take it away.
text:
But for us, parents at a Dorchester school in receivership, UP Academy Holland, and a board member at UP Education Network, the nonprofit school manager that runs the Holland, it has meant transformation. It has meant empowerment. It has meant hope.

And today, we’re desperately clinging to that hope.

As soon as this week, the state education commissioner could elect to take our students’ school out of receivership, jeopardizing all of the gains of the last several years.

We implore state officials to keep a good thing going.

And more broadly, we call on the state Legislature to reject a teachers union-led push to eliminate receivership across the board. Families all over Massachusetts deserve a shot at better schools.

Massachusetts’ receivership law, which dates to 2010, allows the state to step in when a school or district has struggled and to appoint a receiver with the authority to make significant changes.

The law, to be sure, has a mixed record. Receivership hasn’t always worked. But we’ve seen, up close, how it can be done well.

A little over a decade ago, the Commonwealth appointed the UP Education Network to take over the struggling John P. Holland Elementary School in the Bowdoin-Geneva neighborhood of Dorchester. The school became UP Academy Holland.

UP Education was already at work nearby, turning around the old John Marshall Elementary School through a separate partnership with Boston Public Schools. That school was renamed UP Academy Dorchester. Both of these UP academies have turned into schools that the neighborhood can be proud of.

Before UP began its work, the schools struggled with leadership turnover, staffing shortages, and inconsistent academic results. None of these challenges reflected the strength of our community or the potential of our children. We witnessed firsthand what can happen when students benefit from clearer routines — routines established by teachers, staff, and school leaders who have had significant coaching and additional training, and are powered by stronger, more consistent use of data. That’s how UP has instilled in our students a spirit of belonging.

One of us, Christina Qualls, a parent in our community and a school principal, tells the story of her younger sister entering UP Holland significantly behind in reading after time in foster care. As she explains, the family was prepared to request an IEP, or an individualized education program for a student with disabilities, but her sister’s teacher asked for time to understand her as a learner before labeling her needs. Within a year, her sister was reading on grade level. Today she is thriving in high school honors classes. Her experience reflects what’s possible when a school leads with skilled instruction, careful attention, and a belief in students’ potential before anything else.

Now students go home talking about books they are reading and math problems they can solve, and they describe teachers who encourage them. The culture has shifted, and so have the results.

Today, UP Academy Dorchester and UP Academy Holland have risen to the 25th and 20th percentiles, respectively, on a statewide accountability measure of how a school compares with other schools statewide that serve similar grades. The previous iterations of the schools were at the bottom of the rankings. The UP schools are now among the best performing public schools in Dorchester. UP students show some of the strongest academic growth in Boston. They rank first and second statewide in English language arts growth among schools serving high-needs populations, and they outperform the district and the state in English and math growth. The percentage of high-needs students meeting or exceeding standards has doubled since COVID, even as district and state rates remain largely unchanged. Teachers report more substantial support, families report greater trust, and our children show more confidence in their learning.

We also recognize that there is more work ahead. Achievement gaps still exist, and our schools must keep focusing on the needs of students who need extra support. Ongoing improvement will require consistent commitment, stronger collaboration with families, and fair distribution of resources.

These local gains matter, but they also reflect national patterns. Research shows that improving outcomes in high-poverty schools typically rests on the sort of strategy UP has pursued — sustained, targeted investment in leadership, teacher professional education, and schoolwide systems rather than ad hoc fixes. A meta-analysis of 35 turnaround studies found associations between turnaround efforts and gains in attendance, test scores, and graduation when structural changes (leadership, human capital, governance) were implemented.

Our greatest concern now is that our progress could be disrupted by decisions made outside our schools. But UP’s work in Dorchester is exactly the kind of partnership that national research identifies as successful. It is targeted, sustained, grounded in community, and built from the ground up on the belief that improvement is not only possible but measurable. What can often get lost in the worthy debates about schools and their governance and management is the perspective of families who rely on these schools every day.

Massachusetts, like states across the country, has a responsibility to support what works, not disrupt it. When the state decides the fate of UP Academy Holland, it should keep that in mind.

The urgency we feel is shaped not only by the approaching decision — if UP Academy Holland is taken out of receivership, it’s unclear that UP will still be able to run the school — but also by a broader movement in Massachusetts to eliminate receivership entirely. Teachers unions across the state have testified in favor of the so-called THRIVE Act, which would end receivership and require every district currently in it to transition out within a year. As the Boston Globe editorial board recently noted, this push is being led by the Boston Teachers Union, the Massachusetts Teachers Association, and the American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts, all of which argue that receivership is a “failed approach” and advocate for removing the state’s ability to intervene. If that effort succeeds, the partnership that has supported our children’s progress at UP Holland could end by statute, regardless of the outcomes our students are achieving.

This decision determines whether our students’ progress continues or is put at risk. The performance of our students serves as living proof that improvement amid challenging circumstances can be real, that children from communities that have long been underserved can excel, and that families can trust public education when the structures around it are strong.

We ask for the chance to protect what has worked so well.

title: State ending receivership of UP Academy Holland, despite pleas of some parents
text:
Massachusetts education officials announced on Tuesday that the state would end a more than decade-long receivership of UP Academy Holland in Dorchester next year, handing control of the school back to Boston Public Schools.

Many parents and school officials welcomed the news at a board meeting of the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, as they also pleaded with local authorities to continue state support for the school, which improved its test scores and other state accountability measures over the last few years.

The kindergarten through sixth-grade school went from being ranked worse than 99 percent of similar grade schools in 2014, a year into the receivership, to reaching the 20th percentile this year.

Under receivership, the school received coaching and professional development for teachers and school leaders, got help implementing its curriculum, and put in place assessments to track student progress. State oversight also included data platforms to allow the school to track student progress more accurately. And the school implemented strategies to improve attendance and streamline budgeting.

“We ask for the commitment to ensure that those things continue,” Amelia Massoud-Tastor, principal at UP Academy Holland, said at the state board meeting. “We know this work is best done with adequate resources,” she added.

“The school has done a phenomenal job over the last 11 years,” said Daisy Stanley, a parent at Holland. “Now we need to make sure that we continue to get the support that the school had to ensure that this transition goes smoothly,” she added.

Jessica Tang, president of the Massachusetts chapter of the American Federation of Teachers, supported UP Academy’s transition out of receivership.

“Allowing more local input and collaboration is a step in the right direction to ensure the voices of parents and the community are heard as well,” Tang said at Tuesday’s meeting.

Holland’s improved results under the state takeover were an “anomaly in the receivership landscape,” according to Massoud-Tastor. A Globe analysis of test scores, graduation rates, college enrollment, and a dozen other metrics in Lawrence, Holyoke, and Southbridge found that the state failed to meet almost all its stated goals for those districts.

Wary of changes if Boston takes over, however, some parents had gone so far as to request that the school, with more than 600 students, stay in receivership indefinitely.

“Our greatest concern now is that our progress could be disrupted by decisions made outside our schools,” parents Sachia Debrosse, Amanda Nelson, Christina Qualls, and Larae Robinson said in an opinion article published by the Globe.

School officials at Holland warned that the state needed to ensure a smooth transition to Boston’s oversight.

“How we exit matters a lot,” Mike Bower, chief operating officer for Education Network, the nonprofit school manager that runs the Holland, said at the board meeting. “It almost matters as much as how we entered. And unfortunately, we have seen exits happen in the past that did not go very well.”

The goal should be to work together to “ensure that Holland does not lose the progress it has made that it continues to thrive,” he added.

Officials at the state agency said they would sit down with Boston Public Schools Superintendent Mary Skipper to develop an exit strategy.

“I expect the plan will maintain essential flexibilities, autonomies, and the district will commit the necessary resources as the school transitions back to local control,” said Department of Elementary and Secondary Education Commissioner Pedro Martinez.

The state plans to keep monitoring how the school develops through the transition phase, he added. State officials will use a series of “academic milestones and benchmarks” to measure progress.

(This story was corrected on Dec. 17 to clarify that the state did not directly provide assistance to the school.)

Mariana Simões can be reached at mariana.simoes@globe.com. Follow her on X @MariRebuaSimoes.

title: Brown shooting triggers fears among school communities
text:
Two Brown students were killed and nine others wounded in the attack on Saturday by a lone gunman. On Tuesday, Providence police released an enhanced video of a person of interest, after the FBI offered a reward of up to $50,000 for information leading to the identification, arrest, and conviction of the person responsible for the shooting.

While some private schools near Brown canceled school on Monday or for the entire week, Providence public schools remained open. The district canceled all after-school activities and field trips for the rest of the week, “out of an abundance of caution.”

Providence schools added “additional law enforcement support,” Superintendent Javier Montañez said in a letter to families Tuesday. The support included State Police troopers at 10 schools during arrival and dismissal, on top of Providence police deployed around schools near Brown’s campus.

Still, one out of five public school students in Providence were absent on Monday and 16 percent on Tuesday, School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said in a statement.

The absences underscored “the importance of ensuring that families feel safe and confident sending their children to school,” Stephens said.

Governor Dan McKee said he would continue to provide State Police coverage to the schools for the rest of the week. Winter break starts Monday.

“We don’t see anything on the horizon that shows there is another action coming our way,” McKee said. He directed Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green to review K-12 school safety plans.

Providence Mayor Brett Smiley also said parents who are comfortable should send their children to school.

Across New England, teachers, students, and families were still processing news of the shooting and said they felt feel a heightened fear of becoming victims in the future.

Colleges around the area tightened security, as well.

Harvard has begun requiring a university ID swipe to enter campus buildings that were previously open to the public. At Yale, officials increased the presence of campus security and required IDs to enter more gate entrances and doors. And at Emerson College, the school said it was reviewing all safety and security protocols.

High school and elementary teachers went to school this week — the last of the year — worrying about their own students and classrooms, often unsure of how to address the subject with children.

“I saw Brown and I saw Providence in the headlines, it definitely hit me in a little bit of a different way,” said Sydney Chaffee, a Dorchester ninth-grade teacher. “That’s just one state away.”

As Chaffee went about her workday on Monday, the news about the shooting was in the back of her mind, she said. The English and history teacher wondered if students would bring up the news, and how she should address their questions. This time, they didn’t.

“My kids didn’t even mention it,” Chaffee said. “We have become so used to the horror and the tragedy and the inaction, that it just keeps happening and we just keep moving forward because that’s all that we know how to do.”

Chaffee said she was thinking about a new teacher in her school. She thought about the enthusiasm of being new to the profession, and how she didn’t want the news and fear to ruin that experience. At the same time, Chaffee felt the responsibility to ensure new teachers were ready for the reality that they could experience a shooting.

“Our kids shouldn’t go to school and fear that they’re going to be killed,” she said.

On Tuesday, before heading to school, Chaffee checked the news first thing in the morning to see if authorities had found the shooter.

“We don’t dream of lockdown drills. We don’t get into the profession and say, ‘Oh, I can’t wait until I can step into my first classroom and figure out which furniture I’m going to use to block the door,’ ” she said. “We don’t dream of, ‘I can’t wait to be able to console my kids when they’ve lost someone’ or attending our students’ funerals. That’s not why we’re in this field.”

Many teachers across New England followed the news about the Brown shooting on Sunday morning, on the anniversary of the 2012 Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, when a gunman entered an elementary school in Connecticut and killed 26 people.

For Abbey Clements, it was a “tragedy” for another shooting to take place on the same weekend as the anniversary. The retired Connecticut teacher is a survivor of Sandy Hook. Ever since, she has advocated for gun control legislation and created a crisis intervention help line to support educators who survive school shootings.

“Every single teacher in this country worries that gun violence will come to them at any point,” Clements said.

There’s a “look” teachers give one another in the aftermath of school shootings, she said. She experienced it herself after the Uvalde shooting in Texas, which happened in 2022 when she was still teaching.

“It’s like, ‘Can you even believe this continues to happen over and over?’ And without talking, teachers know what that means,” Clements said. “When teachers see these heinous acts of violence happen, they think, ‘Oh my God, this could happen to me and my students.’ ”

Parents also had to decide how to explain to their children what happened at Brown.

Nicole Eaton, a Providence resident whose 7-year-old attends the French American School of Rhode Island, said her daughter felt scared as the family first learned about the shooting.

Eaton, a history professor at Boston College, decided to show her some news coverage.

“I showed her pictures of the police at the campus,” she said. “I showed her the picture of the ambulance. I showed her the picture of the mayor talking. And I talked to her about how they catch people, and how they use evidence to find people, and how this doesn’t happen very often, and that’s why we’re so frustrated and upset.”

Her daughter’s school, which is close to the Brown campus, hired an additional security guard in addition to the local police already patrolling the area. Her school closed on Monday, but reopened on Tuesday.

“Under the circumstances, they’ve done an excellent job,” Eaton said.

title: Boy, 5, dies after being struck by school bus in Standish, Maine
text:
“The complex criminal investigation of this tragic incident has many layers, and involves various investigative partners,” the sheriff’s office said. “The investigative process in these type of incidents can take time to develop, and we ask for your patience as the investigation proceeds.”

The bus was operated by Maine’s Bonny Eagle School District, which operates the largest public sector bus fleet in the state, according to the district’s website.

One student was onboard the bus at the time of the crash, officials said. Cumberland Sheriff Kevin Joyce told WMTW-TV that the other student was Gonzalez’s half-brother.

Edna Libby Elementary School dismissed students after a half-day on Tuesday, and canceled classes on Wednesday, according to district superintendent Clay Gleason.

“In this difficult time please keep those directly impacted in your thoughts — first and foremost the family of the student, as well as the students and staff of Edna Libby," Gleason wrote in a message to parents on Tuesday.

Though the elementary school remained closed Wednesday, Gleason said counselors were on site there and at other schools to support students and other community members.

“The Bonny Eagle community has been deeply impacted by this tragedy and while we can’t change the past, we must move forward together,” he wrote.

Gleason said the district was cooperating with law enforcement and had also opened an internal investigation.

“While I can’t share specifics related to this case, it is standard protocol that any employee would be put on administrative leave while an investigation is underway,” he wrote.

Residents of Standish, roughly a half-hour west of Portland, took to social media to mourn Gonzalez.

“Our hearts are with the family who has suffered the heartbreaking loss of their child,“ Standish town councilor Lisa Struebing said in a Facebook post. ”Please respect their need for privacy while offering care and compassion when welcomed."

Struebing also urged “kindness and support for all impacted, including students, the bus driver, EMTs, faculty, and staff.”

“Let’s support one another with understanding, care, and compassion,” she wrote.

The Second Congregational Church in Norway, Maine, wrote that, just as Maine is a state where “everyone knows someone,” it’s also a place where “when one community is devastated by loss, the pain ripples out to the rest of us.”

“With the painful loss of Simon Gonzalez, a small child who was deeply loved, we pray,” the church wrote. “This has been a hard week for many. Take care of yourselves and each other. Love hard.”

Gonzalez is the second Maine student to die after being hit by a school bus in less than a month. 12-year-old Brayden Callahan was killed on Nov. 25 in Rockland, a city on Penobscot Bay.

Earlier this year, another 5-year-old was struck and killed by a school bus in Boston’s. Hyde Park. Lens Arthur Joseph was on his way home from UP Academy Dorchester when he was struck by his school bus just after it dropped him off.

title: Living with a killer at large
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

The memories endure: The sound. The smell of smoke. The people screaming and running. The dumb luck that kept someone from harm’s way — or the happenstance that put someone else in it. Then the creeping fear, the sheltering in place, when killers remained at large.

These images come from survivors of an attack in New England more than a dozen years ago, but eerily echo in the aftermath of Saturday’s shooting at Brown University — and as we again watch the frustrating hunt for a killer. For four days in April 2013, police struggled to track down the two men behind the bombings near the finish line of the Boston Marathon. And here we are again, four days later, waiting for an arrest.

Back in 2013, a nervous public asked: “What is this world coming to?” Added security worker Guy Dixon, “This is too close to home.”

On Monday, “The sooner we can identify this person, the sooner we can blow this case open,” Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha said.

In the past days, the violence has piled on. The massacre at a Hanukkah celebration on a beach in Australia. The fatal stabbings of a beloved Hollywood icon and his wife, possibly by a troubled adult son. The shooting death of an MIT professor in his Brookline home.

We’re on guard, much like the people of Utah were days after the slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk in September, much like people in Manhattan and elsewhere following last December’s point-blank shooting of health care CEO Brian Thompson.

A killer at large is terrifying, and the wait is harrowing. For four days in 2013, New Englanders were glued to the TV news, staying indoors, checking in on relatives, peeking in their boats in the backyard. After the attack at Brown, we wait to see what happens next.

Varied methods have led to the capture of other suspects. After Kirk’s killing, in which another “person of interest” was released, a man surrendered to authorities late the following night. Five days after the slaying of the CEO of UnitedHealthcare, a tip led to the arrest of the suspect at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pa.

But until those arrests? New videos and new information don’t quell a fear compounded by the cancellation of afterschool activities and university events.

Since the Marathon Bombing, we’ve seen a lot of horror beam across our TVs and phones: school shootings, George Floyd’s murder on a street in Minneapolis, the attempted assassination of a presidential candidate. Readers, we ask: How have you come to live with this? If you made it through the Marathon Bombing and manhunt, please let us know how you endured another time while killers were at large. Did life end up sliding back toward normal little by little, or with a whoosh of relief once the last Marathon bomber was captured?

We could use a whoosh of relief now.

More on the Brown shooting:

The authorities released new video of a man they called a person of interest walking near campus before the attack, but without a clear image of his face. Parents expressed fear about sending their kids to Providence public schools with the shooter at large.

title: Boston Music Awards 2025: Dropkick Murphys, ISHA!, and more win big. See the full list.
text:
“This means the world to us,” Brennan said while accepting the award at Wednesday’s ceremony, noting in his speech that “Boston is such a huge part of who we are.”

Dropkick Murphys, who haven’t secured any titles at the Boston Music Awards since 2012, also picked up wins for video of the year and song of the year (1 million+ streams) for the band’s politically-charged track “Who Will Stand with Us?” from the new album “For the People.”

While Dropkick Murphys led the field with three wins on Wednesday, Boston band Couch, who were nominated in five categories, took home two trophies, including live artist of the year and pop artist of the year.

Rising women hip-hop and R&B performers continue to dominate the new artist of the year category, with Lawrence artist ISHA! taking the 2025 title, shouting out “the Dominicans and the Haitians in the building” while accepting the award (she also performed at the event). The 2024 crown went to Dorchester R&B act Yanna G, while Mattapan rapper Nay $peaks won new artist of the year in 2023.

Rap also dominated the best album categories, with Boston rapper EXITFAME, who also performed at this year’s awards, winning album/EP of the year for “Last Shall Be First.”

“I grew up in Dorchester, Roxbury. And what makes you stay here is the pride of that,” EXITFAME told the Globe backstage at Wednesday’s event, noting how he wants “to bring an eye on the city” with his work.

Meanwhile, Salem rapper Token won the award for album/EP of the year (1 million+ streams) for “I’m Not Supposed to Be Here.”

“I was always insecure about growing up outside of Boston and being an internet kid,” Token said during his acceptance speech. “But where I’m from means a lot to me, and this means a lot to me.”

In a statement from Paul Armstrong, owner and producer of the Boston Music Awards, he praised this year’s nominees and winners for reflecting “the full spectrum of who makes music in Boston right now.”

“It’s been a difficult year in many ways, for a lot of people, and nights like this matter,” said Armstrong. “When things feel heavy, art is often what helps us see a way forward.”

He added, “Our hope is that the Boston Music Awards offered a little light, a sense of connection, and a reminder of the strength that comes from a creative community that truly represents everyone.”

The 2025 edition of the ceremony featured five new categories this year, including the inaugural Margaret Stewart Lindsay music nonprofit of the year award, which honors organizations supporting the creative community. The honor went to the Boston Music Project, a nonprofit that aims to support “the long-term social-emotional and musical success of Boston youth,” according to its website.

“The arts truly are the cornerstone of humanity, and especially right now,” said Chris Schroeder, executive director of the Boston Music Project, while accepting the award on stage. “They play a vital role in helping us to express, amplify, and shape the future that we all want to see.”

Also new for 2025 was the Afro/Caribbean artist of the year category, which took the place of the reggae/ska category. The award went to hip-hop and Afrofusion musician Echezona.

Additional genre-specific winners included Token (hip-hop); Yanna G (R&B); Lia Nicole (Latin); Megan From Work (rock); Hallelujah the Hills (alt/indie); Ezra Furman (singer-songwriter); GA-20 (blues); Samantha Rae (country); Freezepop (dance/electronic); DJ Real P (DJ); Jared Sims (jazz); TREE (metal); Haywire (punk/hardcore); Kier Byrnes & The Kettle Burners (Americana); Tiny Habits (folk); and Miranda Rae (vocalist).

The Boston Globe was honored as well, earning the award for publication of the year, with Globe contributing writer and music editor Victoria Wasylak winning journalist of the year.
