title: 10 memorable musicians, moments, and miscellaneous marvels in 2025
text:
BEST COMMUNITY PERFORMANCE — Noah’s Flood, Boston Lyric Opera

Benjamin Britten’s children’s opera gathered musicians of all ages from several area ensembles into the Ark of Symphony Hall — pint-size beginners who were just learning to read music, poised teenage soloists and string players, masses of children in between, and a warmly enthusiastic audience that joined in with the hymns as taught by music director David Angus. Though it wasn’t without technological stumbles, “Noah’s Flood” was completely unpretentious and genuinely heartwarming, as a community performance should be.

MOST RESTORATIVE CONCERT — The Secret Trio, presented by Ashmont Hill Chamber Music

It seems that to most of the world the Secret Trio’s existence is, in fact, a secret. The group, comprising Macedonian clarinetist Ismail Lumanovski, Armenian oud player Ara Dinkjian, and Turkish kanun player Tamer Pınarbaşı, has a very limited online presence, and the group may never have appeared on my radar if Ashmont Hill Chamber Music hadn’t booked them for an afternoon this past fall. But on my radar they’ll stay; the trio alchemized one part jazz, one part Balkan and Near Eastern traditional music, and a healthy pinch of rock ‘n’ roll, making for an energizing and joyfully virtuosic performance that chased the Sunday scaries away.

BEST OPERATIC PERFORMANCE IN A LEADING ROLE — SeokJong Baek, “Tosca,” Boston Symphony Orchestra

I wrote in July: In Puccini’s “Tosca,” the painter Cavaradossi “often seems more like a plot device and a dispenser of high B-flats than a real character,” especially in contrast to the vain but virtuous Tosca and the preening villain Scarpia. But that wasn’t the case when South Korean tenor SeokJong Baek performed the role opposite Kristine Opolais and Bryn Terfel at Tanglewood; through his supple and searing tenor voice, he conveyed love, pain, and grief that needed no translation.

BEST BREAKOUT PERFORMANCES — Richard Pittsinger, tenor (“Ariodante,” Boston Baroque; “Octavia,” Boston Early Music Festival; “Stellidaura’s Revenge,” Boston Early Music Festival)

On their own, this recent Juilliard graduate’s performances in town this year might not have been star-making. But to each of those, he brought an elegant mode of expression and compelling clarity, and three times makes it a pattern. Things look very promising for this young singer, whose inclination toward the music of Handel might help land him a few more gigs in this Baroque-loving town.

VALKYRIE AWARD FOR WEATHER SYNCHRONICITY — “Symphonie-Fantastique,” Tanglewood Music Center Orchestra with conductor Andris Nelsons vs. Berkshires thunderstorm

The sky was blue as the idyllic third movement began, so when Tanglewood staff ordered the lawn audience to shelter in the Shed because of incoming inclement weather, there were a few confused grumbles. But there was reason to take cover: the wind gradually picked up throughout the ominous “March to the Scaffold,” the limbs on the trees lashed to and fro as “Dream of a Witch’s Sabbath” began — and the instant the lower reaches of the orchestra intoned the first notes of the “Dies Irae,” thunder rattled and the rain came down in sheets, hammering the Shed’s roof as giant church bells tolled backstage. You’d have thought Mother Nature was reading from her own part in the score.

BEST SURPRISE GUEST — Michelle Wu, piano, with Yo-Yo Ma, cello

When Yo-Yo Ma was toting the complete Bach solo cello suites around the world in the late 2010s, the cellist often invited local musicians onstage for an encore. So it wasn’t exactly shocking when, after his performance of the Bach suites at Symphony Hall, Ma announced that a local pianist would be joining him for one more piece. But few if any expected that local pianist to be Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who accompanied Ma in Bach/Gounod’s immortal “Ave Maria.”

PEANUT BUTTER AND PICKLE AWARD FOR UNEXPECTED COLLABORATION THAT ACTUALLY WORKED Víkingur Ólafsson and Yuja Wang, pianists, presented by Celebrity Series of Boston

In the red corner, representing Iceland: Víkingur Ólafsson, one of the more understated and cerebral pianists on the performance circuit, aficionado of Bach and Glass. In the blue corner, representing New York City by way of China: Yuja Wang, a consummate entertainer and connoisseur of sparkle who once performed all four Rachmaninoff concertos — plus the “Rhapsody on a theme of Paganini” — on the same day. What do these two have in common, besides the 88 keys? As it turns out, quite a lot, especially when it comes to 20th century music, and when the pair teamed up for a playful and adventurous two-piano recital at Symphony Hall, they didn’t miss.

MOST FUN NIGHT OUT — Puerto Rico Symphony Orchestra, presented by Boston Symphony Orchestra and Inquilinos Boricuas en Acción

The San Juan-based orchestra celebrated the music of its island home in its first-ever visit to Boston, and the Puerto Rican community showed out in force to do likewise. Flags waved from the balconies, applause between pieces was punctuated with chants of “¡Yo soy Boricua, pa’ que tu lo sepas!” and the orchestra’s musicians hit the stage during intermission to take selfies in the gilded hall.

JOHN C. REILLY AWARD FOR THAT PERSON YOU’RE ALWAYS HAPPY TO SEE ON THE CAST LIST — Dima Slobodeniouk, conductor

Formerly music director of orchestras in Spain and his home country of Finland, Slobodeniouk now seems to be a free agent — and he’s using that freedom to show up with even greater frequency at Symphony Hall and Tanglewood, where he has led performances that consistently rank in the top tier of evenings I spend at the symphony. This calendar year alone, his highlights on the podium included a blazing run at Arvo Pärt’s “Tabula Rasa” with BSO violinists Lucia Lin and Alexander Velinzon, a balanced take on Mozart’s oft-unwieldy “Requiem,” and Roberto Sierra’s roof-raising Concerto for Saxophones and Orchestra with soloist James Carter. Heads up: he’s scheduled to come back this spring for the subscription season’s final program, featuring Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. Wait, am I actually psyched to hear Beethoven’s Ninth?!

title: Families are leaving Boston. What is Boston’s millennial mom mayor doing about that?
text:
A century ago, nearly one in three Bostonians was under the age of 17. Today it’s barely one in eight. While Boston has added nearly 60,000 residents in the last 15 years, the number of children has fallen by about 10,000.

“A big motivating factor in why I ran for mayor in the first place was that exact statistic,” said Wu. “The population was growing, but the number of kids was going down. Moms and dads everywhere across the city can feel why that is true, right?”

From scarce housing to sky-high child-care costs to basic city services that too often seem to make life harder, the deck can seem stacked against parents.

It’s not just in Boston. High-cost cities from San Francisco to New York have seen their child populations decline in recent decades. Nationwide, the number of children under 5 has shrunk since the start of the pandemic. The number of school-age children here ticked up last year, but remains below 2022 levels, and anyone trying to make a big-city more family-friendly is fighting some big trends.

Wu thinks about several “momentous milestones” in a young parent’s life. The first is having the baby, and bringing the child home. The second is when the child starts day care, and parents start paying for it. Then there’s the day you enroll them in school and — you hope — that financial burden lifts. And finally, if your family grows, there’s the day when the stars align and your kids attend the same school and you finally have just one drop-off. It’s a moment, she said, when parents’ quality of life dramatically improves.

Those four moments, Wu said, shape her family policy. So do the concepts of “cost, convenience, and community” — concepts that, as a mom, she lives by too.

Wu said she gets how hard it is to be a parent in the city because she’s been doing it herself for 11 years. But she’s also been mayor for the last four. And things haven’t gotten much easier.

So it’s worth asking: If a millennial mom mayor can’t make Boston better for families, can anyone?

Ironically, over the last 25 years, Boston has become a city for the young.

From 2000 through 2015, the population of 20-to-34 year olds in Boston surged, to become 40 percent of the city’s total makeup. That’s thanks in part to our universities, of course, but also a flood of young people drawn to urban living and good jobs.

Scores of apartment and condo buildings cropped up to house these young professionals. They had amenity rooms and dog spas, but few were designed with children in mind. The newly built Seaport is chock-a-block with brunch spots and venues for “competitive socializing” but has no library, no arts venue, no ballfields.

“There’s this real divergence of Boston really rebounding over the last couple generations,” said Luc Schuster, the head of Boston Indicators, the research arm of The Boston Foundation. “The economy’s thriving. There has been some population growth, but at the same time, we’ve lost kids.”

Now many of those urbanites are in their 30s and 40s, finding it harder to live in Boston with children. Families, of course, have long beat an exodus to the suburbs. But for young people who are committed to city living, it’s been frustrating to watch friends struggle to make it work, or leave altogether.

They’re people like Julia Tutko-Balena, who grew up in Dorchester and now lives in Charlestown with her husband and two kids. She’s thrilled that the city is safer than it was when she was young — “Dorchester used to be very ‘stabby’,” she jokes — and believes Boston is a great place to raise her family. But she says she wishes that more middle-class people like her could find a way to stay.

“They’re people who have lived in the neighborhood and literally helped build the neighborhood,” she said. “They’re getting pushed out because they can’t afford to live [here anymore].”

Growing up in Chicago, Wu moved a lot, her immigrant parents always hunting for the smallest house in the best public school district they could afford. And since Wu first took office, housing, particularly housing for families, has been among her biggest priorities.

It’s also one of the hardest to fix.

She admitted recently that her housing efforts so far have only earned a B+, slowed by standoffs with developers and stymied by sky-high building costs. Rents keep climbing, with the average two-bedroom in Boston now going for $2,495 a month, according to real estate website Apartmentlist.com, up 9 percent since January 2022.

And people are frustrated. A recent poll by advocacy group Abundant Housing found 70 percent of Boston residents say Wu has done just a fair or poor job on housing.

“We have this reputation as this progressive city,” said Abundant Housing executive director Jesse Kanson-Benanav. Most people outside of Boston “don’t understand why we haven’t adopted policies that will accelerate the creation of reasonably priced, moderately-sized, family-sized homes.”

Wu has made some progress on income-restricted units, with more than 5,000 completed or in construction, and 4,000 more in the pipeline — more than have been built in Boston than in any three-year period since the late 1990s. Wu, too, has bolstered programs that help Section 8 voucher-holders buy homes, said Stephanie Ettinger de Cuba, the executive director of Children’s HealthWatch at Boston Medical Center.

Those are real successes, Schuster said, but the need remains for housing that middle-income families can afford.

”A subset of the lowest income families actually is able to remain in the city and attend our schools,” he said. “The big challenge is for families above those income thresholds. Many of them are the ones getting squeezed and moving away.”

For parents that decide to live in the city, securing day care is a major hurdle.

It’s an emotional one too, Wu said. “I remember crying,” she said, even though her sons were at the on-site child care at City Hall. And then there’s the cost. Massachusetts has some of the highest early child-care costs in the country — $22,000 a year, double the national average.

In New York, Democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani won this fall’s mayor’s race this fall in part on an audacious promise of free, high-quality child care for all New York City under age 5. It’s the sort of ambitious progressive policy that one might imagine Mayor Wu rolling out.

But Wu doesn’t go that far, focusing, instead, on a pragmatic approach to the realities of getting child care right for parents who face “the exhaustion of having to juggle everything” — something she knows firsthand. Wu said she kept Mira at her side during the election campaign not for optics but because she and her husband couldn’t figure out “a stable and predictable” child-care situation.

“The mayor is able to see the people who often feel unseen,” said Amy O’Leary, executive director of Strategies for Children, a statewide advocacy group. “Their approach is solutions-based in a world where a lot of things are reacting to problems.”

O’Leary pointed to Wu’s creation of the Office of Early Childhood, one of a handful of municipal-led agencies in the country to focus exclusively on a city’s youngest residents.

The office provides training and financial support to early child-care providers and says 77 new businesses have been licensed as a result. In 2022, Wu changed zoning ordinances to mandate that large developments must include child-care facilities; over 200 sites have opened since. Wu has also expanded paid parental leave for nearly all unionized city employees.

One small but significant solution is Great Starts, a new city website that simply maps all the available child-care options in Boston, allowing parents to filter by who took vouchers and hours they were open.

“It’s hard to over-express how much of Wild West it is for families to even to figure out what is available,” said Elizabeth Leiwant, vice president of public policy and research at Neighborhood Villages, an early education systems change organization. “It was revolutionary for a family to just have a single, easy-to-navigate place where they could go and start to figure out what their options are.”

Since its launch, Great Starts has expanded to become the onboarding site for parents to register for early education slots and public schools at BPS, replacing a trek to register in-person. But simply having an easy-to-navigate website isn’t enough to persuade parents to commit to public schools. The programs have to make sense.

Wherever she can, Wu says, she uses her own lived experience as a parent to shape city policy when it comes to kids. One of Wu’s sons wasn’t able to get a pre-K slot, but under her watch, the city has expanded pre-K programs at BPS, which now serve 53 percent of 4-year-olds in Boston, and 23 percent of 3-year-olds.

Even with that expansion, not all the available slots are full, something Wu ascribes to the practicalities of what parents and young children need: Is the pre-school close to home or a job? Do the hours work? She said she’s pushing to expand offerings to get more families to enroll.

“The data shows that when families get a spot in the Boston pre-K program, they are significantly more likely to stay and enroll in the Boston Public Schools,” Wu said. It’s a “pathway to building a sense of predictability and trust.”

As kids get a little older, the quality of schools starts to matter more, too. Wu’s two sons attend Boston Public Schools, and so when she talks education, it’s personal. More than a third of BPS students attend schools ranked in the bottom 10 percent of Massachusetts schools.

That’s a major sticking point for parents, one evidenced in the demographic data. The number of children in the city drops dramatically — by nearly half — when they turn 5, and the number in BPS schools has fallen by 17,000 in the last quarter-century, to just 46,000. Of those, many are “high-needs” meaning they’re lower-income, have disabilities, or are non-native English speakers. The BPS population has risen slightly in the last three years, which shows modest progress, Schuster said.

In a sign she wants to push harder to strengthen schools in her second term, Wu this fall hosted her first State of the Schools address, announcing more before- and after-school programming, and a goal to have all BPS students learning at grade level by the end of next year. She’s also introduced new math enrichment programs – of which her oldest son is now taking part.

“We are the oldest public school system in the nation,” she said. “And together, it’s time that we make it the best.”

Advocates – and parents – remain in wait-and-see mode. Wu has agitated families by pushing for school closures and consolidations, which she argues have been done to improve the facilities and efficiencies within the sprawling system. (Wu’s sons’ school was part of that consolidation — they now attend the Sarah Roberts Elementary School, which got a $91 million facelift this year).

That frustration stands to continue. Earlier this month, over a hundred protesters chanted “Save Our Schools!” during a Boston School Committee meeting.

But while many parents leave the city for the burbs, that wasn’t the case for Paula Silva, who is from Cape Verde and lived in Brockton and Somerville before moving with her daughter to Boston to take advantage of the city’s academic opportunities.

Silva’s daughter is a strong student at the Mather School in Dorchester, and Silva said her teachers have helped enroll her in leadership and performing arts programs. Now, she said, she’s getting help as she thinks about applying to exam schools.

“I believe here, you have a chance to have a very good education,” Silva said.

In a time when so many parents don’t have extended family nearby to help them raise their children, Wu hopes the city can help combat isolation and build community too. “It’s just too hard, even as two working parents, to make all the pieces fit together,” she said. “You need a larger village.”

It’s the thinking behind Wu’s “Connect Learn Explore” initiative, a free program that’s taught 9,000 kids to bike and nearly 12,000 to swim. And it’s also behind one of Wu’s proudest accomplishments: Boston Family Days, which grants all city residents with children free access to Boston’s cultural institutions on the first two Sundays of the month.

“We’re making it so that you just don’t have to worry about whether you can get into certain programs or find certain opportunities for your kids,” Wu said. “And then finding lots of ways to bring people together.”

Tutko-Balena loves Family Days, and used it to take her kids to the Children’s Museum last month. She said she wants more opportunities to connect with all of the city’s neighborhoods, so that people feel less segregated.

“I think if the city takes care of its people, the people will take care of it,” she said.

Making Boston more family-friendly can pay economic dividends, too, said Jason Kelly, cofounder and CEO of Ginkgo Bioworks. The 44-year-old entrepreneur has a 13-year-old daughter and a 10-year-old son. He’s raising them in Beacon Hill, and says having a mother of three as a mayor matters when it comes to encouraging people to stay, and start companies, in Boston.

“I tell founders all the time ‘remember, you’re going to have kids some day. You should think about the city you want to raise your kids in,’ ” he said.

But for some, the decision to have children can mean making hard choices.

A lifelong Bostonian who works in biotech, Nya grew up in Dorchester and inherited her family’s home in Melville Park (her father paid $178,000 for it in 1988). Nya, who asked for her last name to be withheld to protect her privacy, is 37 and hopes to start a family soon. But even with housing secured, she’s struggling to see how the math can work.

She and her partner have contemplated moving to Washington, D.C., or perhaps Georgia, somewhere they can envision their money going further. She’d love to stay in the city where she grew up, but worries she won’t be able to raise her child here.

“You work really hard to earn your six-figure salary and now it’s become obsolete,” she said. “People at the state and city level lack a true understanding of the Boston economy and what is fueling it.”

Wu says she does, and she’s trying everything she can to make it easier for people like Nya to stay. But she knows it’s an uphill battle. She’s had enough hard conversations with friends telling her they’re leaving the city.

“It’s such a consequential choice to make,” she said. “A lot goes into it. I think sometimes people try to tell me after it’s too late.”

Shirley Leung of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: MWRA’s solution to sewer overflows stirs outrage
text:
This is also an economic issue. Toxic blooms from stormwater runoff recently threatened the Head of the Charles Regatta, and such conditions will imperil other landmark events and economic development if the MWRA compounds the runoff issue by maintaining its current course on CSOs.

We’ve been here before: When Conservation Law Foundation brought its lawsuit to force the cleanup of Boston Harbor, some members of the media called it a waste of billions of dollars. That faulty notion is reprised in the editorial. Yet today the harbor’s revival proves that clean water investments yield extraordinary returns to our economy, such as a value of ecosystem services estimated between $30 billion and $100 billion.

This is also a matter of the rule of law. MWRA deserves credit for magnificent achievements in cleaning up the harbor over decades. From my experience having enforced the federal Clean Water Act throughout those same decades, I would argue that MWRA’s current approach to CSOs violates both the letter and spirit of the law.

Brad Campbell

President and CEO

Conservation Law Foundation

Boston

The writer is former regional administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency’s mid-Atlantic region and former commissioner of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection.

Your recent editorial on the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority’s updated CSO control plan resonated because it recognized what’s driving so much of the public’s emotion: a sincere, shared hope for cleaner, healthier rivers. Those of us who work in water and wastewater feel that same pull. Combined sewer overflows should continue to decline, and this plan was always meant to evolve. The goal — for advocates, MWRA, and our communities — is the same: real improvements in water quality.

The challenge, as your editorial noted, is that progress now requires confronting difficult tradeoffs. After 40 years of major gains, the remaining decisions are more complex — and far more costly. MWRA was created to lead the region’s environmental turnaround, and the MWRA Advisory Board was established alongside it to ensure that those decisions kept affordability in mind — not to block investment but rather to make sure families and communities could sustain it.

When tradeoffs fall directly on households, people deserve clarity about what each dollar accomplishes. MWRA is funded entirely by its communities, which means every dollar becomes a higher sewer bill for the residents who cherish these rivers.

Massachusetts has some of the most engaged, informed residents anywhere. Let’s give them the full story in the formal comment process and trust them to help shape the path forward.

Matthew A. Romero

Executive director

MWRA Advisory Board

Chelsea

The views expressed here are those of the writer and do not represent those of the full advisory board.

The editorial “The MWRA’s tricky balancing act” regurgitates MWRA’s misleading argument for dumping sewage in the Charles River while it misses the heart of the public’s concerns. The agency’s proposal to reclassify the river is no meaningless thing; it’s a permanent concession to have sewage discharged into the Charles forever. The proposal would not only remove any accountability for MWRA to end its discharges. It would actually increase the amount of sewage entering the river in the future as storms worsen. It would be a drastic step backward for a mainstay of Greater Boston that’s taken us decades to bring back to life.

There was no misunderstanding about MWRA, Cambridge, and Somerville’s proposal that has to be “explained” to its critics. The authority faced justified alarm from outraged residents legitimately questioning why we would abandon past cleanup efforts and increase sewage discharges to the river.

The editorial paints solutions as impossible and unrealistic. But the Boston Harbor cleanup — also dismissed as too hard at the time — is now one of metro Boston’s greatest economic wins. Clean water is an investment that pays off.

A sewage-free river is not a pipe dream. It’s what we deserve and what MWRA must deliver.

Emily Norton

Executive director

Charles River Watershed Association

Boston

The proposals on the table from MWRA, Cambridge, and Somerville addressing combined sewer overflows would not get us closer to a swimmable or boatable Charles or Mystic River.

For instance, the proposal does not promise to “eliminate CSOs in the Alewife Brook entirely,” as your editorial claims. It predicts only that there would be no CSOs in a “typical” year of rainfall. So the current proposal essentially guarantees continued releases of CSOs in the Alewife Brook, the Mystic, and the Charles, and probably at an even greater level than now.

As environmental advocates, we understand that costs must be weighed against benefits. But the current proposals provide minimal (and yet to be known) benefits, far less than the editorial asserts.

Massachusetts residents deserve more information and a transparent public process where they can weigh in on whether the costs are worth the benefits for treasured public resources.

The headline that appeared over your editorial online asks: “Is making the Charles swimmable worth the cost?”

For our part, the question is: Is freeing our rivers from sewage worth the cost? Our answer remains a resounding yes.

Patrick Herron

Executive director

Mystic River Watershed Association

Arlington

title: A single box on the doorstep, and his world changed
text:
It was December of 1985 and four-year-old Reggie Nguyenwas adjusting to his new life in Dorchester. It was radically different from anything he had ever known, with snow falling from the sky, and other instances of what felt then like magic.

Reggie and his family were among the third and final wave of “Boat People” to flee Vietnam in the aftermath of the Vietnam war. His strongest memory of the weeks they passed in limbo in a Philippines refugee camp was of a food delivery truck. Every week it came around and the drivers would hand out food with nothing asked in return.

One day that winter, the doorbell rang. There on the doorstep sat a cardboard box. Reggie did not know what to think of this unexpected delivery, except that it was “a gigantic box for a four -year-old.”

Part of him was apprehensive. Just a week earlier, some neighborhood kids had thrown a brick through a window of their home.

But excitement and curiosity won out and Reggie brought the package inside. Opening it, he found action figures, toy trucks and cars, and a strange object that he later learned was a model space shuttle. Being unable to read the letter that accompanied the presents, all Reggie knew then was that he was thrilled.

He especially loved the space shuttle. The Voyager 2 spacecraft was about to make history with its exploration of Uranus and the boy would develop a fascination with the cosmos. The toy fed his sense of wonder, and allowed him to interact with American popular culture. When he started school the next year, he already had shared interests with his classmates.

Back then, his mother worked as a seamstress in Chinatown, where his parents eventually opened a clothing store. Reggie had no concept of Western holiday traditions. The sudden appearance of this mysterious collection of playthings seemed truly a miracle. But it was Globe Santa, made possible through intentional acts of kindness.

Reggie suspects that the Catholic charity that sponsored his family’s immigration applied to Globe Santa on his and his little brother’s behalf. Open-hearted donors sent in money. The Boston Globe was dedicated to ensuring that kids like Reggie had moments of holiday magic.

Nearly 40 years later, Reggie Nguyen, now 44, is a full-time manager for the Brookline Food Pantry. His career is centered on helping struggling families access food and other essential resources.

The pantry serves over 700 households each week—families who, like the Nguyens 40 years ago, are navigating financial hardships. Through Brookline Thrives, a subsidiary of the Pantry, more than 500 students bring home weekend food bags throughout the school year.

When Reggie told pantry volunteers that he was a former Globe Santa recipient, it came to light that many of them were donors. “They told me that they were glad it went to someone; that it made a difference. And oh, it did.”

For Reggie, Globe Santa was more than just “a very fond personal memory” from his first ever Christmas. In retrospect, he knows that Globe Santa’s impact on him lasted much longer than the actual presents.

School scholarships allowed Reggie to pursue his education. He went on to earn a bachelor’s degree in English Literature from UMass Boston.

Before joining the team at the Brookline Food Pantry, Reggie worked at Rosie’s Place, a women’s shelter in Boston. His conviction that helping others matters more than accumulating wealth has been constantly reaffirmed ever since he was just a boy excited about outer space.

The older he gets, Reggie reflects, the more he appreciates that Globe Santa “was something genuinely sweet that happened to me as a young person...bringing joy to a child is precious and that in itself is worth supporting.”

Sophie Arnstein can be reached at sophie.arnstein@gmail.com

For 70 years Globe Santa, a program of the Boston Globe Foundation, has provided gifts to children in need at holiday time. Please consider giving by phone, mail, or online at globesanta.org.

title: ‘It means a lot.’ Holiday gifts donated to 300 needy families in Dorchester
text:
“It means a lot,” she said. “They support my family every year.”

“This is just a helping hand,” she added.

Hall’s family was one of 300 receiving free holiday gifts at the Teen Center Wednesday. At the event, top city and religious officials spoke about the importance of charity, especially during the holiday season.

“What’s most important is people and making sure that everybody is taken care of,” Mayor Michelle Wu said. “If government can be there to help people, if [the] community can come together to help each other ... then the city of Boston is always going to be OK.”

“It’s a beautiful thing to do in a beautiful place, to act with compassion and solidarity, one for another,” Boston Archbishop Richard Henning said.

The event was hosted by Catholic Charities Boston, with support from the Boston Police Department and the Mayor Thomas M. Menino Fund for Boston.

Menino served as mayor from 1993 until January 2014. He died on Oct. 30, 2014. Two of his grandchildren, Samantha and Taylor Menino, now run the toy drive.

In 1993, it began when Menino, Boston’s then newly-elected Mayor, decided to load up his truck with toys for kids in Dorchester on Christmas Eve.

“At that time, the whole Bowdoin and Geneva [area] was not a very good place for people to live,” said Menino’s widow, Angela. “He would pass out the toys to the kids ... he wanted to assure the people that he would be taking care of and helping them.”

“It started off in the back of a Tahoe ... and now it’s grown to this,” said Thomas Menino’s son, Tommy Menino.

The families receiving gifts previously filled out “wish list” forms provided by the Teen Center, according to Samantha Menino.

“They give an age, and they ask like a desired toy, and then they usually put their size for clothes and shoes,” she said. “A lot of kids ask for bikes, Legos, board games.”

On Wednesday, a few dozen brand new bicycles lined the back of a gymnasium and white bags full of gifts dotted the sides. Police officers spoke jovially to one another and smiled against the wind as snow began to fall in the parking lot outside the center.

“I got a 14-year-old here, he attends the teen center,” said Maria Rivera, 63, of Dorchester. “You know they’re safe here. They get fed, they do activities, get help with their homework.

“They’re mentors for our community,” she added.

Rivera, who was picking up headphones, video games, and clothes for her grandchildren and foster children, said she relies on the support of the community to make sure her loved ones get gifts.

“Our community, we’re together, we’re united,” she said. “We’re caring about each other.”

title: Forever renters: For many in Greater Boston, the American dream of homeownership ‘no longer exists’
text:
Harnois is an elementary school teacher in Boston Public Schools; together she and her husband make $175,000 a year. And their monthly rental costs are modest, considerably less than the typical household around here.

“If homes here cost $400,000, we’d be homeowners,” said Harnois, who is 32.

Such is reality now for Greater Boston’s next generation, particularly younger and middle class people.

The cost of buying a home has been steadily rising for decades, and recently it has exploded, growing far faster than incomes.

The typical house in Greater Boston sold for $833,900 in the second quarter of 2025, more than 7.5 times the region’s median household income. Five years ago, a household needed to earn $126,519 a year to afford the median-priced single-family home in this region, according to an analysis by Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Today, that figure has more than doubled, to $259,648.

The result is people who 20, 10, or even 5 years ago would have been able to purchase a home — teachers, nurses, and academics — can hardly even conceive of it.

“The door to homeownership in the Boston area has really been shut,” said Daniel McCue, a senior research associate at Harvard’s housing studies center. “There are hundreds of thousands of people here staring at these numbers saying, ‘Who can actually afford this?’ ”

The consequences are being felt by an entire generation, forced to make a choice their parents did not: Stay in Massachusetts, and rent forever, or leave, and put down roots somewhere less expensive.

“We work really hard, and we feel like we’ve done everything right,” said Harnois. “It is difficult to accept that there is no pathway for us to own a home in the neighborhood I’ve spent my whole life in.”

Since the 1940s, when the 30-year mortgage emerged and made home buying more accessible to many workers, owning a home has been a symbol of success. To achieve the American dream was to work hard, save up, and buy a house, which would serve as both a stable home and a valuable asset that would appreciate with time. For many working class families in Massachusetts, homeownership was the ticket to the middle class.

It was exactly that path that Ben Watts hoped to follow.

Growing up, Watts’s parents did not own their home, a fact he became aware of when he visited friends’ houses as a kid. As he got older, he came to assume that he, someday, would.

“It was ingrained,” said Watts. “That’s what you’re supposed to do, right?”

Now his goal has collided with economic reality. Watts, who is 33, works three jobs — as a bartender and for a French spirits company — and earns nearly $90,000 a year. His rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Belmont, which he splits with his fiancé, is $2,850.

Watts has effectively given up on owning a home. He can hardly find any listings on Zillow for less than $700,000, at least not ones that look like they wouldn’t require tens of thousands of dollars in maintenance. At that cost, Watts would be more than doubling his monthly housing payment, and likely paying at least half of his income toward a mortgage. And that’s after a six-figure down payment, cash he simply does not have.

The prevailing feeling, he said, is resentment.

“I’m being priced out because I’m working to try and make the city that I love better with great bars and restaurants,” said Watts, who grew up in Arlington. “It feels like I’m being told that there’s no place for me here anymore.”

Perhaps what is most frustrating to people like Watts: They know it wasn’t always like this.

Home prices have been on the rise for decades. But the biggest shift in housing affordability began in the aftermath of the pandemic, as home prices rose even faster, and mortgage rates more than doubled, leaving prospective buyers to pay both sky-high total price tags and huge monthly payments.

In 2010, for example, the median home price was $360,800, but the average on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 4.75 percent, meaning the mortgage payment on that median-priced house was only $1,816 a month, almost the same as it was in 2000. Now, with a median house price of $833,900, and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage around 6.79 percent in the second quarter of the year, the monthly mortgage payment on that median-priced house is $5,240 a month — before homeowners insurance, property tax, and mortgage insurance, which can tack on $1,500 more each month.

The shift is pricing a startling number of would-be homeowners out of the market. Roughly 100,000 people who made enough money to afford an entry-level home in 2021 could no longer afford that home in 2025, according to data from Boston Indicators.

“Tell me how many people can afford to buy an almost million dollar single-family home?” said Gail Latimore, executive director of the Codman Square Community Development Corporation. “Tell me how many people can afford to buy an $800,000 house and pay $5,000 a month for the mortgage? We’ve always been an expensive area, but this is unmanageable.”

What happens when so many people are priced out of homeownership all at once?

Right now, a generational wealth divide is emerging, said Albert Saiz, an associate professor of urban economics and real estate at MIT.

While 50 years ago, nearly half of young adults age 25 to 34 in Massachusetts owned a home, today barely one-third do, and a recent analysis by Boston Indicators suggests the true rate is even lower, roughly 24 percent. Those people who were able to buy in the 1970s, ’80s, and ’90s have seen their investments turn into a launching pad for generational wealth: Those homes, in many cases, are now million-dollar nest eggs that have double or tripled in value, particularly in Boston and its suburbs.

“Unless we do something about housing stock — building, building, building — this is a dangerous situation for working class folks who used to depend on housing as their main way to accumulate wealth,” said Saiz.

Take Coire Jones, 38, who makes almost $50,000 doing administrative work at a real estate law firm. Jones sets aside roughly $200 a month, mostly by cutting out extraneous spending, and by choosing to rent a small room in an apartment in Somerville for just $750 a month.

This is not how he pictured things going. Jones’s family has been in Massachusetts for generations, and he loves it here. He graduated from college with a history degree in 2009, in the middle of the Great Recession, and struggled to find a job.

He’s now switched career paths and found stable income. But Jones can do the math. He knows that at his current income, he’ll never be able to afford even a tiny home of his own.

“We millennials were told that you could be whatever you wanted to be and if you went to college you’d be in the middle class,” he said. “I don’t mind renting for the rest of my life. But the foundation of the American economy is that everyone buys a house, and that equity allows you to do a lot of different things and achieve financial stability. And that no longer exists for my generation.”

That doesn’t stop people from trying.

Every year, 200 to 250 people enroll in first-time homebuyer classes at the Chinatown-based Asian Community Development Corporation, one of countless groups that aim to teach would-be buyers the ropes of mortgages, property inspection, and other intricacies of the biggest investment most people will ever make.

In previous years, it was common for 20 to 40 people who took the class to purchase a home, said Angie Liou, the Asian CDC’s executive director. Last year, only six did.

Latimore, of the Codman Square CDC, said a lucky few are able to purchase with the help of down payment and mortgage assistance programs sponsored by the city and other public entities.

Those who aren’t able to buy are left to grapple with what it means that they may never access homeownership.

Some, like Harnois, are willing to stick it out as renters. She is too connected to the neighborhood where she grew up and today works in to consider leaving.

And then there are people like Lillian Rotondo, an East Cambridge resident who works in biotech sales. She said she can’t quite believe the prices of the homes she sees on the market.

She has a familiar story: She and her husband, a chef who works in the Seaport, make good money — roughly $240,000 a year. But it still doesn’t feel like enough to afford a $600,000 or $700,000 place, especially because Rotondo is pregnant with their first child, which they know will be expensive in its own way.

Rotondo’s parents migrated to the US from El Salvador with $20 to their name, she said. Years later, they were able to save up enough to buy a home on Long Island.

It’s important to Rotondo, who is 40, to do the same. And because they cannot afford it here, Rotondo and her husband are going to move, most likely to Rhode Island, somewhere near Providence.

“We have worked hard our entire lives,’ she said. ”We should be able to afford a two-bedroom. So we’ll go somewhere we can.”

title: How two Boston teens are fighting the food waste crisis
text:
Her grandfather lived in China during the Great Chinese Famine, she said, and he witnessed extreme hunger and starvation.

“He would always make sure at the dinner table [that] I finished every last grain, and that’s something that I think is really instilled in me,” Sun said.

His words inspired her to volunteer at First Baptist Church in Jamaica Plain in 2022, where she cooked meals twice a week.

Along the way, she made a startling discovery: community businesses tossing out unsold goods at the end of the day.

“It just felt really rough to me, because I just spent so much time making food, but there was just perfectly fine food being thrown away on the same exact street, so I wanted to try to do something about that,” she said.

Sun and Hennessy, both 17, are seniors at Boston Latin School. Their campaign against food waste began when they were sophomores. The pair asked local businesses to give them the food instead of throwing it out at the end of the night.

They first approached Dunkin’ on Centre Street and then The Real Deal, a family-owned restaurant. And with those willing partners, NoVasta, Latin for “no waste,” was born.

It started out as a small school club whose members volunteer to collect food waste from local businesses and bring it to a drop-off center, such as the church. The club also organizes food drives and raises money to buy items in bulk from wholesalers like Costco.

Over the past two years, NoVasta has become part of the national Zero Waste Coalition. Club chapters have been started at other US schools and abroad.

NoVasta embraces the global goal of reduced food waste and passing legislation to halve food loss and waste by 2030.

“It’s given us a lot of hope to see that even though it’s such a big problem, there are a lot of people — whether it’s students or city councilors or people our age or restaurants — that are willing to work and find ways to contribute to this cause,” Hennessy said.

Nuvana Ivory, who has worked front of house at The Real Deal for two years, has seen Sun and Hennessy come in often to pick up food at the end of the night. The restaurant usually gives any excess food to staff or to homeless people in the area. But the girls’ initiative to eliminate food waste makes her feel good.

“I don’t like to see food go to waste,” she said. “To see the food go to a good cause and not be thrown in the trash is a good opportunity for us to help out.”

Food insecurity is a growing crisis in the United States, with approximately 13.5 percent of US households being food insecure in 2023, up from 12.8 percent in 2022, according to the USDA.

However, while food insecurity is on the rise, millions of tons of food are being thrown away each year, data show.

According to the US Department of Agriculture, food waste makes up between 30 and 40 percent of food supply. In 2019, 66 million tons of food waste were generated in the United States, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

The growing problem prompted Boston City Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata and others to propose an ordinance in 2023 to create a citywide food recovery program.

“More or less of what [is] safe to consume could go to neighborhoods such as East Boston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, High Park that remain underserved by a lack of grocery stores or forcing residents to travel to food pantries on their days off or when they have work,” Zapata said.

Programs to address food waste have been adopted in other cities, such as Washington D.C. Zapata has been working with Sun and Hennessy to try to implement a city-wide food recovery program, which would be established with the ordinance that councilors are working to pass.

“It would compel some of these large food generators to compile their edible leftovers, and then as an effort to utilize what is safe to consume at its highest possible use before it’s sent to be recycled or sent to the landfill,” Zapata said.

While NoVasta started as a school club, it has grown into an international initiative to “turn excess into access.” Through online forums and social media, Sun and Hennessy were able to connect with other high schoolers who noticed the same patterns in their communities: food going to waste while people were going hungry.

“[Students] saw the same overflowing dumpsters in their community, and they saw the same like empty hands on the street that were always just [a few] feet away. So every single student we talked to noticed the same issue in their own city, and they’ve sort of just been waiting for a catalyst to start it. And so we’re really happy that we were that catalyst for them,” Sun said.

title: After decades as a pastor, lawyer, and advocate, Rev. Miniard Culpepper will take on a new role: Boston city councilor
text:
Now, Culpepper is getting ready to add a new line to his resumé. In January, he will be sworn in to elected office for the first time, representing Roxbury-based District 7 on the Boston City Council.

It’s one of the city’s most diverse and historically marginalized districts, and has faced immense turmoil in the last year. The council seat has sat vacant since July, when former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson resigned after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges.

The council is often a launchpad for young politicians with ambitions for higher office, but Culpepper, 72, appears to be flipping that script. The council’s only new member will also be its oldest sitting member, and he comes to the body with decades of advocacy, legal, ministerial, and political experience.

Culpepper said his longstanding community work won him voters’ support.

“The community wanted a voice that they have heard and they can support and that they have confidence” in, Culpepper said.

Representing a council district is similar to leading a parish: They’re both 24/7 jobs, he said.

“Constituents, they call you when they have emergencies. Same thing with church folks,” he said. “What happens now is I don’t stop doing what I’ve been doing, in terms of helping people.”

The mission to serve has been a driving theme throughout his life, and is a thread of his family history, Culpepper said in a recent interview at his home on Seaver Street.

The house is a piece of history itself: His grandparents faced racism when purchasing it in the early 1950s, and were the first Black homeowners on the road, he said. In the 1960s, his mother and grandmother used the small building in the backyard as a day care. This year, it served as Culpepper’s campaign headquarters.

Culpepper remembers his grandfather sitting in the living room when he heard that Martin Luther King Jr. had been killed. The two had protested together, Culpepper said.

Hearing those stories as a child had a profound impact on him.

“How could you be part of a family that fought for civil rights and not have it as part of who you are?” Culpepper said.

Culpepper wants to bring those values to City Hall. He said he plans to push for an ethics committee on the council, a separate city agency focused solely on homelessness, and increased homeownership opportunities for Section 8 voucher holders.

After graduating from Boston Public Schools’ English High School in 1971, Culpepper earned his undergraduate degree from Brandeis University and got involved in politics while getting his law degree from Suffolk University.

He worked on Senator Ted Kennedy’s 1980 run for president and Bill Clinton’s White House bid in 1992. In Washington, D.C., Culpepper worked on Capitol Hill and earned a divinity degree from Howard University in 1988.

By 1995, Culpepper had moved from Washington to Milton with his wife and two young sons, and taken a job as a top lawyer for the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. He also became the senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church, which his grandfather founded in 1939.

Contentious divorce proceedings between Culpepper and his wife briefly divided the church community in 1999, with some parishioners filing a lawsuit to bar Culpepper from church property, while others fiercely defended him, according to a Globe report from the time.

Culpepper’s ex-wife accused him of verbal and emotional abuse, while Culpepper got two restraining orders against her. A judge dismissed the parishioners’ lawsuit against Culpepper less than a month after it was filed.

In Boston’s Black communities and in many political circles, Culpepper is known for his work at HUD and for his civic leadership.

“He’s a very visible person; he’s out in the community a lot,” said Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a native Roxbury resident and political consultant who’s known Culpepper for decades. “He brings a wealth of experience ... [and] has shown his love for the community.”

At HUD, Culpepper sued the Boston Housing Authority for alleged discrimination against tenants of color in the 1990s. It led the city to adopt new civil rights protections.

Culpepper also worked to curb youth violence, particularly after the death of 20-year-old Jahmol Norfleet, a onetime gang member who was shot to death in 2006. Norfleet was killed just months after he and other youth leaders, with the help of Black ministers, including Culpepper, brokered a peace deal between two rival gangs. Norfleet’s death inspired Culpepper to start the Trotter Park Peace Program, which provided activities and paid job opportunities for at-risk youth.

Antoine Goforth, now 39, was Norfleet’s best friend and also involved in a local gang. He said the Trotter Park Peace Program, and his relationship with Culpepper, changed his life. Not only did Culpepper work to get kids jobs and keep them out of trouble, he also developed relationships with them, listened, and earned their respect.

“Whenever we need help with something, he’d be the first person we’d call,” Goforth said. “If Reverend Culpepper wasn’t around, I’d probably be in jail or dead or something like that.”

Cedric White, a close friend and former colleague of Culpepper’s at HUD, said his dedication to advocacy and his community have not waned in the more than two decades they’ve known each other.

“He’s not one to sit around and be idle,” White said. “If there’s an issue that’s not right, he wants to be there to help the cause and stand up for the people.”

In recent years, Culpepper has rallied Black ministers to encourage their communities to get the COVID-19 vaccine, and started a small church farm to grow and distribute free fresh produce. He led protests against the closures of several Walgreens pharmacies in Black neighborhoods, and organized support for migrant families when the state had to temporarily house them in Roxbury’s Melnea Cass Recreation Center.

He also stayed involved in politics, praying over Senator Elizabeth Warren before debates during her presidential run in 2020. After weighing a run for mayor in 2013, Culpepper lost a race for state Senate in 2022.

He said he had no plans to run for office again, until community leaders urged him to run for the District 7 council seat last year.

Joseph Feaster Jr., who has known Culpepper since they worked on Kennedy’s 1994 Senate campaign, said Culpepper’s experience in politics and housing policy, plus his care for the community, will make him an effective councilor.

“Politics requires the ability to oftentimes compromise in order to get what you need to get done for the greater good,” Feaster said. Culpepper’s “going to be able to state his position, he will be able to articulate it well, but he’s also prepared to listen, and that’s the quality many don’t have.”

title: ‘Now the world is paying attention.’ Nigerians in Greater Boston voice hope, doubt after US airstrikes on homeland
text:
On Sunday, Nigerians living in Greater Boston said the sentiment at home is split. Some think the United States is intervening for its own economic and political interests.

“It’s not genuine,” said Kamalu MacPhilips, a devout Christian from eastern Nigeria, standing outside St. Katharine Drexel Parish in Dorchester.

“Trump did not do this because he wants to save Christians, he wants something for himself,” he said. “His mind is always on money, and somehow, he thinks he’s going to get something.”

The United States coordinated with the Nigerian government to launch a series of airstrikes late Thursday against what it called “ISIS terrorists” in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto state where the Lakurawa, a small jihadist group, operates. The number of people injured or killed is unclear, but the US Africa Command said in a statement that initial assessment showed “multiple ISIS terrorists were killed in the ISIS camps.”

Other Nigerians here said that violence affects all residents of the country — and the Nigerian government hasn’t done enough to stop it.

“I’m not a fan of Trump, but people are dying, so he bombed,” said Ifeyinwa Izuchi, who left eastern Nigeria in 1977. “Maybe now the Nigerian government will do something.”

Victoria Awogboro, a Newton resident originally from western Nigeria, said the attack might give Nigerians in the United States a greater sense of security when traveling home.

“The help is needed because this has been going on for a long time and our military seems overwhelmed,” said Awogboro. “If the help is coming now and it’s channeled properly in collaboration with the [Nigerian] government and the military, then that’s a welcome development.”

Standing to her left, Izuchi nodded in agreement, adding that safety concerns while visiting Nigeria have grown in recent years.

“If I want to go home, I’m afraid of kidnapping and terrorists,” she said. “In a country that doesn’t allow its people to carry arms, you have [extremists] walking in the streets with AK-47s and nobody’s stopping them.

“At least now the world is paying attention.”

Trump initially claimed terrorists in the region were targeting Christians in November and threatened military action if the Nigerian government failed to address the alleged religious persecution.

But Trump’s assertion of widespread Christian persecution belies the complicated reality on the ground in Nigeria, one expert said.

“The claims there are that many Christians are specifically targeted for their faith is very, very exaggerated,” said Ladd Serwat, an Africa senior analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, which has monitored the expansion of jihadist groups across Nigeria since 1997.

Data show that 507 Christians died from political violence since 2020, out of a total 53,000 Christians and Muslims since 2009, according to the group.

“Insurgent groups such as Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa often present their campaigns as anti-Christian, but in practice their violence is indiscriminate and devastates entire communities,” Serwat said.

Some of the violence in the region also stems from both economic and religious tensions. Christian farmers and Muslim herders compete for scarce resources, noted Judd Devermont, an Africa Program senior adviser for the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The epicenter of violence in Nigeria is in the northeast, Devermont said, whereas most Nigerian immigrants to the United States hail from southern Nigeria.

While some local groups in Nigeria have direct ties to global extremist organizations, including Al Qaeda and ISIS, others are unaffiliated but embrace the goals of international terrorist organizations, Devermont said.

One of the most prominent terrorist groups in the region is Boko Haram, which has expressed solidarity with Al Qaeda, according to the US Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

The extremist group Lakurawa — which is increasing ties to both the Islamic State and Al Qaeda — is known to operate in Sokoto state, where the United States carried out the strikes.

Devermont called the location of the strikes “a little strange” given Trump’s stated motivation.

“It’s in an area where it’s 90 to 95 percent Muslims,” said Devermont, a former senior director of African affairs at the National Security Council. “It’s not the epicenter of extremist violence.”

MacPhilips said the location of the strikes also raised his suspicions.

“In the north, where the bomb fell, those guys had not seen Boko Haram or anything at all,” he said.

Nimi Wariboko, Walter G. Muelder Professor of Social Ethics and director of the Africa Studies Center at Boston University, said he doubts Trump carried out the attack for “altruistic purposes.”

The nation, and Western powers in general, have economic and strategic interests in Nigeria, he said.

Beyond that, Trump can use messaging that he is protecting Christians around the world to curry favor with his supporters.

“Trump is playing to the evangelical base at home here. He is playing the strong hand of the global defender of Christians and Christianity, and this plays well for his domestic politics,” Wariboko said.

It’s unlikely last week’s strikes alone will help curb terrorist activity in the region, experts said, as such military interventions rarely root out the issues that cause radicalization in the first place.

“Strikes in and of themselves are insufficient,” Devermont said. “It has to be paired with efforts to address what the drivers of extremism are.”

Wariboko said the strikes are “just the beginning.”

“Intelligence and news accounts suggest that the United States may strike again,” he said.

Globe staff writer Jaime Moore-Carrillo contributed to this report. Materials from the Associated Press were also used.

title: Former HR chief Denyse Medlenka takes over for Tim Rowe as CIC chief executive
text:
The Catalyst division aims to bring momentum to CIC’s consulting growth. One example: Maybe a city wants help in activating an underused industrial park. Can CIC provide some guidance without actually opening a CIC-branded shared workspace there?

“We often get asked . . . how do we do it?” Medlenka said. “That is how this other line of service started to come into existence.”

CIC Campuses is also expanding, beyond the 10 cities it currently serves, across 1.5 million square feet of offices and labs. It will open a life sciences campus in Osaka in mid-2026, for example, and is developing plans for a clean-tech hub in Brooklyn.

For Medlenka, the 300-person company’s mission offers great satisfaction. She’s helping entrepreneurs bring their visions to life, while playing an important role in broader economic ecosystems such as CIC’s home base, Cambridge’s Kendall Square. (Medlenka also serves on the Kendall Square Association’s board.)

“I love the idea of helping people live their dream,” Medlenka said.

One thing she doesn’t love: how early the sun sets here. She doesn’t mind the winter temps. The afternoon darkness, though, took some adjusting. (The sun sets more than an hour later in Dallas.) “I was surprised,” she said, “at how intense a 4:19 sunset could be.”

Governor Maura Healey, House Speaker Ron Mariano, Senate President Karen Spilka and other top politicians packed a State House room on Dec. 17 to underscore the findings of a task force assigned to combat antisemitism.

What went unmentioned was a parallel effort among business leaders. This month, around three dozen local executives signed a letter expressing support for the work done by the Special Commission on Combating Antisemitism, reflected in its 73-page report.

The business community engagement began at roundtable discussions held by Andrea Silbert of the Eos Foundation and Sandy Lish of the PR firm Castle Group to discuss antisemitism after the October 2023 Hamas attacks in Israel. (Silbert, who also chairs the Alliance for Business Leadership, got involved as a volunteer and not for Eos.) The attacks also prompted the state Legislature to create the special commission, and the two efforts eventually dovetailed.

Bridging the two was Red Sox executive David Friedman, the only Boston businessperson on the commission and a key participant in the roundtables. The hope with the letter, Friedman said, is to send the message that “this commonwealth takes antisemitism just as seriously as we take other forms of hate.”

Friedman added: “To have all these people jointly say, ‘Yeah, we know this is a big problem and we’re committed to standing up and trying to find solutions,’ I think is really important.”

Bob Marr would often say his greatest achievement was not his business success leading construction firm Marr Cos., but the creation of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester.

Marr died in 2022, but his legacy lives on: Widow Cynthia Marr, who heads up the family foundation, just committed $6.5 million to the Fieldhouse+ project that the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester — not to be confused with the Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston — is building on Columbia Point with the Martin Richard Foundation.

BGCD president Bob Scannell said they have raised $65 million so far, including this latest donation, for the 75,000-square-foot arts-and-recreation complex on Mt. Vernon Street. But tariffs and inflation have driven up the cost to an estimated $75 million. So Scannell needs another $10 million for construction, plus an additional $10 million for operating reserves.

Contractor Lee Kennedy started work this past spring, and it’s on track to open in 2027. Rob Hale and Karen Hale gave $10 million. Other contributors include New Balance, Herb Chambers, and the Corcoran family. The state is kicking in $12 million, along with two federal grants worth $2.5 million.

It’s a shame Marr isn’t around to see the Fieldhouse go up, but Scannell shared the plans with Marr before his death. “He literally had tears in his eyes,” Scannell said. “I can’t think of anyone who cared more about Dorchester than him.”

This wasn’t as good of a bargain as “The Shoe” but it sure is close.

Bill Cummings bought the old United Shoe Machinery factory in Beverly three decades ago for a song — $500,000 — and converted it into a massive 2-million-square foot complex. The purchase helped catapult Cummings into the real estate big leagues. The folks at his firm, Cummings Properties, like to joke that there were more pigeons than people there when they bought it — but that joke is also probably true.

Now, the bargain hunters at Cummings Properties have done it again: They’ve found a suburban corporate headquarters on the cheap that they need to fill up. This one is 330,000 square feet on nearly 55 acres in Bedford, and completely empty.

Cummings won an auction for the two-building complex off Middlesex Turnpike with a $5.6 million bid earlier this month. The office complex, owned by Orion Properties, was built for RSA Security around 25 years ago. RSA eventually moved to nearby Burlington, though Orion kept the property in pristine shape.

Finding another single tenant proved difficult, particularly in this market. (Cybersecurity firm STR had planned to relocate there from Woburn, but that deal fell through.) Cummings is already working on plans to subdivide it, even though the property won’t officially change hands until early January. Cummings typically buys its properties with cash — no debt — and that will be the case here. That enables Cummings to charge lower rents, Cummings president Eric Anderson said, which may help woo tenants.

Because of the parallels with the Shoe, it’s appropriate that Bob Heffernan, deputy field manager at Cummings, was asked to set up an office in the former RSA headquarters to help market the space. Heffernan, Anderson says, noted that Cummings gave him the same assignment 30 years ago to set up shop at the Shoe. This time, he probably won’t have any pigeons to worry about.

The new year will mean a new mayor in Newton — and a new name for the law firm he used to lead.

As Marc Laredo prepares to be sworn in as mayor, taking over for Ruthanne Fuller, he’s wrapping up matters at the Boston firm he cofounded in 1996, now called Laredo, Smith & Kane. In the new year, it will just be Smith Kane as Laredo exits the firm.

Laredo was already starting to step back. A year ago, Matthew Kane took over for Laredo as the 10-person litigation firm’s managing partner, and Kane was added to the firm’s name with little fanfare. There will be a bigger push to promote the latest iteration. (Partner Mark Smith, who joined about 25 years ago, will remain on board.)

Laredo says he’ll miss working with his clients. But the longtime city councilor will now need to spend more time on solving school budget issues, making sure the parks stay green and the trash gets picked upon time, and dealing with other headaches of municipal government. He said: “It’s very important to me that a place I helped build thrives going forward [and] we transition to the next generation.”

title: Man charged with beating elderly neighbor in dispute over wrongly delivered package in Mattapan
text:
A Boston man with a lengthy criminal history was ordered held last week after his 77-year-old neighbor was found allegedly beaten with a swollen eye over a wrongly delivered package, prosecutors said Monday.

Khalil Muhammad, 29, is facing charges of assault and battery on a person over 60 and unarmed robbery, the Suffolk district attorney’s office said in a statement.

He currently has an open case out of East Boston court with the charges of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, assault and battery on a police officer, resisting arrest, and class B possession of narcotics, prosecutors said, on top of being on probation for two other cases from the Dorchester division of Boston Municipal Court.

“Muhammad has a criminal history of violent offenses in both Massachusetts and New York dating back to 2015,” prosecutors said in the statement.

His bail was revoked from the East Boston case during his arraignment in Dorchester court and he was held on a detention detainer due to the probation violations, prosecutors said.

Muhammad’s attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday evening.

Boston police went to 730 Cummins Highway in Mattapan for an assault in progress on Dec. 22 and a witness said a man had assaulted her neighbor and taken his phone, prosecutors said.

The elderly victim was found “badly beaten with his eyes swollen shut, a bleeding cut under one eye, and unable to answer questions” and taken to the hospital, according to the statement.

Muhammad told police that his neighbor allegedly went to his apartment and accused him of “stealing” his package, prosecutors said.

The victim later told officers that he went to get his Amazon package, which was allegedly delivered to Muhammad’s apartment, prosecutors said. Muhammad allegedly “punched him in the face and tore his $700 Motorola phone from his hand,” the statement read.

He was allegedly beaten by Muhammad as he fled upstairs to his apartment, prosecutors said.

“We take all assaults seriously, and the facts present here—an elderly victim suffering considerable injuries after being subjected to an extended attack—are particularly egregious. Escalating an incident of a mis-delivered package to such violence is intolerable,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement.

Muhammad is set to return to court on Jan. 22.

Breanne Kovatch can be reached at breanne.kovatch@globe.com. Follow her @breannekovatch.

title: Unfinished business: Sluggish hiring, AI disruption, tariffs, and sticky inflation to linger into 2026
text:
Tariffs have taken a toll on US small businesses.

Will RFK Jr. help or hinder a ‘Big Tobacco’-style reckoning for ultraprocessed food?

PhDs can’t find work as Boston’s biotech engine sputters.

As another year winds down, forecasts for what comes next are everywhere.

But for the economy, 2026 is shaping up less as a fresh start than as a sequel. The big storylines from 2025 — about jobs, artificial intelligence, and tariffs — have yet to be resolved. Mounting frustration with the high cost of living is poised to be a pivotal issue in November’s midterm elections.

When the ball drops in Times Square on Wednesday night, the TV chyron should read “To be continued.”

Where things stand: Government data released this month after shutdown-related delays offer a snapshot of an economy that looks strong on the surface but fragile underneath.

Gross domestic product expanded at a 4.3 percent annual rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace in two years. Solid gains in consumer spending and exports offset a decline in residential and business investment.

But the top-line numbers mask signs of cooling.

Unemployment is rising and inflation remains elevated. Wage growth is easing and households are saving less than they did earlier in the year, suggesting that incomes aren’t keeping pace with rising costs.

“While top level growth of 4.3 percent looks good prima facie, there are some troubling signs when you pop open the hood,” Boston College economist Brian Bethune said in a note.

Still, the probability of recession remains low — 30 percent, according to economists tracked by Bloomberg, down from 40 percent after President Trump rolled out his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April.

Jobs: The labor market has been sluggish and is expected to remain so next year.

Employers added more than a million fewer jobs in the first 11 months of the year than they did last year. That’s despite GDP growth running near its top sustainable pace.

While layoffs have remained relatively tame, an influx of job seekers nudged US unemployment up to 4.6 percent in November, the highest since 2021.

Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell doesn’t see the jobless rate climbing much further, an assessment shared by most private forecasters.

“We won’t see any kind of a sharper downturn” in employment, he told reporters earlier this month.

The Fed’s optimism stems from its belief that interest rates are now low enough to steady the labor market. (Policymakers have cut their benchmark lending rate by 1.75 percentage points to a range of 3.5–3.75 percent since September 2024.)

AI: Artificial intelligence promises to reshape the economy, but its impact on workers remains a big unknown.

Products such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini improved dramatically, speeding adoption by businesses and consumers. Spending on AI hardware, software, and data centers accelerated economic growth. And AI exuberance spilled into the stock market, raising concerns that a bubble is about to burst.

More importantly, AI poses the threat of massive job losses. Many firms have already curtailed hiring as they assess how they will deploy the technology. Some have laid off workers in anticipation of more widespread AI use.

“Despite concerns about widespread job losses, AI adoption is expected to have only a modest and relatively temporary impact on employment levels,” Goldman Sachs researchers wrote in an August report.

At the other extreme, Dario Amodei, chief executive of AI-maker Anthropic, has said AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 10–20 percent within five years.

“Without intervention, it’s hard to imagine that there won’t be some significant job impact there. And my worry is that it will be broad, and it will be faster than what we’ve seen with previous technology,” Amodei said in an interview that CBS News’ “60 Minutes” aired in November.

Tariffs: All of this — a cooling labor market and a fast-moving AI transition — is unfolding against the backdrop of disruptive trade policy.

Economists initially warned that Trump’s tariffs — a 10 percent baseline import tax plus rates of up to 40 percent on nearly all US trading partners — would light a fire under inflation or cause a recession. It didn’t happen. The president backed off some tariffs and postponed others, and companies rushed to build up inventories while absorbing some or all of their increased costs.

In 2026, tariffs are expected to be a modest drag on GDP. The Conference Board forecasts that year-over-year growth will slow to 1.3 percent in the fourth quarter of next year, down from 1.7 percent this year.

Tariffs will also keep inflation higher than it would otherwise be as US firms pass on more of their increased costs to customers. In September, the Fed projected that its preferred inflation gauge — which excludes often volatile food and energy costs — would rise 2.6 percent next year, up from a June estimate of 2.4 percent. The central bank’s target is 2 percent.

Final thought: A weak labor market, AI disruption, and tariff headwinds are a recipe for uncertainty but not an imminent recession.

But they may well leave Americans frustrated with a slow-moving economy and high prices, especially if tariffs don’t yield the gains in US jobs that Trump promised. If so, the midterm elections could deliver a harsher-than-usual rebuke to Republicans as the party in power.

Welcome to 2026. Don’t be surprised if it feels a lot like 2025.

“The pessimists have just been wrong for so long that people are kind of tired of that schtick.”

— Stock market strategist Ed Yardeni. None of the 21 Wall Street prognosticators surveyed by Bloomberg News is predicting a market decline in 2026.

Crying foul: How a developer’s lawsuit against Cambridge aims to topple affordable housing rules across Massachusetts.

Secret to success: Warren Buffett’s greatest asset is his character, writes biographer Roger Lowenstein.

Dreambuilder: The family foundation of Bob Marr, the construction firm owner who died in 2022, has pledged $6.5 million to help make the Fieldhouse+ project in Dorchester a reality.

Legal twist: The Trump administration has launched investigations into the use of diversity initiatives in hiring and promotion at major US companies, built on the novel use of a federal law meant to punish businesses that cheat the government.

Slamming the door: What America might look like with zero immigration.

Change of address: Google is rolling out a new feature that allows users to change their @gmail.com addresses without losing their data.

$400,000

— The value of lobster meat that vanished en route from a warehouse in Taunton to Costco locations in the Midwest.

It’s been a good year for stocks, though not quite as good as 2023 or 2024.

Going into the final three trading days of 2025, the Standard & Poor’s 500 index had returned 19 percent including dividends. The tech-heavy Nasdaq’s return was 23 percent. For all of last year, the indexes returned 25 percent and 30 percent, respectively.

But even with all the focus on the AI-fueled stock rally, the big gains were found elsewhere this year.

Silver soared 174 percent through Friday, outshining gold, which gained 73. Investors have plowed into both metals as a hedge against political uncertainty and inflation. Silver’s surge also reflects demand from industrial users.

On the downside, the spot price of crude oil at the Cushing, Okla., hub dropped 18 percent. Supply has been steadier than forecast and demand has been weaker than hoped.

After setting a record in October, the bitcoin rally — sparked in part by demand from new exchange traded funds — has faltered. The cryptocurrency was off 6.3 percent for the year as of Friday as investors moved their money to gold, silver, and other better-performing assets.

As always, please remember that past performance is not indicative of future results.

📆 On this date in 1891, Thomas Edison patented a wireless telegraphy system — based on electromagnetic induction and conduction — that anticipated some practical uses of cable-free communication, but it was distinct from the radio technologies developed a decade later.

title: Here’s a look at some of the weirdest local business stories of 2025
text:
Consumer brands often take a turn for the boring under private equity ownership. Apparently, no one at Dunkin’ HQ got the memo. Coolatta-powered marketers dreamed up what they call the “DunKings Cinematic Universe,” maybe Boston’s answer to the Marvel movies. Ben Affleck is Iron Man in another DunKings ad released around Super Bowl time; his Avengers include brother Casey (natch), Bill Belichick with Jordon Hudson, Jeremy Strong (in a vat of coffee beans), and a Wahlberg (Donnie). Who’s next? Maybe Chris Evans joins them for a DCU-Marvel crossover.

The offshore wind industry had nothing to smile about this year, with Donald Trump in the White House, except for one thing: a quote in a Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court ruling, siding with a wind farm developer over a Cape Cod neighbor. The decision, authored by Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt, quotes Simon & Garfunkel’s “The Sound of Silence” by starting off with the lines “And no one dared/Disturb the sound of silence” — a reference to the legal controversy around “cacophonous industrial components” in a Barnstable substation. The SJC even credits the folk-rock duo in a footnote, noting the album (“Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.”), record company (Columbia), and release year (1964). More rock trivia, less legal minutia, please.

The Downtown Boston Alliance keeps getting creative to attract crowds post-pandemic, particularly in the colder months. In 2024, it was floating clown heads. This past year: floating naked pink people, and an illegally parked Nissan Altima with its hood crushed by what looks like a 1960s-era satellite that fell out of the sky.
