There was much online chatter about whether the parking ticket on the windshield was real, and even more after someone ripped the 150-pound satellite off the car, only to discover it too heavy to steal.

Defense company Anduril Industries deployed a strange marketing strategy, blanketing South Station and too many buses to count with billboards proclaiming “Don’t Work at Anduril” (with the “Don’t Work at,” or at least the “Don’t,” made to look like it was spray-painted over the company’s name). There was even a spoof video featuring a disgruntled worker complaining that “here they have you doing actual work.” The intended message: Anduril isn’t for everyone, but please send your resume.

Investment guru Jim Pallotta is known for his previous ownership stakes in the Celtics and the AS Roma soccer team. But in 2025, he was selling something else: a 21,000-square-foot mansion nestled in the Weston woods. The spread, featured in the Wall Street Journal, includes the obligatory swimming pool, outdoor basketball court, and indoor listening room, along with a storage room for his wife’s collection of antique Santas. (The Journal story implied that the figurines were not included in the $38 million list price.)

Were those people on the bridge over the Mass. Turnpike dressed like poop emojis? Yup. The banner they held said “Cut the Crap,” after all. The Charles River Watershed Association deployed these costumed crusaders to pressure the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority to halt the practice of allowing rainwater to mix with sewage in local rivers. (The poop outfits also showed up at a State House hearing on the topic.) As far as the environment is concerned, sometimes you need to give a crap.

Yeah, I hate Southeast Expressway traffic as much as the next commuter. But still. Who thought it was a good idea to start flights between Boston and New Bedford, especially after the South Coast city just started getting commuter rail service to Boston? Cape Air launched the flights in September, and ended them less than two months later. Sure, the trip, gate-to-gate, was only around 35 minutes. But the only thing worse than sitting in your car on I-93 in Dorchester might be standing in Logan, waiting to get through security.

Is the recession finally here? It is if you take CNN at its word that knee-high sneakers from Boston-based Converse are “possibly the most obvious recession indicator of them all.” CNN linked to a TikTok video showing these too-tall shoes in a shop window, with the caption: “this has gotta be a recession indicator.” One commenter wrote: “If I’m paying for a shoe, I’m getting as much shoe as possible.” The CNN report also mentioned the return of canned goods, coupons, and Lady Gaga. With those indicators in mind, CNN somehow missed the latest release of Kowloon-themed sneakers, designed by Tagz Footwear, and what they say about the state of things.

The hoopla leading up to the supposed launch of a Boston Monopoly game may have exceeded the hype for Monopoly owner Hasbro’s decision to move its headquarters to Boston. But manufacturer Top Trumps USA still doesn’t list a Boston game among its 47 city-themed Monopoly editions. No word on why. For now, we’ll have to be content with the 1990s Boston edition (available on eBay), created when BayBank and Filene’s were still around. Strangely, there’s no space for Dunkin’ Donuts, Boston’s closest thing to an actual monopoly.

The Trump-era tariffs made life tough for those in the logistics and shipping industry. Good thing we have drug companies like Takeda around to lighten the mood. Takeda announced plans to be the first biopharmaceutical business to use French boat maker Vela Transport’s wind-powered cargo vessel to ship treatments from Europe to the United States. The trips will take two weeks and help Takeda meet its greenhouse gas emissions goals. Test runs start next year on trimarans that look like racing boats but are in fact something else entirely.

Hasbro wasn’t the only company on the move. Welch’s inked a deal to relocate to Waltham from Concord. The fruit-juice cooperative also set its sights on Manhattan by opening a speakeasy in the West Village to highlight its zero-sugar drinks, with ad agency Superdigital. The space was fitted out to look like a New York City bodega, complete with an analog TV on the counter and an animatronic “bodega cat.” This was purely promotional: The pop-up shop “sold” Zero Sugar-themed lip balm and lunchboxes for zero dollars apiece.

Fall in New England means pumpkins, football, foliage, more pumpkins, hayrides, apple-picking, and now “Spidey D.” Just when you thought it was safe to venture into your local Dunks, the ads reappeared on menu boards and social media accounts featuring the spider doughnut character with random misspelled musings. The ad industry swooned over this “unruly spokes-dessert,” and the purple doughnut sold out at many shops. Next year, let’s see if Dunkin’ can get Ben Affleck in the room with this absurd arachnid.

title: Immigration crackdown, an assisted living facility fire, university tragedy: Some of the top local stories of 2025
text:
The first year of the second Donald Trump presidency brought upheaval to federal food programs, universities, and vaccine policy. A surge of ICE arrests and mass deportations have created fear for immigrants and their families. In March, Tufts University graduate student Rümeysa Öztürk was swarmed by masked agents on a Somerville street and arrested, despite holding a student visa.

Restrictions outlined in President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” mean that over 150,000 Massachusetts residents could see their federal food assistance, also known as SNAP, reduced or cut. Harvard University and the Trump administration went toe-to-toe, with Trump accusing Harvard of pushing liberal ideology and antisemitism and Harvard saying the issue is part of a broader pressure campaign against the school.

Meanwhile, research grants from NIH, NSF, and the Department of Energy were abruptly cut, leaving New England scientists scrambling. And when decades-old federal vaccine guidance changed under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s CDC, Massachusetts published its own recommendations and required insurers to cover the cost of those vaccines.

Tragedy at Brown, Brookline

Two students were killed and nine were injured after a gunman opened fire at Brown University just days before winter break. Scheduled holiday celebrations turned into somber vigils for the slain students, Ella Cook and MukhammadAziz Umurzokov. Then, an MIT physics professor was shot and killed in his Brookline home. A frantic manhunt — in which police pleaded for public assistance in identifying a person of interest — lasted days. Finally, a flood of information led police to a storage locker in New Hampshire, where the gunman, Claudio Manuel Neves Valente, was dead. He was believed to have committed both crimes.

A nightmare in Fall River

On July 13, a pleasant evening was shattered when a fire broke out at Gabriel House, an assisted living facility with 69 residents in Fall River. Flames, heat, and dense, dark smoke quickly tore through the building, killing 10 individuals in the deadliest fire in the state in 41 years. Former residents have since filed wrongful death lawsuits against the facility, its embattled owner Dennis Etzkorn, and the safety equipment provider. And the fire raised questions about the living conditions at Gabriel House, which has a spotty regulatory record and lax emergency procedures.

New Hampshire mom does the unthinkable

Emily Long was open about her struggling on TikTok. Her husband had been diagnosed with glioblastoma, a brain cancer, and she alluded to money concerns in her videos. On Aug. 18, Long shot and killed her husband, two of their children, and then herself. The only survivor was their toddler, 3-year-old James, who was found near his family physically unharmed. After her death, records revealed that Long’s employer had accused her of embezzling more than $600,000. But the Long family, now caring for James, don’t expect to ever understand why she did it.

Skating dreams cut short

An American Airlines midair collision over the Potomac River on Jan. 29 took 67 lives, including six people connected to the Skating Club of Boston. The jet collided with an Army helicopter near Washington, D.C., killing everyone on board. Figure skaters Spencer Lane and Jinna Han were rising stars in the highly competitive sport, traveling with their parents Christine Lane and Jin Han. Veteran coaches Evgenia Shishkova and Vadim Naumov, who represented Russia in the 1994 Olympics, also died in the crash. Months later, grief hangs over the grind of daily training in Norwood.

Retrial draws crowds then acquits Karen Read

Karen Read’s case was retried in Norfolk County Superior Court, drawing a sea of pink supporters outside the courthouse. After a weekslong murder trial, a jury ruled Read was not guilty of murdering her boyfriend, John O’Keefe, a Boston police officer, and not guilty of manslaughter. She was convicted of driving under the influence and sentenced to one year probation. Now, the drama persists, with trial followers speculating about what actually might have happened.

Wu cruises to next term, greater national prominence

Mayor Michelle Wu took a decisive victory in the city’s preliminary election for mayor, winning about 72 percent of the vote and easily securing her second term. Her skills as a politician were tested and proved in Boston and on the national stage. When Wu was called alongside three other Democratic mayors to a congressional hearing on immigration enforcement, Wu appeared at ease, nursing her newborn daughter and firing back at attacks from Republicans. In Boston, Wu was endorsed by the largest Boston police union and her allies filled City Council leadership.

Climate concerns muddy New England waters

As climate change continues to accelerate, New Englanders are feeling the effects. A Boston Globe project chronicled the risk of rising floodwaters in small town, coastal Massachusetts and behind inland levees. The promise of rising seas threatens the buoy that the Seaport gives Boston’s property tax base. Home insurance premiums have surged in coastal communities from Connecticut to Maine as scores of policies have been abruptly dropped. And a new proposal in Boston — dismaying clean river advocates — would allow continued sewage release into the Charles by changing the water quality classification of the river.

An anniversary approaching

As the 250th anniversary of America approaches, the state is planning for a celebration. Already, Lexington and Concord marked the 250th anniversary of the opening battles of the American Revolution with daylong battlefield reenactments. And in Bunker Hill, descendants of veterans from around the country gathered for a parade and battle reenactment, swapping stories of bravery and sacrifice. But organizers fear the planning will be too little, too late. Some lawmakers and historians said Massachusetts has fallen behind other states in local grants and grass-roots programming.

Search for accountability after boy killed by school bus

In April, a Boston Public Schools bus struck and killed 5-year-old Lens Joseph. The bus driver had been in several prior crashes and lacked proper state credentials, city officials announced in May as they launched an independent investigation into the busing contractor. After warning BPS to improve driver training and safety measures, commercial transportation insurer National Interstate refused to renew the district’s coverage because of a rising number of crashes, according to reports obtained by the Globe. Joseph, the Hyde Park kindergartener, was remembered as older than his years, dedicated to his schoolwork and his love of Spider-Man.

Frequenters of Cambridge brothel ring identified

Authorities have sought charges against at least 28 men who they say most frequently exchanged text messages with the Cambridge brothel hot line and made multiple appointments. The brothel network operated for three years in Cambridge, Watertown, and the suburbs of Washington, D.C. After months of judicial delay, some of the men were publicly identified in court, including Paul Toner, a Cambridge city councilor, and James C. Cusack Jr., a local surgical oncologist.

Boston police officers disciplined after Dorchester crash

Three teenagers were killed in a 2024 rollover crash on Morrissey Boulevard, which occurred after accelerating to speeds that reached 106 miles per hour as police continued to follow them. Reports and related video obtained by the Globe show that officers continued to follow the car with lights flashing even after being told to stand down by a supervisor. This year, an internal investigation found the chase to be a violation of department policy: one of the officers was suspended for 30 days, another has since resigned, and a termination decision was pending for the third officer.

Amid the mayhem, some bright spots

After more than nine months in space, Needham-bred astronaut Sunita Williams came back to Earth to an honorary degree and a warm welcome from her dogs. Williams was originally sent to space for an eight-day test flight to the International Space Station, but her stay was extended due to technical difficulties. The first American pope, elected in May, blessed a South Boston baby. The Chicago native also adorned a White Sox cap donated by a newlywed Haverhill couple — diehard Red Sox Fans.

title: Dorchester man arrested on murder charge after Mattapan triple shooting that left woman dead, two injured
text:
A Dorchester man, charged with murder in connection with a triple shooting in Mattapan earlier this year that killed an 18-year old woman and injured two men, was arrested early Tuesday morning. An arrest warrant has been issued for a second suspect, authorities said.

At approximately 6 a.m., members of the Boston Police SWAT Team along with homicide detectives, served an arrest warrant at 260 Ruggles St. in Roxbury and took Dkhari Wornum-Brown, 22, into custody, according to a statement from Boston police.

He was arraigned in the Dorchester division of Boston Municipal Court Tuesday on charges of first-degree murder and carrying an unlicensed firearm, police said.

Judge Rebeca Figueroa ordered that Wornum-Brown be held without bail. His next court date, a probable-cause hearing, was set for Feb. 5, according to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office.

Wornum-Brown was not the shooter, prosecutors said. An arrest warrant has been issued for the alleged gunman. Authorities did not disclose that person’s identity.

Wornum-Brown’s arrest stems from an afternoon shooting in Mattapan on Oct. 11. Police responded to a ShotSpotter activation at 2 Hiawatha Road and found three people suffering from gunshot wounds; all three were taken to local hospitals, authorities said.

According to prosecutors, five people were hanging out on the front porch when two men rode up on a scooter. Wornum-Brown drove the scooter, and the other man hopped off and fired off at least 21 rounds, striking three people. The shooter got back onto the scooter and the two men fled the scene.

Two of the victims were men who suffered nonlife-threatening wounds. But a third victim, 18-year-old G’Kiyah Lewis of Malden, eventually died of her injuries weeks later, police said.

“The violent death of G’Kiyah Lewis is a societal tragedy,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Tuesday. “I’m grateful for the great investigative effort that brought someone forward to answer for this terrible crime and I urge the second suspect to turn himself in before he or anyone else gets hurt.”

Hayden extended his “deepest sympathies to G’Kiyah’s family and friends.”

Investigators used video, GPS tracking, and other circumstantial evidence to identify the alleged suspects, according to the district attorney’s office.

Lewis was a Malden High School senior who loved fashion, the beach, and having her photo taken, her mother, Rehema Grayson, had told The Boston Globe. She was hanging out with her boyfriend and other friends, her mother said, when a bullet went through her arm, grazed her heart, and lodged in her head.

She leaves behind two younger sisters, aged 7 and 15, her mother said.

After her death, Lewis’ organs were donated to three people, a 60-year-old woman and two men in their 40s, her mother said.

Faith leaders and community activists had demanded police action and urged residents to come forward with any information about her killing.

“None of our children should die in the streets,” said the Rev. Kevin Peterson, a community minister and public theologian at Grace Church of All Nations. “No blood should be in the streets of our community.”

Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports. Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com. Follow her @talanez.

title: At Acapella by X, nighttime is the right time
text:
The backstory: This space was long the Blarney Stone, an Irish pub that was a Dorchester institution. Now business partners and longtime friends Freddy Ureña (chef), Yancarlo Fernandez (general manager), and Anthony Cruz (front-of-house manager) have created Acapella, which soft-opened in November and will see its grand opening in January. The “X” is Dorchester native Fernandez’s business group, which also includes a car wash, liquor stores, and Dominican fast-casual PikaloX. Ureña, who grew up in East Boston and attended Le Cordon Bleu in Cambridge, went on to cook in Spain, as a private chef in Dubai, and at area hotel restaurants including Zuma before pivoting to biotech during the pandemic. Acapella is a family affair for him: Wife, Joanna, is also in the kitchen, with daughters Emma and Brianna working as floor manager and bartender, respectively. In opening a venue with an upscale atmosphere, the business partners hope to fill a niche in Fields Corner. “We felt like the community needed something like this,” Ureña says.

What to eat: The menu draws from Ureña’s travels, offering Spanish tapas (patatas bravas, pan con tomate, blistered shishito peppers), tacos, a Turkish salad, and dumplings, along with the likes of steak tips and lobster ravioli. Start with the ceviche, featuring the fish of the day in a bright, refreshing Peruvian leche de tigre marinade, with onions, cilantro, radish, and crunchy toasted corn kernels. Pork and chive dumplings come in a ponzu-soy sauce. Scallops glazed in citrusy butter are delicate bites served on toothpicks for easy hors d’oeuvres-ing. Those who love a cheese-and-charcuterie board will appreciate the generous fried truffle burrata, surrounded by arugula, sliced tomatoes, folds of prosciutto, and toasts, with a ramekin of guava glaze. Grilled skirt steak comes sliced thin with chimichurri sauce, flavorful and nicely cooked, with coarse salt for sprinkling. For the kids: chicken tenders and sliders, both served with fries. Dessert brings the likes of pineapple upside-down cake and Dubai chocolate tres leches.

What to drink: The beverage program is focused on cocktails, with classics (mojitos, margaritas, pisco sours, espresso martinis) alongside house creations like the Fresa Picante (strawberries with mezcal and ancho chile) and La Flor (hibiscus and rum). Perhaps of extra Dry January interest, the mocktails are worthy, not mere afterthoughts: The balanced Felinas (lemonade, apple, ginger beer, and spices) and fruity Citrus & Tonic (grapefruit, guava, rose, and mint) are goblets garnished with fruit and herbs.

The takeaway: A priest, a baby, and a group of women dressed to the nines walk into a bar… A recent midweek visit to Acapella is both perfect setup to a joke and lovely snapshot of the neighborhood. A Berklee student is singing at the front of the room, with its mood lighting, stylish bar, and brick walls painted white. When the weather warms, there will be a patio seating about 80 people. Valet parking is slated for the future, and weekends have been wild, Ureña says, with birthday parties and private events. It seems Fields Corner is ready for its own nighttime scene, and Acapella by X is here to provide.

1505 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-286-4620, www.acapellabyx.com. Appetizers $9-$24, tapas $7-$20, main dishes $26-$45, cocktails $17-$20.

title: First Night Boston puts diversity and culture at center stage
text:
Rios has been attending First Night Boston for the last 38 years and makes a full night of it — after the parade and 7 p.m. fireworks over the Common, dinner at Faneuil Hall follows, and then more fireworks at midnight over Boston Harbor.

“This night is just for me,” Rios said, explaining that it’s a night of solo festivities for her, since she can’t get anyone else to brave the cold. “I love it. We have to celebrate a new year.”

First timers Jon Lutke and family — including his wife, daughter, and son — came from Wisconsin to celebrate the New Year and son Micah’s eighth birthday.

On winter break, they were skiing in New Hampshire when they decided to check out Boston’s celebration. It was the family-centric vibe that attracted them.

“We had heard that this was a pretty good family-friendly event,” Lutke said. “And they had always wanted to come to Boston. So it just worked out.”

For Kim Cook and her four children, ages 7, 10, and two who are 12, it’s “the family time” that makes First Night Boston “special for us,” she said.

Their annual New Year’s Eve trek from Dorchester to downtown Boston for the revelries has become “a family tradition,” she said.

With temperatures in the low 30s descending into the 20s, First Night Boston marked a cold opening to 2026.

As of late Wednesday night, there had been no arrests or any major disruptions related to the festivities, according to Sergeant Detective John Boyle, a spokesperson for Boston police.

Soon after the festivities started at noon, Copley Square was crowded with Bostonians bundled in winter coats to attend celebration, a series of free events and musical performances that, for 50 years, has marked the start of the new year for the city.

Lines formed outside Boston’s landmark Trinity Church to relish musical performances from an orchestra and choir that performed hymns under the church’s majestic golden arches about the day the United States put an end to slavery. The concert, in its 12th year, is held on the same day that President Abraham Lincoln declared the end of slavery in the US in 1863.

This year, the concert marked an important cornerstone in American history as the country turns 250 years old.

“During this significant anniversary, it feels like we are taking a step back as a country because we are taking away so many people’s liberties,” said Allana Matthews, a singer and member of the Unitus Ensemble, which performed during the concert. “Now is the time to show that we will fight for our freedom of speech and our liberty.”

The First Night celebration has come a long way since it first brought together a small group of local artists to ring in the new year in 1976.

Diverging from most New Year’s festivities that centered on loud parties and alcohol, First Night built upon the tradition of elevating community-based initiatives that celebrate culture and American diversity and history instead.

This year’s celebration is occurring during the second Trump administration, which has been widely criticized for challenging free speech protections by deploying federal agents to target protestors supporting Palestinian rights and Black Lives Matter. Trump also came under scrutiny over the past year for restricting civil liberties through an immigration crackdown which the government says has led to the deportation of over 2.5 million people and for nixing federal funding for diversity initiatives.

Still, at Boston’s First Night celebration, diversity was alive and thriving.

People came from all over Greater Boston and beyond to attend Trinity Church’s Emancipation Proclamation event. The pews, which take up every corner of the majestic church, can hold up to 1,400 people. They were so packed that people had to be turned away at the door. Hosted by the Handel and Haydn Society and the Museum of African American History, the event featured orchestra and chorus performances of hymns about the liberation of the slaves and a reading by Massachusetts poet laureate Regie Gibson.

Even in 30-degree weather, the Greater Boston Chinese Cultural Association put together a series of performances in Copley Square that drew dozens of people from all over the city to watch.

Mira Rifai, an analyst from Allston who carries out technical and administrative reviews at a hospital, was taking time off from work and decided to come watch those performances unfold.

“There are so many different cultures in Boston and it’s so cool to see what the city has to offer,” Rifai said. “Events like these remind us that we are all stronger together.”

The celebration featured a traditional fan dance carried out by a group of students from the Angel Dance Company in Weston, and a group of kids from a martial arts studio in Watertown mimicking a lion’s movements in a colorful costume.

Michelle Lin, who owns the Wu An Martial Arts studio that led the Lion dance, said that in China it is typically performed during the lunar new year to usher in good luck for the coming year.

“I want to be hopeful and optimistic for the new year ahead,” Lin said. “There are a lot of people right now that are fearing for their safety for being different. So its important to celebrate diversity right now and maintain an open mind and an open heart.”

Optimism for the year ahead echoed in the minds and hearts of others who came to see the shows.

For 75-year-old Sandra Harris from South Boston, events like First Night are all about bringing people together. Harris is the cofounder of the Coalition to Build Community & End Loneliness and is constantly looking for ways to make people feel included.

She attended an event hosted by A Trike Called Funk, a Boston-based mobile DJ unit, at which street dance performers taught the audience how to move to the beat of the African diaspora in the Americas, swaying to rhythms of hip-hop, salsa, and samba.

“It’s opportunities like these where we get to meet our neighbors and come together to celebrate that we build community,” Harris said, “and I am optimistic that this is a new beginning for all of us and that we will continue to come together in the new year.”

Local artists who thrive on elevating their communities also took center stage at First Night celebrations.

Latoria Boyd, who performs R&B and soul music with the stage name ToriTori, played songs to a crowd of more than 50 people at the Boston Public Library.

The Dorchester native, who now lives in Brockton, said one of her main goals is to give back to the community that has supported her by offering free shows.

“I really feel like I would not be where I am today if it wasn’t for the support of the community,” she said. “I just want to give back.”

Tonya Alanez of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Mayor Michelle Wu, Boston city councilors to be sworn in for new term in office Monday
text:
“We will not appease or abet any threat to our city, and we will not wait for permission to build the world our families deserve,” Wu said. “Boston will be the proof that the nation we fought for is possible — a place where we take care of each other and take on the challenges that matter the most.”

Wu’s second inauguration, following a decisive reelection victory last fall, reaffirmed her considerable influence over Boston politics on a day that kept the face of city leadership largely unchanged and saw one of Wu’s allies elected City Council president. Wu was sworn in at Boston Symphony Hall by Sarah G. Kim, an associate justice of the Massachusetts Superior Court, as her two older children, sons Blaise and Cass, held a Bible beneath her hand. Wu then administered the oath of office to the 13 members of the council, 12 of them incumbents returning to office.

Wu’s remarks — which echoed her past pledges to improve Boston’s education system, tackle its affordability crisis, and protect the job sectors that power the city’s economy — underscored that continuity. Wu said she will spend the next four years continuing to improve school facilities and better city services. And, as the nation prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary, Wu evoked American history as she promised to continue standing against a Trump administration that has repeatedly targeted the Democrat-run city.

“Right now, in some ways, the world feels helplessly stuck — like we know what problems need fixing, but we’ve lost faith we can fix them," Wu said. “Today, the forces we face aren’t British troops on the Common or ships in our harbor, but they demand no less ingenuity.”

Much of Wu’s speech centered on what her administration has already done. Wu said during her second term, she would continue to use “local government as the bedrock for getting results.”

Wu also took some shots at a Trump administration she said has “plundered our economy, ravaged our reputation, and destroyed the lives of our people.” She pledged to defend higher education, life sciences, hospitals, and clean energy — all sectors that the Trump administration has explicitly targeted or defunded.

Wu in the last year has earned support locally and attention nationally for sparring with the Trump administration. Still, her tone on Monday sounded somewhat milder than in some of her election year speeches, when she painted Boston as the defiant vanguard of the Trump resistance.

“God save whoever messes with Boston,” Wu warned in a speech last year. Her message Monday, though, sounded less provocative than defensive — guarded against economic uncertainty and threats from an unpredictable federal administration.

“This is certainly a moment where we have to make some tough choices about what comes next, and be clear that Boston and every community is having to do more with less. But we are going to keep doing more,” Wu told reporters.

Wu in Monday’s address said she plans to expand on some initiatives from her first term, but she did not propose major new programs. She pledged to make the country’s oldest public school system its best by “rightsizing our district” and investing in school facilities. Wu also said the city would “revisit school assignment” to make the process “simpler and more predictable.”

“We refuse to accept that accessing high quality education means crisscrossing our children all over our city rather than ensuring that, in every corner of Boston, the best school is just down the block,” Wu said.

She also touched on the city’s housing production and cost-of-living challenges, though she did not detail any specific new plans for tackling those challenges.

This week marks the official start of Wu’s second four-year term as mayor, and a new two-year term for the council. Monday’s event kicked off a week of planned community gatherings, including story times at libraries around the city, a gathering of faith leaders, and a celebration of small businesses.

Wu, the first woman and person of color elected to lead the city, sailed to victory in November. She appeared unopposed on the general election ballot after challenger Josh Kraft dropped out of the race following a dismal performance in the September preliminary.

A former city councilor who has long wielded influence over the body, Wu also helped council allies secure reelection in November. The panel appears likely to remain friendly to her policy agenda: Every incumbent councilor who sought reelection won in November.

Following Monday’s inauguration ceremony, the council elected Councilor Liz Breadon its new president, in a narrow 7–6 vote that followed a contentious debate. A 66-year-old physical therapist and immigrant from Northern Ireland, Breadon is the first openly gay female councilor and has been an outspoken advocate for LGBTQ+ rights.

Councilor Brian Worrell of Dorchester narrowly lost the election. The contest had been thrown into uncertainty over the weekend after a front-runner for the role, Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, said she would not seek the presidency after all.

There is just one new face on the council this year: Rev. Miniard Culpepper, a longtime Dorchester activist, pastor, and former attorney for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, who was sworn in Monday. He represents Roxbury-based District 7, a seat that had sat vacant for months after former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges last year and resigned from the position in July.

While Wu has yet to detail her full agenda for the next four years, she has indicated one of her top priorities is making Boston Public Schools the “best major city school district” in the country.

It’s an ambitious goal and a daunting challenge: BPS’ persistent problems — including dropping enrollment numbers, decades-old facilities, and stubbornly low test scores — have vexed many of Wu’s predecessors.

Wu insists the district in her first term has made notable progress, while acknowledging that more work is still needed. However, Wu has not identified specific benchmarks or timelines she is targeting to determine success when it comes to improving academic outcomes.

While Wu focused many of her remarks Monday on Boston’s rich history, she closed on a more recent development:her daughter Mira’s first steps. Wu said Mira, who turns one next week, had tried to take a few steps on stage Monday morning, after her first attempt to walk last month ended in a fall.

“Some part of her already knows that progress takes courage — the willingness to take the next step when the ground isn’t certain,” Wu said. “Every one of us, from our earliest days, is living proof that last month’s impossible can become this morning’s milestones — that if we are only willing to try, with a little help from each other, we can build the future our families deserve.”

title: Roxbury teen among four suspects charged in group attack, robbery on Orange Line train, prosecutors say
text:
A Roxbury teenager was arraigned Monday in Boston Municipal Court in connection with a violent group assault and robbery aboard an MBTA Orange Line train earlier this month, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Wednesday.

Mannice Mitchner, 18, pleaded not guilty to charges of unarmed robbery, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and disorderly conduct on a public conveyance stemming from a Dec. 15 attack on an 18-year-old passenger, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Mitchner is one of four teenagers who have been arrested in connection to the attack, prosecutors said. The other three are minors and their names were not released.

Judge Richard Sinnott revoked bail on several open cases involving Mitchner and ordered him to stay away from the victim as well as all MBTA stations and stops, Hayden’s office said.

Mitchner is due back in court Jan. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to court records. His attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Wednesday.

Prosecutors say Mitchner was allegedly part of a group of seven teens who confronted the victim during the evening rush hour and participated in the assault while recording it on a cellphone.

The incident occurred about 5:45 p.m. after the group boarded an Orange Line train at Downtown Crossing. MBTA surveillance video allegedly shows the teens initiating a verbal confrontation with the victim that escalated into violence.

According to prosecutors, five of the teens allegedly punched the victim with closed fists, threw him to the ground, and continued to punch and kick him in the face and stomach. Mitchner is accused of approaching the scene with his phone out to film the attack and kicking the victim in the head.

Prosecutors said the group stole the victim’s shoes and cellphone before fleeing the train at the Massachusetts Avenue station. Two of the seven teens did not physically assault the victim, authorities said.

The victim told police he did not know any of the attackers, officials said.

“This was a frightening experience for this young man and for all the riders who witnessed it,” Hayden said in a statement, adding that surveillance cameras throughout the transit system play a key role in identifying suspects.

Prosecutors said Mitchner has open cases in multiple courts, including West Roxbury, Fall River, Roxbury, and Dorchester, involving charges such as breaking and entering, malicious destruction of property, attempted larceny, and receiving stolen property.

Three of the five juvenile attackers, along with Mitchner, have been arrested, Hayden’s office said.

Transit Police identified suspects through MBTA video footage and prior contacts with some of the juveniles. Additional arrests were made Dec. 16 and Dec. 19 with help from the Boston Police Department’s Youth Violence Strike Force, officials said.

The remaining juveniles are expected to be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: The Great Thaw: Why 2026 is the year Massachusetts real estate finally accepts the new normal
text:
“I think 2025 was the year of transition,” said Ricardo Rodriguez of Coldwell Banker in reference to the political and economic environment, as well as the dust settling around new rules over real estate agent commissions. “What we have is just a new landscape of not only how the business operates, but how the market itself operates. It’s just the new normal.”

The wait-and-see era is officially over. Driven by life events — from marriages to growing families — and a begrudging acceptance of a new economic baseline, the market is poised for a psychological thaw. The question for 2026 is no longer when rates will drop to historic lows (they likely won’t), but how buyers will compete in a landscape where inventory remains critically scarce.

“If you look at the stock market or commodities markets, they’re swinging,” Rodriguez added. “The only one that is not swinging is real estate.”

That stability is a double-edged sword. While it protects property values, it has cemented a barrier to entry that is nearly insurmountable for the middle class. According to Luc Schuster, Executive Director of Boston Indicators and coauthor of the "Greater Boston Housing Report Card 2025," the starter home has effectively vanished.

The report shows that in 2015, 57 municipalities in Greater Boston had a median single-family sale price below $500,000. By 2025, there were only three: Brockton, Halifax, and Wareham. Conversely, Brookline, Wellesley, and Weston now see median prices topping $2 million.

“This shows the entry-level homeownership squeeze,” Schuster said.

While sub-3 percent mortgages are in the rearview mirror, experts envision a critical tipping point.

“If rates get below 6 percent — and stable at 6 percent — you are going to see an increase in buyers rush to the market. You’re also going to see the increase of sellers get on the market,” said Shant Banosian, president at residential mortgage lender Rate. “You can only stall your life to protect your interest rate for so long.”

For those who can’t wait for the Federal Reserve, the 2026 strategy shifts from waiting to creative structuring. Banosian noted a significant rise in the “Bank of Mom and Dad,” fueled by record highs in the stock market.

While cash offers have dipped slightly from their 2024 highs, down payments are rising, a reflection of growing affluence, according to Redfin.

“There is a lot more wealth in the country,” Banosian said. “The parents of first-time homebuyers have a lot more access to capital, and they are willing to gift it to their children.”

For those without a trust fund, the strategy is speed. Cash buyers often demand a discount, leaving an opening for the financed buyer who can move fast. Banosian points to the rise of the “power bid” — a fully underwritten pre-approval that allows buyers to close in as little as two weeks — as a necessary equalizer.

“The two things that we’re trying to combat cash buyers with is certainty and speed,” he added.

Yet, the Greater Boston narrative inevitably circles back to one root problem: supply.

Walk from Back Bay to the Seaport, and you might think Boston is in a building boom amid all the residential projects that are either underway or recently opened. The Greater Boston Housing Report Card highlighted Census Address Counts data showing Greater Boston added more than 70,000 units of housing in the last five years — a “meaningful increase in completions.”

But, those openings are the final delivery of projects permitted years ago. The pipeline for future housing is drying up.

“Permits for future construction are way down in 2025,” Schuster said. “There is real reason to believe we are not going to keep up that pace of new home building in the coming years.”

New housing permits as of July 2025 were down 44 percent from July 2021 levels, according to the Housing Report Card. High interest rates didn’t just scare off buyers; they paralyzed developers, creating a looming supply cliff for 2026 and 2027.

With the supply crunch expected to continue, Kristen Keegan, the 2026 President of the Massachusetts Association of Realtors, suggested buyers look for expanded options, specifically in the condo market. Furthermore, the recent passage of the Affordable Homes Act could allow accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, to squeeze out more inventory, though a construction boom there has yet to materialize.

While the middle market walks a tightrope, the top end occupies a different stratosphere. In 2026, luxury buyers are motivated by a flight to safety.

“Boston has historically been such a stable market, and real estate really is that one place in which people feel comfortable putting a lot of those liquid assets,” Rodriguez said.

However, the era of the glass tower, defined most recently by Winthrop Center and South Station Tower, may be pausing. With construction costs soaring, the math for building 60-story skyscrapers no longer works.

For buyers priced out of the city, the 2026 strategy is geography. Sarah Gustafson, the 2025 president of the Massachusetts Association of Realtors, points to a changing map redefined by infrastructure. The arrival of South Coast Rail has turned Fall River and New Bedford into viable commuter hubs.

But for the true bargain hunter, the compass points west. Gustafson identified Western Massachusetts as perhaps the last stable housing market in the Commonwealth.

The average home value in Springfield is just under $288,000 compared to a little more than $755,000 in Boston, according to Zillow.

“They have just about as much supply as they do people looking for it,” Gustafson said. “Things are moving, but it’s not a frenzied pace.”

Back in Boston, there are reasons for concern heading into the new year, but also reasons to be optimistic about future fluidity. Sellers are listing, buyers are bidding, and the stalemate is being replaced by a pragmatic drive to get on with life.

“I would dare to say [Boston] is the most stable real estate market in the country,” Rodriguez said. “It’s the silver lining to the inventory levels.”

Amid so much economic and political uncertainty, that might be the best news we could hope for.

Some of the region’s real estate agents weighed in on where they forecast the best opportunities for buyers in the new year:

Zechariah Cook, a broker with Douglas Elliman, advises buyers to focus on areas within a 15-minute walk of the Red Line, especially from Savin Hill to Neponset. These pockets offer beaches, parks, local restaurants, grocery options, and quick commutes — all amenities that drive long-term value in a neighborhood that’s continually evolving.

Buyers are drawn to Sherborn for the generously sized homes, larger lots, privacy, and proximity to Boston. Medfield offers similar appeal, with a walkable downtown and a community-driven feel. Parts of Natick, Dedham, and Westwood also stretch buyers’ dollars further while keeping them within a 20- to 35-minute drive of Boston..

Worcester’s rail service, new ballpark, and growing restaurant scene are drawing a new wave of buyers. The South Coast Rail extension is boosting interest in the communities it serves.

Dover, Rochester, and Somersworth, N.H., provide walkability, newer homes, and lower prices while sitting close to Portsmouth and the Massachusetts border.

Douglas Elliman agent Mia Parsons said Woodstock and Quechee remain two of Vermont’s most stable markets. Woodstock saw a significant surge during COVID and continues to grow, while the Quechee Club attracts buyers to its four-season amenities and proximity to Boston.

title: No easy polar plunge this year. Swimmers in Boston met with snow and severe wind chills for New Year’s ocean dip.
text:
Blowing snow quickly covered discarded layers of clothes left on the beach under a coat of ice.

“This is the way the polar plunge should be,” said Weafer shortly after emerging from the choppy sea. “A little snow fall and a little wind. Negative temperatures with the wind chill. The last few years have been unseasonably warm. It was disappointing.”

Jennifer Donati of Brookline said jumping into the frigid water takes the mental commitment of a long-distance runner.

“I used to run marathons, and I did this years ago,” Donati said. “I was one of the original yuppies who came into Southie in the 1990s. We used go out and then do this to sober up in the morning.”

Donati and her daughter, Gemma, both of Brookline, spent New Year’s Eve dining on roast beef and wine and watching the “Stranger Things” finale.

“She told me she (Jennifer) was going to do it,” Gemma said. “Have fun.”

But the daughter’s plans fell through and she was cajoled to join her mom in a bathing suit on the beach in winter.

“I didn’t know it was going to snow,” Gemma said. “I’ve done a few polar plunges in Scotland but I’ve never done one in the snow.”

Brian Lance of Jamaica Plain came out after a night of champagne and enough cheese to insulate him from the cold, he said.

“We are washing away last night and last year,” Lance said. “Jump into a new year with a fresh start.”

Lance used a strategy similar to hundreds around him: Strip down as fast as possible, do a couple of jumps, give a yelp, and sprint into the water as fast as possible.

There were those who rushed in waist deep and rushed back out just as fast. Some disappeared beneath the surface. Very few dared to make a second trip.

“Once you’re in, it’s actually kind of nice,” Lance said. “Getting out is actually kind of painful. You cannot dress fast enough. That’s the key, strip all the cold stuff off and get dry and get warm.”

Dan Monahan, the president of the L Street Brownies, which is now a nonprofit, said the New Year’s Day dip became an annual event in 1904, and the group has been around since 1865. It started as people taking care of themselves, being healthy, and seeking new challenges.

Monahan cringes when people call it a “polar plunge.”

“People can say what they want, but we call it a swim,” Monahan said. “They (Brownies) swim every day out there. Some stay in longer than others. The polar plunge is like fingernails on a chalkboard to us. But that’s all right.”

The L Street Brownies T-shirt sales help raise money for Southies in need, Monahan told the Globe.

“One of the biggest needs for our seniors who live here is that property taxes are tough for them,” he said. “People have to make a decision to pay their rent or buy their food. We are here to pick up any gap we can help out with.”

L Street Tavern owner Mark Medico helps by allowing them to sell shirts from the bar during the New Year’s Day event. Both the Brownies and the Tavern have a common goal: give back to South Boston.

“They’ll come up here with a group and they’ll actually swim out here like a Saturday morning in the summertime,” Medico said. “A lot of them are original Southie people, some are new Southie people, but it’s a good relationship back and forth. We both do things that support the community, whether it’s sports programs, South Boston Hall of Fame, or the St. Patty’s Day Parade — we give back."

Medico, who was working behind the bar, said the popular choice was a thick pint of Guinness and Bloody Mary’s. Orders of Jameson shots were limited.

Sanitized of 2025 with saltwater, Weafer said, “This is Boston.”

title: Years ago, Boston put bus lanes in the middle of this busy street. Has it worked?
text:
According to the T and the city, rush hour bus trips are quicker, cars speed less, and bus riders are pleased — proof that the lanes have been a “successful and impactful project,” in the words of a project summary published last February.

Attitudes among Roxbury residents and workers remain split. Some lane defenders welcome the prioritization of transit and find the lanes convenient. Some critics, however, said the lanes have sown confusion along the street, worsening safety.

Available data paint an ambiguous picture of safety improvements along the segment. The city says the number of crashes that caused injuries declined markedly. Boston police tallies indicate that vehicle collisions overall also declined on average, but only marginally. The T, meanwhile, said its buses have gotten into far more “major” collisions since 2021, an upswing that surprised some experts.

The T faulted the dangerous and illegal maneuvers of nonagency drivers for most of the crashes over the past couple of years. Only one incident, in 2023, “was considered preventable by the bus driver.”

“We are currently exploring updates to the bus lane design to make it more difficult for drivers to enter or cross the bus lane illegally,” the T said.

The agency said it’s already made some tweaks — enhancing physical barriers around platforms, banning left turns, and adjusting signal timing at some intersections, among other changes.

The T and the city plan to spend $37.3 million extending the lanes about a mile north to Ruggles. They intend to break ground in 2026, the T told the Globe.

Boston and the T also intend to carve out bus-exclusive street space along Blue Hill Avenue, in a not-yet-designed overhaul at one point priced at $44 million. The T said construction would begin in 2027 at the earliest, assuming the agency secures a still-pending Small Starts federal grant from the Trump administration worth about $80 million.

Columbus offers a rough template of how Blue Hill Avenue’s lanes may take shape.

From the sky, the lanes give the impression of a blood vessel, bound on either side by gray arteries of street and sidewalk.

There are eight stops in total, four in each direction — narrow islands wedged between the bus and general purpose lanes. The stops, outfitted with shelters, seats, barriers, and digital trip displays, are separated from the sidewalks by the shared lanes, much like some street-level Green Line stations.

Proponents promised that center-running bus lanes would free buses from thickets of traffic, improving their speed and reliability for a bus-reliant neighborhood.

Drivers bearing witness to the buses zipping by would, in time, ditch their cars and hop aboard. Confining the cars that remained to fewer lanes would enhance the street’s safety, according to advocates and some experts.

Stringing the bus lanes through the middle of the road, instead of connecting them to the curb, offers the added benefit of removing parked or turning vehicles from a bus’s path.

“It helps tremendously” with bus operation and reliability, said Zhan Guo, an urban planning and transportation policy professor at New York University.

Cities around the country have explored their potential benefits — from New York City to Eugene, Ore.

Bus lanes have recently attracted the scrutiny of the Trump administration, which this fall pumped the brakes on a bus lane project in New York City over its supposed impacts on freight traffic and emergency vehicles.

The Columbus Avenue rebuild cost $14.5 million, according to the MBTA. The corridor services three routes — the 44, 29, and 22, one of the T’s most popular, according to the agency.

The census estimates that about 30 percent of workers living in the 02119 ZIP code — encompassing much of Roxbury and Columbus Avenue — use public transit to get to work, about four times the state rate. About 28 percent of 02119 residents live below the poverty line, more than double statewide rate.

Expanding bus-specific street space is a pillar of the MBTA’s push to improve the popular service’s speed and reliability. Boston has publicly backed the effort, despite walking back bus lane installations in some parts of the city.

“The best bus-priority systems in the US have center-running lanes,” said Annie Weinstock, president of a New York consultancy specializing in bus infrastructure. “So it’s a very positive step that Boston has done that.”

Some in the Roxbury neighborhood greeted the revamp with skepticism that has only hardened since the lanes opened.

Working the checkout counter at Pina’s Grocery Store, a few yards from the dark red lanes, Maria Martinez griped about their impact on her car commute.

Martinez said she drove to work from Dorchester, a short journey that has been beset with “more traffic” since the buses ate up one lane along Columbus.

“We get to school late, we get to work late,” Martinez said in Spanish.

A city report from 2023 concluded that car trips along the nearly mile-long corridor took, on average, 20 to 40 seconds longer than they did prebus lane. Meanwhile, the study determined, bus lanes shaved around three to four minutes off bus trips during rush hour.

LivableStreets Alliance, a Cambridge transportation advocacy nonprofit, surveyed more than 150 Columbus Avenue bus riders in December 2021, shortly after the lanes went live. Around three-quarters of respondents reported faster and more consistent trips, according to a report summarizing the group’s findings. Just under one-quarter of respondents said they took the bus more frequently after the lanes were introduced.

It’s difficult to definitively pinpoint how exactly the Columbus lanes have impacted bus ridership.

“There is some evidence that with all things equal, [bus] speed increases can result in ridership increases,” said Weinstock, the bus infrastructure expert. “However, there are so many factors here and in other places that you really need to look at a lot [of] data before you can say definitively what caused what.”

Bus ridership plunged across the entire MBTA system during the pandemic — the early heights of which partly overlapped with the lanes’ construction — and has yet to fully recover. The T said the ridership recovery rate of the 22 bus has outpaced the agencywide average, but other lines without center-running bus lanes have also showcased strong rebounds. The 29 and the 44 buses, the other, less popular lines passing through Columbus, have shown weaker recoveries, according to data from TransitMatters, a research and advocacy group.

Still, some in Roxbury appreciate the bus lanes.

“They work well for what they’re meant to do,” said Sol Martinez Guevara, an employee at the Boston Public Library’s Egleston Square branch, a short stroll from where the bus lanes cease at Walnut Avenue and traffic begins to mingle again.

Despite typically biking to work from another part of Roxbury, Guevara appreciated what the lanes signaled about the city’s priorities.

“I feel like that’s just what makes more sense for being more of a public transit oriented city,” Guevara said.

Guevara’s colleague, Dorchester native Mikayla Willingham, largely agreed. She had, for a time, commuted by bus after the lanes were installed, she said.

“I feel like it’s convenient,” Willingham explained, acknowledging that confused or unconcerned drivers will sometimes trespass into bus zones.

For resident Luis Peña, that confusion feeds chaos.

“Boston City Hall’s worst expense has been to spend money on that,” Peña said in Spanish.

Vehicles barrel past the bus stops far faster than speed limits allow, he complained. Impatient drivers habitually veer into the bus lanes to slip around vehicles stationary in the right lane.

On a recent December day, some short bendable posts marking the lane-splits near bus stops were missing, snapped, or bore the marks of frequent beatings.

“It’s very unsafe,” said Peña, as he stood outside his friend’s store by the Weld Avenue stops, at times gesturing toward the road with his cane. “I don’t know why they did that and spent that money.”

The Police Department documented an average of 35.4 crashes annually along the corridor between 2015 and 2019, according to data shared by the agency. There’ve been, on average, 34.7 crashes annually along the stretch between 2022 and 2024. (BPD didn’t detail the types of crashes or their severity.)

The MBTA, meanwhile, documented 13 “major collisions” involving its buses along the Columbus corridor in 2023 and another 13 in 2024. The agency recorded only eight total major collisions between 2018 and 2022, four of them occurring in 2022.

The Globe in late November asked the T and the Transit Police for copies of the crash reports for each incident. Both agencies told the Globe to file a public records request for the documents. The Globe on Dec. 1 requested documentation for all crashes along the segment involving an MBTA bus between 2018 and 2024. The Globe later agreed to narrow the scope of its request to reports relating to the 34 collisions identified by the MBTA, but has yet to receive the reports.

More proactively identifying and punishing scofflaws could help reel in the rule-breakers, some experts said.

“More automated enforcement is a particularly powerful tool,” said Jeffrey Tumlin, a former director of transportation at the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency.

The agency, during Tumlin’s tenure, unveiled center-running bus lanes spanning a long stretch of Van Ness Avenue, a wide thoroughfare running through the heart of San Francisco. Buses experienced markedly fewer collisions along the segment once they began traveling through the lanes, according to an agency report published in April 2025.

Some drivers defied the rules of the new format, Tumlin said, but bus-mounted enforcement cameras helped keep them in line. The T plans to rollout a similar program in 2026.

Boston, meanwhile, maintains Columbus got safer. A July 2023 evaluation concluded that, on average, a larger share of vehicles — about 10 percentage points more — obeyed the corridor’s speed limit after the bus lanes came online.

It noted in a March report that the number of crashes resulting in injuries tumbled across the city in the years before and after the lanes opened. The decline in injury-causing crashes along the Columbus corridor was about 7 percentage points greater than the drop recorded on similar roads citywide, according to the report.

To Maha Aslam, a transit advocate in Greater Boston and bus lane believer, doubt and frustration and concern are understandable responses to drastic changes in a person’s environment.

“We see a lot of resistance from community members, because it changes the way they experience their neighborhood,” Aslam said.

She went on, “In general, people are antichange.”

title: Free skating in Dorchester sets family-focused tone for Wu’s second term
text:
Juliette Jacobs, 8,of Winchester, took a break from skating to explain what she liked most.

“You get to go fast while you’re roller blading around the corners,” she said, adding that she was happy the mayor had held the event “because we’re all having fun together.”

Her parents, Heather and Evan Jacobs, both 45, said events like this send a message about who the city is for.

“Living in an area that has such disparity in wealth, making events available to everyone gives everyone the opportunity to enjoy,” Evan Jacobs said. “It sends a message that you matter.”

The Dorchester event followed a similar free ice skating clinic Friday at the Frog Pond on Boston Common, part of a weeklong slate of family-oriented programming tied to Mayor Michelle Wu’s inauguration for a second term. The schedule also includes library storytimes, free museum days and youth-focused events across the city.

The focus on free, neighborhood-based events comes as Boston continues to grapple with a growing wealth gap, a divide that shapes which families can easily access arts, recreation, and cultural activities. Dorchester, long one of the city’s most diverse neighborhoods, has seen economic and demographic shifts that have put pressure on many families on the wrong side of that widening gap.

Florence Scott, an early-60s Dorchester residentwho brought her 16-year-old twins, Melaki and Myaja, said the skating clinic stood out for how it made young people feel included.

“It’s a positive outlet,” Scott said. “Especially for the teenagers.”

“They may not be exposed to this, and it’s right here. It’s right in the city,” Scott said. “It shows they’re investing in the future for the kids, because they are the future.”

Lorela Shehu, 32, attended the skating event with her husband, Jurgen Shehu, 34, and their 6-year-old son, JJ. The couple, who are originally from Albania, now live in Fenway, where Lorela is a graduate student at Boston University.

“I really appreciate that I’m raising him here,” Lorela Shehu said. “We’ve lived in other parts of the US, and that’s what I appreciate most about Boston, because of all these events and trying to engage families, which we didn’t see in other cities.”

“We kind of feel that we’re part of Boston,” she added. “It’s a good feeling to have.”

Toya Desarmes, 47, of Roxbury, said accessibility is not just about cost, but geography. Many kid-friendly activities, she said, require leaving the city altogether.

“If we bring more activities to the city that the kids have access to, whether it’s free or paid, something that’s local, so they don’t always have to go far,” Desarmes said. “They can use the bus or the train and get there.”

Her son, Alexander, 8, said he was “amazed” when he learned the skating was free. Asked why that mattered, he answered simply: “So everybody could have a chance.”

Noah Woodley, 19, of Milton, came with his girlfriend, Pulane Kgafela, also 19, of Norwood, and said the event felt different from anything he remembered growing up. He said he appreciated the mayor holding the skating clinic in Dorchester, a part of the city with many lower-income residents.

“I haven’t heard of mayors doing this type of stuff,” Woodley said. “Holding this in Dorchester speaks to what type of person she is. I think a lot of people in Dorchester and everywhere will appreciate it.”

Wu arrived midmorning, greeting families and watching skaters circle the rink. Asked what message she hoped to send by starting her second term with neighborhood-based, family events, Wu said the goal was to move beyond ceremony.

“We wanted to make sure that this wasn’t just about a fancy swearing-in ceremony downtown,” Wu said, “but that throughout the neighborhoods, families of every generation could come together and share in the excitement of what it means to build a community.”

“Times are really challenging right now,” she added. “So we have to double down on who we are as a community, and that means being the best city in the country to raise a family.”

title: Healey is picking the wrong fight in opposing rent control
text:
Right now, we are losing moderately priced housing as large investors outbid potential homeowners. In parts of Somerville, more than half of the two- and three-family homes are bought by investors, who spruce up the apartments and either jack up the rents or convert the units to luxury condos. Either way, people with moderate incomes are out, communities are disrupted, and the supply of moderately priced homes shrinks.

Rent control alone certainly won’t solve the housing crisis. But it will keep some people in their homes, and it is one of our few tools to slow the takeover of housing by speculators.

Pat and Alain Jehlen

Somerville

Pat Jehlen is a state senator.

Governor Maura Healey explained that she opposes the rent control ballot question because it would “effectively halt” housing construction.

As a city councilor in Somerville, I worked with a group of tenants a few years ago whose building had just been bought by a corporate landlord. The landlord immediately raised the rent to levels the tenants could not afford.

We met together with the new landlord. One tenant was a preschool teacher whose husband died suddenly of a heart attack. Another had prevented two fires from destroying the building during her decades-long tenure. Another was a recent immigrant and student. We’re not talking new units here — just a huge rent hike and a bunch of great people facing displacement.

I’ve seen this over and over: new owner, giant rent increase, no new units. Elderly people, immigrants with kids in our schools, working families, students — doesn’t matter: gone. I refuse to believe this is fair or has some abstract public benefit.

I wholeheartedly agree that new construction and basic maintenance are critical, and I’ve supported multiple major zoning improvements. But I see no social value in egregious rent increases for no reason, and I believe we should regulate against it.

Ben Ewen-Campen

Ward 3 City Councilor

Somerville

News of Governor Maura Healey’s opposition to rent control came as no surprise. She’s just one in a long line of politicians over decades who have toed the line of real estate industry interests. I’ve been a realtor for more than 22 years, and I’ve learned not to trust the political arm of the National Association of Realtors, which helped create the exclusionary zoning bylaws that it now says need to be reformed.

Although studies have shown that rent control reduces housing production over time, they have also shown that it eases the financial strain on renters in the short term.

We also know that the long-term effect of exclusionary zoning bylaws by municipalities has resulted in today’s housing shortage, and we know that it will take years to reform these bylaws and build enough homes to meet demand and reduce housing costs. So it would be reasonable for Massachusetts to tie rent control to zoning reform and housing production. Simply put: The longer it takes to implement zoning reform and build enough homes, the longer statewide rent control would remain in effect.

Michael Seward

Sunderland

The writer is a licensed real estate broker.

So our governor won’t vote for rent control because it will stop housing production. Really? Since 1994, when a real estate-backed ballot question killed rent control in Massachusetts, the industry has failed to build enough new housing to keep up with demand. Whatever the obstacles have been, it seems rent control wasn’t one of them.

Now high interest rates, high construction costs, high land prices, and heightened risks to our regional economy are cutting production even more. Millions of cost-burdened Massachusetts residents fear they’ll lose their homes. Our governor could help them by supporting affordability measures such as rent control, not by echoing the private housing industry when it cries wolf.

Mike Prokosch

Dorchester

title: Free January events in Boston: Three Kings Day celebration, BLO concert, and more
text:
Immersing yourself in the arts can sometimes be a pricey endeavor, but this week, you can hold onto your savings while appreciating the city’s music, painting, photography, and dance — if you’re willing to participate yourself. Check out a reception for Boston City Hall’s ongoing exhibition featuring the work of eight local Haitian artists, or the Leica retail store’s photography showcase featuring a Harvard artist-in-residence. From a houseplant-palooza to a free line dancing lesson, here are some no-cost activities and events for the week of Jan. 5-11.

GOVERNMENTAL GALLERY Since November, the “Immersion and Representation: The Art of Being” exhibition has been on display in Boston City Hall, featuring eight works by Haitian artists. On Thursday, catch the exhibition’s opening reception, commemorating the 31st anniversary of the Haitian Artists Assembly of Massachusetts, a group of over 40 Haitian artists who are presenting the exhibition. The exhibition is on display through Jan. 30. Jan. 8, 5-7 p.m. Scollay Square Gallery at City Hall, 1 City Hall Square. boston.gov

GIANT STEPS The Boston Rhythm Riders, a line dancing collective that touts the health benefits of simple movement, will host weekly indoor line dancing lessons starting Thursday. At Hyde Park, you can learn casual moves to bust out at your next dance-off for free, while sliding and shuffling around the gymnasium floor. Classes are designed for all levels of familiarity. Thursdays, 6:30-8 p.m. Hyde Park Community Center, 1179 River St. bostonrhythmriders.org

PREMIER PHOTOGRAPHY The Leica Store presents an exhibition by photographer Sarah Schorr, Harvard Center for the Study of World Religions’s artist-in-residence. For its opening night on Friday, Schorr will appear for an artist talk about her latest work, “Ephemeral Field Journal,” which features photographs inspired by Claude Monet’s garden. The exhibition will be on display through March 22. Jan. 9, 6-9 p.m. Leica Store & Gallery, 74 Arlington St. instagram.com/leicagalleryboston

CLASSICAL CLASSICS Boston Landmarks Orchestra presents not one, but two free concerts on Friday and Saturday. The program blends works from the classical and modern playbooks, with a Mozart symphony and a violin concerto from his contemporary Chevalier de Saint-Georges, as well as more recent composers Valerie Coleman, Julia Perry, and others. Friday’s concert takes place in Jamaica Plain, and if you can’t make that, catch Saturday’s concert in Dorchester. RSVP is recommended. Jan. 9, 7-8 p.m. Bethel AME Church, 100 Wachusett St., Jamaica Plain. Jan. 10, 3-4 p.m. Ray and Joan Kroc Center, 650 Dudley St., Dorchester. landmarksorchestra.org

THE GIFT OF GIVING Hyde Square Task Force, a Jamaica Plain-based youth organization dedicated to Afro-Latin culture, hosts its Three Kings Day event, a Christian tradition celebrating the story of the biblical Magi, who give gifts of gold, myrrh, and frankincense to Baby Jesus. At Saturday’s celebration, attendees can create crowns to commemorate the occasion, children will receive surprise treats, and dancing to the live music is encouraged. Jan. 10, 1-3 p.m. Hyde Square Task Force, 30 Sunnyside St. instagram.com/hydesquaretf

PICK A PLANT Whether you’ve got a greenhouse of your own or your home is more in need of plants than the Earth in “WALL-E,” Mahoney’s Garden Center’s celebration of National Houseplant Day can help buff up a collection of any size. On Saturday, the first 100 people to visit the Winchester location can take home a free small houseplant, and other plants will be sold for 20 percent off. You can also learn from Mahoney’s experts: At 10 a.m., find out how to take care of rare household plants, and at 11 a.m., you can ask their experts any questions about care. Jan. 10, 10 a.m.-1 p.m. Mahoney’s Garden Center, 242 Cambridge St., Winchester. mahoneysgarden.com

Check individual event websites for the most up-to-date information.

Ryan Yau can be reached at ryan.yau@globe.com.

title: Former state rep Charley Murphy leads Harvard Street toward new $57 million health center
text:
Murphy teamed up with The Community Builders, a housing developer, and architectural firm Isgenuity to plan a new health center on nearby city-owned land. The 49,000-square-foot facility would be roughly twice the size of Harvard Street’s current location.

Murphy and his team settled on a final design and received city approval. Then there was a not-so-small matter of figuring out how to pay for the $57 million project. Harvard Street will borrow $20 million from South Shore Bank and will use $5 million of its own cash, as well as $8 million from the state’s allocation of federal pandemic assistance funds.

Murphy has been busy fund-raising to pay for the rest, and has all but $4 million accounted for. The biggest private gift, $1.5 million, came from Moderna chief executive Stéphane Bancel and his wife Brenda Bancel, through Bancel Philanthropies. Boston Medical Center, meanwhile, gave $500,000. Murphy hopes to have enough money to close the gap and start construction within the next three months.

“This building has reached the end of its life, so to speak,” Murphy said. “The patients and my staff deserve a better facility.”

Eventually, Murphy is aiming for a phase two that involves leveling a rundown theater on Blue Hill Avenue and working with The Community Builders to replace it with up to 100 apartments across two buildings, and health care space on the ground floor.

One reason Harvard Street has run out of room: Murphy has been on a concerted push to grow the patient base. After rejoining in 2021, he set an ambitious goal of growing that number to 10,000 patients a year, from 7,200.

In early December, Murphy and his roughly 130-person staff pulled it off. Murphy posted a photo on LinkedIn with chief medical officer Tom Karson and a surprised Sissi Maldonado, who was handed flowers to celebrate the moment as Harvard Street’s 10,000th patient in 2025.

Murphy’s not quite ready to hold a similar celebration for Harvard Street’s fund-raising.

“I’m very happy where things are,” he said. “but we’re not there yet.”

Goulston & Storrs wrapped up its 125th year with a new look for a historic name.

The Boston law firm broke with industry conventions by not shortening its name, such as by dropping its ampersand or one of the founders’ names. Instead, its new, more modern logo draws attention to the ampersand, by making it bigger than the other characters, in a more playful font.

Co-managing director Michelle Porter said her colleagues at Goulston & Storrs did consider shortening the name, much like other firms have done over the past two decades.

“We thought about it for sure, but ultimately decided it’s important to who we are, our partnership and our collaborative model,” Porter said.

The 425-person firm worked with Clarity Group Consulting and New York designer Wally Krantz on the redesign of the logo, letterhead, website, and other marketing materials.

In 2024, Goulston & Storrs relocated to One Post Office Square from Atlantic Avenue. Co-managing director Bill Dillon says he can now see the former Milk Street offices of the firm’s founders, Edward Goulston and Leslie Storrs, from the window of his office. Keeping their names in the firm’s identity, Dillon said, was important as a way to honor the firm’s history. Dillon added, ”We have an old school mentality in terms of how we practice law."

Aviation fuel startup Lydian has touched down in Charlestown with a new headquarters in Hood Park.

The venture-backed firm announced it recently left the Engine incubator in Cambridge to open a 25,000-square-foot office and research lab in Charlestown. The 20-person company’s main focus now is developing a low-emissions jet fuel that can be created from carbon dioxide, electricity, and water. Chief executive Joe Rodden says he hopes to double his workforce in 2026. Lydian joins other so-called “tough tech” companies in Hood Park, a complex owned by the Kaneb family, such as ArkeaBio and Indigo Ag.

Rodden, formerly with Form Energy, formed Lydian in 2021 by teaming up with Branko Zugic, who previously led research and development at a battery-tech firm called Open Water Power that was sold to L3 Technologies, now L3Harris Technologies.

Lydian’s tech uses an electrolyzer to break out hydrogen from water, and combines it with carbon dioxide to make jet fuel. The riddle that Rodden’s team is trying to solve is how to create this fuel in an efficient and cost-effective way, with a goal of commercializing it by 2028. The company is backed by VC firms such as Congruent Ventures, Galvanize Climate Solutions, and Union Square Ventures.

While Lydian has already announced a temporary pilot demonstration project in North Carolina, Rodden says Boston is a perfect place to develop this technology because of the region’s universities and research labs.

“For the majority of our hiring, we’re able to pull from the talent here in the Boston area,” says Rodden, who splits his time between San Francisco and Boston. “It’s been a big advantage in that regard.”

Plus, Rodden argues that Lydian and similar startups will draw talent to Boston from other metro areas.

“It’s a great thing to be able to pull those people into Boston,” Rodden says, “and to start to plant the seeds around industrial climate-tech in this area.”

Charles River Apparel launched its consumer business to coincide with two important seasons: holiday shopping, and the New England Patriots.

The Sharon company has historically sold its sweatshirts, jackets, and pullovers through a mix of business partners nationwide, from promotional product distributors to college bookstores to uniform suppliers.

Now, Charles River has opened up a new channel, in part by teaming up with a certain football squad just down the road on Route 1 to co-design a line of Patriots-themed clothing.

The direct-to-consumer launch, including a new website at CharlesRiver.com, is part of a broader effort by new chief executive Jason Lipsett, who recently took over for his father Barry Lipsett in the top job, to modernize the company and build more awareness about the family-owned business.

Lipsett said the launch is off to a solid start, particularly with the Patriots-themed apparel. The team’s strong performance this season has “certainly added to the momentum” of sales, he added. The partnership has meant joining with the Pats in community initiatives at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, including the team’s Winter Wonderland party on Dec. 16.

“The bigger the brand name becomes,” Lipsett said of Charles River, “the more demand and success our customers will have.”

So does this mean Charles River will soon open its own brick-and-mortar stores, too? Not exactly, though Lipsett envisions some kind of year-round showroom in the Boston area eventually. “That’s a long-term goal of mine,” he said, “but it’s not in the immediate future.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
BISHOP ALLEN The brainy Brooklyn-via-Harvard indie pop act dusts off peppy, perky music-blogger-beloved tunes like the raucous “Middle Management” and the jittery “Ciick, Click, Click, Click” for their first run of shows in a decade. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

KEYSHIA COLE In 2005, this Oakland-born R&B belter released her debut, “The Way It Is,” a collection of songs about love and heartbreak that showcased her formidable voice and from-the-gut lyricism; this show will celebrate its 20th anniversary. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

CATE LE BON The Welsh avant-pop auteur’s latest project, “Michaelangelo Dying,” is a gorgeously prickly meditation on anguish and loss centered on her sturdy yet searching alto and saxophonist Euan Hinshelwood’s plaintive wails. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com
