MAURA K. JOHNSTON

ISABEL OLIART, SAMMY WETSTEIN AND ANNE HOOPER TRIO Oliart is the current US National Scottish Fiddle Champion. She’s joined by her teacher Anne Hooper and multi-instrumentalist Sammy Wetstein for a performance of traditional and original Celtic music. Jan. 10, 2 p.m. Free. Center for Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. 617-718-2191, artsatthearmory.org

MICAH P. HINSON You could call Micah P. Hinson an indie-folk artist, but it’s probably more accurate to say, as one reviewer once did, that he resides firmly within his own universe. That universe doesn’t include trips to this part of the world very often, so catch him while you can. Jan. 11, 7 p.m. $15. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. www.therockwell.org

AVA NEAL Judging from the assured, hooky, jangly folk ’n’ pop collected on “Balance Beam,” an album this young Boston-area singer-songwriter released two years ago, she has a promising future. She’ll play music from that album as well as preview songs from an upcoming release this Sunday. Jan. 11, 8 p.m. $10. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729, www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

LUKE WINSLOW-KING Born in Cadillac, Mich., a resident of New Orleans for 15 years, and currently based in Calatayud, Spain, the blues and roots slide guitarist, singer, composer, and lyricist incorporates influences far and wide: from ragtime, Delta blues, and jazz to prewar American folk and Béla Bartók. Jan. 10, 8 p.m. $30-$32. Narrows Center for the Arts, 16 Anawan St., Fall River. narrowscenter.org

TIGER OKOSHI & TRULY TRUE Arts Wayland’s Berklee Faculty Series kicks off 2026 with renowned Japanese trumpeter and Berklee professor Okoshi and his chamber jazz band: vibraphonist Sam Cerra, violinist Louis Thélot, cellist Peter Sumner, and bassist Ferran Rico Andres. Jan. 11, 3 p.m. $20. First Parish in Wayland, 225 Boston Post Road, Wayland. artswayland.com

POINT01 PERCENT PRESENTS Two ensembles featuring adventurous local improvisors: guitarist Gabe Boyarin, violinist Phillip Rawlinson, pianist Anthony Coleman, and drummer Noah Mark perform a new work by Boyarin; three seasoned acolytes of Thelonious Monk — pianist Pandelis Karayorgis, saxophonist Allan Chase, and drummer Luther Gray — play pieces by the great man. Jan. 13, 7:30 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO opens 2026 with concert performances of Samuel Barber’s “Vanessa,” conducted by music director Andris Nelsons and starring Jennifer Holloway as the title character opposite Samantha Hankey as Erika, Anne Sofie von Otter as the Old Baroness, and last-minute additions to the cast Ganson Salmon and Patrick Carfizzi as Anatol and the Old Doctor respectively, stepping in for Pavel Cernovich and Thomas Hampson due to illness. The performances are presented in collaboration with Boston Lyric Opera, whose chorus joins the Tanglewood Festival Chorus for the evening (Jan. 10). Next week’s program opens with BSO principal flutist Lorna McGhee in Allison Loggins-Hull’s “Rhapsody on a Theme by Joni” (as in Mitchell), followed by Bernstein’s “Chichester Psalms” with the Tanglewood Festival Chorus and Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with fan-favorite pianist Seong-Jin Cho (Jan 15-17). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

A FAR CRY x YEEMZ The Jamaica Plain-based string orchestra teams up with singer-songwriter and cellist Yeemz (Yi-Mei Templeman) for a casual and cozy show where audiences are encouraged to move about the space, grab a drink, and absorb the music. Jan. 9, 7:30 p.m., Somerville Armory; Jan. 10, 3 p.m., St. John’s Church, Jamaica Plain. www.afarcry.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Artistic director Jonathan Cohen leads a program featuring the H+H Orchestra and soprano Carolyn Sampson in Mozart’s ecstatic religious piece “Exsultate jubilate” and Telemann’s mythological cantata “Ino,” with a side of Haydn’s Symphony No. 44, “Trauer.” Jan. 9, 7:30 p.m.; Jan. 11, 3 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

A.Z. MADONNA

THE GREAT PRIVATION (HOW TO FLIP TEN CENTS INTO A DOLLAR) Nia Akilah Robinson’s play tells parallel stories of mothers and daughters, set on the same plot of land. The present-day parent-child pair work as counselors at a sleepaway camp in Philadelphia. The other mother and daughter are standing vigil in 1832 by the grave of their newly deceased husband and father. In an era when it was not uncommon for Black corpses to be illegally disinterred by white so-called “resurrectionists” and sold to medical schools, they are determined to protect him from grave robbers. Directed by Mina Morita, “The Great Privation” is a coproduction by Boston’s Company One Theatre and Washington’s Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company, featuring two actors from each city. The Boston-based performers are Marc Pierre and Victoria Omoregie. Jan. 9-31. At the Modern Theatre at Suffolk University, Boston. companyone.org

STOKELY & MARTIN Written and directed by Najee Brown, “Stokely & Martin” imagines a conversation in the afterlife between Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Stokely Carmichael, a passionate advocate of civil rights who popularized the term “Black Power.” Stetson Marshall plays King, and Darren Paul portrays Carmichael. In Brown’s play, they “explore their ideological differences, personal struggles, and shared hopes for Black liberation,” according to press materials. Jan. 16-18. AtMulticultural Arts Center, Cambridge. https://multiculturalartscenter.org/stokely-and-martin/

JOB Josephine Moshiri Elwood plays Jane, a young woman on a leave of absence from her job as a moderator of online content, and Dennis Trainor Jr. plays Loyd, her psychiatrist. The conversation between patient and therapist brings them to some very dark places in this psychological thriller by Max Wolf Friedlich, which is directed by Marianna Bassham. Jan. 16-Feb. 7. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion at the BCA, Boston. 617-933-8600, www.speakeasystage.com

DON AUCOIN

SCREENDANCE ROADSHOW Formerly the Motion State Dance Film Series, this initiative co-curated by Ali Kenner Brodsky and Andy Russ launches its eighth incarnation with this East Providence presentation. Each season, the traveling short dance film series showcases an array of creativity by artists from around the world exploring choreography for the camera, screening the film program at a variety of venues around New England. This kickoff event also features a post-screening talk with the curators. Jan. 15. Free. Myrtle, East Providence, R.I. www.motionstatearts.org/about-screendance-roadshow

FIFTY FAVORITES / FIFTY SEASONS Jacob’s Pillow archivist extraordinaire Norton Owen put together a dazzling compendium of short clips from each of the seasons he has participated in over his remarkable half-century career at the festival. It’s a delightful trip down memory lane for those of us who’ve taken parts of the journey with him. For others, it’s a lively sampler. Annie B-Parson’s opening “occasion piece” from the launch of the new Doris Duke Theatre with a cast of veteran all-stars is priceless. Owen shares more in an online exhibit and podcast as well. https://danceinteractive.jacobspillow.org/playlists/fifty-favorites-fifty-seasons/#1

CONVERSATION IN MOVEMENT While there are few live performances this week, the Loading Dock Gallery continues its group exhibit exploring the relationship between dance and visual art. Captured motion in different media delve into a kind of visual kinesthetic dialogue that embraces form, color, and light. Participating artists include Nino Gordeladze, Dina Mordeno, Ed Porzio, and Johanna Tiemann. Through Jan. 31. Free. Loading Dock Gallery, Lowell. www.theloadingdockgallery.com

ONE MINUTE MOVEMENT SOLOS Mobius is presenting another round of its concert series of finished solos with a provocative twist — each is strictly one minute in length, not an easy task. Jimena Bermejo and Heather Kapplow curated this year’s edition, and the concert includes 18 different artists in a range of styles, from contemporary dance and performance art to a variety of multidisciplinary offerings. Jan. 10. $15. Lilypad, Cambridge. www.mobius.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

OF LIGHT AND AIR: WINSLOW HOMER IN WATERCOLOR Closing soon: “You will see in the future,” Homer once wrote, “I will live by my watercolors.” Not to diminish his grand oil paintings, many of them icons of American culture. But it only takes a moment with a handful of those watercolors to see what he means. Immediate, breathless, and intense, they often feel like stray thoughts captured and committed to paper in the brief moment before they flit away. Homer’s thoughts were rarely without gravitas — the curse of a life lived alongside conflict — and so, too, the watercolors, the largest collection of which is owned by the MFA. For the first time in decades — their fragility limits their exposure to light — 50 of them are out in the open together, an occasion not to be missed, nor seen again for a generation. Through Jan. 19. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

ALLAN ROHAN CRITE Ending soon: Two local exhibitions celebrate Crite, “Urban Glory” at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and “Griot of Boston” at the Boston Athenaeum. For Crite, who painted Roxbury and the city’s Black community with verve and affection for almost 80 years — he died in 2007, just a few years short of his 100th birthday — it’s about time. Along with it comes the first-ever scholarly text on his work, “Allan Rohan Crite: Neighborhood Liturgy,” from Princeton University Press. Crite was a passionate chronicler of both the trials and triumphs of urban Boston’s diverse and dynamic quarters for much of his life, and his official arrival in the canon is more than due. Through Jan. 19 (Gardner) and Jan. 24 (Athenaeum). Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org; Boston Athenaeum, 10½ Beacon St. 617-227-0270, bostonathenaeum.org

HEW LOCKE: PASSAGES Last chance: Boston audiences will remember Locke from “The Procession,” an enormous still life parade of figures at the ICA’s Watershed last summer, mirroring the mass of diverse humanity that’s crisscrossed the globe since the advent of colonialism almost four centuries ago. This exhibition promises to both strengthen and clarify that movement, and its frequent injustices, as a lifelong theme for the Guyanese-British artist, as it draws on a quarter century of his work, right up to now. Through Jan. 11. Yale Center for British Art, 1080 Chapel St., New Haven. 877-274-8278, britishart.yale.edu

MURRAY WHYTE

MAGIC Maybe it’s the advent of AI, or maybe the uncertainty of the times, that has prompted the artworld to lean into mysticism and magic like spiritualists peering into a crystal ball. This group show features colored-pencil emoji drawings by Anna Von Mertens, whose art often examines astronomy and physics, along with psychedelic landscapes by Linda Nagaoka, hex-sign-like paintings by Lena McCarthy, and bright, glittery Rorschach blots by OH Projects. Jan. 10-Feb. 28. Drive-By Projects, 81 Spring St., Watertown.www.drive-byprojects.com

CATE McQUAID

CLOWN PEOPLE PODCAST LIVE TAPING Stand-ups Brieana Woodward and Al Christakis released their first episode of the “Clown People” podcast in 2022. At the Studio, they will tape their 200th official episode with guests Logan O’Brien, Trevor Dion, Gabi Hajos, and Cam Ohh, plus some games and interactive bits. Jan. 9, 9:30 p.m. $13.95-$18.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St.www.thecomedystudio.com

BRIAN SIMPSON “Since I’m a young black man, everybody thinks that my biggest fear is racist cops,” says Austin, Texas, comic Simpson in a spot on Netflix’s “the Standups.” “I’m way more afraid of racist lifeguards.” Jan. 9 at 7 p.m. and Jan 10 at 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. $38.40. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

BLACK COMEDY EXPLOSION Smokey Suarez will be the first headliner for the Black Comedy Explosion’s new night — it has moved from Wednesday nights to Thursday nights. Hosted by Jonathon Gates, music by DJ Wade. Jan. 15, 9 p.m. $15-$20. Carver Den, 80 Talbot Ave., Dorchester. 617-590-8334, Instagram @blackcomedyexplosion

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Where to eat in 2026
text:
January is a time to celebrate fresh beginnings, and one way to embrace that spirit is by visiting new restaurants. There are a number of enticing openings off in the distance to anticipate. For instance, Michelin-starred chef George Mendes will open the tasting menu-focused Agosto in the South End in the summer, with bakery-cafe Baby Sister to follow (named after his son and daughter), while Danny Meyer Italian restaurant Ci Siamo expands from New York to the Seaport.

But in the here and now, diners can choose from sushi, Ethiopian cuisine, American comfort food, and beyond. In Back Bay, for the next month only, the lounge at Uni has been declared Lower Uni, offering four- and 10-course tasting menus. Korean mom-and-pop Park’s Kitchen, which offered takeout and delivery in Roxbury, has closed — to become a brick-and-mortar opening soon: Stay tuned for all your spicy rice cake and handmade dumpling needs. (In the meantime, check out the new Gangnam Spice, specializing in Korean fried chicken and more in Jamaica Plain.) And is it too soon to declare this the year of the neighborhood seafood restaurant? Lobster rolls are surfacing everywhere from Allston (at nouveau New England seafood shack Holdfast) to Watertown (read on).

Here are some restaurants to try in the coming days.

Get Food & Dining Headlines

The Globe's most recent food stories, delivered to your inbox every Wednesday.

Enter Email

Acapella by X

In the longtime Blarney Stone space, something new for Fields Corner: a nightspot with good food and live music, with a generous patio and valet parking coming down the road. Longtime friends Freddy Ureña (chef), Yancarlo Fernandez (general manager), and Anthony Cruz (front-of-house manager) are behind the venture, which offers a menu inspired by Ureña’s travels. Come for ceviche, dumplings, and grilled skirt steak with chimichurri sauce, plus cocktails (with some nice alcohol-free options for Dry January participants). Everyone is here, from babies to priests to friend groups dressed to impress.

1505 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-286-4620, www.acapellabyx.com

Ama at the Atlas

Three years ago, Comfort Kitchen arrived in Dorchester, with a menu that connected cultures, traced trade routes, and brought diners into its expansive worldview. Now, founding husband-wife team Nyacko Pearl Perry and Biplaw Rai and their Pearl & Law Hospitality group expand to Allston. At the Atlas Hotel, Ama is a salute to mothers and others who nurture us through food. (Rai is from Nepal; the restaurant’s name is Nepali for “mother.”) Ama, slated to open this month, features a menu that spans the globe, and the day. Breakfast might bring French toast flavored with Nepali spiced tea, lunch Senegalese-inspired yassa chicken salad sandwiches, dinner tamarind-glazed trout and Berbere-spiced fried chicken.

Atlas Hotel, 40 Western Ave., Allston, www.ama-boston.com

Black Cat Eatery at Wink & Nod

Chef Valentine Howell won a following at modern Greek restaurant Krasi in the Back Bay, then at his Black Cat popup at Jamaica Plain’s Vee Vee, which ended last March. Now Black Cat is on its second life, at South End culinary incubator-slash-speakeasy Wink & Nod. From shrimp ceviche to jackfruit empanadas to red snapper rundown in tomato-coconut broth, Howell’s Afro-Caribbean cuisine is bright and flavorful, a delight to eat and a wakeup for the palate.

3 Appleton St., South End, Boston, 781-435-0394, www.winkandnod.com

Boxfish

When chef Manita Bunnagitkarn moved her popular Cha Yen Thai Cookery across the street in Watertown, it opened up possibilities for the former space. Now it is Boxfish, where Bunnagitkarn offers a seafood-focused menu notable for its originality. Of course there is a lobster roll, the meat poached in brown butter and served on brioche with lemon aioli, as well as clam chowder, a fried fisherman’s platter, and linguine with clams. From there, it goes freewheeling with dishes such as grilled octopus with ube mashed potatoes; fettuccine with uni, brown butter, and nori; and an elegant pan-seared fillet of the day with tomato concasse and beurre blanc. If you’re feeling more surf than turf, try the Boxfish sandwich, featuring shaved ribeye with fontina and caramelized onions.

613 Mount Auburn St., Watertown, www.boxfish.food

Cactus Club Cafe

If you vaguely remember ripping it up at the Cactus Club on Boylston Street back in the day, don’t get excited. This is not a reincarnation of that. Cactus Club Cafe, which is on Boylston Street, is a Canadian export. It looks luxe, it opens for lunch and closes at midnight, and it has a crowd-pleasing menu comprising sushi, rigatoni Bolognese, miso caramel sea bass, burgers and steaks — and somehow much more, plus fun cocktails. If you want to get your OG Cactus Club on, don’t worry, there are tacos and margaritas here too.

500 Boylston St., Back Bay, 617-341-9428, www.cactusclubcafe.com

Cafe Sushi Nisei

Cafe Sushi, beloved in Cambridge, shuttered for dine-in service during the COVID era. Now it has reopened as Cafe Sushi Nisei (“second generation”), with a renovated dining room and sake bar. Brothers Seizi and Kenshi Imura continue to operate the restaurant, along with Seizi’s wife, Mindy Imura; the Imuras’ parents opened it in the mid-’80s and handed it down in 2007. Although the popular omakase menu Cafe Sushi once offered is no longer, the restaurant makes up for it with a focused menu of small plates, sashimi, nigiri, and rolls. Don’t miss the beautiful citrus salmon sashimi, with blood orange and fennel, or the madai nigiri with preserved yuzu.

1105 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, 617-492-0434, www.cafesushicambridge.com/nisei

Gato Exotico

Restaurateur Jason Doo is a nostalgist. His Harvard Square spot, Wusong Road, is an homage to classic tiki bars and Chinese-American restaurants like the one his parents ran, Bobo’s in Malden, when he was a kid. His new foray also reaches back to his childhood — spent hanging out at the very mall where he recently opened Gato Exotico. The CambridgeSide restaurant features a menu of guacamole, enchiladas, and tacos from chef Sergio Enriquez, plus drinks with names like the Tijuana Taxi and the Tres Leches Colada.

100 Cambridgeside Place, Cambridge, 339-229-8787, www.gatoexotico.com

Mesob Restaurant and Bar

Just a few blocks from the Eritrean Community Center in the South End is Mesob, featuring Eritrean and Ethiopian cuisine and named for the traditional woven basket on which shared meals are served. Start with sambusas, then move on to an array of fresh salads and platters of kitfo, timtimo, shiro, and more, served with the flatbread injera. Mesob also offers wine, beer, and cocktails.

1746 Washington St., South End, Boston, 857-305-3468, www.mesobrestaurantboston.com

Moona

For dreamy Middle Eastern fare — platters of labneh, hummus, and olives with pita; feta fritters; lamb kefta; grilled branzino — diners flock to Moona in Cambridge’s Inman Square. Now owner Mohamad El Zein has opened a new branch of the restaurant, nearby in Central Square: It is bigger than the cozy original, with more and new dishes to try. After you’ve feasted on monkfish shish and date molasses-glazed lamb shank with freekeh, try Arabic coffee and rose crème caramel or orange blossom labneh frozen yogurt with kumquat jam for dessert. Cafe service is coming soon.

750 Main St., Central Square, Cambridge, 617-665-5915, www.moonarestaurant.com

Devra First can be reached at devra.first@globe.com. Follow her on Instagram @devra_first.

title: Boston residents line up to get vaccinated at City Hall’s free clinic
text:
The last week of December saw a “very high” spike in flu cases, according to the Department of Health.

In the span of a month, flu cases in Boston rose from 133 cases at the beginning of December to 672 cases the last week of the month, according to the Boston Public Health Commission. During the same timeframe, the percentage of flu-like illnesses in emergency department visits jumped from 2.7 percent to 11.1 percent.

Those totals dipped slightly at the beginning of 2026, with 652 reported flu cases, 20 fewer than the previous week, and 10 percent of total emergency department visits, down by a percentage point less.

However, the totals for the beginning of the year are still above those during the same time in 2025, when there were 326 flu cases reported in the city, and 5.2 percent of emergency department visits due to flu-like illness.

Last year, flu cases statewide spiked around February.

The clinic on Wednesday, inside a room on the eighth floor of City Hall, was staffed with registered nurses from LCG Boston, a nurse staffing agency that runs vaccination sites across Boston. There were almost 30 people already registered within the first 30 minutes.

For Jordan Bordner, a city employee, the convenience of the City Hall location influenced his decision to get vaccinated.

”Everyone should get a flu shot,“ Bordner said. ”It helps you and also everyone that you work with and everyone that you live with.”

There are three more clinics planned for this month:

10 a.m.-2 p.m. Saturday, Josephine A. Fiorentino Community Center, 123 Antwerp St., Brighton

3-7 p.m. Wednesday, BCYF Hyde Park Community Center, 1179 River St., Hyde Park

3-7 p.m. Thursday, BCYF Perkins Community Center, 155 Talbot Ave., Dorchester

The registered nurses have been working in these clinics since September, vaccinating more than 2,500 individuals around Boston as of Dec. 23.

“It’s been quite a long, long season,” said Glendaly Avalo-Valdez, registered nurse with LCG Boston.

Since September, the city has held 27 clinics. Avalo-Valdez said individual clinics typically serve between 30 and 100 people. She has been operating vaccination clinics throughout the city, including Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Brighton.

Other people getting vaccinated, like Maya Lazar, had personal experiences that motivated them to get vaccinated. After Lazar lost her brother because of the flu, she believes annual flu vaccinations are essential.

“I suggest getting your flu shot every single year,” Lazar said. “Specifically, with the strain that’s going around this year, which is pretty bad. So everyone should get their flu shot, it just helps keep other people safe.”

The clinic is also an opportunity for those who weren’t able to get their vaccinations earlier in the season. Zoe Davis, a mom of 11-month-old twins, dropped into the clinic to get both her flu and COVID-19 vaccinations.

“I don’t have either shot so far, I’ve just been busy with my twins,” Davis said.

Davis said she hopes more people will get their flu shots, especially this year. While this year’s vaccine is a partial match to subclade K, doctors and public health officials say getting vaccinated greatly reduces a person’s exposure to severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

“From everything I’ve read, it definitely helps decrease symptoms,” she said. “I know it doesn’t totally prevent you from getting the flu, but I definitely am on board if it can make it better.”

On top of getting vaccinated, local doctors ask people to remember hygienic practices adapted during the pandemic.

This story has been updated to clarify the timing of the city’s flu and COVID-19 clinics.

title: Putting some manners on the Boston City Council
text:
Worrell, who with his brother Chris, a state representative, is one half of what constitutes a prospective political dynasty in Boston, a natural bridge builder in a city that needs more bridges. And I wouldn’t be surprised if Brian Worrell becomes Boston’s first elected Black mayor some day, and he’d be a good one, for myriad reasons.

He comes from a terrific family, who have been an integral part of one of the city’s great traditions, the annual Hewins Street block party in Dorchester, which for more than a half-century has brought together one of the most vibrant, diverse group of people in the city.

But for reasons that seem more political than personal, with Mayor Michelle Wu’s fingerprints all over it, Brian Worrell wasn’t elected City Council president.

Liz Breadon was. And, despite all the politics and wheeling and dealing, that is a good thing.

It is a good thing, some will say, because as the first openly gay president of the Boston City Council, she shows glass ceilings are being shattered in centers of power all over town, even City Hall.

That said, identity politics without substance is just shallow sloganeering. But Liz Breadon is a woman of substance. And her identity, not just her sexuality but where she comes from, is key to understanding what kind of person she is and what kind of leader she could become.

Breadon grew up and came of age in rural Fermanagh, one of the six counties that make up Northern Ireland. While most of the attention during The Troubles — as the Irish, in their penchant for understatement, called their civil war — was focused on urban areas in Belfast and Derry, some of the most pernicious sectarianism and unspeakable atrocities occurred in rural areas like Fermanagh.

Breadon’s father was a farmer, her mother a nurse, and the family also ran a small country store. The civil unrest that launched The Troubles in the late 1960s began when Breadon was about 10 years old.

The ensuing violence led many people to retreat to their tribal enclaves. But Breadon was lucky in that her Protestant family counted many Catholic friends among the customers of their store. And, unlike the vast majority of students in Northern Ireland who attend schools that are segregated by religion and national identity, she went to school with Catholics.

When she embraced her sexuality in her early 20s, she also acknowledged the Protestant and Catholic churches which most people in Northern Ireland called their spiritual homes were irrevocably hostile to gay people.

She came to Boston in 1995, experiencing a liberating, life-affirming personal freedom that was not attainable in her homeland. Years before she joined the council, she and her spouse, Mary McCarthy, who Breadon likes to call “a nice Irish Catholic girl,” were supporters of two women who launched the campaign to bring marriage equality to the Republic of Ireland, which in 2015 became the first country to legalize same-sex marriage by popular vote.

The ballot question came after Katherine Zappone, a native of Seattle, and Ann Louise Gilligan, a native of Ireland and former nun, who fell in love while studying at Boston College, legally challenged the Irish government’s refusal to recognize their marriage in Canada. Breadon and McCarthy held a fund-raiser for the campaign in their Oak Square home.

Unlike most politicians, Breadon knows what it’s like to be told you can’t be yourself.

And, perhaps more than any politician in Boston, past or present, she has seen what happens when incivility takes root, and people retreat to echo chambers, dehumanizing the other side while civil society slides off a cliff.

After Charlie Kirk was assassinated, I wrote a column expressing unease with those who cheered his murder, lamenting, while not excusing Kirk’s divisive rhetoric, that the growing polarization in this country uncomfortably reminded me of what I observed during the more than 20 years I covered the conflict in Northern Ireland.

“I’ve seen what happens when people are so convinced of the righteousness of their side that they dehumanize the other side to the point that not only are they unmoved when someone from the other side is murdered, they actually celebrate it,” I wrote. “I’ve seen this movie before, and have no desire to see it again.”

Not long after that column was published, I heard from Breadon. She noted that her upbringing informed her views and that she was appalled not just by those cheering Kirk’s assassination, but by President Trump’s baselessly and irresponsibly blaming it on Democrats.

“Violence has no place in civil society and it is frightening to hear the President throwing fuel on the fire by openly calling Democrats domestic terrorists,” she wrote in an email to me. “Charlie Kirk was no angel, he profited from peddling misinformation, mistrust and hate, but he did not deserve to die by gun violence.”

Where Liz Breadon comes from, they have a phrase for getting people off their high horses and, as the Irish say, stop acting the muppet. It’s called, “putting manners on them” — not by shaming them as much as emphasizing the importance of empathy, respect and civility.

Here’s hoping she can put some manners on the Boston City Council, and, while she’s at it, the rest of us, too.

title: Dennis Lehane says his Boston is a vanished world
text:
Amazon Music | Apple Podcasts | iHeartRadio | Pocket Casts | Spotify | YouTube

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the Jan. 8 episode.

Kusmer: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer, filling in for Shirley Leung.

Boston is a very diverse and dynamic place, but in Hollywood, a certain vibe often dominates: scrappy, working class, Irish American. I think today’s guest was one of the first people to really paint that picture for the public.

Dennis Lehane is a writer who grew up in Dorchester and wrote some popular books about the neighborhoods of his childhood. There’s “Gone Baby Gone,” “Mystic River,” and many more. More recently, he wrote “Small Mercies,” a book set during busing. His current focus is writing for television. His latest show is called “Smoke” on Apple TV, it stars Jurnee Smollett and Taron Egerton.

It’s a crime show about arson and fire. Dennis said his fascination with fire goes back to when he was in one.

Lehane: I was living in a building where the roof caught fire and the fire alarm system was broken — here in Boston, Charlesgate West overlooking the Charles. There were these homeless people who lived under the off ramp for Storrow Drive, and they came in, they rang all our doorbells, and they banged all these trash cans together. They woke us up and they saved our lives. So, yeah, I’ve stared fire in the face a little bit.

The show is inspired by real things. It’s a real arsonist named John Orr who lived and worked in Glendale, California, in the 1980s.

I just saw it as a way to look at chaos. Like I think our country is in a state of just total chaos right now. I think most people are chaotic in general. It’s just my personal belief, and so I wanted to look at chaos in every shape and form. And then once we came up with, once we leaned into this idea of fire, the big directive I gave to my team was, I’ve seen so much crappy fire out there. Fake fire. And I don’t want one bit of this to look fake.

Kusmer: You mentioned chaos, but what other ideas are you tackling with this new show?

Lehane: Oh, I think there’s a lot in there about, kind of like white grievance politics. You know, there’s two arsonists in this show. And they’re counterpoints for each other. One of them believes himself to be a victim.

The other one truly is a victim of society. That’s not making an excuse for him, but it’s saying that this guy literally had no chance.

The other guy had plenty of chances. He just chose not to take ‘em. And then he wants to sit back and whine about it. So I think that’s in there. We just wanted to look at people who were just really on a collision course with the consequences of hiding who they really are.

Kusmer: Right. And there’s a lot in there about sort of being in and out of control, and how that affects your behavior, and how it changes your personality.

Lehane: A hundred percent. I mean, that’s all to the end of the day. That was my favorite thing about what I do. The Greeks called “in extremis.” And so it’s like in extreme circumstances people are revealed. Nobody knows who they are until they’ve been in a really extreme circumstance. I love this phrase that Comac McCarthy had, which is he believes in “fiction of mortal event.”

I’m not a writer who can write like Henry James about like a crack in the Golden Bowl. Okay. I could care less. You’re rich. Go buy another bowl. I want to write about extreme circumstances with people in extremis. That’s what I’m into.

Kusmer: I think one thing that’s very Lehanian, if I can say, is humor and dialogue. There’s so much banter on your new show, but I think that’s true of your books in general. It’s dark, but it’s also funny. Can you talk to me about the connection between darkness and humor for you?

Lehane: Oh, it’s just how I grew up. I’ve never met a comedian half as funny as at least five people I knew growing up in Dorchester. And you know, my dad was part of a bar culture. He used to bring me into bars all the time and pretend, tell my mother we were at a farmer’s market so he could sneak in and have a drink on a Saturday. So I grew up listening to people talk and tell stories.

The point of any working class story is I got screwed, but I got a little bit of vengeance. Like, I keyed his car. I slept with his sister. So it’s a tragic story — “I got screwed” — but it’s got a little bit of levity in it.

Because the idea is, I think in Irish culture — and that’s where Dorchester and Savin Hill where I grew up and Southie, that’s where we get our sense of humor — they believe that God is a prankster and we’re the joke. We’re the butt of the joke, you know? And so I think that’s something that just goes into my work and I can’t not be funny, as much as my stuff is really dark.

Like the funniest thing is when — “Mystic River” was the first book I wrote that doesn’t seem to have many jokes in it — but when I read it out loud, people almost look for permission because they start to laugh. The voice is actually very funny. But the story is so dark, you’ve got to hear it to laugh.

Kusmer: I always think of Boston humor as like, there’s a lot of like defense mechanisms. It’s sort of like a way of processing pain. I know it’s true everywhere, but I think it’s particularly true here.

Lehane: Oh, it’s particularly true here. I mean, I’m sorry. I went to school down south, and irony and sarcasm dies at the Mason-Dixon line. I mean,I got so tired of people staring at me like they just didn’t, I left. I think I left the South because I got tired of people not getting my jokes

Kusmer: One of many things I found really funny about the new series is that one of your main characters is an aspiring crime writer, but he’s a bit of a hack. What do you think separates good crime writing from mediocre crime writing?

Lehane: No, it’s good writing. It’s just good writing. It’s not crime writing, or romance writing, or anything. I believe that all writing is just either good writing or not good writing. You have to have depth, you have to have depth of character, you have to have depth of language, you have to have depth of story.

I think it has to be honest. Honest writing can get over some real clunky writing. Like if you feel like you’re reading somebody’s authentic experience, even if they don’t choose maybe the best word, you don’t mind. But if I feel inauthenticity in what you’re reading, I throw the book away again. There’s no way I’m reading it. There’s no way I’m watching the show.

Kusmer: How do you train yourself in that way? Like, you know, make sure that you’re staying true and authentic in your own writing?

Lehane: You build, you train. It’s a muscle and it takes, I don’t care what anybody says, the bottom line is it takes 10 years. It takes 10 years to master it. That doesn’t mean that you might not be publishing. I published my first book, eight years in, but I didn’t know what I was doing until I wrote my second. Then I was like, “Oh, okay. Phew. Okay, I think I got this.”

And you gotta be hungry and you gotta be willing to park your vanity at the door. You can have a strong ego about the work, but if you are there, just so people will praise you — like when I go into writer’s classes or I teach and I see somebody who’s in the room basically to be praised — just leave.

That was one of the great training experiences [while writing on] “The Wire.” They had no respect for anybody who needed to be treated with kid gloves. None of us were like that. I mean, I would literally have somebody look at me and say, “I don’t like that idea.” Why? “‘Cause it sucks.” Oh, okay. Well thanks a lot. You know, it was literally like that.

I work almost exclusively with three women in my writing teams. And we washed out all the weak people, and they were all guys. We just got sick of dealing with their egos. I can’t deal with your needs, man.

My head writer will look at me now and say, “That sucks.” And I’ll be like, “Okay. Fair enough. Well, and your idea sucks too.” We’ll go back and forth with each other. You can’t be sensitive. If you’re looking for a safe space, a writers room ain’t it. Let me just put it that way.

Kusmer: We’re in the era of the anti-hero. I feel like that’s almost its own cliché. It’s not just that your characters are anti-heroes. It’s just that they’re really messy people.

Lehane: They’re messy people. How many non-messy people do you know? ‘Cause I don’t. I get so tired of it when I read the bad guys who are so bad, and the good guys who are so good. You know, it’s like I’m bored already. I’m bored saying it, you know? I know messy people.

One of the things I think is the biggest delusion is that we know why we do things. You’ll get to my age. You look back on your life, and the most common thing that you’ll say about most of the major decisions you made is, “What was I thinking? What was I thinking? For God’s sake? I guess it seemed like a good idea at the time, but it was a terrible idea.”

We do things all the time out of instincts, and often those instincts are bad. I think, you know, Taron’s character says it near the end of the show. He says, “You know, all these things we give different names to, it’s just appetite. I’m hungry and I want to eat, and that’s it. There’s your morality.”

And I do believe that pretty, pretty hard.

Kusmer: I wanna talk about Boston now.

Lehane: Yeah!

Kusmer: So you grew up in Dorchester? Savin Hill?

Lehane: Yeah. St. Margaret’s Parish — a little bit below Savin Hill. Edward Square. Those are our stomping grounds.

Kusmer: Did your upbringing look and sound at all like a Dennis Lehane novel?

Lehane: Yeah. Inside my house did not. The tribute to my actual life is Sean’s parents in “Mystic River.” That’s my actual life, except for the fact that his parents aren’t immigrants. My parents are immigrants. You went into my house and you felt safe, and you felt like you weren’t in 1980s Boston — you felt like you were in 1940s Ireland. That was the vibe. I liked that a lot and I felt safe in my home. Without a doubt.

The streets outside were kind of rough. I was 9 when busing happened. I mean, there was just a lot of violence in the streets, a lot of racial violence. Boston was a dirtier town back then.

It wasn’t like now. I mean, I can’t even write a crime novel in Boston anymore because nothing ever happens here, you know? Um. What’d you have one murder last year? It was ridiculous.

Kusmer: Mayor Wu is proud…

Lehane: No, I love it. I love it. It’s a great city. I’d love to have raised my kids here. Yeah. But I’m a homer. I just love it, warts and all.

Kusmer: I can imagine that living, especially living in California, that a lot of your work is kind of rooted in nostalgia for the streets of your childhood?

Lehane: Yeah. It’s a vanished world. That world doesn’t exist anymore. And I write a lot about that with great love and a jaundiced viewpoint. Sometimes it’s like, people say, “Aren’t people angry about your writing?” For the most part, no, because I think I do warts and all.

Kusmer: Yeah.

Lehane: And so yeah, you’ll see the warts. You also see all the wonderful things about it. I loved growing up in a working class town. I loved the feeling of it. I loved the loyalty. I loved the jokes. I loved the sense of family bonds. I loved all of it. I don’t find that in a lot of the rest of the world.

Kusmer: You really capture the character of a certain era of Boston, particularly, you know, those neighborhoods where you grew up. A lot of times people will say that books are like a love letter to a place.

Lehane: Yes.

Kusmer: I’m not sure your Boston based stories are a love letter per se, but because they’re so open about the ugly side of people here, there’s so much abuse, tribalism, prejudice in your books. How do you go about capturing all the different sides of a place?

Lehane: Boston is unlike any other place. It just is. And, and you know, it’s a little bit like Chicago. It’s a little bit like Philly, but it’s its own place. And people are — and I say this as with pride — we’re all just at least a can short of a six pack. We’re all just a little bit off. You know? And I don’t know if that’s the Irish influence or what.

I was in Miami for graduate school, and I remember worrying that I was losing the Boston voice. Right? So I went back home and I ran into a guy and I said, “How you doing?” He’d been kind of a brawler.

And he said, “Uh, I’m good. You know, I got stabbed a couple months ago,” and I was like, “What happened?” He tells me the story. He says, “I was in Faneuil Hall and, and I got into beef with this guy. And anyway, he stabbed me.” And he said, “I dunno what you’ve heard, but it really takes the fight out of a guy.”

And I thought that’s it. That’s the voice. That right there, it’s, “I don’t know what you’ve heard.” Like you may have heard that, you know, getting stabbed is kind of like a hot stone massage, you know? And then the incredible understatement — not “I was praying for my God,” not “it hurt so much.” No. “It kind of takes the fight out of a guy.”

Like that’s the Boston I know. That’s the Boston that is always in my head when I write, and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that my personal favorites — that I think my three best books are written in that voice. There’s only three books I wrote specifically in that narrative voice and it’s “Mystic River,” and “The Drop,” and “Small Mercies.”

And they’re all the same narrator. It’s the same person telling the story, and it’s a guy in a bar. That’s the way I’ve always pictured him. He’s a guy in a bar and he has a really cool story to tell you, and he’s not sentimental and he’s kind of funny, and he’ll take the wind out of you if you are remotely pretentious.

And that’s that voice. And I love writing in that voice, but I’ve only done it three times.

Kusmer: Yeah. I want to talk about “Small Mercies.” After a long hiatus from book writing, you release “Small Mercies” in 2023. It takes place during the Boston busing crisis. What motivated you to set this book during busing and take on these themes: racism, tribalism, in that way?

Lehane: I think it’s the story of the city. I don’t think you can understand the city until you understand busing and what happened. I grew up in it. I was 9. And I saw it firsthand. My neighborhood bordered South Boston.

I had a front row seat for it, and I saw KKK graffiti. I saw “kill all the ‘n-word’” graffiti. I’m 9 years old and I’m like, “What the hell is going on here?” You’re 9, you’re supposed to be a child. And I feel like after that, I wasn’t.

And so I had a lot of anger built up in me because the one weird thing was — and I don’t say this with any pride or anything — I just wasn’t a racist.

And I grew up with racism everywhere. I mean, it was in my house. It was out on the streets. It was in my friends’ houses, it was everywhere. And I just didn’t have it. It was just, I don’t know why. I mean, I probably should have. But I think it’s because my dad constantly would talk against it.

He would just say, you know, “I don’t care if you’re Black, white, green, or purple. You have a place at this table.” I loved my dad and I took all my cues of what to be a man from my father. And so I think I took that from my dad. But what I also saw on the other side was — I very much had a very adult concept very early on, and I believe this to this day — that it is, “Why are we fighting each other? Hmm? We’re both poor.”

Why the hell are we throwing rocks at each other? Why are we fighting each other in the streets? Oh, because it’s in the best interest of the people who actually control this country to keep the poor fighting amongst themselves because if the poor ever figured it out, they could do some damage.

And so it’s very important that the poor never realize that they have much more in common than they have in differences. And that’s why you always see, at times of economic disparity or economic insecurity — I don’t care if it’s Nazi Germany or it’s America — you will always see people playing the race card. Always.

Kusmer: Do you feel like those early memories of feeling so alienated — the kind of emotional imprint that that had on you — how did writing about it help you process what you witnessed?

Lehane: I think that’s what it was. I felt like a spy in an enemy camp, you know? Because I had to listen to all this. It wasn’t like you could stand up and say, “No, no, don’t use the ‘n-word.’” You know, like, you’re gonna beat down, you know? I wasn’t picking any fights, essentially. And so I think I just, I began to bifurcate as a person. And that turned me into a writer.

The two things I think that are most important in my maturation as a writer are coming from Dorchester and busing.

Kusmer: Did writing the book make you realize anything that you hadn’t realized before?

Lehane: Yeah. I finally realized why I was so angry. I’d been walking around my entire life with this pit of rage in me, and it’s very hard to get through, but when you get there, it comes out. And I was like, why? I had great parents. You know, I was never abused. I don’t have any traumatic stories from my childhood. You know what I mean?

Like what? That’s what puts rage in people. Oh, finally, as I’m writing the book, it’s all pouring out of me. And I was like, you’re pissed off about that that summer.

Kusmer: What you were exposed to.

Lehane: Yeah. At 9, what you saw, 9. It’s not fair. And I looked at my own kids and one of whom was around 9 when I started writing the book, and I was like, man, if anybody exposed her to this, you know, I mean, it would be criminal. I would consider it criminal. You know, you’re taking a kid’s innocence away.

And so I’m one of one kid in the city at that time. How many other kids never got it? How many other kids never had a childhood? In some ways because they were watching the adults who they were supposed to look up to throwing bricks at buses with kids in them. I mean, what are you supposed to do with that?

Kusmer: Yeah. So, I don’t need to tell you this, but you know, there’s this national stereotype about Boston, people think of movies like “The Departed,” you know, Affleck movies, obviously your books and movies as well laid the foundation for how people see the city in popular culture. Irish American, insular, working class, sassy, violent. Do you take some credit for sort of how much Boston is seen that way in popular culture?

Lehane: Oh yeah. No, I can’t wash my hands of that one. That’s on me. We even shot “The Drop” in Brooklyn because we just didn’t want to do one more Irish gangster story set in Boston, you know, so we moved it to Brooklyn. Yeah, it’s on me.

Kusmer: How do you feel about sort of being so responsible for how the rest of the country and the world, frankly, see Boston?

Lehane: Well, it’s not just on, I mean, it’s on “The Departed” and…

Kusmer: But I think of them as your successors.

Lehane: I know, I know. Here’s a crazy thing. If there’s a book or a movie, and there’s a bar in it — it happens in Boston, and there’s a gun — people think I wrote it. It doesn’t matter. The number of people who have come up to me and thanked me for writing “The Departed” or “The Town” is, I mean, it’s endless. I’m talking Bostonians. I’ve gotten fan letters for “The Departed,” I’m not kidding. I got a fan letter from a very famous person for “The Departed,” thanking me for how much they loved it.

I can only tell you, I was watching this documentary on Martin Scorsese, and he’s a big idol of mine. And somebody said, “Well, how do you feel about people who say you use too much music in your movies?” And he said, “Then I use too much music, and I probably move the camera too much.” Like you can live with it, I can live with it. What I set out to do when I set out to be a writer, I have far exceeded that, and so I am just grateful as hell

Kusmer: In LA, are you basically “Boston guy”? Like you get a call whenever anyone is setting anything in Boston so they don’t look like an idiot?

Lehane: No. Sometimes I get a little offended. I’m like, “Wait a minute you guys, I’m right here, guys. You guys did ‘The Equalizer’ with my favorite actor? You set it in Boston and nobody called me?” I was a little bit offended, like, “What the hell?” No, they do Boston without me. Plenty of times. Plenty of times.

Kusmer: Do you have any advice for capturing the Boston accent? It’s endlessly talked about. Bad Boston accents in movies.

Lehane: Oh, It’s so bad. It’s so bad.

Kusmer: What, what are the common pitfalls?

Lehane: The biggest one is dragging. It’s not an elongation. It’s an amputation. People don’t say “nevaaahh.” They say “neva.’” You know, they say “foreva,’” you know, it comes out fast, and it’s when you drag it that you get into trouble. And so I think, um, you know, Paul Walter Hauser, who did “Blackbird” with me, he went and did a Matt Damon movie with Matt Damon and Casey Affleck that was on Apple, I think a year ago. I’m forgetting the name of it, but he was like, “Should I do the accent?” And I’m like, “If anybody gives you a look, stop.”

Kusmer: Right. A lot of people would benefit from that advice. Who do you think’s done it best? Non-Bostonians.

Lehane: I’ll tell you who I think is the best and nobody’s seen the movie is the entire cast of “Monument Ave.”

Kusmer: Haven’t seen it.

Lehane: It’s a movie from the ‘90s. Ted Demme made it with Dennis Leary and it’s really wonderful. It’s this very dark crime drama, and I think Leary must have been coaching everybody because Billy Crudup is great. Famke Janssen’s great. I mean, people who are not Bostonians crushed it. Absolutely crushed it. And so that one sticks out to me.

The worst of them is “A Perfect Staaahm.” Diane Lane’s accent is so bad that it affects Mark Wahlberg’s accent, and he grew up here. That’s pretty bad.

Kusmer: It’s a domino effect.

Lehane: Yeah. There was one Mel Gibson made that nobody remembers, called “Edge of Darkness.” And I think they called it “Edge of Darkness” just so they could say “dahkness.” And that was really bad too.

I tell actors: Call the Land Rover dealership in Norwood. Because there’s a woman who answers the phone there. It’s a phone recording — at least she used to be 10 years ago. I loved it. You would call up and she would say, “Thank you for calling Land Rover of Norwood.” You’re like, that’s all you need, man. That’s it. Land Rover of Norwood. You know?

Kusmer: They’re probably like, “We get a lot of calls. We don’t know why. A lot of calls from California.”

Lehane: Yeah.

Kusmer: That’s really good. So in Boston we have a poet laureate, but I would like to name you our crime writer laureate. Do you accept?

Lehane: You’re so kind. I accept. Thank you. Okay, so I’ll be the, I’ll be the the writer laureate, the novelist laureate, the whatever laureate, crime fiction laureate.

Kusmer: We’re honored.

Lehane: Good stuff kid.

title: A leader of a Dorchester-based Cameron Street gang pleads guilty to racketeering and drug charges
text:
A leader of a Dorchester based gang pleaded guilty to racketeering and drug charges Friday in federal court in Boston, the Massachusetts US Attorney’s office said.

Anthony Centeio, also known by the street name “Wheezy,” 37, of Boston and Rehoboth, is charged with conspiracy to participate in a racketeering enterprise; conspiracy to distribute 500 grams of more of cocaine, cocaine base and methamphetamine; and being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition, US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office said in a statement.

The next court date for the Centeio is May 7, at which time sentencing will be discussed, court records show.

Centeio was a leader of Cameron Street, a gang based largely in Dorchester that uses violence and threats of violence to preserve, protect and expand its territory, promote a climate of fear and enhance its reputation, prosecutors said.

In 2022, Centeio was one of 19 alleged Cameron Street members charged in a 39-count federal indictment with crimes that include gun and drug trafficking, illegal gun possession, racketeering conspiracy, and possessing guns in furtherance of drug trafficking , the Globe reported.

Centeio and another Cameron Street member, Daronde Bethea, also known as “Freeze,” tried to shoot and kill a NOB/Wendover gang member in Dorchester in June 2018, prosecutors said. Bethea was sentenced to nearly 24 years in prison for his role in Cameron Street, including the attempted murder in June 2024, the statement said.

Law enforcement recorded controlled purchases of a firearm from Centeio between February 2021 and March 2022, prosecutors said. They also recorded purchases of more than 500 grams of cocaine and cocaine base from Centeio directly or through his cousin and co-defendant Michael Lopes.

Lopes was sentenced to more than four years in prison in May 2024, prosecutors said.

Authorities searched Centeio’s home in Rehoboth in April 2022 and found $25,760 in cash, a Glock .45 caliber semi-automatic pistol, 21 rounds of .45 caliber ammunition, and clothing and jewelry associated with Cameron Street, prosecutors said. Centeio was encountered at Lopes’ residence in Pawtucket, R.I., where hundreds of grams of cocaine, cocaine base and methamphetamine, packaging materials for street level sales and cash were seized.

Adam Sennott can be reached at adam.sennott@globe.com.

title: Agreement halts sale of Rhode Island’s ‘Conjuring’ house, for now
text:
Nicole M. Labonte, an attorney representing Hawes, said the agreement was reached after the notary who notarized both documents “indicated that she would testify that she didn’t notarize them properly.”

“She didn’t do her job as a notary, unfortunately,” Labonte told reporters outside the courtroom. “So we’re conceding that those documents aren’t going to be the documents that my client uses when they do close on the purchase and sale.”

“The intention is still to close on the purchase and sale at some point,” Labonte said. “There would be, at that point, a new warranty deed, new documents for the closing, if we get to that point.”

Filed on Dec. 5, the civil lawsuit seeks to block the sale of the 1677 Round Top Road property, claiming the house’s current owner, Jacqueline Nuñez, of Dorchester, Mass., has experienced serious mental health issues and “lacked the capacity” when she signed the limited power of attorney agreement last year.

The lawsuit was filed by Nuñez’s older sister, Elizabeth Greenhalgh of West Jordan, Utah, and alleges Hawes was aware of Nuñez’s health issues, and that he and a co-defendant, Julia Demay, “are taking advantage of Nuñez’s lack of legal capacity for their own personal and financial gain.”

The lawsuit alleges the power of attorney agreement authorized Demay “to do all things necessary” to sell the home to Hawes for $1.3 million.

However, Hawes, who said last month claims made in the litigation are not supported by facts, said last week the first time he spoke to Demay was in December.

Labonte said Hawes and Demay had “absolutely no connection” to one another before the lawsuit.

Demay, of Middleborough, Mass., could not be reached for comment, and as of Monday, and had no attorney listed in court records.

In a Dec. 7 email included in court filings, Nuñez denied signing the power of attorney agreement, writing, “YIKES! I never signed any such document.”

“Julie Demay is not even an attorney so this is a ridiculous joke or stunt of complete idiocy (I suspect the latter),” Nuñez wrote.

The lawsuit is due back in court on Jan. 27 for a hearing on a preliminary injunction.

In court last month, Hawes had agreed not to close on the sale of property at least until Jan. 7.

Labonte has filed a motion to dismiss the case.

“We argue, first of all, that there’s no standing for [Greenhalgh] to bring the case, but also that the allegations in the complaint are actually, in large part, inaccurate,” Labonte said.

Michael Resnick, an attorney representing Greenhalgh, said “the cause of action that we pled is really aimed at Miss. Nuñez’s legal capacity.”

“There is no claim or count in this lawsuit asserting that [Labonte’s] clients put Miss. Nuñez under undue influence or duress. We have not made that claim,” Resnick said. “Our claim is aimed at Miss. Nuñez’s mental capacity to enter into contracts and other such obligations.”

The lawsuit is the latest development in a string of controversies over the past year and a half surrounding Nuñez and the house made famous by “The Conjuring” horror movie franchise.

In 2024, Nuñez faced allegations of harassment from Hawes, and accusations from former employees who say she owes them money; she allegedly fired one after claiming a spirit told her he was stealing from the business.

In November 2024, the Burrillville Town Council opted not to renew a business license related to the house after Nuñez — who bought the property for about $1.5 million in 2022 — was arrested and charged by local police with allegedly driving a Lexus SUV while intoxicated and leading officers on a chase through town.

According to Greenhalgh’s lawsuit, since January 2024, Nuñez has been “experiencing serious mental health issues that have impaired her judgment and rendered her incapable of understanding the nature and consequences of her actions.” She has been committed to at least three hospitals for psychiatric care, the lawsuit states.

The “Conjuring” house was slated for a foreclosure auction in October 2025, but the event was abruptly canceled after Needham Bank sold the underlying mortgage to YouTuber Elton Castee, through his Summit & Stone LLC, a corporation formed in Rhode Island in September.

Castee, who touts more than 4 million subscribers on his “TFIL” (Traveling to every country in A-Z order) channel on YouTube, along with comedian Matt Rife, purchased the former Connecticut home of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren earlier this year, with its vast collection of allegedly haunted objects.

Castee’s LLC was named as an “interested party” in the ongoing lawsuit. Castee declined to comment on the matter last month.

At the urging of Andrea Perron — whose family was supposedly haunted in the 1970s at the Burrillville home where the Warrens were called in to investigate — Hawes launched a GoFundMe to try to raise money to purchase it at auction.

Hawes has said he is not seeking to make a profit, and the goal is to raise as much money as possible to keep costs down for visitors, and to keep the house in the hands of people who want to preserve it, not exploit it.

The online fundraiser has continued despite the latest developments, and as of Monday had garnered more than $323,000 in donations.

title: Renee Good, killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis, is the latest political martyr of the Trump era
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Protests are a cacophony of signs, slogans, and chants. But at the anti-ICE demonstrations that took place around Boston and across the country over the weekend, one name and face rose above the rest.

In the days since an ICE agent fatally shot her, Renee Good, a 37-year-old Minneapolis woman, has become a rallying cry for Americans’ opposition to the Trump administration’s deportation policies. The network of pro-immigrant groups that organized a demonstration outside Boston City Hall on Saturday, LUCE, gave out signs with a drawing of Good’s face framed by pastel-colored flowers.

“She’s another martyr,” said James Adams, a substance abuse counselor from Townsend who carried a placard that read “Say her name!” Martyr comes from the Greek for “witness.” According to Pietra Adami, a LUCE organizer, that’s exactly what Good was doing. “She saw injustice happening in her neighborhood,” Adami said. “She died trying to protect the community.”

The United States has had political martyrs since before it was a country, and some of Saturday’s protesters sought to summon that history. One held a sign featuring six coffins. Five reproduced a 1770 Paul Revere engraving memorializing the colonists killed in the Boston Massacre. The sixth was labeled with Good’s name.

“In my mind, these two events are linked,” said the protester, a local high school history teacher who identified herself as Michelle, comparing British troops occupying Boston to the thousands of immigration agents the Trump administration has dispatched to Minneapolis.

People who become symbols often fit a sympathetic mold. Activists challenging segregation in Montgomery, Ala., deliberately elevated Rosa Parks, a seamstress who nonviolently refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, as a living embodiment of the civil rights movement. On Saturday, protesters similarly drew on aspects of Good’s biography.

Her citizenship status was one of them. At least 32 people died in immigration detention last year, a two-decade high, and an ICE agent fatally shot a Mexican man named Silverio Villegas González during a September traffic stop near Chicago. But Good “was an American citizen,” said one Cambridge protester, who declined to give his name. “Any of us could have been in that situation.” He carried a sign featuring a still from a cell phone video of Good in her car, speaking kindly to an ICE agent seconds before her death.

Does it help that Good was young, white, and blonde? Possibly. But George Floyd, a Black man murdered in 2020 by a police officer just blocks from where Good was slain last week, also became immortalized. “Charlie Kirk is a face, too,” said Miguel Gomez-Ibanez of Weston, referencing the right-wing activist many conservatives have called a martyr since his killing last year. “It doesn’t have to be a white woman.”

Others noted that Good leaves behind three children. Alanna Floyd, a 28-year-old speech-language pathologist, held up a cardboard sign that read “Then they came for… a mom of three.” It was, Floyd explained, a reference to the poem “First They Came,” which lists groups victimized by the Nazis — socialists, trade unionists, Jews — and condemns Germans’ failure to speak out. “I wanted to highlight who she is,” Floyd said.

Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and others have cast Good as a far-left agitator who tried to run over an ICE agent, but video appears to show her trying to drive away. According to loved ones, Good was a Christian, a poet, and no activist. “We stopped to support our neighbors,” her wife told local media.

Martyrdom can be cynical. The Nazis, fascist Italy, and other autocratic regimes sanctified the dead to buttress their causes. Trump’s allies have bestowed the label on Ashli Babbitt, a 35-year-old QAnon conspiracy theorist who was fatally shot by a police officer while storming the Capitol on Jan. 6.

But even before Good’s death, a growing share of Americans saw the administration’s immigration policies as too extreme. Most disapprove of ICE and say the agency is being “too forceful,” according to a poll released the day Good was killed. Abolishing ICE remains unpopular, but support has spiked since last year.

Still, until now, that opposition has lacked a galvanizing face. “Maybe she’s the first,” said Gomez-Ibanez. “‘Cause you need a face. You gotta personalize it.”
