title: Boston has given out 64 new free liquor licenses. Here’s how they’re changing the city.
text:
When Rai and Perry opened Comfort Kitchen in 2023, the city had just about run out of free licenses unless another restaurant returned theirs. The couple was lucky to get one, and they learned just how much their bottom line depended on beer, wine, and cocktails: Alcohol can be twice as profitable as food.

“Without a liquor license,” Rai added, “we would not have survived.”

Rai and Perry got lucky again when groundbreaking legislation in 2024 created 225 new liquor licenses for Boston. Suddenly, the city finds itself flush with licenses in what could be the biggest expansion of alcoholic permits since the end of Prohibition. The city released the last batch of those licenses on Jan. 1.

Unlike the old system that required restaurant owners to fork over hundreds of thousands of dollars to buy a license from a shuttered restaurant, the new licenses are given out for free. And most are tied to 13 ZIP codes that could use the economic boost of sit-down restaurants including Mattapan, Roxbury, and Hyde Park. These so-called restricted licenses can’t be bought or sold and must be returned to the city after a business closes.

So far, 64 liquor licenses have been approved across 14 neighborhoods, according to the Boston Licensing Board. Fourteen licenses landed in Dorchester, followed by 11 in East Boston, 10 in Jamaica Plain, 6 in Roslindale, and 5 each in Roxbury and the South End.

The new licenses allowed mom-and-pop restaurants and community organizations that had long been priced out of buying a liquor license to get one for free, while others with beer-and-wine permits could upgrade to ones that allowed them to pour cocktails.

Perhaps most exciting: The flood of licenses has unleashed a wave of creativity among restaurant owners and entrepreneurs. They no longer have to open pricey places that cater to the masses to recoup the cost of their license. Concepts that aren’t just Italian cuisine and steak houses will have an easier time getting off the ground now.

With free-flowing licenses come spots like Comfort Kitchen and Ama with inventive global food inspired by Nepal-born Rai. And in Dorchester, there’s JustBook-ish, a bookstore on Dorchester Avenue that serves beer and wine, and Sorrel & Lime, a Caribbean-inspired modern event space on Blue Hill Avenue.

Then there are coffee shops that are becoming vibrant spots at night, too, like Jadu in Jamaica Plain and Gracenote Coffee’s The Listening Room in the Leather District.

Had Gracenote founder Patrick Barter not received a free license, he was preparing to close his popular experiment, The Listening Room, which opened in 2024 in an empty space behind his coffee shop. Barter, who studied jazz drumming at Oberlin College & Conservatory, wanted a place modeled after Tokyo’s jazz kissas, intimate bars where people listen intently to curated vinyl set lists and talking is discouraged.

To operate The Listening Room, Barter had been relying on a series of one-day liquor licenses, but the administrative burden was onerous.

“It wasn’t sustainable,” he said.

Then he heard about the influx of free licenses being offered by the city. The Leather District is not among the designated neighborhoods eligible for licenses, so Barter’s only shot was to win one of the 12 unrestricted licenses, or so-called golden tickets, which can be used anywhere in the city and do not have to be returned.

So far the city has awarded only three unrestricted licenses: The Listening Room, Ama in Allston, and Merengue Express in Mission Hill.

In getting such a valuable license for his tiny backroom club, Barter felt seen by the city. The 50-seat Listening Room is small by design; it doesn’t create a lot of jobs nor generate much tax revenue. That’s in stark contrast to how the city gave out unrestricted licenses a decade ago in what felt like a first-come, first-served basis with permits landing at well-connected, deep-pocketed owners in the Back Bay and the Seaport.

“The motivation for giving us one of the licenses doesn’t seem like it could be financial,” Barter said. “It has to be for what seems to me like the right reasons: supporting interesting and unique, culturally valuable things that are in the process of making Boston a cooler place to live.”

For decades in Boston, demand for liquor licenses has outstripped supply because the state caps the number of liquor licenses the city can have. When the city doesn’t have any free licenses to give out, restaurateurs must buy one from another place that closes, with the scarcity driving prices up over $600,000. That, in turn, has driven young chefs out of Boston to Brookline, Cambridge, and Somerville and other places where liquor licenses are cheaper.

The 2024 infusion of licenses has helped lower the cost of licenses to about $525,000 for those that still need to buy them, said Charlie Perkins, president of the Boston Restaurant Group, who brokers sales of both restaurants and liquor licenses.

“It’s a good thing,” he said.

Perkins still thinks the cost of opening up a restaurant in Boston is too high, making it much harder for young chefs to launch new ideas the way that Gordon Hamersley, Todd English, Jasper White, and others did in the 1980s.

“So all you’re getting are chain restaurants in new developments,” added Perkins. “It’s taking the heart out of the young chefs.”

That is something the city wants to work on, said Segun Idowu, the city’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion.

While the city has reached out to current restaurant owners about the availability of licenses, Idowu said that now it wants to get the word out to developers, encouraging them to include restaurant spaces in new projects now that liquor licenses are easier to come by.

And some neighborhoods, notably Mattapan, still haven’t had many applicants for liquor licenses. Mattapan has only gained one new place to grab a drink — Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant.

That’s something the city wants to stay on top of, making sure the communities that have many licenses left know to take advantage of the opportunity.

“As more and more of these restaurants open as a result of these licenses, then we’ll see a lot more interest from folks because they’ll see that it’s possible,” said Idowu, “and the city will be shaking off that reputation of ‘we’ve got no licenses to give out.’ ”

title: Geoghan preferred preying on poorer children
text:
The telephone call was urgent.

“There is a crisis,” the Rev. Brian M. Flatley, an archdiocesan official, told Dr. Edward Messner, a psychiatrist at Massachusetts General Hospital, on Dec. 30, 1994.

Messner’s notes from that day convey the gravity of the situation: “A priest had admitted abusing minors in the past and has been acting out again recently . . . police and the district attorney are involved . . . The allegations mirror what has come up before.”

Six hours later, the Rev. John J. Geoghan and Messner began regular therapy sessions in which Geoghan admitted to being “drawn by affection and intimacy with boys” and, as an MGH psychologist wrote, “pointed out that his misconduct occurred, `during a time of sexual exploration for this country.’”

In 1995 and 1996, according to court records examined by the Globe Spotlight Team, Geoghan explained why he preyed on children from poorer families: “The children were just so affectionate, I got caught up in their acts of affection. Children from middle-class families never acted like that toward me, so I never got so confused.”

Moreover, court documents that include Geoghan’s psychiatric records contain starkly contradictory assessments of his danger to children from different therapists. He received at least four clean bills of health between 1980 and 1990, a period when the Archdiocese of Boston assigned him three times to parishes despite his record of abuse; but prompted declarations that he was an incurable pedophile after he became a public embarrassment to the archdiocese in the mid-1990s.

For example, Messner’s notes show that Geoghan told him that Flatley, whose job was to deal with priests who had molested children, had branded him “a pedophile, a liar, and a manipulator.”

Collectively, the publicly filed church documents add detailed clinical evidence to what the Globe reported yesterday: Although the 1995 and 1996 psychiatric reports diagnose Geoghan with a deep-rooted sexual perversion, there were ample signs years earlier that he was unfit for parish work.

Yesterday, the Globe reported that Cardinal Bernard F. Law, during his first year in Boston in 1984, assigned Geoghan to St. Julia’s in Weston even though Geoghan had been removed from his two prior parishes for molesting children. In one of those cases, in 1980, Geoghan asserted that his repeated abuse of seven boys in one family, which was disovered that year, was not a “serious” problem. That is according to a church timeline of Geoghan’s career - six parish assignments in 34 years with accusations that he molested more than 130 children.

Law, after celebrating Mass yesterday at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, reiterated the archdiocese’s statement of Friday that he would not comment on Geoghan.

The documents also contain evidence that Geoghan’s false denials of past sexual abuse through the 1960s and much of the 1970s helped justify a critical church decision that freed Geoghan to abuse even more children. In 1989, Geoghan was forced to take a six-month sick leave from St. Julia’s after more accusations of abuse surfaced. But Law soon signed off on a decision to return him to the parish, according to church documents.

The Spotlight reports of today and yesterday are based on public documents filed in connection with 84 civil lawsuits pending against Geoghan and two criminal cases, the first of which is scheduled to go to trial in Middlesex Superior Court next Monday. The archdiocese, Law, and five other bishops are defendants in many of the pending lawsuits, charged with negligence for not properly supervising Geoghan. Already, the archdiocese has settled 50 other lawsuits, paying more than $10 million to Geoghan’s victims.

The multiple accusations against Geoghan represent the largest scandal involving an American Catholic priest since the 1992 disclosure that former priest James Porter had abused more than 100 children in the Fall River Diocese in the 1960s.

The massive number of documents compiled by lawyers handling the 84 remaining civil suits have been under a confidentiality seal sought by the archdiocese. But based on a motion by the Globe, Superior Court Judge Constance M. Sweeney ordered that all the documents be made public. They are scheduled to be released on Jan. 26.

The documents already on public file detail the extent of Geoghan’s lengthy treatment history and make clear the church’s longtime knowledge of his misconduct.

The psychiatric documents offer added insights into Geoghan’s troubled mind and the motivations behind his aberrant actions - often as explained by Geoghan himself.

Geoghan was, by his own assessment, a heterosexual. But he told Messner during his treatment sessions that his victims were usually young prepubescent boys. He said he “avoided girls,” explaining, “I picked the boys because in some way they were the safest, the girls and the mothers would have been more dangerous.”

The records suggest there were early warning signs.

Geoghan, who is 66, attended St. John’s Seminary after graduating from Holy Cross College and was ordained in 1962. Deposition transcripts refer to correspondence from Geoghan’s seminary days in which his superiors conclude he has “pronounced immaturity.”

In an April 1995 session with Messner, Geoghan said that even as a newly ordained priest he would “experience arousal when there was physical closeness” with children.

In a June 1996 psychological assessment, Dr. Mark Blais, a Massachusetts General Hospital psychologist, concluded that Geoghan has a “powerful sense of emotional deprivation and emotional loneliness.”

Medical evaluations of Geoghan, which repeatedly cleared him to return to parish work after incidents of sexual misconduct in the 1970s and ’80s, changed dramatically in the mid-1990s. By then, complaints against Geoghan were being made with unsettling frequency, and it was clear he risked becoming an embarrassment - and financial liability - to the Church.

In December 1984, for example, a month after being reassigned to St. Julia’s in Weston following his removal from St. Brendan’s in Dorchester, Geoghan underwent evaluations by two separate Boston-area psychotherapists. Dr. Robert Mullins declared Geoghan “fully recovered,” and Dr. John H. Brennan advised “no . . . restrictions to his work as a parish priest.”

Not everyone was comfortable with the assignment. Bishop John M. D’Arcy, a popular cleric whose forthright manner rankled Law, according to a friend of D’Arcy, wrote to Law in December 1984 to question Law’s decision assigning Geoghan to St. Julia’s because of his history of sex abuse. He warned that placing Geoghan there might result in further scandal.

Two months later, D’Arcy was gone, transferred to a diocese in Fort Wayne, Ind., which he has headed ever since.

New allegations against Geoghan surfaced within two years, and again in 1989. But Geoghan told Bishop Robert J. Banks in March 1989 that he had “no more sexual attraction to children” and had been “chaste for five years.”

But the church’s own timeline of Geoghan’s misconduct suggests Banks did not believe him. Within weeks, Geoghan was sent to the St. Luke Institute in Suitland, Md., where he was diagnosed with “homosexual pedophilia.” The result: “Told by Bishop Banks he had to leave ministry,” according to a church record.

Instead, Geoghan was put on sick leave the following month, and in August was hospitalized for three months at the Institute of Living, a Hartford treatment center, where he was discharged in November 1989, as “moderately improved.” Banks agreed to send him back to St. Julia’s, subject to approval by another bishop and “BFL” - Cardinal Law.

But during 1995 treatment, psychologists at St. Luke concluded that during the 1989 treatment in Hartford, Geoghan did not tell the truth about the extent of his sexual abuse of children. He denied any incidents before the late 1970s, to include long-running instances of abuse dating to 1962. And the Institute of Living’s report to the archdiocese reflected Geoghan’s lie.

Moreover, the records state that Bishop Banks was “unhappy” with the Institute of Living’s discharge summary because it was “different from what he had understood and based his decision to allow Fr. Geoghan back to work.”

A reply letter from the institute reports: “The probability that he would act out again is quite low. However, we cannot guarantee that it could not reoccur.”

Yet the archdiocese was hit with more complaints in 1991, 1992, and 1994, although the 1992 accusation was dismissed by church officials as “hearsay and vague.”

Law finally removed Geoghan from parish duty in January 1993.

Midway through his treatment with Messner, Geoghan was returned to St. Luke in January 1995. His diagnosis after that 10-day stay was far less optimistic than earlier judgments. “It is our clinical judgment that Father Geoghan has a longstanding and continuing problem with sexual attraction to prepubescent males,” his evaluation reads. “His recognition of the problem and his insight into it is limited.”

Therapists at St. Luke advised that Geoghan have no unsupervised contact with minor males and return for residential treatment, although Geoghan resisted the latter recommendation. Instead, he was sent in July 1995, to Southdown, an Ontario treatment facility, where he stayed for four to six months.

In 1996, Blais, too, submitted a pessimistic evaluation. “Treatment of such a chronic and deeply ingrained condition would need to be lengthy,” he wrote.

Geoghan was removed from the priesthood in 1998.

title: Law on race, ethnicity data broke ground — now let’s gain some
text:
Massachusetts has taken a nationally leading step by requiring more detailed race and ethnicity data collection across state agencies, helping illuminate the distinct needs of communities long hidden by overly broad categories (“New year, new laws from pot to privacy,” Metro, Jan. 2). Realizing the promise of data equity now depends on strong, intentional implementation.

Since the law’s passage, the Asian Pacific Islanders Civic Action Network and partner organizations have been working closely with the Healey-Driscoll administration to help guide implementation. This collaboration matters, and important groundwork has begun. But as the law now takes effect, it is clear that implementation must move forward with greater urgency.

For Asian, Pacific Islander, Black, Latino, immigrant, and other marginalized communities, data disaggregation is not abstract. It directly affects access to food, health care, education, and economic opportunity. Without timely, consistent implementation across agencies, the law risks falling short of its promise.

title: ‘Not how we rock here in Roxbury’: Michelle Wu has a plan for Madison Park, no matter what the neighbors say
text:
Now, you may think this happens all the time. Plans change. No big deal. There’s some truth to that. The difference is that there have been so many promises made — and broken — on this stretch of Tremont Street known as Parcel 3 that to drop a bombshell like this is stunning — and frankly disrespectful of the community process in general and Black voices in particular.

“You’re making a pronouncement right now,” said Tito Jackson, the former city councilor turned cannabis entrepreneur, during the virtual meeting. “You’re telling people what you’re going to do, not asking them what we should do. That’s not how we rock here in Roxbury.”

Wu did not attend the two-hour community meeting on Monday night. She left it up to her planning chief, Kairos Shen, to deliver the shocking news.

This from a mayor who throughout her political career has vowed to blow up the top-down planning process in favor of a more community-oriented approach.

Apparently that was then, this is now.

Shen will have you believe that the sudden about-face is related to the timing of two things: In December, the Massachusetts School Building Authority gave initial approval to help pay for a new Madison Park, which could cost $700 million and make it the most expensive school project in state history. And this week, the Boston Planning & Development Agency is the last chance for the board to renew the designation for the current project on P3, which, at close to 8 acres, is the largest city-owned parcel that’s undeveloped anywhere in Boston.

The planning agency awarded the project, which sits across from the Boston Police Department headquarters and abuts Madison Park’s existing campus, to a team led by HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace in January 2023, but it hasn’t been able to secure financing because of the current glut of lab space and the high cost of construction.

I can understand why Shen, who spent two decades at the planning and development agency under former mayor Tom Menino, is eager to get behind Madison Park. Shen was at the agency when Roxbury leaders began working on a master plan; he has seen over the decades how plan after plan for P3 has evaporated, from a soccer stadium for Robert Kraft’s New England Revolution to a shopping mall anchored by BJ’s Wholesale Club, to offices for Mass General Brigham (then Partners HealthCare), and a new headquarters for the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

That history may help explain why Shen and the city are sprinting toward a project that can get funding at a time when many other developments in Boston are stalled.

But c’mon, has Wu not learned anything from her experience redeveloping White Stadium in Franklin Park or her controversial plan to move the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science to West Roxbury?

In both instances, there was a community uproar and a sense that City Hall just wanted to steamroll projects through. After only eight months, Wu had to pull the plug on her plan to move the O’Bryant across town.

Through sheer political will, she has made headway on White Stadium. Construction has started on the $200-plus million project, but not without riling up residents of Roxbury and Dorchester and drawing a lawsuit from the Emerald Necklace Conservancy that is now before the Supreme Judicial Court. Some of those same opponents showed up at Monday night’s meeting, again saying they’ve been shut out of the process.

Here’s what I fear will get lost in the bungled rollout at P3: Putting Madison Park there is an idea worthy of serious exploration. If anything, Wu and Shen aren’t thinking big enough.

The school, after all, would only take up a portion of the 8-acre site, leaving other parts of it for future development. Maybe HYM and My City of Peace won’t be able to build their full project — 700,000 square feet of life sciences space, 466 units of housing, and a museum and policy center for Embrace Boston — but they could still put something there.

And that’s what the HYM and My City of Peace development team proposed in a statement Monday night. Not an either/or, but a both/and.

“This is a false choice — one that unnecessarily pits education against community investment,“ the statement said. ”This site can, and must, do both."

I’ve been following P3 closely because of the project’s potential to spread the wealth of Boston’s development boom not only to Roxbury but also the people of color who are partners in the project. The city has been taking a page from the so-called Massport model ― which makes diversity a major factor in awarding development rights on agency properties ― and P3 was supposed to be the shining example of that in Boston.

I’m not worried about HYM chief executive Tom O’Brien, who is white and has other projects on his plate, like redeveloping Suffolk Downs in East Boston and Revere. And perhaps cutting O’Brien out of P3 is political payback for contemplating a mayoral run against Wu last year.

But it’s O’Brien’s partners of color — including the Rev. Jeffrey Brown, Dream Collaborative managing principal Greg Minott, and Privé Parking chief executive Ricardo Louis — for whom I feel bad, as well as the people who would have a chance to purchase affordable homes. To them, the current P3 project represented a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

Now what?

I’m sure the Wu administration will continue to make diversity and inclusion a priority in the way it awards development projects. Still I can’t help but think there’s a missed opportunity here to forge a public-private partnership the way Wu did with White Stadium, and create something bigger and better than the city can by going it alone.

What’s more, it didn’t go unnoticed that the fate of P3 is suddenly up on the air in the week leading up to preparations to celebrate Martin Luther King Jr. Day. At the end of Monday’s meeting, Imari Paris Jeffries, chief executive of Embrace Boston — a nonprofit that exists to honor the legacy of King and his wife Coretta Scott King and their time in Boston — reminded us how we shouldn’t forget their commitment to economic justice.

“This holiday is about making good on a promise, especially in a moment where they’re trying to minimize the memory of this holiday, deprioritize this holiday and deprioritize Black History Month and Juneteenth,” said Paris Jeffries. “There is still an opportunity for us to find a solution where the community gets a win, students of Boston get a win, and that we take advantage of the building opportunity in this moment.”

He’s right. We can’t keep telling Roxbury to dream big and then come up short. This history should matter.

title: Man on scooter hit by MBTA bus in South Boston
text:
A man riding a scooter was hit by an MBTA bus in South Boston on Tuesday night, officials said.

The bus was not carrying any passengers when it went through a green light at Old Colony Avenue and Dorchester Street around 10:13 p.m., said Richard Sullivan, superintendent of the MBTA Transit Police.

title: ‘When I came here, it was beautiful’: The cost of Trump attacks on the Somali community
text:
Hilarious, right?

This is what this country is now. It has always been a place where cruelty and racism could flourish. But it’s been a long time since the bigotry was this open, and had the full weight of the federal government behind it.

“When I came here, it was beautiful,” said Abdi Yusuf, head of the Somali Development Center in Dorchester, an immigrant services organization he co-founded 30 years ago. “I fell in love with this country. … I never had to fear anybody.”

Now, he said, Somali Americans “feel we are under attack by the most powerful office in the world, and people are scared.” Some of his clients, who come from many countries, see the videos of masked ICE agents brutalizing and kidnapping people in Minnesota and elsewhere and are afraid to leave their homes.

The president has particular disdain for Somalis, who have the two qualities he and his cultists most despise: They are Black, and they are Muslim.

“Why can’t we have some people from Norway, Sweden?” Trump said at a rally in Pennsylvania in December. “But we always take people from Somalia, places that are a disaster, right? Filthy, dirty, disgusting, ridden with crime.”

This is an administration run by and for white nationalists. Official government communications parrot fascist slogans, urging Real Americans to protect their “one heritage,” recruiting more ICE agents to take their country back, trucking in imagery where all of the heroes are white, and wiping others from the record, including in museums and classrooms.

The administration claims it has seized on Somali immigrants and launched a brutal invasion of Minnesota because dozens of Somali Americans there were involved in a scheme to defraud safety net services — crimes for which they are already being prosecuted and punished.

Meanwhile, this administration’s own operatic corruption is entirely out in the open. There’s nothing Somalis and others can do to avoid Trump’s wrath. Like so many other immigrants, they have followed all the rules, and submitted to extensive vetting, to get here. Most of the people being taken by wilding packs of ICE agents have no criminal histories.

This is about ridding the country of as many non-white people as possible, no matter what it costs us now, and in the decades to come. One in five workers in Massachusetts is foreign-born. A quarter of those who work in education and health care are immigrants. Here, as in other parts of the country, we desperately need them.

“This country is built by immigrants from all over the world,” Yusuf said. “We were always very proud of this. But nowadays it looks like the brown and Black are not so welcome.”

So many immigrants buy into the stories America tells itself: That this is a beacon of freedom and opportunity, where hard work means a chance at a good life for them, and a better one for their children. A citizenship ceremony is the most American place on earth.

Yusuf Abdi fled Somalia as a young man in 2004 after his father, an army general, was assassinated in front of his family by the group that became Al Shabaab. He came to the United States as a refugee and became a citizen in 2014.

“I was very lucky to come to the United States,” Abdi said. A career service manager at the International Institute of New England, in Lowell, Abdi helps resettle other immigrants – he said he’s placed some 5,000 of them in jobs over the years. Along the way, he started a family, earned two graduate degrees, and finally was reunited with his mother and a brother who joined him here.

“Because of the help I got, I always think about what I can contribute back to my new country,” Abdi said.

His new country is fast becoming a place that is no longer worthy of him.

title: Woman ejected from Liberty Hotel bathroom after being accused of being a man files lawsuit
text:
The lawsuit filed Thursday said Baker and Victor were denied the right to use a women’s restroom at the hotel on May 3 by a security guard “because of what Ms. Baker looks like and because they are in a lesbian relationship.”

When the women objected, “the security guard threw them out of the hotel,” the lawsuit stated. The hotel later “panicked” when the pair took to social media to recount their experience, it stated.

“Instead of simply acknowledging its employee’s discriminatory conduct and apologizing, the Liberty Hotel executives agreed to craft a defamatory statement, knowing it was false, suggesting Ms. Baker and Ms. Victor were kicked out of the Liberty Hotel because they had been engaging in obscene conduct in a stall,” the lawsuit said.

Leonard H. Kesten, a lawyer for the women, said the pair were never in the same restroom stall. Despite the previous MCAD settlement, Kesten said, his clients still don’t know who specifically made the false claim against them.

“We’ve always said that we are not going to settle until we know who did it and why,” Kesten said.

In a statement, the hotel’s general manager, Mark Fischer, said the establishment has “apologized several times to Ms. Baker and Ms. Victor about their experience and has spent months working with the Massachusetts Commission Against Discrimination (MCAD) to address what occurred and strengthen its practices.”

“We’ve been candid that we can do better, as it has been and remains that all guests should feel welcome at the Liberty Hotel,” he said. “We recognize that they have a right to bring a lawsuit, but we unequivocally deny discriminating or retaliating against them in any way.”

MCAD brought the complaint against the hotel in June, one month after Baker, of Dorchester, and Victor were ejected from the hotel, where they were attending a Kentucky Derby-themed event.

A security guard questioned Baker about her gender in the women’s restroom, and when she showed her ID indicating that she’s female, “the guard failed to remedy the situation and instead, continued to eject the couple from the premises,” the commission said in its ruling.

The commission said the hotel had retaliated against the couple by issuing “a false statement to the media implying that the women were somehow in violation of the Liberty Hotel’s policies.”

When MCAD initiated its complaint, a spokesperson for the hotel said a review of the incident found that “the employee was in the wrong and his actions were well beyond regrettable.”

“No guest of ours should ever be treated in a manner that is anything other than respectful and welcoming,” the statement said. “We apologize to our guests, and to our community particularly the LGBTQ+ community. We continue to work on making amends with Ansley and Liz while we have taken corrective action and sensitivity training.”

Fischer, the Liberty’s general manager, said after the MCAD settlement that “we deeply regret that our initial statement may have created unintended impressions about the actions of Ansley and Liz.”

In the lawsuit now pending in Suffolk Superior, the women allege they suffered damages “in excess of $10 million,” according to the civil complaint’s cover sheet.

The complaint itself said the women are seeking “to recover actual damages, punitive damages, and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs.”

The hotel hadn’t responded in court to the suit as of Thursday afternoon. No hearings have been scheduled.

Speaking to reporters in June, Baker said she has faced “comments” and “looks” when using the women’s room in the past, but the incident at the Liberty Hotel was her “worst nightmare coming true.”

title: 50 fun things to do in and around Boston this winter
text:
BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO’s spring calendar at Symphony Hall is chock-full as usual; highlights in the near future include an all-John Williams program (Jan 22-25) and the world premiere of BSO composer chair Carlos Simon’s gospel-infused “Good News Mass” (Jan 29 & 31), both conducted by music director Andris Nelsons. Further out, the redoubtable nonagenarian maestro Herbert Blomstedt conducts Brahms’s Symphony No. 4 (March 5-7); Nelsons leads a program of excerpts from John Adams’s “Nixon in China” with soprano Renee Fleming and baritone Thomas Hampson (March 26 -28), and Dima Slobodeniouk jumps on the podium for the season finale, Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. Symphony Hall. (April 30-May 3) 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

VIVO PERFORMING ARTS The organization formerly known as Celebrity Series of Boston offers a substantial orchestral bill this season, bringing the Budapest Festival Orchestra with Iván Fischer, (Feb. 10), the Chicago Symphony Orchestra with Klaus Makela (March 1), and two days later the Vienna Philharmonic with Andris Nelsons. Smaller scale but no less notable options include dynamite Baroque band Ruckus with bass-baritone Davone Tines (Jan. 31), a debut series recital by French soprano Axelle Fanyo (Feb 3), violinist Itzhak Perlman with the Klezmer Conservatory Band (Feb 15), the reliably excellent Danish String Quartet (Feb. 27), and solo piano programs by Conrad Tao (March 15) and Vikingur Olafsson (March 20). Various venues. (617) 482-2595, www.vivoperformingarts.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Artistic director Jonathan Cohen leads H+H’s remaining two mainstage concerts this season; the first has Handel’s “Water Music” as its centerpiece surrounded by music of Bach, Rameau, and Lully (April 10 and 12); the next month brings a program of cantatas and concertos by Bach and Telemann (May 15 & 16). Finally, the H+H Chorus takes its own spotlight concert at Jordan Hall. (May 29 & 31) Various venues. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

A FAR CRY The musician-directed orchestra mounts several concerts with the full group around town this spring, including a program in collaboration with string education program Project STEP (Jan. 31), a Valentine’s Weekend meditation on the shapes of love (Feb. 13 & 14), Copland’s pastoral “Appalachian Spring” alongside Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6 (March 14 & 18), and an evening featuring award-winning tenor Karim Sulayman in composer Karim Al-Zand’s song cycle “The Strangers’ Case.” (May 9) Various venues. 617-553-4887, www.afarcry.org

BOSTON BAROQUE The period instrument orchestra continues its first season without founding director Martin Pearlman on the podium, first with Haydn’s “Lord Nelson Mass” conducted by Bernard Labadie (March 6 & 8), then a staged production of Mozart’s “Idomeneo” directed by Bill Barclay and conducted by David Bates, with David Portillo in the title role opposite Hera Hyesang Park as Ilia and Wendy Bryn Harmer as Elettra. (April 24 & 26). The X-tet chamber ensemble also sorties twice, first for a “Sounds from Spain” program curated by concertmaster Christina Day Martinson and featuring repertoire from the baroque through contemporary periods (Feb. 7), then a Turkey and Ottoman-focused program in collaboration with ensemble DUNYA, with a new work by Mehmet Ali Sanlikol. (May 30 & 31) Various venues. 617-987-8600, www.baroque.boston

ISABELLA STEWART GARDNER MUSEUM Weekend concerts in Calderwood Hall continue apace, bringing in artists including baroque violinist Rachell Ellen Wong with collaborators from her fledgling ensemble Twelfth Night (January 25) the Attacca Quartet (Feb. 22), lutenist Hopkinson Smith with an all-Dowland program (March 8), and guitarist Paul Galbraith, who performs on an eight-string “Brahms guitar” held like a cello (April 5). The museum is also hosting the first event in a new, supposedly more experimental “Thursday Night Music” series, with Signal Ensemble making its Boston debut with Steve Reich’s “Music for 18 Musicians.” (Feb. 26) Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. www.gardnermuseum.org

BOSTON PHILHARMONIC Benjamin Zander leads the Philharmonic first in a twofer of Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 20 (featuring Kristian Bezuidenhout) and Bruckner’s Symphony No. 7 (Feb 13); the season then concludes with Mahler’s ecstatic Symphony No. 3, with British contralto Sarah Connolly and three local choruses. (April 11) The youth arm of the Philharmonic also presents two concerts, the first one of Ives, Debussy and Mahler (Feb. 27) and the second and all-American bill of John Harbison, Gershwin and Copland (May 3). Symphony Hall. 617-236-0999, www.bostonphil.org

LORELEI ENSEMBLE Sometimes it feels like Boston audiences most frequently hear the homegrown Lorelei Ensemble as contributors to larger Boston Symphony Orchestra pieces, so the group’s two-night run in the spotlight at the Institute of Contemporary Art, featuring the world premiere of Christopher Cerrone’s new eight-voice oratorio “Beaufort Scales,” is very much worth marking the calendar. March 20 & 21. Institute of Contemporary Art. www.loreleiensemble.com

ASHMONT HILL CHAMBER MUSIC Local luminaries are the name of the game this spring at Ashmont Hill. New England Conservatory ensemble-in-residence the Borromeo String Quartet throws down a program of Haydn, Britten and Dvořák (Feb. 8), then Harvard University freshman and 2025 National Chopin Competition finalist William Ge plays a solo recital (March 22); finally, the Boston-grown wind and string quartet Hub New Music rolls out an afternoon of contemporary chamber music. (April 12) Peabody Hall, All Saints Church, Dorchester. www.ahchambermusic.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA BLO plans to throw open the doors to its new Opera and Community Studios in Fort Point with March’s performances of Mahler’s “Song of the Earth” featuring mezzo-soprano Raehann Bryce-Davis, tenor Brandon Jovanovich, and actor Ellen Lauren (March 20-29); a fully staged American Revolution-inspired production of Donizetti’s “Daughter of the Regiment” brings the company to the Emerson Colonial Theater (April 24-May 3). The Boston Lyric Opera chorus also joins the Budapest Festival Orchestra for Mahler’s Symphony No. 3 as presented by Vivo Performing Arts (Feb. 10), and Bryce-Davis offers a one-night only solo recital at the Opera and Community Studios (March 24). Various venues. 617-542-6772, www.blo.org

A.Z. MADONNA

GRAND KYIV BALLET’S “SWAN LAKE” This touring Ukrainian ensemble returns with the engaging, spontaneous, well-danced “Swan Lake” it brought to Boston last February. Distinctive touches include the role of the Jester, a quartet of black swans in the final act, and a happy ending; running time is just over two hours, but nothing essential is omitted. Bigger, in other words, is not always better. This time out, Viktor Tomashek and Kateryna Malkovich will be featured in both performances. Jan. 24 at 7 p.m. $54-$69. Huntington Theatre. Feb. 15 at 4 p.m. $48-$108. Emerson Colonial Theatre.www.grandkyivballet.com.ua/en/

TRISHA BROWN DANCE COMPANY Brown, arguably the dean of modern dance, passed away in 2017, but her company, which last appeared here in 2011, continues to celebrate her legacy. The program for the troupe’s Vivo Performing Arts debut spans her career. “Glacial Decoy” (1979) was her first work for a proscenium stage, its five women costumed in long diaphanous dresses designed by Robert Rauschenberg and dancing against a backdrop of his black-and-white photos. “Son of Gone Fishin’” (1981) was Brown’s first proscenium work created to music, a score for computerized organ by Robert Ashley drawn from his opera “Atalanta (Acts of God).” “Rogues” (2011) is one of her last works, a male duet that she created at age 75. Feb. 13 at 8 p.m.; Feb. 14 at 2 p.m. $62-$99. Boston Arts Academy Theater. www.vivoperformingarts.org

“TANGO AFTER DARK” Former World Tango Champions Germán Cornejo and Gisela Galeassi head up a cast of eight tango dancers, two singers, and a seven-piece band playing the music of Argentine tango king Astor Piazzolla. Cornejo and Galeassi have been dancing together since 2011 and were featured on Jennifer Lopez’s reality television series “¡Q’Viva! The Chosen One.” The show comes to Boston from sold-out performances in London. Feb. 20. $45-$76. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

LES BALLETS AFRICAINS In 1949 Paris, Guinean artist Keita Fodeba founded a poetry group that evolved into the African Theater of Keita Fodeba, a dancing, drumming, and storytelling troupe. In 1952, the company took its current name and performed at the Théâtre de l’Étoile; in 1958, it became the national dance company of the Republic of Guinea. It had a run of 48 performances on Broadway in 1959 and subsequently went on to the Edinburgh International Festival. Today the 35-member troupe is an ambassador for African culture as it fuses music, dance, and theater. Feb. 28. $45-$76. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET: “WINTER EXPERIENCE” Both halves of this program have a seasonal component. Crystal Pite’s “The Seasons’ Canon” premiered in 2016 at the Paris Opera Ballet; Boston Ballet first performed it in the fall of 2024. Set to Max Richter’s 2012 recomposition of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” Pite’s ambitious piece calls for 54 dancers. Boston Ballet resident choreographer Jorma Elo created “Le Sacre du Printemps” for the company in 2009; set to Igor Stravinsky’s groundbreaking 1913 score, his version is both original and arresting. March 5–15. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

BALLET RHODE ISLAND: “CURTAIN CALL” Ballet Rhode Island pays a rare visit to Boston with a DanceVisions-curated program of works by Ballet Rhode Island artistic executive director Kathleen Breen Combes, Ballet Rhode Island artistic curator and resident choreographer Yury Yanowsky, independent choreographer Naoko Brown, independent choreographer Ruth Fentroy, Janelle Gilchrist Dance Troupe artistic director Janelle Gilchrist, Dance Currents artistic director Kathy Hassinger, DanceVisions artistic director Margot Parsons, and Boston Liturgical Dance Ensemble artistic director Robert VerEecke. March 7 at 7:30 p.m.; March 8 at 2 p.m. $30. Boston University Dance Theater. balletri.org

GIBNEY COMPANY The New York–based company that Gina Gibney founded in 1991 made its Boston debut at the Institute of Contemporary Art in 2023 with an engaging trio of pieces by Johan Inger, Yue Yin, and Sharon Eyal and Gai Behar. The program this time out begins with “Trio (of six),” William Forsythe’s 2024 reconfiguring of his 1996 “Trio.” Israeli choreographer Roy Assaf’s “A Couple” is a duet excerpted from his 2020 work “Figure No. 16.” Finally, there’s Lucinda Childs’s “Three Dances (for prepared piano) John Cage,” which got its world premiere last year. Set to Cage’s 1944-’45 composition “Three Dances,” Childs’s piece for eight dancers addresses Cage’s minimalist aesthetic. March 13–14 at 8 p.m. $70. Institute of Contemporary Art. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET: “THE DREAM” Over the past 40 years, Boston Ballet has done versions of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” by Bruce Wells and George Balanchine, but this will be the company debut for Frederick Ashton’s one-act, one-hour creation from 1964. The score is drawn from Felix Mendelssohn’s incidental music for Shakespeare’s play. Rounding out the program is the world premiere of former company artist My’Kal Stromile’s “The Leisurely Installation of a New Window,” whose three movements — “Thesis,” “Antithesis,” and “Synthesis” — propose to examine “how individuals and societies live inside systems that no longer resolve cleanly.” March 19–29. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

BALLET RHODE ISLAND: “PURE DANCE” Headlining this bill is “Allegro Brillante,” which George Balanchine created in 1956 to the first movement of Tchaikovsky’s abandoned Third Piano Concerto. Christopher Wheeldon’s “Liturgy” follows; set to Arvo Pärt’s “Fratres,” this duet premiered at New York City Ballet in 2003 with Wendy Whelan and Jock Soto. Closing the program is Yury Yanowsky’s “Fading Creatures,” which he made for Richmond Ballet last year and which was inspired by Salvador Dalí’s “The Persistence of Memory.” March 20–29. $42-$72. Woodman Center, Providence, R.I. balletri.org

JEFFREY GANTZ

SOMETHING IN THE WAY FEST Indie stalwarts Run For Cover Records launched this festival 10 years ago in New York; it’s now a co-production between the label and local promoters Bowery Boston. This year’s lineup will be headlined by post-rock architects Explosions in the Sky and emo standard-bearers Sunny Day Real Estate. Jan. 31 and Feb 1, 1:30 p.m. Roadrunner. somethingintheway.net

SPRINTS Dublin has been a launching pad for some great rock acts over the last decade, and these punkers, whose most recent album “All That Is Over” came out in September, scrambled to the top of the heap quickly; vocalist Karla Chubb possesses the righteous fervency of a preacher-poet, while her bandmates’ perpetual motion adds to the urgency. Feb. 3, 7 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

MESHELL NDEGEOCELLO In 2024, this jazz and neo-soul visionary released “No More Water: The Gospel of James Baldwin,” a musically shape-shifting look at the titular writer-activist and his legacy that will be the focal point of this concert. Feb. 7, 8 p.m. Berklee Performance Center. 617-747-2261, berklee.edu/BPC

MIGUEL “CAOS,” this SoCal polymath’s first album in eight years, grinds and grooves as its central figure grapples with the dark sides of himself and the world around him. This is a Valentine’s Day show and Miguel is one of modern pop’s best live acts, so expect the newer album’s hard-edged tracks to be counterbalanced by sumptuous love songs like the effervescent “Adorn” and the devotion-minded viral hit “Sure Thing.” Feb. 14, 8:30 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

NEW EDITION Roxbury’s original boy band comes home with all six members in tow for a post-Valentine’s Day show featuring Michael Bivins proteges Boyz II Men and soul belter Toni Braxton. Feb. 15, 7 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

JADE Freed from the constraints of girlband drudgery, this former member of “X Factor”-spawned Little Mix made a sweeping statement last year with her solo debut “THAT’S SHOWBIZ BABY!,” a thrill-and-chill ride through modern fame that shows off her powerful voice and deep appreciation of pop’s fringe. Feb. 18, 7 p.m. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

JANE INC. In a short period of time, Toronto synth-pop auteur Carlyn Bezic weathered a car accident, a cancer diagnosis, and a breakup; she channeled those intense experiences into “A RUPTURE A CANYON A BIRTH,” which vibrates with the sort of energy that can only come from winning a staring contest with the abyss. Feb. 18, 7 p.m. Middle East Upstairs, Cambridge. 617-864-3278, mideastoffers.com

ALOFOKE Santo Domingo-born Esmelin Santiago Matías García is known to music aficionados in the Dominican Republic as Alofoke, whose championing of reggaetón, dembow, and hip-hop in the ‘00s led to him becoming one of the country’s most influential media executives. At the Agganis, he’ll be helming a massive dance party as he goes about “reimagining the live event experience.” Feb. 28, 8 p.m. Agganis Arena. 800-745-3000, agganisarena.com

CHARLEY CROCKETT This Texas troubadour has released 15 albums since 2015, including his major-label debut “Lonesome Drifter” and its follow-up “Dollar A Day”—both of which were produced by Shooter Jennings and released last year. Crockett’s honky-tonk-ready tunes are catchy and poignant, with his resonant voice burnishing his tales of everyday people. March 8, 8 p.m. Roadrunner. roadrunnerboston.com

DROPKICK MURPHYS The local punk heroes, who released the rousing “For the People” last July 4, set up shop on Lansdowne Street for their annual St. Patrick’s Day Weekend celebration. The three-evening run at MGM Music Hall at Fenway will be supplemented by a kid-friendly Saturday matinee benefiting their foundation the Claddagh Fund; on the holiday itself, they’ll take over House of Blues. March 13, 7 p.m.; March 14, 2:45 and 7 p.m.; and March 15, 7 p.m. at MGM Music Hall at Fenway. Also March 17, 6 p.m. at the House of Blues Boston. dropkickmurphys.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

KEVIN KLING: UNRAVELED The Minnesota-based performer has said: “There’s the trip you plan … and the trip you take.” In his solo show, Kling delivers his personal take, laced with humor, on his own trip. It’s a life journey that has included a congenital birth disorder and a near-fatal motorcycle accident. Directed by Steven Dietz. Jan. 21-Feb. 8. Merrimack Repertory Theatre, Lowell, in partnership with the Contemporary American Theater Festival. 978-654-4678, tickets.mrt.org

SOME LIKE IT HOT A musical adaptation of the 1959 Billy Wilder classic starring Marilyn Monroe, Tony Curtis, and Jack Lemmon. Two musicians, Jerry and Joe, are unlucky enough to witness a mob hit in Prohibition-era Chicago. So they take it on the lam, disguising themselves as women — Joe becomes Josephine, Jerry becomes Daphne — and join an all-female jazz band that is touring the country by train. Joe falls in love with a singer, Sugar Kane. Meanwhile, the gangsters are in hot pursuit. “Some Like It Hot” boasts a blue-chip creative team, with a book by Matthew López (“The Inheritance”) and Amber Ruffin, music by Marc Shaiman, lyrics by Shaiman and Scott Wittman, and direction and choreography by Casey Nicholaw (“The Book of Mormon”). Jan. 28–Feb. 8. Broadway In Boston. At Citizens Opera House, Boston. broadwayinboston.com

THE MODERATE A drama by Ken Urban (“A Guide for the Homesick”) about a content moderator named Frank Bonner (Nael Nacer) who is ground down by the often-unpleasant material he faces on a daily basis. Frank’s gloomy state is further compounded by his estrangement from his wife, Edith (Celeste Oliva), and son during the COVID lockdown. A chance to revive his spirits presents itself when Frank sets out to help Gus (Sean Wendelken), a teenager who has been creating troubling content about his own home and family life. Directed by Jared Mezzocchi. With a cast that includes Greg Maraio, and Jules Talbot. Feb. 5-March 1. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. 617-576-9278, centralsquaretheater.org

PENELOPE Aimee Doherty stars in a one-woman musical that reimagines Homer’s “Odyssey” from the point of view of Penelope, wife of the long-absent Odysseus, who needs to find ways to cope as Odysseus makes his way back home after the Trojan War. “Penelope” is the brainchild of Alex Bechtel, who told the Globe that he was inspired by his feelings of isolation during the pandemic while he was home in Philadelphia and separated from his romantic partner in Boston. With lyrics and music by Bechtel that ranges from folk to jazz to indie rock, and a book by Bechtel, Grace McLean, and Eva Steinmetz, “Penelope” is directed by Courtney O’Connor, with music direction by Dan Rodriguez. Feb. 6-March 1. Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, lyricstage.com

WE HAD A WORLD Joshua Harmon is one of the most interesting playwrights of the past decade-plus. Boston theatergoers have been able to experience his work via local productions of “Prayer for the French Republic,” “Bad Jews,” “Admission,” and “Significant Other.” In the autobiographical “We Had a World,” Renee, a dying woman (Amy Resnick), calls her grandson, Joshua (Will Conard), with an odd request: that he write a play about their family, and that it be “as bitter and vitriolic as possible.” Also featuring Eva Kaminsky as Ellen, Joshua’s mother. Directed by Keira Fromm. Feb. 12–March 15. Production by The Huntington at the Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

ZABEL IN EXILE R.N. Sandberg is a dramatist of note, and his daughter, Megan Sandberg-Zakian, is a director of note who heads Boston Playwrights’ Theatre. The two have teamed up for the first production of Sandberg’s “Zabel in Exile,” about Armenian feminist writer and activist Zabel Yessayan. Set in 1937 in a Soviet prison where she is awaiting execution, “Zabel in Exile” flashes back to episodes in Yessayan’s life, from her upbringing in Constantinople to the Armenian genocide she witnessed as a reporter. With a cast consisting of June Baboian, Danny Bryck, Sarah Corey, Grace Experience, Anelga Hajjar, and Robert Najarian. Feb. 19-March 8. Boston Playwrights’ Theatre, Boston. www.bostonplaywrights.org

THE BALD SOPRANO and THE LESSON The works of avant-garde playwright Eugène Ionesco, an important figure in what became known as the Theatre of the Absurd, are seldom produced in the Boston area. Hub Theatre Company is attempting to fill that vacuum with a double bill of one-acts. In “The Bald Soprano,” which Ionesco described as an “antiplay,” an evening conversation between two bourgeois British couples degenerates into incoherent gabble. In “The Lesson,” the power imbalance between a middle-aged male professor and a young female student takes a deadly turn. Directed by Bryn Boice. Feb. 20-March 8. Plaza Black Box Theatre, Boston Center for the Arts. Tickets are “Pay-What-You-Can.”www.hubtheatreboston.org

THE THINGS AROUND US A solo musical composed, written, and performed by Ahamefule J. Oluo. Presented at Williamstown Theatre Festival last summer, “The Things Around Us” blends personal stories with a soundscape created live onstage by Oluo, using looping technology to layer in clarinet, trumpet, vocals, and percussive sounds. Feb. 20-22. Presented by ArtsEmerson at the Emerson Paramount Center, Robert J. Orchard Stage, Boston. 617-824-8400, artsemerson.org

THE ANTIQUITIES Jordan Harrison’s exploration of the perils of technology, structured as a journey through multiple time periods, including a near-future in which AI curators at The Museum of Late Human Antiquities reconstruct humanity’s past. Directed by Alex Lonati, with a cast that includes, among others, the always-compelling John Kuntz, Kelsey Fonise, and Jesse Hinson. March 6-28. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion at the BCA, Boston. 617-933-8600, www.speakeasystage.com

WAIT UNTIL DARK An adaptation by Jeffrey Hatcher of Frederick Knott’s suspenseful drama about Susan Hendrix, a blind woman in 1944 Greenwich Village who is terrorized by three hoodlums searching for a doll stuffed with heroin. “Wait Until Dark” premiered on Broadway in 1966, starring Lee Remick, and was revived in 1998 with Marisa Tomei making her Broadway debut. But it’s best known for the 1967 film version with Audrey Hepburn. Jenny S. Lee and Eliza Barmakian, who is legally blind, are splitting the role of Susan and will rotate performances. The hoods will be played by Paul Melendy, Bill Mootos, and Mamadou Toure. Directed by Weylin Symes. March 6-22. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. 781-279-2200, greaterbostonstage.org

DON AUCOIN

MASAKO MIKI: MIDNIGHT MARCH Miki, born in Osaka, is a maker of fantastical felted worlds not entirely of this earth. Using brightly colored fabrics stretched over vaguely humanoid forms set loose in a star-filled universe of her own making, the soft-and-fuzzy sci-fi scene also gives way to a deeper suggestion of a kinder, gentler way to embrace what is different and strange, and to see what’s really universal. Jan. 29 - May 31. MassArt Art Museum, 621 Huntington Ave. 617-879-7333, maam.massart.edu.

DIVINE COLOR: HINDU PRINTS FROM MODERN BENGAL The mass printing industry in India has been alive for decades with wild color and flights of fancy depicting centuries of myths and deities that still play a central role in Indian life. Dismissed as art for their pervasive, throwaway ubiquity, this exhibition reexamines them in the context of not what they are as things, but what they represent, a dynamic culture rushing headlong to the future while holding on to its deep ties to the past. Jan. 31–May 31. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300,www.mfa.org.

AARON T STEPHAN: MURMUR Thousands of cast-concrete cinder blocks will fill the Center for Maine Contemporary Art, the fullest expression of Aaron T Stephan’s long-standing fascination with the rugged, prosaic form. The echo of 1960s Minimalists like Sol LeWitt and Carl Andre, who stacked blocks and fire bricks in neat stacks or straight lines is obvious and intentional. But where those artists pursued precision, Stephan plunges into controlled chaos. Arrayed in heaps, his bricks perform a dizzying perspectival trick: The whole scene is embued with a vanishing point perspective — a trompe l’oeuil sleight of hand seriously at odds with the rough and ready material. Jan. 31 - April 5. Maine Center for Contemporary Art, 21 Winter St., Rockland, Maine. 207-701-5005, www.cmcanow.org.

YINKA SHONIBARE: SANCTUARY Shonibare, a celebrated British-Nigerian artist known for his heady formal engagements with the messy, often brutal entanglements of colonial history, debuts a new installation in the U.S. this winter with “Sanctuary City,” a suite of 18 tabletop architectural models of buildings with known histories as refuges for the vulnerable and persecuted. With inequity always buzzing in the background of the post-colonial world, the piece would never not be relevant; in the current roar of the American mass-deportation experience, it will be more resonant here and now than ever. Feb. 11-Jan. 3, 2027. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434, brandeis.edu/rose

EDMONIA LEWIS: SAID IN STONE Edmonia Lewis studied art in Boston in 1863 and then moved on to Rome a few years later — a feat for a woman artist in an era where few were taken seriously. But it was doubly so for Lewis, who was of mixed race, Black and Indigenous, a set of disadvantages in her time and place that could have sunk her career before it started. That it did not says a lot about her, and this show is a showcase for her gift of sculpting hard stone into flowing, lifelike effigies of a personal slate of concerns: Abolition and social reform, and a dignified representation of Black and Indigenous people most often reduced in art of the time to cliche and disdain. Feb. 14–June 7. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500,

PERSONA: PHOTOGRAPHY AND THE RE-IMAGINED SELF Photography, by its very nature, captures fact: The camera, as they say, doesn’t lie. But it only captures what’s put in front of it, and for at least a century artists have been finding ways to use it to bend reality to their liking. This show, an exploration of performative deception, helps unpack an issue more and more prevalent in our image saturated world: How we can use the camera to capture not who we are, but who we want to be seen to me. Feb. 19-May 10. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org.

BOTH SIDES OF THE LINE: CARMEN HERRERA & LEON POLK SMITH Friends, neighbors, and collaborators, Herrera and Smith, masters of crisp hard-edged abstraction, never quite got the recognition in life that they’re garnering post-humously. (Herrera, all but unnoticed much of her career, was a late life “discovery” for the cognoscenti. She enjoyed her first major museum show at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016, when she was 101.) This show puts them together for the first time, and conjures a little of the deserved glory that eluded them while they were alive. Feb. 21 - July 31. Addison Gallery of American Art at Phillips Academy, 3 Chapel Ave., Andover. 978-749-4015, addison.andover.edu

TECHNOLOGIES OF RELATION Depending who you talk to, the deepening integration of digital technology in our everyday lives has either brought about a utopia of ease and amusement, or a smoking hellscape of invasive despair. And for some, it’s both. This exhibition and its dozen artists purports not to judge — as if that were possible — but rather attempt to demystify its deep insinuation into the everyday, as a means to both understand it, and coax its more noble uses. On view beginning Feb. 21. Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, 1040 Mass MoCA Way, North Adams. 413-662-2111, www.massmoca.org.

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Spanning almost three millenia, 800 BCE right up ‘til now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across era to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. March 6-Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400,www.harvardartmuseum.org.

FRAMING NATURE: GARDENS AND IMAGINATION A cross-cultural, collection-wide display of natural lushness to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the MFA’s “Art in Bloom” celebration, this show promises a gamut of garden-forward glory, both flora and fauna. But because I know you’re wondering: There will be Monets, so plan accordingly. March 15–June 28. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300,www.mfa.org

DERRICK ADAMS: VIEW MASTER Adams is a jubilant polymath with a very specific mission: “What can I reveal that has not been shown?” he told the ICA. “Black people — not entertaining, just being, living. Letting people deal with that as reality.” This show, his first-ever career survey, spans more than 20 years of painting, sculpture, installation, performance, and collage, all of it with a signature ebullience that celebrates the lives of his subjects and captures the joy of the everyday. April 16–Sept. 7. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

MURRAY WHYTE

title: Wild day at the drive-through, a boat gets in trouble, and stolen skis recovered
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police log books (a.k.a. blotters) in our communities.

Captain, the Blackstone Police Department’s comfort dog, has come a long way since joining the force as a puppy in June. His first summer on the job took an unexpected turn in August when he suffered a lower leg fracture while exiting a police vehicle, but it didn’t take long for him to bounce back. He’s since passed the third phase of his training, has been making the rounds at schools and community events, and now has his own line of merch, appearing on trading cards, stickers, patches, and a K-9 calendar. “We’re so happy to welcome Captain back to our ranks,” said Chief Gregory Gilmore. “He’s a remarkable animal, and part of our family here at the Blackstone Police Department.”

On Jan. 2, an employee at the Dunkin’ location on Broad Street in Bridgewater reported that an irate customer in a red sedan had come through the drive-through three times and was banging on the windows. The customer was gone when police arrived at the scene.

At approximately 4 p.m. Jan. 5, Nahant police received a call about a motorboat in the water that appeared to be in distress. It was very cold, the sun was going down, and the vessel — which appeared to have lost power — was drifting toward rocks. The caller said the occupants on board were attempting to paddle the boat to shore. Officers located the vessel and Sergeant Andrew S. Constantine was able to hover a drone over it until State Police and Coast Guard personnel responded to assist. The State Police ended up successfully towing the boat to a nearby ramp.

At 8:03 p.m. Dec. 29, Saugus police received a call from a pedestrian who reported hearing someone knocking on a window of a home on Hilltop Avenue, possibly trying to get her attention. It happened twice while she walked by the building. She was unable to give any description of the individual hitting the window, but she was concerned they might need help. Officers were dispatched to the scene and soon discovered there was no cause for alarm, as the knocking turned out to be the homeowner, who was hanging a wall mount in a room.

A man in Boston went on Facebook Marketplace recently and saw a pair of skis for sale that looked very familiar — for good reason, because the skis belonged to him. Someone had stolen them, and now they were listed for sale. The man contacted police and told them about the online listing. A plan was devised to get the man’s skis back by arranging to meet with the seller (who had an active warrant out for his arrest on an unrelated charge) in the area of Massachusetts Avenue and Washington Street. Officers were directed to the lobby of 155 Northampton St., where they saw the stolen skis propped against a fence, and after confirming that the asking price matched the Facebook Marketplace listing, officers identified themselves as police and placed the suspect under arrest. The stolen skis were recovered and returned to their rightful owner. The suspect, a 43-year-old Dorchester man, was charged with receiving stolen property over $1,200.

If you’re buying or selling something through Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, or any other online platform and you need to meet up in person to complete the sale, make sure you do it safely. The Boston Police Department has designated “Safe Exchange Zones” at police stations across the city that are available 24 hours a day where people can do in-person transactions, and many other police departments offer them, too.

title: Is the Boston accent going, going, Gone Baby Gone?
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Longtime Globe reporter Beth Teitell came here from New York, and almost immediately found herself enchanted by the speech of the receptionists at the Boston Herald, where she worked.

She thought it was a wonder. Better yet, a wicked pissah ... once she figured out what that meant.

How exactly to describe her joy? “You know how when you walk into a relative’s house on Thanksgiving and it smells like Thanksgiving and it feels cozy and right?” she told me. “The accent is the turkey and stuffing of the aural world.”

But today, Beth, fed by a Dartmouth researcher, brings bad news: the accent will at some point make like Leonardo DiCaprio at the end of “The Departed.”

Could it be, as she puts it, that the last person to bark out “pahk the cah in Hahvahd yahd” already has been born?

Time out, Beth: What about Ben and Matt doin’ the bit on Fallon with every Massachusetts town and city? They’re deep in the accent, all the way to Yarmouth. Is that just a party trick?

Are you saying all the parents from Dot and Southie and Charlestown and Malden went into deep suburbia and their kids started taking regulah? And making fun of their parents? And not understanding the beauty of the accent? That Boston sound is “inherent sarcasm,” says Mike Felger from the formerly wall-to-wall accented 98.5 The Sports Hub.

“It’s a romance language,” Felger tells Beth, wistfully.

Even Dorchester native and novelist Dennis Lehane said he misses it on the West Coast. In the latest episode of the “Say More” podcast, he told Globe Opinion: “I tell actors: Call the Land Rover dealership in Norwood. Because there’s a woman who answers the phone there. It’s a phone recording — at least she used to be 10 years ago. I loved it. You would call up and she would say, ‘Thank you for calling Land Rover of Norwood.’ You’re like, that’s all you need, man. That’s it. Land Rover of Norwood.”

Early yesterday, I called the now Jaguar-Land Rover of Norwood, listening intently to the recorded message for what I hoped was the best accent in the region. Sadly, no. Sales manager Mike Fleming said he couldn’t remember when or why they changed their directory message, but he agreed that the use of the accent is fading. At least their current recorded voice omitted the “r” in Norwood, as the good Lord intended.

We need your help to figure this out. We’ve set up a “Boston Accent Tip Line” at 617-798-0874 to get your story. Hey, it might even be used for a followup article.

But first, read: The Boston accent is disappearing. How long will the music linger?
