title: More than haircuts: Inside Massachusetts’ first statewide program aimed at giving detained youths job skills
text:
Skill Up is the first standardized vocational program across all five regions in the DYS system, which serves 12-to 21-year-olds for offenses ranging from trespassing to manslaughter. Previously, young people could get silk-screening, culinary, and carpentry training in a few DYS facilities, but no formal training available to everyone. Now there is a $5.2 million budget and 23 programs across the state, including music production, bicycle repair, and horticulture. Participants earn $15 an hour for up to nine hours of skills training a week – money that’s released when they are.

The job skills and money are important, but the less tangible benefits they gain from the instructors, who also serve as mentors, are just as essential, DYS officials and participants said.

“It wasn’t just haircuts,” said Jamari, 18. “It was getting to know me, wanting to know what I wanted to do with myself, even after.”

“It makes me forget that I’m doing time,” he added. “It makes me feel like I’m just at a barbershop and I’m chopping it up with my friends and my family members.”

The Globe is not fully identifying the youths in state custody, whose criminal records are not public, to avoid having a negative influence on their future prospects.

A number of Skill Up instructors statewide were committed to juvenile treatment facilities in the past, sometimes in the same facilities where they teach, and this shared experience helps build relationships with the young men in the program. The providers also live in the cities where these youths will be released, helping create community bonds that many of them lacked before, said Cecely Reardon, the DYS commissioner, a former public defender.

Bikes not Bombs, the Boston nonprofit that runs the bicycle repair program, lets participants keep the bikes they fix and gives them the chance to apprentice for the nonprofit when they get out. Those in the silk-screening program designed and produced T-shirts for the Big E fair in Springfield last year.

Until recently, youth rehabilitation was focused mainly on education, Reardon said, but it was missing those who weren’t on an academic path.

“They leave here with something no one can ever take away from them,” Reardon said. “If we can help a young person be successful, that’s in the name of public safety.”

Completing vocational, educational, and other risk-reduction programs can reduce recidivism rates by more than half in some cases, according to a recent report by the Massachusetts Department of Correction.

Statewide, approximately 500 young people are in the DYS system, including those awaiting trial and those in treatment units such as the Connelly Center. Some have been released but voluntarily continue to receive services. In all, Skill Up has provided vocational training to more than 430 youths.

Adrian Major, who runs the DreamCutz barbershop with his wife, Alexis, as part of their Dreamcatcher Initiative nonprofit in Dorchester, said barbershops are an ideal training ground because of the therapeutic aspects to getting a hair cut or shave.

The hot towel on your face, the smell of aftershave, the conversation with a barber – all of this can turn a bad day into a good one, Major said.

“It can change a whole dynamic,” he said. “Anything that helps enhance your image makes you really feel better.”

And learning how to provide this service makes students feel good, too.

Major has seen young men progress, from something as small as admitting “my fault” when something goes wrong to opening up about their hopes and dreams. Even just improving their mood over the course of a few hours is a win, he said.

In addition to vocational skills, trainees learn about financial literacy, entrepreneurship, public speaking, and different aspects of employment such as performance reviews. Using proper language is a must in the barbershop: If they swear, they’re expected to do 15 push-ups — and often do so without being asked.

If they act out on the unit, they may stop getting paid temporarily but are still allowed to participate in the program. And the money has been a great motivator.

One trainee was recently involved in a misunderstanding with another resident, which in the past might have turned violent, according to DYS. But the Skill Up participant walked away, and later said he did so because he didn’t want to lose his program privileges.

Overall, morale has improved since the vocational program began, staffers said.

When people are about to leave DYS custody, career navigators help them open bank accounts and find jobs. Over the past few years, roughly 200 former Skill Up participants now out in the community have found full-time employment, officials said. One who learned carpentry skills and got his OSHA certification in treatment now works at Home Depot. Another who learned to silk-screen bought a $600 Cricut machine with his Skill Up earnings and opened an online Etsy business.

For Dante, who grew up in East Boston and was in juvenile treatment facilities from age 16 to 21, the instructors were like big brothers. Dante was released almost a year ago and still has a call with a Dreamcatchers mentor every Friday.

“We could talk to them about whatever, like therapy,” he said. “You see that they come from the same place as you and they’re doing well.”

Reentry “beats down on you,” Dante said, but things have been looking up lately. He recently landed a job as a delivery driver and does dog grooming on the side, with help from the starter kit of clippers, scissors, and combs he got from the program. In fact, it was Adrian Major who first noticed the haircut Dante gave his standard poodle and encouraged him to branch out.

“We create pathways,” said Alexis Major. “It’s about confidence, dignity that they build and they gain.”

Jaaco, 19, has done several Skill Up programs and is currently part of the barbershop crew in Roslindale. Demonstrating his skills on a recent day, he donned a black apron and placed a mannequin head on a tripod. In a matter of seconds, he removed all its hair – called “balding” – with a pair of clippers, using confident back-to-front strokes.

Jaaco has learned patience, respect, and unity through the vocational programs, he said, and his time in the Connelly Center has been instrumental: “This unit has formed me into becoming a better person.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Growing frustration over Boston’s police accountability system on display at community forum
text:
He said OPAT is lagging behind where it should be, largely because Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox has refused to take the agency seriously.

Much of the discussion focused on the contentious relationship between the Boston Police Department and OPAT. The office itself has struggled to get off the ground, although its leaders say they’re turning a corner and finally asserting their authority.

“Movements and changes don’t happen overnight,” said OPAT Executive Director Evandro Carvalho, a former prosecutor who took over leadership of the beleaguered office in 2024.

In response to critics who challenged whether OPAT will ever fulfill its mission, he said progress is absolutely underway as the agency seeks to assert its authority and hold the police accountable.

Some of the promises felt like empty words, said Patricia Hayden, a Dorchester resident who spoke up during the discussion. She bemoaned an ineffective local government that can’t seem to effect meaningful change.

“It’s been 20 years and the same things are happening,” she said. “Our kids are still being killed. They’re still going to jail. There’s no jobs.”

The contention between the police department and OPAT isn’t new. In a September letter to department leadership, OPAT’s Civilian Review Board complained that many Boston police officers have refused to cooperate in its investigations while Cox has often ignored their recommendations.

That includes a case in which the board recommended termination for an officer who detained, tackled and punched a teenager. Instead of getting fired, the officer received a written reprimand for violating the department’s body camera policy.

In a response to the board’s letter last month, Cox promised better collaboration, including efforts to reduce backlogs and improve response times. But he said any discipline decisions must be based on the findings of an internal affairs investigation because of state law, collective bargaining agreements, and department rules and procedures.

A whistleblower lawsuit filed this week also accused Cox of silencing a high-ranking officer who raised concerns about possible corruption and criminal activity in the paid detail and overtime programs.

Deputy Superintendent Marcus S. Eddings said in the lawsuit that he identified 20 officers who should be investigated by the department’s anti-corruption division and 25 who may have violated department rules. Eddings alleges he was demoted in retaliation for reporting detail fraud. A Boston police spokesperson denied the accusation, saying the department investigates all allegations of misconduct and it’s well within the commissioner’s authority to choose members of his command staff.

Cox didn’t attend the forum, though organizers said he was invited.

Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, did participate in the forum, saying he doesn’t “run away from tough conversations” because they often give way to positive change.

While Cox drew criticism for a lackluster approach toward accountability, others said Mayor Michelle Wu should have to answer for the current state of police reform in Boston. Her office has recently touted improved relations between OPAT and the department, saying they’re both “key parts in the City’s public safety infrastructure.”

The office includes the Civilian Review Board, which investigates complaints against officers, and the Internal Affairs Oversight Panel, which reviews police discipline decisions. Carvalho has pledged to make it more effective, efficient, and public-facing. He’s largely been focused on hiring more staff and increasing community engagement.

In an annual report released Sept. 18, officials said they plan to implement the agency’s subpoena power and compel officers to appear for investigative interviews. OPAT was given subpoena power when it was created, a significant allowance that has so far gone unused.

Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia said the office has to assert its independence to build community trust.

“As you continue to do this work, how do we repair that trust?” she said, directing her remarks at Carvalho.

Despite the recent roadblocks, officials sought to reassure the public that police reform has firmly taken hold, even if change is slow. They pledged to keep pushing for better outcomes.

“If you are invested in police reform, these are conversations you should be having with your elected officials, with your mayor, with your city councilors and amongst yourselves,” said former Boston police commander Eddy Chrispin, who alleged in a recent lawsuit that he was demoted after refusing to resign from the Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, a statewide oversight body.

“This can’t be a one-time thing where we walk away and then forget about it,” he said.

title: Today in History: Willie O’Ree becomes first Black NHL player
text:
Today is Sunday, Jan. 18, the 18th day of 2026. There are 347 days left in the year.

Today’s birthdays: Actor-filmmaker Kevin Costner is 71. Actor Mark Rylance is 66. Hockey Hall of Famer Mark Messier is 65. Actor Dave Bautista is 57. Actor Jesse L. Martin is 57. Rock singer Jonathan Davis of Korn is 55. Football Hall of Famer Julius Peppers is 46. Actor Jason Segel is 46. Actor Carlacia Grant is 35. Singer and activist Montana Tucker is 33. Spanish soccer star Aitana Bonmati is 28. Actor Karan Brar is 27.

In 1776, 250 years ago, Henry Knox reached General George Washington in Cambridge after organizing the transport of 60 tons of cannon and other weapons from Fort Ticonderoga in upstate New York via boat and sledges hauled by horse and oxen. The arms were temporarily stored in Framingham; the feat would be a turning point in the American rebel’s siege of Boston, as their eventual placement on Dorchester Heights prompted the British army and navy to abandon Boston.

In 1778, English navigator Captain James Cook reached the present-day Hawaiian Islands, which he dubbed the “Sandwich Islands.”

In 1803, President Thomas Jefferson asked Congress in a confidential message for $2,500 in funding for exploration of Western lands all the way to the Pacific, an early step in the eventual formation of the Lewis and Clark expedition that would ultimately accelerate American expansion westward beyond the Mississippi River.

In 1903, Guglielmo Marconi, the Italian inventor of wireless telegraphy, transmitted from Wellfleet to London the first trans-Atlantic radio transmission, a message from President Theodore Roosevelt to King Edward VII.

In 1911, the first landing of an aircraft on a ship took place as pilot Eugene B. Ely brought his Curtiss biplane in for a safe landing on the deck of the armored cruiser USS Pennsylvania in San Francisco Harbor.

In 1958, Canadian Willie O’Ree became the first Black player in the National Hockey League as he made his debut with the Boston Bruins.

In 1977, scientists identified the bacteria responsible for the deadly form of atypical pneumonia known as Legionnaires’ disease.

In 1990, Washington, D.C., Mayor Marion Barry was arrested after FBI agents caught him smoking crack cocaine in a hotel room in a videotaped sting. (Convicted of drug possession, Barry spent a few months in prison, returning to win a D.C. Council seat in 1992 and his fourth and final mayoral victory in 1994. He died in 2014.)

In 1993, the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday was observed in all 50 states for the first time.

In 1996, Lisa Marie Presley filed for divorce from Michael Jackson, citing “irreconcilable differences” after less than two years of marriage.

In 2013, former Democratic New Orleans Mayor Ray Nagin was indicted on charges that he’d used his office for personal gain, accepting payoffs, free trips and gratuities from contractors while the devastated city was struggling to recover from Hurricane Katrina. (Nagin was later convicted, served time, and was released from prison in 2020.)

In 2019, Jason Van Dyke, the white Chicago police officer who gunned down Black teenager Laquan McDonald in 2014, was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison.

In 2025, a gasoline tanker exploded in Nigeria, killing at least 70 people as individuals sought to transfer gasoline from one tanker into another truck as numerous bystanders looked on.

title: His thoughtful date planning impressed her from the start; their shared faith deepened their bond
text:
That date — dinner at Novara in Milton — had also been a choose-your-own-adventure experience, curated by Shadlee. The software engineer was living and working in Cranston, Rhode Island, but did not hesitate to make the 45-minute drive to meet the accomplished, joyful woman he had matched with on Hinge. “If I’m taking someone out, I’m going to go the distance,” Shadlee says.

While Joanne is a Boston native, she had just moved back to the city that August after having completed her law degree at Howard University in D.C. She was impressed by Shadlee’s curated list of three restaurants, complete with links and brief descriptors for each. Allowing her to choose made the date a chance for “good collaboration,” she says. “It showed me he put a lot of thought into it.”

At Novara, they discovered their shared Christian beliefs and values and Haitian upbringings, learning they both speak Creole.

“He said a few jokes and I was, ‘Oh you’re Haitian,’" remembers Joanne, “because we’re both born here, and [sometimes] there’s varying degrees of how connected [to the culture] you are. The fact that he knew the language was really cool to learn about in person.”

The bond imprinted on her as feeling “safe. ... He was such a comforting presence.” Shadlee, a self-identifying introvert, felt likewise; while he’d been nervous at first, Joanne’s “natural kindness” helped him relax.

“I could be myself and talk about things perfectly fine with her being able to reciprocate,” he says. “I don’t remember the restaurant, I don’t remember the waiter, it felt like it was just the two of us.”

In similar fashion, Shadlee presented his ideas for their second date — which he decided should be experiential, to mix things up. “The date, the time, the link. …. I was just stunned by his level of planning,” Joanne says.

The perfume workshop at the House of Arts & Crafts (now called The Creative Hub) was more intimate than anticipated, though “I’m glad she chose it, because that was my favorite from the list,” says Shadlee. They were the only two in attendance. But they had a “beautiful time,” each creating a unique blend of scents that they named Cest La Vie (her) and The Gentlemen (him). Content from their session wound up on the business’ social media accounts.

“It was great promo for them, but this was our second date,” emphasizes Joanne with a laugh. “They took videos. They turned it into a whole reel. It’s good content for us [now], but I sent that to my friends and was like, ‘Guys…’ It was a lot of pressure.”

For their third date, Joanne invited Shadlee to the Holiday Pops. On the drive home, he parked his car on a well-lit block of Commonwealth Avenue where they continued to talk. (The heat was on, “I’m not trying to freeze her to death,” Shadlee says. “That’d be rude.”) As he drove her back to her house, Shadlee asked the question that had been on his mind all night: “Would you like to be my girlfriend?” Then, they shared their first kiss.

Their faith and their commitment to each other remained constants as the relationship evolved. Weekends included Saturday service; Wednesdays were reserved for devotionals. Shadlee’s back-and-forth from Rhode Island became “something to look forward to, a little bit of a ritual in a sense, and I get to see this beautiful woman.”

For Valentine’s Day, he booked a dinner cruise on Boston Harbor. As they watched the water and live jazz played, Shadlee remembers watching Joanne, thinking: I can see myself being with her forever.

“It’s that level of comfort, safe space, of being open and fully transparent and completely vulnerable,” he says.

They’d been dating eight months when they began pre-engagement counseling.

“I knew we weren’t there yet, but it was powerful to hear people confirm what we felt,” says Joanne. The program was run by a couple married for 15 years, who, upon meeting Shadlee and Joanne, told them: “We sense a safety between you that’s really rare.”

After celebrating their first year together, they attended a marathon of celebrations for family and friends between them — a sprint of nine nuptials, one of them international, and six out of state. Joanne’s uncle’s 50th birthday brought them to New York, where “by the end of the night, [my family] were referring to him as my husband” in Creole. After Shadlee’s brother’s D.C. wedding, the first time Joanne had met his family, he received nothing but rave reviews: “I have not found one person that does not like her. Friends, family, their dog, everybody loves her.”

“I always knew that in my partner, [I wanted] the peace, the sureness, the unwaveringness that I feel with God’s love that has just transformed my life,“ Joanne says. ”I felt that with Shad.”

Shadlee proposed on a private sunset cruise on Martha’s Vineyard on July 12, 2025. Taking a knee surrounded by rose petals, he quoted Colossians 3:14, as Elvis Presley’s “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” the first song they danced to together, played.

Joanne, 33, and Shadlee, 36, wed on October 9, 2025, at St. Mary’s Episcopal Church in Dorchester. The couple opted for an intimate ceremony, planned in three months, with 12 members of their immediate family present. Dinner at the North End’s Florentine Cafe was family-style, served amid illuminated faux grapevines that hang from the ceiling of the restaurant’s downstairs.

“It has a very moody ambiance but very romantic,” says Joanne.

The couple picked the location as a tribute to their upcoming celebration in Italy, where they’ll toast their nuptials with a larger group of family and friends later this year. For their autumn micro-wedding, however, they managed to keep their budget small; Joanne broke down the itemized costs on her social media account, where she typically shares advice for aspiring lawyers.

She arranged white roses from Whole Foods into a sophisticated bouquet and wedding arch; the pair cut into the grocer’s famed Berry Chantilly Cake following their first dance (to Elvis, of course). And they wore the fragrances they’d made.

“We [made the perfumes] so early on in our relationship, and I typically only wear it for special occasions” says Joanne. “It brought back all the memories of love — the adventure, the excitement, the consideration. It made me think of everything that has been such a blessing and lifted the air in my life. It’s the fragrance of love."

title: He’s Boston’s biggest social media food influencer. (But no, he’s not a stay-at-home dad, though he may wannabe.)
text:
You have a sizable following that some people can only dream of having. What brought you to Boston?

My girlfriend at the time, now fiancée, moved up for a biotech job in 2021, and then I followed her up in 2022. I started in Annapolis, Md.

Were you a food person in Annapolis?

This is new. I mean, I was eating a lot, but I was not recording myself. The foodie part started in January 2023.

How did this career unfold?

My best friend does DIY content in his house, and he was getting on me to just start doing content. Somehow, we just landed on doing food reviews, because I wanted to see where the good food was, because I was new to the area. I posted a video, and I think it got like 500 views. And I was like, “Oh, wow, I’m famous!” So I kept posting.

What was your first post, and why do you think it was so popular?

I went to Monica’s, the sandwich place in the North End. I think the premise was like: Is it worth it to pay $20 for a chicken parm sandwich? And I ended up saying yes, because the sandwich was delicious. But I think people related to the affordability aspect, talking through the food.

I think there’s a lot of people — and this is no shade to anyone, obviously — I think there’s a lot of people who kind of cover food and give you more of the aesthetic version. I was just really talking through how I was feeling as I was eating it. I think people related to that. Thank you to all those 500 viewers!

What had you been doing for work, and has this taken over as your full-time job?

At the time, I’d just started a job in consulting. I was a civil engineer by trade. As of August 2025, this is my full-time gig now.

For people who don’t understand how the world of influencing and social media works: How do you make money?

Pretty much all my money comes in through brand partnerships, which you’ll see labeled [in my posts] as paid partnerships. That’s if a larger brand wants me to promote a new product or new dish they’re selling. And some restaurants will pay to promote new locations and things like that.

Outside of that, I don’t charge any restaurant for any review. I pay for my food. I want that genuine, authentic experience. I am able to monetize a bit off of my viewership on TikTok and platforms like Facebook as well. Based on the amount of viewers you get, you get a certain amount per view.

How did you come up with the name wannabe stay-at-home dad? Are you a dad? Do you want to stay at home?

A part of the origin story is that the friend who was peer-pressuring me to do content, we were trying to think through ideas and different ways to do it. At first I was working remotely, and my partner was working in the office, so I was going to pretend to be a stay-at-home dad, or practice to be one. I filmed one video, and it was horrible. I was like: This premise is pretty stupid. So then we just started doing the food videos, and I didn’t have a chance to change my name. It had stuck. I don’t even have a child. … It’s an aspirational thing, totally.

Coming from Maryland, what was your take on the Boston food scene when you got here? How has your viewpoint changed?

I kind of pictured a ton of seafood, some Italian as well, because we had moved into the North End shortly after I got here. I thought those were the main things you’d be able to find. I think one misconception I had was I thought there would be a lack of diversity in Boston’s food scene.

I’ve actually learned that there’s a ton of different foods and different types of cuisines you can find here. You’ve just got to do a little bit of research. I feel like when people are recommending places to people visiting Boston, a lot of people will send you to the North End, and maybe you’ll even get some South End places.

But, similarly to finding more diversity, it was also finding more areas to go to — realizing how much good food is in places like Dorchester, Roxbury, and different areas like that. I kind of opened my eyes. I thought Boston was smaller. I didn’t realize, for example, how big Dorchester is. Dorchester feels like it stretches for miles.

What’s the best restaurant in your neighborhood? Where do you eat for pure pleasure?

I think this will be a popular pick: Rino’s in East Boston. I was a little worried when I first went because they’ve been on TV. It’s very popular. But it is truly an amazing Italian restaurant. I would say it’s the best restaurant over here.

There’s also a ton of great Latino food that you can find in the area, but I think Rino’s is top of the top.

What’s your go-to order?

I would try the chicken parm. If you just don’t want to cook one night and need to get the family fed, take chicken parm to go, put it on the table, and it’ll look like you cooked a big dinner.

And that’s similar with all their portions. Their gnocchi, their Bolognese, is incredible. Everything’s good. I’d say the chicken parm and the Bolognese are two that you’ve got to try.

What’s the most overrated restaurant in Boston, and the most underrated?

Overrated? I’d actually say Galleria Umberto in the North End. And this is not going to be received well. People love it because they have the $2 Sicilian slices. I lived down there for a bit. I tried it multiple times. I just couldn’t get it. And I’m not a big arancini fan, and people say the arancini’s great there. Not for me.

What restaurant do you wish more people knew about?

It’s kind of gotten popular now, but I want it to keep getting more recognition: Comfort Kitchen in Dorchester. I thought it was going to get recognized in the Michelin guide that came out: really great Caribbean food, amazing brunch, amazing dinner. Their jerk duck for dinner is incredible. It’s also really cool, their story. Part of the way they were able to get their brick and mortar is through a platform that allowed community members to invest. It’s a great group of people running it, and I love the food.

Best pizza?

Pizza Project in Brighton has the best pizza I’ve had right now. I feel like people are like, “Oh, it’s out of the way.” Brighton is not that far out of the way. Their pepperoni pizza with hot honey is incredible. And they have this vodka pizza with sesame seed crust, I think, that I’m excited to go back and try.

Best Chinese food?

Dumpling House in Cambridge. I’m a big takeout guy. I do a lot of Chinese takeout. We do huge orders. Obviously, dumplings, of course, are incredible. They’ve got great scallion pancakes.

What about tacos?

So people in East Boston are gonna get mad at me. I’ll say my favorite taco place is probably La Mesa in Chelsea. They do really good birria tacos. It’s between that and Taqueria Jalisco, which is a very popular one in East Boston. I go back and forth, honestly.

How do you decide where you’re going to visit? You try a wide range of places, and I’m guessing you don’t have a bottomless budget.

I wish the process was more refined. I’ll be honest with you. It’s a mix of, if I see a place that is trending, maybe it’s new, and I think people want to see my opinion about it, I’ll go there. So that’s based on things that are popping up in my algorithm. A big source for me is also Reddit. I check Reddit threads all the time. People will post: “Hey, coming to Boston for a few weeks. Where do I find the best burger or the best tacos?” And seeing responses of people who have lived here for a while has been really helpful to me, because I still feel like a tourist at times.

And most of my content is filmed in my car. I get a lot of affordable places. I’m doing a lot of takeout and stuff. That also informs the process.

Do you go in with the intention of ordering a certain item?

Usually, it’ll be a certain dish: I’ve heard this place has a great burger and also maybe try an appetizer. The other day I went to a place and had a great burger, and I got clam chowder because it was cold outside. I’ll try to get a little bit of a sampling of the menu, but most times I’m going in specifically for a certain thing.

How many times a week are you eating out?

I think I’m around four to five times. The way I try to mix it up, just healthwise, is I film a couple places in a day. That way I can take a day in between, or two days in between, to let my body not feel like crap.

How do you actually film yourself? Do you have someone who comes with you? Because this is very artfully done.

I appreciate that. The biggest compliment you can give me is to tell me that it looks artful.

Truthfully, I have this little phone holder in my car that I drop my phone on and then record myself in my driver’s seat. And then when I go out, if I’m sitting down somewhere, I have this little phone holder from Amazon that I can pop up, and then I have a light. I’ve got the classic influencer light that you see at a restaurant that annoys me. I have that, too. I try not to use it too much.

Do people see you coming and know who you are? Do you think you’re getting an objective experience?

If I’m doing takeout and stuff, I’ll try to put my order in ahead of time, just so I can grab it and go. But there’s been times now where I’ve sat down … I’m going to the table, sitting down, ordering, almost hoping no one recognizes me, because, again, my big thing is sharing that authentic experience. I want people who watch my videos to feel like it’s almost like they’re sitting at the table with me, and we’re talking about the food together. It’s not this specific influencer experience, where it’s not going to be the same if you go on your own.

What place has surprised you, in a good way?

I went to The Haven in Jamaica Plain. And that was a deep Reddit thread, where maybe two or three people had said, “Hey, their burger is amazing.”

I think it’s actually a Scottish restaurant. Their burger was incredible. It’s not that I thought it would be bad. I thought, maybe this is a neighborhood staple-type place, where people stand behind it, but it was actually a very good burger, one of the best burgers I probably have had in the area.

Let’s say you’re talking to someone who’s coming to visit for the weekend. Where are you sending them?

First off, I don’t believe you have to eat in Boston proper, right? Because I do genuinely think you can find some great places in Somerville and Cambridge.

I’m sending them to Pizza Project, because everybody comes up here thinking, “Boston’s pizza is terrible.” I think that it’s a great place to prove people wrong. I’m gonna send them to Bred Gourmet. They’ve got great burgers down in Dorchester. They have a location in Kendall Square as well. You can get a little taste of Southern cuisine. They’ve got po’ boys and things like that — some stuff maybe you wouldn’t expect to find in Boston.

And then here’s the one thing that I do think maybe is touristy of me to send them. I’m still gonna send them to the North End to get pastries, because I do genuinely think that’s still an experience. I might not send them to Mike’s Pastry, which, again, might be a controversial opinion, but I’ll probably send them to Modern Pastry for cannoli, because I do think that’s a genuine Boston experience, where the quality meets kind of the expectation.

What about a nice night out?

If you’re having a nice night out, trying to splurge, go to Grill 23.

I was going there with my fiancée. I was going to record, do a video. And I got so caught up in the food. As soon as they brought the bread out, I forgot. I never recorded anything. I just ate, and it was incredible. Now, I’ve got to try to figure out how to get another reservation.

What’s next on your list?

Oh my goodness, I’m forgetting the name of it. Sarma. Sarma is the name of the place I want to go because they have off-menu fried chicken that they serve occasionally. Every video I see of that, I’m like, that’s incredible. I love that idea, to have an off-menu fried chicken. I want to try that. And, of course, I’ve heard great things.

This is another trendy one, the Capri place … I just want to go to see if it’s the real deal. And just because it’s new, it is impossible to get a table right now. The honey bread that they do looks incredible.

What would be your last meal in Boston?

That’s really tough. I’m a big sandwich guy, so honestly, I’m going to go to Figaro’s in Chinatown. The steak and cheese with some chipotle mayo is probably my favorite. It’s so crazy because I put chipotle mayo on so many different things, and I never thought to put it on a steak and cheese until I had it there.

I’m gonna go to Square Deli in Everett and get their Grandma Flo pizza. It’s got homemade meatballs, ricotta. They have incredible pizza dough. I’m not gonna have any room left by the end of this day. By the way, I’m splurging completely. Let me see. I’m gonna go to Carmelina’s in the North End and get a chicken parm. Then, for dessert (I’ve already said the North End desserts; there’s so many other great bakeries) ... actually, I might skip dessert because I feel like I’ve gone too crazy.

Is there any food you hate?

I will never have a blue cheese dish on my channel. And I don’t like truffles. I feel bad, because a lot of places try to jazz up their fries with truffle fries … I can’t stand truffles.

Is there any type of food in the Greater Boston area that we don’t have?

Having some family from the South, I think it’s that Southern cuisine: your fried chicken, your plates like fried chicken, collard greens, mac and cheese, sweet yams, things like that.

Will you spin this career into something else? What’s the dream?

You know, before I was ever doing this, I was a die-hard Food Network and Guy Fieri “Diners, Drive-ins and Dives” fan, all those shows. My dream is to continue to do what I’m doing, but just doing it on a bigger stage and maybe even at the national level.

Interview was edited for clarity.

title: Bristol District Attorney Thomas Quinn says he is not seeking reelection
text:
Bristol District Attorney Thomas M. Quinn III, who led the office when it secured a murder conviction against former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez, said Tuesday that he won’t seek reelection in November.

“After serving almost 12 years as Bristol County District Attorney, I have decided not to seek re-election for a fourth term,” Quinn said in a statement. “It has been a great honor and privilege to serve the citizens of Bristol County.”

He thanked his family and staff and said he had “dedicated my career to the pursuit of justice” in his 40 years as a prosecutor.

“During that time, the courtroom became a second home,” he said. “It is there that I learned the profound responsibility to uphold the law with fairness and integrity.”

Quinn said he had “tried to be a District Attorney who listened, who respected differing perspectives, and who worked to ensure that justice was administered thoughtfully and fairly to all.”

He said he was proud of his office’s accomplishments during his tenure.

“I remain fully committed to carrying out the responsibilities of this office with the same dedication and focus” that have guided my years as a prosecutor, Quinn said. “I will continue to fight for the victims and citizens of Bristol County as I complete my final year in office.”

Quinn, a Democrat, took office in January 2015 after being appointed to the post when his predecessor, Sam Sutter, was elected mayor of Fall River.

That April, his office secured a first-degree murder conviction against Hernandez, who was found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Dorchester resident Odin Lloyd in Attleboro.

Hernandez died by suicide in his prison cell in 2017, days after his acquittal in a separate double murder case in Boston.

Among Quinn’s initiatives as district attorney was a push to reduce the backlog of sexual assault kits awaiting testing.

So far, no Democrats have announced they are running for the office. The sole declared Republican candidate is Seth Aitken.

Quinn is the second sitting DA to announce this month that he’s not running for reelection.

Norfolk District Attorney Michael W. Morrissey, whose office came under heavy criticism for its prosecution of Karen Read, recently said he would not be running for another term, saying “the time is right for me to start a new chapter in my life.”

“Being district attorney is about pursuing justice with integrity and fairness. I am incredibly proud of the meaningful work our office has accomplished, both in the courtroom and throughout the community,” Morrissey wrote in a statement.

Four Democrats have entered the race — defense attorney Jim Barakat, former federal prosecutor Adam Deitch, Craig MacLellan, a Cohasset School Committee member and former state prosecutor, and Djuna Perkins, a former state prosecutor.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: Man who killed teenager in Dorchester in 1994 granted parole from life sentence
text:
A 49-year-old man who was 18 when he fatally shot another teenager in Dorchester during a robbery attempt has been granted parole from his life sentence, records show.

The state’s Parole Board voted 4-1 to grant release to Kevin Denis to a halfway house within two weeks of the decision, according to the panel’s Jan. 12 ruling.

Denis was convicted in 1996 of first-degree murder in the Aug. 19, 1994, shooting of Diron Spence, 17, the ruling said.

First-degree murder normally carries a sentence of life without the possibility of parole. But Denis became parole eligible in January 2024 when the state’s highest court struck down life terms with no chance at release for defendants aged 18 to 20 at the time of their crimes.

As of last week, the Parole Board had granted release to roughly three quarters of the 59 inmates seeking release under the SJC ruling, the Globe reported.

On the day of the killing, the ruling said, Denis approached Spence as he stood with a friend at the corner of McLellan and Bradshaw streets.

Denis demanded money, and Spence’s friend began emptying his pockets while Spence “just stood there,” the ruling said.

“Mr. Denis asked, ‘think I’m playing?’” the decision said. “He then pulled out a .357 Magnum revolver and shot at Mr. Spence from a distance of a few feet.”

Spence’s friend fled as the first shot rang out, according to the ruling.

“Four more shots were fired,” it said. “Three bullets hit Mr. Spence, resulting in a fatal wound to his chest.”

At the time of the murder, Denis suffered from “undiagnosed and untreated mental health” issues, along with “cannabis use disorder,” and “developmental disorders,” the ruling said.

Denis has made strides during his decades behind bars, the board ruled.

“He has invested in self-development by completing approximately 80 programs and earning his bachelor’s degree from Boston University,” the ruling said.

Denis also has a “minimal discipline history” in prison, the decision said.

“He is involved in Restorative Justice practices,” the board said. “He has strong community supports for his reentry.”

The board said it considered testimony opposing Denis’s release from a Suffolk County prosecutor and from Spence’s relatives.

Once he’s released, Denis will have to abide by several conditions including submitting to electronic monitoring for six months, staying off drugs and alcohol, refraining from contacting Spence’s family, and getting “mental health counseling for PTSD, Autism Spectrum Disorder,” the ruling said.

Denis remained incarcerated Tuesday at MCI-Norfolk, a medium-security prison, according to the online Department of Correction database.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: Dorchester teen charged with stealing man’s suitcase and throwing it onto MBTA tracks, causing explosion
text:
A Dorchester teenager is facing charges stemming from an alleged robbery at the State Street MBTA station last week that ended with a suitcase being thrown onto the tracks and igniting an explosion, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Tuesday.

Addonis Reed, 19, was charged with obstructing or endangering a railroad, larceny from a person, unarmed robbery, disorderly conduct, and two counts of malicious destruction of property, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Judge Mark Summerville set bail at $10,000 and revoked Reed’s bail for 60 days on two open cases at Reed’s arraignment Friday in the central division of Boston Municipal Court.

Reed was committed to Suffolk County Jail in lieu of bail and was ordered to stay away from the victim and all MBTA stops, according to court records. It was not immediately clear if he had obtained an attorney.

Prosecutors say the incident occurred at about 11:20 p.m. Jan. 14 at the State Street station at 200 Washington St. when five juveniles “engaged in a confrontation” with an MBTA rider, accusing him of photographing them. The victim denied the allegation, prosecutors said.

Authorities said Reed separated from the group and followed the victim. MBTA security footage allegedly showed Reed taking the victim’s phone and throwing it to the ground several times, breaking it into pieces, prosecutors said.

As the victim attempted to collect his belongings, Reed allegedly grabbed the victim’s suitcase and threw it onto the train tracks, prosecutors said. The suitcase struck the third rail, causing a large explosion and fire, the statement said.

The station was evacuated and train service was suspended as police, fire officials, and MBTA security responded to the scene, prosecutors said.

The victim told officers the suitcase contained two iPads, an Acer laptop, Apple AirPods, and chargers, with a total value of more than $3,000, according to the statement.

Transit police later identified Reed by reviewing security video and matching his description to an individual seen at the State Street station the following day, prosecutors said.

“This is an alarming set of facts, both with the fear that the victim must have experienced during the incident and the destruction of his property and subsequent station evacuation and shutdown in service,” Hayden said in the statement. “I’m grateful for the quick work of transit officers in identifying and arresting this defendant.”

Reed has two other open cases — one in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court on charges of disorderly conduct, assault with a dangerous weapon, and assault on a police officer from December. Another, in BMC Central, includes charges of disorderly conduct, assault with a dangerous weapon, and assault on ambulance personnel from Jan. 6, prosecutors said.

Reed is scheduled to return to court Feb. 20 for a probable cause hearing, prosecutors said.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: The palace intrigue over Segun Idowu’s departure shows that Wu has work to do mending fences with Black leaders
text:
But any time you read for family reasons, you have to wonder if that was the driving factor.

Now some of you will wonder if Idowu is leaving because of a lingering fallout from a City Hall scandal involving Idowu and two city staffers last year. An internal investigation cleared Idowu, who got to keep his job, while the others were fired. One of those former employees sued the city over her termination.

I don’t think it has anything to do with that. If that episode were the problem, Idowu would have left after Wu’s re-election in November, much as other Cabinet members, including chief of streets Jascha Franklin-Hodge, chief of staff Tiffany Chu, and chief communications officer Jessicah Pierre, departed after Wu’s first term.

No, what some say is that Idowu is leaving after a one-two gut punch from Wu to Boston’s Black business and civic leaders: On Jan. 5, city Councilor Brian Worrell lost the City Council presidency after the mayor’s council allies backed another candidate; then on Jan. 12 the city upset many in Roxbury when it announced it would scrap a long-planned lab and housing project on city-owned land to instead build a new Madison Park Technical Vocational School.

Idowu, the story goes, was fed up, and quit. Could it be that simple? Or are Black leaders projecting their own growing frustrations with the mayor? Those frustrations bubbled last February when Josh Kraft challenged Wu in the mayor’s race. Kraft — the longtime leader of the Boys & Girls Club of Boston and son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft — had hoped to capitalize on a recurring strain of dissatisfaction in Black neighborhoods over the quality of schools, rising property taxes, and a controversial redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park. But Idowu stood by her then. Were Worrell and Madison Park really the last straws?

There was only one way to find out. On Tuesday, I asked Idowu if he’s unhappy, perhaps feeling sidelined as a second term begins. The short answer, he said, is no, but he also can’t control how other people are feeling about this moment for the Black community.

“We will always have those experiences,” he told me. “What matters is that we keep our eye on the ball and keep pushing towards progress.”

In other words, Idowu remains an ally of the mayor. You can understand why: she defended him during his darkest moments, amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Idowu maintains his departure has been a long time coming. He told the mayor a year ago — before the misconduct allegations emerged last spring — that he was unlikely to stay the full second term. At the time, his grandmother was in decline, losing mobility and nearing a point where she could no longer live independently.

Idowu’s grandparents helped raise him. He was away in college when his grandfather passed away, and this time he wanted to spend as much time with his grandmother, Frances Lawson, as he could.

Still, Idowu had hoped to give the mayor more time to find a successor and give himself more time to line up another job. He said he has been looking, and he’s hopeful that he will find something by the time he leaves City Hall.

Then he spent last weekend cleaning up his grandmother’s Dorchester apartment after she moved into a nursing home. It all became real: she was never returning and that he needed to make every day with her count. He realized he needed to step down sooner than later.

“I have the opportunity to actually be with her for however long she’s got left,” Idowu told me. “I will not forgive myself if I get the call that she passed away, and I haven’t seen her in two weeks because I’ve been in the office the whole time.”

Idowu made a name for himself as the chief executive of the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts. I got to know him as the thorn in the side of the Walsh administration, pushing the city to do a better job of giving contracts to more businesses owned by women and people of color.

When Wu was elected in November 2021, Idowu was among the first wave of hires she made to her Cabinet. Idowu spearheaded key economic initiatives, such as helping small businesses find retail spaces through the SPACE grant program, increasing supplier diversity for city contracts, growing the number of liquor licenses for restaurants, and helping to attract new companies like Hasbro to Boston. In a statement, the mayor hailed his efforts to spread prosperity across the city and help Boston recover from COVID-19.

“Under Chief Idowu’s leadership, Boston’s neighborhoods have become more vibrant, inclusive, and connected,“ she said. ”His work has helped Boston rebound from the pandemic as a thriving city where companies and their employees want to work and live.”

Idowu also serves as a critical liaison to the Black community, even more so after the departures of other senior Black officials including Pierre, planning chief Arthur Jemison, and environmental chief the Rev. Mariama White-Hammond.

That connection isn’t lost on Black leaders like Imari Paris Jeffries, chief executive of Embrace Boston, a racial justice organization that honors the legacy of Martin Luther King Jr. Some city officials do their job from downtown. Idowu made a point to get out to the neighborhoods.

”He balanced doing the job from City Hall and from the community,” said Paris Jeffries. “That made him acutely aware of what was happening. We hope the administration finds someone with the same connections to the Black community.”

Wu and Idowu may indeed be leaving on good terms, not over frayed relationships in Black business and civic circles. But given how quickly the chatter over his departure turned to those relationships, the mayor should take heed, and find a successor who will help to mend them.

title: The MBTA says it’s still ‘testing’ South Station fare gates. Commuters are calling them ‘obnoxious.’
text:
The gates, only a few weeks old, are the T’s latest major attempt to recoup fares on a historically leaky service. The agency installed gates at North Station in late 2022 to the same end, and, it says, with some success: fare revenues increased, and some riders say commuters have grown accustomed to the change.

Gates at Ruggles and Back Bay are slated for installation this year.

The new South Station fare gates have, at times, stumbled during their first few weeks in operation.

When the gates first went live, the T said “testing” would continue after their launch. Keolis says employees from the gates’ manufacturer “are on site daily to calibrate the technology at the gates and troubleshoot any issues.”

“It’s very normal that these things don’t work perfectly the first time,” said Joshua Schank, a partner at InfraStrategies, a California transportation consultancy.

The gates, in theory, should part when riders scan valid digital passes (daily or monthly), physical cards, or paper tickets. Active military IDs are also accepted.

“There have not been any widespread issues tied to a specific fare type,” a Keolis spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, frustrations for some passengers have festered.

“It’s a pain,” said Randy Whinnery, a 55-year-old Fidelity employee living in Cohasset.

Whinnery failed to open two different gates with his phone before escaping the train platform on a recent January morning.

“It’s early days,” he said, “but one out of five times so far I’ve tried to swipe this thing, it’s worked.”

The gates debuted two days before the new year. It was a less-than-optimal inauguration.

Plenty of passengers passed through without hassle. Some struggled until a station worker hovering nearby intervened. At one point, during a morning influx, a group of gates appeared to momentarily deactivate; workers shepherded riders through a side door.

The T says the South Station fare gates cost about $1.3 million to purchase from the company Scheidt & Bachmann, and another $2 million to install. The agency hopes the investment will pay long-term dividends.

Analysts estimated in 2019 that the T lost about $10 million to $20 million in revenue because of unpaid commuter rail fares. Many commuter rail passengers describe on-train fare checks by conductors as inconsistent.

The state inspector general in 2025 rebuked the T for not doing enough to shore up fare collection on the service.

The commuter rail generated about $133 million in fare revenue in 2024 — almost a third of the agency’s total fare intakes that year, according to the Federal Transit Administration. Fares from all modes covered about 19 percent of the agency’s operating expenses that year.

Some riders have bought into the mission. Others find their belief in the cause dampened by their frustrations with the barriers.

Passage success rates have varied. So too do impressions of the severity of bottlenecks created by the gates.

Kristen McGovern, a 43-year-old Walpole resident working in finance, estimated her phone ticket successfully parts the gates 80 percent of the time. She described queues at the gates as “manageable,” usually not tacking on more than a minute to her journey.

Angela Zaino, a 31-year-old scientist awaiting the Providence train Wednesday, said she’s encountered “a couple of errors” trying to scan the pass on her phone.

“But for the most part, it’s been fine,” she said.

Kayla Medeiros, a 28-year-old social worker living in Mansfield, has spared herself the potential exasperation of phone-scanning by tapping through the gates with a physical CharlieCard.

Still, she says, the confusion and misfortune of others struggling to breach the gates has slowed down her commute.

“I’ve been late for work a couple of times, which is really obnoxious,” Medeiros said.

Riders at South Station must check their tickets at fare gates to enter and exit the train platform. They should still expect to show conductors their tickets once aboard to verify they’re traveling to the appropriate zone (fares vary by distance traveled).

At several points during rush hour crushes in both the early morning and late afternoon, the Globe witnessed Commuter Rail employees stand by open gates and visually check rider tickets, an apparent attempt to ease congestion and get passengers on their way.

The workers functioned, effectively, as human fare gates, yielding an affirming phrase like “Good to go,” instead of a pleasant, high-pitched bing as riders went through.

“Financially, they can’t have one person manning every gate forever,” said commuter Steve Cavagnaro, 46.

Keolis, the company operating the commuter rail, told the Globe that the “passenger concierges” are permanent. They still mill about North Station, where fare gates went online in 2022.

“They worked at South Station before the gates were installed and will continue to be on site at all times gates are in operation,” a Keolis spokesperson wrote.

The T and Keolis had their dress rehearsal at North Station in late 2022. Passengers there also weathered a period of confusion and angst after encountering fare gates for the first time. But the T estimates that fare collection across the lines branching from North Station rose around 15 percent since the gates came online.

“I think people are pretty used to them, for the most part,” said Craig Scheipers, a 37-year-old retail worker living in Salem who had just passed through the North Station gates on a recent weekday morning.

North and South Stations are, of course, quite distinct.

South Station, on a given weekday, services far more riders. Its fare gates, though covered, are also outdoors.

A common evening rush hour ritual involves passengers congregating under the courtyard’s soaring arched ceiling before a large screen. Once the display broadcasts their platform, passengers hustle, at varying speeds, to get through the fare gates.

A mile away, North Station’s gates are packed cozily inside the terminal. Outbound passengers, once past the barriers, can wait out the moments before their departure in an indoor concourse with wooden benches and a Dunkin’.

At South Station, Cavagnaro theorized why the gates struggled to pick up QR codes. “This is outside, so that glass [on the gate sensor] isn’t always perfectly clean, right?”

Though frustrations are simmering for some, Scheipers, the commuter at North Station, trusts his fellow riders from the south will acclimate in time.

“You’ll get used to it,” he said.

title: Franklin Cummings Tech celebrates a new home, and a comeback
text:
“I remember driving by for decades and seeing this lot empty,” said Julius Rogers, a Dorchester native and cybersecurity student. Now, “I tell everyone I feel like I’m working at Google or a startup.”

But the formal opening of the building Thursday is also the culmination of a remarkable turnaround for a school that six years ago was struggling to stay afloat.

The then-Benjamin Franklin Institute of Technology was limping toward a merger with Wentworth that died shortly after becoming public knowledge. At the height of the pandemic, the technical school ran a $5 million deficit and laid off a third of its staff. Student enrollment plummeted. And many feared Franklin Cummings Tech would meet the same fate as over 80 colleges that have gone under since 2020, leaving a gaping hole in the kind of hands-on training that typically pays off in future earnings, particularly for lower-income people of color.

Then it didn’t: Bill and Joyce Cummings donated $12.5 million to the school and called for its renaming to Franklin Cummings Tech. The philanthropists considered a big gift to Harvard or MIT, but chose the two-year school precisely because of its focus on vocational training. That, in turn, ignited a wave of giving that surprised, well, everyone. In four years, the school raised $61 million from 700 donors, including $4 million from City Hall.

“It was amazing after that how they merchandised the fact that they had a Cummings grant,” said Bill Cummings, whose real estate business is based in Woburn. “We were astounded at how much it was.”

Most of the money went toward the new campus in Roxbury, a $75 million building with 68,000 square feet across three floors.

The funds also bolstered scholarships and academic needs as the school moved toward financial stability. It pared down the number of available majors from 22 to 10 to focus its resources on programs with the most potential, and the most student interest. Applications rolled in from longtime Franklin Cummings Tech strongholds — John D. O’Bryant School of Math and Science and Dearborn Academy, for example — as well as charter and private schools that see growing demand among graduates for technical education. In less than five years, enrollment doubled to almost 1,125 students. Staffing rebounded to pre-pandemic levels.

Seemingly overnight, Franklin Cummings Tech became the model for a style of vocational training the Trump administration (and much of the country) is clamoring for. Virtually no one is denied admission to the school, which has long taught mostly men of color, immigrants, and first-generation students. Nearly everyone receives financial aid, and tuition, now $9,500 a semester, has only climbed once in the last eight years. Its outcomes rival more prestigious colleges: Around 80 percent of Franklin Cummings Tech graduates quickly get jobs, with an average starting salary near $60,000, higher than the median income of the neighborhood where the school, and almost one in six students, now resides.

“That’s the joy of the work we’ve done over the past five years: We remain broad access. We’ve remained a majority-minority institution, and we’ve grown quite a bit,” said Franklin Cummings Tech president Aisha Francis. “And we believe there’s still more growth out there — that there’s still market share and demand for the education we offer.”

The renaissance extends not just to the school, but to the part of Roxbury around it.

Where Franklin Cummings Tech now stands was a vacant lot for two decades, after the hardware store Harrison Supply closed in the 2000s. Residents now hope that a wave of teachers and students will eat and shop nearby, and that fresh-faced graduates in biotechnology and business management, for example, staff new businesses that could grow in other major developments rising in the vicinity.

“This is a physical symbol of the absolute resurgence of Nubian Square that is actually in full bloom,” said Richard Taylor, a prominent Boston developer behind the unfinished mixed-used development Nubian Ascends. “This is a story of resiliency, persistence, and a vision to be realized and not deferred in this urban market. You can talk up change in a neighborhood. But to actually make it happen . . . oof.”

It took years, Francis said, and an intentional approach to both economics and architecture.

Forty percent of the construction contracts for the new building were awarded to minority business owners, some from Roxbury or Franklin Cummings Tech alums themselves. The campus hinges around a gleaming central staircase that threads through common study spaces stocked with sound-absorbing furniture. All but one classroom gets natural light, and much of what happens inside the school can be seen from outside. The shop where residents bring their cars in for repairs by automotive students, for the cost of parts alone, connects to a back street on the first floor. The lecturer in the robotics lab is observable from the sidewalk. And the optical shop by the front door — a training outpost for opticianry students that was tucked away on the former campus — will take drop-ins from the community.

“The visibility of the program is something we have been struggling with for the last few years,” said Rhiannon Raymond, an opticianry student in her final semester. “This puts us, literally, front and center.”

Hiding in plain sight throughout are homages to the school’s past and its people. A mural in the entryway depicts the facade of the old South End campus. The veneer cladding on the reception desk is really a collage of discarded chopsticks by a Charlestown business, ChopValue. And the sculptural spectacles affixed to the bike racks — another funky Franklin reference — were created by the Dorchester nonprofit Artists for Humanity. A third-floor ceiling installation depicting blue kites is also a nod to Franklin (and his kite-in-a-thunderstorm experiment), suspended between pieces of wood from the lumber supply company that once sat where the school is today.

Robert Kelchen, a higher education finance expert and professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, called Franklin Cummings Tech “a success story,” with an asterisk. Its turnaround is impressive, but is largely fueled by one-time donations, and the school only has $26 million in the bank.

“The one item to watch out for now is whether they are able to build an endowment out of this in case the supports soften from now on,” he said. “There’s always more to do.”

Maybe the biggest item on the agenda is salvaging the sale of the old South End campus, after a deal to turn it into a senior living community fell through in October. It left Franklin Cummings Tech with less cash on hand.

The sale imploded when what had been billed as an affordable housing development gradually transformed into expensive memory care units, costing upward of $10,000 a month, said Stephen Fox, a South End resident who was on the advisory group for the project.

“Talk about a bait-and-switch,” Fox said. “The whole project was beginning to take on a very different feel from what we originally hoped for.”

Related Beal, the development firm that had the site under contract but ultimately chose not to purchase the property, declined to comment. A joint statement with the school in the fall said the parties “could not agree on a viable business plan that would allow the project to move forward.” The purchase price was never made public, though the site is now assessed at $34 million.

Franklin Cummings Tech found bridge financing to fund the new building, the Boston Guardian reported, and still intends to sell the old campus. It is on the market with the permits for the senior living facility already approved, a spokesperson for the school said.

Francis, confident that a sale will work out, said there are already new bids.

That confidence extends to her as well. A doctorate in English literature and the first female president of the predominantly male institution, Francis seems an unlikely progenitor of its success. But “the leadership” was the reason that Cummings said he made his donation in the first place.

In that way, Francis may have something in common with Franklin, said Bithia Carter, president of the philanthropy nonprofit Give Black Alliance.

The Boston-born inventor and Founding Father gifted 1,000 pounds from his estate to Boston in 1790, specifically to support trade education, and designed the fund to mature in 200 years. Later in his life, Franklin became an ardent “education abolitionist,” dedicated to providing opportunities to all students like the ones who attend Franklin Cummings Tech today.

“He would smile down on this,” Carter said. “By the time he died, he had come to recognize that we need to invest more in all people and recognize their equal capacities. [Francis] is living out the legacy of freeing people, of teaching people to lead their own lives and giving them the tools to do that.”

title: Boston Health Care for the Homeless CEO resigns amid staff layoffs, internal discord
text:
McLaren did not respond to multiple calls for comment, and leaders of the Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program declined to discuss details of his departure.

McLaren’s exit came months after the nonprofit carried out the first layoffs in its 40-year history — a decision that drew widespread opposition from clinicians and others inside the organization, according to four current and former staff who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. His resignation also signals rising strain within the nonprofit as it braces for massive cuts to Medicaid, the government insurance program for the poor that funds most of its services.

While the reasons for his departure remain unclear, employees said McLaren’s lack of clinical experience and top-down management style occasionally put him at odds with staff.

De Las Neuces declined an interview request but said in a written statement Tuesday that the program faced an operating deficit that “required difficult strategic decisions.” The nonprofit in September issued layoff notices to 25 people, or about 4 percent of the agency’s workforce, and moved to close a 20-bed medical respite facility in Jamaica Plain, where people who are homeless can recuperate after hospital stays or injuries.

“I agreed to take on the role of interim CEO because I’ve been part of BHCHP’s senior team for the past 10 years and am deeply committed to the mission of the program,“ De Las Nueces said. ”The focus of our leadership team this year is to preserve clinical services and continue to provide high-quality, comprehensive care for homeless individuals and families in Boston, even in light of anticipated Medicaid cuts.”

De Las Nueces added, “Stan [McLaren] guided us through many tough changes, always keeping patients as our top priority.”

The layoffs have been broadly unpopular within an organization known for its passionate and highly dedicated workforce. Many strongly objected to a move to lay off three front-line recovery coaches who provide one-on-one support to homeless people struggling with addiction, and who play a critical role in helping get them into treatment and on medications (such as methadone or Suboxone) that help suppress their cravings and painful withdrawal symptoms.

Also unpopular, employees said, was a decision by the organization to alter its approach to providing outreach to people outside its main clinic and headquarters at 780 Albany St. in Boston’s South End.

Especially in warmer months, the sidewalks outside the building have been a busy gathering spot for people who are homeless and sometimes using illicit drugs. Last summer, leaders at the nonprofit asked outreach staff to gently redirect people outside into the building lobby to decrease congestion and keep pathways clear.

The move drew criticism from some staff at Boston Health Care for the Homeless, who saw it as a symbolic step back from the organization’s longstanding commitment to street-level outreach and meeting people where they are, even in the toughest conditions. Clinicians said the sidewalk interactions are crucial for building trust with patients experiencing mental health challenges like paranoia, many of whom are unwilling to step inside a medical facility.

“People were . . . angry” over the change, said a physician at the organization who asked to remain anonymous. ”Meeting patients on the sidewalks and in the streets is core to what we do. Those are our people."

Other employees said they objected to a scolding email that McLaren sent to employees soon after the decision was made, in which he criticized unnamed staff for spreading “inaccurate and deeply misleading information” to its partner agencies and state officials.

In the email, obtained by the Globe, McLaren accused staff of falsely claiming that city officials and law enforcement had ordered leadership at the Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program to close all services at Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, also known as Mass. and Cass, an intersection that has long been the epicenter of illicit drug use and homelessness in the city. A spokeswoman for the nonprofit said assertions that the nonprofit had stopped providing outreach at Mass. and Cass are “completely inaccurate.”

In his email to staff, McClaren said the alleged misrepresentations by staff were “damaging our credibility” and “placing us in a precarious position with funders, policymakers, and partner agencies.”

“Let me be clear: this behavior is unacceptable,” McLaren wrote. “If individuals feel they can’t align with the organization’s direction and are prepared to undermine BHCHP by circulating falsehoods to external funders, they should reconsider whether this is the right place for them.”

Several employees said they found McLaren’s email to be excessively vitriolic and a distraction from staff members’ primary concern: That cuts threatened to undermine efforts to build relationships with people living on the streets and get them the help they need.

At the same time, the appointment of De Las Nueces as interim CEO was greeted enthusiastically by many front-line staff members. As a physician and the agency’s chief medical director, De Las Nueces is widely respected within the organization and is seen as someone who would prioritize street outreach, several employees said. She previously served as interim CEO prior to McLaren’s hiring.

“I have worked closely with Dr. Denise De Las Nueces for more than 13 years,” said Dr. Jim O’Connell, founding physician and longtime president of the Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program, in a statement. “She is an astute clinician, an exceptional medical leader, a deeply compassionate physician, and a cherished colleague beloved and respected by our BHCHP staff.”

O’Connell did not respond to requests to comment on McLaren’s resignation.

McLaren’s departure marks the third leadership change since 2022 at the program, which serves more than 10,000 people a year at about 30 clinics and has long embraced a direct-to-the-streets approach to medical care. Last year, the nonprofit provided substance use disorder treatment to more than 1,500 unique patients.

The organization is especially vulnerable to planned reductions in government-funded insurance programs: About three-quarters of its annual budget comes from programs like Medicaid and MassHealth, the state’s Medicaid administrator, according to its website.

In the coming years, steep cuts to Medicaid, enacted by Republicans in their signature policy bill last summer, are expected to destabilize — and even cripple — the finances of medical systems across the country. An influx of patients who can’t find or pay for primary care is about to balloon, experts have warned. In Massachusetts alone, approximately 326,000 Massachusetts residents — almost 5 percent of the entire state population — are expected to lose insurance coverage under new Medicaid restrictions that call for some members to comply with work requirements and recheck their eligibility every six months, according to an analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.

In an interview with the Globe last September, McLaren said that, under one projection, the Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program could lose $30 million to $40 million in Medicaid revenue over a four-year period. The nonprofit is hardly alone in its financial struggles: In the 2024 fiscal year, 16 of 22 health systems in Massachusetts operated in the red, in part because of rising costs and low reimbursement rates, according to an analysis by the Center for Health Information and Analysis, a Massachusetts state agency.

“I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to have worked alongside you during a period of real challenge and change,” McLaren wrote in an email announcing his resignation. “I am proud of the care we provided, the conversations we began, and the way so many of you continued to hold the mission steady even when the work felt heavy.”

De Las Nueces said the decision to enact layoffs was made only after senior leadership at the organization explored multiple ways to boost revenues and improve efficiency. “These efforts, while helpful, were unfortunately not enough to close the financial gap,” she said in a statement.

Prior to joining the program, McLaren served more than three years as president of Carney Hospital in Dorchester. Carney closed its doors in August 2024 after its parent company, Steward Health Care, once the nation’s largest private for-profit hospital chain, filed for bankruptcy after years of alleged financial mismanagement.

Sarah Rahal of the Globe staff contributed to this report.
