title: Faith leaders across Massachusetts urge Governor Healey to take clear stand against immigration enforcement
text:
“Just like all Americans, my attention, my heart, has been in Minneapolis for the last couple of weeks,” said Rabbi Greg Hersh, founding Rabbi of V’ahavatah, a Judaism beyond Zionism synagogue in Cambridge, after the vigil. “I believe firmly that none of us are free until all of us free. None of us are safe, until all of us are safe.”

Good’s death and federal immigration agents’ actions in Minnesota have sparked a national outcry in recent weeks, including among faith leaders. Police arrested about 100 clergy demonstrating against immigration enforcement at Minnesota’s largest airport Friday, organizers estimated, as thousands gathered, despite Arctic temperatures, in downtown Minneapolis to protest the Trump administration’s crackdown. Religious leaders across the country have previously spoken out against ICE raids.

The faith leaders in Boston on Friday wanted Healey to accept their three demands: use her executive powers to protect civil rights, restrict the use of state land for federal immigration enforcement, and establish accountability toward federal actions if they violate constitutional rights.

Following the vigil, the clergy mingled throughout the cathedral hall, reflecting on a prompt displayed on large screens asking how the current political moment had challenged or deepened their faith and what practices they felt called to sustain. With hands on their colleagues’ shoulders, and eyes closed, the clergy all prayed and blessed each other.

“People are fearful and worried about where our society and where our faithful people are headed,” said the Rev. Jeremy Froyen, rector of Grace Church in New Bedford, at the gathering. “But yet, I’m also hearing a lot of joy, not in the sense of being happy with what’s going on, but joy knowing that we’re all together and we’re standing in solidarity.”

By late morning, the Rev. Aaron Payson led the crowd to the State House from the cathedral. People walked in tiny groups through the Commons while discussing the state of the country, possible actions Massachusetts can take, and learning more about other faiths through their leaders.

The Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, pastor of New Roots African Methodist Episcopal Church in Dorchester and core member of MCAN, sang prayer songs on the way along with her other colleagues. She said the gathering had three motives: to stand with the clergy in Minneapolis and all the people in Minnesota, to begin organizing and preparing in case similar things start happening in Massachusetts, and lastly, to get Healey to take action by agreeing to their three demands.

“Part of the point of this is to connect faith communities together so that we are more able to respond both as citizens, but also as people of faith who have a heightened responsibility to care for one another,” she said.

The clergy all gathered at Memorial Hall inside the State House as speakers from multiple faith communities addressed the crowd. The speakers repeatedly urged the Healey administration to take a clear public stand against the use of state resources for federal immigration enforcement.

William Dickerson II, the co-executive director of MCAN and part of the faith tradition Bwete, said the action was intended to demonstrate the collective power of faith communities and push for concrete outcomes.

“We want to make sure that our governor and our public officials are being really mindful of the fact that these kinds of things could happen here,” he said. “See them showing us how they’re going to protect us through public action.”

The Rev. Katie Omberg, an area conference minister in the United Church of Christ, emphasized that the gathering was not partisan, but moral.

“What’s the role of clergy in this? What is our call to do here? Today is answering part of that, which is being brave enough to stand up and call evil, evil,” they said.

Throughout the event, speakers returned to themes of resistance, courage, and unity across traditions.

Sister of Saint Joseph Melinda Pellerin was tasked to speak with the governor regarding MCAN’s demands.

Faith leaders said they hope the gathering marks the beginning of a broader movement across the Commonwealth.

“I hope this is the beginning of a resistance here in Boston,” Hersh said. “Coming together as a wholly religious people and uniting over our shared values to make really important changes so that we can all be safer.”

Materials from the Associated Press were used in this report.

title: Under Segun Idowu, City Hall focused on neighborhood development. Will Mayor Wu now pivot to downtown?
text:
For four years, Idowu did just that, launching new grant programs for local businesses, doling out liquor licenses in parts of town that have few, and connecting far-flung commercial districts to the resources of City Hall. Then, Monday, Idowu announced he will step down at the end of February, to care for his elderly grandmother.

Idowu’s departure comes at a precarious time for Boston’s economy, amid threats to some of the city’s core industries, concerns over the vitality of the Financial District, and declining values of commercial real estate that powers the city’s budget. Now, business leaders are wondering: Will Wu, and whoever she picks to succeed Idowu, continue the neighborhood-focused approach to economic development, or will they pivot to prioritize a downtown that’s still struggling to rebound from the COVID-19 pandemic?

It’s a push-and-pull faced by Boston mayors for decades, from Kevin White’s efforts to revive downtown and the waterfront, to Thomas Menino’s more neighborhood-centric approach, to Martin J. Walsh, who oversaw an era of building all across the city. But Wu, in an interview this week, said downtown and the neighborhoods isn’t an either/or question for her administration.

“That’s a false dichotomy,” Wu said.

“When we invest in downtown, it strengthens our neighborhoods, and when we open and fill neighborhood retail space that also strengthens downtown,” she said. “We need our residents, neighborhood businesses, our large corporations, [and] philanthropic sector all to not only coexist, but cooperate.”

As of now, Wu said, she does not have a replacement for Idowu lined up. Whoever she hires, she said, their top priorities will include filling still-empty storefronts and adapting to Boston’s changing economic landscape amid federal attacks on higher education, health care, and research.

“This continues to be a really challenging and really consequential moment for Boston’s future,” she said. “We are laser focused on driving down the commercial vacancy rates downtown and throughout our commercial areas, and [strengthening] our innovation sector and all the industries that have supported Boston’s economy for centuries and need to [continue to do so] for the next generation.”

That is a slight shift in tone for Wu, who four years ago campaigned on shrinking Boston’s racial wealth gap by investing in communities of color. Catering to downtown and big business interests were not as high on the agenda.

For some Boston business leaders, even that modest shift is likely to be welcome.

Jim Rooney, president and chief executive of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, said Idowu’s tenure has generally been good for the city at large. But he acknowledged that certain segments of Boston’s business community feel like City Hall has neglected the struggles of downtown and not done enough to make Boston’s business environment competitive.

“The view of the business community is that our [city and state] government partners should step up their game with respect to business attraction, retention, growth, expansion,” said Rooney. “And that not enough attention is paid or has been paid to those issues over time.”

The Wu administration has had some big business wins.Hasbro, Lego, and Eli Lilly all moved big facilities to Boston in the last four years, which Idowu said shows that big employers appreciate his and Wu’s “holistic” approach to economic development, prioritizing businesses across the city and improving residents’ quality of life.

“Our strategy was, for the benefit of the commercial cores of the city, it’s important that we have healthy, vibrant neighborhood economies,” Idowu said. “It is not cheaper to move a company to the city of Boston. So why are they doing that? It’s because it’s a place where their employees will want to be.”

Still, for much of her first term, Wu contended with a perception that she is less friendly to big business interests and traditional power brokers than her predecessors. That has played out in clashes over property tax rates on commercial buildings, and over affordable housing and green energy policies that critics argue has stalled new construction.

Those are challenges that Idowu’s eventual successor will have to confront, along with stubbornly high office vacancy rates. Then there are broad economic shifts that are hurting small businesses all over the city, including downtown.

Bessie King, who co-owns the Villa Mexico Cafe in the Financial District with her mother, Julie King, said they received grants from the city to help them survive the roughest parts of the pandemic. But since 2022 they’ve seen City Hall’s emphasis pivot elsewhere.

“They shifted to promoting new businesses or encouraging people to open new businesses without really helping the existing businesses that are trying to survive,” Bessie said.

Last summer, Julie King sent a letter to Idowu saying she was on the verge of closing her quarter-century-old lunch spot. The letter prompted the city to connect the Kings to a small business consultant, who is now helping them update their menu. But Bessie King said it shouldn’t have taken a desperate plea for them to get help. And time is running short.

“For us, 2026 is crucial,” Bessie King said. “If we do not make a profit this year, we will close.”

At the same time, other parts of the city are growing. From Dorchester and Roxbury to Mattapan and Hyde Park, new small businesses are springing up, says state Representative Chris Worrell. He gives a lot of credit to Idowu and a renewed focus from City Hall.

“We are becoming destination boroughs, communities, and that’s [due to] all the investment that Segun has seen into it,” Worrell said. “You see it far and wide when you go into the Black and brown areas of Boston, you see his handprint throughout the city.”

If that was Wu’s goal, Idowu was a natural fit for the job. As president and chief executive of BECMA, Idowu had focused on supporting Black-owned businesses, with the goal of helping marginalized communities build generational wealth. Under his leadership, BECMA and several other advocacy groups in 2021 filed a federal civil rights complaint against the city, after an audit found that just 1.2 percent of the $2.1 billion City Hall spent on contracts between 2014 and 2019 went to Black- and Latino-owned companies.

Then he joined City Hall, aiming to change the system from the inside.

“Segun took the role to be transformational,” said Nicole Obi, his successor at BECMA. “Under his leadership [at City Hall], we saw real progress, whether that was increased contracting with diverse businesses or expanded access to capital, or policies that helped businesses stabilize and grow. That was all by intention.”

Over four years, Idowu and the city nearly doubled the amount in city contracts that went to minority- and women-owned businesses, including a $17 million contract between Boston Public Schools and City Fresh Foods in 2022, the largest contract the city has ever awarded to a Black-owned business.

And when Beacon Hill granted Boston 225 new liquor licenses, Idowu worked to help minority-owned businesses in historically disenfranchised neighborhoods apply for them. He also launched the SPACE Grant program, which doled out COVID-era recovery funds to small businesses to help them move into empty storefronts, not just downtown but all over Boston.

Idowu tackled those efforts with the help of a critical tool: an unprecedented pot of federal pandemic relief dollars. Nearly one-10th of the $560 million Boston received in COVID recovery funds went to Idowu’s Economic Opportunity and Inclusion Cabinet, funding many of Idowu’s marquee initiatives.

Now that money is largely spent, and Wu has warned her department heads to prepare for modest budget cuts. Whoever follows Idowu won’t have the same resources to work with.

Still, Karilyn Crockett, an MIT professor of urban history, public policy, and planning who worked for City Hall for several years under Walsh, said she hopes Wu fills Idowu’s role with someone who will continue his efforts to address longstanding racial disparities in the city’s economic development efforts.

“These were hard-won or hard-fought battles,” Crockett said. “This is a moment to continue this focus and commitment and double down on it.”

For his part, Idowu said he is not at all concerned about leaving behind a vacuum of leadership, even with several major events around the corner, from the FIFA World Cup, Tall Ships, and the country’s 250th anniversary, which are expected to bring a wave of investment and tourism to the city.

“I have tremendous faith in my team,” Idowu said. “I would argue that we’ve been one of the most productive engines of progress in the city in many, many years ... and I think that the person who takes over is going to be standing on a very solid foundation.”

title: Snowstorms are a big test for the MBTA. Did the transit system pass?
text:
I’m not proud, but it was awesome.

Normally, the Southeast Expressway at 8 a.m. is jammed, but not on Wednesday morning. I left at 7:30, dropped off my son at Boston College High School just after 8, and pulled into a garage in downtown Boston by 8:30.

My son has midterms, and putting him on the Red Line felt too risky. That feeling was right. It turns out the Red Line was once again plagued by disabled trains on Wednesday, prompting 30-minute delays.

Many of us are still traumatized by the utter collapse of the transit system during the winter of 2015, when more than 100 inches of snow fell on the region.

It’s made me wonder: Would Phil Eng’s MBTA be different?

Eng has been the best general manager in more than a generation, a guy who has developed a cult following among commuters and who seems to get a standing ovation wherever he goes. He is perhaps Governor Maura Healey’s most important hire. He even wears a second hat these days as the state’s interim transportation secretary. Getting the T back on track has been one of Healey’s biggest achievements in her first term, one she hopes to trumpet during her reelection campaign.

I’m loath to judge the T solely on its worst day amid 23 inches of snow and frigid temperatures. But a transit system’s real test is whether it works when people need it the most and when driving isn’t an option.

This was the biggest snowstorm since Eng took over the T in 2023, and beyond Red Line woes, there have been a raft of cancellations and delays on the commuter rail, including a bunch at North Station Tuesday night.

But one thing is becoming clear: The older the train, the harder it is for it to handle the snow and cold.

The Orange Line, with all of its new cars, is running fairly well. The Green and Blue lines, which also have newer cars, had slight delays on Wednesday. But for riders on the Red Line, it may be a very long winter.

The Red Line has the oldest fleet, with some trains close to 60 years old. Because of delays in getting replacement Red Line cars, only six of 20 train sets in service are new, according to the MBTA.

So when riders hear the conductor talk about a “disabled train,” it’s likely an old Red Line car struggling in the snow. And sometimes, the fix involves having a new train “rescue” an older one by pushing it to the next stop, which creates delays across the Red Line, MBTA chief operating officer Ryan Coholan said.

His advice? “I would highly recommend giving yourself a few extra minutes,” Coholan said.

I wondered if the T should just sideline the oldest Red Line trains on a week like this. That wouldn’t work either, according to the T. The Red Line is the busiest of the subways, about 164,000 passengers on an average weekday. Removing those cars would mean customers would have to wait 45 minutes or more for a train.

Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of advocacy group TransitMatters, said one way the T could ease frustration during the wintry weather is to offer a reduced schedule, in particular on the Red Line. At least that would offer more predictability.

“There are a lot of delays — unexpected and unannounced," Allen-Connelly said. “This is because they committed to running regular service.”

My trip on the T wasn’t a complete disaster on Tuesday. Impressively, the Mattapan Trolley, which connects Milton to the subway system, was running, unlike on Monday when buses had to replace it. I’m told the T had special snow plows running all night to clear the tracks.

And while my morning on the Red Line was a tough one, my Tuesday evening commute was fine. It took only an hour to get from Copley Square to Milton.

Will I get back on public transit? I will have to. I can’t afford the $25 or more to park in a downtown garage. I’m a big fan of the Fairmount commuter rail, and that’s what I’ll return to. I only stopped riding the Fairmount because Eng eliminated the slow zones on the Red Line.

When the T failed us all during the Snowmageddon of 2015, Charlie Baker had just become governor, and he spent much of his first term trying to fix the system. He didn’t campaign on building a better transit system, but he owned the problem, for better or worse.

By contrast, Healey came into office vowing to fix the T, and Eng’s success is a key talking point of her reelection strategy. The T’s struggles test whether “In Phil We Trust” can survive a real winter.

title: Boston digs out: Residents, work crews battle aftermath of historic snowstorm
text:
Southern New England was buried under 23 inches of snow during the storm, making it one of the region’s biggest in decades. The total ranked eighth on record and surpassed the Blizzard of 2005, when 22.5 inches of snow fell in Boston. Forecasters warned that bitter cold will continue through this weekend, limiting snowmelt, while meteorologists also monitored the potential for a nor’easter to develop late in the week.

In past winters, Boston has sometimes removed snow entirely from city streets, transporting it to designated snow farms, empty lots where it can safely melt. City officials have not yet confirmed whether similar measures will be used this year.

Boston Public Works deployed over 900 pieces of equipment to clear streets, Mayor Michelle Wu’s office said in a statement. Workers have focused on clearing intersections, crosswalks and curb ramps, and have coordinated with schools to keep bus routes open. Overnight snow removal operations continued Tuesday, with crews moving large piles to off-road locations. Space savers were set to be collected starting Thursday, along with regular trash collection, Wu’s office said.

Flynn said crews and contractors are limited in how long they can operate within a 24-hour period to ensure safety, noting that city officials have remained in close contact with the Public Works Department throughout the cleanup.

“Our city employees are doing a good job under very difficult circumstances,” he said. “It is the priority that we have to provide the necessary sleep for people that are plowing the streets and contractors. That’s also about public safety.”

The MBTA said service continued through the storm thanks to frontline workers, though delays and disruptions remain. Disabled trains and snow-related switch and signal problems affected the Red, Orange, and Blue lines, while the Green and Mattapan lines were running smoothly, the transit agency said. Many buses remained on snow routes Tuesday and paratransit service have been slowed by uncleared streets as crews continue snow removal efforts.

Similar snow removal efforts were underway in Cambridge on Tuesday, where the city deployed approximately 75 pieces of equipment since the start of the storm, and another 100 pieces were sent out via contractors, according to Jeremy Warnick, a Cambridge spokesperson.

Cambridge’s snow hauling operations began Tuesday night, taking snow to Danehy Park and, if needed, to a second location in Allston owned by Harvard University, Warnick said.

As cleanup continued, the impact of the storm remained visible on Boston’s streets.

In South Boston, plowed side streets were narrowed to single lanes, with parked cars nearly submerged beneath packed snow. Between vehicles, chairs, folding tables, and compost bins were pressed into service as space savers and dotted the curbside.

Sidewalks were even narrower, often incompletely cleared and blocked by snow piled at house entrances. Pedestrians clutched building walls to steady themselves on slick patches.

John MacDougall, a 26-year-old sales analyst and South Boston resident, opted to walk in the street rather than use the slippery sidewalk while returning to his C Street apartment from Stop & Shop.

“I just walked on the main roads, while cars are just blowing right by me,” he said.

MacDougall, who works remotely, said even short trips felt difficult after the storm. The grocery store is less than a mile from his apartment, but snow-covered sidewalks made the walk feel longer.

“The first day after the storm is pretty rough,” he said. “But getting people out here to clear these roads is dangerous for them, and I think they’re doing their best given the large amount of snow we got.”

A few blocks away on West Third Street, Brittani LeBlanc, 27, stood breathless after digging her Toyota Corolla out from a deep snowbank. Originally from Townsend, LeBlanc said she’s accustomed to winter weather, but this was her first major snowstorm living in the city.

“The hardest part is figuring out where to put it all,” she said.

“Somebody said to just put it on the street and they’ll come,” she added, “but I don’t know. I always feel bad doing that.”

LeBlanc said snow plows had passed regularly down her street for nearly 24 hours during the storm, though she had not seen them Tuesday. She credited her neighbors for doing a good job shoveling the sidewalk in front of their homes.

With another storm possible approaching, she offered simple advice.

“I definitely recommend to anybody who is parking to park in a garage spot,” she said, leaning against her open car door.

Flynn noted the importance of resident safety, particularly for seniors and people with disabilities. He urged residents to clear sidewalks, fire hydrants, and crosswalks to maintain access for pedestrians and emergency responders, and encouraged neighbors to help one another.

“And us neighbors help each other out,” LeBlanc said. “[My roommates and I] broke a shovel, and then somebody loaned us theirs.”

In Dorchester, similar scenes played out as snow plows passed through and residents shoveled sidewalks. A Public Works vehicle arrived on Gibson Street carrying salt, while a resident worked her way down the sidewalk clearing snow.

“You’ve got to help your neighbors,” she said.

Thomas McLaughlin, a 70-year-old retiree who previously worked in snow removal, treaded carefully along Gibson Street, noting it was “still hard to walk on” despite cleanup efforts.

“I’m very cautious because I don’t want to fall at this age and break anything,” McLaughlin said. “You take it for granted [that] it’s all soft and mushy, but it could be very slippery.”

Sunny Ortiz, a 27-year-old Roxbury resident who works for a commercial cleaning company, walked along Gibson Street toward a bus stop and said he had largely avoided public transportation due to delays.

Ortiz said he is grateful to the city’s street-clearing efforts.

“You don’t really want to wait 20, 30, 40 minutes for a train ride, so shout out to Mayor Wu,” he said. “The streets were still kind of clear, so I could go on the street and walk, [and] today, you could walk on the sidewalk.”

Ortiz said he had walked across much of Boston in recent days and didn’t mind seeing others enjoying the snow.

“We’ve got another one this week,” he said. “We’ll see how it is, just go day by day.”

title: Parents grapple with second day of school closures: ‘I’m looking at this as a safety measure’
text:
Cheryl Buckman, whose seventh-grade son attends Ruth Batson Academy in Dorchester, said she supported the decision to call off school for a second day.

Nearly 2 feet of snow dropped on Boston, and in her neighborhood, roads and sidewalks remained a sloppy mess, she said.

“There’s no way you can clear it all in one day,” Buckman said. “I’d rather they take the second day. I’m looking at this as a safety measure.”

Boston Public Schools have about 100 buildings to clean up before students return to school, and they need the time to do the work, she said.

Despite the time off, Buckman said her son hasn’t yet grown restless.

“He’s in seventh grade, you’d think he’d be locked into the electronics daily, but no, he’s been outside three times today,” Buckman said.

But for Eugenia Moorehead, a Nubian Square parent of two, the two-day closure made things difficult for her.

“We kind of depend on that school lunch,” Moorehead said. “I remember when we were kids, climbing over mountains of snow.”

“I don’t feel that this is worth it,” she said.

Moorehead said she also has neighbors asking her to watch their kids due to the snow day.

“People can’t afford this right now,” she said. “Child care and food, this is not OK.”

Moorehead’s son attends a school within walking distance, the Higginson/Lewis K-8, while her daughter goes to the much further Gardner Pilot Academy.

She’s confident she could’ve made it work, though.

“We would’ve gotten my baby to school,” she said. “I was born in Mission Hill, I went to school in Brighton, and we made our way to school.”

Jessica Thornton, a Beacon Hill mom, said she figures deciding to call a snow day must be a “difficult and nuanced decision.”

”It will hit some families much harder than others," she said in a text. “For us, I am pleased to have a snow day inside.”

Julianna Barrett, a Boston mother, weighed in on a Facebook post about the decision.

“Boston needs to be closed one more day it’s not safe and they have no where to stand for there buses, my child’s safety comes first!” she wrote.

A social media post by Newton school officials said, “we hate to miss the learning but are worried for student safety accessing sidewalks, schools and parking lots.”

Several parents responded, saying the decision made good sense to them considering the conditions of the roads Monday evening.

The superintendent of Reading Public Schools told families in an email Monday that he understands the decision isn’t “ideal” for them but the school grounds are not in a condition to safely open on Tuesday.

“Our DPW and Facilities teams have been working tirelessly around the clock on snow removal and site preparation, and we are incredibly grateful for their continued efforts and commitment to our schools,” Superintendent Tom Milaschewski wrote. “Despite this work, our buildings and surrounding areas are not yet in a position to open safely for students and staff tomorrow.”

“We recognize that additional closures are not ideal,” he continued. “However, the safety of our students, staff, and families remains our top priority and we must make decisions with that responsibility at the forefront.”

Milaschewski said he anticipated “a regular school opening on Wednesday.”

The situation was the same at Wakefield Public Schools, officials said in an email to families.

“The additional day will allow us to continue clearing and hauling snow away from parking lots and sidewalks to support a safe return for our students and staff,” the email said.

When calling a snow day, school leaders weigh many factors, such as timing and snow fall projections, progress on the cleanup of roads and sidewalks, and other factors.

They also have to consider the mandatory 180-day school calendar. Five snow days are built into the calendar. Any snow days over that limit have to be made up, usually at the end of the school year in June.

Some parents sparred on social media over whether a second snow day is a good or bad idea.

One commenter on Revere’s Facebook page assailed the decision to close for another day.

“This is ridiculous people have to go to work our kids need to be in school!” a poster said. “It’s not even snowing in the ’80s we would go to school in a blizzard this got to stop.”

Others balked at Bassett’s response.

“School isn’t daycare and it’s not the ’80s anymore,” one post said.

Shannon Larson of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: His thoughtful date planning impressed her from the start; their shared faith deepened their bond
text:
That date — dinner at Novara in Milton — had also been a choose-your-own-adventure experience, curated by Shadlee. The software engineer was living and working in Cranston, Rhode Island, but did not hesitate to make the 45-minute drive to meet the accomplished, joyful woman he had matched with on Hinge. “If I’m taking someone out, I’m going to go the distance,” Shadlee says.

While Joanne is a Boston native, she had just moved back to the city that August after having completed her law degree at Howard University in D.C. She was impressed by Shadlee’s curated list of three restaurants, complete with links and brief descriptors for each. Allowing her to choose made the date a chance for “good collaboration,” she says. “It showed me he put a lot of thought into it.”

At Novara, they discovered their shared Christian beliefs and values and Haitian upbringings, learning they both speak Creole.

“He said a few jokes and I was, ‘Oh you’re Haitian,’" remembers Joanne, “because we’re both born here, and [sometimes] there’s varying degrees of how connected [to the culture] you are. The fact that he knew the language was really cool to learn about in person.”

The bond imprinted on her as feeling “safe. ... He was such a comforting presence.” Shadlee, a self-identifying introvert, felt likewise; while he’d been nervous at first, Joanne’s “natural kindness” helped him relax.

“I could be myself and talk about things perfectly fine with her being able to reciprocate,” he says. “I don’t remember the restaurant, I don’t remember the waiter, it felt like it was just the two of us.”

In similar fashion, Shadlee presented his ideas for their second date — which he decided should be experiential, to mix things up. “The date, the time, the link. …. I was just stunned by his level of planning,” Joanne says.

The perfume workshop at the House of Arts & Crafts (now called The Creative Hub) was more intimate than anticipated, though “I’m glad she chose it, because that was my favorite from the list,” says Shadlee. They were the only two in attendance. But they had a “beautiful time,” each creating a unique blend of scents that they named Cest La Vie (her) and The Gentlemen (him). Content from their session wound up on the business’ social media accounts.

“It was great promo for them, but this was our second date,” emphasizes Joanne with a laugh. “They took videos. They turned it into a whole reel. It’s good content for us [now], but I sent that to my friends and was like, ‘Guys…’ It was a lot of pressure.”

For their third date, Joanne invited Shadlee to the Holiday Pops. On the drive home, he parked his car on a well-lit block of Commonwealth Avenue where they continued to talk. (The heat was on, “I’m not trying to freeze her to death,” Shadlee says. “That’d be rude.”) As he drove her back to her house, Shadlee asked the question that had been on his mind all night: “Would you like to be my girlfriend?” Then, they shared their first kiss.

Their faith and their commitment to each other remained constants as the relationship evolved. Weekends included Saturday service; Wednesdays were reserved for devotionals. Shadlee’s back-and-forth from Rhode Island became “something to look forward to, a little bit of a ritual in a sense, and I get to see this beautiful woman.”

For Valentine’s Day, he booked a dinner cruise on Boston Harbor. As they watched the water and live jazz played, Shadlee remembers watching Joanne, thinking: I can see myself being with her forever.

“It’s that level of comfort, safe space, of being open and fully transparent and completely vulnerable,” he says.

They’d been dating eight months when they began pre-engagement counseling.

“I knew we weren’t there yet, but it was powerful to hear people confirm what we felt,” says Joanne. The program was run by a couple married for 15 years, who, upon meeting Shadlee and Joanne, told them: “We sense a safety between you that’s really rare.”

After celebrating their first year together, they attended a marathon of celebrations for family and friends between them — a sprint of nine nuptials, one of them international, and six out of state. Joanne’s uncle’s 50th birthday brought them to New York, where “by the end of the night, [my family] were referring to him as my husband” in Creole. After Shadlee’s brother’s D.C. wedding, the first time Joanne had met his family, he received nothing but rave reviews: “I have not found one person that does not like her. Friends, family, their dog, everybody loves her.”

“I always knew that in my partner, [I wanted] the peace, the sureness, the unwaveringness that I feel with God’s love that has just transformed my life,“ Joanne says. ”I felt that with Shad.”

Shadlee proposed on a private sunset cruise on Martha’s Vineyard on July 12, 2025. Taking a knee surrounded by rose petals, he quoted Colossians 3:14, as Elvis Presley’s “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” the first song they danced to together, played.

Joanne, 33, and Shadlee, 36, wed on October 9, 2025, at St. Mary’s Episcopal Church in Dorchester. The couple opted for an intimate ceremony, planned in three months, with 12 members of their immediate family present. Dinner at the North End’s Florentine Cafe was family-style, served amid illuminated faux grapevines that hang from the ceiling of the restaurant’s downstairs.

“It has a very moody ambiance but very romantic,” says Joanne.

The couple picked the location as a tribute to their upcoming celebration in Italy, where they’ll toast their nuptials with a larger group of family and friends later this year. For their autumn micro-wedding, however, they managed to keep their budget small; Joanne broke down the itemized costs on her social media account, where she typically shares advice for aspiring lawyers.

She arranged white roses from Whole Foods into a sophisticated bouquet and wedding arch; the pair cut into the grocer’s famed Berry Chantilly Cake following their first dance (to Elvis, of course). And they wore the fragrances they’d made.

“We [made the perfumes] so early on in our relationship, and I typically only wear it for special occasions” says Joanne. “It brought back all the memories of love — the adventure, the excitement, the consideration. It made me think of everything that has been such a blessing and lifted the air in my life. It’s the fragrance of love."

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s weddings column.

This story has been updated to correct a photo caption spelling error in the bride’s last name and an error in the weekend day that the couple attended service.

title: BPS warns of hundreds of layoffs under ‘difficult budget year’
text:
The budget for the upcoming fiscal year will be officially presented to the School Committee on Wednesday.

BPS also cut jobs ahead of the 2024-2025 school year budget, when 70 percent of schools saw some reductions in staffing, totaling about 393 full-time equivalent positions.

The latest round of possible job cuts, representing about 4 percent of the district’s total staff, comes after several years of spending increases that were intended to support students recovering from the pandemic and expand services for special education and English language learners.

With city tax revenues under pressure, the Trump administration threatening to slash federal aid to local communities, and now the prospect of fresh job cuts in the schools, challenges are piling up for Mayor Michelle Wu, who recently pledged to make Boston schools the best in country.

Rosie Brenes, 35, of Dorchester, has six children enrolled in Boston Public Schools and worries about the fallout from job cuts.

“I’m just concerned about where they’re going to be cutting things, and how it’s going to affect my children,” Brenes said. “If you want to improve the system, budget-cutting is not the way to go.”

BPS’s expected financial woes come on top of a $53 million shortfall for the current fiscal year, which ends June 30. Skipper, in a memo to staff last month, said that overrun was driven by factors such as rising costs for insurance and transportation, as well as areas such as student food services and filling full-time positions.

Administrators have taken steps to balance this year’s budget, including implementing a hiring freeze for vacant school and central office-based positions, and pausing other spending, Skipper said. The district was trying to protect areas that directly served students, she said.

“These steps should address the shortfall and put us in the best position to meet the challenges of [fiscal 2027], which we know is going to be a difficult budget year,” Skipper said during the Jan. 21 School Committee meeting.

Wu in October announced a call to action to make Boston’s schools the best in the nation, which if accomplished would be a dramatic turnaround for a district that faced receivership just a few years ago. (BPS later entered into an improvement plan with the state to avoid a state takeover. That agreement expired last year, even though the district hadn’t fulfilled all of its commitments.)

Wu has presented few details on how Boston would measure progress or establish deadlines for reaching her goal. She told the Globe in December that she wants to instill “confidence” in families and make BPS their first choice.

Wide achievement gaps persist between BPS’s Black and Latino students compared to white and Asian pupils. More than 40 of Boston’s schools are classified by the state as underperforming, while fewer than one-third of Grade 3 through 8 students meet expectations on the state’s MCAS exams. The district is also working to shutter school buildings, to help lower costs while students attend fewer, larger schools with more diverse offerings.

Haval Abdulrahman, 59, a civil engineer living in Dorchester with two children enrolled in BPS, criticized administrators for considering job cuts after moving to combine some schools and close others.

“They merged schools, closed many elementary schools, and now they talk about additional budget cuts. So that’s not fair,” he said. “They already did something to save money.”

Boston wasn’t able to improve student outcomes despite $454 million in federal pandemic aid to the city’s schools, according to Greg Maynard, executive director of the nonprofit Boston Policy Institute. Now that aid is gone.

“You’re trying to increase student performance while also slashing the budget,” Maynard said. “It’s going to be tough.”

And for Boston Public Schools, which received a budget of nearly $1.6 billion this year — about 40 percent of the city’s fiscal 2026 spending — the challenges are only growing.

Last spring, BPS brokered with the Boston Teachers Union a new contract, which will increase members’ pay by $181 million over three years. Boston Public Schools’ teachers, who earned an average of about $120,000 last year, would receive a 9 percent to 11.5 percent pay increase over the three-year agreement. Classroom paraprofessionals, who on average earn about $45,000, would see a roughly 30 percent increase in pay.

Will Austin, the founder of Boston Schools Fund, a nonprofit working to improve BPS, and a former teacher and principal, said many of the financial issues are out of the district’s control.

Cutting costs for transportation and personnel are the only viable options, Austin said. “Those are two things that you have direct control over and drive most of the cost of the budget,” he said.

The Boston Teachers Union, in a statement to members in January, warned about anticipated job cuts across the district, and called on the city to cover increases in insurance costs.

Erik Berg, the union president, said in an interview that the budget requires more resources.

“We ought to be able to provide our students, our schools with appropriate staffing and funding to meet all students needs,” Berg said. “We can do it. It’s a question of whether we have the will to do it.”

Boston’s public education spending expanded rapidly in recent years, increasing by $400 million between 2020 and this year.

The current year’s budget was a 3.5 percent increase — about $53.4 million — over fiscal 2025, and it focused on priorities such as more funding for special education and instruction for English language learners. Over half of the budget increase was intended to help cover growing costs such as salaries and health insurance.

Bloom, the district’s chief financial officer, told the School Committee in December the upcoming cuts would include positions assigned to the Dever Elementary School, Excel High School, and Mary Lyon Pilot High School, all slated to close at the end of the school year. There are roughly 160 positions at those buildings, he said.

“Across our schools, if we were to include the closures that are happening for this upcoming year, I would anticipate it’s going to be at least three [hundred] to 400 positions, primarily teachers and paraprofessionals in schools, but also some support staff, especially those in schools that are closing just to meet the declining enrollment,” Bloom told committee members.

The district has 10,710 employees, up from 9,266 during the 2019-2020 school year. That expansion included roughly 300 teachers, 230 paraprofessionals, and about 450 support staff, according to the district.

They were added even as BPS’s student enrollment plummeted from more than 53,000 in the 2019-2020 school year to about 46,800 this year, the district reported.

That helped create the current problem, said Mary Tamer, a former School Committee member who was appointed by Mayor Thomas Menino. The district should have focused on offering services that benefited students, such as high dosage tutoring, rather than expanding the ranks of BPS employees.

“None of this is surprising, honestly,” she said.

title: Community activist Monica Cannon-Grant to be sentenced for fraud ‘under the calculated guise of charity’
text:
In an appeal for leniency before learning her fate, Cannon-Grant told the judge she took ”full ownership” of her mistakes, but hoped she would also consider the good she had done for the community.

She told the judge she was “extremely proud” that, through her nonprofit, she had fed 80,000 people during the pandemic and helped others with rental assistance even while hers went unpaid.

The 44-year-old mother of six said it would have a devastating impact on her two youngest children, ages 4 and 7, if she were sent to prison, since they were already suffering from the tragic loss of their father.

Federal prosecutors had recommended an 18-month prison term for Cannon-Grant and portrayed her as a shameless fraudster who stole from people “under the calculated guise of charity,” according to a sentencing memo last week.

“A serious sentence in this case can restore faith in the system,” Assistant US Attorney Dustin Chao told the judge during Thursday’s hearing. “You don’t get to steal if you do good things. You don’t get a pass if you help the community.”

However, Cannon-Grant’s attorney, Emma Notis-McConarty, said it was important for the judge to recognize the good that she had done for so many people.

In a sentencing memorandum filed last week, the defense described her as “a loving mother, wife, and daughter who has dedicated her life to advancing social justice and serving communities in need.”

Cannon-Grant, who ran the nonprofit Violence in Boston Inc., pleaded guilty in September to 18 counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, mail fraud, and tax violations. In exchange, prosecutors agreed to dismiss nine counts related to allegations of mortgage fraud.

She was indicted along with her husband, Clark Grant, in 2022 on charges that they raised more than $1 million for their charity and received nearly $60,000 in pandemic relief funds to provide meals for people in need, but instead spent much of the money on themselves.

In March 2023, Clark Grant was killed in a motorcycle crash in Easton.

The initial indictment charged Cannon-Grant and her husband with three separate schemes: defrauding people who donated money to their nonprofit; illegally collecting an estimated $100,000 in pandemic unemployment benefits while she was working; and lying on a mortgage application.

Additional fraud charges were brought before Clark Grant’s death in 2023.

In 2019, Cannon-Grant’s nonprofit was awarded a $6,000 grant from the Suffolk district attorney’s office to take a group of at-risk young men to a retreat in Philadelphia.

Instead, prosecutors allege, Cannon-Grant and her husband used the money to take a vacation to Maryland, on dining at Bubba Gump Shrimp Co., Shake Shack, and other restaurants, and paying for car rentals, groceries, Walmart purchases, and visits to a Boston nail salon.

Cannon-Grant told the judge she grew up in deep poverty in Dorchester, with an abusive father, and frequently witnessed violence and crime.

She rose to prominence in 2020 after organizing a march in Franklin Park that drew thousands to protest the killing of George Floyd and other Black people at the hands of police. She formed a collaboration with a Dorchester restaurant to distribute more than 1,000 free meals a day to people struggling during the pandemic.

For those efforts, she was honored as a Bostonian of the Year by the Boston Globe Magazine and hailed as the city’s “best social justice advocate” by Boston Magazine.

She started her nonprofit in 2017, operating out of her Roxbury home, but by 2020, it had moved to a sprawling headquarters in Hyde Park.

Cannon-Grant’s lawyers estimated her “fraud-related conduct” involved about $224,000 in loss, and wrote that much of the money was used to “support underserved communities, families, and individuals” and advance social justice.

In a letter urging the judge to sentence Cannon-Grant to probation, Bishop William E. Dickerson II wrote that her organization “fed thousands of people during the Covid pandemic and hundreds of children received wonderful Christmas gifts.”

The death of Cannon-Grant’s husband “continues to be hell,” but she remarried last summer, her lawyers wrote.

Prosecutors allege that after Cannon-Grant collected nearly $400,000 from her late husband’s insurance policy, she made an urgent plea for donations to her GoFundMe account so she wouldn’t lose her home.

Yet, around the same time, prosecutors wrote, she spent almost $100,000 on travel and shopping, including $8,375 in purchases from Louis Vuitton, and trips to St. Thomas and Puerto Rico.

In court Thursday, Notis-McConarty said Cannon-Grant used the insurance policy money for funeral expenses and to support her family.

title: Can Boston still weather winter storms?
text:
In addition, the storm has strained or exhausted municipal snow budgets in Eastern Massachusetts. Officials in Framingham and Taunton, for example, now have exceeded their snow-removal budget for this winter, even as another storm is expected to strike the area this weekend.

One thing is certain: After several mild winters, the muscle, sweat, and community response needed to dig out from a big snowstorm have been tested anew, residents said.

“We need more plows on the road, a little more salt. There’s still a bunch of snow left over here and a bunch of snowbanks,” said Jay Jay Mosley, 30, of F Street. “All residents of Boston will appreciate it, especially here in Southie.”

In Cambridge, crews had already plowed all city-owned roadways and expected to complete sidewalk cleanup by the end of Thursday, spokesman Jeremy Warnick said Wednesday.

Nearly 200 pieces of equipment, including about 100 contracted units, were deployed during the storm, Warnick said. Overnight snow-hauling operations are expected to cost roughly $250,000 per night through at least Friday, he added.

Not everyone in Cambridge, however, could see a cleared street outside their windows.

Rob Yonkers, for one, still saw a storm-tossed sea of snow Wednesday, days after the biggest storm in four years had blanketed her side street in North Cambridge.

A city plow had come through Alberta Terrace only once, Yonkers said. And in its wake, cars had been buried in tall white bunkers, parking spaces vanished, and weary shovelers were forced to toss piles of travel-slowing snow into an already narrow road.

“A lot of the people on my street have given up, haven’t even tried to get their cars out anymore,” said Yonkers, a 30-year-old singer. “There’s just a huge snow pile in the street because no one knows where to put it.”

Following several years of mild winters, adjusting to a big snowfall can wreak havoc with the routine.

Where to toss the snow from driveways and sidewalks can be an awkward choice between courtesy and necessity. Patience wears thin all around. And public-works crews are prodding their muscle memory to stimulate old plowing skills.

“It’s like hit or miss,” Andrew Plifka, a 26-year-old South Boston resident, said of snow-removal efforts near his home on E Street. “Obviously, there’s a lot of snow, and there’s not many places for it to go. But the corners especially are pretty bad.”

Former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh said he recognizes the strain and challenges faced by both the city and its constituents in the aftermath of a big storm.

“It’s complicated, it’s hard, it’s not easy,” said Walsh, who lives in the Lower Mills section of Dorchester. “You have to think of a lot of things when a storm like this happens — canceling schools, plowing, emergency apparatus.”

“We’re watching the Patriots in the AFC Championship game” when the storm began Sunday, “and they’re out there working hard,” Walsh added.

Independent snow-removal contractors also have been helping residents dig out, including solo operators handling sidewalks, steps, and driveways in hard-hit neighborhoods.

Gabriel Ramos, a 27-year-old Malden resident, said he began clearing snow Sunday night and continued Monday as the heavy snowfall continued.

“I’m a one-man team,” said Ramos, an Army veteran who uses a snow blower and helped clear sidewalks, steps, small driveways, and cars.

Ramos, who works in IT, said snow removal is his winter side-job to earn extra money, and that residents appear to be adjusting to the irritation and inconvenience.

“I think everybody’s picking it back up again and getting used to the amount of snow that’s out there,” Ramos said. With another storm possible this weekend, the part-time snow warrior is prepared to take on more work.

The MBTA also has been plagued by slowdowns and interruptions, much to the dismay of commuters who have waited in bitter cold for less-frequent service.

At the Broadway station Wednesday, would-be riders huffed and grumbled after an announcement that the next Red Line train to Alewife would be delayed by nearly a half-hour because of a disabled train at JFK/UMass.

Among them was Jack Malespini, a 30-year-old who commutes to Massachusetts General Hospital. Service had been more reliable during the storm itself, he said, but delays had worsened since.

“Today is the worst for me,” Malespini said Wednesday.

But for some lifelong Bostonians, the scrambled routines and inconveniences of a big winter storm are to be expected in a traditional New England climate, all while warming temperatures might mean fewer of them occur.

“We’ve been walloped with the first significant snowstorm in four or five years, and maybe people forget about it a little bit,” said John Tobin Jr. of West Roxbury, a former Boston city councilor.

“I was out there shoveling and using muscles I hadn’t used, and didn’t realize I had, that had atrophied over the last four years,” Tobin said with a chuckle.

Overall, he added, the city’s cleanup seemed to go well.

“These men and women are out there busting their humps and are in their trucks for 12 and 14 hours at a time,” Tobin said. “It’s hard work.”

Amid the toil, and the dreary prospect of another round of digging, some residents looked ahead to reaping a reward on Feb. 8, when the New England Patriots face the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl.

“Go, Pats!” Mosely, the South Boston resident, shouted as he shoveled. “Let’s go, Drake Maye. Let’s win a championship!”

title: After last week’s massive snowstorm, a weary region braces for another wintry blast
text:
“The 8 to 12 inches that fell on the Cape last Sunday may see another 6 inches pile on top of the snow pack” beginning Sunday morning “and lasting through much of the day,” said Globe meteorologist Ken Mahan.

Mahan said areas along the South Shore and South Coast that received as much as two feet of snow last weekend could get another three to six inches Sunday.

Boston and its suburbs are expected to be largely spared this time around, according to the National Weather Service, which said in a Friday advisory that forecasters expect lighter “accumulating snow with lesser overall impact further north and west into the Boston-Providence corridor Sunday.”

In Chatham, officials with the town’s Department of Public Works met Friday to discuss preparations for the upcoming storm, which could cause flooding significant enough to force evacuations, director Robert Faley said.

“We are kind of the spit on the elbow of Cape Cod, so we’re out there where we are vulnerable to some of these events,” he said.

Faley said officials will closely monitor the tides, wind speed, and wind direction, which he said makes flood-prone areas more vulnerable to erosion.

Normally, Chatham’s coastline is vulnerable to winds from the south, Faley said.

“But if it’s a wrap-around [wind], from a nor’easter, and the winds come out of the northeast, then it’s a whole different set of vulnerable areas that we’re monitoring,” he said.

Overall, town officials and residents are fatigued heading into a second round of severe weather, he said.

Public works staff are still clearing snow from sidewalks and parking lots, he said. At the same time, they’ll need to take a break in order to be “prepared and well-rested” ahead of Sunday’s storm, he said.

“People are ready for spring to show its face,” Faley said.

On Nantucket, officials are bracing for more drifts from wind-swept snow at a time when the island’s having trouble fully replenishing its road salt supply, said Andrew Patnode, the public works director.

“The wind will whip through and blow snow off of [open] areas and across our roads,” he said.

Normally, the town tries to keep its main salt barn filled to the top. But with salt in high demand these days, the most recent delivery came not by barge but by truck.

“We’re running a little low, so we wanted to replenish,” he said. “But we didn’t get a full shipment.”

Finding areas to dump cleared snow is also becoming a problem, he said. he said. Officials have begun leaving it in beach parking lots, Patnode said.

“Since we just got eight to 10 inches this past Sunday, it’s obviously becoming pretty difficult for us to find room for this snow, especially on our historic narrow downtown streets,” he said.

Salt shortages have also affected Falmouth.

The town’s main salt barn was two-thirds empty Friday, although it had just received three to four truckloads earlier in the day, James Kempton, the deputy director of Falmouth’s department of public works.

But Falmouth may still share some of its supply with neighboring towns that are facing steeper shortages, Kempton said. He was optimistic Falmouth will have enough salt for this weekend and said he’s grateful it’s only expected to snow about two to five inches on his community.

Earlier this week, some on Cape Cod were worried the storm could drop another foot, he said.

“We’re in good shape for the next one, we are thankful it’s not going to be another foot of snow though,” he said.

He said crews worked long hours on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday clearing snow from last week’s storm.

“The town of Falmouth is thankful that we have a lot of dedicated employees,” Kempton said.

In Maynard, officials said ongoing snow removal operations from the last storm could be complicated by this weekend’s successor.

The town’s DPW had scheduled another snow removal operation on Sunday night, but only under clear skies.

The “operation is weather dependent due to the potential of another predicted storm that may take place on Sunday night,” town officials said Thursday.

Officials assured residents that the town understands their frustration.

“We understand storm events like this can be stressful and challenging to our residents’ daily life,” the statement said. “We will continue to utilize all of our resources and work hard to improve the conditions of the community for vehicle and pedestrian use.”

The weather pattern is also disrupting the repair schedule on the MBTA’s Red Line, with officials saying Wednesday they were cancelling planned repair work on the Red Line this weekend due to the punishing weather.

“Riders are reminded that this weekend’s (January 31 - February 1) scheduled Red Line service suspension between Broadway and North Quincy on the Braintree Branch and Broadway and Ashmont on the Ashmont Branch has been canceled due to the lingering impacts of the recent winter storm and the potential weather for the weekend,” the MBTA said. “Regularly scheduled Red Line service will operate this weekend.”

In Marshfield, DPW crews worked for 51 hours straight this week to repair a water main break, and on Tuesday night they were “sent home for some well-deserved rest,” the town’s public works superintendent, Ken Ryan, said in a statement posted to Facebook.

Crews along the South Shore and Cape Cod can expect more pressing work on Sunday, forecasters said.

“Greatest overall impacts from accumulating snow and gusty winds are across South Shore, Cape Cod and the Islands Sunday and Sunday night," the National Weather Service said Friday in an advisory.

On the Cape in Sandwich, officials warned Thursday that Sunday’s storm could bring flooding.

“There is potential for moderate flooding around high tides Sunday into Monday,” officials said. “Water could be 1-3 feet deep.”

Officials urged residents to keep “safe near the water, secure loose items, and keep an eye on updates from the National Weather Service.”

In Fall River, officials took to social media this week in hopes of hiring more plow drivers, as well as to inform residents that a parking ban will remain in place with more snow on the way.

“The parking ban remains in effect as we continue the clearing and hauling of snow,” officials said. “We ask for your patience and cooperation as we continue to clean up from one major storm while facing the possibility of another weekend storm on the way.”

The storm could also threaten ferry travel to and from Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard, according to the Steamship Authority.

title: Free February events: Valentine’s Day, school break, and more
text:
HEARTS AND CRAFTS Winthrop Center, an event space in Downtown Boston, hosts festive family fun, including free arts and crafts such as heart-shaped cookie decorating, friendship bracelet making, and handprint bouquet painting. Kids can also write postcards to their loved ones and send them from the center’s mailbox. The event will also feature a Polaroid photo booth and a live DJ. Heart-shaped pizzas from Gatto Pazzo, starting at $11.50, will be available for purchase. Feb. 14, noon-2 p.m. Free. The Connector at Winthrop Center, East Entrance: 115 Federal St., West Entrance: 250 Devonshire St. theconnectorwc.com

FIND YOUR LOVE STORY Have a loved one pick out your next read at Harvard Bookstore’s Valentine’s Book Swap. Split up and choose a book for your shopping partner before reuniting to share your selections. For an added layer of mystery, attendees can create a Blind Date with a Book by wrapping their picks and writing clues on the packaging for the recipient to guess. The store will provide free wrapping materials, markers, and labels. Registered attendees will receive a 20 percent off coupon that can be used during the event. The shop will also offer a photo booth and bookmarks from The Amora Experience, a company that organizes bonding activities for couples, to take home. Feb. 14, noon-2 p.m. Free. Harvard Book Store, 1256 Massachusetts Ave. harvard.com

ROMANCE READERS Lovestruck Books and Cafe celebrates its one-year anniversary with a weekend-long event. Beginning Valentine’s month with a bang, the romance bookstore’s final day of festivities includes pop-up author visits, with free George Howell coffee samples and temporary tattoos. With any purchase, attendees will receive a limited edition Lovestruck postcard they can send from the store. Book lovers can also purchase limited edition anniversary merchandise. From noon-4 p.m., Somerville embroidery shop, KEEPER, will offer custom name stitching free with the purchase of a Lovestruck anniversary tote bag. The store will offer different pop-up shops throughout the day, including permanent jewelry from Spark by Simone. Additionally, from 1-3 p.m., attendees can share a moment or memory with Iman Khondker, who will write a custom poem for them for $15. RSVP on Eventbrite to reserve a spot. Feb 1, 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Free. Lovestruck Books and Cafe, 44 Brattle St., Cambridge. lovestruckbooks.com/events

HEARTS, HARVARD, AND HISTORY Cambridge local Ananda Montoly hosts a romance-themed walking tour of Harvard Square, including information about the filming of the 1970 romantic drama “Love Story” on the Harvard campus and Bob Dylan’s connections to the neighborhood. The tour will also feature sweet stops at local businesses like Le Macaron French Pastries and chocolatier L.A. Burdick. Feb. 14, noon-2 p.m. Free. Meet outside of Zinneken’s Belgian Waffles, 1154 Massachusetts Ave. cambridgeusa.org/event

ART SHOWCASE Artist Edie Tang invites Boston to see her portraits and floral paintings. Instead of hanging her art on the walls, Tang will present the work using models, who will move around the space carrying the pieces. During the event, Tang will also paint flowers onto dresses live for attendees to observe. DJ Simply Dennis will perform. Light snacks and drinks will be served. Feb. 14, 4-6:30 p.m. Free. Bogosplit, 100 Huntington Ave. bogosplit.com

FAMILY FESTIVAL The Foundry community center in Kendall presents a week of free, family arts and STEM activities. The fourth annual festival centers around the theme of “Pathways” and features activities for all age groups, from a circus show to a Kenyan Coffee Tasting. The lineup includes craft workshops, dance classes, cooking classes, scientific activities, and theatrical performances. Feb. 14-21, various times. Free. The Foundry, 101 Rogers St.Cambridge. cambridgefoundry.org/events/festival

MUSEUM AMUSEMENTS The Old State House and Old South Meeting House will host daily family activities for kids off from school during February vacation week. Each day features different hands-on entertainment, many with historical themes, including quill making and tavern games. All throughout the week, the museums will host scavenger hunts, gallery talks, and coloring. Feb. 16-20, 10:30 a.m.- 2:30 p.m. Included for adults with museum admission price. Free for children 12 and under. Old State House, 206 Washington St. and Old South Meeting House, 310 Washington St. revolutionaryspaces.org

STORYTIME AND SIGNING Celebrate Lunar New Year with author Sylvia Chen, who will read her children’s book “Sparkles for Sunny” at Beacon Hill Books and Cafe. The story follows Sunny, a little girl tired of wearing her sister’s hand-me-downs and determined to find a way to express her style for this year’s Lunar New Year party. After the reading, there will be a book signing and activity featuring traditional red paper envelopes. The book will be available in store for purchase. Attendees must reserve a spot on Eventbrite. Feb. 17, 10-11 a.m. Free. Beacon Hill Books and Cafe, 71 Charles St. bhbooks.com

BUILDING BUDDIES Channel your inner engineer at the Waterworks Museum’s “Catapults and Cotton Balls” event. The museum invites families to learn about parabolic motion through construction crafts, including making a popsicle stick and wooden spoon catapult and a launcher out of cardboard tubes and a balloon. Builders can then test their creations by using them to launch cotton balls at plastic cup targets. Reservations through Eventbrite are requested. Feb. 21, 10 a.m.-2 p.m. Free. Metropolitan Waterworks Museum, 2450 Beacon St. waterworksmuseum.org

HISTORY HUNT The Wayland Museum and Historical Society invites families to explore its “Red, White, and ‘I Do’” wedding dress exhibition with a scavenger hunt. The activity will guide visitors through the museum’s collection, from examining a garment’s fabric to finding details on a teapot from 1723. The museum will also offer an origami heart craft attendees can take home. Feb. 14, 10 a.m.-2 p.m. Free. Wayland Museum and Historical Society, 12 Cochituate Road. Wayland.waylandmuseum.org

Their Winter Fitness Series includes sessions in Bota Fogo Dance, yoga, tai chi, kids dance fitness, walking groups, strength and balance workouts, and line dancing. No registration required. Multiple dates and locations. See website for details. Free. boston.gov/events

FEEL THE BEAT Soulfire Movement, a Dorchester-based dance fitness company, invites attendees to dance, sweat, and meditate as part of their free eight-week class series. The class focuses on mindfulness and includes three parts: a 45-minute cardio dance workout, a yoga stretch, and a sound bath meditation. Register for any session on Eventbrite. Thursdays Feb. 5-March 26, 6-8 p.m. Free. Fields Corner Yoga, 1532B Dorchester Ave. soulfiremovement.com

SWEAT AND SHOP Roll out your yoga mat for February workout classes with fitness lifestyle brand Vuori. The Hingham store will host High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) and yoga sculpt. After each session, attendees can enjoy refreshments from local businesses, such as Pour Coffee after the sculpt yoga class and Press Juice Bar following the HIIT session. Register on Eventbrite to reserve a spot. Yoga sculpt: Feb. 7, 8:30-10 a.m. HIIT: Feb. 22, 9-11 a.m. Free. Vuori, 94 Derby St., Hingham. derbystshops.com/tenants/vuori/

CARDIO FOR A CAUSE Get your Valentine’s Day workout in at Orange Theory while supporting Stepping Strong, Brigham and Women’s Hospital’s Boston Marathon team raising money for trauma research. The strength and cardio training class will be led by Emily Long, a physician who is running this year’s marathon for the charity. The session will follow the Orange Theory class format, incorporating treadmill, weights, and rowers. Post workout refreshments will be provided. Feb. 14, 2-3 p.m. $35 donation suggested. Orangetheory Fitness, 88 Van Ness St. Reserve a spot by making a donation at events.brighamandwomens.org and going to eventbrite.com.

PARK PARTY Get cozy at Moakley Park’s Winter Warmer event. Boston Harbor Now hosts an afternoon of activities including creating fleece scarfs, making dream catchers, and an artwork treasure hunt. The event will also feature entertainment from DJ and dance duo A Trike Called Funk and free hot chocolate, tea, popcorn, and fruit. Feb. 7, 2-4 p.m. Free. Moakley Park, 1005 Columbia Road. bostonharbornow.org

SKATE DATE Lace up for special free ice skating days at the Frog Pond. Over the course of the month, the rink will host two adult yoga on ice classes, open to all skating experience levels. For an all-ages activity, the rink’s Skating With Friends day will also include free admission and skate rentals, as well as complimentary hot chocolate. Iceflow: Feb. 1 and 8, 7:30 a.m. Register on Eventbrite. Skating at Lunch: Feb. 5 and 12, noon-2 p.m. Skating with Friends: Feb. 15, 10 a.m.-8 p.m. Free. Boston Common Frog Pond, 38 Beacon St. friendsofthepublicgarden.org

SNOWBOARDING SHOWDOWN Watch snowboarders compete at the Red Bull Heavy Metal finals. In the annual competition, athletes tackle obstacles more commonly seen in skate parks, including tricks on handrails, stairs, and fences. The winners of the Minneapolis and Pittsburgh qualifiers will face off in three separate events at City Hall Plaza. Feb. 21, 2:30-5:30 p.m. Free. City Hall Plaza, 1 City Hall Square. redbull.com/events

GROUNDHOGS AND THE GREAT OUTDOORS Celebrate Groundhog Day with a guided hike at Greenwood Park. Roland “Boot” Boutwell, a guide from Friends of the Middlesex Fells Reservation, will share a groundhog story, nature-themed poems, and information on winter plant identification and natural history. Register on Eventbrite. Feb. 2, 9:15-11:30 a.m. Free. Greenwood Park, 176 Pond St. friendsofthefells.org

title: Cape Cod braces for winds as Nor’easter skirts New England
text:
As Greater Boston continues digging out from its biggest snowstorm in four years, some residents saw light nor’easter snow showers and howling winds across southeastern New England Sunday.

The region avoided the brunt of the system, with the most intense core of the storm remaining well offshore. Cape Cod and the Islands saw the greatest effects, but even there, impacts were limited and far from anything extraordinary, meteorologists say.

“A week ago, we were watching this potential coastal nor’easter [that] could hit us or could not,” Kyle Pederson, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said Sunday night. “Boston just saw some flurries with a trace of snow but nothing measurable.”

National Weather Service meteorologists said scattered snow showers brought a coating of 2 inches of snow to Plymouth County, with inland towns seeing flurries and slick spots on side streets. A winter weather advisory for the region was canceled Sunday morning, except for Nantucket, which saw wind gusts as high as 62 miles per hour Sunday afternoon.

A high wind warning was set to stay in effect until 4 a.m. Monday as northerly gusts were forecast to reach 40 to 50 miles per hour across Cape Cod and up to 60 miles per hour on Nantucket, prompting concerns about blowing snow, low visibility, and hazardous conditions for anyone venturing out in the afternoon.

On Sunday morning, thousands of Patriots fans stuffed hand warmers into their socks and shoes ahead of the team’s Super Bowl send-off rally at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

With temperatures in the single digits, the two-hour event tested even the hardiest supporters.

“Earlier in the week the forecast was calling for snow, so we were a little skeptical about coming,” said Alex Montalvo, of Worcester. “But on Friday it looked pretty clear, so we made the decision to hunker down, take it easy, and get ready to see the Pats off.”

“We weren’t worried about the cold,” said Kyle Knox, of Uxbridge. “It’s New England, you have to be prepared.”

As of late Sunday night, 50 flights were canceled and 206 were delayed at Boston Logan Airport, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking website. Cape Air accounted for the most disruptions, with 22 cancellations and 10 delays.

The snow, even though light, came on the heels of a major winter storm that buried the region last month. Logan Airport recorded more than 23 inches of snow, one of the top 10 single-storm totals on record, and many cities and towns are still clearing heaps of snow out of intersections and driveways.

In addition to the wind over the weekend, the region saw coastal flooding with beach erosion along the eastern Massachusetts coast. Pockets of moderate coastal flooding in Nantucket were only aggravated by the weather Sunday, with multiple reports of coastal flooding through the day.

“Nantucket was mainly the area that saw the worst of it,” Pederson said. “Central Avenue in Scituate had some minor coastal flooding, but was still passable.”

On Monday, the Fall River/New Bedford Commuter Rail Line will operate on a reduced “severe weather schedule” following additional snowfall on the South Coast and continued extreme cold, according to the MBTA and Keolis, the company that operates the commuter rail. Service will be reduced to meet demand for essential workers while limiting trains’ exposure to storm conditions and providing access for cleanup crews, officials said.

Crews installed heaters near Orient Heights and Ashmont stations and deployed jet snow blowers along the Braintree Branch, a spokesperson said.

MBTA and Keolis crews will salt and sand passenger areas, clear snow, and respond to incidents, transit officials said in a statement. The MBTA advises passengers to plan for extra travel time and exercise caution on platforms, in parking lots, and when boarding or exiting trains.

This week, temperatures will be “warmer” compared to what the region has experienced recently, the National Weather Service said. But another “arctic blast” is expected next weekend, with strong winds and very cold conditions.

“It doesn’t look like it was too terribly bad today,” Pederson said. “The wind’s actually already starting to die down.”
