title: From a lot of Masshole drivers to $1 million apartments: How a gas station’s demise represents a changing Boston
text:
In 1974, Morris’ son Stan moved the gas station to its current location, just a half-mile down Washington, and through the decades Hatoff’s became a Boston institution, sometimes serving drivers who belonged in one.

Cheap gas attracts, well, it just attracts, like flies to a light.

When I learned from Adam Gaffin’s terrific local news site Universal Hub that Hatoff’s was headed for the great cheap gas station heap in the sky, I jumped in my Subaru Crosstrek, still in my flannel pajamas and OluKai slippers, and drove from rural Vermont to the urban mecca of cheap gas, flooring it through Egleston Square, worried the pumps would be dry by the time I got there.

Alas, they weren’t. There is no official closing date. And it was impossible to tell if this was one last mad dash to Hatoff’s, because it was its usual crazy self. Like an open air market in one of those Indiana Jones movies, where anything can happen at any time, and probably will.

Drivers often approach a pump with their gas tank on the other side of their vehicle. This results in some drivers pulling three-point turns, to get their gas tanks lined up with the pumps, in a very tight space. This necessitates the kind of driving usually associated with the bumper cars at Canobie Lake Park.

But, still, it’s kind of amazing to observe the intricacy of the creative thinking and driving, like watching a ballet or a symphony, if the ballerinas, oboe players, and violinists were Masshole drivers.

I strategically placed my car at Pump 12, in the lane closest to Washington Street, facing Egleston Square, so I could make a quick getaway.

But, it turns out, Pump 12 was the slowest gas pump ever made. Pump 12 was eking gas with a velocity normally associated with pouring maple syrup on pancakes. It took forever. Well, it felt like forever, and it was frickin’ freezing.

Standing there, shivering in the cold, executing a fill-up with the speed of donating a pint of blood, I looked around Hatoff’s. In a city that is still very segregated, it may be the most integrated spot in Boston. There’s every kind of people, color, creed, city folk pumping good music, suburbanites pumping cheap gas.

Because everybody, no matter what they look like, no matter where they’re from, likes a bargain. And Hatoff’s remains a bargain when it comes to gas in the city.

After filling up, I drove down Centre Street in JP and noticed that Gibbs and JP Oil were selling gas for less than many places in the city, but not nearly as cheap as Hatoff’s.

Hatoff’s is slated to become — take a wild guess — housing. The $90 million project is aimed at building 230 apartments, the same kind of fate that engulfed the late and lamented Doyle’s, just blocks down Washington from Hatoff’s.

Doyle’s was a neighborhood tavern that dated back to the 1880s and was one of JP’s most enduring institutions.

It was depressing, frankly, thinking back to a Doyle’s where we toasted holidays and late friends from the Globe newsroom; where when my kids were young we met Cathy Mayo, a great JP lady, and her adopted son, Delmace, a disabled Haitian kid who grew up to become an elite para-athlete; where over all those years we shot the breeze with Gerry Burke Sr., the longtime proprietor of Doyle’s, who in the 1980s became the first publican to sell Sam Adams Lager.

Jim Koch, the Sam Adams founder, had just opened a craft brewery at the old Haffenreffer brewery on Amory Street. Gerry and Jim cut some JP kind of deal.

Doyle’s had the best collection of political memorabilia in the city. You’d half expect to see James Michael Curley, Kevin White, Ray Flynn, Tom Menino, and Marty Walsh come through the front door, arm in arm, as all those mayors, not to mention their coatholders, spent more than a little time in Doyle’s.

Doyle’s hosted more politicians and would-be politicians, the famous and the infamous, than any place in Boston, right up there with the Eire Pub in Adams Village in Dorchester.

Alas, that great JP bar where you could get a Pickwick Ale for short money is long gone, replaced by wood framing and blue tarp. The whole block is going to be transformed into 29 condominiums. Starting price? Well over $1 million. Six of the apartments are deemed “affordable.”

But, then, what the heck is affordable in the city of Boston?

It was a great relief to drive by the next block from Doyle’s and see the Midway Cafe is still going strong. Live music, great local musicians, good crowd. The Midway is JPAF, which means JP as ... well, I can’t print the rest.

There are places like the Midway and Hatoff’s and Doyle’s and, further afield, Simco’s, the hot dog kings in Mattapan, Sullivan’s on Castle Island, J.J. Foley’s in the South End, where the bartenders still wear ties, so many other places in Charlestown, Brighton, Allston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Beacon Hill, Hyde Park, Back Bay, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and East Boston that define neighborhoods and traditions. And with increasing regularity, the places that defined neighborhoods are giving way to condos and apartments.

The city’s biggest need, housing, is the biggest driver of change, and maybe that’s the way it has to be, the way it’s always been, the way it always will be.

But there’s also something to be said about losing the things and places and people that made Boston distinctive, neighborhoods that were ethnic and assimilated, places where people who don’t look like each other can, if only briefly, interact with civility and even joy, places where Joe and Nemo’s was valued over McDonald’s, where Vietnamese guys still fish off the pier on Castle Island while Southie guys in scally caps and hoodies walk by nodding approvingly.

It’s neither sad nor happy. It’s just what it is.

Cities change. Even Boston. Things change.

title: Looking back at ‘The Warriors,’ the quintessentially New York movie inspiring the Patriots’ winning season
text:
You see, last week I read an article in this very paper about coach Mike Vrabel and his players repeatedly referring to “The Warriors,” specifically actor David Patrick Kelly’s immortal taunt: “Warriors! Come out to play!” That line is quite often the only thing people know about the movie, and it wasn’t even in the script. Kelly improvised it on the spot for his character, Luther, an enemy of the titular gang, and created something iconic in the process. People chant it all the time, especially if they have a few beer bottles hanging around that they can clink together with their fingers, as Kelly does in the film.

I am confused by all of this. I mean, if the Yankees started chanting dialogue from your buddy Ben Affleck’s movie, “The Town,” I’d disown them for invoking a movie as closely associated with Boston as that one is. That’s how much of a New York movie “The Warriors” is. But far be it for me to question the reasoning behind a team’s rallying cry. After all, it got the Patriots to the Super Bowl.

What I found far more flabbergasting was Vrabel’s comment that nobody knew what he was talking about when he first referenced “The Warriors.” “I had to actually show the movie,” he said. His comment reminded me that the reason I know all about the movie is because I saw it opening weekend at the Loews Jersey in my hometown of Jersey City. Which means I am far older than every player on the Patriots. I’m also older than Mike Vrabel.

But I digress. The best I can do here is give a primer on “The Warriors” for those of you who first heard about the film from your hometown heroes. It’s a favorite film of mine, and one of only two movies I’ve attended dressed as one of its characters (the other is “The Rocky Horror Picture Show”).

The plot of “The Warriors” is simple. At a summit designed to form an alliance between all the gangs of New York, the leader of the Gramercy Riffs gang, Cyrus, is shot and killed by Luther, who runs the Rogues gang. Luther frames the Warriors for the truce-breaking crime, leading the Riffs to put out a contract on the Warriors.

As a result, every rival gang wants to off them. Led by their War Chief, Swan (Michael Beck), the Warriors must make their way from the Bronx to their safe home turf of Coney Island. Throughout their journey, they violently face off with several other gangs. There’s a memorable death in the subway; much of this film takes place on the rapidly deteriorating 1970s era MTA. And the film’s lone female main character, Mercy (“Too Close for Comfort”'s Deborah Van Valkenburgh), turns out to be more complexly drawn than expected.

Yurick’s far more serious book was influenced by Greek tragedy. Hill keeps that angle, but everything else about “The Warriors” is extremely stylized, from its dystopian look to its unforgettable, graffiti-sprayed poster title logo. One version of the posters, which contained only the logo, was specifically designed to look like real graffiti on the MTA subway station walls. There was certainly enough of the real thing back in 1979.

Hill has written, produced, and directed movies as varied as “Alien,” the Depression-era boxing drama “Hard Times,” and the violent cop buddy comedy “48 Hrs.” But I’ve always said Hill’s movies, regardless of genre, were westerns under the skin. This one has a twisted nod to “High Noon.” Nobody believes the Warriors are innocent, so no help in defeating their rivals is forthcoming. Making matters worse, there’s an omniscient Greek god of sorts, a radio DJ whose lips occasionally fill the screen to taunt our heroes and tell rival gangs where they are.

We never see anything besides her blood red lipstick-covered mouth, but that instantly recognizable voice is unmistakable. Those velvety tones belong to the late, great Lynne Thigpen, Morgan Freeman’s antagonist in “Lean on Me” (for us Gen Xers), and the Chief on “Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego” (for you millennials). Thigpen gives “The Warriors” an icy coolness that overshadows the assorted gangs and their memorable outfits.

Speaking of memorable outfits, one of the gangs who target the Warriors is the Baseball Furies. They control Riverside Park on the West Side of Manhattan. With their painted faces, baseball bats, caps, and pinstripe uniforms that resemble the Yankees’ attire, these guys are my favorite gang. Each set has a specific uniform that’s perfect for cosplaying at fan-filled midnight screenings. The Warriors themselves have buttonless vests that show off their abs.

Eventually, the Warriors make it back to Coney Island, where Luther issues his immortal taunt. At the midnight screening I attended as a Baseball Fury back in 2019, someone brought bottles into the theater and recreated that scene. Surprisingly, everyone let that guy have the floor; I expected the entire theater to say the lines, but he was the only one who did.

Such friendly camaraderie wasn’t present at theaters when “The Warriors” opened 40 years earlier. In fact, several violent incidents and riots occurred at screenings attended by real-life rival gangs in New York City, Los Angeles, and Boston. A major fight broke out at my Jersey City screening on opening weekend. Two of these incidents proved fatal, including one in Dorchester. Two weeks after the film’s opening, State Senator Michael LoPresti Jr. from East Boston requested an investigation into having the film banned in Boston.

A skittish Paramount (the studio that released “The Warriors”) temporarily pulled all marketing from TV and radio, and offered to pay for any vandalism theaters incurred. Security was increased at several theaters as well. Nowadays, a movie would never cause this sort of controversy, but back then, it only added to the street cred of a soon-to-be-cult classic.

Though it received many negative reviews (and a positive one from Pauline Kael, who also referenced “The Blackboard Jungle” in her review), “The Warriors” made money at the box office and had a long shelf life. It inspired a concept musical album co-written by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2023, as well as video games and comic books. Several remakes were considered, but none were made, because how can you make a better movie than this one? It’s a product of its time, lightning in a bottle that can’t be recreated.

Let’s see if the movie’s mojo still works for the Patriots when they come out to play on the home field of my beloved San Francisco 49ers in Santa Clara on Super Bowl Sunday. Until then, to quote Lynne Thigpen’s DJ, “I guess the only thing I can do is play you a song.”

Odie Henderson is the Boston Globe's film critic.

title: In Greater Boston, a temporary court reprieve and a legal limbo for Haitians
text:
In and around Boston, home to the country’s third-largest Haitian community, there were signs of relief in the immediate aftermath of the judge’s decision.

But the anxiety and panic — and confusion — that led up to Tuesday’s planned end to TPS still loomed, as no one knows what will happen next. One health care company executive noted the “chaos” this week as his office had to notify 24 Haitian workers that they would have to be fired because of the change in their legal status. Then, Tuesday, his staff scrambled to let them know they still had jobs — virtually all of them returned to work, said John Randall, chief executive of Amego, Inc., a nonprofit that operates in locations east of Worcester and south of Boston.

“Everyone is in a holding pattern, but they’re still employable and legal today,” Randall said Tuesday afternoon. “They are living in states of uncertainty.”

Public officials and immigrants’ rights advocates have long warned of the humanitarian harm, but also the financial impacts the end of TPS could have on the local economy.

Some of those who could lose their jobs at Amego have worked there for up to a decade, Randall said. More than a dozen other workers have quit in recent months, anticipating the expiration of their legal status.

“This is just a write-off of an entire section of our workforce,” Randall said.

At the same time, Haitian immigrants and advocates have balked at the notion of sending people back to Haiti, which continues to be convulsed by bloody unrest.

Additionally, advocates report TPS holders are afraid to leave their homes because they don’t want to be picked up by immigration authorities.

Nicole Albert runs the Gilbert Albert Community Center in Dorchester, which provides English for Speakers of Other Languages [ESOL] lessons to immigrants, many of them from Haiti. Late last month, she noticed classes were getting “smaller and smaller.” Typically, the center sees 200 students a week. By late January, the number had dropped to 40.

“People were starting to hide, thinking, ‘I don’t want to get deported and then my kids stay behind,’” she said.

The legal limbo, with the cancellation of TPS before the courts, could create confusion over people’s work status. But Haitian employees with this status are indeed still authorized to work, said Leslie Ditrani, a Cambridge immigration attorney who runs Pathway for Immigrant Workers.

Employers and Haitian workers with TPS don’t need to reverify documents, request new ones, or take any other action, she said.

Some employers had already ended the employment of Haitian workers with TPS in the months leading up to Tuesday’s deadline. More than 100 Haitian TPS holders have already lost their jobs at Logan Airport. One airport worker who was let go last summer testified at a recent TPS hearing that he had been driving for Uber to help support his family; he shares a bedroom with his wife and daughter in a shared apartment on the North Shore. His wife, who works as a caretaker, also has TPS and had expected to lose her job on Tuesday.

Road to Responsibility, a developmental disabilities provider based in Marshfield, had already lost 100 Haitian workers since last summer when their work authorizations expired or they opted to leave the country on their own. On Monday, the company sent out termination letters to the 18 remaining employees with Haitian TPS, but called them first thing Tuesday morning to tell them to disregard the notices.

“People were so ecstatic that they still had a job, people crying on the phone,” said chief executive Christopher White. “We told all the workers, ‘Look, this could stay in place for a day, a week, a month, we just don’t know how this is going to go. But we’re just so glad you’re going to be with us.’”

Some Haitian employees had been “hoping to hide out” in the country, White said, while others said they were going to Canada or back to Haiti. “Most of the Haitians I know have said the last place on earth they want to go back to is Haiti,” he said.

To make up for staff losses at Road to Responsibility, which serves 1,000 people across Southeastern Massachusetts, White has turned to temporary staff and asked existing employees to pick up extra shifts, but the costs — $24,000 every two weeks in additional overtime pay — and the burnout are adding up. The people the organization serves have noticed the absence of the Haitian workers, some of whom have been there for a decade.

“These are good, hard-working people,” White said. “They’ve been paying taxes, trying to do all the right things, who were invited into this country by the federal government and now are being rousted out like they’re all criminals.”

Dr. Karen Scanlan learned Monday afternoon that the expiration of TPS status for Haitians would affect a woman who has become particularly close to her daughter over the past year. Scanlan’s daughter, Tory, 27, is nonverbal and severely autistic, and this worker at the Foxborough group home where she lives is among those who help with basic tasks, including washing and eating.

“It’s just heartbreaking to me that she can’t work because of this,” said Scanlan Monday, before the court-ordered pause. “It’s hard enough to find these dedicated, kind people to take care of our children.”

Indeed, more than half of nursing assistants and almost half of personal care attendants in Greater Boston are immigrants, many of them from Haiti, according to Boston Indicators, the Boston Foundation’s research arm.

The rate of immigrants coming to Massachusetts dropped by half in 2025 compared to the past few years, while growth in the labor force slowed, according to the UMass Donahue Institute in Amherst.

Last week, in the days leading up to the Feb. 3 deadline, one Haitian TPS holder, a 51-year-old Dorchester resident, spoke about what made her flee her homeland: gang members broke into her house in Haiti and killed her partner, a slaying she said she witnessed. She spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of being targeted by immigration authorities. She described the killing of her loved one as senseless.

“They came to [the] neighborhood and entered houses and killed people,” she said through an interpreter.

She is here with her 15-year-old daughter, and tried to define the worry she felt as the TPS saga unfolds.

“I don’t have anywhere to go,” she said.

title: ‘I’d rather overpay and be comfortable.’ As mid-budget gyms die out, patrons face tough choices.
text:
Now, fitness offerings for the middle class seem more limited than ever.

Rami Esrawi, 29, uses the New York Sports Club on Boylston Street, one of the few remaining in the city. For a dental student’s budget, it’s affordable enough. But the experience, he said, has been undermined by seemingly constant headaches and inconveniences: towel shortages, locker doors falling apart, saunas inoperable for months at a time.

In one sense, it’s a reflection of the fortunes of New York Sports Club, which operated as Boston Sports Clubs until its parent company went bankrupt in 2020 amid a flurry of legal troubles. Since then, the company has shrunk its footprint from more than 30 gyms in New England to three.

Esrawi said there aren’t many options to go elsewhere.

“I don’t need a personal trainer, I don’t need a ton of workout classes,” he said. ”I‘m looking for something that’s under $100, that has the amenities I like, and that has a good crowd.”

“I feel like Boston lacks that,” he added.

Esrawi is not alone. Increasingly, many gym-goers are having to choose between cheap budget gyms they don’t want, or paying a premium for boutique amenities they don’t need. Those who can afford to pay more are upgrading, and those who can’t are pivoting to budget options.

Joshua Bold, 22, gets access to classes, towels, a sauna, steam room, pool, and sports courts at luxury Equinox Sports Club, where memberships start around $200 monthly, though he noted he doesn’t regularly use all those facilities. Comfort and cleanliness are where he gets value — all things he felt were lacking at his last gym, which cost $50 to $55 a month.

“I’d rather overpay and be comfortable than cheap out and dread going,” Bold said, adding that he’s “paying for the things I don’t want to deal with.”

New York Sports Club spokesperson Kari Saitowitz said that while the pandemic may feel like “ancient history,” it was an inflection point for NYSC and many other Boston gyms. For one thing, weakened attendance made it harder to justify expensive rents, such as for the Downtown Crossing location that closed in May.

“You can’t easily just contract your square footage when membership softens,” she said.

A former Boston Sports Club in the South End underwent a similar transformation. Now a SoWa Health + Wellness, its memberships are $190 per month. Meanwhile, other BSC locations have been supplanted by low-budget alternatives, with New Hampshire-based Planet Fitness filling one in Back Bay and another in Central Square, and Crunch Fitness ($9-$19 per month) taking over spaces in Allston and Dorchester.

Other gyms with similar offerings and price ranges, such as the sprawling Boston Athletic Club in South Boston, have also closed. The YMCA still operates 10 midpriced locations in the city, though some locations tend to draw large crowds at peak hours. Aside from those, alternatives are few and far between.

Esrawi said his priorities are twofold: affordability and accessibility. But cheaper options, he said, are often too crowded at peak times for his taste. And for someone who’s still in school, more expensive options are out of the question.

It’s part of a national trend, according to financial analysis firm William Blair: The mid-tier has lost market share to “high-volume, low-price” options, the Planet Fitnesses and Crunches of the world.

“There’s almost a premium brand expectation on a midprice gym because they are seen as a full-service gym,” Saitowitz said. “Clean locker rooms, good hours, great equipment, a strong staff, knowledgeable trainers.”

Oftentimes, she said, low-budget gyms don’t carry those same expectations, while premium players charge higher fees to help cover those expenses.

At the same time, many younger gym-goers are choosing to shell out more money for premium gyms and boutique fitness studios, while spending remains strong among millennials and older patrons.

Though some luxury clubs don’t have a strong footprint in New England as a whole, they are highly concentrated within the city. Equinox, one of the most visible brands in the premium fitness world, operates four of its five Massachusetts locations in Boston; the fifth is in Newton’s Chestnut Hill.

Life Time, another luxury fitness outfit, costs $349 a month for its amenities, which include a cold plunge, red light recovery, and two floors of workout equipment at a former Boston Sports Club in the Prudential Center mall.

“It is a higher price point initially when you look at it,” said Kyle Hollander, the club’s general manager. “But if you’re coming consistently every day, you get a lot more than what you would [anywhere else].”

Sam Batchelder, a 24-year-old South End native, said his Life Time membership is his highest monthly expense. But as an online fitness coach and daily gym-goer, the value is more than worth it.

“It’s my new country club,” Batchelder said.

Batchelder, Bold, and other luxury gym-goers said socializing and community were main drivers in their decision to join a higher-end club. That much is backed up by a recent report by industry firm Les Mills, which found that “experience and ambiance” are core drivers of attendance for younger fitness enthusiasts.

John Atwood, a Natick-based fitness industry consultant, said the thinking is simple, for those who can afford it: “If this is incredibly important to your lifestyle, if you’re going to come to this place three times a week, then isn’t it worth it to spend a little bit more money?”

How young people choose to spend may matter a lot to the fitness industry. A 2025 report from the Health & Fitness Association, a Boston-based industry group, found that 25-to-44-year-olds now represent the largest gym-going population, or roughly a third of all membership. Millennials still buy the most premium gym memberships at 48 percent, though the large size and spending habits of Gen Z suggest that trend may soon skew younger.

“The trend where that age group is seeing this as a necessity and not as a luxury is definitely accurate,” said Parham Javaheri, president of club operations and chief property development officer at Life Time.

Data also shows Gen Z leans toward the kinds of workouts that can get pricey, with 43 percent of boutique studio membership being 25-and-unders.

Saitowitz, of New York Sports Club, said that despite the brand’s struggles there will always be demand for a full-service gym for those who decide against, or can’t afford, premium options.

“What we’re looking to do is provide enough value to that consumer, that they want to and can justify spending what we charge,” she said.

It remains to be seen if that will be enough to keep members like Esrawi. For now, he’s content paying his $55 membership. But as for when he’ll consider somewhere else?

“When I start making money,” he said.

title: Mayor Wu says White Stadium overhaul’s cost to taxpayers rising to $135 million
text:
At an event Friday Wu attributed the cost increases to inflation, tariffs, and expensive design changes based on feedback from neighbors and other members of the park community.

“The primary driver of why this project got more expensive is because we heard from community members that there were all of these dreams and hopes and goals, and we decided to make the project better and therefore more expensive in response to that,” Wu said.

Those additional items, Wu said, include a kitchen in a community room, and dedicated storage space for the school sports teams. The city has also made some more costly design choices, opting to put in a grass field rather than less-expensive artificial turf, for example.

But, the mayor added, Boston’s contracts with construction companies include maximum costs provisions, so the exposure for taxpayers will not go beyond $135 million.

“This is the final budget,” Wu said, adding the White Stadium project followed the city’s usual process that evolves from a placeholder figure that is little more than an estimate into a hard number based on design changes and bids from contractors.

“There is a guaranteed maximum price contract that is required when bidders submit their bid, and so that $135 [million] is locked by a contract,” Wu said.

But the project’s critics, who have proposed a less expensive design that would be fully paid for with public funds, say they are still not on board. The White Stadium project has been challenged in court by the environmental nonprofit the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and more than 20 residents, who argue the city’s plans amount to privatization of public land and could violate environmental protections. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court agreed in December to take up the case after a lower court sided with the city.

“Luckily, no foundation has been poured, no steel has been framed, and no walls have been built,” said Louis Elisa, a Dorchester resident and member of the Franklin Park Defenders, one of the groups that has sued to stop the project. “There is still plenty of time for the city to reconsider this fatally flawed project, and instead build a much more affordable, fully public high school stadium that meets the needs of BPS students and their families — not those of professional athletes and their investors.”

Wu has touted the project as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to give Boston Public Schools students and residents access to a world-class facility, while splitting the cost of the upgrade with a private entity that will bring a professional women’s sports team inside the city.

She argued Friday that the higher cost is worth it for BPS students.

“Our Boston kids deserve nothing less than the best,” Wu said. “This creates the chance for the facilities to match their talent and their potential.”

The project became a flash point in Wu’s reelection campaign last year when opponent Josh Kraft unearthed what he said was an internal projection showing the city might spend as much as $170 million on the project. Wu dismissed that assertion as not ”grounded in reality,” saying it was produced as a “worst case” scenario.

Demolition of the old stadium began in early 2025, when workers removed the entirety of the original structure, with the exception of the facade of the west grandstand.

The construction site was abuzz with activity midday Friday under a light dusting of snow. Yellow excavators and bucket loaders deposited dirt into dump trucks while construction workers in hard hats and fluorescent vests criss-crossed the property. Work on the foundation and utility services is underway, and construction on the new stadium itself is scheduled for the end of March, according to the city.

Should the Massachusetts high court block or disrupt the construction plans, Wu said the city has contingencies in the lease agreement. If the team backed out for any reason, for example, it would owe Boston tens of millions of dollars, which the city could use to finish the facility for students only.

The stadium deal does have backing from many members of the community, including some school athletes. Camila Restrepo, a junior and varsity soccer player at the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science, took advantage of Wu’s press conference Friday to demonstrate her skills, juggling the soccer ball with her feet some 50 times before addressing the room.

Boston’s investment in women’s sports and high school athletics “shows students like me that our dreams are worth supporting,” Restrepo said.

Restrepo’s dream is to one day play for Boston Legacy FC — “so Miss Jennifer, please keep me in mind,” she told the team’s co-owner Jennifer Epstein, as the room erupted into laughter.

A beaming Wu tallied how long it might be before Restrepo could join the team.

“Six years from now, we’re going to be cheering Camila on at White Stadium,” Wu said, “and everyone better be there!”

title: ‘You cannot erase us’: Roxbury square renamed for historic Twelfth Baptist Church
text:
In the year since President Trump began his second term, his administration has removed Martin Luther King Jr. Day and Juneteenth from the National Park Service’s list of national holidays with free admission and ordered the agency to review materials related to slavery and racial injustice at certain sites. He has also issued executive orders targeting the National Museum of African American History and Culture and directing changes to content focused on slavery and racial history within Smithsonian institutions.

In Boston, after Trump signed a sweeping executive order directing federal agencies to end DEI initiatives tied to federal grants and contracts, Northeastern University removed language and initiatives from its DEI webpage and the Harvard Graduate School of Education closed its DEI office altogether.

But as crowds shivered through the unveiling of the bright blue “Twelfth Baptist Church Square” sign, churchgoers said the marker will help secure New England’s oldest Black Baptist congregation into public memory.

Historian and author Dart Adams said permanent recognition of the church’s past — including its role on the Underground Railroad and in shaping the early ministry of King — is essential to protecting its future.

“You can not erase us if we keep record of what we’ve done,” Adams said from behind the pulpit Sunday morning. “It’s our honor to have a marker declaring that Twelfth Baptist Church … is proof that Boston, especially Black Boston, will always survive and thrive.”

For worshippers packed into the pews, the renaming brought solace after what they described as a racially charged start to Black History Month, when Trump shared a social media video depicting former president Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes.

Adonica-Curmazuela Chaplin, who officially joined the parish this week, said she hopes the renaming is a step toward recognizing Black history year-round, not just in February.

“If my history isn’t recorded and known, they will deny it like they’re trying to do it now,” said Chaplin, 79, of Roxbury. “We have leaders in Washington that refuse to tell the truth of our history. We can do it, but it has to be printed.”

The message echoed one expressed by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who sat in the chancel for more than two hours as Bodrick and other speakers addressed the congregation. It was the second time this month the two appeared together, following the city’s annual Black History Month celebration at City Hall, where Bodrick delivered an impassioned call for equity and justice for Boston’s Black community.

“What we’re here to do today is to make sure that as you’re going about your daily walk, not a single person will miss the reminder of the history that lives right here in this community,” said Wu. “Every month is Black History Month.”

Dozens of phones rose into the air as the crowd gathered outside the church, waiting for the brown paper concealing the new sign to be pulled away. The crowd cheered when a city worker climbed a ladder and sliced through the covering, revealing the marker.

Jaronzie Harris clapped as the sign came into view, exchanging excited words with fellow congregants. Having joined less than a year ago, she said the kindness and outspokenness of Twelfth Baptist members have insulated her from the rest of the world.

“I feel blessed to be in a community that’s pushing back on what the federal administration has been doing to censor the past,” said Harris, 38, who lives in Dorchester. “There’s erasure on a national scale, but it means a lot that the city is recognizing us and supporting us.”

Beside her, Violet Britton, a Roxbury resident who has attended Twelfth Baptist Church since she was a young child, stood in disbelief.

“My vocabulary isn’t extensive enough to explain how I felt,” said Britton, 81. “Something opened inside me.”

Speaking to the hundreds who gathered for his sermon, Bodrick urged worshippers to continue speaking openly about their struggles and perseverance. Assuming younger generations will automatically know the history that came before them, he said, is one of the “tragedies” of the modern day.

“We believe in memory, we believe in faith, we believe that truth prepares the next generation,” he said. “And we refuse to let the next generation walk into the future ignorant of their past.”

title: In challenging times, CNN has been rising to the occasion
text:
CNN has come in for plenty of criticism over the years. And much of that criticism has been justified. We don’t have enough space here to list the network’s many boneheaded personnel moves, coverage gaffes, and self-inflicted wounds.

But present-day CNN does valuable work, day in and day out, in a national atmosphere charged with partisan rancor.

The decimation of The Washington Post in the past week should remind us not to take for granted the dwindling number of news organizations committed to independent reporting. Such media outlets can be weakened in a heartbeat if an owner is as unprincipled as Jeff Bezos has shown himself to be.

Remember, we’ve got three more years of the Trump administration to go. If democracy is to remain afloat, CNN might need to play a crucial role.

Right now, the network’s status is up in the air as its parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), remains the subject of a fierce bidding war between corporate giants Netflix and Paramount Skydance.

But on the journalistic end of the spectrum, it’s worth noting how CNN has taken pains to stock its anchor desks with those who have proven their mettle as reporters — they’re not just deskbound bloviators.

Kaitlan Collins, who is CNN’s chief White House correspondent and anchors her own nightly political program, is a study in poise under pressure, even when being harangued by the Neanderthal-in-Chief for not smiling enough.

Even-keeled Dana Bash leans on her many years as a political reporter in putting elected officials on the spot, without grandstanding. She often prefaces a question by saying “With respect,” then pressing on until she gets an answer.

Jake Tapper’s mixture of gravitas and wit make him a must-watch. Reporting last week on Trump’s racist Truth Social post about former president Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama, Tapper hit the perfect notes of disgust, incredulity, and reportorial inquiry into how that post came to be.

Manu Raju is the network’s chief congressional correspondent and an anchor of “Inside Politics Sunday.” So we see Raju chasing elected officials through the halls of the Capitol and asking them hard questions, and then breaking down the latest issues, informed by his own reporting, on his show.

Anderson Cooper, Abby Phillip, Kasie Hunt, Erin Burnett, and Wolf Blitzer also draw extensively on their reporting experience in their anchor roles.

As anchor of a morning show, Audie Cornish has been the same steady, unflappable presence she was on NPR. Reporter and election-night voting-map analyst John King talks politics with the directness of the Dorchester guy he is.

When it comes to expert commentators, CNN also boasts a strong roster.

As the heart-rending Nancy Guthrie story has unfolded, law enforcement analyst John Miller has been insightful, while also using his deep sources to keep abreast of new developments.

National security analyst (and former Globe columnist) Juliette Kayyem is smart, sensible, and able to respond quickly to breaking news about complex events. Dr. Sanjay Gupta was an indispensable voice of expertise during the COVID pandemic, and has long played a similar role on other medical issues. At a time when the US Department of Health and Human Services is headed by Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has spent years undermining confidence in childhood vaccinations, Gupta is even more vital.

So is the rest of the CNN team. At least in theory. CNN has screwed up before, and they will probably screw up again. But there are going to be many varieties of crazy coming our way in the next few years, and we’re going to need them to be at their best. As they say in the TV biz, stay tuned.

Don Aucoin can be reached at donald.aucoin@globe.com. Follow him @GlobeAucoin.

title: Eight restaurants to visit for Lunar New Year
text:
Grasshopper

Opened: 1997

When word came that this beloved meatless restaurant had to leave its longtime location on North Beacon Street in Allston, vegans and those who love them went into mourning. But the day was saved when owners Hoai Nguyen and Linh Le were able to relocate Grasshopper to the 88 Food Connection. Fans old and new can still get their fix of dishes like vegi-chicken fingers, barbecue veggie pork, crispy taro nest, and the No Name, made with nuggets of gluten and bearing a strong resemblance to General Tso’s. And Grasshopper still offers its monthly Third Sunday Buffets, all you can eat for about $16.

88 Food Connection, 1 Brighton Ave., Allston, 617-254-8883, www.grasshoppervegan.com

Penang

Opened: 1996

Owners June and Suan Lee Cheah expanded from New York to Boston with this Malaysian restaurant 30 years ago, and Chinatown diners have been feasting on Hainanese chicken, nasi lemak, and beef rendang ever since. Whatever else you order, the meal isn’t complete without roti canai, thin pancakes to dip in a rich chicken curry. After all these years, it’s still fun to eat in a restaurant made to look like a traditional timber house, peeking into the open kitchen to watch the chefs at work.

685 Washington St., Chinatown, Boston, 617-451-6373, www.penangcuisineboston.com; 569 Moody St., Waltham, 781-899-2100, www.penangwalthamma.com

Ba Le

Opened: 1996

Run by Jennifer Nguyen, this family business has expanded in recent years from Dorchester to Quincy and Malden. The main attraction is always banh mi, Vietnamese sandwiches that stand above the rest thanks to fresh-baked baguettes, house-made mayonnaise, crisp pickled vegetables, and a plethora of fillings and combinations. Spring rolls, noodle dishes, rice plates, and more are also available, along with assorted pastries, smoothies, and other desserts and snacks. This time of year, you’re also likely to find banh tet or banh chung, stuffed rice cakes wrapped in banana leaves, a New Year’s tradition.

1052 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-265-7171; 99 Asian Supermarket, 60 Broadway, Malden, 781-480-4184; Kam Man Food, 219 Quincy Ave., Quincy, 617-773-8053; www.balebanhmiboston.com

Peach Farm

Opened: 1995

Maybe it was Lydia Shire who started it. Peach Farm, open late, has long been an after-work favorite of local chefs. But you can come any time, for just-out-of-the-tank seafood and other Chinese dishes. You can’t go wrong with salt-and-pepper anything, tender eel in black bean sauce, sizzling flounder, or lobster with ginger and scallion. But really, you kind of can’t go wrong with anything.

4 Tyler St., Chinatown, Boston, 617-482-3332, www.peachfarmseafood.com

Koreana

Opened: 1992

For many Boston diners who didn’t grow up with Korean food, Koreana offered a first taste of kimchi, galbi, bulgogi, bibimbap, and more. Decades on, you can still pull up to the Cambridge restaurant for grilled meats, bubbling stews, bottles of soju, and a slew of banchan, or side dishes.

158 Prospect St., Central Square, Cambridge, 617-576-8661, www.koreanaboston.com

Pho Hoa Anh Hong

Opened: 1992

A pioneer of Fields Corner’s Vietnamese food scene, Thanh Le opened Pho Hoa after arriving in the United States from Vietnam in the ’80s. The restaurant remains in the family today, an anchor of what is now the Boston Little Saigon cultural district. Come for the pho, of course, noodle soups laden with every cut of beef, chicken, or seafood. But you’ll also find vermicelli dishes, rice plates, hot pot, and other specialties. A few years back, Pho Hoa and another neighborhood fixture, Anh Hong, partnered under one roof; now Anh Hong’s seven-course beef menus are available too.

1370 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-287-9746, www.phohoarestaurant.com

Taiwan Cafe

Opened: 1989

Knowledgeable lunchers beeline for the blue awning up a steep, short flight of stairs to Taiwan Cafe, where midday dishes are a steal. Bring a friend and order three for $34.95, plus half-price appetizers. There’s a lengthy menu of Taiwanese dishes to explore at dinner, too: Pan-fried dumplings, roast beef and scallion pancake rolls, braised eggplant with basil, and beef noodle soup are just the beginning.

34 Oxford St., Chinatown, Boston, 617-426-8181

Kowloon Restaurant

Opened: 1950

The Kowloon: It’s a legacy, it’s a landmark, it’s a way of life. The Wong family launched the business in 1950, and it’s growing even now, with a tiki bar coming to Revere Beach in the fabled warmer months. You come to the Kowloon to be at the Kowloon, with its many rooms and elaborate decor, but also for comedy shows, pu pu platters, wings, maybe even sushi — and definitely a colorful cocktail or two. You know it, you probably love it, and best of all it’s still here.

948 Broadway, Saugus, 781-233-0077, www.kowloonrestaurant.com

title: Residents are steaming about snowbanks — and some neighborhoods are angrier than others
text:
“In Seaport, the streets are completely clean, and over here, it’s not,” he said.

Though plows have been working to clear Boston streets for the past two weeks after a massive storm dumped nearly two feet of snow on the city, some areas have been the site of repeated complaints to 311, according to available city data.

The city received 7,922 snow-related complaints from the first snow storm on Jan. 24 to the most recent on Monday, according to a Globe analysis.

The highest volume of complaints was concentrated in neighborhoods such as Dorchester, South Boston, and the South End, according to a Globe analysis. Residents in those neighborhoods, it would seem, are more frustrated with snow removal efforts than those living elsewhere.

“The deeper you go in, the more it snowed,” said 22-year-old Andrew Frisbie, pointing up towards the winding side streets of Mission Hill. “Touching on that a little more would be great.”

In the South End the area around Montgomery Street and Tremont, registered 15 separate complaints from last Saturday to this Monday, per city data.

Another area, along Allston and Medford streets in Charlestown, saw residents make 14 separate complaints over the same period, the data shows. And in South Boston, along the intersection of Dorchester and West Fourth streets, there were roughly 12 complaints.

For comparison, there were no areas in the Seaport with anywhere near the same volume of complaints over the past weekend.

In a statement Wednesday morning, city officials said crews had been working “day and night” to clear snow from main thoroughfares, business districts, and transit hubs, “covering every neighborhood across Boston.”

They also said that in certain areas such as the Seaport and the Back Bay, larger property owners often contract with private companies to remove snow.

For Uphams Corner residents trying to reach the JFK/UMass MBTA station, the only viable path along Sydney Street is on the roadway itself. The sidewalk, which runs next to Interstate 93, remains fully covered in snow.

“It’s obtrusive, for sure,” said Moseley Street resident Jason Dorce. “There are some parts that you have to walk out into the street to then get back to another cleared spot.”

Removal crews have largely cleared the street, but massive snowbanks in nearby parking lots are still giving drivers a headache, he said.

Boston maintains 13 snow farms across the city, using snow melting machines to speed up the process. Officials said the city would “proactively continue working with our local and state partners to identify additional locations” to dump snow.

Some residents still remember the massive snow pile in the Seaport from the storm of 2015, which did not fully melt until July of that year.

“There’s only so many places to put it,” Dorce said. “Until it all melts, and it goes down the drain.”

Part of the problem, officials have said, is that the average temperature in the city has remained well below freezing for well over two weeks, until a Wednesday warm spell brought a return to more seasonal weather.

“Unlike recent years, where the temperature has been dipping up and down and Mother Nature helps us get rid of the snow a bit, this [snowfall] has stuck,” said Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, during a Tuesday interview on GBH’s “Boston Public Radio.”

Starting Jan. 24, temperatures in the city stayed at or below freezing for nine consecutive days, according to Globe meteorologist Ken Mahan. Until Wednesday, the few days to briefly rise above freezing were not enough to cause significant melt-off.

The streak of cold weather, though, is not necessarily uncommon, Mahan said.

“Most of the weeks or longer streaks of subfreezing temperatures coincided with or followed some of the biggest snowstorms of the year,” he said. “In fact, the colder it gets, the fluffier the snow can become, making it pile up even higher at the surface.”

The most recent two-week stretch of freezing weather was February 2015, when two major snowstorms dropped over a foot of snow each, Mahan said. That stretch was part of “Snowmageddon,” a three-week period where more than 7 feet of snow paralyzed the region.

Residents awoke Wednesday morning to dripping rooftops and slush streets, spurring hope for a coming thaw to finally make street corners accessible again. Temperatures could hit 40 degrees.

“Even though its technically still colder than normal, it’s a relief,” Mahan said. “It’s still warmer than what we’re used to [over the past few weeks].”

City officials have said that, while the city is responsible for clearing snow from public roadways, sidewalks are generally the responsibility of property owners. As of Wednesday, the city said it had issued 3,626 snow removal violations, including 138 violations to the MBTA.

That doesn’t sit well with certain residents.

“I’ve never understood how the city can say homeowners have to remove snow on sidewalks, which are city property,” said Marcia Peters, a 50-year resident of Jamaica Plain. “I know it’s an ordinance, but how does that work?”

Some residents have gone as far as organizing their own snow-clearing efforts, such as the Boston Cyclists Union, which cleared several blocks of bike lanes near Boston University on Friday, according to social media.

“Commonwealth Avenue is one of the most used bike lanes in the city, and yet it’s completely unusable as it currently stands,” the group wrote.

Wu, speaking on GBH, acknowledged that the current snow removal system is “complicated” and “maybe inefficient.”

“It’s no good to the mom [with] a stroller if three of the houses on the street have cleared their sidewalk, and one in the middle hasn’t,” she said.

City councilors, including Brian Worrell and Enrique Pepén, have floated various measures to improve the city’s removal efforts, such as a volunteer “snow corps” modeled off other cities.

title: Today in History: Clinton acquitted in impeachment trial
text:
Today is Thursday, Feb. 12, the 43rd day of 2026. There are 322 days left in the year.

Birthdays: Film director Costa-Gavras is 93. Author Judy Blume is 88. Former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak is 84. Country singer Moe Bandy is 82. Musician Michael McDonald is 74. Actor-talk show host Arsenio Hall is 70. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh is 61. Actor Josh Brolin is 58. Filmmaker Darren Aronofsky is 57. Actor Christina Ricci is 46. Rapper Gucci Mane is 46. Actor Jennifer Stone is 33. Pro wrestler Jaida Parker is 27.

In 1554, Lady Jane Grey, who had claimed the throne of England for nine days, and her husband, Guildford Dudley, were beheaded after being condemned for high treason.

In 1776, 250 years ago, General George Washington and his artillery expert, Henry Knox, slipped across the isthmus south of Boston to Dorchester Heights and started mapping out where the rebel army would place the cannons that Knox delivered from Fort Ticonderoga. Their eventual fortification of the drumlin hills, along with a fierce nor’easter, prompted the British to evacuate Boston in March and retreat to Halifax in Canada.

In 1809, Abraham Lincoln, the 16th president of the United States, was born in a log cabin at Sinking Spring Farm near Hodgenville, Kentucky.

In 1877, in the first public demonstration of his telephone invention, Alexander Graham Bell made a call before a crowd at Lyceum Hall in Salem to his office in Boston.

In 1909, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) was founded in New York City.

In 1912, Pu Yi, the last emperor of China, abdicated, marking the end of the Qing Dynasty.

In 1914, groundbreaking took place for the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.

In 1934, Bill Russell was born in West Monroe, La. The Celtic great and civil rights figure died in 2022.

In 1999, the Senate voted to acquit President Bill Clinton in his impeachment trial on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice.

In 2002, former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milošević went on trial in The Hague, charged with genocide and war crimes. (Milošević died in 2006 before the trial could conclude).

In 2016, Pope Francis embraced Patriarch Kirill in the first meeting between a pontiff and the head of the Russian Orthodox Church. The meeting in Havana was a landmark development in the 1,000-year schism that has divided Christianity.

In 2019, Mexico’s most notorious drug lord, Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, was convicted in New York of running an industrial-scale drug smuggling operation, murder and money laundering. (Guzman is currently serving a life sentence at the federal supermax prison facility in Florence, Colorado.)

title: How Liz Walker found her higher purpose
text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the Feb. 12 episode.

Anna Kusmer: Welcome to Say More from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer.

If you lived around Boston in the 1980s or 1990s, you will probably recognize this voice.

Yes, that is the Liz Walker.

She was the first Black woman to co-anchor a TV newscast in Boston. In 2005, she left the news and went to church.

After TV, Reverend Liz Walker was the pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian Church. As a pastor, she found her higher calling, mixing faith with the power of talking. And between ICE raids, natural disasters and the mental health crisis, we need places to talk more than ever.

Her new project is called “Can We Talk.” Her book about the project, “No One Left Alone,” takes us into the church walls to sit beside grieving parishioners, healing together through conversation.

Welcome Liz, thanks for being here.

Liz Walker: It is an honor to be with you, Anna. Thanks for having me.

Kusmer: I want to talk about this new book and the project that inspired it. At the center of the book, as a young man named Cory Johnson. Can you tell me his story and why it became so important to your ministry?

Walker: Well, the first thing to tell you is that as a reporter, I covered this neighborhood often.

Roxbury, as we all know, is kind of the center of the — I hate to say Black, so I’ll say urban — community, and it’s a community that’s changing. When I went there in 2011, that neighborhood had been in the midst of what I’m going call gang violence, so that may not be accurate, but there was gun violence and lots of young people had died.

Seventy-five people had died between 2010 and 2011 in Boston. Many of them, most of them from Roxbury, and one of them was Cory Johnson. I had covered stories on shootings in that neighborhood, but I didn’t know the full story. You usually started on the news on a weekend.

Often, it was, “Another shooting in Roxbury, details at 11.”

So going back in as a minister and learning more about these young men who were dying, especially Cory because he was a member of the church and a promising young man. He had two children, two young girls, worked at the YMCA, worked in the community centers, and he was a typical youth, but he was really looking for a bright future. He and his brother went out to a party one night, and he didn’t come home. He was killed, and the murderer was never found. The circumstances have always been mysterious.

I wanted to know about Cory when I got to the church because I could see that his family was still grieving. I got there a year after he was killed.

Kusmer: One of your first events as pastor was like a one year anniversary of Cory’s death, and I think you were talking to his mother and that was that part of what inspired, sort of what came next?

Walker: Yeah. Because at this memorial service, a year after Cory was killed, and right after I got to the church, his mother asked me to pray at the memorial service. It was at the Boston Kroc Center in Dorchester, and the whole point of the memorial service was balloons and music. But underneath this, kind of party atmosphere and celebration, you could feel the pain.

There’s no way to go on when you — or at least there’s no way to go on in a healthy direction — when you haven’t dealt with some of the things that are holding you down. And this family was, and still is, trying to figure their way through this grief.

They’re a large family from Trinidad and Tobago. To see them try to put their best face on, in the wake of this violent death, broke my heart.

Kusmer: You say, and it really struck me in the book, that you didn’t know how to talk to someone whose loved one had been murdered when you were first talking to Debra at that event.

You were a journalist in Boston for decades, so obviously you literally knew how to talk to someone about hard things, but you felt like you were missing something in this new role.

Walker: Absolutely.

Kusmer: Can you talk about what you feel like you were missing?

Walker: Well, first of all, journalists, usually — now I’m old school and it may have changed in the last 5,000 years since I was on television — but you go to the scene of a horror show, or you go to the scene of a horrible situation and you usually say, “How did it feel?” which would make sense in a very kind of a superficial way.

But it’s really not quite the way to handle someone who just saw their love die.

So that’s what I mean about, what do you say?

And I think that in a culture that we have, we really don’t know how to address grief. What do we do? Do we come in and say, “He’s in a better place?” Do we come in and say, “You’re going to be all right?”

That’s not what you need to say. So that’s what I meant. I thought I knew what to say. I think we all think we know what to say, but in fact, talking in that way is not necessarily helpful. And so that was another part of this book: What do we say? How can we support our neighbors when they’re going through things?

And that’s what I learned, and that’s what I share.

Kusmer: So this project that came out of this realization is called “Can We Talk.” Can you describe what “Can We Talk” is, the sort of the form it took, and just what that actually looked like to be in the room there?

Walker: So we wanted to do something more than the usual fair, and I don’t say that with disrespect. When a person is killed or dies in our community, the church plans the funeral, the church works with the family, we talk to the police. We try to do everything we can to ease the burden of the family.

But what happens is after the funeral, maybe we bring covered dishes over, maybe we pray with the family, but at some point, life goes on for us. Life does not go on for the family. So this “Can We Talk” idea came from talking to mental health experts, funeral directors, and of course this family about, what would help you a little bit? After all of this is happening, how can we help you?

And talking really to psychologists because grief needs to be taken care of, it needs to be tended. Doesn’t mean it’ll go away, but it can be handled and managed so that you can cope, knowing that you are going through this.

So in talking to them, one of the ideas came up, “Well, why don’t we have something like Alcoholics Anonymous for people who are grieving?”

The similarity is only in the fact that this is a kind of a drop in group. It’s in the basement of the church. It’s not church, but it gives a safe — and we consider sacred — space for people to just release some of their pain.

These are gatherings we started monthly. We have food and we have a mental health worker on site who usually does it pro bono. We have companions — other people who have gone through trauma themselves, but have been trained in some basics of trauma education to identify what trauma is — identifying what you can do, as a neighbor, as a friend.

We tried it and the outpouring was amazing that first time. People just showed up. People heard we had a sign on the church wall outside, that was our only marketing plan.

People showed up and they talked about violence last week and about violence 20 years ago that they just were told to get over and move on, or they told themselves that.

But, it was always there because untreated trauma, any wound, needs at some point, light and air to heal. And if you don’t give it that, it can fester and it can get much worse.

Kusmer: The goal of this project, I think, maybe in a romantic sense we might think, “Oh, we want people to have these cathartic breakthroughs where they do relieve themselves of grief.”

But I think it’s not like that, you know? And I think of Debra, Cory’s mother, you kind of follow her throughout the book, her coming to these sessions.

What do you kind of define as progress for somebody who’s attending these events?

Walker: We had an event in New Bedford and Debra got up and spoke and so I listened to her very closely and I’ve watched her over the years, and she says that for her it is the ability to even talk about this incident that has given her a little space inside.

When Cory was first killed, she got a call in the middle of the night and she said she knew almost immediately something was wrong. When she got to the hospital, and this was back in 2010, and realized her son was gone, she said a part of her just shut down, just numb. There were no words for what she was going through.

Somehow over the years she kept working. She did what she had to do, but she never entered that space that was shut down. She said that went on for four years. So the idea of confronting your boogeyman, your darkness, your pain, your worst moment, it’s not about ending that moment, but it’s about finding a way through and then somehow integrating that into your life.

She will never be happy or get over Cory’s death. And she said that there are days now when she goes into a dark hole. She can’t help it, but she knows a way out.

The other thing she said that was very stunning to me, and it was nothing I even thought about, was that telling her story she sees now helps other people. And last night in New Bedford, it was extraordinary. People, probably about 30 or 40 people, were at this church and they listened to Debra talk, and then we tried a little, “Can We Talk” with them. And people started sharing things.

One man talked about being shot during busing and never having gone to the hospital. He was so ashamed. The things that we carry. So that’s what I think the healing is. A thing we talk about in Black religious tradition is God is a God of making a way out of no way. When you think there’s absolutely nothing, I’m going to be able to survive this.

Debra decided, “I’ll just have to live like this. I’ll have to live with this darkness. That’s just gonna be life.” And she says, a little of the darkness has lifted and she’s found a place to kind of deal with the death just a little easier.

So it’s not going to change. You’re right. It’s not big, but these are things.

I think one more thing you didn’t ask, but I’m going to tell you anyway, the idea of telling your story. We live in a culture, and this has always been the case, where other people define us, they define Cory: “at-risk young man, gang member.” That wasn’t who Cory was, so she gets to define who she is and who her son was.

Kusmer: And I imagine in a church setting where a lot of us might visualize a pastor speaking down to the congregation, this is maybe a new dynamic for a lot of people. They’re the ones speaking and they’re the lead, directing the conversation. I imagine that’s an interesting dynamic for you as well as a pastor.

Walker: I talk about these experiences in very dramatic terms, but it has been a life change for me because we are listening.

As a preacher, I love to preach. I could preach right now, but that’s not what you invited me for. But the goal here is to learn, to listen and to listen deeply because, part of the problem we’re in, the mess we’re in now is that so many people feel unheard. And that affects everything. And so this is a way for people to feel heard, to feel honored, to have dignity restored. And I’m not just talking about Black people or poor people or people of color. There are many people who just don’t feel heard. And this is a way to help kind of reach them and listen.

Kusmer: Liz, you grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas in the 1950s and 1960s, and you went to high school at Little Rock Central, which is famous for being the high school of the Little Rock Nine, where nine Black teenagers were sent to this all white school as part of integration after Brown v. the Board of Education. They were met with racist backlash. What was it like to be on the front lines of desegregation at such a young age?

Walker: I lived in the neighborhood around the school, at least within a mile of the school.

My brother and I have talked about this, “Are we just making this up or is this true?” But we remember the troops driving into — well, that’s a traumatic sight to see — government troops and guns and all these Jeeps and all that stuff.

So I think we do, I think that’s a real memory, not just imagination coming in when we were very young.

And then later my father, who was a part of the Civil Rights leadership in the city, wanted me to desegregate — be a part of the desegregation, the integration of these schools, because they did it in 1957 at Little Rock Central.

Then they shut down the schools and then they started it back up, grade by grade. And that’s how this was still going on all that time. So I was supposed to be in the seventh grade in 1963, and this was the year that they were desegregating the seventh grade. So they’d worked their way from the 12th grade down, and it was horrible.

Now, when the Little Rock Nine were in the news, the thing about them was, as horrible as their situation was, and it was certainly horrible, there were cameras, there was attention, there were interviews. They had Daisy Bates.

There was something to hold all of that chaos. By the time I got to the seventh grade, your father took you to the school or maybe you went with a group. I was not sent with a group. And you went and you were on your own. So there was no organized thing, at least not for me.

The reason I think I was not involved in that was right at the beginning of the school year, my father died.

So my family was thrown into its own personal chaos and the rules, whatever the rule, whatever he had in mind, who knows? But I felt very much on my own and so that was a traumatizing time for me. It was a time when puberty was coming, a time when most kids are thinking about dating.

It felt like the frontline of a war and there were only maybe in the whole school of 800 students, maybe 50 Blacks. I don’t think there were that many organized picnics or anything because I guess life just went on.

And, I really suffered from that, and other kids suffered from that, from being the only one in a class or being spit on. There were just all kinds of stories. I know that that has impacted me all my life, compounded by the trauma of losing my father.

And again, back in the day, there were no psychologists, there were no counseling services. You went to the funeral and my mother, my stepmother was grieving herself, she didn’t have time.

It was just shut down in my soul and has just begun to come up — of how I struggled with it since this program started. I tell people that and they look at me, but I think a lot of us hold our stuff to ourselves because we don’t know what to do with it, so we hold our pain inside.

Kusmer: What did the group, “Can We Talk,” unlock for you?

Walker: It unlocked the fact that I was not dealing with some issues. There was always this hole and it really came out in relationships, or the lack thereof, because I never went to a therapist. I never put a frame or a context around that time. I never even thought about the time I went through. You just got over it and moved on.

The year of 1963 was probably one of the worst years for this country. That was the year John F. Kennedy was killed. That was the year that the four girls were killed in Birmingham, Alabama. All hell had broken. We were in the Vietnam War. We look back on that time now as a defining moment in American history, and it affected all of us.

Kusmer: When I was a child growing up here in Boston, you were famous for being a local TV news anchor. What drew you to the calling of news?

Walker: Interesting. I have no idea. I wish I did. I think I always wanted to write, and I think one of the healing parts of my childhood was when I went to Central High School because by the time I got to Central, things had calmed down. One of the classes I took was journalism. I always liked to write little poems and things like that as a child, but I never thought that was going to amount to anything because I didn’t think it could. But I had a journalism teacher, Charles Lance. I was in his class and there was some project, and this was probably the 10th grade and he said, “You can write.”

Nobody had told me I could do anything, including my parents. When people say that to you, it can stick with you. That was kind of a way forward for me. I put everything into writing then.

Kusmer: What made you leave the anchor chair to go to Harvard Divinity School?

Walker: That’s another mystery in my life. I went to Sudan in 2001.

Kusmer: Is this a journalistic assignment?

Walker: I assigned myself this. Some people in Boston had been invited to go and observe and explore allegations of slavery in South Sudan. This was going on for decades, these allegations. And so a group went, and I was invited with them. I thought I’d do a documentary.

I went to my news director, and television news then, and now, was not looking at why we are gonna go all the way to South Sudan to do a story. “We cover local news.”

But I got mad and I decided, “You know what? I’m gonna do this myself.” So I took my own camera and it was on that journey that the people I went with Reverend Dr. Gloria White-Hammond and Pastor Ray Hammond, who are still two outstanding community leaders in Boston, medical doctors and ministers.

And I went with them and they kind of defined how I reacted to what I saw as a call. They said, “Oh no, this is God calling you. There’s something you should do.”

Kusmer: What in Sudan sort of created this shift for you?

Walker: I never had seen that kind of trauma, physical trauma. We went to villages where you could actually see the hollowed out piece where the bomb hit.

Kusmer: Wow.

Walker: Because this was the north against the south. I’d never been that close to that. I was never that close to a conflict, and so that kind of opened me up to the misery of the world.

Kusmer: Do you feel like you hit a wall with the tools of journalism? That then ministry felt like sort of an evolution of maybe what you had?

Walker: I do believe that I hit a wall of journalism because you sit there behind the camera and you’re watching this scene go on and this woman’s talking about gang rape and you’re thinking —

And telling the story is huge! This is important.

But remember, Hurricane Katrina hit, and when Katrina hit, people were waving white flags on rooftops that were covered with water and people were begging for help. And it seemed a little odd that TV cameras were just shooting that when I’m actually asking you to save my life. At some point there, the needs are beyond that idea of some objective and removed storyteller.

People are desperate for help, and your job is only to tell the story. I think storytelling is important, but sometimes you wanted —

Kusmer: — to do more.

Walker: I wanted to do more. That’s all.

Kusmer: Yeah, that makes sense. What do you think your dad would say if he knew you became a minister?

Walker: I wonder. I think he’d be going, “Girl…”

Kusmer: Why?

Walker: Well, I wonder if I became a minister because my dad was a minister and that’s all I remember.

I am not running around with some dramatic, “I’ve been called by God.” I kind of wonder was that just kind of trying to figure out what my dad was doing?

It has been the most satisfying role and it has been a role of kind of swimming in the deep end of the pool as opposed to on the side and taking the picture and really seeing the human condition, and seeing the commonality in it.

It crosses all kinds of barriers that you think. We have more in common. And you hear it and it sounds like a platitude, but it’s so true. That’s how I guess you get to platitudes. We have so much more in common as human beings than we think. And now when we are dividing the world into “us” and “them.” I think more than ever somebody’s got to say, “That’s not exactly what’s going on here, because we are all suffering.”

Kusmer: It’s funny because although you are technically a local celebrity, as a teenager, I was actually more in awe of your son because I went to Brookline High School with Nick. He was, and is, a phenomenal singer and actor. I still think about his performance in the musical “Ragtime,” which he was in as a senior.

Walker: Oh, that was huge.

Kusmer: Yeah. He was amazing in that. And I actually remember that he would walk down the streets next to Brookline High School, maybe he was walking home, and he would sing at the top of his lungs. I’m sure you remember that, too. And like an angel, the most gorgeous voice. First of all, you must be so proud of him.

Walker: I am very proud. I’m in awe of Nick. So many people remember him in Brookline walking down. I used to say, “Nick, be careful about that. People are gonna think you’re crazy singing at the top of [your] lungs.”

But that was his gift and he just did it.

Kusmer: Yeah. I mean, there’s so much in your book about humility, and I’m just curious about what you’ve learned from your son and your own parenting experiences.

Walker: Well, I’ve learned a lot from my son. I’ve learned that, you know, I wanted Nick to just be a regular kid that would just stay in the lines, because that’s what I wanted to do. And Nick had a sense of purpose early on. He wanted to sing and he only wanted to go to New York. And it wasn’t about, I look back now, I don’t think it was so much about fortune and fame. It was just about his gift.

Kusmer: Sharing his gift.

Walker: I really think so. That may be naïve.

So I learned that from him — the idea of purpose in our lives. And it is not an easy profession because there’s so many times of being down, so many times of being out. He was in “Hamilton” and that was huge, but he’s been struggling and hustling for a long time. And every victory is a big victory because he has been struggling and hustling. So, I talk a lot about purpose and trauma and grief can take us away from our sense of purpose.

And, “How do you restore that?” is important.

Kusmer: You have a whole chapter in your book about the power of music. I was wondering if you have a musical note to reflect on.

Walker: Oh, gosh. That’s a great, that’s such a great, great question. The song is “Golden.”

You know who I’m talking about — ”living my life like it’s golden.”

Kusmer: Jill Scott.

Walker: Jill Scott. I like Jill Scott, anything she does, because I love her voice. But that song is, you know, it’s just how we can take on a different kind of position and state of mind in life no matter what happens to you. It’s about just living your life, with swimming in the deep end, trying and taking risks, and not being afraid because there’s so much to make us afraid of everything.

And so “living my life like it’s golden” is a step out of that fear for me.

Kusmer: Liz Walker was the longtime pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian Church here in Boston. Her new book is called “No One Left Alone”, about the project “Can We Talk.” Thank you so much, Liz, for sharing with us. It’s been an honor to speak with you.

Walker: Anna, it’s been really delightful talking to you and I wish you the best.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.
