title: For better or worse, Wu’s bet on White Stadium will define her legacy
text:
What about building a more modest alternative for the exclusive use of Boston schoolchildren and opposing teams — one that includes a regulation track, a field for high school football and soccer games, and a field house with lockers and showers? Opponents say that can be done for $29 million. But the Wu administration dismisses that option, saying the cost would be much higher than that, while producing no formal bids or cost estimates to back up such a conclusion.

It’s Wu’s way or the highway — and dare I say there’s something slightly Trumpian about that attitude?

Ignoring the critics, the cost, and legal arguments against it, President Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House in order to build a ballroom. After adding his name onto the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Trump recently announced plans to rebuild it, no matter what detractors have to say about it.

Unlike the East Wing or the Kennedy Center, there’s no question White Stadium warranted demolishment. Built in 1949, it was once an urban jewel. After falling into extreme disrepair, it stood as a sad commentary on city priorities about Franklin Park and school sports.

Rebuilding it is now a legacy project that will define Wu’s mayoralty, and she appears to be willing to take the heat and risks that go with it.

The women’s soccer team could fail to gain a following, collapse financially, or exit Boston. Or it could be such a success that it needs a larger venue, like the professional soccer stadium planned for the New England Revolution in Everett. Either way, the Wu administration insists the city is protected.

As for cost, Wu now insists that it’s “locked.” However, in the Contrarian Boston, Scott Van Voorhis suggested that’s not accurate because guaranteed maximum price agreements don’t preclude or stop contractors from billing for change orders that would increase the cost. In the end, the public will eventually find out who is right about that, just like it did with the Big Dig.

To be fair, great vision often requires a great leap of faith. Past Boston mayors have taken on legacy projects that proved the skeptics wrong. Kevin White turned crumbling warehouses into Quincy Market, a popular tourist destination that revitalized downtown Boston, which is again in need of creative revitalization. Tom Menino championed a convention center in South Boston that spurred development of a new luxury neighborhood and entertainment district, known as the Seaport.

With White Stadium, Wu is looking beyond downtown, to a part of the city that could greatly benefit from attention and investment. According to Wu, the newly renovated stadium “will deliver the largest community benefits deal in Boston’s history.” With the city committed to $135 million, Boston Legacy, which will lease the stadium from the city, is putting in $190 million.

Construction is slated to begin at the end of March, and the project is expected to create more than 500 construction jobs. There are promises to share the work with local businesses in the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park, including Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, and Roxbury. Some $43 million in contracts are also allocated to minority and women-run businesses. It all sounds great.

The city still faces a legal challenge from the Franklin Park Defenders, who have joined the Emerald Necklace Conservancy to sue the city over the stadium plan, arguing that it’s an illegal use of park land. The case is now before the Supreme Judicial Court. For the plaintiffs, it is the last stand.

If the city wins, it will be Wu’s way, for better or worse.

Will it be all that she promised, from an investment in the future of Boston Public Schools to an economic boom for a long-neglected part of the city? Most of all, will it be what Boston student athletes need and deserve?

Because of the need to maintain pristine field conditions for the pro soccer team, high school football won’t be played there until November, the end of the season. Wu officials say high school soccer games can be played on the field. But questions are still being raised about how long high school games can coexist with professional games before field quality becomes an issue. As with the final cost, the truth about shared usage will eventually be known, too.

In the end, that truth will be Wu’s legacy.

title: Craft spirits distillery to replace beer garden on Rose Kennedy Greenway
text:
A craft spirits distillery is set to replace the longtime beer garden on the Rose Kennedy Greenway, park officials announced.

Dorchester-based Boston Harbor Distillery will start serving its signature craft spirits and cocktails on the Greenway this spring, the Rose Kennedy Greenway Conservancy said Thursday.

“Our goal has always been to create spirits that tell a story of Boston and its harbor,” Rhonda Kallman, the distillery’s founder, said in a statement. “We’re delighted to bring Boston Harbor Distillery to the Greenway, a place that embodies the heart of the city. This partnership gives us the opportunity to share our craft with both Downtown neighbors and visitors from around the world, creating memorable experiences in a space that celebrates community, connection, and the vibrancy of Boston.”

The new spot will supplant the former Trillium Brewing beer garden, which held the lease at the corner of High Street and Atlantic Avenue for nearly a decade, park officials said. When it was established, it was the city’s first public beer garden.

Park officials said Boston Harbor Distillery was selected after a competitive bid process.

“We’re very grateful for the role Trillium Brewing played in helping to establish our beverage gardens and in welcoming so many visitors to the park,” said Eileen Ong, the conservancy’s director of programs and outreach. “Their creativity and partnership shaped a program that has become a beloved seasonal destination and helped spark the growth and popularity of beer gardens across the city.”

A Trillium spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment.

In addition to its locally inspired whiskey, rum and liqueurs, Boston Harbor Distillery will also serve cocktails, mocktails, beer, wine, and locally produced snacks.

Trillium, which also has locations in Canton, Fort Point, and Fenway, opened a new winter beer garden inside Winthrop Center on Federal Street last month.

title: ‘Half hearted action won’t protect us.’ Why some want Beacon Hill to do more to fight back against ICE
text:
If so, many of you have asked, what can be done to protect the people who live here from federal overreach? It’s a question that gained new urgency after federal agents shot and killed two US citizens in Minneapolis.

Two weeks ago, Governor Maura Healey stood in front of dozens of elected officials, community leaders, and immigration advocates to announce a series of measures to restrict ICE enforcement tactics in the state — taking what looks to me to be her strongest public stance yet against Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

She filed a bill to keep ICE out of churches, schools, courthouses, and other sensitive locations. Healey also ​​signed an executive order barring ICE from making civil arrests in nonpublic areas of state facilities such as state hospitals or social services buildings and using state property for immigration enforcement activity.

“People have been killed,” Healey said.

Many applauded Healey’s moves. But some fellow Democrats and community groups pressed her to go further, as my colleagues Samantha J. Gross and Matt Stout have reported.

And when you look around the country, there is evidence that some blue states are moving more aggressively against ICE.

In Maryland, state legislators recently passed a bill that bans contracts between local law enforcement and ICE to facilitate immigration arrests, which now awaits Governor Wes Moore’s signature. New Mexico and New York are looking at similar legislation, too.

Last year, Governor Gavin Newsom made California the first state in the country to prohibit federal law enforcement from wearing masks after he signed the bill into law, though a federal judge struck down the law in a decision this week. The judge said California can still demand that officials show identification.

Back in Massachusetts, some have noted that the state’s Department of Corrections has a contract with ICE, formally called a 287(g) agreement, that allows prison system officials to identify undocumented immigrants eligible for deportation and turn them over to ICE. It’s the same kind of partnership Maryland lawmakers moved to ban.

Massachusetts is the sole state with a Democratic Governor and an electorate that rejected Trump in 2024 where a state agency is participating in the 287(g) program, according to recent reporting from Bolts Magazine. Healey has defended this contract, but largely forbade the state from entering into new agreements with ICE in her recent announcement.

Other Democratic-led states have recently been shutting down existing 287(g) agreements, including in Virginia, where newly-installed Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, last week issued a directive withdrawing state agencies from these contracts.

Healey’s office has defended the governor’s record on the issue.

“Over the past year, Governor Healey has led a strong and coordinated response to President Trump’s attacks on our immigrant communities, on public safety, and on the rights and freedoms of every Massachusetts resident,” Karissa Hand, a Healey spokesperson, told me in a statement. “Governor Healey will continue to work closely with community organizations and law enforcement to protect the people of Massachusetts from ICE’s abuses.”

The governor also on Friday issued a strong statement urging N.H. Governor Kelly Ayotte to oppose the federal effort to convert a Merrimack, N.H., warehouse into a detainment center.

“We should be opposing ICE’s tactics, not allowing them to expand. We certainly should not be allowing ICE to build new human warehouses when they can’t be trusted to keep people safe and protect due process. I oppose this in the strongest possible terms, and I am demanding that Governor Ayotte do everything in her power to block a new ICE facility.”

Advocates who want Healey to do more aren’t giving up.

On Thursday, a group of advocates renewed their calls for increased action from Beacon Hill. A delegation from the Faith Leaders Caucus of the Massachusetts Communities Action Network (MCAN) arrived at the State House, asking for a meeting with the Governor — both to thank her for the steps she’s already taken, but also to ask for more. The delegation, among other things, wants the state create a some meaningful way for residents to report incidents where they think ICE may be doing something illegal.

“The moment of truth for us could be rather soon,” said Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, a Founding Pastor of the New Roots AME Church in Dorchester. “While we are grateful for what [Healey] has done, we still also feel it’s insufficient.”

White-Hammond held a poster that she asked staff at the State House to deliver to the Governor. It depicted a piece of a broken heart.

“This moment is heartbreaking,” the poster read. “Governor Healey, half hearted action won’t protect us.”

I feel like all my rights are violated. There is not a plan on how to get help or to be protected on the case of abuse. Things are totally out of control. People are afraid to speak.

title: Man accused of double murder in Brockton last year arrested in Mexico
text:
A man suspected of killing two teenagers outside of a Brockton mall last year was arrested in Mexico, bringing an end to an extensive international manhunt, officials said.

Davinci Leonard, 23, faces double first-degree murder charges and a myriad of gun charges in connection with the March shooting that killed 15-year-old Tymari Albertson and 18-year-old Cevannah Alvarez outside a Chipotle restaurant, the Plymouth district attorney’s office said in a release last week. The shooting occurred following a fight that began outside the mall.

“This was a lengthy and thorough investigation which took officers up and down the east coast, west to Michigan and California, and then onto Haiti, and ultimately to Mexico,” District Attorney Timothy Cruz said. “I commend all those involved for their hard work and determination on this case.”

Following his capture, Mexican and California authorities expelled Leonard to San Diego, where he was taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals Service. He is scheduled to be transported to Massachusetts for arraignment in Brockton District Court next week.

The U.S. Marshals had offered a reward of up to $7,500 for information leading to the arrest, and two others were previously arrested on suspicion of helping him escape, officials said.

David Mosley-Lott, 32, of Quincy and Jaylen Speed, 25, of Dorchester, were found to have been in contact with Leonard in the days after the shooting, officials said. Mosley-Lott was charged with one count of accessory after the fact and intimidation of a witness. Speed was charged with one count of accessory after the fact.

The investigation, led by Massachusetts State Police and Brockton Police, included extensive witness interviews, surveillance footage analysis, and crime scene examination.

Brockton typically has among the highest homicide rates per capita in the state, but the city’s overall violent crime rate relatively remained level from 2019 through 2023, according to the state’s crime data dashboard. Homicides jumped from four in 2020 to eight in 2021, with elevated numbers persisting through 2024.

“Two young people have lost their lives on Saturday night, and our hearts go out to their families,” Cruz said shortly after the incident last year. “This is a senseless loss of life, and one death via gun violence is too many.”

title: ‘It feels like home’: Vietnamese community rings in Lunar New Year at Tet in Boston
text:
“It’s as close as you can get,” added his wife, Van Nguyen, also 39, who joined him in the United States just last year.

The Lunar New Year — known as the Spring Festival in China, Tet in Vietnam, and Seollal in Korea — is a major festival celebrated in several Asian countries and in diaspora communities around the world.

Organized by the Vietnamese American Community of Massachusetts and the New England Intercollegiate Vietnamese Student Association, the festival remains the region’s largest Vietnamese Lunar New Year celebration. On Sunday, it filled the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center in South Boston, a space nearly 10 times larger than last year’s venue.

The added room gave vendors more space as they sold food, clothing, books, and crafts from rows of booths, and allowed volunteers to run children’s activities without the crush of past crowds. For several attendees, the move felt like a recognition of the sizable Vietnamese community that has grown in the city over the past few decades.

“I came when it was really small, but I remember thinking that it felt like home,” said Windy Pham, 33, a Vietnamese immigrant who first attended the Tet festival in 2016. “I’ve been so proud to see it grow. It’s really rewarding to see how the city is supporting and promoting our culture.”

Pham founded Little Ant World, a company that publishes bilingual children’s books and hosts cultural events. More than a dozen of her titles were displayed Sunday at the booth she staffed with her husband and her 4-year-old daughter, Alyssa.

As more Vietnamese families have settled in neighborhoods such as Dorchester and Quincy, Pham said city leaders have helped provide gathering spaces for the community. That push to preserve cultural traditions, she added, has fueled demand for her books.

“A couple of parents actually bought the whole library because they’ve really invested in the culture,” Pham said. “They want to have the next generation carry out these traditions, because otherwise, we’ll lose it.”

Near the edge of the convention center, Thanh Truong watched families line up to pose for photos beneath colorful origami cranes. He sat beside his 6-year-old son, Tyler, who preferred to observe from a distance.

Born in Vietnam, Truong moved to Chelsea as a child and recently relocated to Saugus. He brought his son to the festival hoping to strengthen his connection to his heritage and said he plans to return each year until they can travel to Vietnam together.

“As soon as he walked in, he loved it,” said Truong, 47, of his son. “He has special needs, but this opened his eyes, and as soon as we put on his traditional outfit, he didn’t want to take it off.”

In front of a miniature wooden barn labeled “Lucky Horse Ranch,” Liam Wong, 8, paused to inspect an inflatable horse. He wore the uniform from his Vietnamese martial arts class, the performance he was most excited to watch that afternoon.

Wong, who lives in Quincy, said he had never seen so many Vietnamese people in one place before attending Tet in Boston. The experience deepened his excitement for the holiday, his favorite of the year.

“There’s so many fun things,” Wong said, sipping on a cup of bubble tea. “It feels like a party.”

Near the stage, crowds gathered for the lion dance, a traditional costumed performance meant to ward off evil spirits. Nearby, Delilah Dao, 18, held what she called “authentic coffee” in one hand and a hefty bánh mì sandwich in the other.

Dao, who was born in Boston, said many of the Vietnamese relatives and friends now live across the country. This annual festival offers a rare chance to see the community come together, she said.

“In a way, even though I wasn’t born in Vietnam, it kind of feels like home,” she said. “I just love it.”

Material from the Associated Press was used in this report.

title: When Mass. legalized weed, it promised to help communities harmed by the war on drugs. Has it gone far enough?
text:
There’s no question that the playing field is more level than it otherwise would be. Licenses to deliver marijuana have so far been awarded solely to equity applicants, and a recent report found more than half of delivery businesses are owned by people of color. Cannabis cafe licenses, approved in December, will also go exclusively to equity entrepreneurs and other small operators for the first five years, allowing people to legally smoke marijuana in public. The social equity trust fund, which is turning cannabis tax dollars into a form of reparations, has doled out nearly $29 million in grants of up to $500,000 apiece, with another round set to be awarded soon.

But many equity participants don’t have access to the resources it takes to survive in an increasingly corporate industry dominated by white, wealthy investors. Some have prison records; others jumped in with little business experience.

And the volatility of the industry isn’t helping. Retail prices have fallen sharply and competition is increasing. Taxes remain punishingly high, and many banks still refuse to work with cannabis businesses due to the federal ban. The state’s Cannabis Control Commission has even started discussing a freeze on new licenses.

Massachusetts has been heralded as a pioneer in cannabis equity, but being first has come with a steep learning curve. In New York, for instance, where recreational pot sales began about three years ago, strict rules were put in place to limit the power of big cannabis companies. There, retail licenses were initially awarded exclusively to equity applicants, whereas equity dispensaries here had to compete right out of the gate with well-funded medical marijuana providers that had been in business for years, often in prime locations.

Shannon O’Brien, chair of the Cannabis Control Commission, acknowledged the programs have not been fully successful.

“We have not met the mission of promoting social equity,” she said.

Of the nearly 21,000 people working in the cannabis industry around the state, 7 percent of general employees identify as Black and almost 10 percent as Latino — lower shares than in the overall population. Senior-level roles are even less diverse.

Ruben Seyde is the son of Mexican immigrants and grew up in Fitchburg, one of the areas the state considers disproportionately impacted by marijuana arrests. After joining the social equity program, Seyde launched his Clinton-based delivery business, Delivered Inc., in 2023, and thought he’d be able to break even within six months. But an initial rule requiring two workers per vehicle, intended to prevent robberies, drove up costs, and restrictions on delivering to certain communities have limited revenues.

At this point, Seyde, 30, doesn’t expect to turn a profit until the end of this year.

“The way that the social equity program was pitched to a lot of us was that it would be an opportunity to build generational wealth or to build some start of stability at a minimum,” he said. “The dreams we pictured at the beginning have changed significantly.”

Other efforts around the country are also coming up short. More than a dozen states with equity programs have helped expand access to cannabis licenses and limit corporate dominance, but converting them into operational businesses, with power to help shape the market, has been a much bigger challenge.

“They create a lot of false hope, and in a lot of ways they set people up for failure,” said Cory Waggoner, chief executive of Higher Yields Cannabis Consulting, a Denver firm that works with social equity businesses around the country. “Most of [the equity programs] fall flat on their face.”

In Massachusetts, the two main equity efforts are the economic empowerment initiative, which expedited the licensing process in 2018, and the ongoing social equity program, which has provided free training and reduced fees, along with nonlicense tracks for budtenders and other jobs, to nearly 1,200 people.

In Worcester, Ulysses Youngblood has used this boost to create a small empire. At Major Bloom, employees make everything from gummies to topical ointments in a gleaming stainless-steel manufacturing kitchen. They sell those products in a storefront brightened by vibrant paintings and also deliver them to customers’ doors. Having three licenses is key to having a sustainable enterprise, said Youngblood, who was kicked out of college for marijuana-related offenses and later got his MBA and worked in corporate sales. Anything else is a “pipe dream.” But many people don’t have the money to do this.

It cost Youngblood $1.4 million to get up and running, much of which he borrowed from an entrepreneur he played college football with. Because Youngblood had to keep a majority ownership stake to be part of the economic empowerment program, he wasn’t able to turn to investors looking for a sizable share in the business — a conundrum many equity participants face.

Major Bloom’s production manager, Sheldon Straker, had less luck with the social equity program. He wanted to commercialize his patent for a process to make tinctures, but without tools such as an incubator program, his idea never got off the ground.

Training is a huge component of the program, O’Brien said, pointing to an extensive curriculum for every type of license, all the way up to classes targeting investors and creating brand awareness.

But for Straker, without a way to test his business model, the program didn’t go far enough.

“There’s more to the equation of fulfilling this equity promise than just giving people access to education,” he said, the scent of weed thick in the air.

The recreational cannabis industry has generated more than $8.8 billion in sales since 2018, but revenues have essentially plateaued over the past two years. Taxes paid by businesses, on the other hand, are still sky-high, with an effective rate of 60 to 80 percent. Owners could get some relief now that marijuana is on track to be downgraded to a Schedule III drug federally, which would allow them to deduct expenses such as rent and wages.

Meanwhile, lawmakers are debating whether to raise the retail license cap from three to as many as six, which could have a significant impact on equity operators.

Increasing the limit could make the market more attractive for well-funded companies — some of which have already tried to skirt the license cap — opening the door to owning a larger slice of the industry.

Equity entrepreneurs are floundering as it is, said Chris Fevry, whose partner in the delivery company Dris has social equity status. An operation allowed to have six dispensaries would “consume everyone,” he said, and push out small businesses.

At the same time, the existing limit could make it harder for owners to sell. Payton Shubrick, chief executive and founder of 6 Brick’s dispensary in Springfield, said people assumed she was on track to be a millionaire when she got her license. But it would have made more sense financially to stay at her corporate job, where she could have continued padding her retirement account and building up generational wealth.

She’d like to have the same opportunity to cash in that other companies have, but the three-store license cap limits the number of potential buyers. If she owned a pizza shop, with far fewer regulations, she said, it wouldn’t be a problem.

“Having license caps in cannabis has created a dynamic where many groups are struggling and don’t have an exit strategy,” she said. “There’s no one to sell to.”

Kobie Evans, co-owner of Pure Oasis, the state’s first Black-owned dispensary and the first pot shop to open in Boston, disputes this, noting several recent sales. Evans, a former real estate agent from Dorchester, had been counting on a sizable award from the trust fund to open his third dispensary, in Brighton. But when he only got $50,000 — with little explanation why — he was forced to turn to a high-interest loan.

“We’re kind of out over our skis because we thought for sure that we’d get funding,” he said.

Some business owners admit to being overly reliant on the fund. Ryan Cohen said it was a “death sentence” when his $300,000 grant application was denied — and he didn’t know why; he closed his Hudson delivery operation six months later.

Cities with robust support systems have seen more success. In Boston, where an ordinance requires one equity license to be approved for every nonequity license, and equity operators get free assistance from architects, lawyers, and other experts, half the licensed cannabis enterprises are equity businesses.

Adding licenses for public marijuana consumption to the mix — going just to equity applicants at first — represents one of the biggest opportunities since the industry was legalized, said Shekia Scott, who designed the CCC’s social equity program and is now the senior cannabis industry manager for the city of Boston. Cannabis cafes will provide a legal space for occupants of federal public housing — as well as tourists and other renters — to partake and also allow operators to further broaden their customer base by partnering with coffee shops and other mainstream businesses.

But being the only license holders hasn’t been enough for equity owners in the delivery business, which accounts for nearly a third of all equity licenses. A December report from the Donahue Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst found some successes but noted that the exclusivity policy hadn’t provided the low barrier to entry or financial feasibility that was intended.

In the beginning of the recreational cannabis industry, equity was all about giving everyone a fair shot at a license, said Damian Fagon, policy director at the Parabola Center for Law and Policy, a cannabis policy think tank based in Malden. But in New York, where Fagon directs the Bronx Cannabis Hub, equity has evolved into an economic development project.

Unlike in Massachusetts, companies that run retail shops in New York aren’t allowed to own cultivation or manufacturing businesses, limiting market control for big players with deep pockets; exclusive arrangements are prohibited, meaning one dispensary with the financial means can’t corner the market on a popular brand. These guardrails help equity owners compete and gain market power, Fagon said.

“Access doesn’t just mean a license,” he said. “It means a viable small business that you can hold onto for generations and has a real stake in shaping the market.”

title: How a Hyde Park basketball program is bringing sport and community together
text:
These days, Mair is the starting point guard at Duke and one of the top success stories to emerge from Hercule’s work with young athletes. Mair said each time she comes back to Boston, she visits Hercule to work with and speak to girls in his programs.

In 2021, Hercule founded The Hoops Collaborative, a nonprofit based in Hyde Park that provides free, advanced basketball clinics and games for all ages and skill levels. Along with training, the program invites local community leaders and speakers to each session and supplies participants with food and self-care products.

“Them seeing that collaboration within itself means a lot,” Mair said. “Giving to the community as people have given back to me, I think it just means a lot.

“Over the years, he started doing more and more for the community as he got more opportunities and more supplies from people who are donating.”

Mair isn’t the only player for whom working with Hercule helped them reach another level. His program alumni include Denia Davis-Stewart of Merrimack, Darion Jordan-Thomas of UMass Lowell, and Valentina Pepic of Niagara.

Hercule, an O’Bryant High School graduate and 2001 UMass Boston alumnus, played for the Beacons all four years as a walk-on, and was named most improved and most valuable player in his senior season. He began coaching with the UMass Boston women’s team as an assistant in 2004, and later shifted to the high school level with boys and girls at East Boston High School for seven years, then New Mission for two seasons, before moving to English High in 2015.

In his fifth year of coaching, Hercule decided he wanted to bring resources to his students away from the court when they started expressing interests outside of the game.

That became his inspiration in launching Herc42Skills.

“There’s more than the game that surrounds basketball, there’s so many different avenues you can attack,” he said. “I know different people from all walks of life through the game of basketball.”

Though Herc42Skills caters to all youth, The Hoops Collaborative, held at Match Community Day Charter School, has a special focus on young women. Hercule noticed early on that many girls were reluctant to join his clinics out of fear of slowing the program or a lack of confidence.

“I wanted to just create a program where we had a beginner and a pro in the program at the same time,” he said.

On game days at The Hoops Collaborative, girls from six local schools pack the gym with their families, coaches, and referees, and play three games a night. Live music and food is provided. Community leaders and special guests connect with participants after training, to close drills and practices.

The goal for the collaborative is to use sports as a catalyst to give girls a head start on mentorship, career development, self care, and civic engagement.

“You can only be what you can see,” Hercule said.

Guest speakers have ranged from attorneys, law enforcement, firefighters, professional players such as Celtics star Jayson Tatum, and local leaders, including Mayor Michelle Wu. In November, the program received recognition from congresswoman Ayanna Pressley and shared the court with the Celtics during pregame.

“We can create a lane and affect as many young people as possible,” Hercule said.

Outside of the evening events, the program keeps participants engaged through Sunday dinners, tours of NBA facilities, trips to WNBA games, and donation drives.

Parents have been the biggest advocates of Hercule’s programming, saying their children have seen many benefits from being involved.

“He makes sure everybody leaves with something, whether it’s advice or connecting them with someone,” said Rob Bullock, whose children, Taylor (12) and Robert (15), have been involved since the collaborative’s inception.

“To be connected with people through the sport she loves, that teaches her how important and how valuable she is has been amazing,” Bullock said of his daughter.

Youth empowerment and mental care is one of the most appreciated benefits of the program for parents. The collaborative also brings therapists to the program to help children who have experienced traumas.

Shannon Boon’s 10-year-old daughter, Catherine, has found ways to open up through these services. Boon’s husband died in 2018, and it was difficult for her two children. Boon said the counselors can “mentor you in sports and at the same we can talk about what’s going on in your life.”

“That’s going to bridge a gap where they wouldn’t be open to discussing things, to developing a therapeutic relationship if it wasn’t coming from that approach,” she added.

Boon, who is white and has biracial children, said her daughter also experiences a strong sense of belonging, and she is eager to attend all programs Hercule is leading.

Boon said of all the sports programs in which her children participate, Hercule’s is the best. Affordability (the programs are free) is a leading factor.

“It can be difficult, if you have a talented athlete, to find programming that’s feasible if you have mid to lower income,” she said.

Catherine Boon often has to play with students a few grades ahead of her to find a challenge, but with the collaborative, quality training that will push her skills is easily accessible. All coaches and leaders in the collaborative are volunteers.

Parents are hoping programs such as The Hoops Collaborative see more funding from the city and donors. Hercule is looking to keep his network across the city active with his students and open doors on and off the court.

“It’s not just what The Hoops Collaborative can do on a weekly basis,” Boon said. “It’s that exponential reach that it has for the future.”

title: Why is this year’s St. Patrick’s Day parade going the opposite way? The answer goes back to 1776.
text:
Sound familiar? You’d be excused for forgetting that in years past, the parade kicked off at the Broadway MBTA Station and headed southeast, turning around up City Point, before heading west through Telegraph Hill and ending at Andrew.

Unless you’re particularly concerned about watching the parade go left-to-right rather than right-to-left, it may not seem like much of a change. (The one “real” change is an extra stretch tacked on to the end of the parade, a few blocks past the Broadway MBTA Station on A Street.)

But some locals are welcoming the decision — and, given the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day (the withdrawal of British troops from Boston in 1776), celebrating its historical implications.

“The residents of Andrew Square are thrilled about this,” said Linda Zablocki, president of the Andrew Square Civic Association.

For starters, Zablocki said, it’s a return to tradition. Originally, the parade kicked off in Andrew Square and worked its way north toward Broadway. It was reversed in 1988 to start on Broadway and head south, the Globe reported.

But the change is especially poignant given that this St. Patrick’s Day will also be the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day — the day the British army fled the city of Boston on March 17, 1776.

Over the winter of 1775–76, dozens of cannons captured from the British at Fort Ticonderoga in upstate New York were hauled over the Berkshires and across Massachusetts. George Washington, commander of the Continental Army, used the cannons to fortify the Dorchester Heights, atop what is now South Boston’s Telegraph Hill.

Under the cover of darkness, the colonists dragged the cannons from Roxbury to the peak of the heights. In the process, they marched through an area identified as the modern Andrew Square, up what are now Dorchester and Telegraph Streets — a march that closely mirrors the new climb of the parade.

“If that hadn’t happened, we’d all be speaking in a British accent right now,” Zablocki said.

City Councilor Ed Flynn, who represents the neighborhood, said the change was “fitting and proper” for the occasion, especially given the build-up to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence later this year.

“We’re proud of our history in South Boston, and we recognize the historic time we’re in and the contributions made up at Dorchester Heights,” Flynn said. “It’s about celebrating not only Boston history, but American history.”

Flynn said that residents of Andrew Square had petitioned for the change in light of the anniversary, and that parade organizers viewed it as a “fair request.”

The South Boston Allied War Veterans Council, which runs the parade, did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday.

Zablocki also suggested the change would contribute to a more orderly atmosphere in Andrew Square; rowdiness, she said, tends to be worse at the end of the parade route than at the start.

“But that’s a problem everywhere in the city,” she added.

The St. Patrick’s Day parade, which has historically drawn roughly a million people into the city, has gained a mixed reputation among South Boston residents. Past parades have been criticized for rampant drinking, violent brawls, and other displays of public indecency.

That’s been the case for years — as far back as the 1970s, residents were bemoaning public drinking, the Globe reported. In 2016, then-Mayor Marty Walsh tried to shorten the parade route in the name of public safety, but his efforts were blocked by a federal judge who ordered the city to allow the event to proceed along its typical route.

Last year, police warned there would be “zero tolerance” for misconduct at the parade. Flynn acknowledged that the 2025 festivities were an improvement from previous years.

“We’re preparing and continuing to meet with city, state and federal officials,” he said. “This is not a Mardi Gras atmosphere.”

This year, parade organizers have also added a specific-place for “family-friendly viewing,” at Medal of Honor Park along Broadway.

“We wanted to make sure that families, and [especially] our military families, are respected,” Flynn said. “And that there’s an opportunity for them to watch the parade in a safe and healthy environment.”

The parade won’t be the only commemoration of Evacuation Day. On March 17, a procession of re-enactors and public figures will march through South Boston and re-dedicate the Dorchester Heights monument, a spokesperson announced on Tuesday.

The event, the spokesperson said, will culminate in celebratory cannon fire.

title: Alpha Kappa Alpha sisters who joined sorority as Boston college students ‘come home’ for conference
text:
Women returning to Boston, some after many years, are embracing the nostalgia of their campus days, members said.

“We’re feeling lots of energy to be in Boston,” said Spearman, who joined AKA in 1984. “When we were in school together, we used to visit each other’s campuses.”

Alumni will network this weekend with AKA members from about 15 local chapters, including Harvard, Northeastern, and Suffolk universities, organizers said.

The high cost of securing a conference space, along with lodging and food, had been an impediment to holding the event in Boston in recent years, members said.

Boston has changed in many ways since AKA last held a conference here in 1997, women said, pointing to more local groups and businesses that welcome, or are led by, people of color.

Black Bostonians who are part of the sorority want to highlight that shift for members who have lived elsewhere since college, members said.

“There are a lot of institutions in Boston that are celebrating Black Americans,” said Kafi Meadows, another graduate of Wellesley College. “We want to showcase the diversity of Boston for the members of our sorority.”

Alpha Kappa Alpha was founded in 1908 at Howard University in Washington, D.C. It has been a collegiate and professional home for generations of Black women, with members including former Vice President Kamala Harris, Nobel Prize-winning author Toni Morrison, tennis champion Althea Gibson, civil rights leader Coretta Scott King, and poet Maya Angelou.

AKA members said their Boston chapters are especially valuable for African-American students, who are traditionally underrepresented in the city.

“Being able to create that collective community and find a critical mass and also pour back into the undergraduate community was definitely a highlight,” said 36-year-old Farrah Belizaire, who graduated from Boston University in 2011 after growing up in Brockton.

This year, attendees are also celebrating the Boston area’s main group for AKA college graduates, which marks its 100th anniversary.

Founded in 1926, the Psi Omega Chapter builds on the legacy of college-educated Black women who called Boston home and dedicated themselves to the sisterhood throughout the 20th century, Meadows said.

“All of this is legacy. We’re building on those who came before us and we’re creating something for the generations that come up behind us,” said Meadows, 54, who grew up in Dorchester.

While many may associate AKA with Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) that are spread across the South, there is a special community of Black collegiate life in Boston, members said.

“Black fraternity and sorority life often has more visibility and is ingrained a little bit more in the southern parts of our country,” said Belizaire, who lives in Randolph and has helped run the sorority’s chapter for southeast Massachusetts. “But a lot of our organizations have had just as much of an impact in the northeastern parts of the country, where we’re not always as strongly represented in numbers.”

The conference kicked off Thursday with a donation drive for Paige Academy Community Cultural Center and Home for Little Wanderers, according to the sorority.

On Saturday, performers will put on a step show “homecoming takeover” dance party featuring DJ Kid Capri.

Members of other Black Greek-letter organizations and members of the public can purchase tickets for the Saturday party on Eventbrite.

title: While peers enjoy week off, some Boston students study for first health care certifications
text:
“Some people, during break, they don’t have anything to do,” said Calvin Grayson, a Grade 11 student from Dorchester Center. “It allows us to study for something that’s really important for our lives.”

The school, a longstanding in-district charter school, is in the early stages of a new partnership with Mass General Brigham announced in 2024. The partnership, funded by a $38 million grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies, aims to help fill the more than 13,000 health care vacancies across the state and give more Boston students a path to the middle class.

Grayson, for example, now lists his potential future hospital jobs like items on a grocery list, up to one day becoming a surgeon. As a nursing aide, Grayson could work through college and medical school, he said, exactly the sort of outcome school leaders hope for.

The review week is the latest innovation enabled by the Mass General Brigham partnership, which is also slated to double enrollment, add additional state-approved career training programs, and offer students critical hands-on experience in hospitals and nursing homes

For Mass General Brigham, the partnership is intended to help them fill staff shortages. They have more than 2,000 staff vacancies each year. Acute hospital staff shortages that arose during the pandemic have abated somewhat, but problems persist, with more than 13,000 vacancies for positions such as nurses and technicians at hospitals across the state.

But the hospital network also hopes career programs such as health assisting, which includes the CNA certification, will offer economic mobility for the students, said H. Kay Howard, Mass General Brigham’s director of health careers training.

“There’s all these different roles, many of which don’t require a college degree ... but then have tremendous pathways for growth,” Howard said. It “gives them really strong choices.”

Health care has become the driver of US job growth, accounting for nearly two-thirds of new jobs in January.

About three-quarters of Edward M. Kennedy students are low-income, and more than 90 percent are Black or Latino. Nearly all graduate on time and a larger faction go on to college than in Boston as a whole.

Many certified nursing assistants work in long-term care facilities, helping residents eat and wash and taking note of any changing needs or symptoms. Alongside the exam, nursing aides need on-site training, which Edward M. Kennedy students are getting through six weeks of shadowing nursing aides.

Ghyani Burris-Rowell, another student at the bootcamp, said she’d like to one day open her own nursing home with her mom.

“I really love old folks,” she said. “I just enjoy giving them that care. It’s what you would want for yourself, but you might not be in the state to do for yourself.”

Burris-Rowell said she’s missing her February break and all the extra sleep she’d be getting. “But I know I’m going to appreciate it," she added.

During the bootcamp, students begin each morning with a 75-minute practice test for the knowledge portion of the aide exam. Teachers then lead reviews of the material or guide students through practices of the skills portion of the exam.

In Burris-Rowell’s class, students broke down the process of emptying a urine bag in extreme detail. One girl politely introduced herself to the mannequin patient and asked for permission before pulling a privacy curtain in behind her. Two others deliberated on the volume of the urine they collected.

An instructor gave a boy his trick for removing a gown without contaminating himself.

“Imagine it’s the dirtiest thing on the front of you, that you don’t want to touch,” he said.

Most of the skills are simple, but the dozens of different steps add up. Whether students use their training to work in nursing homes or hospitals or they pursue further education, it will give them more choices, said Annemarie Tesora, a registered nurse and teacher at the school.

In the first year of the hospital partnership, 51 students in grades 11 and 12 passed the CNA exam. This year, 52 more, all in Grade 11, are eligible to take it. As seniors, they will bring their skills to weeklong stints at Mass General Brigham hospitals.

The school will add a medical assisting program next year, with students picking between the current health assisting pathway and the new medical assisting option in Grade 9. Students who follow that program will be able to get jobs or further education in areas including X-ray technology and sterile handling of surgical tools.

Like many career-oriented high schools around Massachusetts, Edward M. Kennedy leaders have plans to expand further. Currently, the school serves just 424 students, but it has long had hundreds of students on its waitlist.

The city is currently seeking a new site, with a goal of moving in the fall of 2028. Enrollment would double, classrooms would have space for model hospital rooms that meet standards of care, and the school would add a third career program, biotech. Students in that pathway could go on to laboratory science or pathology roles.

During the summer, the state also approved a partnership for the school to offer courses from Bunker Hill Community College.

For years, Tesora taught the same health assisting course at Northeast Metro Tech, a vocational high school in Wakefield. She called her Boston students’ experience “unparalleled.”

“There’s no other school around that’s doing what EMK is doing,” she said. “They get such great experiences.”

title: MBTA announces several service suspensions for signal upgrades in March
text:
The Red Line will be suspended from Broadway to Ashmont station during the weekend of Feb. 21-22 for signal upgrades and modernization work.

Free shuttle buses will run to all stations between Broadway and Ashmont.

Commuters traveling to Downtown Crossing from Ashmont should plan for at least an additional 40 minutes of travel.

The Orange Line will be suspended between Back Bay and Forest Hills for nine days, between Feb. 28 and Mar. 8.

Free and accessible shuttle buses will be available, but commuters should plan for extra travel time.

Riders are also encouraged to consider the commuter rail for free service. The trip between Forest Hills and Back Bay takes about 10 minutes, the MBTA said.

The MBTA will be working on commuter rail lines during weekends in February and March as part of the North Station Terminal Area Signal System Improvement Project. The proposed budget for the project is $45.2 million.

“This project is replacing the obsolete signal system that controls the movement of MBTA Commuter Rail and Amtrak trains in and out of North Station with a new, state-of-the-art microprocessor system that requires less maintenance and reduces failures and train delays,” the MBTA said.

The suspensions on the four lines will take place on Feb. 21–22, Feb. 28–March 1, March 7–8, March 21–22, and March 28–29.

On those days, Fitchburg line service will be suspended between North Station and Porter.

Riders can take the Red Line from Porter, then switch to the Green Line at Park Street to arrive at North Station.

On the Haverhill line, service will be suspended between North Station and Oak Grove.

The MBTA recommends riders take the Orange Line instead.

On the Lowell line, service between North Station and Anderson/Woburn will be suspended, as will Newburyport/Rockport line service between North Station and Swampscott.

Free shuttle buses will be available.

title: Man who raped two women in Dorchester in 1994 is granted parole from life sentence
text:
He committed the assaults on the evening of Sept. 16, 1994, when he was 30, the ruling said.

Just after 6 p.m., Kelley rang the doorbell of a 76-year-old woman who was expecting a visiting nurse to come and care for her ill husband.

However, when she looked out the blinds she saw Kelley, who had done repair work at her residence on multiple occasions, the ruling said.

When she opened the door, Kelley said he had material for a contractor meeting him at the residence to do work.

The woman let Kelley inside, and he grabbed her from behind and put his arm around her neck, the ruling said. He told her he had a gun and knife and forced her to the kitchen area.

Kelley hit her with a bottle and frying pan and also slapped and threatened to kill her, telling her to “keep quiet and shut [her mouth],” the ruling said.

He forced her to the second floor where he repeatedly raped her, the ruling said. He also took about $75, “stating that he was a drug addict who needed a fix and that he would kill her because he did not mind dying,” the ruling said.

At some point after 7:30 p.m., the visiting nurse rang the doorbell and entered the home. She encountered Kelley, who forced her upstairs at knifepoint, telling the 31-year-old to remove her clothes because he was going to rape her, the ruling said.

Kelley told the nurse that he “could kill her,” the ruling said, and he claimed that he “had killed a police officer before.”

He later threw her on a bed and raped her, according to the ruling.

“Mr. Kelley then took both women downstairs, where he went through their pocketbooks looking for money,” the ruling said. “He locked them both in the bathroom and barricaded the door. He ripped the phones out of the walls and fled the scene.”

The board had rejected Kelley’s four prior bids for release before his fifth hearing went forward in September, officials said.

He has completed sex offender treatment and other rehabilitative programs, the ruling said.

“Mr. Kelley’s offense was directly related to addiction,” the decision said. “He has been sober for 30 years. Mr. Kelley demonstrated further insight into his pattern of offending and invested in Restorative Justice practices.”

He’s also gone more than 11 years without any disciplinary reports, the board said.

Once he’s out, he’ll have to abide by several conditions including maintaining a nightly curfew, staying off drugs and alcohol, refraining from contacting the victims’ families, and participating in mental health counseling for “adjustment, depression and anger management,” the ruling said.

Kelley will also have to comply with mandatory sex offender conditions, the ruling said.

He remained incarcerated Thursday at the North Central Correctional Institution, a minimum- and medium-security facility in Gardner, according to a Department of Correction database.

title: The sting (and promise) of speed cameras
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

The news about cameras tracking and ticketing speeding drivers has stirred our readers. Some of you sent missives in support (“we use it for tolls, why not?”) and in opposition (“it’s un-American,” “it jacks up insurance premiums”).

Here are a few views, and I’ve asked the Globe’s Matt Stout to answer concerns — and look at next steps.

Reader Amy Sutherland is pro-speed cameras, “especially if they can nail people turning right from the far left lane!” In fact, she’d be OK with cameras on sidewalks to capture e-bikes whooshing around pedestrians.

Richard Nichols compares speed cameras to ATMs, sold to us as helpful but emerging as a profit-maker that banks (or communities with speed cameras) increasingly rely upon for revenue.

For Jonathan Soroff, it’s all about improving our miserable traffic flow. Citing one example, he writes that cameras should be used to ticket “drivers who block the box during rush hour.”

David: Matt, where do we go from here? What’s the next step for the Massachusetts proposal?

Matt Stout: There could be a few — or none. It depends on what state lawmakers do. Governor Maura Healey included her proposal to allow speed cameras in school zones and construction zones in her budget proposal, which lawmakers will rewrite and debate through the spring. Other bills allowing for cameras to catch not only those speeding but also motorists who drive through a red light or “block the box,” still are working their way through the Legislature and have yet to surface for a vote in either the House or Senate. For either to survive, they’d have to win approval in both chambers by the end of July.

What limits would be placed on speed cameras, or would they be up to the communities’ discretion?

That depends on the proposal. Healey’s plan would limit them to school and construction zones, and would cap cameras in any town or city to one camera per 5,000 residents. The other bills would require a city council or select board to approve where cameras go only after they hold a public hearing.

Are supporters aware of the aversion to growing Big Brother tracing of us, from Ring networks or faulty AI face-recognition used by ICE?

Supporters argue that cameras are already everywhere and in some cases — such as police departments’ use of license plate readers — are not regulated in a way speed cameras would under their proposal. As one state representative put it: “We’ve got a universal dragnet, which is fine, but actually enforcing the law is something that we can’t do.”

How much of a difference do supporters say the speed cameras would make?

They argue it could make a big difference. Lawmakers and proponents say that first off, their proposal isn’t about generating a new piggy bank for towns and cities — their proposal would require that any net revenue flow to a state trust fund. Also, cameras can alter driver behavior and ultimately help make the roads safer.

That’s not to say they’re popular. Their introduction can often spark fierce pushback, especially in the beginning; look no further than Providence, where one resident in 2018 called it “political terrorism.” Eight years later, cameras are still around Rhode Island, albeit with mixed results, according to data compiled by Rhode Island’s NBC 10.

Readers, the Globe will be keeping a (human) eye on this.
