title: R.I. legislators take aim at private equity in health care amid Fatima, Roger Williams hospitals crisis
text:
But Rhode Island can’t stop there, because private equity and corporate medicine could very well endanger other hospitals and medical facilities in the state, jeopardizing the health of some of Rhode Island’s most vulnerable residents, Senator Linda L. Ujifusa said Thursday.

Ujifusa, a Portsmouth Democrat, and Representative Kathleen A. Fogarty, a South Kingstown Democrat, have filed two bills aimed at protecting Rhode Island’s health care system from the abuses they see in private equity ownership and the corporate practice of medicine, which Ujifusa called “a national issue.”

“We have important hospitals that are at risk of following the same path as Fatima and Roger Williams,” Ujifusa said, noting that South County Hospital has been facing financial problems, like many hospitals. “We are trying to shift from crisis response to early prevention.”

In January, Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey signed into law a bill touted as a first-in-the-nation effort to monitor and rein in private equity in the hospital industry. The goal is to prevent the sort of profiteering that critics say contributed to the financial collapse of Steward Health Care, the loss of hospitals in Dorchester and Ayer, and at least 15 patient deaths.

Ujifusa said the Rhode Island legislation would not go as far as the new Massachusetts law, but it would create a “transparency and early warning” system that could potentially prevent private equity from buying up Rhode Island hospitals in the future.

The bill would require health care entities to provide the attorney general and the state Health Department with certain financial and organizational information before transactions take place.

State officials could then conduct a review, and the entities involved in the deal would have to show that “the transaction will not result in a significant reduction in competition, increase in cost, or harm to access, quality, or equity.”

State officials would have the power to approve the transaction, approve it with conditions, or reject it.

The bill would add to the powers that the attorney general and the Health Department already have over such transactions under the Hospital Conversions Act, as well as under anti-trust and consumer protection laws, Ujifusa said.

“This legislation strengthens transparency, oversight, and accountability for private corporate actors that can currently extract profits from Rhode Island health care providers with little public scrutiny, often at the expense of patients, health care workers, and community stability,” Fogarty said in a statement.

Ujifusa said Rhode Island cannot pretend that the crisis facing Our Lady of Fatima and Roger Williams Medical Center is a “one-off situation.”

“It is a national issue,” she said. “Private equity has harmed hospitals across the country, including next door with Massachusetts and the Steward hospitals.”

Ujifusa said she believes private equity should not be involved in health care.

“Health care is such a fundamental right,” she said. “It should not ever be treated as just a business, even though it sometimes is, because lives are at stake, and we should never put private profits above public health.”

She said the Rhode Island bills are based on model legislation developed by the National Academy for State Health Policy, and they’re informed by analyses conducted by researchers at the Center for Advancing Health Policy through Research at the Brown University School of Public Health.

Ujifusa said the legislation matters to all Rhode Islanders because any hospital closure has a big impact in such a small state. For example, when Memorial Hospital closed in Pawtucket, the emergency rooms at The Miriam Hospital and Rhode Island Hospital in Providence saw a significant influx, she said.

It’s important for the state to take legislative action, Ujifusa said, because there are virtually no federal laws that restrict private equity in health care.

Ujifusa and Fogarty also have introduced the Rhode Island Ban on the Corporate Practice of Medicine Act.

That bill would prohibit entities without health care provider licenses to own a medical practice or employ health care licensees, or to indirectly or directly interfere with the professional judgment of a licensee.

The legislators said that bill targets “corporate rollups” that consolidate independent medical practices under centralized corporate ownership or management.

“These arrangements allow non-clinical entities to influence medical decision-making without being subject to the same professional, ethical, or public accountability standards as licensed health care providers,” they said in a statement.

Such corporate structures “weaken clinical independence, obscure responsibility for patient outcomes, and allow corporate owners to profit from health care delivery while avoiding accountability for harms affecting patients, workers, and communities,” the legislators said.

Ujifusa said corporate control of health care can distort clinical decision-making, diverting resources away from patient care and into shareholder pockets. “When profit comes before patients, people get hurt and lives are put at risk,” she said.

title: ‘It’s so hard just to survive’: How Gen Zers in Greater Boston are making it
text:
Many who choose to stay are living lean. The Globe spoke with several twentysomethings to better understand how they are managing high costs. Some said they have grown accustomed to skipping meals, or putting off medical appointments. Others track their expenses with the precision of accountants, and still come up short.

Here are a few of their stories.

Josie Golder lives in a 200-square-foot attic in Beacon Hill. The heat is spotty, the ceiling slanted. Located directly above an empty storefront, the space has just enough room to squeeze a full-sized bed in and little else.

When Golder graduated from law school at Northeastern University last spring, many of her peers flocked to cushy jobs at corporate firms, where they’re making around $200,000 a year, she said. She chose a less lucrative path — working for the city in employment and labor law — but one that allows her to make an impact on the community and pay the bills.

She tries to keep her weekly expenses to less than $250 so she can pay off her law school loans as quickly as possible — handing over about $1,000 every month.

“I have a spending tracker,” she said. “I’m very on top of things.”

After two years, the rent on her tiny studio is still less than $2,000 a month, and her landlord has promised to not raise it. To keep laundry costs down, Golder washes her clothes in the bathtub with a portable washer and dryer.

Though small, her place is close to public transportation, plenty of stores, and her City Hall office, where she’s required to work in-person five days a week.

For work clothes, she primarily thrifts at Goodwill and Covet, a consignment shop where she sells items in exchange for a discount on future purchases. She buys most of her groceries at the budget-friendly Trader Joe’s and meal preps daily.

Golder puts some savings aside for emergencies when she can. She likes to catch a movie at the Alamo Drafthouse in the Seaport on a Tuesday, when tickets are cheaper.

Golder said she’s in a fortunate position compared to many others.

“I recognize my privilege,” she said. “It’s crazy how people the same age can be on such different trajectories.”

A breakup last summer prompted Ella Halpine to consider living on her own in Boston.

But even cramped studios were going to break the bank for Halpine, who makes around $57,000 a year as a graphic designer at a Boston nonprofit. So she packed up her bags and two cats — Dolly and Carl, named for Dolly Parton and her late husband Carl Dean — and moved into a 450-square-foot studio apartment in Worcester.

Adjusting to life without roommates — and the move itself — presented new challenges. Halpine has amassed almost $10,000 in credit card debt in the past year, adding to her nearly $14,000 in student loan debt.

She meticulously tracks every cent in an elaborate spreadsheet and aims to keep her monthly budget around $3,700, which includes $1,500 for rent, $250 for groceries, and $200 for utilities. Much of her income goes toward paying down debt.

“I usually have to move things around constantly or figure out how I can make a couple extra dollars and commissions for the month,” Halpine said.

Ahead of trips to the supermarket, she loads up on coupons. Occasionally, she allows herself a small treat, like mangoes or a bag of gummy bears. A vegetarian, Halpine typically prepares meals of vegetables, eggs, beans, and rice for the week.

She chose to live next to a train station and commutes to Boston an hour and a half each way a few days every week, a long ride she spends drawing. When she gets home, she said, she collapses on her bed from exhaustion.

The majority of her friends live in the Boston area, but these days, Halpine sees them far less than she’d like. They are struggling to make it work financially, too.

“I don’t know a single person that is able to live alone” in Boston, she said.

Meanwhile, Halpine has become a big fan of Worcester.

The bus is free. The city is less hectic. The art scene, particularly the museum, is vibrant. And the library is among the best she’s ever seen. Halpine will poke around its archives for hours and check out movies, shows, and books — for free.

“Unless something drastic happens, I don’t see myself being able to move back to the Greater Boston area,” she said.

Halpine wrestles with her uncertain future.

Her parents often talk about how valuable travel was during their early adulthood, but the cost of going anywhere now seems astronomical. She has always dreamed of owning a home with a garden, but that vision seems to wilt with each passing day. For now, she just wants to get off the wait list to join her local community garden.

“I was not anticipating being almost 30 and being so far from what I thought was a relatively modest goal,” Halpine said. “Not knowing when or if that will be part of my life plan anymore is really devastating.”

Jordan Elliott often agonizes about life after college. A senior studying communications at Emerson, he’s set to graduate this spring.

He hopes to have a job lined up by then.

At the moment, he works part time at an upscale grocery store making $18 an hour and attends classes four days a week. The schedules often overlap, forcing him into a delicate balancing act of keeping his grades up and earning his next paycheck.

“It’s so hard just to survive. Just to live, you’ve gotta give three different people like $150 to $300,” Elliott said. “I’m trying to still be a kid, but I can’t do that anymore.”

Elliott and his girlfriend, Rebecca Dontje, have contemplated signing up for an EBT card for food benefits. He has developed a habit of skipping meals to save money and neglects going to the doctor, fearing a high bill.

“I’m just distraught because I don’t see this changing any time soon,” Elliott said.

His parents, immigrants from the Caribbean, continue to provide him with support. They buy some of his clothes, and passed down a fully paid-off car.

“They help me with money frequently,” Elliott said. “I really do appreciate them.”

They’ve also offered for Elliott, who says he hasn’t taken out any student loans, and Dontje to live free in a one-bedroom property they own in Dorchester after graduation. The young couple is debating between moving there or staying where they are, in a home her parents own in Cambridge, where they are responsible for paying utilities and any extras, which usually amounts to about $400 a month. Come May, the young couple would have to start paying rent, too.

“At the end of the day, however we can save money, we need to do that,” Elliott said. “We’ve been together for three years now, so we’re trying to build a life together.”

Elliott had his sights set on a career in radio broadcasting, but because funding for public media was slashed, he’s considering other roles.

He has applied to more than 100 jobs since his junior year and says he’s been met with rejections and silence. Still, Elliott returns to LinkedIn every day, desperate to find a new posting to apply to or a connection to expand his network.

“It hurts a lot,” he said. “But you gotta keep moving.”

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Paula Ayala López moved to Boston a little over two years ago after a monthslong job search.

She doesn’t see herself here long term. Everything is just too expensive.

“I have been fortunate enough that I am financially doing well enough now, but I am very aware of the fact that I am reaching the cusp of that,” she said.

When she finally landed her role as a graphic designer, making $67,000 a year, Ayala López was presented with a spur-of-the-moment opportunity to live with three of her friends in a triple-decker unit in Dorchester. She and her roommates split expenses to cut costs, sharing a family plan on Instacart for groceries. But their rent increased by $200 with each renewal, a trend that worried Ayala López.

In September, she and her partner moved into an 800-square-foot, two-bedroom apartment in Brighton, paying $1,300 each for rent. The ceiling leaked for two months. The carbon monoxide alarm didn’t work for weeks. Many maintenance requests have gone unanswered, she said.

“This isn’t worth the amount that I’m paying,” she said.

Every month, they pay $80 to $90 on electricity. They scored a student deal for internet, which costs them about $50. Both remain on their family phone plans.

Ayala López, who mostly works remote, commutes to her job downtown on public transit. Her workplace reimburses half of what she spends on her CharlieCard.

Ayala López tracks her money closely and abides by the 50/30/20 budget rule — allocating 50 percent of her income toward necessities, 30 percent toward “wants,” and 20 percent to savings. She said she often ends up spending more on necessities.

“It definitely comes into play a lot when it comes to like, ‘Can I go out this month?’ ” Ayala López said. “Or do I need to reduce the amount of groceries that I’m buying?”

Ayala López cooks all her meals. Instant ramen is her go-to cheap and quick dinner.

She’s grateful to her younger self for attending a public university in Puerto Rico, where she received a Pell Grant and didn’t need to take out loans. Although she wants to pursue an advanced degree, the costs are just too high.

Ayala López thought she would own a house by now. She has accepted it’s only a matter of time before she’s priced out of Boston. Within a few years, she thinks she will move with her partner somewhere else, very likely out of Massachusetts.

“It’s not sustainable for me to stay here,” Ayala López said. “Which is sad in some respects. I’ve built my communities in Boston and friendships and all this stuff.”

Correction: A previous version of this story misspelled Jordan Elliott’s last name. The Globe regrets the error.

title: At Boston’s snow farms, blizzards meet a watery end
text:
Few people in Eastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island might share that sentiment, following two big, recent storms that have made this winter the snowiest in Boston in a decade. But more might be on the way early next week.

Thanks to the mechanical melters, thousands of truckloads of the white stuff have been transformed almost instantaneously into water at 14 “snow farms” from Hyde Park to East Boston.

“This is a tool in our tool kit now,” said Nick Gove, the city’s interim chief of streets. “And we’re going on the second decade of that. Both the state and the city got into snow farms in a big way in 2015,” which was known as “Snowmageddon.”

In that winter, which brought a record-breaking 110 inches of snow to the city, a snow farm in the Seaport in South Boston famously did not see its last clump of dirty slush disappear until July.

Gove doesn’t think Boston is due for a repeat, but he does believe the final bits of months-old snow will not become a puddle until late April.

“It’s been a long week, a long month,” Gove, who had been roaming the city, said in an interview from his car.

Despite the heavy snow this year, Gove said, the city has not had to ask the state for permission to dump any into Boston Harbor, a practice banned by the state Department of Environmental Protection in 1997. However, at the snow farms the melt is funneled down storm drains, which lead to a system that sometimes can get overwhelmed and discharge into rivers and streams.

Even for the harbor, officials left room for emergency exceptions.

“If we were to get another blizzard this size,” Gove said, “we would potentially be looking to ask” for that option.

By midafternoon Friday, the city had hauled 3,587 truckloads of snow, or approximately 59,344 cubic yards, to snow farms at locations ranging from Bunker Hill Community College in Charlestown, to the former Bayside Expo Center in Dorchester, to the old Edison power plant in South Boston.

The number of farms still being used has dropped by one, to 13, said Anne Roach, spokeswoman for the city’s streets department.

Front-end loaders, backhoes, and 10-wheel dump trucks have been put to work, Gove said, in an expensive, days-long effort to haul the snow to a medley of city, state, and privately owned sites.

The snow farms are dispersed throughout Boston to shorten the haul routes from each neighborhood. And with 802 miles of roadways, easier access to the snow farms makes a difference, Gove said as a warmer sun shined Friday.

“We’re now getting a good assist from Mother Nature — a lot of solar melt, which is a big help,” Gove said.

In West Roxbury off the VFW Parkway, the melter has been chugging away. Plenty of work had been done there by Friday afternoon, and plenty remained. A wall of snow about 400 feet long and 20 feet high waited for its quick transformation to liquid.

In a nonstop routine, a backhoe returned over and over to pluck bulging chunks of speckled snow from a steep, gray mound. Within minutes, the snow had been dumped into the melting tub, only to leave a minute later as a gushing stream of water.

A truck with reserves of diesel fuel was stationed nearby to keep the melter running.

“They’re very, very efficient,” O’Connor said, nodding toward an 80-ton-an-hour guzzler humming away in front of him.

Put in too much snow at once, O’Connor said, and an oversize load could gum up the works. Make it a bit less bulky, and the result will be a smoothly running, snow-chomping success.

“You’ve got to be patient,” O’Connor said.

Kevin Walsh of the Boston Water and Sewer Commission stopped by Friday to inspect the operation — an unending cycle of dump, melt, repeat — and took a few photographs.

“We’re making sure it goes into the storm drains,” said Walsh, adding that erosion-control measures are in place at each of the snow farms.

O’Connor said that a second melter was expected at the site, and that the melting would continue into the night. If all went well, O’Connor said, the rest of the snow might be gone this weekend.

And when might he sleep? “When we can.”

title: State revives long-stalled plans to redevelop Shattuck Hospital site at Franklin Park
text:
On Thursday evening, nearly 100 residents from neighborhoods bordering Franklin Park — including Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan — poured into the Brooke High School auditorium in Mattapan for the first in a series of state-led public listening sessions on the future of the Shattuck Hospital campus.

Residents brought a range of competing visions for the site. Some want to restore the entire tree-lined expanse to open green space, with a meadow lined with paths to walk dogs and relax. Others propose new housing for seniors or military veterans. Still others long for a recreation center with a pool or ice rink, a place to socialize and help keep youths off the streets. Suggestions have also included a community garden, an urgent care clinic, and a 24-hour pharmacy.

For their part, officials in the Healey administration said they are committed to hearing all viewpoints and have no set plans for the site, effectively restarting community outreach efforts that began in 2018. But the Shattuck grounds are restricted under a 1949 state law for “public health” uses, and the state has already said it plans to issue a new request for proposals focused on supportive housing, a service that helps people out of homelessness and addiction by pairing stable housing with counseling, case management, and employment assistance.

For many residents who live next to the 527-acre Franklin Park, long considered the crown jewel of Frederick Law Olmsted’s network of public parks known as the Emerald Necklace, any proposal with the words “supportive housing” is a nonstarter.

“It’s going to be a fight,” said Louis Elisa, 76, who lives next to Franklin Park and heads the Roxbury-based Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association, during one of his regular walks through the park on Wednesday. “There is deep distrust that the state truly cares what people who live here think.”

Much of this distrust traces back to the last round of community discussions about what to do with the Shattuck site.

The state had called for 75 to 100 supportive housing units when it requested proposals in June 2021 for redeveloping the Shattuck. But the state received just one response, from a coalition of nonprofits led by Boston Medical Center. At 370 pages, that bid far surpassed expectations: It called for 446 treatment and emergency shelter beds and 405 units of supportive housing for individuals and families, as well as outpatient programs serving up to 400 people a day.

The grandiose plan faltered in part because of its size and timing. It was introduced amid mounting community reports of open-air drug use and discarded needles along the western edge of Franklin Park. Neighborhood groups largely blamed those problems on the 2022 opening of an 18-unit cottage village on the hospital grounds for people experiencing homelessness and addiction, arguing that the new housing drew illicit drug use to the park.

Public safety concerns were also heightened after Jean McGuire, a 91-year-old civil rights pioneer who was the first Black woman elected to the Boston School Committee, was stabbed multiple times in the fall of 2022 while walking her dog at the park. McGuire survived but the assailant was never caught.

The BMC-led plan also drew criticism from some addiction treatment specialists, who argued that housing hundreds of patients in one location was not therapeutic and echoed the outdated practice of isolating people in large state institutions, disconnected from society and support networks.

The state’s Executive Office of Health and Human Services said in a statement Wednesday that the earlier proposal, which would have cost $550 million, is “no longer feasible” because the BMC-led coalition behind the project was not able to identify a viable funding model.

Meanwhile, the state will work to relocate the Shattuck’s 268 medical and psychiatric beds to the East Newton Pavilion, a large medical facility in Boston’s South End that is under construction, in 2027.

Many residents still fear the state seeks to transform the land beside the storied Franklin Park into a catch-all repository for the city’s intersecting struggles with homelessness, untreated mental illness, and addiction.

“We are not against services and supports, but we are against dumping people behind a treasured park,” said Renee Stacey Welch, whose family has lived next to Franklin Park for five decades and is chair of the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Council. “Who wants to live next to a community of active drug users?”

At the forum on Thursday, tensions occasionally flared as residents and park lovers sparred with several advocates pushing for more housing for those battling addiction, with speakers sometimes shouting at each other across the room. The debate carried on in the high school parking lot long after the meeting adjourned. “Why do all these programs have to be concentrated near our park?” said Shawn Nelson, a Roxbury resident, his frustration evident.

A coalition representing some 600 residents living near Franklin Park came to Thursday’s meeting armed with data and detailed maps of Boston showing their communities shouldering a disproportionate share of the city’s homeless housing.

Those residents had identified 167 facilities in Boston that provide supportive housing for people with substance use disorders, and estimate 70 percent of them are in the neighborhoods bordering Franklin Park. As a percentage of their population, the park’s adjacent neighborhoods have nearly five times as many supportive housing units as predominantly white neighborhoods of Boston, they calculated.

“We are witnessing a new form of geographic redlining: the hyper-concentration of statewide social burdens in majority-minority neighborhoods,” said Rory Coffey, a resident of Jamaica Plain and founder of the Coalition for Region-wide Services Beyond Franklin Park, or CORES, which did the property analysis. “True equity means every community in the state acts as a partner in recovery, so no single corridor is forced to become a sacrifice zone.”

Several members of a separate community coalition — which is calling for at least 200 units of supportive housing and substance use recovery services at the Shattuck site — also spoke up at the hearing. Wearing purple shirts saying “Our Neighbors Are Dying!,” they described the toll of the overdose crisis and the critical shortage of long-term supports for people struggling to maintain their recovery.

Shameeka Moreno, an addiction counselor from Dorchester and member of the coalition, described how access to supportive housing could have prevented the overdose death in 2023 of her 43-year-old cousin, who had long struggled with cocaine and alcohol addiction and was chronically homeless. “The number of people dying because they lack adequate support systems is astronomical,” Moreno said. “The situation is dire.”

Some of the community’s opposition to supportive housing is rooted in Franklin Park’s long history, and the way state and local officials have carved it up over time for various uses. Beyond the Shattuck Hospital, the park is home to a zoo, a large golf course, and a city parks maintenance yard.

Moreover, the city’s plan to redevelop the aging White Stadium on the other side of Franklin Park into a 10,000-seat stadium for a professional soccer team has upset some neighbors and park advocates, who argue it is an inappropriate infringement; conservationists are concerned it will lead to the removal of more than 140 trees from the park.

Today, 40 percent of Franklin Park’s land is inaccessible for free public use, according to the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, a nonprofit park stewardship group.

Former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, who lives a mile from Franklin Park in Dorchester, fondly remembers walking the park’s paths with her two young sons and taking in the vibrant colors of the annual Caribbean and kite festivals. On summer days, her children would fly their own kites and mingle with the men playing dominoes on the benches.

“That park has meant everything to this community, and we deserve a voice in shaping what happens here,” Wilkerson said.

State Representative Chris Worrell, a Democrat from Dorchester, has been among those pushing for a statewide strategy for addressing the critical shortfall of supportive housing.

“We want beautiful things too,“ Worrell said, referring to some of the ideas being floated for the Shattuck site. ”It’s not that my community is against [supportive housing] — but we already are bearing the brunt of it."

title: Days after blizzard, Mattapan Square remained packed with snow, residents say
text:
“The traffic is clear, the roads are clear,” Mattapan resident Sonya Lee, 61, said as she was leaving the square toward River Street. “It’s much better now compared to when we first had the snow storm. It was awful. It was terrible.”

On Tuesday, the City Council will discuss how Boston can improve on its response to recent snowstorms, including the creation of a citywide “snow corps” to assist elderly or disabled people clear their sidewalks, and the possible purchasing of more snow melting machines.

As of Saturday, less than a week after last Monday’s blizzard delivered 17 inches in Boston, Public Works had taken 3,855 truckloads of snow from streets and intersections to 13 snow farms across Boston, the city said Monday. In early February, almost two weeks after the first snowstorm dumped nearly 2 feet of snow on Jan. 25 and Jan. 26, Mayor Michelle Wu reported more than 6,200 truckloads of snow had been cleared.

Throughout the week, Public Works crews used skid steers during the day to clear crosswalks, intersections, and curb ramps, the city said. Larger equipment was sent out at night to remove snow across Boston neighborhoods, including Mattapan, according to the city.

The city did not respond to an interview request about cleanup at Mattapan Square, in particular.

Councilor Enrique Pepén, who represents District 5, including Hyde Park, Mattapan, and Roslindale, said his office has received many complaints about snow removal across the district. He noted that sidewalk clearing in Boston has historically been the responsibility of property owners.

“If there’s a house and there’s a sidewalk right in front of it . . . whoever owns that house has to shovel that sidewalk,” he said.

The same applies to business owners, property management companies, state agencies, and the MBTA.

However, Pepén acknowledged that responsibility can become unclear in certain areas, particularly where ownership is not obvious.

“That’s a question we’re going to ask on Tuesday,” Pepén said.

Pepén said he supports the creation of a “snow corps” program, similar the one in New York City, which would allow Boston to hire shovelers on demand during major storms.

“Whenever there’s a snowstorm, we really need to make sure that it’s not just for streets that are plowed,” Pepén said. “That our sidewalks, they’re OK, especially near our intersections. We want to make sure that everyone’s safe.”

Meanwhile, Councilor Brian Worrell of District 4, which includes Mattapan, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, and Roslindale, is calling on the MBTA to include sidewalk snow clearance in its next commuter rail contract. Worrell’s proposal highlights ongoing safety issues for pedestrians and people with disabilities, especially at Fairmount Line stations.

Last Thursday afternoon, sidewalks near Mattapan Square and the MBTA station were covered in ice, although the main sidewalks in the square were cleared out. While some pedestrians carefully shuffled across the slick surface, others chose to step directly into the roadway to avoid the difficult terrain.

“Any time someone has to walk out into moving traffic, it puts everyone at risk, regardless of your age,” Iman Solomon, 77, a retired teacher and resident of Milton, said last week.

Soloman said the icy conditions are especially dangerous for seniors.

“In past years, I’ve actually had fallen a few times to where it’s done permanent damage to my right shoulder and also some back injuries,” Soloman said. “It’s treacherous out here for anyone who is a senior. The thought of falling is always there.”

Last week, conditions were particularly difficult near the intersection of Blue Hill Avenue, Cummins Highway, and River Street. On one sidewalk, pedestrians faced a snowy dilemma: navigate a narrow, icy uphill path that had not been shoveled, or step into a large puddle in the road. Crosswalks outside the Mattapan T station lacked curb openings that forced people to walk through the accumulated snow, following in others’ footsteps, or squeeze through narrow paths between snow banks. In some cases, medians between crosswalks had not been cleared, forcing pedestrians into the street.

Lloyd Malcolm, 98, who has lived in Mattapan for 70 years, said he was concerned about the lingering snow, for himself but also for others in the community.

“If they leave it here, people are going to be having more accidents,” he said. “Everyday there’s accident in this town.”

By Monday morning, sidewalks and crosswalks were all cleared and pedestrians were able to walk around the square freely.

Josiane Rosamond, 74, who lives on River Street in Mattapan, said she observed visible cleanup efforts.

“There’s been a lot of effort to really keep things easy for people because you have a lot of pedestrians going through here,” Rosamond said Monday as she was walked toward the bus station.

She recalled last Thursday, when workers were clearing snow between parked cars and along sidewalks. Earlier in the week, she had to cross the street to avoid the large puddle that made passage difficult. By Saturday, she said, the are was a noticeable improvement.

“The puddle was no longer there,” Rosamond said. “The sidewalk is totally clean. Everything is fine.”

While some residents describe a smooth recovery, others question how the cleanup unfolded.

“Resources we’re lacking,” Marc Simon, 30, who sells cellphones in Mattapan Square, said Monday. “It did take a while for the cleanup to occur.”

Last week, Simon, who works at the store nearly everyday from open to close, said he and a coworker created narrow pathways for customers before additional clearing was done.

“I don’t see the city doing as much as they should,” Simon said. “I see citizens trying to figure it out themselves.”

title: Why the city should buy Boston’s Crane Ledge Woods
text:
Protection of natural places is not a default “no” to all housing. The Crane Ledge Woods Coalition has endorsed Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s Squares + Streets initiative to support housing, public space, small business, and culture, for example.

The community-based Squares + Streets approach would allow the development of an estimated 1,000 new units in the heart of Hyde Park, directing density to sites near transit and walkable business districts. While mindful of the serious risk of displacement of residents, this streamlines development approval where housing is best located, through new construction, adaptive reuse of historic buildings, and reinvestment in our city’s neighborhoods.

In contrast, the housing proposed at Crane Ledge Woods would require clear-cutting 14 acres of tree canopy, destroying a vital carbon-sequestering cooling zone and wildlife refuge, to build a car-centric, gated heat island. This is not a model of sustainable or equitable development for Boston or the Commonwealth.

Protecting woodlands like Crane Ledge while increasing housing density near transit and walkable main streets are necessary complements. Our woodlands provide measurable public benefits for residents: They sequester carbon, absorb water and protect against flooding, cool neighborhoods during increasingly dangerous heat waves, filter air pollution, buffer sound, and provide a home for wildlife and spaces for all to enjoy.

At a time when local action to address climate change is an undeniable imperative, development decisions must withstand stringent scrutiny when irreplaceable natural resources are at stake.

The Crane Ledge Woods Coalition was formed in 2021 and now includes more than 50 organizations citywide, from City Life/Vida Urbana to the Boston Building Trades Council. Through an open, inclusive process respectful of all views, we have developed an alternative vision: The city should purchase the land for permanent conservation, with owner Jubilee Christian Church and its development partner compensated fairly.

Climate action plans adopted by Wu and Governor Maura Healey identify preserving woodlands as among the most cost-effective strategies to address climate change and advance environmental justice. As elected officials pursue ambitious targets, destroying 14 acres of woodland in our own backyard seems at odds with our stated values.

Boston has a tradition of far-sighted civic vision, from the Emerald Necklace and the “People Before Highways” movement to the Rose Kennedy Greenway and Neponset River Bike Path. In building these spaces, elected officials working together with residents set aside conventional thinking and recommitted themselves to sustaining the commons.

Crane Ledge Woods presents another once-in-a-generation opportunity. With legal hurdles resolved and the Boston Planning and Development Agency board’s reluctant approval last September allowing for an accurate appraisal of the value of the land, which should be undertaken as soon as possible, achieving conservation of Crane Ledge Woods is within reach.

For a public benefit purchase, the city is bound by appraised value. While each property is different, and the first step is an on-site no-obligation appraisal, recent city parkland acquisitions have been in the $12 per square foot range, which for the 24-acre Crane Ledge Woods would be $12.7 million, or 0.5 percent of the city’s annual capital budget. For context, Boston’s $4.2 billion capital budget has 433 individual project line items.

As an inland green infrastructure project with many additional public benefits, a Crane Ledge Woods acquisition would fall in the low-to-middle range of the city’s climate-focused capital projects. Wu is now uniquely positioned to deliver a widely supported acquisition of Crane Ledge. Mass Audubon, the state’s leading conservation organization, has developed a concept plan for these woods. Through its capital budget, the city has the means to achieve this goal.

An inspiring civic vision is not the exclusive property of our predecessors. Our hope is for a Boston that leads the way: building equitably while protecting our natural spaces. In a city where nearly every parcel faces development pressure, preserving our last wild places is an investment in our collective well-being, our environmental resilience, and our connection to the natural world that sustains us all.

title: After losing coverage for GLP-1 drugs, Mass. patients face difficult choice: $500 a month, or fear of regaining weight
text:
“It was definitely not a willpower thing,” he said. “It was chemical. [Zepbound] gave my body the biological help it needed to overcome the weight gain.”

Like Tierno, more than 40,000 customers of the state’s two biggest insurers, Blue Cross and Point32Health, have lost coverage of GLP-1s for obesity this year, according to the latest data provided by the companies. An unspecified number of customers of smaller insurers have also lost the benefit, according to the Massachusetts Association of Health Plans.

Their ranks will rise given a vote Thursday to end coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss by the Group Insurance Commission, which provides insurance to over 460,000 state employees, retirees, and relatives. MassHealth, the state’s Medicaid program, could also make a similar move in upcoming months. Overall, about 140,400 patients with obesity were prescribed the medications in 2024 in Massachusetts, the Globe has reported. That class of medicines includes Zepbound, Wegovy, Ozempic, and Mounjaro.

With the end of insurance coverage, people who have spent decades trying to lose weight, including by undergoing surgery to shrink their stomachs, are scrounging for ways to afford to pay out-of-pocket for GLP-1s, or exercising and counting calories in the hopes of keeping the weight off without the drugs.

“I don’t take this medicine for the fun of it. I take it because I need it,” said Michelle Markert, a 55-year-old interior designer in Newton who lost at least 35 pounds on GLP-1s before insurers ended the benefit.

Markert said she used to pay $80 for her monthly prescription under her plan with Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, which is owned by Point32Health. Now Markert, who switched to Blue Cross this year, will pay $500 a month out of pocket, the equivalent of a car payment.

“That $420 is going to have to come from somewhere else,” she said. “I’ll think twice about going out to eat or even going out to the movies.”

Blue Cross, the state’s largest insurer, said it has notified 25,670 members so far that they no longer qualify for GLP-1s for obesity. The second-largest insurer, Point32Health, has notified more than 15,000 of its members that they have lost eligibility. Both still cover GLP-1 drugs for diabetes.

Tierno, who has struggled with his weight since childhood, said the trend doesn’t make sense given the costly long-term consequences of obesity. When he began taking Zepbound, he had high blood pressure and blood sugar levels classified as prediabetic. Now he doesn’t.

“For me, this has literally been a miracle drug,” he said. “It was not just about weight loss for vanity. It truly was a health issue.”

Doctors who treat people with obesity agree.

Dr. Paul Copeland, an endocrinologist and obesity medicine specialist at the Massachusetts General Hospital Weight Center, said GLP-1s have given many of his patients their first opportunity to improve their health and quality of life. Now, he spends much of his time trying to cobble together weight loss regimens with far less effective drugs.

Some of his patients who lost coverage have started to regain weight, he said. He worries they will suffer serious health consequences. A recent study projected that people who stop taking GLP-1s would regain their lost weight within about 18 months.

“There are substantial dangers in having these medications pulled away from patients,” said Copeland. “Not only is there a rapid weight gain for most patients, but there is documented re-worsening of comorbidities such as cardiovascular risk factors.”

The new insurance restrictions have fueled the use of direct-to-consumer programs such as NovoCare and LillyDirect, where prices range from $149 to $449 a month, depending on the drug and dosage. (Prices are similar on the new government website, TrumpRx.gov.)

Unfortunately, Copeland said, such programs are leading to a two-tier system that disadvantages those who can’t afford those prices.

Insurers, for their part, blame the situation on the two pharmaceutical giants that dominate the GLP-1 market: Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk.

Those companies, insurers say, have charged exorbitant amounts for the weight loss medicines, and the costs to insurers were unsustainable. Zepbound and Lilly’s rival drug Wegovy have list prices ranging from about $900 to more than $1,300 a month.

Blue Cross said it spent $515 million on GLP-1s in 2025, up from $140 million in 2023. The cost of the drugs was projected to reach nearly $1 billion this year if the insurer hadn’t restricted coverage. Point32Health has experienced a similar trend.

Facing steep losses from GLP-1 costs, both insurers shed hundreds of employees from their workforces last year.

When Blue Cross and Point32Health stopped coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss, they said employers with 100 workers or more could keep coverage by paying extra. But, only 20 percent of employers chose to maintain coverage, which was “telling,” said Blue Cross spokesperson Amy McHugh.

“Lowering the cost of GLP-1 medications to a reasonable level based on the overall health improvements and cost savings they bring is the single most important step toward removing the primary barrier to coverage,” she said.

Novo acknowledged insurers’ criticism last week when it announced plans to cut the list price for GLP-1s by up to half in 2027.

“Private and public payers, as well as patients, want access and have been calling for lower list prices,” Jamey Millar, Novo’s executive vice president for US operations, said. “Our actions today answer that call.”

But Novo executives also faced competitive pressures. Novo initially dominated the GLP-1 market, but Lilly has overtaken it with more effective drugs.

Lilly has given no indication it will lower list prices. A company spokesperson said Lilly is disappointed insurers are denying coverage of medications for the “serious, chronic disease” of obesity. Even without insurance, the spokesperson said, customers can get Zepbound from LillyDirect starting at $299 a month for the lowest dosage.

Like Tierno, several Massachusetts residents on GLP-1s say they can’t afford that.

Robert Atterbury, an audiology office coordinator who lives in Dorchester, said he has lost 20 pounds on GLP-1s and now weighs about 250 pounds. Zepbound had cost him about $30 a month with his Harvard Pilgrim insurance. Paying hundreds of dollars per month isn’t in his budget.

His weight is “inching back up,” he said, and he’s worried about heart disease and diabetes, as he has high blood pressure.

“The drug company and the health insurer made the decision for me,” said Atterbury, 60. “I had nothing to do with it except not making enough to be able to afford to pay for it out of pocket.”

Susan Elsbree, a 55-year-old public relations executive in Jamaica Plain, also lost her insurance coverage of Zepbound.

She said she was furious because she has lost 35 pounds, lowered her blood pressure, and no longer needs cortisone shots for her arthritic knees. She had struggled to shed weight for years, exercising at least five days a week — doing hot yoga and playing tennis — but nothing worked like the GLP-1.

She can afford to pay $199 a month to continue to get Zepbound through Mochi Health, a telehealth platform.

She lamented, though, that the health gap is widening between the haves and have-nots. “I’m furious with the insurance companies,” she said. “This is about equity as much as anything else.”

title: Mapping Boston: See how neighborhoods differ in race, income, and housing
text:
Dorchester remains by far the largest Boston neighborhood in both population and land area, with more than 126,000 residents — nearly a fifth of Boston’s total population. The next most populous neighborhood, Roxbury, has fewer than half as many residents, at roughly 50,000. Bay Village is the smallest, with about 1,600.

For this analysis, the Globe used neighborhood boundaries created by the city that align with census tracts, allowing for more precise comparisons across communities.

While Boston has been a majority-minority city since the turn of the century, many of its neighborhoods remain racially segregated, the latest data show.

In Mattapan, roughly 92 percent of residents identify as people of color, including about 70 percent who identify as Black. The overall racial composition has remained relatively stable over the past decade, though the neighborhood has seen growth in Haitian and Latino immigrant communities.

East Boston has the highest share of Latino residents, at just over half of its population. It also has by far the highest share of residents who identify as multiracial — about 43 percent, more than twice the next-highest neighborhood, Dorchester.

By contrast, the North End and Beacon Hill have the highest shares of white residents, each at nearly 90 percent.

Massachusetts is the richest state in the country, but Boston’s prosperity is unevenly distributed. The share of households earning more than $200,000 a year — the top income tier in census data — varies widely.

The Seaport, also known as the South Boston Waterfront, has the highest concentration of high-income households, with more than 40 percent earning above that threshold. The neighborhood is also one of Boston’s fastest-growing areas, filled with luxury towers, high-end offices, and new retail development.

Buildings in the Seaport account for roughly one-tenth of Boston’s property tax base. But rising sea levels and increasing flood risk threaten that concentration of wealth.

South Boston and Charlestown were long considered working-class neighborhoods, but now rank close behind Seaport in the share of wealthy residents — a dramatic transformation in recent decades. Mission Hill and Longwood have the lowest shares of high earners.

The share of children has been declining for years in Boston and across Massachusetts, contributing to a drop of about 70,000 public school students over the past two decades — an 8 percent decline statewide.

The highest concentrations of residents under 18 are clustered in the southern part of the city, including Dorchester, Mattapan, and West Roxbury, where children make up just over 20 percent of the population.

Longwood has the smallest share of children, at about 2.7 percent, along with other neighborhoods closer to downtown, such as the North End and Back Bay.

More than six in 10 housing units in Boston are renter-occupied, and renters are especially concentrated in the city’s densest and most student-heavy neighborhoods.

In Chinatown, more than 90 percent of occupied housing units are renter-occupied — the highest share in the city. Allston and Fenway are close behind.

In contrast, more residential neighborhoods on the city’s outskirts, including Hyde Park and West Roxbury, have renter shares of 40 percent or less.

Boston’s population has fluctuated in recent years, particularly during the COVID pandemic, but several neighborhoods have seen large infusions of Asian and Latino residents that are reshaping parts of the city.

Chinatown and East Boston have the highest shares of foreign-born residents — about 51 percent and 45 percent, respectively. In Chinatown, many foreign-born residents are of Asian origin; in East Boston, most are Latino.

Material from prior Globe stories was used in this report.

title: Roxbury to commemorate 250th anniversary of Henry Knox’s Noble Train of Artillery march on Saturday
text:
Revolution 250, the organizing committee of the state’s celebration, has partnered with multiple community groups, including Boston 250 and Unitarian Universalist Urban Ministry, to celebrate Knox.

The event is part of Knox Trail 250, a statewide observance that has made its way across Massachusetts. Local communities have held celebrations on the date that Knox marched through, such as Feb. 8 in Framingham.

In the winter of 1775-76, Knox, a 25-year-old Boston bookseller, hauled away British cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston. The cannons were positioned at Dorchester Heights, ultimately forcing the British troops to evacuate the city on March 17, 1776.

“You don’t get to declare independence without first commemorating Evacuation Day,” said Jonathan Lane, executive director of Revolution 250. “And you don’t get to Evacuation Day without telling the story of Henry Knox and his Noble Train of Artillery.”

Knox’s ties to Roxbury are significant. Before his expedition, he built fortifications in the neighborhood that caught the eye of Washington, launching his role as an officer in the artillery.

“Within a year, he was the Brigadier General of the artillery,” Lane said. “He has a meteoric rise, but that was Washington’s style.”

The events Saturday will begin at 2 p.m. with a procession from Fenway High School to John Eliot Square. Marchers will include colonial militia reenactors, patriots of color, a fife and drum unit, and the Hamilton-Garrett drumline. Two teams of Clydesdale horses will pull sleds and cannons, echoing Knox’s original winter trek.

Organizers said the event will stand apart from other Knox Trail events across Massachusetts and New York.

“We … wanted it to really feel true to what Roxbury has been and what it continues to be today as a the hub of Black Boston and a center of revolutionary thought and action,” said Alex Meadow, deputy director of partnerships in the mayor’s office.

Formal programs will be held at the Dillaway-Thomas House. Alongside Knox’s story, the programs will highlight Black patriots who fought in the Revolutionary War and explore the experiences of free, enslaved, and Indigenous people during the Siege of Boston. Black reenactors from the Living History Company and local historians, artists, and poets will participate as well.

A speaking program is planned to begin at 3 p.m. at the First Parish Church, recently reopened after a multiyear renovation. Mayor Michelle Wu is expected to attend and announce the launch of the Boston Historic Markers Program.

The event will conclude with a 15-minute light projection show as a part of the Boston Beacon initiative.

The Roxbury event is one of two Knox-related observances in Boston this month, alongside the annual Dorchester Heights ceremony on March 17. Both are part of Boston 250, the city’s public-private effort to mark its role in the nation’s founding. For Meadow, the theme running through Boston 250 is “everyday revolutionaries.”

“Henry Knox was a bookseller who went to Boston Public Schools,” Meadow said. “An important piece of this for us is through our events and through our programs, helping people realize that they hold power themselves.”

title: Haitian man living in Boston dies in ICE custody, family says
text:
In mid-February, Damas told personnel at the Florence facility that he had a toothache, but he was not sent to a dentist, his brother Presly Nelson said in an interview.

Damas was seeking asylum and had entered the country legally through a Joe Biden-era humanitarian parole program for Haitians in 2024, Nelson said.

Damas died Monday at a Scottsdale hospital, after the family chose to take him off life support. He had been receiving treatment for more than 10 days, his family said. The detention center had only given Damas over-the-counter medication for his pain, according to his family.

Damas had two sons in Boston, the youngest of whom is a 13-year-old in seventh grade.

“It’s like treating a human being like they’re nobody,” Nelson said. “As an American, I’m very ashamed, I’m very disheartened.”

Over the weekend, Nelson rushed from Boston to Arizona to see his brother after receiving a call from the hospital that Damas was in critical condition and might not have much time left. In the hospital, Nelson found his brother on life support. Still, Damas was handcuffed to the hospital bed, had a chain on his body, and two security officers were stationed by his room, Nelson said.

“He could barely blink his eyes — he was in a vegetative state, motionless, on life support,” Nelson, 47, said. “But he still had handcuffs on . . . it was so hurtful.”

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Friday that it alerted Damas’ family about his worsening conditioning as well as Congress after his death. The statement confirmed Damas was held to be deported, though he had appealed. The department also said it provided adequate medical care.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the statement said. “At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.”

But Damas’s death sparked outrage among lawmakers in Massachusetts and Arizona. On Thursday, Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, along with Representative Ayanna Pressley, wrote a letter to homeland security Secretary Kristi Noem and ICE acting director Todd Lyons demanding a full investigation. They also called on the DHS to provide proper medical treatment care to detainees as a matter of standard.

The letter was sent the same day Noem was fired by President Trump amid mounting criticism of her leadership of DHS. Damas is at least the 10th person to die in ICE custody this year, the lawmakers said.

After Damas first informed staff of his nagging tooth pain, he visited the health clinic at the detention center over the course of Feb. 17 and Feb. 18. He was given over-the-counter medications but was reportedly denied dental treatment, according to the lawmakers. Several days later, Damas told his family that his condition had worsened and he could no longer speak properly. He informed them he would finally be taken to a hospital, the letter states.

On Feb. 20, staff at the HonorHealth John C. Lincoln Medical Center told his family that Damas was suffering from pneumonia and had been placed on life support in the intensive care unit, where he remained in critical condition, according to the letter. But for days after that, neither family nor lawmakers received clear updates on his medical condition and whereabouts, they said.

As the family continued to press for updates, Markey reached out to ICE on the their behalf. “ICE did not provide satisfactory answers,” and officials said they could not release information unless a privacy form was signed, lawmakers say in the letter.

“Senator Markey had made clear that a Privacy Release Form was impossible given that it was unclear where Mr. Damas was located and if he was even alive,” the letter says.

Several days later, the family learned that Damas had been transferred to a nearby hospital, and was scheduled for surgery on Feb. 26. He died on March 2.

Damas, who worked as a mechanic in Haiti, and his sons had fled gang violence in their native country, his family told the Globe. Nelson had sponsored Damas to come to the US in February 2024, and the family lived in Dorchester. Damas and his sons thought they had reached safety here, Nelson said, and they were excited for the 13-year-old’s education in Boston.

“It was like a dream come true when they came,” Nelson said. “It was a relief, considering all the turmoil that’s been going on in Haiti.”

Now, the family, and the boys, are left devastated.

Massachusetts District Court records show that Damas was arrested in September and charged with assault and battery, a misdemeanor. His family said that police took Damas to the station after he gave what they characterized as a slap on the back of the son’s head following a misunderstanding.

Damas was quickly released after the family posted bail, but ICE officers had arrived to the police precinct to detain him. “An officer came out and said, ‘I’m sorry, he was picked up by a federal agent,’ ” Nelson said.

Nelson and his twin brother, Presner Nelson, said they were in close touch with an immigration attorney to try to get their brother out of detention. Damas called both of his brothers, his children, and his mother back in Boston often, remaining positive about his chances to reunite with them, his family said.

“He was hopeful that one day he was going to come back home,” said Presner Nelson.

His family alleges that ICE did not provide Damas with timely medical care. This allowed the untreated toothache “to become a deadly infection,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter. And from Boston, the brothers, and their mother, spent their time constantly calling the detention facility and the hospital trying to get more information. And they were often stonewalled, they said.

Damas‘s death, the lawmakers said, was “a tragedy and likely, a highly preventable one.”

His death comes amid growing concerns about the conditions inside federal immigration detention centers, with last year marking the deadliest in ICE history in over two decades, lawmakers said.

The Florence detention center where Damas was held is operated by CoreCivic, a massive private prison operator, which contracts with ICE across the country.

Presly Nelson has lived in the US for almost three decades, and became an American citizen after first moving here on a scholarship to study in Wisconsin. He had hoped his brother and his nephews would be able to experience the America he had come to love — a country that embraced people from all over the world.

“That was the compassionate country that I’ve come to appreciate and respect,” Nelson said. “This country is great because of its diversity, and without it, I think we become weaker and weaker.”

Now, Nelson wonders: “If he [Damas] were still back in Haiti, he would not have died like this.”

After his brother passed away, Nelson received a call from an official at ICE, he said. The agency was requesting his address, so they could send him a letter of condolence. While he appreciated the call and passed along his address, he felt it was too little, much too late.

“What’s that going to do for me,” Nelson said. “Is the letter going to bring my brother back to life?”

The original online version of this article was updated to include a statement from the Department of Homeland Security.

title: Ly Y of Quincy, journalist who wrote of escaping Cambodia’s genocide, dies at 83
text:
Before the Khmer Rouge’s reign of terror, Mr. Ly had worked in Cambodia for The Associated Press. Then he began assisting reporters from the Globe and Chicago Tribune as an interpreter and as one of the local “fixers” — invaluable colleagues who guided and supported foreign correspondents through dangerous reporting assignments and unpredictable negotiations.

“I know that they educated us, or Ly did, on how to deal with soldiers,” recalled Matthew V. Storin, then a Globe reporter in Phnom Penh and later the newspaper’s editor-in-chief. “We had to buy [soldiers] bottles of Remy Martin brandy just to get information sometimes.”

Mr. Ly, who chronicled his family’s journey from Cambodia’s notorious Killing Fields to Boston in Globe newspaper articles and a memoir, died Feb. 26 in South Shore Hospital in Weymouth, about 13 months after suffering a major stroke. He was 83 and had lived in Quincy for many years.

In 2000, he published “Heaven Becomes Hell: A Survivor’s Story of Life Under the Khmer Rouge.”

“Unless you see something like this through the eyes of someone who’s experienced it, you really can’t begin to grasp it,” John S. Driscoll, a former editor-in-chief of the Globe who edited the memoir, said when the book was published.

During the genocide of the Khmer Rouge regime, led by the dictator Pol Pot, about 2 million people — roughly a third of Cambodia’s population — died between 1975 and 1979 from forced labor, mass executions, starvation, and the lack of basic amenities.

As a journalist before the genocide, Mr. Ly was valued for his intelligence and experience.

“My dad spoke four languages: Cambodian, French, English, and Thai,” said his son, Johnny Sim Ly of Woodcliff Lake, N.J.

But when the Khmer Rouge took over, Mr. Ly was forced into menial labor. He had to lie about his background to avoid being killed at a time when soldiers targeted intellectuals and those who had worked with Americans.

Interrogated by an official one day, “I pretended to neither speak nor write any foreign language,” Mr. Ly wrote in a December 1980 Globe article, after his family had arrived in Boston.

The genocide took an enormous toll on Mr. Ly’s family. In “Heaven Becomes Hell,” he wrote about the joy his family had felt, just before the Khmer Rouge regime, when Prasat, his first child, was born.

Mr. Ly wrote that his son “was precious to me. He was the only hope for my future. I could see in his eyes that he would be thirsty for knowledge.”

As a toddler, Prasat was among many who became very ill. Mr. Ly wrote about how the family struggled without success to care for him with almost no medicine.

After Prasat died, Mr. Ly wrote that he carefully placed him “in a tiny grave, a cubic meter big, and I did not forget to plant a piece of wood there as a marker, so that I could come back to pray for him again. That is an image that I shall never forget. Then I said goodbye in silence.”

Mr. Ly was born on May 18, 1942, in Reap, in Cambodia’s Prey Veng Province. His mother was Cheng Sim. His father, Y Heng, had been a district chief and was reduced to menial farm labor during the Khmer Rouge regime.

In Cambodia, Mr. Ly was known as Y Ly, his birth name. Johnny said that when his father immigrated to the United States, he was told that for purposes of official records here he could not use a single letter as his first name, so his name was reversed from Y Ly to Ly Y.

Foreign correspondents in Cambodia had turned to Mr. Ly for his fluency in languages and for his expertise in many other matters.

“The greatest value of Ly was that he knew everybody, he knew the territory,” Storin said. “He knew where to go, he knew what was safe and what was not safe.”

When Storin returned to the United States, he lost touch with Mr. Ly during the Khmer Rouge regime, but he didn’t forget his friend.

“I had a black and white photo of Ly that I literally kept on my dresser for five years, it just was lying there,” he said.

Mr. Ly had married Chantra Try in 1971. During the genocide, they were forced to leave Phnom Penh and walked for days to villages where they were enslaved.

When the Vietnamese military invaded Cambodia in 1978 and overthrew the Khmer Rouge, Mr. Ly “was the one who had the vision, the courage to try to escape,” Johnny said. “He said, ‘If we stay, we’re definitely going to die.’”

Mr. Ly led his family on a days-long trek by foot to a Thai refugee camp, bringing with him his wife, her three brothers — Hak, Huot, and Heng Meng — and their father, Chour L. Chheng.

Meanwhile in Boston, Storin had lunch one day in 1980 with Sydney Schanberg, a New York Times correspondent who had won a Pulitzer Prize for his Cambodia reporting, and Dith Pran, a photojournalist who had worked with Schanberg in Cambodia much in the way Mr. Ly had worked with Storin.

At the end of the lunch, Storin showed Dith – who had escaped Cambodia’s Killing Fields – the photo of Mr. Ly that he had kept on his dresser. Dith recognized Mr. Ly and said he was in a refugee camp in Thailand.

Storin then arranged for Mr. Ly and his family — which by then included Mr. Ly’s two children — to move to Boston, where they initially lived in Dorchester.

“They came in November 1980 with the clothes on their back, one kilo of rice, and a few trinkets they had used to trade with the people along the way of the refugee trail,” Storin said.

In the United States, Mr. Ly worked for a time at the Globe and became a leader of Greater Boston’s Cambodian community.

“He helped to bring a lot of people from Cambodia over,” said Johnny, who added that his father also helped launch and wrote for the Bodhipriks News, published in Greater Boston and circulated among New England’s Cambodian immigrants.

Along with “Heaven Becomes Hell,” Mr. Ly wrote other books, including the memoir “Becoming American.”

“It was a heroic life in certain ways,” Storin said.

In addition to his wife and his son, Mr. Ly leaves a daughter, Outtra Sim Ly of Woodcliff Lake, N.J.; a sister, Y Sokkom of Phnom Penh; and a brother, Y Leng, of Cambodia’s Kandal Province.

Family and friends will gather at 7:30 a.m. Saturday at Dolan Funeral in Chelmsford, where Buddhist monks will lead a Seeing the Light ceremony at 8:30 before a procession to the crematory.

The cremation ceremony will be at 9:15, after which the gathering will go to Triaratanaram Temple in North Chelmsford for a 10:30 prayer session with the monks.

“To our family, he was the leader. He was the one who had the vision, the courage to try to escape and leave,” Johnny said.

His voice breaking, Johnny added that when his father was “on his death bed, while he was passing, one of the things people were thanking him for was that without him, none of us would be here.”
