title: Reenactors commemorate Henry Knox’s 1776 winter expedition to haul cannons to Boston
text:
Saturday’s commemoration was the latest in a series of reenactments across the state leading up to the 250th anniversary of American independence in 2026. Organizers also used the event to recognize the contributions of Black Bostonians to the city’s history.

The celebration, part of the City of Boston’s Boston 250 Initiative, kicked off from Fenway High School with a procession of militia reenactors, a fife and drum corps, and the Hamilton-Garrett Drumline. The group marched to the church, where local historians reflected on Knox’s ties to the neighborhood.

Several speakers explored the lives of free, enslaved, and Indigenous people during the Siege of Boston. The experiences of Black Americans during the Revolution, said historian Dart Adams, are often left out of the narrative.

“Black Bostonians constantly feel erased,” Adams said.

The crowd applauded as he listed Black residents credited with shaping the city’s history. The cheering grew louder when Wu announced the city’s plan to invest $650,000 in an effort to “uncover the hidden histories” of Boston.

The funding will support the installation of more than two dozen historic markers and a program allowing community members to research and propose new ones, she said.

“This year we have an opportunity to shine a light in those spaces, on those sacrifices, on those individuals, and that collective action,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll.

Revolution 250, the organizing group behind the state’s anniversary celebration, partnered with several community groups, including Boston 250 and the Unitarian Universalist Urban Ministry, to host the event. It was part of Knox Trail 250, a statewide observance in which communities hold events on the dates Knox passed through their towns.

Boston will host another Knox-related event this month, the annual Dorchester Heights ceremony on March 17. But several attendees found Saturday’s festivities especially meaningful for neighborhood residents, since many of the 250th commemorations have been held in other parts of the city.

“We’re so happy to see the history of this neighborhood being celebrated,” said Randy Foote, 77, who moved to the area in 1968 and taught history at Roxbury Community College. “It’s a tremendously historical place, but it gets forgotten.”

Foote, who said he’s “all about Henry Knox,” lives in a home that overlooks the area where troops positioned the cannons that ultimately forced the British evacuation.

His favorite moment of Saturday’s celebration came when he stepped inside the First Church. The Knox event marked the first gathering in the building since the completion of a multiyear restoration, and Foote was not the only one pausing to admire the fresh white paint and gleaming fixtures.

“I love seeing the horses and all, but seeing this church so beautiful and so alive is so heartwarming,” said Foote, who also leads tour groups along the Freedom Trail. “It just knocks me out what they’ve done.”

Though Saturday wasn’t the first time Foote had retraced the final leg of Knox’s route, the event gave many attendees a reason to explore it themselves. Some, despite years in the neighborhood, said they had never stepped inside the First Church.

Sean Burke, a Dorchester native, climbed the church steps for the first time wearing a 250th anniversary scarf and several patriotic pins on his cap. A self-proclaimed history buff, Burke said he attends reenactments whenever he can.

“You can’t go wrong with a live cannon demonstration,” said Burke, 38. “That’s always something you don’t think you’d hear in Roxbury. It’s usually a little more quiet.”

Burke has made several trips to Lexington and Concord over the past year and attended the lantern ceremony at Old North Church last April. He encouraged community members to get out and take part in events that highlight the country’s history, especially when they are happening close to home.

“It’s very fitting, in this time and political climate, to remember your history and to learn it,” he said. “Living here, we’re so blessed. It’s literally saturated with history. It’d be a shame for people not to partake.”

After the remarks, attendees inside the Putnam Street church turned their attention to a light show that illuminated the space. The immersive program highlighted the past, present, and future of Roxbury’s revolutionary spirit through light projections, live music, and multimedia art curated by local artists and historians.

“I love seeing the horses,” said Foote’s wife, Nel, 73. “But my actual favorite thing is seeing so many people come together in our neighborhood to acknowledge it.”

title: ‘It makes it feel like our needs aren’t as important.’ Disabled residents say Boston could have done better in removing snow.
text:
Jerry Boyd, 56, a West Roxbury resident who has cerebral palsy, uses MBTA RIDE, a door-to-door paratransit service, but said he couldn’t reach the vehicle in his motorized wheelchair when sidewalks weren’t cleared.

“I applaud the city on those efforts, but definitely more work needs to be done,” Boyd said. “We can’t be caught off guard in future winters like the city seemed to be this year.”

Curb cuts, sloped ramps built into sidewalks at intersections, are especially critical because they allow people using wheelchairs and other mobility devices to move safely from the sidewalk to the street.

“When we find curb cuts not shoveled out or sidewalks not with a wide enough path, it makes it feel like our needs aren’t as important,” Boyd said.

Councilor Ed Flynn called snow cleanup a civil rights issue.

“You judge a snowstorm on how accessible the streets and sidewalks are for persons with disabilities and seniors,” Flynn said.

The city did not respond to an interview request to address complaints from residents with disabilities. However, it defended its snow removal operations.

“We recognize the major impact that snow has on people with disabilities,” Disability Commissioner Kristen McCosh said in a statement. “We make every effort to maintain accessible paths of travel by ensuring that City resources are focused on sidewalks, curb ramps, and crosswalks.”

During the two major snowstorms, the city conducted targeted snow removal in priority areas, including Boston Public Schools locations, major thoroughfares, intersections, curb ramps, and public squares, according to Boston Public Works.

Crews have removed 10,444 truckloads of snow from city streets this season, 6,566 loads in January and 3,878 in February, according to Public Works. The Public Works Code Enforcement Division has issued 5,870 snow removal violations across both storms, the department said.

Of the 311 cases reported to the city each month, 59 percent in January and 53 percent in February were related to snow, according to Public Works.

“Every winter storm presents a unique set of challenges,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said in a statement. “We remain open to feedback and will continue to iterate on our snow removal strategies within our fiscal and staff constraints.”

Osaghae said the Boston Code of Ordinances requires property owners to clear snow, slush, and ice from sidewalks and curb ramps around their property. The ordinance requires a minimum 42-inch-wide path to be cleared for people using wheelchairs and pushing strollers.

“We need to have a finalized ‘who to go to’ when this situation is happening,” said Daniela Depina, 45, who is wary of stepping out of her Dorchester home and onto the icy, snow-ridden sidewalk.

Depina, who is visually impaired, has rescheduled medical appointments, skipped grocery store runs, and even paid someone to take her 11-year-old daughter, Mariah, to school, because the ground outside her home was not fully shoveled, she said. She called 311 after the January storm and said she didn’t get answers about who was responsible for clearing her sidewalk.

“I had to sit on my butt to get down my stairs, because that’s how bad it was,” said Depina, a disability peer advocate at the Boston Center for Independent Living. “If everywhere you call you’re getting the runaround, it’s almost feeling like the door is being shut.”

Gabrielle Mondestin, chief communications officer for the MBTA, said in a statement that its RIDE service is affected “even after the snow has stopped falling.” Drivers may struggle to pull over or park near a customer’s destination, and it can be difficult to deploy vehicle lifts when piled snow blocks the curb, she said.

Crystal Evans, 45, of Braintree, who has a neuromuscular disease and uses a ventilator to breathe, travels to Boston three to six days a week for health care. She gets medical transportation through her insurance company, but it has been unreliable, so Evans opts for the buses and trains.

Evans, who shoveled Braintree sidewalks using her motorized wheelchair in 2015, said piles of snow made the curb cuts inaccessible and crosswalk buttons impossible to reach from her chair.

“When we’re dependent on a sidewalk plow, then things like signs and light posts, the plows can’t navigate,” Evans said. “Then they just stop, back off, go into the street, and we don’t have that continuous path of travel.”

She said snowbanks left at traffic islands were another concern for her as she crossed intersections.

“As a wheelchair user, you don’t know if a car is going to come around the corner or not,” she said. “I’m lower than the snowbanks.”

William O’Donnell, 42, a peer support leader who lives in Quincy, was particularly fearful of having to walk into the street with Juno, his guide dog.

“The dog is trying to guide you around obstacles,” O’Donnell said. “Often, there’s not a straight way you can go, and then they have to dodge traffic, worry about getting you around the cars.”

When he walked in the street, O’Donnell said he could feel the heat of the cars traveling next to him, less than an arm’s length away. He suggested that if municipalities have to build snowbanks at the edges of the streets, they can keep them off of curb cuts or use melting machines to eliminate them.

Casandra Xavier, a 36-year-old disability advocate who was born with blindness and hearing loss, said city officials should take accessibility into account when clearing snow because they never know when they might need it.

“No one is exempt from acquiring a disability in this life,” she said. “We are not asking for a favor. We’re just simply reminding everyone of our rights as persons with disabilities, that we too should have access to our environment freely and comfortably.”

title: Many neighbors welcome supportive housing, treatment at Shattuck site
text:
Re “At Franklin Park, again a split over land use: Shattuck future fires fears of neighbors” (Page A1, March 1): Readers of the article about plans by the state to redevelop the Shattuck Hospital site may have been left with the impression that neighbors overwhelmingly oppose supportive housing and addiction treatment there. While there are some mobilizing against housing and treatment on the Shattuck campus, there is also a large, multiracial coalition, Housing and Health on Morton Street, that strongly supports housing and treatment at this site.

We are both members of this coalition, which sees Morton Street redevelopment as a crucial step in tackling our communities’ critical housing and health care needs. In contrast to the article’s framing, our group is made up not of “several advocates” but, rather, of hundreds of residents of Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, and Jamaica Plain.

People of color or immigrants represent more than 70 percent of our coalition’s base. Member groups include African Community Economic Development of New England, Agencia ALPHA (serving Latino residents), New England Community Project (Dorchester), Reclaim Roxbury, and True Alliance Center (serving the Haitian community).

At the Feb. 26 listening session covered by the article, besides “calling for at least 200 units of supportive housing and substance use recovery services at the Shattuck campus,” as the reporter noted, we also urged the state to build on its earlier Vision Plan (from 2019-20), developed with a community advisory board, that incorporated substantial input from surrounding communities and identified key needs and priorities.

Shameeka Moreno

Dorchester

Clare Okalany

Roxbury

Moreno is an organizer with the Boston Tenant Coalition. Okalany is head of operations for African Community Economic Development of New England.

title: ‘A total unicorn situation’: Why aren’t there more places like Bow Market?
text:
“One of my friends says Bow Market’s the center of the universe,” said regular patron Sam Farnsworth on a recent Friday.

Somewhere between a small business incubator, a food court, and a European-style piazza, Bow Market stands as a bright spot in the Boston area’s brick-and-mortar landscape — a stark contrast to the struggling food halls and shopping malls dotting the region. But even in a region desperate for fresh retail and commercial real estate concepts, Bow Market remains just about as singular as it was when Baum and Boyes-Watson — two local thirty-somethings who run the market full time — pitched it a decade ago. That’s because all the things that make Bow the draw that it is, from its quirky use of real estate to its unique vendor mix, are also what can make it so challenging for homegrown projects like it to get all the “yeses” they need to come to life.

“There are people like us in every neighborhood and every downtown,” said Boyes-Watson. “All of these projects dance on a knife’s edge. All of them do. If you made it slightly easier, you might trip someone over into saying, ‘I’m doing this,’ versus not doing it.”

In the years since the pair founded Bow, construction costs have gotten pricier, and the financing environment is tougher. But the Bow Market founders said the far more crucial and elusive ingredient is flexibility from city hall on jumping through the legion of regulatory hoops.

“Something like this does need a champion in the local government, I think, to get it done,” said George Proakis, Somerville’s former planning chief and now the city manager of Watertown. “It’s not the thing your average zoning officer has seen.”

Proakis worked with Baum and Boyes-Watson to jigsaw the project into being, while still ensuring it wouldn’t be “locked in amber,” Baum said, and that it could evolve over time.

But that sort of municipal patience for projects that aren’t one-size-fits-all can be fleeting, the pair said.

In 2023, Bow said it would expand by about 6,000 square feet, spilling out onto Somerville Avenue. By the time it announced the expansion, Somerville had revamped its zoning code, and both Proakis and former Somerville mayor Joseph Curtatone, another supporter of Bow, had left City Hall. Baum and Boyes-Watson got the expansion done, but the whole process felt more complicated than just a few years earlier, they said, in a way that they believe would be all but impenetrable for others aspiring to create similar projects without the deepest of pockets.

“I think if we tried to do it today,” said Boyes-Watson of Bow, “we would have a way harder time.”

Part of the goal of Bow, its founders say, is for the markets’ triumphs to ripple outward to the local economy. Since opening in 2018, Bow has seeded the area with a bevy of its “alumni” who have graduated to their own standalone storefronts. But without the regulatory wiggle room granted to Bow’s owners, some of those businesses might never have opened in the market.

“I actually had absolutely no interest in opening a brick-and-mortar,” said Lauren Friel, the owner of Bow’s Rebel Rebel wine bar.

Vendors have been drawn to Bow by a few different factors: the relatively affordable rent (from about $1,300–$5,000 a month for most spaces); the manageable amount of inventory it takes to fill the storefronts (as small as 155 square feet); and the lease length (as short as a year, compared to five-year commitments common at other commercial spaces).

What ultimately sold Friel, however, was the fact that the market vendors were able to share a liquor license.

“There was just no other opportunity that existed anywhere in the city that didn’t require a half-a-million-dollar investment,” she said.

Three James Beard Awards nods and two new wine bars later, she still maintains she never would have become a proprietor had it not been for Bow, which she described as “a total unicorn situation.”

Those unicorns don’t always materialize. Boyes-Watson was also part of the team behind Starlight Square, a temporary pandemic-era space that opened in 2020 to host performances and small business markets on a municipal parking lot in Cambridge’s Central Square. Cambridge later awarded the team $500,000 in American Rescue Plan Act funding to go toward developing a permanent civic space modeled on Starlight.

“That would have been another Bow Market,” said Mark Boyes-Watson, Matthew’s father and the architect behind Bow and Starlight.

But asa 2024 city report recommended the Starlight site be developed into “a mixed-use building” — with housing, retail, a public plaza, and performance space — Cambridge reallocated Starlight’s funding to another arts-focused applicant. Starlight’s temporary structure soon shut down.

Later that year, the city put out a “request for information” seeking redevelopment ideas for the site. It got six responses, but progress has since been quiet.

“The City remains deeply committed to activating Central Square and making it a place the community gathers,” City of Cambridge spokesperson Jeremy Warnick said in an emailed statement.

A new project in Lowell is a testament to what can happen when all the stars align. After the owners of Mill No. 5, an eclectic indoor bazaar, announced in late 2024 that the market would close, some of the vendors banded together to find a new home.

“We didn’t know what it was called yet, we didn’t know where it was going to be, but we were very excited to do it on our own, because we knew we could manage it and we could make it happen,” said Jennifer Simone, who ran the artist collective Hive & Forge in Mill No. 5.

The business owners turned to the city, which offered funds and other support. In November, within a year of Mill No. 5’s closure, the newly formed Hive Public Market debuted in a 13,775-square-foot space on the ground floor of Lowell’s historic Hildreth Building. The market’s dozen or so shops — selling everything from video games to stationery to kitchenwares — are a mix of vendors from Mill No. 5 and new entrants.

“The owners are really the people that were making this happen,” said Thomas Golden, Lowell’s city manager. “We, the city, stood behind getting to ‘yes.’ ”

Back at Bow, many vendors, along with other observers, said the market’s special sauce is Baum and Boyes-Watson themselves.

“They’re a uniquely determined group of people, both to set this up and to continue to run it for all these years,” said Proakis.

Vendors said the pair are near-constant fixtures at Bow, as likely to work with entrepreneurs on a storefront expansion as they are to shovel snow in the courtyard.

“They really wanted, I think, to create a space that felt like a place that they wanted to be at,” said Brittany Lajoie, general manager at Remnant Brewing, the market’s anchor. “An owner, operator, developer who actually has a personal stake definitely feels different.”

The pair said people occasionally reach out looking for advice on developing similar concepts in other neighborhoods. More often, though, they’re approached by people who want them to helicopter into a new area and create Bow 2.0. It’s a request that, the pair must break to them, is futile.

“The folks that are going to be able to do this are the people that exist already in a community,” said Baum. “Don’t call us to come down to Dorchester and do it again. That doesn’t work. We don’t live there.”

title: After waiting out winter for a sunny day, Boston finally got one Tuesday
text:
From Carson Beach to Charles River Esplanade and Boston Common, people ditched puffer jackets for tank tops, shorts, and T-shirts to take advantage of the unseasonably warm weather.

Some were out biking, strolling, running, or reading a book under the sun; others sat around with friends or just by themselves.

“I am definitely enjoying the sunshine and the lack of clouds,” said Christina Fleisch, 26, who recently moved to Dorchester and sat near Carson Beach.

For many, the day truly felt like spring break after a long winter in which 61.5 inches of snow fell in Boston. Much of the snow has melted, but there are still piles and patches left on city streets.

“It’s very funny to be outside when it’s very warm, and there’s still snow on the ground,” said Kiran Hinze, a 30-year-old housing counselor at the Boston Common.

Nyx McDougle, 25, said the winter was really hard this year compared to the past couple years. McDougle said they wanted to come out to enjoy the first few strong rays of sun.

“Just wanted to get out, get my feet in the sand, get my skin exposed to the warm air,” McDougle said as they were lying down on a mat at Carson Beach.

They planned on spending the afternoon at the beach and brought a few books and a LEGO set.

For others, the sunshine was an excuse to slow down and spend time together.

Kerry Byrne, 39, who works for the City of Boston, sat near Carson Beach, with her parents, enjoying a lunch by the water while recovering from a broken leg.

“I’m almost two months into recovery, so [I] figured just to get down here and get some fresh air,” Byrne said as she planned on having chicken salad and tuna fish prepared by her mother for lunch.

Nearby, at the University of Massachusetts Boston campus, students also took advantage of the spring-like day between classes.

Liz Prochazka, a 21-year-old biology major, and her boyfriend, Ethan Rickard, a 20-year-old history major, walked hand-in-hand along the waterfront before classes.

“It’s very nice compared to the heavy snow and cold breeze, except for the giant mountains of dirty snow,” Prochazka said as she pointed out to a few lingering snow piles.

“Drove into school kind of late, but then we just went on a walk, because it’s just a nice day,” Rickard said.

Skie Manda, a 22-year-old graduate student, had been waiting for a sunny day to start training for the Boston Marathon.

“It was really hard for me to practice because it was really cold for the past couple of months,” Manda said. “This is my first run of the season. I’ve been doing pretty good so far.”

Downtown, workers stepped away from their offices for a quick dose of fresh air and sunshine at the Charles River Esplanade and the Boston Common.

Mike Lavin, 31, an auditor, spent his lunch break on the esplanade, which is just a 15-minute walk from his workplace. He usually comes down there around three times a week during the summer.

“The vitamin C feels so good, and guess that it’s definitely a mood booster,” Lavin said as he sat on a bench near the river. “I definitely feel a difference in my day when I’m able to get out here.”

Hinze walked through the Common during their lunch break. They planned to spend their entire break at the park and try to step on the grass if it isn’t very muddy.

“I’m very glad that we have the 70-degree weather,” they said. “I hope we have a few more days.”

Julia Klopfer, 27, a nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, met a friend for a five-mile run along the river on her day off. In the morning, she enjoyed the sun along with a cup of coffee on her front porch.

“It’s nice to feel the sun on my skin and just have a little bit of a respite from all the cold weather and watching all the snow melt,” Klopfer said as she waited for her friend near the river.

Northeastern students Perris Fisher, 24, and Elise Turner, 24, decided to have a picnic. They got coffee and EL Jefe’s and came to the Common.

“It was a beautiful girl’s day,” Turner said.

Some brought their pets outside to enjoy a rare warm day in March.

Jeff Neale, 37, came down to the esplanade with his mother’s cat, Jack Jack.

“This little guy’s been inside all winter and crying to get out,” Neale said, looking down at the fluffy grey cat he’s been looking after. “The dock here is not too much noise, so I figured [I’d] give it a try.”

At the Public Garden, Paul John, 38, played baseball with his five-year-old son, Harry, on his day off.

“He’s kind of been cooped in a little bit because of the storms and the weather, but we’re enjoying the weather and have some fun today,” said John, who works as an accountant. “Hopefully it holds up. I think we’re going to have a fantastic summer this year.”

While many embraced the warmth, most knew they could not be fooled by Mother Nature. Forecasts show colder temperatures returning next week. Still, for one day, Bostonians were happy to forget about winter.

“You better get it before it’s gone,” said David Byrne, 71, who was out having lunch with family near Carson Beach.

title: Wu announces millions in funding for immigrant organizations in Boston
text:
“Whether your family has been here for generations, or you are a new resident in our city — we will not let anyone storm into Boston and disrupt our community,“ Wu said at a press conference at City Hall. “With today’s announcement, we’re showing that the best way to keep our city safe is for us to come together as one. History is clear, when Boston stands together, no matter the odds, no matter the monarch, justice wins.”

About a month ago, Wu also signed an executive order that prohibited federal immigration officials from detaining people on municipal property, proposed ways to protect protestors, and stated that law enforcement would investigate allegations of agents breaking local or state laws.

On Tuesday, more than a dozen leaders from community organizations stood next to Wu and other city officials, including City Council President Liz Breadon, Councilor Enrique J. Pepén, and Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune.

Louijeune, the daughter of Haitian immigrants and the first Haitian American elected to Boston municipal government, greeted the crowd in English, Spanish, Haitian Creole, Chinese, and Portuguese. The funding announced on Tuesday, Louijeune said, would be essential to protecting immigrant groups in Boston — particularly when communities are on high alert.

“Vigilance requires resources,” Louijeune said. “People’s livelihoods are at stake, people’s families are at stake, and we have to use the resources to the social capital that we have, to make sure that we are standing up for those who are most vulnerable.”

Louijeune specifically reference the case of Emmanuel Damas, a Haitian immigrant who was living in Boston when he was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year. In early March, he died in ICE custody at a hospital in Arizona, near the detention center where he had been held for months. He had a toothache which led to a deadly infection after being left untreated, his family said. The Department of Homeland Security has contended that Damas received adequate medical care.

Damas leaves behind several family members in Dorchester, including his 13-year-old son, the Globe reported. Louijeune extended condolences to Damas’s family, and said she had recently met with them.

“There is absolutely no reason why someone should be dying from a toothache,” Louijeune said. “This statement of us all standing together in solidarity, is showing that we stand with people like Emmanuel Damas and his family — and we stand up against the harms that are being created by this administration."

Groups who would be distributed some of the funding included the Massachusetts Immigrant and Refugee Advocacy Coalition, the Mattapan-based Immigrant Family Services Institute, the Chinese Progressive Association, and the Mabel Center for Immigrant Justice, which provides immigrants with pro bono legal representation.

Lee Pelton, the CEO and president of The Boston Foundation — which as of last year had $1.7 billion in assets — thanked Wu for her recent executive orders regarding immigration policy, and noted that The Boston Foundation has assisted immigrants since its founding more than 100 years ago. And the Foundation would continue to do so, especially under the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies, Pelton said.

The federal government’s actions in places like Chicago, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and Maine, Pelton said, have made it clear that this moment calls “for truth telling, for mutual aid, for courage, and for resolve.”

“Moments like this remind us of something critically important,” he said. “Boston has always been a city shaped by immigrants. When our immigrant neighbors are threatened or vulnerable, we do not stand aside. We step forward. They are us, and we are them.”

title: No pot of gold: Collins investors fighting over St. Patrick’s Day auction for Southie site
text:
Andrew Collins, who is the identical twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, spent years assembling the Dot Ave. parcels and pitching the concept of a life-science campus there. That vision stayed abstract; Andrew Collins never formally proposed a project to the city. Senator Collins has said he has no connection with his brother’s real estate business.

Now the Dot Ave. land, and its ownership, is at the heart of the legal imbroglio facing Andrew Collins and his various business entities that the Globe first reported last year. A dozen suits in state and federal court allege Collins owes investors a combined $149 million; Collins has denied wrongdoing.

Together, the Dot Ave. parcels set for auction have an assessed value of $20.4 million. Just who owns the property, however, depends on who you ask.

The foreclosure auction notice heralds the land as a “major Boston development opportunity” being sold at the behest of those that own its mortgage, a partnership connected to New York real estate firms J.T. Magen & Co. and Extell Development. The companies and their development adviser, The HYM Investment Group, previously told the Globe that Collins has no financial interest in the South Boston property.

Collins disputes this, maintaining that his stake in the LLCs that the city assessor lists as the property’s owner gives him a cut of whatever happens to the property.

What’s more, last fall a Suffolk Superior Court judge ordered the county sheriff to sell the Dot Ave. property parcel-by-parcel to pay back an $8.6 million judgment in favor of Collins investors Divas Pant and Dhiraj Bora. An appeal is pending in that case.

Bora and Pant allege that J.T. Magen and Extell are “working in concert ... to violate and circumvent a court order” that could drastically limit their ability to collect on that judgment, their attorneys wrote in a March 6 court filing.

“Defendants are using the foreclosure sale for an illegitimate or ulterior purpose,” attorneys David A. Russcol and Nina L. Pickering-Cook wrote. “If the foreclosure sale is allowed to proceed ... the Pant/Bora Judgment would be eviscerated, as Collins is likely unable to satisfy the Pant/Bora Judgment other than by the sale of the Properties.”

In a recent letter to Russcol, an attorney for the J.T. Magen and Extell partnership acknowledged as much, saying Pant and Bora’s judgment “of course is subordinate to the mortgage” and that any funds from the sale would go to pay off the mortgage before their debt.

The auction includes an option to buy two additional properties that Collins did not assemble, including a drive-thru Dunkin’ Donuts. A company affiliated with J.T. Magen purchased the two lots at 370 Dot Ave. and 75 Old Colony Ave. in late 2023 for $25 million, more than four times their assessed value, according to a Suffolk County deed.

Through an attorney, Collins said he intends to challenge the auction.

“Action will be taken promptly to protect the interests of relevant entities in which Mr. Collins is involved at those locations,” attorney Raymond P. Ausrotas said in an email.

J.T. Magen and Extell have until Thursday to respond to Pant and Bora’s injunction — just days before St. Patrick’s Day.

title: Boston pubs and restaurants that make you feel like you are in Ireland
text:
Sharon Carey

General manager, Carrie Nation

Where do you go?

There’s a little pub called The Druid and it’s amazing. It’s a little hole in the wall, and there’s just such an Irish vibe to it. It’s friendly, the staff are lovely, the food’s great, and it’s tiny. And also I’m a massive fan of Emmets. Another bar, the Brendan Behan, is really cool as well. I like the smaller little nooks and the little bars. It reminds you of a pub at home. The only thing missing is the fireplace, where you’re sitting by the fire on a cold winter night, sipping Irish coffee, chatting with your friends, having the craic.

What do you order?

Shepherd’s pie. You know us Irish and our meat and potatoes, right? Actually, I make it all the time. When you mash the potatoes, you have to use the Kerrygold Irish butter and the full-fat milk. Shepherd’s pie is technically lamb, but not gonna lie, I do use beef. My other half is definitely a Guinness drinker. He will get a Guinness whether we’re at The Druid or Emmets or The Dubliner. I love a good Irish coffee. Emmets does a good one. The Druid does as well.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in a little town called Carndonagh in County Donegal. I came in 2005 to the US, for work, I suppose, excitement, I was young and wanted to travel. All them things. It’s a small town. It’s definitely got a little bit smaller. While I was growing up, I think there were something like 13 bars in our town, which is quite a lot for the size of it. That’s gone down in numbers a lot through the years. It’s very rural, an Irish little town. Everybody knew everybody, and if you didn’t know them personally, you knew their brother or sister or mother or granny. It’s definitely a close-knit community. It’s like that in Boston, as well, though. There’s such a huge Irish connection here, from all over. Everybody supports and tries to help each other out.

CJ Crawford

Bartender, The Druid

Where do you go?

The Druid!

What do you order?

The fish and chips and a pint of Guinness. Oh, and don’t forget the curry sauce. Make sure you say that.

What’s your hometown?

Liscannor in County Clare. It’s just in the shadow of the Cliffs of Moher, so it’s a lovely spot. It’s definitely somewhere you want to go, whenever you get here.

Mary Kiely

Director of operations and co-owner, The James, Essex

Where do you go?

If I was to think about my favorite Irish bar, I would probably say The Druid in Cambridge. The food menu is great, the Guinness is great, it’s a great people-watching place, and the music is great. It’s always a good time. I also really like Devlin’s and The Abbey, which are closer to my home, and Porter Cafe in West Roxbury.

What do you order?

I like to try fish and chips in most restaurants I go to, especially the Irish ones. What makes a good fish and chips, I think, is a light, crispy batter, the tartar sauce has to be really good, and crispy fries. I like Guinness, especially in March, and I also love a good Irish coffee. But usually I like to drink sauvignon blanc, French if they have it. Not really Irish! (Laughs.) We’ll be drinking a lot of Guinness this week.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in Cork city. Cork is great. It’s a pretty big city with good nightlife and lots of restaurants. It’s a college town, so there are a lot of young people, and it’s always been kind of vibrant. My dad is from the country and I have aunts and uncles spread out all around the county of Cork; I spent a lot of time in Kinsale, and my cousin runs a pub in Drimoleague.

Aidan McGee

Chef and partner, The Dubliner and McGonagle’s

Where do you go?

I usually find Emmets Irish Pub on Beacon Hill is really, really good. It’s been around well over 20 years, and it keeps that small pub feel about it. It’s got that old-school Boston Irish vibe. You can get Irish cider in there. The bartenders are all Irish. It’s a very simple, homely kind of vibe, like I’d get sitting in my local in Donegal.

What do you order?

The sausage roll is my go-to if I’m just having a snack. We call it a sausage roll, here you call it pigs in a blanket. It’s nice, flaky pastry. It’s always fresh. I’m having the fish and chips if I’m extra-hungry. The fish and chips is really good.

What’s your hometown?

It’s in the northwest of Ireland, Donegal Town, right on the border to Northern Ireland. It’s an amazing place, very scenic, very rustic and rugged. National Geographic once voted it the most sought-after place, so we get loads of tourists coming from all over the world, but the locals never change. That hospitality is still there. The people are amazing. If your car breaks down, they’ll give you a lift or fix it for you. It’s that kind of country vibe. There’s very simply cooked fresh fish and loads of pubs that are just amazing. They don’t try to be anything they’re not. They’ve evolved, but they haven’t really changed.

Amy O’Sullivan

Server and bartender, Mr. Dooley’s

Where do you go?

I come right here into Mr. Dooley’s. That is the answer. If you ask me where I would like to go when I’m feeling homesick, it’s right in here. There’s very good Irish food in The Dubliner and McGonagle’s, too.

What do you order?

Beef stew and a pint of Guinness.

What’s your hometown?

Bantry, West Cork. It’s beautiful, stunning. Have you been? Well, you’ll have to do it now for your paper.

Dermot Quinn

Owner, Greenhills Bakery

Where do you go?

Obviously the Greenhills Bakery. Then you’ve got the Irish pubs. On St. Patrick’s week, we just find someplace with Irish music downtown. There’s The Banshee, another place down on Dorchester Ave. My wife (and Greenhills co-owner), Cindy Quinn, is from Holden. We met downtown in an Irish pub back in ’89. It’s not there anymore but it was up the street from Mr. Dooley’s.

What do you order?

We feature our Irish boiling bacon. That’s a favorite growing up. It’s like the rashers from Ireland, but boiled not fried. It’s a tradition in Ireland. Corned beef was not a staple in our diet growing up. It was either ham or boiling bacon. We boil it for like two hours and use the juices from the boiling bacon to make a white sauce, like a bechamel, with parsley. Then we serve it with cabbage and carrots and turnips and potatoes and stuff like that. We serve boiled dinner every Thursday, and we give out two slices of soda bread. Americans don’t really eat the white sauce, that’s more of an Irish thing.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in County Offaly, out in the country. We grew up taking care of the farm. I’m one of 12 children. We had to fight for our space growing up. We fed the calves and pigs and did the farm work, sowed the potatoes, picked the potatoes, and took care of all the vegetables. My grandmother and mother always made the breads every day, made the butter, milked the cows and took the cream off the milk, then used the buttermilk to make the bread. It was a culture we grew up with. My grandmother passed away on Jan. 12, 1990. I had gone home to see her a month before. I said, “Granny, give me the recipe for the brown bread.” I came back not thinking I was ever going to use this recipe, then two months later I was trying it out in our apartment. There was a butcher shop in South Boston; we brought him down some brown bread and scones. He wanted more and more and more, then I had to rent a kitchen and it snowballed. We had our grand opening with Mayor Flynn 35 years ago.

Kevin Treanor

Owner, Chemist Cocktail Bar, Hugh O’Neill’s, The Merchant, and the Phoenix Landing

Where do you go?

I like the Phoenix Landing, where the Guinness I think is the best. Also The Druid, where I used to bartend. On St. Patrick’s Day, we give out real shamrocks that we order from a florist here in Cambridge.

What do you order?

I know it’s an American thing, but I do like my corned beef dinner. We didn’t have that growing up. A pint of Guinness and an Irish breakfast or corned beef dinner. At the Phoenix Landing, the Irish breakfast is one of our biggest sellers. We even have it on the main menu.

What’s your hometown?

I’m from Monaghan, Monaghan town. It hasn’t changed a whole lot. It’s very working class. The biggest manufacturer there now would be a company called Combilift: Those things that carry a forklift on the back of a truck, they come from Monaghan. It’s one of our claims to fame. The other is we have the biggest export of ducklings and mushrooms. It’s a nice, quiet spot. I love it, but people have never heard of it. I arrived here in San Francisco in the early ’90s and I didn’t know anything about St. Patrick’s Day. In Ireland, it was a religious holiday. We’d go to Mass and there was no drinking afterward. Now, of course, they do what the Americans do. I thought: People are celebrating St. Patrick’s Day like this? I thought this was fabulous, and I still do!

title: The unsolved murder of Kendric Price, a beloved youth mentor gunned down on his childhood street in Dorchester
text:
“I’m not saying I can change the world,” Price told the Globe in 2012. “But I’m planning to make a difference one child at a time.”

He also coached basketball, first as an assistant coach at Roxbury Community College and University of Massachusetts Boston, and later as a head coach at Brooke High School.

In March 2019, Price was settling into his new job at Cristo Rey Boston High School and getting ready to move into a new apartment in downtown Boston when he was killed on Greenwood Street, the street he grew up on in Dorchester.

He was 32.

No one has ever been charged with his killing.

His mother, Carol Price, remembers the last time she saw him.

It was Friday night, and she cooked him one of his favorite dishes for dinner: sauteed chicken with onions, green peppers, rice, broccoli, and cheese.

“That day, he came home, he said he was tired. ‘But it’s a good tired,’ he said,” she recalled.

Price told his mother he was going to stay in and take it easy that night.

“He said he was not going out at all,” she said.

But for some reason, after his mother went to sleep, he changed his mind and decided to stop by a garage at 12A Greenwood St., just down the street from his mother’s house. The garage was a known party spot,according to Globe reports at the time.

“It was a party, an after-hours type of thing,” she said.

That’s where he was when gunfire broke out shortly before 3 a.m.

Officers found his body riddled with gunshot wounds, according to police. A police report did not indicate that anyone else was wounded.

For a long time, Price kept thinking that if she had only been awake, she could have stopped him before he went out the door.

“I beat myself up for a long time,” she said.

She still wonders who was at the party when her son was shot.

After her son was killed, many people came to her to show their support while she was grieving, she said. But no one spoke about what actually transpired that night, leading her to assume that witnesses did not come forward and “no one told the police anything.”

When she spoke to investigators right after his death, she pleaded with them to find out what happened and arrest whoever was responsible for taking her son’s life.

“Please do not let this become a cold case,” she said. “I want justice for my son.”

Seven years later, she is still waiting.

“I’d love for someone who knows something to please come forward,” she said. “This perpetrator has probably killed other people since. He needs to be held accountable.”

Carol Price doesn’t like using the word “anniversary” to describe the date of her son’s death. For her, March 2 is a “trauma-versary,” a day she relives the pain and anguish she felt when she learned she had lost her son.

Price had so many opportunities ahead of him and should have had a bright future, she said.

She recalled how busy he always was with school, sports, and other extracurricular activities. And that’s exactly what she wanted: for him to pursue his interests and stay out of trouble.

“I always thought, I don’t ever want the streets to get my son,” she said. “And unfortunately he went to a party, and that’s what happened.”

Carol Price still lives on the same street where her son was murdered and has to pass by the garage where he spent his last moments.

She can’t help but wonder what could have been.

“Kendric came back to Boston,” she said. “He chose to come back and help those who were left behind.”

So she tries to turn her pain into something productive, by giving back to the community like Price did.

She continues to run Big Business Network because it helps people and “reminds me of him,” she said.

Boston police say they continue to investigate Price’s murder.

“It’s an open and active investigation,” said John Boyle, a spokesperson for the Boston Police Department. “We urge anyone to come forward with information, no matter how little they think it is.”

Anyone with information about the murder of Kendric Price can call Boston police homicide detectives at 617-343-4470. Those wishing to leave an anonymous tip can call CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS or text the word ‘TIP’ to 27463.

title: Just six days of war in Iran cost us $11.3 billion. ‘What the [expletive] is wrong with us?’
text:
It adds up!

But, as we all keep hearing, freedom isn’t free. Just how not-free has been difficult to pin down so far. There have been higher estimates, but most experts seem to agree that, in addition to the loss of seven US service members, we’ve been burning through at least $1 billion a day since we joined Israel to attack Iran on February 28. Pentagon officials told Congress on Tuesday that the first six days alone cost $11.3 billion. Wheeeeeeee!

It can be hard for anyone not named Musk or Bezos to understand numbers that big.

Here, Richard Kogan, a budget expert at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, was helpful. According to his math, a billion a day is more than the federal government spends on all State Department, embassy, and foreign aid programs. He said it’s about what we spend on programs for NASA, scientific research, natural resources, environment, agriculture, commerce, and transportation infrastructure put together. A billion a day is more than double what we spend on all federal education and job training programs, including Pell grants and federal K-12 school aid to states. It is twice our daily spend on all VA hospitals and health care for veterans.

For perspective closer to home: The city of Boston’s entire operating budget was $4.6 billion for 2025. A few days’ worth of Iran spending could cover it.

It costs $60 million per year to run the Codman Square community health center, which serves 23,000 patients each year, and $33.6 million to operate the Food Bank of Western Massachusetts. You could fund them both for 10 years with what we’re spending in a day to level Iran. One billion dollars could buy school lunches for 1.8 million American children for a year.

Poof go the billions. Down come the bombs. Up come the body counts.

Congressman Jim McGovern has been working these numbers, too, and he hates them.

“What the [expletive] is wrong with us,” he said. “It’s just all screwed up.”

The Worcester Democrat has devoted his career to making sure hungry people get fed in the richest country on the planet. Year after year, he pushes for more funding for food stamps, school lunches, and food pantries, and year after year, Congress refuses to do enough. So it’s especially galling for him to see money that could be feeding American children being used to kill Iranian ones.

Reached between stops delivering Meals on Wheels to seniors in Millbury on Wednesday morning, McGovern rattled off the figures: The United States has already spent in Iran more money than the federal government spends on our 1,500 community health centers, more than it spends on Head Start programs for preschoolers each year, and three times what it spends on fuel assistance for low income households annually. McGovern said we have already spent enough in Iran to fund the entire Meals on Wheels program for a decade.

“We spend pennies on everything else, yet when it comes to war, there’s no limit,” he said. “How is this America First?”

The congressman points out that everybody was all “America First” when it came to slashing global food aid and lifesaving USAID health programs designed to uplift poor people around the world. Now, however, “We hear not a peep,” he said.

Well, it wouldn’t be the first time Republicans have done a 180 to align themselves with the whims of the capricious cult leader in the White House. President Trump broke his many promises not to get us into any wars, but most of his fellow Republicans wouldn’t dream of calling him on it. Actually, this isn’t a war, they argue on TV, as the footage of the widening conflagration plays on the split screen. Or, we’ve been at war for decades. Or, Iran started it, or was going to. Or, it’s just about over already.

Almost two weeks in, they can’t even get their story straight about why we attacked in the first place. All of which is making it more difficult to justify how much taxpayer money they’re spending there in our names.

History shows that Americans have a pretty high tolerance for deaths in the Middle East. But when raining destruction upon others costs them real money, even gung-ho types start to get wobbly. Voters might not be able to always get their heads around the billions it takes to destroy mosques and fuel depots, but we can sure understand $3.58 a gallon at the gas pump.

Like Trump, a few game Republicans, like Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, have been telling Americans that they should suck it up. Marshall, who argued last year that Iran was nowhere near nuclear weapons capability, now says he was wrong. Why? Because the White House says so.

“Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices,” he said on CNN, of spiking gas prices. “This is one of the prices of war.”

Oh well then, by all means, let’s pay it. What’s a billion-plus a day, when our cause must be so righteous, so just?

If only they could tell us what it is.

title: Life expectancy gap between Black residents and other Bostonians has doubled over the past decade
text:
Community leaders say the loss of years for Black residents is fueled by systemic racism in Boston, which has led to community divestment and residential segregation.

“It’s always going to be different numbers for us, because the Black and Brown community is always overlooked,” said Lovelee Harvey, 56, a senior recovery coach at Metro Boston Alive, a nonprofit recovery center in Roxbury.

Over the last few months, the Boston Public Health Commission organized state mortality data by race and ethnicity to develop its life expectancy analysis, part of its “Live Long and Well” agenda, which examines how systemic racism has created this public health crisis.

A longer report containing more detailed data is expected to be released in April, said Dr. Bisola Ojikutu, executive director of the Boston Public Health Commission.

We broke down the “Closing the Gap” report, released Feb. 27; here are five takeaways.

The life expectancy gap is widening: Since 2013, Black residents maintained living around 78 years, while the rest of Boston’s life expectancy rose from about 81 to 85 years.

Black men, in particular, have the lowest life expectancy compared to all other groups, according to the report. Between 2022 and 2024, they lived about 9.3 fewer years than other men in Boston.

Black women have the lowest life expectancy compared to all other women, having lived about 6.4 years fewer than other women from 2022 to 2024.

“We think about the drivers of life expectancy, and we know that those are social and structural determinants of health,” Ojikutu said.

Black residents have maintained the lowest life expectancy of all major racial groups in Boston, at around 76 years in the latest period from 2022 to 2024, according to state data.

Meanwhile, Asian residents had the highest life expectancy of about 88 years from 2022 to 2024.

Life expectancy for all groups declined during the COVID-19 pandemic from 2019 to 2021, but have since rebounded.

The life expectancy gap between Black residents and other Bostonians has doubled over the past decade — from 3.3 years to 6.6 years.

“That should concern everyone,” said Winston Bodrick, executive director of the Roxbury YMCA and a member of the Live Long and Well Advisory Council, a new group of community leaders who will help guide efforts to close the gap. “Life expectancy is one of the most fundamental measures of how well the community is doing, so that was a real drawback for me.”

Ojikutu said the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Black residents lost more years of life than other groups, as well as a steep increase in overdose mortality, particularly among Black men, contributed to the gap’s doubling.

Unintentional drug overdoses — the product of substance use disorder and a drug supply that is frequently contaminated, such as with fentanyl — were the leading cause of premature death for Black men in Boston from 2022 to 2024. They have led the causes of premature deaths since 2020.

Negative stigma surrounding substance abuse may trigger feelings of shame for those struggling with addiction, discouraging them from seeking treatment, Ojikutu said. Greg Davis, a former heroin and cocaine user, said those feelings would only intensify his addiction.

“Each time those feelings kicked up for me, I sedated myself, which I believe is what’s going on with a lot of these folks who are still addicted,” said Davis, founder and president of Metro Boston Alive.

Davis added that many struggling with addiction don’t seek help because “they don’t trust the system.”

Now 41 years clean, Davis, 76, is exceeding the report’s average life expectancy for Black men.

Harvey, who described himself as a former “more user” — “If somebody had more, I would use it,” he said with a hearty laugh — overdosed more than 10 times during his active addiction. He recalled being angry about being given Narcan on multiple occasions, but now, he distributes Narcan on the streets every day.

Heart disease and cancer were nearly as significant, followed by homicide and several other health conditions.

Systemic barriers have contributed to these chronic diseases going unchecked, said Dr. Christopher Lathan, chief clinical access officer for the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and a member of the Live Long and Well Advisory Council. They are present in every stage of health care: prevention, screening and treatment.

Being unable to take time off work, or not having a primary care clinician at all, can hinder receiving a health screening.

“You can’t just stop your life and then focus on the cancer, which is what a lot of folks who have any means will do,” Lathan said.

Bodrick, of the Roxbury YMCA, said institutions like the YMCA play a “critical role” in addressing the life expectancy disparity by promoting physical health and wellness.

“We provide safe spaces for physical activity, youth development, community development, as well as preventative wellness programming,” Bodrick said. “These moments may look small, but together, I think they shape lives.”

Communities in Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan have the lowest life expectancies in Boston, Ojikutu said.

A 2023 report by the BPHC found a 23-year difference in average life expectancy between Roxbury and Back Bay. In Dorchester, that gap is approximately 20 years, and in Mattapan, the gap is approximately 18 years, Ojikutu said.

These neighborhoods are home to majority-Black populations, according to the Globe’s neighborhood census maps. Mattapan has the largest share of Black residents, with 69.8 percent, while Black residents make up 42.9 percent of Roxbury and 36 percent of Dorchester.

These are also not wealthy neighborhoods, according to the Globe maps. Only 8.9 percent of Roxbury households earn more than $200,000 a year, compared to 13.7 percent in Mattapan and 15.4 percent in Dorchester.

The city pledged on Feb. 27 to contribute $2 million toward medical screenings and other preventative programs to curb the widening life expectancy gap, adding to the $10 million investment from the Atrius Health Equity Foundation in 2024 focused on increasing economic opportunity in neighborhoods with lower life expectancies.

To reduce drug overdoses, Harvey said the community needs the right people to “educate in a loving, caring, culturally competent way.” He hopes the city will promote education and economical development, and give a “fair share” to underprivileged communities.

Lathan, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said tackling food deserts and creating community health centers, among other efforts, can promote screenings and other forms of prevention.

“We have a government, both city and state, that’s really interested in trying to alleviate the barriers,” Lathan said. “Hope should not be restricted to just affluent communities. Hope should be accessible to all.”

title: A hawk goes on the lam, a man plows snow on protestors, and friends fight over a dirt bike
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police blotters in our communities.

Back in January, a man reported that his red-tailed hawk had gone missing and was last seen in Medfield. Fast forward about a month later, and Trixie was found safe in Millis and returned to her owner. Millis/Medway animal control shared the good news on social media on Feb. 25, and thanked everyone who reached out to animal control Officer Kelley Ward after they noticed the red-tailed hawk was wearing a bell. “That small detail made a big difference,” the post said. “ACO Ward remembered that Trixie had gone missing from a nearby town and was able to track down her owner and reunite them. This is a perfect example of why reporting unusual wildlife behavior matters and how teamwork makes all the difference.”

At 2:19 a.m. Feb. 18, Beverly police checked on a potentially disabled vehicle near the intersection of Elliott Street and McPherson Drive. According to the log entry, police checked out the situation and the vehicle wasn’t broken down; it was “just a citizen admiring a duck.”

On Feb. 18, police got a call from someone who reported seeing two masked men inside a black van at the Skug River parking area on Salem Street in Andover. Police arrived and determined that there were ski masks pulled over the headrests of the van, but there was no one inside. Although it turned out to be nothing, police said calls like this one are important. “We would rather respond to 100 of these calls and have nothing wrong, than not receive a call when something was noticed to be out of the ordinary,” police wrote on social media. “So … if you see something, please say something.”

At 12:30 a.m. Feb. 7, when Watertown police were dispatched to a report of a fight unfolding on Maplewood Street, officers arrived to find two men yelling at each other over a motorized dirt bike that was on the ground between them. One of the men told police that his friend had agreed to buy the bike for $1,300, but when he handed him the money for it, he noticed the slogan “For Motion Picture Use Only” was stamped on the bills — a telltale sign that the cash was counterfeit. He alleged his pal then tried to grab the bike, and that’s when they started fighting. The fellow who allegedly tried using bogus bills for the purchase was identified as a 19-year-old Dorchester resident. He was arrested on charges of attempting to commit a crime, unarmed robbery, disturbing the peace, and possession of counterfeit notes.

A 65-year-old man is facing criminal charges after he allegedly used his plow to throw slush and snow on anti-ICE protestors who were gathered at Chapman Park in Rockland, Maine, on Feb. 21. Police said the man drove his truck, with the plow down, in close proximity to approximately 75 people at the park, where they were holding their demonstration. “This action caused snow and ice to strike multiple people, some with enough force to knock them to the ground,” Rockland police wrote in a social media post. “No one saw it coming,” one of the participants said in an interview with News Center Maine. “People heard the ‘thunk’ of that blade hitting the pavement. And immediately it started throwing up this wall of cold, slushy, brownish muck on everybody.” Such demonstrations have become a weekly occurrence at the park, with participants holding signs featuring slogans such as “Save Democracy,” “Clear ICE From Our Streets,” and “Impeach Trump.” Police said they would be increasing their presence at the group’s upcoming gatherings.

title: Headed to the St. Patrick’s parade on Sunday? Here’s how to get there, and when parking restrictions begin.
text:
Don’t drive to this year’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade in South Boston.

That’s the message from city officials ahead of Sunday’s event, which is expected to draw nearly a million attendees. Almost two dozen road closures will take effect around the parade route starting Sunday morning, as the city sends public transportation into overdrive to help carry the merry multitudes.

This year’s St. Patrick’s Day Parade, traveling its old route in reverse, will begin at 11:30 a.m. in Andrew Square, covering three-and-a-half miles of South Boston streets before ending near the Broadway Station Red Line Stop.

According to the city’s website, parade attendees are strongly encouraged to bike, take public transit, or walk to the event. The MBTA has announced it will offer free shuttles from South Station to and from parade areas between 9:30 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Sunday. The T is also running “rush hour service” on the Red Line between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. as revelers travel into Boston and back home.

South Boston residents with permit stickers on their vehicles can park at The Marine Park Garage at 12 Drydock Ave. for a reduced rate between Saturday night at 6 p.m. and Sunday at 8 p.m., according to the city’s advisory.

Parking restrictions, 22 in all, will take effect on Sunday, with towing enforcement beginning at 2 a.m. Sunday morning.

title: Lawmakers call for more answers from ICE about Haitian man’s death
text:
Damas’s family has deep roots in Boston; two of his brothers, his mother, and his two sons live in the city. Damas, 56, was living with his sons and mother in Dorchester before he was arrested by ICE in September, after a domestic incident.

ICE then transported Damas more than 2,000 miles away to the Florence Correctional Center in Arizona. Damas told staff at the facility that he had a toothache around mid-February — which he had spoken of in phone calls to his family — but was not taken to see a dentist, his brother Presly Nelson told me.

When I checked in this week, Nelson shared that the brothers have been spending much of their time trying to care for their 76-year-old mother, who hasn’t been sleeping or eating, and is experiencing bouts of depression. They’re also looking after Damas’s 13-year-old son, looking for mental health services for him, and trying to encourage him to still attend middle school despite all that’s happened.

Most of all, the family is pressing for more information from the federal government about how such a tragedy could follow a mere toothache.

“Right now, you know as much as I do,” Nelson told me, “which is nothing.”

Damas was seeking asylum and had entered the country legally through a Biden-era humanitarian parole program for Haitians in 2024, according to his family, and was fleeing gang violence back home in Haiti. His initial asylum claim was denied by an immigration judge in January who ordered him deported; Damas appealed.

ICE has reached out only to confirm Nelson’s address in order to mail him Damas’s belongings — and to send a letter of condolence, Nelson said. “I have no idea what happened while [Damas] was in custody in the last two weeks before he was hospitalized,” Nelson said. “I’m still in the dark.”

Last week, ICE released a statement about Damas’s death, saying that he was transferred to different hospitals to receive higher levels of care. ICE said the agency alerted Damas’s family as his condition worsened and notified Congress after his death. Damas was facing criminal charges for assault and battery, according to ICE and Massachusetts district court records.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the statement said. “At no time during detention is a detained alien denied emergency care.”

2025 was the deadliest year for people held in immigration detention in more than two decades, with more 30 people dying in ICE custody. Since January of this year, at least 11 people have died in ICE custody, according to agency news releases.

Lawmakers in Massachusetts and Arizona have called for more answers from ICE about Damas’s death. Last week, Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, along with Representative Ayanna Pressley, wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and ICE acting director Todd Lyons demanding a full investigation.

Markey told the Globe in a statement Thursday that Damas’s death “was a terrible, preventable tragedy.”

“It is critical that immigrants in ICE’s custody receive timely and proper medical care,” Markey said.

Now, the family is having to pay for an autopsy, Nelson said, and for his body to be flown back to Boston. They will hold a vigil for Damas next week.

Nelson asked that the people of Boston keep his family “in their thoughts and prayers.”

“I don’t know what really happened, but I’d like to have a fair and honest investigation. And whatever the investigation gives us, we will let it be,” Nelson said. “I don’t know, maybe it was all fair, maybe it wasn’t. So only a fair investigation will tell us exactly what happened.”

Great! But the Fascist Trump Regime will build the detention facility elsewhere. The attack on immigrants is a spearhead of a whole fascist program being carried out in the US.
