title: The 2026 Sox: You gotta have faith
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Even after four World Series titles this century, skepticism remains in a Red Sox fan’s blood.

And last season ended with a loss to the dastardly Yankees in the wild-card round, an unacceptable outcome that in the pre-championships past would have led to the pursuit of the biggest names available.

Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow did not take that approach. But the approach he did take, dearest skeptics, may well have been one that will make the Red Sox a better all-around team this season. Here are three reasons why you should have faith in these ’26 Sox:

The ascent of Roman Anthony: When he came to the plate with two outs in the ninth inning and the United States trailing Venezuela, 3-2, in the World Baseball Classic championship game last week, many Red Sox fans had the same thought: He’s going deep. Walk-off homer. A USA baseball hero at the age of 21.

It did not work out that way – Anthony struck out on a 99 mph fastball — but the expectation made all the sense in the world. Anthony’s arrival from the minor leagues last June was much-heralded — he was considered the top prospect in baseball — and yet he somehow exceeded expectations, batting .292 with 8 home runs and an .849 OPS in 53 games before an oblique injury ended his season in September.

He was arguably the US’s best player at the WBC, and with good health, he will be one of the best in the American League this season. The Red Sox’ next homegrown superstar is here, people.

An improved defense: The Red Sox’ outfield defense has been mostly excellent in recent seasons, with Wilyer Abreu winning two Gold Gloves and Ceddanne Rafaela and Jarren Duran one apiece. But their infield defense? That was often another story, with some infielders often fielding as if their gloves were welded from a different metal. Steel, maybe. Or iron.

This season, infield defense should go from a detriment to a strength. Willson Contreras is a significant defensive upgrade at first base, while smooth Marcelo Mayer earned the starting second base job. Reliable Trevor Story remains at short, while potential fan-favorite Caleb Durbin, acquired in a trade with the Brewers, takes over at third for the departed Alex Bregman. The result: the Red Sox should play much crisper games this season.

Starting pitching quality and depth: Three seasons ago, the Red Sox’ Opening Day starter was 36-year-old bargain-bin pickup Corey Kluber. He had a 7.04 ERA in 15 games that season and threw his final major league pitch in June.

That October, Craig Breslow was hired as chief baseball officer, and his greatest success since has been building up the Red Sox’ major league staff and pitching program. On Wednesday, Garrett Crochet, the runner-up for the American League Cy Young award last season, will make his second Opening Day start for the Red Sox. He is followed in the rotation by veteran offseason pickups Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez, holdover Brayan Bello, and Johan Oviedo, with an array of promising pitchers, including lefties Connelly Early and Peyton Tolle, waiting in the wings.

The Red Sox? With pitching depth?

Our grandfathers never would have believed it.

In yesterday’s Starting Point, Globe reporter Shelley Murphy invited reader questions about gangster James “Whitey” Bulger. Here’s one question, and Shelley’s answer:

Q. I read somewhere that during the Boston busing crisis, Bulger was planning on blowing up a school bus full of Black students coming to South Boston schools. I’d love to know more about this. Warmly, Yolette Ibokette.

A. Thank you for your kind email. Whitey vehemently opposed court-ordered desegregation of Boston’s schools and went on a rampage behind the scenes, though I never confirmed any stories about him threatening to blow up a bus full of children.

I wrote a story for the Globe in 2001 linking Bulger to the firebombing of John F. Kennedy’s birthplace in Brookline in 1974 and the torching a year later of a school near the home of Judge W. Arthur Garrity, Jr. That story was based on an account provided to me by a Bulger associate. He also confirmed that he was with Bulger when the pair of them fired machine guns into the Globe because of its editorial support for school desegregation.

After Bulger’s capture in 2011, he wrote letters to a former friend who served time with him in Alcatraz, confirming my earlier story. In the letters, shared with us, Bulger boasted about throwing a Molotov cocktail into Kennedy’s birthplace in retaliation for senator Ted Kennedy’s outspoken support for school desegregation — and spray-painting “Bus Teddy” on the sidewalk outside. He also admitted to torching the school near Garrity’s house, and shooting at the Globe.

Thank you for being a Globe reader, Shelley Murphy.

title: After a midseason turnaround in 2025, Franklin baseball ready to return to elite status
text:
In a new season, the Panthers, ranked No. 6 in the Globe’s preseason Top 20, are ready to build on a successful stretch run a season ago.

The goal is for a program that won the Super 8 title in 2018 and made back-to-back title games in 2022 and 2023 to get back to that point.

“Just after a couple scrimmages, looking at the team, I’m really excited for this season,” said senior captain Sean Kryzak.

Last spring, Franklin took down fifth-seeded Xaverian and battled to the last out with No. 4 King Philip in the quarterfinal, losing on a walkoff. They worked their turnaround well, and it provided valuable varsity experience for the young squad.

“We just put our head down,” senior captain Jack Sullivan said. “Any adversity we faced, we made it through. We made the elite eight, in a game we definitely wish we had back, but I think that just prepared us mentally for this season.”

Leading the way are senior captains Sullivan, Kryzak, and DJ Silverstein. Sullivan, a Globe All-Scholastic honorable mention a season ago, hit .358 with 29 hits and is heading to Babson in the fall.

He — like many of the Panthers — takes a ton of pride in representing the community.

“It’s not just the high school,” Sullivan said. “It’s all those youth kids that come watch the games. … At the end of the day, our goal is to win a state championship, and that’s what we’re here to do.”

Silverstein (Bentley) is the Panthers’ ace — he pitched 55 innings last spring with a 2.42 ERA as a righty with a 6-foot-3-inch frame.

Kryzak (Brandeis) provides a veteran presence in the outfield and on the mound. Junior Owen Pennini is a crucial outfielder, and sophomore first baseman Patrick Luizzi led the Hockomock League with 22 RBIs a season ago. Junior Joe Goguen returns behind the plate, as does senior Drake McAlpine at third.

“Coach Brown — the greatest coach — always talks about the compound effect,” Kryzak said. “Repeated work, doing it over and over. Make sure you’re doing it right and it has a positive outcome. Especially to bring together the younger guys last year, it’ll hopefully follow through this year. And it seems like it will.”

A public school does not typically “gain” kids. There are graduation losses, and departures to the preps and privates. Teams rely on players from town.

It helps to do it in Franklin.

“Some people say baseball’s fading and this and that, but it’s strong in Franklin,” Brown said. “Franklin’s a baseball town. It’s a great town, and a great community.”

It’s a very tough task to win the Hockomock League — last spring, the league produced four of the top 12 seeds in the Division 1 tournament (Taunton, King Philip, Attleboro, and Franklin) and four of the top 14 seeds in Division 2 (North Attleboro, Mansfield, Canton, and Milford).

But iron sharpens iron.

“We’re definitely held to a higher standard than a lot of other programs with the recent success,” Silverstein said. “That helps with the development a lot. It prepares younger guys well to step up when their number’s called.”

▪ Did you enjoy following Brody Bumila’s basketball exploits for Bishop Feehan in the Division 1 tournament? Well, baseball season is his preferred time of year.

The 6-9 senior lefthander, committed to Texas, is generating plenty of well-deserved buzz. He’ll finally pitch again at the high school level this spring, after only hitting last year because of injury. Expect standing-room only when he’s on the hill.

Baseball America recently named him the No. 29 high school prospect in the country for the 2026 MLB Draft, and the No. 6 lefthanded pitcher.

▪ A refresher: Chelmsford is the reigning Division 1 champion, a thrilling run as the No. 14 seed. Walpole claimed the town’s first baseball title in Division 2, as did Pioneer Valley in Division 5. North Reading won Division 3, and Millbury claimed Division 4.

▪ A few big-name programs have realigned for the new season, the most significant of which is Plymouth North moving up to Division 1. The Eagles won the 2024 Division 2 title and were the top seed in last year’s tournament.

King Philip has moved back down to Division 2 after a year in Division 1, which saw the Warriors advance to the state semifinals.

Division 3 top seed St. Mary’s moved back up to Division 2, and Division 4 runner-up Lynnfield moved up to Division 3.

Monday, Charlestown at Latin Academy, 3:30 p.m. – The Townies surprised last year in both the Boston City League and Division 5, and will get an early test.

Monday, No. 6 Franklin at No. 17 King Philip, 4 p.m. – A rematch of last year’s Division 1 quarterfinal, these Hockomock League rivals will once again contend.

Tuesday, North Andover at No. 11 BC High, 4 p.m. – A good season-opening test in nonleague action as the Scarlet Knights make the trip down to Dorchester.

Wednesday, No. 15 Chelmsford at No. 10 St. John’s Prep, 4 p.m. – Title defenses don’t start much harder: the Lions travel to Danvers to face the Eagles in nonleague action.

Thursday, Milton at No. 14 St. Mary’s, 4 p.m. – Two perennial contenders clash, and now it’s a Division 2 matchup.

title: Woman sentenced to 15 to 20 years for fatal stabbing in downtown Boston
text:
Prosecutors said Sheppard was killed around 11:30 p.m. on the night in question.

She had been on Boston Common with a friend and the two encountered Partsch as they were leaving, prosecutors said.

Partsch and Sheppard had “engaged in a series of social media exchanges” before the encounter in which Partsch had threatened her and sought to goad her into a fight, prosecutors said.

“Evidence indicates that the two had not met in person prior to that day,” prosecutors said.

As Sheppard approached the Park Street MBTA stop, Partsch confronted her with a knife, prosecutors said. As the two fought, Partsch stabbed her several times in the face, head, and torso. The fight was captured on video, prosecutors said.

Partsch fled the scene and Sheppard was later pronounced dead at an area hospital, prosecutors said.

“Jazreanna Sheppard was poignantly and eloquently remembered by her family and friends today, remembered as a compassionate daughter, sister, cousin, and mother who was taken from everyone’s lives in a senseless, impossible-to-understand moment of violence,” Hayden said in a statement.

The statement also quoted Judge Mary Ames, who addressed the defendant from the bench as she handed down the sentence.

“It’s the senselessness of this act, the senselessness of the act that you committed, Ms. Partsch,” Ames said. “And I hope now that you see the consequences of what you’ve done to this family — a child who will not grow up knowing his mother except through this beautiful family who will keep her memory alive.”

Several of Sheppard’s relatives gave victim impact statements, prosecutors said, including one who described Sheppard as a “deeply loved human being” whose “heart was poured into everyone around her.”

In an impact statement submitted to the court, Sheppard’s cousin, Noemi Negron, noted that Sheppard’s child is now without her mother.

“Our family continues to struggle with the reality that her life was taken so suddenly and senselessly,” Negron wrote.

Sheppard’s son “deserves his mother, and our family deserves the chance to see her continue to grow and thrive,” Negron wrote. “While he is surrounded by love and care, there is no replacing the loss he will carry.”

title: Croft promised an affordable private school. But the math never added up.
text:
What’s more, the price was right. Tuition was thousands less than top-flight private schools — and Given was known to offer steep discounts to families of more modest means.

What Given had created seemed almost too good to be true: A private school without exorbitant costs or moral compromises. And somehow he had managed to do it for a fraction of the price of his competitors.

Families flocked to the school. Given opened in 2018 with 20 kindergartners in Providence. Nownearly 600 students ranging from preschool to middle school are enrolled in Boston and Providence.

Demand was so high by late last year, the school was hiring for a dozen new positions and looking to open a new school in Cambridge and expand in the South End. Details about how Croft would afford the growth were scant, but Given assured parents in a September email that the school’s “financial performance” was “strong.”

Just over five months later, Croft’s board dropped a bombshell.

It was not.

Given had mismanaged the school’s budget for years, keeping two sets of books, and hiding $13 million in debt, the board said. He allegedly forged a $500,000 letter of credit, meant to be a security deposit for a South End lease. And with so much debt, Given sold bonds to parents, promising they could invest in their children’s school while also earning a virtually guaranteed investment return. Then, according to one lawsuit, Given sold a second set of bonds to cover payments from the first — the very definition of a Ponzi scheme.

Croft’s board members say they didn’t know anything was amiss until Given alerted them in early March, after the school’s bank detected a forged document and called the police.

Boston police have said they are investigating. The school’s four-member board, which did not respond to a Boston Globe interview request, suspended Given and has suggested federal and state investigations are underway. Along the way, The Croft School was effectively left broke, facing closure in a matter of weeks.

Given, 45, hasn’t been charged with a crime and, in a statement released last month through his lawyers, said he’s cooperating with the school’s investigation. Given, who did not respond to an interview request, “has never used any school funds for his own personal benefit,” the statement said. When a reporter knocked on his door Tuesday, no one answered.

Many parents remain devoutly loyal to Croft and its teachers, and leapt into a fund-raising campaign to keep the Boston schools open. But parents — in conversations and text chats, over coffee, and waiting to pick up their kids from school — have also been grappling with another topic.

Why would Given risk it all? His reputation, the schools he built, the futures of hundreds of students.

Allison Cox, whose 8-year-old son attends Croft, said Given clearly believed in the school’s mission, but somehow got in over his head.

“Scott conflated hope with facts. I feel like he really believed that it would work,” Cox said. “I think it was hubris.”

Given, a graduate of Dartmouth College and a Harvard Business School alum, was already a prominent education entrepreneur when he was in his thirties.

The nonprofit he started in 2010, UP Education Network, took over failing schools in Boston and Lawrence. It raised millions of dollars from prominent Boston foundations and philanthropists.

In some cases, the organization pulled off remarkable turnarounds. Josh Angrist, an MIT economist and Nobel laureate who studies public education, said his research showed that UP’s first school, which replaced the Gavin middle school in South Boston, was “outstanding.” In its first year, UP nearly doubled the percentage of students who demonstrated math proficiency on the state’s annual test.

Given’s reputation grew beyond education circles. The Dartmouth Class of 2002 honored him with an award for distinguished alumni. Given told the alumni newsletter at the time that he planned to quadruple the size of his UP Education Network, growing it to 20 schools by 2020.

He acknowledged the challenge of running turnaround schools inside big, bureaucratic school districts. “It can be brutally difficult and this requires thick skin and a relentless work ethic,” Given said.

Ultimately, he did not quadruple UP, and some of the schools’ methods were controversial. Like many charter schools of the 2010s, UP’s schools were strict about discipline. Given resigned in 2016 after a WBUR report showed that one of his success stories in Dorchester had issued 68 suspensions to kindergartners, more than any other Massachusetts school.

That controversy may not have been all that pushed Given out. People who know him say he seemed burned out after more than a decade working in public education.

He also became a father and has said he launched Croft, in part, because he wanted to create a school where he would like to send his own children. After opening the Providence school in 2018, he founded the Jamaica Plain location close to his family’s current home in Wellesley, and enrolled his children there.

He named it in honor of Harold Croft, a respected teacher and track coach in Reading.

Croft was going to be different than UP. Instead of a nonprofit aimed at turning around failing schools, this new institution would be a for-profit company, and its financials would remain largely private.

Given told parents and employees the enterprise was backed by private funders who believed in the mission — as well as what he described as sizable, low-interest loans from himself and his father.

Rebecca Ullman, a parent of two Croft students, said Given was a constant presence at the Jamaica Plain location.

“Scott was very present in the life of the Croft school,” Ullman said. “He was an engaged school leader, absolutely.”

At the beginning, Croft’s annual tuition was $18,000 a year, lower than the cost of some day-care centers. Financial aid made it even more affordable for many families.

But Croft also managed to provide offerings that a large, sprawling school district like Boston simply could not match.

One section on Croft’s website, titled “Convenience,” reads like a wishlist for work-weary parents: Hourlong drop off windows, extended day programs, and child care on holidays. At the Jamaica Plain location, there was also a “family cafe” with free Wi-Fi, coffee, tea, and snacks.

The website said Croft strove to be “the most-parent centric school in the world.”

Edith Bazile, chairperson of the Boston Special Education Parent Advisory Council, said schools outside the traditional public system can promise the kind of personalized engagement many parents seek.

“It’s the seductive pull of a school that says, ‘I’m going to give you a different experience, I’m going to celebrate you by not just educating your student in a certain way, I’m going to address your needs as family,’ “ Bazile said. “They market family and community engagement.”

For loyal Boston Public Schools parents like Jennie McDonald-Brown, Croft’s resources were just too appealing to pass up. She was heavily involved with Boston schools before moving her son, now in the fourth grade, to Croft two years ago.

“Most of my dear friends are BPS school leaders and educators, and some of the most talented, passionate educators I’ve ever met still. And so this was a really, really difficult decision for us,” she said. “And I think what it boils down to is, my son was in a class with 26 kids, and at Croft, he was in a class of 13.”

Many Croft parents had once been committed to keeping their children in public schools. But for one reason or another, they’d decided to change course. Some found it difficult to develop relationships with their children’s public school teachers, who generally managed much bigger classes than teachers at Croft.

Josiane Martinez, whose 8-year-old son attends Croft, is married to another woman of color. Martinez said other members of the LGBTQ community sent their children to Croft because the school cultivated a nurturing environment.

“I felt comfortable sending my son there, knowing that he was going to be embraced for everything that he is,” Martinez said, “and he’s been thriving.”

The school advertised an ethos aligned with many parents’ worldview. It was committed to inclusion and billed itself as reflecting the diversity of its community. The school said that 39 percent of its students were nonwhite, although that is a lower share than almost all of Boston’s public elementary schools.

Maria Fernandes, whose son is enrolled in Croft’s third grade, said the school’s staff work with his learning style.

“I knew Black educators who are sending their kids here [and] that for me was a gold stamp, and I said, ‘That’s where I want to send my kid,’” Fernandes recalled.

In time, some parents began to wonder how Croft could afford to be so generous.

Although tuition eventually climbed to $35,000, that is still some $14,000 less than the Park School in Brookline. Croft also charges qualifying families less, including discounts for siblings.

“I don’t see how that translates into an extractive, profit making model,” said Eileen Connor, a Croft parent who runs the Project on Predatory Student Lending, which represents student borrowers at for-profit schools. “It would be a miracle if it broke even.”

In the summer of 2024, Given emailed Croft parents with an unusual pitch. He wanted parents to put up a million dollars to fund improvements, characterizing it as a supplement to the school’s traditional financing. Given offered to sell bonds with a 12.5 percent annual return and virtually zero risk.

In his email, Given told families a $100,000, four-year loan would be repaid along with $50,000 in interest.

The bonds were a “‘win-win’ for Croft and for our families,” he wrote.

Paul Crockett responded to the offer, according to court records. “[C]an you pencil me in for $100k?” he wrote to Given. Crockett would eventually invest $160,000 in the bonds, according to a lawsuit he filed last month.

Then, beginning late last year, Given made a series of financial maneuvers that would lead to his downfall.

In late October, Given began selling a second round of “Croft Bonds” to parents. Two months later, as the school’s debts mounted, Given forged the $500,000 bank letter of credit, according to Croft’s board — using Leader Bank letterhead to make it appear legitimate.

The day after Christmas, he made another move to raise cash fast. He moved up the deadline for the next year’s tuition payments, forcing parents to cough up thousands of dollars five weeks ahead of schedule.

Despite the infusion of cash, the cracks soon began to show.

In January, Given notified families that Croft would abandon its plan to expand into Cambridge. The next month, he attempted to back out of the lease for Croft’s new South End building, according to a lawsuit filed by the landlord.

The landlord, Washington Associates, tried to cash in the allegedly forged letter of credit Given had offered as a security deposit. According to the landlord’s lawsuit, Leader Bank discovered the forgery, and called the Boston Police Department.

In early March, Given confessed to a member of Croft’s board that he had forged the letter of credit and concealed the true amount of the school’s debt, according to statements issued by the board. The board has not answered questions about its oversight, leaving parents to wonder how it could all go wrong.

“How does one person manage to keep two sets of books and get this far down what appears to be a fraud without anyone raising an alarm?” said Croft parent Matt Donohue.

In the end, many families remain baffled that Given would put the school’s survival and so much else at risk.

Croft’s immediate future remains uncertain.

Parents at Croft’s Jamaica Plain location said they have raised enough money — more than a million dollars — to keep their school running through June. In the South End, parents were confident they’d reach a similar fund-raising goal.

Providence parents have raised enough to stay open through April and were optimistic they would find the money to stay afloat until summer.

But those are all short-term fixes. Keeping the school running permanently will be the next challenge. The parents’ groups that organized the fund-raising say they will be exploring options like turning Croft into a nonprofit.

Cox, like many parents, has been left with the challenge of explaining the crisis to her children. She settled on a simple lesson of right and wrong.

Don’t lie to solve a problem, Cox told her 8-year-old son.

“You have to ask for help instead,” Cox explained to him. “That’s what Scott didn’t do.”

Christopher Huffaker and Steph Machado of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: I made a career with carbs. Now they make me sick.
text:
No, I don’t have celiac disease (I was tested already), so it’s just a sensitivity. But it’s one that makes you feel tired, bloated, and a little sick after eating gluten. It affects everything: My face was puffy when I ate gluten, brain fog and migraines made concentrating difficult, and my tummy would hurt for days.

I tried eliminating everything else first, in denial that it would ever be my favorite foods that made me feel this way. Was it the dairy? The sugar? No, it was the gluten.

In theory, keeping gluten out of my diet might sound manageable. Just a little lifestyle tweak, right? A minor inconvenience? In practice, it’s a full-time mental exercise.

Every meal now begins with reconnaissance. I scan menus differently, looking for clues: Could there be hidden flour in that sauce or gravy, breadcrumbs in a meatball, soy sauce in a marinade? I’ve learned that gluten is less an ingredient and more a lifestyle choice that the food industry made on my behalf long ago. It’s everywhere. It’s sneaky. It’s rich and decadent. It is, frankly, a little rude.

Dining out, which used to be the easiest and absolutely most fun part of my job, has become a series of negotiations.

“Is this fried? Do you use a shared fryer?”

“Do you have gluten-free pasta?”

“Can you not bread the eggplant?”

“Do you have Tamari for my sushi?”

There’s a moment that I feel like every gluten-free person knows when the waiter has to go “check with the kitchen.” That’s when you realize dinner just got complicated.

Oftentimes, I find myself staring into the depths of the bread basket on the table, watching others frost their slices with copious amounts of butter. At many places, I desperately ask the server the question – “what here is gluten free?” – and I get a finger over the menu, circling around the salads. Great, I’m a rabbit for the day.

There is also the humiliation of realizing how much of your personality was built on bread. I make my own pasta at home, and even bought a shirt that says “HOT GIRLS EAT BREAD.” I’m an adventurous eater, who will try anything and everything once, who never met a carb she didn’t like, and who believed the best way to get to know a place was to eat your way through it, and speak to the staff who run their eating establishments.

Now, I am the person asking if the tortilla chips are truly gluten free, or just in spirit.

By no means am I perfect with this new diet. Will I happily suffer after eating my favorite cacio e pepe at Oberlin, the roni island pizza (pepperoni, cherry peppers, and hot honey) from Pizza Marvin, bahn mi from Asian Bakery, a stack of pancakes from a diner, mole, dumplings around Boston’s Chinatown? Yes, yes I will.

But I’ve found some great spots that cater to these new needs: Verveine Cafe & Bakery in Cambridge is an entirely gluten-free bakery, and their bread and ube brownies make me feel like I’m not missing out on anything. Nicks on Broadway in Providence has gluten-free crostini and biscuits that taste just as good as his “real” ones (no, really, they do). Eataly, thankfully, has the best selection of gluten-free pastas I can find to make at home. And I’ve been gravitating a lot toward Vietnamese food, much of which is naturally gluten free. Le Madeline in Quincy and Gao in Dorchester have been seeing a lot more of me. I’m ordering poke bowls, crudo, and sushi, my true comfort food, more than ever.

But it’s different now.

I obviously still love going out, and trying new food. But these days, before I take a bite, I find myself doing something I never used to do. I have to hesitate.

Where do you eat gluten-free food? Send me recommendations from around New England at Alexa.Gagosz@globe.com.

title: Long-envisioned jazz club secures public backing to open in Roxbury
text:
MassDevelopment said it would provide a $380,000 equipment loan, with an additional $1.63 million in loan financing from M&T Bank and a $450,000 credit enhancement offered by the city. The Boston Foundation will guarantee financing through its Business Equity Fund.

The project is expected to create 26 new full-time jobs, officials said.

“This project demonstrates what is possible through the collaboration of public, private and philanthropic partners,” said Eric Paley, the state’s economic development secretary who also chairs the MassDevelopment board. “JazzUrbane Cafe will bring a new cultural destination to Nubian Square, expanding access to live music while adding to the neighborhood’s rich artistic tradition.”

JazzUrbane shares its name with a recording studio; both were founded by Bill Banfield, a jazz guitarist, producer, and professor emeritus at Berklee College of Music.

The club bills itself as a venue dedicated to spotlighting local and national artists “who define and celebrate the diverse cultural traditions that make Boston a unique and global city.” In addition to live music, it will also offer film screenings, dance, theater, and multimedia installations.

“We believe our company will be a force in contributing to how the next iterations of cultural development in Boston will be implemented,” Banfield said in the statement. “The JazzUrbane Cafe is positioned at the center of Nubian, in the heartbeat of the city, where we can serve and uplift the soul of our great city and be a temple for the entire community.”

It’s been a long road for the planned venue, which was first announced in 2019 by Mayor Marty Walsh as part of a renewed investment into the area, then known as Dudley Square.

The club received zoning board approval in 2022, with an eye towards a June 2023 opening; according to city records, however, it did not receive a liquor license until early last year.

The prospective club is already a member of the Ujima Good Business Alliance, a local development group that includes District 7 Tavern and the Dorchester Food Co-op.

“We are pleased that other actors in our ecosystem see the same immense promise and viability of this venture that we do,” Nia K. Evans, Ujima’s executive director, said in a statement.

At one point, JazzUrbane’s long list of backers also included Nia Grace, a restauranteur behind Grace by Nia in the Seaport and the new Uptown Social on Columbus Avenue. (Grace did not return a request for comment, nor did Banfield.)

The club is scheduled to open in May, Evans said.

Nubian Square itself doesn’t have much of a history of live music — unless you count church, said Byron Rushing, current president of the Roxbury Historical Society and a former state representative. But the nearby South End was once the hub of the city’s jazz scene, populated by clubs like Wally’s and its long-gone neighbors — Estelle’s, the Savoy, and the Hi-Hat, he said.

“With its location and historic facade, JazzUrbane will help shape the heart of Nubian Square,” said Orlando Watkins, chief program officer for the Boston Foundation.

The Bolling Building, renamed in 2015 after the first Black person elected president of the Boston City Council, once housed a well-known furniture store. The flatiron-style building — its decline, renovation, and eventual reopening — became a symbol of the rebounding fortunes of what was then known as Dudley Square.

title: Battle lines drawn in court clash over White Stadium
text:
Massachusetts needed the Public Lands Preservation Act, which was passed in 2022, to end attempts to circumvent what previously had been state policy. The law mandates that, before obtaining a two-thirds legislative majority as required under Article 97, there shall be a public process, an alternatives analysis showing that the project is not viable elsewhere, and provision of compensatory land for the land being taken. The only mandate of this law that this project has met is the public process.

The Kraft Group, which owns Gillette Stadium, the New England Revolution, and a proposed 24,000-seat Everett soccer stadium, supports the city. The Revs’ argument that the plaintiff’s success may endanger other public-private partnerships lacks merit. Conversely, we see the defendant’s success in the lawsuit as gutting the Public Lands Preservation Act.

Meanwhile, Boston Legacy’s March 14 inaugural game drew a league record crowd of 30,207 to Gillette, raising the possibility that an 11,000-seat White Stadium is obsolete before it opens. As economist Andrew Zimbalist wrote in CommonWealth Beacon in December, only two National Women’s Soccer League stadiums have fewer than 20,000 seats, and all but one city hosting men’s and women’s teams share venues.

Keeping White Stadium public respects the law on preserving public lands in letter and spirit. Sharing Everett is just common sense.

Doug Pizzi

Executive director

Mass Parks for All

Boston

Call me petty, but I’m exhausted by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy’s protracted legal battle against the White Stadium redevelopment (“A local nonprofit crossed Wu. Then its permit for a fund-raiser was denied,” Editorial, March 23). The suggestion that the Wu administration is being petty in denying a permit for the group’s annual fund-raiser, traditionally held at Franklin Park, may be valid, but it pales next to the conservancy’s own pettiness in choosing to wage this legal fight at all.

From the outset, its combative approach has left Boston’s broader nonprofit sector wondering how an organization loses the plot this badly. The tedious legal battles to halt decades-overdue renovations reveal a profound lack of perspective on what a public-private partnership of this scale actually requires.

Polls have shown greater public support for the city’s plan than opposition. Advocates are right to push for cost accountability and community input, but the conservancy has drifted far from its own mission, steered by out-of-touch board members who don’t live near the park and a president with shallow roots in Boston.

It’s high time the conservancy abandon its protracted legal battle, wasting both its own money and that of taxpayers. The group is standing in the way of Boston’s students, a well-supported mayoral administration, and long-overdue progress for one of the city’s most neglected public spaces.

Denying a fund-raiser permit may be petty. Denying a generation of Boston’s students a stadium they deserve is shameful.

Brenden McHenry

Dorchester

title: Conman or family man? Court documents offer contrasting views of an Irish contractor who defrauded homeowners.
text:
Prosecutors are asking US District Court Chief Judge John J. “Jack” McConnell Jr. to sentence O’Brien to four years and eight months in prison, the maximum allowed by the plea deal. But O’Brien’s defense attorney, Todd A. Spodek, is asking the judge to give O’Brien just three years behind bars.

According to federal authorities and defense attorneys, “traveling conmen fraud” cases reflect an increasingly familiar scheme also seen in New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania.

In a sentencing memorandum, interim US Attorney Charles C. Calenda’s office said O’Brien told his parents he was moving his young family to the United States in the summer of 2021 to “seek out better financial opportunities.”

“But from the very beginning,” Assistant US Attorney Taylor A. Dean wrote, “his version of the ‘American dream’ relied on deceit and exploitation.”

O’Brien entered the United States under a tourist visa that authorized him to remain in the country until Oct. 19, 2021. But he overstayed that visa and “engaged in a complex scheme of deceit” over the next 3½ years, according to the sentencing memorandum.

Prosecutors said O’Brien used a “charming demeanor” to convince homeowners to drain their savings and retirement accounts to pay for unnecessary home repairs. He often approached victims outside their homes, claiming he had noticed some small repairs he could fix, but those minor fixes quickly mushroomed into major projects, prosecutors said.

Many victims reported that O’Brien used “scare tactics” to convince them to pay larger and larger sums. He warned victims that their homes would collapse if they didn’t act fast, and in some cases, he and his crew caused the damage he offered to fix, prosecutors wrote.

O’Brien admitted to defrauding at least 80 homeowners in Rhode Island and Massachusetts between July 2021 and March 2025. But prosecutors estimate that number is “significantly greater,” and they submitted a list of more than 110 victim names to probation officials.

O’Brien used the proceeds to “feed a lavish lifestyle filled with luxury vehicles, expensive vacations, pricey beauty treatments, and an extravagant monthly entertainment budget, the likes of which most Americans can only dream,” prosecutors wrote.

O’Brien not only harmed homeowners, he also “engaged in labor exploitation,” using day laborers who often did not speak English and who were reluctant to complain about his supervision, according to prosecutors. One victim reported that O’Brien’s laborers did not wear respirators while performing work in her basement, and one laborer said he had not been paid in three weeks.

As the fraud grew, O’Brien used a check-cashing company in Dorchester, Mass., to cash victims’ checks rather than deposit them into his bank account. He then used that cash to buy Rolex watches from known money-launderers to conceal the proceeds, prosecutors said.

“He is a man who knew what he was doing,” prosecutors wrote, “a man who had contacts around the world who could help him pull off the fraud and who had a network of like-minded colleagues who were similarly engaged in this type of scheme across the United States.”

Prosecutors described O’Brien as “an organizer or leader of criminal activity involving five or more participants,” saying he directed multiple money launderers to assist him with his crime and used other suspected members of the “Traveling Conmen Fraud Group” to defraud his victims.

The FBI said groups of Irish or United Kingdom nationals have been entering the United States illegally or overstaying tourist visas, soliciting construction work, and overcharging homeowners. They go door-to-door, introducing themselves to homeowners — who are often elderly individuals — claiming to notice damage that needs to be repaired immediately.

In addition to 56 months in prison, prosecutors asked the judge to order O’Brien to forfeit $5,565 in cash, plus property described as Rose Cottage in Telford, England, and to make restitution to victims.

But the defense asked the judge for a sentence of 36 months, challenging the prosecution’s sentencing guideline calculations.

For example, the defense challenged the calculation of how much victims lost. “Regardless of O’Brien’s fraud, the fact remains that there were real crews performing real construction and providing measurable value to homeowners,” the defense attorney wrote.

Also, supporters submitted letters offering a starkly different portrayal of O’Brien.

“My son is not a criminal,” wrote his father, John O’Brien Sr. “John is the type of man who goes to church every Sunday, who hugs and kisses his kids goodnight, who tells his wife and kids he loves them before he goes to work every morning, a man who goes above and beyond to help complete strangers in [their] hour of need.”

O’Brien is married and has three children, ages 7, 4, and 2, according to court documents.

His father said O’Brien grew up in a part of Ireland that had “gangs of youths always looking for young lads to bully into the drugs dealing and dangerous life-threatening situations.” But he said he kept his son away from that life.

His brother, Thomas O’Brien, wrote that, “Putting him in prison is like putting a goldfish in a shark tank.”

His aunt, Margaret Ann O’Brien, wrote that he collected money in a bucket in Dublin to help her raise funds for homeless people in Ireland and Ethiopia. “I am sure he will get back to this selfless work after this bridge is crossed,” she wrote.

The Rev. Stephen Monaghan wrote to the court, saying, “I have only ever known John to be a very reliable and very hard-working man. While he may have acted outside the rules and regulations of his visa, I have only ever known him to be a decent young man.”

Senator Eileen Flynn, a memberof the upper house of the Irish Parliament, described O’Brien as “a man whose kindness and strength of character have been evident throughout his life.”

“John went to America with the best of intentions and to create a new life for himself,” Flynn wrote. “Given the current circumstances, it would be best, if possible, to have John O’Brien back in Ireland for the support of his community and for the benefit of his young family.”

title: I never sounded like a news anchor. Turns out that was the point.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Can I share a secret?

When I was younger, I wanted to be someone who was behind a microphone or in front of a camera. I dreamed of hosting my own TV or radio show.

But then, reality set in. ​The people I saw on TV were nothing like me. As a tomboy from Dorchester, a total Dot Rat at heart, I didn’t see where I would ever fit in.

I didn’t look or sound like a news anchor. And I certainly didn’t want to dress like one.

So I set those ambitions aside and just concentrated on doing good journalism.

Over the years that I’ve worked at the Globe, I’ve always jumped at the chance to work on videos. Whenever I had an opportunity to be on camera, I gladly took it, and cherished every moment.

Such was the case last Tuesday, when I was asked to do a video about a story I was working on: a mansion in Beverly that had been robbed.

I happily agreed, and my colleague Raphael Chinca, one of the Globe’s Emmy Award-winning multimedia producers, set up a camera in the newsroom and filmed me talking about the robbery. The video was posted on social media, and by the next day, it had been viewed over a million times.

Comments — about my voice, and how I pronounced certain words, and how I was wearing an Adidas track jacket while delivering a serious news report — were pouring in. And they haven’t stopped.

I had no idea that my Boston accent and choice of fashion would spark so much discussion online. Honestly, I was shocked ... by both the sheer volume of comments, and how overwhelmingly positive they’ve been.

Lots of people commented that my voice reminded them of home. Others said my casual demeanor made it feel like they were listening to a friend telling them a story.

Many people messaged me privately, saying that they had given up on the news and no longer trusted mainstream media, but they felt like they could trust me.

I was so happy to hear that. It’s given me a lot of hope, and it’s making me realize that there could be a place for this Dot Rat after all.

I hope to continue to do more video reports for the Globe, and I hope you’ll join me by following our social media accounts.
