title: Bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue still make sense
text:
Blue Hill Avenue has remained largely unchanged for the past 60 years, since the streetcar tracks that once ran down the center were removed. The roadway starts at Warren Street in Roxbury, bisects Dorchester and Mattapan, and is as wide as a highway, with four lanes of driving, two parking lanes, and an intermittent median strip. Double-parking, especially for businesses receiving deliveries, is an endemic problem with little enforcement.

City planners and designers have known for years that the most important upgrades for pedestrian and transit infrastructure just wouldn’t be feasible if buses remained reliant on curbside bus stops; there’s too much demand with double-parked cars, buses, pedestrians, cyclists, and businesses all vying for space — which is why the federal grant process has focused on the center-running approach.

Now, bolstered by federal money, it all boils down to those center lanes. Mayor Michelle Wu can either push forward with those plans, helping unclog some of the most high-traffic bus lines in the city and unlocking tens of millions of dollars for other improvements; or keep the roadway largely as it is, pecking at its problems through small initiatives like fixing sidewalks, adding lighting, and resurfacing the street.

Facing those two options, this editorial board stands where it did in 2022: in support of center-running bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue. While this project will never reach unanimous community support, the center-running bus lanes maximize pedestrian safety, preserve the most amount of parking, and cut down the truly disastrous wait times for public transit during rush hour. Keeping Blue Hill Avenue largely unchanged would be its own form of failure; a crash requiring a Boston EMS ambulance happens every three days along the road, according to the city.

The most recent community feedback regarding the project was collected by the MBTA in 2024; while a sizable portion of community members strongly disagreed that the project would meet its goals, they were outnumbered by those who either somewhat or strongly agreed that the project would improve the roadway. The margins were slim, but those in agreement made up the majority.

In Denver, a former highway called Colfax Avenue is facing a dilemma similar to Blue Hill Avenue. Just like Blue Hill, Colfax Avenue is a major city thoroughfare hosting some of the highest-trafficked bus routes in the city. It suffers from clogged lanes, a lack of pedestrian infrastructure, and very little greenery. It also once hosted streetcar tracks and was left with little investment after they were torn out.

That 10-mile project began its buildout in 2024, giving Boston a model. The project in Denver includes small-business relief grants to offset the harms that ongoing construction can cause. With a new pot of cash, Boston should look into ways to support the small businesses that would face direct impacts during the most intensive construction phases.

Construction on the corridor will be a necessary disruption for meaningful change. Luckily, these impacts are something that smart city planning can mitigate. Understanding seasonal high times for businesses, factoring in Boston Public Schools transportation schedules, and even knowing the dates of special community events that provide bumps for local business can help mitigate the damaging impacts of construction.

There are other, local projects that provide a guide as well. The center bus lanes on nearby Columbus Avenue did drastically improve transit times for bus riders at a modest negative cost to drivers.

Any decision the city makes now is going to disappoint someone. Local City Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell, as well as other leaders, say the constituents they represent are against this plan. They believe their constituents deserve large-scale investment on their terms, and this project, like a previous attempt to rework the avenue under former governor Deval Patrick, is a mandate from outside the community.

But many residents do support it — the majority, if the T’s survey is to be believed. As the Dorchester Reporter has noted in its recent coverage, young people are largely in favor of improving this stretch. And while construction will strain the businesses that are the beating heart of this corridor, if they are supported, they will be able to benefit from an influx of investment, customers, and community growth brought by a safer main street.

title: Man who fatally shot 16-year-old in Dorchester in 2008 granted parole from life sentence
text:
First-degree murder normally carries a life sentence without the possibility of parole, but Grier became eligible to seek release after the state’s highest court in 2024 struck down life terms with no chance at parole for defendants aged 18 to 20 at the time of their crimes.

Grier was 20 when he killed Barboza, the ruling said.

It said Grier on the evening of Nov. 30, 2008, had encountered Barboza inside a Dorchester store, where the two exchanged words, leaving Grier “upset.”

The ruling didn’t detail what was said between the two.

The following day, the decision said, Grier and Barboza encountered each other again as Barboza exited a store on Washington Street.

Barboza and Grier walked toward a street corner, and when Barboza reached the corner, Grier shot him, causing the teen to fall to the ground, the ruling said.

Grier, the board said, “continued to fire” at Barboza, striking him once in the head and twice in his legs. Barboza was later pronounced dead at an area hospital.

The four board members who voted to free Grier were moved by his progress behind bars, according to the ruling.

“Mr. Grier presented with insight into the causative factors that led to his gang affiliation and offending behavior,” the ruling said.

It said he began “to invest in self development” before the 2024 court ruling made him eligible to seek release as a convicted killer.

“Mr. Grier also invested in education - earning his associates degree,” the board said, without naming the institution that conferred the degree.

He also “developed occupational skills” in an effort to prepare himself for reentry into society, the decision said.

“Mr. Grier also has a support system to assist him with his transition,” the ruling said.

It said the board heard testimony in support of parole from a social worker and from Grier’s relatives, as well as testimony opposing his release from Barboza’s family.

Once he’s out, Grier will have to abide by several conditions including maintaining a nightly curfew, submitting to electronic monitoring for six months, staying off drugs and booze, having no contact with Barboza’s family, and enrolling in “mental health counseling for adjustment,” the ruling said.

A cousin of Barboza’s, Deja Anye, had posted a tribute to Facebook to the slain teenager in 2014, writing that he was shot the day before his birthday.

“The next day was his 17th birthday, but instead of celebrating with his friends and family, he was lying in a hospital bed with a bullet in his head,” Anye wrote. “He was gone. Nobody told me, but I knew. I heard the late-night crying and talk of family deaths, I couldn’t believe it. The person I grew up with, shared laughs with, was gone... No goodbye, no nothing. Matter of fact, the last time I [saw] him I said, ‘Hey De’Andre!’ ... My aunt, De’Andre’s mom, is one of the strongest women I’ve ever met. She is my hero and her son is my family’s guardian angel. I will make them both proud.”

title: ‘Pets shouldn’t be a privilege.’ As cost of living rises, demand grows for pet food pantries.
text:
YmaNini LaCourt wouldn’t know what she would do without her dog Mizzo, a small Chihuahua-mix with an adorable underbite.

But after losing her job during the pandemic, LaCourt has been working part time for less than $20 an hour, not nearly enough to cover her expenses, including food for a pet she describes as “part of me, part of my life, part of my world.”

LaCourt, 65, is among hundreds of pet owners increasingly turning to local pet food pantries to make ends meet. As the cost of living in the Boston area continues to climb, and with recent federal cuts to programs that help low-income Americans, including SNAP and Medicaid, more people would be forced to give up their furry family members without this kind of assistance, according to the food pantries.

“Pets are part of people’s families, and we’re really focused on keeping families together,” said Edward Schettino, president of the Animal Rescue League of Boston, which runs the Keep Pets SAFE program. SAFE stands for Supporting Animals and Families Everyday and its pantry serves pet owners in Dorchester, Mattapan, and Roxbury.

“When people struggle, pets struggle,” Schettino added.

Demand for the SAFE program and a statewide equivalent run by the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (MSPCA) has surged this year compared to 2025, according to the nonprofits.

When money is tight, many pet owners sacrifice their own needs to buy a bag of kibble, animal advocates said. Some may feed their pet before eating a meal themselves.

Like LaCourt, many people in Massachusetts got pets during the pandemic to keep them company while spending more time at home.

Alyssa Krieger, director of community outreach for Boston’s MSPCA, said the group distributed 2.8 million pet meals across Massachusetts in 2024. In 2025, the number jumped to 3.5 million, she said.

Krieger said their clients typically get half of their pet’s monthly food from the program, visiting sites such as the Lawrence YMCA, Hyde Park’s Helping Plates and the Falmouth Service Center to pick up a bag of kibble provided by the MSPCA.

Pet owners seek out the program about two to four times per year, she said, and receive around $50 worth of food each time.

“People are using it when they really, really need it because life is nearly impossible in Massachusetts right now,” Krieger said.

Over the past several years, Krieger has talked to hundreds of pet owners at distribution sites in parks and parking lots. Often with their dogs in tow, the owners tell Krieger how thankful they are for the help.

“Those conversations really have taught me that pet ownership shouldn’t just be a privilege for people with a lot of money,” Krieger said.

In Boston, the ARL makes more than 25 deliveries per month, both to people’s homes and the offices of Action for Boston Community Development, a social services nonprofit, Schettino said.

The program focuses on dog and cat food, as well as cat litter. It also honors requests for food for birds, rabbits, guinea pigs, and other less common pets.

Monthly deliveries of about $80 worth of cat food and litter have helped Dorchester resident Betty Strickland pay off her 2019 Toyota Yaris, she said.

Strickland’s husband died in 2018 from health problems that began more than a decade earlier when he was shot in the stomach when their home was robbed, she said.

A friend decided Strickland needed a pet for company and gave her Leah, a long-haired white and tabby.

“She’s such a good kitty, I mean she’s so good, there’s certain things she knows not to do," said Strickland, adding that Leah provides “so much” company for her.

Because Leah had several teeth removed because of dental problems she developed as a kitten living on the street, she only eats canned cat food, said Strickland, 73.

Leah’s expensive taste, as well as her well-mannered behavior, leads neighbors to address her using a royal honorific.

The cat has her own kitchen chair, the only piece of furniture she’s allowed on.

“She really is a princess,” Strickland said.

Strickland’s monthly income, from her pension and Social Security, amounts to less than $2,000. Without the rescue league, she’d be spending nearly $100 a month on canned cat food and litter, she said.

“It makes it easier for me to spend money someplace else,” Strickland said.

Both Strickland and LaCourt receive housing assistance, which covers roughly two-thirds of their rent. A set percentage of their monthly income covers the final third.

LaCourt could work full time now, but she’s hesitant. The more she earns each month, the greater percentage of her income must go toward her rent. She already pays $1,000 toward the monthly cost of her two-bedroom apartment.

LaCourt’s 20-year-old daughter would contribute more to the household budget, but her hours at T.J. Maxx were recently cut to one day a week after her store on Newbury Street shut down and she was moved to another location.

That means that for now, the assistance is giving LaCourt’s family some much-needed peace of mind.

“I’d be lost without them, they’re so helpful,” she said.

Claire Thornton can be reached at claire.thornton@globe.com. Follow Claire on X @claire_thornto.

title: From teardown to new dream home: build in N.H., assemble in Mass., pocket the savings
text:
Worldwide, prefabricated construction is booming in part driven by increased demand for sustainable homes. In Massachusetts, which has set steep, legally binding targets to reduce greenhouse gases that drive climate change, housing is responsible for about 30 percent of the state’s total energy use.

For their project in Somerville, Buntel and Graber reached out to the New Hampshire firm Bensonwood to build their dream home, which would include two home offices, a second living area upstairs, and striking, exposed New England timber-framing. And the kicker: the home would generate enough electricity to power itself, a big incentive in a state where residents pay the highest electricity rates in the continental United States.

When the various pieces of the couple’s home — walls with windows and doors and a roof — arrived on a truck, they were fixed together like Legos. The design and internal wiring made it extra easy for the couple to add solar panels, cork floors that retain heat, and a heat pump, to both generate power and cut their energy consumption.

“We were delighted to discover that we produce way more energy than we use,” Graber said of her new home.

Bensonwood’s brand called Unity Homes, is run out of a factory in Keene, N.H. Homebuyers can choose from one of five models, then make modifications. The models all have Swedish names, acknowledging that country’s leadership in offsite construction.

Other local prefab designers with an environmental bent include Green Staxx, which turned to a factory in Quebec to construct modular units for installation in a Newton apartment building, and BrightBuilt Home, which offers net-zero design options.

Bensonwood founder Tedd Benson said his company aims to “make a building you could eat” by using organic materials such as wood and cellulose, a recycled insulation product. He added that factory building significantly reduces waste.

“We’re not filling up a dumpster on a job site,” Benson said.

Elsewhere in Greater Boston, Bensonwood also recently designed 12 affordable housing units in Dorchester and three student residences at Tufts University and the Wellesley College Science Complex.

For consumers, prefab homes can be significantly cheaper, though plenty of variables affect the bottom line. For Buntel and Graber, a prefab was more affordable than a deep energy retrofit would’ve been. Plus, they got a brand new home.

The real cost gain for prefabs, though, is time saved.

“Monday, there was a hole in the ground. Thursday, I could walk up to the second floor,” Graber said.

But John Ferrante, CEO of the Associated General Contractors of Massachusetts, noted some downsides. Meeting building codes can be difficult when shipping components to various cities, and the local workforce may feel jobs are being taken away, Ferrante said.

There are also limits to how architecturally ambitious or creative you can get with a preset menu of design choices.

Still, Ferrante says the growing prefab trend will keep growing because “everybody in the industry is looking for ways to control the cost of construction.”

And if people can dramatically cut their energy bills through a prefab design, all the more incentive.

Between their solar panels and energy efficiency upgrades, the Somerville couple is generating a surplus of electricity. Eversource gives them credits for excess energy production, which they can dip into during the winter months if they use more than they produce. The couple also gifts some credits, essentially free energy, to the Somerville Homeless Coalition.

“Imagine if everyone was giving some electricity to people who needed it,” Buntel said.

Environmentally conscious homeowners can also retrofit existing homes. John Sterman, a professor at MIT’s Sloan School of Management and director of the school’s sustainability initiative, took that approach when he did a deep energy retrofit on his 1920s Lexington home. He replaced all the windows and installed a heat pump and solar panels, among other renovations, to turn his home into a personal “power plant.”

Sterman concedes: this took a lot of time and money. While he wasn’t about to rip down his historic home, Sterman adds that in many cases “you’re better off doing a tear down and a rebuild.”

Buntel and Graber hold on to the memory of the fixer upper they started with. A framed illustration of the original house is displayed over a collection of potted plants, and on a nearby bookshelf sits a wooden sign with a heartfelt message to their teardown on Trull Street: “Old Ugly Trull. Mourned not missed.”

Graber said maximizing sustainability and lowering their carbon footprint is a responsibility they take seriously.

“This isn’t just a nice-to-have,” she said. “This is truly a need-to-have. ... It’s just how to make it more accessible.”

title: US hospitals are emerging from bankruptcy only to falter again
text:
The bankruptcy of Steward Health Care walloped the Massachusetts health care landscape. Six of its hospital campuses in the state were taken over by new operators, while two others — Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer — closed their doors after Steward’s financial implosion. Meanwhile, in Rhode Island just last month, the Centurion Foundation took over Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital, two safety-net hospitals that had become cash-strapped under Prospect Medical Holdings ownership.

The renewed strain also underscores a broader problem in the hospital industry: bankruptcy is often proving to be less a reset than a handoff. Distressed facilities are being passed to new operators, often with lease relief, asset sales, or emergency financing to keep them open. Even as overall health care Chapter 11 filings fell in 2025, hospital bankruptcies rose, according to Gibbins Advisors, suggesting many hospitals remain financially fragile even after leaving court.

Some of the former Steward hospitals taken over by Michael Sarian and Faisal Gill — two executives chosen by MPT to run the facilities — have been hit in recent months with lawsuits from vendors and service providers, court filings show. The unpaid bills span a wide range of basic services, including medical staffing, physician coverage, plumbing, fire protection, and security systems.

HSA and NOR recently removed Sarian as chief executive officer and replaced him with Gill, even as the hospitals themselves were dealing with growing operational and financial strain. The two executives are now fighting in court, trading accusations of improper fund transfers and a conspiracy to replace Sarian at the helm of the companies.

MPT has said it expects the former Steward and Prospect hospitals sold to HSA and NOR Healthcare Systems Corp. — another company created by Sarian and Gill to take over several Prospect hospitals in California — to resume paying full rent by the end of this year and that Sarian’s companies would be better operators than their predecessors.

MPT didn’t respond to requests for comment.

“Under Mike’s leadership we had issues which right now I am working with vendors to correct,” Gill said in an email, adding that he’s secured an additional $30 million for new equipment at the HSA hospitals.

Trane Technologies plc, Johnson Controls International, and other service providers have filed liens against some of the hospitals, according to court records. Equipment lessors are trying to recover their machines. Several vendors and health care companies have said they stopped providing services altogether.

The strain extends beyond vendor disputes. In Texas, hospitals run by Healthcare Systems of America, or HSA, one of the operating companies tied to Sarian and Gill, are also behind on tax payments owed to two counties, court papers show. In Florida, meanwhile, an employee at one HSA hospital alleged in a whistleblower lawsuit that managers told him to mislead government regulators about building-safety violations and refused to pay to repair an elevator. HSA denies the allegations, Gill said in an email, and has moved to dismiss the complaint. The company argues the plaintiff failed to show that the relevant statute was violated.

For patients and the communities around these facilities, the risk is that mounting financial stress starts to show up in everyday care. When hospitals miss payments to vendors and service providers cut back, they can struggle to maintain equipment, staff departments, and keep up with repairs, basic building operations, and other routine functions essential to patient care.

Medical staff at some HSA hospitals in Florida continue to contend with broken equipment and lack of supplies, but HSA has been more responsive when they raised concerns than Steward had been, DeQuasia Canales, a union official who represents workers at a number of HSA facilities, told Bloomberg in an interview. “That’s a low bar,” said Canales, referencing deterioration in facilities run by Steward.

The management dispute has added another layer of uncertainty. In February, MPT sent HSA a notice of default over unpaid rent and other obligations, including delinquent Texas taxes. In a California lawsuit filed in February, seeking to remove Sarian as chief executive officer, NOR alleged that it bounced $4 million of checks to health care providers in January and had built up about $20 million in unpaid payroll taxes over time. In response to questions from Bloomberg, Gill said NOR is now current on the payroll tax liability, which he said had built up under Prospect’s ownership.

A spokesperson and a lawyer for Prospect didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Gill, in court papers, has accused Sarian of improperly moving more than $50 million out of NOR and another company the two manage and transferring the funds to HSA, which is solely owned by him, since 2021. Sarian, in an email, said claims that he siphoned money out of the businesses are false, and his lawyer said he has been the victim of deceptive colleagues.

Sarian, in his own court filings, has accused Gill and a minority investor of working together to force him out and take control of part of his ownership stake in the companies.

Those accusations remain contested, and the executive feud may take time to sort out in court. But the more immediate problem for MPT is that the hospitals it helped rescue are again facing missed payments and questions about day-to-day operations. The turmoil is another test of whether the operators it backed can stabilize the facilities and restore rent.

title: ‘History matters’: As 250th looms, Rob Waldron launches video contest for students
text:
“I was worried, particularly having grown up with the history [of the state], that the history is not necessarily getting out there,” Waldron said. “What can I do in my philanthropy, in my time, to get the kids engaged again?”

ICivics will narrow down the finalists, and then a panel of more than a dozen judges will pick the top three. They include Pam Everhart at video-contest cosponsor Fidelity Investments, Vertex CEO Reshma Kewalramani, Pops conductor Keith Lockhart, and Boston Foundation president Lee Pelton.

Ever since Waldron stepped down as chief executive of Curriculum Associates at the start of 2025, he has followed his passion for history. (Kelly Sia took over at the Billerica firm, and Waldron remains its chairman.) He joined the boards of the Massachusetts Historical Society and the Adams Presidential Center, and launched a startup with Dean Serrentino called Historiq that uses AI to help accelerate archival processing and digitization.

“History matters,” Waldron said. “It teaches us how we should be as citizens, and what we’re going to hand the next generation.”

Let’s make a deal.

That was House Speaker Ron Mariano’s message to the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce on Thursday, regarding the income tax cut question currently headed to the ballot in November.

Mariano sees the proposal to cut the income tax rate to 4 percent as catastrophic to the state’s budget. Proponents, including some business groups such as the Massachusetts High Technology Council, think otherwise, and argue it would improve the state’s competitiveness.

Mariano wants a deal this spring that would be good enough to persuade proponents to pull the question from the ballot — although it’s not clear what that deal would entail.

So Mariano publicly turned to the chamber and its chief executive, Jim Rooney, for help. The chamber has remained neutral, at least up to this point, and it has board members on both sides.

“We’re on the precipice,” Mariano told the crowd at the Fairmont Copley Plaza hotel. “We need the help of the business community that is watching this unfold.”

Mariano said the state simply can’t afford such a big tax cut that will translate to a major loss in services and cuts to school budgets, economic development, and infrastructure spending.

“The House shares your concerns about affordability and competitiveness, but the ballot question simply isn’t an answer to either of those challenges,” Mariano added. “It’s my hope that the folks who are pushing this ballot question are willing to sit down with us and consider alternatives to their current approach.”

Wonder Group is opening as many as 30 “food hall” locations in Greater Boston this year, but CommonWealth Kitchen won’t be celebrating its arrival.

New York-based Wonder, a venture-backed business that offers multiple food brands under one roof, sparked unusual pushback from CWK soon after its first Boston-area openings in February.

Normally, CWK’s blog and email newsletters promote food startups fostered by the Dorchester-based nonprofit incubator. But in this email, executive director Jen Faigel did something unusual by expressing concern about Wonder’s authenticity.

Faigel said she spoke up because she views Wonder as exemplifying the “commodification” of food, and how private investments can enter a market, outspend local businesses, and upend a business model. “If small and independent restaurants and caterers had Wonder’s marketing resources,” she added, “Boston’s food scene would be on much sounder footing.”

Launched in 2018 by former Walmart executive Marc Lore, Wonder is in the midst of a major growth spurt — thanks in part to a $600 million investment round last year. Boston-area executive Courtney Lawrie, formerly with Wayfair, is helping lead this push. She says Wonder now is up to more than 100 locations in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic regions, up from 35 in early 2025, with an eye on reaching 200 by the end of 2026.

Wonder combines aspects of a food hall and a ghost kitchen; diners can choose from up to 20 different menus, including some with ties to celebrity chefs, with take-out, delivery, and dine-in options. The company also acquired several food startups in the past few years: the Grubhub delivery business, Blue Apron meal kits, and the Boston-born Spyce robot salad maker.

Lawrie said CWK’s commentary doesn’t reflect Wonder and its mission, to “make great food more accessible.” She said Wonder’s approach is rooted in “flavor-driven, chef-inspired meals” and has received warm welcomes in the communities where its stores have opened.

Around Greater Boston, it’s hard to miss that Jordan’s Furniture sure looks different in its latest ad campaign.

The logo was significantly redesigned for the first time in decades with a more modern look. The “J” is in lower-case now. The word “Furniture” is gone. The new tagline is: “We get you. We got you.”

But the biggest change might be this: Eliot Tatelman’s role as the Taunton-based chain’s spokesperson has been diminished.

That’s not necessarily a surprise. Tatelman retired last year, at age 79, leaving his sons Josh and Michael in charge. (Now, Josh Tatelman is the sole CEO.) Tatelman is willing to participate in the ads, but we won’t see as much of him now.

He’s still considered part of the on-camera cast, though sometimes he only handles the voiceovers. In one TV ad, Tatelman narrates with his instantly recognizable Boston accent. However, we don’t see him. Instead, we see anonymous actors celebrating life’s moments, and maybe considering a sofa or mattress for purchase.

Expect more of these ads in the coming days, weeks, and months. An internal team led by Jordan’s marketing executive, Linda SanGiacomo, designed the campaign, working with Tim Vaccarino and others at TBWA\Chiat\Day Boston (formerly MullenLowe). Pretty Awesome, a production business in Boston, helped out.

SanGiacomo said the Jordan’s marketers are trying to keep alive the spirit of fun and friendliness that Tatelman embodies. He’ll continue to appear in ads, she added, “until he tells us he doesn’t want to anymore.”

Massachusetts employers in general still seem gloomy about the economic outlook, but not the executives at Citizens Financial Group.

CEO Bruce Van Saun told investors in January that he sees solid GDP growth in 2026, stable unemployment, and maybe even a slide in inflation. Of course, that was before the Iran war upended assumptions a bit.

Still, Van Saun largely remained optimistic in his remarks to employees, provided the Iran situation gets resolved soon, as he completed his annual tour last week of 14 major Citizens markets by meeting with around 600 employees at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

“Every year, you hope you get a calm year,” Van Saun said. “It’s usually by March [that] the hope dies.”

The COVID-19 pandemic hit in March 2020, while Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in March 2023. Last year, the Trump administration’s tariffs kept executives up at night. This year? The United States and Israel launched airstrikes on Feb. 28, and the bombing and chaos were relentless in the month that followed, with a tenuous peace coming into place only last week. “March,” Van Saun conceded, “has not been my favorite month.”

title: The fine art of enriching Boston
text:
Leslie founded two nonprofits — Dorchester Community Center for the Visual Arts, better known as DotArt, in 1998, and Living Art, in 2015. They were small, even by local nonprofit standards — not the type of organization you’d typically read about in the business section.

They had an outsize impact, but Leslie rarely got the recognition she deserved for bringing art to communities, even as schools cut back on such “extras.” No matter. For her, teaching artmaking was a labor of love. And she helped make Boston a better place to live and raise a family.

Today’s newsletter is my way of honoring Leslie, who died March 24 at her home in Stoneham, where she had moved to be closer to family. She was 90.

Welcome to Dorchester

My wife and I met Leslie in December 1989. We’d just moved to the Ashmont section of Dorchester. Leslie knocked on the door, welcomed us to the neighborhood, and offered an invite to her annual New Year’s Day party.

Leslie lived a few houses away, and she was thrilled we’d landed from New York with two small children in tow. She and her husband at the time had a young son and were members of a babysitting cooperative. She was quick to recruit us into the co-op — and we were glad she did. We met people who became longtime friends and introduced us to other Dorchester families.

An unstoppable force

The essential thing to know about Leslie: She was a fighter — determined, unyielding, never one to take no for an answer. Even those who loved her knew she could be a pain in the butt.

That strong will was evident when she battled tuberculosis as a young girl in Dublin. She was bedridden for four years and spent most of that time in a body cast.

During that period, “drawing became a crucial way to realize her ideas about herself and the world,” her ex-husband, Paul Dobbs, said in an email. “This was quite possibly the crucible that created her passion for teaching, or, more specifically, for advocating artmaking as a tool for self-realization.”

Leslie was accepted at Ireland’s National College of Art and Design at 14, and later attended the famed École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. When she returned to Dublin, Leslie taught art while establishing herself as an acclaimed painter.

Coming to America

Leslie came to the US in 1973 to become a graduate student at Boston University. She taught undergraduate art classes at BU and Massachusetts College of Art and Design, where she was later appointed an assistant professor.

It was at BU that Leslie met Dobbs, an archivist, whom she would marry in 1977. A decade later, they adopted an infant, Adam, from Honduras. Leslie lived for several months in a Honduran Mennonite colony while the adoption papers were completed. She was already in her 50s.

In 1992, Leslie created The Children’s Studio in Dorchester, where she and others taught young children to draw, paint, and sculpt. That led to the formation of DotArt six years later.

Leslie focused on portrait paintings, done on hollow-core doors, and figurative sculptures in papier-mâché on simple armatures.

“Leslie also made the creation of these portraits a ‘paying job’ by securing funding from the city of Boston and charitable foundations (including the Boston Foundation) to create and manage summer jobs for teens,” according to an obituary by family friend Mark Farrington.

Moving on

Leslie left DotArt in 2012 after a consultant recommended the organization hire a new executive director with better organizational skills. Leslie was notoriously late for everything. (I would kid her about operating on “MacWeeney Time.”)

While a persuasive fundraiser, Leslie didn’t care much for the paperwork that many institutional donors wanted to see detailing how their grant money was spent and the results achieved, said Evan Hershenson, DotArt’s executive officer and treasurer.

A few years after leaving DotArt, she started Living Art, which recruited police officers, firefighters, EMTs, and veterans to pose for portraits.

Her genius was the ability to provide “new art opportunities in so many mediums,” Hershenson said. “She knew how to bring art into a lot of different spaces. And the one constant was creating a safe space where you wouldn’t be judged on your work.”

A Funeral Mass for Leslie will be held April 25, 10 a.m., at the Paulist Center, 5 Park St. in Boston, with an informal gathering afterward to celebrate and appreciate Leslie’s remarkable life.

title: It isn’t sexist to say it: Rachael Rollins messed up
text:
The report also concluded that Rollins “knowingly and willfully made a false statement of material fact under oath” and generally “lacked candor.” According to the report, she also attended a Democratic Party fund-raiser featuring then-first lady Jill Biden “without required department approval and contrary to ethics advice she received,” a violation of the Hatch Act.

The US Office of Special Counsel also released a report of what it called her “egregious transgressions.”

When Rollins announced she would be resigning her position, her lawyer described the findings as mostly “minor process fouls.” Now that she appears to be launching a run against Hayden, she has taken to social media to suggest that as a woman, she is being held to a different standard than a man.

It’s true that Hayden paid a $5,000 civil fine for an ethics violation in 2024 after the state Ethics Commission found that he used his official position to try to discredit Arroyo. But Hayden also signed a disposition agreement in which he admitted the violation and waived his right to a hearing.

After taking responsibility for his actions, Hayden left it at that. Rollins is still trying to equivocate and deflect responsibility, and that’s a mistake.

As the first Black woman elected as Suffolk County district attorney and the first Black woman to become the region’s top federal prosecutor, she broke ground in many important ways. She pivoted away from punishment toward fighting the societal causes of crime and released a list of nonviolent crimes she said she wouldn’t prosecute. But over time, she gave critics of that approach too many weapons to use against her.

During her first run for Suffolk County DA in 2018, the Boston Herald first reported she had been charged with receiving stolen property while she was a college student. In response, her campaign said that the “minor” arrest did not affect her career as a prosecutor but has “informed how she views criminal justice reform.” The misdemeanor charge, which dated back to 1991, was eventually continued without a finding and dropped.

A stint as chief legal counsel at Massport from 2013 to 2015 ended with what CommonWealth Beacon described as “a puzzling coda” — a $175,000 severance agreement and a $45,000 education benefit that have never been explained to the public.

When Rollins was Suffolk County DA, a Dorchester resident filed a complaint alleging that Rollins threatened her and inappropriately flashed blue lights at her during a 2020 Christmas Eve confrontation at the South Bay shopping center. Then-Attorney General Maura Healey launched a review that found no civil rights or criminal violations, which is not the same thing as saying nothing happened. The matter was referred to the state Ethics Commission, which ultimately cleared her.

In January 2021, Rollins yelled at a television news crew that approached her in front of her home, seeking comment about the traffic incident. Telling them to “get out of here,” she added, “You know what I’ll do? I’ll call the police on you and make an allegation and we’ll see how that works out for you.” That from a prosecutor who listed trespass as a crime she wouldn’t prosecute in the name of criminal justice reform.

Some will say that because of race and gender, she was judged more harshly for reactions such as those connected to the alleged road rage incident. But I think she was also granted leeway because of her progressive agenda. The Globe, for example, endorsed her for DA, describing the charge of receiving stolen property as “a minor brush with the law as a college student” and emphasizing her ability to “push the office in new directions.”

With backing from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey, who hailed her as a national leader in transforming the criminal justice system, Rollins was nominated by President Biden to be the region’s top federal prosecutor. Then came the scathing reports by two watchdog agencies about her conduct in that job.

The Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers voted to publicly reprimand Rollins, with three of the 12 members finding the punishment too lenient and a fourth member recusing herself, the Globe reported at the time. When Rollins agreed to the public reprimand, she admitted to improperly disclosing confidential information to a Herald reporter about an investigation into Hayden. But still, according to the Globe report, she told the board she “erroneously thought she had discretion to disclose the matter without prior authorization pursuant to DOJ manual.”

She has been working at Roxbury Community College as executive director of a program focused on helping formerly incarcerated people for an annual salary of $96,000.

Does she deserve a second chance as a prosecutor? That’s up to the voters.

But she did mess up. Better to just admit that.

title: What do former grisly mob haunts say about modern day Greater Boston?
text:
Like so many formerly gritty spots throughout the region, the building’s interior has become something else entirely. It’s dominated by a mural of people being baptized in a river, flanked by screens welcoming worshipers to the church. The carpet is purple, as are the seats. During one recent Sunday service, about 20 people were in attendance.

The Rev. Collin Green led them in prayer and song. After the service, he acknowledged the sordid history of the property, bringing up the prior owner and longtime leader of the Winter Hill Gang, the late Howie Winter, unprompted. He said the neighborhood is no longer a place where people need to look over their shoulder.

“It’s changed,” he said. “It’s not that way. God is in the building.”

But not all the changes from how it was to how it is are for the better. He mentioned the local housing crunch, saying one congregant, who grew up in Somerville, travels to attend services from Worcester, where housing is more affordable.

It’s a transformation playing out across the region. As Greater Boston has gentrified, it has become less of a backdrop for working-class, clannish noirs that hinge on loyalty and limited life choices directed by Ben Affleck or Martin Scorsese. It’s now more of a hub of gentrifying young professionals, skyrocketing housing costs, and concerns about displacement.

Holly Simione, 56, grew up a short walk away from the former Somerville garage-turned-church. When she was a kid, she knew who the “bad guys” were in the neighborhood. While she was in middle school, a man on the run from police hid in her yard. Simione was on the porch, she recalled. He pointed a gun at her but didn’t fire. That was the neighborhood back then.

“I remember being mindful of people but not being afraid of them,” she said.

Now, Marshall Street itself has two dozen properties assessed at more than $1 million, according to city records. Winter Hill, according to some residents, may be home to some of the last slices of un-gentrified Somerville, but is not immune to the market forces that have seen rents skyrocket locally. Others say, no, Winter Hill has already been gentrified, just not as much as, say, Davis Square. They all agree the neighborhood is not what it used to be. And it’s hardly alone.

Down Interstate 93 in South Boston is the former location of Triple O’s Lounge, a hive of misdeeds. In another age, here is where James “Whitey” Bulger held court, a bookmaker disappeared, at least one bar fight led to a gangland slaying, and a Bulger protégé worked the door. It is now a joint called Fox & the Knife, where you can order $38 scallops. Not your grandfather’s Southie, to say the least.

In the same neighborhood, the so-called Haunty, a notorious cottage where mobsters killed and buried bodies in the basement, has been razed. In its stead, there are condominiums, all of them assessed at more than $1.7 million. (One of the units sold for $1.9 million in 2022.)

“It was always going to be replaced by something like this,” said Joshua Lown a post-doctoral research associate at Boston University’s Initiative on Cities, as he stood next to the building that replaced the Haunty.

A mob associate of Bulger’s once testified that he said he stood guard as Bulger killed Arthur “Bucky” Barrett, 45; Deborah Hussey, 26; and John McIntyre, 32, on separate occasions inside the Haunty. Their bodies were buried in the dirt cellar. When the house was being sold, they were exhumed and buried on Halloween night 1985 near Florian Hall.

Now at the address, there is a new building featuring a bump-out on a corner, an architectural flick to historic housing in Boston, Lown said in an interview.

“There’s some nod to the triple-decker look,” said Lown.

Gentrification, he said, can be a squishy term.

“Nobody is saying ‘I don’t want nice stuff,’” he said. “What they’re saying is we resist nice stuff because it often brings displacement.”

In the Seaport, the pier where Bulger gunned down two people has become a testament to Boston’s nouveau riche. Nearby are gleaming towers of glass housing biotech companies, trendy cocktail places, and expensive apartments to house the people who work, eat, and drink around there. Much of the neighborhood used to be parking lots.

In Dorchester last year, one restaurant found out what can happen when you fail to account for the grimmer chapters of the city’s history. The owner of Savin Bar and Kitchen was forced to take down a photo of Bulger after local outcry. Neighborhood residents had said the Bulger photo was especially inappropriate considering the mobster brutally killed Eddie Connors, who owned Bulldogs, a restaurant on the same site in the early 1970s.

Farther north, the North End’s Prince Street was once home to the Mafia in Boston. There, federal authorities raided and bugged what was the headquarters of the Angiulo family in the early 1980s. Some things haven’t changed; the building remains in the Angiulo family to this day, according to records with the Suffolk Registry of Deeds. But much has. For one, the North End is considerably less Italian than it was in the heyday of the Boston branch of the Mafia. And the neighborhood, like so much of the city, has been battered by gentrification.

The biggest crime on Prince Street nowadays may be a $19 espresso martini.

Six miles away, there is a house on Guild Street in Medford where a Mafia induction was recorded by federal agents decades ago — a singular coup for American law enforcement.

Here, on Oct. 29, 1989, blood was drawn from each of the inductees’ trigger fingers, a holy card with the image of a family saint was burned, and gangsters recited an oath: “As burns this saint so will burn my soul. I enter alive into this organization and leave it dead.”

There are no indications of that past nowadays, as the neighborhood is a solidly middle-class, suburban enclave just off the Fellsway. Here, gangsters may have come and gone, but real estate remains a good investment. The house where the induction ceremony took place was sold in 2019 for $600,000 and is now likely worth more.

“It comes down to the money,” said Joe Leeman, a retired Boston police lieutenant who is a historic tour guide in Boston. “Everything is so expensive to live here ... so there’s not a lot of nonsense anymore.”

Leeman grew up in Charlestown but has lived in South Boston for years. Both neighborhoods, once home to the more rough-and-tumble elements of the city’s milieu, have evolved. His property value has gone up drastically over the past 10 years, he said.

While Boston’s cost of living is a chief deterrent for organized crime, there may be other factors at play. Namely, the government has legalized some sectors that were key for organized crime for decades. Sports betting is legal in Massachusetts, which cuts into illicit loan sharking and betting operations. Recreational marijuana is also a legal reality in the state, although Leeman acknowledges that the market for harder, still illegal drugs is still very much there.

If the paths for a neighborhood are between remaining intertwined with organized crime and gentrification, Leeman said, without question, the latter is better.

But, nowadays, he said, “There’s no organized crime to speak of.”

Back in Winter Hill, so much has changed for long-term residents like Simione.

“As it should,” she said.

Still, she said, “I was OK with ‘Slummerville.’”

She paused for a moment.

“That’s where I grew up.”

Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Pure Oasis, state’s first Black-owned pot shop, abruptly closes six years after being first to open in Boston
text:
“We were kind of dead in the water,” Evans said in an interview. “I didn’t want to keep staff in the lurch not knowing how long it would take before the hold would be lifted off.”

Evans said he faced a vortex of troubles. A bill that recently passed in the Legislature would double the marijuana stores companies can own, which he said will give an advantage to large, well-funded, out-of-state corporations. A well-heeled competitor who can afford to undercut his prices recently got approval for a downtown store neighboring his. And persistent economic woes caused by dwindling customer spending, plummeting prices, and oversupply in the weed market forced a tough decision to close, Evans said. Pure Oasis has also faced a slew of lawsuits over alleged unpaid debts, court records show.

“I kind of felt like the landscape of cannabis, especially for equity and small operators, was changing,” Evans said. “At one point, equity operators were celebrated, and now we felt like there was no one to turn to.”

Pure Oasis’ problems came amid broader industry turmoil. Thirteen stores shuttered last fiscal year, more than all previous years combined, state data show. A record 24 cannabis companies in January were in receivership, a process similar to bankruptcy, the latest reports show.

Pure Oasis was also working to open a third store in Brighton, a move Evans said could still be possible through loans. Financing the expansion in 2025, he added, strained the business, causing a cascade of missed payments.

Evans, a real estate agent, and his business partner, Kevin Hart, a hospital administrative director, had entered the pot business because of the state’s pioneering marijuana legalization law. Massachusetts was the first in the nation to require that communities hit hardest by marijuana arrests be given full access to the industry. Many states followed suit.

Now, six years after opening his first store, Evans said he feels “abandoned by lawmakers.”

On March 25, the Boston Cannabis Boardgranted approval for Curaleaf, a large national cannabis chain, to open a block and a half from Pure Oasis in downtown, contingent on Curaleaf’s plan to offer downtown equity businesses discounts, officials said. A sweeping cannabis reform bill recently passed by the Legislature would ultimately increase the number of pot shops any entity can own from three to six.

Evans said large companies will now consolidate and wipe out “all the small mom-and-pops.” Attempts by equity operators to lobby for a smaller license cap increase “fell on deaf ears,” he said.

Evans is still looking to reopen his Dorchester store, likely with the help of an operating partner. The top priority remains lifting the tax lien and paying staff, he said.

If Evans and Hart couldn’t succeed, that’s a bad sign for others in the state’s social equity programs with less education and business experience, said Laury Lucien, a social equity advocate who advises the Cannabis Control Commission.

“These guys from Pure Oasis, they’re very intelligent human beings,” Lucien said. “That’s what’s so heartbreaking about it.”

Marissa Reese, a budtender at Grove Hall, said customers asked if a closure was coming in recent months.

“But we thought because they were the first dispensary, they would be protected,” Reese said. “Nobody expected this.”

Pure Oasis was part of the state’s economic empowerment program. That program fast-tracked license approvals for entrepreneurs from disproportionately Black and Latino communities with high rates of marijuana arrests.

In 2025, the company was selected to receive $50,000 through the state’s social equity fund, despite applying for more than $1 million to cover costs for its third dispensary in Brighton, Evans said. To make up the remaining funds, Pure Oasis diverted money from daily operations last year, Evans said. In February he also told the Globe he had taken out a high-interest loan.

Last month, the social equity fund awarded Pure Oasis another $300,000, the maximum amount allowed.

Evans said he planned to use that money to pay the taxes owed.

But the grant money has yet to arrive, with no clear timeline, he added. (A spokesperson for the Executive Office of Economic Development said awardees were notified that the contracting process to be able to receive the money is set to start soon.)

The company has tried unsuccessfully to set up a payment plan with the Department of Revenue, Evans said.

The Department of Revenue declined to comment, citing taxpayer confidentiality.

Last year, Pure Oasis owed another $178,000 in state taxes, which was paid, records show. The company had a different federal tax lien for $4.1 million filed in August 2024, records show, but the company structured a payment plan to resolve it, Evans said.

Still, taxes represent just the beginning of the cannabis seller’s financial woes.

On April 8, a judge ordered Pure Oasis to pay nearly $2.3 million to resolve defaulted mortgage payments on an industrial space in Dighton, outside Taunton, court records show.

That day, signs appeared in the downtown store’s windows saying “closed temporarily,” and Evans emailed employees to say the business had exhausted “every option” and needed to shut down immediately.

“It was totally abrupt,” said Josue Soto Lora, an inventory worker at the Grove Hall store. “It was just an email saying, ‘Hey, we’re closed.’”

Many workers are trying to file for unemployment and get their final paychecks. Some have sent complaints to the attorney general’s office over the money they’re owed, former employees said. A spokesperson for the attorney general said the office was aware of the matter.

The company also faces four pending lawsuits over alleged debts totaling more than $320,000 for cannabis products, construction costs, and contractor services. Separately, in recent months, courts have ordered Pure Oasis to pay roughly $120,500 in unpaid rent and $66,000 for pot product debts, records show.

The company had paid its bills on time for years, but beginning in June 2025 debt issues escalated, with more than $1 million in unpaid debts accumulating in the past six months, said Mike Blumenthal, executive director of Cannabiz Credit Association, which collects self-reported invoice data from more than 130 businesses in Massachusetts.

Across the state, unpaid debt issues among cannabis companies have ballooned in recent years. The recently passed cannabis reform legislation, currently awaiting Governor Maura Healey’s signature, would ramp up debt enforcement by publicizing delinquent companies and restricting their activities, though not until 2028.

Joe Baker, who worked the front desk at the downtown Pure Oasis, said the company was served lawsuits multiple times in his eight months there.

“I honestly didn’t see it coming as far as getting closed down because in my head, I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you probably just didn’t pay some money,’” Baker said. “I didn’t know the depth of how crazy it was.”

Pure Oasis’grand opening in Dorchester in March 2020, with state officials in attendance and lines around the block, was heralded as a proud milestone for the state’s social equity programs.

Lucien, the advocate for social equity in cannabis, said she hopes the state doubles down on its efforts to support disadvantaged businesses, even if these remedies didn’t work in time to save Boston’s first equity retailer.

She said multiple social equity companies are being “kept afloat” by the state’s social equity fund, a recent measure aimed at bolstering these businesses amid high federal taxes and a lack of bank loans. She said the fund is helping address financial pressures for equity operators, though regulatory strains remain. Some, such as Pure Oasis, may not have gotten their financial lifeline soon enough, Lucien added.

“It might have been a little bit too late for them, perhaps,” she said. “So long as marijuana is federally prohibited and banks are not making loans available to people, we’re going to see this happening quite a bit.”

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to reflect that Pure Oasis was selected to receive $50,000 in 2025.

title: Wu appoints Rodney Marshall as Boston’s first Black fire commissioner
text:
As recently as two years ago, the department’s effort torecruit more women and people of color was still struggling through fits and smarts: 71 percent of that academy class was white and 93 percent were men. Demographic data the city posts online show that 73 percent of the department’s employees is white, even though 44 percent of the city population is.

“We’re going to make this a job that’s equal for everyone,” Marshall said Thursday. “Men, women, people of color — whoever wants this job is going to have the opportunity.”

He pointed to the department’s efforts to recruit new firefighters from all of the city’s neighborhoods through the cadet program, as well as its Teen Academy — a paid summer job program for 14- to 18 year-olds that introduces youth to fire services.

The mayor’s office did not immediately provide updated demographic data for the department or its most recent fire cadet class.

“It’s important that we reflect who we are in public safety, in our schools, in the cabinet, and wherever there’s positions of power in the city,” said state Senator Lydia Edwards of East Boston, who has previously criticized the department for its handling of reports of racial and gender discrimination.

But while Marshall’s appointment marks a turning point, Edwards said, she is most impressed by the Boston native’s decades of service, which has earned him the deep respect of his peers.

Wu on Thursday thanked Burke for his leadership, calling him “a shining example of what it means to be a public servant.” She said it is an “honor” to appoint Marshall as his successor.

“He served all across our city in East Boston, Back Bay, Brighton, South Boston, and has seen firsthand the needs of our neighborhoods and the people who call them home,” Wu said of Marshall. ”Rodney has earned a reputation as someone who earns trust, and that’s the kind of leadership this department, the oldest and the best, deserves."

Burke also celebrated Marshall’s promotion, saying he has personally witnessed Marshall’s “steady leadership, sound judgment, and commitment to our mission” over his four years as fire commissioner.

“My title might have been Commissioner, but Chief Marshall and myself were equals,” Burke said. “We did everything together. His instincts were unbelievable when things got tough, ... and I’m proud that it’s him. It couldn’t be a better day.”

Marshall first joined the fire department in 1991, before rising through the ranks to become deputy fire chief in 2022. He was recognized by the department in 1998 for saving several lives during a six-alarm fire, and earned another commendation for rescuing people trapped in a bus in 2013, according to Wu’s office.

Marshall also designed and launched the fire department’s cadet program, which aims to recruit young Boston residents.

Marshall is a Grove Hall native and graduate of Boston College.

Joined by his family, friends, and colleagues on Thursday, Marshall emphasized his commitment to prioritizing the health and safety of Boston residents and his fellow firefighters.

“It takes a team to assemble a 50-foot ladder and stand it up; it takes a team to stretch a two-and-a-half hose line down the hallway; and it’s the strength of that team that makes the difference between life and death on this job,” Marshall said. “I take this job very seriously. I love this department, and I love this city.”

Marshall’s appointment comes after Wu has seen the departure of several high-profile Black officials from her administration in recent months. Jessicah Pierre, Wu’s former chief of communications, left the administration last November after Wu resoundingly won a second term. Segun Idowu, the city’s former chief of economic opportunity and inclusion, resigned from his job in January.

Then last month, Wu’s tourism chief, John Borders IV, stepped down for a role with Boston’s new women’s professional soccer team, Boston Legacy FC.

The Boston Fire Department has long faced criticism for its purportedly change-resistant culture, and lack of diversity, as well as reports of racial discrimination, and sexual harassment and assault.

In early February, 12 elected officials of color, including City Councilor Brian Worrell, sent a letter to Wu urging her to name the city’s first Black fire commissioner.

Marshall’s appointment is well-deserved based solely on his resume, Worrell told the Globe, but it’s also “an inspiration, and it continues to show that Boston will not be a city that sets barriers on any of their residents.”

“This is us continuing to take that step in the right direction, making sure that we create a fire department that is reflective of every neighborhood in the city and that every resident could see themselves in,” Worrell said.

The city hosted the announcement of Marshall’s appointment Thursday at the Berkshire Partners Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club in Dorchester, where his two children attend after school programs.

Whenever he picks them up while in uniform, Marshall said it sparks the curiosity of other kids.

“I love these questions because they present an opportunity to have a conversation about this job, this profession, and this department,” Marshall said. “These conversations open kids’ eyes to what’s possible, and to considering a path” they didn’t know existed.

Marshall said that, as a child growing up, he didn’t know what firefighters did, and remembers walking past a fire house on Washington Street that always had its doors closed. This summer, he said he plans to issue a directive for all fire stations to keep their doors open during the warm months.

“I want city kids, kids from every neighborhood, to be able to walk in, see the trucks, talk to the firefighters, and experience the wonder and excitement of seeing this job up close,” Marshall said.

His hope, he said, is that one of those children will grow up and land the department’s top job — like he did.

title: Another week, more proof Massachusetts is losing its edge
text:
School daze: Hampshire College, a small liberal arts school that has been under financial pressure for years, said it would close after the fall semester.

Enrollment at the Amherst campus has declined by half since the early 2000s to about 625 students, according to Hampshire president Jennifer Chrisler.

Its closing is part of a broader trend within higher education, in which smaller private colleges in particular have struggled, while the soaring costs of tuition have prompted more families to question the value of a four-year degree, write the Globe’s Brooke Hauser and Diti Kohli. By one new estimate, more than one-quarter of all private colleges in the US could close or be forced to merge within the next 10 years.

Fewer high school graduates are choosing to go to college amid a “public discussion in this country about the value of a liberal arts education,” Chrisler told The New York Times.

Moreover, higher education is facing an enrollment cliff. The number of college-age students will fall about 15 percent through 2029, according to Carleton College economist Nathan D. Grawe.

The implications for Massachusetts are large. Fifty-nine private, nonprofit colleges and universities contributed $71.1 billion to the state’s economic output, supported more than 320,000 jobs, and generated $2.4 billion in annual tax revenue, according to a 2023 study by Econsult Solutions for the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts.

Texas toast: When it comes to venture financing, Austin is hot on Boston’s heels.

Texas startups gathered $5.8 billion from venture capital investors in the first three months of the year, topping the $5.3 billion for Massachusetts startups, according to research firm PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association.

My colleague Aaron Pressman says it’s likely the first time ever that the Bay State has fallen behind the Lone Star State. In the previous four years, Massachusetts held an average quarterly advantage of $2 billion quarterly over Texas.

Though it may just be a slip in the rankings, and Massachusetts startups could pull back ahead for the rest of the year, the news comes as the state is dealing with several major challenges, Aaron reports. And it continues the narrative of decline for the state that invented venture capital investing and ranked behind only California as recently as 2013, when New York’s position as a capital of finance and media helped it pull ahead.

Trump administration policies, including research cuts and hostility to climate-change initiatives, have hurt the biotech and green-tech industries. The state hasn’t been a player in AI, which is sucking up hundreds of billions of dollars in investments. Texas, meanwhile, has emerged as a power in defense tech, robotics, and energy.

The financing slowdown matters because venture capital is the lifeblood of the life sciences, biotech, and technology sectors at the heart of the state’s high-end economy. Jobs, workers — and tax revenues — will go where that money flows.

Rent ruckus: Sky-high housing costs put the state at a competitive disadvantage to lower-cost rivals, and that disadvantage is getting worse.

A statewide rent control initiative likely headed to the November ballot is being sold as a fix. It isn’t.

The proposal would limit annual rent hikes to the rate of inflation, with a cap of 5 percent. But controlling rents won’t build a single new unit. And by capping landlord returns, it discourages the new construction that is the only real path to keeping rents in check. It would also depress property values, straining municipal budgets.

Last month I argued that the measure is a bad idea. This week, a group of mayors made their case against the initiative.

“What is especially ominous about the proposed ballot question is that it applies not just to the red-hot Boston housing market, but everywhere else in the Commonwealth,” New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell warned. “In Greater New Bedford and other regions where housing developers at times struggle to make their numbers work, it would effectively shut down housing production.”

Mayors from Worcester, Lawrence, Quincy, and Revere also oppose the initiative.

The solution to Massachusetts’ housing crisis isn’t a limit on what landlords can charge. It’s a combination of development incentives and zoning changes that make it easier and more profitable to build.

Final thought: None of this week’s developments — one soft quarter for venture capital, one college closing, one ballot initiative that hasn’t passed — is fatal on its own.

But the trends continue to move in the wrong direction.

title: Five new TV shows and movies to stream this weekend
text:
Starring Wahlberg and directed by New England’s own Peter Farrelly, the new comedy “Balls Up” hit Prime Video this week. The Dorchester native joins forces with actor Paul Walter Hauser to play a pair of marketing executives who come up with a condom concept that probably wouldn’t fly in a high school health class but nonetheless helps them score a World Cup sponsorship deal in Brazil. Things quickly turn chaotic as the duo get into drunken antics at a game. “Balls Up” also stars Benjamin Bratt, Molly Shannon, Sacha Baron Cohen, and Eric André. Available on Prime Video

After playing second fiddle to her famous father in streaming hits like “Happy Gilmore 2” and “Jay Kelly,” Sadie Sandler gets the chance to take on a leading role in the new comedy “Roommates,” arriving Friday on Netflix. The daughter of New Hampshire native Adam Sandler plays college student Devon, who finds herself butting heads with her roommate Celeste (Chloe East) following a falling out between the dorm room buddies. The comedy also features Nick Kroll, Natasha Lyonne, and “Saturday Night Live” cast member Sarah Sherman. Available on Netflix

For fans who need more “Love Island” in their lives, the spinoff “Beyond the Villa” kicked off its second season on Peacock this week. The latest installment takes a look at how “Love Island” season 7 cast members are faring following their stint on the main series, including Everett native Bryan Arenales, who won the reality show with Amaya Espinal. Sadly, the couple broke up last year. Available on Peacock

The season 2 finale of “The Pitt” streams on HBO Max this week, and there’s a lot left to wrap up for the hospital drama. At the top of the list is what’s going on with Noah Wyle’s Dr. Robby as he continues down a self-destructive path ahead of a planned sabbatical, plus the uncertain health situation surrounding his replacement Dr. Al-Hashimi (Sepideh Moafi). But for fans, the biggest remaining question has to be: What’s happening with Baby Jane Doe?!? Available on HBO Max

Long a bitter rival of the Celtics, late Lakers legend Jerry West gets the spotlight in the new documentary film “The Logo,” now streaming on Prime Video. An Olympic gold medalist, Hall of Famer, and the inspiration behind the silhouette used in the NBA’s logo, West had an impact on and off the court that cannot be understated. The documentary examines the former NBA champion’s legacy, featuring stories of West as told by Michael Jordan, Magic Johnson, Shaquille O’Neal, and more. Available on Prime Video

title: Locals react to the advancement of a bill that would protect Haitians from deportation
text:
Hello newsletter subscribers! A quick programming note before we dive into the news — we are going to start delivering Immigration Unmasked every other week for the near future. The pace of ICE-related news in New England has slowed a bit, and while it remains an urgent focus for us, this schedule makes sense to us for now. Rest assured, if the situation on the ground changes, we’ll adjust as needed.

I write to you with some updates on a crucial measure that currently shields some 350,000 Haitian nationals across the US from deportation.

The Trump administration since last year has worked to terminate this special class of legal protections granted to Haitians — as well as Hondurans, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans. Formally called Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, the program shields immigrants whose home countries are undergoing armed conflict, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary country conditions, from deportation.

President Trump’s effort to end TPS protection, part of his wider crackdown on legal immigration, has faced mounting legal challenges. The Supreme Court is expected to rule on the case this summer.

Haitians in this country, however, potentially have another lifeline on the horizon. On Thursday, the US House passed bipartisan legislation to extend this status for Haitians through 2029, my colleague Julian E.J. Sorapuru in Washington reported. In a somewhat surprising move, 10 Republicans sided with Democrats, breaking party lines.

In Boston, Haitian American advocates and community leaders were heartened. “It’s a wonderful moment,” said Geralde Gabeau, the executive director of Immigrant Family Services Institute Inc., a Mattapan-based nonprofit and one of the leading groups supporting Haitians in Boston.

Greater Boston has the third largest Haitian diaspora in the country, following Florida and New York. An estimated 45,000 Haitian TPS holders live in Massachusetts, where many work in health care, across nursing homes and hospitals in the region.

Many Haitians in Massachusetts have been living in the region for decades, with some relying on TPS since 2010, when the US government designated Haitian nationals for these protections after an earthquake devastated the country. Now, deadly violence grips the country, with gangs controlling as much as 90% of the country’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

Many Haitians have told me it is too unsafe for them to return, and as the Trump administration has tried to roll back their deportation protections, they’re not sure what comes next for them. The House vote seemed to offer some comfort.

“Knowing all the pain, all of the anxiety and all of the issues that our community is facing – to me, it’s such a big relief for them to know there is hope,” Gabeau told me on Thursday after the House voted on the legislation.

Massachusetts Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat who is the co-chair for the House Haiti Caucus, has been a staunch advocate in Washington for Haitians under TPS. She pushed forward despite many obstacles, using a procedural measure called a discharge petition in order to get a vote.

Gabeau has been collaborating with Pressley and others to drive the discharge petition forward, even as many people initially had doubts. But they had to try anyway – and now, she said: “We’re going to do everything in our power to get to the finish line.”

On Thursday, Carline Desire had been watching the results of the House vote closely. She leads the Association of Haitian Women in Boston, a Dorchester-based group that works to advance social and economic opportunities for Haitian women across the area. Desire said that Thursday’s vote represented a major step forward for a community that has spent the last year “really on edge.”

She was especially reassured to see that the legislation had bipartisan support. “We are a nation of immigrants. Most immigrants have just been phenomenal in enhancing so many different aspects of our society,” she told me. “There are some who really meet across the aisle to make sure that we do the right thing as a nation.”

Still, the bill faces difficult odds in the Senate, where the legislation needs 60 votes to pass. Advocates in Boston are pushing for the momentum to continue.

“The urgency remains clear: Haitian families cannot wait,” said Ruthzee Louijeune, an at-large city councilor in Boston and the first Haitian American elected to Boston municipal government. “We call on the Senate to move without delay and deliver protections that reflect the realities on the ground.”

It’s time to get back home. ... I’ve really always put my family first."
