title: 26.TRUE Marathon offers community, comebacks, and culture beyond Boston’s main route
text:
Powder was one of 400 runners who participated in 26.TRUE on Saturday, a racing event designed as a more inclusive option to the Boston Marathon that takes the runner through the “real” city.

The event, which features a half and full marathon, was held for the first time during the COVID-19 pandemic when PIONEERS Run Crew, Boston’s first Black and brown-led running community, put together a race for runners who’d registered for the canceled Boston Marathon. It was supposed to be a one-time event, but garnered so much interest that it’s now in its sixth year.

Aliese Lash, an event organizer, said 26.TRUE is dedicated to celebrating predominantly Black and brown neighborhoods including Dorchester, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan, which are usually overlooked during marathon weekend.

“These [neighborhoods] are historically underrepresented in running culture,” Lash said. “Something we care a lot about is how to make running more equitable and accessible to people of color and people who may not see themselves as elite, strong runners.”

Unlike traditional road races, 26.TRUE does not receive city-mandated road closures. Participants run on sidewalks and are encouraged to follow pedestrian rules. The marathon requires no qualifying standards, and runners register on a first-come, first-served basis and pay a $100 fee to cover overhead costs. Runners are able to complete 26.TRUE’s full or half-marathon options at their own pace without fear of having nobody left at the finish line.

This year 400 runners participated, the largest number in the event’s history, Lash said.

“We’re really centering it to be a tour of the city as opposed to a competitive race,” Lash said. “26.TRUE is so beautiful because the course itself gives runners a chance to really see the sights, smells, sounds, and culture of the parts of the city that we really love. This is what we call home.”

At the finish line, a block party was in full swing with a DJ, food trucks, and a recovery tent. Runners embraced family and friends and congratulated one another.

Near the finish line, Kelvin Velez stood holding a sign that read, “Jackie! Free tacos at the finish line!”

Velez said that Jackie is his “amazing” younger sister. While she’s not a regular runner, she always tries new things, he said.

“I’m the older brother, so I have her back, of course,” Velez said.

Later, when Jackie Velez crossed the finish line, she said completing the half-marathon was a personal goal of hers that she wanted to make by the time she turned 40 next month.

“This opportunity came, and I just signed up and started training,” she said.

Elsewhere at the block party, Whitney Polich greeted her friend Dylan Reyes, who had just completed the full route, with a sign reading, “Dylan runs on Dunkin!”

Reyes, of Boston, began running two years ago after reaching a low point in his life. He joined PIONEERS Run Crew and said the community helped carry him through.

The 26.TRUE route had excellent energy that kept him and other runners going, he said.

“You get to see so much of the historic parts of the city and so many people are out on their porches cheering,” he said. “It’s just a good vibe, everyone’s happy.”

Reyes is a fan of his friend’s poster, but he swapped Dunkin’ for a Modelo.

“No coffee now, but alcohol is great!” Reyes said, lifting his glass.

Volunteer coordinator Molly Ryan said the event’s 150 volunteers were essential to make 26.TRUE happen. Volunteers handle everything from bib pickup and registration to medal distribution and crowd support.

“Nothing would happen without the volunteers,” Ryan said. “It’s definitely a community effort.”

Powder said she plans to run the full marathon next year. Part of the reason she ran 26.TRUE was for its empowering community. Within the group, she’s seen runners become motivated to take risks like starting businesses and finishing school.

“Running is just the starting point, but the finish line is endless,” she said.

title: Head Start looks for help from Mass. in its mission to help young children
text:
In Massachusetts, roughly 1,300 slots for children across Head Start’s 28 agencies have been eliminated in the last three years because federal funding has plateaued over that time, while the cost of running the program continues to rise, according to the Massachusetts Head Start Association. Nationally, Head Start enrollment dropped from 1.1 million kids in 2013 to around 785,000 in 2022, according to research by the Annie E. Casey Foundation.

“If they didn’t get into a Head Start program, they would be sitting at home,” said Brittany Acosta, a Head Start parent in Dorchester.

It’s teachers are drastically underpaid, and there’s a serious need for a rainy day-type fund should the federal government shut down again, the association says. As they’ve done in years past, state lawmakers have offered to provide financial relief, but the Massachusetts Head Start Association’s request for 3 percent above the amount it received last year, an additional $4.6 million to help its staff keep up with the state’s rising cost of living, so far has not been allocated.

Last year, President Trump’s leaked budget proposal revealed he considered eliminating Head Start entirely. Then, in the summer, he cut off Head Start enrollment for immigrants without legal status. And during the fall’s government shutdown, four Head Start centers in Massachusetts closed because they couldn’t access their funding.

Trump’s latest budget proposal shows a fourth year without increasing funding for the program, which was established in the mid-1960s.

Michelle Haimowitz, executive director of the Massachusetts Head Start Association, said the program doesn’t want to eliminate more child slots than it already has, but paying teachers a competitive salary is equally important in order to keep them from leaving for higher paying jobs. Head Start teachers make under $50,000 annually compared to over $85,000 for the average Massachusetts kindergarten teacher.

“It’s an impossible choice,” Haimowitz said. “When we reduce the size of our programs, we’re not reducing the size of the need.”

Massachusetts is one of few states that supplements federal funding for Head Start, and last year it increased the program’s state grant from $5 million to $20 million, adding to the $189 million in federal aid it receives in this state.

“We can’t run a program without giving staff a raise for three years,” Haimowitz said. “Our next fight now is not just for survival, but it’s for thriving and growth.”

The Massachusetts House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday released its budget, which doesn’t grant Head Start’s request of a 3 percent boost. But state Representative Christopher Worrell filed an amendment for additional funding. Worrell, whose district covers parts of Dorchester and Roxbury, said he loves Head Start’s embrace of culture, recalling one visit to a center where he could smell staff cooking stew chicken, a traditional Caribbean dish.

“I’ve been to dozens of schools throughout the district, and you don’t get that home-cooked meal,” Worrell said. “[The state is] stepping up and doing the best we can with what we have.”

At the Action for Boston Community Development’s Head Start and Early Head Start center in Dorchester, the children of Classroom 7 arrived one Monday morning and dove into bins of magnetic tiles before their teachers, Paola Polanco and Leolina Rasundar Chinnappa, served breakfast. Acosta dropped off her 4-year-old daughter, Violeta, before reporting to her teaching position at the center, where several other Head Start parents also work.

“It’s important for all Head Start parents to have the opportunity to give their child an experience in a learning environment before they actually start kindergarten,” Acosta said.

Beyond providing early education and care to children of low-income families, from birth to age 5, the program helps them access other resources, including mental health services, SNAP benefits, homelessness assistance, and employment opportunities.

It also serves as daycare for parents who might not be able to afford it, while they’re at work.

Research has shown the importance of preschool in a child’s development with one 2023 study, focused on Boston public preschools, finding that it improves student behavior and increases the likelihood of high school graduation and college enrollment.

For Rickencia Clerveaux and Christopher Mclean, the Dorchester Head Start center is the only place they feel comfortable sending their 3-year-old son, Shontz, who is on the autism spectrum. Shontz’s stimming — repetitive movements that stimulate the senses — has reduced, and his speech has improved since he joined the center in 2024, Clerveaux said.

His parents say he’s also come out of his shell. Mclean now drops his son off and gets a simple “bye” as Shontz joins his classmates, he said.

He and Clerveaux said they appreciate the specialized attention Shontz can receive from teachers, such as when staff identified that Shontz might have hearing issues. His parents were able to follow up with their doctor and get Shontz to have surgery to improve his hearing.

“It’s a safe net for parents,” Clerveaux said. “There’s so many ways that him being here helps him grow better.”

Without Head Start, Clerveaux said a lot of pressure would be put on parents to find care for their children, “knowing that they’re already struggling or not getting the ends to meet.”

“That’s a burden for everybody in the community,” she said. “If there’s no funding, there’s no daycare and parents cannot work.”

title: From across Boston they flock to play for Latin Academy boys’ tennis, a co-op of 29 schools
text:
“I’ve done a lot of different things in my life, but there’s no question in my mind that the youth development aspect of what I’ve done with kids and tennis in Boston is the most important work I’ve ever done,” said Crane, who has dedicated the last 30 years of his life to youth tennis.

Once upon a time, Crane served as a sports journalist for the New York Post, the defender general of Vermont, and the executive director of the Massachusetts State Ethics Commission.

He has been the head boys’ tennis coach at Latin Academy since 2009, and last season led the Dragons to their first Division 3 semifinal appearance in program history.

This season, the Dragons are trying to repeat that success, and are doing so with players from five Boston high schools (Latin Academy, O’Bryant, Josiah Quincy Upper, East Boston, and New Mission).

Sophomore Mayfre Moreta, a New Mission student, has never crossed paths in the school hallways with his doubles partner, Gio Waterman, who attends Latin Academy, but the pair still managed to rally from a set down to clinch the deciding No. 2 doubles point in last year’s D3 quarterfinals.

“I think [that win] speaks to our identity as a program,” said Waterman. “It’s so nice to play with all these new guys from other city schools. We share that bond of representing the city of Boston.”

Along with the unique co-op structure, Crane runs a no-cut program that carries roughly 35 kids ranging from seventh to 12th grade every year who vary from beginners to experienced tournament players.

“We don’t cut because we want to teach kids from all over the city how to play the game,” said Crane. “We want to give them a sport that they’ll play for the rest of their lives.”

Matteus Washington, a Latin Academy senior, is in his sixth, and final, year with the program. Although Washington has dueled the state’s top players at No. 1 singles this season, he is just as proud that he gets to lead his teammates every day.

“It’s really cool to see how the seventh-graders of this generation look so much like I did in seventh grade,” said Washington, who has posted a 3-3 record this year. “It’s super eye-opening and enriching to be a part of their development.”

Crane recognizes that the team’s makeup is unique and oftentimes difficult to manage.

“Logistically, it’s difficult. The kids are coming from all over the city, and they can’t all show up at the same time because their schools get out at different times,” said Crane.

But above all, Crane is thankful he can give his kids — many of whom come from low-income situations — the chance to play tennis, as well as offer them summer jobs at Tenacity, Sportsmen’s, Franklin Park Tennis Association, and other tennis facilities around the city.

“What motivates me the most is getting to know these kids, building relationships with them, and figuring out how I can be of help to them. I want to help them grow, help them succeed on and off the court, and help them get ready for the rest of their lives.”

▪ Emily Cilley has yet to lose a match as the head coach of the Swampscott girls.

In Cilley’s first year with the program, the Big Blue (4-0) have put last season’s second-round loss to Dover-Sherborn in the rearview mirror.

Key to their success have been sophomore stars Nikki Carr and Ginger Gregoire. Carr has been dominant at first singles, posting a 4-0 record without dropping a set, and Gregoire has been a great option at second singles, logging a 3-1 record and securing the deciding 3-6, 6-1, 6-1 victory in the season opener against Bishop Fenwick.

“They are both very disciplined players who understand the balance between being cautious and being patient,” said Cilley. “Their technical skills are on point, and they aren’t intimidated by the person across from them.”

The Big Blue’s strong start has catapulted them to the top of the Northeastern Conference. They’ll look to continue their unbeaten streak against St. Mary’s next Saturday.

▪ The girls of Central Catholic are off to their best start in program history.

The Raiders boast a 6-0 record after taking down Lowell 5-0 on Saturday morning. The win was their fifth sweep of the season, with the only non-sweep coming in a 4-1 victory over Notre Dame (Tyngsborough).

Morgan Bateman has looked unstoppable at second singles, as she is yet to drop a set, and Ella Asmar has been just as impressive at third singles, posting an undefeated record.

Although Haley Wolters was responsible for the only loss by a Raiders player this season, she has logged impressive victories at first singles, such as a 6-2, 6-3 win against Chelmsford and a 6-1, 6-1 triumph over Lowell.

The Raiders have a chance to extend their winning streak to nine with matches against North Andover, Lowell, and Haverhill on the horizon, before they clash with undefeated Andover on April 30.

title: Why hasn’t Boston built a Vietnamese memorial yet?
text:
Ngọc-Trân Vũ is a Vietnamese artist, cultural organizer, and strategist based in Dorchester who leads the “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” public art initiative.

I came to Boston as the daughter of a Vietnamese refugee family, including a South Vietnamese veteran, who arrived in 1992 through the US Humanitarian Operation Program. My family first resettled in Dorchester’s Neponset-Port Norfolk neighborhood with support from the International Rescue Committee. Over time, the seven of us also lived in Columbia Point and South Boston’s Old Colony Housing Project before eventually finding our way to Fields Corner, the heart of the Vietnamese community in Boston and New England.

Like many in our community, I grew up in the aftermath of war. I inherited stories of rupture, migration, survival, grief, and rebuilding that were not always spoken but were transmitted through gesture, silence, sacrifice, ritual, and love. Those histories shaped how I understand family, community, and what it means to build a life after displacement. They also shape how I understand public memory.

Boston often speaks of being a “city of belonging.” I believe that aspiration matters. But belonging must be felt in the places we shape, the histories we honor, and the stories we choose to make visible on public land.

For all that Vietnamese families have contributed to the city, there is still no permanent public marker in the heart of Boston’s Little Saigon Cultural District that honors the Vietnamese diaspora and the refugee journeys that brought so many families here.

That is why the proposed “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” at Town Field Park in Dorchester matters so deeply right now.

This is not just a public art project. It is an offering. It is a call to remember, to repair, and to root a history in the public landscape of the city we now call home. It is also a chance for Boston to recognize the Vietnamese diaspora not as a footnote but as part of the living fabric of this city, a community whose labor, memory, resilience, and presence have shaped Dorchester across generations.

The absence of such a marker matters.

The year 1975 marked a profound rupture for Vietnamese people around the world. It marked loss, forced displacement, separation, and the beginning of rebuilding under painful conditions. More than 50 years later, that history still lives in our bodies, our homes, our small businesses, our places of worship, our memories, and our intergenerational relationships. In Fields Corner and throughout Dorchester, Vietnamese families have built lives with resilience and care. We have created culture and community even when public recognition has lagged behind.

A memorial at Town Field Park would help change that.

Public memory is never neutral. What a city chooses to mark permanently on public land reveals whose lives are seen, whose histories are valued, and who is recognized as belonging. For immigrant and refugee communities, especially in this political moment, visibility is not symbolic alone. It is deeply civic. It tells our elders that their journeys matter. It tells younger generations that their histories deserve space. And it tells the broader public that Dorchester’s story is incomplete without the Vietnamese community.

Town Field Park is the heart of a neighborhood where our families have built businesses, raised children, organized community life, and sustained cultural traditions over decades. Our story is rooted here. The “1975: A Vietnamese Diaspora Memorial” would be a public site for remembrance, reflection, learning, gathering, and intergenerational connection in the very district where our histories continue to unfold.

This matters not only for Vietnamese families but also for our neighbors in Dorchester and across the city.

A permanent cultural marker would help recognize Boston’s Little Saigon as an arts and cultural destination in a part of Dorchester that is too often overlooked. It would invite residents, students, and visitors to spend time in the district, learn its history, and support local businesses. It would strengthen neighborhood identity, deepen civic pride, and contribute to the kind of place-based cultural vitality that helps communities thrive. This is what happens when public art is community-driven and grounded in real histories. It becomes more than art. It becomes civic infrastructure for belonging.

Over the past three years, community members, coalition partners, artists, small-business supporters, and cultural organizations have helped shape this vision. What is needed now is for the city of Boston to make room for it on public land, yet so far the city has been largely unresponsive.

If Boston truly wants to be a city of belonging, this is the moment to take action.

title: Tracking the celebrities and notables running the 2026 Boston Marathon
text:
Clinton, 46, the daughter of former president Bill Clinton and former secretary of state Hillary Clinton, took on the Boston Marathon for the first time.

When she completed the race, she was greeted by her famous parents at the finish, who gave her a Marathon medal.

Chelsea Clinton is an author, advocate, and the vice chair of the Clinton Foundation, a philanthropic organization aimed at addressing global problems. Clinton has run several marathons and ran as a qualified participant at Boston.

Her finish time was not available.

This was the third time the former Bruins captain and NHL Hall of Famer has taken on Boston.

Chara, 49, made the storied road race his first marathon ever in 2023, then ran it again in 2024. Since, he has run several marathons across the world, and recently became a World Marathon Major Six Star finisher. This year, Chara is running in support of the Thomas E. Smith Foundation, an organization dedicated to advancing comprehensive and compassionate care for people affected by paralysis.

Chara finished in 3:18:00.

The Needham native and trailblazing astronaut fell in love with the Boston Marathon as a child and has run it multiple times, including unofficially as a 17-year-old, and on a treadmill while aboard the International Space Station, where she became the first human to complete a marathon in orbit.

A former Navy captain and longtime runner who now lives in rural Maine, Williams, 60, ran from Hopkinton to Boston more than a year after her space mission unexpectedly stretched from weeks into months. Retired from her nearly three-decade-long career with NASA, Williams recently spoke with the Globe about the race.

“I’m a little slow, but I feel good and am happy to get out there to try it,” she said with a laugh.

Williams completed the journey in 5:52:49.

Herren, 50, a Fall River native and promising basketball star whose addiction to heroin derailed his career with the Celtics, ran with his wife, Heather, to honor 15 years of the addiction recovery nonprofit they founded. He finished in 5:12:13.

The Herren Project was started in 2011 after Herren got sober, and he’s running “to raise money so more people can find recovery, more families can heal, and more stories can come full circle,” the couple said on their fund-raising website.

“It’s a full circle moment for both of us — a celebration of healing, love, and the life we’ve worked so hard to reclaim. It’s also about every person still struggling and every family grieving the loss of a loved one,” they said.

DaRosa, a multi-instrumentalist for the Dropkick Murphys, the popular Boston-bred Celtic punk band, ran this year in support of the Claddagh Fund, a charitable foundation founded by frontman Ken Casey. The 43-year-old told Boston.com that, since getting sober several years ago, running has become a form of meditation that has helped him feel more present and grounded. His one lighthearted goal, DaRosa said, is to beat Oprah’s marathon time. He narrowly eclipsed her 4:29:15 mark at the 2024 Mesa Marathon in Arizona.

DaRosa crossed the finish line in 3:40:32.

Dick and Rick Hoyt were a staple of the Boston Marathon. Between 1980 and 2014, Team Hoyt — the father-son duo — completed 32 of the prestigious races together, with Dick pushing Rick in his wheelchair through the 26.2-mile course and across the finish line. Together, the two became running legends. Rick, a quadriplegic who had cerebral palsy, died in May 2023, two years after his father.

The Hoyt family has remained dedicated to upholding their legacy. Troy Hoyt, one of Dick’s grandsons, has run the past three Marathons in Dick and Rick’s honor. He has raised money for Team Hoyt, part of the Hoyt Foundation, which was formed with the goal of building “the individual character, self-confidence, and self-esteem of America’s young people with disabilities through inclusion in all facets of daily life,” its website says.

Hoyt finished in 4:35:35.

Arenales, an Everett native and last year’s winner of the reality show “Love Island USA,” finished his Boston debut in 4:06:49. While he has run three marathons previously, Arenales, 29, calls Boston his “dream race.”

“I can’t wait. It’s literally a dream come true, what that race means to the city and the state of Mass. I’m Boston Strong till I die,” he said on Instagram recently, noting it will be his third world major. “I just can’t wait until I get that medal around my neck and, just to be able to share that moment with my dad and family and friends.”

Green, 40, is among the most popular running influencers in the Boston area. The Cambridge mom of three injects humor into her clips, which feature quick-cut, rapid-fire monologues that poke fun at the sometimes overly serious attitude with which people approach the sport.

Green finished in 3:50:17.

Linden was back at it again this year.

The two-time Olympian has run the Marathon a dozen times before, including last year, when she placed 17th in her final race as a professional. In 2018, on one of the coldest and most rain-soaked race days in recent memory, Linden became the first American woman to win Boston in more than 30 years.

This time around, Linden, 42, a beloved figure in the running world who has turned to trail running and ultrarunning, is returning to Boston to pace her husband.

She raced just a week after finishing third at the Marathon Des Sables, a six-day, 250-kilometer competition across the Sahara Desert. She also will be taking on the London Marathon.

Linden finished in 2:35:49.

The three-time Olympian and Connecticut native is one of the most accomplished athletes in the history of women’s soccer, and finished in 5:16:32.

Lilly, 54, who holds the world record for the most number of international appearances and last played professionally for the Boston Breakers, ran for fellow soccer legend Mia Hamm’s foundation, which supports families in need of transplants and advances opportunities for women in sports.

The Celtics broadcaster and play-by-play commentator ran Boston — his first-ever marathon — last year and followed up with a 3:28:25 run this year. Carter ran for the Celtics Shamrock Foundation’s Green Runs Deep team, which raised money for the Martin Richard Foundation and Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester’s Fieldhouse+ project, a new athletic and community facility being built in Dorchester, according to his fund-raising website.

Burnett, a meteorologist and weather producer for WCVB, ran Boston for the first time in support of the Special Olympics, which helps provide training and competition opportunities for athletes with disabilities. He clocked in at 5:57:32.

Burfoot, the former editor-in-chief of Runner’s World and 1968 Boston Marathon winner, has competed in the fabled road race many times over the years. Now 79, the running legend returned with a time of 5:11:29.

McGillivray, the longtime race director of the Boston Marathon, ran from Hopkinton to Boston for the 54th time on Monday. This year, he raced alongside three of his children — Max, Luke, and Elle — to support his Finish Strong Foundation, which aims to inspire youth through running, reading, and kindness.

They also ran in honor of Susan Hurley, who participated in numerous Boston Athletic Association events and united athletes as part of her CharityTeams organization. She died of ovarian cancer in November.

“I know that as I run this year, she will be looking down on me providing the same support,” said Max McGillivray, one of Hurley and Dave McGillivray’s two sons, in a recent interview with 7News.

McGillivray finished in 4:46:02.

title: This Boston-made chai tea is sweeping local cafes
text:
Vishal Thapar and Rohini Sen know chai. Combined, the couple estimates they have made about 500,000 cups of the spiced tea in their lives.

However, after emigrating from India, Thapar and Sen noticed the lack of what they considered high-quality chai in the United States. They took matters into their own hands and in 2015 launched Boston Chai Party, selling chai concentrate made from authentic Indian spices.

According to Thapar and Sen, Boston Chai Party is the first East Coast company producing unsweetened chai concentrate without preservatives or additives. In addition to its being sold online, the tea has become a staple in popular Boston-area establishments like Café La Paz, Davis Square Hand Crafted Donuts & Bagels, Goldilox Bagels in Medford, Third Cliff Bakery in Jamaica Plain, and The Mill Cafe in Arlington. Recently, the tea became available at all Flour Bakery locations.

While starting their business, the couple learned that most products in the tea industry come from large international brokers and distributors. As a result, “by the time the tea comes to you, it’s gone through four or five different channels and hands, and most of it is two or three years old,” Thapar explained.

With Boston Chai Party, Thapar and Sen streamlined this process by working directly with tea estates, bypassing the wholesalers. They began to make trips to India to meet with farmers and pluckers, who harvest tea leaves.

They now primarily work with a farm in Assam, India, a location they chose because of their connection to the workers.

“They’re just wonderful, lovely people. The owner of the farm, he takes such good care of them.” said Sen. “It just resonated with us, the environment and the atmosphere and the sense of belonging and the sense of pride that they take in each and every tea leaf that they grow.”

The couple and their children now make regular visits to the farm. Over the course of these trips, Thapar described the workers becoming “part of [their] extended family.”

“It’s a huge motivation for us to run this chai business, to basically go back every year, give them updates, show them how their hard work is translating to actual consumption over here,” said Sen.

Thapar and Sen work to help the Assam community through initiatives like donating feminine hygiene products and distributing supplies to a school that many of the pluckers’ children attend.

While they source their ingredients in India, they make the concentrate itself in Boston. In both places, the couple prioritizes working with businesses and organizations they feel a connection with.

“The center of everything is the relationship[s] that we build as part of this,” said Thapar. “To me, that is more precious than the business itself.”

Using Thapar and Sen’s recipe, the company produces its chai with CommonWealth Kitchen, a nonprofit in Dorchester. It also works with Community Work Services, an organization that helps people find employment opportunities, to fulfill orders.

Even before they launched the company, chai was a big part of the couple’s lives.

“Growing up, our neighbors would come over at the drop of a hat — not appointment based, very spontaneous — just to come have chai,” said Sen. “Chai would signal, ‘OK, put everything aside, time for a break.’”

For the business owners, chai serves as an icebreaker and creates a simple, informal occasion for people to come together. In their own household, Sen and Thapar even use it as a peace offering after arguments.

The couple met in graduate school at the University of Connecticut, and both work in the health care industry doing cancer research. Their medical background taught them about the health benefits of chai, which has been shown to support gut health and boost immunity.

Currently, Thapar and Sen are expanding the business to sell other types of tea, including varieties designed for health benefits like Chamomile Lavender Sleep Support and Honey Lemon Cough & Cold Relief. Since most tea estates specialize in one particular variety, they have begun working with other farms across India to source these new ingredients.

In the future, Thapar and Sen hope to continue expanding their selections and work with tea farmers from other countries like Sri Lanka and Japan.

title: 50 years ago this week, a radical group bombed the Suffolk courthouse in Boston, deepening the city’s turmoil
text:
“It’s inconceivable that somebody would put a bomb in a public place like that,” Narine, 88, said at his Brockton home.

The bombing, which investigators later linked to a broader series of attacks across New England in the months that followed, came at a volatile time in Boston, as the city grappled with racial tensions from school desegregation, economic decline, and deep uncertainty about the future.

Nearly two dozen people were injured in the blast, and while the attack has largely faded into history, for victims such as Narine the consequences have lasted for decades.

The explosion, fueled by at least six sticks of dynamite, ripped apart the courthouse’s second floor, just feet away from where Narine was in line.

“I was close to it . . . too close,” he said, sitting in his living room alongside his wife, Samali Kajubi.

Narine lost his left leg, and his left elbow was shattered so badly it no longer has a joint, he said. He suffered severe burns on his right leg that left deep scars.

Narine was rushed to Massachusetts General Hospital, where he awoke to find his right leg suspended in traction. His other leg was wrapped in bandages that were soaked in blood. A surgeon later told him he only survived the blast because he was in good physical shape.

The explosion knocked down parts of the ceiling, smashed walls and office partitions, and brought down large sections of marble.

In the immediate aftermath, authorities searched for a man who was seen running from the building after leaving a package, but the search was later called off after investigators were given conflicting descriptions of the suspect.

Narine said there was no sign of danger before the blast. He said he later learned that a warning call had been made to the courthouse before the explosion, but the building was never fully cleared, a lapse that Robert Allison, a history professor at Suffolk University, said reflected the lack of coordinated security protocols at the time.

The Globe reported that a courthouse operator had answered a telephone call from a woman who warned that a bomb would go off in 20 minutes. Allison said courthouse officials struggled to determine how seriously to take the threat, or how to respond, and did not order a full evacuation.

“Today, there would be a way of tracking where the phone call was made and who made it,” Allison said. “You couldn’t do that then.”

Court officials believed that if there were a bomb, it would be on the upper floors near a courtroom, and people on those levels were warned of the threat, according to Allison. But people on the lower levels were not notified.

“There was much less of a coordinated response,” he said. “These are things we learn through painful experience.”

Narine said there was no indication of a threat when he entered the courthouse and bounded up the steps to the second floor.

“One or two phone calls had been made, but nobody took the opportunity to say, ‘No, you can’t come in,’ ” he said.

Boston in the mid-1970s was a different city than it is today. Still reeling from the turmoil of court-ordered school desegregation and years of economic stagnation, the city “hadn’t yet figured out what it was going to do next,” Allison said.

The bombing happened just a day before a planned “March for Peace,” part of a broader effort by Mayor Kevin White to mark the nation’s bicentennial and project a sense of unity and renewal.

But the courthouse attack was only the beginning.

In the weeks that followed, radical groups launched a series of attacks across New England against symbols of authority, violence that investigators later connected to the courthouse bombing.

Explosions hit a power facility in Maine in May, and another courthouse in Lowell was bombed in June, injuring a custodian. On a single day in early July, bombs struck an Eastern Airlines plane at Logan Airport, a National Guard armory in Dorchester, and a courthouse in Newburyport. A post office in Seabrook, N.H., was also hit.

Over time, investigators focused on a group that included three figures who were allegedly tied to a radical underground network called the Sam Melville/Jonathan Jackson Unit, later to be known as United Freedom Front. The group allegedly carried out bombings and robberies along the East Coast in the 1970s and early 1980s.

“There was a proliferation of these left-wing groups that wanted to overthrow the government, and they didn’t have a whole lot of coordination among them,” Allison said.

For years, no arrests were made in the courthouse bombing. But more than a decade later, federal authorities launched a sweeping prosecution that charged the three with seditious conspiracy and racketeering tied to a string of bombings, including the attack on the courthouse.

The federal trial in Springfield lasted months, becoming the longest and most expensive trial in state history, the Globe reported. It seemed like a long-awaited chance for justice, but the jury was unable to reach a verdict, and a mistrial was declared in November 1989.

Prosecutors considered trying the case again, according to Globe reports from the time, but the defendants were already serving lengthy federal sentences for other bombings. A retrial would be costly and, in the government’s view, unlikely to change the outcome in a meaningful way.

The lack of a resolution is one reason the bombing has faded from modern memory, Allison said.

“You really can’t write history until you know the end,” Allison said.

Narine tried to find justice another way.

A jury found that courthouse officials had been negligent in their response to the threat and awarded Narine $1.5 million. But the state appealed and the award was overturned, apparently because Narine had not established which government entity at the city, state, or federal level was ultimately responsible.

“The court found that there was negligence,” he recalled. “But who was responsible for negligence? I didn’t prove that.”

Narine turned to state politicians for help, and at one point he was offered $100,000 by the Legislature, he said. But he refused, believing it did not properly compensate him for his loss.

The bombing changed the course of Narine’s life but didn’t diminish his ambition. At the time, he was attending Roxbury Community College at night while working days at Tufts University. He finished his degree and later continued his education at Boston University, where he studied creative writing and discovered a love for writing stories. He published a couple of books and built a life around reading and creativity.

Narine learned to walk with a prosthetic, but has faced chronic pain since the attack. He raised a family and has grandchildren now. He still drives; a few years ago he drove alone from Massachusetts to Philadelphia to visit a dying friend.

He said that he rarely thinks about the bombing, and that he “didn’t sustain anger over it.”

But Narine remains frustrated that what happened to him and others in the courthouse that day was never fully explained and over time largely forgotten.

“I lost my leg for no good reason,” he said. “Changed my life, absolutely, with a lot of pain behind it.”

Emily Sweeney and Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Boston teenagers sentenced in Dorchester shooting that killed father, injured son
text:
Two Boston men were sentenced to serve 18 to 22 years in state prison for a 2024 shooting in Dorchester that killed a man and injured his son, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Wednesday.

Manuel Guerrero, 19 and Luis Perez, 18, pleaded guilty to manslaughter, armed assault to murder, and home invasion on Tuesday ahead of their trial, which was scheduled to begin next week, prosecutors said in a statement.

Both teenagers were charged with shooting the father and son though it is unclear who actually fired the shots.

On August 12, 2024, Guerrero and Perez were seen on surveillance video getting out of a Kia Forte at the intersection of Trent and Clarkson streets, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said Guerrero and Perez walked up to the third floor of a home on Trent Street and knocked on the door. Leudis Concepcion, 20, opened the door, saw the two masked men with guns, and quickly closed it.

Prosecutors allege that one of the men fired two shots through the door, striking Concepcion in the arm.

Hearing the shots from outside, Concepcion’s father, Leudis Mejia Sanchez, 49, ran up the stairs as Guerrero and Perez ran down, and was shot in the chest at close range, prosecutors said.

Guerrero and Perez ran back to the Kia and drove to Inwood Street, where they got out and walked toward Geneva Avenue, prosecutors said. They were caught on video without their masks, leading investigators to identify them, according to prosecutors.

A few days later, the Kia was found in a Zipcar parking space. Police traced the men’s location through GPS information from the rental car and a GPS monitoring bracelet Perez was wearing for an unrelated armed robbery, prosecutors said.

“The combination of surveillance technology and strong investigative work led to the identification and arrest of these defendants and their eventual confession,” Hayden said. “I extend my deepest sympathies to the family and friends of Leudis Mejia Sanchez, whose last act in life was a valiant effort to help his son.”

In court on Tuesday, Mejia Sanchez’s family remembered him for his “kindness and spirit,” prosecutors said. They described him as a “community leader, a person who touched countless lives with selflessness, always prioritizing others.”

Hannah Goeke can be reached at hannah.goeke@globe.com.

title: Parking fees? Congestion pricing? Mayor Wu’s new climate plan will study ways to discourage driving into Boston.
text:
Wu, who ran as a champion for climate issues, faced criticism early in her tenure for not moving faster on climate policy, and did not release a climate plan until her second term. Wu allies said Monday the new plan delivers the comprehensive agenda they had been waiting for, and lays out a clear path to achieving the city’s long-held emissions targets.

“We need to do more than just envision,” Wu said at a news conference, standing before a view of the city from the East Boston Waterfront. “We are taking action.”

The city plans to achieve these cuts primarily by curtailing emissions from buildings and transportation, which account for almost all the city’s greenhouse gas emissions. As the city implements BERDO — an ordinance that requires large buildings to reduce their emissions — officials said they will expand programs supporting building owners as they come into compliance. To reduce emissions from smaller buildings, the city will convene a task force to decarbonize restaurants and consider expanding a program that helps residents switch to electric stoves.

On transportation, the city wants to shift Bostonians away from driving toward walking, biking, and public transportation, while increasing the share of electric cars to about 20 percent of all vehicles. The city will expand electric vehicle charging stations in municipal lots and curbside locations with the goal of ensuring every resident is within a five-minute walk of a station by 2030.

Officials also plan to secure permanent funding for three existing fare-free bus routes and study parking fees, tolls, and congestion charges to dissuade private vehicle trips.

While Wu’s plan offers few specifics, she is all but certain to face resistance to any proposal for congestion pricing or increased fees.

“The economy of Boston is struggling,” said city Councilor Ed Flynn. “Now is not the time for an expensive expansion of city regulations.”

In particular, charging drivers more to use the roads has long been a hard sell in Massachusetts. In 2024, former state transportation secretary Monica Tibbits-Nutt caused an uproar when she mentioned the possibility of tolling vehicles at the state’s borders. Governor Maura Healey promptly walked back the idea and rebuked the secretary for a “very poor choice of words.”

While the plan suggests further study, some said the city should take stronger steps.

Joan Fitzgerald, a Northeastern University public policy and urban affairs professor, noted that Boston has struggled to reduce its transportation emissions. Though she supports congestion pricing, she said the measure would likely face political headwinds and require state approval.

“The city should start enforcing actions that make the things that they have, such as the bus rapid transit, work better,” she said.

The plan also includes previously announced initiatives such as studying the feasibility of harnessing thermal energy from the Boston Harbor and the Charles and Mystic rivers. And the city intends to join a FEMA program that officials say will reduce flood insurance premiums.

Officials said Monday they believe this plan will put Boston on track to reach its 2030 target of cutting emissions in half — an encouraging, and perhaps unexpected, finding given the dismantling of federal climate policy under the Trump administration. In 2022, NU researchers, including Fitzgerald, concluded that the end-of-decade emissions goal was out of reach, barring a dramatic pivot from the city and other leaders.

City climate officials on Monday, though, projected a more optimistic tone. Since 2005, Boston has already reduced its emissions by about 20 percent, the report said. Officials said if they successfully implement existing policies and programs, the city will slash emissions by about 48 percent by 2030 without adding new requirements.

Not everyone was convinced that Boston is on track for those targets.

“Very similar to the Commonwealth and the nation, I think that we are going to be challenged to hit our goal,” said John Walkey, director of climate justice and waterfront initiatives at GreenRoots, an environmental justice group.

He said the initiatives could face funding challenges, especially if the economy takes a turn for the worse. And, he added, the city’s bureaucracy sometimes needs to “get out of its own way.”

Brian Swett, Boston’s chief climate officer, acknowledged implementing existing initiatives successfully will be “a big lift.”

The city has already taken most of the easy steps to decarbonize, Wu said.

“The first steps are the easiest ones, and then every additional percentage towards the end gets harder and harder and harder to do,” she said.

The plan also maps out a strategy for Boston to combat the accelerating impacts of climate change on residents, including worsening heat waves, heavy downpours, and coastal flooding. These impacts aren’t felt equally across the city, officials noted, disproportionately burdening the most vulnerable communities.

By 2030, the city is targeting a 25 percent reduction in heat-related emergency room visits during heat waves. Wu said she will advocate for the state to set a “maximum indoor temperature” during heat emergencies, including preventing utilities from disconnecting customers during periods of extreme heat. To assess how best to combat flooding of basement units, the city has launched a pilot program in Dorchester.

Wu was elected in 2021 on a promise to deliver Boston a “Green New Deal,” a proposal to decarbonize while boosting economic opportunity and combatting inequities. Her campaign plan, from before her first bid for mayor, set far more ambitious targets: zeroing out municipal emissions by 2024 and powering Boston fully on renewables by 2030.

When asked about those earlier ambitious targets, Swett said the city had sought to set goals that are “both ambitious but achievable.”

“There are tweaks to goals over time based on things that may be outside of our control,” he said.

Nonetheless, some climate activists praised the plan as ambitious and credited the mayor for her leadership. They said Boston needed an actionable plan to meet its goals, not additional future targets.

Larry Chretien, executive director of the Green Energy Consumers Alliance, a climate nonprofit, said Wu’s plan creates opportunities for Boston to put “put points on the board,” and keeps the door open for more ambitious targets in the future.

“She’s not backing away from climate commitments,” he said of the mayor.

Lindsey Butler, the executive director of the Boston Green Ribbon Commission, said at the news conference, “At a time when so many leaders have failed us on climate, we continue to be pushed forward.”

title: Domestic violence calls for lifesaving solutions
text:
As Renée Graham highlighted in her column “The most deadly place for women and children: a family home” (Opinion, April 22), domestic violence is unfortunately all too prevalent. This is why domestic violence programs are integral to our public safety. They provide not just mental health counseling and support services but also practical safety planning as well. Advocates help survivors develop an exit plan that, for many, can be lifesaving. They work with survivors to secure housing, gather documents, connect with support, and prepare to take legal action.

As Safiyah Riddle and Corey Williams of the Associated Press noted in a news report in the same edition (“Series of fatal cases spur calls for action,” Page A2), certain communities are disproportionately affected by this violence. This is why investments in programs that are imbedded in a community, have the trust of local residents, and can provide culturally specific services are essential to supporting victims and survivors of domestic violence.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

The Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance administers federal dollars to programs that provide free, direct services to crime victims. These include domestic violence organizations, sexual assault programs, and homicide bereavement programs. Due to federal funding shortfalls, programs are receiving, on average, a 35 percent reduction in funding beginning July 1.

These cuts will decimate our victim service infrastructure in Massachusetts, with programs already planning layoffs as a result of the cuts. Access to lifesaving services is on the line.

State legislators have an opportunity to fix this. As the Massachusetts House of Representatives is set to debate the state budget, we urge lawmakers to include the line item Targeting Resources for Underserved Survivors of Trauma, or TRUST Line. This $13.8 million investment would mitigate grant cuts and ensure that programs would be able to continue providing services without interruption.

Liam Lowney

Executive director

Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance

Boston

MOVA is an independent state agency governed by the Victim and Witness Assistance Board.

There’s an important issue that many might have overlooked in coverage of the deadly domestic violence cases involving Black mothers in Virginia and Louisiana: The traditional way many people and policy makers address domestic violence may not work for Black women, in part because it fails to recognize their history with and distrust of law enforcement and their desire to heal their entire family (“Series of fatal cases spur calls for action”).

Black survivors want options that do not include incarceration or prosecution. They have seen lives destroyed by responses involving criminal-legal systems that don’t fix the problem or address the source of the abuse but, rather, perpetuate a 400-year cycle of state violence against Black bodies.

In Massachusetts, Black survivors experience a severe lack of culturally specific services and responses. The Massachusetts Women of Color Network’s Keeping Black Women Alive project, in its 2021 report, has identified alternative responses to systems within harm-reduction models that effectively meet the emergent needs of Black survivors of domestic and sexual violence.

Survivors need to see that support exists in culturally aware environments, with people who look like them and understand what they have been through.

Deborah Collins

President and CEO

Brookview House

Dorchester Center

title: How Boston’s fringe theater companies are making it work
text:
“But there’s something thrilling about the live communal experience that is only happening right now,” he says. “There’s an electric charge between artists and the audience that’s exciting to be a part of. That’s what we have to double down on.”

Doubling down on an appealing communal experience starts with stories an artist feels must be told.

For Psych Drama Company, which produces only one or two plays each year, “theater offers a communal place to talk about complex emotions so we don’t act on them,” says Wendy Lippe, Psych’s producing artistic director and a practicing therapist. Psych Drama’s mission is to integrate theater and psychology, encouraging audience members to share their observations during post-show discussions.

“We choose plays that explore the dialectical tensions we live with every day — light and dark, love and hate. They are better tolerated when we hold them collectively,” she says.

Small theater companies also serve as petri dishes for experimentation — allowing playwrights to try out ideas or push the boundaries of the form. By nurturing new work, they invest in the next generation of theater and prevent the art form from getting stale.

“We’re interested in creating new hybrids of theater and performance,” says Charlotte Meehan, cofounder and executive artistic director of Sleeping Weazel, which is known for multimedia performances.

To accomplish this, Meehan says her company works in “increasing iterations, with workshops and cabarets” as the piece develops.

Investing in the development process is also fundamental to Punctuate4 Productions, says president and artistic director Myriam Cyr.

The company’s projects range from historic dramas, including “Saltonstall’s Trial” and “The Abolitionist’s Refrain” to a musical, “Thru Hike,” based on Appalachian Trail adventures, and adaptations of stories by Agatha Christie and Arthur Conan Doyle.

“We like to be incubators for new work, but we’re also committed to seeing these works have a life beyond us,” says Cyr, who as a freelance director and with Punctuate4 Productions collaborates with a wide range of playwrights, theaters, cultural organizations, and international artists willing to participate in the development process. This iterative, collaborative journey is, says Cyr, “an investment in the next generation of theatrical expression, allowing the form to meet the moment.”

Some companies meet the moment by rooting their work in Boston neighborhoods.

Even with a 30-year track record, Company One’s commitment to community and to nurturing new work keeps them producing stories that resonate within those communities.

“Our loyalty to neighborhoods transcends specific spaces,” says Summer L. Williams, associate artistic director and cofounder of the company. “We’ve developed deep partnerships with the City of Boston, the Boston Public Library, and the BCA, and we are thoughtful about looking at who’s left out of the conversation, what issues community leaders are interested in, and then what story is the best fit for a particular venue.”

Small and fringe companies lack anchor venues and move from one available space to another, adding another pressure to their decision making.

“I am grateful to produce at the BCA, and have a ‘summer home’ at Club Café,” says Lauren Elias, founder and producing artistic director of Hub Theatre Company, “but the space dictates the kind of play that will work.”

“I like to balance thought-provoking plays with theatrical Cheetos,” Elias says. “[The late] Spiro Veloudos taught me that you have to earn the audience’s trust. When you do good work, they are more likely to come to something less well known.”

Danielle Fauteux Jacques founded and has served as Chelsea-based Apollinaire Theatre’s artistic director for 30 years, and is currently co-directing “Dido of Idaho” through May 10. Fauteux Jacques says that when they’re considering titles, the question is simple: “Would we want to see it?” But rather than rely on her own taste, Apollinaire invites a group of people currently involved with the theater to suggest play titles, and then meet and talk about them.

“It tends to be about eight to 10 people who meet two, three times a week for six weeks,” she says. “It’s not a fixed group, but can include actors, designers, anyone involved in behind-the-scenes work. Having different minds in the room opens the discussion up to different viewpoints or ways to stage things within the fringe aesthetic.”

Other small and fringe companies have a culturally specific focus, while understanding how to amplify their stories by partnering with other, more established organizations. Front Porch Arts Collective, CHUANG Stage, and Teatro Chelsea each emerged in response to a desire to tell the stories of communities whose voices haven’t been heard.

“Boston doesn’t get enough credit for how diverse it is,” says Maurice Emmanuel Parent, cofounder and producing artistic director at Front Porch, Boston’s only professional Black theater company. “It’s healthy that Boston is now home to three theater companies telling stories about the specific cultural fabric of the community.”

Teatro Chelsea was launched with support from Apollinaire Theatre, which provides performance space, while CHUANG Stage partners with performing and community organizations based on the story.

Hernandez says Teatro Chelsea pays attention to other Latino stories being produced across the country. In addition to mounting their own productions, like the recent “The Beautiful Land I Seek,” the company partnered with Gloucester Stage for “Hombres” and Front Porch for a reading of the musical “Cubamor.”

“Our goal is to produce two full-length shows and the [New Play] Festival each year,” Hernandez says. “We are driven by the stories. The right partners allow us to do more than what we could do on our own.”

Alison Yueming Qu, CHUANG Stage’s executive director, says her company is New England’s first Asian-American theater company to focus on pan-Asian narratives.

“We have our eyes out for bilingual and multilingual stories, and our choice of plays reflects our commitment to producing Asian-American playwrights with a passion for community and locality.”

CHUANG Stage also produces a very intentional roster of events at PAU Arts in Chinatown; last year, it partnered with Company One and Umbrella Stage for “Learning How to Read by Moonlight,” reaching the large Filipino population in Metro West.

“As we grow, we are looking for other neighborhoods where we can produce culturally specific work,” says Qu. “We’d like to reach the Vietnamese community in Dorchester, the Korean community in Allston.

“Every single story has a space it belongs to,” she says. “I find a lot of joy in making those connections.”
