title: After a surge of affordable housing development in Boston, the money that helps pay for it all is drying up
text:
“The city relies on commercial development to provide funding for affordable housing,” said Matthew Kiefer, a land-use attorney for Goulston & Storrs in Boston who frequently represents developers. “The effect of the recent fall-off in construction is that there is just going to be less money available for affordable housing.”

Construction of both commercial development and market-rate housing — two of the top funders of new subsidized units in Boston —has slowed to a crawl as broad shifts in the economy have made it more difficult for developers to build. Few new office and lab projects, which provide millions of dollars in payments to the city’s affordable housing fund, filed plans with the city in 2024 and 2025. And while the city has shoveled money from the COVID-era American Rescue Plan Act funding into subsidized housing projects, that money, too, is running out.

City housing officials are bracing for the possibility that they will be able to fund fewer affordable housing projects in the years to come if the development slowdown persists, dimming one remaining bright spot of Boston’s construction industry.

Development has long been a key economic engine for Boston. The city boasts one of the most valuable markets for new construction in the US, and officials over the years have increasingly sought to take advantage of that status, charging fees to builders to help finance other policy priorities.

That includes affordable housing.

The city’s inclusionary development policy, for example, requires developers of market-rate housing to set aside 20 percent of the units in their projects at affordable rents, or pay a sum equivalent to what it would cost to build that many affordable units.

And Boston’s “linkage” policy requires commercial developers to pay a fixed amount based on the size of their project. A 200,000-square-foot lab project, for instance, would owe the city a little more than $4.6 million in linkage payments.

Those two policies will account for around one-third of the city’s nearly $95 million in funding for subsidized development and preservation in the 2026 fiscal year, and around 42 percent of that budget in the 2027 fiscal year.

Tying so much funding to affordable housing construction can be a highly effective strategy in times of plenty.

In 2022, at the peak of a lab building boom, developers in Boston filed applications for dozens of new projects that were due to pay the city an estimated $61.4 million.

In 2024, buoyed by that surge, the Neighborhood Housing Trust — the city’s fund for affordable housing development — received around $17 million in payments.

All of that money — as well as the $91 million in COVID recovery funding Mayor Michelle Wu allocated for new affordable housing development — helped pay for one of the most prosperous periods for affordable housing development in recent memory.

Between 2021 and 2023, the city permitted 3,488 new income-restricted units, the most in any three-year period since at least the late 1990s. And more is on the way, with some 4,504 units in the pipeline as of December 2025.

“It has been a wonderful couple of years,” said Sheila Dillon, the city’s housing chief. “We have been able to fund a lot of really excellent projects that our residents need.”

In 2023, the city looked to lean even more on commercial development for affordable housing money, raising the proportion of affordable units required in market-rate developments under the IDP from 13 percent to 20 percent, and doubling linkage payment requirements for lab projects.

The idea was to tap into the prosperity that developers were enjoying. When building boomed in Boston, city officials said, money should be set aside to help build homes for low- and middle-income residents, not just those who work in fancy new lab buildings or who could afford luxury condos.

“Developers are making money from these periods of economic prosperity, and it makes sense that that prosperity should be used to benefit people who need it,” said Kiefer. “As a taxpayer in the city of Boston, I would much rather you tap development to fund affordable housing than raise my taxes.”

But those policies “effectively tie this essential public benefit to the health of the macroeconomy,” Kiefer said.

While the city still received around $16 million in 2025 in payments from projects permitted in previous years, payments to the Neighborhood Housing Trust are expected to decline in 2026, as new housing and commercial development in the city have fallen to their lowest level in recent memory.

Only a few projects with linkage obligations filed applications with the city in 2024 and 2025, with $3.6 million in payments expected from projects filed in 2024, and just $2.1 million from those filed in 2025, a drop off of over $59 million compared to 2022.

The decline comes at a time when affordable developers need more money from local and state governments than ever to get their projects off the ground.

Generally, affordable housing development is an expensive endeavor — even more so than market-rate construction — because projects have to meet rigorous energy, accessibility, and design standards. These days, developers of those projects are also grappling with the same factors that have driven the market-rate development decline lately, namely the rising cost of materials.

“There is a lot that goes into building affordable housing,” said Emily Haber, CEO of the Massachusetts Association of Community Development Corporations. “It’s a balance because you want to make the best use of limited funds, but you want to make sure you’re building something high quality with that funding that is going to last for decades.”

The West End library project, for instance, was projected to cost more than $835,000 per unit when it was first proposed in 2023, without factoring in the cost of building the library on the bottom floors. Those costs have since gone up.

Meanwhile, competition is increasing, because some developers who are struggling to finance their market-rate housing projects are these days considering using subsidies to make their projects work. In Dorchester, Samuels & Associates rearranged the two-building second phase of its nearly 500-unit mixed-use DOT Block project. Both buildings were initially planned to be market-rate with a small number of affordable units, but the developer instead made a deal with the city to make one building entirely market-rate to make it easier to finance, and the other entirely affordable so it could tap federal, state, and city subsidies.

While affordable developments utilize a mix of subsidies from the local, state, and federal governments, Boston’s network of small nonprofit developers that build many of the city’s neighborhood-level projects leans hard on city money.

After receiving money from the state, Fenway Forward, a community development corporation in Boston’s Fenway neighborhood, still needed roughly $3 million from the city to break ground and begin building 24 homes for low-income families on the site of a vacant commercial building on Queensberry Street last year.

“When you’re building 24 units of deeply subsidized housing . . . it is expensive and complicated . . . because of the discounted rents,” said Suneeth John, Fenway Forward’s deputy director and head of real estate. “Without both the city and the state contributing, we don’t have a project.”

title: R.I. judge dismisses lawsuit to block ‘Ghost Hunters’ star from purchasing ‘Conjuring’ house
text:
In court on Wednesday afternoon, Signore granted the motion filed by Hawes, finding in part that Greenhalgh did not have legal standing in the case. Signore dismissed the lawsuit without prejudice.

“This is a process that we shouldn’t have had to go through to close on this property,” Hawes said in an interview after the hearing. “We should have been able to close on Dec. 5, but instead of getting a payoff total, we got hit with lawsuits. And it’s just ridiculous, and I’m happy that the Rhode Island court system has seen through it.”

Michael Resnick, an attorney representing Greenhalgh, who was not in court on Wednesday, said, “The case is still alive.” Resnick said Greenhalgh is “actively seeking” to be appointed as a guardian of Nuñez, of Dorchester, Mass., in Suffolk Probate and Family Court in Boston.

“If that happens, the case is going to be even more alive,” Resnick said.

Signore also granted Hawes’s real estate attorney, Jonathan Lynch, and the firm that employs him, Percy Law Group, a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

Greenhalgh had also filed a motion to dismiss a countersuit filed by Hawes. Signore dismissed some of the counterclaims, but allowed others to continue.

Nuñez, who was also not in court, did not immediately return a request for comment. Julia Demay, who was named as a defendant in the case, was not present at the courthouse and had no attorney listed.

The lawsuit was filed on Dec. 5, 2025, and argued Nuñez had been “experiencing serious mental health issues that have impaired her judgment” when she signed a warranty deed and power of attorney agreement to sell the property to Hawes for $1.3 million in October 2025.

The lawsuit said Nuñez has since been committed to at least three hospitals for psychiatric care in Rhode Island and Massachusetts, and that she had been “experiencing and/or operating under various delusions, including but not limited to, that she owns the Property outright and that she is ‘The Savior of Humanity.’”

As the case played out in court, Hawes agreed not to use the documents Nuñez allegedly signed in October to close on the house. His attorney, Nicole M. Labonte, said in January that a notary who notarized them indicated she had not notarized them properly.

Nuñez, in an email included in court filings, denied signing the power of attorney agreement.

Labonte said Wednesday Nuñez signed a deed in December to transfer the property over to Hawes, along with an affidavit of the seller, with a different notary.

Asked when he may try to close on the property, Hawes said he was going to speak with his attorney.

“As of right now, it looks like we can,” Hawes said. “We have the property insured. We’ve been maintaining the property up to this point. So once my attorney tells me what … they think is the next option, then that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”

Just before the house was slated to move to a foreclosure auction in October 2025, Needham Bank sold the underlying mortgage to YouTuber Elton Castee through his Summit & Stone LLC, a corporation formed in Rhode Island in September, property records show.

Last year, Castee, who touts more than 4 million subscribers on his “TFIL (Traveling to every country in A-Z order)" channel on YouTube, along with comedian Matt Rife, purchased the former Connecticut home of paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren, with its vast collection of allegedly haunted objects.

In January, Summit & Stone filed a petition asking the court to place Bale Fire LLC into receivership, a process similar to bankruptcy in state court, citing an outstanding balance on “The Conjuring” house mortgage of approximately $1.2 million. A judge denied the motion in February.

Needham Bank filed a lawsuit in November 2025 seeking to rectify how, after it sold the loan to Summit & Stone, the bank mistakenly discharged the mortgage. The lawsuit, in which Hawes is listed as an interested party, remains pending.

“There’s no court order stopping the closing from being completed,” Labonte said. “The only thing stopping it from being completed is the fact that there’s no specific bank who will accept the money for this mortgage.”

Jonathan Joseph Lucido, an attorney representing Summit & Stone, said he had no comment on Wednesday.

When the house was slated for auction last year, Hawes, at the urging of Andrea Perron — whose family was supposedly haunted in the 1970s at the home — launched a GoFundMe to raise money to try to purchase it.

Hawes has said he is not seeking to make a profit, and the goal is to raise as much money as possible to keep costs down for visitors and to keep the house in the hands of people who want to preserve it, not exploit it.

The fund-raiser had raised more than $330,000 as of Wednesday.

“Thousands of people came together to make this happen,” Hawes said outside the courtroom on Wednesday.

“A lot of people are going to be seeing some inside information, and a lot of the stuff that’s been going on behind the scenes that we haven’t been able to talk about,” he said. “But now, with where we stand, at least in the near future, we’re going to make everything available.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
NEWDAD This Galway trio, who released their second full-length, “After,” last year, makes moody, atmospheric gauze-gaze that spins into thrashy territory at its most intense moments. May 2, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

DRY CLEANING One of the best post-post-punk bands of recent years, this London outfit released “Secret Love,” its stellar third album, in January; vocalist Florence Shaw’s fractured, elliptically melodic poetry is framed by jagged guitars and start-stop rhythms, creating a cracked-mirror vision of pop. May 5, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

FAKEMINK London-based producer and MC Vincenzo Nischal Camille Bhatia has become one of the UK underground hip-hop scene’s breakout stars during his short career; his beats have the homespun intricacy of bedroom pop and the blown-out sonics of rage rap, while his rhymes feel free-associative and swaggering. May 5, 8 p.m. Roadrunner Boston. roadrunnerboston.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

TANYA DONELLY AND CHRIS BROKAW Two Boston vets join forces to venture into old-time music — and I mean really old-time; they’ve just issued a collaborative EP, “The Undone Is Done Again,” wherein they reimagine a handful of medieval madrigals. They’ll be joined by Elizabeth Steen to perform the EP Friday, along with some of their own material. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $35. First Church Congregational, 11 Garden St., Cambridge. 617-876-4275. www.globalartslive.org

KIMON KIRK AND SYD STRAW Boston expat Kirk is in the habit of returning to the area periodically to show us what he’s been up to musically. His latest visit this Friday brings two treats: First, he’ll be previewing an upcoming album, “Bikini Jardine;” second, he and his band will be backing up a set from the fabulous Syd Straw. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $15. Sally O’Brien’s, 335 Somerville Ave., Somerville. 617-666-3589. www.sallyobriensbar.com

LEAH BLEVINS Leah Blevins teamed up with Dan Auerbach to make her new record, “All Dressed Up,” and what resulted was a marvelous collection that mixes straight country (you want country hurt? Try “Lonely”) with timeless country-soul. She kicks off a tour in support of the album in Cambridge next Tuesday. May 5, 8 p.m. $20. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729. www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

HELLBENDER Helmed by saxophonist Jared Sims, the Boston Music Awards 2025 Jazz Artist of the Year, this fiery quintet boasts a compositionally canny and invigoratingly improvisatory spirit that takes the ball from 1970s Miles Davis and runs with it. Featuring guitarists Andrew Stern and Jeffrey Lockhart, keyboardist James Rohr, bassist Jesse Williams, and drummer Randy Wooten. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $30.15-$41.79. Regattabar. regattabarjazz.com

TIGER MOAN BATTLE OF THE BONES Singer and multi-instrumentalist Amy Kucharik and her vintage blues outfit hold a first Sunday residency featuring special guests. This time, it’s a duel between two local trombone talents: Tiger Moan’s own Tim Lewandowski and guest Sara Honeywell. May 3, 7:30 p.m. $20-$25. The Burren Back Room, 247 Elm St., Somerville. burren.com/music

THE EDMAR COLÓN QUARTET The accomplished Puerto Rican saxophonist, pianist, and composer — whose collaborators include Wayne Shorter, Teri Lyne Carrington, and The Boston Pops — fronts a first-rate band comprising keyboardist Maxim Lubarsky, bassist Oscar Stagnaro, and drummer Mark Walker. May 7, 6 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St. longlivebeerworks.com/boston

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA Dima Slobodeniouk leads the BSO in its final Symphony Hall concert of the spring season, featuring the Tanglewood Festival Chorus in John Adams’s majestic “Harmonium” and Beethoven’s beloved Symphony No. 9. April 30-May 3. Symphony Hall. www.bso.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA John de los Santos’s English-language production of Donizetti’s zany rom-com “Daughter of the Regiment” is around for one more weekend; last weekend’s opening proved the ample comedic chops of both the translated book and the excellent cast (standouts: Brenda Rae as Marie and Sandra Piques Eddy as Widow Berkenfeld). It’s well worth your time. Emerson Colonial Theatre. May 1, 7:30 p.m.; May 3, 3 p.m. www.blo.org

BACK BAY CHORALE The chorus’s 50th anniversary season concludes with Orff’s epic “Carmina Burana,” as the long-running community chorus teams up with singers, orchestra, and dancers from Boston Conservatory at Berklee as well as the Boston Children’s Chorus. Stephen Spinelli conducts. May 1, 8 p.m. Symphony Hall. www.bbcboston.org

A.Z. MADONNA

BEETHOVEN Valeriy Pecheykin’s play focuses on 17 crucial scenes from the life of Ludwig van Beethoven, underscoring the composer’s refusal to surrender in the face of his increasing deafness. Performed in Russian with English subtitles, it features live performances of Beethoven’s music and original compositions by Sarah Infini Takagi. Directed by Yana Gladkikh. May 1-10. Arlekin Players Theatre, Needham. 617-942-0022, www.arlekinplayers.com

SOMETHING ROTTEN! The enormous shadow of William Shakespeare (Jared Troilo) hangs over the playwriting and acting efforts of Nick Bottom (Ryan Mardesich) and his brother Nigel (Ohad Ashkenazi) in Elizabethan England. So Nick decides they should focus their efforts on a new genre called a … musical. With music and lyrics by Wayne Kirkpatrick and Karey Kirkpatrick, and a book by Karey Kirkpatrick and John O’Farrell. Directed by Ilana Toeplitz Ranson with musical direction by Katya Stanislavskaya. May 1-June 7. Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, www.lyricstage.com

GEM OF THE OCEAN What the late August Wilson always wanted us to understand is that emancipation is not the same as freedom. That’s a truth experienced firsthand by the characters in Wilson’s “Gem of the Ocean,” several of whom had formerly been enslaved and are now barely getting by in 1904 Pittsburgh. Under the direction of Monica White Ndounou, “Gem of the Ocean” does not disappoint for the most part, though it does suffer from Wilson’s compulsion to add one more digression, one more freewheeling monologue. Featuring Regine Vital as Aunt Ester, a mystical “soul cleanser”; Joshua Lee Robinson as Citizen Barlow, a young man who seeks absolution for ​a death he inadvertently caused in Alabama​; Jonathan Kitt as Solly Two Kings, who helped enslaved people escape on the Underground Railroad after he escaped slavery himself; and Kadahj Bennett as Caesar Wilks, a constable so iron-fisted he makes Inspector Javert of “Les Miserables” look like a dues-paying member of the ACLU. Through May 17. Actors’ Shakespeare Project in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall. 617-241-2200, ActorsShakespeareProject.org

SWEPT AWAY A musical about a 19th-century shipwreck and its aftermath, “Swept Away” is a should-see, maybe even a must-see, for, among other reasons: the variety and sheer energy of the indie-folk music by The Avett Brothers, coupled with the emotional directness of their ardent lyrics. The bravura direction by Jeremy Johnson, who stages scenes of stillness and tumult with equal deftness — the squall/shipwreck scene is a doozy — while smoothly transitioning among the musical’s radical mood shifts. The textured performances by the four principals: Peter DiMaggio as the ragged, haunted Mate; Christopher Chew as the curmudgeonly Captain; Max Connor as Little Brother, in flight from farm life and avid for adventure; and Bishop Levesque as Big Brother, a religious and initially starchy man locked in fraternal combat that conceals a deep love for Little Brother. Through May 23. SpeakEasy Stage Company at Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, speakeasystage.com

DON AUCOIN

BILL T. JONES / ARNIE ZANE COMPANY “History of Collage,” which blended dance with music and spoken word to explore identity, community, and creativity, was the last piece Jones and Zane created together before Zane died in 1988. Last year, Jones remounted the work on members of his current company, and this weekend they bring “Collage Revisited” to Western Mass. as part of an ongoing legacy project. The concert also features “Story/,” set to the music of Franz Schubert. May 1. $20-$75. UMass Fine Arts Center, Amherst. https://arts.umass.edu/performing-arts/events/bill-t-jones-arnie-zane-company-2526

PANTOS PROJECT DANCE Under the direction of Kat Pantos, the company’s annual spring showcase, “without you,” examines the impact of time’s passage as it explores themes of love, loss, and friendship in new works by Carolyn Breton-Pantos and Marissa Masson. In addition to the professional company and the adult collective, called the ensemble, the concert highlights the pre-professional youth troupe MOVERS. May 2. $55. Boston University Dance Theater. www.pantosprojectdance.com

TONY WILLIAMS’ DORCHESTER DANCE FEST The dedicated Williams brings together a variety of artistic talent, including his own City Ballet of Boston, for a celebratory afternoon of music and dance, from ballet and modern to jazz. This free, family-oriented event is designed to highlight the creativity, spirit, and rich diversity of the community and beyond. May 2. Free. The Strand Theatre, Dorchester. www.cityballetofboston.org

BOSTON BALLET SPRING EXPERIENCE This upcoming mixed repertory program puts Boston Ballet’s versatility and artistic depth on full display through three very different works, including the return of principal dancer Lia Cirio’s “After,” featuring a life-size sculpture by John Farrell. Jerome Robbins’s “Dances at a Gathering” weaves together a masterful series of solos, duets, and group sequences set to piano pieces by Frédéric Chopin. William Forsythe’s 1992 “Herman Schmerman,” set to an electronic score by longtime collaborator Thom Willems, pairs the inimitable choreographer’s technical rigor with an edgy playful wit. May 7-17. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

FRAMING NATURE: GARDENS AND IMAGINATION A cross-cultural, collection-wide display of natural lushness to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the MFA’s “Art in Bloom” celebration, this show promises a gamut of garden-forward glory, both flora and fauna. But because I know you’re wondering: There will be Monets, so plan accordingly. Through June 28. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW The Black Arts Movement came to be in a critical time in 1960s and ’70s America as the civil rights movement had given way to more forceful ideas around Black rights. In Boston, those ideas found root in the African American Masters Artist in Residence Program, founded by the firebrand artist and activist Dana Chandler. This show charts the organization’s long evolution through decades of cultural and racial tumult, and its unwavering devotion to the cause of Black representation. Through Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

AMERICAN IMPRESSIONISM In the mid-19th century, the Hudson River School of painters, led by Thomas Cole, adopted the heroic frame of their European Romantic forbears to craft a beatific vision of the American landscape that was often at odds with reality. While Americans fawned over their imagined idylls, Europeans were rushing headlong into Modernism as artists like Edgar Dègas and Claude Monet dropped Impressionism, frank and immediate, like a bomb into polite French establishment painting. It would take a while for the US to catch up, but they did, and with some masters of their own, many of whom you’ll see here: James McNeill Whistler, John Singer Sargent, and Childe Hassam, among others. Through June 7. Yale University Art Gallery, 1111 Chapel St., New Haven. 203-432-0601, https://artgallery.yale.edu/

MURRAY WHYTE

BOSTON UNIVERSITY MASTER OF FINE ARTS PAINTING THESIS EXHIBITION We’ve arrived at the sweet spot in the calendar for discovering new talent. Several MFA thesis exhibitions are open or opening soon. Besides BU right now, see work by artists from Massachusetts College of Art and Design at MassArt x SoWA (460 Harrison Ave.) through May 17. The School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University’s show runs May 5-17 at Aidekman Arts Center, 40 Talbot Ave., Medford. At Faye G., Jo, and James Stone Gallery, 855 Commonwealth Ave., through May 17.www.bu.edu/cfa/news/bu-art-galleries

CATE McQUAID

SAM JAY Now that we have been told aliens are real, former Boston comic Jay feels they are being a bit disrespectful, showing up in Vegas on a Sunday afternoon or at a mall in Miami. “I’m a ’90s kid, that’s not how my aliens roll,” she said a few weeks ago at the Melbourne International Comedy Festival. “This is how my aliens rolled — Iowa, cornfield, 3 a.m. One farmer.”May 2, 7 p.m. $37-$55. The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St.www.thewilbur.com

JOSH OCEAN THOMAS The New York comic says his mother can’t tell when a video is AI, which leads to some interesting conversations. She once called him in a panic, saying, “A man was just eaten on the subway by an octopus!” He said, “No, mom, that’s AI, and she’s like, ‘How do you know?’” May 1-2, 7 p.m., 9 p.m., and 11 p.m. $30. Goofs Comedy Club, 432 McGrath Highway, Somerville. www.goofscomedy.com

CERTIFIED GOLD The Comedy Studio’s signature showcase show features Matt McArthur, Holly Johnston, AJ Hapenny, Harrison Green, and Will Smalley on Friday and Green, Carolyn Riley, Sky Nockels, Zachary Morin, Dan Boulger, and Alex Giampapa on Saturday.May 1-2, 7:15 p.m. $29.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Boston’s next fire commissioner lives in Canton, but ‘will comply’ with city’s residency mandate, officials say
text:
A Boston Fire Department spokesperson told the Globe on Thursday that Marshall, who was born and raised in Dorchester, was referring to his family and community ties when he answered the question of where he lived. The Globe requested an interview with Marshall, but Wu’s office did not make him available.

For decades, the city’s municipal code has required that city workers live in Boston as a condition of their employment, but the rule is often disregarded or only selectively enforced. There are also various exceptions to the rule: State law exempts teachers from the mandate, and many of the city’s union contracts — including those of the fire department and Boston’s largest police union — allow members to move out of the city after 10 years of service.

The code also exempts firefighters who are appointed to senior management positions, subject to the residency rule, if they are promoted from a union-covered role and have already met the 10-year residency requirement. That exemption means Marshall does not appear to have been in violation of the rule in recent years, as he served as one of the fire department’s chiefs of operations.

The residency requirement does apply, however, to the city’s department heads and cabinet chiefs, including the fire commissioner, but allows for a grace period of six months for appointees to move within city limits, according to the city code.

Veronica Yoo, the city’s chief of communications, emphasized that timeline in response to questions from the Globe about Marshall’s residency, though she did not answer questions about when Marshall plans to move.

“Like his two immediate predecessors before him, incoming Commissioner Marshall will comply with the [residency] requirement,” Yoo told the Globe in a statement Thursday.

Marshall is far from the only senior mayoral appointee to face the prospect of moving upon their promotion. Many officials in former mayor Martin J. Walsh’s administration — including former Boston Redevelopment Authority director Brian Golden, top aide Joseph Rull, and former corporation counsel Eugene L. O’Flaherty — kept homes outside the city during their time at City Hall.

Current Fire Commissioner Paul Burke, who was slated to retire from the role Thursday, moved from his home in Norwell to Roslindale when he was appointed to the job in 2022.

The city’s residency requirement has also been the subject of debate as Boston’s cost of living has skyrocketed, with officials questioning whether the rule places too heavy a burden on city workers, particularly those making lower wages. Wu issued hundreds of waivers of the requirement in her first term in a bid to fill chronically vacant, essential positions — including for lifeguard roles at city pools.

Marshall is set to earn an annual salary of $318,000 per year as Boston’s fire commissioner, according to his employment contract.

Public property records show that Marshall purchased a four-bedroom home in Canton in 1993 and, in December 2020, signed a homestead declaration stating that he and his wife live in, or intend to live in, the home as their primary residence.

According to state campaign finance records, Marshall also made two donations to former Suffolk County district attorney Daniel Conley in 2013 and 2015, listing his Canton property as his home address.

Marshall, 58, is listed under a Dorchester zip code in the city’s payroll records from 2025. Boston property records list Marshall’s parents as the owners of a home in Dorchester, and court documents show Marshall and his two siblings inherited the home when his mother died last year. Those court documents, which Marshall signed last summer, list his address as his Canton home.

At the announcement of his appointment, Wu, other elected officials, and many of Marshall’s colleagues praised him for his decades of service to the city, saying he is widely and deeply respected in the department for his leadership.

The city hosted the event at the Berkshire Partners Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club in Dorchester, where Marshall said his two children attend after-school programs.

Marshall first joined the fire department in 1991, before rising through the ranks to become deputy fire chief in 2022.

He was recognized by the department in 1998 for saving several lives during a six-alarm fire, and earned another commendation for rescuing people trapped in a bus in 2013, according to Wu’s office. He also designed and launched the fire department’s cadet program, which aims to recruit young Boston residents.

His appointment as the city’s first Black fire commissioner marks a historic moment for the department, which has long struggled to diversify its ranks and faced years of allegations of sexism and racism.

Andrew Ryan of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Disgusting and beloved: Remembering Boston punk haven The Rat
text:
When he was 16, Richie Parsons, a Dorchester native, flipped through a copy of the Boston Phoenix and spotted an ad for the $8.95 double LP.

Too young to get into the clubs, Parsons bought the record instead. He played it to death, falling through a portal into Boston’s underground.

The bands on the album became Parsons’s “local rock ’n’ roll heroes,” a model for the path that would turn him into one of Boston’s punk rock veterans.

Today, Parsons said, the album functions as a period piece that “really captured the whole scene.” He looks back on the album fondly, crediting it with his first exposure to Boston bands.

Jim Harold, the club’s tough but protective owner, curated the album’s track list, selecting the hardest-working bands. Among them was The Boize, with their song “I Want Sex,” an accurate portrayal of the club’s seedy underbelly.

Another was “Who Needs You,” on which The Real Kids angrily sing about a former lover who has moved on.

“The best thing I ever did was get rid of you,” lead singer John Felice growls into the microphone.

Songs like “At the Rat” and “Boy from Nowhere” name-drop Kenmore Square to enthusiastic screams from the crowd.

At the time, Parsons was working in Filene’s department Store in Downtown Crossing. A co-worker’s boyfriend played in one of The Rat’s bands, and Parsons gathered stories.

“I used to come home and tell my guitar player, ‘I heard about this band and this guy, and they’re playing at this club,’” Parsons said. “It was all the different people from the ‘Live at the Rat’ album.”

On March 16, 1977, The Runaways, the all-female rock band featuring Joan Jett, played their final night at The Rat. An advertisement noted reservations would be held until 8 p.m.

Parsons was desperate to go. Still underage, he called the club and promised he wouldn’t drink. Somehow, it worked.

His English teacher lent him his 35-millimeter camera. Equipped with a roll of slides and a roll of black and whites, Parsons had his first Rat night.

“It was all Boston rock ’n’ roll from there on for me,” Parsons said.

The club itself was a fire hazard. The floors were sticky with beer. The air hung thick with sweat and smoke. The bathrooms were layered with grime. At one point, a urinal was ripped from the wall. Instead of fixing it, men simply used the hole left in the floor.

It was disgusting and beloved.

“That was the charm of it all,” one clubgoer said.

When Kathei Logue, who would later become an influential booking agent for the club, first heard the live album, she was electrified. She remembers playing it at home as her daughter danced to its rhythm.

“I discovered there’s music happening that doesn’t sound like all this stuff I don’t like,” Logue said in an interview. “That wasn’t what was being played on the radio.”

By 1978, she was booking local bands and chasing the newest sounds.

The energy preserved on “Live at the Rat” extended beyond the stage as bands tried and failed to break into the industry, moving without shame.

Across the city in Boston’s long-gone Combat Zone, Elizabeth Brawner danced at the Naked I Cabaret, under the name Kendra Wild. She and another dancer shared an apartment in Kenmore Square, a 2-minute walk from The Rat.

When they weren’t working, they were at the club: dancing, partying, bringing musicians back to their apartment.

“It was the most incredible time of my life,” Brawner said in an interview.

The same recklessness and defiance pulsing through the album’s tracks spilled into Boston’s streets.

Brawner found power in the spandex, leather, and the women who came in to get drunk and find someone to go home with.

“They were outside of the box, didn’t follow the script,” she said. “It was a bubble of creativity.”

The Rathskeller closed in November 1997, after decades of fueling not only punk rockers but lovers of new wave, hardcore, and ska.

In its place now stands Hotel Commonwealth, which pays homage with its Rat Suite. Initially, the hotel hired a specialty firm to locate memorabilia from The Rat.

After six months, the team found nothing, and the suite plan was almost scrapped. Then Henry Santoro, a GBH radio producer and host and an avid member of The Rat community, stepped in.

Santoro secured Willie Alexander’s sticker- and graffiti-covered keyboard that was practically glued to the stage. Any band could play it.

Once word spread that the “godfather of punk” had donated his signature piece, artifacts began pouring in.

“It got to the point where we amassed so much stuff that they had enough [to] switch stuff out,” Santoro said in an interview.

Ken Casey of the Dropkick Murphys donated a signed guitar. Parsons handed over photographs. Dicky Barrett of The Mighty Mighty Bosstones contributed a plaid suit.

Santoro even tracked down the club’s comically ugly 2-foot-tall papier-mache rat, once perched at the end of the bar. An Ohio homeowner had it, and he agreed to sell the sculpture for a few thousand dollars, the only item the hotel paid for.

In 2013, Peter Rinnig, former owner of QRST, a screenprint shop, teamed up with Jim Harold to remaster “Live at the Rat” on CD. They sold around 1,000 copies.

“Somebody was smart enough to roll tape and get these bands to perform,” Santoro said. “It really meant something.”

Nearly five decades since The Rat’s start, longtime rockers remain enthralled. A Facebook group dedicated to The Rathskeller keeps the memories alive, and members scavenge for new scraps of shared histories.

“It was like a home for misfits,” Santoro said. “And we were the misfits.”

title: Emaciated, hypothermic dog rescued in Dorchester prompts MSPCA-Angell investigation
text:
The MSPCA-Angell is asking for the public’s help to learn more about a hypothermic, severely underweight stray dog found in Dorchester in late April.

Animal control officers brought the dog, a Cane Corso mix, to the Angell Animal Medical Center in Boston on April 22.

Veterinarians said the dog, which staff has named Balboa, arrived in critical condition.

“When Balboa first arrived at our emergency room, he was weak and significantly underweight — to the point that his ribs and hip bones were clearly visible,” Dr. Emily Hussey said in a press release on Friday.

The dog’s body temperature was very low, according to veterinarians.

A dog’s normal body temperature ranges from 101 to 102.5 degrees, and hypothermia can set in when that drops below 95 degrees, officials said.

Balboa’s temperature was just 94.4 degrees upon arrival.

“Thankfully, Balboa came to us when he did,” said Mike Keiley, MSPCA-Angell’s vice president of animal protection. “Our veterinary staff were able to begin stabilizing him by providing heat and offering supportive care.”

Now stable, Balboa has been transferred from the medical center’s intensive care unit to the organization’s animal care and adoption facility, where he continues to recover.

Keiley said it will take time for the dog to regain its health, and food must be reintroduced slowly to avoid refeeding syndrome, a potentially dangerous condition caused by rapid intake of nutrition after being malnourished.

Before becoming available for adoption, Balboa will enter foster care so staff can monitor his recovery and understand his behavior in a home environment. He will later return to the shelter for neutering before being placed for adoption.

The organization’s law enforcement officers are working with Boston Animal Control to determine how the dog came to be malnourished and potentially abandoned. The MSPCA-Angell is asking anyone with information about the dog’s background to come forward. Officials also urge pet owners to seek assistance through MSPCA programs.

“There are still a number of unanswered questions about Balboa’s past. It’s possible his former owner was struggling to care for him,” Keiley said. “If that’s the case, we want them — and anyone else facing a difficult time — to know that we’re here to help connect them with resources.”

Aayushi Datta can be reached at aayushi.datta@globe.com.

title: This Nepalese restaurateur is rewriting the rules of Boston hospitality
text:
Rai’s breakthrough came in 2023, when he co-launched Dorchester’s five-star Comfort Kitchen along with his wife, Nyacko Pearl Perry. Together, they now run Pearl & Law Hospitality, striving to create restaurants that feel like extensions of home. Their latest projects are inside Allston’s Atlas Hotel: There’s Ama, serving global comfort food, and the brand-new Foxglove Terrace, a rooftop sanctuary with live music and glittery city views. We talked about his hospitality philosophy, his opinion on Boston diners, and his most-loathed sushi roll.

What appealed to you about opening in a hotel?

We were definitely thinking of opening a second location and were looking for the right partner. Tishman, the developer, actually reached out to us about this project, and it really made sense.

To be candid about opening restaurants, it’s a very heavy undertaking financially. This project made sense to us because it was already built into a hotel. It’s also serving the Harvard Business School community. It’s a built-in economy. On the internal side, we have a very talented team that needed growth in a different capacity, and this felt like the right fit.

How would you describe the new restaurants to a friend?

Ama, in its literal translation, means mother in Nepali. The whole concept is built on motherhood and caregiving. My mother works at Comfort Kitchen as a prep person, and she really sustained [my wife]’s health during pregnancy by making Nepali chicken soup, a recovery soup. It was very deep and meaningful on that level. And we have a lot of female leadership in our company.

In our world, caregiving is usually not really the front and center in our conversations, but it’s a very meaningful act. The whole point is: We should start seeing this industry as a caregiving industry versus just a service industry.

Foxglove is named after a flower. It’s both medicinal and poisonous. It flowers every other year. It just happened to be in our driveway one summer, and we liked it. Foxglove is definitely a younger version of motherhood, the fruit of caregiving: excitement and joy. Our food is focused on local, sustainable seafood. It’s on a rooftop overlooking Cambridge and Boston. Once we get our entertainment license, we’ll have live music.

What inspired you to enter this industry?

I was born and raised in Nepal, and I have family in Cambridge, and they invited me for Thanksgiving, Christmas, summer vacations.

My very first job was working at Darwin’s, which is no longer in operation. I worked in places like Charlie’s Kitchen and Hi-Rise. I liked the culture. It was really young and vibrant.

What was your first impression of Boston?

I gravitate toward walking cities, where everything is close. It really drew me in, more than any other city in the States. And I really felt that people in Boston are straightforward. They will not mince their words. I’m the same way: very straightforward, very kind, and hospitable.

What’s missing from the Boston food scene, and what does Boston do well?

This one is going to be a little spicy.

I like spicy, and salty.

When I travel to hospitality conferences and summits, one thing that I really see that’s missing is people showing up for you. We have so many great restaurants and concepts. When I [say] showing up, you have to be there in person. You’ve got to bring your body there. You cannot just like a post or share with friends. We have to be present, we’ve got to partake, and it can’t be in silos. And Boston is in many ways, just in geography, very segregated, and I think that makes it a little more difficult. For instance, Cambridge and Dorchester: It might as well be South Carolina and New York. But they’re like a mile apart.

I won’t name the restaurant we went to in Connecticut. It’s a James Beard winner. It was good: really good food and service. I feel like Boston has that but does not get the accolades or exposure.

What’s the hang up? What’s going on?

Maybe it’s this story of Boston itself being an old city and stale. It just pulls us back. And I really think our branding for Boston needs a little update. We’ve got such good seafood here, but that’s rarely mentioned.

How do we fix that?

I think it’s a collective effort. When I think of media in general, and now also influencers, social media folks, I think we spend a lot of time just talking about how beautiful this restaurant is … I think it’s a collective effort, talking about what makes Boston unique, and what really puts us out there. How can we compete with South Carolina, New York City, LA? We have our own brand. We have our own uniqueness. We do things well; we have great chefs.

How would you describe Boston customers?

Loyal during summers and not very loyal during winters. You know, this is something that I’ve been studying for a while. It’s the start of May. Now, restaurants are gearing up for patio season. Everyone is going to get their guests in.

There’s something about the winter in New England. I lived in Minnesota for a couple years. I feel like people there have ways to engage even during the harshest of winters. I’m talking about myself, too: I don’t like getting out during the dead of winter, and I think that’s the time restaurants really need support because it’s so slow.

Where do you like to eat when you’re not working?

It’s changed over time, just because now we have a 3½-year-old. It’s: Where can we take our toddler and be OK? We like the Dumpling House in Central Square. They’ve been there forever. My son loves to eat dumplings, rice, and noodles. We love it, too.

We live in Hyde Park, and Exodus Bagels is one place we love. And then we have Midnight Morning, a brunch restaurant space in Roslindale. It’s really dependent on our lifestyle at the moment.

Is there a restaurant that you really miss that no longer exists?

Yes, where Nyacko and I went for our very first date: City Girl in Inman Square. They had really good brunch and pasta. I don’t remember what we ate. Obviously, they had great food, but it’s just the space, the emotions that we had at that time, how they made us feel. It was such a small, intimate space. I love small, intimate spaces: two servers on the floor and three in the kitchen. You can really feel the energy. But I think they’d been running that restaurant for 15 or 16 years, and it’s taxing.

Speaking of taxing, what’s your advice for someone contemplating opening a restaurant?

For someone not in the industry and who wants to open a restaurant: You should work in a restaurant for at least three months. There’s a very romanticized version of what this business is. It’s a lot of hard work, raw emotions, and the industry itself is very fickle. No holidays.

For someone already in the industry, my advice would be to start with something small, like a pop-up that really would test their concept.

What do you like about this business?

I think this really grounds me in many ways. I don’t imagine myself working 9-to-5 in front of a desk. I come across so many people. I get to work with people from all different backgrounds. It really fuels my passion.

I was raised by a community, and that’s where I feel safe. It’s in my DNA. It’s a very natural thing for me to be in a space like this, meeting chefs, farmers, purveyors, all on a single mission of serving friends and family.

What would you eat for your last meal?

That would have to be my mom’s cooking. Rice, pork belly curry, and mustard greens.

Is there any food that you cannot stand?

My wife and I have this joke. Whenever we go to a sushi place, my wife loves California rolls. And if I were to pick any sushi roll, that would be the last one. They just do not vibe with me. There’s something off-putting about California rolls. I’d rather spend money on something different.

Interview was edited and condensed.

title: 10 of the most promising new restaurants for spring
text:
Avra Estiatorio

Nick Tsoulos grew up in coastal Nafpaktos, Greece, fishing with his family and grilling what they caught for dinner. The Avra restaurants he runs with partner Nick Pashalis are inspired by his hometown — loosely. Avra Estiatorio is an export from New York, with branches in Beverly Hills, Dallas, and Miami, and now here in the Lyrik development at the burgeoning intersection of Newbury Street and Mass. Ave. Expect white tablecloths, spiraling stairs, faux olive trees, and fresh seafood — on the grill, in sashimi and ceviche, and on display over ice in the “fish market.” After feasting on oysters and Greek-inspired small plates, choose a whole fish to be grilled and dressed with lemony ladolemono sauce. Boston seems to have an insatiable appetite these days for modern, stylish Greek fare — see: Kaia, Kava, Krasi, and a few that don’t even start with “K” — so there’s an audience here. Is there such a thing as too many? Maybe a good question for the city’s 86,000 steakhouses.

400 Newbury St., Back Bay, Boston, 617-592-8888, www.theavragroup.com/avra-boston

Dalia

The decor is the star at this South Boston stunner from chef Nicholas Dixon and Broadway Restaurant Group (Capri, Prima). No detail has been overlooked, from the retractable glass ceiling in the dining room to the gallery of pet portraits in the fireside lounge. But the heart of this Spanish restaurant is the open kitchen, where a team of chefs cooks octopus tendrils and wagyu beef over live flames. If you can get a reservation at all right now, aim for a seat overlooking the show, where you can sip sherry and sangria while gobbling potato chips with jamon, garlicky shrimp, mini burgers, and hamachi crudo. If Dalia is all about Being Here, the food is a fine supporting player.

429 West Broadway, South Boston, 617-752-0429, www.daliaboston.com

Foxglove Terrace

Earlier this year, Pearl & Law Hospitality Group — behind Comfort Kitchen in Dorchester — began to grow, opening Ama at the Atlas Hotel in Allston. Now they’ve found a way to top it, literally, with Foxglove Terrace, a rooftop cocktail bar open Wednesday through Sunday. Exit the elevator on the 16th floor and find yourself in a space with panoramic views, works by contemporary artists, and dishes and drinks that draw from world influences. It’s open now, so the secret is out, but Pearl & Law has tried to protect its sky-high baby — and you — from the omnipresent, mystery-wrecking gaze of devices. They want this space to be intimate, and visitors to be present with one another. Is this a nice thing we can still have in the year 2026? Please approach with buy-in, for the sake of your experience and ours. We all have to just disconnect and dance, sometimes.

40 Western Ave., Allston, 617-675-8881, Instagram @foxglove.terrace

La Tavernetta

This is the latest chapter in the evolution of chef Douglass Williams, who cooked at Radius and Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and Paris before opening MIDA, first in the South End, then all over town, including East Boston. Wave from its pier to La Tavernetta, Williams’s new wharfside Italian tavern across the way, open 11 a.m. to midnight (1 a.m. Fridays and Saturdays). Find a make-you-a-regular menu with an it’s-an-occasion view: oysters, skewers, wings with caramel-chile sauce, sandwiches like a porchetta Reuben, plus a little pasta and some proteins from the grill with sides. The filling for the house stromboli changes on the regular. There’s plenty of crisp white wine for summer drinking, plus a full cocktail program with low- and no-alcohol options. I don’t know why your spritz comes in a glass shaped like a handbag, but don’t fight it. That patio is going to be the place — or at least a place — this summer.

45 Lewis St., East Boston, 617-600-8922, www.latavernettaeastie.com

Maple & Ash

Find me the market report that says Boston should be the next destination for your schmancy steakhouse. So many of these are opening. Maple & Ash, out of Chicago and into the Seaport, distinguishes itself with live flames: seafood over smoldering coals, wood-fired steaks and chops. Listen, if you’re going all out on steakhouse fare, you might as well go somewhere with caviar, pull-apart Japanese milk buns, fire-roasted seafood towers, ricotta agnolotti with truffles (official menu name: Pillows of Love), and a 45-day dry-aged porterhouse known as The Eisenhower. The $175 four-course “I Don’t Give a F*@k Just Feed Me” menu might be the way to go.

131 Seaport Boulevard, Seaport, Boston, 617-362-8881, www.mapleandash.com

Rosa y Marigold

Before her death in 2023, the great poet Louise Glück was a regular at Somerville Peruvian restaurant Celeste, run by JuanMa Calderón and Maria Rondeau. (A filmmaker and architect, respectively, they are also behind La Royal in Cambridge and Esmeralda in Vermont.) The pair named their new restaurant Rosa y Marigold, after their friend’s final work. Glück would have appreciated its Celeste-like menu, replete with ceviches, causas (potato terrines), whole fried branzino with salsa criolla, and Chinese-Peruvian dishes such as fried rice with seafood. Everything goes well with a frothy purple Newbury Sour, made with Pisco and named for Rosa y Marigold’s location at the Lyrik. The restaurant is also open for brunch and lunch, with live jazz several times a week.

400 Newbury St., Back Bay, Boston, 617-356-3780, www.rosaymarigold.com

Uptown Social

This venue has history. It was legendary soul food restaurant Bob the Chef’s. It was Darryl’s Corner Bar & Kitchen. Now it’s Uptown Social, a continuation of the story, told by partners Nia Grace (Grace by Nia) and Donnell Singleton. The focus is very much still on live music, Southern-style hospitality, and food for the soul. Chef Chelven Randolph turns out a menu of pickled deviled eggs, wood-roasted beets with goat cheese and hot honey, lamb ribs, and pork chops with succotash. Sip a Player’s Club cocktail (pineapple vodka with passionfruit and cava), sit back, and open your ears.

604 Columbus Ave., South End, Boston, 617-506-8111, www.uptownsocialboston.com

Willie’s

Oh, nothing, just a cool little restaurant serving Boston’s favorite foods, pizza and pasta, from the folks behind Somaek, Sushi @ Temple Records, and Zurito (right next door, on Beacon Hill). Chef Jamie Bissonnette is throwing pies — the perfectly pared-back P.C.T. (pizza con tomate, hold the mozz); pepperoni with pink vodka sauce; one topped with ramps, fried egg, and Spanish chorizo. A napa cabbage Caesar, a grinder stuffed with Italian and Spanish meats and cheeses plus cherry peppers, fried chicken with Calabrian chile oil and onion soup mayo, hand-cut spaghetti carbonara with bottarga and yuzu kosho ... It’s the most right-on, Bissonnette-iest Italian menu since, well, his last Italian menu. We are here for it.

20 Charles St., Beacon Hill, Boston, 617-982-6613, www.williesboston.com

The Zebra Room

There’s Yvonne’s, the supper club that’s been a Downtown Crossing scene since 2015. And now there’s the Zebra Room, located beneath Yvonne’s. It’s a steakhouse writ small, with just 10 tables and a bar (in the vein of nearby Bogie’s Place, the not-so-secret steakhouse you enter through the Wig Shop). Request a reservation up to 14 days in advance and cross your fingers for a seat in the very red room, where you will drink ice-cold martinis and feast on Gruyere popovers, tuna carpaccio, salads for the table, prime rib, wagyu steaks, and baked lobster Savannah, a nod to the classic served at Locke-Ober, the historic tenant of this space.

4 Winter Place, Downtown Crossing, Boston, www.zebraroom.com

title: Boston College High School to start enrolling sixth graders in fall 2027
text:
In the fall of 2027, Boston College High School intends to add sixth grade to its offerings at the all boys, Jesuit-run Catholic preparatory school in Dorchester.

The move is meant to “strengthen its approach to student formation by reaching boys earlier in their middle school years,” and to align with the structure of the majority of other districts across Greater Boston, school officials said in a statement Wednesday.

“At BC High, our commitment to cura personalis, the care for the whole person, calls us to meet students earlier in their development,” President Grace Cotter Regan said in the statement. “Beginning in sixth grade allows us to more fully accompany our students and support their formation during one of the most important stages of their growth.”

The expansion builds on the prestigious private school’s Arrupe Division, established in September 2007, to include seventh and eighth grades at the 160-year old school.

The addition of the Arrupe Division “has deepened BC High’s commitment to formation and education at a critical stage of development, helping students grow academically, spiritually, and socially within the Jesuit tradition,” the school’s statement said.

Including sixth graders among the student body is aimed at introducing “habits of reflection, service, and academic curiosity at a formative stage, giving students more time to internalize the school’s Jesuit values,” school officials said.

The shift also is reflective of how a majority of other schools are designed, with middle school beginning in sixth grade, the statement said.

Administrators said that a longer runway leading up to high school grades will help students build stronger academic foundations while reducing the social and academic anxiety that can come with frequent transitions.

“Students will benefit from a more gradual progression into the expectations of high school, along with increased opportunities to form friendships, explore activities and develop confidence in an all-boys environment,” officials said.

The decision comes after more than 18 months of research and “thoughtful reflection,” the statement said.

The Board of Trustees voted in January to create a sixth grade set to open in the Fall of 2027.

“This decision reflects thoughtful planning and a clear understanding of where education is headed,” Board Chair Paul Donato said in the statement. “By expanding to sixth grade, BC High is strengthening its ability to serve young men and ensuring the long-term vitality of our mission.”

Robert Hamblet, head of the school’s Arrupe Division, said “sixth graders are at a pivotal stage of growth, and it’s our responsibility to meet them there with intention and purpose.”

“We are building an environment where boys are supported, known, and encouraged to be themselves — where they can still play, still find joy, and develop a real eagerness to learn,“ Hamblet said in the statement. ”At the same time, we challenge them in ways that are positive and meaningful, because that’s how they grow. This is a critical moment in their development, and it’s a privilege to shape a program that responds to who they are and who they are becoming.”

title: Dorchester man found guilty in 2023 Caribbean parade shooting that injured eight
text:
A Dorchester man who was involved in a gunfight that injured eight people at the 2023 J’Ouvert Caribbean parade, and who later fled to Georgia, was sentenced Thursday to life in prison following two trials, prosecutors said.

Gerald Vick Jr., 33, was convicted by a Suffolk County jury Wednesday on one charge of carrying a machine gun, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Vick was convicted last month on charges of carrying a firearm without a license (second offense), carrying a loaded firearm without a license, and possession of a large capacity feeding device, the statement said.

A second jury convicted Vick on one count of possession of a machine gun on Wednesday.

He was charged as a habitual offender for being convicted of two prior violent crimes, the statement said.

The sentence of life in prison carries the possibility of parole in 15 years, the statement said.

Vick was originally due to stand trial in December 2024. On the night before his trial was to start, Vick removed his GPS monitoring bracelet.

He fled and was apprehended in Georgia six months later, the statement said.

According to the statement, two other men have been charged in the shooting.

Dwayne Francis, 31, of Dorchester, was arrested on several firearm-related charges. He is scheduled for trial on June 1.

Sebastian Monteiro, 22, of Boston, pleaded guilty in October 2024 to several firearm-related charges. He was sentenced to four years in state prison with one year of probation upon release.

On Aug. 26, 2023, police on patrol at the J’Ouvert Caribbean parade saw two groups congregating on opposite sides of Talbot Avenue, officials said.

Francis and Monteiro were part of one group, and Vick was part of the opposing group.

According to officials, Francis was yelling into his phone while staring at Vick’s group and grasping something inside his hoodie.

Shots rang out as officers approached, and eight people were shot. There were no fatalities, according to the statement.

Camille Bugayong can be reached at camille.bugayong@globe.com.

title: Black residents upset at Wu’s policies are directing their ire at a new target: Boston city councilors of color
text:
The tension — and outright political threats — underscored the escalating frustration bubbling up in pockets of the Black community. Among the sore points are the mayor’s push to redevelop White Stadium in Franklin Park, redesign Blue Hill Avenue, block the return of an elected School Committee, and try to relocate the John D. O’Bryant exam school from Roxbury to West Roxbury, which Wu ultimately walked back.

Some prominent Black political activists have long chafed at what they view as Wu trying to sell Black residents on her policies rather than develop initiatives with them from the start.

Wu, in turn, has touted efforts to build collaborative relationships with community leaders and city councilors. And despite those criticisms, she enjoyed deep wells of support in the election last year, easily dispatching challenger Josh Kraft. Although Kraft aggressively courted Black voters, Wu won three out of every four votes in wards 12 and 14, considered the heart of the city’s Black community.

Still, frustrated activists are now going beyond focusing on the mayor, and are bringing pressure on her allies of color on the council, namely Louijeune, Pepén, and Santana, whom they accuse of advancing her agenda without sufficient scrutiny or pushback.

“We want them to be a check on the mayor’s power, and [vote] based on our interests, not hers,” said Rodney Singleton, a Roxbury native and longtime community advocate. The councilors of color, Singleton said, “more than anyone else, should understand our pain.”

For much of the forum, the councilors listened as residents aired their grievances. Exclamations of support or outrage regularly filled the room of some 120 attendees.

Culpepper, the councilor whose district includes Roxbury and parts of Dorchester, Fenway, and the South End, later told the Globe that the frustration Black residents have with elected leaders is valid, and appears widespread.

Candidates “run for office . . . standing for the most vulnerable at the ballot box,” he said. “But then when it comes to the administration and the council floor, [some] buckle.”

Three of the six councilors of color did not respond to repeated requests for comment for this story. Louijeune declined an interview request. But last fall during the city election cycle, she said councilors still hold the mayor accountable even if they don’t oppose or actively try to undermine her agenda, pointing to changes they made to Wu’s 2025 and 2026 budget proposals.

Louijeune has also at times broken from the Wu-allied bloc of councilors, including voting for a symbolic, nonbinding resolution early last year to halt Wu’s White Stadium project.

Wu’s office defended her record representing Black residents, noting her administration has invested money to support Black businesses, jobs for Black youth, and housing.

In each instance, said Michael Osaghae, a Wu spokesperson, it’s come with “direct input from residents and a comprehensive community engagement process.”

To be sure, like any constituency, Boston’s Black voters are not a monolith, and Wu’s supporters argue that her vocal group of critics does not necessarily represent the opinions of the majority of Black voters.

State Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who backs both the mayor’s Blue Hill Avenue and White Stadium redevelopments, said he believes working with Wu — particularly in cases when the votes aren’t there on the council to overrule her — is a more effective way for councilors to deliver results.

“Holding the mayor accountable cannot simply just be for show,” Holmes said. He said elected officials, the councilors included, ultimately have to listen to all their constituents, not just the naysayers. “I wouldn’t want my city councilor standing up just to be obstructionist.”

Still, many Black residents say they are still upset Wu vetoed a bill that would have converted the appointed School Committee to an elected one, despite overwhelming approval by voters in 2021 for the change. They also saw Wu’s proposal to move the O’Bryant, the city’s most diverse exam school, to the mostly white neighborhood of West Roxbury as a critical misstep, one Wu later reversed in response to intense backlash.

Several influential Black leaders also remain adamantly opposed to Wu’s effort to redevelop Boston Public Schools’ White Stadium in partnership with a professional women’s soccer team. And Black residents continue to be split on the $160-plus-million plan to overhaul Blue Hill Avenue, because the federal and state funds backing the project are contingent on the design including a controversial center-running bus lane.

Most recently, Wu sparked an uproar in the Black community when her administration announced its plans to cancel a long-stalled but community-backed lab and affordable housing project on a large plot of land in Roxbury known as P3. Instead, she proposed using the site as a potential location for a new Madison Park Technical High School.

But developments at the start of the year particularly rankled Black leaders. Those who spoke to the Globe all pointed to the vote for president of the City Council in January as a key motivating factor to mobilize to hold councilors’ feet to the fire.

The morning of the vote, former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, a leader of the coalition seeking to hold the councilors accountable, said she was sure Worrell would be the next council president, which would make him just the second Black man ever to hold the title. Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, the front-runner who had claimed she had the votes for weeks, unexpectedly dropped out the night before — after three of her supporters defected to Worrell, who then became the only candidate still in the race.

Worrell, whose district includes parts of Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roslindale, had pitched himself as a leader “independent” of the mayor, and built a coalition of support that included her most outspoken antagonists on the council. He is considered well-respected by his peers for his prior leadership of the council’s budget-making committee.

Instead, a white woman,Councilor Liz Breadon narrowly emerged as president after two Wu-allied councilors convinced her to run on the eve of the vote. Three councilors of color — Louijeune, Pepén, and Santana — backed her over Worrell.

“It was a community-wide slap in the face,” Wilkerson said, likening it to a public humiliation of a Black man and the many Black residents who were excited to see him in the leadership position. “I don’t think that the councilors who didn’t support him understood the concern, the anger about what happened.”

Worrell did not respond to requests for comment.

The politicking for the presidency typically happens behind closed doors and well in advance of the vote. But it was unusually public, last minute, and messy this year, and left some councilors frustrated and surprised by the outcome.

“It felt like it was rigged from the get-go, so I was happy to see the pushback from [the] community,” Mejia said. “It was a missed opportunity to really validate Black leadership in Boston.”

Roughly two months later, Wilkerson organized a private meeting in March with five of the six councilors of color — Pepén did not attend — and roughly 30 Black community advocates, to demand the elected officials explain their decision.

Michael Curry, chief executive of the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers, moderated the closed-door talk, and said the councilors’ responses varied: Some struggled to answer, while others attributed their choice to internal council politics and relationships, he said.

“The bottom line is . . . there’s an obligation of elected officials to meet people where they are and address their concerns,” Curry said. “And if they’re making a decision that is adverse to the interests of their constituents, they’ve got to be able to respond and explain why.”

But he also credited the councilors for being willing to face criticism, both at the private gathering in March and at the public forum weeks later, where they endured more than 90 minutes of scrutiny and confrontation.

“What they got in both of those meetings was raw, unfiltered, passionate feedback,“ Curry said. ”Hopefully they adjust their approach to getting feedback based on those conversations.”

title: This Boston writer’s love of twisty tales and edgy characters began in Dorchester
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Even back when he was growing up in the Ashmont section of Dorchester, Patrick Radden Keefe was thinking about whose stories get told — and whose don’t.

When he was 16 years old, in the Milton Academy student newspaper, he wrote about the death of a groundskeeper that he felt others had ignored.

“We didn’t act as though a member of our community had died,” Keefe told me. The murdered man was from Keefe’s own neighborhood.

“Those kinds of contrasts probably imprinted themselves on some level in my DNA.”

The stories he tells

There’s a similar dynamic at play in his latest best-seller “London Falling,” about a 19-year-old who lived a double life, posing as a Russian oligarch’s multimillionaire son to shoot up the city’s social ladder.

Keefe came to the Globe offices to talk to me on the Say More podcast. When I asked him about his writing influences, he said he was transformed by a 1995 New Yorker essay called “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Black Man” by Henry Lewis Gates Jr., which was a reflection about race in America during the OJ Simpson trial.

“That was the first time that I got to the end of an article and then went back to the beginning and took it apart,” said Keefe. “I was trying to deconstruct the magic trick and figure out how he did it. That was a piece that really kind of changed my trajectory.”

Bluffing toward danger

Keefe has employed a similar magic in his new book, which starts with the murky, devastating moment in 2019 in which 19-year-old Zac Brettler fell to his death from a luxury apartment building in central London. His body was found washed up on the shores of the Thames, and his family was shocked to learn about his double life, about him lying to just about everyone.

The book unravels those lies and tells a story about how the mega-wealthy operate in the world’s richest cities.

Keefe was surprised the upper-middle-class British Zac flirted with danger by posing as a super-rich foreigner’s son, but it told a profound story about the changing culture of places like London.

“The book is really about reinvention,” said Keefe. “It’s about the way in which the city of London reinvented itself over the last few decades to become the kind of place where a kid who sort of has everything and a lot of opportunities ahead of him would aspire to be the son of a Russian oligarch.”
