title: ‘All that feels very close to home’: How Patrick Radden Keefe’s crime stories took him from Dorchester to Belfast and London
text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the May 7 episode of “Say More.”

Anna Kusmer: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion, I’m Anna Kusmer.

You might know him from his best selling book “Say Nothing,” about The Troubles in Northern Ireland.

Patrick Radden Keefe writes nonfiction page-turners about crime and family secrets.

He’s also known for the book “Empire of Pain,” which takes on the Sackler family and their role in America’s opioid crisis. He’s written countless essays in The New Yorker magazine.

Keefe’s new book starts with the devastating moment a young man, 19-year-old Zac Brettler, falls to his death from a luxury apartment building in London. He is found washed up on the shores of the Thames River, and his family is shocked to learn he’s been living a double life, and lying to just about everyone. The book unravels those lies and tells a story about how the mega-wealthy operate in the world’s richest cities. I should also mention Keefe is from here, he grew up in Dorchester.

Welcome, Patrick, to the Boston Globe studios.

Patrick Radden Keefe: It’s great to be with you.

Kusmer: I want to start by talking about your new book, “London Falling,” and the main character Zac Brettler. How did you first learn about him and decide you wanted to dig into his story?

Keefe: I came to it in a weird way. I was living in London in the summer of 2023. I had written “Say Nothing,” which came out in 2019, and we were turning that book into a limited series, which is now on Hulu. So I was producing the series. I moved my family over to London and I was on set one day. I got to chatting with a stranger, a guy I hadn’t met before. He was a visitor to the set just that day.

I have a tendency as a reporter to start conversations with strangers. Much to my children’s embarrassment, I get in the back of an Uber and start interrogating the driver. I did on this occasion just start chatting with the guy and told him what I did, that I’m a journalist with The New Yorker, that I write these big investigative narrative pieces. And he said, “I might have a story for you.”

Kusmer: So, what did he say?

Keefe: What the guy said was, “There’s a family here in London who I’m very close with, who in 2019 had this tragedy. They lost a child. They lost their son, Zac. He was 19 years old, and he died in mysterious circumstances. He went off the balcony of this luxury apartment building overlooking the Thames, and he died in the river. After he died, his parents, Matthew and Rachelle, made this startling discovery. They learned that unbeknownst to them, their teenage son had been living this double life and that he’d been moving around London at age 18 and 19 pretending that he was the son of a billionaire Russian oligarch, which he wasn’t. And he got mixed up with some pretty dicey people and he wound up dead.”

The guy had basically said that much to me when I knew, if the family would talk to me, this is a story I have to write.

Kusmer: As you say, Zac was this 19-year-old who created this elaborate web of lies. He was in these fancy British prep schools. Can you talk a little bit more about how he got in over his head? What actually happened? What happens between this web of lies and him falling (or jumping) off the balcony?

Keefe: Zac was a fascinating kid because from an early age he was a type that probably a lot of people would recognize. He was sort of a chatty, funny, precocious, zingy little kid. He was the life of the party. He would tell stories. He was almost like a stand-up comic. He could keep people entertained, very at ease in his own skin, good at talking to adults.

Zac found that he was surrounded by these kids at this new school who were the children of oligarchs. They were really wealthy kids who were macho. They had a swagger and drove around in fancy cars. They partied at nice hotels.

Zac was an upper-middle-class kid. This was a kid who was pretty lucky in the grand scheme of things, but compared to these kids, he felt poor. He started initially to tell these stories about his family. He would say, “Oh, we live in a mansion. My father’s an arms dealer. He drives two Range Rovers.”

He would tell these little stories. Then eventually he graduated to bigger lies that he told to adults where he claimed that he was the son of a Russian oligarch, that he was poised to inherit hundreds of millions of dollars.

I think part of the reason for this is that he wanted to get past the velvet rope. He wanted to get into the room where it was happening and he thought, “If I hustle a little and tell a little lie about who I am, it’s amazing. Suddenly these grown-ups are really interested in me. I’m not just some kid.”

He was so good at it. He tricked Russians into thinking he was Russian.

Kusmer: He put on a fake Russian accent and actually tricked Russians.

Keefe: He had a few words here and there of Russian. He was very capable when it came to tricking people about who he was.

Kusmer: How did he end up dead?

Keefe: He ends up meeting these two guys. Initially, he meets a guy named Akbar Shamji. On paper, Akbar was this really impressive guy. He was in his 40s, a very handsome, charming guy. He’d gone to Cambridge University. He had a very posh accent. He came from a wealthy family. He lived in Mayfair, which is a really fancy neighborhood in London. In fact, he lived on Mount Street, which is the fanciest street in Mayfair.

He seemed like an international businessman and he took a shine to Zac. He had a real estate project that he was working on in Lisbon and he was looking for investors. He meets Zac originally thinking this is a kid who could invest some of his family’s money in my real estate project. They start spending a lot of time together. Eventually, Akbar introduces Zac to this other guy named Verinder Sharma, who lives in this fancy building on the Thames. This is the building where Zac dies — a really expensive building, typical of a certain kind of building in London these days where it’s empty most of the time because most of the really expensive units are owned by wealthy foreigners who don’t live there for much of the year. Verinder Sharma seemed like a retired businessman.

But the interesting thing about this story is that Zac wasn’t the only one pretending to be something that he wasn’t. Akbar Shamji, it turns out, actually was a bit of a charlatan and had just declared bankruptcy before he met Zac.

Verinder Sharma, who was playing the part of this guy living out his comfortable retirement, was a gangster. He was a leg breaker. He was a guy who would dangle people off of buildings. He’d been involved in murders. He was better known in the underworld by his nickname, which was “Indian Dave.”

Zac ends up in this apartment with these guys. They had believed that he was this billionaire kid, and it’s basically right around the time that he dies that they start to figure out that maybe he’s not who he was pretending to be.

Kusmer: This is an extremely interesting story about these personalities and people colliding. You didn’t just write an essay about them; you turned it into a whole book. What made this story book-worthy? Can you tell me a little bit about the themes and the bigger dynamics that you dug into?

Keefe: I write for The New Yorker magazine; that’s my day job. I write these long pieces for the magazine. The nice thing about having all the real estate they give me to write long pieces is that most of the time when I finish a piece, I get to the end and I think, “I have said everything you could possibly say about this subject.”

There have been four times in 20 years when I’ve gotten to the end of a piece and thought, “Boy, I just scratched the surface. There’s more to this.”

The book is really about reinvention. It’s about the way in which the city of London reinvented itself over the last few decades to become the kind of place where a kid who sort of has everything and a lot of opportunities ahead of him would aspire to be the son of a Russian oligarch. It’s a weird turn of events, but also about the personal reinvention of people in the city.

There’s Zac, who reinvents himself as Zac Ismailov, this billionaire Russian, but also there’s the story of Zac’s two grandfathers who survived the Holocaust. This is Rachelle’s father and Matthew’s father. Both grandfathers survived the Holocaust. They lost virtually their whole families, and then they arrive in London as teenagers and they have to decide, “Who am I going to be? What’s the life that I’m going to lead now that I’m solo in the world?”

On a deeper level, that’s a metaphor for adolescence in general. This book started out as a mystery, really a thriller, but it became a book about parenting and about grief and about what it’s like to realize as a parent that you might have this fantasy that your child is like clay and you can mold them into the person you want them to be. But the reality is they reach adolescence and they become their own person. Sometimes that person can be a stranger to you, which is what happened with Zac.

My relationship with the Brettlers is ongoing. We launched the book in New York City at the 92nd Street Y a couple of weeks ago and they were in the audience. They came over from England to be there for it. There are things in the book that are uncomfortable for them knowing that stuff is in there, yet they’re supportive of what I’ve done, and I don’t think they regret having placed that trust in me. That means a lot to me.

Kusmer: I think it’s also the radicalness of opening everything in light of the fact that this is a story about obfuscation. On a more macro level, a lot of the obfuscation and lies in this book are about what’s going on in a city like London — mega-wealth out of control. It is everywhere in the world, but particularly in these megacities.

I think the book felt especially salient today because [it raises this question of], “How are the mega-wealthy just so untouchable?”

When I was talking about this book with my husband, Jeffrey Epstein kept coming up as an example of how this class of people just feels so untouchable. Can you talk about some of the themes that felt really of this moment?

Keefe: I think it’s a great observation. When I am writing a book, I don’t want it to feel like an op-ed or an argument. But at the same time, of course, I’m living in this world and I want to write something that feels relevant. Part of the reason I was drawn to this story is that it felt very much like a story of this moment. There were a couple of respects in which that was true.

One is that Zac Brettler was a kid who grew up on Instagram. He had a lot of admiration for people who were really wealthy, but it wasn’t a traditional sense of working hard and slowly accumulating savings. His favorite movie was “The Wolf of Wall Street.” He had an attraction to a certain sort of “hustle bro” who is looking to cut corners and make money by any means necessary.

Kusmer: He didn’t see it as a cautionary tale. He saw it as a manual.

Keefe: He absolutely saw it as that, to a point where when Zac turned 18, he incorporated his own business and named it after the crooked brokerage firm in “The Wolf of Wall Street.” I don’t think he was totally crazy to think that’s how you get ahead today.

Without getting too far off track, you can be a con man and lie reflexively and pretend you’re a success when really you’re a failure, and if you keep faking it till you make it, you can reach the highest levels. People do.

That’s one side of things. But specifically to your question, it’s also a story about the super-rich and the way in which they achieve escape velocity in our culture where they don’t live in any one jurisdiction where they can be held to account. Akbar Shamji is getting chased around the world by creditors, but he basically claims he doesn’t have any assets, even though he lives in a $12 million apartment. It’s not really his because it’s not in his name. All the assets are in trusts and shell corporations.

It turns out the apartment that Zac fell out of, is this mystery apartment where another guy dies a year later. Who owns the apartment? It wasn’t owned by the guy who was living there. It was being loaned to him by another businessman. But that guy also didn’t own it because it was owned by a shell company. And who is the beneficial owner of the shell company? It took me some digging to figure that out, but it turns out it’s a Saudi princess. The whole thing is smoke and mirrors.

Kusmer: And to bring it back to this specific story, it’s the Brettlers in their grief trying to find justice. These smoke and mirrors make it essentially impossible to figure out who is responsible.

Keefe: I think that the Brettlers had a set of expectations when they came into this.

Now I should say, they are well-off, live in a nice neighborhood, they’re white, well-educated and have a ton of connections. And maybe because of all that, they had a set of assumptions about living in a big city like London — if something goes wrong, you call the police and the system will step in to help you. I think they would today say that was a very naïve assumption that they had.

But part of this story is about them learning that the city that they love, the city that they live in, has already made a deal with the devil. When it all goes wrong for them, there’s nobody to call.

Kusmer: So Patrick, you are “OFD.”

Keefe: I am.

Kusmer: Originally from Dorchester.

Keefe: Proudly so.

Kusmer: In one of your essays you actually define OFDs as “proud to be from there, but also proud to have left.” Is that you?

Keefe: I’m not proud to have left. What I was trying to get at in that article — which was about Braintree actually — was how it was full of people who were OFD.

When I encountered people growing up, particularly when I was still living in Dorchester, there was always this little bit of weirdness for people telling you they were originally from Dorchester. I always felt like you’d get a little bit of both. They were proud they were from there, but also proud to have it in their rearview mirror. For me, still living there at the time, it already struck me as a little strange.

Kusmer: You went to Milton Academy. I know some people who went to Milton. I grew up in Brookline, and I’ll say I see it as one of the fanciest schools in the area. When I was putting all these things together, I thought a little bit of Zac in your book going to these fancy prep schools. I’m curious if you had a culture shock going from Dorchester to Milton. It’s actually not geographically that far, but I imagine culturally it was a bit of a jump.

Keefe: No, I mean you’ve put your finger on it. The strangeness was that it was 10 minutes geographically but it was a world away. Those two environments were very different.

Dorchester is a big neighborhood that is diverse in every imaginable way. It was a very different environment from Milton, but I was nevertheless very privileged by the standards of Dorchester. I grew up in a big old Victorian house a block from Ashmont Station.

A guy wrote an article about me in The New York Times a few weeks ago when the book came out and ended up quoting an article I wrote when I was 16 years old for the Milton Academy student newspaper. I think it was 1992 or 1993.

It was about how there was a groundskeeper at Milton Academy who was from Dorchester, and he got shot in Dorchester and killed. The school, it felt to me at the time, kind of moved on. We didn’t act as though a member of our community had died. The oddness was that he’s from this neighborhood 10 minutes away, which is also the neighborhood where I grew up. Those kinds of contrasts probably imprint themselves on my DNA. In a strange way, I feel as though that tiny bit of friction still informs my work today.

Kusmer: Have you considered writing about Boston’s criminal underworld or Boston crime history? I noticed in your essays you reference Whitey Bulger and the Sugar Hill Gang. There’s obviously a rich text here.

Keefe: I have a bit. I wrote an essay for The New Yorker about Whitey Bulger. All that feels very close to home. Whitey was at large when I was growing up and he loomed very large in the popular imagination in Dorchester. When I published that essay, some people were unhappy about the way I characterized Billy Bulger and his relationship with his brother, but I thought it was pretty interesting.

Kusmer: For “Say Nothing,” that took you into the Boston College archives. I was really interested in that.

Keefe: With “Say Nothing,” the book came out in 2019 and I truly thought it was going to be a book for nobody. The Troubles was one of those subjects that people had very strong, clear views on, and I felt a huge amount of ambivalence. I published that book, and I was full of ambivalence, thinking nobody was going to read it. I remember doing the first few events here in Boston and being nervous because of the huge Irish American community.

The book takes a fairly skeptical view of Gerry Adams, who in some corners of my community growing up was regarded as a real hero. In a kind of unambivalent, unambiguous way, he was regarded as a hero. I was shocked, truly, that the book became a bestseller, was turned into a TV series, and is still being read now.

Kusmer: Why do you think that happened? What were you wrong about?

Keefe: Well, I think there’s a bunch of things. I think a lot of people had never really engaged with the issue beyond the bumper sticker version and were welcome to the idea of a book that’s pretty accessible, anybody can pick it up. Some of it is that there were more people who shared my ambivalence than I knew.

I think a big part of it is that enough time has passed now. I think occasionally what happens is when you’re in the crucible of a conflict, there’s a sense of “us and them” and people put on ideological blinders. They can sort of see things in a slightly monochromatic way. Then enough time passes that it becomes safe to look back.

Honestly, some of it is also about age. I’ve been back to Belfast a few times and went to the Belfast Book Festival to talk about the book. There were these big sold-out crowds, but most of the people who came were young people in their 20s and 30s. They would come and get me to sign their books and would say, “I was born after this stuff. My parents lived through this, but they never talk about it.”

Kusmer: They want to understand them better’

I don’t want to overly project here, but do you think there’s also the appeal to Americans of reading about civil war when trying to understand the fracturing of our own communities right now?

Keefe: For sure. I should say that when I was writing the book, it wasn’t on my mind.

I was writing the book in 2015, 2016, and 2017, and I felt like I was describing something very foreign in time and space. The interesting thing was when the book came out and you had Black Lives Matter protests and militarized police on the streets shooting tear gas at marchers, suddenly all the iconography — especially from the early chapters of the book which are about the birth of The Troubles growing out of a civil rights movement in Northern Ireland and the really heavy-handed tactics by the British — suddenly felt very familiar.

I guess I would say that “Say Nothing” is a very dark story, but the miracle is that The Troubles ended. It was a three-decade grinding conflict that people thought would never end, and it ended.

Now, part of what the book is about in the end, is that it’s a pretty cold peace. If you go to Belfast today, it’s not that everyone is holding hands and loves each other, but it is a peace and the peace is held.

Kusmer: I want to talk to you now about your influences. You are really well known for your skills in narrative nonfiction writing. Recently, for The New Yorker’s 100-year anniversary, you wrote a piece about Truman Capote. I think people would consider him a pioneer of the genre. Who do you think are the best to ever do narrative nonfiction?

Keefe: Oh, man. For sure Truman Capote. Robert Caro would be a big one for me. I read “The Power Broker” when I moved to New York in my late teens. My dad gave it to me when I went to college and I read it over the course of a summer. It’s a 1,000-page book. It’s a tome. It takes some doing. I don’t even know that I could read a book like that over the course of a summer now. But I did and I loved it and it’s always lingered with me. I go back to his work a lot.

Strangely enough, the piece that did it for me was when I was a first-year student at Columbia in the fall of 1995. The O.J. Simpson verdict — this is how old I am — came down and Henry Louis Gates Jr. published a piece in The New Yorker called “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Black Man.”

He basically was interviewing prominent Black cultural and political figures about their views on the verdict and the O.J. trial.

I had read The New Yorker starting in high school. I liked the idea of being a writer. I liked the idea of being a New Yorker writer, but that was the first time that I got to the end of an article and then went back to the beginning and took it apart.

I counted how many people he interviewed and looked at who he talked to more than once. “This is interesting. He waits to bring in this person until the end.”

I was trying to deconstruct the magic trick and figure out how he did. That was a piece that really kind of changed my trajectory a little bit.

Kusmer: I’ve been asking some of my journalist groups what I should ask Patrick Radden Keefe. One thing that kept coming up from the male journalists was your modeling career. How did you become a J.Crew model?

Keefe: “Career” might be a slightly strong word.

Kusmer: Everyone’s like, “How did he do that?” How did that come to be?”

Keefe: That’s too funny

Kusmer: So many people asked me about it. They were like, “You gotta ask him about the J. Crew stuff. Does he get to keep the pants?”

Keefe: Not only did I get to keep the clothes, but I get a 30 percent discount. I think it’s forever? They told me it’s a year, but it’s been more than a year and it still works.

Here’s a story about the power of legacy media. It came along because there was a guy who works with J. Crew who knows me and said, “Would you want to do this? It’d be fun and take half a day.”

So I did it and then they, J. Crew, put out the spread on Instagram. I got a few notes, but not all that much. Then The New York Times wrote about it and everybody suddenly noticed. It’s a funny thing, like when a tree falls in the woods. Truly I think it’s The New York Times article that people noticed.

Yeah, listen, it was fun. I don’t think it’s going to become a second career, but as a one-time thing, I enjoyed it.

Kusmer: Good work if you can get it.

Keefe: Exactly.

Kusmer: Patrick Radden Keefe is a writer for The New Yorker. His new book is “London Falling.” It’s so good. [Listeners] should read it. Thank you so much, Patrick, for joining me.

Keefe: What a pleasure.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

Listen to more Say More episodes here and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

title: With UMass chancellor, Michlewitz and Moran head to the Vatican to talk climate
text:
The fact Michlewitz and Moran have been invited to the Vatican underscores how extensive the Legislature’s climate efforts have been. (A UMass Boston spokesperson said they will pay for the travel from their campaign accounts.) In every two-year session, it seems lawmakers will serve up a major omnibus climate-and-energy bill. The sausage-making isn’t pretty and doesn’t always go as planned. But the reality is: They’re making progress — even if it’s in fits and starts.

This delegation to the Vatican, which also includes public health expert Ashish Jha, underscores something else: the rising prominence of UMass Boston under Suárez-Orozco’s direction. He’s a renowned immigration scholar who arrived at the Dorchester campus, at age 63, amid some leadership and financial turmoil there six years ago.

Suárez-Orozco, who speaks with an Argentinian accent and comes armed with more quotes than a Bartlett’s, quickly set about building bridges to Boston’s business community. One obvious goal: to help cultivate career opportunities for many of the 12,000 undergraduates at UMass Boston, long considered a commuter school. These connections lead to internships, jobs, and mentorship.

Sometimes they lead to important donations, too, like gifts from New Balance owner Jim Davis and tech entrepreneur Paul English to establish UMass Boston centers to study sports business and artificial intelligence, respectively.

Suárez-Orozco’s work in the pontifical academy, where he has served on its council since 2019, ensures some ideas from Massachusetts appear on a world stage. He helped bring Governor Maura Healey and Mayor Michelle Wu to a climate summit at the Vatican in 2024, and another Massachusetts delegation to discuss AI there a year ago.

This time, the topic will be climate legislation. For Moran and Michlewitz, it really starts with the Global Warming Solutions Act, in 2008; that bill made Massachusetts one of the first states in the country with aggressive goals to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050. That same year, the Legislature passed the Green Communities Act, which helped spur more renewable energy and a new home efficiency program known as Mass Save.

That set the stage for a 2016 clean-energy law establishing a state-overseen competition to secure contracts that could finance a giant power line to draw hydroelectricity here from Quebec and an offshore wind farm south of Martha’s Vineyard.

No one expected either project to take this long. But we are talking about New England. While the projects turned into epics, for various reasons, they have reached completion this year. The NECEC line was charged up in January, delivering the equivalent of up to 20 percent of Massachusetts’ electricity, and the Vineyard Wind project is essentially done and sending electricity to the shore, with some punch list items and payment issues to work through.

Meanwhile, Mass Save is back in the Beacon Hill debate. House leaders recently took some heat for a provision in their latest energy bill that calls for a reduction in the program budget, to make it more sustainable while giving constituents a break on their utility bills. Senate leaders, expected to be more supportive of Mass Save funding, have not yet released their version.

It’s partly the messy back-and-forth that makes this matter of interest to the Vatican, which has a keen interest in government models that can be replicated around the world. Michlewitz says the past two decades of legislation have proven that pursuing a climate resiliency agenda can also be good for the local economy. He says the papal academy’s invite offers an opportunity to elevate this work to a constituency in size and scope that’s well beyond what he could have imagined.

This will be the latest session on the urgency of climate change that the papal academy has held in various locations during the past two years, including one at the UMass Boston campus last year. The aim is assembling a list of best practices at the Vatican next year.

Suárez-Orozco plays down his role in all of this. He’s just a modest convener, or so he would say, a scholar at heart, albeit one who is quick to cite Einstein or Eliot in everyday conversation. He gets excited when he can get back to his research, like a presentation he’s giving next month on how climate change has forced the migration of vulnerable populations.

He also likes to say that climate change is coming to a neighborhood near you — something he can witness from his perch on UMass Boston’s coastal campus — regardless of whether the federal government recognizes it.

Massachusetts, in the grand scheme, is relatively small, with far fewer people than the Los Angeles metro area, where Suárez-Orozco previously worked. But the ideas that we produce? They’re worth sharing, especially when confronting an issue as broadly challenging as this one.

title: Three Boston shootings in 24 hours leave one dead, four injured
text:
One person is dead and four others are injured following a string of shootings in Boston over the weekend, with the most recent seriously injuring a woman in Dorchester on Sunday night, according to Boston police.

All three shootings are considered separate incidents, according to police. No arrests have been made.

The latest shooting occurred Sunday around 6:41 p.m., when police responded to the area of 69 Kingsdale St. after multiple reports of gunshots, Boston police said in a statement.

Police found a man and a woman suffering from gunshot wounds, police said. The woman suffered serious, life-threatening injuries, while the man suffered injuries not believed to be life-threatening, police said.

Both victims were transported to local hospitals, police said.

“At this time, it is a very active investigation,” Boston Police Superintendent Paul McLaughlin said at a press briefing in Dorchester. “We are canvassing the area, looking for witnesses, victims, and video, and we encourage anyone who witnessed or knows anything about the incident to contact the homicide unit.”

Jennifer Boves, 37, who lives in a multi-unit building next door to where police said the shooting occurred, said she returned home Sunday evening to find her street blocked off by police tape and cruisers.

“The fact of me not even being able to park in my house or my apartment, it was just very concerning,” Boves said. “I have a 2-year-old, so it’s pretty scary.”

Jeff Lincoln, 31, who said he recently purchased a rental property across the street, echoed those concerns. He was in the neighborhood to take out the trash when he saw police cruisers and tape blocking his way.

“They’re all great families, with kids and stuff,” Lincoln said of his tenants. “I want them to have a safe area that they can live in. I’m definitely concerned.”

Two other shootings took place in the city from Saturday night into Sunday morning, according to Boston police.

The first occurred around 11:39 p.m. on Saturday night, when police responded to a report of a person shot at 28 Woolson St. in Mattapan, Boston police said in a statement.

When officers arrived, they found a man who had been shot outside, according to the statement. Boston EMS responded and pronounced the victim dead, police said. The victim’s name was not released.

Later, around 2 a.m. Sunday, Boston police responded to a shooting on Geneva Avenue in Dorchester, according to a police spokesperson. Arriving officers found two victims suffering from gunshot wounds near the intersection of Geneva Avenue and Everton Street.

Both victims were taken to local hospitals for further evaluation, police said. No further information on their conditions was released.

Collin Robisheaux can be reached at collin.robisheaux@globe.com. Follow him on Twitter @ColRobisheaux. Nathan Metcalf can be reached at nathan.metcalf@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @natpat_123.

title: Mother’s Day Walk for Peace marks 30 years in Boston
text:
“It was bittersweet, of course, but my son’s heart is still beating,” Johnson said in an interview Sunday night.

On Sunday, Johnson walked through Dorchester alongside family and friends wearing red shirts emblazoned with the number five — a tribute to her son’s favorite color and his artist name, “5ive” — during the 30th annual Mother’s Day Walk for Peace.

The 5k walk brings together families, survivors, and community members to honor loved ones lost to violence while raising money for the Peace Institute, whose work includes crisis response, long-term grief support, youth programming, and advocacy for families affected by homicide.

“It’s a space for me to turn the tragedy into a purpose of love, to uplift my son and show him how much he was loved,” Johnson said.

The event Sunday came hours after a pair of shootings were reported in Boston, including one in Mattapan on Saturday night, where a man was killed. The other shooting was reported in Dorchester early Sunday and left two people with injuries, according to police. Later Sunday night, two people were hospitalized with injuries after a shooting on Kingsdale Street in Boston.

The walk traces its origins back to 1996, when Chaplain Clementina Chéry organized the first gathering three years after her 15-year-old son, Louis D. Brown, was killed by stray gunfire in Dorchester while on his way to a Teens Against Gang Violence meeting.

What began as a small group of grieving mothers has since grown into a major annual event and the centerpiece of the Peace Institute’s work.

“This year’s walk was an incredible reflection of what 30 years of community, resilience, and collective action can accomplish,” Chéry, the institute’s chief executive and president, said in a statement. “Seeing thousands of people come together to honor loved ones while investing in peace and healing is deeply powerful and reminds us why this work is so important.”

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden attended Sunday’s walk alongside members of his staff, a spokesperson for his office said.

“One of the primary factors in Boston’s historically low crime rate is the participation of community members at all levels,” Hayden said in a statement. “This march is a perfect example of residents coming together to advocate for a safer society.”

Mayor Michelle Wu also attended the walk and praised those who have helped sustain the event over three decades.

“This incredible group of moms and survivors have channeled the deepest pain into the most impactful sense of purpose, and have changed our city, and continue to do so every day,” Wu said at the event, according to audio of her remarks provided by her office.

To mark the event’s 30th anniversary, organizers hosted the walk’s first post-race community rally at Town Field Park, featuring live music by Angelena and the Unit along with food vendors, mocktails, and family activities.

Luis Antonio Thompson, a senior producer in the Peace Institute’s production department and Brown’s cousin, said organizers wanted to turn the event into more of a gathering place.

“In years past, people would walk the route and then go home, and this year we said, ‘What if we made it a destination?” Thompson said. “It was received pretty well.”

The walk had raised roughly $467,000 by Sunday evening, about 78 percent of the institute’s $600,000 fundraising goal, according to Thompson. Fundraising for the event will continue through Father’s Day, as it does each year, he said.

Anthony Potter, who said he grew up with Brown and attended the walk for the first time in more than two decades, said the event reflected his friend’s vision for the city.

“Boston is very different from when we grew up; things were a lot more separated, even segregated,” said Potter. “To see so many different people come together for a unified purpose is the vision that Louis had.”

title: White Mass: The Boston stories Hollywood misses
text:
Boston does not have a shortage of film and television set here. It has a shortage of Boston in them.

For decades, the camera has returned to the same corridor: cops, robbers, political operators, and a certain strain of white working-class male volatility.

We all know the cinematic trope. “The Friends of Eddie Coyle.” “Mystic River.” “The Departed.” “The Town.” “Black Mass.” Each set in a Boston that functions less as a real city than as a mythology — the most usable canvas for white urban toughness in contemporary American cinema.

You can watch a decade’s worth of Boston films and never meaningfully enter Chinatown as a lived neighborhood. Never see Dominican hair salons or Brazilian flags. And never step inside the kind of Jamaican restaurant or bodega that anchors entire blocks.

Yet Boston has the second-largest Dominican population in the United States. Its public schools are around 85 percent nonwhite. Its immigrant communities are central to the city’s daily life.

Bostonians who move elsewhere often hear some version of “I didn’t know there were [fill in the blank] people in Boston.” Others are met with surprise when they mention that Donnie Yen or Donna Summer came from here. That disbelief comes from decades of selective storytelling.

This matters because it narrows the public imagination of who belongs here. If Boston is consistently depicted as white ethnic grievance, institutional scandal, and blue-collar combustion, then its academic density, immigrant vitality, artistic ecosystems, and multiracial civic life recede from national view. That distortion shapes perception. Perception shapes who feels welcome. Who feels welcome shapes who arrives, who invests, and who stays.

The pattern holds across comedies, legal dramas, medical procedurals, prestige thrillers, and romantic comedies. “Cheers” is about a white bar. “Ally McBeal” and “Boston Legal” are largely white law series. “St. Elsewhere” is a predominantly white hospital drama. “Fever Pitch” is a romcom built around a particular Red Sox fan demographic, the same stratum celebrated in “Celtic Pride.” “Boston Public” depicts a school system that is more white than it is in reality and filters that world almost entirely through white characters’ eyes.

There are exceptions. “Blue Hill Avenue,” a movie released in 2001, was set in the heart of Black Boston and has been cited as a different kind of story about the city. But “Blue Hill Avenue” was shot largely in St. John, New Brunswick — which may explain why its Roxbury feels like a place no Roxbury resident would recognize.

The TV series “Rizzoli & Isles” used contemporary Roxbury and Dorchester settings — but that’s a partial credit, because the show was still a procedural drama told from the point of view of two white women.

The pattern runs in both directions. When Hollywood does tell a story that originated in Black Boston, the city itself often disappears. The LL Cool J film “In Too Deep,” based on the real story of Roxbury drug kingpin Darryl “God” Whiting, was set in Cincinnati. TV’s “Survivor’s Remorse,” which followed a Boston family navigating sudden wealth and fame, relocated them to Atlanta for its entire run.

Because Boston isn’t sprawling, class, race, and power exist in close physical proximity. That should produce narrative friction we rarely see. Instead, Boston often appears as a generic tough Northeast city. Outside of “Good Will Hunting” and “The Social Network,” our intellectual infrastructure is rarely treated as cinematic.

Crime is marketable. Corruption is marketable. The mythology of Whitey Bulger is marketable. Non-rhotic accents are marketable.

But so are other realities — ones that have never received the same institutional backing.

In the late 1990s, clergy, community organizers, and police collaborated in what became known as The Boston Miracle, helping reduce youth gun homicides to historic lows. In 1999 and 2000, the city recorded just one youth-related gun homicide, after averaging dozens during the crack epidemic. That story had genuine stakes, real tension, moral ambiguity, and fragile coalition-building across communities that distrusted one another. When it finally did reach the screen, as “City on a Hill,” law enforcement figures were romanticized and community leaders reduced.

Long before civil rights icons were monuments, they were students here — dating, studying, organizing. Think of W.E.B. DuBois, the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., (future Atlanta mayor) Maynard Jackson, Malcolm X. Boston has been at the forefront of national movements since the abolitionists. But incubation is quieter than confrontation. It’s harder to package than a climactic courtroom scene or an urban gunfight. It is, apparently, harder to finance.

The Massachusetts film tax incentives of the early 2000s drew significant production to the region and helped establish a self-sustaining infrastructure — locations, crews, institutional knowledge — that reinforced the archetype already in place. That archetype, once profitable, became self-protecting. A multicultural Boston — Caribbean-inflected, academic, immigrant, artistic — would require new storytelling frameworks, new casting assumptions, new marketing language. It would complicate a mythology that studios already know how to sell.

TV and film have never fictionalized or cast Melnea Cass, Ruth Batson, Mel King, the Rev. Eugene Rivers, Tommie Atkins, or the Rev. Michael Haynes. Local fixtures, in most cases for three decades. Boston street cred only sells if it’s earned via violence.

What of the activists, educators, and coaches who were household names locally but invisible nationally? Or the Boston Shootout, the prestigious high school basketball tournament that drew elite talent from major US cities for nearly three decades? Its origin story alone would make compelling cinema. The Chinese tongs, or secret societies, that shaped early Chinatown power structures? The layered histories of Puerto Rican enterprise and upward mobility running alongside — and sometimes in conflict with — neighborhood gangs?

Contrast this with what other American cities are permitted to be on screen. Los Angeles can be “Room 222,” “Sanford & Son,” and “Boyz n the Hood” — comedy, domestic life, and tragedy across generations. Not just “L.A. Law.” Chicago can be “Good Times,” “The Chi,” and “Chicago Fire” — not only “Chicago Hope.” Baltimore is “Roc,” “Homicide,” and “The Wire” — not merely “Diner,” “Avalon,” and “Liberty Heights.” Each city carries multiple ethnic and emotional identities on screen. Each city gets to show Black, Asian, and Latino life in its full range: everyday, comic, tragic, aspirational, routine.

Boston is rarely afforded that breadth. Doing so would complicate the brand.

title: Series of Boston shootings alarm residents after relatively peaceful period
text:
“Oh my goodness,” he said Monday afternoon, upon learning the shooting was fatal.

Legros, 69, who immigrated from Haiti decades ago, said his neighborhood has gotten safer in recent years. He often sees police cruisers patrolling the area, which adds to a sense of security.

He said he hopes detectives conduct a thorough investigation and figure out what happened Saturday night.

The unusual spike in gun violence marred Mother’s Day weekend in Boston, leaving residents unsettled. In addition to the Woolson Street shooting, a double shooting Sunday evening left a woman with life-threatening injuries.

Officials have said they believe the weekend shootings were all separate incidents, not connected.

As of Sunday, there have been two fatal shootings in Boston this year, compared to six in the same time frame last year, according to Boston police crime data; There were 26 nonfatal shootings in the same period this year, compared to 30 in that time in 2025. Over the last five years, the city reports an average of 41 shooting victims by this time each year, according to the data.

Police said two men were first shot shortly after 2 a.m. Sunday as they rode motor scooters down Geneva Avenue in Dorchester, a police report said. It did not disclose their ages. One of the men shouted twice to responding officers, “I’ve been shot,” according to the report.

The violence continued Monday, when a gunman opened fire along Memorial Drive in Cambridge, injuring at least one person.

Police who responded to the Geneva Avenue shooting found “two mini motorbikes laid out in the street” in an intersection, police said. The report said a witness told police he saw two people running up Geneva Avenue toward Columbia Road.

Officers proceeded in that direction in their cruiser and were soon flagged down by one of the victims. The person had sustained what appeared to be a gunshot wound to his right shoulder.

He told officers a group of people exited a parked car and a masked assailant fired multiple shots, police said.

Both victims were taken to an area hospital for evaluation, police said. Their conditions weren’t immediately available Monday.

The attack closely followed the fatal shooting in Mattapan, police said. In that case, the victim was pronounced dead at the scene.

A police report did not disclose the man’s name or age, but officials said in a statement that he was an adult.

The third shooting occurred around 6:48 p.m. Sunday on Kingsdale Street in Dorchester.

Police responded to the area after receiving “multiple reports of gunshots” and found a man and woman who were both wounded, authorities said.

The woman suffered serious, life-threatening injuries, while the man’s injuries were not considered life-threatening, police said. Their conditions weren’t available Monday.

Neighbors on Kingsdale Street said the double shooting unfolded on the porch of a triple decker. Yellow police tape was tied across the front steps Monday afternoon. A man in a work uniform said he was there to change the locks; he said a cleaning crew had come earlier.

Around 1 p.m. Monday, a swarm of police cars suddenly descended on the street. Both uniformed and plainclothes officers rushed to the rear of the house as more backup cruisers arrived.

According to Boston police transmissions, officers were looking for a suspect in the shooting. They searched the home without success. A group of people eventually left the home, along with several responding officers.

The street was otherwise quiet, with the occasional pedestrian, people walking dogs or heading home from the store.

There have been some instances of violence in recent years, “but in general, this neighborhood is good,” said Anna Walsh, who lives down the block, speaking with Telemundo Boston.

No arrests have been made in any of the weekend shootings.

John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Suspect in Cambridge shooting couldn’t ‘care less if innocent people get hurt,’ officer warned in 2021
text:
Brown, who lives in Dorchester, was confronted by a state Trooper and an armed Marine veteran, who shot him several times in the extremities. Brown is in custody at a Boston hospital.

The shooting in broad daylight appeared to confirm the worst fears police had about Brown, according to testimony from his sentencing hearing nearly five years ago.

“Mr. Tyler Brown [couldn’t] care less if innocent people get hurt,” Boston police officer Edward Gately III said at Brown’s sentencing in Suffolk Superior Court on Aug. 18, 2021.

During his delivery of an emotional victim impact statement, Gately recounted how Brown fired an estimated 17 rounds at four officers on a Saturday afternoon on May 16, 2020, as they responded to reports of a man threatening people with a gun.

Gately said he was “a firm believer” that when Brown gets out, “he will hurt or … kill someone," according to a recording of the hearing obtained by the Globe.

Gately implored Superior Court Judge Janet L. Sanders to give Brown the maximum sentence, calling him “a very dangerous individual who doesn’t care who he hurts.”

Brown was on probation at the time of the May 2020 shooting. He had been released from prison in January 2020 after serving six years for the stabbing.

“He has shown us how well he has done while he was out on probation for his stabbing,” Gately said, his voice cracking with emotion. “Probation apparently means nothing [to] Mr. Tyler Brown, nor does the value of life.”

Brown has a long criminal history in the Boston area. He took a deal in the May 2020 shooting case, pleading guilty to eight charges.

Prosecutors asked for at least 10 years behind bars, but Brown received a maximum of six years, with credit for about 18 months time served.

The sentence immediately was criticized by both the Suffolk District Attorney at the time, Rachael Rollins, and Boston Police Superintendent-in-Chief Gregory Long. They said the sentence did not reflect the magnitude of the offense.

Judge Sanders said she felt a decade in lock up was too harsh.

Speaking from the bench, Sanders told Brown she was taking a chance by sentencing him to six years, especially since he was admitting to shooting at officers. She also acknowledged Gately’s emotional plea.

Sanders considered a number of factors before announcing her decision, according to an audio recording of the hearing obtained by The Globe.

First, there was a consequential change to Brown’s criminal record after prosecutors moved to vacate his 2009 conviction for cocaine distribution. Brown was among the thousands of defendants whose cases were compromised in the state drug lab scandal involving Annie Dookhan, a former state chemist who admitted to tampering with samples.

Without that conviction on his record, Brown could no longer face a sentence enhancement for armed career criminals; he also no longer qualified for a mandatory 10-year sentence, prosecutors said.

Sanders said many criminal defendants have terrible childhoods during which they experienced abuse — as did Brown. Many also have psychiatric issues, the judge said.

She listed letters of support for Brown , including from then-Acting Mayor Kim Janey’s Office of Returning Citizens, which helps formerly incarcerated people. She said that Despite being incarcerated for much of his adult life, Brown still forged a strong relationship with his two children, the judge noted. He had reached out for mental health treatment just days before the May 2020 shooting, when resources were scarce because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What set Brown apart to her, Sanders said, were the letters of support from family members, from Kevin Sibley, who then worked for the mayor, along with two other self-help organizations for incarcerated people Brown was involved with.

Sanders quoted the letter from the mayor’s Returning Citizens Office: “We believe that Tyler, if he’s provided with reliable opportunities for personal growth, he will be a valuable contributing member of our community.”

“I don’t see letters like that,” the judge said.

But a Superior Court probation officer also called for a lengthy sentence, saying Brown had an eight-page criminal record in Massachusetts, as well as convictions in New Hampshire and Michigan for drug charges, possession of a dangerous weapon, armed robbery, escape through violence, and assault of a prison employee.

“What’s most concerning,” the probation officer said, were the similarities between the stabbing and the May 2020 shooting.

“They both involve Mr. Brown approaching a group of individuals unknown to him and asking, ‘Where are you from,’ followed by the showing or use of a weapon,” the probation officer said. “Probation believes that Mr. Brown is a danger to the community due to his random acts of violence towards strangers.”

Sanders said she was going to rely on her own intuition and trust Brown to make positive decisions in the future.

“While it’s certainly incredibly serious to be shooting at a police officer, there is a difference between shooting at a police officer and shooting a police officer, and the reality is that nobody was injured,” Sanders said.

“I do think that he was out there wildly shooting,” she said. “But I’m not so sure that he was really intending to hurt any particular person, particularly when one understands or takes into account the fact there are mental health issues.”

Sanders reiterated to Brown, “I’m kind of taking a chance on you.”

“I can’t look into a crystal ball and figure out what’s going to happen once you get out. But I do understand that I am taking on risk here, and I just pray that, you know, my intuitions are right and that you have the ability, the smarts, the will, the support, not to go out there and endanger other people like you have in the past.”

Sanders ordered that all of Brown’s charges, including his probation violation, run concurrently with the six-year sentence, and that he serve three years of probation after his release.

The Massachusetts Parole Board agreed to Brown’s prison release on March 26 last year, and Brown was released from MCI-Shirley on May 21. He was allowed to serve the remainder of his sentence under parole supervision.

Members of the parole board noted that while Brown was incarcerated, he had completed a violence reduction program and other classes through a Tufts University program.

Brown is “remorseful about the part he played in the offense, and realizes that this offense could have worked out,” according to a copy of theboard’s ruling.

Brown suffers from mental health disorders, including PTSD, depression and anxiety, and takes medications daily, the ruling said.

Upon release, Brown was ordered to attend classes at Tufts University, attend mental-health counseling, take his medications, and undergo testing for alcohol and illegal drugs, the ruling said.

Now, less than a year later, Brown is facing two counts of armed assault with intent to murder and firearms offenses for Monday’s shooting. His arraignment date has not been scheduled yet.

title: A new open-air market is set to open in Dorchester this summer. Here’s where.
text:
A new Sunday outdoor market is set to open in Dorchester later this month, organizers said.

Organizers for “Dot Fun Day” said they are recruiting vendors and working on securing final approvals to open on May 24. The market is set to occupy the lot of the former Dorchester Tire property at 1160 Dorchester Ave. in Savin Hill.

The site, just a few minutes north of Fields Corner and Boston’s Little Saigon district, is expected to include a diverse range of food and cultural offerings, organizers said.

“We want this to become like a part of everyone’s Sunday routine,” said Tam Le, a local business owner and one of the organizers behind the market. “You know, having this third space where the whole community can come together. Everyone knows everyone, everyone’s hanging out — we stop by the market, we grab a couple things, we say hi to our neighbors.”

The plan was first announced at a meeting of the Columbia-Savin Hill Civic Association last week, according to the Dorchester Reporter.

A spokesperson for the city’s licensing board said Monday that the organizers were currently going through the special events process.

Le, who owns Pho Hoa Restaurant in Fields Corner and Lê Madeline in Quincy, said the rest of the organizing team includes Piter Brandao, owner of Pleasant Entertainment and a member of the city’s Black Men and Boys Commission, as well as Joel Kamm and Kevin DePina.

“We’re very much a part of the community,” Le said. “[This] is so new that, you know, we have an idea of what we want to be, but we [also] want input from the community. We want to grow with whatever the wants and needs are of the community.”

Dorchester Tire closed in 2021 after nearly 60 years of operation. Since then, the vacant property has hosted other community events, such as a community cookout in August.

At one point, the building was envisioned as the home of Le’s Vietnamese coffee roaster, Lêgacy Càphê. Those plans have since changed, Le said; now he is looking for a way to “activate the entire property.”

Vendors at the outdoor market will include dessert boutique Lizzie’s Bakery and pop-up kitchen D’ Burger, Le said, as well as various arts and crafts stores. Organizers are also working to obtain a temporary liquor license for an outdoor beer garden, he added.

Aside from a few minor permitting concerns, he said there was “nothing we see that’s going to get in the way of us opening up.”

If all goes well, the market will run every Sunday through October, Le said.

“We may start off with just a handful of vendors, but we hope to grow it to full capacity over the first two months,” he said.

title: A history of violence, mental illness, and drug use: What we know about the suspected Cambridge gunman
text:
Brown was released on parole last year for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in 2020. He was reportedly suicidal in the hours leading up to the Memorial Drive shooting. Brown was released from a psychiatric hospital Friday and was reportedly using crack cocaine, court filings show.

A parole officer called 911 Monday and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester.

title: How did the alleged Memorial Drive shooter obtain a gun?
text:
Brown, 46, of Dorchester, is on dual parole and probation for a host of violent offenses, including armed assault to murder. His criminal history means it was illegal for Brown to possess any gun whatsoever, never mind the multi-caliber BCI-Defense Model FF-15 authorities allege he used in the shooting, according to court documents.

“The state and federal laws are straightforward: if you have a felony conviction, you cannot legally purchase, possess, or carry a firearm,” said Elisabeth Ryan, the Boston-based policy counsel at Everytown for Gun Safety, in a statement. “This individual should never have had access to a gun.”

George W. Vien, a former federal prosecutor, concurred, saying that federal law prohibits someone with a felony conviction from possessing any firearm or ammunition, regardless of the style of gun.

“It’s really clear cut,” he said.

Additionally, Massachusetts law prohibits sale and possession of assault weapons, such as a Colt AR-15 or an AK-47. The law also bans weapons that have internal functional components that “are substantially similar to the construction or configuration of a weapon that is expressly banned under the law.” But there are exceptions, including grandfathering clauses.

Massachusetts law bars specific military-style weapons and their duplicates and any semiautomatic weapons with at least two identifying features — such as a folding or telescoping stock, a bayonet mount, a grenade launcher, or an ammunition magazine that attaches to a pistol.

But could a local resident who is not a convicted felon buy this particular gun in Massachusetts? Given carveouts the state has in its gun laws, the answer remains unclear. Messages left with the Middlesex district attorney’s office, State Police, and the governor’s office were not returned Wednesday.

The gun also has a serial number, according to court documents, raising the possibility that it could be traced. A Globe review of two decades worth of state data for gun dealer transactions, personal transfers, and gun registrations in Massachusetts turned up no results for a firearm with the gun’s serial number.

According to a statement of facts from a State Police trooper, Brown’s parole officer called Boston police shortly after noon on Monday to report concerns with Brown.

Brown had previously served multiple stints behind bars, including one for a May 2020 shooting in the South End that involved four Boston police officers.

The trooper noted in the report that Brown’s parole officer spoke to him through a video call on Monday, during which the parole officer saw Brown waving a round a “semi-automatic rifle” while in a kitchen that was not his own.

The State Police report offers other details to the immediate run-up to the shooting, noting that Brown had been released from a local psychiatric hospital on Friday, and that he had been previously diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, and depression.

Brown, who has a history of crack cocaine use, according to authorities, had a drug test scheduled for Monday and told his parole officer that he had relapsed and was ready to end his life.

Massachusetts is considered to have among the most stringent gun laws in the nation. According to Everytown, the state is one of a few to bar gun purchases by people with outstanding warrants and one of a few to require secure storage for any firearm not in the owner’s immediate control.

Still, violence in Massachusetts can be affected by weaker gun laws elsewhere, said Ruth Zakarin, chief executive for the Massachusetts Coalition to Prevent Gun Violence.

“We’re impacted by weaker gun laws in other states,” she said. “We’re impacted by the fact that what we have in Massachusetts is not what we have on the federal level.”

If someone can’t legally purchase a gun, there are myriad ways to illicitly possess one. They can be stolen, straw-purchased, where someone purchases a gun legally, attests that the gun is for them, but in reality they are buying it for someone else, or guns could be trafficked in from somewhere else, perhaps a location that has more lax gun ownership laws, according to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Untraceable, 3-D printed guns have also been on the uptick in the US.

Brandon del Pozo, a medical professor at Brown University and a member of the Regional Gun Violence Research Consortium, said the weapon Brown used “appears to be a variant of the AR-15, a lightly modified version of the US military’s standard combat rifle.”

“Despite stricter laws in Massachusetts, they are easy to purchase throughout the country, including in the region here. Convicted felons are precluded from buying a weapon like this, but the background checks that would prohibit it aren’t required at private sales or gun shows many states, or when the system takes too long to return the results,” he said.

Such loopholes, said del Pozo, “mean that nearly anyone, including convicted felons and people with severe mental illness, can buy one of these weapons designed for combat.”

Warren Eller, a professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice, lamented that “the gun legislation that we pass doesn’t really affect the causal reasons of why people go out and shoot.”

“Anyone in our country can get a hold of any thing they want to depending on the amount of effort you put into it,” he said. “The question is what kind of impediments can we put up now to stop these sorts of things. The day and age to stop illicit use of firearms through simply banning purchases is long, long gone.”

title: Person shot four times in Roxbury, Boston’s fifth shooting in four days

Authorities said the victim described the shooter as wearing a black sweatshirt but couldn’t get a “good look” at him.

His condition wasn’t immediately available Wednesday afternoon.

Tuesday’s shootings continued a spate of recent gun violence in Boston that included a fatality, police said.

On Saturday night, a person was shot in Mattapan and later died, police said. Authorities identified the man as Michael Jacob, 30, of Randolph.

Shortly after 2 a.m. on Sunday, two people were shot while riding motor scooters down Geneva Avenue in Dorchester, according to a police report.

Both victims sustained injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.

Also Sunday, a man and woman were shot on Kingsdale Street in Dorchester. The woman remained in critical condition Tuesday while the man suffered injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening, police said.

No arrests have been made in any of the five shootings, police said.

title: A rare El Niño is approaching. Here’s what it could mean for New England.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Super, historic, record-setting.

Those are just some of the words meteorologists are using to describe what is expected to develop across the Equatorial Pacific in the coming months.

Quick refresher: El Niño develops when winds weaken and sea surface temperatures surge across the Equatorial Pacific near South America — and this one may affect us bigtime.

Here are the four biggest things you need to know:

1. This could be one of the strongest El Niños on record

Nearly every major forecast model shows a significant El Niño developing by late 2026, with ocean temperatures potentially rising around 3 degrees Celsius above average. That would place this event among the strongest ever observed, rivaling the legendary 1877-78 El Niño.

Why does that matter? El Niño acts like a giant atmospheric heat engine. It tends to bring wetter conditions to the Southern US, leading to floods, while the northern tier often turns warmer and drier, increasing drought and wildfire risks out West.

2. New England may feel the effects by late summer

There’s usually a delay between El Niño forming and its impacts reaching New England. But by late summer and fall, we could see hotter, more humid weather settle in.

That may translate to more heat waves, sticky nights, and an increase in heavy downpours and thunderstorms. Coastal storms could also become more frequent later in the year as the jet stream grows more active.

3. Winter could turn warmer and wetter

Historically, strong El Niño winters favor milder temperatures across New England. That doesn’t eliminate snow, but it often means more mixed precipitation and rain events, especially near the coast.

At the same time, El Niño winters can still produce major nor’easters. Some of New England’s biggest storms have occurred during strong El Niño years.

4. Hurricane season may quiet down

Strong El Niño patterns typically increase wind shear over the Atlantic, making it harder for hurricanes to organize and strengthen.

That could lead to a slightly quieter-than-average Atlantic hurricane season overall, although, as always, it only takes one storm to make it memorable. After all, Hurricane Bob did make landfall in New England during an El Niño year (1991).

So, quieter hurricane seasons, maybe? Hey, you wanted a silver lining, right?

▪ Entering the day four goals shy of the school record, Wellesley senior Tara Battaglino reached the mark during a 14-5 girls’ lacrosse win over Brookline. Battaglino passed former WNBA guard Blake Dietrick’s mark of 331, set in 2010.

▪ Wakefield softball delivered No. 15 Georgetown its first loss, a 9-5 defeat on the shoulders of Kathryn Sliski, who homered and surpassed 300 career strikeouts.

Gretel Marshall, Rockport — The junior homered and drove in four runs to help her own cause as she fanned 10 Vikings during a 14-13 softball win vs. Lynn English.

Reese Taylor, Apponequet — The sophomore continued a torrid stretch, homering, scoring two runs, stealing two bases, and driving in two runs in an 8-4 softball win over New Bedford that also saw her strike out five and allow three earned runs.

A multisport athlete who starred on the football field as well, the 6-foot, 190-pound outfielder and running back totaled 1,614 yards and 22 touchdowns on the ground as a junior, giving him 27 total touchdowns and more than 2,000 yards of offense while leading the Sailors to the Division 4 Super Bowl crown.

Nascimento, who played at Everett and Norwich, served as defensive coordinator under John Dubzinski last decade. His brother, Jason Nascimento, was the coach at Medford from 2012-18.

Nascimento will take over for Frank Roche, who left after three years with the Spy Ponders to take over at Belmont Hill. Arlington finished 7-4 last year but did not make the Division 1 tournament.

“I am incredibly honored to be named the head coach of boys’ hockey at Nauset,” O’Connor said in a statement. “I am looking forward to maintaining and building on the established culture from the past four seasons.”

O’Connor was a captain at Arlington Catholic and Southern New Hampshire, while also spending a postgrad year at South Kent. He is the youth hockey director for the Northeast Generals and has coached at Mt. St. Charles (R.I.) and with the Neponset River Rats.

“Somerset Berkley holds a special place in my heart,” Sousa said in a statement. “The soccer program played a major role in my life and helped shape the path of my career. I’m honored for the opportunity to give back to a community that means so much to me and help student-athletes grow both on and off the field.”

St. Mary’s has won a state title in at least one sport for 19 consecutive years, with its boys’ basketball team capturing the Division 2 title in March.
