title: City officials are ramping up anti-violence efforts ahead of summer through youth jobs and more
text:
The city has recorded five homicides so far in 2026, with just two involving guns, according to Police Commissioner Michael Cox. He said violent crime is down slightly compared to last year and shootings have decreased.

But summer brings a heightened risk of violence because of additional daylight hours, more outdoor events, school vacation, and hot weather that can shorten people’s fuses, Cox said. He asked residents to contact police if they have any public safety concerns.

“I can’t emphasize enough, if you see something, say something,” he said.

Officials said they’re taking a holistic approach to crime-fighting — year-round, but with a special focus on summer.

“Safety is a citywide effort, not just a City Hall effort,” Wu said. “We know that real safety doesn’t come from just making statements or proclamations. It comes from the entire community building it together.”

That means investing in impacted communities, addressing trauma, expanding access to addiction services, improving outdoor spaces, and focusing on workforce development.

This year, “every Boston Public Schools student who wants a paid summer job will get one,” Wu said.

After receiving a $1 million grant from the nonprofit Cummings Foundation last year, the city has focused on strengthening partnerships with local hospital systems to provide robust support for gunshot victims in the immediate aftermath of a shooting, among other initiatives, said Isaac Yablo, senior adviser for community safety and director of the Boston Public Health Commission’s Office of Violence Prevention.

Another $1 million will help them keep the momentum going, officials said.

But the Wu administration’s efforts aren’t enough, said a handful of critics who showed up at the press conference with handmade signs to protest proposed budget cuts to a year-round afterschool youth jobs program. Wu’s proposed budget for next year would eliminate 1,800 city-funded positions for teens and young adults.

“This one is going to really affect the community,” said Janiah Lee, 19.

She said some young people rely on the paychecks: “It’s not just for people to get fresh kicks and stuff. Some people are actually helping their family members with bills, et cetera.”

Wu has said that massive fiscal challenges meant incredibly difficult choices in the proposed budget, but her administration is still prioritizing youth employment through the summer program and other efforts.

“We are working alongside key community anchors to sustain year-round opportunities for our young people,” her office said in a statement Wednesday.

title: Boston police officer indicted on manslaughter charge in connection with fatal shooting of carjacking suspect
text:
The now-suspended officer was released on personal recognizance following his March arraignment in Roxbury Municipal Court. The indictment moves the case to Suffolk Superior Court, where O’Malley will be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

King was shot while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Prosecutors determined that O’Malley had no justification for shooting at a moving vehicle.

“It is disappointing that the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office is choosing to second-guess an officer whose only goal was to protect the public,” O’Malley’s lawyer, David Yannetti, previously said in a statement. “We will continue to vigorously defend this officer and this case.”

Yannetti, best known for his successful defense of Karen Read, added in court papers that the “main issue in this case will be who the aggressor really was and whether Officer O’Malley acted in lawful defense.”

Yannetti filed several defense motions in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court in an effort to illustrate “King’s mayhem and reign of terror,” spanning nearly two decades and resulting in more than 17 criminal cases across Massachusetts, court records show.

Over the years, King has been charged with strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carjacking, breaking and entering, gun offenses, and resisting arrest, according to court filings.

At the time of his death, King was free on bail for at least three separate felony cases and had active warrants for his arrest, court records said.

Yannetti is seeking King’s mental health, criminal, and court records from all his past cases, recordings from police body-worn and dash cameras, the medical examiner’s file on King, along with statements taken from O’Malley and witnesses at the scene of the shooting.

O’Malley told investigators that when he shot King, he feared for his own life and for the life of another officer at the scene, believing his colleague was about to be run over.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood. About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached and tried to drive away, police said.

King opened the car window, but did not turn the vehicle off. O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” a police report said.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, the report said.

King’s family has said he was experiencing a mental health crisis in the hours leading up to the deadly encounter.

In court filings, Yannetti said King gave “O’Malley no choice that night.”

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti wrote. “When facing an extremely dangerous threat, there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

“If a man is going to assault and carjack an innocent woman, then threaten the lives and safety of the public and a police officer, that man needs to be stopped — whether he is in his right mind or not,” a defense motion stated.

But Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said in court in March that investigators determined O’Malley’s explanation wasn’t reasonable, citing witness testimony and footage from police body cameras.

The other officer, Polumbaum, said, “was in greater danger of being struck by those bullets than he ever was by the car.”

While the law affords police officers deference for split-second decisions, “we keep in mind the law and common sense,” he said.

Immediately after firing the shots, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” according to the police report. He later told investigators he believed the other officer “was going to be crushed by the suspect’s vehicle,” according to the police report.

However, investigating officers concluded that O’Malley’s statement “was not factually true.” State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

In March, responding to a question from reporters about whether the officers should have allowed the suspect to drive away, Hayden said that “in this circumstance, that might have been prudent.”

Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney representing King’s family, said he welcomed the indictment.

“For months, Stephenson King Jr.’s loved ones have been grieving the devastating loss of a son, a family member and a man whose life mattered deeply, while also fighting for the transparency and accountability they deserve,” Crump said. “The arrest, manslaughter charge, and now this indictment against the officer involved sends a powerful message about the seriousness of this case.”

Crump said the family “knows that accountability cannot stop here. They deserve the full truth about what happened to Stephenson and a justice system willing to fully examine every decision that led to his death. We will continue standing beside them and demanding transparency, truth and justice every step of the way.”

Lea Skene of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Cutting GLP-1 access hurts patients, and insurers, long-term
text:
While health insurers celebrate rebounding profits, let’s not lose sight of the fact that people are being denied access to needed treatments for a chronic disease (“Insurers rebound after cuts in coverage,” Page A1, May 16).

For many patients, GLP-1 medicines are the first tools proven to help them manage obesity and by extension the 200-plus health conditions associated with it. I lost 128 pounds with a GLP-1 medication. Access to this care changed my life.

There is a state proposal to take these same treatments away from patients with low incomes who are disproportionately affected by obesity and cannot pay out of pocket.

Cutting care that prevents emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and complications from obesity only means we’ll need to pay for the disease later. And that cost will be more than a dollar amount.

Let’s encourage our state leaders and legislators to act with compassion and with an eye toward the promise of improved public health and long-term savings these medicines offer.

Michael Donnelly-Boylen

Dorchester

The writer is a patient advocate with the Obesity Action Coalition.

title: Boston still runs on Dunkin’. But a new coffee culture is taking hold.
text:
“I never thought coffee could taste like that,” the 35-year-old said.

He’s been trying to convince Boston of the same ever since.

Katisomsakul is part of a new generation of immigrant and Asian American entrepreneurs rethinking the traditional cafe with scrappy pop-ups and temporary concepts inside bars, gyms, and galleries across Boston. Together, they’re trying to transform a city long defined by convenience coffee into one driven by craft and cultural identity, even as the economics of Boston are increasingly stacked against them.

Even as independent operators like Katisomsakul are multiplying, commercial rents are soaring and chains are quickly adapting to trends.

But while Boston may still run on Dunkin’, its next generation of coffee drinkers increasingly wants something else.

Nearing closing time at Newbery, there was hardly an empty seat. Customers sipped light roasts, lingering over them like tea. Next door, Dunkin’ didn’t have a single customer sitting inside.

“The coffee scene is changing,” said Katisomsakul. “The industry has been ready for it. Finally, so is Boston.”

Whether Boston’s new wave of independent operators can survive may be another question entirely.

“At this rate, it’s going to be a whole lot of major corporations versus an army of independents,” said Tam Le, owner of Càphê Collective, a new Vietnamese cafe attached to a Cambridge art gallery. “National brands are knocking on Boston’s doorsteps. Those players will always have the marketing budgets, consultants, and ability to quickly add new items.”

Boston’s current coffee boom didn’t emerge out of nowhere. The city’s most recent coffee movement arrived in the 2000s and early 2010s, when specialty shops such as George Howell Coffee, Thinking Cup, Pavement Coffeehouse, and Barismo introduced single-origin beans and meticulous pour-overs.

But while craft coffee has long flourished in other Northeast cities, these previous spurts struggled to penetrate beyond Boston’s affluent neighborhoods. Some locals viewed $8 pour-overs as elitist and for yuppie newcomers, while Dunkin’ remained synonymous with the city’s working-class identity.

Today’s wave reflects a broader shift toward Thai beans, Vietnamese coffee, Japanese matcha, and social media-driven aesthetics where bright colors, white fluffy cold foam, and sweeter flavors reflect the tastes of a younger, more diverse Boston.

“Starbucks created coffee culture. But Generation Z and millennials don’t know anything other than coffee culture,” said Brian Warrener, director of the Center for Beverage Education & Innovation at Johnson & Wales University.

He said the region’s younger generation isn’t ashamed to swap the “difficult to consume” drinks such as bitter black coffee, hoppy IPAs, and dry wine with lots of tannins, for lighter, smoother, and sweeter choices.

“Starbucks and Dunkin’ now represent a commoditization of that culture. These generations expect more, and want everything to be an experience,” he said.

Americans are drinking more coffee, with 66 percent of adults reportedly drinking a cup every day. A recent Toast analysis found a bump in barista-crafted drinks that many people don’t have the skills or time to make at home. Latte orders rose 4 percent in 2025, while regular drip coffee sales fell by nearly the same amount.

Many of the same trends driving Boston’s indie coffee boom are also being rapidly adopted by the chains the newcomers are taking on.

Blank Street Coffee, the venture capital-backed chain that’s expanding rapidly, has embraced Gen Z-focused matcha drinks, now accounting for 50 percent of its business.

Starbucks and Dunkin’, which is attempting to go public for a third time, still dominate the market. But both chains have recently closed underperforming stores, are reconsidering their retail footprint, and introduced trendier items, such as dirty soda and protein-rich drinks.

Many of Boston’s newest coffee businesses don’t have a permanent address as owners avoid costs of traditional storefronts. Even established operators said Boston is becoming increasingly difficult.

“The challenge is finding locations and rents that actually can sustain an independent business,” said Andy LoPilato, CEO of Pavement Coffeehouse, a local chain still owned by its founder.

For many entering Boston’s coffee scene, the math behind opening a traditional cafe no longer works.

“We looked at different places all over Boston and surrounding areas, and it all ranges from $6,000 at the lowest to $22,000 a month,” to rent a retail space, said Najma Mohamed, who cofounded Espresso East, a yellow coffee truck that’s parked along the Neponset Greenway Trail, behind a CrossFit in Dorchester. It’s not visible from the street, but customers line up for lattes with flavors like maple sea salt, pistachio, Dutch cookie, and even baklava.

The coffee truck also serves a fig matcha that uses tea from a Japanese farm the owners have traveled to. That’s a menu that would have been considered nearly unthinkable at an indie shop two decades ago when French vanilla, mocha, and hazelnut were largely the only flavors. Then, being an aficionado meant being a purist.

Mohamed and her sister, who were born in Kenya, started planning Espresso East in 2023, in their early 20s. They pulled personal loans, credit cards, and their savings to make it happen. Opening a truck dramatically lowered the barrier. The sisters now own the truck debt-free. A brick-and-mortar would have required a weightier upfront investment between rent, build-outs, utilities, permits, and staffing.

“We stopped doing the math as soon as we saw the monthly lease amount alone,” said Mohamed.

On a recent Saturday, Simon Ngo and Tiffany Zheng were in Kenmore Square at The Handle Bar, vigorously whisking matcha powder to serve dozens of sweaty young people who had just finished a workout class. This spring, they launched Nomu, a roaming pop-up cafe serving ceremonial-grade Uji matcha, after traveling to Japan and learning about the tea.

Sarah Chan, 25, snagged one. “It’s nice to get matcha from an Asian-owned business by people who know what they’re doing,” said Chan.

Young Bostonians “see rising prices and want to actually know where the ingredients are coming from,” said Ngo, an East Boston native whose parents immigrated from Vietnam. “If they’re paying seven to eight dollars for a drink, they want to know it’s one of the best things they’re going to find in Boston.”

Le, of Càphê Collective, also owns Lê Madeline in Quincy. He remembers a moment after opening his first shop in Dorchester a decade ago where “typical blue collar Dunkin’ customers” first tried Vietnamese coffee.

“They were converted,” said Le.

Back at Merai in Brookline, Katisomsakul will soon take Newbery Street down a more traditional route, poised to open a storefront this summer. It’s a feat he never could have imagined — or afforded — when he started hosting pop-ups last year.

“I got my start selling coffee bags on a corner,” said Katisomsakul. “I think this is the beginning for coffee in Boston. I’m just a small piece of the movement.”

title: Memorial Drive shooting suspect declared dangerous, ordered held without bail
text:
During the hearing Thursday morning in Cambridge District Court, Middlesex prosecutors played a short video showing Brown allegedly opening fire on Memorial Drive. The popping of gunshots rang out in an otherwise silent courtroom.

Citing the video and Brown’s criminal history dating back to his teen years, Assistant Middlesex District Attorney Nicole L. Allain argued he should be held without bail under the state’s dangerousness law.

District Court Judge David E. Frank agreed.

Brown’s public defender Carolyn I. McGowan didn’t challenge the dangerousness request.

But McGowan said there would be a vigorous defense at trial.

“There are miles to go in this case,” she said, also appearing via video conference from Brown’s bedside.

From the hospital bed, Brown wore a face mask and kept the covers pulled up to his chin. He didn’t speak during the hearing but appeared somewhat more alert than during his arraignment last week. He’s being treated for gunshot wounds to his “lower extremities,” officials have said.

Speaking from the bench, the judge said the information provided by prosecutors led him to conclude that Brown poses a danger to the public.

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime on May 11, not long after a Massachusetts parole officer called 911 to report that Brown was suicidal and armed with an assault rifle. The officer said Brown had an extensive criminal record, including a 2020 shootout with Boston police in the South End, along with a history of crack cocaine use and mental health problems. He had recently been discharged from a psychiatric hospital.

His long and complicated history with the criminal justice system includes a 2021 sentencing decision that has repeatedly drawn criticism for its apparent leniency. After the 2020 shootout with Boston police officers in the South End, now retired Superior Court judge Janet L. Sanders sentenced him to six years in prison, less than the 10-year sentence prosecutors had requested. Sanders had said she was persuaded by Brown’s intellectual gifts, his commitment to fatherhood, and promises to keep his life on track.

When Brown was released in May 2025, he was accepted into a yearlong re-entry program through the Tufts University Prison Initiative, but officials said he stopped attending in February.

In the hours preceding the Memorial Drive shooting, Brown repeatedly told his parole officer he was suicidal and displayed the assault rifle he allegedly later used, according to police and prosecutors.

The officer called 911 and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester, but he wasn’t home when officers got there. Boston police pinged his phone and tracked him to Cambridge.

Less than two hours after the 911 call, Brown began randomly shooting while walking down Memorial Drive, according to prosecutors. Panicked motorists ran for cover, some hiding under their cars.

Brown has been charged in Cambridge District Court with six felonies and two misdemeanors, including assault to murder, attempted assault and battery with a firearm, and gun and ammunition charges.

He pleaded not guilty last week, also from his hospital bed, appearing heavily medicated during a relatively short arraignment hearing.

In court on Thursday, prosecutors cited Brown’s long criminal history, including convictions from other states. Records show he was charged with armed robbery as a teenager in 1994. In 1999, he was charged with assaulting a Michigan corrections employee and escaping from jail. His other convictions include drug and gun offenses in Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

The May 2020 police shooting unfolded after someone called 911 and said a man was “talking crazy” and carrying a gun, according to court records. The caller and three other people were moving stuff into an apartment on Northampton Street when the man approached them, asked where they were from multiple times, then told them to “call your boys” and reached into his bag — where he had a firearm, a police report says.

When Boston police responded and found Brown a block away in the South End, he “appeared agitated,” leading officers to believe he could be an “emotionally disturbed person,” according to court records. He then pushed one of the officers, threw his backpack, and started running, according to police. During the ensuing chase, he started shooting at officers, who fired back. No one was injured and Brown was taken into custody.

In the immediate aftermath of the shootout, one of the responding officers, who said he was in shock, wondered aloud how he’d escaped uninjured, court records say. Brown responded with something to the effect of: “I don’t know, I can’t shoot,” according to the records.

That was a few months after Brown had been released from prison after serving time for a 2014 stabbing.

Brown “had been keeping up with his mental health conditions during his initial months on probation, but with the COVID outbreak, had lacked the ability to maintain services and had suffered from a deteriorated mental state as a result,” the records say.

Police reports describe somewhat similar circumstances in the stabbing case, which also took place in the South End. Brown approached a group of people and asked them: “Where you boys from,” according to a police report. He stabbed one man in the stomach, chased them with a knife, and then stabbed another man in the chest, police said.

title: Fire crews remove man from elevator shaft at Fields Corner MBTA station
text:
Boston firefighters removed a man who was apparently trapped inside an elevator shaft at the Fields Corner MBTA station, officials said Saturday.

The man gained access to the station “either late [Friday] night or in the early hours of [Saturday] morning,” according to Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan. After entering from the roof, the man eventually became stuck in the front portion of the shaft.

Witnesses eventually heard banging and called for assistance, according to WCVB-TV.

The man, whose name was not released, told rescuers he was homeless and had been seeking a place to sleep when he entered the station, Sullivan said. He is expected to face trespassing charges.

The Boston Fire Department did not return a request for comment Saturday night.

No further information was immediately available

title: Prom is crazy expensive. This fairy-prom mother gives students their storybook dance for free.
text:
Over the last decade, Rapo’s charity,Giving the Glam, has helped over a thousand Massachusetts students afford the dance of their dreams. She gives high schoolers free ballgowns and suits expertly fitted by seamstresses; a glam squad for hair, nails, and makeup; and even a ride in a Ferrari with a police escort to the party.

As prices surge on everything fromtomatoes to coffee to beef, more parents can’t dish out the $1,000 it typically costs for a storybook prom. Teens are left scouring for gowns, borrowing outfits from relatives, and embellishing old dresses with tricks from TikTok. But people like Rapo are stepping in to fill an increasing need because they believe every student deserves that fairy tale.

Last week, prom festivities kicked off at midday at Rapo’s sprawling house in Dover, about 15 miles outside Boston. It was the big night for seniors at Cristo Rey, a Catholic high school in Dorchester that serves families with limited economic means.

In Rapo’s living room, two long tables were covered in an array of high heels, designer clutches, and men’s dress shoes. More tables held a rainbow of nail polish, lipsticks, and enough makeup to fill a stand at a Sephora. One at a time, 45 high school seniors rushed into the pop-up dressing room to try on bow-ties and necklaces covered in rhinestones.

“I never thought prom day would be like this,” said senior Abdiel Reyes. “It feels like I’m in the movies.”

Upstairs in a guest bedroom, Acosta had a fresh manicure and hair blowout when she slipped into a $600 gown that had been altered just for her. Like all the other teens, she will get to keep the dress.

“I feel like I’m glowing,” Acosta said.

Her mother, a social worker named Aracelis Acosta, was relieved when the school announced it was partnering with Giving the Glam.

“With everything being so expensive,” Aracelis Acosta said, “I wasn’t sure I could give her the prom she always deserved.”

One of the charity’s volunteers, who all wore black T-shirts with the nonprofit’s logo, knelt down before Acosta to help her adjust the straps on her black heels. Another volunteer, Josias Barbosa, closed his Loov Concept salon in Medford to curl and style students’ hair for the big night.

They were part of an army of 25 helpers who had traveled from as far away as Fall River and Nashua, N.H., to give students the royal prom treatment. Most of the volunteers grew up struggling in Brazil and want to help those who need a lift.

That’s what inspired Rapo to launch her charity. She grew up in Favela do Aço, a dense, low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, and she sees herself in today’s urban high schoolers.

“I want them to feel like a million bucks,” Rapo said.

The cost of prom has nearly doubled over the last 16 years, according to research by Jay Zagorsky of Boston University’s Questrom School of Business. The big ticket items include outfits, accessories, salon visits, and limo rides. Tickets to the dance can range from $30 to $150 in Massachusetts.

A number of local organizations work to make prom memorable on a budget. Anton’s Cleaners helps spearhead Belle of the Ball, which provides used prom dresses and accessories free of charge to higher schoolers.

Hundreds of girls referred by their schools flock to Hynes Convention Center every year to sift through thousands of donated gowns. A swarm of volunteers act as personal stylists, helping them find the perfect dress, shoes, and bag.

Demand has surged since the pandemic, according to Anton’s marketing director, Stephanie Littefield. They now invite 1,800 students to participate, up from 1,200 in 2019.

“Everything is expensive today,” Littlefield said.

The issue goes beyond cost, said Shauna King, a marketing teacher at Plymouth South High School. Students are spending more because they want their photos to meet the impossible standards they see online, King said.

King runs the Massachusetts chapter of Becca’s Closet, a national initiative that helps students find gowns. A dressing room built into Plymouth South High School allows students from all over the state to make an appointment and browse through donated dresses.

Rapo at Giving the Glam doesn’t rely on used outfits or do-it-yourself projects. The charity provides brand new gowns and celebrity quality makeovers. Rapo typically spends between $700 and $1,000 on each student, she said, and raises between $150,000 and $200,000 every year to make it happen.

“Helping kids afford the prom of their dreams isn’t about the money,” Rapo said. “It’s about teaching them to give back to the community.“

Earlier this month, Giving the Glam helped teens at Brockton High School, many of whom have lived in homeless shelters or were in foster care.

Marc Laviolette, 19, walked into the dance in a shiny pink suit that Rapo’s team helped him pick out. He said he never felt “so loved” by his classmates.

“They told me I should have been nominated for prom king,” Laviolette said. “I got my dream prom.”

title: ‘One of our best’: Boston firefighter killed battling three-alarm fire in Dorchester
text:
The fire broke out about 8 p.m. Saturday, and five residents were home at the time. All residents escaped safely without injury, though all were displaced.

The blaze spread through all three floors and burned through the roof, according to the Boston Fire Department, which said firefighters deployed “multiple ground and aerial ladders” to keep the flames from spreading to neighboring homes. Video posted to social media showed flames shooting from the roof of the building.

By 8:32 p.m., officials said the heavy fire had been “knocked down,” with crews continuing an aggressive interior and exterior attack to contain the blaze.

A mayday call went out for an injured firefighter. Minutes later, a second alert reported that the firefighter was being transported to a hospital under police escort, where he was later pronounced dead.

Fire officials said they could not provide additional details because an investigation into the fire and Kilduff’s death remained ongoing.

Early Sunday, rows of firefighters, police officers, and other personnel stood at attention as Kilduff’s body was loaded into an ambulance and taken from the hospital to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

On Sunday night, despite steady rain, dozens of firefighters and police officers lined Albany Street outside the medical examiner’s office to honor Kilduff during a dignified transfer to a funeral home in West Roxbury. Flashing blue police lights and red firetrucks illuminated the street as a hearse carrying Kilduff slowly pulled away under escort.

Kilduff, a father of two, was a third-generation Boston firefighter and a US Marine veteran. He was remembered not only for his 24 years with the Boston Fire Department, but also for the compassion and energy he brought to volunteer work supporting families of fallen service members and first responders.

Kilduff — known as “BK” — was assigned to Rescue Company 2 and was a “quintessential rescue man,” Kelly said. He is the first Boston firefighter to die in the line of duty in more than a decade.

“He’s probably been to more fires than any firefighter currently employed by the Boston Fire Department and in this region,” Kelly said, adding the crew hasn’t slept since the fire.

On Sunday afternoon, firefighters at the fire station in Egleston Square hung black drapes from the bay doors and laid flowers on the ground.

The crew described Kilduff as the lifeblood of the station — “the guy that took care of everything” — who even kept retirees looped in to firehouse events.

On the floor near a fire rig was an outline of Kilduff’s shoes where he had left them the night of the fire, his initials “BK” inside.

“We gotta write ‘too big to fill’ on them,” Kelly said.

Inside the Rescue 2 break room on Sunday, the men who worked alongside Kilduff described him as the kind of rescuer who was either already at a trapped firefighter’s side, or sprinting toward them.

“That would be the only two modes BK would be in,” Kelly said.

Rescue 2 is a specialized company that responds to dangerous situations involving firefighters in distress. Kelly said Kilduff was among the few firefighters appointed directly to the unit because of his skill and experience.

Victor Gaybor, another Rescue 2 firefighter who was at the fire Saturday night, recalled his final interaction with Kilduff.

“We were on that fire floor in the back porch and like we always do, we take a moment and just bust each other’s chops a bit, we’d lighten the whole situation,” Gaybor said. “I went back downstairs to report to my lieutenant at the time, and what happened, happened. We just went out to see what we can do for BK.”

As they traded stories about Kilduff’s jokes and his “excellent” cooking, members of Rescue 2 team said they considered themselves family and felt as if they had lost a brother.

Kilduff’s two children were traveling and unable to reach the hospital Saturday night, Kelly said, adding that Rescue 2 would fully support the family.

Funeral arrangements were still being finalized Sunday, but union officials said services would likely take place this week.

“He’ll be buried with the highest honors available in the city and within our union,” said Sam Dillon, president of the Boston Firefighters Local 718.

On Saturday morning, before the fatal blaze, Kilduff helped rescue a homeless man “who was trapped in a confined space of an MBTA yard,” Kelly said.

Kilduff was also credited with helping save the life of a fellow firefighter who suffered cardiac arrest while battling a fire more than a month ago. Dillon said Kilduff rode to the hospital with the firefighter and performed CPR.

Michelle Caroline, a former volunteer coordinator for the Gary Sinise Foundation, said Kilduff became one of the organization’s core volunteers helping families of fallen military and first responders.

“He never backed down from a challenge and stepped in whenever or wherever needed,” Caroline said.

By Sunday afternoon, a small memorial had begun to take shape along the metal fence outside the home on Treadway Road. A photo of Kilduff smiling in his firefighter’s uniform sat above flowers, candles, toy firetrucks, and American and Irish flags.

Katelyn McCabe, 33, who lives across the street, said she spent much of Sunday helping build the memorial, including printing and framing a photo of Kilduff at a nearby Walgreens.

“Sometimes people say, ‘That’s what they signed up for,’ but you still expect them to come home,” McCabe said. She said her late grandfather served as a district fire chief in Boston.

McCabe said she came outside soon after the fire broke out and was there when Kilduff fell.

“I heard the impact, and then I heard ‘Mayday,’” she said. “I just can’t get it out of my mind.”

Nearby, a lone firetruck remained stationed outside the three-story home, where the charred interior was visible through shattered upper-floor windows.

Phat Dao, 56, was visiting a friend when he stepped outside Saturday night to find Treadway Road crowded with firetrucks as flames and smoke poured from the building.

Standing in the rain near Kilduff’s memorial Sunday, Dao said the firefighter’s death hit him hard because “he died helping people.”

“He’s a hero,” Dao said.

Kilduff’s father, who served as a Boston fire lieutenant, died in 2008, according to his obituary. The elder Robert Kilduff served as Local 718 vice president and founded the local’s Children’s Fund.

“Boston lost a hero,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement Sunday morning. “The Kilduff family has given everything in service to this country and this city. ... Boston will forever honor Firefighter Kilduff’s dedication and service with the most profound gratitude.”

Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall said Kilduff was a “firefighter’s firefighter.”

“It’s going to stick with us for a long time,” he said. “There’s no routine fire, there’s no routine call. And you’re never truly safe until you get home.”

On Sunday morning, Governor Maura Healey ordered US and Massachusetts flags lowered to half-staff at all state buildings in honor of Kilduff.

“His death serves as a reminder of the dangers firefighters face every day when they put their lives on the line to keep our communities safe,” Healey said in a statement.

Edward Kelly, general president of the International Association of Fire Fighters, called Kilduff the union’s “unsung hero.”

“He did everything behind the scenes for our union,” Kelly said. “He mentored fire unions all throughout the state. He was just someone that left an indelible mark.”

The last two Boston firefighters killed in the line of duty were Lieutenant Edward J. Walsh Jr. and Michael R. Kennedy, who died in 2014 while battling a nine-alarm blaze in the Back Bay.

At the time, Kilduff spoke to the Globe about the somber rituals held to honor fallen firefighters, including the black shroud draped across uniform badges, the honor guard, and the bagpipes.

“It’s a show of respect for the family, and it’s a tribute from us as firefighters,” said Kilduff, then the director of operations for the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts. “It’s really hard to explain, except to say that our job, if you break it all down to the bare bones, [is that] we show up at somebody’s really bad day and try to make it a little better.”

Globe correspondent Adam Sennott contributed to this report.

title: ‘We’re going to need four people to replace him’: Community mourns Boston firefighter killed in line of duty
text:
On the brick wall of the Rescue Co. 2 firehouse in Roxbury, five plaques commemorate the lives of Boston firemen from that unit who have died in the line of duty. The newest plaque remembers the oldest tragedy, the death of Charles Buchanan in 1947. Buchanan only got a plaque in 2022 after a modern-day fireman dove deep in the archives and asked the fire commissioner to honor him.

What that modern-day fireman didn’t know then was that in just a few years his own plaque would be the sixth to be mounted on that brick wall.

Robert Kilduff Jr. died Saturday after suffering severe injuries working to extinguish a blaze on Treadway Road in Dorchester. On Memorial Day, residents and firefighters stopped by the firehouse to pay their respects, leaving flowers, American flags, and even a firetruck toy.

Kilduff’s colleagues say they are devastated by his loss, remembering him as a model citizen who went above and beyond his duties. A third-generation Boston fireman, he knew all the dates and details of historical fires in the city and acted as the firehouse’s informal historian. Serving the community was his calling, his colleagues said.

“We’re going to need four people to replace him,” said Lieutenant Glenn McGillivray. “His character is extremely difficult to replace. We can get another body in here, but it’s not going to be BK.”

Among his colleagues, the 53-year-old West Roxbury resident was known as BK or Bobby.

McGillivray said Kilduff was going back to school to get a degree in fire science. He was constantly learning, “trying to better himself, better the job, better the firehouse. That was BK,” McGillivray said.

Kilduff was admired for being an excellent problem solver, finding simple solutions for complicated situations, said Lieutenant Gilbert Quinchia. Most firemen aspired to be like him, he said.

“This is where he wanted to be,” Quinchia said. “This was his calling. He was happy to be here every day.”

At the firehouse Monday, Quinchia welcomed community members who wanted to show solidarity to the men currently working. A mother with her daughters carrying American flags. A couple with their son carrying flowers. Residents who knew Kilduff.

Quinchia said a resident who stopped by the firehouse remembered Kilduff from a time he helped her with a car fire. Quinchia said people don’t usually remember firefighters’ names and faces. That’s how special Kilduff was to the community, he said.

While the firehouse is open and serving the community, its members are mourning.

“If you can somehow relate to losing a close family member, that’s how we feel,” Quinchia said. “Not losing a coworker, that’s a very different thing. We lost family.”

In 2022, when Kilduff honored Buchanan, Kilduff told The Boston Globe firefighters’ work is “unique.”

“We show up on people’s really bad days, and try to make them a little bit better,” Kilduff said then.

Kilduff was so proud to recognize Buchanan in 2022 that he framed a news article about the event and put it up on the firehouse’s wall, Quinchia said.

The Professional Firefighters of Massachusetts has organized a fund-raiser for Kilduff. The GoFundMe page intends to support his two children Mason and Hanna Jane, the International Association of Firefighters said in a statement Monday.

“Kilduff served the people of Boston for 24 years and came from a family with deep roots in the fire service,” the union said. “He was a Marine, a father, and a proud member of the Boston Fire Department and Boston Firefighters IAFF Local 718.”

The Greg Hill Foundation has also set up a fund-raising page for Kilduff’s family, raising over $19,000 as of Monday. And the Tunnel to Towers Foundation said it would pay off the remaining mortgage on his home and support educational expenses for his children.

The Saturday blaze spread through all three floors of a Dorchester house and burned through the roof, according to the Fire Department. Five residents were home when the fire broke out and escaped safely without injury.

A wake will be held Sunday at St. Theresa of Avila Parish in West Roxbury, with a funeral Mass at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross in the South End on Monday.

It was not yet clear when Kilduff‘s plaque will be added to the firehouse’s wall.

Hannah Goeke contributed to this report.

Marcela Rodrigues can be reached at marcela.rodrigues@globe.com.

title: ‘Mayday, mayday, mayday’: Radio calls show urgent response to blaze that led to death of Boston firefighter
text:
“The men and women that come out to do this ... we’re not safe until we actually get home,” Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall said at a press conference early Sunday morning, hours after Kilduff’s death. “You could be returning from a fire, you could be returning from a call, but you’re never truly safe until you’re home.”

A 24-year veteran of the force, Kilduff was the first Boston firefighter to die in the line of duty in over a decade. He was a member of Rescue Company 2, a specialized unit that responds to dangerous situations involving firefighters in distress.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation, officials said.

Radio transmissions, videos, and photos captured the urgent response Saturday night.

8:05 p.m. — A fire box was struck in the Savin Hill area of Dorchester. Within a few minutes, dispatchers identified the building as 18 Treadway Road; the fire is on the third floor.

8:10 p.m. — The first ladder engines reach Treadway Road. Firefighters report “smoke showing” from a 2 1/2 story wood-frame building, according to radio transmissions from Broadcastify. The fire is concentrated in the rear of the home.

8:12 p.m. — Firefighters called in a second alarm.

8:14 p.m. — One firefighter, requesting another water line to the rear of the building, warned in a radio transmission that “the rear stairs are very narrow.”

8:15 p.m. — By this point, the blaze had spread to the front of the building, with large flames seen bursting through the roof of the home. Ladders are attacking the fire through the roof.

8:20 p.m. — Firefighters began “making a push onto [the] third floor,” per radio transmissions.

8:21 p.m. — The fire was raised to a third alarm.

8:27 p.m. — A firefighter said in a radio transmission that the heavy fire appeared to be “knocked down.” He advised, though, that “all companies” were still working the scene.

8:33 p.m. — Another firefighter again warned about access to the upper floors of the home. “Can you have all members use caution on those rear stairs? They’re very compromised at this point,” he said. “Rear stairs.”

8:38 p.m. — Dispatchers gave the all clear for third-alarm fire companies to begin withdrawing from the scene.

8:48 p.m — The Boston Fire Department posted photos of the rear of the home, showing a visible fire damage and a gutted back porch. “Great job to stop the fire from traveling to the adjacent homes,” the department wrote.

8:50 p.m. — A firefighter called in a mayday to report that Kilduff had fallen three stories. “Mayday, mayday, mayday; we had a member go off the third floor porch.”

8:51 p.m. – All firefighters were ordered off the porch.

8:52 p.m. — Boston EMS transmissions reported “an injured firefighter off the roof.” A firefighter, urgency in his voice, pressed dispatchers to have police clear a path to Boston Medical Center — “now.”

8:58 p.m. — EMS reported that one firefighter, in critical condition, was being transported to the emergency room at Boston Medical Center.

12:03 a.m. — Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall announced that the injured firefighter had died, identifying him as Robert Kilduff Jr.

John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed.

title: Boston community groups protest Mayor Wu’s $4.9 billion budget proposal over cut grants
text:
They also demanded that the Boston City Council reject the mayor’s budget proposal to pressure her to increase spending to continue the programs. An effort by some councilors to do so failed after the the body deadlocked on a vote last week, with the councilors split on how to push back on Wu’s planned cuts. The council has the power to reject, reduce, or change certain line items in the mayor’s budget proposal, as long as the amendments do not increase the total amount the mayor is proposing to spend.

Following the rally Tuesday, around 100 protesters signed up to testify and speak out against Wu’s spending plan at a council budget hearing that stretched into the late hours of the evening.

Carliz Mañana, 18, a high school senior from Dorchester, said she got a job at the nonprofit Youth Justice and Power Union through the city’s year-round youth jobs program, which now is at risk of ending next school year.

“It’s honestly meant so much to me. . . . [Without it] I would be in a different crowd, I would be doing different things, I wouldn’t know anything about what’s going on in my community,” Mañana said in an interview.

“I want the mayor and all of the city councilors to know that if you don’t fund the community (programs) . . . you’re disappointing all of us and we’re not going to back off,” she continued.

Wu’s office did not provide a statement in response to the Globe’s request for comment Tuesday.

Wu and other city officials have warned for months that Boston, like many cities across the state, is facing a challenging and tight budget season, as it grapples with skyrocketing costs related to health insurance and snow removal, along with extensive state tax-cap restrictions on how municipalities can raise revenue.

Wu is already seeking the council’s approval to use $70 million from the city’s emergency reserves to cover deficits in the city’s and Boston Public Schools’ current budgets.

Some councilors have suggested that Wu’s administration either use less conservative revenue projections, or dip into the city’s so-called “rainy day” reserves, to fund the programs in jeopardy. Wu has said she does not plan to do either, calling the alternatives “fiscally irresponsible,” to the outrage of some protesters.

“What is it still sitting there for? These are rainy days, these are storming days, that’s what it’s for,” Teri Trotman, a 62-year-old Dorchester resident, told The Boston Globe. “People need to be able to live, and if you’re cutting all their programs, that means you don’t care, you don’t care about the city that you’re the mayor of.”

Protesters argued that many of the grant programs direct resources to marginalized communities — such as low-income residents, seniors, Black and brown students, and immigrants — who are already struggling to make ends meet, or facing attacks by the Trump administration.

They also emphasized that Wu’s move to end the year-round youth jobs program comes after the School Committee approved a plan to cut 300 to 400 staff jobs, citing significant cost increases and financial challenges due to declining enrollment.

“Our students only have one life. . . . They can’t redo these vital years, and if we take [resources] away from them, we’re going to see the impact later,” said Lea Serena, vice president of the Boston Teachers Union. “Find more money and put it where it belongs.”

Wu has previously described her budget proposal as “tough” but necessary belt-tightening to protect essential city services amid surging costs.

Wu’s administration has also noted that her plan maintains funding for a number of initiatives — including a program that guarantees summer jobs for BPS students; new recruit classes for police, fire, and EMS; weekend and evening hours at libraries and youth and family centers; and free English language classes for adults through the Boston Public Library.

Jaya Savita, 29, executive director of the Asian Pacific Islanders Civic Action Network, said she understands the city is facing financial challenges, but she can’t support a budget that increases the Police Department budget, but cuts funding for senior programming, youth jobs, housing support, food access, and immigrant communities.

“I understand that [Wu is], in theory, between a rock and a hard place, but I’m disappointed,” Savita said. “This isn’t the mayor I voted for.”

title: Winthrop man charged with manslaughter in wife’s death says shooting was an accident, gun ‘just went off’
text:
“I can’t do this,” the relative said.

According to a police report, Brewer told investigators that his wife was lying in bed when he removed a gun from the pocket of a jacket while standing next to the bed. Brewer said that neither the jacket nor the gun belonged to him, according to police.

Brewer said he was holding the gun when it “just went off,” police said. He denied touching or pulling the trigger.

Officers had responded to a 911 call at the Beacon Street apartment shortly after 8:30 p.m. and found the couple inside. The woman was lying on a bed with an apparent gunshot wound to the abdomen, according to a police report.

Berry-Brewer was conscious and told officers that her husband had shot her but described the shooting as “an accident.”

She was taken to Massachusetts General Hospital, where she died a short time later, police said.

A woman told police she went to the apartment after hearing a loud bang she believed was a gunshot. She knocked on the door and Brewer eventually let her inside, where she provided Berry-Brewer medical aid, police said.

Police recovered a Smith & Wesson gun in the apartment, she said. Brewer was also charged with illegal gun possession.

Brewer’s lawyer, Lorenz Perez, told reporters that his client insists the shooting was an accident. He said the gun was found in a bag, not a jacket, but declined to comment on where the weapon came from.

The couple married on May 1, according to a longtime friend.

They met when Berry-Brewer was working as a medical assistant at Massachusetts General Hospital in 2023. Brewer was being treated for a bacterial infection.

By 2024, they were a couple, and in 2025, Berry-Brewer wrote to a judge, asking that he be released from jail, where he was being held for allegedly stabbing a man on the steps of a church near Boston Common, court records show.

“Sean gave me back my humanity. Made me want and expect more from myself. He asked for my help; in doing so, he aided me,” she wrote. “I have no qualms about standing firm, in defense of a person who I believe in. A person I am sure will leave this world greater than he found it.”

Brewer has a history of homelessness, mental illness, and violence, court records show. In 2024, he allegedly stabbed a fellow homeless man during an argument on the steps of St. Paul’s Church in Boston, according to court records.

Brewer spent nearly two years in custody, while also serving a separate Middlesex Superior Court sentence, until Feb. 18, when Hayden’s office dropped the stabbing charge because the victim would not testify.

“Yeah, like I said, I no longer want to go further,” the alleged victim told prosecutors. “I’ll find him on the streets.”

Berry-Brewer’s letter of support was filed in connection with the 2024 case, records show. At the time, his defense attorney cited the “long-term and highly supportive relationship” between the two as justification for Brewer’s release.

The judge refused to free him at the time, but he was released Feb. 18 after prosecutors dropped the case because the victim refused to testify, records show.

In the same case file, Brewer described his life, writing that he became homeless when he was 13 but still managed to reach the 11th grade at Dorchester High School.

He was married and became a father in his 20s, but was soon overwhelmed by his mental illnesses, including bipolar disorder, that led to substance abuse, homelessness, and interaction with the criminal justice system, according to a letter Brewer wrote to a judge and court records.

Judge Debra A. DelVecchio set bail for the manslaughter charge at $100,000 and revoked Brewer’s bail on pending charges of assault and battery on a police officer.

Teneesha Singletary said she and Berry-Brewer met in the first grade at Agassiz Elementary School in Jamaica Plain, and remained close friends for the rest of their lives.

When Singletary’s first child was born, she asked Berry-Brewer to be the girl’s godmother.

“If there’s one word I could use to describe her, it would be ‘irreplaceable,’” said Singletary, 48. “There will be a hole in my life for the rest of my life.”

As young women, she and Berry-Brewer were active in Black civic life and attended New Covenant Christian Church, now Jubilee Christian Church, in Mattapan, Singletary said. Berry-Brewer loved being in nature and immersing herself in music and literature, she said.

Berry-Brewer worked at Mass General and moved to Winthrop from Beacon Hill in the past year, according to Singletary.

Singletary and her family moved to Georgia about eight years ago, but the two friends stayed in close touch, she said. She said she had never met Sean Brewer.

“If he indeed did this, he has no idea the trail of devastation he has left,” Singletary said.

John R. Ellement of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: 18-year-old allegedly punches police officer in face outside Dorchester party
text:
A Boston police officer was punched in the face during a confrontation with four men who were allegedly standing guard at a party in Dorchester on Monday, police said.

The officer and other members of the Youth Violence Strike Force were patrolling in the Geneva Avenue area around 9:30 p.m. Monday, which led them to the intersection of Westville Avenue and Boyd Street, where a party was being thrown nearby, police said in a statement.

“As officers conducted a U-turn, they observed a group of four males standing completely still on all four corners of the intersection, police said. “The four individuals who appeared to be standing guard acting as security for the party on Westville Street. The males were all wearing hoods with masks covering their faces.”

Officers stepped out of their vehicles, approached the four people, “and engaged in casual conversation,” police said. At that point, one of the four ran away, police said.

“When an officer tried to prevent the male’s flight, the suspect turned around and punched the officer in the face with a closed fist,” police said.

Armanti Perez-Taylor, 18, of Dorchester, was quickly taken into custody and charged with assault and battery on a police officer and resisting arrest, police said.

Meanwhile, other officers arrived and “attempted to frisk” a second man on the street corner and “immediately felt the handle of a firearm inside” his waistband, police said.

As officers tried to take him into custody, Khyier Winfield Young, 18, allegedly tried to grab ahold of the gun during a brief struggle, police said.

After his arrest, police allegedly recovered a 9mm pistol loaded with nine bullets. The gun had been reported stolen, police said.

The remaining people at the scene were identified and released.

Young was charged with several gun violations, including carrying a loaded firearm without a license and receiving stolen property. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday in Dorchester Municipal Court, where bail was set at $1,000 and he was ordered to wear a GPS monitoring bracelet, court records show.

Perez-Taylor pleaded not guilty at the Dorchester courthouse Tuesday and was released on personal recognizance, ordered to wear a GPS monitoring device, and abide by a 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew, records show.

John R. Ellement can be reached at john.ellement@globe.com. Follow him @JREbosglobe.

title: Popular Open Newbury Street events will be scaled back this summer, Mayor Wu says
text:
The city piloted Open Newbury Street in 2016. That event — where the tony Back Bay street was blocked off to cars so pedestrians could wander freely among vendors and businesses — was so successful it continued to grow over the years, and expanded to other neighborhoods in 2022.

Last year, Newbury Street was closed on 10 summer Sundays and once in the winter for a holiday stroll. Open Streets events were also held in the summer and fall in Roxbury, Hyde Park, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Jamaica Plain.

Last week, the city announced four Open Streets events planned for this year, starting with Jamaica Plain on Aug. 2, then Mattapan on Sept. 12, Allston/Brighton on Oct. 4, and Roslindale on Oct. 18.

Meanwhile, dates for Open Newbury Street are still being finalized, Wu said on Reddit.

In addition to some of the larger events on the calendar, Wu said neighborhood block parties will also be held this summer, and that World Cup watch parties will be hosted by small businesses and the city.

“We expect to have the same number of Open Newbury dates as we always do,” Marcela Dwork, Wu’s press secretary, said by email.

Meg Mainzer-Cohen, president of the Back Bay Association, which represents businesses in the neighborhood, said the organization has asked for fewer Open Newbury Street events in the past and continues to be in close communication with city officials about the dates for this year.

Although “there’s a lot of support” for Open Newbury Street events among retailers and restaurants on the street, Mainzer-Cohen said some have expressed concerns about there being too many in previous years.

Some businesses, like hair salons and bakeries, are less dependent on foot traffic, Mainzer-Cohen said. Outside vendors have also set up shop in front of stores before, causing confusion, she added.

“This is about a balanced approach,” she said. “We were happy to see some give and take.”

Boston has faced public criticism over its World Cup preparations compared to other cities, such as Philadelphia, where the marketing rollout has been smoothly run and well-funded. Meanwhile, Boston officials are currently locked in a battle with state transportation officials over closing a section of Summer Street to vehicle traffic for all seven local World Cup matches.

Wu said the Open Streets series will return to its regular programming next year.

“Each year we look at the entire calendar,” she said. “Once we close the books on FIFA and this big summer of mega events, we’ll be back in 2027 with more of a regular Open Streets schedule (and Open Newbury too)!”

Still, her response was met with some pushback online.

Echoing complaints dating back to her reelection bid last year that Wu has pulled back on her public transit and safe streets agenda, some bemoaned the lack of communication from her administration about Open Streets.

“Why hasn’t there been any proactive communication from your office about these street related initiatives? Lately it only seems like you make a statement when there’s enough social media outcry,” one person on Reddit replied to Wu. “I’m seeing cities across the country do way more in terms of street closures and pedestrian plazas. They’re not acting like they’re limited by these big events, they’re going all out because of them.”

title: ‘The light of our family’: Dorchester shooting victim had just launched career as a union carpenter
text:
Bala, 22, was fatally shot around 1 a.m. Friday after celebrating his friend’s graduation in Dorchester. Boston police officers responded to reports of gunfire on Bowdoin Street and found Bala with a gunshot wound, officials said.

By the time Dominique Bala arrived at the hospital, his son was already gone.

“I don’t know how this happened,” he said, shaking his head slowly.

Police have released few details about the shooting, including whether they believe the victim was targeted. No arrests have been made. Officials said homicide detectives are actively investigating.

Bala grew up in Boston, where his parents settled after immigrating from Senegal. He played basketball at Charlestown High School, loved to travel, and hoped to start his own business someday, his dad said.

“He was the light of our family,” Dominique Bala said during an interview Wednesday at his Dorchester home. “He was my only son.”

Overwhelmed with grief, he keeps returning to those lighthearted text threads, rereading them almost in disbelief. He scrolls past inside jokes, social media links, laughing emojis, and old family pictures — Gio playing basketball and posing with his youth soccer team.

Bala would often send photos and videos from work, showcasing his developing carpentry skills; they discussed flooring installation techniques, trading best practices.

Bala had joined a carpenters union after completing the rigorous training program, his father said. “He respected the work.”

He recently joked about how his muscles had grown from all the heavy lifting, Dominique Bala said, smiling at the happy memory.

The father said he doesn’t know how to process this grief.

Near the shooting scene, a sprawling memorial display has taken shape, covering the sidewalk with dozens of candles, flowers, balloons, and liquor bottles. There are also signs of Bala’s newfound passion: various tools, a mini construction helmet, and leather work boots covered in written messages.

“You were so excited about your new journey,” someone wrote in permanent marker.

In addition to construction, Bala worked part-time for a party rental company. He had been a car salesman and a security guard in the past, according to his dad.

“He knew how to hustle,” Dominique Bala said. “That work ethic he got from me.”

After moving to the United States in 1989, Dominique Bala worked as a contractor for the Navy before joining the federal government’s General Services Administration. He also picked up handyman jobs on the weekends, like painting and installing floors. And his son often wanted to come along for the ride, Dominique Bala said.

“We did so many things together,” he added.

In the hours before his death, Giovanni Bala went to a Cape Verdean restaurant in Dorchester, one of the family’s favorite spots, his dad said. He said a group was leaving when gunfire broke out.

Surveillance footage obtained by WCVB-TV shows the gunfight unfolding in a nearby parking lot, with multiple gunmen opening fire and ducking behind cars as bystanders scatter and run for cover.

Bala was shot in the chest, according to a police report. He was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

His death comes as city officials ramp up anti-violence efforts ahead of summer, when shootings often spike.

During a press conference last week to discuss those efforts, officials said gun violence is trending downward this year in Boston, which consistently ranks among the safest major cities in the country. Mayor Michelle Wu reiterated her administration’s holistic approach to crime-fighting, focused on addressing the root causes of violence through social services, workforce development, and other resources.

Bala was “well liked, hardworking, good to his family and friends,” state Senator Liz Miranda said in a social media post earlier this week. She said Dorchester residents and the local Cape Verdean community are deeply mourning the loss.

“This young man did everything right and he wasn’t able to go back home to his family,” she wrote. “Now is the time to double down on all fronts to ensure kids from our neighborhoods can enjoy themselves safely.”

title: Development would bring needed health care, housing to former Carney Hospital
text:
What will be important as the plan moves forward is ensuring the right mix of medical services — services that residents need and can access.

Carney Hospital sits on 12.8 acres of land in Dorchester owned by Apollo Global Management, a New York-based private equity firm.

The developers plan to demolish the existing hospital buildings. They would build a new 350,000-square-foot health care building, an education building geared toward training nurses, 200 units of senior housing, and 300 units of family housing, in addition to retail and open space. The senior housing is expected to include a memory care unit, assisted living units, and independent living units. The project is estimated to cost around $850 million, with at least the health care facility completed by 2030.

To their credit, the developers have been actively engaging the local community, holding around 35 community meetings before taking the first step in the city of Boston permitting process by filing a letter of intent on May 20. Although Apollo hasn’t garnered much local good will, due to its role in Steward’s operations and bankruptcy, HYM CEO Thomas O’Brien is a longtime Boston area developer and civic leader, while the Rev. Jeffrey Brown of My City at Peace also has deep roots in Boston city affairs.

Many of the decisions about the health care center will be made by its eventual operator. O’Brien told the editorial board he expects it will be run by a major local health system — he’s talking to Mass General Brigham, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Boston Medical Center, and Brown University Health. According to the developers, the health care center would not be a hospital but would include a yet-undetermined mix of services, potentially including emergency and urgent care, behavioral and mental health care, imaging services, primary care, or specialty care. (The housing on the site will be managed by HYM, who would hire an outside operator to run the senior housing.)

As the health system — and state health care regulators — considers any proposal, it should take into account the recommendations of a Dorchester Health Planning Working Group report and ensure that the site offers the services the surrounding communities need the most: namely, primary care, behavioral and mental health care, and emergency and urgent care.

When Carney Hospital was open, it had 50 inpatient psychiatric beds. Although the hospital also had medical-surgical beds, the most common reasons patients were hospitalized at Carney were for mental health disorders, including bipolar disorders and schizophrenia. Carney’s emergency department had around 30,000 visits a year, although the data suggest many of those could have been avoided with timely access to urgent or primary care.

Since Carney closed, the working group found, other local hospital emergency departments have been increasingly crowded while community health centers have had longer wait times. Codman Square Health Center is reporting a 4.5 month wait for a primary care physician.

The lack of those services today is a reason Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s office says any development must include health care uses that fill the gaps left by Carney’s closure. “Any proposal must include a committed health care partner with the capacity to deliver and sustain these critical services in the long term, so that residents and families have the care they deserve and are not left without options again,” a Wu spokesperson said in a statement sent to the editorial board.

Importantly, the health care system should also commit to ensuring that the services are accessible to patients with a variety of Medicaid plans. More than 70 percent of Carney Hospital patients had government health insurance, often MassHealth.

There may be community pushback on the size of the housing development. David Keenan, a member of the Dorchester Lower Mills Civic Association, told the editorial board he worries about traffic based on the number of family units being proposed. While developers should work with community members to address specific concerns, Boston and Massachusetts badly need more housing, including the type of one- to three-bedroom units this development is expected to generate. Developers say the housing would include 100 units for sale and 200 rental units, mostly market-rate housing with 20 percent income-restricted to adhere to Boston’s inclusionary zoning requirements.

The city of Boston should move expeditiously to consider the project. If the mix of services is right, the project has the potential to be a twofer — filling the gaps in health care created by Carney Hospital’s closure while moving the city toward its housing goals.

title: ‘He gave me a voice’: Roscoe Baker remembered as basketball star, community icon, champion of Boston’s young dreamers
text:
Tributes flowed last week for Baker, a Roxbury-raised resident of Dorchester who died May 17 of complications from an April stroke. He was 88.

Friends remembered him as a local basketball star, a community icon, a champion of the city’s young dreamers. One of Boston’s best all-around athletes of the 1950s and ’60s, he spent the following decades showing others how to be great.

“People called him the unofficial mayor of Boston,” said his daughter, Jillian Baker. “He was a tall guy with a big personality who really cared about his students, the community, the homeless, and how sports can be an avenue for youth to excel.”

Baker was a multisport star at Roxbury Memorial High, as a basketball guard, football quarterback, baseball pitcher, and track athlete. He led Delaware State basketball in scoring as a senior in 1961. Upon returning home, he filled it up for the semi-pro South End Bruins, coached by Jack Crump.

“Roscoe was a legend,” said teammate Ray Flynn of South Boston, the future Boston mayor. “I admired him. It was his sportsmanship on the court.”

Baker became a player-coach and a referee, working hundreds of college games over 50-plus years (including as one of the first officials in the Big East). In 1974, he did a Celtics-Bulls game at the Garden next to friend Ken Hudson, the NBA’s first Black full-time official.

Those two also combined, with others including Harris, Clarence “Jeep” Jones, Wayne Embry, and Rudy Cabral, in 1969 to create the Boston Neighborhood Basketball League. In a time where the city was torn apart by racial strife, the BNBL brought together different neighborhoods to compete on the outdoor courts.

“It took away the negativity of the busing era,” Harris said. “If you rode around the city at night, you’d see kids playing under the lights, teams of mixed races, making friendships that lasted for life.”

That group in 1972 formed the Boston Shootout, which quickly became America’s premier grassroots basketball tournament. Over the decades, it attracted the likes of Adrian Dantley, Tree Rollins, Patrick Ewing, Chris Mullin, Grant Hill, Kobe Bryant, Antoine Walker, and Paul Pierce.

In the hottest summer days, “it had a calming effect,” said Albert Holland, former principal at Burke High (now Holland Tech). “It really helped Boston move from a point where we were angry at each other to a point where we could sit together and watch great basketball.”

Baker was born in Thomasville, Ga., on July 29, 1937, to Edwina Baker Curtis. He grew up in the Roxbury home of Barbadian immigrants Gustavus and Edna Haynes, whose four sons each answered their callings. Vincent was a journalist and jazz historian. Roy was a world-renowned jazz drummer. Douglas was a musician and World War II veteran.

Michael, the oldest, served 40 years as the pastor at Twelfth Baptist, and was a friend of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. He was in high school when he invited Baker, then a grade-schooler, to live with the family. Baker’s mother, a singer, was moving out of the area. “He wanted to stay and play sports,” said his daughter, Jessica Moore. “I think he saw a future and an opportunity for himself, even at a young age, in Boston.”

The community leader Mel King once told the Globe that Rev. Haynes constantly challenged him and other Black men around him to serve the community and understand their power, to “recognize our capacity to make a difference.”

Baker, who taught at Timilty Middle School after graduating college, in 1968 became the first Black director of the Roxbury Boys Club. Among those he guided were two young girls from Roxbury, Andrea Swain and her sister, Lisa.

Hanging out at the club in the early ’70s, they wondered why they were not allowed to swim. Baker encouraged them to speak out. Girls soon joined various activities at the club. In 1981, the Roxbury Boys Club allowed girls as full members, and changed its name to reflect that — the first Boys Club in the country to do so. Soon, other affiliates did the same.

“He gave me a voice,” said Swain, 61, now chief impact officer of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston.

In the early ’80s, Burke High was in dire straights. Drugs and gangs rattled the pillars on its facade. Its academics were crumbling. In 1986, Holland brought in Baker as a teacher and dean of discipline to help him turn the school around.

“Encouraging kids to go to class and to do the right thing, he was just a special person that cared about individuals, and everywhere he went, he’d make you laugh or put a smile on your face. He left such an imprint on your heart,” said Brandy Cruthird, a late-80s basketball star at what is now the Dr. Albert D. Holland Technical High School.

The original plan at Burke, she added, was to dedicate the school gym to Holland, but Baker’s passionate speech about Holland’s impact helped convince decision-makers to rename the entire school.

Charlie Titus, 76, grew up in Columbia Point, and later Roxbury, in the ’60s. He remembered a community that was united in its struggle for progress, and pushed forward by leaders such as Baker.

Titus listened, staying in school and on the court. He wound up becoming UMass Boston’s first athletic director, founding the men’s basketball team, and coaching for 29 years. He is in the St. Michael’s College and UMB Halls of Fame.

“That doesn’t happen to me without people like Roscoe Baker, Mike Haynes, Jeep Jones,” he said. “They were 24/7 youth workers. Their days never ended. They were always around, taking us places, taking us down south to the HBCUs, to jobs. They were just there — they were a part of your life.”

Baker leaves behind his daughters, Jessica Moore, of Boston, and Jillian Baker, of Los Angeles; a son, Roscoe Baker Jr., of Kissimmee, Fla.; three grandchildren; and numerous family members and friends.

A funeral will be held Friday, May 29, at the Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, with a viewing from 9:30-11 a.m., and a service from 11 a.m.-noon.

title: Healey issues guidance for schools, churches, and other locations in dealing with ICE
text:
The guidance was promised by an executive order Healey signed in January, which sought to prohibit ICE agents from making arrests in nonpublic areas of state facilities and barred the use of state property for immigration enforcement staging.

Healey unveiled that order when she filed legislation that would ban federal immigration enforcement from entering churches, schools, courthouses, and other locations. The Massachusetts House and Senate have each passed differing versions of wide-ranging immigration bills designed to be a bulwark against the Trump administration’s deportation operation.

The guidance spells out how schools, child care centers, health care facilities, and places of worship have the right to require federal immigration officials to present any warrants before entering a facility, and deny access to nonpublic areas without a valid judicial warrant. It also recommends that facilities have lawyers on call and train staff on how to respond if federal immigration officers show up at their places of work.

Healey said she hopes the guidance will help restore any drops in school enrollment, attendance at places of worship, and patients seeking medical care, which she said have taken a dip in communities with high immigration populations.

“These are the noble care professions that society depends on each and every day,” the Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, founding pastor of the New Roots AME Church in Dorchester, said at the State House on Thursday. “This advisory gives practical guidance on how we honor the laws of this land.”

The guidance outlines the kinds of signage that places can post to clearly designate nonpublic areas, as well as advice on adopting written visitor policies and procedures.

It also urges employees and staff to “remain calm” and to “never attempt to physically interfere” with ICE agents, and instead contact the highest-ranking staff member on site, who should call an attorney.

The guidance asks that staff members document their actions, as well as information about the ICE agents, and contact the families of children who may have witnessed the interaction.

The state also offers examples of what are considered public and nonpublic spaces. Offices, classrooms, stairwells, and nursery and play areas are all nonpublic, according to the guidance. So are storage areas, athletic fields, parking lots, dormitories, research labs, and exam rooms.

Katie Murphy, a Brigham and Women’s Hospital nurse and president of the Massachusetts Nurses Association, said her colleagues have for months seen patients skipping regular appointments while others wait to go to the emergency room for care to avoid potentially being detained by ICE.

The guidance from the Healey administration offers extra comfort, she said, though health care providers are more concerned with patients deferring care than ICE showing up.

“They are not going to their appointments, [and] they are not going to the emergency department until they are really sick,” she said. “This puts even a greater strain on a failing system.”

Gladys Vega, the head of Chelsea-based La Colaborativa, said the guidance is a welcome step in her community, which she said has seen ICE agents show up in a school parking lot, grocery store, and food distribution line.

La Colaborativa also runs a health clinic in collaboration with Mass General Brigham, which sees patients with varying immigration statuses.

“As an organization that serves thousands of residents and operates a small practice, we have been deeply concerned about the privacy, the dignity, and the health of our community members,” said Vega, who worked with the administration on the guidelines. “We are constantly very nervous about it.”

Lauren Cook — chief executive of Ellis Early Learning, which operates three child care facilities in Boston — said the guidance is helpful, though she worries about child care centers like hers that don’t have ready access to legal counsel.

Nonprofits often rely on pro bono help, which can take days to find, Cook said.

Even so, “it’s helpful to be able to use this as . . . a guidepost against what we have already established,” she said, noting that her team had stitched together a hodgepodge ICE response plan from a variety of sources.

Ellis lost two beloved teachers in recent months because their work authorizations weren’t renewed.

Healey on Thursday said she couldn’t say how this guidance would be enforced in a situation where federal agents clash with, say, a faith leader or a school employee.
