“I expect this to not be an issue, because I expect them to actually follow the regulations,” she said of federal officials. “Should they not do that, and I would be very disappointed if I saw that . . . that will be immediately reported to the attorney general’s office and to our office, and appropriate action will be taken.”

Healey’s taken other steps to push back on ICE operations, including creating a portal with the AG’s office where residents can report alleged misconduct by ICE. She’s publicly demanded ICE stop deportation flights out of Hanscom Field, called for an extension of temporary protected status for Haitian immigrants, and opposed a since-scrapped plan for an ICE detention center in southern New Hampshire.

Earlier this year, the governor also prohibited the state from entering into any new agreements with ICE unless there is a public safety need. Her own Department of Correction is the only entity in Massachusetts that has an existing deal with ICE. It allows local law enforcement to act as deputized immigration agents for the purpose of identifying noncitizens who could be eligible for deportation once they complete their sentences.

She said at the time that she supported the existing agreement, which was implemented in 2007, because if someone is incarcerated in a state prison, they’ve “done something pretty bad.”

The DOC’s agreement is among 12 such arrangements between federal immigration agents and state prison systems around the country, and Massachusetts is one of only two of those states — Arizona being the other — that are currently led by a Democratic governor.

title: At UMass commencement, diversity and artificial intelligence took center stage
text:
Graduation caps decorated with glitter flashed in the bright sun Thursday morning as the University of Massachusetts Boston celebrated its 58th commencement with graduates hailing from more than 133 countries.

The campus overlooking Dorchester Bay teemed with families as some 2,740 undergraduates accepted their diplomas and began the next chapter of their lives. As speakers addressed the crowd, references to the diversity of the graduating class emerged as theme.

Madeeha Masroor Syeda, who delivered remarks on behalf of the class of 2026, told her fellow graduates that her achievement was rooted in the sacrifices of her immigrant parents. She used her moment at the podium to highlight those who have been denied similar opportunities.

“There are young people around the world with the same dreams and potential, who do not have the safety or freedom to sit where we are today,” Syeda said. “Many may never get to experience a day like this.”

Students, some shaking with enthusiasm, lined up for their turn to walk across the stage.

“I feel very excited to be done, but also slightly nervous for the real world,” said graduate Olivia Hill, who studied nursing. “I hope to get a really nice job that I enjoy.”

The campus grounds were lined with flower bouquets as parents beamed with pride.

“It’s very emotional,” said Jen Clark, mother of a graduating senior. “You’re proud of yourself and you’re proud of your son, and it was everything. I just had a great day.”

The ceremony began with a welcome from chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco.

“Beacons, you did it. You made it. You earned it,” Suárez-Orozco said. “Take everything that UMass Boston has offered you, go out with it into the world fiercely, boldly.”

Students radiated joy as they crossed the stage to collect their diplomas, many donning graduation stoles embroidered with the flags of the countries they represented.

The celebration came against a backdrop of growing uncertainty about whether that global reach can be sustained for schools like UMass Boston, which saw about 250 fewer international students arrive on campus last fall, a 17 percent drop from 2024.

“UMass Boston is the most diverse public university in New England, and the third most diverse university in the United States of America,” said Senator Edward J. Markey, who received the Chancellor’s Medal.

Like at other commencements this season, the mention of Artificial Intelligence drew jeers and boos, highlighting the unease that looms over a class entering the workforce at a time of heightened uncertainty.

“We live in a world of growing disinformation, distrust of science, devaluing of higher education, of your degrees and of overpromises of AI without a full reckoning of its threats,” Suárez-Orozco said.

Syeda, the class speaker, received the John F. Kennedy Award for Academic Excellence, which is given to the graduate who best exemplifies academic excellence, commitment to service, and good citizenship.

“As we step into this next chapter of our lives, we are no longer just the ones being guided; we are becoming the ones others will look to for guidance,” Syeda said. “We will be the ones who will mentor, who will teach, who will give people a place to belong.”

A drizzle began to form as the ceremony neared its end and families embraced their graduates.

“It is an honor for me to see her graduate, because she worked hard, she worked full time and she went to school full time,” said Elmire Guillaume, cousin of a graduate. “She made it through and we’re very proud of her.”

Thai Theodoro can be reached at thai.theorodo@globe.com.

title: With two weeks to go, Wu and state still deadlocked over transit plans for World Cup
text:
With city and state officials tight-lipped, tens of thousands of World Cup fans remain in limbo as they seek a clearer picture of traffic and pedestrian plans outside South Station when the Cup kicks off, with the first game at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough slated for June 13. T officials expect as many as 20,000 fans could ride trains for each of the seven games slated in Foxborough.

Two weeks ago, state transportation officials informed City Hall that they intend to take the unusual step of temporarily occupying part of Summer Street — between South Station and Fort Point Channel — and closing it off to vehicle traffic for 10 hours at a time on match days, according to a May 15 letter from Eng.

But Boston officials said in a statement last week that the plan is an “inappropriate use of eminent domain to bypass the permitting process for roadways under local jurisdiction.”

A spokesperson for Wu did not respond this week to multiple requests for comment on the dispute.

The stalemate is the latest in a string of coordination breakdowns and other missteps surrounding Boston’s World Cup preparations. It began early this year with a months-long standoff between Boston Soccer 26, the host committee, and the town of Foxborough over security costs at Gillette. The dispute was eventually resolved to Foxborough’s liking, but not before drawing unwanted international attention and briefly casting doubt over whether the event would even proceed.

Meanwhile, dozens of Massachusetts towns and cities that were awarded $10 million in state grants in March to support local watch parties and other celebrations spent months waiting for vital permits needed to move forward. Without the public-viewing licenses from FIFA, soccer’s global governing body, communities could not finalize their plans. As the tournament neared, some municipalities began considering scaling back or canceling events altogether.

FIFA officials finally issued most of the licenses within the past week. As of Thursday, all but one of the 17 organizations that received state grants had obtained the licenses for the roughly two dozen watch parties or confirmed they didn’t need one, according to state officials.

Even so, the approvals came so late that many communities say they are now scrambling to finalize important details, including hiring local food vendors and musical performers.

“It’s crazy that an event this large would not have more organization behind it and more forethought,” said Jackey West Devine, executive director of a nonprofit, Fields Corner Main Street, that finally received a license from FIFA on Tuesday for a watch party on June 21 in Dorchester. “This is history in the making, after all.”

Speaking at the T’s board meeting Thursday, Eng called the World Cup “an unprecedented event” and said he expected the state and city would reach a resolution, though he offered no timeline.

“I’m confident that with the ongoing dialogue that we have with the city, we will find a resolution to how to balance the needs of our riders, the visitors, the enhanced service that we intend to ride the thousands of people that we are ready to carry, as well as the users and the people that live around our system at South Station,” Eng said.

Yet two Boston city councilors said this week that they were surprised crowd control measures at South Station had not been resolved by now.

The lack of preparation is particularly jarring, they said, given that most host cities resolved transportation issues months ago. Other cities have also shown greater willingness to block off streets for Cup-related events. Houston, for instance, plans to designate some 30 blocks of streets near its soccer stadium. In New York, officials are planning significant traffic disruptions to accommodate Cup-related traffic, with multiple streets and lanes in Manhattan closed on game days.

Talks over how to manage crowds at South Station have stretched on for months. The question of closing Summer Street surfaced as early as February, when Eng toured the station with local law enforcement officials. The urgency grew after an international friendly game in late March between Brazil and France, what was seen as a test run for the tournament. Officials concluded South Station needed an “additional footprint” to handle the crowds.

Among the problems: there was not enough space, pedestrians trying to pass through were obstructed, and access for emergency vehicles and personnel was compromised.

“The friendly match is where we saw . . . the crowds did end up on the streets, so we know from that perspective the sidewalks were insufficient,” Eng said in a short briefing with reporters after Thursday’s board meeting.

As of Wednesday, more than 37,000 train tickets had been sold across the first five games of the tournament, which is about a third of the total tickets on sale.

Of those sales, some 11,500 tickets were for the first game on June 13 between Scotland and Haiti.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper said Wednesday that the city and the T should be able to “strike a happy medium” between fully shutting down a busy thoroughfare for 10 hours on match days and restricting traffic during peak crowd periods. He said the agency should identify those hours when the largest numbers of fans are expected to use South Station to travel to the games, and focus traffic restrictions around those times to minimize disruption for commuters.

Boston has already agreed to allow the T to close a portion of Summer Street to traffic for the first match on June 13, and the third match on June 19 between Scotland and Morocco. However, the two sides remain at odds over whether — and when — traffic restrictions should be imposed for the remaining five games.

“No matter what, it’s going to be difficult,” Culpepper said of crowd control efforts at South Station. “Here’s the question: Do you cut off the street for those who depend on it and use it every day, just for the World Cup? Or do you look at the times when it’s most used for the games? Why close the street in the mornings, when there won’t be games?”

Ed Flynn, the South Boston district councilor, said he was frustrated that negotiations between the T and city officials have taken place behind closed doors, with little transparency and no clear resolution in sight.

“This should have been resolved five or six months ago,” Flynn said. “But it wasn’t resolved, so here we are, just days from the World Cup, and we don’t have a clear public safety and logistical plan in place for getting people to and from the games.”

title: Blasts from the past, a bunny is rescued, and stolen ATVs recovered
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police blotters in our communities.

The Massachusetts State Police bomb squad traveled to Nantucket earlier this month after some World War II-era rockets turned up on the island off the Cape. The rockets, which were once used in military training exercises, were discovered in an eroding sand dune. State fire officials said that although the rockets were “old and degraded,” they were still potentially dangerous, so the State Police, along with the Nantucket Fire Department and the US Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit 12, “conducted a controlled explosion to mitigate the hazard.”

Police recently rescued a rabbit that was stuck in a fence in back of a home at 132 Beacon St. in Chelsea. “The little guy was having a real hare emergency and needed some-bunny to help,” police wrote on social media. “Our officers hopped into action, carefully cut the fence, and freed the furry friend without any further bunny business. At the Chelsea Police Department, we answer all types of calls for service. Whether it is a serious emergency, a community concern, or a rabbit rescue that needed a little hop-eration, every call matters.” Police shared video of the rescue and publicly thanked Officer Jonathan Maldonado and the caller who notified them that the rabbit needed help. “No bunny gets left behind!” police wrote.

At about 3:30 p.m. on May 2, the Groton Fire Department was dispatched to assist a pregnant woman who was going into labor in the parking lot of a local business in town. With the help of Groton Fire Lieutenant Tyler Shute, Firefighter-EMT Chris Braun, and EMT Gibson McCullagh, the baby was safely delivered in the mother’s vehicle, according to Groton Fire Chief Arthur Cheeks. The woman and her newborn boy were then taken to UMass Memorial Medical Center in Worcester. “The Groton Fire Department would like to congratulate the family on their new addition, and commend Lt. Shute, Firefighter Braun and EMT McCullagh and all other responders, who helped ensure a safe birth in challenging circumstances,” said Cheeks. “We are pleased to hear that mom and baby are recovering well. It is an honor to be able to provide care to people in the most pivotal, positive moments of their lives.”

The Boston Police Department’s auto theft unit recently teamed up with Milton police to investigate the theft of off-road vehicles that had allegedly been sold — and then promptly stolen — through fraudulent Facebook Marketplace sales. Police say the alleged scam worked like this: The buyers allegedly wrote bad checks to purchase the vehicles, and by the time the sellers realized they couldn’t cash the checks, it was too late, because their ATVs were long gone. As a result of the investigation, police arrested two males on charges of larceny of a motor vehicle, forgery of a check, and uttering a false check. Police also said a search warrant for a home on Woodgate Street in Dorchester led to the recovery of three allegedly stolen ATVs, and a search warrant at a home on Sprague Street in Dedham led to the recovery of a dirt bike.

Emily Sweeney can be reached at emily.sweeney@globe.com. Follow her @emilysweeney and on Instagram @emilysweeney22.

title: Former Fed chair Powell, Minnesota Twin Cities community leaders accept JFK Profile in Courage awards
text:
Powell received the award “for protecting the independence” of the Fed despite Trump’s aggressive efforts to try to force him to lower interest rates and to get him to resign when he would not.

The people of Minnesota’s Twin Cities also received the award for “peacefully defending” human rights and immigrants in their community during a Trump administration immigration enforcement surge that included federal agents killing two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during protests there in January.

Four Twin Cities community leaders — Iman Yusuf Abdulle, Natalie Ehret, Carolina Ortiz, and Zena Stenvik — accepted Sunday night on behalf of the residents of Minneapolis and Saint Paul.

“Joining Chicago, Portland, and other communities, their compassion and unwavering commitment to the ideals that sustain our democracy inspired communities across this country and forced the federal government to back down,” Caroline Kennedy, honorary president of the JFK Library Foundation, told the crowd. “We especially remember the courage of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who gave their lives for their community and our country.”

The award choices led to unusually strong demand for this year’s award ceremony, which was moved to a tent outside the library for capacity reasons for only the third time. The other occasions were in 2017, when former President Barack Obama received the award, and in 2019, when the recipient was then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Among the attendees Sunday were Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, and three members of Renee Good’s family — her father, Tim Ganger, brother Brent Ganger, and sister Anna Ganger Collins.

Powell was an unusual choice for the award, created in 1989 to recognize “public servants who have made courageous decisions of conscience without regard for the personal or professional consequences.” Many past recipients, such as Obama, Pelosi, and last year’s honoree, former Vice President Mike Pence, were elected officials.

“He is not an elected official, and these are not ordinary times,” Jack Schlossberg, Caroline Kennedy’s son and a member of the Profile in Courage Award committee, said in introducing Powell. “His commitment to the public interest never wavered.”

A lawyer and former investment banker who served President George H.W. Bush’s Treasury Department, Powell is a soft-spoken government official who led the nation’s central bank for eight years ending May 22. Despite initially appointing him to the job, Trump quickly turned on Powell in mid-2018 when the Fed began inching up its benchmark interest rate to head off potential inflation.

Then, as in Trump’s second term, Powell refused to give into the pressure.

While the Fed has made mistakes in the difficult task of monetary policy, the public expects “we will make our decisions based only on our best economic analysis of what would most benefit the people we serve.

“We do not take into account the fortunes of any political party or politician in making those decisions,” Powell said.

The Fed was created by Congress as a uniquely independent federal agency so that it would make decisions based on what’s good for the economy and not for short-term political reasons. Interest rate decisions are made by a 12-member board, but the chair is highly influential and publicly explains the Fed’s actions.

Powell was reappointed to a second four-year term by President Joe Biden in 2022. When Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he wanted the Fed to significantly lower rates to spur more economic growth. But Trump’s high tariffs led to concerns among economists about price increases, and the Fed moved cautiously.

Trump was infuriated. He publicly derided Powell as “stupid,” a “knucklehead,” and a “stubborn moron” while calling on him to resign and musing about firing him. But Fed board members can only be fired “for cause,” not for policy disputes.

So Trump tried to find a reason last year, focusing on the rising cost of renovating and expanding the Fed’s Washington, D.C., headquarters.

He increased the pressure on Powell and the Fed by attempting to fire another member of the central bank’s Board of Governors, Lisa Cook, because of mortgage fraud allegations she denies. Trump’s unprecedented move was put on hold by a federal judge pending Cook’s legal challenge, which the Supreme Court is deciding. Cook attended Sunday night’s ceremony.

Then in January, Powell revealed that the Justice Department was conducting a criminal investigation into whether he had lied to Congress about the renovation.

Still, Powell refused to resign as chair before his term ended May 22. Trump nominated his replacement, Kevin Warsh, who was recently sworn in to succeed him. But Powell broke with tradition and opted to remain on the Fed board until the criminal investigation is over, denying Trump another seat to fill. His separate 14-year board term doesn’t end until 2028.

Powell described President Kennedy as “an inspiring public servant” and “a towering figure in my early life.”

“Partisan political differences are normal — indeed essential — in a thriving democracy,“ Powell said. ”But we ought to be united in our commitment to the higher principles that define our nation. Chief among them is respect for the rule of law."

title: Free June events: Pride Month, Father’s Day, and more
text:
BEACH BASH Head to Revere for its fifth annual Beach Pride Celebration. The outdoor seaside party — in case of rain, revelers will relocate to the Marriott’s Springhill Suites — will feature face-painting, a photo booth, and live DJ and drag performances. Bring your (most sand-friendly) dancing shoes. June 28, 1-6 p.m. Free. Waterfront Square, 500 Ocean Ave, Revere. revere.org

DANCING QUEENS Somerville returns for their annual “Big Gay Dance Party,” featuring drag performances, music from DJ Live, and LGBTQ organizations tabling. This year’s event is themed “Gender Euphoria,” and the organizers encourage guests to dress up whatever makes the feel the most like themselves. June 27, 4:30-8:30 p.m. Free. Union Square Plaza, 90 Union Sq., Somerville. somervilleartscouncil.org/events

PRIDE RIDE Bike lovers, put on your helmets for a community ride celebrating Pride. The Cycle Loft shop hosts a cruise down Vine Brook and Minuteman Bikeway. They will also offer free snacks, drinks, stickers, and temporary tattoos. June 7, 9 a.m.-12 p.m. Free. Cycle Loft, 43 Middlesex Turnpike, Burlington. trekbikes.com/cycle-loft

ZOO-TIFUL Spend a family day among giraffes, red pandas, flamingos and more. In celebration of Father’s Day, dads will get in for free to the Stone Zoo and Franklin Park Zoo. Tickets are required for all other attendees and can be purchased online or in person. June 21, 9 a.m.- 6 p.m. Free for fathers. Franklin Park Zoo, 1 Franklin Park Rd. and Stone Zoo, 149 Pond St., Stoneham. zoonewengland.org

DRAWINGS FOR DAD Need a no-cost (but from the heart) present for pops? Head to the Hyde Park Branch of the Boston Public Library for their Father’s Day Crafts event. The library will provide all materials to make cards and other paper crafts. June 20, 9:30-11:30 a.m. Free. Hyde Park Branch of the Boston Public Library, 35 Harvard Ave., Hyde Park. bpl.bibliocommons.com/events

SYMPHONIC SUNDAY Boston Modern Orchestra Project (BMOP) hosts a free Father’s Day Concert at New England Conservatory’s Jordan Hall. Conducted by BMOP artistic director Gil Rose, the ensemble will play works composed by modern American composers, including “Miami Variations” from Pulitzer Prize winner Paul Moravec, “History of the World” by John Aylward, and Avner Dorman’s concerto “Inner Fire,” featuring cellist Kristina Reiko Cooper. June 21, 7-9 p.m. Free. Jordan Hall, New England Conservatory of Music, 30 Gainsborough St. bmop.org

FOOD FEST For the foodie fathers, head over to the Rose Kennedy Greenway for an Asian Food Festival. Attendees can purchase street food, bubble tea, desserts, grilled items, and a variety of other items from different Asian cultures. The event will also feature free entertainment, including Taekwondo demonstrations, cultural dance performances, and a guest Japanese singer. For brewery lovers, the event will also feature a beer garden from Thai company Singha Beer featuring games and merchandise giveaways. June 20, 11 a.m.-7 p.m. and June 21, 11 a.m.-6 p.m. Free. Rose Kennedy Greenway. rosekennedygreenway.org

FAMILY FUN Enjoy the warmer weather at MIT Open Space’s summer party. The outdoor event will feature free soft serve ice cream, herb planting with a horticulturist, a drop-in sketching activity with Blue Mouse Gallery art school, and a performance from the Continuum Dance Project. June 24, 12-2 p.m. Free. Kendall/MIT Open Space, 292 Main St., Cambridge. openspace.mit.edu

BANDS AND BREWS Bask in the sunshine with live music, cornhole, and Giant Jenga at Sam Summer Saturdays. Each week, a musician will take the stage at the Samuel Adams Boston Brewery beer garden. Artists scheduled to perform this month include Pittsfield singer-songwriter Autumn Phoenix (June 6 and 27) and R&B and soul artist Tenille Ja’Nae (June 13 and 20). For seasonal eat and drink, attendees can purchase burgers, hot dogs, and Samuel Adams summer ale. Multiple dates, 1-4 p.m. Free. Samuel Adams Boston Brewery, 30 Germania St. samadamsbostonbrewery.com

ANCHORS AWAY For the aspiring sea captains in your life, Charlestown Marina and Boston Harbor Shipyard and Marina invite families to board a ship, make nautical bracelets, and meet representatives from local sailing schools and clubs during their Massachusetts Kids Boating and Fishing Week celebrations. Attendees at Charlestown Marina can also enjoy hot dogs, hamburgers, and chips. Charlestown Marina: June 6, 11 a.m.-2 p.m. Pier 6, 1 8th St. Boston Harbor Shipyard and Marina: June 7, 11 a.m.-2 p.m. 256 Marginal St. Free. masskidsboatingday.org

SUMMER SOLSTICE Mount Auburn Cemetery celebrates the longest day of the year with meditations, live music, and more. Throughout the day, the cemetery will host both free and ticketed activities. No-cost events include an outdoor meditation in the facility’s Hazel Dell (registration required) and a bat net demonstration from Tufts University biology instructor Dr. Chris Richardson. The celebration ends with a pay-what-you-can performance of Celtic and Middle Eastern inspired music from guitarist Ira Klein, the cemetery’s artist in residence, and fiddle player Cate Byrne. June 21, 10 a.m.-7:30 p.m. Free. Mount Auburn Cemetery, 580 Mount Auburn St, Cambridge. mountauburn.org

GREENWAY GAINS The Rose Kennedy Greenway becomes a free fitness hub this season. From parkour to children’s yoga, the park offers something for everyone. Additional classes include mat pilates, Zumba, yoga, barre, and HIIT workouts. Multiple dates and locations. Free. rosekennedygreenway.org

WATERSIDE WORKOUTS Put on your gym clothes and head to South Boston for a waterfront fitness workout. Sessions include dance workouts, yoga (bring your own mat), and revamp training, a method that combines resistance band exercises, cardio dance, and bodyweight workouts. Multiple dates, 5:30-6:30 p.m. Free. 9 World Trade Center Ave. massport.com/community/events

PARK SERIES During the summer, Boston Parks hosts daily outdoor fitness classes in locations like the Frog Pond, Hynes Playground, and Christopher Columbus Park. Workouts include yoga, Zumba, dance fitness, strength training, and tai chi. Multiple dates and locations. Free, registration recommended. boston.gov/events

SUFFOLK DOWNS SWEAT The Blue Line Flex series returns to Suffolk Downs. From June to September, the Yard at Beachmont Square will host a variety of fitness classes every Tuesday and Saturday from local fitness studios and instructors. Offerings include pilates, yoga, boxing, cardio dance, and high intensity interval training. Saturday sessions will also feature music from a DJ. Multiple dates, Tuesdays, 6 p.m. and Saturdays, 10 a.m. Free, registration required. The Yard at Beachmont Square, 10 Suffolk Downs Blvd., Revere. atsuffolkdowns.com

Correction: Because of a reporting error, a listing in the June edition of Boston at a Bargain incorrectly stated the class schedule for Blue Line Flex at Suffolk Downs. They will be hosted on Tuesdays and Saturdays through September. The Globe regrets the error.

title: ‘Nobody was outside the bounds of his compassion,’ daughter of Boston firefighter says at his funeral
text:
A 24-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department and third-generation firefighter, Kilduff was killed May 23 when he fell from a third-story window during a three-alarm blaze in Dorchester. He was 53.

Kilduff — or “BK,” as he was affectionately known at the firehouse — died as he lived: helping others, his family and colleagues said during the service, which was held at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross in the South End.

“My dad is my hero. He’s the hero everyone says he is, and I’ll miss him forever,” said his son, Mason Kilduff. “He taught us all how to live, and now he’s taught us how to die.”

Kilduff served in the Marines before becoming a firefighter, coached youth football, and mentored younger first responders. Above all, he showed up for his family, loved ones said.

When Kilduff responded to that Dorchester fire, he unwittingly answered the final call, a call from above, summoning him home for good, said Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall.

Kilduff served with the department’s Rescue Company 2, a specialized unit that responds to particularly dangerous situations, including firefighters in distress.

“While Bobby is worthy of the title hero many times over, he would never want you to call him that,” Marshall said. “He would prefer to be known for being a great dad, a great partner, a mentor, a brother firefighter, a friend. He was truly a light in this world.”

Just moments before his fatal fall, Kilduff alerted other firefighters to tenuous conditions as the engulfed structure became unstable, said Lieutenant Greg Kelly. Five residents of the house also escaped without injury.

“His very last act was to push two firefighters out of the dangerous area,” Kelly said.

In the 48 hours preceding that call, Kilduff likely saved two other lives, officials have said. One was a young woman threatening to jump off a building in the Fenway. The other was a homeless man who became trapped in a confined space in a Dorchester MBTA yard. Kilduff was also credited with helping save a fellow firefighter who suffered cardiac arrest while responding to a call several weeks ago.

“My dad represents everything our world can be if we look out for each other,” said his daughter, Hanna Jane Kilduff, 24, who’s pursuing a master’s degree in education. “Nobody was outside the bounds of his compassion.”

She said he consistently encouraged her to take risks and prioritize her own joy.

Always a diehard Boston sports fan, Kilduff shared that passion with his son, a Marine currently stationed in North Carolina.

“We’re both Boston guys forever,” said Mason Kilduff, 22. Their common interests led to frequent phone calls, discussing “the most recent news in Boston sports, what we would do to fix the Red Sox,” and other pressing issues.

Mason Kilduff said he still has the dozens of letters his dad sent him during bootcamp.

Later during the service, Richard G. Henning, archbishop of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Boston, addressed the Kilduff children directly.

“We heard you speak so beautifully about the ways in which your father, your beloved, shaped you. But I think it’s fair to say that in a very real sense you shaped him as well,” Henning said. “He knew what he was fighting for. It was ever and always you.”

Shortly after Henning spoke, fire officials rang a ceremonial bell to commemorate Kilduff; his helmet rested on the coffin.

He was a prankster during downtime, said firefighter Vic Gaybor, but the “one I wanted by my side” during emergencies.

At the Rescue Company 2 firehouse in Roxbury, Kilduff was known as the company’s informal historian. He could recite dates and details of historical fires in the city, and he was often the first to honor those killed in the line of duty.

It just doesn’t feel right to honor a fallen brother without him, said Sam Dillon, president of Local 718, the Boston firefighters’ union.

“I hope we got it right,” he said. “Brother, I hope we made you proud. And we’ll never stop trying.”

Hours before the funeral was set to begin Monday morning, throngs of firefighters parked in a Dorchester lot and boarded buses that brought them downtown.

“Rest in peace firefighter Robert Kilduff,” read the bus marquees.

A giant American flag hung over Washington Street, suspended between two firetruck ladders. Bagpipe music echoed through the neighborhood on an unseasonably cold, dreary morning. When Kilduff’s casket arrived outside the cathedral, some of his closest colleagues served as pallbearers, proceeding carefully up the church steps.

It was a level of fanfare Kilduff would have found excessive, said his longtime partner, Jess Spruell.

“He probably wouldn’t want us standing here, focusing on what he did. Because for him, helping people wasn’t about being called a hero,” she said. “It was about caring. It was about showing up, being there for others. It was about doing what was right.”

Kilduff embodied the spirit of Boston, a city built on the principle “that our people will show up for one another,” Mayor Michelle Wu said during her remarks.

“Boston has never lost the faith that when we call, someone will come,” she said. “When one of our protectors lays down their life in service to our city, every heart in Boston feels the pain of that loss.”

Members of the public also came to pay their respects.

“It’s very emotional,” said Mary Reardon, 61, whose late father worked alongside Kilduff’s grandfather in the department. “I have a lot of respect for firefighters, for what they do and what they sacrifice.”

After the service, Kilduff’s casket was transported down the church steps and loaded again atop Engine 42. The clouds had dissipated as morning turned to afternoon, giving way to bright sunshine. It was time for one last ride.

title: Trump faces new inflation warning from bond market, adding to midterm challenges. Follow live updates.
text:
By the Associated Press

The second lady told ABC News of her husband: “I think he would make a great anything he’d like to be.”

She said she’d been asked a couple of times about misconceptions of the vice president, and said, “I think people don’t understand what a fundamentally gentle person he is.”

By the Associated Press

Asked during an interview with ABC News if she’d like to see Vice President JD Vance run for president, second lady Usha Vance offered a careful dodge.

“I’m not a particularly ambitious person,” she said, after a pause. “I would like to see him happy.”

The second lady added of her husband, “I would like to see him making contributions that matter. And whatever form that takes is a form that I’ll be supportive of.”

By the Associated Press

In another of a series of moves restricting media access at the Pentagon, the Defense Department has declared that its press office is now a classified space inaccessible to journalists.

On X, acting Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez confirmed the move, saying there was “nothing controversial” about it and that it came because speechwriters, who use classified material, were now occupying the space.

“The Pentagon Press Office has been redesignated as a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility due to speechwriters from the Office of the Secretary of War sharing the facility,” Valdez wrote.

By the Associated Press

That’s according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss the president’s thinking.

The potential retreat is a recognition of the legal setbacks the fund has encountered since it was announced two weeks ago, as well as a mounting political backlash from Republicans concerned by a perceived lack of oversight of the money disbursement and the potential for payouts to participants in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.

The Justice Department has said it would temporarily pause its implementation to comply with a court order.

By the New York Times

At 37, James Talarico has become one of the Democratic Party’s fastest-rising stars in part by talking about his identity as a Christian. Unlike some politicians who forge politically strategic relationships with faith leaders deep into their careers, Talarico has an authentic lifelong relationship with a local pastor, and speaks easily about his personal faith.

As the Democratic base becomes increasingly secular, Talarico’s faith-forward approach is unusual for a white Democrat. And it seems to be working. He won a competitive primary in March and outpaced his Republican rivals in fundraising. Some polls before the Republican runoff last week put him ahead of the state’s scandal-plagued attorney general, Ken Paxton, whom some analysts in the state see as a relatively weak opponent.

But as the race intensifies, Talarico’s religious identity is also coming under new scrutiny. He is a seminary student at a progressive institution in Austin. And he has injected unusually complex theological arguments into discussions of progressive policy. In return, political and theological conservatives have called Talarico a heretic, compared him to the serpent in the Garden of Eden and suggested he could be the Antichrist.

READ MORE

By the Associated Press

The Trump administration on Monday provided more details for how Americans on Medicaid will be able to claim exemptions from new work mandates.

A new rule reveals that starting in 2028, if health or government data doesn’t prove exemptions, some Medicaid enrollees will need to prove they are eligible with documentation.

The rule also puts forth a stricter-than-expected definition for who can qualify for exemptions based on being “medically frail.” To meet that qualification, a person’s health condition must significantly impair their ability to comply with the work requirements, according to the text of the rule.

The work requirements were part of a 2025 law. Starting in 2027, they’ll require some working-age Medicaid participants to work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or be enrolled in school at least half the time.

States have warned implementing the changes will be expensive and time consuming. Advocates say they’ll cause millions to lose their health insurance.

Monday’s rule will be open to public comment before it is finalized.

By the Associated Press

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently blocked the promotions of at least seven Navy officers who had been selected by a board of senior Navy admirals.

The net result of Hegseth’s intervention is a slate of 22 nominees to be one-star admirals that bears little resemblance to the broader force these officers will help lead.

Two of the officers removed by Hegseth from the promotion list are women, and two are Black men. An additional three are white men.

Hegseth’s actions, which appear to violate the rules governing a promotion system that is supposed to be apolitical and merit-based, were described by four current and former defense officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters.

By the Associated Press

The White House says the president will head to Chippewa County, located in the northwest part of the state.

The trip will highlight the administration’s efforts to benefit farmers, particularly on taxes and trade.

“Wisconsin families put their faith in President Trump in 2024, and he has spent every single day since taking office fighting and delivering for them,” White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said.

The visit is part of a series of trips that are intended for Trump to promote his economic agenda and achievements.

By the Associated Press

The Trump administration said Monday it will comply with a court ruling temporarily blocking a nearly $1.8 billion fund meant to compensate allies of the president, effectively agreeing to pause the plan for at least two weeks after setbacks in the courts and a fierce backlash from Republicans who objected to potential payouts to participants in the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.

The announcement from the Justice Department comes in response to a Friday court ruling by a federal judge in Virginia who ordered plans for the fund halted pending additional arguments later this month. The department said in a statement that it “disagrees strongly” with the ruling but would abide by it.

The Trump administration had defended the $1.776 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund,” established to resolve Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns, as an appropriate corrective measure to make up for what officials insist was a weaponized law enforcement during the Biden administration.

By the Associated Press

Senate Majority Leader John Thune indicated Monday he was hopeful the White House would move to drop the $1.776 billion settlement fund designed to compensate Trump’s allies.

“I do think the best way to handle it is if the administration decides to shut it down themselves,” Thune told reporters.

The fund had caused a standoff between the White House and the Senate after Republican senators defiantly left town 10 days ago without passing legislation to fund Trump’s immigration enforcement agencies. The Senate returns today.

By the Associated Press

The State Department plans to drastically slash the number of US embassies and consulates in Africa that can process visas for foreigners seeking to come to the United States.

The almost 50 US embassies and consulates that are processing visa applications will be reduced to 20 in the coming weeks, according to three US officials and an internal memo obtained by The Associated Press. There is not yet a set date for the change, but it is expected in June, according to the officials, who were not authorized to comment to the media and spoke on condition of anonymity.

By the Associated Press

President Trump said Monday that Israel and Hezbollah have agreed to dial back fighting after he held talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and communicated with the Lebanon-militant group through mediators.

Trump announced the development in a social media post following his call with Netanyahu.

By the Associated Press

A Trump administration policy illegally banned transgender troops from military service, a divided panel of federal appeal court judges ruled on Monday.

The majority opinion by a three-judge panel from the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia circuit upholds a March 2025 ruling by US District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington, D.C. Reyes concluded that President Donald Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.

The administration appealed after Reyes issued a preliminary injunction requested by attorneys for six transgender people who are active-duty service members and two others seeking to join the military. The appeal court’s majority decided that the injunction should be narrowed to the plaintiffs currently serving in the military but not those seeking to join.

By the Associated Press

Tina Peters, the former clerk convicted of participating in a scheme to chase election conspiracy theories promulgated by President Trump, was released from prison Monday after the president successfully pressured Colorado’s Democratic governor into commuting her sentence.

Peters’ release was confirmed by the Colorado Department of Corrections. The state agency said it would have no more information about the 70-year-old inmate. Her sentence was shortened by Colorado Gov. Jared Polis last month after Trump waged a lengthy pressure campaign against the governor and his state.

By the Associated Press

Former Colorado elections clerk and conspiracy theorist Tina Peters is scheduled to be released from prison Monday after serving less than a quarter of a nine-year sentence for her role in a scheme to copy her county’s election system.

Colorado Governor Jared Polis, a Democrat, commuted Peters’ sentence last month following pressure from President Trump.

The Colorado Department of Corrections would not confirm the time of Peters’ release, and a representative for her attorney said Peters would not speak to the media when she’s freed.

Peters was the first local election official to be charged with breaching security after the 2020 election. She snuck in an outside computer expert affiliated with My Pillow Chief Executive Mike Lindell — who himself denied that Trump lost the White House in 2020 — and the person copied the county’s Dominion Voting Systems computer server as it was updated in 2021.

READ MORE

By the Associated Press

Oil prices are rising following the latest fighting to threaten the US-Iran ceasefire, but Wall Street isn’t very worried.

The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 percent early Monday, falling a bit below the record it set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 166 points, and the Nasdaq composite was little changed.

Brent crude climbed 4.7 percent, and Treasury yields moved higher in the bond market. Tech stocks held up better than the rest of the market.

Science Applications International Corp. soared after becoming the latest US company to report bigger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

By the Associated Press

A standoff between the White House and the Senate remains unresolved after Republican senators defiantly left town 10 days ago without passing legislation to fund President Trump’s immigration enforcement agencies.

Senate Republicans who are returning to Washington on Monday say they won’t have the votes to pass the Homeland Security spending bill until the White House works with them to place parameters on the new $1.776 billion settlement fund designed to compensate Trump’s allies. But Trump has shown little interest in doing so, even after a judge temporarily halted any payouts.

It’s unclear how they’ll settle the dispute.

By Jim Puzzanghera, Globe Staff

After withstanding unprecedented attacks from President Trump, former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell accepted the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award Sunday night and warned of the economic risks of allowing a president to remove officials at the independent central bank over policy differences.

“The public would lose faith that the central bank will make decisions based only on what’s best for all Americans. The Fed’s credibility would be lost,” Powell said during a ceremony at the JFK Presidential Library and Museum in Dorchester.

READ MORE

By the Associated Press

Trump on Saturday branded the federal judge who blocked his renovation of the Kennedy Center as “an anti Trump Hater” and predicted that the nation’s premier performing arts center, which he wanted to shutter for a two-year overhaul, will “soon be closed, probably never to open again.”

In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Trump fumed about the Friday decision from US District Judge Christopher Cooper, who also ordered Trump’s name removed from the center. Clearly angered by his latest legal setback, he said it was “impossible for me to be treated fairly,” tying Cooper’s ruling to earlier losses, including the Supreme Court’s rejection in February of his sweeping tariffs.

His post aimed to make the case for the project even as he says he’s giving up on it. Hours after Cooper’s decision, Trump said he was backing away from the renovations and making arrangements to relinquish control to Congress of what, until the Republican president’s second term, had been known as the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

By the Associated Press

The United States bombed Iranian radar and drone control sites in Iran after Tehran shot down an American MQ-1 Predator drone this weekend, the American military said Monday. Iran acknowledged launching a retaliatory strike, while Kuwait said it was intercepting incoming drone and missile fire.

The dueling attacks reflect the fragility of a weekslong cease-fire in the Iran war, which has seen repeated attacks even as American and Iranian officials try to negotiate a deal to extend it. Iran has maintained its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz in the meantime, disrupting global energy supplies as a fifth of all oil and natural gas traded once passed through the narrow mouth of the Persian Gulf.

READ MORE

By the Associated Press

The world is getting more uptight about lending money to President Trump’s government — causing interest rates to climb in ways that are worsening affordability pressures, hampering economic growth, and creating a new risk for Republicans in November’s midterm elections.

The energy price spike triggered by the Iran war has seeped into the price of bonds that help fund the US government. Interest rates on a 10-year US Treasury note are topping 4.44 percent, up from 3.95 percent before the war started at the end of February. Average mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels in nine months, while auto sales are slumping.

The challenge is global in scale, as interest rates have risen for multiple countries as the world has been adjusting to the prospect of higher inflation, mounting questions about the sustainability of government debt, and a dramatic surge in investment in artificial intelligence.

title: Trump 3.0? Mass. GOP voters say they’re split on ‘illegal’ idea
text:
But even if he were to try to run again … would Republican voters still want him?

A new Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll found that, at least in Massachusetts, they’re literally split. Close to 47 percent of the 465 likely GOP primary voters surveyed said they would vote for Trump again, while another 47 percent said they wouldn’t.

The virtually dead-even divide reflects some cracks in the president’s support within his own party, said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center.

“We’re back to a divided GOP regarding Trump,” he said. Half of likely GOP voters “are solidly loyal, while the other half either want to move on from Trump, or oppose the hypothetical because they know it’s not possible by law.”

Even some of the loyalists aren’t holding their breath for a third Trump term, though.

“I would vote for him again,” said Heather Zimmerman, a Republican voter from North Hatfield. “But it’s illegal, so he can’t do it.”

Charles Sweeney, 68, of Merrimac, said he would support Trump for another term — if the Constitution allowed.

“Which is kind of debatable at this point,” Sweeney, an independent voter, said.

Trump mused for months about seeking a third term in the White House — a proposition likely to run him smack into the 22nd Amendment (the one that says that no one can be elected president more than twice). At least one ally, podcaster and former Trump White House aide Steve Bannon, hinted at “a plan” to help elect Trump to the White House in 2028, and last year, Trump told NBC News that he was “not joking” and “there are methods” for him to seek another term.

But he’s since backed off the rhetoric, at least publicly, telling reporters last fall that it’s “pretty clear” he’s termed out.

Massachusetts might not be the most apt place to gauge the Republican president’s popularity, but he still has a grip on the party’s grassroots here. More than 63 percent of those surveyed in the Suffolk poll rated his job performance as good or excellent.

“I’ll take Trump, just because I like a lot of the things he does,” said Craig Lane, a Republican from Newburyport. “But I think the talk of a third term is more just theater.”

Here are some other notable numbers from the poll:

— 32 percentage points: How much Mike Minogue, the former medical device company executive, leads former MBTA chief administrator Brian Shortsleeve in a head-to-head matchup in the party’s gubernatorial primary. Around 45 percent of likely GOP primary voters — both Republicans and independents — said they would vote for Minogue, compared to roughly 13 percent who are backing Shortsleeve.

Another 40 percent are still undecided, but the race is Mingoue’s to lose, Paleologos said.

“To use an MBTA analogy, it’s like Minogue is one stop away from Government Center, and Shortsleeve is stuck on the platform in Braintree,” he said.

— 46 percent: The percentage of voters who said they had never heard of the GOP’s de facto US Senate nominee John Deaton. That’s gotta be a bit of an ego hit for Deaton, who isn’t a total newcomer to the Massachusetts political scene. He challenged US Senator Elizabeth Warren in 2024, who defeated him 60-40 percent.

— 61 percent: Former GOP Governor Charlie Baker’s favorability among the likely primary electorate. That’s not far off the 69 percent who view Trump favorably.

— 36 percent: The percentage of voters excited about Secretary of State/Trump administration multi-tool Marco Rubio as a potential presidential candidate in 2028. Rubio generated the most excitement among those surveyed in the poll, followed by Vice President JD Vance (28 percent).

The poll, conducted between May 26 and May 29, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. Live callers reached respondents via mobile and landline phones.

$UPER PAC ATTACK: A pro-Seth Moulton super PAC is wading into the US Senate primary between the congressman and Senator Ed Markey, knocking Markey on — you guessed it — his age and tenure in Washington.

The PAC, Advance Progress, tapped one of Markey’s old State House colleagues to help hammer home the message with an ad that begins airing Tuesday on broadcast, cable and digital platforms. The PAC is putting $1.5 million behind the ad, according to Matt McKenna, a spokesperson for the group.

“Ed Markey and I got into politics together more than 50 years ago,” Michael Connolly, who served with Markey in the state legislature for nearly four years in the 1970s, says in the direct-to-camera video.

“I was proud when he got elected to Congress, but it’s time for the next generation to lead,” says Connolly, who also served as secretary of state for four terms, says in the 30-second spot. “You’ve got to know when to pass the torch. Part of serving is knowing when to step aside, that’s why I retired.”

Not long ago, Connolly was in Markey’s camp. He donated $1,000 to his old colleague in 2020, when Markey beat back a different generational change challenge from then-Representative Joe Kennedy III.

“Ed’s a friend, but it’s time to move on,” Connolly says in the ad, before closing: “People shouldn’t stay in Washington too long. It’s bad for your health.”

Advance Progress raised $1.3 million as of the end of March, records show, including $250,000 donations from David Peeler, a senior advisor at the Boston-based private equity firm Berkshire Partners, and Richard Wells, a director at the tech investment firm, Insight Partners.

It’s the second outside group spending money in Massachusetts to knock Markey for his roughly 50-year tenure in Washington. A dark-money group led by a Moulton donor started airing ads that diagnosed Markey (and a couple of other older senators) with a fictional ailment: “Chronic Reelection Disorder.”

Markey’s not alone, though. The pro-Markey Commonwealth Together PAC began airing ads earlier this year, targeting Moulton for not being progressive enough and accusing the Salem Democrat of changing with the political winds.

SIGNED, SEALED… Republican attorney general hopeful Michael Walsh has submitted just enough signatures to make the September primary ballot, according to the secretary of state’s office. But Walsh — one of three GOP candidates who had signatures flagged by local clerks over possible forgery concerns — could still come up short. Of the 10,600 signatures he submitted, 1,058 from Scituate and Weymouth were set aside because of potential issues. Someone (an incumbent opponent perhaps?) could challenge his signatures by filing a complaint with the State Ballot Law Commission by 5 p.m. Friday.

RENTAL AGREEMENT?: One of the most closely watched ballot questions might not make it to the ballot after all. Rent control advocates are circulating a compromise that, if embraced by the real estate industry and lawmakers, could prompt them to drop their ballot push, according to the opposition campaign.

“We were formally contacted by the Yes campaign on Sunday with language that differs from the proposed ballot question,” Conor Yunits, chair of the Housing for Massachusetts campaign that’s opposing the question, said in a statement. “In good faith, we will review their proposal. Our campaign is focused on policies that protect property owners, renters, housing production, and community budgets.”

Andrew Farnitano, a consultant on the Keep Massachusetts Home campaign behind the ballot question, said the group is “continuing to have productive conversations with members of the real estate industry and are hopeful that we can reach agreement on a legislative compromise.”

The details of what could make it into any potential compromise weren’t clear Monday night.

SHERIFFS STICK-UP: Mass. sheriffs’ offices’ finances like the ‘wild west,’ in need of reform, inspector general finds by Sean Cotter, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts sheriffs are running their offices’ finances like the “wild west,” including millions of dollars passing through off-the-books bank accounts, illegal spending, and scant oversight, the Office of the Inspector General said in a scathing report released Monday by the state watchdog.

BATTLING AI: Her boyfriend created illicit images of her teen daughter. In Massachusetts, that’s not a crime. by Janelle Nanos, The Boston Globe: While other states have updated their laws to address the rise of fake nudes and obscene AI-generated images of children, Massachusetts is one of only five states that has not.

Have questions about how to talk to children about online safety after the Globe’s “Trapped in the Dark Web” series? Join the discussion with criminal justice experts and the reporters behind the stories Tuesday at 1 p.m. Sign up here!

JOBS REPORT: Boston reaches deals with private employers to provide hundreds of jobs for teens by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: Mayor Michelle Wu said the city has reached agreements with employers to provide nearly 500 paid school-year jobs for Boston students, framing it as the start of an effort to plug a hole created by a $5.5 million spending cut next year that would effectively kill the city’s current afterschool jobs initiative.

IN MEMORIAM: Funeral for fallen Boston firefighter honors his legacy of service by Lea Skene and Travis Andersen, The Boston Globe: Thousands of firefighters donned their navy dress uniforms on a cloudy Monday morning and poured into Boston’s South End, lining Washington Street ahead of a funeral Mass for their fallen brother, Robert “Bobby” Kilduff Jr., a 24-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, who was killed May 23 when he fell from a third-story window during a three-alarm blaze in Dorchester.

Quincy city councilors are looking to undo Mayor Tom Koch’s $126,000 raise amid concerns about its pension impact by Peter Blandino, The Patriot Ledger.

Hampshire College may not have funds to complete its final fall semester by Brooke Hauser, The Boston Globe.

How did the Mass Save energy efficiency program become so politicized? by Miriam Wasser, WBUR.

Western Mass housing advocates say the 46% decline in shelter stays isn’t all good news by Sam Ferland, Greenfield Recorder.

Thanks for reading The Scrum.

title: For $579,000, an unfinished 1800s carriage house condo
text:
In Boston, an 1,800-square-foot house for $579,000 is a rare bargain, especially an attractive, free-standing house in a nice neighborhood.

The structure at 8 Pine Street in the Mount Neponset neighborhood of Hyde Park is just that — but there’s a catch. It’s completely unfinished on the inside.

As is, artists could use it as a spacious and private studio; antiques dealers and interior designers would find it useful for furniture storage; it could serve as grand place to keep a collectible vehicle. Or, given permission by the City of Boston (and with some TLC), you could even live here.

“It can’t be a commercial enterprise, like a store,” said Christopher Lydon, the realtor with Milton’s William Raveis Real Estate, who is listing the property. “Its legal designation is as a barn. But, if you got a variance from the Zoning Board of Appeals, you could turn it into a really nice residence.”

While it is a solid gambrel-roofed building with a lot of historic charm, it’s just a shell. The interior contains little more than four walls, studs, rough flooring, ceiling joists, and rudimentary plumbing and wiring.

“Often, buyers are seduced by an attractive purchase price. But they need to know that it will involve effort, and they have to have a plan,” said Robb Cohen, a long-time real estate broker with Engel and Völkers in Boston.

In April, a heavily burned Dorchester house that would need to be mostly gutted or torn down sold for $776,000.

That being said, it does present the possibility for the next owners to make it their own. “They can put their own stamp on it, whether as a residence or as a work place,” said Cohen.

The barn that is for sale is a condominium with a monthly fee of $110.

Laid out in 1858, Maple, Oak, Pine, and Walnut Streets were part of a new development named for the area’s various kinds of trees by the Real Estate & Building Company. This barn, unit 4, was built in 1884. By 1912, Hyde Park had become the southernmost part of Boston, but traces of its history remain, including this building. The house it once served is long gone and the surrounding land was subdivided and filled with newer construction. One of those newer buildings is a classic Boston triple-decker; it and the old carriage house now comprise a four-unit condominium complex.

“This property has proved attractive to a lot of people,” Lydon said. “This is a free-standing condominium with a deeded off-street parking spot.”

He believes that the building’s original use was as a horse stable and that it became a carriage house when the population moved from horse-drawn to automotive transportation. Over the years, it retained its wide barn doors and entrance ramp, a side door, and a substantial rubble stone foundation. But it never became a studio or a home.

For a person who needs work or storage space, or who wants to build a home of their own, this could be a rare opportunity.

“But you do have to know what you are doing,” Cohen warns. “You don’t want to build a million-dollar kitchen in a half-million dollar house.”

title: In Boston, a Haitian rallying cry, and a local hero, ahead of the World Cup
text:
But in the speakeasy of Hue, it is sung with gusto, an outpouring of joy. The patrons were there to celebrate Haiti at the World Cup and toast a sporting hero who has roots in both Haiti and Massachusetts: a forward for the national team, Frantzdy Pierrot, 31, who went to high school at the northern end of the Orange Line.

The World Cup can have this effect on people — national pride, mixed with bittersweet history, and a heavy dose of delight. And yes, there is discussion of the soccer, or football, as pretty much the rest of the world calls it. The tactics, the predictions, the strengths and weaknesses of the various squads.

But the sheer scale of the tournament is so culturally impactful that the talk inevitably turns to the personal. Ostensibly, people are talking about soccer, but really they’re talking about their childhood, their country’s history and culture, and how it fits in with the game. The tournament is simply a rhetorical entry point to all that.

For Haitians of a certain age, their Dave Roberts moment came in 1974, when their country qualified for the Cup. They were playing Italy, a European footballing superpower. The goal came shortly after halftime via Route 1 football: there is a clearing header from the Haitian central defense, then a straightforward through-ball that Haitian forward Emmanuel “Manno” Sanon latches onto.

He rounds the renowned Italian goalkeeper, Dino Zoff, and puts the ball in the net. Haiti 1, Italy 0. It broke Zoff’s lengthy string of scoreless games.

In Port-au-Prince, there was bedlam, Lucien, 62, recalled. He can still remember walking to his friend’s house to watch. Televisions were a relative rarity at the time in Haiti, and his buddy had the appliance that conveyed the match in real-time. He remembered that on the walk, all the radios in the street were tuned to the game. After the goal, there was the shouting and jumping. General elation.

The result of the game is typically a footnote in these recollections. (Italy won 3-1.) As is the case with the rest of the tournament for the national team. (Haiti failed to earn a single point and was cumulatively outscored 14 to 2.) But for Haitians, Sanon’s goal was enough proof that they belonged on soccer’s global stage.

More than half a century has passed since that goal. Haiti has failed to qualify for every World Cup since. Until now.

And there is, of course, a Massachusetts connection that goes beyond the team’s June 13 clash with Scotland at Gillette Stadium and the local diaspora’s jubilation at the upcoming tournament. Frantzdy Pierrot spent his formative years here in Massachusetts, attending middle school and high school in Melrose, before a stop playing college soccer at Northeastern University.

Ten miles north of Boston is where Pierrot’s family sought a better life.

“Melrose gave me everything,” Pierrot said at Hue.

When they moved from Haiti, the focus was education for him, not athletics, said Pierrot. His father drove a bus and worked other jobs, including one at Logan Airport, sometimes only sleeping four or five hours a night to make ends meet.

Nowadays, his father, Destine, is sure that uprooting his family to Melrose was the right move. Asked what he will feel when his son walks onto the field, and the Haitian national anthem is played before the first World Cup match, he answers simply, “Happy.”

The meet-and-greet at the Back Bay bar came shortly after Pierrot was feted as a sporting hero during a ceremony at the State House. Governor Maura Healey said he represented “the very best of” the Commonwealth, all the while declaring a statewide day in his honor. Former coaches recalled his dogged determination and unshakable self-belief. The Melrose High School marching band struck up a version of “Sweet Caroline.”

He fielded questions in English and Haitian Creole from the press and posed for photos with admirers decked out in Haiti jerseys and signed autographs.

Pierrot’s soccer journey has taken him overseas, with stints in Belgium, France, Israel, Greece, and, most recently, Turkey. He has played Champions League soccer against some of Europe’s biggest clubs, including Juventus, Paris Saint-Germain, and Benfica.

It’s a long way from Bas-Limbé, a community on Haiti’s northern coast, about 140 miles away from Port-au-Prince. That is where his family’s roots are. It’s where he recalled playing soccer in the streets barefoot, using whatever was around as a ball, including spherical fruit.

“Football gave us happiness,” he told the State House crowd.

Nowadays, Haiti remains a nation rocked by turmoil, with gangs controlling much of the capital. In recent years, the national team’s home stadium was overrun by gangs and vandalized and the national soccer training center was set ablaze. The violent instability has also meant that the Haitian national team had to qualify for the World Cup, all the while playing their home games abroad.

The Haitian diaspora, too, has weathered hardship, namely federal hostility toward immigrants. Greater Boston, which is home to the third-largest Haitian community in the United States, has not been spared the pain, as tens of thousands of immigrants in the state wonder whether they will be deported to a country riven by chaos.

For Pierrot, the Cup offers him and his teammates an opportunity to show that there is more to Haiti than horrific headlines and news dispatches. For Haitians, both at home and abroad, the Cup offers a respite.

“It means so much,” said Boston City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, a Haitian American.

After the event at Hue and the State House ceremony, Lucien hosted a local access television program to discuss Haiti at the World Cup inside an Egleston Square media studio.

Among his guests was Donnet Desilus, a 65-year-old Dorchester resident who once captained the Haitian national team.

He spoke about what the United States has given his family: four college educations for his children, three of whom went to Ivy League schools. And like everyone else in the local Haitian community, he talked glowingly about what the competition means for Haiti.

“It’s the best thing for the country,” he said.

But he is measured when talking about the team’s chances.

Haiti’s initial opponents include Brazil, which has won more World Cups than any other nation. Morocco made it to the semifinals of the most recent Cup four years ago and was recently — and controversially — crowned champion of Africa. Scotland earned its trip here through the gauntlet of European qualification.

“It’s a tough group,” he said.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated Frantzdy Pierrot’s role on the team. He is a forward. Johny Placide is the captain.

title: Escalating their feud, Wu endorses state Senator Nick Collins’ primary challenger
text:
Wu on Wednesday said Gayle would be a “powerful, principled voice” in the Senate who “has stood with our families even when state legislators have not.”

She went even further at a news conference trumpeting her support, commending Gayle’s years of grass-roots advocacy work in Boston while criticizing the Senate for “offloading their elected power to unelected corporate interests to negotiate against Boston families.”

“We are tired of our own senators blocking solutions that came out of a vote of the City Council and the House of Representatives, town halls, meetings, organizing unions, faith leaders — everyone coming together to say we need relief and we need help now,” Wu added. “We’re tired of feeling like ballot initiatives are the only way to get anything to happen up there.”

Collins represents the First Suffolk District, which is anchored by Dorchester and South Boston. He is the second Democrat in the Senate to face a challenge with roots in Wu’s City Hall: Will Brownsberger, who also opposed Wu’s tax shift proposal, is being challenged by Daniel Lander, a former Wu aide.

While Wu has not yet weighed in on that race, on Wednesday she signaled she would be active in Gayle’s campaign effort and encouraged voters to rally behind her.

“This is going to be a fun election cycle,” Wu said.

Vanessa Woo, a spokesperson for Collins’s campaign, said the incumbent has built a record of fighting for Boston’s underserved populations, saying he’s addressed mental health and substance use crises and helped provide “working families tax relief,” among a series of other priorities.

“He will continue to do what he does every day,” Woo said, including “partnering with community leaders to address the challenges residents face.”

Brownsberger, meanwhile, is from Belmont but his district includes part of Boston.

“I’m just focused on serving the people in my district and making sure that people are aware of the hard work we’re doing,” Brownsberger said Wednesday. “And that’s about all I have to say.”

Wu’s decision to directly align herself against a fellow Democratic incumbent could test both her sway among city voters who overwhelmingly gave her a second term, and her standing in the State House, where she has trusted allies in the House but fraught relations with Senate leaders.

Senate President Karen Spilka declined to comment on Wu’s remarks after appearing at a Pride flag-raising event at the State House.

“I’m not here for politics,” she said.

Collins, considered a conservative Democrat in the Senate dominated by progressive voices, once weighed a run for mayor in 2021. Wu went on to win the office that fall.

A married mother of four, the 47-year-old Gayle has lived in Dorchester or the South End for more than 20 years, according to her campaign, and currently works as the senior director of advocacy and family partnerships at Neighborhood Villages, a Boston-based early education and child care nonprofit.

Wu’s entrance into the race aside, Collins appears to be operating from a position of strength. An internal poll circulated by his campaign showed that 82 percent of the roughly 800 people surveyed said they would vote for Collins in the primary election, compared to 10 percent for Gayle and 9 percent for Juwan Skeens, who is also running in the Democratic contest.

Collins also had $92,000 on hand at the end of last month — Gayle had about $15,600 at the end of April, according to her most recent filings — giving him a cash advantage in a contest where tens of thousands of dollars can be a major difference-maker.

As South Boston’s senator, he also hosts the annual St. Patrick’s Day Breakfast, one of the city’s most hallowed, if sometimes awkward, political traditions. Wu skipped the breakfast in March, prompting Collins to joke about Wu’s absence that “she found it just a little bit too taxing.”

Gayle on Wednesday said that she is “honored” to have the mayor’s support and cast Collins as prioritizing the needs of “the wealthiest residents.”

“When I talk to folks across this district, the number one thing they bring up is housing and affordability,” Gayle said. “I’m on your side.”

Wu’s endorsement could offer a much-needed boost to Gayle as she challenges Collins, an established sitting lawmaker who has served in elected office on Beacon Hill for more than 15 years.

Wu’s influence on Gayle’s campaign is already apparent. Gayle’s campaign manager, Maccon Bonner, worked for two years as Wu’s liaison to the Back Bay, Beacon Hill, Fenway, and Mission Hill until Gayle hired him this year.

Wu’s endorsement, particularly for first-time candidates, has proven powerful and influential in the past.

In the 2023 municipal election, Wu backed four new City Council candidates, all of whom won council seats that November.

In 2024, Wu endorsed longtime public defender and first-time candidate Allison Cartwright in her successful bid to be clerk of the Suffolk County Supreme Judicial Court against sitting city councilor Erin Murphy. Cartwright also had the backing of US Representative Ayanna Pressley and Attorney General Andrea Campbell, bringing an unusually high level of attention to a race typically far below the average voter’s radar.

Then last fall, as Wu easily rolled to reelection, her close allies on the council again held onto their seats by fairly wide margins with her support, including Councilor at Large Henry Santana, who was seen as the most vulnerable incumbent in last year’s election.

Kelly Garrity of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: More than 500 readers shared stories of never having COVID. Here’s what we found.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Six years since the pandemic began, most people have tested positive at least once.

It’s become a near-universal experience — a shared disruption that reshaped daily life, work, family, and health. And yet, there’s a group of people who say they’ve managed to avoid it entirely. No positive test. No unmistakable illness. Nothing.

Who are these so-called COVID “superdodgers”?

Responses from more than 500 of you revealed a wide spectrum of experiences and beliefs. Some of you described taking rigorous precautions long after others relaxed — still masking, avoiding crowds, carefully managing risk. Others said you eventually returned to normal routines but somehow never got sick. A number of you credited luck. Some pointed to faith. Others shared detailed personal regimens: UV lights for disinfecting mail, multiple daily showers, vitamin stacks, nasal sprays, strict isolation, or giving up travel altogether.

Reading through your messages, one thing became clear: There isn’t a single story here. There are hundreds.

Still, how?

I began digging deeper by speaking to many of you, but also with a coalition of international researchers and local scientists who have spent years trying to answer the same question. Why do some people seem to escape infection, even after repeated exposures?

Is it behavior? Biology? Timing? Or something we don’t fully understand yet?

It turns out, the answers are complicated and may challenge some assumptions. In some cases, what feels like certainty may be less clear-cut. In others, emerging science offers intriguing clues about immunity, genetics, and how the virus interacts with the body.

This is just the beginning of that exploration. I’ll share what I’ve learned from your stories and from the science about what it really means to be a “superdodger” of COVID-19.

What started this?

For a while, I thought I might be a “superdodger” myself. I was living in Detroit, one of the hardest-hit cities by the pandemic, reporting from COVID units while also caring for my parents in in-home hospice. I also quarantined with my husband three separate times when he had the virus, and I never tested positive. It felt impossible.

That changed after I moved to Boston. In October, I felt the worst sickness of my life. I remember the disbelief when the urgent care provider told me I was positive with COVID… I actually asked them to run the test again. I resonate with many of your stories and do believe there’s something special here.
