title: Over 40 Mass. cities and towns host a version of Porchfest. Why is the event so popular?
text:
This Saturday, at least four Massachusetts communities will host a Porchfest of their own, including Newton, Medford, Franklin, and Dorchester (“Dorchfest”). Arlington and the Fenway neighborhood are coming up on June 20, and the second annual Cambridge Porchfest is set for July 11.

Greene keeps a spreadsheet listing all the Porchfests she’s aware of.

“I like to track things,” she said. By her count, seven states haven’t hosted one yet, but there have been two in Australia.

Cleveland was the second place to host a Porchfest, in 2009, after a couple who’d been living in Ithaca brought the idea with them. In 2011, Somerville became the first city in Massachusetts to embrace Porchfest. That one has grown so large — more than 500 bands performed this year alone — that many Bostonians assume Somerville is where it all started.

Elle Marrone is executive director of Greater Ashmont Main Street, a nonprofit that supports Dorchester’s economic viability through pop-ups and other “activations.” After serving as fiscal sponsors for Dorchfest for a few years, Greater Ashmont Main Street became the host organization last year.

Marrone grew up in Arlington, and her husband, Matt Weinburg, is from Sudbury. They embraced Dorchester’s diversity from the moment they moved in.

“We really did fall in love with the neighborhood hanging out on porches,” she said.

In Norfolk County, the Town of Franklin (as it’s officially known, though it now has city government) will host its third Porchfest this weekend. Mixing private residences with municipal spaces in Franklin’s Cultural District, this Porchfest is another example of local leadership combining neighborliness with civic boosterism.

“What’s unique about us is we’re not only on porches but on town property,” said John Lopresti, chair of Franklin’s Cultural District Committee. They’ll have music on the Franklin Town Common, at the Historical Museum, and on the steps of the Franklin Public Library, the nation’s first.

“We wanted to expand it, really bring the beauty of Franklin [by] showcasing these historical assets,” Lopresti said.

On the last Sunday of May, the North Shore city of Beverly — one of the latest communities in Massachusetts to adopt the Porchfest model — celebrated its second annual event a day later than originally planned, after Saturday’s wind and rain necessitated a postponement. In the residential neighborhood of Ryal Side, the Danvers River provided the backdrop for the Jonee Earthquake Band, a trio that played a rowdy mix of punk, rockabilly, and surf-rock while perched atop a garage.

The band’s piratical namesake, Jonee, who alternated between electric and pedal steel guitar, noted that the band didn’t expect donations but would be glad to sell anything from their merch table.

“And if you can’t afford anything,” he joked, “enjoy windowshopping!”

A few blocks around the corner, a crowd of at least a few hundred people mingled behind police tape to listen to Wood & Bone, a professional soul and Americana band with traces of Van Morrison and Ray LaMontagne in their original songs. A tangle of bikes of all sizes rested on the street at the edge of the crowd.

Amid that throng, Ace and Alan Foulds wore shirts advertising their own Porchfest, in Reading. The town will host its eighth annual Porchfest on June 27.

The Foulds try to visit as many Porchfests as they can, for inspiration. They helped bring the concept to Reading in 2019 as part of the town’s 375th anniversary celebration. During the COVID-19 pandemic, they organized a Porchfest online.

One of the joys of Porchfest is learning which of your neighbors make music, said Alan, who serves as Reading’s town moderator.

“It’s like, ‘I didn’t know you played the pennywhistle!’” he said.

In Ithaca, Greene worked for many years at the Kitchen Theatre Company, where the tagline was “Important conversations happen in the kitchen.”

“I’m very soaked in that philosophy,” she said. To her, Porchfest is a prime example of community building through the arts: “Not that it was a conscious plan, but I do like things that bring people together.”

After Greene’s initial Porchfest partner, Gretchen Hildreth, stepped aside, she recruited another neighbor, Andy Adelewitz, to pick up the slack. He was in a heavy metal band that played an acoustic set at an early Porchfest in Ithaca. By now, they’ve amassed a group of around 100 volunteers to help organize each year.

The Ithaca group is still surprised at how far the concept has traveled. There’s a store in Ithaca that now sells “Porch Fest” summer lager, produced by Framingham’s Jack’s Abby brewery.

Back in Beverly, a high school rock band led by guitarist Silas Bellino held court from the front porch of his family’s home. They played a loose, spirited set ranging from covers of Neil Young and the Allman Brothers to Mountain’s “Mississippi Queen.”

“Anybody have a cowbell, or any cowbell-adjacent items?” Silas asked the crowd, as a group of younger kids played hacky sack in the street.

Erin Cherry, who teaches in the city’s elementary school music program, was on hand to support Silas, who has been volunteering in her classroom.

She introduced herself to Silas’s father, Guy Bellino, who teaches political science at nearby Salem State University. Silas has been a joy to have in the music room, Cherry said.

“That makes me feel so good,” said Bellino, beaming.

title: Meet Latoya Gayle, the woman who wants to unseat state Senator Nick Collins
text:
But to the supporters who packed an Italian restaurant near Ashmont Wednesday morning to watch Wu offer her endorsement, Gayle offers more than just an opportunity to unseat a foe.

To her supporters, Gayle is viewed as a candidate who will fight for residents they say Collins ignores.

“My experience has been he’s unserious,” said Kate Warren Barnes, a longtime community advocate and college lecturer. “He’s unserious, he’s unresponsive, and he hasn’t been the solutions-focused leader that this district needs.”

Gayle, 47, has spent years as an advocate for families and young children. Currently, she works as director of advocacy for a nonprofit called Neighborhood Villages, pushing for changes in the state’s child care system.

Like a surprising number of influential Black Bostonians, Gayle grew up in Springfield, as the youngest of seven sisters. She has raised her own family of four children in the South End and in Dorchester, where the family now lives.

Her parents migrated to Massachusetts from Alabama, seeking refuge from the oppressive racial politics of the Deep South. She said her run for office has been inspired, in part, by a feeling the progress her parents’ generation fought for is slipping away.

“I think people my age grew up and we were taught so many things that we’re dealing with today were behind us,” Gayle told me. “And not that the world is perfect, but that we weren’t gonna go back. And it seems like we’re on a backwards trajectory right now.”

For years, friends had casually suggested she think about running for office, but she had always brushed the idea aside. She was already involved as a Boston Public Schools parent active in educational issues and raising her family. But this year she finally came to believe that she had reached the right moment in her life to go for it.

That was largely driven by her feeling Collins was too conservative on many issues, among them rent stabilization and driver’s licenses for undocumented immigrants. She’s running to be a more progressive, community-centered voice.

The First Suffolk district has an interesting history. For years the domain of legendary powerbroker William M. Bulger, it was redrawn long ago to reflect a changing population. Bulger was followed by Linda Dorcena Forry, a Haitian American, who held the seat for five years, until being succeeded by Collins in 2018.

In perception, it has reverted to being a seat identified with South Boston because of Collins. But the district also includes part of the South End, Chinatown, downtown, and much of Dorchester, making it one of the most diverse in the Massachusetts Senate. That’s a big part of the reason Collins, who gradually become a darling of the downtown business establishment, is viewed as perhaps more vulnerable than his supporters assume.

As for the mayor, the mutual contempt between Collins and Wu is hardly a secret. Not only did he expend every possible ounce of political capital to kill Wu’s attempts to raise revenue by shifting more of the property tax burden away from residential homeowners and onto commercial property, he relentlessly attacked Wu in the process.

That played well behind closed doors at the State House, where cities and towns are often treated like pawns. But Wu is clearly betting that it will prove less popular with voters.

In endorsing Gayle Wednesday, she openly accused Collins of siding with corporate interests at the expense of his constituents in a sleazy backroom negotiation.

“We are tired of the state Senate saying no to everything,” she said. “We are tired of our state Senate offloading their elective power to unelected corporate interests to negotiate against Boston families.”

Gayle is a definite underdog in a race against a well-known and well-funded incumbent. But Wu’s support is beyond valuable. And underdogs sometimes win.

Gayle said this moment demands change. And she believes she can be that change.

“If there’s ever a time to do it, now is that time.”

title: Wu’s Beacon Hill power play could come with a price
text:
But the state Senate race she waded into Wednesday may be her biggest gamble yet — one that’ll test the bounds of her influence in the city, and, win or lose, could have damaging side effects on Beacon Hill.

Wu escalated her long-running feud with South Boston Senator Nick Collins, endorsing child care advocate Latoya Gayle in her primary bid to unseat him. Wu and Collins’ long-running beef hit its peak late last year, after the conservative Democrat (again) blocked her attempts to get property tax legislation passed on Beacon Hill. (You can catch up on the drawn-out drama here, here, here, and here.)

The endorsement wasn’t exactly a surprise. Those in Wu’s political orbit have for months been quietly supporting Gayle, a first-time candidate who lives in Dorchester and whose campaign manager, Maccon Bonner, served in Wu’s administration before joining the campaign. But in putting her name — and fiery criticisms of the entire Senate — behind the effort to oust Collins, the mayor officially opened a new front in her battle with the upper chamber. It was a moment she seemed to revel in.

“This is going to be a fun election cycle,” she said.

Gayle faces an otherwise uphill battle. Collins is well-known in the district, and has a significant cash advantage. He had $92,000 in his campaign account at the end of last month to Gayle’s $15,500. Shortly after Wu’s endorsement, his campaign began circulating an internal poll that showed that 82 percent of the roughly 800 people surveyed said they would vote for him in the primary, compared to 10 percent for Gayle. (Collins’ campaign didn’t respond to questions about details of the poll, including its margin of error or how it was conducted).

It’s not the first time Wu has backed apparent underdogs and won. She helped install several allies on the City Council in 2023, and aided political unknown Allison Cartwright in her defeat of sitting City Councilor Erin Murphy in a 2024 race for the oft-ignored role of clerk Suffolk County Supreme Judicial Court.

Still, this one will test her clout in some of the less-friendly areas of the city toward her. Seven of the nine precincts where her opponent, Josh Kraft, outperformed her in last year’s preliminary election were in South Boston.

“Mayor Wu is arguably the most influential figure in Boston politics right now, and this is about whether that popularity translates into influence in a state legislative race,” said Kate Norton, a political consultant who previously worked for former mayor, Martin J. Walsh. “By weighing in against Collins, she’s putting her political capital on the line. He’s a well-established incumbent who has really strong support in the neighborhood.”

Collins isn’t the only one caught in the mayor’s crosshairs. State Senator Will Brownsberger, the other member of the Senate’s Boston delegation who spoke out publicly against her property tax shift bill, is facing a challenge from former Wu aide, Daniel Lander. Though Wu has yet to weigh in directly on that race, Lander’s campaign finance reports are peppered with donations from those in the Wu-inverse.

Senate President Karen Spilka declined to address the Gayle endorsement at an unrelated event Wednesday. But she’s been quietly helping Collins and Brownsberger, one of her top deputies, by making calls to union leaders to rally their support for them, according to two people with knowledge of the calls.

Taken together, the races have the feel of a revenge tour, a risky game for a mayor who needs buy-in from both chambers of the state Legislature if she wants to get some of her biggest priorities passed.

Then again, many of those priorities already seem stuck in neutral.

“The question really is,” Norton said, “what does she have to lose?”

SURVEY SAYS: It’s anyone’s game in the Democratic primary for Massachusetts’ Sixth Congressional District — but state Representative Tram Nguyen may have a slight edge in the six-person field, at least according to a poll her campaign commissioned.

The poll of 400 likely Democratic primary voters in the North Shore-anchored district found Nguyen, of Andover, leading with 28 percent of support from those surveyed. Dan Koh, a former White House aide, notched the second most support at 18 percent, while the rest of the field all fell under 10 percent. The poll, conducted between May 26-27, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.89 percentage points, according to a memo from the campaign.

It’s the second internal poll that has Nguyen, the only current elected official in the race, leading. A March survey that John Beccia’s campaign released had Nguyen at 13 percent to 10 percent apiece for Beccia and Koh, though that was within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus roughly 5 percentage points.

Another internal poll software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck’s campaign released last month had the software engineer leading the field, but only after voters read “candidate bios” that read like campaign lit for some (Andres-Beck) and oppo hits for others (Koh).

Nguyen’s poll, conducted by Workbench Strategy (which has done work for Zohran Mamdani’s New York mayoral campaign) also included results after voters read “all positive biographical statements” about the candidates. But unlike Andres-Beck’s survey, it included the results without them.

BALLOT BUSTERS: Officials with the Massachusetts Democratic party are looking to knock two Republican candidates for statewide office off the ballot after they submitted signatures flagged by local clerks over possible forgery concerns to the Secretary of State’s office this week.

Adam Roof, the state Democratic Party’s executive director, filed complaints with the State Ballot Law Commission on Wednesday, alleging that “numerous” certified signatures both Republican attorney general hopeful Michael Walsh and lieutenant governor candidate Anne Manning Martin handed in by Tuesday’s deadline had been “fraudulently obtained.”

Neither candidate has much wiggle room should any of their signatures get discounted: Both submitted around 10,600 signatures — just over the 10,000 threshold to qualify for the September ballot — and each had more than 1,000 flagged by clerks. The ramifications could go beyond just the ballot: Knowingly submitting fake signatures is against the law.

POUR DECISIONS: Add Spilka, the Senate’s top Democrat, to the list of pols supporting a proposal to keep drinks flowing until 3 a.m. this summer as the state gets ready to host a handful of World Cup games. In fact, Spilka’s office hinted that the Senate may want to let the liquor flow even more freely (read: happy hour).

The Ashland Democrat “supports giving cities and towns the option to shift last call to 3 a.m. this summer, and more widely giving local officials the flexibility to loosen up our antiquated alcohol consumption laws,” a Spilka spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.

It’s possible her chamber could soon get something to consider. House lawmakers on a legislative committee rewrote and unanimously advanced a narrowed version of the legislation on Wednesday that would allow bars, with local approval, to push last call to 3 a.m., starting Monday and lasting until July 31.

The House and the Senate are both holding formal sessions on Thursday.

Both Wu and Governor Maura Healey say they back the idea. Actual bartenders, not so much.

RECORDS SCRATCH: Transparency fight escalates as House votes to limit its exposure to audit, public records requests by Chris Lisinski, CommonWealth Beacon: Massachusetts House leaders are attempting to chart a path forward on a pair of overlapping transparency fights. In the process, they seem to have set off an even greater conflagration. “This is, to me, kind of like a shit sandwich with extra pickles,” said House Minority Leader Brad Jones.

MONEY MATTERS: City Council delays vote on Wu’s $4.9 billion budget proposal, approves using $70 million of reserves to plug budget gaps by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: The Boston City Council voted Wednesday to postpone a planned vote on the mayor’s budget proposal until next week, delaying action on a spending plan that has divided the council and drawn intense pushback from community groups.

RENTAL ASSISTANCE: Mayor Wu endorses compromise rent control proposal, saying it would ‘avoid a messy ballot initiative’ by Andrew Brinker, The Boston Globe: Wu on Wednesday threw her support behind a compromise rent control proposal that tenant advocates and a group of high-powered real estate developers unveiled earlier this week in a bid to avoid a brutal ballot fight this fall.

title: Enjoy walking around Boston? A new 80-mile circuit lets you do exactly that.
text:
Unlike traditional nature paths, the walking trail network uses “green spaces, built environments, and walkable connections between them,” said Miles Howard, the group’s founder and director.

“Our hope in launching this trail is encouraging people to think beyond arbitrary lines of demarcation,” Howard said. “This whole area is far more interconnected in a physical and geographic sense than one might realize, and walking is a fantastic way to discover that firsthand.”

Howard gained national attention for his work designing two other trails that run through Boston — the original Walking City Trail and the City on the Hills Trail.

Official maps and guides for the Boston Boundless Trail will launch online on June 6, which is National Trails Day. The maps can be downloaded from BostonTrails.org and will be compatible with Google Maps and the popular map platform AllTrails, Howard said.

Other than turn-by-turn instructions, which can be used on smartphones or printed out, hikers will be on their own, Howard said. There are no signposts.

“We recommend pairing one of the maps with the turn-by-turn directions, so that you’re not constantly looking at your phone on the trail,” he said.

Howard recently answered a few questions about the new urban loop trail.

What is an urban hike?

One of the key differences between just going for a walk and going for an urban hike is that you’re really prioritizing interesting scenery over efficiency and directness.

An urban hike can be any place where you know the features are more built up, but where you’re constantly looking around and thinking, ‘I have an inclination to walk through here.’

I would guesstimate that the trail is about 60 percent paved and 40 percent dirt.

But some of the dirt sections are really going to have a lot of rustic elements, like roots and rocks.

How did you come up with the Boston Boundless Trail?

When you look at a map of the Boston area, you can see parks and conservation lands and gardens that could be interesting features for a route.

But you really can’t get a sense of how all this is going to feel as a curated sequential experience until you actually go out and try walking it.

One of the most fun planning elements happens in areas where there are no obvious walkable connections in sight. I have to think, like, ‘OK, how do we do this? Is it even possible to do this?’

That element of discovering how a map translates to real life is part of the fun. It kind of feels like you’ve stumbled across something that’s been lost or forgotten when you find a walkable means of getting somewhere.

So there’s the theoretical phase, which is mapping it out, and then there’s the translation to real-life phase, where you’re actually going out and walking it.

How long is the trail?

It is going to be an 80- to 90-mile loop.

The longest section of the 12 is going to be the third section that goes from East Milton to the Trailside Museum in the Blue Hills, and it’s also going to have the most elevation gain by far.

How hard is it to navigate the trail?

The number of junctions and turns one will encounter is comparable to what you might experience on a backcountry trail. There will be more of them in residential areas though.

I can’t really say how hard or easy it is to follow the route because it’s subjective for each person, but we have found that offering multiple navigation resources makes this wholly doable for most trail users.

Can you walk me through the 12 sections?

Section 1: Long Wharf North to Savin Hill Beach in Dorchester

Section 2: Savin Hill Beach to East Milton Square

Section 3: East Milton Square to Blue Hills Trailside Museum

Section 4: Blue Hills Trailside Museum to Riverdale Park in Dedham

Section 5: Riverdale Park to Waban Station in Newton

Section 6: Waban Station to Oak Square in Brighton

Section 7: Oak Square to Davis Square in Somerville

Section 8: Davis Square to Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown

Section 9: Bunker Hill Monument to Chelsea Square

Section 10: Chelsea Square to Revere Beach

Section 11: Revere Beach to Beachmont Station in Revere

Section 12: Beachmont Station to Lewis Mall Wharf in East Boston

And hikers can take the MBTA ferry from East Boston back to Long Wharf if they want to complete the full loop.

What are some highlights?

The trail is going to utilize the core of the Skyline Trail in the Blue Hill Reservation, which will definitely be the most challenging part by far.

To get out of the Blue Hills, on the west side, to get into Hyde Park and Dedham, we’re actually going to be utilizing the lost highway of the I-95 connector that was partially built that exists in those woods now. You can basically link up to it via the west end of the Skyline Trail, walk the old overgrown highway through the woods for a bit, and then follow the green corridor where the rest of it was supposed to be built to get out of the woods. It’s such a cool piece of Boston history.

The trail will utilize paths along the Malden River in Everett and also take you past the Potato Shed Memorial in Charlestown.

The trail also takes people through marshes and over water crossings.

Can cycling enthusiasts bike the trail?

There are more stretches of this trail than prior Walking City Trails that can be thoroughly biked, and we are going to be including an overlay with the finalized Google map of the route that will show stretches where you can bike.

But there are definitely portions where biking is not going to be feasible.

How would you recommend amateur hikers tackle the loop?

For beginner hikers approaching this with cross-trainers, a bag, and a couple bottles of water, most of the trail is going to be very natural territory.

The 12 segments range anywhere from just under 5 miles to almost 10 miles in length, so they’re going to want to ideally cut most of those trail segments in half. We do designate a suggested halfway point for each segment in case people want to divvy it up into shorter hikes.

We also list connections to public transit.

This is going to be something that, while great in distance, has a lot of outdoor territory that will feel very entry level for a lot of people.

What if someone wants to tackle the whole trail in separate chunks?

It’s obviously very subjective, but I’m going to estimate that the average person might want to do under 5 miles in a day. Basically, my guess is that it would probably take them somewhere between 21 to 24 sectioned hikes to do the whole thing.

title: On rent control, the real estate industry faces a big decision: Deal or no deal?
text:
And we have a special deal for Power Play readers: free registration to the Globe’s 2026 Tech Innovation Summit on Tuesday in Boston. Just use the code “POWERPLAY” when you register here.

Featuring: Gil Winn, Corey Thomas, Sal Lupoli, Tamara Small, Greg Vasil, Alicia Barton, Sharon Durkan, Shannon Liss-Riordan, Ian Bowles, Miceal Chamberlain, Rhonda Pacheco, Brian McGrory, and more.

The local real estate industry is facing the most consequential decision it may make for a long time: Deal or no deal?

So far there’s no consensus among developers, landlords, and real estate agents, as they stare down a July 1 deadline for a compromise that would keep what would be one of the nation’s strictest rent control policies from reaching the ballot this fall.

That’s because the proposed compromise would usher in something industry leaders have long resisted: limits on annual rent increases. They have the money and the motivation to go all the way to defeat the measure in November, which would ensure it can’t be brought back to the voters for another six years.

But sensing that might be too risky of a path, a small faction broke off this spring to work on an alternative that could prompt rent-control supporters to drop the ballot question. The faction includes several prominent developers: WinnCompanies CEO Gil Winn, HYM Investment Group managing partner Tom O’Brien, Lupoli Companies CEO Sal Lupoli, and The Builder Coalition executive director Dave Madan.

The proposed compromise they’ve crafted would allow rent control in Massachusetts for the first time since the 1990s, but it’s a more modest version than what’s headed for the ballot. The new proposal would allow towns to opt in to a program capping annual rent increases at 5 percent plus inflation, up to 10 percent, and exempting new construction for 15 years. It’s far looser than the ballot measure, which would mandate a statewide cap limiting rent increases to the rate of inflation, or 5 percent, whichever is lower.

Advocates sent the new language to Beacon Hill on Tuesday, offering to withdraw their ballot measure if it’s passed into law by the end of the month. That’s going to be a tough sell. House Speaker Ron Mariano is no fan of rent control, and he and Senate President Karen Spilka are unlikely to get on board without buy-in from key real estate groups – NAIOP Massachusetts, the Mass. Association of Realtors, and the Greater Boston Real Estate Board.

Now the ball’s in their court.

NAIOP chief executive Tamara Small says her members and advisers spotted a number of red flags in their review of the proposed legislation, and they’re “digging into it to understand what it means.” When might NAIOP decide? All Small would say on that: “Relatively soon.”

The Greater Boston Real Estate Board is an umbrella group, with five boards it needs to satisfy. Greg Vasil, GBREB’s chief executive, knows time is of the essence. But proffering a deal at the eleventh hour, he says, shows no consideration for the steps an organization like his must take to review. His projection: “It may take us a couple of weeks.”

Then there’s the Realtors group. While they will consider the proposal, general counsel Justin Davidson said his group remains committed to fighting rent control.

These groups have been the financial backbone of the “no on rent control” campaign, and they have been confident, deciding just three weeks ago not to cut a deal with rent control supporters. The no campaign is well on track to raise the $30 million pledged to fight the ballot measure, and has viewed any compromise offered by rent control supporters as a sign of weakness.

But not everyone agrees. Early polling suggests a majority of voters support rent control, and the stakes are huge. That has some in the real estate industry wondering if cutting a deal is better than risking defeat.

That’s why Winn decided on his own to seek an alternative proposal that the real estate community could live with. Winn, whose company builds and manages affordable housing projects, first began reaching out to nonprofit partners, such as community development corporations, with ties to tenant groups. More recently, he called developers O’Brien, Lupoli, and Madan.

Winn’s goal, we’re told, was to craft a framework that could jumpstart a meaningful conversation with the rest of the real estate industry and lawmakers. Talks began to ramp up between the CDCs and the rent control supporters in March, and by the end of last week, Winn helped facilitate compromise language that tenant advocates have signed off on, transforming the debate.

The real work begins now, as the industry groups review a proposal that they would have dismissed out of hand not that long ago. Will the clock run out on everyone? Tick, tick, tick.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Teachers and staff at the Croft School in Jamaica Plain have been fighting with the board over getting fully paid as the for-profit private school prepares to shut its doors on June 12. Now they’ve escalated that fight by filing a lawsuit in Suffolk Superior Court on Thursday against the school, its founder Scott Given, and board member Michael Goldstein. Plaintiffs Matthew Salisbury, Sade Freeland, and Jennifer Elson are seeking class action status, and being represented by Shannon Liss-Riordan’s law firm known for recovering millions of dollars in back pay for waitresses, truck drivers, janitors and others. The lawsuit alleges that the Croft school is refusing to pay about 40 teachers and staff their salary for the full academic year – amounting to each losing thousands of dollars. “We’ve earned our pay, and now we want to hold them accountable for their wrongdoings,” said Elson, a school counselor. A board spokesman declined comment. The Croft school has been in disarray since March after the board accused Given of mismanaging $13 million and keeping two sets of financial books. The school, which has locations in Providence and Boston, filed for bankruptcy Friday morning to liquidate its assets.

Boston city councilor Sharon Durkan has a plan to jump-start sluggish housing construction: Get rid of the minimum off-street parking mandates. Requiring parking, the thinking goes, simply adds to construction costs, giving developers one more reason to sit on the sidelines. Somerville and Cambridge have done it. Why not Boston? The proposal was aired in a public hearing on Thursday at City Hall. Several years ago, the city ended parking minimums for affordable housing projects. And now Durkan, who represents several downtown neighborhoods, believes she has more than half of the 13-person council on board with dropping them altogether. Southie’s Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy of Dorchester, who hail from neighborhoods where many residents regularly drive and park on the streets, are publicly opposed; Flynn said removing the parking requirement will not address the city’s housing crisis and instead will “worsen our existing parking crisis.”

Want to watch the parade of “Tall Ships” along Boston Harbor on Saturday, July 11? You may want to save up your doubloons. Sail Boston Inc., a nonprofit, is setting up bleachers on Massport’s Fish Pier to provide a prime viewing spot. The tickets cost $225 for general admission and $375 for premium seats, which at least includes lunch (at that rate, you bet it includes lobster rolls). Despite the steep price, Sail Boston spokesman George Regan says the group isn’t making a profit on these tickets; those grandstands cost money to put up, and Regan argues the tickets are still “cheaper than a good seat at Fenway Park.” But if you want to watch for free, Massport is offering waterfront viewing space to the public in the Ray Flynn industrial park in South Boston nearby and at Piers Park in East Boston.

First, CommonWealth Kitchen lamented the arrival of Wonder, the venture-backed ghost-kitchen/food hall operator. Now, the Dorchester nonprofit food startup incubator is warning about another “big money” player: giant food supplier Sysco and its $29 billion deal to buy Jetro Restaurant Depot. CWK sounded the alarm last week, blasting the deal and raising the question: “What happens to us when the giant gets even bigger?” CWK chief executive Jen Faigel says Sysco is not particularly friendly to smaller businesses, unlike a cash-and-carry warehouse like Restaurant Depot. She calls the merger “another example of corporate consolidation gone wild at the expense of the little guys.” Not to fret, says a Sysco spokesperson: The company has no plans to raise prices at Restaurant Depot, or hurt its service, and it will operate Restaurant Depot, which has five Greater Boston locations, as a standalone business under the Sysco umbrella.

No good deed goes unpunished. You know the feeling. And it’s a good bet that Corey Thomas does, too. As chief executive of Boston cybersecurity company Rapid7, he took on a number of leadership roles in local civic circles. Notably, Thomas sits on the board of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (after a stint as chair), and he’s wrapping up his role as chairman of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, a two-year term that ends this month as BofA’s Miceal Chamberlain takes over.

Rapid7’s stock took a tumble in 2024. That prompted activist investor JANA Partners to start buying up shares and shaming management. In particular, JANA criticized Thomas’s prominent board service, calling it a distraction from the all-consuming job of a public company chief executive.

JANA and Rapid7 settled their differences last year, and put three JANA-backed directors on the board. The fallout became clear this week when the company announced Thomas had been replaced as CEO by one of the new board members, Wael Mohamed. Thomas will remain with the Rapid7 board as executive chairman.

The idea that a CEO who is civically engaged is somehow harming shareholders is silly. These extracurricular activities help develop networks and valuable relationships in communities where their companies are located. Conversely, public company CEOs provide an important voice in civic conversations. It was even more essential for Thomas, one of the few Black CEOs of a public company, to hold prominent civic posts because it showed how Boston welcomes diverse leadership. It would be a shame if JANA’s attack discourages other C-suite types in Boston from taking on these time-consuming but critically important roles. We shouldn’t let activist investors dictate what’s important for building a better Boston.

title: Dot Day Parade, Dorchfest bring Boston’s largest neighborhood together for a weekend of celebration
text:
The 120th-annual Dorchester Day Parade caps a weekend of festivities that included Dorchfest, a porchfest-style music festival, and the Dorchester Day 5K, which raises money for local charities and youth programs. Together, the events serve as a reunion for residents and a tribute to the community’s history.

Dot Day’s genesis dates to 1905, when organizers launched a parade to commemorate the founding of Boston’s largest neighborhood, according to the Dorchester Reporter. More than a century later, what began as a single procession has grown into a multiday tradition.

On Saturday, hundreds of people packed Ashmont and Adams Village for the fifth year of Dorchfest. Bands and solo performers played from porches, driveways, and front yards as crowds wandered from block to block, stopping to listen and dance.

“We come every year,” said Carla Alvarez, swaying to salsa music near Bushnell Street. “The music is amazing.”

As he held his 2-year-old son in his arms on Saturday, Winston Jones, of Lower Mills, spoke of Dorchester’s diversity. He said events like Dorchfest and the parade celebrate the mix of communities that has long defined the neighborhood.

“Music is a great organizer, a great way to bring different cultures, families, all sorts of levels of age together,” said Jones, 38. “You walk up a block, and you see people you see at the park or people you go to the gym with.”

Dorchester is home to large Cape Verdean, Latino, Black, Vietnamese, and Irish communities. Though the neighborhood has seen less luxury development than other corners of Boston, some longtime residents say new condominium projects and rising housing costs have reshaped parts of the area.

“We’ve lost a lot of folks because of displacement and gentrification,” said T. Michael Thomas, founder of The People’s Academy, a nonprofit that trains underserved youth and adults for trade careers. “The parade means everything because it highlights diversity, community, and family. It promotes it and it shows it.”

Matthew Milhomme, 42, has witnessed a different side of Dorchester’s evolution. Sitting along the parade route as traditional Vietnamese dancers glided past, he said he’s watched new businesses open and public infrastructure improve since moving into the home where his wife has lived since 2013.

He said the parade serves as a showcase for local groups and organizations, giving his family a chance to reconnect with the locality.

“I love looking at all the different parts of our community,” Milhomme said. “But our neighborhood hasn’t changed, it’s been the same people that were there before us.”

As marching bands blared and dancers twirled past, Edward Bordenave clapped from the sidelines alongside his wife and daughter, who recently traded their Dorchester home for one in Milton. Having spent nearly a decade in the neighborhood, Bordenave said celebrating local changes is one reason he’ll keep coming back for Dot Day.

“It’s good to be back seeing familiar faces and seeing the parade again,” said Bordenave, 40. “I just hope that the cultural fabric of Dorchester still remains.”

Dorchester crowns an honorary mayor each year. The title goes to the community member who raises the most money for the parade, with every dollar donated counting as a vote.

This year, that honor belonged to Nolan, a Dorchester native and lifelong resident who spent Sunday atop a float surrounded by friends, family members, and children from the youth sports teams she coaches. Near the Ashmont fire station, a large group of supporters cheered as her float passed by.

“If you’re not from here, you might not get it, but if you come and stay a bit, you learn that everyone feels a deep sense of pride to be from here,” said Nolan, who raised more than $18,000 for the parade committee. “There’s so many different groups and people that make Dorchester so special, so it’s awesome to be able to see that represented through the parade year in and year out.”

Among them was Myles King, who bounced excitedly on the curb as a pack of motorcycles roared past.

At 8 years old, King hasn’t lived through the decades of change that older locals describe. But somehow, he expressed the same pride in Dorchester that so many lifelong residents share.

“My neighborhood is kind, weird, and peaceful,” King said. “I just like living here.”

Boston Globe correspondent Aayushi Datta contributed to this report.

title: Boston’s new approach to special education may be leaving out the kids who need it most
text:
“Now my son can write his name for the first time without guidance,” Whyte said.

The Henderson was once hailed as a model of inclusive education, drawing scholars from as far as Germany and Brazil to observe how students with and without disabilities learned side by side. But soon the kindergarten-through-12th-grade school will stop serving as a long-term destination for Boston’s most vulnerable students.

After next year, the city plans to eliminate Henderson’s high school grades amid declining enrollment and a budget crunch. A similar institution in Brighton, the Mary Lyon, is shutting its high school this year.

The closures come as Boston Public Schools is in the final stages of a once-in-a-generation transformation of special education. The plan includes a shift away from high schools like Henderson that specialize in teaching students with disabilities. Instead, city officials envision making all classrooms inclusive environments.

Some parents and educators worry that with Boston schools poised for layoffs, there won’t be enough staff in every classroom to meet the needs of children, like Julian, with more severe disabilities.

Boston Public Schools agreed in 2022 to overhaul special education after the state found that services for students with disabilities were in “systemic disarray.” Another audit determined that too often children with disabilities were being segregated from their classmates and taught in separate classrooms.

When Superintendent Mary Skipper presented a solution in 2023, she outlined an urgent plan to fix longstanding problems.

“We can no longer be a district where students need to travel to a certain school with a certain program in another neighborhood, sometimes far away from home, to get the services they need,” Skipper said. “All Boston Public Schools must be inclusive.”

The goal was to educate students with disabilities in general education classes whenever possible by 2027. Boston has made progress, but about one of every three students with disabilities is still mostly learning separately from other children, according to state data.

And many of these children are still struggling. More than 90 percent of students with disabilities from third to fifth grades are not meeting expectations in reading on the most recent state MCAS tests.

Some studies have found that general education students perform just as well in inclusion classes, but others found negative effects on students who are struggling academically.

City officials say the new approach to special education is designed to meet the needs of all children.

“This is a student-centered approach,” said Simone Wright, Boston’s deputy superintendent of academics.

Parents welcome a system built around individual kids, but they fear there won’t be enough staff to make it work, especially for students with more severe disabilities. Across Boston next year, schools are slated to eliminate 147 full-time special education positions as the city faces growing financial challenges.

The cuts are due in part to the closure of a handful of schools, and city officials downplayed the repercussions.

“We feel really confident saying student services and supports will not be impacted by any staffing reductions,” Wright said.

The Roosevelt K-8 school in Hyde Park is set to lose four special education teachers and four classroom aides, according to Noah Patel, a sixth-grade math and science teacher. Staff have been told, Patel said, that next year they will group most children with disabilities from kindergarten to fourth grade in the same classroom.

“It feels like we are going backwards,” Patel said.

In Jamaica Plain, the Curley School used to have two teachers at all times in core classes such as English and math. With the cuts, third-grade teacher Kafunda Banks said three teachers will have to divide their time between two classrooms.

That sentiment was echoed at 15 schools surveyed by Megan Murray, a third-grade special education teacher at the Holmes School in Dorchester who is writing her dissertation about the overhaul of special education.

“Teachers felt like they are tasked with the impossible mission of providing instruction to all students without the resources they need to make it work,” said Murray, who is studying at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

Across the country, more students are being diagnosed with disabilities. In Boston, 24 percent of public school students had one this year, up from 21 percent in 2020, according to state data.

Given that rise, advocates expressed concern about the planned closure of the two specialized high schools.

“If you take the Henderson and the Mary Lyon away, we won’t have many schools that can handle” students with more severe disabilities, said Elaine Meehan, a Mary Lyon board member.

At both high schools, students with disabilities make up over a third of the population. For decades, they have learned alongside their typically developing peers. The model had a simple secret: They had more staff.

In core subjects such as math and English, two teachers work together in a classroom at all times and at least one of them must have a degree in special education.

However, a budget shortfall driven by raises for staff, rising special education costs, and other factors prompted administrators to propose cutting up to 400 jobs districtwide next school year, including more than 100 classroom aides.

At the same time, enrollment across the city has steadily dropped, a trend that officials said has had an acute impact on the Henderson.

Over the past three years, 45 percent of eighth-graders did not continue there into high school. The Henderson had the smallest ninth to 12th grade population in the entire city, according to Boston Public Schools.

Some parents blame the Henderson’s enrollment drop on the school’s inability to recover after a 16-year-old student brutally assaulted its principal in 2021. The city increased security and added more social workers, but some thought more could be done.

Some parents say they have no choice but to go elsewhere. Mae Colanti, a lively third-grader with Down syndrome, is leaving the Henderson, according to her parents, Cristina and Michael Colanti. Currently at the school, one aide is bouncing among three classrooms and Mae, who has a hard time transitioning to new activities, needs more support, her parents said.

Mae’s parents made the difficult decision to move her next year to Roslindale’s George Conley School. She will be taught in a separate classroom where children with disabilities are grouped together.

Other parents fear that the changes will force them to seek placements outside of Boston. Under the law, if local public schools can’t meet a child’s needs, the city must pay the tuition to send them to a private institution.

This year, Boston Public Schools budgeted $49 million to send 450 students to private schools. Rising tuition costs have become a significant strain on the city’s school budget, officials have said.

If children with more severe disabilities can’t find a placement under the new special education model “out of district costs are only going to grow,” said Victoria Crisp, a special education advocate and former administrator at Boston Public Schools.

That includes Deanna Webb, a former Henderson teacher, who said that for eight years the school has been the best place for her daughter, who has Down syndrome and autism.

“A student like my daughter,” Webb said, “would be learning in a separate environment if she weren’t at the Henderson.”

title: Marty Walsh’s labor relations, North Shore edition
text:
Walsh, the former Boston mayor and current executive director of the NHL Players’ Association, has been leaning on local labor leaders as their members weigh which candidate to endorse to replace US Representative Seth Moulton. And in many cases, it seems to be helping.

Koh has endorsements from more than 30 unions, and can now add another one to the list. Members of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, the umbrella organization representing more than 700 unions and labor groups around the state, voted to endorse him Friday.

In announcing the group’s backing Monday, AFL-CIO president Chrissy Lynch highlighted Koh’s history with Walsh overseeing “a City Hall in Boston that brought in historic economic development that secured tens of thousands of union jobs,” as well as his work in former president Joe Biden’s labor department. (Koh followed Walsh there when the then-mayor left City Hall).

Walsh — whose labor credits include a stretch as the head of the Building and Construction Trades Council — insists he’s not twisting any arms.

“I’ve definitely made some calls for Dan, but most of it’s been him,” he said in a phone interview Sunday.

Walsh has been poking his head into the state’s political scene since he left for (er, started commuting to) D.C. He endorsed Boston City Councilor John FitzGerald in his successful 2023 campaign, and got behind former city councilor Frank Baker’s comeback bid and Alexandra Valdez’s council campaign last year, though both fell short in November. The Dorchester native pounded the pavement for Koh in 2018, when Koh was running for the open seat in the Third Congressional District.

“The first time he ran for Congress, obviously, I was helpful there because people didn’t really know who he was at the time, other than being my chief of staff,” Walsh said. “This is a whole different ball game. This one is really about Dan’s relationships.”

But not all labor groups are breaking Walsh’s Koh’s way.

The SEIU State Council, a coalition of 1199 SEIU, SEIU Local 509, SEIU Local 32BJ and the SEIU Committee of Interns and Residents, announced Monday it’s backing state Representative Tram Nguyen in the Sixth District primary, a move that Harris Gruman, the SEIU State Council’s executive director, acknowledged might ruffle Walsh’s feathers.

“I think [Walsh] would like us to respond to what he did for us in the past, which was very good,” and Gruman, nodding to Walsh’s record when he was a state representative for nearly 17 years. “But he wasn’t at the forum because he wasn’t a candidate. People were judging the candidates, not judging who is supporting the candidates.”

Nguyen has also nabbed support from United Auto Workers International, three local affiliates of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, the Boston Carmen’s Union Local 589, and all four local United Food and Commercial Workers chapters in the state. And Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former congressional aide also vying in the Democratic primary, scored support from the influential Massachusetts Teachers Association.

The SEIU council backed Nguyen, Gruman said, because she has been at the State House for years “making sure that our members are protected and get fair treatment and livable wages and benefits.”

LABOR INTENSIVE: The AFL-CIO also voted to endorse Governor Maura Healey and US Senator Ed Markey, who’s facing a primary challenge from Moulton. The picks weren’t totally surprising, but it’s a big deal for both campaigns — particularly Healey, by whom some union officials have felt a little let down. For Markey, it’s one more thing to help quell any momentum for Moulton.

NO SMALL PARTS: Attention suburban dads with a little free time! You could star in a campaign ad for John Beccia, the Lynnfield Democrat and fintech executive running for Moulton’s Sixth District seat.

Beccia’s campaign put out a call for actors to perform in three ads it’s set to film this week. Roles include:

— “Waitress in a diner,” who has what the casting call describes as “one line in conversation with John Beccia,” for a spot titled, “Scam Likely.”

— Male and female roles in an ad dubbed “You Beccia,” where a couple, in front of their home, speak one line to the camera. (His campaign has used the slogan so voters know to pronounce his last name as “betcha.”)

— Or, this Oscar-worthy assignment: “A suburban Dad at a gas station filling up his tank. No dialogue.”

The gigs pay between $500 and $750 for about five hours of work, according to the listing. Though the casting call says it’s for “non-union” actors — after the AFL-CIO asked Democratic campaigns this year not to hire non-union actors, per an email viewed by the Globe — a spokesperson for Beccia’s campaign said it’s paying actors through the Screen Actors Guild, and that the production company posted the ad without giving the campaign a heads up.

Some Democrats are publicly putting some distance between themselves and scandal-plagued Maine US Senate hopeful Graham Platner after last week’s New York Times reports about his past relationships, which followed a Wall Street Journal report about explicit texts he had exchanged with several women.

Not Senator Elizabeth Warren, though.

Warren recorded a robocall for Platner’s campaign to help get out the vote ahead of Tuesday’s primary, according to a spokesperson for the senator.

“Hi — it’s Elizabeth Warren, calling to ask you to VOTE for Graham Platner this Tuesday, June 9th,” she says in the message, per the transcript shared with the Globe.

“Graham is a veteran and an oyster farmer running for Senate to dream big and fight hard for working people in Maine. We need to take on corruption in Washington,” Warren says. “We need to defeat Susan Collins. And we need every Democrat to get out there and vote for Graham Platner!”

She’s not the only one standing by the embattled Platner. US Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat,defended him on the Sunday cable circuit, and US Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii was scheduled to hold a virtual fundraiser for Platner on Sunday, per POLITICO.

RELATED READ: This lobster boat captain from Down East quit Platner’s campaign, but hasn’t left it behind by Sam Brodey and James Pindell, The Boston Globe: Genevieve McDonald — a former state legislator, lobbyist, and trailblazing lobsterman turned political operative — has become a catalytic character in the dramatic story of Graham Platner’s candidacy. After publicly quitting the campaign in the wake of the first wave of negative headlines about Platner that revealed his offensive online posts and his Nazi symbol tattoo, McDonald became the source behind a New York Times piece alleging the newly married Platner had, as of last year, been exchanging explicit texts with as many as a dozen women.

ANOTHER LOCAL ANGLE: Massachusetts accounts for 4th-most contributions to Graham Platner’s campaign by Tim Dunn, Boston Herald.

ANOTHER ROUND FOR LAST CALL: The good news for those hoping for a later last call this summer: The state Senate on Monday plans to advance its version of the legislation the House fast-tracked last week that would let the liquor flow at bars and restaurants until 3 a.m. and permit public drinking in designated districts, according to a person familiar with the chamber’s plans.

But the Senate wants to stretch the timeline further, letting cities and towns keep the new public consumption rules in place through Labor Day. The House legislation would sunset at the end of July.

The bad news: That means lawmakers (who aren’t famous for their speedy negotiations) will have to reach a compromise before the bill hits Healey’s desk. The World Cup kicks off Thursday. No pressure.

SIGNATURE MOVES: To get on the Mass. ballot, incumbent Democrats got a hand from their public employees by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: Over the course of several weeks this spring, at least seven public employees working under Secretary of State William F. Galvin popped into city or town halls on weekdays to file paperwork to help get the eight-term incumbent back on the ballot. For House Speaker Ron Mariano, it was his chief of staff who helped handle the political task; for state Auditor Diana DiZoglio, an intern in her taxpayer-funded office chipped in. Four aides to Attorney General Andrea Campbell, including her office’s top communications official, submitted documents to help ensure she could run for reelection. Officials say the work was done on vacation, personal, or comp time, but the practice highlights the delicate dance they have to do to avoid illegally mixing political and public work.

TAX TALK: All 3 candidates for Mass. governor promise transparency. They also say they won’t release their tax returns. by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: The three major party candidates for governor refused requests from the Globe to disclose five years’ worth of their personal tax returns, a denial made all the more notable as their personal wealth and demands for transparency are animating this race.

FAMILY MATTERS: Former state Senator Dean Tran’s sister sentenced to 2 years supervised release, must pay $40K fine by Colleen Cronin, Boston Herald: Tuyet Martin, the sister of former state Senator Dean Tran, will have to pay $40,000 and spend two years under supervised release for her role in a scheme involving the ex-legislator. Martin wrote a fake employment offer letter for her brother that he used to obtain Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, federal prosecutors said.

AUDIT LATEST: DiZoglio calls for Mariano to resign, asks Healey’s help in audit fight by Katie Lannan, GBH News: After the Massachusetts House passed a bill last week that would narrow the scope of a voter-approved audit of the state Legislature, state Auditor Diana DiZoglio called for House Speaker Ron Mariano to step down from his job, and for Healey to veto the bill if it reaches her desk.

MassHealth to defund homeless health care program that serves thousands statewide by Tori Bedford, GBH News.

Mass. bills would ban PFAS in food packaging, kid’s toys and more by Barbara Moran, WBUR.

Israel and Iran exchange strikes in most serious escalation since April ceasefire by Patrick Quinn, Siddharth Karthikeyan and Hrvoje Hranjski, The Associated Press.

Ahead of World Cup, officials announce safety plans and ask for public’s help by Sean Cotter, The Boston Globe.

Massachusetts cities facing steepest layoffs since the Great Recession, observers say by Spencer Buell, The Boston Globe.

title: Three MBTA bus routes to remain free through end of year
text:
Three MBTA bus routes will remain free to ride through the end of the year, Mayor Michelle Wu and the MBTA announced Tuesday, just weeks before the fare-free pilot program was again set to run out of funding.

Spokespeople for the Wu administration and the transit agency did not immediately make clear Tuesday how much the program’s temporary extension would cost.

City and state officials indicated that money used for the MBTA’s reduced fare program would cover the plan to temporarily extend the program for bus routes 23, 28, and 29, which go through Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury. Wu’s office said in a statement that the reduced fare program “resulted in cost savings that are being applied to deliver this extension through the end of the year.”

City officials also said that they plan on “working this summer and fall on options for the fare free program in 2027.”

“There’s no such thing as free,” said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board. “It just means someone else is paying for it, and every trip on the MBTA is already significantly subsidized.”

Wu’s office on Tuesday touted the program’s success, saying riders have taken nearly 23,000 fare-free trips every weekday on the three bus routes since the start of the year. All-door boarding on the buses has cut times at stops by 20 percent, according to the city.

“We’re proud to partner with the MBTA to extend this successful program as we continue building a more reliable, accessible, and affordable transportation system across Boston,” Wu said in a statement.

Wu first eliminated fares on the three bus routes in March 2022, when she used $8 million in federal pandemic relief dollars to fund the program.

Then, in February 2024, Wu again used federal COVID-19 funds to reimburse the MBTA and continue the pilot program for an additional two years.

That money was set to run out at the end of February, but roughly a week before, city officials announced that enough of those funds remained to pay for the program through the end of this month.

Transit advocates have fretted over the program’s long-term future and from where officials could pull money to keep rides free on the three bus routes.

Seth Gadbois, a transportation attorney for the Conservation Law Foundation, applauded the extension of “this essential program.” But Gadbois said it feels “a little like we’re driving in circles when it comes to long-term solutions.”

“We bought four months of this back in February, and here we are buying six months more now,” Gadbois said. “Especially at a time when many transit advocates see the administration’s commitments to climate safety and justice missing from the budget, this is a promising and important step, but riders need and deserve more long-term certainty.”

Reggie Ramos, the executive director of the nonprofit Transportation for Massachusetts, said she was not surprised officials wanted to extend the fare-free routes through the end of this year, calling it a “wildly popular program that has proven to be a lifeline for that corridor.”

“Beyond the extension of this program, the real and critical questions are: How do we make programs like this sustainable and how do we ensure that the service these buses provide are at a level that is dignified and truly reliable?” Ramos said in a statement.

Transit advocates have pushed Wu and city officials to find a long-term, sustainable funding source to continue the program. In February, Wu’s office said the city is discussing the future of the program with the MBTA.

Supporters of the three fare-free routes have pointed to city statistics that show more than one-quarter of riders on the routes save $20 or more per month, savings they can put toward other expenses.

City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune said the routes are used “ heavily by our working-class and Black and Brown residents.”

“We’re helping families save money, making it easier for people to get to work, school, and essential services, and continuing to build a more equitable and connected city,” she said in a statement provided by Wu’s office.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
LA MATINEE DE FUZZ This Sunday-afternoon celebration of the distortion pedal includes the pummeling Queens outfit Skeeter de Milo along with three Bay State bands: sludge-punkers BEDTIMEMAGIC, psych shredders Astrai Bitch, and euphoria-corevisionaries Sapling. June 14, 2 p.m. O’Brien’s Pub. 617-782-6245, obrienspubboston.com

BLEACHERS Pop whisperer Jack Antonoff’s long-running alt-rock project released its fifth album, “everyone for ten minutes,” last month; it combines diary-of-a-star lyrics with kitchen-sink production while strenuously channeling fellow New Jerseyan Bruce Springsteen. June 16 and 17, 8:30 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway.crossroadspresents.com

LAMBRINI GIRLS The take-no-prisoners Brits, whose debut full-length, “Who Let the Dogs Out,” was one of punk’s 2025 highlights, bring their spiky basslines and righteous sneers across the Atlantic. June 17, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

Folk, World & Country

THE MEKONS/THE SADIES A fantastic double-pairing: The never-idle Jon Langford returns with venerable sonic shapeshifters the Mekons — the band that started it all for him — while alt-country’s Swiss Army Knife the Sadies soldier on in the wake of the untimely death of member Dallas Good four years ago. June 12, 8 p.m. $45. The Sinclair, 52 Church St., Cambridge. 888-929-7849, www.axs.com

THE GOLDEN HOURS A new band formed by the members of David Wax Museum and the Lowland Hum, the Golden Hours has an unusual origin story: It grew out of its members engaging in what they describe as an “immersive, blindfolded concert experience.” The results were such that a band was formed, a debut album (suitably titled “Terra Nova”) recorded, and a full-blown tour undertaken. June 12, 8 p.m. $40. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 617-492-7679. www.passim.org

JOSIAH AND THE BONNEVILLES The “Bonnevilles” in Josiah Leming’s band name doesn’t encompass just the people he plays with, but the people who come to his shows as well: “The only goal for me is to make something real and honest that can get people through the day,” he says. He’s touring in support of his latest, “As Is.” June 17, 8 p.m. $30. House of Blues, 15 Lansdowne St. 800-653-8000. www.ticketmaster.com

STUART MUNRO

MAYNARD JAZZFEST The fifth annual edition of this musical jamboree will feature performances by master trombonist Brian Thomas and his funky big band, the BT Allstars; eclectic, Boston-based jazz sextet Subject2Change; and Arlington’s own scorching, horn-powered Latin group Gringo Kings. Food and drink will be available for purchase. June 13, 12:30-5 p.m. Free. Veteran’s Memorial Park, 35 Summer St., Maynard. instagram.com/p/DWCcy0WiTWg/

RICK ESTRIN & THE NIGHTCATS This dynamic, multiple Blues Award-winning outfit is led by veteran Estrin, a superb songwriter, soulful singer, and scorching harmonica player. June 13, 8 p.m. $35-$37. Narrows Center for the Arts, 16 Anawan St., Fall River. narrowscenter.org

IZE TRIO For a unique spin on the jazz piano trio, this international group — American pianist Chase Morrin, Cypriot percussionist George Lernis, and Palestinian cellist Naseem Alatrash — combines jazz, Middle Eastern, and classical traditions. This gig, with special guest saxophonist Gregory Groover Jr., celebrates their latest album, “Global Prayer,” an exuberantly spiritual follow-up to their 2024 debut, “The Global Suites.” June 14, 6 p.m. $30.15-$41.79. Regattabar, Cambridge. regattabarjazz.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

ROCKPORT MUSIC A full weekend of music by the sea; Friday evening brings a Brahms celebration for opening night with an array of soloists including festival director Barry Shiffman, while the next morning puts cellist Mira Kardan on stage for a one-hour program with pianist Micah Yui. Saturday evening features a solo recital by the celebrated pianist Simone Dinnerstein, performing Bach, Rameau, and more; Sunday offers an all-Schubert evening with violinist Benjamin Beilman, cellist David Finckel, and pianist Wu Han. Shalin Liu Performance Center, Rockport. 978-546-7391, www.rockportmusic.org

SHE WAS THERE The two days of “She Was There” incorporate a film screening and panel discussion at the West End Museum curated by the Roxbury International Film Festival, and a concert the following afternoon at the Museum of African American History presented by Castle of our Skins and Boston Lyric Opera, featuring music and poetry by and about Black women. Cambridge-raised playwright Lenelle Moïse (“K-I-S-S-I-N-G”) narrates; American soprano Kearstin Piper Brown sings. June 13 (screening/discussion) and June 14 (concert). www.blo.org

MUSIC IN BLOOM Wander through the New England Botanic Garden at golden hour as spring gives way to summer, while small ensembles of musicians stationed throughout the gardens perform short sets of pieces by over a dozen living composers. Stopping to smell the flowers is encouraged. To visit all the musicians’ stations, you’ll probably have to walk a half mile; skip the heels for this one. Presented by Juventas New Music Ensemble and New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill. June 14 and 21, 6 p.m. Rain dates June 15 and 22. New England Botanic Garden, Boylston. https://nebg.org/

A.Z. MADONNA

IN OLD AGE The widowed Abasiama Ufot (Ebony Marshall-Oliver), whom Boston audiences have gotten to know from earlier installments in Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play Ufot Family Cycle about three generations of a Nigerian-American family, develops a late-in-life spiritual bond with Azell Abernathy (Marvin Bell), a gentle-spirited carpenter. Directed by Dawn M. Simmons. June 13–28. Production by Front Porch Arts Collective. Presented by ArtsEmerson at Emerson Paramount Center, Jackie Liebergott Black Box Theatre. 617-824-8400, ArtsEmerson.org

EUREKA DAY It’s a testament to Jonathan Spector’s skill that he managed to make his play as funny as it is while wading into the charged territory of mandatory vaccinations. That “Eureka Day” manages to (mostly) survive his wrongheaded decision to suddenly inject one character’s past tragedy into the mix is a testament to the play’s overall strength. With a topnotch cast directed by Margot Bordelon, “Eureka Day” mines quite a few laughs from the spectacle of well-meaning progressives tying themselves in lexical knots as they try to process events that defy ideological pigeonholes. Through June 28. Production by The Huntington. At Huntington Theatre. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

MY HOME ON THE MOON There’s much to savor in cara hinh’s production of Minna Lee’s clever sci-fi comedy, a marriage of whimsy and serious inquiry into where our tech overlords are taking us, whether we give them permission to or not. Set in a struggling Vietnamese restaurant in a rapidly gentrifying area, “My Home on the Moon” wants us to understand the value of heritage and community, and the degree to which food can underpin both — and, ultimately, to realize how precarious the balance can be if the goal is to maintain ethnic and cultural traditions. Lee’s play is, at bottom, an argument for humanity. And these days we can use as many of those as we can get. Through June 20. Production by CHUANG Stage. At Plaza Theatre, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-297-7161, www.chuangstage.org

DELIRIUM As chaos envelops the outside world, a man (Andrey Burkovskiy) and a woman (Chulpan Khamatova) are mired in a perpetual, petty argument. Eventually, as “the boundaries between reality and delusion dissolve,” according to press materials, “conflict becomes connection, and contradiction becomes a form of devotion.” Igor Golyak directs his own adaptation of Eugène Ionesco’s “Frenzy for Two, or More.” June 18-July 2. Arlekin Players Theatre. At Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. www.arlekinplayers.com

DON AUCOIN

FLAMENCO BOSTON St. Ignatius Concert Series closes its season with a presentation by Flamenco Boston. Through intimate, carefully crafted performances, the company aims to highlight the art form of Southern Spain through a style of flamenco that forefronts its deep, authentic traditions. The concert features dancers Cristina Candela and Elisabet Torras, Anthony Tran on guitar, and Barbara Martinez as the vocalist. June 12. Free ($20-$30 suggested donation). St. Ignatius of Loyola Catholic Church, Newton. www.stignatiuschestnuthill.org/concerts

¡BAILAREMOS! Flamenco Dance Project directed by Sabrina Avilés and Yuling Spanish Dance led by Yu-Ling Hu present this annual showcase celebrating the rhythm and passion of the art of flamenco. Both companies are dedicated to building community and increasing appreciation of flamenco music and dance while elevating diversity and accessibility. The evening features live music by Alfonso Cid and Dustin Carlson. June 13. $33. The Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org

BLACK SWAN It’s official. American Repertory Theater’s new musical adaptation of the 2010 film of the same name is generating lots of buzz and has been extended an additional week. Tony Award-winning choreographer Sonya Tayeh not only crafted the high-voltage movement but directs this world premiere production, a psychological thriller about ambition and power in the ballet world. It features music and lyrics by Obie Award winner Dave Malloy (“Moby-Dick,” “The Great Comet”) and a book by Guggenheim Fellow Jen Silverman. Through July 12, $43 and up. Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. www.americanrepertorytheater.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

AN EXQUISITE EYE: INTRODUCING THE ASO O. TAVITIAN COLLECTION Opening this week: The Clark Art Institute made a splash in 2024 when it announced it had received a coveted private collection from the Aso O. Tavitian Foundation, named for the late software billionaire who was also once a member of its board of trustees. A trove of 331 artworks by renowned European artists from the 15th to the 19th century — Peter Paul Rubens, Elisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun, and Jan Van Eyck top the marquee — the gift came with a $45 million check to fund a curator to care for them and a new wing to house them. This summer the Clark offers a long look before its permanent home is set to be complete in late 2027. Through Feb. 21, 2027. Clark Art Institute, 225 South St., Williamstown. 413-458-2303, clarkart.edu

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Spanning almost three millenia, 800 BCE right up till now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across eras to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. Through Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, www.harvardartmuseum.org

AMERICAN IMPRESSIONISM Last chance: In the mid-19th century, the Hudson River School of painters, led by Thomas Cole, adopted the heroic frame of their European Romantic forbears to craft a beatific vision of the American landscape that was often at odds with reality. While Americans fawned over their imagined idylls, Europeans were rushing headlong into Modernism as artists like Edgar Dègas and Claude Monet dropped Impressionism, frank and immediate, like a bomb into polite French establishment painting. It would take a while for the US to catch up, but they did, and with some masters of their own, many of whom you’ll see here: James McNeill Whistler, John Singer Sargent, and Childe Hassam, among others. Through June 14. Yale University Art Gallery, 1111 Chapel St., New Haven. 203-432-0601, https://artgallery.yale.edu/

MURRAY WHYTE

LEARNING WITH TREES Curator Martina Tanga partnered with the nonprofit Tree Boston to organize this celebration of what trees can teach us. The show, on view at City Hall and at the Dorchester gallery Hallspace, features artists such as Joel Janowitz, Clint Baclawski, and the artists’ collaborative just practice — Amanda Ugorji and Sophie Weston Chien, and considers the beauty, spiritual symbolism, environmental necessity, and companionship trees provide.Through Aug. 14. Scollay Square Gallery, Boston City Hall, 1 City Hall Square.www.boston.gov/departments/arts-and-culture/scollay-square-gallery

CATE McQUAID

LAUGHS FOR DAVE: A BOSTON COMEDY BENEFIT While longtime Boston comedian turned Boston Duck Tour guide Dave McDonough is undergoing cancer treatments, his buddies Dan Boulger and Christine Hurley are throwing a benefit to help him pay the bills, with other comics possibly dropping in. June 12, 7:30 p.m. $33.85. Venues II, 277 Ocean St., Marshfield. www.bostoncomedyfest.com

MY FRIEND KATY Comedian and “Ted Lasso” writer Jamie Lee uses comedy to tell the dark story of her best friend dying unexpectedly 20 years ago in college, and her subsequent investigation into that death, for this one-person show. June 13, 9:30 p.m. $20-$25. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. www.therockwell.org

TAWANDA GONA One of Gona’s formative moments as a comedian was playing the Comedy Studio’s original location on the third floor of the Hong Kong six nights a week for a month for the “comic-in-residence” program. Now he’s returning from New York to headline the new club location. June 14, 6 p.m. $23.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Homestead cafe in Dorchester to close after decade in business
text:
Following a decade of pouring stacks of latte art, Dorchester’s home.stead bakery and cafe will shut its doors later this month.

On Thursday, the shop announced on Instagram that it would cease operations after June 20.

“We invite you to stop by for your favorite cup of coffee or pastry and to say goodbyes,” the post said.

The cafe, on the corner of Dorchester Avenue and Adams Street, became a neighborhood gathering place after opening in 2016 — hosting dance parties, bicycling events, and art shows.

When home.stead opened, there weren’t many similar community hangouts.

“It filled a void. There was nothing else like it at the time,” said Adam Myerson, a customer who lives in the neighborhood. “But now there are other options nearby.”

Myerson and his friends donated money for home.stead to jump-start its build-out.

“A lot of people will be sad to see it go,” Myerson said.

In the post announcing its closure, home.stead staff thanked the shop’s neighbors.

“We are deeply grateful for the friendships and support that you have given us over the years,” the announcement said. “It has truly been a privilege to have known you, and we would love to stay in touch.”

A previous version of this story incorrectly described the upcoming event schedule at the cafe.

Redmond Bernhold can be reached at redmond.bernhold@globe.com.

title: Opponents of Blue Hill Ave. bus lane ask Trump administration to rescind $80m
text:
“The Wu administration’s unwillingness to listen to its most vulnerable residents continues a pattern of racist governance that Black Bostonians are all too familiar with,” Reggie Stewart, a Dorchester resident and chair of the Environmental and Climate Justice Committee of the Boston NAACP, said at a press conference Friday morning about the Blue Hill Ave. project. “We support better public transit, safer streets, and real investments in communities that have been neglected for generations, but investment does not mean forcing a harmful project onto Black neighborhoods after the people who live, work, worship, and run businesses there have said no to it.”

Residents are concerned the road redesign will decrease parking along Blue Hill Avenue, limit travel to one lane in spots, and remove trees along the thoroughfare, which could lead to more pollution and add to an already heightened rate of respiratory ailments among nearby residents.

What the community needs, according to the Coalition for Responsible Transportation Policy, which requested the revocation of federal funding, is for the city to lobby the MBTA to extend the Orange Line to Mattapan Square as well as beyond Forest Hills into Roslindale.

A light rail was supposed to be installed after the elevated Orange Line was taken down in the 1980s, coalition members said, but the Silver Line bus route was eventually added instead — one of many transportation-related “broken promises” to the Black community, they said.

Federal money for Blue Hill Avenue has been scrapped before. In 2009, the state withdrew an application for a federal grant for the 28X rapid transit bus line following significant opposition from the community.

In a statement, the Wu administration said the plan for roadway improvements would continue to evolve during the ongoing community process.

“The city is working closely with community leaders, residents, and the MBTA to deploy federally-awarded funds to make much-needed improvements to Blue Hill Avenue, beautify the roadway, speed up commutes, and expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor,” city officials said in a statement.

The US Department of Transportation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russell Holmes, the state representative from Mattapan who supports the proposed developments around his neighborhood, pushed back against the idea that they were being built on the backs of the Black community.
