“All of these developments are being done for Black people,” he said. “The rest of this city, it’s exploding in development, and for so long it felt like there was … nothing happening in the communities that I represent."

“Black people need to also be a part of this development and a part of this economic change that’s happening in Boston.”

But on Thursday night, city officials got an earful during a contentious meeting in Dorchester about the transportation plan for the White Stadium redevelopment in Franklin Park. Residents were upset at the plan to restrict parking on game days and require visitors to Franklin Park to request parking passes, according to the Dorchester Reporter, while people in surrounding neighborhoods would have to get resident permits to park in front of their homes.

“People like me, particularly Black people like me, who are homeowners, who pay taxes, cannot be anywhere around here celebrating birthdays, a regular cookout, a Little League team ... on game days,” one woman at the meeting said.

The city’s $325 million bid to redevelop White Stadium for a professional women’s soccer team is facing a legal challenge over whether it’s an impermissible use of a public park. The question before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court is whether the project is a renovation of an aging facility or a new arena altogether.

Dorchester residents are also up in arms about a proposal from the state to build a campus for hundreds of people dealing with mental illness and addiction at Shattuck Hospital, adjacent to Franklin Park. One resident called the plan “a new form of geographic redlining” that would concentrate social burdens in the city’s majority-minority neighborhoods.

Speaking at the press conference about Blue Hill Avenue, Louis Elisa, president of the Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association said all those projects would be built “on the backs of the Black community.”

“Stop trying to fool people that this means anything to the residents of Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan,” Elisa said of the bus lane. “This proposed project, which will bring a lot of money to the city of Boston for construction, will do very little to improve the quality of life along Blue Hill Avenue.”

“Stop trying to destroy the Black community,” he added. “Stop the aggressive takeover.”

A project to improve sidewalks and add bike lanes to Cummins Highway in Mattapan, which has taken years and caused major disruptions, has added to worries about construction projects in the area.

The coalition opposed to the bus lane said the “last straw” was a meeting Mayor Michelle Wu held a few weeks ago about the Blue Hill Avenue revitalization without inviting community advocates or two city councilors, Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper, who have been critical of the project.

The coalition said Wu hasn’t met with residents or business owners in person about their concerns, despite the city holding 100-plus meetings about it in the past several years.

“I just want you to understand the extraordinary moment that we’re in, where a predominantly Black community … out of sheer frustration, have thrown up their hands and decided to prevail to the Trump administration for relief,” Dianne Wilkerson, a Dorchester resident and former state senator, said at the press conference.

Asking for the federal funds to be withdrawn, she said, is the only way to get the city to the table to discuss a plan that will help the community.

Globe correspondent Chloe Pisani contributed to this report.

title: Soccer fans crowd South Station as Boston’s World Cup kickoff looms. Follow live updates.
text:
Read more World Cup stories

By Thai Theodoro, Jaden Perry, and Camilo Fonseca, Boston Globe

Maybe it’s too early to tell if all the pre-World Cup headaches were worth it. But if Day 1 is anything to go by, Boston did more than survive — it made hosting the tournament almost look easy.

The city swelled with soccer-mad fans on Saturday, with thousands boarding trains to Foxborough and thousands more crowding together in restaurants and at muggy outdoor watch parties.

So much was riding on the first of Boston’s seven World Cup match-days, with lingering questions about preparations and the ever-present fear of a transit meltdown. It remained to be seen whether the city’s efforts would end in embarrassment — or worse, disaster.

Instead, the day went off (mostly) without a hitch.

Fans complained about high prices, long lines, and crowded trains without air conditioning. But when the first train returned to South Station just before midnight, it seemed much had gone smoothly.

“I was really shocked at how organized they were, and on time, and smooth,” said Rosalvo Valcimond, 37. “All the fans, and all the different cultures all together in the same train — everyone was supportive and respectful.”

As of late Saturday night, Boston police said they had made no Fan Fest-related arrests. State Police also said there were no arrests to report at 9 p.m.

Instead, the first day of Boston’s World Cup festivities was orchestrated by the thunder of Scottish bagpipes and the lively beat of Haitian drums. Aside from those long lines outside South Station, where 20,000 fans queued up for their sold-out commuter rail trains, there was little in the way of distress or disturbances.

READ MORE

By Jaden Perry and Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondents

Spilling off packed trains at South Station, Scotland fans were riding high after the team’s first World Cup win since 1990.

“[It’s] been 28 years since Scotland qualified for the World Cup, but my son and I are together, and we saw Scotland win,” said Drummond Welsh, who was draped in a Scottish flag.

Chanting as they exited South Station, some fans went straight for McDonald’s for an after-game snack. Others scattered.

Steven Rehnie was not impressed with the transportation. His train was packed and had no air conditioning, Rehnie said, describing it as a “nightmare” getting into the stadium.

“It seemed badly organized, but [it was] amazing to go to the first World Cup game,” Rehnie said.

Many Haitian fans stepped off the train at South Station wearing disappointed expressions after the loss.

But Rosalvo Valcimond, 37, had good things to say about Boston’s first day of hosting the World Cup.

“I was really shocked at how organized they were, and on time, and smooth,” Valcimond said. “All the fans, and all the different cultures all together in the same train — everyone was supportive and respectful.”

By Frank Dell’Apa, Globe Correspondent

European teams fully expect to succeed at the World Cup, and for good reason. Eight of the last 10 finalists have been European, and they’ve won four of the last five titles.

They are favored again this time, but they’ve seldom made such a slow start.

Until Scotland’s 1-0 victory over Haiti before a crowd of 64,106 Saturday night, Euro teams had been winless in this World Cup. Sure, the heavyweights — the Dutch and Germans — don’t get started until Sunday. But it usually doesn’t take this long for Europe to flex its muscles. In Qatar, its teams had compiled a 3-0-3 record after the first three days.

Scotland, though, showed how even an average European team can efficiently achieve a result against an inexperienced foe. The Scots got started quickly, with John McGinn’s backheel to Andy Robertson setting up Scott McTominay. Then, McTominay slammed a drive off the right post following a Ben Gannon-Doak feed in the 17th minute. Finally, Che Adams controlled a long ball, and McGinn’s deflected shot got past Haitian keeper Johnny Placide in the 28th minute.

And that was that.

READ MORE

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

The first World Cup train arrived in South Station just before midnight, making the return trip from Foxborough.

A fleet of special trains are carrying some 20,000 fans who saw Scotland best Haiti by a score of 1-0.

“The train coming back home was easy, it was so nice,” said Douglas Bogv, 64, who moved from Scotland to the US 25 years ago. “Everything was coordinated.”

Bogv said the train back from Foxborough was a different experience than the one departing from South Station. To get to the game, he waited in line for about an hour.

But coming back, he said, there was even enough space for passengers to all sit comfortably.

“I have never seen so many Scottish people in my life,” Bogv said.

Column by Tara Sullivan

The clock had just crossed the 78th minute when Haiti striker Frantzdy Pierrot lifted his 6-foot-4-inch body from the green grass below. He rose above Scotland defender Grant Hanley and put his head on the ball. It sailed toward the Scottish net and, for just a moment, it seemed Pierrot was about to bring a storybook ending to life inside Boston Stadium, otherwise known as Gillette.

Alas, the ball sailed wide left, effectively taking Haiti’s chances with it. Scotland won Boston’s World Cup opening night, via both a 1-0 scoreline in Group C play and via their countless kilts and never-ending songs.

Yet there amid the sound of bagpipes and choruses of Loch Lomond were plenty of scenes of love for another great Boston diaspora, the one to which Pierrot belongs. As banners, posters, flags, and jerseys in support of Haiti proudly made their way down Route 1, into the stadium parking lots, and eventually into the stands, the extra love for Pierrot spoke to the special resonance he has with Boston.

Officially, Pierrot is here to lead the country of his birth onto one of the world’s greatest sporting stages.

Emotionally, he is here to represent the best kind of dream his adopted country can offer.

“It’s like he’s coming home again,” said Dean Serino, who coached Pierrot at Melrose High.

READ MORE

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Staff

Scottish fans erupted as the final whistle blew, throwing their hands into the air and filling Fan Fest at City Hall Plaza with cheers and hugs among blue jerseys.

Scotland fended off some close calls and delivered the Tartan Army the result it had waited decades to see. Their team won to open the country’s first World Cup appearance since 1998.

Fans had spent the day marching through Boston in kilts and filling the city’s streets with bagpipes. Now it was time for even more beers.

Callum Liddle, 29, came from Scotland with his best friend, father, and father-in-law. His group exchanged hugs and high fives with all the fellow Kilt wearers around them.

“It’s the best day of my life,” Liddle said.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

Full time here in Foxborough, and the first World Cup game at Gillette Stadium finishes Scotland 1, Haiti 0. John McGinn’s deflected finish in the first half holds up as the winner after a back-and-forth affair. A first win at a World Cup since 1990 leaves the Scots top of Group C, with Brazil and Morocco having drawn earlier in the day.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

Despite Haiti not yet scoring a goal, Haitian fans at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center in the Seaport remain hopeful.

“Haiti’s always on the news for something bad, OK,” said fan Judeline Jaboin. “So now we’re in the World Cup. It’s a big thing for us, even if they don’t win tonight. “

Wearing a fitted blue-and-red cap, Jaboin added: “That’s why I’m here, to support my country.”

Scotland fans also found reasons to cheer, but were still on edge about how close the match has been.

“Scotland aren’t playing too well,” said fan Grant Medland, who is visiting Boston for the games. “I feel that the fact that Haiti having too much possession is worrying me a wee bit, but we’re lucky to be in front.”

Check out the action at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — I popped down to the concourse for the early part of the second half, and while Scotland still leads — 1-0 at the second-half hydration break — there’s some nerves in the Scottish crowd. “Long way to go,” one Scot told another. “We’ve been here before,” another said. This would be a huge win for Scotland, which will struggle to get a result against Morocco or or Brazil and would love to bank 3 points tonight in Foxborough.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

The halftime whistle settled over Fan Fest like a release valve.

After more than 45 minutes glued to the screens, fans finally looked away from the ball.

As the break began, Mayor Michelle Wu stepped to the microphone as a mix of cheers and booing filled City Hall Plaza.

“To all of our friends from Haiti and Scotland,” Wu said. “We are so happy you landed here.”

Fans welcomed the break from the tension of the game. They got up to line up for the bathroom stalls.

Soccer fanatics talked through every close call before the second half could pull everyone back in.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

Fans squeezed through the narrow gaps left open in the crowd, brushing past a sea of jerseys, flags, and police officers.

Two girls in Brazil jerseys stopped to hand Boston police officers stickers with Brazilian flags.

Around them, languages bled into one another, creating a constant hum of celebration. People seemed to recognize each other not by name, but by color and crest.

“Hey Brazil! Let’s take a selfie,” a fan in a Colombia jersey shouted.

Screams rose, hands went up, and fans raced toward each other, hugging in celebration, as Scotland scored its first goal of the game.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

John McGinn opens the scoring in the 28th minute, and the Scots are going wild for their first World Cup goal for a generation. A rebound fell to the Scotland midfielder at the edge of the penalty area, and his deflected effort found the back of the net to make it 1-0. We’re going to be hearing that “Super John McGinn” song plenty this evening.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — Midway through the first half, it remains 0-0 at the game’s first hydration break. Both teams had quick chances in quick succession, with Scotland’s Scott McTominay coming closest to opening the scoring with a first-time effort that rattled the post. Haiti has been dangerous too, particularly with crosses from out wide that have threatened the Scotland box.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

In the Seaport, the watch party is packed with fans for Haiti and Scotland at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center.

Standing shoulder to shoulder, fans clutched their flags and kids jumped in excitement.

Every near goal elicits cheering and an air of strong anticipation. With the speakers turned up to the max, it feels as if we’re in the stadium watching from the bleachers.

“OOOOOOOO,” the crowd yelled when Scotland nearly missed a goal.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — This crowd may be skewing Scottish — 75 percent to 25 percent would be our rough estimate — but the Haitians are making themselves heard, especially when Haiti has managed to break in transition. The chants of “Haiti! Haiti!” accompanied by hundreds of waving Haitian flags, have helped contribute to a great atmosphere here in Foxborough. It’s still 0-0 after 16 minutes.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

For the first time in 32 years, a World Cup match is underway here in Foxborough. It’s a packed house — even for a 9 p.m. kickoff — as Haiti and Scotland both make their long-awaited returns to the biggest stage in the sport.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — I’m not sure ever quite seen anything like that playing of the Scottish national anthem. Tens of thousands of Scots belted out “Flower of Scotland” at the top of their lungs, and the noise would give you goosebumps.

It’s a special atmosphere ahead of kickoff here at Gillette Stadium.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

It’s a Haitian party at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center.

To everyone’s surprise, famous kompa singer Alan Cavé is here, throwing a concert for fans just an hour before the team plays on the world stage in 52 years.

As fans take swigs of beer and sip their drinks, they wave their Haitian flags under blue and red lights.

By Michael Silverman, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — There were lines, there was heat and there were aromas, but Ryan and Vicki White had one the hard part: They completed their train trip from South Station to Foxborough.

The couple packed up their Subaru Ascent minivan with their 3-month-old baby and grandparents and drove from Burlington, Vt., to Boston at 9 a.m. Saturday morning.

After checking into their hotel, they soaked in bustling downtown Boston before reaching the train station.

“That’s the most kilts I’ve ever seen, it never crossed my mind that it would be a thing,” said Vicki.

Then, it was time to line up.

“I think we were walking for more than 20 minutes in loops,” said Ryan. “I kept thinking we had arrived but you looked up and there were four more loops, each 200 yards long.”

He said the operation was well-organized and a bit like being in a line at Disney World “but with less theming.”

Their 5:45 train left at 6:30.

“We had no AC for the first 30 minutes,” said Ryan. “They made us sweat it out for a little bit.”

There was the heat, and there was an aroma.

“There were probably a couple thousand people on the train and the [conductor] says: ‘There’s two bathrooms in the front and one in the back,’” said Ryan. “That bathroom in the back did not smell that good.”

The White’s spoke not long after reaching the back of another long queue: the one to get into Boston Stadium.

“I hope this line doesn’t last too long,” said Ryan.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

Fan Fest on City Hall Plaza was filling up fast 30 minutes before the Scotland and Haiti game kicked off.

Fans crowded around the big screen, which switched to pan over the crowd.

Scotland fans sang and waved their arms in the air as they waited for the game to start.

By Michael Silverman, Globe Staff

Gordon Mills and Ewan Dalgleish looked drained and relieved.

Inside Gillette Stadium at last about 90 minutes before kickoff, the friends had completed a train journey that felt a little too long.

“This was the killer,” said Mills about the ticket scanning and security line that they endured after their delayed train from South Station reached Foxborough. “It took us longer again from South Station to here than it took us to drive from Plattsburgh, New York, to Boston yesterday — and that includes a lovely ferry we took from Plattsburgh,” said Mills, who like Dalgleish is originally from Scotland and lives in Ottawa, Canada.

The two have a hotel room near South Station. They got to South Station five minutes before their 5:00 train and then stood in line before getting on that 5 p.m. at 6:20.

After waiting on the still train for 15 minutes, wheels finally started to roll and the train took 40 minutes to reach Foxborough.

“It was just a train ride,” said Dalgleish. “The AC was working and people were singing.”

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe Staff

Any lingering concern about demand for World Cup train service was put aside on Saturday, after the MBTA announced that tickets for all 14 of its express trains to Foxborough were sold out.

All 20,000 train seats for the Scotland-Haiti match had been sold by Friday night, according to Jake O’Neill, a commuter rail spokesperson.

Tickets first went on sale on April 8, with online demand reaching unprecedented levels, the agency said. Within 24 hours, ticket sales for the Haiti vs. Scotland match had beat the record of the most special event train tickets sold to any individual event at Gillette Stadium.

Fans were required to offer proof they had a same-day match ticket to secure their seat on the commuter rail.

The last Foxborough-bound train departed South Station at 6:15 p.m.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

Strangely, the United States national anthem was just played — 52 minutes before kickoff, which isn’t a typical timeline for the national anthems — and drew a few boos from this heavily Scottish crowd.

The cheers came a few moments later, though, as the Scotland goalkeepers came out to warm up. The Scottish fans have been singing in the concourse all evening and are bursting at the seams awaiting their team’s return to the World Cup after 28 years.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

Energy is building up at the Haiti-Scotland watch party, where they are pulling out more chairs to accommodate the crowd.

Melissa Sapini, Miss Universe Haiti, took to the stage at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center and asked Haitian fans to make some noise.

“Tonight is about more [than] celebrating Haitian pride,” Sapini said. It’s about “honoring our heritage, connecting generations, supporting local businesses, and showing the world our strength, the spirit of our community.”

Then former state representative Marie St. Fleur took the microphone to extol the first Haitian team to play in the World Cup in more than 50 years.

“They’re going to leave it all on the field at Boston Stadium this evening,” St.Fleur said.

She revved up the Haitians in the room, chanting and lifting spirits, but she didn’t leave out Scottish fans. Calling on both groups, each group waved their flags with spirited chants.

“Now let’s celebrate our culture in the best way Haitians do it with music and dance,” St. Fleur said, which followed a bass-boosted, floor shaking celebration of Kompa and Scottish hits.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

Scotland fans Dazz Bartley and Camy McPhee took a break from festivities inside a classic Boston establishment: Dunkin’.

“The menu is not as extensive as it is in the UK,” Bartley said.

The two decided to go to Dunkin because prices everywhere else were too high. The friends said they paid $45 for three drinks and a soda earlier.

Bartley, who is half Jamaican and half English, said Boston is “a bit like London.”

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

Inside Boston Fan Fest, three children darted through the crowd, dancing and waving hand fans adorned with the Haitian flag.

Kayla Saint-Cyr, 7, Keilanj Saint-Cyr, 5, and Ava Paul, 6, all of Boston, could hardly contain their excitement.

“We’re going to be on the news!” they said in unison.

The free watch party at the Thomas M. Menino Convention & Exhibition Center gave families a place to take in the World Cup atmosphere without making the trip to Foxborough.

Asked what she hoped for from the tournament, Kayla offered an answer that could unite both crowds at the watch party.

“I hope that all of the teams win and get a trophy and a medal,” Kayla said.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

The Dubliner Irish bar in downtown Boston was unusually packed for 7 p.m. Friday, with the line outside extending beyond the bar’s exterior. Fans crowded around several TV screens, all broadcasting the World Cup match.

Both Brazil and Scotland fans showed out to the bar, mingling with each other during halftime.

Hugo Santos and Luis Martins only met today, but watching Brazil in the World Cup has already made them “family,” Santos said.

Santos, from Rio de Janeiro, said soccer “changed his life” when he got to come to Fisher College in Boston on a soccer scholarship.

Martins is from Brazil — he predicted the country would win 3-1 in its game against Morocco.

“Brazil is nervous,” Santos said. “The badge of Brazil is heavy, it’s a way of life.”

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Staff

Chatter filled the room as families streamed into Boston’s Fan Zone to watch Haiti take on Scotland. Over the crowd floated the tune “Haïti Chérie” – “Beloved Haiti” – its guitar melodies swaying like a neighborhood celebration, carrying equal parts nostalgia and excitement for Haitian fans.

Alexsandra Wiafe, 46, of Salem, arrived at the Thomas M. Menino Convention & Exhibition Center with her two children, ages 7 and 11, and her best friend, eager for kickoff.

“I’m really excited, I’m anxious and I can’t wait till the game starts,” Wiafe said.

Wiafe said she learned about the watch party on Instagram and was drawn to its family-friendly atmosphere.

“A lot of the other ones they’re for adults,” she said.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

It’s been nothing but positivity here at Gillette Stadium, even between opposing fans. We’ve already seen plenty of camaraderie here in Foxborough, where Scotland and Haiti fans are snapping photos together, wishing each other luck, and trading hugs and high-fives.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

At the City Hall Plaza Fan Fest around 6 p.m. Saturday, the number of fans sporting Brazil’s yellow and green colors was giving the mass of Scotland supporters a run for their money.

Isabella Shannon and Hunter Cole watched the match between Brazil and Morocco on a massive screen. Shannon is from Brazil, and Cole is American.

“I kind of dragged him out here,” she joked.

The couple registered for Fan Fest for the food offerings and to watch the game with a crowd.

“Brazil is really good,” Shannon said. “I wanted to see it on a big screen.”

Livia and Benjamin Vieira watched the game intently, dressed head to toe in the colors of the Brazilian flag.

When Morocco scored the first goal of the game, Benjamin gripped his head in frustration.

He did not want to talk about the game. Livia Vieira said it would just “stress him out.”

“Brazil is not playing well,” Livia said, adding that the team has been making lots of mistakes. The pair are “very big fans” of the country’s soccer team.

By Thai Theodoro and Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondents

Fans hoping to catch a train at South Station were still packed along Summer Street with the last ride to Foxborough scheduled to depart at 6 p.m.

Brendan Kavanagh, 36, of Boston, said he was not worried about getting to the game early.

“I’m just excited to be going to a World Cup game in my home city,” Kavanagh said.

A Liverpool fan, Kavanagh said he is rooting for Scotland because of Andy Robertson, the team’s captain and longtime Liverpool left back. His friends, who came with him, are rooting for Haiti.

“For Scotland and Haiti, it’s a pleasure to be at the World Cup, so everyone’s just happy to be at it. Hopefully, it’s a good game,” Kavanagh said.

Beer cans and to-go boxes littered the ground near the line for the train.

With half of his face painted in the red and blue colors, Chris Bassett said he figured he’d root for the “underdog” because he has a British-motivated rivalry with Scotland.

“I think no matter who wins, it’s just a really fun event for people to come together and experience a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be able to see games in the U.S,” Bassett said.

By Thai Theodoro and Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondents

One family became impatient with the line at South Station.

As drivers across the street yelled “$400 for six people or $250 for four people,” the family ran to get into one of the cars.

Nearby, Steve Doss was working the register at the Land of Beer Wine and Spirits store inside South Station.

“Something’s going on. I can’t quite figure it out,” Doss joked, adding sarcastically that it was only “a hair” busier than usual.

Doss said it was a pleasant day at work and everyone was in a good mood.

“I feel a bit underdressed,” he said about his numerous customers in kilts.

Several food trucks were also parked in Dewey Square as fans lined up for the train to Boston Stadium. One was serving Haitian food, while another served crepes.

The state’s Department of Transportation had set up a table to hand out bug repellent wipes, sunscreen, and hand sanitizer.

As boarding groups checked in at South Station — the latest one, E, was scheduled for 5:45 — the crowd at the waiting area started to dwindle.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

When Victoria Brissot, 29, left Haiti for the United States 16 years ago, she said she never imagined she would one day watch her home country take the field on soccer’s biggest stage.

“This is history. I am part of history. This is beautiful,” said Brissot, of Boston.

Brissot felt pride for her country as the glitter and paintings across her cheeks in the colors of the Haitian flag caught the afternoon light.

Haiti enters today’s matchup as the underdog, ranked 83rd in the world compared with Scotland’s 42nd in FIFA’s official rankings. But for many Haitian fans, the moment carries meaning beyond soccer.

For Brissot, simply seeing Haiti reach this moment on the world stage was enough.

“They did the best that they could, and they got us here, which is more than enough,” she said. “I’m super proud of them. Super, super proud.”

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff

A spokesperson for Keolis, the operator of the MBTA’s commuter rail, said passengers for trains to Foxborough were arriving at South Station “well before their boarding time, which is leading to longer lines.”

But the spokesperson said queueing was “proceeding as planned” and trains were departing South Station on time and arriving at Foxborough “on or ahead of schedule.”

“All ticketed passengers will be accommodated on board Boston Stadium trains,” the spokesperson said in a statement to the Globe.

Tickets from South Station to Boston Stadium required an advance reservation, and passengers selected a boarding group with a corresponding arrival time, according to the spokesperson.

Take a look at the live traffic map near Gillette Stadium here.

By Thai Theodoro and Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondents

Ker Vens, 33, of Cambridge, arrived at South Station with his Haitian-American family dressed in matching Haitian jerseys.

Vens said his family had so far waited about 40 minutes to board a train to Foxborough and were already nearing the station’s entrance.

Before heading out, Vens said the group celebrated the Haitian way by gathering for a house party and taking plenty of photos.

“We expect to win,” he said.

Vens didn’t hesitate when asked if he felt intimidated by the large presence of Scottish fans in kilts compared to those wearing Haiti’s red jersey.

“We’ve faced worse,” he said.

Others in line were getting antsy. Several supporters of Scotland said they would rather pay for an $80 Uber ride than continue waiting to enter South Station.

Elsewhere near South Station, one fan exclaimed, “This is [expletive] wild” as he walked along the line down Congress Street. He was only about halfway to the back of it.

Another said “Crikey!” when they saw the end of the line stretching down Summer Street.

“This is a disgrace,” one Scottish fan, who declined to give his name, said. Waving at two kids standing at his side, he joked, “We were in France when this line started.”

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

PROVIDENCE — The buses parked on either side of the street, so they can get the beer on to the buses, a steward said on the loudspeaker.

There were nearly two dozen yellow school buses that picked up the hundreds of fans that had congregated near the state Capitol to head to the game.

“No Scotland, no party,” chants would occasionally break out.

Paul Smith, 63, is from Edinburgh. This is his sixth World Cup. His first was in 1982 in Spain. He has been to all the tournaments that featured Scotland. But this is his first tournament this century.

“For it to be a success, we have to get out of the group. And to be very successful to make it to the round of 16,” he said. “If we don’t win today, we are knackered.”

He is apprehensive.

“You think we should win but there has been so many disasters for Scotland,” he said as he waited to get on one of the buses. There was a delay because they were waiting on beer and wine.

There was a bit of cash left over from the renting of the buses, so they decided to use to get some drinks.

At about 4:30 p.m., the buses left downtown Providence in a line yellow and headed out.

Next stop Foxborough.

“No Scotland, no party,” the fans chanted.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

At South Station, the line to board trains started at Summer Street, wrapped around from the intersection of Atlantic Avenue and stretched the length of Congress Street before looping to Dorchester Street and ending on the other side of Summer Street.

People walking to join the end of the line were shocked when it continued wrapping around multiple streets.

Elie Ciril, who came with his wife and three kids from Miami, said the line was “unexpected.”

“It goes to show the excitement” and popularity of the World Cup, he said, also joking that “for every 10 Scottish guys, there’s one Haiti fan.”

“It’s not fair,” he said, laughing.

The line was moving quickly at around 5 p.m. The Ciril family had joined about 10 minutes before they crossed from Summer Street to Dorchester Avenue.

“I’ve never seen anything like this,” Vicki Krupp said from the back of the line at 5 p.m. Saturday. She said her time slot to arrive at South Station was between 5 and 5:30 p.m., and she and her husband arrived right on the dot.“I have faith that Keolis will move this along quickly,” the Massachusetts local and Haiti fan said.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

I’m riding the train down to cover tonight’s game. All is pretty peaceful — everyone has a seat on our carriage and aside from some chatting here and there, not too much noise.

Most of the drama is surrounding the wait for the bathroom; the line extends through about four carriages and is only getting longer.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

PROVIDENCE — Hundreds of Scotland’s Tartan Army fans congregated by the state Capitol to board buses to Foxborough, about 20 miles away from downtown Providence, for their country’s game against Haiti later tonight.

Some of the supporters wore Scotland’s new away jersey.

“Is it orange, salmon pink? We have the same debate. We do not know,” said Maggie Dawson, 54, from Aushterarder in central Scotland. “It’s the color of winners in the first game. In the next games, we will play in our traditional blue.”

Dawson was among the throngs of fans waiting for the buses as a Scottish bagpipe band serenaded them with music.

Bryan Harris, 51, of Dundee, Scotland, said he was feeling nervous excitement as he waited for the bus.

“Twenty-eight years we’ve been waiting for this. Last time in 1998, I was in France as a student. I didn’t think it would take this long to qualify again,” he said. “This is the biggest game. Forget Morocco. Forget Brazil. Three points against Haiti should get us through to the next round. We’ve never done it before. It’d be history in the making.”

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

As a group of Scotland fans passed four people carrying Haitian flags, one yelled, “I hope you guys lose, but best of luck!”

“You don’t mean that,” Johnny Thermoncy laughed in reply.

The group of Haiti fans was getting a lot of attention outside of Fan Fest on Saturday as Scottish supporters flooded downtown Boston.

“It’s fun, actually,” Max Bem, a friend of Thermoncy’s, said of the rivalry. “They were chanting when they saw us, but at one point they were like, ’Hey, come over here, let’s take a picture.’”

Bem grew up playing soccer and said his love for the sport is “in his blood.”

Thermoncy said he’s glad Haiti is getting international attention, which he said the country needs as it endures a humanitarian crisis.

“The country, the Haitian people, they need that fervor, they need that support,” he said.

The last time Haiti played in the World Cup was 1974, making the day even more special for fans.

“We have a lot of Haitians coming from everywhere to watch the game and support Haiti,” Thermoncy said. “Maybe with that support, that would send a message to the country to get back on its feet, to get better.”

As the 9 p.m. kickoff between Haiti and Scotland inches closer, crowds are swelling at South Station in Boston, where fans are boarding the commuter rail to get to Foxborough, and in Providence, where fans will ride buses to Gillette Stadium.

Are you traveling to the game? Let us know about your experience in the comments.

By Avery Hill, Globe Correspondent

One ride through Boston will let you know that the Scots travel well. Fenway Park is no exception.

Whether it was in or outside of the stadium, a kilt, sporran, or Scottish flag could be spotted at every turn on Friday night for the Red Sox’ 10-1 win over the Rangers.

Many Scottish fans don’t have previous experience with the World Cup, as it’s been 28 years since the nation’s last appearance, but what do they know about baseball? For many, not much.

“One of the American guys that I work with, he was actually saying if you hear the ball whistling, duck,” Dannie Buchan of Fraserburgh, Scotland, said.

READ MORE

Earlier this morning on talkSPORT, a popular British sports talk radio station, reporter Shebahn Aherne said there were dozens of fans waiting outside the Dubliner near City Hall Plaza.

It was 9 a.m. The bar wasn’t set to open for another two hours.

talkSPORT reported more than 24,000 Scotland fans had traveled to Boston to watch Scotland-Haiti at Gillette Stadium on Sunday night.

To kill time before kickoff, a bagpiper came by to play for those gathered at the bar. Watch:

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

Connor Hardy, the Boston police officer who went viral for juggling a soccer ball with World Cup fans earlier on Saturday, has had some practice. The 14-year veteran of the department played soccer in high school and at St. Anselm College in New Hampshire.

“I had a little background,” he joked, standing inside Fan Fest Saturday afternoon.

Hardy said he saw a group of American and Scottish fans playing soccer together, getting “revved up” for tonight’s game, and decided to join.

“When I went over there, I think they originally thought I was gonna steal the ball and be the fun police,” he said. “I actually just kind of did my thing with them, and it was fun, and it turned out funny.”

Hardy said he never expected to go viral. The video of him showing off his juggling skills before getting swarmed by fans has garnered millions of views on social media.

“Never something I thought would happen,” he said. “It’s all good fun though — it’s great, the World Cup here in Boston.”

What’s the scene like at Gillette? Our reporters are on the way. For now, take a look at our live traffic tracker.

By Emily Spatz, Globe Correspondent

Soccer fans packed Downtown Boston Saturday afternoon just ahead of the matchup between Qatar and Switzerland at 3 p.m. Scottish supporters filled Union Street — some singing and dancing, others relaxing in the shade before heading to Foxborough this evening.

Scottish flags and kilts were everywhere. People clutched clear bags — the only ones allowed in Boston Stadium for the games — adorned with Scottish paraphernalia as they moved between bars.

Kids played with inflatable soccer balls, kicking them in the air to cheers from the crowd.

At City Hall Plaza, Benedita Melgaço and Carolina Melgaço stood out against a sea of blue and white in their bright yellow Brazilian jerseys.

The two traveled from Brazil to watch their country play in the 6 p.m. match against Morocco in New Jersey tonight. They chose Boston because they have family here.

They didn’t know Scotland was playing today, but figured so because of the mass of fans.

“I have never seen so many Scottish people. Only in Scotland,” Benedita, who is Carolina’s aunt, joked.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

Jean Zephir, 33, was at the official FIFA-designated Providence Fan Fest with his family, including Henley, 1.

He was enjoying Joé Dwèt Filé’s “Kompa” playing at the park and getting ready to cheer for Haiti later tonight at the game against Scotland at Foxborough.

“To have Haiti at the World Cup is like a miracle,” he said. “To have Haiti back is fantastic.”

He came to check out the fan fest where Amapiano and Soca sounds blasted through the air. Zephir plans to drive to Foxborough later this afternoon.

His nephew John St. Franc, 11, supports Brazil at the World Cup.

“I like Neymar,” he said.

Zephir plans to meet up with friends at the stadium.

“I feel like it’s a battle, and Haiti is a winner. To be part of the World Cup is a chance for us to show how great we are,” he said. “People see that Haiti is the worst. But being in the World Cup, we proved to the world how great we are, and we are still alive.”

Seide Richemond, 35, grew up in Haiti and moved to the U.S. at 13. He now lives in Central Falls, R.I.

He came to the fan fest in downtown Providence on his way to the game later today.

“As a kid growing up watching the sport, the idea of seeing Haiti at the World Cup was unimaginable, an event of a lifetime not to be missed,” he said.

He is heading to the game later with his brother and expects Haiti to pull off an upset.

“As far as celebrations go, no one can beat Haiti,” Richemond said. “Haitians love celebrating, and at the game it’s going to be a celebration of our culture.”

By Michael Silverman, Globe Staff

Kevin Clark never lost faith that Saturday’s first World Cup game in these parts would actually take place at Boston Stadium.

But after FIFA’s venue operations director was mostly finished showing off the pristine checkerboard grass field, the locker rooms Scotland and Haiti will be using, the sprawling Stadium Fan Experience, and more to the media on Thursday, he admitted that much of the drama that preceded kickoff this year did not make fulfilling an already tall order any easier.

“Operationally, no, there weren’t any delays,” said Clark about how, for months, the Town of Foxborough held up granting the entertainment license FIFA and the Kraft Group needed. “We also don’t have any time to lose, so we needed to basically carry on unimpeded. Otherwise, we wouldn’t be able to deliver this on Saturday.”

The “pretty sizable flip” in attitude and morale that came with the license’s approval in mid-March translated into the transformation of Gillette Stadium into the FIFA-approved venue it is today.

It is match-ready.

After working their way through a warren of fencing, barrier-lined queue zones, gates, and metal detectors, fans will still recognize the stadium. The Patriots’ six championship banners above the south scoreboard haven’t gone anywhere.

Inside the seating bowl, just about the only other signage visible to the naked eye will say “FIFA,” “World Cup,” “Boston,” or one of FIFA’s top sponsors.

“I just want the game on Saturday to come and then I’ll be 100 percent proud, but I’m really proud,” said Greg Whately, venue pitch manager of how the field is taking shape. “This is the pinnacle for any player. We’re giving them the stage to perform, so we have to give them the proper stage.”

READ MORE

Photos by Jessica Rinaldi, Globe Staff

These tried-and-true soccer bars in the Boston area will be ready for legions of fans, regardless of your team allegiance.

With big screen televisions, specialty drinks, and delicious noshables, these spots are perfect for immersing in the excitement without having to shell out for tickets. Check out the list here.

By Matt Porter, Globe Staff

He walked 500 miles. Then he walked 500 more.

For Craig Ferguson, that was only the beginning.

Since late February, the Scottish soccer superfan has been walking across America, more than 3,100 miles from Los Angeles to Boston, to accomplish two goals: raise money for mental health services in his country, and arrive in time for Scotland’s opener against Haiti on Saturday — the Scots’ first World Cup match in 28 years.

As a vehicle for celebration and donation, the 22-year-old hiked the world’s fourth-widest nation. He is believed to be the first to go coast-to-coast in a kilt.

“Adventure, that’s the heart of it,” said Ferguson, a content creator from Paisley, the town west of Glasgow known for its teardrop textile. “Being able to tell my kids one day that I walked across an entire country like the US is pretty cool to me.”

When he arrived there on Friday, it was his 109th day on the road. He has taken six rest days in that time. His longest day covered more than 40 miles, some 82,000 steps, and nearly 12 hours. He has climbed nearly 3,000 feet on some days while burning upward of 4,500 calories.

READ MORE

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

The World’s Largest Soccer Ball is officially in Boston, adding another point on the scoreboard for the World Cup host city.

The 47-foot-tall soccer ball was officially given the title Friday, at an event held in East Boston. The achievement was officiated by Guinness World Records.

“Go big or go home in Boston,” Mayor Michelle Wu said to a crowd of people in Piers Park, where the soccer ball stands.

The Guinness World Record official adjudicator, Andy Glass, joined Wu on stage. And, after her speech, he awarded the city with Guinness’ celebrated plaque.

“There’s one more exciting thing to see in East Boston,” Wu said.

Throughout the event, the giant blue ball loomed over the speakers. Tethered by long wires to fixate its place on stage, the inflatable is printed with the silhouettes of the world’s continents — a tribute to those coming here for the tournament from across the world.

“We’re welcoming the world to Boston,” said Senator Lydia Edwards, who represents the East Boston area. “It’s just incredible that the world will be able to see what we get to see every day, which is a beautiful, vibrant green city that is welcoming to all.”

Over the next week, the ball will remain inflated at Piers Park.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

PROVIDENCE — Conrad Balatoni, 35, and his son, Theo, 9, arrived in downtown Providence from Edinburgh on Friday. They chose to travel to Providence because it was cheaper and closer to Boston Stadium in Foxborough.

Balatoni said he “promised” Theo that if the Scottish national team qualified for the World Cup, he’d bring his son to the United States to see them play.

“It’s really special. I have never seen a Scotland game live, so I am excited that my first one will be a World Cup match,” Theo said.

Balatoni said the trip is special for him because he also played professional soccer in the Scottish Premier League.

“It’s good seeing boys I played with, such as Scott McKenna, who plays center back, playing at the highest level in World Football,” Balatoni said. “It’s a testament to the hard work they’ve put in to get to the highest level and give us Scottish fans something special to experience.”

Balatoni had one more promise for Theo.

“What if they go to the final?” Theo asked his dad.

“If they go to the final, we’ll go,” Conrad said.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

PROVIDENCE — Hours before Scotland was scheduled to take to the field, Chris McLeish, 45, and his brother-in-law Dave Paton were getting ready to head into the G Pub in downtown Providence around 11 a.m.

The duo from Glasgow arrived in Boston the night before and plan to head to Foxborough later this afternoon. But the pair stopped off for a pint first.

“We are hoping for a good time,” McLeish said while sporting the jersey of Scotland’s Scott McTominay. “A Scotland victory and a good time. No Scotland, no party. It’s a Tartan Army slogan.”

At a street festival near the pub, Jack McKenzie, 14, from Alloa in Central Scotland, and his cousin Derren Douglas, 12, were with their parents enjoying the bright, hot start to the day. The group plans to head to the game around 2 p.m.

“We expect to win [tonight], and if we win, we’ll have a big chance of going through,” McKenzie said.

By Frank Dell’Apa, Globe Correspondent

Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay has recovered from a stomach ailment and is expected to play against Haiti in a World Cup Group C game on Saturday night.

McTominay arrived in Boston from Charlotte, N.C., on a separate flight, accompanied by a doctor, then practiced with the team Friday at the Revolution Training Center. (Training visitors included restauranteur Gordon Ramsay, who played for Rangers on a trial basis in the 1980s.)

McTominay, 29, converted a key goal off a bicycle kick in a 4-2 win over Denmark that clinched qualification in November.

“I’ve got 26 superstars here. To try to put so much onto one person is not fair,” Scotland coach Steve Clarke said. “We are delighted with Scott’s abilities and what he can bring to the team. But we are going to need another 15 to bring the same if we want to have a positive tournament.”

After transferring from Manchester United to Napoli two years ago, McTominay emerged among the top attacking midfielders in Serie A and on the international stage. Until recently, though, Clarke had McTominay lining up on the back line for Scotland.

“Some daft head coach put him as a center half five years ago,” Clarke said.

Scotland, which last competed in the finals in 1998, has been revived under Clarke’s coaching.

“It’s going to be a difficult game. First time in 28 years we’ve been here, first time for Haiti since 1974. They’re also a proud nation. They’re going to be here 100 percent committed, same as we are,” he said. “And we know they have qualities that can cause us problems on the pitch, so we have to deal with those problems and we have to try and bring our best game to the pitch when we have the ball. If we can do that, then, hopefully that will be enough to win the game.

“It’s going to be a squad World Cup. The starting team is important, [but] I think you’ll find a lot of games the team that finishes the game is every bit as important, if not more important.”

By Frank Dell’Apa, Globe Correspondent

Haiti’s World Cup qualifying experiences have been unique. In 1974, it played host to the CONCACAF World Cup qualifying tournament, all matches contested at Stade Sylvio Cator in Port-au-Prince. Les Grenadiers advanced to the finals for the first time, but lost all three games in Germany.

This time, Haiti played all its qualifiers on the road, becoming the first country to make it to the finals that way.

“Today, it’s a whole different story,” Haiti coach Sebastian Migne said. “It is different from the 1974 era, and it is up to us to rise to the challenge.”

Migne said earning at least a point “would be a huge reward for the garçons, and even if we didn’t score any points [in the first two games], with the new rules, the best eight [third-place teams] advance. But we hope to accomplish that tomorrow, if possible playing nice soccer, so we can take the fans with us, and cultivate excitement around us. There are always teams like this, and we could be one.”

Migne called forward Frantzdy Pierrot, born in Cap Haïtien and raised in Melrose, “one of the pillars” of the team.

“What is great for him, he is currently at his best,” Migne said. “And he is in his hometown for his first game in the World Cup. That adds to the motivation and to the pressure, and I trust him to manage that.”

By Katie McInerney, Globe Staff

Most fans headed to Saturday’s World Cup game probably have tickets already — and for good reason: Tickets on sale right now are well over $1,000 and are likely to climb as kickoff approaches.

If you’re planning to head to the game, you better have your travel planned. Tickets to take the commuter rail to the stadium are sold out.

title: For Boston’s Cabo Verdeans, finally, a seat at the World Cup table
text:
At the back of the pub, the cheers went up again when Coleta walked in, 23 minutes after kickoff, wearing the jersey of Cabo Verde’s national team.

“Traffic,” he said, rolling his eyes, taking a seat at the bar that Butler had saved for him. “There was an accident on the Expressway.”

Everybody nodded knowingly, because they’ve all been there before.

But, as a native of Cabo Verde, Coleta had never been in this position before: sitting down to a World Cup that includes the Blue Sharks, Cabo Verde’s national team.

Coleta is 62 years old. He works for the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority. He was born on Fogo, one of Cabo Verde’s islands. Fogo means fire in Portuguese, and the island has an active volcano. But like so many other Cabo Verdeans, Coleta and his family left the archipelago off the coast of West Africa for Boston not because they feared an eruption but because they longed for opportunity.

“I was 12 when I got here, to Boston,” he said. “Soccer was all I knew. It was my life.”

In high school, he played on one of those great Madison Park teams that won a city championship, then transferred to Boston Tech.

He played semi-pro, but any dreams of going beyond that broke down along with his gimpy right knee.

“It’s hard to explain today, but when I was a kid, soccer was everything in the Cabo Verdean community,” he said. “We didn’t play basketball, no baseball, no football. Now it’s different, Cabo Verdean kids are playing everything.”

With a population of around 500,000 people, and a diaspora that is estimated at 700,000 to 1 million, Cabo Verde never got near a seat at the World Cup table.

Portugal colonized Cabo Verde, and even after the island won its independence in 1975, the exploitation of natural resources extended to taking the island’s best players, Coleta said.

The last few generations, however, have produced young men who want to play for their country.

“We’ve got some really good players,” Coleta said, including those who qualify to play for the country through their parents. “We’ve got a guy, Pico Lopes, who grew up in Ireland and is the captain of Shamrock Rovers, right Ray?”

Butler, a native of Ireland who knows the League of Ireland well, leaned in.

“He’s a very good center back,” Butler said of Lopes.

The good people of Crumlin, the Dublin neighborhood where Lopes grew up, and where his Cabo-Verdean-born father settled, gave him a rousing send-off the other day.

Both Butler and Coleta like that symmetry, because the Irish and Cabo Verdeans share an immigrant history in Boston.

Marty Walsh, whose parents were from the Gaeltacht in Connemara, an Irish-speaking region, was the first Boston mayor whose parents’ native language was not English. He once told me when he looked at the Cabo Verdean kids playing basketball at the Boys and Girls Club in Dorchester near where he grew up, he saw Irish kids from a century before.

“Poor kids from a colonized island that couldn’t provide them jobs,” Walsh said. “A lot of them came to Boston to make a life for themselves and their families.”

The Irish struggled when first arriving in Boston in large numbers. But they assimilated and went on to run the town.

Immigrants from Cabo Verde faced similar struggles, but the community has become one of the most enduring and vibrant in the city.

In more recent years, many Cabo Verdeans who used to live in Dorchester have moved to Brockton, Coleta said, because the cost of housing in Boston continued to soar.

That means the Cabo Verde team is being cheered on in Brockton and Pawtucket and other places in New England as loudly as in Dorchester.

Cabo Verde plays its first game Monday, in Atlanta, against Spain, one of the favorites to win the World Cup, in what is billed as a David vs. Goliath matchup.

Coleta will be there, part of a group of 14 guys who grew up together in Dorchester, playing soccer on Franklin Field, where a slide tackle left the outside of your thigh looking like it had a run-in with a giant cheese grater.

As immigrant kids who grew up in Boston, they’re used to being underdogs.

“We grew up together. We played together. We scored goals together. But nothing can top this, watching Cabo Verde in the World Cup together,” Coleta said.

Coleta and his childhood buddies were at Cesaria’s, the Dorchester restaurant on Bowdoin Street, to watch the qualifying match when Cabo Verde punched its ticket to the World Cup last October.

“I would compare it to what Americans felt when the US hockey team beat the Soviet Union in the Olympics,” Coleta said. “It was more than just a game. It was a moment in history, a feeling you never forget, a pride bursting out of your chest. It was like the day my son was born, that feeling.”

Coleta and his buddies went back to Cesaria’s Friday, but it wasn’t a late night.

They had to get up Saturday morning for the flight to Atlanta, to cheer on the Blue Sharks, to remember where they came from, to celebrate where they landed, and to chase this idea, this crazy idea, that says anything’s possible.

title: Fifth-graders spot n-word printed in school dictionary, sparking parent backlash in Milton
text:
While the district is taking steps to address the incident, many parents say they want stronger, sustained commitments from the district to address racial discrimination in the schools. They launched a website, Milton Reckoning, which includes several demands to prevent racial incidents and properly address them if they occur.

“To me it’s not about this incident, it’s about the pattern of incidents,” said Somaneh Diemé, the parent who created the website on behalf of parents and whose son attends the fifth grade at Tucker. ”How do we respond to it and how do we protect each other?”

The dictionary’s entry for the n-word also included “a racist and offensive definition,” according to an email the school’s principal sent to families of fifth-graders in the French immersion program earlier this month that was obtained by the Globe.

“We recognize the weight, history, and impact of this racial slur and understand how deeply hurtful it can be,” Celeste Hoeg, the principal, wrote. “The presence of this language in a school resource is unacceptable.”

On Wednesday, scores of parents and community members from different racial backgrounds showed up at dismissal wearing red shirts — the school color — to show solidarity with Black students. It’s not how many parents envisioned the school year ending for their children, especially fifth-graders who will be heading to middle school next fall.

“For fifth-graders this will be one of the last memories they will leave Tucker with,” Diemé said, as he proudly scanned the turnout creating a sea of red on the playground. “We just want to support the kids, show them we care, and we are united.”

Racial controversy has become all too familiar in Milton, a middle-class community along the borders of Dorchester and Mattapan.

In 2020, a backlash emerged after a middle school teacher was suspended for referencing police racism during a lesson following the killing of George Floyd. A year later, Pierce Middle School students walked out after a student said a racial slur in an online video. And in 2023, the district got hit with a discrimination lawsuit involving a math program geared for students from marginalized racial groups.

Several parents say their children also have encountered racial slurs at Tucker, even though diversity and inclusion are widely embraced there.

“It’s unacceptable for this to be a rite of passage for Black students in Milton or anywhere,” said Vernée Wilkinson, who has a child at Tucker. “More proactive measures need to be put into place.”

Milton is not the only district grappling with discrimination as the school year winds down.

Lynnfield parents have been pushing district leaders to do more to address racial incidents, including racial slurs and bullying, which have persisted despite efforts by the district to prevent them. A new incident emerged Thursday evening at Lynnfield High School where a racial slur targeting Black people was found written on a bathroom stall door, prompting a school district and police investigation, according to an email Lynnfield’s superintendent sent to the community that night, which was obtained by the Globe.

Milton also has launched an internal investigation into the Tucker School incident. John Phelan, Milton’s interim superintendent, said the district is working with Tucker families to address their concerns and agreed to form a working group of educators and families to execute an action plan, including a review of district policies.

“We acknowledge that there is clearly more work to be done to ensure that every child feels safe, welcome, and supported, and to ensure that any racist behavior or language will be addressed swiftly and thoroughly,” he said in a statement to the Globe.

Phelan said he could only share limited information, citing privacy concerns, but noted an investigation determined staff adhered to district policies and procedures. The dictionary, he said, has been removed from the classroom. The district is now conducting a review of books in all the schools.

When the incident first came to light, parents were frustrated about the school’s lack of communication and rumors swirled about what happened.

Initially, the school only notified parents in the French immersion program, according to parents, resulting in confusion among other parents left out.

Lauren Brown, a parent, said broader communication would have been helpful. Her child is Black, but is not in the French immersion program, leaving her to rely on word of mouth rather than concrete details from a school communication.

”The cost of staying silent is that you now have eroded trust," she said. “There’s no transparency.“

Many parents and other community members are seeking eight demands to foster a more supportive learning environment for students of all racial backgrounds across the entire school district, such as a formal and transparent racial incident response protocol, anti-racism training for staff, and mandatory anti-racism education for white students and their families, according to their website, Milton Reckoning.

“This is not a Black problem,” according to the website. ”The children who appear to need support are the white children who, in many cases, have not been taught the history, weight, and consequence of racist language and behavior.”

The quick mobilization is reminiscent of the boon in community activism in Milton six years ago amid a nationwide racial reckoning, said Régine Jean-Charles, a Milton resident and director of Africana Studies at Northeastern University.

“I’m elated that parents are actively engaged and inspired to start a new initiative,” she said, but added it’s frustrating that the cycle of racial incidents hasn’t stopped, despite previous attempts. “We should not have to keep re-inventing the wheel over and over again.”

title: Tiny Cape Verde ties powerhouse Spain, shocking World Cup and sending local fans into celebrations
text:
“We Cape Verdeans, we are all on the same vibrations. We are about to win. We all want to win. We’ve already won,” said Neila Teixeira, 24, who celebrated in Brockton.

The celebration comes as World Cup fever has taken over Boston. In total, 2 million people are expected in the city this summer for the festivities.

Most recently, Scottish fans celebrated their Saturday win at Boston Stadium, with the Tartan Army marching from Back Bay Fens to Fenway Park for Scottish Celebration Night.

Now, it was Cape Verde’s turn.

“This is history being made. Remember that we are made for this. Forget that one percent chance. Ninety-nine percent fate,” said Keila Rodrigues, 30, as the final whistle blew.

The matchup was lopsided on paper. Spain, the 2010 World Cup champion, entered the tournament ranked third in FIFA’s men’s rankings.

Cape Verde was ranked 64th and arrived as the third-smallest country by population, with just over 500,000 residents, to ever compete in the world’s greatest sporting spectacle.

At Ann’s Palace in downtown Brockton, fans showed up to watch the game donning Cape Verde’s blue jersey, as some waved the country’s flag.

Analisa Gomes, 32, took the day off to come to Ann’s Palace to watch the game. “First win, that’s all we are waiting for. A lot of faith,” she said, as the game played out.

Alissa Teixeira, 27, also took the day off. She was with her friend, and they were sipping on Shirley Temples.

“I was born and raised in Cape Verde. This is a dream come true. My expectation is for us to do our best, no matter the result,” she said. At the 36th minute, when the Cape Verdean keeper made a save, the room erupted in cheers as if they had scored a goal. Towards the end of the half, as Cape Verde made a breakaway, almost everyone was on their feet even as the end of the attack fizzled out.

And as Cape Verde kept Spain at bay, chants of “Ole, Ole, Ole” broke out.

“We made history,” Taija Walker-Monteiro said as she waved the Cape Verdean flag.

In Dorchester, where many of Greater Boston’s more than 22,000 residents with Cape Verdean ties live, Spanish jerseys were scarce at the watch party. As the match began, Mayor Michelle Wu stopped by to greet fans and visit local vendors participating in the event, including Sweet Glam and Tutu’s Art.

The park became a sea of blue, red, and white. Children waved Cape Verdean flags, families danced between chants, and DJ James Fortes, 36, known as mez.wav, kept the crowd moving with a mix of Spanish-language hits and Cape Verdean Creole music.

That sense of community stretched beyond the fans themselves. Police officers assigned to the event joined residents for an impromptu pickup soccer before kickoff and later settled into the crowd to watch the game, cheering alongside lifelong supporters.

“Everybody online was saying that Spain was gonna beat us by 6 or 7 points, and they didn’t,” said Natalie Varela, 18, who was elated after the historic game. “We gotta show them, we gotta protect the small island, everybody doubting us.”

After Spain was held scoreless for the match, many fans left optimistic about what could come next for the small island nation.

Varela is already making plans, she said. She and her family will travel to Texas for Cape Verde’s match against Saudi Arabia.

“I’m gonna wear my pride, my flag, everything. I am very excited,” she said.

With the underdogs holding their ground against one of soccer’s global powers, it became increasingly difficult for many not to be swept up in the belief that this World Cup may still hold more winning chapters for the small nation.

That belief extended beyond the Cape Verdean community. Alexis Rojas, 38, from Colombia, wore a Cape Verde jersey to the watch party. Years of making friends with Cape Verdeans in Dorchester, he said, made him excited to cheer for the country’s first World Cup.

“Not letting Spain, one of the favorite teams, score and being their first time, I think this is an amazing performance,” said Rojas.

Even with a draw, many said it felt like a win.

Tony Barbosa, 38, came to watch the game with his brother, Eric Barbosa, 28.

“This is our first time being in the World Cup after gaining independence, and we feel like it’s a huge opportunity to get known on the world stage,” said Tony Barbosa. “I’ve already won the World Cup by even being here.”

The brothers said that though the result mattered, simply seeing Cape Verde on soccer’s biggest stage carried its own significance.

“It was crazy to see Cape Verde versus Spain to begin with, that we were paired against them [in the] first game,” Eric Barbosa said. “They might have been underestimating our team because we’re the underdog and they’re the best.”

Almost every advance by Cape Verde sparked cheers loud enough to make some passerby think a goal had been scored.

“I’m emotional right now, 50 years in the making, history in the making,” said Cibele Lutaaya, 40, who moved to the US at 11 years old.

Spain took 17 shots to Cape Verde’s four. Cape Verde’s 40-year-old goalkeeper Josimar José Évora Dias, known as Vozinha, made eight saves, while Spain’s keeper made one.

“Honestly, I think we might expect to win the next game,” said Fortes. “It was a beautiful day.”

After this match, Cape Verde is scheduled to face Uruguay in Florida on Jun. 21, followed by a game against Saudi Arabia in Texas on Jun. 26.

title: Maybe this meeting actually is an email
text:
Governor Maura Healey’s calendar has been littered with swearing-in ceremonies, media appearances, and events with everyone from mayors to international dignitaries.

Two people mostly missing from her schedule this year? Senate President Karen Spilka and House Speaker Ron Mariano.

Beacon Hill’s “Big Three” — who largely dictate what becomes law, what doesn’t, and what policies Massachusetts’ 7.1 million residents feel most — have spent remarkably little time together in the same room this year. The three Democrats haven’t held their traditional leadership meeting since March — and that in-person confab was the only one they’ve held in more than six months.

The closed-door sit-downs between the governor, speaker, and Senate president were once a semi-regular feature of governing on Beacon Hill. So much so, former Governor Charlie Baker’s office regularly referred to it as the “weekly leadership meeting” on his public schedule. This year, it’s closer to a semi-annual tradition.

The practice dates back decades to former Republican Governor Bill Weld’s time in office, and the habit began informally. Weld agreed to grab drinks at the Charles Hotel with then-House Speaker Charles Flaherty and then-Senate President William Bulger, Weld said in a 2017 interview, after which they all agreed to meet every Monday at 3:15 p.m.

The meetings — part dealmaking, part relationship-building — continued for years, including through former Deval Patrick and Baker’s administrations.

They’ve long served a variety of purposes. For the press covering Beacon Hill, they’re an (increasingly rare) opportunity to get the State House’s most important figures afterward in one place to ask questions.

They could be sources of political intrigue. (See Patrick’s alleged comments to lawmakers about a federal prosecutor investigating Beacon Hill.) They can be “special‚” as Healey described her first one, or even a way to make a quick buck if you’re a betting man like late state Senate President Thomas Birmingham. And in past retellings, they’re all but essential.

When the COVID-19 pandemic put a pause on in-person meetings — whether you were a governor or not — Baker openly lamented the loss.

“The fact that I haven’t seen Karen Spilka and Ron Mariano in person except maybe at one event for a couple of minutes … and that we don’t sit down and eat stale cookies and drink bad coffee once a week, I think is a problem,” Baker said during a 2021 GBH radio interview. “Human beings see each other as people when they spend time with each other in person.”

Take a spin through the governor’s recent calendars — which lists, among other things, meetings and calls with state and elected officials — and it appears she’s spent more time traveling to the Super Bowl in February or catching the France vs. Brazil friendly in March than she has meeting in-person with Spilka and Mariano. (Her daily calendar also shows no scheduled calls with either legislator, although some items are redacted.)

There’s no shortage of things to talk about, or things Healey wants lawmakers to pass from her own agenda. And with all three up for reelection this fall, it’s all the more motivation to get some of those things done before November — hypothetically at least; Spilka and Mariano aren’t facing any opponents this year.

But the Big Three’s lone meeting so far this year is a new low for the group. Healey, Spilka, and Mariano held eight leadership meetings in 2025, including three times before June, according to a Globe review of Healey’s schedules. In 2024, they met six times, including four times by mid-June.

It’s a significant drop-off from the Baker era. By this time in 2022 — an election year, Baker’s last in office, and with the end of formal lawmaking looming — he had met with Spilka and Mariano 10 times, according to a review of Baker’s public schedules from then.

Perhaps this well-worn public show of open communication loses its draw (or need) when everyone is from the same party. Healey once said she found it “kind of funny those meetings get covered” by reporters.

Or maybe it’s easier for a Democratic governor to get what she wants by playing both sides individually. That was more or less former Governor Michael Dukakis’s strategy, given there was always, as he put it to the Herald in 2014, “a certain amount of tension between the House and Senate, even though Democrats controlled both branches.”

Healey, Spilka and Mariano’s offices say they’re still in regular touch.

“The Governor, Speaker and Senate President are in frequent communication about shared priorities and delivering results for the people of Massachusetts,” their offices said in a joint statement in response to questions from the Globe. “They remain focused on lowering costs, creating jobs and moving the state forward.”

But as one legislator put it back in 2021, staying in touch by phone and email, “does not meet the same level of meeting in person, and the interpersonal relationship.”

The politician? Karen Spilka.

2030 WATCH: Attorney General Andrea Campbell has sued Trump more than 50 times. Democrats say they hear ‘a future governor or senator.’ by Anjali Huynh, The Boston Globe: Andrea Campbell has sued the federal government more than 50 times since Trump took office last year, using millions of dollars in additional taxpayer funding to hire attorneys and form the state-level bulwark that, more often than not, beats the administration in court. That has earned her regular praise — and buzz about her potential for higher office — from fellow Democrats.

ENDORSEMENT ALERT: The pro-housing group Abundant Housing Massachusetts is throwing its support behind an interesting mix of legislative candidates in Democratic primaries this election cycle.

The group is backing one challenger, Newton City Councilor Alison Leary, who’s looking to unseat state Representative John Lawn, a 15-year incumbent. AHMA is also endorsing state Senator Will Brownsberger, who’s facing a challenge from Daniel Lander, a former aide to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, and Cambridge Vice-Mayor Burhan Azeem, who’s chasing the Democratic nomination in the crowded race to replace outgoing state Senator Pat Jehlen.

PICKING SIDES: Some of the city’s current and former Black elected officials are choosing sides in the Democratic primary that’s pitting state Senator Nick Collins against two challengers, the Wu-backed Latoya Gayle and repeat candidate Juwan Skeens. Former state Representative Marie St. Fleur and current state representatives Brandy Fluker-Reid and Chynah Tyler are among those hosting a fundraiser for Collins on Wednesday, the Dorchester Reporter’s Yawu Miller reports.

LABOR PAINS: Unions in uproar over Gov’s plans to tap pension fund for economic development grants by Tim Dunn, Boston Herald: Unions and fiscal watchdogs are in uproar over a proposal in Healey’s economic development bill that would tap the state’s pension system to the tune of $50 million to $100 million to fund economic development grants across Massachusetts. Both the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 509 and the National Association of Government Employees (NAGE) expressed their “firm opposition” to the provision in a letter earlier this month.

OVERSIGHT FIGHT: Amid friction with Boston police, watchdog agency again tries to flex its authority by Lea Skene, the Boston Globe: After two recent fatal police shootings, Boston’s civilian oversight agency is calling for an updated policy that would require the department to release body-camera footage within a specific timeframe, increasing transparency in the wake of officer violence. In a memo sent to Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox, the city’s Office of Police Accountability and Transparency called on the department to release bodycam footage to the office within seven days and publicly within 30 days, bringing Boston police more in line with other major law enforcement agencies across the country.

SPENDING SPAT: Mayor Wu says council’s budget changes could lead to layoffs by Eve Zuckoff, WBUR: Wu is warning the city could face layoffs, particularly in the transportation department, after the city council passed a slew of amendments to the mayor’s proposed budget. Wu said city officials warned the Council that any amendments beyond a package that was developed by Ways and Means Chair Ben Weber would result in layoffs. Weber said he’d discussed with the mayor’s office restoring $8.2 million for immigrants, housing, seniors, the arts and more. But Councilor John FitzGerald worked with other members of the body frustrated by how much was left out of Weber’s amendments, and proposed restoring an additional $2.3 million in funding.

ETHICAL QUESTIONS: Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn renews push for ethics reform by Gayla Cawley, Boston Herald: Ed Flynn said the public has “lost complete faith” in the Council.

A tentative deal is reached to end the Iran war and Trump orders a stop to the US naval blockade by Munir Ahmed, Julia Frankel, Abby Sewell and Will Weissert, Associated Press.

Despite pre-game worries, Day 1 of the World Cup goes (mostly) without a hitch for Boston by Thai Theodoro, Jaden Perry, Camilo Fonseca and Allyson Chiu, The Boston Globe.

Judge re-opens lawsuit over the way eBay terrorized Natick couple after settlement talks break down via Universal Hub.

As the World Cup begins, Boston hotel prices are dropping by Isabel Hart, Boston Business Journal.

The White House UFC fight is another Trump birthday spectacle by Jim Puzzanghera, The Boston Globe.
