title: Eddie Andelman, the voluble voice who pioneered sports talk radio in Boston in the early 1970s, has died
text:
But he was best known for his founding role in “The Sports Huddle,” a call-in discussion among Mr. Andelman and friends Jim McCarthy and Mark Witkin that began in 1969 and came to define the genre.

“I caused riots,” said Mr. Andelman, who was the most outspoken and outrageous member of the trio. “Nobody was doing the kind of stuff I did.”

His talk-show fame was a fluke, he said.

“I was sitting at a bar talking sports with my buddies and some guy was listening to us,” Mr. Andelman recalled. “I told him to butt out. He said he owned a radio station and liked what I was saying and how I was saying it.”

So Mr. Andelman and his friends ended up with a Sunday night show on WUNR, a small Brookline station.

“We followed the Portuguese Hour,” he said. “That was our lead-in. On the first night, none of the phones worked. Just unreal.”

Mr. Andelman and his colleagues, who were unpaid, sold ads for the show. While one caller told them, “You sound like three guys in a gin mill,” that was the essence of “The Sports Huddle’s” popularity.

“We told the listeners, you will be the stars of this show,” Mr. Andelman said. “We have two goals: to put fun back in sports and to look out for the fans.”

When ”The Sports Huddle” moved to WBZ radio, whose 50,000-watt signal reached 26 states, its audience expanded rapidly. And after WBZ (which Mr. Andelman said stood for “Wyoming Blasting and Zoning”) dropped the show in 1971, it was quickly picked up by WEEI.

By then, “The Sports Huddle,” which began with calliope music and used a ticking time-bomb sound effect to warn chatty callers that they’d overstayed their time, had become a Sunday night habit for sports addicts.

Mr. Andelman was the clear star.

“Even when he was bad, he sounded good,” Witkin said. “Because he was a natural.”

Like McCarthy, who was an insurance executive, and Witkin, who was an attorney, Mr. Andelman was a white-collar professional; he was involved in commercial real estate development.

“My success wasn’t handed to me,” he said. “Whatever I got is mine. I had no nannies.”

Among Mr. Andelman’s investments was a lucrative partnership in the New England Harness Raceway and adjacent acreage in Foxborough.

“One of the reasons I was successful in radio is because I never gave a damn if I was fired because I knew I could make a living doing something else,” he said.

Mr. Andelman, who had a business degree from Boston University and an MBA from Northeastern, grew up in Dorchester and Brookline in a family where money was a constant concern.

“His father was not successful until later in life,” his wife, Judi, said. “So he really is conflicted about whether he’s really comfortable or whether he’s going down the tubes tomorrow.”

Mr. Andelman had an instinctive distrust of sports owners, who he believed were hypocrites.

“Every owner has made the same speech since I was 2 years old,” he said. “This is not my team. It belongs to the fans and I’m just a caretaker.”

Mr. Andelman was particularly critical of Red Sox and Bruins ownership, who he said were charging fans high prices to sit in rundown facilities.

“Fenway Park is a bad ballpark,” he said. “They’ve put lipstick on a pig. Tourists love it because they come once every 10 years. Everybody else hates it.”

Mr. Andelman, who was hardly a hockey fan, ripped the old Boston Garden for its rats and unwelcoming atmosphere.

“The Garden also has no escalators and no air conditioning,” he said. “But it does have rude ushers, winos, and stalactites.”

While he was undeniably popular, Mr. Andelman’s acerbic style was not universally appreciated, which he accepted.

“If everyone is happy with what I’ve done, I’m not doing my job,” he said. “But I’m my own worst critic. If I do a bad show, no one has to tell me about it.”

Humor was central to “The Sports Huddle’s” appeal.

“There’s no Pulitzer Prize for sports talk radio,” Mr. Andelman said. “And there shouldn’t be.”

When the Patriots were struggling in the early ’70s, the hosts called Buckingham Palace to ask for a couple of guards.

They also initiated a “Superfoot” contest for British soccer players in the search for a placekicker and came up with Mike Walker, a Lancashire bricklayer who earned the job.

After five years with WEEI, the program moved to WHDH for 15 years before the station and Mr. Andelman, who had his own show, parted company.

“They’ve got no promotion, no money to spend,” he said. “I mean, it’s been a nightmare for the last five years.”

In 1991, he returned to WEEI, which had adopted an all-sports format.

“It’s still a marvel to me that people listen to me and take this stuff seriously when I don’t take it seriously,” Mr. Andelman said.

Four years later, after he had left “The Sports Huddle,” Mr. Andelman was paired with Bruins broadcaster Dale Arnold on “The A Team,” but their partnership didn’t click.

“I wanted to create a high-energy odd couple of radio, two people who were totally different,” said program manager Glenn Ordway, who was looking to boost ratings. “Eddie didn’t believe in that philosophy.”

Nor did Mr. Andelman believe in the confrontational format that sports talk had adopted.

“Radio should be a theater of the mind, not screaming and stupidity,” he said.

So after a decade at WEEI, which he said had “too many people who are not trained and not educated,” Mr. Andelman left at the end of 2001 and decamped to an afternoon show on WWZN.

“I would like to restore sports radio to a high enough intellectual level and try to reach people,” he said. “I’ve made my bones trying to be creative, trying to be innovative, not piling on and beating the crap out of all the athletes.”

Yet sports analytics left Mr. Andelman cold.

“There are too many computers in studios today,” he said. “You can’t have a fun conversation if you’re always looking up facts and figures.”

After WWZN abandoned local programming in 2005, Mr. Andelman revived “The Sports Huddle” on WTKK with new cohosts Bill Fairweather and Mike Donovan. He retired in 2010.

Mr. Andelman was inducted into the Massachusetts Broadcasters Hall of Fame in 2011.

In addition to his wife, Mr. Andelman leaves three sons David, Daniel, and Michael; and seven grandchildren.

Services will be held at 11 a.m. Wednesday at Stanetsky Memorial Chapel in Canton, with burial at Sharon Memorial Park. Shiva will be held at a later date, according to the funeral home.

Outlasting Mr. Andelman’s on-air career was the annual Hot Dog Safari, which he conceived in 1989 as a bus tour for fans to determine the area’s best frankfurters.

Over the years, the safari raised millions of dollars for the Joey Fund to find a cure for cystic fibrosis.

“Even the health nuts got involved,” Mr. Andelman said. “Some guy brought in tofu hot dogs. Can you imagine?”

title: Teachers forced to spritz water on students, turn off lights as some classrooms in Boston top 100 degrees
text:
Earlier this week, after the heat broke, temperatures remained stubbornly high in some schools. On Monday, with outside temperatures comfortably in the 70s, nine classrooms across six schools registered temperatures in the 90s, according to the temperature sensors.

“It’s awful,” said Pedro Salines, who has a 9-year-old third grader at the Mather. “It’s a crucial thing for there to be air conditioning in school with little kids.”

Other schools with hot classrooms included Mozart Elementary, Mel King Preparatory High School, and Holland High School of Technology.

In a statement, Boston Public Schools said it was working closely with the leaders of schools that lack air conditioning to keep a close eye on temperatures inside school buildings and classrooms.

“We understand the concerns families may have during periods of high heat, and we are committed to supporting the health, safety, and comfort of our students and staff to the greatest extent possible,” said schools spokesperson Samara Pinto.

Climate change has made it more challenging to keep students cool in old buildings. Five of the last six years have seen above-average temperatures for the months of June and September, said Ken Mahan, The Boston Globe’s lead meteorologist.

“This June has seen high temperatures 10 degrees higher than average,” said Mahan, making it the third hottest June on record so far.

Over the past 30 years, temperatures have jumped an average of 2 degrees.

Across Massachusetts, 17 percent of schools do not have a cooling system, according to a state survey published last year.

Boston officials said 100 of the city’s schools now have air conditioning available in some capacity, a number that has increased dramatically. An order filed in the City Council in January 2025 said that the number of schools with cooling systems nearly tripled in three years.

Next year, three Boston schools are scheduled for air conditioning upgrades: Phineas Bates Elementary School in Roslindale and the Thomas J. Kenny School and Joseph Lee K-8 School in Dorchester, according to the city.

The issue is more complicated at the Mather, which is the oldest public elementary school in North America. Officials said the building has “extremely limited electrical capacity,” which makes it impossible to install a facility-wide air conditioning system.

During the recent spike in temperatures, school officials said at the Mather they moved students and staff to classrooms with lower temperatures. They said they also brought in more than two dozen additional fans, extra water, and gave students additional breaks to keep them and staff as comfortable as possible.

This week, Rizzo and five other Mather parents petitioned for a new cooling system at the school. Standing outside the school with clipboards, they collected signatures from other parents to push the city to do something.

They decided to take action after their children came home complaining about the heat last week. After spending the day inside the school, students emerged drenched in sweat and wrapped in wet paper towels that failed to keep them dry.

Some teachers turned off lights to minimize any additional heat. Rizzo’s first grader told his mother last week: “Mommy, we spent the day in the dark today.”

Other teachers periodically sprayed students with water, parents said.

Nevika Pinyochon, a teacher’s aide and lunch monitor, has a 10-year-old daughter in the Mather’s fourth grade. Pinyochon said last week, students complained of headaches and nausea.

“It’s so hot,” said Pinyochon, who stayed home from work Thursday because of the temperature. “The school tried to do the best they could. Opening windows and spraying kids, we refilled the bottles of water. It’s too much.”

In February, a member of the Mather’s parent council emailed school officials to ask about a number of issues with the building, including accessibility in the four-story school without an elevator and the lack of air conditioning.

The response was not encouraging.

“In regards to the air conditioning and accessibility both of these are longer term,” wrote Brian Forde Jr., Boston Public Schools’ chief operating officer. “I do not have a timeline present as we balance these needs across the district’s aging infrastructure.”

Moses Park, a pastor who has three children at the Mather, described the lack of air conditioning as “an issue of inequity and injustice.”

“I’m not surprised that a school that serves Black and brown students who come from a wide variety of immigrant backgrounds got the short end of the stick,” Park said. “It’s a basic human right. It’s symptomatic of a deeper issue.”

title: Former postal worker admits to stashing years of undelivered mail in rented locker, officials say
text:
A former mail carrier with routes in Brighton, Dorchester, and Mattapan has admitted to stashing thousands of pieces of undelivered mail in a personal storage locker, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

Khalea Turner, 29, of Hull, pleaded guilty Monday to one charge of obstructing mail, US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office said in a statement. Turner, a former Postal Service employee, will be sentenced at a later date.

Between November 2022 and January of this year, Turner failed to deliver roughly 14,700 pieces of mail assigned to routes in the three areas of Boston , along with the Fort Point neighborhood, the statement said. Instead, he stored the undelivered mail in a rented U-Haul storage locker in Weymouth.

Investigators who recovered the mail on Jan. 9 found US passports, jury notifications, government checks, education documents, and immigration paperwork intended for customers on Turner’s routes, according to Foley’s office.

The case comes amid years of complaints about chronic mail delays and inconsistent Postal Service delivery across Boston, according to previous Globe reports. Some residents have said they could not rely on prescriptions arriving on time, while others report waiting weeks for bills and government documents.

In 2024, Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, Representative Ayanna Pressley, and seven other members of Massachusetts’ congressional delegation pointed to reports of lost mail and delivery delays in Roxbury, Somerville, Brookline, and other communities as evidence of ongoing postal service problems, the Globe reported. Later that year, audits by the Postal Service’s inspector general found significant operational issues at mail facilities in South Boston and Fort Point, including mail left unprocessed for days and packages that were handled improperly.

Turner faces up to six months in prison, one year of supervised release, and a $5,000 fine for the obstruction of mail charge, according to the statement.

Lila Hempel-Edgers can be reached at lila.hempeledgers@globe.com. Follow her on X @hempeledgers and on Instagram @lila_hempel_edgers.

title: Boston’s next World Cup game kicks off at 6 p.m. Follow live updates.
text:
Read more World Cup stories

By Chloe Pisani, Globe Correspondent

The first commuter rail train bringing fans back to Boston pulled into South Station shortly before 9 p.m. Tuesday.

It arrived about an hour after the Iraq-Norway game ended in Foxborough. Norway won, 4-1.

Hundreds rushed off the train, streaming onto buses, subway cars, taxis, rideshare vehicles and even pedicabs.

Fans said the transit process to and from the game was surprisingly painless.

“It was excellent,” said Kate Weisburg, 30, from New York. “Everything was really smooth.”

Weisburg said she is considering attending another game because her train experience was so easy.

Riders paid $80 for a round-trip ticket. Fans said the express trains took about 40 to 50 minutes each way.

Joseph Mirsky, 27, of Chicago, also attended a game in New Jersey, where he said the transit to the stadium was far worse compared to Boston.

“The transport [in New Jersey] was really bad, some of the worst I’ve ever seen,” Mirsky said. “But here it was awesome. It was obviously a little longer, but very organized.”

While the train tickets were pricey, it far beat driving, said Milton Gholston, 35 of Revere.

“Obviously it costs more than a normal transit ride, which is kind of frustrating, but it is what it is.”

By Nicole Yang, Globe Staff

The crowd waiting to catch the train from the stadium back to Boston is absolutely packed, even an hour after the final whistle. Lucky for those in line, that giant screen in broadcasting the Argentina-Algeria game.

By Ben Volin, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — There aren’t too many deals to be had during this year’s World Cup, with ticket prices often stretching well into the four figures. But the fans who trekked to Foxborough Tuesday evening for Norway-Iraq got their money’s worth.

In one of the cheaper matches of the World Cup, the heavily pro-Norway crowd was treated to a delightful match, with Norway fighting off several furious Iraq chances to emerge with a 4-1 victory in the Group I opener for both squads.

And the man everyone came to see delivered in a big way, with Norway’s Erling Haaland, the hulking, ponytailed, 6-foot-5-inch striker for Manchester City, accounting for two goals in the first half, in the 29th and 43rd minutes. Norway put the match away with goals in the 76th and 97th minutes.

READ MORE

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

With just a few seconds to play, Norway makes it 4-1 on what looked like an Iraqi own goal.

The Norwegians dominated much of the early proceedings before finding the opening goal from — who else — Erling Haaland, in the 29th minute. The Iraqis responded excellently through the rest of the first half, first finding an equalizer through an Ayman Hussein header, then nearly finding another goal in the dying moments of the half. Norway still led at halftime, though, after a calamitous miscommunication between an Iraqi center back and his goalkeeper handed Haaland his second goal on a silver platter. Leo Østigard made it 3-1 in the second half with a header from a corner, and an own goal made it 4-1 in the final seconds.

A 4-1 win puts Norway top of Group C along with France, which beat Senegal 3-1 earlier in the day, yet Norway will be top on goal difference. Norway will face Senegal in New York/New Jersey on Monday, a couple hours after France faces Iraq in Philadelphia.

By Cam Kerry, Globe Staff

Erling Haaland, in his World Cup debut, almost capitalized on sloppy play to cap off a hat trick. Haaland’s pressure created a turnover, springing him free in on goal. Iraq goalkeeper Jalal Hassan came off his line and denied Haaland, keeping Iraq’s slim hopes for a point out of the match alive.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — Only a few minutes after the hydration break and Norway has doubled its lead, as defender Leo Østigard powered a header home from a corner to make it 3-1 in the 77th minute. The Iraqis have a lot of work to do to get anything from this game.

By Cam Kerry, Globe Staff

The teams have traded possession of the ball, but no Grade-A chances have emerged for either side since an action-packed first half. In the 70th minute, it’s still 2-1 in favor of Norway.

By Cam Kerry

The ball is rolling again. Norway looks to see out a result for three points, while Iraq tries to climb back into the match.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

Bit of trouble with the pitch at halftime — one sprinkler at the edge of one of the penalty boxes has gone rogue, spewing out a brownish-looking liquid onto the grass. They’ve cut the sprinklers for now, but a big brown stain remains, which seems to be a mixture of water and the sand that’s under the pitch.

And now a stadium staffer has taken a cartoonish fall trying to run over to help with the mess at the edge of the penalty box. Not exactly a seamless halftime thus far.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — Iraq very nearly finds another equalizer in the dying seconds of the first half — Ali Al Hamadi was through on goal but had his shot blocked by a desperation tackle, then Akam Hashem blasted a volley inches over the bar. Hashem’s effort hit the top of the net, and more than a few fans thought it had hit the back of the net instead.

After 45 minutes, Norway still leads 2-1 after a busy half in Foxborough.

by Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — As quickly as Iraq leveled the score, Norway is back in front just as quickly. It’s a horrible error from both defender Zaid Tahseen, who played a lazy backpass, and goalkeeper Jalal Hassan, who hesitates too long and smashes an attempted clearance off of Erling Haaland and into his own net. It’ll go down as a second goal for Haaland, but that was all on the Iraqis, who trail once again. It’s 2-1 in the final minutes of the second half.

By Amin Touri and Cam Kerry, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — Iraq hasn’t possessed much of the ball in the first half, but the Lions of Mesopotamia are suddenly level as Ayman Hussein rises highest to head home the equalizer for Iraq. You can see what it means to the Iraqis — much of the bench went to celebrate the goal. It’s 1-1 with 40 minutes played in Foxborough.

Hussein, the team’s captain, scored the clincher against Bolivia in the intercontinental playoffs to send Iraq to its first World Cup since 1986.

By Cam Kerry, Globe Staff

Erling Haaland slides in behind the defense, getting his left leg on a sublime cross from David Møller Wolfe, who overlapped with Antonio Nusa. It’s Norway’s first goal in the World Cup since 1998, good for the lead in the 29th minute.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

At the first-half hydration break, the score remains 0-0 between Iraq and Norway in Foxborough. The fans don’t particularly appreciate the stoppage — fans of Norway in particular were booing as the teams left the pitch. Singing “Livin’ on a Prayer” during the break seems to have lifted their spirits, though.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

Fans of Iraq and Norway filled in to Fan Fest at City Hall Plaza, replacing the French and Senegalese fans who cleared out.

“It’s a very cool experience. It’s unique, almost, because we haven’t been in the World Cup since [1986], so it’s a cool experience,” said 16-year-old Iraqi fan Ali Raheem. “We get to be in the World Cup, even if we don’t win games, even if we don’t score goals. It’s the experience.”

The match is important for Norway too, seeing that the Landslaget haven’t graced the world stage since 1998.

“I think Iraq has a great team too and I think that they’re really gonna put up a strong fight,” Dallas Smith said, wrapped in Norway’s bright red flag. “[It’s] really fun to see everybody excited and playing,” Smith said, acknowledging the significance of this game for both countries.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

There’s little surprise about which jersey is most popular in the crowd — shirts with “Haaland” on the back are everywhere. There’s more Norway shirts than any other (reading “Braut Haaland,”, including his mother’s last name), but there also plenty from his club, English Premier League’s Manchester City, as well as his previous teams, Borussia Dortmund of Germany and RB Salzburg of Austria. The big striker has already threatened the Iraqi box twice in the first 10 minutes in his typical style — bulldozing through defenders.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

At kickoff, this place is just about filled out, with perhaps a handful of empty seats here and there if you squint toward the nosebleeds. This seemed like the most likely game to have a little trouble selling tickets, between the lack of a marquee matchup and a less than ideal kickoff time, but that doesn’t appear to be the case.

By Cam Kerry, Globe Staff

Iraq launches the ball out of bounds deep into Norwegian territory, kicking off the opening match for both teams.

By Amin Touri, Globe Staff

FOXBOROUGH — The first thing I’ve noticed on the concourse this evening: There appear to be far more “neutral” fans here tonight than for Saturday’s Haiti-Scotland game. Norwegian and Iraqi jerseys certainly have a plurality, but there are plenty of other shirts — United States, Mexico, Greece, Thailand, a dozen different club jerseys, the list goes on.

Perhaps it’s because the tickets for this game were among the lowest of any of the games in Foxborough, but this seems like the general public’s choice to get a glimpse at the local World Cup.

by Ariela Lopez, Globe Correspondent

Dallas Smith and James McConnell traveled to Boston this week from Minneapolis to support not one but two World Cup teams whose fan bases have descended on the city.

McConnell is Scottish. Smith’s grandparents are Norwegian. Both sported Norwegian flags at the Fan Festival at City Hall Plaza, where they plan to watch the evening’s match between Norway and Iraq.

Yesterday, they went to a pop-up ‘Norgefest’ celebration by Rowes Wharf. The day before, they watched the Scottish Tartan Army procession.

“I think Boston has been doing a great job hosting,” Smith said.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

The crowd at Boston’s Fan Festival bursts into applause as substitute Bradley Barcola scored two minutes after being subbed on for France. Les Blues took the lead 16 minutes prior to Barcola’s 82nd minute strike, when Kylian Mbappé finished Michael Olise’s clever pass.

By Nicole Yang, Globe Staff

The longest line inside the stadium is undoubtedly the one for this small merchandise stand, which features a limited selection of tournament-, country-, and game-specific items.

The lines for concessions are pretty manageable.

By Nicole Yang, Globe Staff

The limited amount of parking spots at Boston Stadium (5,000 in comparison to the usual 20,000 for Patriots games) means the tailgating largely happens away from the actual parking lots.

Along Route 1 there were plenty of lively sites, including this robust section of Norwegian fans.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe Correspondent

Most soccer fanatics pick one favorite in a World Cup game and go all in.

That is not the case for Mohammed Missouri, executive director of the Office of Neighborhood Services for the city of Boston. Being Iraqi-Norwegian turned Bostonian means today he is living the best of all worlds.

“It’s a good day for me no matter what,” he said.

Missouri, 42, was born in Baghdad, Iraq, and moved to Norway as a result of the Gulf War when he turned 8 years old, he said.

READ MORE

By Ariela Lopez, Globe Correspondent

Ahmed Naser traveled to Boston from Ottawa to support Iraq in the Lions of Mesopotamia’s match against Norway in Foxborough on Tuesday.

Naser, who was born in Iraq’s capital of Baghdad, does not have a ticket to the game this evening. Instead, he’s planning to watch the match from the Fan Festival downtown.

Naser said he recognizes that the Iraqi team, which has qualified for the World Cup only once before, faces tough opposition in the tournament.

“Our group is very hard,” he said. “We’re not expecting something crazy.”

Naser said he hopes for a draw as tonight’s result.

By Jaden Perry, Globe Correspondent

As a cool breeze swept through the Fan Festival, fans continued to trickle in as concession stands and gift shops opened their registers. Award-winning singer and Boston native Lisa Bello took to the stage, helping fans settle in.

Nearly 20 kids, teens, and adults juggled a soccer ball, with each successful bounce invoking celebratory shouting.

As the game started, fans zoned in on the jumbo screen.

“A lot of people have been hating on him,” said Matthew Fleury, 19, about his favorite player from France, Kylian Mbappé. “I want to see him win another World Cup and prove people wrong.”

By Ariela Lopez, Globe Correspondent

The match between France and Senegal is set to begin at 3 p.m., and some fans plan to watch from the Fan Festival.

Mamadou Gaye, 47, lives in Lawrence, Mass. and was born in Senegal. He came to the Fan Festival with some friends and has met even more Senegalese fans in the crowd.

“If they keep making it fun, maybe I’ll go to more,” Gaye said about the Fan Festival.

The Fan Festivals will continue through June 27.

By Ariela Lopez, Globe Correspondent

The FIFA Fan Festival at City Hall Plaza has just begun, and hundreds of jersey-clad fans are already enjoying food and music — and trying to get some shade — at the party.

Martín Morales and his family, who are visiting the United States from Quito, Ecuador, for the World Cup, came to Boston for the day.

“We were wondering what to do in the area, and most of us didn’t know Boston,” Morales said.

Wearing Messi jerseys to support Argentina in its match against Algeria tonight, his family is waiting in line at the Fan Festival to get a coveted custom collectible bracelet.

Signs at the event estimate the line is more than an hour long.

By Claire Thornton, Globe Staff

Rows of metal barriers meant to contain World Cup fans standing in line went unused for hours on Tuesday. Thousands of fans moved steadily, without any log jams.

Out of four lines set up ahead of the Norway-Iraq game, only one was put to use.

Around 1 p.m. on Tuesday, officials shortened the line further, so that fans walked through fewer rows of metal barriers before entering South Station.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

Inside South Station, fans patiently waited their turn to be ushered through.

They cheered when the turnstiles were opened and they made their way to the trains.

Conor, 12, and Graham, 11, were with Conor’s parents Amanda and Kevin Robertson. They are from Hingham and were at South Station heading to the game to support Norway.

“There were a lot of people, but it’s been efficient,” Graham said.

“It’s been seamless, well-run, so far no issue,” Amanda said.

Conor who was wearing a Manchester City kit said he was going to the game to watch Erling Haaland of Norway.

“We are both left-footed strikers,” Conor said.

“I think he is going to score,” Graham said.

By Claire Thornton, Globe Staff

Ali Al Sabea wore Iraq’s national flag over his shoulders as he helped his parents navigate World Cup crowds outside South Station.

The 19-year-old studies engineering at Iowa State University, and said his parents live in Illinois. They emigrated to the US from Iraq three years ago.

Al Sabea said he saw videos of Iraqi fans gathering on Monday night to celebrate their country’s historic World Cup appearance ahead of Tuesday’s game. He would have been among them if he and his parents arrived in Boston earlier, he said.

Al Sabea, who got to town on Monday night, said Iraqi fans are looking forward to having fun during the match.

“We’re friendly, we like to get to know people from other countries,” Al Sabea said.

Other young men smiled and cheered outside South Station, greeting each other as “habibi,” a term of endearment. They were excited to support the Iraqi national team, but in their own way.

Ari Balata wore the Kurdish flag around his shoulders and a Kurdish emblem on his chest, showing support for the autonomous region within Iraq.

Several players on the Iraqi team are Kurdish, said his brother, 27-year-old Warheal Balata.

“You’ve got to show up your people,” said Warheal, who said his parents are from Kurdistan.

As of 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, you can land a ticket for Tuesday’s Iraq-Norway game for $420 on StubHub.

Saturday’s game in Foxborough was at capacity with 64,146 listed as the official attendance.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

The MBTA sold out of commuter rail tickets for Saturday’s Haiti-Scotland game. The demand for Norway-Iraq on Tuesday was much lower, with about 11,000 sold according to Joe Pesaturo, an MBTA spokesperson, who was standing outside South Station as fans queued.

As of 1 p.m., more than half the ticket-holders had already boarded trains. The first trains left around noon.

“People started arriving early, and it’s been a steady but not crowded group of people,” Pesaturo said.

By Milton Valencia, Globe Staff

This non-ticket holding commuter rail passenger (me) was able to board the regularly scheduled 1:12 p.m. Providence train pretty smoothly.

There is a special section cordoned off for the stadium trains, and queues were set up directing people there. And with a prolonged schedule, there did not seem to be much of a wait. Volunteers called out: “Are you going to the game? You can board any time you want.”

None of the delays seen on Saturday seemed to be in place as of now. It was business as usual at South Station.

And even if you’re not on the way to the game, you can still catch the vibe. Food trucks are set up, and volunteers are passing out free water and sun screen, as well as hand sanitizer. A rainbow of soccer jerseys, mostly supporting Iraq and Norway, dot the crowd as police officers in yellow gear direct people away from Summer Street, where the queues are set up.

And as I write this, the train starts moving. On time.

Here’s a look at our live traffic tracker for Foxborough. Backups are beginning to form on both sides of Route 1 entering Gillette Stadium.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

Mouin Al-Masoodi, 38, wore his Iraqi national team jersey while walking along Purchase Street with his daughter Dana, 11, on Tuesday.

They arrived in Boston from Oklahoma Monday night and are staying downtown. They plan to head to the game later Tuesday. For both tickets they paid $780.

“This for me is pure resilience and unity, because the Iraqi people unite around the football team,” Mouin said.

This is the first time that Iraq is back at the World Cup after 40 years.

“These are the top football teams in the world, it’s a bit unlucky to be in this group, but I hope we put in a good game,” he said.

Dana is looking forward to seeing the atmosphere at the World Cup.

“I love soccer and I play it, and I wanted to see a game and see how professionals do it, Dana said. “I am very thankful that I came with my dad.”

This is their first live football game together.

“This is an amazing opportunity to see the national team in the US,” he said. “This is an amazing opportunity for Dana to connect with her heritage. She is a proud American but also proud of her Iraqi roots.”

By Chris Serres, Globe Staff

Following crowded conditions and long lines for Saturday’s World Cup game, officials with Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration and the MBTA have held multiple meetings and will continue to evaluate South Station street closures for the rest of the World Cup, a spokesperson for the mayor’s office said.

For Tuesday’s game, the second of seven World Cup matches in Boston, the MBTA will closed Summer Street from Purchase Street at Dewey Square to Dorchester Avenue, on Tuesday from 7 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

Additional Summer Street closures will be done on outbound travel lanes from Surface Road to Atlantic Avenue.

They have agreed to close the same streets for this Friday’s 6 p.m. game between Scotland and Morocco, because officials are expecting much larger crowds.

As for the remaining five games, the city and the MBTA have not settled on a specific plan, but have agreed to base any decisions on what streets to close around South Station based on crowd size.

“[Tuesday] is big, because it’s the first [match] during the weekday with commuters,” the mayor’s spokesperson said. “We’ll evaluate how today goes, and see what the crowd looks like for an early game, and make adjustments.”

By Claire Thornton, Globe Staff

Three Norwegian visitors boarding a Red Line train car at Downtown Crossing on Tuesday said the T is a good public transit system, but perhaps not the best they’ve experienced.

Kristoffer Sandstad, of Oslo, said one proud Bostonian hyped up the T while speaking with him over the weekend.

“We met this local guy who was maybe a bit of a show-boast, and he told us that this tram system is the best in the world,” Sandstad said.

“I don’t know if we agree, but it’s pretty good,” he said.

Sandstad, along with friends Lars Manengen and Jonas Alme, came to the World Cup to celebrate that they’re all turning 40 this year.

Even if the T isn’t the world’s best, Sandstad said, their time on public transit has been “perfect” since arriving in Boston on Saturday.

The gang said they’re part of a larger group of eight who bought game tickets together. Some paid $60 and some paid $400 for the tickets they were allotted by a lottery system.

By Omar Mohammed, Globe Staff

On Tuesday morning at South Station there appeared to be a lot more Norwegian fans than Iraqi supporters.

But two siblings showed up dressed to support their country.

Ibrahim Al-Ali, 15, traveled with his sister Sarah, 22, all the way from Dearborn, Mich. The pair had just landed in Boston for the game. They plan tohead straight back to Michigan on a 5 a.m. Wednesday flight.

They only decided to get the tickets two days ago.

Why?

“It’s Iraq, it’s our country,” Sarah said.

They both are excited and didn’t expect to see Iraq play at a World Cup in the US.

They paid about $180 each for their tickets.

Ibrahim said he plans to show his cousins in Iraq all the videos he plans to take at the game when they travel back to the country after they get home from Boston.

“It’s kinda like a duty, what we are doing,” he said. “It took a lot for Iraq to qualify and lots of family wanted to come but had problems with visas. We are here to show up for them.”

By Redmond Bernhold, Globe Correspondent

How do you outdrink St. Patrick’s Day in Boston?

Inviting Scots to town is a good start.

This past weekend, Scottish fans stopped downtown before trekking to the World Cup match in Foxborough. On their way, they emptied bars and liquor stores of Corona, Budweiser, Coors, seltzers, ciders, and Tennent’s Lager, Scotland’s most popular beer, according to interviews with business owners.

“We’ve been here for over 30 years, and we’ve never seen anything like it,” said Noelle Somers, chief operating officer at Hennessy’s Bar in downtown. “We tripled St. Patrick’s Day.”

Boston’s energy has been electric, especially after a long winter. Many Scottish patrons learned the names of Hennessy’s bartenders, hugged them, gave generous tips, and drank for hours, Somers said — adding that she rarely sees energy like that in the bar.

“They brought fun back that was lost,” she said.

On Sunday night, Hennessy’s sold out of beer. The bar got a delivery to re-up Monday, and another one is slated for Thursday — in time for the next weekend of soccer matches.

By Milton Valencia, Globe Staff

When you arrive at South Station you see the city popping — even before the first train is scheduled to depart for Foxborough for Tuesday’s Iraq-Norway game.

Iraqi fans are waving flags, while several Norway fans posed for a photos wearing viking hats. Several vendors set up food trucks and informational booths, as non-ticket holders went about their daily commute.

title: Could the postal center next to South Station move at last? The US postmaster may be open to it.
text:
For most of this century, Massachusetts officials have been debating whether, and how, to move the sprawling US Postal Service annex next to South Station. Now the future of the massive complex is once again up for discussion among state and federal leaders.

Representative Stephen Lynch this week told The Globe that US Postmaster General David Steiner has expressed willingness to sell the 1.3 million-square-foot mail sorting facility and relocate its operations. Such a move would clear the way for even more large-scale development alongside the region’s busiest transportation hub, and perhaps an expansion of South Station itself.

Steiner assumed the top position at the US Postal Service last year, following Louis DeJoy’s resignation, and his openness to a sale came as a surprise to the congressman. Lynch said he and Steiner have even visited a property in South Boston near the Reserved Channel that could hold the vast sorting center.

When Texas development giant Hines last year opened its 51-story South Station Tower, the project included a refurbished train platform and larger bus terminal that expanded capacity by 50 percent, but no expansion of train tracks. Compared with the $1.6 billion expansion and renovation of New York City’s Moynihan Train Hall — a head house for Penn Station — and a similar “multibillion” dollar redevelopment at Washington, D.C.’s Union Station, Boston’s South Station is something of “the stepchild on that whole process,” Lynch said.

“If we had that extra land and that opportunity, we could really, really increase the amount of train traffic and people traveling by rail,” Lynch said, adding that an expansion could also hold space for cargo trains.

The Postal Annex has long hemmed in South Station. Government leaders for decades have discussed relocating the facility, a low and long property that stretches across 15 acres along Dorchester Avenue and Fort Point Channel across from former Gillette parking lots.

Moving the mail-sorting facility would open up space for more tracks at South Station, expanding from 13 tracks to as many as 21, and would likely include air rights to develop commercial or residential buildings above that expansion. The South Station Tower stretches 690 feet above the station’s existing tracks, and there would likely be room for another skyscraper above a track expansion, Lynch said.

Still, there is a long, and expensive, road ahead before any of this becomes a reality. The South Station Tower took around half a century to develop, from discussions in the 1970s until the tower’s opening last year. And moving the sorting facility to South Boston would likely require the support of the Massachusetts Port Authority, which owns large stretches of land off Summer Street beyond the Menino Convention and Exhibition Center.

The land long considered to be an option for a relocated mail-sorting center is tucked between E and Summer streets near the Reserved Channel heading into South Boston. Massport acquired a four-acre parcel at 525 E St. in 2022 and owns a combined 22 acres along that stretch, according to Boston assessing records.

The property is currently something of an industrial no-man’s-land and sits adjacent to the 42-acre site where developer Oxford Properties has pitched an eight-building, 1.7 million-square-foot mixed-use development. Oxford has leased 38 acres from Massport for the project, which the city is reviewing.

Massport chief executive Rich Davey said the organization is keeping a close eye on any discussions around South Station. In the 15 years since he started his tenure as the state’s transportation secretary under Governor Deval Patrick, Davey has watched the South Boston waterfront transform from dirt parking lots into a neighborhood that powers 10 percent of Boston’s property-tax base.

“The neighborhood’s changed dramatically,” he said.

It’s important USPS find a suitable site for mail sorting and distribution, he said. And while Massport would support a postal service facility on its South Boston land, Davey wonders whether it’s the highest and best use for the property.

“We’ll be prepared to support [a mail-sorting facility] if that’s the best use, but I also think we’re starting to really think about, for the first time, what would it be if it wasn’t a post office?” Davey said. “We’re going to keep a close eye on it.”

Catherine Carlock can be reached at catherine.carlock@globe.com. Follow her @bycathcarlock.

title: ‘I just wanted to see him happy’: Boston police cadet helps man with cane cross the street before a parting handshake
text:
A few days ago, a Boston police officer gained social media fame for displaying his soccer ball juggling skills to a group of World Cup fans at City Hall Plaza.

On Thursday, a new video showed another delightful scene, as aBoston police cadet helped a man with a cane cross the street before a parting handshake.

The brief clip, which the police department posted to social media with the message “Community Policing takes many forms!” shows an older gentleman in a beige-colored suit walking gingerly with a cane through a bustling intersection.

The exact location wasn’t specified, but it looked like a busy stretch of downtown, which has lately been packed with international visitors taking in the soccer tournament.

Walking beside the pedestrian is Willians Varela, a native of Cape Verde who moved to Dorchester about four years ago, police said. Varela keeps stride with the older man as the two appear to have a cordial conversation.

Other pedestrians and a driver are seen passing the two, who eventually shake hands before the older man continues on his way.

Cadets are not licensed officers but perform a variety of duties as part of a two-year training program with an eye toward possibly becoming sworn officers, which requires a separate Civil Service exam as well as successful completion of Boston Police Academy training.

Varela plans to join the next academy class.

In a statement, Varela recounted his meeting with the older man.

“As I was doing the traffic, it was a busy day,” Varela said. “I saw the gentleman walking by himself, so I gave him a compliment. I told him that I like his suit!”

He said he asked the man “if he minded if I walked across the street with him. He thanked me and said it was kind of unusual to see a young person as an officer. I told I am not an officer yet and explained the Boston Police Cadet program and he told me to keep up the good work.”

The man said he used to live on Beacon Hill where “they had a lot of officers helping people out,” Varela said. “He said it makes him happy to see young people joining law enforcement.”

Varela said the moment harkened back to conversations he used to have with his late grandfather.

“It took a little longer for us to cross the street because our conversation was taking a little longer,” Varela said. “I just wanted to see him happy. I had a Grandpa and when he was alive, I really enjoyed talking to him, so it was nice for me. I think it was a good conversation for both of us.”

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: The World Cup is an international celebration. There are lasting lessons in that.
text:
But, in my defense, nobody told me about the Tartan Army.

It wasn’t until last week, when I saw downtown invaded by men in kilts and felt the energy that hit our town like a hurricane, that I suddenly began to get it.

No Scotland No Party!

But of course, it isn’t just the Scots infusing the city with this badly needed energy. The huge Fan Fest installation on City Hall Plaza reflects the breadth of the revelry.

It’s Haitians cheering an unexpected strong performance against Scotland Saturday night. It’s been Cape Verdeans across Dorchester celebrating perhaps the greatest day in the history of Cape Verdean football Monday, a scoreless draw against mighty Spain.

It’s fans from Norway “rowing” up escalators at South Station.

In perhaps the most unexpected development, there were even alarming reports of Boston running out of beer given the thirsty onslaught of revelers — or at least running low.

If you really want to see a city, it doesn’t hurt to see it through the fresh eyes of people who don’t live here. It’s easy for us to forget that we live in a really fun city. Our new international friends have made it easy to remember, whether they intend to or not.

Ask anyone who was in Fenway Sunday night, watching thousands of Scots who probably know as much about baseball strategy as I know about offsides in soccer, having the time of their lives, singing along to “Dancing Queen.”

Their Boston has been warm and welcoming, and full of newfound friends. Not the version of the US that had led many people, especially on social media, to urge foreign travelers to think twice about coming to America.

This comes at an interesting moment. We’ve spent years now listening to our xenophobe-in-chief demonize people from outside the country.

What started out as a purported push for stronger borders was quickly revealed for what it is. It was never just a bid to curb “illegal” immigration. It was about the systematic denigration of people who don’t fit President Trump’s notion of who deserves to come here.

Sure, I recognize that people here for the World Cup are tourists, not immigrants. Even so, they are demonstrating on an hourly basis how much better letting people in is than shutting them out.

Turns out building a big tent is a lot more fun than building a wall.

Not to be overlooked, even for a second, is that some of the most passionate revelers in Boston are people who have been here all along.

Massachusetts has among the largest Haitian and Cape Verdean communities in the United States. And that Haitian community, in particular, has been literally fighting for its existence in the time of Trump.

For those communities, this is a moment of pure joy.

John Barros, the interim executive director of the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority, hosted a watch party at the Menino Center for the Cape Verde match, joined by “a couple thousand of my closest friends.”

Like most Cape Verdeans, he’s still glowing with pride from his team’s performance.

“Most of our talent plays for other countries,” he noted. “We had hard-working dreamers on our team representing the American story: If you work hard and work together, you can achieve the impossible. People are riding high on that narrative that the little guy can get it done.”

You could argue that immigration policy and the World Cup have nothing to do with one another. But there is no way to reconcile the images of vibrancy and joy that have gripped all of us this past week with a constant message that people from outside are almost always a problem.

Not that facts seem to sway these people, but part of me wishes that some of the so-called immigration hard-liners in Washington could be in Boston this week to see what the people they denounce actually bring to a city.

For that matter, to a country.

title: Six years after closing during the pandemic, this Irish pub is eyeing a return to Mission Hill
text:
“We have a lot of work to do,” said Scott Prince, one of the partners in the venture. “But so far, the experience has been really great. I’m very hopeful that our vision will become a reality.”

Prince, 40, knows his way around a bar; he’s poured drinks at The Banshee in Dorchester for the past eight years. Before that, he lived on Mission Hill and worked at another neighborhood staple, the Puddingstone Tavern.

The original Flann O’Brien’s, known for its rusting statue of its Irish poet namesake (since auctioned off), closed in December 2020 after being open since at least the early 1990s. But Prince said his memories of it are still strong.

“It was a place where you kind of got lost in,” he said. “You would go in for a brunch, right, and you’re hanging out, you’re watching whatever, and before you know it, it’s 6 o’clock.”

That getaway feel is “kind of what we want” to bring back, he said.

Prince said that after he found out that Yellow Door was closing, he brought the idea of bringing Flann’s back to Ray Butler and Michael Vaughan, who run The Banshee as well as Brick & Beam Tavern in Quincy. Butler and Vaughan agreed to partner with Prince to resurrect the bar, which they too had frequented in the 1990s.

“It was nostalgic to them, so it was kind of the perfect opportunity for all of us,” Prince said. “When that opportunity came up, you know, we kind of pounced on it.”

Since Flann’s heyday, Mission Hill has seen plenty of change. But Prince said the bar will reflect both the old and the new.

“Flann’s brought a ton of people together,” he said. “You would get Irish immigrants, hospital workers, college kids, Mission Hill [locals]. It was just a place where people from all walks of life would come and hang out. That’s the biggest thing. If we can get back to that, I think that’d be a great success for us.”

Prince said the owners are working to secure a liquor license; a prospective transfer is slated for review before the city’s licensing board on June 24.

If all goes well, he said, the pub will be ready to reopen by the end of the year.

By staying in the bar’s original location, Flann O’Brien’s will be opening just down the street from Puddingstone Tavern. But Prince said he isn’t trying to push out his old stomping ground; on the contrary, he had nothing but praise for the Puddingstone and its owner, Harry Walsh.

“Learning from Harry is [learning] how to run a restaurant, but also be a great person,” he said. “I think that he kind of embodies what Mission Hill’s about. Obviously, there will be a little bit of competition, but I think at the end of the day it’s healthy for Mission Hill and for all the restaurants in the area.”

title: ‘A reminder of why this work matters.’ AJ Dybantsa, top NBA draft pick, refects on lessons learned at Brockton Catholic school.
text:
AJ Dybantsa, the possible top pick in Tuesday’s NBA Draft, recalled the valued he learned at Trinity Catholic Academy in Brockton during a recent talk sponsored by the Campaign for Catholic Schools.

Dybantsa said at the talk last week he doesn’t “lose confidence on the court” as he knows what he is “capable on the court.”

“Everyone has a bad game, but you have to have a short memory,” he said, according to a video of the June 16 event held at the UMass Club in Boston. “That doesn’t impact my confidence, because I know what I can do out there.”

Dybantsa went to elementary school at Trinity Academy, and spent his freshman year of high school at St. Sebastian’s in Needham, before heading off to prep schools in California and Utah.

The 19-year-old played this past year at Brigham Young University in Utah, where he led men’s college basketball in scoring nationally.

The event also featured Dybantsa’s father, Ace Dybantsa, and remarks from Dana Barros, a former NBA All-Star from Mattapan who starred at Boston College. Barros is a trustee of the Campaign for Catholic Schools, the nonprofit said in a statement.

“The evening highlighted the role CCS’ Trinity Catholic Academy played in AJ’s development and the broader mission of Campaign for Catholic Schools,” the statement said.

The Campaign for Catholic Schools sponsor Trinity Catholic in Brockton and St. John Paul Catholic Academy in Dorchester. The schools serve students in grades pre-K to eighth.

Ace Dybantsa said there were moments in his son’s life where he put academics and “personal responsibility” ahead of basketball, according to the statement.

The campaign was founded in 2007 by businessman Jack Connors as part of a “plan to reinvigorate urban Catholic schools” in Greater Boston.

Every student in a CCS-supported school receives reduced tuition and more than 70 percent of families receive financial aid or “scholarship support” on top of that, CCS said.

Bob Atchinson, the CCS chair, said the event featuring AJ and Ace Dybantsa “was a reminder of why this work matters.“

”Every child deserves the opportunity to attend a school where they are known, valued, and believed in.”

Breanne Kovatch can be reached at breanne.kovatch@globe.com. Follow her @breannekovatch.

title: ‘A true national holiday’: Boston celebrates Juneteenth in Franklin Park
text:
“Black people, people of color, we are the ones who created the country. So I think there is significance because of what is going on in society, with the government, and just the racism and the misogyny,” said Dixon, an artist.

Solonlair Gbolor, who was selling his custom-designed African-style clothing, praised people’s dedication to community and eagerness to come out for this event and celebrate Juneteenth, officially June 19, during the 250th anniversary, which gave people “a lot to look back at and a lot to look forward to.”

“The fact that people can gather together, in celebration of this historic day, Juneteenth, and as we go toward the country’s independence, it’s a good sign,” he said.

Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021 under the Biden administration. The day celebrates June 19, 1865, when Union soldiers told emancipated slaves in Galveston, Texas, that they were free. That news was brought about two months after the Confederacy had surrendered in the Civil War and more than two years after President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation freeing slaves in the South.

Massachusetts made the day a state holiday in 2020 under a bill signed by former Governor Charlie Baker, a two-term Republican.

In Boston on Saturday, music blared as grills across Playstead Park were fired up to cook chicken or hot dogs. Members of the local radio station 98.1 FM, the Urban Heat, blasted music and pumped up the crowd as people danced.

Governor Maura Healey arrived around 3 p.m. after Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll and Mayor Michelle Wu had already weaved their way through the crowd, shaking hands and chatting with constituents.

Healey took time to walk through a school bus serving as a mobile museum on school desegregation that had been set up next to the NAACP Boston tent.

Healey said she was happy to be among the crowd celebrating Juneteenth.

“Obviously, Juneteenth, Freedom Day, we’ve got to remember what that history was about, and we have to honor it every day, and the work to advance civil rights continues here in Massachusetts and across the United States,” she told reporters.

Sharon Butler-Charles, an author, was showing off books she had written and her wellness products at the festival. Butler-Charles said people should use the day to understand their “beginning and how blessed we are to be separated from that.”

“Not to the extent that we’ve forgotten, but to celebrate the blood, sweat, and tears of our ancestors and what they went through, so that we can stand on their shoulders and be here today talking about it and celebrating what they went through,” Butler-Charles said.

Bernadine Kirkland, 63, of Dorchester said she was using the day to honor “our rich cultural heritage.”

“I love the celebrations. I love ... the significance of them, and just being out here and being able to celebrate,” Kirkland said.

Dixon, the artist, said events like the one in Franklin Park allowed people to “see us in the light that we always are in.”

She was happy Juneteenth was “highlighted in a way where people now know it is a true national holiday and know what it’s about.”

title: ‘That could’ve been me’: Mattapan community horrified, devastated after fatal crash
text:
A body covered with a white sheet lay in the street outside a lawyer’s office and a pizza shop. The scene, King said, left her rattled.

“It’s really devastating, and it’s scary because it’s close to home,” said King, 31, who works at a sneaker store across from the scene of the crash.

“We are devastated by the senseless act of violence on Blue Hill Avenue that took a woman’s life, left others injured, and has shaken the Mattapan community and our City,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement. “Our hearts are with the victim’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as everyone impacted by this terrible tragedy.”

Saturday’s episode began unfolding with a crash just up the road.

Matos was driving near Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street when he collided with another vehicle, police said in a statement Sunday. He then abandoned his damaged car and fled to a nearby car wash, where he allegedly pulled a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel, and drove the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square.

Matos allegedly sped down the avenue, driving on the sidewalk before hitting the female pedestrian and crashing into another vehicle at the intersection of Blue Hill Avenue and Fairway Street, according to police.

Police said Matos allegedly drove away from that collision and continued down Blue Hill Avenue before coming to a stop after striking an MBTA bus.

“The suspect was then forcibly removed from the vehicle and restrained by several community members until officers arrived at the scene,” police said.

Genara Peters, 56, was working in Super Dollar on Blue Hill Avenue when she heard a commotion outside. People, Peters said, were “running up and down the street.”

“I asked my customers what’s going on. They say someone got hit,” she said. “I was sad, and I was scared, because it’s right by the store.”

When police arrived around 2 p.m., they found the woman and a vehicle crashed into the side of an MBTA bus. Matos was taken into custody.

He is expected to be arraigned in Dorchester District Court Monday.

The woman’s name was not immediately released pending notification of her family, police said.

Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan said in an email that the MBTA will not “make any statements and/or comments which may interfere with an active and ongoing investigation,” citing the “seriousness of the incident and the tragic loss of life.”

Police said they made another arrest Saturday night after a man was seen entering the taped-off crime scene and recording video of the area while laughing. The man, identified Sunday as Robert Monestime, 21, of Braintree, will be arraigned in Dorchester District Court on charges of disturbing the peace and interfering with a police officer, authorities said.

Other local officials decried Saturday’s murder.

Boston City Councilor At-Large Erin Murphy said the death was the result of “a violent and reckless chain of events.”

“No one should ever be put in danger simply walking through their neighborhood,” Murphy said in a statement.

Boston City Councilor Enrique Pepén, who represents the district that includes Mattapan, praised the bystanders who rushed to help in the aftermath of the crash.

“Their actions reflect the care and concern so many of our community members have for one another,” Pepén said in a statement.

Some people said the crash left them worried for their own safety.

“When I heard it was really sad and really horrifying,” said Mia Mahhan, 26, who works at Finest Int’l Market on Blue Hill Avenue. “We need to have more security. I’m just hoping we can walk safely and move around safely.”

On Sunday afternoon, the busy road lined with stores, food markets, and restaurants showed little sign of the fatal car collision. A few people strolled on the sidewalks as cars and motorcycles streamed down both sides of the six-lane avenue.

While there wasn’t a piece of police tape in sight, King said she felt “a little bit traumatized.”

“That could’ve been me,” she said.

Camilo Fonseca of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: BAMS Festival looks to keep its ‘Momentum’ during a year away from Franklin Park
text:
“There are shifting priorities for the City of Boston around what to support at this time,” said BAMS Festival founder and executive director Catherine T. Morris. “We maintain that our communities deserve access to the arts.”

A fund-raising message posted to the BAMS Festival website said that both “reductions in municipal funding and corporate investment have left a gap in our financial resources.” It noted that the organization considered canceling the event entirely, but instead was able to reduce some production expenses with this year’s move.

Morris explained that Play Playe is built “around the art of play. We don’t do enough of that.”

“It was born to center games, opportunities to activate creativity, and to try something new and meet someone new,” she added. “It’s important that we know each other and don’t forget the core elements of our humanity.”

That means board, card, and hand games as well as team challenges. Returning to the event are BAMS Festival staples such as dance lessons — which range from crumping to bachata to the Black line dancing of Boston Rhythm Riders — small business and arts vendors, and a “Soul Food Row” of food options. The indoor KidChella stage, curated by several area organizations, will showcase local youth talent.

Morris said that holding the event at The Record Co. will bring new visitors to that branch of the Boston music nonprofit, which rents out practice and creative spaces to local artists. The building, located at 55 Morrissey Blvd., is slated for redevelopment.

The event’s entertainment will be centered around DJs, who Morris said are “the lifeblood of any party. They help to mobilize communities. These are DJs who are community-centered and play music for the people. They’re not about ego.”

Topping the bill is hip-hop royalty DJ Jazzy Jeff, who will be appearing the week before he reunites with Will Smith as part of Philadelphia’s celebration of America’s 250th anniversary. The DJ will also participate in a June 25 “Artdacity: Check Ya Self” conversation at Converse’s headquarters on Lovejoy Wharf, which will discuss issues related to health and wellness in the creative community.

Also appearing will be Junior Rodigan, who for decades has been the region’s leading reggae and Caribbean music selector. Rodigan told the Globe that he is excited to be part of a “concept of bringing top DJs from various genres together, so we can showcase what we do at nightclubs in front of family audiences.”

A wide spectrum of house and dance music will be represented by Kelvin Sylvester, a Boston DJ, artist, songwriter, and producer whose soulful approach has earned him overseas tours and airplay for his deep, infectious grooves, which include collaborations with fellow Bostonian Lee Wilson.

“For the BAMS Fest set I am going to take people on a musical journey with different time stamps,” said Sylvester, who is excited to see younger house DJs adopt the all-vinyl approach that he’s long championed. “It’s good that a new generation is discovering music that’s not overstimulating, keeps your attention, tells a story and still slaps!”

Some additional Momentum events include a tribute to pioneering hip-hop producer J Dilla at City Winery, multiple events co-produced with the poetry and open mic organization FreeVerse, and a roller skating party at the venerable Chez Vous roller rink in Dorchester, the kind of community institution that Morris said BAMS Festival tries to partner with.

Another such institution is the Community Art Center in Cambridge. On Thursday the center will, as part of Momentum, celebrate the opening of the photo exhibit “A Place Called Home | Our Voice, Our Stories, Our Legacy,” at the Street Theory Gallery & Collective in Central Square. CAC executive director Erin Muirhead McCarty said the exhibit collects images taken in Cambridge’s Port neighborhood between the 1970s and early 2000s by youth photographers.

While most art exhibits involve a handful of curators, McCarty said that the CAC “invited the community into the building to help us curate the images,” resulting in an exhibit of “photos that seemed to resonate with the largest swath of people.” The attendees of those sessions are included in the list of 18 co-curators.

BAMS Festival is seeking to raise $95,000 to make up for its current shortfall. As for whether BAMS Festival will be back in Franklin Park next year, Morris encouraged the community to “stay tuned.”

“We don’t know where the city will be next year, but our goal is to maintain the integrity and the scale and the offering of BAMS Festival, as well as year-round programming.”

title: Man shot in Dorchester Sunday night, marking end of violent weekend
text:
A man was shot and critically injured in Dorchester on Sunday, marking an end to a violent weekend in the city.

Around 10:45 p.m., officers went to 445 Quincy St., where they found a man lying in the driveway with gunshot wounds, police said in a statement.

The man “was conscious and able to talk,” police said.

He was taken to a local hospital and was initially listed as stable, police said. But when his vital signs dropped, “full notifications were requested” meaning homicide detectives were called in to investigate, police said.

The man was in critical condition Monday and was undergoing surgery, police said.

Two other people suffered graze wounds from the gunfire, police said.

No arrests have been made.

The shooting came after a woman was killed in Mattapan Square by a man who drove into her as she was walking, police said.

He had already crashed one car and hijacked a second, police said.

Ibraim Matos, 37, of Hyde Park, is slated to be arraigned in Dorchester Municipal Court Monday on charges of murder, carjacking, and leaving the scene of two crashes.

On Friday around 11:30 p.m., a man was shot in Charlestown near 100 Hood Park. Police said he will survive his injuries.

Earlier on Friday, a body was found near 100 Malcolm X Boulevard in Roxbury.

No additional information on the Charlestown and Roxbury incidents were immediately available Monday.

This is a developing story.

title: Mabinty Janneh was headed to the bank. But moments after she stepped off the bus, chaos ensued.
text:
Prosecutors said she was dragged several hundred feet after being struck. She was later pronounced dead on the scene.

Ibraim Matos, 37, pleaded not guilty Monday to a host of charges associated with the deadly crash. He allegedly carjacked someone Saturday afternoon and sped off in the stolen vehicle, then struck and killed Janneh, stopping only after he hit an MBTA bus.

The Hyde Park man was ordered held without bail and sent to Bridgewater State Hospital for a mental health evaluation. Doctors there will determine whether he’s mentally competent to stand trial after a preliminary assessment raised questions about his psychological state, court officials said.

Authorities have provided little information to indicate what may have prompted the deadly rampage.

As Matos appeared in Dorchester District Court for his arraignment, a large group of Janneh’s relatives filed into the courtroom and watched the proceedings from the gallery, struggling to make sense of the tragedy.

During a brief statement to reporters afterward, Janneh’s cousin Ahmad Thorley said she was loved. He asked for privacy while the family grieves.

“We are still saddened, shocked, and disturbed about this event and the loss of our loved one,” he said, standing on the courthouse steps as other relatives looked on, some wiping away tears. “We would like to thank the Mattapan community for intervening and preventing more loss of life.”

In court, Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ursula Knight described how the violence unfolded.

Matos was driving his own vehicle near Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street when he collided with another car, according to police and prosecutors.

He abandoned his damaged Acura and ran to a nearby car wash. There, he allegedly yanked a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel and drove off again, traveling the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square shortly after 2 p.m., authorities said.

Encountering traffic, he then “intentionally drove up on the sidewalk, which was pedestrian-filled,” Knight said.

Meanwhile, Janneh was stepping off the bus.

When she saw Matos speeding down the sidewalk, she and other pedestrians desperately tried to get out of the way, ducking into doorways and otherwise seeking cover, the prosecutor said.

“Unfortunately, however, she could not outrun the defendant’s car,” Knight said. “She was overtaken by him.”

She said Janneh was dragged “several hundred feet” as Matos continued driving — “until her lifeless body was ultimately dislodged.” He ultimately ran into another vehicle and then a bus, which stopped his rampage, she said.

That’s when a group of bystanders forcibly removed Matos from the vehicle and restrained him until officers arrived.

“It’s impossible to overstate the peril posed by this man’s actions when so many people were out and about enjoying a beautiful summer Saturday,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Monday.

Matos is charged with murder, carjacking, and leaving the scene of two crashes.

Janneh’s family members declined an interview Monday. Tributes poured in on social media, from loved ones in the US and her native Sierra Leone.

“Mabinty was a beautiful soul whose kindness, love, and hardworking spirit touched everyone who had the privilege of knowing her,” the family wrote on a GoFundMe page seeking donations for burial and other costs. “She was a devoted family member, a loyal friend, and someone who always put others before herself.”

Records show Matos has a long criminal history in the Boston area, including assault charges. Prosecutors said the previous charges are largely domestic in nature, with several restraining orders against him.

A court-appointed mental health professional testified Monday that a preliminary assessment led her to recommend further psychological evaluation. In terms of his factual understanding of the charges he faces, Matos seemed confused and became “overwhelmed and tearful” during their interaction, she said.

She said he reported suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. She also mentioned possible schizophrenia and past hospitalizations.

Judge Erika Reis ordered Matos to undergo evaluation at the state-run mental hospital in Bridgewater. She set his next court appearance for July 10.

In Mattapan Monday afternoon, Fernandez X-Press Car Wash was busy; cars filled the small parking lot where Matos allegedly terrorized customers Saturday.

Owner Yancarlo Fernandez, 36, said he wasn’t there at the time but saw videos circulating online.

“The staff called me when it happened,” he said, describing how the carjacking victim screamed when Matos accosted her. He had initially tried to steal a different car, but switched gears after realizing it was locked, Fernandez said.

Mattapan resident Michelle Vargas, 48, said the fatal crash has traumatized the neighborhood, but she took comfort in the fact that Matos was quickly arrested.

“He needs to be held accountable for what he did,” she said.

Travis Andersen of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Seth Moulton’s campaign is all but dropping hints for super PACs
text:
With just over 10 weeks until the primary against US Senator Ed Markey, Moulton’s campaign has turned to a practice known as “red-boxing,” a wink-and-nod communication tactic campaigns use to legally get around rules barring coordination between campaigns and super PACs.

Moulton’s messaging plan is all laid out in a discreetly placed section of his campaign website, and framed in a tidy red box. And if the reader happens to work for a super PAC backing Moulton’s bid, who knows, that message could pop up in ads in the run-up to the Sept. 1 primary.

Anyone can access the page, though you’ll have to dig around to find it. Scroll past a section titled “Meet Seth Moulton,” his policy platform, a donation button, a section for news clips, and another highlighting the campaign’s social media platforms, and underneath directions for how to donate by mail, alllllll the way at the bottom on the webpage, there is a “media info” link — tucked right next to the campaign’s privacy policy — that has the game plan.

Moulton’s campaign wants messages targeting Democratic primary voters in the last six weeks of the election, letting them know about his stance to abolish ICE, his plans to “make life more affordable for working people,” and his views on President Trump’s foreign policy. A month out from election day, the campaign wants to convince unenrolled voters to know that Moulton is on a mission to “stop the gerontocracy in Washington,” and that it’s vital they pull a Democratic primary ballot.

The page also includes a link to an unlisted YouTube video stocked with silent B-roll footage of Moulton shaking hands with and greeting people at an anti-war rally, marching in a Pride parade, and working delegates at the state Democratic convention — ready-made material for any outside group looking to cut an ad.

A spokesperson for Moulton’s campaign pointed out that it “can’t control what our supporters do.”

“[We] hope that they stay focused on delivering a positive message about Seth and his progressive vision for Massachusetts and the country,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Red-boxing gets its name from the literal red boxes campaigns use to highlight information they hope outside groups will notice. It’s a practice that has become increasingly common among Democrats who also tend to spend a fair amount of time arguing that campaign finance laws need tightening. There aren’t any federal laws explicitly barring the practice, but groups like the Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Campaign Legal Center say it’s a no-no.

Unlike campaigns, where donors are limited in how much they can give a candidate, super PACs can raise and spend unlimited funds. Advance Progress, the super PAC backing Moulton, has spent nearly $1.5 million so far this year. Some of the largest donations came from David Peeler, a senior advisor at the Boston-based private equity firm Berkshire Partners, and Richard Wells, a director at the tech investment firm, Insight Partners, who each donated $250,000, records show.

A separate group, MA Progress Action, has also jumped into the race with ads that bear a striking resemblance to the PAC’s anti-Markey campaign messaging. Because the organization is a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, it isn’t required to publicly disclose its donors — and technically has to serve a public purpose beyond politics, something campaign watchdogshave argued it isn’t doing.

THIS MEANS WAR: Mayor Michelle Wu has dominated elections in her own backyard, whether it’s herself or helping one of her allies on the ballot. Now she’s testing whether her political clout travels beyond city limits.

Wu on Monday formally endorsed Daniel Lander, her former aide, in his primary challenge against state Senator William Brownsberger, one of the key lawmakers who helped sink the mayor’s (several) attempts to pass tax legislation on Beacon Hill.

The move marks Wu’s second foray into a Democratic state Senate primary this cycle. Earlier this month, she endorsed Latoya Gayle, the child care advocate and community activist challenging longtime Wu rival, state Senator Nick Collins, for his South Boston/Dorchester-centered district.

Brownsberger may present a tougher test for Wu’s coattails. Unlike Collins, whose district is entirely within Boston, much of Brownsberger’s territory lies outside the city, stretching into communities like Cambridge, Watertown, and Belmont, where Wu’s political brand is less established.

Brownsberger, one of Senate President Karen Spilka’s top deputies, also has the backing of Governor Maura Healey. The governor notably stayed out of Wu’s reelection race last year, when she cruised to victory after her chief rival, Josh Kraft, ended his campaign soon after the September preliminary election. Lander, meanwhile, nabbed an endorsement from US Senator Elizabeth Warren last week. (He worked on Warren’s 2020 presidential campaign.)

More on the endorsement from the Globe’s Samantha J. Gross.

The lack of an endorsement is the latest setback for McKee, who has been trailing former CVS executive Helena Buonanno Foulkes in the polls and in fundraising. When asked by a Globe reporter if she had confidence in Eng’s leadership, she said, “Absolutely.” She did not take additional questions. A MBTA spokesperson previously described the hair-pulling incident involving an employee as an “insensitive interaction” that occurred while saying goodbye after an agency team dinner.

Eng, also the general manager of the MBTA, said earlier this week that the dinner in November 2024 was a “team-building exercise at a restaurant” with the MBTA’s executive team and their spouses. “The incident that happened two years ago is something that I’ve apologized for,” he said Friday. “I understand now, in hindsight, that it was insensitive.”

IN HIS DEFENSE: Frustrated by coverage of the Legislature’s ongoing audit battle, House Speaker Ron Mariano is firing back. In a CommonWealth Beacon op-ed on Sunday, Mariano accused state Auditor Diana DiZoglio of being driven by “political ambition and personal grievances” and pushed back on media coverage he argues has skewed public understanding of the fight.
