EMAIL CHAIN REACTION: How the ballot question to cut Massachusetts’ income tax fell apart over email by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: In emails last August, a top lawyer in Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office traded proposed wording for a summary of a ballot question to cut Massachusetts’ state income tax with an attorney representing the authors of the proposal. At Assistant Attorney General Grace Gohlke’s invitation, Kevin Martin, a Goodwin Procter attorney, suggested language that did not mention an indirect but critical outcome of the ballot question: that it would also slash the tax rate on long-term capital gains. The omission ultimately spelled the end of the tax cut proposal.

title: City councilors propose extending Orange Line beneath Blue Hill Avenue
text:
Blue Hill Avenue is one of Boston’s main arteries, traveling from Milton into the city through predominantly Black neighborhoods. Situated between the existing Orange and Red Lines, the neighborhoods are predominantly served by bus service, not rail.

“What we are proposing is to remedy this train desert ... so that we can enjoy the same kind of transportation that everyone else in the state enjoys,” Culpepper said.

Worrell and Culpepper said they met with State Transportation Secretary Phil Eng on Tuesday morning to present the idea. They said Eng committed to studying the proposal. A spokesperson for Eng said state officials are committed to looking at the proposal through the Program for Mass Transportation, the MBTA’s long-range capital plan.

Culpepper also said he had presented his idea to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who he said “does like it.”

In a statement Tuesday afternoon, a spokesperson for Wu said she was “open to discussing potential future rail options.” A second statement later Tuesday evening, however, sounded a more skeptical note.

“Digging new miles of subway tunnel under City streets would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment,” the spokesperson said. “Today, Boston has an opportunity to deliver more immediate improvements and beautification of the Blue Hill Ave corridor.”

Culpepper and Worrell did not present a timeline or a cost estimate for their proposal, saying they want to work with state transit experts to determine both. In a mock-up the councilors distributed Tuesday, they proposed adding a branch of the Orange Line that would head south from Ruggles Station and make several stops along Blue Hill Avenue, including Grove Hall, the Franklin Park Zoo, and Mattapan Square.

The pitch for a new, longer Orange Line that would bring rail service to more Black Bostonians comes as many in the Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester neighborhoods that branch off Blue Hill Avenue reject a longstanding plan to add dedicated bus lanes up the center of the congested street, alongside trees, lighting, shortened crosswalks, and bike lanes. Proponents of the plan say it will speed up bus travel and bring critical safety improvements, while critics argue it will add to traffic and threaten small businesses along the corridor. Earlier this month, some neighbors who oppose the plan went so far as to ask the Trump administration to rescind $80 million that had been allocated for the project.

Decades ago, a street car ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square, but it was ripped out in the mid-20th century. In 2009, the state proposed, and residents rejected, an earlier plan for “bus rapid transit.”

Worrell and Culpepper said they did not explicitly discuss the bus lane proposal with Eng on Tuesday, but they have been clear that they oppose it.

The energy in fighting the bus lane proposal makes now a good time to pitch something else, Worrell said: “We’ve always needed it, and I think this is the time.”

With the Orange Line idea, Worrell said, “we are trying to bring a new idea and a new proposal to the table.”

“And a better proposal,” Culpepper added. “A more efficient proposal. It might cost a little bit more, but this is the best way the community will get the best and efficient transportation, just like the rest of the state.”

title: Milton leaders look to buy Labouré College for potential early education center
text:
Milton town and school officials are hurrying to analyze the potential purchase of Labouré College, a private nursing school closing this summer, with an eye toward converting it into a prekindergarten and kindergarten.

The School Committee voted earlier this month to explore design options to build an early education center at the school in time to potentially bid on the campus when it goes up for sale in August.

If the School Committee determines it wants the property, the Select Board would have to decide to buy it by early August to get any needed financing on the town ballot in November, School Building Committee Chairman Sean O’Rourke told the School Committee June 3.

“I think it’s a great asset for the town. That’s my personal opinion,” O’Rourke said. “Does it work for a school? That’s kind of what we’re all trying to figure out.”

The 134-year-old Catholic college is set to close this summer amid financial headwinds, with its nursing programs to be absorbed by nearby Curry College. Like many small private colleges across the region, the school’s enrollment has dropped rapidly in recent years.

Earlier this month, the Quincy City Council rejected Mayor Thomas Koch’s plan to buy the campus of the former Eastern Nazarene College, which closed in 2025. Koch had proposed paying $22.5 million for campus, but several city councilors expressed concern about Quincy’s existing debt.

Milton is one of relatively few Boston-area school districts with a growing enrollment, causing space constraints across the district. Its student population has grown by about 200 over the last decade, to more than 4,350 students, while Massachusetts as a whole recently reported its lowest enrollment in 30 years.

That means that while many Massachusetts districts are considering school closures, Milton is now simultaneously pursuing two options to add classroom space: the potential Labouré purchase joins an existing process of seeking state funds for a new elementary or middle school.

The town was accepted into the state school building agency’s pipeline in December 2024 with a goal of getting partial reimbursement for a new or renovated school. Other than Labouré, the main option officials are considering is an all-new school near Milton High School.

The Labouré site could be renovated with the same state assistance, but only for the previously proposed elementary or middle school project, unless the town restarts the long process to get state funds.

District leadership recommended considering the site for an early education center, which would free up space at every elementary school and potentially save on operating costs, according to a presentation to the School Committee.

“If the schools can make it work, then great,” said interim Superintendent John Phelan. “If not, it can be a town asset that can be utilized by the town in another way.”

Buying and renovating Labouré without state help could cost Milton some money — the state may reimburse about 28 percent of the district’s costs on a new project — but could also be completed much more quickly. A year and a half after being accepted into the Massachusetts School Building Authority pipeline, the district is still in very early planning stages, as construction with state funding can take years.

The Labouré campus has three buildings, with both classrooms and office space. O’Rourke recommended renovating just one building for students, in the hopes of not triggering costly energy code upgrades in the other two structures.

On June 15, the School Building Committee voted to hire contractors to evaluate potential costs and design options. Little design work could be done before the Select Board would have to purchase the buildings, one member noted. That means the town will have little information on how costly renovations might be.

The district will continue to pursue state funding in parallel to the Labouré purchase, O’Rourke told the School Committee.

Labouré College itself purchased the Milton site, formerly home to Aquinas College, in 2012. The nursing school had previously been located in Dorchester.

Christopher Huffaker can be reached at christopher.huffaker@globe.com. Follow him @huffakingit.

title: Rolling back this Massachusetts gun law would only be the beginning
text:
For me, gun violence is not an abstract issue. Day to day, I work with survivors of gun violence from Boston and New England, who can never fully escape the memory of those lost to gunfire.

Gun violence in America is all too common, and shootings often spike in the summer. Cities, like Boston, are successfully fighting gun violence with violence-prevention programming, but the crisis remains urgent. Despite a decline in homicide rates in Boston compared to this time last year, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan saw five shootings in four days in May.

Meanwhile, the gun lobby has been working to dismantle Massachusetts’ critical public safety laws. An alliance of political operatives, a gun shop owner, and the state’s gun lobby, operating as the “Civil Rights Coalition,” gathered enough signatures to force the upcoming statewide referendum to repeal the “Act Modernizing Firearm Laws.”

This landmark legislative package addressed critical gaps in the state’s laws by outlawing build-it-yourself, unserialized firearms; empowering clinicians and school administrators to file Extreme Risk Protection Orders to remove a gun when a person poses serious danger; and strengthening the state ban on the possession, transfer, and sale of assault-style firearms.

If this law were to be repealed, communities would be less equipped to stop shootings. Without a comprehensive legal framework to remove a gun from a dangerous situation, school officials and doctors, who are using Extreme Risk Protection Orders for deescalation, would have their hands tied even when they see clear warning signs.

The act also created a public dashboard to track the state’s landscape of gun-related incidents, supported the state’s firearm registration system and violence prevention infrastructure, and required evidence-based firearm safety courses for gun owners. Now, for example, the Basic Firearms Safety Course covers secure gun storage, suicide-prevention education, disengagement tactics, and live-fire training.

These changes are already yielding tangible results. Local law enforcement report that the law has given them tools to curb gun violence by dismantling the supply chains for unserialized guns and Glock switches that transform pistols into automatic weapons. Research by the National Policing Institute has found that unserialized guns are the weapons of choice for those barred from purchasing firearms, from high schoolers to people with violent histories.

This referendum is bigger than Massachusetts. The gun lobby is using the state to test a new strategy to erode gun safety laws across the country. If it succeeds in rolling back good public safety laws here, it will probably push other states to follow, putting even more Americans in more danger.

Violence and hate, abetted by unfettered access to guns, are a scourge on the nation. Massachusetts has embraced tools that save lives. Voters should keep them strong by defeating the ballot question in November.

title: ‘Why aren’t they listening?’: For many Black residents, this Blue Hill Avenue transit plan repeats old problems
text:
On a street where everyone is battling for space, and every inch is contested, this barren strip sits right in the center of everything, in most places entirely useless. The cracked concrete is a reminder of the inaction and disinvestment that’s made this crucial artery through Black Boston so frustrating and dangerous to navigate.

“Cambridge has beautiful streets and bike lanes, beautiful bus stops, all that,” said Glorian Lee, 18, who lives near Franklin Park and takes the 28 bus down Blue Hill Avenue every day. “Why can we not have the same thing?”

City and state officials say they finally have a plan to make things better. They see the neglected median as the key to transforming Blue Hill Avenue into something like the functional, even pleasant boulevard it was 80 years ago. The pitch is this: Take the beleaguered buses out of the side lane of traffic, where they get stuck behind the double-parkers and right-turners, and put them in the exclusive, unencumbered center, in new dedicated bus lanes. There, they can move more swiftly, ferrying the people of Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester — who are some of the heaviest users of public transit, but suffer through some of the least reliable service — to and from their schools, jobs, and dentist appointments. It’s the anchor of a larger plan for the avenue that also includes trees, crosswalks, streetlights, and new sidewalks.

After decades of stops and starts, the money for improvements is finally there. The federal government has come through with grants totaling $95 million, while the state and city are set to kick in $51 million and $18 million, respectively. But Mayor Michelle Wu has gone quiet on the center bus lane proposal, caught between competing pressures to remake the city’s streets for the better and to avoid alienating the Black voters already frustrated with her.

The trouble is, many people in the neighborhoods branching out from Blue Hill Avenue are deeply opposed to this plan, a skepticism wrought by decades of broken promises and worse. They fear that adding a bus lane and removing some dedicated travel lanes would slow car commutes that are impossible already, or that street improvements could limit parking and gut the local businesses that are the spirit of the corridor. Alongside promises of better lighting and safer crosswalks, the latest version of the plan also includes bike lanes — which to many represent the first, galloping horseman of the gentrification apocalypse. Some neighbors have gone so far as to ask the Trump administration to rescind $80 million in federal funding, an effort to halt the project.

Supporters say they do not anticipate any harmful effects on businesses, and officials intend to preserve as much as 90 percent of parking. But those assurances do little for communities that have every reason to doubt what the government says. The MBTA in 2025 spent $300,000 on a traffic analysis, but never released it to the public, adding to worries about what officials have planned.

When a corridor is neglected for so long, promises to improve it can feel like something nefarious. Many in Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester say they feel like the plan for a center-running bus lane — along with other government efforts to increase housing and boost businesses along the avenue — is being forced on them despite protests.

Which is to say, the current debate is about much more than a bus lane. It’s about trust, and what happens when the government has done so little to help and so much to harm a neighborhood that it has little credibility left. It’s about who gets a say in Blue Hill Avenue’s future.

“Why are we even here tonight? They already know that we don’t want this,” said West Ward, 25, at a March community meeting on the bus lane. “Why aren’t they listening to the people who live here?”

The story of Blue Hill Avenue is a story of disinvestment. Once home to Jewish neighborhoods, the corridor swiftly transformed in the mid-20th century when racist housing policies funneled Black residents there, as banks refused to give them home loans elsewhere in the city. Now, its neighborhoods are home to some of Boston’s most diverse communities, Black families who trace their roots here back generations and newer arrivals from Haiti or Cape Verde.

A century ago, a streetcar ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square. Families queued up to ride it through a vibrant cultural corridor with meat markets, furniture stores, synagogues, and historic theaters. But in the 1950s, as cars became more prevalent and white families left the city for the suburbs, authorities ripped out the streetcar and redesigned the avenue to add a traffic lane in each direction. The new setup made it easier for commuters to travel in and out from the suburbs in their cars. But it also made Blue Hill Avenue less of a destination for shopping and dining, and did little for the people who lived there.

They “pull the trolleys out, and create this road, that is a huge road, that’s designed to get people through my neighborhood and not to my neighborhood,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat.

As long ago as the 1970s, city and state transit officials recognized that removing the trolley had condemned the neighborhoods to poor public transit — a “major [factor] contributing to the deterioration of the Blue Hill Avenue community,” according to a city report from that time. Archival documents show officials wanted to restore the trolley and even weighed extending the Orange Line beneath the corridor.

“Fixed-rail trolley service is the preferred technology,” a 1979 report concluded. “It has to be made easy for Corridor residents and others to reach these important destinations.”

The plan for rail was ultimately rejected as costly and infeasible.

As the decades wore on, trains and trolleys expanded elsewhere in the MBTA system, including an extension of the Green Line into Somerville that took three decades and cost $2.3 billion. But rail never returned to Blue Hill Avenue.

It was not the only time such transit was taken from Boston’s Black communities.

“When they took the Orange Line away from Nubian Square, we were supposed to have a replacement, and we never got that,” said City Councilor Brian Worrell, who argues his constituents deserve subway service, not just buses. “It’s like we’ve been redlined out of the rapid rail infrastructure — and you’re talking about one of the highest transit rider corridors. Why doesn’t Blue Hill Ave. get what Dorchester Ave. has?"

By 2009, when at last federal funding was available for a project to refurbish the street, the proposal was for “bus rapid transit” called the 28X, after the 28 bus route that ran up the corridor.

Rail “was never feasible,” said Jim Aloisi, who shepherded the effort as transportation secretary under Governor Deval Patrick. “I heard those voices back then, and we had plenty of discussions about it, but I just had to politely say, ‘I know that’s what you think you want, or what you want, but that’s not feasible.’”

Instead, Aloisi said, he wanted to prove to residents of the corridor that the 28X bus could be “really, really, really good, and function as well as light rail.”

Skeptics in the neighborhood felt like they were being presented with a fully formed plan — one with no room for their feedback to shape it, said Vivien Morris, a longtime community leader in Mattapan who recalled the opposition.

“That’s been our history — being treated negatively and pushed around town,” she said. “That’s why if the initiative came through the city, then people feel like, first we have to push back in order to make sure that our voices are heard.”

The 28X quickly fell apart. Facing widespread opposition from neighbors, Massachusetts turned down the federal money, leaving Blue Hill Avenue’s problems to fester.

Not everyone in the community was happy to see the 28X project die. Its collapse inspired Holmes to run for state representative. Now, he keeps a rendering of the rejected route in his office.

“I’m still just in disbelief that we made that decision,” Holmes said. Elected officials had turned down tens of millions of dollars, he said, when “what we should be doing is bringing resources back to our Black neighborhood that has been under-resourced and under-delivered to for decades.”

In 2019, Boston officials decided to try again. Recognizing the failures of the previous, state-run effort, the city under Mayor Marty Walsh took a more active role in planning the bus project, hoping to rebuild trust in the skeptical communities around Blue Hill Avenue.

“This is a part of the city that has been underserved over the last several decades,” Vineet Gupta, the city Transportation Department’s planning director, told GBH News at the time. “We really want to start learning from people who live in the corridor.”

But after seven years, hundreds of survey responses, and thousands of public comments, trust is still frayed, and residents remain dubious that the plan will help them. Meanwhile, the consequences of inaction on Blue Hill Avenue plague everyone who lives near it.

The corridor is one of Boston’s most dangerous, with a collision requiring EMS transport every three days on average, according to city data. For pedestrians, crossing the wide street can be treacherous. And driving it is a singularly maddening experience.

“I do whatever I can to avoid Blue Hill Ave.,” said Ihioma Breneus, 42, who lives in Mattapan.

Residents and commuters complain about the traffic, particularly during peak times; they gripe about double- sometimes triple-parking; they fear for their safety, and their kids’ safety, when they cross the street or, God forbid, ride a bike.

“Blue Hill Avenue is as unsafe today as it was 50 years ago,” said Tiffany Cogell, who grew up in Roxbury and now heads the Boston Cyclists Union. As a kid, she recalled, she was never allowed to cross the wide street — meaning though she lived just a few minutes away, she couldn’t get to Franklin Park on foot. “There is no reason in the world that I’m about to be 57 years old, and Blue Hill Avenue doesn’t feel any different or safer than it did when I was a little girl.”

If there is consensus on the problems, though, there is still no consensus on the solution. Neighbors are sharply divided on, if not overwhelmingly opposed to, the center-running bus plan. An analysis prepared for the MBTA found the plan would speed up the 28 bus by as much as 15 minutes at peak times, while slowing down cars by as much as six minutes during the morning rush, in part because the latest version of the plan would get rid of some traffic lanes. Critics fret over that increase, and argue officials should make other improvements — more trees, safer crosswalks, better lights — without changing the bus path.

“Nobody’s asking for it,” Breneus said of the center lane. Many fear the revamp could bring gentrification, and say the city isn’t doing enough to prevent that.

Two city councilors who represent Dorchester and Roxbury are still pushing for rail, not bus service, along Blue Hill Avenue. Worrell and Councilor Miniard Culpepper on Tuesday unveiled a plan to extend the Orange Line beneath the corridor. Officials owe their neighborhoods faster, better transit, they said.

“We want them to live up to their promise from 40 years ago,” Culpepper said.

But even if political leaders were to embrace the idea — and Wu has already sounded skeptical — any rail expansion would be costly and time-intensive. For some, the bus lane at least offers a quicker answer to Blue Hill Avenue’s problems.

Lee, the 18-year-old, lives in Dorchester, just a few miles from his part-time job in Mattapan Square. The bus ride should take about half an hour, but one recent Thursday, Lee left home two hours early, knowing he could be delayed. Once, he said, he was so late for work that he missed his two-hour shift entirely.

At his stop near Franklin Park, Lee tracked the bus on an app, knowing that the schedule is merely a suggestion.

“Another bus bunching!” he lamented, referring to delays that made his bus arrive at the same time as the one scheduled for 15 minutes later. That day, he made it to work before his shift started. But he often thinks about all the things he could do with the luxury of a bit more time.

There is a clear generational divide between younger transit users who take the bus and want a better one, and older commuters who drive. At a public meeting this spring, former state senator Dianne Wilkerson described the center bus lane as yet another unwanted change that officials were inflicting on her community.

“Nobody takes a bus to go pick up the pizza,” she said. “Nobody takes a bus to go pick up their kids. … That’s not how anybody lives. So we will not have this forced on us.”

It hasn’t helped that the Blue Hill Avenue plan is being debated alongside two other controversial developments nearby. Wu is pushing to turn Franklin Park’s White Stadium into a professional soccer venue, and the mayor also caused uproar when she shelved a plan for a life sciences and affordable housing project in Roxbury in favor of building a new high school on the site.

“You have three projects affecting a really marginalized community, and at this point they feel really unheard,” said Chevanese VanDyke, 46, who lives in Dorchester. “No bus is going to make up for that.”

For transit officials who want the project to go forward, the next few months will be about persuading people like VanDyke. The MBTA has promised more public engagement, and planners emphasize the design is far from final, meaning some of the more unpopular features in early sketches may change. The MBTA won’t go ahead with the project if Wu doesn’t want it, and for the mayor, there are landmines everywhere. Elected with the support of Boston’s Black communities and its transit advocates, she has now alienated swaths of both. Any choice she makes on Blue Hill Avenue could further incense at least one group.

Aloisi blamed critics for exaggerating how much parking might be lost, and how much businesses might suffer.

“Do you want to condemn those bus riders, those transit-dependent residents of the city, to a lifetime of substandard transit access on the altar of false information?” he said. “This is really a moral responsibility to make something like this happen and not to let it fail again.”

For Blue Hill Avenue to get better, Holmes said, it has to change. Beautifying the streets and leaving the traffic setup as is will not solve the problems, he said.

Alongside the bus lane, he’d like to see two traffic lanes in each direction, and as much parking retained as possible. He can live with losing some trees from the plan.

“We’re not going to have any bike lanes,” Holmes added. “Forget that.”

Those tweaks could assuage some fears about congestion and gentrification.

“So much of this is the Black community saying, ‘We don’t trust that this is for our community,’” Holmes said. “‘Is this for us?’ And I say the answer is, ‘Yes. Don’t move.’”

The distrust is hard to get around. But if the city and state don’t have a record of doing right by Black neighborhoods, Holmes said, “at least I do.”

He can see a future where the government, with the support of the neighborhood, fixes a problem it helped create. “You’re going to see young folks going to and from school on the buses,” he said. “You’re going to see those who are in most need.”

That’s who the improvements are for, Holmes emphasized. “We’re looking to serve the people who live in our community.”

Now, he just has to convince them, too.

title: The best things to do in and around Boston this weekend
text:
On tap this weekend: boogie down in Cambridge, celebrate Pride Month, plus World Cup fun continues. — Matt Juul

BOSTON FAN ZONE If you couldn’t get tickets to see Norway vs. France in Foxborough, you can catch all of the World Cup action at the Lawn on D’s watch party. If the match gets you in the competitive spirit, check out the event’s game selection, including cornhole, mini golf, and foosball. June 26, noon. 420 D St. 877-393-3393. signatureboston.com — Annie Sarlin

CAMBRIDGE CITY DANCE PARTY Shake off the week at the 26th annual Cambridge City Dance Party. Enjoy music from local DJs, interactive activities, and a sunset light show at this all-ages dance party. June 26, 6-10 p.m. Free. Central Square, 344 Broadway, Cambridge. cambridgeusa.org — Gitana Savage

QUEER HISTORY WEST END PRIDE PARTY In celebration of its new queer history exhibit, the West End Museum hosts a Pride-themed party at Dorchester Brewing Company. The event will be emceed by drag artist Axel Starcock and feature information on historic local LGBTQ activists, educators, and community spaces. June 26, 6:30-8:30 p.m. 1250 Massachusetts Ave. 617-723-2125. thewestendmuseum.org — AS

BOSTON GROWN-UPS MUSEUM If you’re having some summer camp nostalgia, the Boston Children’s Museum has the solution. Head to the museum for a special after-hours grown-ups-only night. Kick off the evening with a ride on the harbor in animal pedal boats, then keep the party going with a series of summer camp-themed activities, including tug-of-war, friendship bracelet making, and more. Food and drinks are also available for purchase. June 26, 7 p.m. $33.85. 21+. Boston Children’s Museum, 308 Congress St. eventbrite.com — GS

ROXBURY POETRY FESTIVAL Spend your Saturday channeling your inner poet at the Roxbury Poetry Festival. Sponsored by the Mayor’s Office of Arts & Culture, the event offers workshops, featured speakers, a slam poetry competition, and complimentary lunch at this free, daylong event. June 27, 10 a.m.-10 p.m. Free. Bruce C. Bolling Building, 2300 Washington St. boston.gov — GS

FAMILY FUN DAY Celebrate summer with bounce houses, magic shows, music, and more at Somerville’s 20th annual free Family Fun Day. The event will also include cornhole, soccer, basketball, and other games, as well as crafts like water bottle decorating and stuffed animal coloring. June 27, 1-4 p.m. 541 Broadway, Somerville. 617-625-6600. somervillema.gov — AS

SUMMER SATURDAY MOVIE NIGHT Who lives in a pineapple under the sea? Catch the Bikini Bottom gang at this free outdoor screening of “The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants” at Urban Park’s first Summer Saturday film of the season. Listen to music from a DJ before settling down on the lawn to watch SpongeBob’s adventures as he follows the Flying Dutchman and his ghostly pirate ship into the deep ocean. June 27, 4 p.m., movie starts at 6 p.m. 325 Main St., Cambridge. 617-491-0709. kendallcenter.com — AS

MAYOR WU’S WORLD CUP WATCH PARTY Keep the World Cup energy going at Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s free watch party for the Colombia vs. Portugal match. Head to East Boston Memorial Stadium to cheer on your team. June 27, 7-10 p.m. Free. East Boston Memorial Stadium, 143 Porter St. boston.gov — GS

BOSTON FUNNY Tony V headlines the inaugural event in this planned monthly comedy series at the Royal Sonesta, under the Boston Funny banner. He’ll be joined by a host of Boston favorites, including Jimmy Dunn, Carolyn Plummer, and Will Noonan. June 27, 8 p.m. $28.52. The Royal Sonesta, 40 Edwin H. Land Blvd., Cambridge. bostonfunny.com — Nick A. Zaino III

BOSTON THAI TASTE Head to Boston Common for a festival honoring Thai culture. Sample dishes like pad thai, mango sticky rice, and papaya salad from food vendors, watch Muay Thai kickboxing, listen to DJ sets, and catch live performances of traditional Thai dance and Isan music. June 28, 11 a.m.-7 p.m. 139 Tremont St. nathikaevents.com — AS

5TH ANNUAL REVERE BEACH PRIDE CELEBRATION As Pride Month nears its end, celebrate in the sun at the fifth annual Revere Beach Pride Celebration. Enjoy drag and dance performances and do some shopping from a selection of local LGBTQ+ and ally organizations. June 28, 1-6 p.m. Free. Waterfront Square, between 400-500 Ocean Ave., Revere. revere.org — GS

48-HOUR ONE-ACT PLAY FESTIVAL The Rockwell hosts its second annual 48-Hour One-Act Play Festival, featuring theatrical performances from LGBTQ+ actors who, as the name suggests, only had 48 hours to conceptualize, write, and rehearse their material. June 28, 6 p.m. $18.87. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. therockwell.org — GS

KABOOM COMEDY AND VARIETY Boston has a small but mighty vaudeville/variety scene with occasional independent shows at different theaters. Kaboom is where they all perform on a regular basis, hosted by two of the most prominent variety acts, Alex Feldman and Colin Campbell. June 28, 7 p.m. $18.95-$29.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com — NZ

ONE LONG EARRING The band is getting back together! Maybe. That’s the plan in this musical comedy about a fictional band reuniting after an ugly public breakup years ago at the Labia Majora Festival. June 28, 7:30 p.m. $50.25-$54.90. The Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, 55 Davis Square, Somerville. 617-245-2900, crystalballroomboston.com — NZ

JACOB’S PILLOW DANCE FESTIVAL The Berkshires summer dance event recently kicked off, with this weekend’s programming featuring performances from the Paul Taylor Dance Company (through June 28), Uppercut Dance Theater (through June 26), the School at Jacob’s Pillow’s Contemporary Ballet Performance Ensemble (June 27), and Shamell Pitts’s company TRIBE(through June 28). On June 27, Pitts will also host a “PillowTalk” discussing his inspirations behind “Touch of RED,” which the company will perform at the festival. Through Aug. 30. 358 George Carter Road, Becket. 413-243-9919. jacobspillow.org — AS

IN OLD AGE The widowed Abasiama Bassey (Ebony Marshall-Oliver), whom Boston audiences have gotten to know as a key figure in Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play cycle about three generations of a Nigerian-American family, develops a late-in-life spiritual bond with Azell Abernathy (Marvin Bell), a gentle-spirited contractor. Directed by Dawn M. Simmons. Through June 28. Production by Front Porch Arts Collective. Presented by ArtsEmerson at Emerson Paramount Center, Jackie Liebergott Black Box Theatre, 559 Washington St. 617-824-8400, artsemerson.org

EUREKA DAY It’s a testament to Jonathan Spector’s skill that he managed to make his play as funny as it is while wading into the charged territory of mandatory vaccinations. That “Eureka Day” manages to (mostly) survive his wrongheaded decision to suddenly inject one character’s past tragedy into the mix is a testament to the play’s overall strength. With a topnotch cast directed by Margot Bordelon, “Eureka Day” mines quite a few laughs from the spectacle of well-meaning progressives tying themselves in lexical knots as they try to process events that defy ideological pigeonholes. Through June 28. Production by The Huntington. At Huntington Theatre, 264 Huntington Ave. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

BAD BOOKS After discovering her teenage son with a book she considers obscene, a mother (Aimee Doherty) confronts a local librarian (Therese Plaehn). Matters quickly escalate, and soon the entire town is embroiled in the dispute. Sharyn Rothstein’s play is directed by M. Bevin O’Gara. Through June 27. Gloucester Stage Company. At Natti-Willsky Performance Center, 267 East Main St., Gloucester. 978-281-4433, gloucesterstage.com

ENSEMBLE ALTERA As the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence approaches, the Providence-based professional chamber choir debuts “Declarations,” an evening-length piece by composer Piers Connor Kennedy based on texts by a tapestry of American writers including Thomas Jefferson, Tracy K. Smith, Langston Hughes, and Iñupiaq poet dg nanouk okpik. June 27, 7 p.m., Old South Church, 645 Boylston St.; June 28, 3 p.m., First Baptist Church, 75 N Main St., Providence. ensemblealtera.com

ROCKPORT CHAMBER MUSIC FESTIVAL The Galvin Cello Quartet opens up the weekend early at the Shalin Liu Performance Center, featuring a free hourlong family concert Friday morning (perfect if the kids are out of school) — then, for the grown-ups and Broadway babies, Upstairs on Main hosts a Pride Month cabaret on Friday night with vocalist Thom Smoker and pianist Nick Place. Saturday begins with “The Nightingale’s Sonata” in the morning, narrated by Thomas Wolf and based on his book of the same name about violinist Lea Luboshutz; that evening, 2025 Banff Competition winners the Poeisis Quartet splash down with a new music-focused program. Sunday afternoon, violinist Augustin Hadelich (you’ve maybe seen him with the BSO) takes the spotlight with a mini-solo recital before intermission, Tchaikovsky’s “Souvenir de Florence” after. Through July 12. Shalin Liu Performance Center, 37 Main St., Rockport. 978-546-7391, rockportmusic.org

MAGGIE O’FARRELL Our critic adored O’Farrell’s new book, “Land” — even calling it better than her beloved “Hamnet,” the source material for the gorgeous recent film. Local readers will have the chance to hear from the author herself, in conversation with local superstar Celeste Ng (“Everything I Never Told You”), on Saturday. June 27, 7 p.m. $45.09 (includes copy of the book). First Parish Church, 1446 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge. 617-661-1515, harvard.com

PAUL SIMON Solid Sound Festival isn’t the only major music event in Western Massachusetts this weekend. Paul Simon heads to Tanglewood for two shows — Saturday and Sunday — on his extended “A Quiet Celebration” tour, which visited the Boch Center Wang Theatre last summer. Read more about upcoming concerts in this week’s Sound Check. June 27-28. Tanglewood, Koussevitzky Music Shed, 297 West St., Lenox. bso.org

MUSEUM OF FINE ARTS: AMERICA AT 250 A celebratory occasion turned fraught and contentious by a radical turn in American government, the semiquincentennial this summer is shaping up to be yet another battleground in the daily culture war grind. At the MFA, there’s no backing down: It turned down a $400,000 federal grant for the full do-over of its just-opened 18th-century Art of the Americas galleries for fear of government interference, and has gone ahead with its vision of an inspiring, imperfect, still-in-progress democracy with much left to aspire to — a far more hopeful view than the simple-minded celebration the administration touts. Ongoing. Museum of Fine Arts, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

LOOKING FOR AMERICA, FEATURING HANK WILLIS THOMAS Thomas will be best known to Bostonians for "The Embrace", the colossal bronze memorial to Coretta Scott King and Martin Luther King Jr. on Boston Common. But Thomas has spent a career contemplating the thornier elements of American history and culture, and this is the latest installment on the theme, in time for the country’s 250th. The exhibition will focus on collaboration and community, critical through struggle, and will include contributions from artists including Karinne Smith and Hector René Membreño-Canales, and his mother, the esteemed historian Deborah Willis. ThroughJuly 19. Ogunquit Museum, 543 Shore Road, Ogunquit, Maine. 207-646-4909, ogunquitmuseum.org

DANNY LYON: THE BIKERIDERS In creating one of the definitive documentary photography projects of the 1960s, Danny Lyons joined the Chicago Outlaws Motorcycle Club while still an undergraduate at the University of Chicago to capture his subjects from the inside. The result, a raw portrait of a subculture that helped define a generation of America, is now a totem of the form. Through Aug. 16. Currier Museum of Art, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

FIFA FAN FESTIVAL BOSTON Looking for another World Cup-themed event? Head to City Hall Plaza for the final days of the FIFA Fan Festival, the city’s central World Cup gathering spot. On Friday, you can catch Norway vs. France at 3 p.m. and Cape Verde vs. Saudi Arabia at 8 p.m., while Saturday’s games include Panama vs. England at 5 p.m., Colombia vs. Portugal at 7:30 p.m., and Jordan vs. Argentina at 10 p.m. A range of local food and drink offerings will also be available for purchase. On Saturday, DJ Jazzy Jeff headlines the 2026 Play Playe event at Dorchester’s the Record Co., which invites the community to compete in a variety of board and card games, video game arcade, and spades tournament. The event also includes dance lessons and a vendor market. Other weekend activities include a Caribbean rave experience, an after-hours event at the Fuller Craft Museum, and slam poetry performances. Through June 28. Multiple locations. bamsfest.org — AS

title: After 38 years, the nicest guy at the State House calls it quits
text:
But all good runs come to an end, whether you’re Ted Williams, Elma Lewis, Arthur Fiedler, Tom Menino, or Casimir “Chip” Zigulis.

And so, this week, Chip’s run comes to an end. He put in his papers and, after 38 years as a State House page, he is officially retired.

“I had a blast,” he told me, sitting in his chair, second from the right, under the rostrum in the House chambers, where he outlasted a half-dozen speakers and not a few chairmen of Ways and Means.

He was an institution within an institution.

“Chip,” House Speaker Ron Mariano said, “represents so much of what is great about this institution — a place where folks from all walks of life can come together to better the Commonwealth that we all love."

Chip Zigulis came from a walk of life very different than all the pages who preceded him.

He was the first person with an intellectual disability, with any disability, to serve as a State House page.

Many moons ago, Jim Brett, then a state rep from Dorchester, and probably the best mayor the city of Boston never had, was shooting the breeze with then Speaker George Keverian about the state’s efforts to help the disabled community.

“I was telling George, you know, we spend all this money on programs for the disabled, why don’t we hire some of them?” Brett recalled. “And George was like, ‘What kind of job are you thinking?’ ”

Brett, whose brother Jack had an intellectual disability, had thought about it long and hard.

“A page,” he told the speaker.

The pages sit in four chairs under the rostrum in the House, Brett reasoned, facing the 160 legislators in the chamber.

“When they’d look at the page,” Brett explained, “they’d see he or she is no different than anybody else. It would take the ‘dis’ off the word, and all you’d see is their ability.”

Then Keverian asked, “Do you have anyone in mind?”

Brett had Chip Zigulis in mind.

Shortly before meeting with Keverian, Brett had met with Chip and his mother after he was mugged, not far from their home in Dorchester.

“My mother sent me to the store,” Chip said. “Some guys jumped me. They took 23 dollars off me.”

They punched Chip so hard his hearing aids popped out.

Brett, whose brother Jack’s intellectual disability made him especially empathetic toward those like Jack, was moved by Chip’s story, a guy just trying to make a living, trying to help his mom.

Chip had been working for the Marriott Long Wharf but jumped at the chance to work at the State House in 1988.

It was the same year he represented Massachusetts in the Special Olympics, in figure skating. Ten years later, he represented the state in tennis. He also got to play a friendly match against Monica Seles.

“She said I was pretty good,” he said. “She’s a nice lady.”

Chip Zigulis is the Forrest Gump of the State House, one of those guys who just happens to be there when famous people are about, and they gravitate to him. He got an uncredited role in “Good Will Hunting” and met Robin Williams and Matt Damon.

When he met Williams, he imitated the actor’s catchphrase from “Mork and Mindy,” the old sitcom that made Williams famous.

“I said, ‘Nanu, Nanu.’ And he said, ‘I don’t do that anymore.’ But he couldn’t have been nicer to me.”

Before he became governor of California, Arnold Schwarzenegger was pushing physical fitness when he visited then Governor Bill Weld. Not long after, Schwarzenegger was hugging Chip and they went over to the Common and did pushups together.

Chip met his wife, Janet, at Bible study, and when they got married 25 years ago all the big shots from Beacon Hill showed up.

“Jim Brett was there,” Chip said. “George Keverian, Tom Finneran. They all came.”

He says Charlie Flaherty was the funniest speaker, Finneran the sharpest, and Keverian the kindest.

“Charlie would tell me, ‘I’m gonna tell you something but you can’t tell anybody’,” he said. “George was a very nice gentleman. The one thing I didn’t appreciate was them making fun of George for his weight. It was very disrespectful to George. If you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything at all.”

That kind of sums up Chip Zigulis. If he can’t say something nice, he just doesn’t say anything.

He loves Jim Brett.

The feeling is mutual. Brett left the Legislature and went on to become, very appropriately, a member and then chairman of the President’s Committee for People with Intellectual Disabilities under three presidents. He did the same, heading the state’s commission on those with intellectual disabilities, under governors both Democrat and Republican. He has spent his life trying to help disabled people into the mainstream and independence, a living, active memorial to his brother Jack.

Brett gets emotional talking about Chip Zigulis.

“Like all people with disabilities, all he wanted was a chance,” Brett said. “He got the chance, and he did the job, he lived a life of independence, and made a difference, and just by being who he was, he made people happy. Every day, the public and the members met Chip’s smile.”

It’s not been all sunshine and roses.

About five years ago, Chip finished work, crossed Beacon Street, and walked down through the Common to Park Street Station, to take the Red Line home. Some guys mugged him near the station.

“They were not nice,” he said.

But Chip Zigulis is, and that’s the difference.

He is 63, and could have worked longer, but he’s had some health problems, was hospitalized for a while, and it led him to take retirement sooner than me might have wanted.

“I’m really gonna miss this place, the people here,” he said, looking around at the chamber where names of the great and good watch over those who make laws. “Not just the speakers and the big guys, but the little guys. They were good to me, and I tried to be good to them.”

Chip Zigulis was better than good.

He was the best.

title: Two Boston city councilors pitched a plan to extend the Orange Line. The map they used was full of AI-generated mistakes.
text:
The two said they had met with MBTA General Manager Phil Eng, also the state’s interim transportation secretary, who had been receptive to the idea. At a news conference, they shared a mock-up of one possible route: an Orange Line extension from Ruggles to Mattapan Square.

It didn’t take long, though, for observers to notice a few problems with the map the councilors presented.

For one thing, it’s missing the Charles River, and locates Aquarium station on a brand-new island in Boston Harbor. (Maybe the Zakim Bridge was dammed to flood the Financial District?)

That’s to say nothing of the lines themselves; the Green Line’s B branch has somehow added two Kent Street stops (the third, and the original, still marked correctly on the C branch), while the E branch seemingly runs express from Hynes Convention Center all the way to Heath Street. The Mattapan Line runs in reverse, and the Red Line’s Braintree branch has disappeared altogether.

Even the Orange Line seems somewhat bare bones, skipping three stops between Chinatown and Ruggles, and then running straight on (or rather, dipping slightly) to Forest Hills.

The slapdash mistakes pointed clearly to one culprit: artificial intelligence.

And as with anything that seems AI-generated, social media commenters were quick to poke fun.

“Green line stop consolidation has gone too far,” one commenter wrote on X.

“They evaporated Boston University,” another mused.

(Northeastern University, for the record, was also “evaporated.”)

The slapdash map has also raised more serious questions about the proposal. Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of advocacy group TransitMatters, told WBUR that commuters on Blue Hill Avenue “deserve better than a concept that appears to have been assembled over a weekend.”

On Wednesday, Culpepper’s office acknowledged the map was produced by a large-language model, based on various hand-drawn proposals drawn up over the past several months.

Both councilors said the mistakes on the map did not detract from the merits of the proposal.

In a joint statement Wednesday afternoon, the two councilors characterized the map as a “conversation starter” with the MBTA “to make a case for why this should and could be studied.”

“The map we shared is just an initial vision of what’s possible, not a final plan,” the councilors wrote. “We leveraged AI to combine a number of iterative, hand-drawn maps to bring a vision to life during our meeting.”

Culpepper’s office said the proposed Orange Line stations in the mock-up were not randomly generated by AI, but deliberately selected over the course of several months of discussions.

The map, the councilors suggested, was just a visual aid. Only a formal prospectus from the MBTA, they said, would be able to “properly show constituents what rapid rail transit could look like in a corridor that has only ever been given bus options for half a century.”

“We left that meeting with an alignment from the MBTA that this was indeed possible,” they said.

In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Worrell acknowledged the map had been “upgraded” by AI, while sharing an earlier “handmade” proposal.

“No matter the map, the point remains the same: There is a gaping hole for rail in this section of Boston that aligns with economic, environmental and educational inequalities,” Worrell wrote.

The map shared by Worrell also gives a clearer idea where the proposed Orange Line stations would go: following Warren Street to MLK Boulevard and Grove Hall, before cutting down Blue Hill Avenue to Mattapan Square. (The Talbot Avenue and Morton Street stops, at least on Worrell’s map, would be west of the commuter rail stations of the same name.)

An extension of the Orange Line along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor would connect parts of Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, predominantly Black neighborhoods, with the rest of the city. The MBTA said this week it’s committed to exploring the idea further.

Culpepper and Worrell said that a timeline or a cost estimate for the proposal would be available only after consultation with state experts.

The Orange Line pitch comes after fierce debate over plans to add a dedicated bus lane up the center of the frequently congested Blue Hill Avenue,. That plan has sparked deep opposition in certain quarters, with critics arguing it will worsen traffic and threaten small businesses along the corridor.

Culpepper and Worrell have emerged as vocal opponents of the proposed bus lane, although they said they did not explicitly address the issue with Eng on Tuesday.

Decades ago, a street car ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square, but it was ripped out in the mid-20th century. In 2009, the state proposed, and residents rejected, an earlier plan for “bus rapid transit.”

“This ask for rapid rail options has been a core feature of our proposal since day one,” the councilors said in Wednesday’s statement. “The bus should always have been the floor, not the ceiling, for a community that has experienced over 40 years of transportation inequity and broken promises.”

title: From Brockton to the NBA, a basketball prodigy revels in his roots
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

On the biggest night of his life, AJ Dybantsa wore his pride on his chest.

His strikingly modern double-breasted suit — closed with a ribbon, embroidered with delicate florals — was a statement. But the pins adorning his jacket were the message.

Over his heart, connected with silver links, were the flags of Jamaica, his mother’s birthplace, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where his father was born. And on the right lapel, Dybantsa wore a blue-and-white pin with “TC5,” in honor of the late Terrence Clarke.

On a night that was all about where he’s going — Dybantsa became the first Massachusetts-born No. 1 overall pick in the NBA Draft on Tuesday — he showed everyone where he’s from.

Dybantsa’s parents were the guiding forces in his journey, from their home in Brockton to basketball’s biggest stage.

And Clarke, a Dorchester native and projected first-round pick who died in a car crash just weeks before the 2021 draft, was a source of inspiration.

So when Dybantsa walked across the Barclays Center stage to shake NBA commissioner Adam Silver’s hand, it was both a culmination of one family’s journey and a coronation for an entire era of Massachusetts basketball.

“I just try to put on for my state,” Dybantsa said. “Brockton bred, 508. I do everything for them. I like helping back in the community and giving the kids hope.

“There’s a lot of kids that play basketball out there and think that they can’t make it, but once they see me, they can be like, ‘OK.’ They might have some hope. It doesn’t necessarily have to be basketball, but anything they do. If they want to be a doctor, an engineer, anything. I’ll just try to be that role model.”

The fact that Dybantsa is the first born-and-raised Bay Stater to go No. 1 is even more striking when you consider the long list of Massachusetts basketball talent that came before. Most notable among them is Hall of Famer Patrick Ewing — also a No. 1 pick — who was born in Jamaica and starred at Cambridge Rindge and Latin.

For his part, Dybantsa checks all the boxes for the modern NBA prospect, from his 6’9” frame and pro-level scoring ability to his basketball IQ and social media following, which has already made him one of the game’s more recognizable faces.

His journey to draft night reads like a fast lane to stardom: Dybantsa left St. Sebastian’s School in Needham to join Prolific Prep in Napa, Calif., then spent his final high school season at Utah Prep, where he played a schedule that crisscrossed the country.

He spent one season at Brigham Young University, playing for head coach Kevin Young, a savvy basketball mind with endorsements from NBA stars including Kevin Durant and Devin Booker.

Despite those whirlwind travels, Dybantsa remained proudly tied to home. And every step of the way, Dybantsa had his father, Anicet Dybantsa Sr., next to him.

Dybantsa was the only player in the draft who wasn’t represented by an agent. Instead, his father retired from his job as a police officer and moved with him to Utah to handle his son’s affairs.

So it was fitting that when Dybantsa’s selection was announced, Silver addressed him not as AJ, but by the name father and son share.

“Without him,” AJ said, “I wouldn’t be here.”

title: At retrial, man convicted of murder in fatal Dorchester home invasion in 2015
text:
A man was convicted of first-degree murder Friday for his role in a 2015 Dorchester home invasion that left one man fatally stabbed and shot, with his fiancée suffering a gunshot wound to the head in the presence of their infant, officials said.

Victor Arrington, 40, whose first trial in 2024 ended in a hung jury, was convicted at his retrial of murder as well as several lesser charges in the slaying of Richard Long, 37, who was killed on March 31, 2015, the Suffolk District Attorney’s office said in a statement.

Arrington’s lawyers didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. He faces a mandatory sentence of life without parole at a June 30 hearing, records show.

All first-degree murder convictions are reviewed by the state’s highest court on appeal.

Prosecutors said Arrington and two other men had planned to assault and a rob a man who lived on Harvard Street in Dorchester but broke into the wrong home and encountered Long, a union ironworker.

They forced Long and his fiancée into their bedroom and tied them up with electrical cords, and then decided to kill the couple to cover their tracks once they realized they were in the wrong residence, prosecutors said.

The assailants stabbed Long and fatally shot him in the head. They also shot Long’s partner in the head in the presence of the couple’s infant child, according to prosecutors.

They doused the couple with bleach and set fire to the kitchen before fleeing, prosecutors said. Long died at the scene, but his fiancée somehow regained consciousness and climbed the stairs to a neighbor’s apartment to get help.

Arrington was arrested in July 2015 but his case moved slowly as both sides fought over whether the jury could view his location history on his iPhone, which a judge ultimately granted, prosecutors said.

A co-defendant, James Boyd, 33, is expected to plead guilty on July 1 to home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, and two counts of kidnapping, prosecutors said.

They said the third suspect was identified but never charged since he was killed in April 2015. He wasn’t named on Friday.

“This team effort helped secure a just verdict in an extraordinarily harrowing case, notable not only for its shocking violence against completely innocent victims but also for the precedent it set in the use of advanced digital evidence,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “But most important of all is the opportunity for Richard Long’s family and loved ones to see someone held accountable for this terrible crime.”

An online obituary for Long described him as a devoted father.

“His children were his joy and he took every opportunity to spend time with them, never hesitating to hug them and express his love. Richard made people feel special,” the tribute stated.

title: ‘She’ll be known as a Bostonian’: Family and friends mourn woman killed in Mattapan carjacking crash
text:
A cousin said the crowd’s intervention is a testament to Janneh’s impact on those she met in Boston.

“She’ll be known as a Bostonian,” Ahmad Thorley, the cousin, said in an interview outside the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center in Roxbury, where the afternoon service was held.

“The fact of the matter is the people did not delay. They did not waste time. They went immediately,” he said. “That’s the humanitarian feeling of the community.”

Following the service, Janneh’s casket was put into a black SUV bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City. From there, her body was to be flown to Sierra Leone, where her parents and siblings live. They plan to bury her, Thorley said.

“Everybody that she touched and everybody that she talked to, surrounded herself [and] laughed with was able to give their last respects to her as she continues on to her journey back home to be buried,” he said.

Janneh was born in Sierra Leone and lived in Ohio before moving to Massachusetts in 2023, another cousin said.

On June 20, she took a bus to Mattapan Square to visit a bank to send money to her parents and then take a lesson at a driving school, Thorley said.

That’s when authorities allege Ibraim Matos drove a carjacked vehicle onto the sidewalk on Blue Hill Avenue, struck Janneh, and dragged her several hundred feet. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Matos, 37, of Hyde Park, was arraigned last Monday in Dorchester Municipal Court, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and other charges.

He was ordered held without bail and sent to Bridgewater State Hospital to undergo an evaluation to determine his competency to stand trial. His next court appearance is July 10.

Thorley said he lives near the crash site and learned about the collision on social media, but initially did not know the victim was Janneh.

That day, Thorley said he had been at a cookout in Brockton celebrating his niece’s high school graduation. An aunt called him and told him the crash killed Janneh.

“The police had contacted her,” Thorley said. “She was crying.”

The deadly collision was part of a chaotic string of events that culminated with onlookers forcing Matos from the carjacked vehicle.

During the arraignment, a prosecutor said Matos was driving his own vehicle near Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street when he collided at about 2 p.m. with another car, abandoned his damaged Acura, and ran to a nearby car wash.

There, Matos allegedly yanked a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel, and drove off again, traveling the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square.

As he approached traffic, a prosecutor said Matos “intentionally” drove onto a sidewalk filled with pedestrians, who desperately tried to get out of his way.

Janneh, who had just stepped off a bus, could not get to safety in time and was dragged “until her lifeless body was ultimately dislodged,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ursula Knight said in court.

Matos then crashed into another vehicle and a bus before his car came to a stop and witnesses surrounded him, according to the prosecution.

Thorley said Janneh’s parents have seen video footage of witnesses restraining Matos.

Representatives from the funeral home handling Janneh’s services called her a “martyr,” he said.

“That could have been anybody,” Thorley said.

Janneh’s service came hours after more violence erupted near the crash site.

At about 1:45 a.m., gunfire activated a gunshot detection system along Blue Hill Avenue.

Officers found four people suffering from gunshot wounds, including one who was mortally wounded, Boston police said. A fifth gunshot victim went to a hospital outside Boston with “non-life-threatening injuries,” police said. He was later transferred to another hospital.

Thorley said Janneh relocated to Massachusetts because she had many relatives here and lived in Dorchester. A day before she died, she moved into their uncle’s home, he said.

A GoFundMe campaign to raise money for her burial costs had raised more than $12,000 by Saturday.

Mbalu Tarawally, one of Janneh’s aunts, said she hopes her niece is at peace.

“We need justice for Mabinty,” she said.

At Janneh’s service, mourners prayed to Allah to show her mercy and grant her forgiveness. Her closest relatives dressed in white.

A funeral program included a photograph of Janneh dressed in a white kaftan embellished with a red and green floral pattern. An emerald green head wrap offset her curly hair.

Pins featuring the same photograph were also distributed.

A cousin said Janneh enjoyed modeling and the photograph was from a shoot conducted on her birthday in April.

“She was loved,” said the cousin, who is also named Mabinty Janneh. “Every time she’s around everybody, she was so, so kind. Everyone can testify to that.”

She said her cousin was interested in travel and braided hair. Thorley said she worked in Boston aiding people with developmental disabilities.

Another aunt, Aminata Bangura, said her niece was loving.

“She loved everybody,” she said.

title: With GateDrop, Tim Near peddles an alternative to energy drinks
text:
“It’s a dream realized,” said Near, who previously worked as a product manager for several tech firms. “It’s like everything I’ve ever wanted: to see products on shelves and have friends call me up and say, ‘I just took a few GateDrops and it made my day.’ ”

Near is based in Manchester, N.H., though for now the company’s roughly one-dozen staffers work remotely. Near and Tyrell came up with the recipe for GateDrop while training for a half marathon. They contract with a factory in Utah to make and package the gummies, but are hoping to eventually move that work to New Hampshire. They sell four-gummy packages for $2.99 in stores, or $14.99 for a 25-gummy pack.

With caffeine derived from natural sources and no artificial sweeteners, Near is hoping GateDrop’s appeal broadens beyond athletes to anyone who wants a healthy pick-me-up during the day.

Global Partners vice president Jac Moskalik said GateDrop is a natural product for inclusion among its roughly 50 local vendors that get shelf space. Moskalik started carrying it at the suggestion of Alltown Fresh merchandising director Nina Peters. Among other local brands that sell through Global: Chatham Ice Cream Bars and cookies from Fancypants Baking Co., as well as some foods cooked up at the CommonWealth Kitchen incubator in Dorchester.

“To me, it’s a point of differentiation,” Moskalik said of carrying local brands like GateDrop. “When you go into one of our stores, it’s almost a little bit of a treasure hunt.”

John Fish and Cyndy Fish appreciated the care and attention Cyndy’s mom received from Cape Cod Healthcare before she died. So when it came to return the favor, there was no question they would break out the checkbook.

The Fishes are giving the nonprofit $20 million, its largest-ever donation. As a result, its flagship Hyannis facility, located roughly 7 miles away from their Osterville home, will be renamed the Cynthia G. and John F. Fish Campus at Cape Cod Hospital.

The money will be used for new initiatives focused on elder care, as well as overall patient care and expanded community access. John Fish, chief executive at Suffolk Construction, said he’s been particularly impressed by what Cape Cod Healthcare chief executive Michael Lauf has done while leading the hospital. He hopes the donation will encourage others to give as well.

“We need as a community to send a signal how important Cape Cod Healthcare is to our community and the importance of quality health care in our backyard,” Fish said.

Fish sits on a number of corporate boards, including the Brigham and Women’s Hospital board and the executive committee for the Brigham’s parent organization, Mass General Brigham. Cape Cod Healthcare, he added, simply doesn’t get enough credit for what it does.

“Cyndy and I have always felt it’s one of those underdog institutions in Massachusetts because it is overshadowed by the academic medical centers,” Fish said. “[But] at the end of the day, we’ve got an institution that really provides a high level of quality care and patient outcomes.”

Has peace finally arrived on the south bank of the Charles?

Sure seems so, judging from the mood at a ribbon-cutting at OneMilestone last week. That’s the fancy new lab building that Tishman Speyer and Bellco Capital recently finished on Harvard-owned land along Western Avenue, across from Harvard Business School in Allston.

Harvard University once had a fraught relationship with its Allston neighbors, dating back at least to when it used a straw buyer to secretly gobble up properties there. More recently, state Representative Mike Moran held up a bill that would have allowed a Harvard-funded drainpipe to the Charles River, hoping to obtain more info about Harvard’s future plans for its undeveloped Allston land.

Moran, now the House majority leader, offered a more conciliatory tone at the ribbon-cutting, to celebrate the 900,000-square-foot first phase of Harvard’s Enterprise Research Campus. It’s the rare example of big private-sector construction actually going forward in Boston right now. Moran noted that Mayor Michelle Wu, another speaker at the event, was a senior at Harvard in 2007 when neighbors were meeting about the project. (Wu’s planning chief, Kairos Shen, recalled how he brought his then-infant daughter to a project meeting in 2009.)

Moran said when he first took office in 2005, the Harvard-Allston relationship was quite strained. “As a matter of fact,” Moran said, “you wouldn’t catch me dead at a Harvard ribbon-cutting in those years.”

Moran noticed a change, though, when Drew Faust became Harvard’s president in 2007. Moran said Faust worked to improve those ties during her 11 years as president, as did successor Larry Bacow and current president Alan Garber.

“We’ve come a long way with our relationship: the community, the electeds, and Harvard,” Moran said. “Let’s just keep that going . . . so we can have more ribbon-cuttings like this.”

Allston Civic Association president Tony D’Isidoro credited Tishman Speyer chief executive Rob Speyer for wanting the campus to fit with the neighborhood and “be the furthest thing from a technology fortress.” The first phase includes the lab building, with Roche recently moving in as the first tenant, along with apartments, a hotel, and the David Rubenstein Treehouse conference center.

D’Isidoro also thanked the team at Tishman Speyer, a New York development firm, for not ribbing him about the New York Knicks’ recent championship.

“Not one person from your team has come up to me and said, ‘How about those Knicks?’” D’Isidoro joked. “They know we’re hurting right now and we’re very sensitive to that.”

While the Supreme Judicial Court tossed rent control off the November ballot, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu says the need for reform has not gone away.

Speaking with political reporter Jon Keller last week, Wu talked about the remaining importance of legislation that would prevent landlords from charging onerous rent increases. She has her own bill pending at the State House to limit rent increases in Boston to no more than 10 percent annually — nowhere near as stringent as the statewide measure that the SJC rejected.

“It certainly wasn’t my idea to write the language how it was and to put it on the ballot,” Wu said at the State House News Service-hosted event. “But what I try to reflect is that when you are out in Boston, . . . people are desperately trying to hang on to afford to live in our communities.”

Keller asked: What’s next?

Wu responded: “The need is out there for legislation statewide that allows for cities and towns to help community members remain community members.”

Wu lamented that her rent control bill is one of several City Hall petitions that have run into resistance at the State House. She has also tried for a bill that would shift more of Boston’s property tax burden onto commercial property taxpayers, and off homeowners, and a transfer fee on transactions over $2 million to raise money for affordable housing.

Wu said she can empathize with the rent-control organizers.

“It’s not because all of a sudden, people, you know, decided it was such a fun hobby to collect tens of thousands of signatures,” Wu said. “It’s because the level of frustration about inaction at the state level, at the State House, has reached a boiling point.”

title: Man gets life in prison for role in violent Dorchester home invasion that left man dead, woman seriously hurt
text:
Among those who delivered powerful victim-impact statements Monday before Arrington was formally sentenced was Long’s oldest son, Richard Long Jr., according to a statement from Suffolk District Attorny Kevin R. Hayden’s office.

“At 12 years old, I still needed my dad,” Long Jr. said, according to the statement. “My siblings needed my dad. We needed his guidance, his protection, his encouragement, and simply his presence. Instead, because of the defendant’s actions, we had to learn how to grow up without him. When I think about my father, I don’t first think about the day he died. I think about the man he was when he was alive.”

Long Jr. said his devoted father “picked me up from school almost every day. Those rides home weren’t just transportation—they were moments I got to spend with my dad. At the time, they seemed ordinary. Today, they are some of the memories I treasure most because I never knew how few of them I would have."

Prosecutors said Arrington and two other men had planned to assault and a rob a man who lived on Harvard Street in Dorchester but broke into the wrong home and encountered Long.

They forced Long and his fiancée into their bedroom and tied them up with electrical cords, and then decided to kill the couple to cover their tracks once they realized they were in the wrong residence, prosecutors said.

The assailants stabbed Long and fatally shot him in the head. They also shot Long’s partner in the head in the presence of the couple’s infant child, according to prosecutors.

They doused the couple with bleach and set fire to the kitchen before fleeing, prosecutors said. Long died at the scene, but his fiancée somehow regained consciousness and climbed the stairs to a neighbor’s apartment to get help.

Arrington was arrested in July 2015 but his case moved slowly as both sides fought over whether the jury could view his location history on his iPhone, which a judge ultimately granted, prosecutors said.

A co-defendant, James Boyd, 33, is expected to plead guilty on July 1 to home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, and two counts of kidnapping, prosecutors said.

They said the third suspect was identified but never charged since he was killed in April 2015.

Long’s partner who survived the ruthless attack also Tuesday submitted a victim impact statement, which her sister read during the sentencing hearing, according to Hayden’s office, which didn’t name the survivor.

““Ever since the incident, I have had to live with the psychological, emotional, and physical impact of this horrific crime,” the woman wrote. “What happened that day changed every part of my life and devastated me to my core. Even now, years later, I continue to experience nightmares and moments where I relive the fear, helplessness, and terror of what happened. Home was once the place where I felt safest, but that sense of security was taken from me. Every day, I am fearful of being alone in my home and, at times, even fearful of being there with my family. ... Today, I find myself questioning whether opening our doors could somehow lead to tragedy again,” the surviving victim wrote.

A now 12-year-old son of the couple, who was the infant present in the home during the attack, told the court Tuesday that losing his father before even getting a chance to know him was devastating.

“The sudden and tragic loss of my father just weeks after my birth created a void that shaped every aspect of my upbringing,” said the boy, according to the statement. “His absence wasn’t a distant memory but a constant, emptiness that defined my earliest experiences. I grew up without his guidance, his love, or his presence, which left me feeling different from my peers. This early trauma manifested in deep sense of insecurity, as the most fundamental bond was severed before it even had a chance to form.”

Arrington’s first trial in 2024 had ended in a hung jury before jurors convicted him last week at retrial, officials said.

Hayden said Tuesday in a statement that words of Long’s loved ones were “remarkable for their grace, eloquence and remembrance.”

“But more than anything their words and memories are searing reminders of the vast, unending grief carried by all survivors of homicide victims,” Hayden said. “They are calls for us, all of us as a society, to work ever harder at reducing violence in our communities.”

title: Want to retreat from the heat? Here’s which Boston pools are open, closed this summer.
text:
For the first time in years, a vast majority of Boston’s public pools will be open this season, providing a free space for families to cool off as the summer heat approaches.

This comes as the city has spent millions in recent years to fix and clean up neighborhood pools — some of which closed for multiple summers — and as the Wu administration expands free youth swim lessons.

“This has been a major project over the last five years. When our administration started, there was a lot of work that we had to dig out from,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Monday at the Hennigan Community Center Pool reopening. “Some of them, the pools had been kept going much longer than they should have been.”

Last year, nine of the city’s 20 pools were closed for repairs or renovations. This summer, six of them will be closed: Mirabella Pool, Blackstone, Holland, Curtis Hall, Leahy-Holloran, and Mildred Avenue.

Among the six closed pools, operated by Boston Centers for Youth and Families, four — Mirabella in the North End, Blackstone in the South End, Curtis Hall in Jamaica Plain, and Holland in Dorchester — are closed for unspecified repairs.

Leahy-Holloran in Dorchester is closed during construction at the adjacent Richard J. Murphy K-8 School, and the Mildred Avenue pool in Mattapan is expected to open sometime in July.

For residents not close to a city pool, Boston currently has some 70 splash pads spread throughout the city for kids to cool off.

Prompted by concerns over some of the city’s public pool conditions, the Boston City Council is holding a virtual hearing Monday on the “conditions, operations and access” to BCYF pools.

Last month, the city reopened the Hennigan pool in Jamaica Plain, which had been closed for years due to maintenance issues and renovations. Its nearly six-year closure sparked community protests, as residents pushed for the repair and reopening of the natatorium, which primarily serves the largely Latino and Black Hyde Square community.

On Monday, Mayor Wu took a dip in the refurbished pool, which was fitted with new gutters, ventilation systems, and floor tiles, among other improvements.

“It’s really because of years of advocacy, feedback, and community participation in shaping all the different parts of this that now, the Hennigan is back and better than ever,” Wu said at the pool’s reopening celebration.

Two years ago, Wu also attended the opening of Clougherty pool in Charlestown — a pool that had closed for a two-year renovation. Before its remodeling, the pool had a faulty filtration system, sizzling concrete that burned to the touch, and a leaking tank. Post-renovation, residents likened it to a country club.

Reaffirming the mayor’s commitment to expanding access to swimming, the city announced in June a collective grant of over $100,000 to 11 nonprofits to cover free swimming lessons for Boston’s youth.

Expanding access to swimming lessons and free community pools could be a matter of life or death for some children. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, drowning is the leading cause of death for children under 5.

Eryn-Ashlei Bailey of the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Council said community pools are especially important in disadvantaged communities.

“Other students are advantaged in that they have access to private swim clubs where they can practice during school breaks, school vacations, summer vacations,” Bailey said.

And then there’s the matter of the sweltering summer weather, Bailey said.

“The question becomes, if we didn’t have this pool, if we didn’t have this resource, how would people cool off in the really, really hot weather?” Bailey said.

Jaden Perry can be reached at jaden.perry@globe.com.

title: Cracking down on blight protects all communities, not just Back Bay
text:
The Globe’s editorial on the decaying Boylston Street buildings exposes a broader failure in Boston’s approach to property neglect (“Back Bay blight: The city should do more to address crumbling buildings,” Editorial, June 28). When a structure is marked with a red “X” because firefighters cannot safely enter, and when scaffolding is required to keep pedestrians safe from falling debris, the problem is no longer cosmetic, it is systemic. Yet Boston lacks the legal tools to compel action from absentee commercial owners or investors who allow their properties to deteriorate for years.

Other cities, such as Springfield, have adopted blight ordinances and taxes that require owners to maintain their buildings or face escalating penalties. Boston has no such mechanism. As a result, neighborhoods across the city — not only Back Bay, but Mattapan, Dorchester, East Boston, and Hyde Park — are forced to live with vacant storefronts, unsafe structures, and non‑owner‑occupied residential buildings that depress local business activity and undermine community stability.

title: Revving the ‘economic engine’ of the state’s Black community
text:
