Summer Eats is a federally funded food assistance initiative that provides healthy free meals to kids and teens throughout the summer months. This year’s program has expanded its scope from 33 meal locations last year to 62 across Allston, Brighton, Back Bay, Chinatown, Dorchester, East Boston, Fenway, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, Roxbury, South Boston, West Roxbury, Roslindale, North End, Charlestown, and Bay Village.

You can see the full list of spots here.

“In Boston, we believe in taking every possible step for access to fresh, healthy food. The Boston Summer Eats program ensures our young people get nutritious food even when school isn’t in session,” Wu said in a release.

“Summer doesn’t have to mean empty stomachs or worried parents,” added Erin McAleer, president of Project Bread, which is an program partner. “Summer Eats is a vital resource ensuring kids and teens in Boston and beyond have access to nutritious meals when school is out.”

Dorchester has the most meal locations at 13. The individual hours and operating days of each location vary, though the majority are open Monday through Friday, offering breakfast from 8:00 a.m. to 10 a.m. and lunch from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.

All meals must all be consumed on-site. “Grab and go,” options are no longer allowed due to updated federal regulations, officials said, though all meals will follow USDA guidelines and include milk, fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins.

Many of the meals will be prepared at the Boston Public Schools’ Central Kitchen in Dorchester by BPS culinary staff, the release said.

The initiative is a partnership between the Mayor’s Office, Boston Public Schools, the YMCA of Greater Boston, Boston Centers for Youth & Families, and Project Bread and is open to all youths 18 and under.

Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism.

title: Brockton man arraigned in 2017 Boston murder after nine years on the run, officials say
text:
A Brockton man wanted in a fatal 2017 Boston shooting was returned to Massachusetts and arraigned on murder charges after nine years on the run, prosecutors said Wednesday.

Alan Marcus Lewis, 40, was arraigned on first-degree murder and felony firearms charges in Suffolk Superior Court on Wednesday, the Suffolk District Attorney’s office said.

He was arrested on July 1 in Charlotte, N.C., and returned to Massachusetts this week, capping what the U.S. Marshals Service described as a multi-year investigation.

Lewis was wanted for the fatal shooting of Brent Stevenson, 37, in Boston near Symphony Hall in 2017.

At approximately 6:38 p.m. on November 6, 2017, police responded to reports of shots fired in the area of Massachusetts Avenue and Boylston Street.

Police said that Stevenson was driving along Massachusetts Avenue when he was shot multiple times, ultimately crashing the vehicle near 333 Massachusetts Ave. He was pronounced dead at a local hospital.

In March 2018, Lewis was charged with felony murder and gun offenses stemming from the incident, according to court records. Police released his name that August but did not indicate a motive for the killing.

In June 2024, authorities offered a $5,000 reward for information leading to Lewis’s arrest.

According to new details shared this week, a U.S. Marshals’ fugitive task force later determined that Lewis had moved to Houston, where he was “living under multiple assumed identities and had established a new life and family.”

Shortly after he was tracked to Houston, he fled Texas and was later located in Charlotte, N.C., authorities said.

“This arrest sends a clear message to violent fugitives everywhere: no matter how long you run or where you hide, the United States Marshals Service will never stop pursuing you,” Dennis Matulewicz, acting U.S. Marshal for the District of Massachusetts, said in a statement.

In 2018, Stevenson’s younger brother, Lawrence, recalled watching his brother, nicknamed “Randy,” die in the hospital after the shooting.

“The world doesn’t stop for you just because you have traumatic loss,” said Stevenson, who at the time helped with grief counseling at a Dorchester institute for families dealing with traumatic violence. “We have to get through our days regardless. We have to.”

Correction: Due to a reporting error, a previous version of this story misidentified Lawrence Stevenson as the victim’s older brother.

Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism.

title: Midwives break ground ceremonially for Boston’s first freestanding birth center in Roxbury
text:
“It’s about honoring the ancestors of this land as this is going to be a portal,” said Luana Morales, who set up a bed of flowers and presided over the ceremony. “It’s about respecting the people of this neighborhood with beauty, dignity, and integrity.”

Freestanding birth centers offer a different model from hospitals: a home-like setting where midwives — licensed providers trained to support patients through pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period — lead care for low-risk pregnancies. The centers typically offer longer appointments than hospitals, have fewer patients, and most work with doulas, nonmedical professionals who provide physical and emotional support.

Some residents cited Roxbury’s high rates of maternal complications and the disproportionate risks faced by Black residents as reasons to establish birth centers as an alternative to hospital-based care. Neighborhood Birth Center’s founder Nashira Baril said her hope is that the center will fill a gap in maternal health care and address racial inequities within the health system by expanding access to comprehensive, insurance-covered midwifery care.

Board members hailed from Somerville to Salem, and many guests could be overheard saying “This isn’t just ceremonial, we’re actually breaking ground” and “It feels so real. It’s alive, not just a Zoom meeting.”

More than $10 million has been raised for the nonprofit birthing center, but more than $3 million is still needed.

“Boston has never had a freestanding birth center, despite well-documented poor outcomes and persistent racial inequities in perinatal health outcomes and growing demand for midwifery-led care,” said Baril, who has a master’s in maternal and child health from Boston University School of Public Health and serves on the state’s Maternal Health Task Force.

“Just hard hats and five shovels weren’t fitting for this occasion that has been years in the making. We invite everyone because that’s who it’s for,” she added.

Neighborhood Birth Center is being built on four parcels: 23 Kearsarge Avenue and 10, 14, and 18 Winthrop Street. There will be a two-story “home” center with four birth suites that will provide prenatal, birth, postpartum, newborn, and reproductive health services. Leaders say it’ll also serve as a hub for family education, postpartum support, community programming, and student midwifery training.

The center will serve more than birthing families but also plans to provide parenting classes, care for menopause, for people who want preventative services, or help with fertility. It will also have a community gathering space and host a house-in-residency for up to four training midwives learning at the center.

It is slated to open in the fall of next year.

Birth centers do have limitations, since they are designed for low-risk pregnancies and do not typically include physicians or OB/GYNs as part of routine care. They also have restrictions on the procedures they can offer, including the use of epidural anesthesia and surgical interventions. If complications arise during childbirth, patients are transferred to a hospital.

Neighborhood Birth Center is close to Warren Street and is nearby both Boston Medical Center and the Longwood Medical multiplex for quick transfers if needed.

Care will be led by certified nurse-midwives, supported by a team of doulas. Doula services are covered by MassHealth.

The groundbreaking comes as Massachusetts faces growing concern over maternal health access and outcomes. Hospitals across the state have shuttered 13 maternity units, totaling more than 100 beds, over the past decade. Maternal health inequities are widening despite years of state investment, with Black families disproportionately affected by complications and unequal access to care.

State leaders, including Governor Maura Healey, have pointed to birth centers as a lower-cost, lower-intervention alternative for people with low-risk pregnancies and have allocated millions of dollars in funding to support them.

Roxbury is especially meaningful for a center as it has among the highest rates of morbidity, along with Mattapan and Dorchester, said Jo-Anna L. Rorie, who has been a CNM for 37 years. She described how the neighborhood has to rely on BMC because Carney Hospital and St. Margaret Hospital closed.

“Roxbury is important because it has a rich history of Jamaican, African, and Caribbean immigrants and people from down south. This is where redlining took place, and birthing centers offer a feasibility for the community,” Rorie said.

Tara Register Curry, who lives across the street from the birthing center, said neighborhood residents are generally supportive of the birthing center, but not everyone understands its vision, she said.

“People need to look past just having a baby here,” said Curry, a mother of two girls. “This will be a place of community gathering, families seeking services and education, and providing that not just to the neighborhood, but to Boston. We go through more after having a baby, and this can be a safe place of support.”

title: DOGE cuts threatened a series of plays made with the NPS. Company One stepped in to fill the gap
text:
Now, Company One has picked up the baton from the National Parks of Boston and Plays in Place and is carrying the series forward, producing “A New Era,” at the Strand Theatre in Dorchester from July 18 to August 8, a year after it was originally scheduled to premiere as a site-specific show at King’s Chapel Parish House. The story centers on the launching of the First National Conference of Colored Women in 1895, which took place in Boston, and highlights the strategizing of seven Black women, led by renowned Boston abolitionist, suffragist, and newspaper editor Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin, to build a unified coalition of women from across the country who have diverging priorities and views.

Patrick Gabridge, producing artistic director at Plays in Place, says that deep budget and staffing cuts at the National Park Service driven by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) led to a loss of funding for the series’ second installment. “The budget got greatly reduced, the staff was all shaken up, priorities drifted and many things changed,” he says. “It’s a result of the [Trump] administration changing their view on the National Park Service.” National Parks of Boston deputy superintendent Liza Stearns, who had championed the series at NPS, retired from her post, he says.

So when Company One wanted to step in and produce the play, Gabridge was thrilled. “We were like, ‘If you can do it, that would be amazing, because the story needs to get out there,’” he says. “It’s a moment that so few people have ever heard of.”

Summer L. Williams, Company One’s associate artistic director, is directing the play and was involved in its development. She says it’s a good match for Company’s One mission as a home for social justice, community building, public engagement, and for elevating marginalized and alternative narratives. “It felt like such a shame for the work on this really worthy project to be stalled,” Williams says. “And it felt like a perfect fit for us as we were thinking about our programming … in relationship to the 250th anniversary [of the nation’s birth].”

“I’m just impressed by how they walk the talk,” ADEkoje says of Company One’s commitment to “public art for public good.”

When Gabridge first recruited ADEkoje, a playwright, screenwriter, and actress, to pen a play for “Suffrage in Black and White,” he suggested a few possible characters. Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin, ADEkoje says, “did not appeal to me at the beginning because I was like, ‘Oh, she’s part of the Black Boston elite, and I’m more interested in working class warriors.’”

But as she read more about her trailblazing accomplishments, she was attracted to Ruffin’s passion, determination, and belief that the world could change. She had created the nation’s first newspaper by and for Black women, The Woman’s Era, that she published and edited. She founded the Woman’s Era Club and organized the first-ever national conference of Black women in 1895, in Boston, which led to the founding of the nation’s first national organization of Black women. “It’s her earnestness that made me say, ‘You know what? I can rock with this because she’s really trying.’”

Ruffin’s primary goal was to pass a law to stop lynching in the South, and her strategy was to ally with white women in the suffrage movement to enact anti-lynching legislation and eventually win the right to vote. In 1869, she had joined with abolitionists Julia Ward Howe and Lucy Stone to form the American Woman Suffrage Association, so she saw how forging alliances could prove successful. “Josephine’s main argument is we need to align with these white women because they’re angry and they’re fighting for the same thing,” ADEkoje says, “and if we bring our numbers to them, then they will stand with us when we’re trying to trounce lynching.”

Not all the characters agree. The Black women with roots in the South “think Josephine is living in a bit of a fantasy,” says Patrice Jean-Baptiste, who plays Ruffin. “They believe she doesn’t have a full picture of what it is to experience the atrocities of living in the South, and therefore her insistence on connecting with white women is laughable, and in fact offensive and foolish.”

But Ruffin, Williams says, “grasped the power of a multiracial approach. She understood the power of people banding together for what’s necessary to make change ... Black women have always been about building coalitions for the betterment of everyone in this country.”

Given that they’re putting on a show that had already been the victim of DOGE cuts and that federal arts funding has been under attack, are the artists involved in “A New Era” worried about any blowback?

“I mean, as much risk as there is in doing anything where you are full-throatedly naming what you’re prioritizing,” Williams says, “and that you’re prioritizing a story that centers Black women who are at the helm of trying to steer the course of this nation in a better direction. I don’t know if I care that someone is upset that this history is being brought to the surface and discussed in a way that is highly relevant to what we are encountering now.”

Jean-Baptiste says that efforts to quiet dissent won’t work. “You can’t quiet people down. You’re not going to shut people up,” she says. “We’re going to do it. Don’t tell us we can’t in a world where you’re starting to turn back rights and disenfranchise Black people. Let us get louder.”

ADEkoje points out the irony that the creation of this play was funded by a government that’s now removing what it deems “improper ideology,” including the erasure of Black history, from federal museums, parks and monuments. “NPS’s funding was paramount to this even happening. So I thank NPS for all the work that they’ve been doing to preserve the truth of our country.”

Despite budget cuts at the National Park Service, Gabridge hasn’t given up on producing the third installment of “Suffrage in Black and White,” Ginger Lazarus’s “Nothing But Victory!” Written to be performed at Faneuil Hall, the play unfolds in 1915 just after the failure of an amendment that would have granted women the right to vote in Massachusetts, as the leaders of the suffrage movement debate potential changes in strategy and some troubling compromises.

“There are still staff members [at NPS] who have been deeply involved with this project and really want to see it happen,” Gabridge says. “So I would say it’s not dead. It’s just on pause until the situation changes budgetarily and politically. To activate Faneuil Hall in that way would be stunning.”

A NEW ERA

title: Mind the gap: What to know about the MBTA’s looming summer shutdowns, including next week on the Red Line
text:
The agency is offering other options, too. An express shuttle, for example, will be in place to ferry people directly between Harvard Square and South Station via the Massachusetts Turnpike.

But the subway shutdown is expected to have a significant impact on how commuters, tourists, and others get around downtown Boston and Cambridge for the last leg of July. (A remarkably similar closure of the Orange Line is coming in late August, too. And other closures are hitting the Green Line. But more on those later.)

The Red Line stoppage begins just days after World Cup tourists departed Boston after the tournament’s July 9 quarterfinal match in Foxborough, and those enjoying the sight of historic military vessels see the spectacle end on Thursday.

Regular Red Line service will resume on July 30.

The MBTA is continuing to repair train tracks underground, upgrade the Red Line’s 50-year-old signal infrastructure, and replace floating slabs — hulking concrete pieces on rubber discs that absorb trains’ sounds and vibration.

“This regular, planned renewal and revitalization work is ongoing and continuous, ensuring the long-term stability of our infrastructure and preserving the system for future generations of riders,” the T wrote in a June statement.

Slab work, in particular, can be “time-consuming” and requires longer train diversions “to allow enough time for the cement to cure,” according to a 2024 video the T released to explain its repairs.

There are about 5,600 primary slabs (and 11,200 secondary slabs atop those) on the Red Line alone. During the shutdown, approximately 18 primary floating slabs and six secondary slabs are planned to be completely replaced, T spokesperson Lisa Battiston said.

Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of transit advocacy group TransitMatters, said floating slabs have posed “recurring issues” for the T since 2011.

“Decades of [water] infiltration in the tunnels have eroded and cracked the concrete,” she said.

T officials are also partway through a $296 million project to complete a new digital signal system on both the Red and Orange lines by the year’s end. The agency has vowed that once it fully transitions to a new digitized system, riders will “experience a more reliable trip” and shorter wait times.

Currently, roughly one-third of T delays can be traced back to signal problems, instances where the analog network connecting electrical equipment functions improperly.

In January, the T said that crews had completed signal work on 12 of 14 locations on the Red Line. Battiston, the T spokesperson, said signal work will take place at the Porter Square and Central Square stations during the shutdown.

Additional signal improvements were also completed in May, the Globe reported, between service suspensions on the southern half of the Red Line and Mattapan Line.

The July shutdown will also allow the T to do renovations to Alewife’s open-air station, stairway repairs at Kendall/MIT, and inspections of the Red Line tunnels, Battiston said.

Be prepared for delays.

The City of Cambridge wrote in a statement that it anticipates “significant impacts to travel throughout the region during the closure” and encourages residents, commuters, and tourists alike to plan ahead, build in additional travel time, and “consider alternative travel options when possible.”

That could mean a lot more people taking Ubers, riding bicycles, or simply hoofing it to work or a dinner out.

T officials estimate it will take more than an hour to get from Park Street to Alewife via one of the shuttles. That’s a trip that, on average, takes about 20 minutes now on the subway, according to data from TransitMatters.

In addition to its free shuttles, the T is encouraging riders to use an array of buses — including the 69, 87, 88, 89, 91, and 109 lines in Cambridge — to connect to the Green Line during the shutdown.

The Fitchburg commuter rail line will also be fare-free between Porter Square and North Station, the T said. (There are, of course, regular fares beyond Porter Square.)

The T says no.

But the 10-day closure is something of a flashback for Red Line riders, who suffered through a bout of shutdowns in 2023 and 2024 before the end of most slow zones systemwide.

Today, the Red Line is doing relatively well. Its speed and service have improved remarkably in the last three years, according to T data, though the ridership of the system’s most popular line never rebounded to its prepandemic high of roughly 210,000 paid rides daily, according to TransitMatters data.

Trains are consistently running at 24 miles per hour this month. Since January, TransitMatters has documented only three brief slow zones on the Red Line between Porter Square and Davis Square northbound; North Quincy and JFK-UMass northbound; and Savin Hill and Fields Corner southbound.

In June, 89 percent of Red Line riders reached their destination within five minutes of the expected time, according to a T dashboard.

But that experience will change, at least temporarily, for many riders navigating the Red Line after Tuesday.

There is, just not on the Red Line.

A large part of the Orange Line will close, too, for 11 days at the end of August, with service shuttering between the Oak Grove and Back Bay Station for track and signal repairs. Free shuttles will run from Aug. 20-30 between Oak Grove and North Station, though stations will also be closed beyond North Station, too.

And like the Red Line, long waits await. The T said those traveling to Downtown Crossing from Oak Grove should plan for an extra 70 minutes on top of their normal commute.

On the Green Line, service will be suspended for parts of each of the branches the weekend of Aug. 1. Inbound trains will not stop at Summit Avenue from Monday to Aug. 7, and trains will bypass Brandon Hall in both directions from Aug. 17 to Oct. 20.

Symphony Station is also closed until summer 2029 for a three-year, $151 million accessibility rebuild.

And even the commuter rail is not spared: The Needham commuter rail line was scheduled to be down from Friday night through the weekend for a bridge replacement and then again the weekend of Aug. 14. The Framingham/Worcester line is closed between Worcester and Grafton from Aug. 5-11.

title: Man charged with shooting at Boston police officers had pending warrant for assault, records show
text:
The man who allegedly fired at police officers in Dorchester on Wednesday was wanted for an assault with a dangerous weapon and was recently declared mentally incompetent in another criminal case, records show.

Rasiel J. Carbuccia, 20, allegedly opened fire with a ghost gun at two officers near the intersection of Devon and Laredo streets around 9:11 p.m., police said Thursday.

Carbuccia was arraigned Thursday in Dorchester Municipal Court on multiple charges, including two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon, possession of a ghost gun, and illegal possession of firearms, records show. Not guilty pleas were entered on his behalf.

He was ordered held by Judge Thomas S. Kaplanes pending a dangerousness hearing set for July 28, records show.

In a statement Thursday, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox praised the officers “for the immense bravery and professionalism they displayed.”

“This incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers our officers face every day to protect this community,” Cox said.

The windshield of a marked police cruiser sustained ballistic damage, police said. Police later recovered a handgun with a spent shell casing jammed in the chamber, officials said. It had an extended magazine with 16 rounds. Police also recovered a bullet in the middle of the street where the incident originated, according to a police report.

After officers attempted to conduct a “subject stop,” near Devon and Laredo Streets, Carbuccia, of Jamaica Plain, allegedly opened fire and ran from the officers, leading to a foot chase over fences and through backyards that ended on Stanwood Street, the report stated.

Carbuccia was taken into custody. The ghost gun, a homemade weapon that does not have a serial number, was recovered on Devon Street, police said.

Two of the officers Carbuccia allegedly fired at were not physically injured but were taken to a Boston hospital for observation, police said.

“We are profoundly grateful that both officers escaped physical injury and were able to return home safely to their families at the end of their shift,” Cox said.

On July 6, a warrant was issued for Carbuccia’s arrest in Roxbury Municipal Court, where he was charged with one count of assault with a dangerous weapon. The warrant was still active on Wednesday night, records show.

According to court records, the state Department of Mental Health sought court permission in 2024 to treat Carbuccia with seven antipsychotic drugs without his permission. He was 17 and being treated at Boston Children’s Hospital on an in-patient basis, records show.

A judge agreed and his mother, Rosalba Carbuccia, was appointed as his guardian. She was tasked with ensuring her son was compliant with medication protocols, records show.

The order was extended in May 2025 after Carbuccia was examined by a doctor who recommended changes in his medication regimen, records show.

The mental health department stopped providing services in April 2025, according to court records, which provided no explanation for the termination.

Carbuccia was also facing a larceny case in East Boston from August and an assault and battery charge in Boston Municipal Court filed in November, records show.

Since being charged in both cases, Carbuccia was either being held on bail at the Nashua Street Jail or undergoing mental health care at the Solomon Carter Fuller Mental Health Center, according to court records.

In the East Boston case, he was found incompetent to stand trial in February and Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office eventually dropped the case, records show.

The second case is still pending. Carbuccia was released on personal recognizance on June 9, records show. His bail was revoked Thursday following the Dorchester arrest, records show.

Details of those incidents were not immediately available Thursday.

Nick Stoico of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Roxbury library branch renamed in honor of Boston’s first black woman TV reporter
text:
As a reporter at WBZ-TV, Shaw covered stories largely ignored by other media outlets. From 1969 to 2000, she reported on issues such as Boston’s school busing crisis, the women’s rights movement, and Dorchester housing hearings.

Shaw was a lifelong resident of Roxbury. She died in 2024 at age of 90.

The Shaw-Roxbury Library was originally named after Thomas Dudley, a 17th-century governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose family has been linked to the slave trade. The name was changed in 2020 to the Roxbury Branch. The request for a third name change originated from a petition from the community in 2025.

“She was a strong advocate for the library and a voice in its previous renovation,” David Leonard, president of the Boston Public Library, said at Saturday’s ceremony. “She could be equally warm and welcoming and connecting, but also would leave you in no uncertain terms about what she expected you to do for the community.”

Shaw’s long-time neighbor, The Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, said that while Shaw was not big on accolades she would feel deeply honored by the library’s name change. It was a place she visited regularly for years.

“The library was far more than the place where she picked up books. She was here all the time,” White-Hammond, pastor and founder of the New Roots AME Church in Dorchester, told the crowd. “She would stop by if she saw you. We would listen to this Walkman, which is not really what you were supposed to be doing in the library. So we were trying to hide it, but she would correct us, lovingly, right?”

Shaw was not only a voracious reader but a long-time activist. After her community organizing years in the ’60s she worked at Action for Boston Community Development, which supports low-income residents in Greater Boston, according to her obituary. She went on to become a contributing host on “Say Brother,” a public affairs program that focused on issues that mattered deeply to Boston’s Black community.

Shaw will be remembered as a reporter who showed compassion, said Catrina Cooley, 60, who watched the ceremony from a camping chair in the crowd.

After Cooley’s parents were struck and killed by a drunken driver in 1982, she recalled, Shaw came to the family home and sat on the couch with shocked and grieving relatives.

“She was very patient with us,” Cooley said. “She was one of the first Black reporters who we knew was going to tell the story, right.”

Wu’s office announced the name change in honor of Shaw in June 2025 after the BPL’s Board of Trustees voted with a vast majority in favor of the decision.

While Shaw “was deeply loved by the community,” some Roxbury residents had supported renaming the branch the Nubian Library to better reflect the surrounding district, and to honor Shaw and other civil rights and community leaders inside the building.

“We have been saying that there should be a wall of honor in the library,” Sadiki Kambon, lead organizer of the Nubian Square Coalition, said in a phone interview Saturday. ”Sarah-Ann’s name should be on there. They could name a room after her but not the entire facility.”

Leonard said trustees discussed the name “Nubian Library” twice.

“In practice, we actually like referring to it now as the Shaw-Roxbury branch of the Boston Public Library at Nubian Square because we think that respects both the service area for the library as all of Roxbury, but also recognizes that geographically we are located in Nubian Square,” he said.

Listening to the community was important to Shaw, White-Hammond said. When there was a community meeting at the library and Shaw happened to be in the building, she would never fail to stop by, she said.

“She’d sit down. She’d listen to what people were debating and talking about,” White-Hammond said.

“I think if we made it just about the moment and the name becomes totally ceremonial, she’d be annoyed,” she added. “But as long as we receive her name on the building and recognize that as an opportunity to continue that legacy, I think she’d be really proud.”

title: Extreme heat events prompt Boston, others to eye cooling policies
text:
Massachusetts is facing a sobering reality: Climate change-driven extreme heat events are prompting Boston to consider solutions similar to those of Sunbelt cities (“Debating a rule for renters to keep cool: City considers a maximum limit on temperature,” Page A1, July 4). When it comes to setting maximum indoor temperature regulations, Massachusetts municipalities already have the authority to do so on their own.

Establishing a statewide maximum indoor temperature should remain the primary public health goal, but local boards of health are empowered to reform their sanitary codes. While that process can be slow, even demonstrating local interest could help accelerate broader statewide action. However, these changes must be coupled with additional support for renters to improve cooling and incentives for landlords.

At Boston University School of Public Health, we are studying the impact of indoor and outdoor temperatures and cooling strategies in Massachusetts and other hot cities. We’ve contributed to a report of the Barr Foundation, the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, and Frontline Solutions that outlines several steps to inform future conversations about resilience to extreme heat.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

We must start treating extreme heat like the public health emergency it is. Making reforms now, rather than scrambling during the next crisis, will establish the preparedness infrastructure necessary to keep our communities safe.

Madeleine K. Scammell

Chelsea

The writer is a professor of environmental health and interim associate dean for policy and practice at the Boston University School of Public Health.

Recent coverage in the Globe underscores the growing public health and safety risks posed by extreme indoor heat across Massachusetts (“Debating a rule for renters to keep cool”). While renters are the focus of the story, it’s important to underscore that many of those same residents are also working jobs without adequate heat protections.

To protect Massachusetts’ workers, we must invest in their well-being at home and at work. That means taking meaningful steps to incorporate occupational heat protection and enforcement to safeguard the Commonwealth’s most vulnerable workers. The recent report setting a policy agenda on heat resilience, to which our organization contributed, offers several recommendations to improve worker protection and accountability during our hottest months.

Thankfully, we are moving in the right direction. This year, we partnered with the City of Boston on a series of training sessions to help implement the city’s first-ever ordinance mandating heat-illness protection plans for workers. While this momentum is promising, we need statewide solutions to protect residents and workers during extreme heat events, which are increasingly becoming a public health crisis.

Tatiana Begault

Executive director

Massachusetts Coalition for Occupational Safety and Health

Dorchester

title: In ‘A New Era,’ a lively look at back at Boston’s Black suffragist past
text:
“If you want to send a message, try Western Union.” These words were uttered by Frank Capra, whose movies, it should be said, were not above sending the occasional message. But the point is clear enough: Art should be art, uplift should be uplift, and one should exercise caution when mixing the two.

Skill and passion, however, can work just as well. “A New Era,” Miranda Austen ADEkoje’s new play that had its world premiere at the Strand Theatre in Dorchester over the weekend, places a historical movement and moment — the fight for Black and women’s suffrage in 1890s Boston — in the service of a story crackling with ideas and conflict. In a crisp two hours, the Company One production wrestles with the compromises often required to make progress, and the complexity of issues that always overlap no matter how badly some seek to keep them confined to their own lanes. “A New Era” reminds us that ideals are dynamic, not static, and that coalitions, not individuals, usually get things done.

Those coalitions can be hard to build, as Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin finds out here. The real-life Boston suffragist, journalist, and activist, played here by Patrice Jean-Baptiste, wants to expand the advocacy work of her Women’s Era Club to a national level. Much of the play takes place in her tasteful Beacon Hill home (scenic design by Janie E. Howland), where she hosts friends and fellow Women’s Era Club members in plotting next steps. Those include the work of the National Federation of Afro American Women, which advocated for education, temperance, and anti-lynching laws as well as suffrage. Those latter two intertwined items are of the utmost importance here: Even after the passage of the 14th Amendment in 1868, Black Americans could scarcely vote in much of the country — women didn’t win the vote until 1920 — and lynchings became a common occurrence in the wake of Reconstruction’s collapse.

If this is starting to sound like a civics lesson, “A New Era” is anything but. Josephine has two ideological adversaries here, although, befitting the complexity of the relationships in the play, they’re also allies. One is Gertrude Sampson (MaConnia Chesser), a proud, brightly attired Bostonian of a family with generations of residence in the city, who has no qualms about dropping the N-word to describe the recent Southern arrivals she views as bringing the race down. The other is Margaret Murray Washington (a luminous Sydney Alicia Jackson), the third wife of Booker T. Washington and a savvy political player in her own right, who shares some of her husband’s accommodationist streak.

“A New Era” ventures outside Josephine’s home to the public sphere of convention halls, where happily anachronistic needle drops including Chaka Khan’s “I’m Every Woman” and Lauryn Hill’s “Everything Is Everything” make implicit connections to yesterday and today. A haunting video montage of lynching headlines, some quite recent, serves a similar purpose. But “A New Era” really comes to life when Josephine squares off with Gertrude, then Margaret, over what their goals might be and how to achieve them. Not coincidentally, these moments also contain ADEkoje’s sharpest writing. “This is Boston,” Gertrude reminds Josephine. “Activism and elitism are kissing cousins.” Later, Josephine challenges Margaret: “If uplift is all we need, why are we still hanging from trees?”

Director Summer L. Williams keeps the dialogue-heavy action moving, and uses the sizable Strand stage to illustrate character dynamics, as when she isolates Josephine away from the rest of the cast in moments when it seems her influence is waning. Costume designer Nia Safarr Banks creates a variety of looks that speak to both traditionalism and defiance. I have one lighting quibble: the decision to keep the house lights partially up throughout much of the play calls attention to the difference between the play’s public and private moments, but it also gets distracting. The theatrical illusion suffers when you can clearly see the people sitting in front of and beside you.

If “A New Era” isn’t a mere history lesson, the history it explores is nonetheless important, especially at a time when erasure of Black history and culture has become institutionalized at the highest levels of government. These battles were real, and the act of remembrance is crucial. All the better when they arrive in the form of good drama.

A NEW ERA

Play by Miranda Austen ADEkoje. Directed by Summer L. Williams. At the Strand Theatre, Dorchester. Pay what you can. https://companyone.org.

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of MaConnia Chesser and Summer L. Williams’s names. The Globe regrets the error.

title: BPS enrollment has fallen by 3,000 students in the last two years as birthrates decline and immigration slows
text:
Over the last 25 years, Boston Public School enrollment has plunged 30 percent to just over 44,000 students, according to the most recent state data. Fewer kindergarteners are entering the school system and some of the larger classes are graduating high school, city officials said.

In the past, declining enrollment was partially offset by new arrivals, including immigrant families, but that influx has also waned.

Students learning English comprise a third of Boston’s total enrollment, state data show.

Their numbers dropped by 10 percent in the last two years to 15,500, according to the city. That decline includes nearly 1,400 fewer native Spanish speakers and 114 students whose first language is Vietnamese.

Despite the decline, “no broad changes” are planned to the school’s programs for students who are learning English, said Boston Public Schools spokesperson Samara Pinto. Administrators anticipate 37 fewer educators will teach English as a second language next year, with final staffing depending on enrollment and student needs.

“We remain committed to providing the services and supports” that non-native English speakers need, Samara added.

School officials have reaffirmed their commitment to place over 1,000 students in bilingual programs by 2033.

City schools are pressing ahead with plans to launch 16 programs that provide some instruction in the native languages of many of Boston’s immigrants. At least 11 Boston public schools offer classes taught in Spanish, Mandarin, Vietnamese, Haitian Creole, and other languages.

In the fall, Boston will launch a new program at the Lilla G. Frederick Elementary school in Dorchester, where kindergarteners will learn in both English and Cape Verdean Creole. The plan is to expand the offer to the other grades over time.

Some advocates have criticized these bilingual efforts because they say it can be difficult for immigrants to get seats in a program in their native language.

Studies have shown that instruction in two languages boosts academic development. Seventy-four percent of those enrolled in Boston’s bilingual programs are non-native English speakers, according to Boston Public Schools.

“More affluent” families who primarily speak English “are clamoring for these spots,” said Ari Branz, organizing director of an immigrant support network at St. Stephens Church in the South End.

Many of these programs have long waiting lists with some parents holding out for two or three years before their child is given a seat. But most immigrant families “do not know that these bilingual programs exist,” Branz added.

Boston Public Schools has many types of seats available for non-native English speakers, Pinto noted, and will continue to monitor enrollment trends “to strategically expand access” to these families.

Almost all students learning English struggle academically. Less than 10 percent fully met or exceeded academic standards in math and English in grades 3 through 8, according to the state’s most recent standardized tests.

Like most school districts, Boston had a difficult budget season driven in part by the drop in enrollment. With the most recent school year completed, the city plans to close four schools and merge two others. Hundreds of teachers and classroom aides are bracing for layoffs after the school system cut positions in the coming academic year.

The cuts mark the second time in three years that Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration has eliminated school staff amid declining enrollment and rising costs.

The reductions will affect all students, with a particular impact on non-native English speakers and other immigrants. Now more than ever, Boston schools should do all they can to support these students who face additional challenges, said John Mudd, a former member of the School Committee’s task force on English learners.

“With the Trump administration cracking down on immigration,” Mudd said, “we should be doing the best we can to keep these kids in the system by making sure they reach their ultimate potential.”

Christopher Huffaker of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the share of non-native English speakers enrolled in Boston Public Schools’ bilingual programs. It is 74 percent.

title: Federal agent charged with assaulting juvenile girl in Boston, police say
text:
A federal agent was arrested and charged last week with assaulting a juvenile girl in an alleged domestic violence incident in Mattapan, court records show.

Leonel Ledesma, 39, was arraigned Friday in Dorchester Municipal Court on one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, a felony, and assault and battery, a misdemeanor, records show.

He pleaded not guilty and was released on personal recognizance, records show.

He was arrested Thursday.

According to a police report filed in court, Ledesma’s wife, Yessica Ledesma, said she and her husband are both “federal agents.”

The report did not indicate what agency, and it could not immediately be determined. Leonel Ledesma’s employer was left blank on the department’s booking sheet and criminal application, records show.

Around 11:24 p.m. on Thursday, police were called to a residence on Oakridge Street, records show.

The girl, who is not related to the couple, told police that Leonel Ledesma tried to take her phone and slammed it on a table during an argument, before flipping a table, which hit her left leg.

Police saw ”minor bruising" on her right thigh and left shin, according to the report.

The couple denied making any physical contact with the girl, whose age and relationship to the couple was redacted in the police report.

Yessica Ledesma said the girl threw her food into her husband’s face and acted aggressively to both of them during the confrontation. She told police the girl “had been caught doing drugs and that her behavior is out of control.”

Yessica Ledesma said she told the girl to go to her room and as she passed by the couple “pushed both the suspect and her and walked into the room.”

Leonel Ledesma, who lives in Heber, Calif., said the teenager had repeatedly displayed “disrespectful” behavior toward him.

“Leonel stated that the victim began to disrespect him and he informed her that if it continued, he was going to take her phone away,” police said. “She stated that he grabbed the phone from her and she threw the food she was eating at him.”

He denied any physical contact took place.

Police, however, identified Leonel Ledesma as the “dominant aggressor” in the altercation.

The juvenile was taken to Boston Children’s Hospital for evaluation Thursday, police wrote. Her mother planned to fly to Boston from San Diego on Friday, police said.

title: A multi-million dollar complex is being built in Mattapan. Local homeowners ask, why now?
text:
It’s the type of street where everyone knows everyone. The kind of place, older residents say, where you want to raise a family. Where football games are played at the park, and there’s neighborhood trick-or-treating. When Patricia Venter moved here decades ago, she liked that it seemed “nice and quiet.”

But last year, the explosions started. Months of sporadic dynamite blasts, followed by excavators clawing dirt and rock, disturbing the neighborhood and remaking the empty lot at the end of Culbert Street into what will soon become an affordable housing complex of 41 apartments.

Some in the city view the project as a much-needed addition to the housing stock in Boston, which continues to wrestle with an unrelenting housing crisis.

Not so on Culbert Street, where seemingly everyone loathes what’s happening and worries it’ll forever change the dynamic of the little enclave they beat the odds to build. They worry about parking, traffic, and how the size of the project will affect day-to-day life on Culbert.

Here may be a case study in how fraught building new housing can be in a city known for its stubborn resistance to change and well-documented history of racism. Experts say the region needs more housing of every stripe. Yet, there is a push and pull in neighborhoods throughout the region between the need for more housing and the fear of displacement, change, and what it will bring.

Such tension is even more fraught along Blue Hill Avenue, the longtime geographic spine of Black Boston that has for decades suffered from political disinvestment and is now undergoing large-scale change. The city is planning to inject $160 million into the corridor to add a center bus lane, plant more trees, and improve the crosswalks, a controversial plan that the city says will transform the boulevard’s transit infrastructure and revive the commercial corridor.

On Culbert, though, some of those changes are being met with heavy skepticism, with residents feeling as though this large housing project in particular is being foisted upon them, regardless of their objections.

Some residents here were content with the lot at the end of their street remaining empty. Others say they aren’t opposed to development of that space, but it is simply too large a building for their neighborhood. Critics say they’re being asked to shoulder an outsized burden in the city’s efforts to address the housing crisis.

Thousands of housing units have already been added to the corridor in recent years, including the new development under construction at the end of Culbert Street.

City officials acknowledge that the construction process can be hard on the neighbors, but the long-term benefits for those who need affordable housing are too great.

“Transforming a long-vacant site near public transit into 41 affordable homes is a meaningful investment in Mattapan’s future,” said Sheila A. Dillon, the city’s chief of housing.

Residents say the development is proof that the powers that be — developers and city government — are not listening to them.

The complaints are various: Dynamite has driven rats onto their properties, the commotion of heavy machinery has disrupted their day-to-day lives, and the influx of new residents will turn the tiny street into a parking lot.

Dane Fletcher, who grew up on the street and whose parents still live there, feels city authorities have downplayed residents’ concerns.

“Despite our earnest pleas to the city, we were blatantly bulldozed,” he said. “How can the city possibly make right the wrong that was done to the generation of residents that still live here?”

And there’s a wider question the city must contend with: How to develop the housing the city needs responsibly?

***

Patricia Venter and her husband, William, moved to Culbert Street in the early 1970s. At the time, Mattapan was still a predominantly white enclave, but those demographics were starting to shift.

In the 1930s, redlining kept Black residents and other racial and ethnic minorities out of certain neighborhoods, including Mattapan. Though it was outlawed in the late 1960s, discriminatory lending persisted for decades.

Then came the blockbusting. For decades, Mattapan had been predominantly Jewish, until real estate agents stoked fears of racial integration among white homeowners so they could buy their properties for cheap and, in turn, sell them to Black families at higher prices.

Change came rapidly: The neighborhood went from 78 percent white in 1970 to 70 percent Black in 1980.

“Jews sold their homes to unscrupulous speculators for less than market value, while [Blacks], eager to participate in the ‘American Dream,’ were forced to pay inflated prices,” wrote authors Hillel Levine and Lawrence Harmon in their book “The Death of an American Jewish Community.”

Nowadays, more than two-thirds of Mattapan’s residents identify as Black.

It is also a historically marginalized neighborhood. Yet, residents of Culbert Street managed to carve out a middle-class existence for their families.

Venter has fond memories of Culbert Street through the decades: birthday parties for her three boys and sports at the park. She understands that things change, she said, pointing out that two nearby churches used to be a grocery mart and a funeral home. But how that change is undertaken matters, she said.

“We were not given the proper consideration,” Venter said. “That’s a big project. I don’t think the humanitarian element was addressed properly.”

City officials acknowledge the challenges posed by construction in residential neighborhoods. But they also say the final project is a result of listening to community concerns about size and density: They reduced the scale from 48 to 41 units, added parking spaces, and created a special loading zone for delivery drivers.

And the units will be for working-class families, the city said, with units available for households making 30 to 60 percent of the area median income, or $49,000 to $97,000 for a family of four. Five other units are set aside for local homeless families.

“These new apartments, including one-, two-, and three-bedroom homes, will be within reach for Boston families who might otherwise spend more than half their income on housing, including residents transitioning out of homelessness and those working full-time at minimum wage,” Dillon said.

But that’s no comfort to those living through the construction. Esmie James, an 86-year-old retiree who has lived on the street for nearly 50 years, said that during one round of dynamite blasting, her furnace pipe exploded. The blasting is necessary because a prominent rock ledge dominated the site, leading some longtime neighbors to believe development there was impossible.

The months of wintertime blasting, which ended in late February, troubled residents because the neighborhood has a documented issue with natural gas leaks. National Grid reported 16 new leaks within a half-mile radius of the construction site between September 2025 and March 2026.

The city said proper precautions were taken, including a Boston Fire Department detail at each of the blasts and sniff testing for natural gas before and after each explosion.

Despite those safeguards, some residents report recent cracks in their foundations or their floorboards and cabinets becoming separated. They wonder aloud if the explosions caused them.

The company in charge of the blasting at the site, Maine Drilling and Blasting, did not respond to requests for comment. Fire and public safety officials have said that all the blasting that occurred was done within the city’s sound and vibration requirements, and such work is not uncommon in a region with so much ledge.

City officials parry other criticisms of the project, too, saying the plot was vacant and filled with trash before construction. There is a rodent mitigation plan in place, and the tree canopy has been maintained, all while building much-needed affordable housing on the site.

Multiple levels of government have invested in the project. The city has spent more than $2.4 million, while the state has invested $2.6 million, and state and federal tax credits for the initiative total $14.3 million. (Private lender financing tops $28 million, according to the city.)

The developer, Lincoln Avenue Communities, which specializes in affordable housing projects, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. During public hearings last year, developers framed the project as a win-win, saying that, because the lot was vacant, the proposal was “development without displacement.”

***

It’s an undeniable reality that cities change, and Blue Hill Avenue, a 4-mile-long thoroughfare that slices through Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury, is no different. There are housing developments and sizable construction sites up and down the corridor.

Part of that change stems from the Blue Hill Action Plan, in which the city is seeking to sell about 30 small city-owned vacant lots along the corridor to local developers to build housing units, commercial property, or community spaces to revitalize the avenue. Many of the lots sat vacant for decades and had been seized by the city for tax liens.

The city’s Office of Housing says Boston remains committed to the plan, with the city owning 29 parcels along the corridor. Eighteen have designated developers, according to the city.

Between 2015 and 2025, nearly 2,000 housing units were built in the corridor, and the city spent nearly $70 million. It hasn’t been enough. Greater Boston continues to struggle with a housing crisis. Bostonians have relocated from the neighborhoods where they grew up to places well outside of the city.

Data show that Brockton, Randolph, and Avon now have the highest share of Black residents in the state. At the same time, Boston continues to lose Black residents, as more and more are priced out.

“I don’t think the question is if we need housing. We absolutely need more housing,” said Ruth Georges, a local community advocate. “I think it’s how we do that; that is still a question that has yet to be solved in a way that homeowners feel is intentional.”

State Representative Russell Holmes is among the politicians who do not want to see his constituents have to move out of the city. Holmes, a Democrat who lives in Mattapan, emphasizes the need for housing density along the avenue. It’s necessary to make the communities work, he said, to help ensure people can stay in the city if they want, and to support businesses there.

For Holmes, multiple things can be true simultaneously. He is happy with the number of units the Blue Hill Avenue project is adding to the local housing stock, but is critical of the way the proposal was “slammed onto the community.” The developers, he said, were not attentive to the neighbors’ needs. Most concerning for residents, he said, was the noise from the construction, as well as the construction vehicles associated with it. More conversation with neighbors, he said, could have smoothed over some of those issues.

Not all housing projects along the avenue have been met with stiff local resistance. If some residents point to the project at the end of Culbert as a case study in how not to effectively engage with stakeholders, there is another project that locals cite as a welcome addition to the neighborhood.

About a mile north of Culbert Street and the 1471 Blue Hill Ave. project on the corner, three buildings are currently under construction. They will house 30 condominiums to be sold at below-market rateS. (The project includes six parking spaces.) There’s also commercial space in each of the buildings, and during the planning process, community members heard pitches from various businesses, all of which were incentivized to have some sort of roots in Boston. Mattapan residents were able to recommend the ones they liked best.

During the permitting process, the developer, DVM Housing Partners, worked with a neighbor to grant them official access to a slice of land they had been using as a driveway for years, but was actually within the property lines of the redevelopment proposal.

In October, DVM also threw a block party and invited residents to celebrate the project.

For Neldine Torres, a nurse practitioner who serves on the board of the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Council, that project exemplified responsible development.

“Any development project should probably take notes in terms of knowing how to engage with the community and listen,” she said.

The president and founder of DVM, Dariela Villon-Maga, knows the avenue well. She grew up in Grove Hall, currently lives in Mattapan, and has an office near Roxbury’s Nubian Square.

She explains the paradox of development in Boston’s Black and brown communities: After decades of disinvestment, investment can be viewed skeptically, particularly if it comes from a developer with no roots in the city. (Lincoln Avenue Communities lists four office locations on its website; none are in New England.)

People ask, “Who is this for?” she said. There are fears of gentrification and displacement.

Of course, people want nice amenities and housing in their neighborhoods, but there is also a level of paranoia that is justified, she said.

“External investment makes longtime residents ask, ‘What’s coming next?’” she said. “There’s a fear of ‘why now?’”

Back on Culbert Street, that fear has morphed into outrage.

David Venter has become the face of the opposition to the project, emailing city officials and developers, speaking out at public hearings, and penning a letter to the editor in The Dorchester Reporter.

Venter recently bought the house he grew up in from his mother so that she can live out her days there. He fears that the new apartments at the end of the block will undermine the feel of community that has developed over the decades.

“It really is a village,” he said.

He rejects the notion that the local opposition is grounded in NIMBYism. For him, the project is adding insult to historical injury. Decades of institutional racism shaped the neighborhood: redlining prevented Black people from moving there, blockbusting meant they had to pay a premium to buy there, and disinvestment kept home values low.

“You didn’t want us,” said Venter, who works in communications for a nonprofit home health care company. “You wouldn’t give us any loans for our houses. We had to do it on our own. We were self-sufficient.”

He paused. “Now this.”

title: ‘It’s time to drop the hammer on them’: BPS fines transport company over $400,000 for late or missed buses
text:
But despite more coming on time, some buses still came more than an hour late, or not at all.

In May, nearly 500 of these “blown trips,” triggered $184,000 in damages, even as combined on-time percentages hit 90 percent that month.

The fines, first reported by WBUR in April and again last week, have led parents and local officials to call for the state to increase its oversight of Massachusetts’ largest school district, just years after local officials narrowly averted a state takeover of BPS following reports of “entrenched dysfunction,” extending from staffing issues to the districts’ tardy buses.

That compromise created a remedial improvement agreement with the district, which the state let expire last summer even as the city failed to hit other goals beyond reliable buses, including improving special education and ESL programs.

Cheryl Buckman, a BPS parent and advocate, created a petition this week calling for the state to again intervene on busing and for BPS to consider terminating service with the company, which has been its sole busing provider since 2013.

“Why weren’t [these] guys fined a long time ago?” said Buckman, whose petition on Wednesday had 20 signatures. “I believe it’s time to drop the hammer on them.”

Per their contract, the district can charge Transdev $500 for any no-show or overly late trips, district transportation director Daniel Rosengard told City Council members in a March session discussing bus lateness. Transdev can also secure bonuses by being on-time.

Using this price calculation, the district likely left millions on the table by not enforcing fines across previous years.

Last fiscal year, BPS allocated $189 million to transportation, at least $21 million of which went directly to Transdev for management expenses, Rosengard told the Council members.

Following ramped up enforcement, Transdev’s end to last school year was among its strongest ever.

In June, the company achieved a month of bus service that was on time 95 percent of mornings, for the first time satisfying the minimum target BPS promised state officials they would realize along all routes in their now-expired improvement agreement from 2022.

June also had the smallest number of blown trips at 197. For reference, district buses complete roughly 3,000 total routes each school day, according to a 2025 progress report.

In a statement, Transdev spokesperson Mischa Wanek-Libman said the company has made various improvements over the past year, including hiring 40 additional drivers and training 750 drivers in safety and defensive driving courses.

“While we recognize there is more work to do, these improvements reflect our continued investment in safety, service, and accountability,” Wanek-Libman said.

In a statement Monday, a district spokesperson said the fines “address an uptick we were seeing in the number of uncovered trips even as overall [on-time performance] was continuing to improve.”

But some in the community said they haven’t felt like performance is improving, and see the fines as proof of that.

Theresa Delehanty, 66, who helps two of her elementary-age grandchildren catch the bus in South Boston each morning, said the bus didn’t arrive at all five times last school year, more than ever before.

Transdev service began to seriously regress around last December, necessitating the start of fines, Rosengard also told city councilors in March.

In an open letter to state education officials published Friday, City Councilor-At-Large Erin Murphy expressed frustration with BPS officials.

She said she has repeatedly received the same kind of “local assurances,” about transportation but without “sufficient answers and meaningful change,” and now wants the state to do its own review.

“The need for these fines,” Murphy added, “confirms that the district and its contractor are still failing to meet basic expectations.”

In a statement on Monday, a district spokesperson wrote that BPS, “continues to work closely with Transdev to ensure that during the 2026-27 school year we build on the record high on-time performance seen this past school year.”

Addressing why fines only began this year, the spokesperson said that “while our experience has shown that non-performance damages are not always the most effective tool at our disposal, we use them strategically when necessary to maintain accountability.”

So far, “this targeted use of damages” had led to “a significant reduction in uncovered trips,” the spokesperson added.

The district’s busing protocols and its relationship with Transdev have come under intensified scrutiny over the last year, following the death of Lens Arthur Joseph, a 5-year-old Hyde Park student who was struck by Transdev driver Jean Charles shortly after afternoon drop-off in April 2025. It was later revealed that Charles, who tried to flee the scene of the crash, was also driving with an expired state certification.

A WBUR and ProPublica report released last month exposed further issues at Transdev. According to their investigation the company did not properly identify its role in 42 fatal crashes, including the one that killed Joseph, in federal databases.

In Boston alone, they identified 71 serious school bus crashes involving the company which weren’t reported using its name.

An independent probe last year revealed a collective failure by BPS and Transdev to properly document and track training requirements and accident reports.

New safety recommendations were adopted at the start of last school year, but parents like Buckman said they don’t trust that Transdev is being held accountable.

“Sorry just does not cut it anymore,” she added. “There is [a] huge fracture between BPS families and BPS itself.”

BPS is also Transdev’s only school bus client, and the company was the only bidder for the district’s most recent five-year busing contract, signed in 2023.

According to a district spokesperson, multiple vendors were invited to bid in 2021, but only Transdev submitted an offer.

First Student, which provided district busing before Transdev, was also plagued by chronic delay issues. In 2012, the Globe reported 37 percent of its buses were arriving up to an hour late and the firm was fined $800,000 as a result.

title: Representative Pressley says she’s ‘devastated’ by death of teenager found in rental property owned by her husband
text:
Representative Ayanna Pressley said Tuesday that she’s “devastated” by the death of a teenager who was found in a Mattapan rental property owned by her husband.

“I am devastated about the death of Yoseliani Marte, an 18-year-old with so many dreams ahead of her, her life cut short by domestic violence,” Pressley said in a statement.

The Democratic lawmaker said that as a parent of a teenager herself, “the thought of a young person violently losing their life in this way is beyond crushing.”

Pressley said she stands with “our community and everyone who loved Yoseliani as we grieve this deep loss. May we all honor her life and humanity and extend compassion to her loved ones as they navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

Police haven’t publicly identified Marte as the victim in the case, but her mother, Elenie Ocasio, told Boston 25 News on Monday that an assailant had “put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house, and left her to die.”

No arrests have been made.

Police said there’s “absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property.”

Property records show the seven-bedroom home where Marte was found is owned by Pressley’s husband, Conan Harris. Pressley and Harris live in the Hyde Park section of Boston, according to the lawmaker’s website.

Shortly before 2 p.m. on Saturday, two officers responded to a radio call for a person shot at 25 Malta St., according to the report.

Another officer working the front desk of a police station in Hyde Park “took a walk-in report” of a person shot at an apartment in the building.

The victim was found in a bedroom inside that unit, the report said.

Shea Butter Smoothies, a Dorchester juice bar where Marte worked, posted a heartfelt remembrance of her to Facebook on Monday.

“Liani was a brilliant and motivated young lady whose passion and dedication had a profound impact on our team and the work we do,” the business said. “Her innovative ideas, particularly in enhancing Shea Butter Smoothies, brought a unique touch that our customers adored. She approached every project with enthusiasm, creativity, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”

She also “brought joy and positivity to our workplace. Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many,” the post said. “She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

To honor her life and support her relatives as they grieve, the business said, “we will be donating 50% of the proceeds from every purchase of the Big Papi smoothie to assist with her funeral costs. We encourage our community to join us in this effort, as we remember the beautiful person she was. ... Rest in peace, Yoseliani. You will always be remembered.”

title: Safe streets in Boston require more than choosing sides
text:
Given that sequence, it seems fair to conclude that politics played some role in Wu’s retreat from unabashed champion of bus and bike lanes to something less ardent and more politically pragmatic — a retreat that is now drawing harsh criticism from cycling advocates after the tragic death of Louisa Gag, a city transportation planner who was killed while riding her bike on July 9. In Gag’s memory and honor, Wu has pledged to review safety designs for the section of Tremont Street where Gag was killed and greater enforcement of laws regarding bike lanes that are blocked by illegally parked cars.

What should not be lost in the emotion of the moment is the need for balance and openness to different points of view when it comes to creating safe streets for everyone. The perception that both were lacking under Wu gave Kraft an opportunity on the bike lane issue. While he was never able to capitalize on it beyond the loud cheers he got for mentioning it at his announcement, he did force Wu to acknowledge there is more than one side to the bicycle lane debate. It’s the side of businesses that say they lose customer parking spaces to bike lanes as well as the side of pedestrians who dodge people on bicycles, e-bikes, and scooters who ignore red lights and other rules of the road.

To cycling advocates, those are fighting words. From where I sit — which is usually not on a bicycle — they see no other side to the issue, just energy-hogging barbarians. While I respect those who believe cycling is the best way to save the planet, an all-or-nothing perspective defies the reality of Boston’s jumble of streets and the need to share them with cars and trucks because everyone can’t or won’t ride a bike. Unless the city somehow builds protected tunnels for cyclists, they are going up against vehicles that weigh thousands of pounds. That’s inherently unsafe. Speed limits and attention to traffic signals should be enforced on the motorist side, but risk is part of cycling.

Of course, the city should also do what it can to address roads that are especially unsafe. For example, in 2023, the city said that section of Tremont Street in Mission Hill where Gag was killed needed improvements, such as wider sidewalks, more protections for cyclists, and measures to slow traffic. Whether it simply got lost in a bureaucratic shuffle, or was put off because of election year politics, the project has not advanced.

Kraft never posed any real threat to Wu. Early polls showed she was ahead of him by 14 points. She beat him by a 49-point margin in the September preliminary election and he dropped out shortly afterward.

Yet despite her big political win, the perception that Wu does not listen to all sides persists and continues to fuel criticism of the way she pursues transportation policy. That’s the case with her $135-million proposal to add center-running bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue. The pushback is now so strong that opponents asked the Trump administration to withhold $80 million in federal funding that’s allocated for the project.

Bill Forry, executive editor and co-publisher of The Dorchester Reporter, recently wrote that complaints from opponents about a lack of public input on the Blue Hill bus project don’t “pass the sniff test.” His review of news articles in The Reporter chronicled 18 forums, open houses, and hearings over the past four years, plus pop-up workshops and “street team” engagement.

Yet quantity doesn’t trump quality. If people don’t feel they are being listened to, that’s a problem for a mayor. For Wu, it’s a consistent problem on any number of issues, from bike and bus lanes to renovating White Stadium.

From a personal perspective, this has to be a difficult moment for Wu. Gag worked for her as a policy fellow and intern when Wu was a Boston city councilor, then took on a role as a city transportation planner who oversaw bike-share policies and road safety improvements.

She will want to do the right thing for the cycling community. But she shouldn’t make the same mistake she did before and shut out Bostonians with a different point of view.

Some may have cheered Kraft’s words about bike lanes. But like it or not, she’s their mayor, too.

title: ‘Should I just close everything?’: Why a restaurant owner’s tearful video went viral
text:
“What is all of this for?” he said, crying in the video. “You’re hoping that everything works out. Your hopes and dreams and all your sacrifices now will pay off.”

Pham and his wife, Yeanie Bach, originally an IT specialist and photographer, opened their first restaurant, Banh Mi Oi, in West Roxbury in July 2020. Since then, the two have opened a second Banh Mi Oi in Waltham, Greenhaus Cafe in Roxbury Crossing, Phinista Cafe in Fenway, Vang Coffee Bar in Quincy, and Yeanie’s Burgers and Social in Dorchester. They are hoping to open a second Yeanie’s in West Roxbury in the coming weeks.

Pham posted the video as a “PSA” to anyone looking to become a small business owner. “The entire company is literally on your shoulders,” he said in an interview with Boston.com. “Some days it gets really messy and it gets really heavy. There is no work-life balance.”

He never expected the video to go viral and receive an “insane” response in the comments — more than 4,000 on Instagram — and in his DMs, he said.

The video was “probably one of the lowest points of my life [and it] became one of the most heartfelt moments I’ve ever had,” he said in a follow-up video on July 17, thanking everyone for their words of support.

Pham believes the video resonated with so many people because they face similar struggles as business owners: paying off debt, supporting staff members, managing equipment issues, and ensuring customer satisfaction all while trying to invest back into the community.

The food industry is a particularly “hard” industry right now, Pham said. “There’s this really weird shift [in] mindset where food can’t be more expensive because people are making less money,” but then restaurants lose profits and risk potential closure.

In the video, Pham also shared that his main struggle is living 500 miles away from his wife and daughter and only getting to see them for one week every month. Pham lives in West Roxbury, but his wife moved to the D.C.-area so their daughter can grow up closer to family.

“I’m sacrificing being with my wife and daughter on my birthday. They’re 500 miles away,” he said in the video. “But I need to put the business first. I need to be here to make sure we are supporting the team.”

“Every time I come back to my daughter or I talk to her on FaceTime, she’s different. … Her hair’s a little bit longer, her face is different,” Pham said in the second video.

Although he continues to be apart from his family, Pham said he isn’t sure the sacrifice is “worth it yet.” He continued, “The only thing that keeps me going right now is the difference that we’re making in our neighborhood[s].”

Police arrested Jeremie two months later when the same boys spotted Jeremie near Copley Square and their father contacted the police, records show.

title: Dorchester man allegedly shot friend ‘in confusion of a gunfight,’ prosecutors say
text:
Just after 1 a.m. on May 22, Ferrer pulled his car into a parking lot on Bowdoin Street and a “gunfight erupted between Ferrer and his friends and another group,” Assistant District Attorney Cailin Campbell said in a statement Thursday.

Surveillance video obtained by WCVB-TV showed roughly a dozen people running for cover as gunshots rang out, followed by more gunfire as people crouched for cover.

A ShotSpotter detection device in the area recorded five shots, according to a police report. Police found two guns and multiple vehicles were shot, the report said.

“In the confusion of the gunfight, Ferrer shot the victim, his friend, Giovanni Bala,” Campbell said.

Bala later died from “multiple gunshot wounds to the torso,” including a fatal wound to the upper chest, according to a police report.

In an interview Friday, Ferrer’s lawyer, Bradford Stanton, said that he intends to challenge the prosecution’s charge of premediated murder, saying it was “inappropriate given the circumstances.”

Ferrer had a valid license to carry a gun, Stanton said.

“I don’t believe a lawful firearm owner acting in self-defense should be charged,” he said. “Someone shot at him and he returned fire. Tragically his friend was caught in the crossfire.”

Ferrer had no previous criminal record, according to a police report.

A spokesperson for the Suffolk District Attorney’s office declined to comment further on the murder charge, but said they believe it is supported by the evidence.

“When illegal guns are in the hands of people perfectly willing to use them — especially in a situation like this, where numerous people are firing at each other—terrible and tragic outcomes are inevitable,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a news release Thursday.

“Here, the outcome is a defendant charged with the death of his own friend,” Hayden said.

Bala’s father, Dominique Bala, said his son had gone to a Cape Verdean restaurant and was leaving with a group of people when gunfire broke out.

Bala, who grew up in Boston after his parents immigrated from Senegal, attended Charlestown High School where he played basketball, his father said. He loved traveling and one day hoped to start his own business, having recently completed union carpenter training.

“He was the light of our family,” Bala said in an interview. On the morning of the shooting, his only son texted him: “Good morning dad have a good day love you.”

In May, community members set up a memorial to Bala on Bowdoin Street that included dozens of candles, flowers, balloons, and liquor bottles, as well as a miniature construction helmet and leather work boots in honor of his passion for carpentry.

Ferrer is due back in court on August 19.
