title: Marty Walsh wades into Michelle Wu’s fight with Beacon Hill
text:
Walsh’s endorsement adds another layer of political intrigue to a race already packed with it. Lander is one of two challengers whom Wu is backing against two Democratic state senators — Brownsberger and South Boston’s Nick Collins — after they helped block her repeated attempts to push property tax legislation through Beacon Hill.

Walsh and Brownsberger aren’t an obvious political pairing. Walsh is a dyed-in-the-wool union leader from Dorchester with lunch-pail roots and a reputation as an old-school Boston power broker. Brownsberger is a Harvard-educated lawyer from Belmont known for unknotting wonky issues and who was among those who cast doubt on a State House staff unionization effort.

But the two Democrats go way back. The pair served together as state representatives, and worked out of the same office in their early days in the chamber, Walsh said. Their relationship lasted even after Walsh left the State House for City Hall, and Brownsberger won his state Senate seat.

“When I was mayor, he was one of the guys I’d call if I needed anything — budget stuff, legislation we had. Everything we did, I’d call Will,” Walsh said. Walsh, now executive director of the NHL Players’ Association, will hold a press conference Monday afternoon with Brownsberger outside the State House.

“Will is going to tell you how it is. You know where he stands, and he doesn’t play games,” Walsh said. “He’s a good guy. He’s a good person. And I think he deserves to be in the state Senate.”

So, seriously, don’t read into this, Walsh insists.

“This isn’t Walsh vs. Wu,” he said. “This is Marty Walsh supporting his friend Will Brownsberger who he’s known since he’s been elected as a state rep.”

Buuuut …. it’s hard not to read into it, at least a little, given Wu and Walsh’s history.

The almost-mayoral rivals — Wu and Walsh appeared to be headed for a showdown in the 2021 mayoral race before Walsh was tapped to join president Joe Biden’s Cabinet — have spent the past few years circling each other politically.

Last year’s City Council election was the latest example. Wu leveraged her political operation to help get City Councilor Henry Santana reelected, while Walsh endorsed former city councilor Frank Baker, who sought a council comeback after forgoing reelection in 2023.

Super PACs with ties to both emerged in the race, in which Santana ultimately won an at-large seat over Baker. (Walsh and Wu were aligned on one candidate, Alexandra Valdez, whom Walsh endorsed and Wu said she voted for.)

How much either endorsement will move votes in the state Senate race is unclear. Brownsberger’s district covers Allston and Brighton and part of Boston’s Fenway neighborhood, but also includes parts of Cambridge, Watertown, and Belmont, where Brownsberger lives.

Wu’s push to oust Brownsberger and Collins is a major test of not only the length of her political coattails, but also her ability to reshape a Senate that’s regularly stood in her way.

Brownsberger, in a statement, said he has “always valued Marty’s judgment and willingness to roll up his sleeves and solve problems.”

“We have had a great working relationship,” he added. As for his working relationship with the current mayor ... that’s admittedly “a little bit strained.”

PARTY FOUL: Steve Kerrigan, head of Mass. Democratic Party, charged with drunken driving last month by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: Steve Kerrigan, the chairman of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, was charged with drunken driving last month and admitted that prosecutors had enough evidence to convict him after he was pulled over in Southborough, according to court records.

Kerrigan, 54, pleaded to sufficient facts on June 15 in Westborough District Court, a common outcome in drunken driving cases under which Kerrigan will have his case continued without a finding for a year. He also lost his license for 45 days. Kerrigan told the police officer that he was driving home from a restaurant. The officer wrote in a report that he was unable to smell alcohol on Kerrigan “due to an overwhelming odor of cologne.”

Governor Maura Healey said in a statement that she had spoken to Kerrigan, “and told him how unacceptable this is.”

PROGRESSIVE MESSAGE: US Representative Pramila Jayapal is endorsing Senator Ed Markey for reelection as he faces a primary challenge from Representative Seth Moulton.

Markey is “the only progressive in this race,” Jayapal, a Washington Democrat and the former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said in a statement shared by Markey’s campaign. The endorsement is the latest move by Markey’s camp to frame the 80-year-old incumbent as the race’s progressive choice.

FITN DOA? The DNC may snub the N.H. primary once again — and make the same mistakes once again by James Pindell, The Boston Globe: An elite group of Democratic National Committee members are set to meet — and likely vote — Friday on a plan for first state presidential primaries in the 2028 presidential election.

ANOTHER CHAPTER FOR 62F: Massachusetts’s tax cap law — and the refunds it can deliver taxpayers — will live to see another day.

State senators on Thursday night pulled back an amendment to their sweeping economic development bill that would have repealed the decades-old law known as Chapter 62F — not a totally surprising move given the tough election-year optics of blocking money from potentially flowing back into taxpayers’ pockets.

But lawmakers didn’t leave the 1980’s-era law untouched. Senators instead passed a redrafted version of the proposal from state Senator Jason Lewis that is designed to effectively blunt the impact of a ballot question going before voters in November that would make it easier to trigger refunds to taxpayers.

The law, as it currently stands, is intended to limit state tax revenue growth to the growth of total wages and salaries and return any excess to taxpayers. That’s calculated by looking at the previous year’s cap, and then adding the adjustment for wage and salary growth, according to an analysis from Tufts University’s Center for State Policy Analysis.

The ballot question would reshape the law by setting the cap each year based on the actual revenue collected — a tweak, the analysis found, that could trigger three to five times as many refunds and return as much as 15 times as much money to taxpayers.

To taxpayers, that could be very appealing. To lawmakers who must build the state budget each year, not so much.

Enter the Senate’s 11th-hour proposal. The new version senators embraced Thursday adds what Lewis called “an additional test” to determine if and when refunds can start flowing. It would prevent tax givebacks if net tax revenues in the fiscal year are less than 7.5 percent of the total statewide personal income for the calendar year.

In other words, before voters weigh whether to make it easier to get a refund, the Senate wants to make it that much harder.

Though it’s a step down from the full-on repeal senators first floated, the ballot question backers weren’t placated.

The amendment as passed “would weaken the law months before voters consider a ballot question to strengthen it, undermining the ballot process and further eroding public trust in state government,” Taxpayers for an Affordable Massachusetts, the campaign behind the question, said in a statement late Thursday night.

FUN TIMES: The Senate also passed parts of its so-called “fun agenda” on Thursday, approving a measure that would lift Massachusetts’s decades-old ban on happy hour and another allowing towns and cities a local option for keeping public drinking districts.

FOR THE RECORD: Mass. Senate proposal would make records in governor’s office and Legislature public, with limits by Anjali Huynh, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts lawmakers are moving closer to widening the state’s public records laws, with the Senate preparing to vote on legislation that would make some of the Legislature’s own records available as well as those of the governor’s office.

The Senate’s proposal, released by Democratic leaders on Thursday, is similar to a version passed by the House last month, and comes months before voters will weigh a ballot question that would go further in opening the Legislature’s records to the public.

But while Democratic leaders and several good government groups cast the legislative proposals as recognition of the public’s right to know, sponsors of the ballot proposal took a dimmer view, arguing the measures would reveal little about the Legislature’s workings that the public can’t already get.

SPOTLIGHT UPDATE: Attorney general is probing MassHousing grant program highlighted in Spotlight investigation by Joey Flechas and Gordon Russell, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office is investigating apparent fraud and a conflict of interest in a state housing grant program, problems highlighted in a recent Globe Spotlight Team investigation that found a trail of shoddy and incomplete work where there should have been fully renovated apartments.

A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office confirmed it received a referral on trouble in the MassHousing program, which aimed to rehabilitate rundown affordable housing units in struggling mill towns. It was unclear where the referral came from; officials from MassHousing declined to comment on whether the agency asked for the investigation.

BUDDING DEFENSE: Suffolk sheriff says he didn’t break law in court filings about corruption case against him by Danny McDonald, The Boston Globe: Court filings on Thursday in the federal corruption case against Suffolk Sheriff Steven W. Tompkins offered a glimpse of what his defense will be should the matter proceed to trial, with his attorney saying there was no quid pro quo in the sheriff’s dealings with a cannabis company.

In the brief, which is essentially a roadmap of Tompkins’s legal defense in the case, Tompkins’s attorney Martin G. Weinberg said his client’s dealings with Ascend Mass represented “a business transaction, at full market value, with a longtime friend that had nothing to do with Mr. Tompkins’s official position.”

Take a look at the newest renderings of the state’s $2.1 billion Sagamore Bridge by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe.

title: Seeking a path forward for Blue Hill Avenue
text:
Re “Blue Hill Avenue transit: Bus or rail?” (Opinion, July 13): The dueling op-eds in the Globe’s July 13 edition — “Community deserves rail, not another bus debate,” by Boston City Councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper, and “Don’t jeopardize bus project waiting for rail,” by former state transportation secretary James Aloisi — show the chasm between a former bureaucrat and community leaders who point to decades of being told they should be grateful for crumbs instead of an objective analysis of transit options that could yield a full loaf.

Worrell and Culpepper are right that Blue Hill Avenue’s more than 30,000 daily transit users deserve the comprehensive analysis the Commonwealth has done for other routes serving other communities. Aloisi, who directs the MIT Transit Research Consortium, bizarrely says a subway is a “blunt mobility instrument” and focuses on the goal of improving “the bus rider experience.”

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

The goal is to improve mobility for all. We need to look at alternatives and evaluate ridership, cost, environmental impacts, viability of construction, and other factors instead of pouring our energy into tinkering with the bus network.

Buses are the lowest-capacity mode with the least potential to shape land use and development. Why the fixation on buses? Because they are cheap to implement. Big thinkers like these city councilors have been told that buses are what you get. It’s long past time to see a study identify the best alternative for the corridor.

Anne McKinnon

Jamaica Plain

Amsterdam is an old city built around a canal system that makes straight roads practically impossible, but planners have engineered a practical solution that incorporates light rail, autos and light trucks, bicycles (lots of them), and pedestrians. Many of the major streets are configured as follows: sidewalk, bike lane, auto lane, tram, auto lane, bike lane, sidewalk. It would seem that the wide expanses of Blue Hill Avenue, Seaver Street, and Washington Street would be ideal for a similar configuration, incorporating light rail or Silver Line buses while connecting Nubian Square and Mattapan Square.

Lucius C. Michel

North Andover

I cannot overstate the need for presenting more study-based options for the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, including rapid transit, and notwithstanding the costs. Our community has working-class and lower-income families who are major public transit users.

Sentiments expressed by Councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper are important, chief among them the history of unkept promises of transportation improvements for Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan.

I can still recall the neglected Orange Line slowly creeping around the Ferdinand Building into what was then Dudley Station because of the way the track leaned. It was still the best way to get to work downtown on time. Then it was gone altogether.

We know that plans of any kind will take years to be implemented. The road to gaining community agreement on a plan must be paved with a demonstration of ongoing commitment through action and investment, not one big gamble every 40 years that has as much of a chance of being a loss as a win.

Why not start spending the money that’s been set aside now on traffic infrastructure and enforcement improvements along the existing corridor, better bus scheduling, preparing businesses for changes, designing pollution controls, and other enhancements?

Laura Younger

Dorchester

The former state secretary of transportation needed a member of his staff to drive him to Mattapan Square so that he could assess “the poor quality of service on the 28 bus”? Seriously? I might have suggested a walk from the state office at Park Plaza to the Red Line at South Station, then a train to Ashmont, and then the Mattapan Trolley.

Paul Stewart

Quincy

title: The T paratransit service changed its bag policy. RIDE users say it’s made grocery shopping nearly impossible.
text:
Implemented last August, the rules have radically upended the routines of some RIDE customers, people with disabilities who have few options to get around otherwise. They used to be able to stow all their shopping either in the rear of a van or the trunk of a RIDE sedan, but patrons must now fit their folded carts and belongings within their own sitting area, often jammed in by their feet or resting on their stomachs.

So widespread is the frustration over the rules that more than 50 RIDE patrons showed up at an MBTA board meeting this month wearing T-shirts and carrying signs that read, “Secure Our Dignity.”

T officials argue the limitations make the RIDE safer and faster for the roughly 4,000 weekly riders who use the shared door-to-door service. Fewer bags, T officials said, leave more space for wheelchairs and walkers and prevent the possibility of produce and eggs shifting around in traffic.

Yet dozens of riders and transit advocates argue the policy has resulted in inconvenient and painful consequences. Seniors who can only carry so much say they are going without heavier items such as milk or laundry detergent; some disabled riders stack grocery bags on their stomachs and feet, leaving them in an uncomfortable, if not, embarrassing position.

“It cuts off your circulation if the bag is heavy and sitting on your legs,” said Valerie Best, a 77-year-old RIDE customer who lives in Mattapan. “Once the bag fell and my packages were rolling up and down the aisle. Just talking about it — it almost brings me to tears.”

While RIDE drivers are still allowed to assist riders, they are limited to items up to 15 pounds that can be carried “in one arm and in one trip.”

The Massachusetts Senior Action Council met with MBTA officials several times and demonstrated how the policy leaves riders cramped. But advocates say their calls to reverse the most restrictive rules had largely gone unheard.

After the demonstration at the July T board meeting, general manager Phillip Eng said the policy will be reviewed in the coming weeks. T board member Chanda Smart said the potential worst-case scenario for RIDE customers — being left without a ride home — is “unacceptable.”

Maya Bingaman, a T spokesperson, said in a statement the agency is “exploring several options that strike a balance between transporting customers and their items, maintaining safety, and operating a high quality, efficient transportation system.”

The RIDE charges either $3.35 or $5.60 for eligible riders from 58 communities. Its service has long been plagued by issues with contractors and staffing shortages, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic. Wait-times were long, and drivers often arrived late or canceled altogether, the Globe reported.

T data show that on-time performance has improved and now is up to 98 percent. The RIDE last summer also rolled out a new online booking service the T says will help make it more efficient.

“It’s never been a perfect service,” said Carolyn Villers, an organizer with the Massachusetts Senior Action Council. But, she said, the RIDE is a lifeline for its riders who need to get to senior centers, dialysis appointments, and social visits to friends and family, especially as many food assistance programs and other welfare benefits face federal cuts.

“People were blindsided by this rule,” Villers said. “At a time when there are cutbacks on safety net programs, the T making it impossible for people to care for themselves in this way is especially troubling.”

Federal paratransit guidance requires drivers to assist people getting on and off vehicles, but whether they should also help with packages and carts is “not specifically addressed,” said Kenneth Shiotani, a senior staff attorney at the National Disability Rights Network. While he “understands” the T policy, he thinks it’s “a little too stringent.”

“Paratransit is by definition slow getting on and slow getting off. They may need extra time and help with even minor levels of packaging,” he said of riders. “Being more flexible” — and allowing riders to carry on larger grocery orders — “makes more sense,” he said.

For Katherine Stearns and her husband, the policy change has quadrupled the Lynn couple’s transportation costs.

She uses a wheelchair, and he has health issues of his own. They take the RIDE to the nearby Market Basket to stock up: They typically fill one foldable cart with food they can store in two freezers and feed them for a month. Now, she said, they have to ride the service about once a week and pay all four times in order to stay within the bag limits. The couple is on a limited income of under $1,200 a month.

“It’s terribly unfair,” Stearns said. At the local Lynn senior center, “everyone is complaining that the RIDE is useless now.”

Nika Lea Tomicic — a transit advocate at the Riders’ Transportation Access Group, a T advisory group — said the policy contradicts the core promise of the RIDE: providing dependable transit service for older and disabled people.

“It’s about not understanding the RIDE user and their perspective as someone who uses this service to have an independent-living style,” she said. The T is “thinking instead that this is some van that scoops folks up and can take as many as possible to maximize efficiency.”

In extreme cases, riders have reported being refused RIDE service for having too many bags, advocates and three riders told the Globe. The T policy says “any customers violating policy will be no-showed and will not be sent another vehicle.”

Elizabeth Gillaspie saw that almost happen. She frequently accompanies a friend suffering from a heart and stomach aneurysm and said they were once turned away from a RIDE vehicle outside a Revere grocery store in September for having too many items — five grocery bags in all.

The T ultimately sent another ride, when her friend “was crying and in tears,” Gillaspie said.

Daniela Depina, who is visually impaired and has been a RIDE user for 22 years, said limiting herself to two grocery bags per ride is difficult for her family of five.

But what’s worse, she said, is that the people who were impacted were scarcely consulted about the policy changes.

“I wish that when this decision was made, they had included persons with disabilities and our seniors,” Depina said. “To eliminate shopping carts and say this is a safety issue, without hearing from us, is wrong.”

title: Sea of Puerto Rican flags, street dancing, and more at Boston’s annual Puerto Rican parade
text:
“Seeing the families and the friends, they all come out and enjoy … It’s like a family reunion,” said Hector Pantoja, 40, a warehouse worker who has come to the event all his life. “[We] love each other.”

The parade is put on every year by The Puerto Rican Festival of Massachusetts, an organization founded in 1967 to promote belonging and cultural affirmation for Puerto Ricans in the area. It serves as the culminating event for the organization’s annual two-day Puerto Rican Festival, which in the past attracted more than 50,000 attendees, according to the organization’s website.

Massachusetts has the fifth-largest Puerto Rican population in the United States, according to 2023 data from the Boston Planning and Development Agency.

Near the front of the parade, just behind a group marching with a welcome sign, a tow truck decorated for Lulu’s Barbershop threw bags of candy towards the crowd. Elsewhere, a man dressed in Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl outfit waved at the crowd. Throughout the procession, several young dance groups, whose members wore long flowing skirts and cheer uniforms, twirled and jumped.

“It is a big deal. It feels like we’re back home,” Christina Colon, 34, a freelance UX/UI designer from Dorchester, said. “Honestly, it’s rough because I feel like Boston is slightly segregated … It does feel good because we don’t see this on a regular basis, especially when you’re at the inner, inner city like, let’s say, downtown.”

She added that this year, the parade seemed to include “more of our culture” such as “the dances, the history of it, some of the up-and-coming artists.”

Local politicians and activists attended the event, too. One group encouraging young people to consider a career in law enforcement marched in black shirts reading “Injustice everywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.”

Another group, standing on the back of a junk removal truck, carried red and black signs reading “No human being is illegal” and “No one is free when others are oppressed.”

Other groups walked in support of political candidates up for election, including a group for Massachusetts treasurer candidate Elizabeth Dionne and a group for Suffolk County district attorney candidate Linda Champion.

For community coordinator Veronica Bowens-Wiggins, 52, from South End, it was nice to see representatives in person rather than through a flier.

“They’re actually trying to give you a small token of who they are personally. And I think that’s important,” she said.

But for Myrna Santana, 50, who has been coming to the parade since childhood, the event was less about politics and more about community enjoyment.

“We always keep politics on the side when it’s [time] to have fun as family, as neighbors. … You just have to have fun as a community,” she said.

As the parade continued, a group of men on horses trotted by. One man pulled his horse to the side to greet three women with their iPhones out, filming, the horse’s nostrils getting up close to the cameras.

At the end of the procession, dozens and dozens of cars drove by, their doors opened or removed entirely— many balanced large speakers on their roofs.

But, even after the parade ended, festivities felt far from over. On building stoops, people sat, blasting music, waving flags, and chatting.

“People are going to be calling out of work tomorrow because it’s going to be a good night,” Jason Rodriguez, 30, from Jamaica Plains, said. “Puerto Ricans are very prideful people, so the fact that the community is this loud and this proud makes sense.”

title: Swimmer who drowned in Milford quarry identified as Boston teenager
text:
The swimmer who drowned over the weekend at a Milford quarry was identified Monday as a Boston teenager.

Yanick Rodrigues, 17, drowned at the Shadowbrook Quarries, while swimming with a friend Saturday, officials said.

His body was recovered on Sunday.

After immigrating from Cape Verde in 2016, Rodrigues attended Madison Park High School in Roxbury, where he was a star soccer player, according to a report by WCVB-TV.

His death comes less than a week after local officials issued a warning about the dangers of the quarries, a popular spot where swimming is forbidden.

On July 19, an 18-year-old woman fell about 12 feet from a ledge onto jagged rocks. The woman, who said she briefly lost consciousness after the fall, was found bleeding in several places, police said. She was flown to UMass Memorial Medical Center for treatment.

“While we’re thankful this incident did not have an even more tragic outcome, it serves as an important reminder that the Quarries are not a safe place for recreation,” Milford’s police chief, Robert Tusino, said in a statement last week.

“The steep rock faces, unstable terrain, and limited access for emergency responders create an extremely dangerous environment where a single misstep can have life-altering consequences for civilians and responders,” he said.

Other swimmers have drowned at quarries in Milford over the years.

In 2014, an 18-year-old from Providencejumped into Fletcher’s Quarry and did not resurface. The teen’s body was found a day later about 70 feet down and 10 feet away from the cliff. At the time, the death was the second at a local quarry since 2007, and the fourth in almost two decades.

Last summer, police said they would be cracking down on trespassing at local quarries by threatening thousands of dollars in fines.

title: Asian lifestyle retailers are reshaping some of Boston’s most coveted shopping districts
text:
These high-profile openings reflect a larger shift in Boston: Concepts that once held appeal mostly among East Asian immigrants, Asian Americans, and other cultural enthusiasts are becoming mainstream.

The new entrants to Boston retail have been urged on by landlords who are eager to revive empty storefronts. And they’re finding an eager audience among a young generation of consumers raised on social media, anime, K-pop, and international cuisine.

“Boston’s retail market definitely needed some new blood,” said Peng Jia, who owns MoreFun, a toy mecca, in Back Bay and Cambridge, with a third location on the way in Allston.

Amy Pei, a Northeastern University marketing professor, said social media has meant global trends travel much more quickly. Instead of encountering skincare from Korea through friends or while traveling abroad, shoppers now see them through influencers — watching videos of skincare regimens, product reviews, and house tours. By the time retail shops open, the demand already exists, she said.

The trend began in Boston, as it has in other cities, with dining. In the late 1800s, an early wave of immigration from China began, establishing Boston’s Chinatown. There, restaurants served familiar dishes to the mostly men who lived and worked in the neighborhood, marking one of the earliest examples of food trends making their way from Asia. Over the past several decades, immigrants and international students have expanded the market for new concepts.

“Food is always the conduit,” said Arnold Byun, the co-founder of MAUM Market, a pop-up featuring dozens of Asian-owned small businesses. “Then comes the retail.”

In recent years, broad consumer curiosity has expanded from food to fashion, art, beauty, and other products. Landlords and retail brokers see it as an opportunity.

“Generally speaking, the retail market is starved for new concepts. So everybody’s very excited to see these new retailers coming to the market,” said Sara Taylor, a partner at Newton-based Blackline Retail Group. She helped broker the deal to get Teso Life to sign a 10-year lease for downtown.

The appetite extends well beyond Boston. Asian food alone in the US is now a $37 billion market, and it’s growing annually, outpacing the broader food sector, according to BDA Partners, a research investment banking advisory firm. Sales of Asian food products in the US are expected to reach $51.3 billion by 2031.

H Mart, which opened its first Boston-area store in 2014 and has become a $2 billion powerhouse, now it has five area supermarkets stretching from Burlington to Quincy. In 2020, 99 Ranch Marketopened in a former Quincy Big Y space, where shoppers can now find about 100 different kinds of soy sauces and live goby fish. Newcomers such as Hashi Market are expanding into Cambridge and Brookline this year, while products that were once considered speciality items — from chili crisp and seaweed snacks to kimchi — have become everyday staples.

Boston’s embrace of Asian cuisines including Vietnamese, Thai, Taiwanese, and Japanese now spans from neighborhood restaurants to Michelin-recognized dining, helping transform areas around Quincy, Cambridge, and Dorchester’s Fields Corner (which is sometimes referred to as “Little Saigon”).

Chef Peter Nguyen is reimagining Vietnamese food at Lê Madeleine in Quincy, while Laurence Louie transformed his family’s Hong Kong bakery into Rubato, a modern café inspired by Cantonese comfort food. Last year, 10 of the 26 local restaurants recognized by the Michelin guide served Asian-inspired food or were Asian-owned.

Boston’s growing appetite for Asian food is what convinced Byun that the city was ready for MAUM Market. The idea first started in 2022 in Los Angeles and then later New York, coming off the pandemic as Byun said he noticed many Asian businesses bubbling up.

At MAUM’s first Boston pop-up last summer, about 6,000 attended in just a few hours. On a recent Sunday, MAUM hosted its second annual market in the Seaport, where 45 local vendors participated, selling goods such as gaming accessories, jewelry, art, plushy anime characters, and ceramics.

Because of the turnout, the company is expanding in Boston, and it is poised to host three pop-ups in 2027, putting it in scope with MAUM’s plans for New York City and Los Angeles.

Pei, at Northeastern, said some consumers associate Korean and Japanese products with quality and innovation, helping explain why demand has persisted beyond fleeting social media trends. “If they weren’t good, this wouldn’t have lasted,” she said.

Cy Kwok, a general manager of Teso Life, said that’s led to a natural broadening of the target market. “People are curious about this culture, and we’re bringing it into the community and educating them.”

Demographic shifts are also expanding the customer base. From 2010 to 2020, Massachusetts residents identifying as Asian grew from 307,000 to 504,000. In recent years, they’re also moving to wealthier suburbs, such as Lexington, where Asian Americans account for a third of the population. Students from Asia also make up a large share of Boston’s international student population. Nationally, Asian Americans represent one of the country’s fastest-growing consumer groups, with roughly $1.4 trillion in buying power, according to global data firm Nielsen.

That growth has also expanded the customer base for businesses selling Asian products, even while retailers are drawing shoppers far beyond Asian immigrant and Asian American communities.

What many of these concepts share is that they ask customers to do more than just shop for goods. At Memory Shop, visitors spend 20 to 30 minutes posing for photos, decorating prints, and hanging out, even though a single photo session itself lasts less than three minutes. At Anime Zakka, also on Newbury Street, rows of gacha toy machines that dispense mystery prizes like quirky miniatures or anime figures encourage customers to linger.

“I think that’s exactly where retail is slowly moving towards,” said Brian Cheung, Memory Shop’s owner. He has two stores now, and is opening a third on Harvard Avenue in Allston, known for its retail options, this summer. “Making shopping feel more like an experience is just something that Asian retailers do the best.”

For years, Boston was an afterthought for many of these concepts, said Byun. Today, entrepreneurs and national chains alike see Boston as a city worth investing in.

“You always heard about LA and New York, but that’s it,” said Byun of MAUM. “Now people are looking way outside of New York.”

“For us,” he added. “We’re doubling down in Boston.”

title: In Milton, a 1929 bank gets a second life as a neighborhood market
text:
“We didn’t really need another restaurant around here... We needed a market like this,” said Kerrigan, who opened Steel & Rye in an old and largely empty auto dealership in 2012.

Perched up on a hill overlooking Dorchester’s Lower Mills, Two Pence Market will be part café, part neighborhood grocer where shoppers can pick up prepared meals, local produce, pantry staples, and fresh pasta. Or they can linger over breakfast, lunch, coffee, or scoops of Toscanini’s Ice Cream before browsing through a collection of wine and spirits to bring home. But behind shelves of groceries is a broader bet that the locally-owned businesses — not the highest-paying commercial tenants — can help revive Milton Village.

Wild, who lives in Milton and owns the building as well as several others that surround the market, said he purchased the property not knowing initially what would go in it.

“Certainly, I have a vision for everything in the Village, and knew that this [building] was kind of the cornerstone, a really important piece,” said Wild, who lives in Milton with his wife and three young children. His vision stretches beyond the market itself; he imagines closing some streets to cars for pop-up markets and other neighborhood events overlooking the Neponset River and Mattapan trolley tracks.

Buying the building before settling on a tenant, he said, was partly about “avoid[ing] it getting in the wrong hands.” He wanted an independent operator, not a national chain.

Instead, they’ll sell goods from local farms, like seasonal greens from the historic Allandale Farm, which dates back to the late 1700s in Chestnut Hill; and strawberries, blueberries, and peaches from Ward’s Berry Farm, a family-owned 175-acre farm in Sharon. They’ll have a self-serve coffee station using coffee from Fazenda Coffee Roasters of Dedham, along with black iced tea, a peach iced tea, and a lemongrass lemonade on draft.

Floral arrangements from Vow & Vine, whose owner creates arrangements out of her home in Dorchester, will line outdoor shelves next to the market’s front door and throughout the market. Fruits and vegetables will be piled up inside an old banking cart the owners found inside an old vault in the basement.

That same vault has been redeveloped into a workable, professional kitchen where they had to cut through 14-inch concrete walls. And they reused as much as they could from the original bank, such as the chandeliers and other lighting that were refurbished and hung from the ceiling.

Banking statements, a flyer advertising safe deposit boxes, and money bags from the early 1900s are framed in a hallway by the bathrooms. The fireplace has been reactivated, and people can lounge around it with coffee or a lunch. An upstairs vault has become “the bottle shop,” where shoppers can browse more than 200 wine labels, some local beer, and 120 spirit brands.

“We’re not looking to be a package store,” said Kerrigan. “We’re really looking to say: Here are three IPAs we love, three pilsners we love, a few non-alcoholic brands... showcasing stuff that’s local or small production.”

Alison Hearn, whose resumé includes Ten Tables in Cambridge, for Barbara Lynch’s restaurants, and Myers & Chang in Boston, will oversee the culinary program alongside Joy.

While shoppers can grab meals and bring them home, they can also order off the menu — filled with smoothies, breakfast sandwiches, farro bowls and poke, soups, and more — and eat them inside or outside on the market’s patio.

And there’s been plenty of buzz and anticipation for Two Pence to open. During a Globe interview with the three owners, neighbors pressed their faces against the front doors while peering inside, trying to catch a glimpse of when it might open. At one point, Larry Moulter, the former chairman of Boston Garden, strolled into the market wandered in with the same question.

Standing outside the restored bank and overlooking Milton Village, Wild gestured toward the market behind him.

“I had another [tenant] that would have paid more in rent... But it’s not about that,” said Wild, while standing outside of the market and looking over the neighborhood. “I believe in building up this Village for the long-term, and I know what’s possible.”

He pointed toward the front doors.

“Opening this,” said Wild, “Is the next step in that vision.”

title: ‘My family, we are all upside down’: Relatives mourn man killed on Boston Common as ‘beautiful son’
text:
“He never got mad, he never said no, he was never getting in people’s face,” Desrosiers said. “None of my boys ever get into an argument where it was heated or to a fight. We were very blessed.”

Sanon was beginning to build a life of his own after moving away from his childhood home to his own apartment in Norwood, Desrosiers said, when he was killed just after 5 a.m. outside the Boylston Green Line station, allegedly by a homeless man with a history of violence and mental health issues.

“My family, we are all upside down,” Desrosiers said, adding he wished he had been with Sanon that day to protect him. “I feel so powerless, because if I was there it would have been a different story.”

Sanon was a graduate of West Roxbury High School who worked various food service jobs and enjoyed playing basketball, Desrosiers said. He last worked at a Moroccan restaurant that closed in 2024 and was living off state assistance, Desrosiers said.

“He was a very helpful man. You have an issue, you need help? He’s going to be the first one to step up,” Desrosiers said. Sanon always called him “Mmai,” he recalled, because he couldn’t pronounce his name properly when he first came to live with him in 2004 after emigrating from Port-au-Prince.

Ashlie A. Jeremie, 27, the man charged with killing Sanon, had reportedly stopped taking the medication he was prescribed for a diagnosis of “bipolar disorder with psychotic features,” prosecutors said at his arraignment last week.

Jeremie was ordered held without bail and sent to Bridgewater State Hospital for a 20-day mental health assessment to determine if he can stand trial.

He had previously been examined by clinicians at Bridgewater last year in connection with an assault and battery case in Dorchester Municipal Court, records show, and had been released into the homeless shelter system from federal custody just 16 days before Sanon’s murder.

It remains unclear what led to the fatal encounter or why Sanon was on the Common so early in the morning.

Just over an hour before the attack, police had been called to Tufts Medical Center to remove Jeremie after he reportedly harassed staff members. Jeremie was later apprehended after assaulting a 21-year-old Boston University student with a stolen jackhammer bit in Chinatown.

For Desrosiers and other grieving relatives, the investigation so far has raised many questions about what happened to Sanon, and why his alleged attacker had been allowed to walk the street.

“They just talk to the same guy and let him go, and the same guy prior has a history of bad stuff,” Desrosiers said. “To me it’s negligence.”

While he had gotten his own place, Sanon lived only a short walk away from his parents’ house in Norwood and remained close with them and his brothers, whom he would talk with every day, Desrosiers said.

But in the week before his death, family members had lost touch with Sanon, who had only recently gotten a cellphone. Desrosiers was in Florida for his mother’s funeral and returned the day before his stepson’s death.

“All that’s a gray area, we don’t know what he was doing,” Desrosiers said, adding his stepson’s attacker was a “completely random person,” unknown to the family.

“For some reason he was so heated, so mad, [that he attacked] whoever was close to him at that time,” Desrosiers said. “Unfortunately, it was my beautiful son Jonathan. He didn’t even have a chance to run, a chance to fight. It could [have] been anybody.”

title: Can the Clancy trial not become a circus?
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Judge William F. Sullivan has a delicate path to walk.

He’s presiding over the high-profile trial of Lindsay Clancy for the killings of her three children. And he does so with the unenviable task of navigating between the public’s long-held right to view court proceedings and the necessity to avoid a circus that could upend them.

Clancy, of Duxbury, does not deny she killed her children, but is pleading not guilty under what’s commonly known as the insanity defense. Her lawyer maintains she should not be held criminally responsible because she was so deep in the throes of postpartum depression and psychosis.

The case has drawn intense attention for the unfathomable crime alleged, and also what it may spotlight about the way the health system treats women and, in particular, mothers.

Harrowing listening

The trial is expected to run as long as two months, and already Sullivan’s balancing act faces two tests. The first is expected to come this morning, when the court will hear the 911 call that Clancy’s husband, Patrick Clancy, made when he arrived home from getting take-out. He found his three children strangled in their basement and his then-wife severely injured following a suicide attempt outside the home.

From prosecutors’ statements and court records, we know the broad strokes: Patrick Clancy stayed on the phone as he first saw Lindsay Clancy, and then still as he discovered his children dead or dying. It will be harrowing listening, if admissible evidence that will give the jury more information about what happened that night in January 2023.

So Sullivan is allowing it to be played in court — but not livestreamed and widely broadcast, as much of the rest of the trial is. Only those present can hear it. The media can report on it, but not record it.

A controlled crime scene

The second test of balance is the jury’s viewing of the Clancys’ former home, expected later in the week. On Tuesday, Sullivan deemed it to be limited to lawyers on both sides, court staff, and the 18-person jury, six of whom will be designated as alternates when deliberations start.

Sullivan also ordered that Duxbury and State Police will be responsible for securing the area before jurors arrive, and for keeping unauthorized “third parties” off the premises during the view. He also decided jurors will be allowed “to visually inspect the outside of the property as well as . . . the basement, all rooms on the first floor, and all rooms on the second floor of the premises.”

They won’t be permitted to “open closet doors, touch any items within the premises, or disturb items,” Sullivan wrote.

This can work. Two years ago, I covered the first trial of Karen Read, the Mansfield woman who was tried twice and ultimately acquitted of the death of her boyfriend, Boston Police officer John O’Keefe. That trial was, if anything, even more closely watched and controversial than this one, driven by claims of police corruption and a coverup.

A break in the circus

In spring 2023, those of us in the media cohort covering the Read trial followed the jury as they were bused to the scene of O’Keefe’s death outside of a Canton home. Police kept us — and some of the non-media spectators who regularly attended the trial — down the street, probably a few hundred feet away as the jurors, attorneys, and even the judge milled about outside the home where O’Keefe’s body was found. A crowd watched from afar, but didn’t interfere.

The trial was a circus, but the crime scene view went fine.

Shelley Murphy and Travis Andersen of Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: The best things to do in and around Boston this weekend
text:
JAWS Courtesy of the Boston Public Library, catch a free screening of 1975’s “Jaws,” directed by Academy Award winner Steven Spielberg and starring Roy Scheider, Robert Shaw, and Richard Dreyfuss. Known for its haunting score composed by the legendary John Williams, as well as its iconic New England setting (the movie was filmed on Martha’s Vineyard), the summer classic screens at BPL’s Charlestown location. July 31, 2 p.m. Free. BPL Charlestown, 179 Main St., Charlestown. bpl.bibliocommons.com — Daisy Levine

PARANORMAL CIRQUE SPECTER In a fusion of cabaret and theater, acrobats, illusionists, and performers bring a paranormal circus show to Boston, presented by Cirque Italia. No one under 13 is permitted at the show, while guests ages 13 to 17 must be accompanied by an adult. July 31-Aug. 3. Tickets start at $20. Suffolk Downs, 525 William F. McClellan Highway, East Boston. paranormalcirque.com — Janira Skrbkova

RAT CITY ARTS FESTIVAL A grassroots celebration of local artists, poets, and musicians returns to the Allston-Brighton area for its fifth year while also promoting neighborhood rodent mitigation. The lineup includes nu metal band Cheem and alternative rock band Makeout Palace. Aug. 1, 3-10 p.m. Free. Charles River Speedway, 525 Western Ave., Brighton.ratcityartsfestival.com — JS

SOULFUL BLISS Head to the Seaport this weekend for a celebration of music, culture, community, and joy. Organized by Boston-based event agency AfroDesiaCity, relive the R&B sounds of the ’90s and 2000s while enjoying live performances, DJs, art, community storytelling, and artisan markets. Aug. 1, 4-10 p.m. Viaduct Plaza, 9 World Trade Center Ave. afrodesiacity.com/event-details/soulful-bliss-2026-seaport — DL

KEVIN NEALON “Do you know what the most stressful job in the world is?” asks former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Nealon. “Air traffic controller. But not if you don’t take it seriously.” Aug. 1, 7 p.m. $45-$59.The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St. thewilbur.com — Nick A. Zaino III

ESTHER KU Ku started her stand-up career in Boston before appearing on shows like “Girl Code” and “Wild ’N Out.” She doesn’t get back to town often, and she is headlining with a great supporting group in Dan Crohn, Zach Stewart, and Chef Phil. Aug. 1, 9 p.m. $39.90. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, laughboston.com — NZ

ROARING TWENTIES LAWN PARTY Jazz, vintage vendors, and flappers take over Ipswich this weekend, creating a Gatsby-esque 1920s-themed summer bash. On hand will be music, dancing, contests, fashion parades, food and beverage vendors, and more. Aug. 1-2, 2-8 p.m. Tickets start at $52. Castle on the Crane Estate, 290 Argilla Road, Ipswich. roaringtwentieslawnparty.org — DL

DINE OUT BOSTON Meet Boston’s semiannual restaurant week returns this summer featuring multi-course fixed-price lunch and dinner menus across almost 200 participating establishments. Among the hot spots making their Dine Out debuts are Rosa y Marigold, Maple & Ash, and Fallow Kin. Aug. 1-15. Various locations.meetboston.com/dine-out-boston — JS

ZAC BROWN BAND AT FENWAY Joined by special guest Old Crow Medicine Show, Zac Brown Band returns to Fenway Park for the latest stop of its “Love & Fear Tour.” The concert marks the country group’s 15th time playing the beloved ballpark. Read more about the latest concerts coming to the Boston area in this week’s Sound Check column. Aug. 2, 7 p.m. Tickets start at $89. Fenway Park, 4 Jersey St. mlb.com/redsox/tickets/concerts/zac-brown-band — DL

HAVE FUN, BE YOURSELF In 2024, Andrew Mayer brought this one-person show to Edinburgh Fringe; now he is recording it as special. The story centers on Mayer’s struggles to stop resisting his nervousness and just be himself, played out in three dates over the course of six years, and the relief he felt at the end of that process.Aug. 2, 7 p.m. $20-$25. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. therockwell.org — NZ

TANGLEWOOD This weekend’s flagship event at Tanglewood is surely Saturday’s semi-staged performance of Mozart’s madcap “The Marriage of Figaro,” featuring music director Andris Nelsons on the podium, and an ensemble cast including baritone Michael Sumuel as Figaro, Nikola Hillebrand as Susanna, and Hanna-Elisabeth Müller as the Countess; in the director’s chair is James Darrah Black, who also stage-directed the Handel and Haydn Society’s excellent 2022 “Figaro” at Symphony Hall. Friday evening, Finnish composer-conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen visits the podium for a program of Wagner’s Prelude and “Liebestod” from “Tristan and Isolde,” Sibelius’s Symphony No. 7, and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 5, “Emperor,” the latter featuring pianist Yefim Bronfman. Sunday, Nelsons ends his summer stint at Tanglewood with a visit from violinist Joshua Bell, performing Bruch’s “Scottish Fantasy,” and Tuesday afternoon into evening unites all the BSO and Tanglewood-based ensembles — and many more local groups too — as the grounds come alive for Tanglewood on Parade, this year curated by Yo-Yo Ma. Tanglewood, Lenox. 617-266-1200, tanglewood.org

BOSTON LANDMARKS ORCHESTRA Landmarks steps out of its usual Wednesday evening Hatch Shell timeslot this week, traveling to Jamaica Plain and Roxbury to present a program including Max Richter’s recomposition of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” Mozart’s Symphony No. 40, and several shorter pieces by Florence Price, William Grant Still, Gabriela Lena Frank, and Julia Perry. As with everything this orchestra does, attendance is free, but given the limited space of the indoor venues, online registration in advance is recommended. July 31, 7 p.m., Bethel AME Church, 100 Wachusett St., Jamaica Plain. Aug. 1, 3 p.m., Twelfth Baptist Church, 160 Warren St., Roxbury. landmarksorchestra.org

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW Closing this week: The Black Arts Movement came to be in a critical time in 1960s and ’70s America when the civil rights movement had given way to more forceful ideas around Black rights. In Boston, those ideas found root in the African American Masters Artist in Residence Program, founded by the firebrand artist and activist Dana Chandler. This show charts the organization’s long evolution through decades of cultural and racial tumult, and its unwavering devotion to the cause of Black representation. Through Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Closing this week: Spanning almost three millennia, 800 BCE right up till now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across eras to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. Through Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, harvardartmuseums.org

SPRAY: JULES OLITSKI IN THE 1960s Closing soon: Olitski represented the United States at the Venice Biennale in 1966 and was the first living artist ever to have a solo exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1969, but his long-ago star turn hasn’t been as enduring as New York abstract painting peers like Mark Rothko or Jackson Pollock. This exhibition is a chance to wonder why: A showcase of his signature spray-painted canvases from that era, rendered in mesmerizingly loose fogs of color, the show is a rare opportunity to contemplate his fade from renown. Through Aug. 9. Currier Museum, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

DEAD GIRL’S QUINCEAÑERA In the premiere of a dark comedy by Haitian-American playwright and screenwriter Phanésia Pharel (“The Waterfall”), a teenage girl disappears during her quinceañera celebration, triggering an investigation by her three best friends in which they set about “interrogating suspects, spinning increasingly wild theories, and roasting one another along the way,” according to press materials. Directed by Melia Bensussen. Aug. 5-29. Coproduction by Barrington Stage Company, Goodman Theatre, and Hartford Stage. St. Germain Stage, 36 Linden St., Pittsfield. 413-242-6411, barringtonstageco.org

A NEW ERA Miranda Austen ADEkoje’s new play about the Black suffragist movement in 1890s Boston deftly avoids the trap of “message” art by telling a rich story full of complex, conflicted characters. The world premiere production from Company One focuses on the real-life Boston suffragist, journalist, and activist Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin (played here by Patrice Jean-Baptiste) as she tries to build coalitions without sacrificing her ideals. You can feel the ideas crackling as the drama builds. Through Aug. 8. Pay what you can. Strand Theatre, 543 Columbia Road, Dorchester. companyone.org

COMING OUT PERFECT Richard Mercado’s debut YA graphic novel, “Coming Out Perfect,” is autobiographical and extremely poignant, funny, and charming. His previous minicomic, “I Owe It to My Parents to Not Come Out” won accolades, and this more expanded version will win readers’ hearts. He’ll read at All She Wrote Books on Sunday. Aug. 2, 5 p.m. Tickets are on an income-based sliding scale and include a copy of the book. 75 Washington St., Somerville. allshewrotebooks.com

BETRAYAL The three lead performances are as exquisitely controlled as Shana Gozansky’s direction in this fine production of Harold Pinter’s 1978 drama of infidelity, which famously unspools in reverse chronology. In tracing the entwined lives of lovers Jerry (Michael Underhill) and Emma (Liza Giangrande, remarkable once again) and Emma’s husband, Robert (Tanner Efinger), Gozansky does not overdo the famed “Pinter pause.” But she does allow space within Pinter’s characteristically spare dialogue for meaning to take shape between the words as “Betrayal” winds its way backward from 1977 to 1968 in London and Venice. The production reminds us that there’s seldom anything small about Pinter’s small talk. Also featuring invaluable contributions from composer and sound designer Julian Crocamo. Through Aug. 1. Gloucester Stage Company. Natti-Willsky Performance Center, 267 East Main St., Gloucester. 978-281-4433, gloucesterstage.com — Don Aucoin

BUYER & CELLAR Inspired by the strange-but-true fact that Barbra Streisand had a private shopping mall built in a basement on her Malibu estate, this comedy by Jonathan Tolins stars Victor L. Shopov as a struggling actor hired to work at the mall — which has only one customer. Directed by Daniel Bourque. Through Aug. 1. Hub Theatre Company. Club Café, 209 Columbus Ave. hubtheatreboston.org — DA

title: What makes Boston so safe? Black pastors have different theories.
text:
There used to be a homicide in Boston, on average, every 58 hours. A man was found beaten and strangled to death in Savin Hill Park one Saturday afternoon in July, a pregnant woman found shot in the face on Neponset Avenue a few hours later. The year was 1990.

And at the forefront of fighting this vicious scourge of violence were Black clergymen, working with residents, advocates, and police to help bring about a huge dip in street violence, in what was eventually dubbed the Boston Miracle.

Now, more than three decades later, homicides in Boston are down nearly 80 percent from 1990, with fewer shootings and assaults than comparable American cities.

Those statistics beg the question: What makes a city safe?

It’s an inquiry with a multifaceted — and sometimes elusive — answer that keeps local ministers out on the streets on hot July evenings, talking to any stranger who will listen and some who won’t, and meeting with local police and other community leaders to dissect the problem in granular detail.

For Randy Muhammad, the solution to street violence in every era starts with being out on the streets. So on a recent Monday, he approached the type of crowd plenty of people would walk by and avoid eye contact. He sees an opportunity.

The group of men and women were hanging outside Ashmont T station. Some drank beers in brown paper bags, others nips of liquor. One guy rolled a joint. Another wore a balaclava obscuring his face despite the July heat.

Muhammad, senior minister for the Nation of Islam’s Muhammad Mosque No. 11 in Grove Hall, was on an hour-long peace walk through this section of Dorchester with about 30 others. The group walks the streets every Monday night.

“More unites us than divides us,” Muhammad tells those who are here. “We’re an example that we can come together, regardless of what neighborhood you come from.”

Boston, strictly by the numbers, is a safe American city. In 2024, The Economist declared it the safest major city in the nation, a distinction some, though not all, advocates scoff at. After all, if there are still shots being fired on your block, what good is that label?

Muhammad is acutely aware of this.

“It don’t feel safe to everybody,” he said, “but numbers don’t lie.”

This year, those numbers look like this: total shooting incidents in Boston for the year, as of July 19, were at 53, the same tally for the same time frame last year, but below the five-year average of 68. Homicides are down, both year over year and when compared to the five-year average: 13 so far this year, compared to 21 last year over the same period. The five-year average is 17. Those are a fraction of the killings that gripped so many neighborhoods decades ago.

While homicides are also down elsewhere in the US, the number of slayings in Boston is much lower than in cities of comparable size, like Baltimore and Washington, D.C., and much lower than smaller cities like New Orleans.

Among the Black ministers who have done this street-level outreach work, there is little consensus over what has kept street violence in Boston down.

Some credit police engagement with various communities, and the willingness of city officials, nonprofit advocates, and clergy to collaborate and identify shooters and would-be shooters and try to encourage them to choose a different life path.

Some church leaders offer a simple explanation: maybe a critical mass of the really bad guys are locked up or have been rehabilitated.

Others, among 10 clergy interviewed, hail the impact of after-school and extracurricular programming. Some highlight the importance of summer jobs.

“It takes a job to stop a bullet,” said City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, senior pastor of Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church.

Yet others point to gentrification, suggesting that the escalating cost of living may have pushed out some would-be shooters. Some even cite the quality of hospitals, in keeping some gunshot victims from being another murder stat.

Or maybe it’s a combination of all of those factors.

* * *

It was not always this way. In 1990, Boston saw a record-breaking 152 homicides. The driver of that bloodshed was the introduction of crack cocaine in the late 1980s. As that market developed, so did turf-based gangs and the wars that went along with them, according to research from Christopher Winship, a sociology professor at Harvard University.

Boston had a street violence problem, and some people wondered aloud if that level of bloodshed was going to become a permanent reality.

It didn’t. Between 1990 and 1996, homicides in the city dropped about 60 percent. Many city stakeholders believe the decline in violence was driven, at least in part, by Black clergy, according to Harvard research, specifically a consortium of churches known as the Ten-Point Coalition.

Some faith-based leaders participated in Operation Ceasefire, an initiative from the mid-1990s that saw a “fully institutionalized collaboration” among various agencies, including Boston police and outreach workers. It focused on offering gang members ways out, and threatening them with federal sentences in prisons far from their families if they continued to be violent, according to past Globe coverage.

The dip in street violence during the 1990s was eventually called the Boston Miracle, and underpinning it was the street outreach work of Black ministers, who, in working with at-risk youth, “projected a sense of fairness.” Because people trusted them, the Black clergy created “an umbrella of legitimacy for fair and just policing.”

“The police cannot be effective if their activities are not perceived as legitimate by the community,” one of Winship’s research publications stated.

An outgrowth of that effort in the 1990s can still be seen in the basement of Roxbury’s Charles Street AME Church, every Wednesday morning. There, police, including members of the city’s gang unit, probation officers, sheriff’s deputies, representatives from the district attorney’s office, nonprofit staffers, and clergy convene to discuss crime in the city. These weekly meetings have continued since 1998, and some credit the collaboration fostered by such regular communication as helping prevent and mitigate street violence.

“That level of collaboration had never existed anywhere,” said the Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III, pastor at Azusa Christian Community, who founded the weekly meeting during the 1990s and was a leader in the Ten-Point Coalition.

Bishop John M. Borders III, of Morning Star Baptist Church in Mattapan, agrees that cooperation between the political, law enforcement, and pastoral classes of Boston is key. He recalls years in the early 1990s when he would preside over funerals for 25 to 30 murder victims.

“It was a way of life for me,” he said this summer. “It became personally exhausting and I suffered depression as a result of grieving with those families for so many years. So many deaths.”

One of those funerals would become the flashpoint for action and the partnerships lauded by so many in the city. In 1992, a funeral on a Thursday night for a 20-year-old victim of a drive-by shooting was interrupted when a group of young men stabbed a mourner.

Globe coverage of the violence paints a picture of hysteria and chaos: one person was chased through a parking lot and fired several shots from a handgun, one of which went through the open church door and lodged in a wall. Another mourner was pursued by youths up a church aisle toward the altar, almost tripping over the casket before being cornered in an alcove, where the assailants mauled him.

The funeral violence shook Boston, and prompted hundreds of clergy to come together. That spirit of collaboration continues to this day.

“It was the tipping point for the city,” Borders said.

Like Borders, Bishop William E. Dickerson II, senior pastor for Greater Love Tabernacle in Dorchester, has done hundreds of funerals for homicide victims. He grew up in Boston. He knows the city’s history of racism, including a stark racial wealth gap. One doesn’t have to be a scholar to see the link between affluence and reduced levels of street violence.

He has done street-level outreach and is not above getting confrontational to drive his points home, particularly during funeral services.

“You see your boy lying in the casket?” he demonstrated during an interview. “What y’all going to do? Go right back to the block?”

The Rev. Jeffrey Brown, associate pastor at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury and a leader of the Ten-Point Coalition in the 1990s, did street-level ministry work throughout the worst violence of past decades and understood that locking people up was not going to be enough.

Collaboration was key. Sometimes, it meant police allowing clergy to work with gang members to get them on a better track rather than arresting them. Other times, it was city officials securing a job for a young person who was at risk of making some terrible choices.

Brown acknowledged that some people, no matter how they are approached, “are going to do what they’re going to do.” But he estimates that cohort to be a small percentage of those wrapped up in the criminal underground, say 2 to 4 percent.

His message to those embedded in street life was always the same: “The potential of your worth has yet to be seen.”

* * *

Back on the streets of Ashmont, Muhammad, the Nation of Islam minister, is handing out fliers promoting a mediation and conflict resolution hot line.

He’s wearing a bright orange T-shirt emblazoned with a quote from Louis Farrakhan, the Nation of Islam leader who attracted controversy in years past for antisemitic, homophobic, and misogynistic rhetoric. The quote itself is unobjectionable: “Making our communities safe & decent places to live.”

The idea behind events such as the peace walk is to build a rapport with community members, he said. That way, when it comes to disputes that could end in violence, his group can act as a neutral third party.

“We offer an exit ramp,” said Muhammad. Oftentimes, he said, “we’re the only voice of deescalation.”

Muhammad and others will talk to everyone they come across in their walks: men and women, old and young, Black and white. Some cajole strangers to join them on Mondays for the peace walk.

“We have to be vigilant, stay on it,” he said of street violence in Boston. “If you’re not out here being proactive, it just takes an instant . . . it can change.”

Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Death of teenager found in Mattapan rental property owned by Pressley’s husband ruled a homicide
text:
The state medical examiner on Thursday ruled that the death of a teenager who was found July 18 in a Mattapan rental property owned by Representative Ayanna Pressley’s husband was a homicide, police said.

Police also formally identified the victim as Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, 18, of Boston.

No arrests have been made; police officials have said there’s “absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property” on Malta Street.

Pressley and her husband, Conan Harris, live in the Hyde Park section of Boston, according to her website.

“The Boston Police Department Homicide Unit is actively investigating the facts and circumstances surrounding this incident,” officials said in a statement Thursday.

Ocasio’s mother, Elenie Ocasio, previously told Boston 25 News that a perpetrator fatally shot her daughter in an act of domestic violence.

“He put a gun to her head, took my baby in that house, and left her to die,” she told the station.

She had identified her daughter at the time as Yoseliani Marte.

Pressley said in a recent statement that she is “devastated about the death of Yoseliani Marte, an 18-year-old with so many dreams ahead of her, her life cut short by domestic violence.”

Police have released no information about a suspect.

Pressley said that as a parent of a teenager herself, “the thought of a young person violently losing their life in this way is beyond crushing.”

The lawmaker said she stands with “our community and everyone who loved Yoseliani as we grieve this deep loss. May we all honor her life and humanity and extend compassion to her loved ones as they navigate this heartbreaking tragedy.”

Shea Butter Smoothies, a Dorchester juice bar where Marte worked, posted a heartfelt remembrance of her to Facebook on July 20.

“Liani was a brilliant and motivated young lady whose passion and dedication had a profound impact on our team and the work we do,” the business said. “Her innovative ideas, particularly in enhancing Shea Butter Smoothies, brought a unique touch that our customers adored. She approached every project with enthusiasm, creativity, and an unwavering commitment to excellence.”

She also “brought joy and positivity to our workplace. Her infectious laughter, kindness, and willingness to help others made her not just a colleague, but a cherished friend to many,” the post said. “She will be missed immensely, and her legacy will live on in the hearts of those who had the privilege of knowing her.”

To honor her life and support her relatives as they grieve, the business said, “we will be donating 50 percent of the proceeds from every purchase of the Big Papi smoothie to assist with her funeral costs. We encourage our community to join us in this effort, as we remember the beautiful person she was. ... Rest in peace, Yoseliani. You will always be remembered.”

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: A field guide to the Legislature’s last formal sessions, for now
text:
That doesn’t mean Friday will be quiet.

Legislators slapped a lot more on the table Thursday. The House added bills covering road safety, prosthetics, and licenses to the docket for Friday. The Senate passed its version of public records legislation Thursday, and teed up a likely vote on Friday for a bill that supporters say would furtherexpand abortion access. And negotiators checked other items off of their to-do list, striking deals on legislation that would set new standards and protections for home care workers and reshapechild welfare laws.

House Speaker Ron Mariano struck an optimistic-ish note Thursday. “There’s less of a potential for us to be here at 3:30 in the morning like we were last [session],” he told reporters. (The House actually adjourned at 9:19 a.m,. on Aug. 1 in 2024 after an all-night final formal session.)

Still, no one really knows how the day (and night) will go. So for the lobbyists, staffers, lawmakers, and assorted State House denizens settling in for whatever Friday turns into, we put together a list of do’s-and-don’ts to survive the last scheduled formal session.

Do lower your expectations. Waiting on a deal to finally pop on the Legislature’s energy affordability bill? Hoping to see movement on the policy-packed economic development bill? Don’t hold your breath. Lawmakers could reach agreements and vote to pass bills that are already being negotiated behind closed doors, but it’s more likely they spend the next 17 hours (and maybe beyond) getting bills into so-called conference committees instead of pulling almost-finished products out of them.

Don’t lower your caffeine intake.

Do take your time getting to the State House. You probably have time to see a matinee of “The Odyssey.” In IMAX. In Rhode Island. Most of the real action probably won’t start until later in the day.

Don’t make any Friday night plans. Even if they don’t drag things out until 3:30 a.m., on Saturday, Beacon Hill lawmakers have a tendency to start late and end late. And with that in mind …

Do remember that time is an illusion. Technically, legislators have to finish moving things into closed-door negotiations by midnight to keep them in play for the remainder of the two-year session. But time often works differently on the last night of the session, and lawmakers can extend the clock for as long as they want, technically keeping it July 31 until, say, 9:19 a.m. the next day.

Don’t panic if the bill you’re watching doesn’t land on the governor’s desk by Friday night. Lawmakers have until early January to finish work on anything that survives Friday’s deadline — though with the November election looming, there’s plenty of incentive to wrap things up sooner.

Do keep an eye on the more than 1,000 bills that were awaiting action from the House and Senate budget committees as of Thursday.

Don’t expect most of those to pass. While legislative leaders likely will try to get a range of legislation into conference committees so they have more fodder to trade for things they actually want to pass, most of the bills that aren’t already on the move face long odds of surviving this session.

Do take some comfort in knowing the session has to end at some point. Right? RIGHT???

Don’t hit The 21st Amendment until that actually happens.

PRIMARY OBJECTIVES: Leaders We Deserve, the group created by gun control activist David Hogg that helps challengers taking on sitting Democrats, on Thursday dipped into the one of the Legislature’s most closely watched primaries, endorsing Daniel Lander, the former Michelle Wu aide now challenging state Senator William Brownsberger for his Boston-area seat.

Lander is the second Massachusetts candidate the group has gotten behind ahead of the Sept. 1 primary. Leaders We Deserve is also boosting Patrick Roath, the Jamaica Plain attorney challenging US Representative Stephen Lynch in Massachusetts’s Eighth Congressional District. The PAC has spent more than $100,000 on Roath’s behalf so far, according to federal election records.

Hogg’s group has actually put its name behind more state-level candidates than federal ones, according to its website, so far backing more than two dozen state representative and senate hopefuls, some of whom have been successful.

That said, it also wasn’t immediately clear whether the organization would put the same amount of attention and resources behind Lander that Hogg and his PAC have for Roath. On its website, Leaders We Deserve touts Lander as a “problem solver at heart‚” though the praise comes with a flub: The group says he’ll “bring the fight for working people to Springfield.” (The State House, of course, is in Boston.)

ANOTHER ONE: California Representative Ro Khanna is endorsing US Senator Ed Markey for reelection, adding another prominent progressive lawmaker to the 80-year-old incumbent’s list of supporters.

NATURAL RESOURCES: An effort to boost nature, backed by big-money donors, lands in the middle of Mass.’s ballot question mania by Jordan Wolman, CommonWealth Beacon: For one of the most under-the-radar ballot questions of the nine slated to go before voters this fall, the case is pretty simple. A coalition of environmental groups is asking voters to greenlight the innocuous task of setting aside tax revenues that are already collected from the sale of sporting goods and steer them toward conservation.

While leaders of the ballot campaign seem confident that it will enjoy broad support from voters, they have relied on just a handful of very deep-pocketed individuals to get the measure in front of voters in the first place, giving critics a fresh example of the ability of wealthy donors to shape the ballot question process. In fact, it’s powered in large part by one person. Kirsten Waerstad, a Belmont resident who appears to have very little else in the way of political giving, dropped a $800,000 donation to the campaign in September — the third-largest contribution this cycle from an individual donor who isn’t themselves running for office.

ROAD WORK: Wu names longtime City Hall veteran Chris Osgood interim chief of streets by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: Wu is appointing longtime City Hall veteran Chris Osgood to be the city’s new interim chief of streets and lead a department that has grappled since early last year with a broad slowdown of major streets projects, plummeting staff morale, and fierce criticism from transit advocates.

The mayor also announced a group of eight advisors, all of whom have extensive experience in City Hall and transit work, to team with Osgood to determine how to adjust and improve the city’s so-called Streets Cabinet’s operations.

The personnel changes came with separate announcements that the city and the MBTA will begin to host a series of community meetings to gather feedback on an updated design for the overhaul of Blue Hill Avenue — a new proposal that incorporates feedback and concerns raised by some residents over the past three years.

COMMON CONCERNS: Downtown Boston wants more police. The question is how to get them by Irene Rotondo, MassLive: After a series of shootings and a deadly attack near the Boston Common, neighborhood advocates and business leaders are calling for a larger police presence in the downtown area. And while stakeholders agree more officers are needed, whether the Boston Police Department has enough personnel to significantly increase its presence downtown without affecting coverage elsewhere remains to be seen.

CRANE PAIN: Construction costs are creating a backlog of projects stuck in neutral by Grant Welker, Boston Business Journal: Boston is facing both local and worldwide challenges, reaching an especially slow point for new construction. Permitted projects such as the 6-million-square-foot Dorchester Bay City and a 1.8-million-square-foot project on the Mystic River in Charlestown were already seen as unlikely to begin construction this year. And that was before the year began, with a war in Iran and the subsequent spike in fuel costs, along with other challenges.

Death of teenager found in Mattapan rental property owned by Pressley’s husband ruled a homicide by Travis Andersen, The Boston Globe.

Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden says the work is ‘not done’ as he runs for a second term by Amanda Keane, GBH News.

Cerberus, former Steward Health Care private equity owner, settles with creditors by Yogev Toby, The Boston Globe.

Appeals court tosses Covid-era curbside-dining lawsuit by North End restaurants, but throws them one slim possible lifeline via Universal Hub.

Stoughton police chief and town manager placed on paid leave amid allegations of interference and harassment by Bryan Hecht, The Boston Globe.

Why changes to an MBTA bus route are so important for this Boston neighborhood by Will Katcher, MassLive.

Boston to host National Urban Rat Summit this fall by Marc Fortier, NBC10 Boston.

The Dean of Massachusetts mayors by Hallie Claflin, CommonWealth Beacon.
