title: The Globe picked the best things to do in Boston. Here are the spots readers say we missed.
text:
GLOBE MAGAZINE

The Globe picked the best things to do in Boston. Here are the spots readers say we missed.

From bookstores to coffee shops, here are some of our readers’ favorite suggestions.

For a third year running, Globe reporters and correspondents searched for the best Boston has to offer. From bookstores to specialty markets, The Boston Globe’s Best of the Best awards for 2026 highlighted the hottest in a city buzzing with bucket list attractions. In response, we received a myriad of reader reactions: “Really? Aren’t those mostly obvious?” one reader commented on our list of the best things to do around Boston. We focused our picks on Boston, plus neighboring areas including Brookline, Cambridge, and Somerville. But it seems we missed out on some gems farther afield: “Funny how the SouthCoast doesn’t exist at the Globe,” commented another reader on our new list of can’t-miss cultural festivals. We get the message. Here are some of your top picks (comments are lightly edited).

We’re on the same page with readers about these top bookstores.

Get Globe Magazine

An engaging blend of award-winning narrative journalism, opinion, lifestyle, travel, recipes, and advice.

Enter Email

“Beacon Hill Books is a great bookstore that you missed. It also has a cafe in a wonderful setting with a wait list.” Elaine Clark, Danvers

“Beacon Hill Bookstore on Charles Street is certainly worthy of being on the list IMHO.” BostonGnome posted on bostonglobe.com

Details: 71 Charles Street, Boston, 617-945-4713, bhbooks.com

“By contrast, the Grolier Poetry Book Shop feels like it could be the personal library of a sagely old English professor who throws tea parties where you talk about Keats and may or may not have magical powers. Tucked away down a Harvard Square side street, it’s easy to spend a quiet hour there among the floor-to-ceiling shelves, flipping through volumes. The staff are great — they’ve introduced me to a number of titles over the years that have become my favorites, and they’re incredibly dedicated to making the space a locus of community for poetry-lovers. Even if poetry’s a tough sell for you, I’d say go in anyway, take in the atmosphere for a bit, and then ask whoever’s at the counter if they have any recs.” Jeremy Holt, Washington, D.C. (formerly of Watertown)

Details: 6 Plympton Street, Cambridge, 617-547-4648, grolierpoetrybookshop.org

“WHY is the I AM Books bookstore on Salem Street in the North End NEVER on this list? I find that hard to believe. It is a delightful shop and you do NOT have to be Italian to enjoy it OR find something fun to read. They even have a discount section.” Laurel Florio, Boston

Details: 124 Salem Street, Boston, 617-530-1106, iambooksboston.com

“The MIT Press Bookstore in Kendall Square is a veritable candy-shop of eclectic small-press and university-press titles that it’s hard to come across elsewhere and which collectively embody that very MIT spirit of bold, slightly madcap creativity and play. If there’s any place that can inspire you, as it did me, to impulse-buy a critical anthropology of house parties or a history of UFOs in world culture, it’s here.” Jeremy Holt, Washington, D.C. (formerly of Watertown)

Details: 314 Main Street, Cambridge, 617- 253-5249, mitpressbookstore.mit.edu

Details: 338 Newbury Street, Boston, 617-267-8688, tridentbookscafe.com

Start your morning out right at one of these local favorite coffee shops.

“Cannonball Cafe!! An amazing spot for coffee, matcha, smoothies, and daily fresh baked goods. It’s a must-stop for me on the way to work or on weekends if I spy the line isn’t too long. The creativity of the owner, Rachel, and the deliciousness of the drinks cannot be topped.” Cheryl Hall, Boston

Details: 383 Dorchester Avenue, Boston, 617-910-5533, cannonballcafe.com

“Nine Bar in Somerville makes great lattes! (And Somerville could use more coffeehouse choices!)” this is my name posted on bostonglobe.com

Details: 11 Holland Street, Somerville, 617-764-1915

“Phin Coffee House on High Street downtown is a top 5er missing from this list imo. Their citrus espresso alone gets them there, although everything they do is perfect. Highly recommended.” Kntmssnr posted on bostonglobe.com

Details: 10 High Street, Boston, 617-500-9150, phincoffeehouse.com

Find exactly what you bargained for with these reader-recommended thrift stores.

“Lighthouse Thrift. Enjoy the beach and great thrifting!” vintagewear posted on bostonglobe.com

Details: 126 Bridge Road, Salisbury, 978-465-1141, lighthousethrift.org

“Marblehead has the Magic Hat, GREAT place particularly for clothing as my wife can attest. She’s found so many great items, many with original price tags still attached.” JIROW posted on bostonglobe.com

“A big miss from this list is Root for Us Records, now in Newton at the corner of Elliot and Rt. 9. Excellent inventory of new and top-notch used vinyl of all genres. Knowledgeable staff. Very good store … And no, I have no affiliation with the store other than my love of vinyl.” gmfeld37 posted on bostonglobe.com

title: Tips for soaking up the rays and exhaling all that stress
text:
War in Iran, and the high gas prices it has brought, is one place to start. ICE killings and general uncertainty about the direction of the country under President Trump is another. Democracy is being threatened and violence is condoned. Bad news streams 24/7.

Then again, things have been worse. The country was fiercely divided by the bloodshed of the Civil War and the politics and lives lost in Vietnam. The Great Depression brought bread lines before the New Deal.

And, more recently, the COVID-19 pandemic claimed 1.2 million American lives and radically changed how we live and work.

In an unscientific survey, the Globe interviewed folks relaxing outdoors. Maybe something someone says here can help reduce our stress.

Chris Cuddy is barefoot, sitting on a park bench in Marblehead’s Crocker Park reading a book on a Sunday afternoon.

He says that last night he got in a long debate in a café with a friend about Trump and he regrets it.

“He’s just going on and on about Trump and I’m like, ‘dude, I just want to read a book now,’” he says.

“Whether you like him or not, it’s too much,” says Cuddy. who calls the president “a clown.”

But even the book he’s reading “The Typewriter and the Guillotine” by Mark Braude, makes him think of Trump.

It’s about Janet Flanner, a New Yorker writer in Paris sounding the alarm about the rise of fascism before World War II. She profiles German Chancellor Adolf Hitler as a megalomaniac with mystical tendencies and no common sense.

“She starts seeing that this Hitler guy is coming up and he’s up to no good, but no one believes her, so don’t worry about him,’' he says.

Sound familiar?

“I wish he would just go away,” he says of the president.

With that off his chest, he pauses, and gazes out over spectacular Marblehead Harbor.

“I like the children’s laughter and watching the birds. It calms me down,” says Cuddy, a creative director and author of children’s books. “And I like random conversations like this. It makes you realize this is what life is about.”

Mark Kahn, strumming a guitar at nearby Devereaux Beach, says he watches the news, “as little as possible. I play the guitar, I bike, and I swim.”

Instead of doing an interview, he sings a Frank Zappa song, “Take Your Clothes Off When You Dance.”

He smiles when he sings the lyrics: “There will come a time when every evil that we know will be an evil that we can rise above!”

Joining in the impromptu jam is Joseph Edwin Downy, 2, playing the cymbals. “He’s obsessed with music.” says Emilie Flores, his mother. “He literally will dance to any beat.”

They keep the music turned up and shield him from the bad news on the tube.

“I’m just taking it one thing at a time, one day at a time. Trying to make sure he sees the positive,” she says. “It’s kind of impossible not to have him see something dark but even if he does, we try to at least make sure he’s understanding of it.’’

On Revere Beach, when people ask Richard Salvo, 80, how he reduces stress, he tells them to go fly a kite. Literally.

Salvo, a retired building supply salesman from Saugus, had just launched a half dozen bright kites. He gets them airborne and anchors them in a stake buried in sand. Then relaxes in a beach chair.

“I bring my book, but then I get antsy after a while, so I get up and check my kites … then I go back to reading my book.”

It’s a Chase Fulton spy novel. He’s also a big Trump supporter, one of the 77 million Americans who voted for him in 2024. Salvo still supports him.

“The only thing I blame the president for is he’s not a politician, but he proved that a businessman could run the country better than a politician.”

“What’s ruining the world is social media right now. People will say things they would never say to your face.”

His advice to relax is simple: “Enjoy life,” he says. “And it doesn’t hurt to pray once in a while.”

At Skaket Beach in Orleans, Brian Convery crafts a pair of fire breathing sand dragons with his friend, Ed Foisy. It takes them three hours and then they place flares inside the sculptures’ mouths and light them at sunset.

Convery deliberately sculpts them below the high tide line, so they get swallowed by the ocean. That’s a life lesson, he says.

“Everything is temporary,” he says.

The art encourages conversations and keeps kids away from their iPhones.

“It’s just people saying, ‘wow, I never saw anything like this before.’ It’s fun. And what we are missing is fun.”

In Quincy, Erica Norman, a jewelry store manager, runs through a tunnel of trees along the city’s riverwalk next to the Neponset. She’s listening to Billy Joel sing “We Didn’t Start the Fire” with its chorus, “It was always burning since the world’s been turning.”

But she believes people are nastier these days.

“There’s terrible people out there getting brainwashed left and right, and you just want to find people that are like-minded. You can’t get away from it so running is just a way to clear my head.”

Keith Jones, 61, of Concord loves to bike to Walden Pond and swim in its warm, gentle waters.

He says he channels the pond’s onetime neighbor, Henry David Thoreau, but is not very optimistic for our future.

“I don’t think human beings can fix a broken world,” he says.

He is also concerned about AI. “We evolved from an agrarian society to an industrial society. Now we’re a technical society where machines are starting to do work for us and think for us. And what will that do to the human species is a complete unknown.”

A recovering addict, he’s gone back to school to be an addiction counselor “to offer people hope,” he says. “Life is stressful. It’s ebbs and flows. And I’ve lived long enough to know that with every trough, there’s going to be a peak. … It’s one of life’s lessons,” he says.

title: Independent restaurants keep closing. Boston, make it stop.
text:
Restaurants close, as surely as they open. The closing of these particular restaurants feels notable. They are successful. They helped turn their corner of the South End into a dining destination. They’ve been open for a decade, with loyal followings. And they are run by one of Boston’s strongest, most-experienced hospitality teams — the kind of people who pay back investors and give back to the community.

If the bottom line doesn’t work for them, who can it work for?

Boston dining feels as if it has reached a tipping point. This is a city where a liquor license can sell for more than half a million dollars. Rent and other expenses keep rising while thin margins narrow further. The cost of ingredients fluctuates so dramatically, restaurants can’t update their menu prices fast enough to keep up. And well-known, well-funded out-of-town businesses — Cactus Club Cafe (Canada), Hawksmoor (London), Major Food Group (New York), Union Square Hospitality Group (New York) — are moving in at a rapid rate, replicating concepts that already exist elsewhere.

They see Boston as an opportunity. Developers and landlords see them as a good bet. Small, local, independent restaurants keep fighting. Over the last year, in fact, they’ve noticeably upped their game — perhaps in response to the presence of the Michelin Guide, which included Boston for the first time in 2025. But the landscape is much more challenging than it was when places like Biba, Clio, Hamersley’s Bistro, L’Espalier, Olives, Radius, Rialto, and so many others flourished here.

In March, I received a message from the team behind Nine, the restaurant that took over the former No. 9 Park space in Beacon Hill. “Since opening, we’ve had our share of ups and downs in this economy, but we’re so proud of the team that’s stuck with us through it all,” it read. “It would mean everything to be able to reward that loyalty with a busy, thriving restaurant — especially before the bigger city chains start moving in.” That was not to be. Nine closed in June, after less than a year in business.

A month later, Seaport restaurant Chickadee followed, after eight years at the industrial end of the neighborhood. Another excellent independent restaurant with experienced operators, gone.

“It’s an expensive city to live in, so people are tightening the belt. People are leaving, unfortunately,” said Chickadee chef and co-owner John DaSilva. “The labor shortage, too . . . . With the talent gap and lack of training, it’s almost like we as operators are hiring line cooks as sous chefs and sous chefs as chefs de cuisine.”

Just above us is Portland. Just below us is Providence, home to culinary school Johnson & Wales. Both cities have excellent, interesting dining scenes where independent businesses can thrive. Both offer a lower cost of living and operating.

“We see articles comparing Boston [dining] to Portland and Providence. Often people are putting us at No. 3,” DaSilva said. “Maybe you’re a young cook who went to Johnson & Wales. You used to come to Boston. Now it’s, why would you, when they’re doing cool and interesting [things] in Providence or Portland — or New York? If Boston is almost as expensive, you might as well move to New York and work for the best chefs in the country.”

This doesn’t scream “world-class city.”

When the Michelin Guide announced its results for Boston, 311 Omakase received one star; six restaurants received a Bib Gourmand designation, connoting good value; and 19 restaurants were “recommended.” Even just a decade ago, Michelin would have found many more restaurants to consider. Tourism marketing bureau Meet Boston reportedly spent $1 million to bring the prestigious dining awards here for three years. But if the city isn’t friendly to the kind of restaurants that win those awards, why bother? This year, there wasn’t a single Boston nominee for the James Beard Awards.

Things need to change, before it is too late. Boston’s character is at stake.

That’s not hyperbole. The flavor of a city’s restaurant landscape helps determine the flavor of the city itself. A diverse, risk-taking, high-quality dining scene — a “cool” dining scene — brings in visitors and their dollars. More important, it attracts residents and keeps them here. It makes a city a desirable place to call home. It makes our high residential rents seem more worth it. Restaurants are where we gather, what we line up for, what we follow (almost) as closely as sports. They are the center of our weekend plans and social lives.

It won’t feel like Boston anymore if we can’t say: Hey, want to meet for dim sum in Chinatown, tacos in East Boston, pho in Fields Corner, Haitian food in Mattapan, Italian food in the North End, cocktails in South Boston, dinner in the South End? It won’t feel like Boston anymore if the hot new restaurant is always an outpost of a chain, or another iteration of a dominant restaurant group’s aesthetic, just with different spices.

There are many good landlords in this city, and Lynch and DaSilva stress their strong relationships with theirs. But we cannot count on landlords to prioritize local, independent restaurants without incentive or requirement. We cannot make it solely diners’ responsibility to keep their favorite restaurants in business — especially as dining grows ever more expensive, and diners’ dollars dearer.

We need intentional, concerted plans and policies from the city itself in order to reverse course.

Easier said than done, and Boston is certainly working on it — creating free liquor licenses, starting entrepreneur training programs like the new BizUnlocked, which graduated its first class this summer, and more.

I recently had a rich and lively conversation with City Councilor Brian Worrell about what might help. He spoke of streamlining the notoriously onerous permitting process, making restaurant and transportation hours later, connecting more neighborhoods by rail, including skills like culinary arts in the public school curriculum, creating more cultural districts like Little Saigon in Dorchester, and creating pathways for business owners to purchase their spaces, thus keeping expenses more predictable.

There is a will. There are ways. But the restaurant scene needs to be someone’s priority. Boston has had a food czar and a nightlife czar. It needs a dedicated person to drive change and find solutions, and to work with and coordinate all of the city’s stakeholders, in the name of creating the rich, diverse, soulful, ambitious, exciting, and uniquely Boston restaurant scene the entire city deserves.

Boston needs a restaurant czar.

title: Milton schools aggressively investigate residency. Black students face more scrutiny, records show.
text:
Black students accounted for 12 of the 15 Tucker students investigated during the school year that began in fall 2024.

Across all Milton schools, nearly half the children investigated that year were Black in a town where Black students account for less than 12 percent of enrollment.

And in the previous academic year, more than half of students expelled from Milton schools over residency issues were Black, including nine from Tucker.

Milton’s tactics stand out compared to other school districts. In some cases, the town pays police officers to conduct surveillance of children’s homes, going so far as to inspect the student’s bedroom, as part of residency investigations.

By contrast, officials from seven other local school districts said they do not use police for residency checks.

Milton interim schools Superintendent John Phelan said the town does not target families because of their race but acknowledged that some students have been scrutinized more than others.

“The School Committee and I have considered that there may be any number of factors that contribute to overrepresentation of some groups in residency investigations and removals,” Phelan said in an email.

Camille Sanabria-Cooper, a Black Milton resident with two children in the schools, said the disparate enforcement made her question the town’s commitment to all children.

“Do they really have investment in our Black and Brown kids?” Sanabria-Cooper said. “They deserve the same treatment that other kids have.”

Even a Milton school official questioned the fairness of the town’s tactics after noting that one-quarter of the students expelled during one school year were allowed to reenroll.

“If 25 percent of removals come back to the system,” Vy Vu, Milton’s director of data and analytics, asked in a September 2024 email to then-superintendent Peter Burrows and others, “then is our removal process efficient, accurate, equitable?”

That same month in an email to school officials, a parent whose son was expelled that same month expressed disbelief.

“I am a tax paying resident of Milton,” the parent wrote. “What does this say about the culture of our school?”

Massachusetts schools are funded in part by local taxes and state law allows officials to expel children who do not live in a school district, which are generally defined by municipal boundaries. In Milton, the residency requirement is enforced by the school registrar and two Milton police officers who work as school resource officers during the academic year.

Phelan and School Committee Chairperson Mark Loring declined interview requests. In a statement, Phelan said he would not address how residency investigations were handled prior to his appointment in June 2025.

In his statement, Phelan said he has been personally involved in every residency case during his tenure to ensure fairness.

The records provided by the town show that since Phelan took charge, officials stopped tracking the race and other characteristics of students investigated. That made it impossible to determine whether children were scrutinized equitably.

Better data collection is a top priority, said Phelan, adding that a staffer was hired to help families navigate the process and avoid unnecessary investigations.

During Phelan’s first year, Milton conducted at least 32 residency investigations, five involving police. Ten students have been expelled. And since 2022, Milton police officers have been involved in at least 33 residency investigations, according to town records.

Police Chief John King also declined to be interviewed and would not make his officers available for comment. In an email, King said the two officers work full time for schools when they are open and are otherwise assigned to the Police Department. The officers are each paid roughly $125,000 annually, which includes almost $15,000 to serve as school resource officers, according to King and Milton payroll records.

When assigned to the schools, the officers conduct surveillance and home visits for residency investigations. But King said that for that work they do not wear police uniforms or drive cruisers.

“They do not use police equipment,” King said. “They identify as working for the schools.”

But a Black mother of a Milton student disputed King’s account. The mother resides outside Milton, but her child lives with a grandparent in town and attends Milton schools. She spoke on the condition of anonymity because she feared retaliation.

In 2022, a Milton police officer in full uniform arrived in a marked cruiser to conduct a home residency check at the grandmother’s house, she said.

It lasted less than five minutes: She showed the officer her son’s bedroom, and the officer left, she said. The officer never presented a warrant, but the mother felt she had no choice but to consent to the search.

“It’s an intimidation tactic,” said the mother, adding, “you feel almost like you’re a criminal, and you haven’t done anything wrong.”

Another former Tucker parent, Jean Ambroise, who is Black and grew up in Milton, said a town police officer searched his home in 2018 to confirm his three children lived there.

Police may surveil families at their homes repeatedly at mealtimes and on weekends, records show. Home visits are typically scheduled with families in advance, according to Superintendent Phelan.

Civil rights watchdogs were alarmed by the practice.

“The district should not be sending an officer to a private home to investigate a civil violation unless they have a warrant supported by probable cause,” said Katy Naples-Mitchell of the American Civil Liberties Union.

The state education department doesn’t track how schools enforce residency requirements, but most districts require parents to submit documents to prove where they live. Many school systems, including Boston and Milton, have tip lines to allow anonymous report violators.

However, school superintendents in the suburbs of Newton and Wellesley said they don’t use police officers to investigate school residency complaints.

And in Needham, Superintendent Daniel Gutekanst estimated his town has had up to 25 residency cases over the last two decades. Police were involved in perhaps two of them, he said.

Like Needham, Newton, and Wellesley, the high-performing schools in Milton have long lured parents of means to the suburbs.

But unlike those communities, Milton does not belong to Metco, a 60-year-old program that buses Boston kids to schools in 33 suburbs. A lawsuit filed in May seeks to expand Metco into more communities as a way to reduce racial segregation, arguing that municipal school district boundaries have created an inequitable education system.

Black Milton parents say it is widely known that enforcement of the residency policy focuses in the vicinity of Tucker Elementary near the Mattapan border.

“Black people are being followed, and it’s happened for many years,” said Somaneh Bouba Diemé, founder of Milton Reckoning. “It’s more harassment for people than anything.”

This fall, Milton schools will begin using new software to match the addresses of enrolled students against current public records. The goal is to ensure that local tax dollars are only paying to educate students who live in Milton.

It was not clear how this change would affect the town’s broader investigative efforts.

Milton, which was once part of Dorchester, has a population of more than 28,000. The town remains inextricably linked to the city: It is home to 4,500 commuters who work in Boston, including more than 300 city employees.

In response to a record request about the school residency policy, Milton released nearly 180 pages of documents, which included emails between administrators and parents, and spreadsheets tracking the cases of individual students. Large sections of the documents were heavily redacted.

The level of detail and the type of information varied widely by year, making it difficult to assess whether the investigations were equitable, according to the records.

When officials did track race, disparities were apparent. In the school year that began in fall 2024, officials scrutinized the residency of 103 students, 47 of them Black and 18 white.

The prior academic year, a spreadsheet tracked characteristics of expelled students that included race, gender, income level, whether they were non-native English speakers, and whether they had special education plans.

That year officials kicked out two dozen children for residency violations: Records show 14 were Black and five white.

Emails suggest the investigations caused tensions among staff and administrators.

“It is certainly difficult enough to do this job and to also have to deal with school personnel upset that I am doing my job,” wrote Sarina Burke, the schools registrar who takes the lead on investigating families, in a January 2022 email.

In an email later that year, then-acting superintendent Janet Sheehan wrote it was a “red flag” that a child whose family had immigrated to the United States was living with an aunt in Milton. A police officer conducted a home visit: The child and her mother both had bedrooms, Burke reported.

The family would be placed on a “residency watch,” wrote Burke, who vowed to “keep this on my radar.”

In November 2024 an investigator for the state Education Department contacted Milton about a parent’s complaint over its residency enforcement. Milton’s director of student services, Danielle Wetmore, objected in an email to a colleague.

“Residency is a local issue, so they should not be interfering,” Wetmore said, writing that the state investigator “is particularly difficult and pushes all complaints through.”

In recent years, school administrators have been under pressure to more vigorously screen students to ensure they are Milton residents. One official, Timothy Lyons, demanded in 2024 that all families face a residency audit.

“I would volunteer time to come and do it myself,” said Lyons, then a member of the Warrant Committee, which helps oversee town finances. “That’s how much I believe we have a problem.”

In 2025, Milton added another verification, so now families must prove residency at the third grade, as well as when they enter the school system and before grades 6, and 9. The town can require documentation from families beyond a signed lease or mortgage statement, photo identification, and a current utility bill.

Historically it has been up to families to establish that they live in town.

“It’s not our job to prove what community the kids live in,” then-superintendent James F. Jette, who is Black, told a colleague in a February 2022 email. “On the contrary, it is their job to prove that the kids live in Milton.”

Katie Johnston of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Man killed in daytime shooting in Dorchester, police say
text:
Police Superintendent Paul McLaughlin told reporters that officers were called to the scene and found a man suffering from multiple gunshot wounds.

The man was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead just before noon, police said.

There were no immediate arrests.

“We’re very early on, less than two hours from that time and still doing a very active investigation,” McLaughlin said. He asked anyone with video or information about the shooting to contact police.

“We have witnesses,” he said. But “We’ll be out here for a while canvassing.”

McLaughlin said the shooting does not appear to be random.

“I don’t believe there’s a danger to the rest of the community,” he said. “This was a situation where [the] parties are known in one way or another.”

Investigators appeared to focus on the steps of an apartment complex, where yellow evidence markers were placed.

Police tape blocked off the road in front of the complex and a liquor store next door.

Hector Acevedo, 47, said he was friends with the person who was shot. He described him as a young man who had emigrated from the Dominican Republic less than two years ago.

Acevedo, who lives in nearby Grove Hall, said that he had hung out with the victim in front of the apartments just a few hours before the shooting.

When Acevedo came back later, he was shocked to learn what had happened.

“I heard a lot of noise, but I didn’t think it was my friend,” Acevedo said as he sat with other neighbors a few doors down from the crime scene. “Maybe they [went after] the wrong person, because [he was] not the kind of person to be a big criminal.”

The man’s death, if ruled a homicide, would be the 19th slaying in the city this year, compared with 22 at this time last year, police said.

On Monday, a person was killed and four others were injured in a shooting outside a Hyde Park restaurant. Oliver C. Derima, 27, of Randolph, has been charged with murder and was ordered held without bail Tuesday.

“Clearly, we’ve had a few incidents recently. We have a lot of detectives assigned to this, and we’ll be looking to put this case together as quickly as we possibly can,” McLaughlin said, referring to Wednesday’s shooting.

“The biggest thing that we look at, especially when it comes to retaliatory violence, is we look to try to get that shooter off the street as quickly as we can,” McLaughlin added.

The shooting occurred not far from the Franklin Park Zoo, one of the city’s most popular destinations.

At the entrance to the zoo , people said the daytime violence was unsettling.

Kathy Foote, of Gloucester, said she was driving to the zoo with her family a few hours earlier when she had to pull over as police cruisers passed by on their way to the scene of the shooting.

“It’s scary, especially when you’re riding through,” Foote said.

Nick Stoico of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Beacon Hill’s biggest defender may be Healey
text:
Collins is facing two Democrats in September, most notably Latoya Gayle, a Michelle Wu-backed activist from Dorchester. Rush is confronting his first primary challenge since winning his Senate seat in 2010, this time from Hyde Park attorney Persis Yu.

Add those to the list of at-risk incumbents Healey is backing this cycle. She has already endorsed state Senator William Brownsberger, a Belmont Democrat facing another Wu-endorsed challenger, Daniel Lander. The governor, according to her campaign, has also lined up behind state Representative Marjorie Decker, who is facing a rematch from Evan MacKay, the Democratic Socialists of America-backed challenger who nearly ousted her in 2024. Earlier this week, Healey endorsed state Representative John Lawn, backing the veteran lawmaker in his primary against Newton City Councilor Alison Leary.

And she’s throwing her support behind state Representative Christine Barber in the crowded race to replace state Senator Patricia Jehlen.

None of those candidates are obvious underdogs, and most are the more moderate picks (relatively speaking) in their respective races. Backing them over insurgent newcomers is also reflective of the realities the Healey is facing in her role as governor. Even if lawmakers occasionally drag their feet on (or ignore) some of her legislative priorities, Healey needs like-minded allies in office in order to get her priorities passed — a circumstance she nodded to in statements Wednesday announcing several of the endorsements.

She said it’s a “privilege to work alongside” Barber. Her administration’s attempts to tackle the state’s high housing costs? She “couldn’t do it without legislative partners” like Collins. And Rush “has been critical in passing laws that help regular people,” she said.

It’s also a notably more cautious approach for the Arlington Democrat, who hasn’t always shied away from political risk. As attorney general, Healey was one of the first high-profile politicians to throw her weight behind Ayanna Pressley in her successful attempt to oust then-US Representative Mike Capuano, a 10-term incumbent.

Four years later, with her own gubernatorial primary all but wrapped up, she deployed her campaign operation to help lift Andrea Campbell to victory in the heated and expensive Democratic primary for attorney general.

Her strategy now sits in sharp contrast to Wu. The Boston mayor spent much of her first term using her political power to elect allies to the city council — which paid off when she needed votes to muscle through priorities or stop proposals in their tracks. Now, she’s seeing just how far that political operation can travel, backing Lander in a district anchored by Boston suburbs and Gayle in another that treads on territory in the city that hasn’t been particularly friendly to her.

Wu is simultaneously escalating a simmering power struggle on Beacon Hill, putting herself on the opposite side of legislative leaders — and now, Healey.

Whether Healey’s endorsements amount to more than a press release remains to be seen. She has a reelection campaign of her own to run, and it’s unclear how much time she’ll devote to, say, appearing at campaign events for legislative allies.

Healey is also notably passing on endorsing in what’s arguably the state’s most closely watched primary: the US Senate contest pitting Senator Ed Markey against Representative Seth Moulton.

“I have respect for both of them,” Healey told WBUR in June, “and that’ll be for the voters of Massachusetts to decide.”

IN OTHER ENDORSEMENT NEWS: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark is endorsing Brownsberger for reelection, the latest Democratic heavyweight to back the veteran state senator’s reelection bid.

The duo have a little bit of history: Brownsberger and Clark squared off in the 2013 scramble for the then-open Fifth Congressional District seat, a Democratic primary that Clark ultimately won. The two had served in the state Senate together for roughly two years to that point.

“Will is one of the most effective legislators I have had the privilege to work alongside,” Clark said in a statement shared by Brownsberger’s campaign. “He shows up, does the work, and never stops fighting for our neighbors.”

CROSSING PARTY LINES: Former governor and NCAA president Charlie Baker is still playing in Massachusetts politics — and not just on the Republican side.

Baker and former lieutenant governor Karyn Polito are headlining a Boston fundraiser for Democratic state Representative Chris Markey next week amid Markey’s run for Bristol County District Attorney, according to an invitation obtained by the Globe.

Markey does have a GOP opponent. Seth Aitken, a Swansea resident and attorney, launched his campaign last summer. But the Dartmouth Democrat and Baker have a history: Markey was one of a handful of Democratic state representatives who endorsed Baker during his successful 2018 reelection campaign.

PROGRE$$IVE CHANGE: Pressley is heading back to her hometown this fall to headline a fundraiser for Citizen Action/Illinois, a public interest group pushing progressive policies in the state.

Ticket prices for the Sept. 18 event in Chicago range from $250 to $10,000, according to a copy of the invite the Globe’s James Pindell got a hold of.

CHECK IT: A lot of accusations were lobbed during Markey and Moulton’s chippy debate Monday. WBUR’s Anthony Brooks fact-checked some of the biggest claims each candidate made — including Moulton’s Epstein files comments.

LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION: Suffolk DA candidates Linda Champion, Rachael Rollins defend their residency ahead of election by Gayla Cawley, Boston Herald: Suffolk DA candidate and Norfolk County homeowner Linda Champion said she moved to Boston in April, but didn’t achieve full occupancy until May. She confirmed to the Herald that she registered her campaign and took out nomination papers to run for Suffolk DA while using her new Hyde Park address before the home was issued an occupancy permit by the City of Boston.

Rachael Rollins, the former Suffolk County district attorney seeking the office again, is listed on the state elections website as being registered at a Roxbury address for the Sept. 1 Democratic primary, though property records show that she has declared her homestead or primary residence in Medford since 2003.

LOWELL REPORT: Massachusetts House primary spotlights Lowell’s growing Cambodian political influence by Trajan Warren, GBH News: In recent years, one Massachusetts House district in Lowell has become a contest of Cambodian leadership. This fall’s primary will be no different. Tara Hong, the 26-year-old incumbent, is a first-term state representative. He ousted state Representative Rady Mom in 2024 after trying to unseat the incumbent two years before, at age 22. But Sokhary Chau could keep Hong from a second term. The 53-year-old, a Lowell city councilor, was the first Cambodian to become mayor of an American city when he was chosen by the Lowell City Council in 2022.

SAFETY FIRST: Downtown attacks prompt civic leaders to hold new meetings on public safety by Jon Chesto, The Boston Globe: The mood seemed cautiously optimistic, maybe even hopeful, when civic and business leaders gathered at Emerson’s Cutler Majestic Theatre to discuss public safety in the downtown last October. The takeaway: Concerted efforts to address everything from shoplifting to drug dealing in Boston’s central business district seemed to be working.

But flash forward nine months, and the same old concerns are reemerging — concerns that could get in the way of ensuring downtown Boston is a thriving residential and commercial hub. Downtown’s prominent stakeholders in government, nonprofits, business, and law enforcement will gather again on Wednesday in the biggest summit to address the issue since that event at the Cutler last fall.

CAM COURTERS: Boston police, district attorney sued over fatal shooting video by Sean Cotter, The Boston Globe: A progressive advocacy group is suing the Suffolk County district attorney’s office and Boston Police Department, seeking the release of impounded video showing a police officer shooting a man to death earlier this year.

Lawyers for Civil Rights is seeking the release of the police body-worn camera footage showing the death of Stephenson King, a 39-year-old man Officer Nicholas O’Malley shot during a traffic stop on March 11 following a reported carjacking. The shooting led to a public outcry for more information — and to criminal charges. The Suffolk DA’s office announced a manslaughter charge against O’Malley less than two weeks after King’s death. It was the first time in three decades a police officer was charged with an on-duty killing.

WU ON STREETS: ‘I am furious’: Wu reflects on city planner killed while cycling, talks about street safety plans by Shannon Larson, The Boston Globe: The death of Louisa Gag, a Roslindale native who was responsible for helping improve roadways and expand city bikes, sparked furor from residents and cycling advocates. They demanded swift action from Wu, who ran for mayor as a champion for transit infrastructure, and said the tragedy could have been prevented.

“I’m never going to get over it,” an emotional Wu said on “Morning Edition” Tuesday. “I will always have Louisa on my heart as long as I am able to do anything to try to fix and improve our community.”

SPOT THE DIFFERENCE: In spring, Cambridge officials turned ShotSpotter off. Now, they’re turning it back on. by Spencer Buell, The Boston Globe: Depending on the audience, it was either a flip-flop under pressure, or a show of humility from elected leaders willing to give the public more say in how decisions are made.

This company should be in Massachusetts by Emma Platoff, The Boston Globe.

Nearly 15 years after student discipline reform, school suspensions in Mass. are falling. Are emergency removals taking their place? by Hallie Claflin, CommonWealth Beacon.

Liberty Junction defends its Springfield courthouse bid in legal filing by Jeanette DeForge, The Republican.

2 hospital operators in talks to take over Norwood Hospital, says Lynch by Priyanka Dayal McCluskey, WBUR.

Advocates frustrated over lawmakers’ failure to pass PFAS legislation by Craig LeMoult, GBH News.

title: Man charged in fatal shooting on Blue Hill Avenue; third murder suspect arrested this week by Boston police
text:
The victim was identified Thursday as Victor Armani Arias Rivera, 20. According to a police report, Huynh showed up outside the house on Blue Hill Avenue asking about a stolen bike. Arias Rivera was among a group of people sitting outside on the steps. Huynh walked up to him and said, “give me the bike, where’s the bike,” according to the report. When the victim denied having it, Huynh shot him twice, then fled the area on a motorcycle, the report says.

“This was a brazen, brutal shooting that took a young man’s life and showed yet again how illegal guns in the hands of people willing to use them are a menace to our city,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Thursday morning, thanking investigators for their recent work.

The shooting marked the 19th homicide in Boston in 2026, compared with 22 at this time last year, police said.

Huynh was held without bail after his arraignment Thursday in Dorchester District Court. A large group of Arias Rivera’s family members attended the hearing, some wiping away tears as prosecutors outlined the case. They left the courthouse without speaking to reporters.

Detectives interviewed his friend, who accompanied Huynh to Blue Hill Avenue on Wednesday morning after he “received a phone call stating that his stolen bike” was in that area, the police report says. The friend told police the bike had been stolen a few days earlier, adding that he agreed to go with Huynh to try and retrieve it.

After they interacted with the people outside and looked around the house for the bike, Huynh “pulled out a gun and shot the victim,” police wrote. Huynh’s friend yelled, “Why did you do that,” according to another witness statement cited in the report.

The friend then called another person and told them about the shooting, according to police. That person called Huynh, told him to turn himself in, and sent an Uber to pick him up in Quincy and bring him to Boston Police Headquarters, according to the report. The person told police that Huynh turned himself in because he “made a bad decision,” the report says.

During a brief interview with detectives, Huynh admitted to the shooting, according to prosecutors. He told police: “I guess I shot somebody ... I just snapped, blacked out,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ashlee Mastrangelo said in court.

Also on Thursday, two men were arraigned in another daytime shooting that took place July 15 on York Street in Dorchester. The victim in that case, Breidy Martinez, was riding a motorized scooter when a gunman opened fire, killing him, according to police. Martinez, 29, died on the scene.

Prosecutors said two men in a Jeep were following Martinez “for a period of time” before the vehicle’s passenger jumped out and fired five rounds, one of which struck him in the back of the head.

Hensly Dominique Jeanty, 32, and Dradae Montissol, 26, both pleaded not guilty and were held without bail. They also appeared Thursday in Dorchester District Court.

Prosecutors haven’t determined who was the driver and who was the shooter — a point raised by Jeanty’s defense attorney, George E. Murphy Jr.

“They don’t know, but here we are — he’s charged with murder,” Murphy said.

Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Kaitlin Tolbert said the issue is “legally immaterial” because the driver “actively participated in following Mr. Martinez” before the shooting took place.

No motive has been disclosed in the case. Authorities also haven’t disclosed any potential relationship between the victim and suspects. Prosecutors said they used traffic cameras to track the Jeep.

The recent gun violence has drawn an outcry from police union leadership and some elected officials who believe the department’s staffing issues are hampering their ability to prevent crime. While acknowledging the uptick, city leaders have noted that violence remains relatively low, especially compared to other major cities.

Earlier this week, a Randolph man pleaded not guilty to murder and related gun charges in a shooting overnight Monday outside a Hyde Park restaurant that left one person dead and four others injured. The suspect, Oliver C. Derima, 27, was among those wounded in gunfire during the chaotic sequence of events. He was ordered held without bail during a court appearance Tuesday.

In another incident, police on Tuesday identified a man who was fatally shot in East Boston over the weekend as Joseph Gabriel Lucas Gomez, 21.

He was found shot in the area of 464 Meridian St. at about 1:24 a.m. on Sunday, police said in a statement.

That shooting came following a violent Fourth of July weekend that left two people dead and 11 others injured in gunfire.

title: What happens to a rural community after its hospital closes?
text:
When Steward Health Care closed Nashoba Valley Medical Center outside of Ayer on Aug. 31, 2024, residents clamored to save it, pushing for its purchase by another hospital operator or for the state to take it over by eminent domain and transfer it to another operator. Some nearby homes still have signs reading “No hospital 2024, No Healey 2026,” expressing the frustration many felt that Governor Maura Healey let it close. But ask many in the region today what should happen to the vacant building, and the response tends to be a shrug. Health care providers and community-based organizations have largely moved on to seeking other ways to fill the health care gaps.

“It’s owned by Apollo,” said Chelsey Patriss, executive director of the Health Equity Partnership of North Central Massachusetts, referring to the New York-based investment firm that acquired the property during Steward’s bankruptcy. “We don’t get to decide what happens with it.”

The loss of the hospital was felt in myriad ways by residents of small towns like Ayer, Pepperell, Shirley, and Groton. It was Ayer’s biggest employer, with around 500 employees, according to Ayer Town Manager Robert Pontbriand, and its closure left the town with between $250,000 and $300,000 less in annual property tax revenue because a vacant hospital is worth less than an operational one. Patriss said residents lost further trust in the health system, with the hospital closure coming less than a year after UMass Memorial Health HealthAlliance-Clinton Hospital in Leominster eliminated its maternity unit.

The biggest concrete impact is on emergency services. Ambulances now have to travel to UMass hospital in Leominster or Emerson Hospital in Concord, each about 15 miles from Nashoba Valley Medical Center. A report by the Nashoba Valley Health Planning Working Group found that as of February 2025, the median emergency medical services transport time in the region had increased from 12 minutes to 17 minutes.

But that metric understates the actual impact in the most affected communities. Ayer Fire Chief Timothy Johnston said the typical time ambulances took between leaving for a call and returning to the station in Ayer went from between 20 and 40 minutes when Nashoba Valley was open to one to two hours after the closure. Johnston said the department had four people working 24/7 before the closure, but as calls took longer, the department relied more on on-call firefighters and mutual aid. Since the closure, the department has received about $1 million in state aid, which it used to buy a paramedic vehicle and hire two more firefighters to work each day shift.

Another lingering impact is the loss of primary care and specialty doctors. While Bookmark Medical, formerly Revere Medical, acquired Steward’s physicians, Patriss said some doctors retired or took jobs elsewhere.

Jenna Montgomery, public health educator for Nashoba Associated Boards of Health, a regional health department that works on behalf of 15 towns’ boards of health, said her father, who lives in Townsend, had a Steward primary care doctor in Townsend. It took him six months to find a new doctor in Sudbury, nearly an hour away.

Montgomery said the boards of health, working with consumer health care advocacy group Health Care for All, held focus groups with residents after the hospital closure and found people were delaying or skipping care. Montgomery said a common refrain was, “I’m not going to doctors’ appointments because I couldn’t be bothered to deal with the logistics to figure it out.”

Providers are working to address these shortages. A big improvement should come when UMass Memorial Health opens a satellite emergency facility in Groton in February 2027 with 16 treatment rooms, imaging, and a helipad and private ambulance to transport people to area hospitals. “A big piece of what we’re doing is to support local EMS crews so they don’t have to make long travel times to other area hospitals,” UMass Medical Center President Justin Precourt said.

Emerson Health President and CEO Christine Schuster said Emerson is rotating more specialists through its Littleton office and adding five new clinicians plus mammography services to a Groton primary care office.

One ongoing problem is transportation. The region has minimal public transit, and most people have cars — but not everyone. Patriss said senior centers that provide rides to older adults have had to turn down requests or eliminate rides to social events or grocery stores to accommodate the need for medical transportation.

A lingering reminder of the hospital loss still sits in Ayer: the hospital’s vacant shell. Although parts of the campus were sold and remain in use as a nursing home and doctors’ offices, the main building is empty. Both UMass Memorial and Emerson Health considered buying the hospital but couldn’t make it work financially.

At the other hospital Steward closed during its bankruptcy, Carney Hospital in Dorchester, developers are advancing a proposal to build housing and a medical building.

The Ayer site is zoned for medical services, and Pontbriand, the town manager, said he hopes the site can be used to serve the region’s growing, aging population. Nashoba Valley Medical Center had a geriatric psychiatric ward, which hasn’t been replaced. It provided medical care to the region’s three prisons. A report by the Nashoba Valley Health Planning Working Group identified an ongoing lack of mental health and addiction services.

The challenge will be finding an operator that can make money there given the cost of removing or renovating the hospital building. “In Boston, there are many more people you might be able to bring to the table to finance a big project like that. It’s hard the farther you get from Boston,” said Amie Shei, president and CEO of the Health Foundation of Central Massachusetts.

Shei said the region’s residents are accustomed to traveling far distances and struggling to access health care. Even before the hospital closure, a Community Health Needs Assessment by the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health found, based on 2022 data, that there are far fewer primary care physicians and mental health providers per capita in the region than in Massachusetts overall. The closure of Nashoba Valley Medical Center made those problems worse. Two years later, finding solutions to help the most vulnerable residents remains a work in process.

Correction: The description of Apollo and how it obtained the property has been corrected.

title: 12-year-old seriously injured while subway surfing on Red Line
text:
A 12-year-old boy was seriously injured after he climbed onto the roof of a Red Line car and attempted to “subway surf” while the train was moving around 1 a.m. Tuesday, according to MBTA Transit Police.

The child boarded the train at the JFK/UMass station in Dorchester just before 1 a.m., said Transit Police Superintendent Richard Sullivan in a statement. He fell off the car and onto the ground shortly after.

The boy sustained a serious but not life-threatening head injury, Sullivan said.

“Our thoughts and prayers are with this child, and it is our sincere hope he makes a full recovery,” he said. “This incident underscores the inherent extreme danger of ‘train surfing.’ It could literally cost you your life.”

Transit Police are continuing to investigate.

Train surfing is a dangerous practice that involves riding on top of speeding trains. In 2014, a teen faced criminal charges after he was seen surfing — and doing a handstand on — the roof of an Orange Line car. More recently, in 2023, a young man was captured on video standing on top of a Red Line car heading toward North Quincy Station as it moved across a bridge.

The thrill-seeking act has risen in popularity among young people in cities nationwide in recent years, spurred on by sensational videos shared on social media. And it has proven deadly. In New York City, five people were killed while subway surfing last year, and a 14-year-old boy was fatally injured in May, ABC News reported.

Shannon Larson can be reached at shannon.larson@globe.com. Follow her @shannonlarson98.

title: Stray puppy has leg amputated after being hit by driver in Dorchester, officials said
text:
A stray puppy that was hit by a car in Dorchester last week had one of her back legs amputated this week and is recovering at a veterinary facility, MSPCA-Angell said.

Lark, a 5-month old Siberian Husky, was hit on Friday evening on Geneva Avenue, officials said. The driver did not stop or report the accident, the animal welfare group said in a statement Tuesday.

Boston Animal Control is investigating.

After the crash, animal control officials brought the dog to Angell Animal Medical Center in Jamaica Plain, where it was treated for severe injuries, including an extensive fracture and “degloving” of her back leg, officials wrote.

After cleaning the dog’s injury, taking X-rays, and putting it on pain medication and antibiotics, officials determined the damage was “too significant for her leg to be saved,” and performed an amputation on Monday, officials said.

Mike Keiley, vice president of animal protection for MSPCA-Angell, said officials are trying to identify Lark’s owner as well as the driver who hit her.

“It’s possible Lark has a family out there who’s been searching for her,” he said. “If that’s the case, we want them to know she’s safe and receiving the care she needs.”

If the dog isn’t claimed within seven days, officials will begin searching for an adopter after she receives medical clearance, Keiley said.

Anyone with information regarding the driver who hit the dog is urged to contact Boston Animal Control at (617) 635-5348, while anyone who thinks they recognize her or may be her owner can contact MSPCA-Angell’s Boston Adoption Center at (617) 522-5055.

Updates on her adoption will be posted to the organization’s website and social media, and interested adopters can contact officials there.

The puppy has “shown us what a fighter she is,” Keiley said. “We’re grateful to give her a chance at the long, happy life she deserves.”

title: The Somerville Theatre celebrates Catherine O’Hara, and more local arts news
text:
It’s been nearly nine months since the death of the much-loved comic actress. The weekend of Aug. 21-23, the Somerville Theatre, in Davis Square, will showcase O’Hara’s antic legacy with screenings of “Beetlejuice” and a selection of “SCTV” greatest hits (Aug. 21), a double feature of “Waiting for Guffman” and “After Hours” — forgot she’s in that one, didn’t you? (Aug. 22), and a double feature of “Best in Show” and “A Mighty Wind” (Aug. 23). That evening, the Crystal Ballroom, in the Somerville building, will host “Catherine O’Hara Tribute: Home for the Holidays (all of them!),” which one participant describes as “a variety show-cum-costume party.” — Mark Feeney

The Boston Public Art Triennial

When life feels weighty, buoyant art is an antidote. On Friday, Aug. 10 artist crystal bi launched “perfect memory,” a Boston Public Art Triennial project, into Dorchester Bay from Carson Beach. Made from bamboo and ethereal fabric, the artwork asks viewers to reflect on lineage: Who dreamed you here, and who are you dreaming into the future? It will be on view off the Harborwalk at Fox Point Pavilion and Boat Dock at University of Massachusetts Boston through Sept. 11. 6- 8 p.m. Registration required. (www.eventbrite.com/e/crystal-bi-perfect-memory-sunset-picnic-and-kayak-tour-umass-boston-tickets-1995789286481)

Get Starting Point

A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday.

Enter Email

And this is heaven: Heather Kapplow’s inflatable installation “Better Angels” pops up at Waterfront Park Aug. 21 and 22,offering grace and sanctuary courtesy of the Triennial. The title echoes Abraham Lincoln’s first inaugural address on the cusp of the Civil War: “We are not enemies, but friends,” he said, and predicted that “the better angels of our nature”would ultimately hold sway.

Pete, Head of Security (Kapplow’s take on Saint Peter) greets visitors at blow-up golden gates and invites them to reflect on their ideals and any obstacles to achieving them. Inside, time spent amid fluffy clouds invites witnessing, sharing, self-reflection, and acceptance.

Finally, there’s “Float,” curator Robin Hauck’s frothy summer show at FPAC Art Space (through Aug. 22), with works by artists such as Adria Arch and Cicely Carew — a drifty respite from a hot and challenging world. — Cate McQuaid

Hitting double figures

In 1976, Leica, the renowned German camera maker, opened the first of what are now 28 galleries worldwide. It opened a Boston branch in September 2016. To celebrate its 10th anniversary, and the galleries’ 50th, Leica Gallery Boston is exhibiting “Community Garden.” It features the work of 13 photographers who’ve shown at the gallery. Among them are Constantine Manos, Mary Ellen Mark, Alex Webb, and Rebecca Norris Webb. Also included are contributions from four emerging photographers: Mav Fernandez, Raphael Lehnen, Artemisia Luk, and AbdoulNasser Mika. “Community Garden” runs from Aug. 14-Oct. 18. Leica Gallery Boston, 74 Arlington St., 857-305-3609, leicagalleryboston.com — Mark Feeney

Mysterious Skin returns

Scott Heim’s “Mysterious Skin” was published in 1995 and quickly became a gen X cult classic, treasured for its honesty, empathy, and eerie beauty. Following two Kansas boys as they mature into adulthood and reckon with the legacy of sexual abuse, the novel established Heim as a master of unsettling landscapes and disturbing events: Kansas, UFOs, New York, AIDS. The movie version, directed by Gregg Araki and starring Joseph Gordon-Levitt, came out in 2004 to rave reviews (the New York Times’s A.O. Scott called it “a gorgeous, heartbreaking and utterly convincing work of art”).

Now the film is being re-released in a 4K restoration, and the book has both a newly released paperback edition and a new unabridged audiobook. Heim, 59, a Kansas native who lives in Roslindale, says the experience is “Surreal! I started writing the book when I was 25, and it’s a huge honor to even have the book in print still, let alone have the film get produced and make an impact. So now to see this ‘new generation’ of fans seeing the movie and making TikToks about it — a lot of whom are younger than I was when I wrote the book — is especially wild, and humbling.” The film opens Friday at the Seaport Alamo, and Heim will introduce it at an event August 25 at Coolidge Corner. — Kate Tuttle

title: ‘The organizing power we need is in this room’: How a local protest music series became a hit
text:
In July, the one-year anniversary was celebrated at the more capacious, newly opened Opera + Community Studios in Boston’s Fort Point neighborhood. The series moves back to the Burren Aug. 18.

“Which Side?” began when Joyce Linehan found herself confronting a second term of President Trump. The famously proactive Linehan — former chief of policy and planning for Mayor Marty Walsh and longtime community organizer with deep roots in the Boston rock scene — faced questions from her set: “What are we gonna do?”

She realized, “For the first time in my life I had absolutely no idea.” (Linehan was recently appointed chief of staff at the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority.)

Linehan now jokes that, in the midst of these discussions, a book fell off its shelf and hit her on the head: “Which Side Are You On? 20th Century American History in 100 Protest Songs,” by James Sullivan, a regular Globe contributor and Emerson College teacher. She had presented Sullivan and his book in the ongoing series of readings in her Ashmont living room.

She had her answer: organize protest-music concerts.

One of the truths that Sullivan and Linehan hold self-evident is that, contrary to common perceptions, protest music is not dead. That, yes, protest songs are still being written. The “Which Side?” events are organized around songs old and new. Six acts are asked to perform two songs each, one cover and one original.

Sometimes, as Sullivan said at July’s event, the “protest” content of a particular song is a matter of context. The first “Which Side?” show opened with guitarist Jon Butcher playing Jimi Hendrix’s hellacious arrangement of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

It’s also a matter of interpretation. At the Fort Point show, Sullivan pointed out that the Falmouth-born Wellesley grad and professor Katharine Lee Bates wrote the poem that became the lyrics to “America the Beautiful” as a patriotic protest, citing the line “God mend thine ev’ry flaw.” There’s also the malleable meaning of “Born in the USA,” depending on who is singing it and for what.

One of the hallmarks of the event has been Sullivan’s role as an ad hoc talent scout. He found the OG’s — four formerly incarcerated men — through his work with Emerson’s prison education program at MCI-Norfolk.

As for performers that Sullivan booked in previous months, he saw the singer Salyse portray Coretta Scott King in the play “Stokely and Martin” at the Multicultural Arts Center in Cambridge, where she sang Billie Holiday’s “Strange Fruit.” At “Which Side?,” she sang “Dog Days Are Over” by Florence + The Machine. He heard the Guatemalan singer-songwriter Mercedes Escobar sing the Staple Singers’ “Freedom Highway” at a Folk Americana Roots Hall of Fame event at the Boch Center. Escobar in turn brought along the octogenarian Kossoy Sisters, identical twins Irene and Ellen, whose involvement in the folk scene goes back to Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie. They sang a haunting a cappella version of the Guthrie favorite “Hobo’s Lullaby.”

Linehan, meanwhile, has drawn on her years as club wrangler to recruit echt-Boston indie artists like the Bags, the Cavedogs, Barrence Whitfield, and Thalia Zedek. The “Which Side?” house band — comprising Boston music scene ringers — is the wryly-named Paid Protestors.

So, what’s the good of singing protest songs in the face of the Trump administration?

“I see this as an organizing exercise,” Linehan told the crowd at Fort Point last month, in keeping with her feelings about the social uses of music. “I don’t know what we’re organizing for, but one of my labor activist friends says, ‘We need to keep that muscle limber, because we’re going to need it at some point.’”

The “Which Side” events include speakers in the breaks between songs. At the July event, those included Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, the ACLU’s Kade Crockford, and Boston lawyer, public policy expert, and civil rights activist Ted Landsmark. There are often less established but nonetheless important speakers, like one man who talked at a previous event about his experience of being unhoused for 14 months. Guests can offer inspiring words of solidarity, or, in the case of Crockford, specific paths of action, like enrolling in the ACLU’s program for training election poll monitors.

At the July event, Linehan allowed that much of the effect provided by “Which Side?” is “therapeutic.”

But the event also gives each attendee a specific “assignment.”

“I want you to meet two people [tonight] that you’ve never met before and talk to them a little about what brings them joy and what makes them anxious,” Linehan said. “Because at some point you’re going to need to know where everybody is; you’re going to need to know who has help to give and who needs help. Because we are a community.”

The final speaker of the night was Landsmark, famously known for a Pulitzer Prize-winning photo by Stanley Forman of Landsmark being attacked by a flag-wielding anti-busing protestor on City Hall Plaza.

Throughout the night, images of the American flag had been shown on a video screen above the stage. At one point, the screen showed the infamous image of the attack on Landsmark.

Landsmark talked about how that photo had embarrassed the city and inspired action, and he talked about the importance of the arts in building community. The image changed to Landsmark smiling on his couch at home with his prize collection of American banjos — “the definitive American musical instrument,” he said — from a recent Globe story by Sullivan.

He told the audience, “All the organizing power we need is in this room.”

WHICH SIDE? A Protest Music Teach-Out

With Damon & Naomi, the Hazel Project, the Croaks, Dom the Composer, Eric Martin, Emily Marvosh, the Paid Protesters. At The Burren, 247 Elm St., Somerville, Tuesday, Aug. 18, 8 p.m. Tickets: Pay what you want ($5 minimum). whichside.boston

title: Dominican Parade and Festival fills Franklin Park with cultural pride
text:
A Dominican flag soared through the air Sunday, leading a parade through Jamaica Plain to celebrate Dominican heritage and culture in New England.

Thousands gathered to cheer on the floats, praise the dancers, and wear Dominican flags as capes at the annual Dominican Parade and Festival. The parade, which ended in Franklin Park, was created to showcase the “vibrant culture and traditions of the Dominican,” according to the website of Casa de la Cultura Dominicana en Boston, the nonprofit that organized the event.

“We’ve been celebrating this event for 40 years,” said Alejandro Guzmán, a youth coordinator for Casa de la Cultura. “Now, we’re trying to develop it and make it a safe place for the community.”

Before the parade officially began at 11 a.m., the celebration was already underway. Loud music played from cars waiting to join the procession, and people danced on the sidewalks.

The streets were draped in the Dominican flag, and people arrived decked out in red, white, and blue. Several people pushed carts selling red, white, and blue items. Others waved beaded necklaces, flags, hats, and towels.

Floats, dancers, advocacy organizations, and cars adorned with bass boosters proceeded along the parade route, winding through the streets. Several groups attended Sunday’s event, including the Consulate General of the Dominican Republic, MeetBoston, a visitor services organization that promotes events around the city, and America’s Food Basket, a grocery store chain co-op. As the groups passed by on their floats, members threw beads and candy into the crowds, while the Boston Public Schools float tossed beach balls that some people bounced along the sidewalk.

“This means a lot,” Guzmán said. ”Not only because I’m part of [Casa de la Cultura Dominicana en Boston], but because I’m Dominican."

He explained that the two main goals for this year’s festival were to enjoy the festival and keep everyone safe.

In recent years, violence has erupted at the festival, and in 2024, five people were shot as the celebration wound down. Ahead of this year’s event, city officials pledged to keep the festival safe.

Scattered among attendees, Boston police could be seen walking around during the event, periodically stopping by the force’s booth and chatting with attendees.

At the festival’s stage, performances throughout the day featured dancers from Latin dance schools, several DJ sets, and Toño Rosario, a Dominican merengue artist.

Rosario was Nicolas Gonzalez’s favorite performance of the day. Gonzalez was behind a booth selling flavored drinks in cups that resembled pineapples and skulls.

“We’ve been doing [our business] for almost 10 years,” said Gonzalez, who runs Tropicana Prestige, a frozen juice vendor. This year’s festival was his sixth time selling the drinks, which come in four different flavors.

“My mom and dad used to make these drinks,” he said. “And then it was my turn to work.”

Just a few booths down, Juan Marte was selling a variety of tequeños, arepas, and hot dogs. Marte owns Don Tequeño y Doña Arepa, a Venezuelan and Dominican Latin restaurant with locations in Dorchester and Jamaica Plain.

The couple started their business from their home during the COVID-19 pandemic, and Sunday’s event marked the restaurant’s first time selling food at the festival.

“We were so surprised to see how much the community was welcoming of something new in the city,” he said.

As the day carried on, Latin music filled the air while people relaxed on the grass. Near the front of the stage, some people danced to the music as a few kids kicked a soccer ball around nearby.

When a new performer took the stage, the crowd erupted in cheers, coupled with the revving of motorcycle engines as people popped wheelies and raced down a side street.

“When you see all the people, not just the Dominican people, when you see everybody on the streets, appreciate the culture that makes you feel something on the inside,” Guzmán said.

Katie Cressman can be reached at katherine.cressman@globe.com.

title: Clementina Chéry: ‘Every homicide creates a ripple effect’
text:
Thank you for highlighting the contributions of Boston’s ministerial community to public safety (“Decades on, a constant voice for peace,” Page A1, Aug. 2).

As the mother of Louis D. Brown, my 15-year-old son murdered in Dorchester in 1993, I lived this history. Boston recorded 152 homicides in 1990. By 1996, that number had fallen to 61, and juvenile homicides declined dramatically. This progress grew from partnerships among clergy, police, prosecutors, probation, public health officials, community organizations, youth, and families, and included implementation of the Louis D. Brown Peace Curriculum in Boston schools.

That history matters today.

But numbers tell only part of the story. Every homicide creates a ripple effect, expanding the circle of trauma to parents, children, spouses, siblings, grandparents, friends, neighbors, and others whose lives are forever changed.

Our response to violence must include a survivor-centered focus that recognizes healing — of individuals, families, and communities — as essential to interrupting cycles of violence that plague our neighborhoods. This involves faithfully supporting those affected by violence throughout the criminal justice process and beyond, engaging community members to discourage retaliation, and showing survivors that their loved ones’ lives mattered.

Prevention, intervention, enforcement, and faith partnerships matter. So does healing. A survivor-centered homicide response is a necessary component of public safety.

Chaplain Clementina Chéry

President and chief executive officer

Louis D. Brown Peace Institute

Dorchester

title: Here’s how the money came together to fund the Boston Fed report on economic inequity
text:
Several sponsors that had approached the Fed made it happen. The Barr Foundation kicked in $1.3 million, while The Boston Foundation provided $450,000 and handled the contract with Mathematica, according to Keith Mahoney at TBF. The Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce and Eastern Bank each chipped in $250,000. Mahoney also said a city resiliency fund established by then-mayor Marty Walsh with private donations during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic provided another $65,000.

The bottom line: Things haven’t changed all that much from 2015. The wealth gap remains huge between white ($549,000 in net wealth) and Black families ($7,800), though it’s even more pronounced when comparing homeowners ($790,000) to renters ($1,500), or households led by Latinos ($1,200) to white families.

“We were not expecting the report would yield different results in terms of inequity,” said Eastern executive chair Bob Rivers. “I’m fine with updating the study ... to give it more credibility but believed the answers were going to be fundamentally the same.”

Jim Rooney, chief executive of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, said the report’s findings reinforced that homeownership is a big driver of wealth here, and making it easier for people to achieve that should remain a chamber priority. “Do we need yet another reason to double down on housing production?” Rooney said.

The work, to some extent, can be traced back to a 2015 meeting at McKenna’s in Savin Hill between Rooney and Walsh. Over breakfast, they lamented Boston’s racial wealth gap and vowed to put City Hall and the chamber to work to address it. Walsh, for example, then brought on Karilyn Crockett as the city’s first chief of equity. And Rooney later launched the Pacesetters program connecting small-business contractors with large enterprises in need of their services.

Separately, the 2015 report spurred civic leaders to create the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts and prompted Eastern to launch a business equity fund through its foundation.

Through it all, though, the hope for more thorough research continued. Finally, following the racial reckoning and the Black Lives Matter protests early in the pandemic, the Boston Fed and the report sponsors got to work in 2022. By that point, Crockett had left City Hall to teach at MIT, and was working with the chamber on a consulting basis.

The initial budget for the report was set at $1.5 million. But costs grew as the parameters expanded, and both the Barr and Boston foundations kicked in more money.

“The fact there were more than 5,000 households that participated in this, that’s a great indication of people’s willingness to share their personal and financial data,” Crockett said. “We now have a snapshot of how households are doing in terms of their wealth, in terms of their economic status.”

Lee Pelton had also made a push for the 2015 report to be revisited after he became president of The Boston Foundation in 2021. The timing of the report’s release is good for Pelton, as he plan to retire at the end of this month, though Mahoney says it’s purely a coincidence.

The big question hanging over everyone: What’s next?

Rivers, for one, can’t help but admit frustration that more hasn’t been done to address wealth inequity since the 2015 report. He hopes this time will be different.

“I think the last time we missed the moment,” Rivers said. “We shouldn’t miss the moment again.”
