title: Sosik leads Hometown Financial, the state’s fastest growing bank, to new heights
text:
Next up: completing the purchase of Primary Bank in New Hampshire, Hometown Financial’s ninth acquisition in the past 10 years, while preparing to convert from a mutual bank to a shareholder-owned one in early 2027. Hometown Financial’s depositors will be able to buy shares before the general public, and some of the newfound capital will be used for the Primary purchase.

“You’ve got this industry that has very low margins,” Sosik said. “Scale becomes absolutely critical. . . . While margins were shrinking, expenses have been rising, in some cases dramatically.”

Mergers, Sosik adds, allow the bank to broaden its footprint and community impact. “It’s about us wanting to be here for a very long time to serve our communities,” Sosik said.

TruNorth will have about $7 billion in assets, before Primary’s $700 million-plus gets factored in. That’s around four times the combined assets in 2015 when Hometown Bank and Easthampton Savings Bank came together under Hometown Financial.

Sosik got his start by joining the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. as a bank examiner after graduating from Bentley in the early 1990s. Several years later, the board at a small bank that eventually became Hometown Bank was looking for a new chief executive, and recruited him for the job. Sosik moved to Easthampton Savings in 2013 and from there started building Hometown Financial through a series of mergers and acquisitions.

State law requires banks that convert to public ownership wait for three years before they can be sold. Sosik said he has no intention of selling as soon as he is legally able, as other community banks have done.

“We have a very different mission here,” Sosik said. “Ours is to continue to grow the company and be here for our communities for a long time.”

The 2015 report highlighting wealth inequities between Black and white households in the area sure got Boston talking.

The finding from the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston that the typical household led by a US-born Black person had $8 in wealth compared to nearly $250,000 for white households was a stark illustration of the disparity. But it wasn’t great statistical science: The poll included only around 70 US-born Black households, and about 400 in total.

Last week, the Boston Fed released a more substantial report involving 5,000-plus households across the state. To pull it off, the Fed needed $2.3 million for the survey work by consultancy Mathematica.

Several sponsors made it happen. The Barr Foundation contributed $1.3 million, while The Boston Foundation provided $450,000 and handled the contract with Mathematica, according to Keith Mahoney at TBF. The Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce and Eastern Bank each chipped in $250,000. Mahoney also said a city resiliency fund established by then-Mayor Marty Walsh with private donations during the COVID-19 pandemic provided another $65,000.

Things haven’t changed all that much from 2015. The wealth gap remains huge between white ($549,000 in median net wealth) and Black families ($7,800), though it’s even more pronounced when comparing homeowners of all races ($790,000) to renters ($1,500).

“I [was] fine with updating the study . . . to give it more credibility, but believed the answers were going to be fundamentally the same,” Eastern executive chair Bob Rivers said.

Greater Boston Chamber chief executive Jim Rooney said the new report underscores how homeownership is a big driver of wealth, and that making it easier for people to buy a home should remain a chamber priority.

The discussions, to some extent, can be traced back to a 2015 meeting at McKenna’s Cafe in Savin Hill between Rooney and Walsh. There, they lamented Boston’s wealth gap and vowed to address it. Walsh brought on Karilyn Crockett as the city’s first chief of equity, for example, and Rooney launched a program connecting small-business contractors with large enterprises in need of their services. The 2015 report also led to the creation of the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts and prompted Eastern to launch a business equity fund.

The hope for more thorough research continued. Finally, following the Black Lives Matter protests early in the pandemic, the Boston Fed and report sponsors got to work. By that point, Crockett had left City Hall to teach at MIT, and was working with the chamber on a consulting basis.

The report’s initial budget was $1.5 million. But costs grew as parameters expanded; the Barr and Boston foundations kicked in more money.

It represents good timing for Lee Pelton, who pushed for updated Fed research after becoming president of The Boston Foundation in 2021. Pelton is about to retire, though Mahoney said the report’s release during his last month is just coincidental.

So what’s next?

“I think the last time we missed the moment,” Rivers said. “We shouldn’t miss the moment again.”

Form Energy is ushering in C-suite changes along with a massive round of equity investments.

Last week, Somerville-based Form announced it had secured $750 million, in part to help power the expansion of its factory in Weirton, West Virginia, where it makes utility-scale batteries and is racking up orders.

Form also said it has a new chief financial officer, Navneet Govil, replacing Charlotte Beard (who left last year), and a new chief operating officer, Wes Sloan. Form president Ted Wiley also had been the operating chief, but will relinquish that title to Sloan. Govil most recently worked at SoftBank Investment Advisers, while Sloan joins from Panasonic Energy Corp. of North America.

The C-suite now is spread across Form’s three main locations: Somerville, Weirton, and Berkeley, Calif. Chief executive Mateo Jaramillo is primarily based in West Virginia, and Sloan will be there, too. Govil will work out of the Berkeley office.

Meanwhile, the leadership team based in Somerville includes Wiley, Billy Woodford (chief technology officer), Yet-Ming Chiang (chief science officer), and Marco Ferrara (chief digital officer). Woodford, Wiley, and Jaramillo spend time at all three locations.

Pete Frates died seven years ago from ALS, but the need to raise money toward the goal he’s best known for — that elusive cure — has not abated at all.

It’s why NWN, a fast-growing IT provider based in Boston, took up the cause. Chief marketing officer Andrew Gilman said he met with Frates’ parents about four years ago, as well as with writer Casey Sherman, to explore ways to highlight the “Ice Bucket Challenge” that is now synonymous with ALS. They wanted to bring the fund-raising initiative back into the public eye, after it subsided following Frates’s death.

They were eyeing the 10-year anniversary of when Frates, Pat Quinn of New York, and friends took the original “challenge” viral to raise money for ALS research. The 2024 anniversary event ended up happening at Fenway Park, featuring Governor Maura Healey and Red Sox president Sam Kennedy, thanks in part to NWN’s sponsorship. The company also sponsored the installation of a Pete Frates exhibit at the TD Garden’s Sports Museum last year.

Now, NWN is at it again, sponsoring a live reading of Sherman’s feature film script about Frates, based on a book Sherman co-authored with Dave Wedge. The event, hosted by comedian Lenny Clarke, took place on Monday night at the Willowbend golf club in Mashpee. Sherman hopes to generate donations and awareness for the Pete Frates Foundation. (Sherman is currently shopping the movie concept around to potential studios and directors.)

“It’s important that we find new ways to engage in the community to keep the fight in the forefront and to continue to raise funds . . . and to keep Pete’s memory alive,” Gilman said. “This is the beginning of a Hollywood moment for something that inspired the world when it first came out 12 years ago.”

title: The chef behind Dorchester’s cult-favorite Italian restaurant is opening a second café and wine bar
text:
The expansion comes as Boston’s Italian restaurant scene is getting bigger and more corporate, while Quaresima is purposefully small and entirely self-funded. The new restaurant is also the product of an unusually community-driven process, with the landlord asking neighbors to weigh in on what should fill a vacant storefront.

“I really want to create a space outside with some tables and chairs, like a small bistro you’d find in Paris. That’s the picture I’ve had in my mind,” said Quaresima in an exclusive interview with the Globe.

The empty storefront wasn’t simply another vacancy that Quaresima happened to stumble upon, despite looking for the past year for the right space for a second location. Its landlord, developer and Dorchester resident Travis Lee, saw an opportunity to bring in another local operator when his longtime tenant closed in June. Over the years, he’s made a practice of asking community members and neighbors what they want in the storefronts he owns, and, in some cases, letting them help him decide who actually moves in.

When the roughly 1,000-square-foot storefront became available, Lee said he circulated the opportunity among people in his network and heard from five interested parties, including Quaresima and a mother-daughter team behind the concept of Café Bleu. After interviewing the candidates, he narrowed the field to Quaresima and Café Bleu and asked people to weigh in.

Lee’s approach is unusual in a city where commercial real estate is often a costly numbers game, and where many independent restaurants can’t survive — let alone open a second location — because of the high rent costs for a business that already has such thin margins.

“I think it’s the right thing to bring people that live and have invested themselves into a specific geographic community into the process,” said Lee. “But I also think it’s good business.”

Lee’s model has produced a string of neighborhood businesses, which included the now-shuttered 50 Kitchen, Fresh Food Generation, the store Just Bookish, and more.

For this prominent corner location in the historic Lenane building, the neighborhood’s newest restaurant will be a second outpost from one of Dorchester’s most exciting culinary names. For Lee, that meant betting on a chef whose first restaurant had already demonstrated that the neighborhood would show up for him and fill his seats.

Over Easter weekend in 2023, Quaresima opened Via Cannuccia, naming it after his childhood street just south of Rome in the seaside town of Anzio. He’s built a career working in restaurants in Italy and France and came to the United States in 2013 to work at Petit Robert Bistro, a Parisian-style bistro in the South End.

Since striking out on his own in Dorchester — a neighborhood with a food culture shaped by generations of Irish, Cantonese, and Vietnamese immigrants — Quaresima quickly developed a particularly loyal following among restaurant professionals. On their days off, chefs, servers, and bartenders from across the city regularly fill the tables at Via Cannuccia, eating Italian food that hasn’t been Americanized. “I don’t put meatballs on top of spaghetti, and I won’t ever put chicken parmesan on the menu,” said Quaresima. “We serve traditional Italian dishes.”

Quaresima said Bottega Cannuccia will be a place where guests can stop in for fresh pastries, like butter croissants, cookies, muffins, scones, cinnamon rolls, sfogliatella, and his favorite pastry, zeppola, which is a rich Italian cream puff that’s served warm, filled with pastry cream and dusted with powdered sugar. He’ll serve sandwiches with Cannuccia’s homemade bread, salads, Italian espresso, and tea from Mariage Frères, a French tea house from Paris that was founded in 1854.

At night, the Bottega will serve cheese and charcuterie boards, crostinis, fresh soups, and dishes like bruschetta with smoked trout and sweet potato and saffron aioli, and a crocchetta di pasta alla carbonara. The wine list will focus on Italian grapes, such as Montepulciano d’Abruzzo, Vermentino from Sardegna, and Nero d’Avola from Sicily. There will be a handful of cocktails, Italian and American beers, ciders, and a selection of Italian amari, cordials, and digestifs.

While restaurant groups are spending millions opening sprawling Italian-focused concepts around the city, Quaresima is taking a very different approach, funding the 30-seat neighborhood shop entirely by him and his wife, Tsedenia Kiros.

“I think parts of the restaurant scene in Boston has lost some of its charm with these really big spaces,” said Quaresima. “It’s why I went with little spaces. They’re unique here. And you have to be attentive [to] all the details.”

title: Darryl Whiting, once a crack-dealing ‘God’ and the scourge of Roxbury, has died. Here’s what locals say about his ruinous legacy.
text:
“I’m not a romantic; at the end of the day, his legacy is [expletive] crack cocaine,” said Jamarhl Crawford, who grew up in Roxbury and dealt drugs as a teenager, before becoming a community activist and organizer. “He was just a crack dealer.”

Whiting, for all his imprint locally, was not from Boston. He came here from New York in the 1980s and took over the Orchard Park housing development in Roxbury, eventually turning it into his personal trap house. There, he preyed upon the weaknesses of drug-addicted mothers surviving on government assistance to gain the use of their apartments to move significant amounts of narcotics.

“Basically, he came into Orchard Park, got rid of the old dealers, and either you were buying from him or selling for him,” said Crawford.

The operation was 24-7, with Whiting’s organization eventually becoming the largest supplier of cocaine in Roxbury, authorities said at the time.

By the time his New York Boys organization was dismantled by law enforcement in the early 1990s, the group was grossing more than $6 million a year in drug sales and controlled about $11 million in local real estate, according to federal court testimony. Whiting owned and operated a video store, sneaker shop, and barbershop, all on Warren Street in Roxbury, as well as the Crown Social and Recreation Hall on Geneva Avenue in Grove Hall.

At one point, Whiting’s organization had about 75 members, according to court testimony from someone who worked for him, including women who acted as drug mules, bringing hard drugs from New York to packing houses in Boston. There were also people who processed and packed cocaine, runners, and street-level sellers, all ultimately answering to him.

His rise in the Boston underworld inspired LL Cool J’s character in the 1999 crime thriller “In Too Deep.” And some of Whiting’s tale has become blurred with fiction locally.

Some observers from his era have suggested that Whiting was the one person most responsible for bringing wholesale amounts of crack cocaine to the streets of Boston. Others are adamant that that is an urban myth, a reductive oversimplification, and a fundamental misreading of Boston street life during the 1980s.

Whatever the reality, a Boston police commissioner once described him as “an evil person.” To the head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration office in Boston, he was “a piece of trash.” A different investigator labeled him “a city’s worst nightmare.” Newspapers dubbed him a criminal mastermind.

The head federal prosecutor in Boston once gave his case higher priority than that of New England Mafia boss Raymond “Junior” Patriarca.

His larger-than-life story sometimes had elements of a Hollywood noir script.

During one court appearance, he announced to the gathered press, “Call this the second trial of Jesus Christ!” He once struck a cop with a ring shaped like a ram’s head. Police said he went by many names: God, G, Rah.

Taking down his operation was a massive undertaking: In 1990, 250 federal agents and police raided locations in Roxbury, including Orchard Park, Dorchester, and Mattapan, arresting 18. Whiting was already behind bars when that happened, serving an assault and battery sentence at the Deer Island House of Correction.

Ultimately, Whiting became the first person in Massachusetts to receive a life sentence for selling narcotics.

The Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III has worked on street violence prevention and mitigation in Boston for decades. To him, Whiting was among the dominant underworld forces that circulated hard drugs throughout Black Boston, ripping apart families and ruining lives.

“There wasn’t anybody comparable to what he was doing,” Rivers said this past week.

Whiting’s rise to the top of the Boston drug trade corresponded with a historic spike in street violence in the city. In 1989, there were 100 homicides in the city. The next year, the number was 152. Such street violence, according to researchers, was fueled by the crack cocaine trade and the turf-based conflicts it fostered.

Rivers said Whiting’s organization was part of the milieu that increased the bloodshed on the streets of Boston.

“There was no question about that,” he said.

Like so many underworld figures, he leaned into the Robin Hood trope, projecting an image of someone who cared about Black communities in a city that had a very real history of racism.

He once put on a free rap concert for more than 1,000 teenagers at Dorchester’s Strand Theatre. There were also free trips to amusement parks for youths, Christmas parties, Easter egg hunts, barbecues, weekend brunches, and gifts of sports equipment. One registered nurse testified in court that his Grove Hall club doubled as a day care center for homeless mothers and offered youth programs and health care counseling.

But for one retired Boston police officer who grew up in Orchard Park, Whiting’s legacy is no different from James “Whitey” Bulger, the mobster who lorded over South Boston’s underworld for years and corrupted the local FBI office. Crack turned their home into a “zombieland,” they said.

Speaking on the condition of anonymity because they feared reprisals on their relatives, the former cop said it’s true that Whiting would buy people groceries and pay their bills when they were tight on money. But once he did someone a favor, that meant they owed him. For the Orchard Park native, Whiting was a “wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

“He did all that, but he had his own agenda,” said the retiree. “He was helping himself. He was making his money.”

Court testimony painted an even darker and more violent picture. One former member of his organization said under oath that discipline was instilled with violence, saying he was beaten on Whiting’s command at least three times.

A woman testified she became addicted to crack after agreeing to let Whiting’s gang use her apartment to set up a drug-dealing operation. The woman said she earned $350 a week for allowing drugs to be processed and packaged in the apartment she shared with her two small children. She also admitted to torturing a suspected informant on behalf of Whiting’s gang, saying the person was burned on the forehead with a curling iron “for a long time.”

Boston political consultant Joyce Ferriabough Bolling recalled feeling “horrible for the Orchard Park community” during Whiting’s heyday, which was marked by rampant and brazen drug peddling in and around the development that was colloquially known as “OP.”

“I wondered why the police or somebody in authority didn’t move on closing down God’s in-your-face operation,” she said.

His legacy is a dark one, according to Ferriabough Bolling, as it took at least two generations to clean up the crack scourge in Boston.

“I hope he made his peace with the real God,” she said.

Jeremiah Manion of Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Jack Bulger epitomized the privilege and burden of family
text:
Bill helped him land a good job with a good pension.

Whitey cost him that pension, enlisting him in a harebrained scheme to help Whitey stay out of prison after Whitey went on the lam in 1994.

In 1938, Jack was a newborn when his family moved into the Old Harbor development at 41 Logan Way, just around the corner from St. Monica’s Church.

He will, as his family noted in his obituary, “be remembered for his generosity, humor, and fierce loyalty.”

If that last quality defined him, it also helped and cost him in equal measure.

In 1964, Jack accompanied their father, James, for whom Whitey was named, to visit Whitey after he was transferred to the federal prison in Lewisburg, Pa. It was the last time the elder Bulger would see his wayward son.

Bill Bulger said his father never had a good day after Whitey went to prison. James Bulger did not live long enough to see his son emerge from prison and become the city’s most powerful, and lethal, gangster.

Bill Bulger became a powerful figure himself, on Beacon Hill, ascending to Senate president in 1978.

With his politician brother’s considerable influence, Jack became clerk-magistrate of the Boston Juvenile Court in 1982, a job that he held until his retirement in 2001.

But even as an officer of the court, Jack Bulger didn’t hesitate to help his gangster brother after Whitey went on the lam in 1994. He paid the monthly rental fee for a safe deposit box Whitey kept at a bank in Clearwater, Fla., and he spoke with Whitey twice in prearranged telephone calls while Whitey was on the run.

Jack Bulger lied twice before federal grand juries investigating Whitey, insisting he hadn’t spoken to his fugitive brother since Whitey took off, and that he didn’t know where he hid his money.

During one of those phone calls, Jack agreed to help Whitey obtain phony IDs to use on the run.

Even though Jack was nine years younger than Whitey, they bore enough of a resemblance to make the scheme somewhat plausible. Whitey instructed Kevin Weeks, his top lieutenant, to go to Jack’s home in Southie to take photos with Jack wearing a fake mustache.

When Weeks delivered the fake ID to Whitey at the Water Tower in Chicago, Whitey frowned. The photo was all wrong. Whitey’s mustache was pencil thin. Jack’s was big and bushy. It looked like he had a caterpillar on his lip.

The task force trying to find Whitey put traces on the phones of Bill and Jack, but a corrupt state cop told Whitey’s partner in crime, Stevie Flemmi, about it. Flemmi, whose parents were Bill Bulger’s neighbors, gave them the heads up.

What the cops couldn’t do Whitey did unwittingly, using traceable phone cards to call his brothers, which put them in compromising positions.

In a letter to a friend after he was captured in 2011, Whitey acknowledged he screwed up.

“I put the heat on people,” he admitted. “My brother Jack was trapped.”

After it emerged that he had admitted to a grand jury that he had spoken to his brother while Whitey was on the run, Bill was forced to resign as president of the University of Massachusetts, the sweet sinecure he had secured after his tenure as Senate president.

But Bill was able to keep his annual $274,539 pension.

Jack wasn’t as lucky. In 2003, Jack was sentenced to six months in prison and six months of house arrest for lying to two grand juries and thwarting efforts to capture his brother.

He was stripped of his pension, which was not even a quarter of Bill’s. Loyalty to Whitey had cost Jack his freedom and his income, and it cost Bill his job and, in the eyes of many, his good name.

It was a heavy price to pay for the Bulger credo of family above all else.

While Whitey was willing to forgive Teresa Stanley, his longtime companion who spoke to the authorities after deciding she didn’t want to spend her life on the lam with him, Jack was less forgiving.

During an interview for the book Shelley Murphy and I wrote about Whitey, Stanley told us that Jack Bulger confronted her once while walking on Castle Island and snarled, “I wish you were dead. Look at what you’ve done, all the trouble you caused.”

That was pretty rich, because Teresa Stanley didn’t cause any trouble. Whitey did.

That was something that neither Jack nor Bill were able to fully acknowledge. They remembered the funny, fiercely loyal, and protective brother who stuck up for little kids and carried the groceries of older neighbors.

But it was Whitey who murdered people. It was Whitey who made millions by allowing drug dealers to operate freely in Southie as long as they paid him tribute, while his family perpetuated the myth that Whitey was the Robin Hood of Southie, that he kept the drugs out of Southie.

It was Whitey who made their lives difficult, not the State Police and DEA agents who finally held Whitey to account, not the reporters who wrote about his exploits, not the big bad world outside of Southie.

They were enthusiastic purveyors of Southie exceptionalism, the myth that Southie was God’s country, the best neighborhood in the city, while Whitey’s criminal activity rotted the neighborhood from within, like termites.

When Whitey was convicted of murder and myriad crimes in the courthouse on the waterfront named for his old neighbor, Joe Moakley, he gave a thumbs up to Jack as he was led out of the courtroom.

Whatever you think of them, the Bulger brothers had longevity in their genes. Whitey was 89 when he was murdered in a West Virginia prison in 2018. Jack made it to 88.

Bill is, at 92, the last one standing.

The Bulger brothers lived long, long lives, a blessing not afforded to so many of Whitey’s victims.

title: I know how to drive in a rotary. Probably.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

I see you honking at me with your New York plates, guy, but I know how to drive on a rotary. Trust me, pal. Born and bred. Rotaries are our state bird, probably.

So I don’t know what you’re getting at leaning on your horn there. Relax, guy, I’m in the right lane ‘cause I’m getting off the second exit. That’s how it’s done around here. I know the sign just says something like “yield” or “enter if you dare.” But I assure you there are rules because right after you flipped me off I immediately looked ‘em up in the state driving handbook because I will not stop trying to win an argument even if all parties are no longer present.

Don’t worry, I didn’t Google ‘em while I was driving. As soon as it was safe, I double-parked.

Why us?

“Rotaries are much more common in Massachusetts than in other parts of the country,” the section of the official Massachusetts Driver’s Manual begins, a clear dig at you and your stupid yellow license plate. And if the rotary has multiple lanes, like that one where we exchanged fingers, then “for a quarter-turn, or to continue straight ahead, enter the rotary from the right lane.”

Boom. Roasted. I need to bang a U-ey and go find that clown. Tell me how to drive on a rotary? Listen pal, lemme explain how it works, cause it’s so simple even someone from a place where you can’t make a right on red will follow it.

If you’re gonna be blocking anyone in the inside lane from getting off, you can’t be in the outside lane. You still with me? So if you’re getting off the first exit, no problem. Ain’t blocking no one, and youse can both exit together.

‘Simple manners’

Same if you’re going straight and hopping off the second exit, like you seen me doing. Not sure if your little brain can follow along here, but same logic applies. I’m gettin’ off, so anyone in the inside lane is either exiting with me, or continuing around to I-don’t-care-because-I-ain’t-in-their-way. It’s simple manners.

“For a three-quarter-turn, or a U-turn, enter the rotary from the left lane. Travel through the middle or inner lane.” So you ain’t blocking anyone from getting off!

It’s a perfect system, pal. So where was you coming from that you dare honk at me like I was blocking you? I’m not a blocker, buddy. That’s you clowns. You and Connecticut. Gotta be on your toes around them blue plates.

I seen you coming around the rotary on the inside, but the right lane was open so I hopped in. Pretty sure that’s the definition of “yield.” There’s no way I could be blocking you from getting off, because if there’s one thing we know in this state, it’s how to drive.

Since I know you’re too dumb to follow this, I’ll draw you a picture.

Now that I look at it, I suppose that if you was getting off the third or fourth exit, and if that happened to be my first exit but I was going to the second, there might be a moment where those rules don’t make sense. Am I a blocker? That can’t be right. My mother didn’t raise no blockers.

‘Wicked confusing’

Hold up, is that why the state is doing that thing where they paint a million lines all over rotaries when no one’s looking? Don’t know if you’ve seen these, but they’re wicked confusing unless you’re in the right lane, cause then they just make you get off the first exit.

Wait a sec. Is that why they done that? Are we trying to paint our way out of a corner? Just sneak in with a Statie detail and a paint roller and quietly pretend like they didn’t raise an entire state of blockers?

Did I just lose an argument to a New Yorker? This ain’t right; I never lose arguments in my head.

But hey, maybe next time use your blinker, huh? I’m not a mind-reader, guy.

title: White Stadium victory frees Wu’s second term from a political thicket
text:
It all adds up to a big win for Wu, who has faced more than a year of allegations that she was stuffing an unpopular and possibly illegitimate idea down the throat of a community that didn’t want it. The prospect of losing must have been nightmarish for her.

It’s fair to say that White Stadium was an unlikely choice for a crusade. The stadium has been a mess for years, but somehow it became a mess everyone had learned to live with. Plans to improve it had been floated and discarded without fanfare or outrage. It was as though everyone had decided it wasn’t great, but it was good enough.

Politically, it didn’t help Wu that the catalyst for this project was bringing a women’s professional soccer team to Franklin Park. Though Boston Legacy FC has committed to paying $190 million of the cost of the $325 million project, the claim the city was somehow selling out the community around Franklin Park resonated in some quarters. Many would argue that Wu could have chosen a more worthy cause for a 2 ½ year dogfight.

For my part, I became an advocate for restoring White Stadium years ago. Unlike some so-called advocates, I’ve toured White Stadium multiple times and was shocked by its decrepitude. I supported construction magnate John Fish’s idea of renovating it in 2013 - which died a quiet death after Mayor Thomas M. Menino left office before it could be realized. And I’ve never changed my mind that a new White Stadium would be a great benefit for the young people of Boston.

I give Wu’s courtroom adversaries, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, great credit for its deep concern about Franklin Park. It fought this battle for principled reasons, and the finished product will be better for its advocacy.

Of course, no ruling will change the fact that a large and vocal contingent of neighboring residents are uneasy with the White Stadium renovation.

It’s up to the city to prove the many remaining issues of access can be resolved without placing an undue burden on residents. Wu should expect to be held to her promises this will be an economic engine for Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, beginning with the awarding of contracts to renovate and operate it. And that this will be a facility for Boston Public School students first, and for a soccer team second.

Those are the reasons this project is worth it.

As for Wu, it’s fair to say the start of her second term has been a slog. After her resounding victory in the mayor’s race last year, Wu immediately became the target of criticism. Black activists have argued that she is both too inaccessible and too inflexible. Progressives say she isn’t going far enough in pushing their issues. Even cyclists are bitterly critical, even though Wu is literally the first champion of their causes to occupy the mayor’s office.

But wins like Tuesday’s offer an opportunity to reset. Instead of debating what happens if Wu loses the White Stadium case, the conversation can now move to what the renovation can bring to Boston. It can dampen the talk that she’s damaged politically, or headed to some other work opportunity.

The truth is that Wu, for better or worse, is the same person who destroyed Josh Kraft a year ago, the same person who has never, in fact, had a single close race in her political career.

We might not know for years whether White Stadium was a visionary idea or a lousy idea. But what we know today is that Wu took a considerable political risk, stuck to her guns, and won.

title: ‘Full steam ahead’: Wu takes victory lap after end of White Stadium legal battle
text:
The SJC’s decision eliminated the final legal hurdle for the controversial project, effectively clearing the path forward for construction to continue. The redeveloped stadium, which the city is partnering with the professional women’s soccer team Boston Legacy FC to deliver, will be the new hub for Boston Public Schools athletics and the home stadium for the women’s soccer team.

The city committed to covering $135 million of the project’s estimated price tag. Boston Legacy FC is expected to pay about $190 million.

Officials from Boston Legacy FC, top City Hall staff, and local and state leaders joined Wu on Thursday to celebrate the SJC’s decision.

“We are charting a course that teams and cities around the country are already looking to,” Wu said at a news conference behind the William J. Devine Golf Course clubhouse, situated on the other end of Franklin Park from the stadium.

The project has generated substantial scrutiny and opposition over the past three years, as critics raised concerns about the project’s rising price tag, the city’s partnership with a private entity, and the decision to locate a professional sports complex in Franklin Park.

Wu has framed the project as an extraordinary opportunity to overhaul the more than 75-year-old dilapidated stadium and give Boston Public Schools students and city residents access to a professional-grade sports facility, without taxpayers having to shoulder the full cost.

She said “generations” of Boston Public Schools families have been asking the city to renovate the aging stadium. “Our Boston kids deserve the very best, and as a city, we can never apologize for fighting to give it to them,” she said.

But the project’s opponents, who filed the initial lawsuit to stop the project in February of 2024, argued it violates constitutional parkland protections, and that the neighborhoods around Franklin Park are not an appropriate place for a professional sports stadium.

The Supreme Judicial Court ruled Wednesday that the stadium site is a school facility, not parkland, and therefore not subject to those protections.

Still, even with that legal victory in hand, it remains unclear when the stadium will be finished and ready to host games and practices, either for students or professionals.

Wu did not directly answer questions Thursday about the project’s timeline and target completion date, but said construction work is happening on the site six days a week and meeting planned milestones.

She indicated that the lawsuit over the project had caused some delays.

“It’s undeniable that the litigation process has been a distraction and took significant resources and time and energy,” Wu said. “So we are evaluating closely, and we’ll be working to really fully assess what that means for the remainder of the schedule.”

Wu and Boston Legacy FC owner Jennifer Epstein on Thursday also did not answer questions about whether the professional women’s team plans to host any home games at White Stadium during the 2027 National Women’s Soccer League season, which begins in February.

The team is currently playing all of its home games this season at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

Work on the stadium began in early 2025 with the demolition of the old facility, and on Thursday, construction appeared to be back in full swing.

The sound of clangs, beeps, and crashes filled the air as excavators rumbled across the site. Two red cranes towered over dozens of laborers in hard hats and fluorescent T-shirts and vests, helping lift long metal rods.

As construction continues, a group of elected and community leaders that make up the White Stadium Neighborhood Advisory Council will finalize transportation plans for the 20 Boston Legacy FC game days, Wu said.

Residents can share their input on traffic management plans, including game-day parking restrictions, at four community meetings the city is planning to host in Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, and Dorchester this fall.

title: Hip-hop therapy is uncommon in the US. This Roxbury nonprofit wants to change that.
text:
In the 2010s, CSR adopted a program called Beats Rhymes and Life (BRL), an initiative that uses hip-hop clinics to address mental health and community wellness for children and young adults. These clinics, which last about 10 weeks each semester, involve writing workshops, hip-hop education, and other exercises that build communication skills.

CSR currently uses the program to work with clients between the ages of 14 and 24 who may not want to receive treatment through traditional therapeutic services.

Artist coordinators and registered local clinicians create programming that is hip-hop inspired and addresses issues students might be experiencing at home, such as substance abuse and depression. Staff use tools like a visual “hip-hop timeline” and songwriting exercises to teach students how the genre has been used to address oppression in Black and brown communities for decades.

The program is the first of its kind in Massachusetts, and similar programs are extremely uncommon in other parts of the country. Representatives from CSR say that shouldn’t be the case.

According to Stephanie Sabins, the lead clinician for BRL, the creative process in therapy creates opportunities for “healthy risks” and helps people understand themselves.

“Some of the best conversations I’ve ever had with youth are in these groups,” she added.

Sabins, who has worked in the program for five years, thinks hip-hop therapy is still making its case as a respected approach to improving mental health.

“We are actively decolonizing therapy,” said Candice Watch, BRL’s director. “Storytelling is actually what hip-hop has always been, and that is an actual form of therapy.”

Therapy doesn’t have to look like the traditional medical model, Watch explained. She said using an already known form of cultural expression — such as hip-hop — is sometimes more effective than talk therapy or other clinical treatments.

Each cohort is encouraged to write about whatever they want in their songs. Heartbreak, stress, and grief are among the many topics. That creative autonomy helps participants develop social skills, creativity, and self-assurance.

Students like Luis “Louie” Colon are reaping the benefits.

Colon, a 22-year-old Roxbury native, started the program in the spring. He struggled with public speaking and, at times, connecting with and relating to his peers. BRL changed that.

He said BRL is one of “the only things I really had where I can be with my peers, laugh, joke, and have fun.”

When Colon’s not in BRL sessions, he’s pursuing a career in photography and visual art. Making time for his personal life is difficult. Dwindling support for artistry leaves Colon feeling like he’s fighting an uphill battle and often alone.

“We all go through the same stuff, but being here, I was happy,” he said.

Clinicians say that relatability is crucial in participants’ mental health.

Alan-Michael Chest is a Massachusetts-licensed mental health counselor and musician. He incorporates music and culture into his practice.

“Music offers vulnerability without judgment,” Chest said.

At age 7, Chest wrote his first rap: a song about struggling to understand crime in America. He said the creative process must be a part of therapy: “It’s really meeting a client where they’re at, and it’s really changing the framework for therapy altogether.”

BRL reaches participants through local grassroots organizations and city programs that work with youth at risk, such as Spoke Art and You Got This Center. Several programs can’t pay for partnerships with CSR, or can’t give kids stipends to participate, which makes getting people to participate in the clinics more challenging. When BRL loses participation numbers, the program itself is at risk; a portion of BRL’s grant funding is based on the number of young people it serves.

In 2021, BRL built a studio in a van to bring the program to prospective artists’ backyard. Budget cuts have kept the van off the streets because it needs repairs.

For staff, demonstrating to the public that BRL offers an important model for therapy is a challenge, but one that keeps them inspired.

Michael “Big Mike” Mendes, BRL’s main teacher-artist, has been making music and drawing since he was a kid. Growing up in Dorchester and coming from a Cape Verdean family, art has always been how he communicated best.

Mendes said BRL’s mission isn’t making artists, but introducing a new channel of healthy expression. He believes hip-hop is a key path to inspire new leaders.

“Through rapping and teaching people how to rap, we’re getting them to find their confidence, have conversations that they’re not having, and develop healthy relationships with adults,” he concluded.

This article has been updated to correct the names of Michael “Big Mike” Mendes and Luis “Louie” Colon, Colon’s age, and how many years Stephanie Sabins has been with BRL. The caption has also been updated to reflect correct event information.

title: Joshua Báez’s skill and hard work makes Cardinals’ debut star a victory for Boston baseball community
text:
Báez started his high school career at Cristo Rey High in Dorchester, then transferred to Snowden International School in the Back Bay.

His emerging baseball talent led Báez to Dexter Southfield in Brookline for the 2020 season. That season was canceled by the pandemic, but Báez continued to improve.

Báez played summer ball for The BASE in Roxbury and embraced their commitment to academics, ultimately committing to play for Vanderbilt.

There weren’t many ballfields in the greater Boston area that Báez didn’t play on at some point.

“The first time I saw him take batting practice, my jaw dropped,” said Dan Donato, who coaches baseball and hockey at Dexter Southfield and is the brother of former Bruins winger and Harvard coach, Ted Donato. “He had massive power. He was somebody who could hit 20 home runs in his sleep.”

And a powerful right arm, too. Major League teams saw Báez as almost a perfect draft pick because if he didn’t hit, he could move to the mound and take advantage of his 98 mile-per-hour fastball.

Craig Breslow, then working for the Cubs, was among the scouts and team officials who came to watch Báez play in 2021. But he fell into the second round after an inconsistent senior season.

The Red Sox were interested, but had the fourth pick that season and used it on Marcelo Mayer. Their mistake was taking University of Florida outfielder Jud Fabian early in the second round. He didn’t sign.

The Cardinals took Báez with the 54th pick. His apprenticeship in the minors was longer than expected — 452 games over parts of six seasons — because of injuries and a high strikeout rate. But Báez had a strong 2025, and it continued with Triple-A Memphis this season.

“[The Cardinals] told him a few weeks ago that he was a big part of their future. And once he was called up, they wanted him there for good,” Donato said.

Donato played in the minors for the Yankees, Mariners, and Rays from 1995-98, reaching Triple-A. He knew a five-tool player when he saw one, having shared the field with Derek Jeter and Bernie Williams, among others, during spring training.

“Josh ran a 6.31 60 [yard dash], and Bernie Williams was 6.7. In the outfield he’d go the gap as smooth as Ceddanne Rafaela and make a throw right to the bag,” Donato said. “He had all the skill, and he worked harder than anybody I had ever watched.”

Báez came of age at a time when baseball talent in the Boston area was at a high level. Boston College outfielder Sal Frelick was a first-round pick in 2021. Maryland’s Sean Burke, who played at St. John’s (Shrewsbury), was a third-round pick that year.

Future All-Stars Ben Rice, Cam Schlittler, and Shane Smith also emerged during that period.

“There were always pitchers from the Northeast, but there are more indoor facilities now, and players can work on baseball all year. For somebody like Josh, that was huge,” Donato said. “It’s different now than when I was coming up. It’s super competitive now. In our league, we have pitchers throwing 88-93.”

Landmark days are nothing new for Báez. He hit four home runs for Memphis on June 16, the third anniversary of his father’s passing. His mother, Yris, was at the game.

José Manuel Báez, known as “El Bronco” in the Dominican Republic, was an accomplished semi-pro baseball and softball player known for his power. His son promised him he would make it to the majors, and he did.

Báez was 0 for 17 in the four games after his debut. He came off the bench on Wednesday, singled to end his skid, then drew a walk. On Friday in Philadelphia, he blasted the first pitch he saw for a two-run homer.

“He’s going to be fine,” Donato said. “He’s shown what he’s made of.”

Without fail, new Red Sox catcher Adley Rutschman makes it a habit to meet the pitcher as he’s coming off the mound at the end of an inning to offer a few words of encouragement.

The exchange usually comes along the baseline and lasts only a few seconds.

“I really don’t know when it started, but I’ve always done it,” Rutschman said.

It’s a habit he picked up from his father. Randy Rutschman was a catcher at Linfield University in Oregon who later coached and played semi-pro ball in the West Coast League.

“He kept playing after college just because he liked baseball so much,” Rutschman said. “I think I was 6 when he stopped playing, but I remember him doing that with the pitchers.”

Rutschman said his message is usually something along the lines of, “Great job, let’s keep it going,” or “We’re going to get through this,” if it’s a rough inning.

Rather than wait until they get to the dugout, Rutschman says what’s on his mind right away.

“It’s different, but I like it,” Payton Tolle said. “He takes care of the pitcher.”

A few other observations on the Red Sox:

⋅ According to Baseball Reference, Wyatt Olds was the 23,757th player to appear in a major league game when he pitched for the Sox on Monday.

The 27-year-old righthander got the news that morning, too late for any of his family or friends from Oklahoma to get to Fenway Park. But his wife and four-month-old son were there.

Olds had started to wonder if the day would ever happen. He was drafted in 2021 out of the University of Oklahoma, and this was his third season in Triple-A and sixth in the minors. Olds also had not been pitching particularly well of late for the WooSox.

But he struck out James McCann and Jordan Lawlar, both swinging, on nine pitches, then retired Tim Tawa on a weak groundout.

“The Lord works in crazy ways,” Olds said. “Just happy to be here. I’m glad I did this with the Red Sox.”

His new teammates celebrated the occasion in the clubhouse. As Triple-A manager, Chad Tracy was accustomed to telling players they had been called up. But until this year he had not watched any of his players make their debut in person.

“It’s really cool,” Tracy said. “To be part of that is a lot of fun.”

When he took the mound in front of a sellout crowd, Olds said he remembered his college coach, Skip Johnson, always saying to take big moments one pitch at a time.

“That was all I was thinking, just make the next one,” he said. “He really imprinted that on us. It worked for me.”

Olds had a ball and a lineup card to take back to his family. He couldn’t stop smiling as he spoke about his day.

“I told the guys that was the most fun I ever had in my life,” he said.

⋅ The Sox set a major-league record winning 15 consecutive games against teams with a winning record before Wednesday’s loss against the Diamondbacks. Joe Cronin and the 1933 Washington Senators were the last team to record 14 straight victories against above-.500 foes.

⋅ Tanner Houck said in spring training that his goal was to return from Tommy John surgery this season, even though the Sox thought it was unlikely. It still might be a long shot, but Houck is moving closer to a minor league rehabilitation assignment and could be a relief option before the year is out.

Houck has a 2.68 ERA in 33 career relief appearances in the majors, with 9.6 strikeouts per nine innings.

⋅ He’s never made the major leagues, and it doesn’t seem likely he will this season, but Triple-A Worcester outfielder Braiden Ward is sure an interesting player.

The 27-year-old leads the International League with 53 stolen bases in 60 attempts. He also has been hit by a pitch 28 times, the most in the minors. Ward has scored 64 runs and had a .362 on-base percentage.

⋅ The “Sell the team” chants at Fenway Park have dissipated, but there is a chance John Henry and FSG could sell Liverpool.

According to reports from England, the investment group that purchased an approximately 38-percent stake in the club earlier this month has the option to acquire a controlling interest over the next year.

That alliance, called 1892 Holdings, includes British-Indian billionaire Amit Bhatia, Jeff Bezos, and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

FSG sold its interest in the Pittsburgh Penguins last year after four years of ownership. Henry also owns the Globe.

The passing of Tommy John earlier this month sparked a discussion about if he should be in the Hall of Fame, given the combination of a successful career and having ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction surgery named after him.

Everybody in baseball, from the amateur ranks on up, knows about Tommy John even if they aren’t familiar with all the details of this career.

But when it comes to the Hall of Fame, less is more.

Only players, managers, team or league executives, and umpires can be Hall of Famers. Broadcasters and writers are honored by the Hall every year with awards voted on by their peers but aren’t inducted.

Still, they are recognized on the stage and have their moment in the spotlight. It’s special.

The late Dr. Frank Jobe changed the course of the game in 1974 when he performed what was revolutionary surgery on John by replacing his elbow ligament with a tendon from his left wrist.

Jobe was recognized by the Hall during the 2013 induction ceremony with John in attendance. One of Jobe’s proteges, Dr. Neal ElAttrache, spoke. Jobe passed away less than a year later. They had their moment.

The Hall has also given out the Buck O’Neil Lifetime Achievement Award since 2008, “to honor an individual whose extraordinary efforts enhanced baseball’s positive impact on society, broadened the game’s appeal, and whose character, integrity and dignity are comparable to the qualities exhibited by O’Neil.”

O’Neil was a player and manager in the Negro American League, and later a revered scout and coach. He was the first recipient of the award, which is given every three years.

Roland Hemond (2011), Joe Garagiola (2014), Rachel Robinson (2017), David Montgomery (2020), Carl Erskine (2023), and Bill White (2026) have been honored in the years since.

Ballpark architect Janet Marie Smith should also be on that list, along with notable coaches — Dave Duncan, Leo Mazzone, and Ron Washington come to mind — scouts, and others in the game who don’t fit neatly into a particular category.

The Cubs went into the weekend with a five-game lead in the National League wild-card race. Pete Crow-Armstrong is having an MVP-type season with 32 home runs and 31 stolen bases through 129 games. He’s already at 7.8 bWAR. Alex Bregman has played a big role, too. He has a .964 OPS and 25 RBIs in 32 games since the All-Star break while playing Gold Glove-level defense at third base. After a slow start, Bregman is again leading another team to the postseason. “You can’t fake it through 162 games,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “It’s a credit to how he works every single day.” … The Diamondbacks gave Ketel Marte a seven-year, $116.5 million extension before the 2025 season, the kind of contract that is essentially a partnership with the player and a sign of trust. It helps explain why manager Torey Lovullo looked so exasperated and angry at Fenway Park on Monday when he didn’t know where Marte was. Marte just didn’t show up for the game and didn’t give any explanation. “There was very little coming back,” Lovullo said when asked what Marte had told the team. Marte was placed on the unpaid restricted list and was later moved to the injured list because of a knee issue. Diamondbacks CEO Derrick Hall, who was in Boston, called the latest situation “bizarre” and said the team wanted an explanation. Marte also was on the restricted list last season when he returned to the Dominican Republic without permission after his home in Arizona was broken into during the All-Star break … The Mariners have been a wreck, but entered the weekend only three games out of a wild-card spot. The odds are against them, but 13 of Seattle’s final 15 games are against the Angels, Athletics, and Rockies. Cal Raleigh was somehow 5 of 48 with 18 strikeouts in his first 16 games this month … Jordan Walker won the Home Run Derby and has hit five home runs for the Cardinals since, blasting his 27th of the season Friday night … Duquette Consulting, owned by former MLB executive Dan Duquette, is collaborating with Lorenzo Garmendia and Gradum Gswing — the hitting development company Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin employed to help turn his season around after a slow start. The goal is to bring the company’s model to other MLB players and teams. Durbin worked directly with Garmendia at the company’s facility in Waltham. Gswing has centers in nine states … Received an email a few days ago from an online sportsbook listing prop bets for the Little League World Series. It included over/under odds on strikeouts for specific pitchers. How does anybody think that is a good idea? Meanwhile, MLB’s Field of Dreams Game in Iowa earlier this month was played on a field with advertisements for FanDuel and BetMGM on the outfield fences. That was unintentionally amusing. If you recall the film, one of the main characters is the ghost of Shoeless Joe Jackson, who wants to play ball again after being banned for fixing the 1919 World Series … Happy birthday to Mike Boddicker, who is 69. The righthander was 39-22 with a 3.49 ERA over 83 games for the Red Sox from 1988-90. The Sox sent Brady Anderson and 21-year-old prospect Curt Schilling to the Orioles for Boddicker at the ’88 trade deadline. Boddicker had a 2.63 ERA down the stretch to help the Sox win the division by a game over the Tigers. The Sox were then swept by the Athletics in the ALCS, with Boddicker taking the loss in Game 3. Boddicker left the Sox as a free agent. In all, he played 14 seasons and won 134 games, and a World Series with Baltimore in 1983 when he pitched a three-hitter in a 4-1 win over the Phillies in Game 2.

title: Today, pay what you can at these Boston-area restaurants
text:
If dining out feels increasingly steep these days, here’s an opportunity that may be within your reach.

Today, Aug. 26, restaurants around the world are participating in Paga Lo Que Puedas, or Pay What You Can: a global hospitality initiative started by Mexico City restaurant Masala y Maíz that invites diners to eat what they want and pay what they’re able to.

Local participants include Dorchester’s Comfort Kitchen and Barra in Union Square, which will be joining the effort with more than 100 other restaurants across 13 countries.

“We really want people to come on that day that wouldn’t normally feel like they could come,” said Nyacko Pearl Perry, a cofounder of Comfort Kitchen. “We would like our space to welcome them.”

One of Comfort Kitchen’s ongoing challenges, Perry said, is maintaining a high quality of food and service while offering a price point that still makes sense for everyone.

Enter Email

“We consider ourselves to be pushing up against what fine dining is,” she said. “We want to create luxurious experiences, but we don’t want to be stuffy. We don’t want people to feel like they can’t come in.”

For the promotion to be financially viable for both patrons and staff, restaurants are hoping for community support. Diners who can afford to pay more are encouraged to do so. Comfort Kitchen’s team is creating an internal “safety net” based on the staff’s average earnings on a Wednesday night. They’ll supplement the tips that come in.

Perry acknowledged that many restaurants wouldn’t be able to participate given their already razor-thin margins. Her cofounder and husband, Biplaw Rai, is also thinking about what restaurateurs can learn from the experience, and plans to share the day’s data with fellow restaurants.

“We are hoping ... that we learn new things on consumer behaviors and how people are paying,” Rai said. “And if people are being more generous.”

Barra co-owner Paola Ibarra said her restaurant has tried to offer more affordable bites and drinks as people spend less, even outside of this particular promotion. She said that small, independent places like Barra have been affected financially, but they still want to be “close to” the community, regardless of price.

“We’re OK with running the risk,” she said. “If the risk is someone says, ‘I can’t pay a lot,’ we’re happy to share the cost with other customers. It’s a good initiative, and we’re ready to try it.”

Barra, 23a Bow St., Somerville, hola@barraunionsquare.com
