title: The Globe’s housing reporter thought he’d have an edge finding an apartment. He had no idea what was coming.
text:
So there I was, with neither a boatload of money nor sufficient sleep, weaving between pedestrians on Bennington Street, desperate to fill out an application before someone else did.

This is what it takes to find an apartment around here.

As The Boston Globe’s housing reporter, I spend my professional life writing about Massachusetts’ intractable housing problem, and how it warps the lives of so many people in this state — especially renters.

But the ever-rising cost of housing is big in my personal life, too. Countless friends have moved away because rents are too high; others complain about the city’s notorious Sept. 1 shuffle — when about two-thirds of all the leases in Boston turn over.

Finding a new apartment is, in a word, a nightmare. Every decent listing seemingly has 50 interested applicants. Some brokers still try to charge steep (and mostly now-illegal) fees. And the rent itself soars higher every year.

For years, I have managed to avoid the anguish of a housing search here by staying put in my charming-if-slightly-tattered apartment in an East Boston three-decker. But I have finally outgrown that place, and my partner — Globe transportation reporter Diti Kohli — and I decided in March that it was time to look for somewhere new.

I initially dismissed the seriousness of this endeavor, and volunteered to head our search. As someone who writes about housing for a living, I figured I would be uniquely equipped to navigate Boston’s frenetic rental market.

I had no idea what lay in store.

The apartment in Magoun Square was a great find — a first-floor unit in a little multifamily building steps from the Green Line extension.

It met much of what we were looking for: Outdoor space, a good kitchen, plenty of windows for our cat, Mittens. With friends nearby, Somerville was our preferred neighborhood. And at $2,700 a month, it was in our price range.

The challenge, of course, would be beating out dozens of other applicants.

Half the trouble of apartment hunting here — if you want to avoid a several-thousand-dollar broker fee, that is — is poring through the sheer volume of listings online. There are dozens of websites, from local brokerages to national sites like Apartments.com, with thousands of apartments to choose from.

It’s no simple feat to figure out what is a real, available apartment, and what isn’t. It requires backgrounding landlords and brokers, finding an actual person to set up a tour, ensuring move-in timing works — all while hoping that some better-financed renter doesn’t beat you to the punch.

As it turned out, shockingly few of the thousands of apartments listed online were available on our timeline, or fit even a few of our criteria we had established. For those, competition was fierce. And many landlords and brokers didn’t return messages.

When they did, there were often issues, like that some were charging broker fees, which was a nonstarter. (Massachusetts mostly outlawed tenant-paid broker fees last year, but some brokers still charge them, sometimes through a loophole with so-called “open listings” that are shared by multiple brokers, or in apparent violation of the law in other instances.)

“Does the landlord have any flexibility on the broker fee?” I had asked the broker of one Somerville apartment.

This broker actually wrote me back.

“No.”

Before long, apartment-hunting became something of a full-time job. I turned on Zillow notifications for new listings in our preferred neighborhoods — Somerville, Jamaica Plain, perhaps Dorchester.

Each buzz of my phone sent my heart rate soaring. Maybe this was the place? But our search quickly fell into a tiresome pattern: Either a listing would be for a place that wouldn’t work for us, or it would be somewhere that looked right, but the landlord would already be swamped with applications. March drifted into April, and apartments available for Sept. 1 move-ins were quickly getting scooped up.

So when Bethany, the owner of that apartment in Magoun Square, messaged me back to set up a tour, the stakes suddenly felt very high.

It may sound ridiculous, but I spent two days rehearsing what I would say to her.

The night before the tour, I could barely sleep.

When we arrived at the apartment, a woman who looked to be around 30 and had clearly just finished her own tour was outside chatting with Bethany, laughing and looking very personable. I muttered something to Diti about her apparent charm offensive, and offered the woman a smile as we walked in. She did not smile back.

Without a word, it felt like she was telling us: “This place is mine.”

Bethany, a kind woman whose arms were full of tattoos and appeared very much like the sort of person who would own a building in Somerville, explained that she already had more than a dozen tours lined up, with more to come.

We tried our best to be charming. We asked questions and chatted about Bethany’s impending move to Portugal. I sprinted home from the Blue Line and returned our application as soon as it landed in our inbox.

But I just had a feeling that we weren’t getting this place. And sure enough, three days later, Bethany wrote back.

Good afternoon,

Thank you for the application. We just signed a lease.

Good luck in your search!

Ouch.

I realized at that point that I had probably let the search process get to me more than was reasonable. But this is an experience shared by many Boston 20-somethings, including those who make significantly more money than Diti and me.

There is an argument to be made that a tight housing market is a good thing — a sign that, despite the region’s recent struggles, demand to live here remains high. Indeed while rents have been dropping in some other high-cost rental markets lately, they’re still rising in Greater Boston.

At the same time, when 20- and 30-somethings with professional jobs can’t find an apartment, it’s a clear sign the region simply doesn’t have enough homes for the people who want to live here. When young professionals struggle to find housing at their tier of the housing market, it puts even more pressure on working-class families, who are leaving the region due to cost pressures in increasing numbers.

I decided after the Magoun Square debacle that I needed to shift my strategy away from Zillow searches, and perhaps focus on Jamaica Plain, where I hoped competition might be less intense. I started wandering neighborhoods hunting for “for rent” signs, and even turned to a platform I had previously shunned: Craigslist.

There, small landlords were advertising units in old multifamily buildings — the sort of buildings that Diti and I love.

After a few failed attempts, I stumbled upon a broker who seemed to exclusively work with small landlords. I perused her portfolio and found a unit that almost seemed too good to be true: A 1,000 square-foot two-bedroom in an old triple-decker near an Orange Line station. It had a front porch, a walk-in pantry, and some interesting built-in quirks like a stained-glass window.

The broker answered her phone after one ring, and offered to show us the place the following day. On the tour, she said the apartment had been on the market for a few weeks, and while a couple of people had liked it, no one had yet applied.

She handed us a paper application form and told us to email the completed version to her as soon as possible.

Driving home, Diti and I talked about how much we both loved the place. So we pulled over at a Dunkin’, filled out the application by hand, and emailed it back.

A few days later the broker texted.

The owner wants to meet you on Sunday . . . to go forward!

A few days later, we met our new landlords — a couple who have lived in Jamaica Plain and owned the triple decker for decades — at JP Licks on Centre Street, and signed the lease.

We recently got the keys, and though we aren’t moving for a few more weeks (to avoid the peak Sept. 1 moving costs), we stopped by the other day to plan and clean.

As we sat there munching on a pastry from what will be one of our new neighborhood cafes, I realized that there was still one thing I had forgotten to do.

I pulled out my phone and deleted the Zillow app.

title: Dolly Parton reminded us what it means to be a good American
text:
Her appeal — not necessarily her music, but the whole ouvre of her as a human being — cut across all sorts of cultures and divides, in all sorts of countries.

It was often said that at her concerts, it wouldn’t be unusual to see a drag queen and a guy wearing a trucker’s cap with a Confederate flag on it in the same audience.

And yet she was intuitively sensitive to how some of her down-home themes came across. When she learned that the word “Dixie” made some folks, especially Black folks, uncomfortable because of its connection to the Confederacy and slavery, she ordered it removed from the Dixie Stampede dining spots at her theme parks in Tennessee and Missouri.

“There’s such a thing as innocent ignorance, and so many of us are guilty of that,” Parton told Billboard in 2018 after the name change. “When they said ‘Dixie’ was an offensive word, I thought, ‘Well, I don’t want to offend anybody. This is a business. We’ll just call it ‘The Stampede.’ As soon as you realize that [something] is a problem, you should fix it. Don’t be a dumbass.”

“That’s where my heart is,” she added. “I would never dream of hurting anybody on purpose.”

In saying that, she offered a life lesson as profound as anything Jesus, Mohammed or the Buddha ever said: Don’t be a dumbass. And don’t hurt people on purpose.

Like many women of her era, she was wildly underestimated while rising in a music industry dominated by men.

She had a great line when people suggested she was just a dumb blonde: she said she wasn’t dumb, and she wasn’t a blonde.

She grew up, one of 12 children, in a one-room cabin in the Great Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee. Her father, a poor farmer, paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal.

Her father never learned to read or write. She considered him the smartest man she ever met, but recognized that his illiteracy made his life very difficult.

That is why she threw so much of her passion and her money into promoting children’s literacy, not just in this country but in several others.

In a country where class divisions are often dismissed, lest it contradict the myth that every American is born equal and has the same chances in life, Dolly Parton knew that was, as she’d put it, pure bunk.

She never forgot where she came from, or that poverty did the same thing to the human spirit whether it was in Appalachia, the Bronx, Dorchester, or the slums of Calcutta.

Deprivation wasn’t the worst part of being poor, she said; the worst part was the shame.

It was her humble roots, and being constantly underestimated, that seemed to drive her most, and there’s nothing more American than that.

Her embrace of any and all others was also quintessentially American. She embodied the words that united the 13 original American states, the words that remain on US currency, e pluribus unum: out of many, one.

She believed deeply in the American concept of identity, the idea that Americans can maintain diverse identities while sharing a common, collective identity and purpose.

That’s why she wouldn’t hurt anyone on purpose. Because if you hurt another person on purpose, she believed, you were hurting yourself.

And that’s why she was so loved and respected by such an array of different people, from not just this country, but all over the world.

She was never fond of the word feminist, but her ability to build a successful career in an entertainment industry dominated by men made her a role model, especially for American women.

How many people, men or women, would say no to Elvis?

Dolly did.

In 1974, at the height of his fame, Elvis Presley wanted to record the song she wrote, “I Will Always Love You.” Parton was thrilled, because she admired Presley so much.

But when, right before the recording session, Presley’s manager insisted he would record it only if he was entitled to at least half of the publishing rights, Parton walked away.

She cried, but she stuck to her principle.

When Whitney Houston covered “I Will Always Love You” in 1992, it became an international hit, and in the end Parton collected some $10 million in royalties from that rendition in just the 1990s alone.

She used some of that money to build an office complex in a Black neighborhood in Nashville.

She did it to honor Whitney Houston, telling an interviewer, “I just thought, ‘This was great. I’m going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well.’ ”

My people as well. How American is that?

Parton’s embrace of the LGBTQ+ community was similar in outlook. If her Christian faith was central to her own identity, she couldn’t understand how people who call themselves Christian could hate queer and transgender people.

“I try to love everybody,” she said.

It is probably not news that Americans are not especially popular around the world these days. It’s easy to blame it all on Donald Trump, who insults other countries and projects the kind of American exceptionalism that denigrates others.

But for all its great achievements, for all its many great people, this country has done plenty of things around the world that aren’t good and have nothing to do with Donald Trump.

In more recent times, we’ve become a more cruel country, a bad neighbor, a place less serious and taken less seriously abroad.

That in and of itself is a reason to celebrate Dolly Parton’s life, and to mourn her passing. She was loved because, as she put it, she tried to love everybody.

She reminded us what it means to be a good American, a good person, a good soul. She was all that, and more.

title: The Massachusetts primary races we’re watching
text:
By Joan Vennochi

What do President Trump and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu have in common?

Both have a zeal for endorsing candidates of their choice to try to control election outcomes — and with that zeal, the confidence to test their own clout.

State Senators Nick Collins and Will Brownsberger, both Democrats, now face Wu-backed primary opponents because they did not support the mayor’s proposal to shift some of Boston’s property tax burden from residents to commercial property owners. Daniel Lander, a former Wu aide, is taking on Brownsberger, while Latoya Gayle, a community activist and first-time candidate is challenging Collins with Wu’s blessing.

While these contests do test the power of insurgency against incumbency, because of Wu’s involvement, the debate has focused more about the role that Boston lawmakers should play in pushing the mayor’s agenda. There is palpable tension between Wu and the two senators, especially Collins, who during the fight over her property tax legislation accused Wu of using “fear and manipulation” in her ultimately unsuccessful bid to get the proposal through the Legislature.

After serving eight years in the House, Collins won election to the state Senate in 2018 and now represents a district that includes South Boston, Dorchester, the South End, Chinatown and parts of Roxbury, Mattapan and the Back Bay. Brownsberger, a 20-year veteran of the Legislature, is a key part of Senate leadership, and represents a district that includes parts of Boston and Cambridge, along with all of Watertown and Belmont. Sounding less than eager for this fight with Wu, Brownsberger recently told the Globe editorial board, “I’m not quarreling with the mayor. The minute we can have peace in the valley, I will embrace peace in the valley.”

But peace does not seem to be Wu’s priority right now and, in a way, that’s understandable. Her power is at its height. She ran unopposed in her 2025 reelection campaign, after she bested challenger Josh Kraft by 49 points in the preliminary election and he dropped out. She has a track record of success when it comes to endorsing Boston City Council candidates. Watching congressional candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sweep to victory may have also encouraged her to test her own political muscle.

Yet the stakes are different for Wu than they were for Mamdani. If either Gayle or Lander win, she gets credit. But that credit won’t win Wu any more friends in the Senate or any more support on Beacon Hill for her tax proposal. Indeed, it may produce the opposite.

But she’s all-in with Lander and Gayle, just like Trump is all-in with Darline Graham, naming her interim US senator in South Carolina after her brother, longtime Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly last month. Trump then backed her in Tuesday’s special run-off election.

At least Trump’s backing of Darline Graham is motivated partly by his loyalty to her late brother. Wu’s backing of Lander and Gayle is strictly a matter of payback politics.

Is there no way to build bridges instead? Wu seems to share Trump’s view that there isn’t.

By Abdallah Fayyad

What interests me in next week’s Massachusetts primaries? There is, of course, the Democratic Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton. There’s the race for Suffolk County district attorney, pitting the incumbent Kevin Hayden against his controversy-prone predecessor, Rachael Rollins, and Linda Champion. And there’s the Republican gubernatorial primary that will give us a temperature check on the post-Jim Lyons Massachusetts GOP.

But the primary result that I’m especially eager to see will come from the Eighth congressional district. The current Democratic representative, Stephen Lynch, is the kind of incumbent that up-and-coming Democrats have been trying to oust. At 71, he’s older than the average House member, he’s been in Congress for a quarter of a century, and he’s more conservative than the party’s base. Meanwhile, his challenger, Patrick Roath, is an energetic 39-year-old lawyer who is knocking Lynch for votes that haven’t aged well — like his opposition to the President Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act.

Polling in congressional primaries isn’t easy, and there have only been a couple in the Eighth. These polls, which aren’t independent, show that the race is tightening. In February, a poll sponsored by Roath found that he was trailing Lynch by 26 points. But earlier this month, a poll by a PAC affiliated with Roath found that he’s only down by 7 points. Some close observers are calling the race a toss-up.

Given the dearth of independent data, it is possible that Lynch might cruise to reelection, or that Roath could manage an upset. And while Roath, who served in Governor Deval Patrick’s administration, is still the underdog, he has a lot going for him. A relative unknown just a year ago, he’s been active on the campaign trail compared to Lynch, who has run a relatively quiet campaign. And since Lynch first got elected to Congress, the Democratic base has drifted away from his style of politics and is looking for younger and more progressive candidates. Voters also want spirited fighters who can do more to stand up to Trump, and Roath is hoping to convince just enough of them that he’s in better shape to do that than the incumbent.

Earlier in the race, in an apparent dig at Roath, Lynch said, “Nowadays, kids get up in the morning, and they think they see a member of Congress in the mirror — no experience, no leadership, no accountability.” Next week, we’ll see whether voters agree with Lynch, or whether they think it’s time for a new kid on the block.

By Kara Bettis Carvalho

I’ll be following three races closely on Sept. 1. First up: the GOP gubernatorial primary, because the outcome will reveal the state of moderate Republicanism in Massachusetts.

The two candidates, Mike Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve, are similar in some ways — both are military veterans who advocate growing jobs and support cutting government waste and taxes. But their differences underscore some of the lasting tensions in the state Republican Party.

Minogue, a wealthy biotech executive and philanthropist who is backed by the state GOP, contributed generously to President Donald Trump’s inaugural fund and is conservative on social issues, including abortion. Shortsleeve, a venture capitalist who managed the MBTA under former Governor Charlie Baker, falls more comfortably in the traditional New England Republican camp, supporting abortion rights, for instance.

Polls have shown Minogue comfortably ahead, and his allies have pressed his opponent to drop out of the race. While Minogue touts his party’s support, Shortsleeve argues that he has a more realistic chance of unseating Governor Maura Healey, in no small part because of Minogue’s opposition to abortion. (Healey is not facing a primary challenge.)

Second: I’ll be watching the Democratic primary in the Fourth Congressional District, which includes towns from Brookline to my city of Fall River. Like many races nationwide, Democratic voters in the Fourth will choose between a more moderate Democrat, Representative Jake Auchincloss, and one with more left-wing values — Jason Poulos.

Auchincloss has not faced a primary opponent since he was elected to replace Representative Joe Kennedy III in 2020. He is a former Marine and Newton City Councilor who has garnered a reputation for working pragmatically across the aisle and sometimes criticizing his party’s progressive wing.

Poulos, a Sherborn resident and AI researcher, is running on a more progressive platform that includes canceling student debt and providing universal basic income. Though he has said he is a member of Democratic Socialists of America, he also contends that he is not running as a democratic socialist in this race. Voters can judge for themselves what that means.

Third, I’m watching the Republican primary for the First Bristol and Plymouth District State Senate seat, which covers the South Coast towns of Fall River, Somerset, Swansea, Westport, Freetown, Rochester and Lakeville. It’s the only contested Senate Republican primary in the state, and by some accounts the first time the district has had a contested Republican primary seat in decades.

Gabriel “Boomer” Amaral, a realtor from Fall River who lost the mayoral race in 2025 by 225 votes, is running against Somerset resident Manny Silva, a former information technology manager who works as a pastor. The outcome could hint at the type of red shift the South Coast has seen in recent years, evidenced by Fall River voting for Trump in 2024. While both candidates are conservative, Amaral has expressed frustration with the left’s focus on “social justice issues” and says he wants to help working-class families. Silva has talked about improving government transparency and reducing taxes.

For either man, unseating the Democratic incumbent, Senator Manuel Rodrigues, will be a steep challenge. Rodrigues, a 16-year incumbent who is chair of the powerful Senate Ways and Means Committee, is unopposed in the Democratic primary and has raised $225,000 in campaign contributions. The two Republicans, meanwhile, have less than $30,000 between them.

title: Boston police commissioner says officers will be on alert for Caribbean celebrations; urges people not to bring weapons
text:
Scooters are also prohibited, and the roads around Franklin Park will be closed to traffic and parking.

The Caribbean Carnival, a parade that begins at 1 p.m. at Warren Street and MLK Jr. Boulevard in Roxbury, will travel up Blue Hill Avenue before reaching Franklin Park, Cox said.

The event will have a firm cutoff time of 6 p.m., he said.

The carnival is preceded by another parade, known as J’ouvert, which begins at 6:30 a.m. at Shattuck Hospital, cutting through Franklin Park before ending at 10 a.m. at the parking lot of the Franklin Park Zoo.

In previous years, the morning procession has been the backdrop for various violent incidents, most notably in 2023 when eight people were wounded from gunfire between two rival groups.

Mayor Michelle Wu and community leaders denounced the violence at the time.

That followed fatal J’ouvert shootings in 2015 and 2014, which also happened in the hours just before or during the parade.

After the 2023 shooting, officials changed the parade route to avoid Talbot Avenue, where some of the previous shootings had taken place, Cox said. Now the festivities cut through Franklin Park, he said.

“Since we’ve moved it from Talbot Avenue, I don’t think we’ve had any incidents associated with it,” Cox said.

The carnival has also been marred by violence. In 2022, a man was killed when a gunman drove into a crowd and opened fire as people dispersed from the event following an earlier verbal altercation.

The shooter was later sentenced to 15 years in prison, the Globe reported.

Cox said police will continue to implement safety measures during the carnival.

Ahead of the city’s annual Dominican Parade on Aug. 16, Cox made a similar pledge, saying police would be out in force to prevent violence.

After that event concluded, police near Franklin Park apprehended a 20-year-old Dorchester man who was allegedly trying to conceal a loaded gun.

Police reported no violence during the parade.

Cox said that the training that helped officers make that arrest will prove critical again Saturday.

“The goal is for people not to bring [guns] here in the first place,” he said. But “our officers are trained on how to both observe folks that might be having them and then more importantly how to retrieve it from them in a safe way.”

Addressing a rise in stabbings in the city, Cox said that officers are aware of the threat.

“If you think there are a lot of guns in the world I would say there are exponentially more knives,” he said. “You can make a weapon out of anything. The reality is it’s a choice, and that’s what we’re trying to tell people — don’t make that choice.”

John R. Ellement of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Markey had an ‘iPad’ moment. Experts question whether it’s enough to bolster Moulton’s age pitch in Senate primary.
text:
Perhaps now more than ever, the nation’s aging political class is under renewed scrutiny, and Markey is not immune.

But while Moulton, 47, has made Markey’s age a central part of his “pass the torch” campaign, those potentially viral clips illustrating his argument on the need for generational change have been otherwise rare. Markey, across three debates, regularly jostled with his younger challenger, lobbed well-rehearsed retorts, and, last week, was quick to note his support from even younger representatives.

It’s all left some experts to question: Will the message ultimately break through?

That, they say, depends. Samuel Moyn, a Yale University professor and author of “Gerontocracy in America,” said in an interview that while age matters to many voters, if an older candidate doesn’t risk imminent “cognitive decline or outright death,” they will likely have a leg up in fending off those attacks.

Moulton and Markey are more similar than they are different on paper: They both agree that ICE should be abolished, that there should be better access to health care, and that women should be able to have abortions.

In a recent campaign ad, Moulton even said: “Senator Markey and I want the same things,” though, he argues, “wanting isn’t winning.”

“This is the lesson of this contest,” Moyn speculated. “If you have two people who are ideologically very similar and the older candidate is high functioning enough, he will win.”

Since the beginning of the campaign, Moulton has tried to convince voters that Markey is too old to serve another six-year term — by its end, he’ll be 86. He has challenged Markey to disclose his health records, called for a “serious conversation about” age limits in Congress, and suggested term limits for committee chairs.

In April, a dark money group led by a Moulton donor ran a 30-second ad titled “Diagnosis,” which featured an actor playing a doctor who warns of a fictional ailment called “Chronic Reelection Disorder.” The PAC ran a similar ad that aired before the August debate, showing a time-lapse of photos of Markey during his 50 years in Congress.

If he wins, Markey wouldn’t be the oldest senator in the chamber. Republican Chuck Grassley is the oldest sitting senator at the age of 92, followed by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who turns 85 next month. Sanders has endorsed Markey and is scheduled to rally with him Saturday in Dorchester. The average age of a senator at the start of last year was just under 64.

In other races, it often was a defining moment — a health scare or public flub — that provided a touchstone for arguments for a younger option. Connecticut voters recently ousted longtime Representative John Larson, who froze mid-sentence for nearly 20 seconds during a speech on the House floor in February 2025. Larson, 78, said it was due to a partial seizure.

Perhaps most famous was former President Joe Biden’s debate performance in June 2024. Biden sounded hoarse, frequently lost his train of thought, and made factual errors, all but crippling many Democrats’ confidence in him. Biden ultimately withdrew from the race, and that November, President Trump won a second term over Vice President Kamala Harris.

But this Senate primary has lacked a relative show-me moment, watchers say.

Markey has also proven he can beat a younger candidate. At 40, Representative Joseph P. Kennedy III lost the Senate primary to Markey, 74 at the time.

While Kennedy was decidedly younger, Markey had successfully rebranded himself as the hip, progressive fighter with endorsements from rising stars like New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the youth-led Sunrise Movement for climate action. By the time Election Day rolled around, Markey was polling 10 points ahead of Kennedy among voters 35 and younger.

David D’Alessandro, the former chief executive of John Hancock, recently penned an op-ed making a case for younger leaders on Beacon Hill. But he contends that Moulton is “oversimplifying” the age issue.

“His argument is coming out as, ‘He’s old, I’m young, vote for me,’ ” D’Alessandro said. “Markey was beatable with the right candidate.”

The age argument is also “a proxy or a straw man” that challengers wield against incumbent politicians instead of focusing on structural issues like campaign finance reform or party recruitment, said Tracey Gendron, chair of Virginia Commonwealth University’s Department of Gerontology.

“Age alone is an insufficient measure of competency,” said Gendron, author of the book “Ageism Unmasked.” “It’s also an insufficient measure of health.”

Gendron said the focus on age has “blown up” since Biden’s failed reelection campaign, and warned that age is used as a political cudgel without regard to a specific diagnosis or condition. Voters, she said, can get distracted by what she called essentially a nonissue.

While there are certain people in office who “won’t let go of power,” she said, blaming a candidate’s age is too simplistic.

“I’m going to vote for somebody based on how well they ideologically match with my values,” she said. “To take somebody down based on age . . . that is not only a value but an antithesis.”

So far, the odds are in the older candidate’s favor. Recent polling showed Markey leading Moulton by double digits ahead of the Sept. 1 primary. And nearly half of the 500 voters surveyed in a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll said that all else being equal, Markey’s age “makes no difference” in their choice.

By comparison, 33 percent of voters said the senator’s age would make them less likely to vote for him, while 11 percent said they would not vote for Markey because of his age.

Gendron said this is likely because Democratic primary voters don’t see a problem with Markey’s record or see an urgent need for change. Plus, she said, “there is no typical 80-year-old.”

“We tend to group people into ‘the elderly’ and think that older people are a monolith,” she said. “To think all people of a certain age are just a certain way doesn’t make sense.”

title: South Boston man to face sentencing in 2023 Dorchester murder
text:
A South Boston man convicted of first-degree murder for inciting a 2023 shooting in Dorchester that left a 41-year-old man dead is scheduled to be sentenced Friday in Suffolk Superior Court.

A jury convicted Patrick M. Harland, 41, on Tuesday for his role in the killing of Curtis M. Effee on Geneva Avenue on Dec. 30, 2023, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Superior Court Judge Christopher P. Belezos, who oversaw the trial, is scheduled to preside over the sentencing. Harland faces a mandatory life without parole sentence. His conviction will be reviewed by the Supreme Judicial Court.

According to prosecutors, Harland and his then-girlfriend verbally argued with Effee and a woman over the use of a vehicle. Harland summoned Dasahn Crowder, his girlfriend’s relative, to Geneva Avenue where Effee, 41, lived. Tyreese Robinson accompanied Crowder, prosecutors said.

Harland, Crowder, and Robinson began fighting with Effee, and Harland brandished a knife at him, prosecutors said. Crowder opened fire with a gun, fatally wounding Effee, prosecutors said. At least two children were nearby at the time of the shooting, officials said.

Crowder and Robinson were arrested the following day, while Harland was not found until March 25, 2024, prosecutors said.

After the shooting, Harland’s girlfriend split up with him, prosecutors said. While being sought by police, Harland threatened her, her children, and her mother, prosecutors said. He also “posted a fake missing person’s bulletin including her minor children’s names and ages and the address of her workplace,” prosecutors said.

Crowder, 23, of Quincy, and Robinson, 21, of Randolph, pleaded guilty in June to manslaughter, illegal gun possession, and six counts of armed assault with intent to murder.

They were sentenced to up to 30 years in prison.

In a statement, Hayden called the shooting a “tragic example of a dispute leading to a horrible act of violence ... the elevation of this situation by rash and poor decision-making caused extraordinary harm to the people involved and to the entire community.”

John R. Ellement can be reached at john.ellement@globe.com. Follow him @JREbosglobe.

title: Quincy quarries hit new heights, bat gets inside a home, and handgun is found in a flower planter
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police blotters in our communities.

People of a certain age may remember when the Quincy quarries were filled with water and young people would congregate there to jump off the graffitti-covered rocky ledges and swim. The quarries have since been filled with dirt and are now used by rock climbers and as a training site for the Massachusetts Firefighting Academy’s Technical Rescue Program, which was recently there to conduct a rope rescue instructor improvement session. The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services recently posted photos of the training, and wrote: “Strong work by the instructors and support staff who made it happen!”

On Aug. 1, Lincoln police received an emergency call from a phone that had an automated crash detection feature that had been activated. “While resources were en route, the involved party was able to report that there was no crash,” police wrote. “The calling party had left their phone on the roof of their vehicle resulting in the crash detection service being activated after the phone had fallen into the roadway.”

At approximately 8:48 a.m. on Aug. 17, Boston police officers responded after someone picking up trash and cleaning the flower planters outside Tufts Health Sciences Campus in Chinatown found a handgun in one of the planters. “Detectives arrived on scene and secured the firearm which was determined to be a Davis Industries P-380 semi-automatic handgun loaded with six rounds of live ammunition,” police wrote. “As detectives began their investigation, they were able to determine the unknown suspect had discarded the firearm before boarding a Silver Line Bus in the afternoon on August 14. The suspect later returned to the planter where he discarded the firearm, before realizing it was no longer where he had left it. Detectives acquired images of the suspect and dispersed them to officers throughout the area.” On Aug. 24, officers arrested a 55-year-old Dorchester man who allegedly ditched the gun in the planter and charged him with several offenses, including carrying a loaded firearm without a license, possession of a firearm with a defaced serial number, and improper storage of a firearm.

On Aug. 3, Lincoln police got a call from a resident of South Great Road who reported that a bat had gotten into their home. “Officers did the best they could but were unable to locate the animal,” the log entry stated. Police then got another call from the same residence. “A caller reported the bat in their house had not made its way out,” the log entry stated. “An officer assisted by opening a door. The bat eventually made its way outside.”

What’s up with all these wrong-way drivers lately? Yet another occurrence of this dangerous and potentially deadly phenomenon was reported on July 9, when a trooper from the State Police barracks in Middleborough was alerted to a driver traveling north in the southbound lanes of Route 24 in Freetown. “The caller reported nearly being struck head-on while traveling in the left travel lane,” police wrote. “The Trooper responded immediately and located the vehicle stopped in the median, facing the wrong direction.” The woman behind the wheel “exhibited numerous signs of impairment and performed poorly on Standardized Field Sobriety Tests,” and was subsequently arrested for operating under the influence of liquor, police wrote.

Emily Sweeney can be reached at emily.sweeney@globe.com. Follow her @emilysweeney and on Instagram @emilysweeney22.

title: ‘I’m not a puppet.’ For Lander and Gayle, Wu’s backing against state Senate incumbents comes with boost — and tough questions.
text:
At forums or debates, Lander and Gayle have had to vouch for their independence, and even motivations for simply running. Collins, a South Boston Democrat, has used Wu’s endorsements as something like fodder, arguing voters don’t want a “blind loyalist” to City Hall. Business leaders have questioned whether Wu’s influence in Brownsberger’s district outside Boston is a help or perhaps a hindrance.

“I’m not a puppet for anybody,” Gayle, a Dorchester Democrat, said at a recent candidate forum. “I stand here on my own, and I welcome the endorsement of anybody who thinks that I’m a great candidate and that I’m going to represent this community. ... I am not a proxy for the mayor.”

The dynamic is an unusual one, particularly for legislative races that tend to rise and fall on candidates’ résumés and experience, and the needs of a specific district.

The races, though, are unusual in themselves. Wu made waves in the Boston political universe when she endorsed Lander, her former policy adviser, and Gayle, an education advocate, against two fellow Democrats representing her city who have also been among her top political adversaries on Beacon Hill. Brownsberger, the Senate’s No. 3 Democrat, and Collins repeatedly helped block her bid to shift more of the city’s property tax burden onto commercial real estate to ease property tax spikes for homeowners.

Wu has argued that Lander and Gayle would better represent Boston residents’ interests in a Legislature where other measures she’s pushed, such as bills to limit rent increases in Boston or impose a tax on high-dollar real estate sales, have stalled.

“This is about an agenda that our residents need to see relief and action on, and the pace that the Senate seems to find acceptable is not connected to real life in Boston,” Wu told the Globe.

It’s meant Wu has hung over the race, both figuratively and oftentimes, literally. Last weekend, she rallied with volunteers for Gayle and Lander in separate events, saying the Senate needs “new leaders who are eager to run towards problems with big ideas and with huge vision.” As the two candidates took questions at various forums in the days before, Wu often wasn’t far from people’s lips.

If Brownsberger had voted the way the mayor wanted, Lander was asked during a debate hosted by the Charles River Regional Chamber, would he still be running for office? And should the business community be worried that Wu will instruct Lander how to vote?

“I started thinking about running for this office at the end of the legislative session two years ago,” Lander, who lives in Fenway, said, calling it a “five-car pileup.”

In a Globe interview, Lander said people in the district — who currently are represented by someone in the top rungs of Senate leadership — are “hungry for a Legislature that isn’t just going to listen to leadership.”

“Those are the people I’m going to listen to every single day who are, like, really frustrated with how hard it is to live here,” he said.

Some are still skeptical. Greg Reibman, chief executive at the Charles River Regional Chamber, said it’s unclear whether Lander’s embrace of Wu helps him in the district’s other corners of Watertown, Cambridge, and Belmont.

“Or,” Reibman said, “if his ties hurt him.”

At a candidate forum in Dorchester, moderators and attendees alike also pressed Gayle for reassurance that she would prioritize her constituents’ interests over those of her powerful political backer.

Gayle insisted that the mayor endorsed her because of Gayle’s reputation in the community and record of education advocacy work. The next night, at an event hosted by a local Democratic ward, when asked about what relationship the First Suffolk District senator should have with City Hill, Gayle preached collaboration. Juwan Skeens, another challenger, said it should be a connection with a “backbone.” Collins emphasized “independence.”

“It’s important to be an advocate for the people, not for an individual. Not for a politician, not to be a ‘yes’ person, or to carry the water of an individual,” Collins said, without mentioning Wu directly. “I don’t think this district deserves a blind loyalist.”

Collins, in turn, has leaned on his labor support, emphasized his work to build coalitions and secure state funding for Boston in his 15 years in elected office, and touted endorsements from Governor Maura Healey, state auditor Diana DiZoglio, and several Boston-area state representatives. He told the Globe he doesn’t take Wu’s criticisms of him personally — their fight over tax legislation has often bled fully into public view — but argued that it “speaks to an inability to compromise.”

“I have working relationships with people who I don’t agree with 100 percent; I think what you see differently is [the] mayor wants you to agree with her 100 percent,” Collins said.

Gayle has firmly disputed the characterization that voters are concerned about Wu’s influence. Wu is also coming off her dominant reelection effort, clearing out her competition after last year’s preliminary before coasting to a second term in November.

“The scrutiny is from a loud minority of people,” Gayle said. “It is not from everyday voters.”

Instead, residents are concerned about the rising costs of housing, utilities, groceries, and child care, Gayle said, arguing Collins had not done enough to address those issues or protect residents against Trump administration policies. She also said it was she who reached out to Wu to ask for her endorsement after she launched her campaign because she felt they were aligned on those values.

“If and when there comes a time that me and the mayor disagree, we’ll cross that bridge when we come to it,” Gayle said. “We are both strong, independent women, mothers raising our families in this city, and I think we’re excited to have the chance to work together on those things. There’s not an expectation that either one of us owes the other one for something.”

The talk also shouldn’t distract from what candidates say are the wider issues their voters care about, or what they, themselves, can bring. For Brownsberger and Lander, creating more affordable housing in the Senate district has become a key issue, and created stark differences; Lander, for example, supports lifting a ban on rent control while Brownsberger opposes it.

Brownsberger, of Belmont, said his campaign has “never been about a quarrel with the mayor.” As he sat on a stoop in Watertown last week making the case to one local resident, Brownsberger said his years at the State House have put him “in a great position to get a lot down and to continue to get a lot done.”

“I’m past climbing the ladder,” he said. “I’m growing like a tree, just putting down the roots, spreading out the branches, and taking care of what’s around.”

He later told the Globe he will work with Wu “when she’s ready.”

“I’m honestly baffled as to why the mayor seems so eager to tear down a fellow public servant,” he said.

Lander, in turn, has said he has “deep ties” to the other cities and towns in the district and would bring a fresh, younger perspective to the Senate.

“When I win, it is going to send a really loud message to all senators basically, most of whom do not have challengers or don’t have competitive elections, that there’s a cost to legislative dysfunction and inaction,” Lander said.

He has leaned heavily on Wu, too, including a mention of her endorsement in his well-oiled pitch at the door to potential supporters. At Sarah Baker’s doorstep in Watertown last week, Lander pointed to ongoing talks over legislation that would ban student cellphone use in public schools. With the school year starting, Lander tried to use it as an example of how bills “don’t move” at the State House.

“There is no urgency,” Lander said.

title: Senator Markey fields national progressives to make his case in primary race against Moulton
text:
Sanders also described Markey as someone who is “prepared to stand up to the greed, the irresponsibility, the arrogance of the billionaire class.”

“[They are] a class that thinks they are entitled to it all,” Sanders said. “Ed grew up in a trade union family. He knows what the working class in this country is going through. And I am very proud to call him a colleague, and I want to see him return to the United States Senate.”

Moulton has long argued that Markey is too old to serve another term and should “pass the torch” to a younger generation. Moulton’s argument aligns with a national trend in which voters have shifted toward younger, more progressive candidates over older incumbents.

But Markey and his supporters have instead tried to center his progressive values. He leaned into that idea on Saturday, calling his event the “greatest gathering of progressive voices on one stage, our progressive palooza.”

“They are all here, all assembled because we’re coming down to a referendum here in Massachusetts on who should be the senator for the next six years on the floor of the Senate, partnering with [Senator] Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders every single day,” Markey said.

Warren said Markey is a “progressive, a fighter that Massachusetts can depend on.”

“Are you ready to elect someone who has got the guts to stand up to giant corporate executives, to billionaires, to Republicans, to the president of the United States, and say enough screwing American families, we are here to fight back?” Warren said at the union hall.

During a rally on Lynn Common Saturday, Moulton waved off Markey’s gathering of progressives as the “political establishment” supporting him. Instead, Moulton pointed to his own event, dubbed “rally for the next generation,” that featured a bounce house.

“That’s why we’re here with the bouncy house,” Moulton told the Globe. “We’re focused on the next generation. We want to do things that bring in people to politics who don’t always get involved. This is not about an insider game. This is about being with the people.”

Markey’s surrogates, however, took close aim at Moulton’s politics on Saturday. Representative Ayanna Pressley called on voters to bring their friends and families to the polls to vote for Markey and, in the process, took an apparent snipe at Moulton.

“Only 100 people have the rarefied opportunity of serving in the United States Senate at a time. One hundred individual people. We can’t afford anyone on our side of the aisle to be mediocre. The roster is simply too small,” she said.

Moulton shrugged off Pressley’s comments.

“I don’t care,” he said. “I mean, was she talking about Senator Markey’s view on AI? How can you have a senator who deregulated the internet, made it unsafe for our kids, and now doesn’t even understand what AI is?”

But Pressley also criticized Moulton’s past comments on transgender children in sports. In a New York Times article following the 2024 election, Moulton said he would not want his two young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”

“Massachusetts Democrats don’t pander or throw their neighbors under the bus. Massachusetts Democrats don’t antagonize children or mumble half apologies. We stand up straight, and we fight like hell,” she said, in an apparent reference to the remarks.

Pressley was more direct in her attack on Moulton in an email she sent to supporters on Saturday.

“He suggested that Democrats throw these vulnerable children under the bus for the sake of political expediency. And he used disgusting, dehumanizing, misgendering language in the process,” she wrote in the email. “Disqualifying, disqualifying, disqualifying.”

Moulton has apologized for the remarks, including during his final televised debate with Markey earlier this month. In that appearance, Moulton said he was “sorry” if he hurt anyone “because that was not my intention.”

He also accused Markey of running a “very negative campaign from day one.”

“It’s kind of shocking that after 50 years in Washington, rather than being able to talk about his record, he just has to try to distort mine, and frankly, distort his own,” Moulton told the Globe.

Sam Brodey of the Globe staff contributed reporting.

title: David Hogg wants to oust sitting Democrats. The Eighth District — and its incumbent Stephen Lynch — may be his biggest target.
text:
“This race is not about Stephen Lynch’s age — it’s about his track record,” Hogg told roughly 40 Roath supporters in Roslindale, including state Representative Sam Montaño, Boston City Councilors Enrique Pepén and Ben Weber, and members of the Boston Teachers Union.

“I would not be here right now if this race was not very close,” Hogg said.

That dynamic has pushed the primary into a stratosphere of races nationwide testing voters’ appetite for replacing longtime Democratic incumbents with younger, often more progressive voices.

Roath, who has pledged to bring a “future-oriented, optimistic vision” to Congress, is one of 47 candidates Leaders We Deserve has endorsed this cycle in congressional and state legislative races from Texas to Minnesota. The PAC is also backing Daniel Lander in his challenge to state Senator William Brownsberger in the Massachusetts Legislature, and Hogg is planning to headline an event for Lander on Monday alongside Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.

Of the candidates the PAC has backed, 34 have won a primary or general election so far, though many were uncontested, intraparty races. Hogg said many of the incumbents the group planned to target ultimately retired, in a year that has seen a staggering number of incumbents exiting Congress.

That’s put a heavier focus on the Eighth District. Hogg’s group has poured at least $470,000 into the primary as of last week — which is among the most the group says it has spent on behalf of a candidate this cycle. That’s included nine mailers, including one that refers to Lynch as “MAGA’s favorite Democrat.”

Roath and Hogg have repeatedly criticized past votes Lynch took on immigration and health care, which the congressman has defended throughout the campaign. And Lynch has dismissed many of the attacks as “ridiculous stuff that you hear in the middle of a campaign.” He has repeatedly decried the money Leaders We Deserve and other groups have spent on Roath’s behalf, and Lynch’s campaign has charged that Hogg’s group has been “lying about his record in Congress.”

Lynch has repeatedly pointed to the Trump administration dubbing him an “ICE agitator” and his enduring support from unions such as the Massachusetts AFL-CIO and groups that back left-leaning candidates, such as the Planned Parenthood Action Fund.

“Money in politics is probably the most insidious impact and danger to our democracy right now,” Lynch said during a forum in Weymouth this month, the only one where both candidates appeared together on stage this campaign. “My opponent has had four mailings. You probably got them all, and they’re all from PACs that he’s working with.”

Lynch said on a radio program Thursday that he has done about two dozen town halls with senior centers and councils on aging and that he’s spent the last seven weeks knocking on doors. This weekend, he attended Norwood Day alongside State Senator Mike Rush, also facing a primary challenge to his left.

“It seems like we’re fighting amongst ourselves, the Democrats, rather than focusing on getting back into this government,” Lynch said during an interview with the Boston Neighborhood Network on Thursday, adding that he’s a moderate trying to keep other moderates “in the Democratic column.”

“We don’t want to be the party of protesters,” he said.

Hogg made a name for himself nationally leading protests against gun violence. After graduating from Harvard University in 2023, he then turned his attention to the Democratic Party. He briefly served as a DNC co-vice chair beginning in February 2025, before stepping down that June amid criticism from Democratic leaders who disagreed with his plans to get involved in races against sitting Democrats.

Hogg said his group backs candidates under the age of 45 for Congress and those under 35 in state legislatures with certain progressive beliefs, such as supporting Medicare for All.

Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist based in Washington, D.C., said that while he believes Hogg has his finger on the pulse of the change Democrats are looking for, “he has taken a pretty adversarial tone toward not just the establishment.”

“He’s not exactly pitching a big-tent version of the Democratic Party,” Lehrich said.

He pointed to Hogg’s support of some longshot candidates, such as Deja Foxx, a content creator who lost her Democratic primary in Arizona last year by nearly 40 percentage points. But Lynch, he said, is a “good target” for Hogg: “He’s a pretty centrist voice in a blue seat for a long time.”

Roath has leaned into criticisms that Lynch hasn’t been active enough for the district, which stretches from Boston south of the city. “This is a place that should be fighting above its weight,” he said.

In a Roslindale neighborhood with mailboxes stuffed with mailers and lawn signs, Hogg had a much warmer reception than he’s used to getting on social media Sunday afternoon.

“I’ve been waiting my whole life for this kid to grow up,” one woman said of Hogg, after stopping to ask Roath about his outside funding.

“You can be my hero if you vote for Patrick,” Hogg replied.

Hogg has said he was drawn to the race after watching a clip of Lynch last year sparring with a protester upset with Democrats’ response to Trump, during which Lynch said, “I’m elected. You want to decide that? You need to run for Congress.”

In Hogg’s view, Democrats’ “No. 1 guiding philosophy is risk aversion.”

“The reality is, it is so hard to defeat a Democratic incumbent,” he said. But he added that if one does “get defeated, it’s because [they] genuinely aren’t doing the work.”

title: ‘He was the heart of the city.’ Fans descend upon Boston Common for Jaylen Brown’s 741 Frequency Fest.
text:
Fans lined up across the Common to buy shoes from Brown’s company 741 Performance. One fan in line, Yasmine Bonei, of Chelsea, was excited to get the shoes and celebrate Brown.

“As a Boston person for the last nine years, it’s kind of sad seeing him leave Boston,” Bonei said. “I know in Philadelphia he’s gonna do great things.”

“Razor” Ramon Jamal, a barber cutting hair at Marvelous Barber Lounge for the event, said the lounge was participating to give back to the community.

“It’s just a great event to give back to Boston, especially with somebody that was so renowned to the city,” Jamal said.

A stage was erected in the center of the celebration where artists including the Boston Public Schools marching band, local R&B artist Yanna G, and Grammy Award-winning artist Lil Jon performed for the crowd of fans.

“Jaylen Brown was the heart of the city, the heart of the team, obviously, very appreciative of the times that we had,” said Tariq Longsworth, of Dorchester.

Longsworth was sad to see Brown leave, but seeing the number of people who came out to support Brown meant a lot.

“I can’t wait to see when seven goes up in the rafters,” Longsworth said.

Chris Breen traveled from Toronto for the event. He was donning Celtics gear from head to toe and had even dyed his beard dark green.

“When he came in, he and the rest of the team, they changed everything,” Breen said. “We had gone through some changes since the 2008 championship, some ups and downs, then they won a championship.”

Johannes Becker became a Celtics fan once she and her husband moved from Munich, Germany. She named her child, Liam Jalen, after Brown, for what he represents.

“He’s one of the smart players; he has brains, and he stands up for the community. He does a lot for the community,” Becker said. “He speaks his mind, and that really resonated with us.”

Before Brown stepped onto the stage, he walked around the event signing items for fans. People moved closer, hoping for a chance to meet their hero. Some fans were even wearing 76ers merch.

When Brown walked onto the stage, he was met with a roar from the crowd. Fans waved flags and jerseys as he spoke.

“I’m at a loss for words. When I got to this city, I said I’m gonna go to war for this city,” Brown said. ”I met so many great people here, people that helped me in the community, that motivated me on my journey, people that have supported me even when I didn’t support myself at times. So, I just want to say thank you to Boston."

Toward the end of the event, Brown performed a song he had created with A$AP Ferg called “Just Do It.” After Brown thanked the crowd, he invited out rap superstar Lil Baby.

The event ended with Boston Mayor Michelle Wu coming on stage to share how much she and the city appreciate Brown.

“I have seen him not just in the Garden, but I have gotten to see him in our schools, in our parks, and in our classrooms, Wu said, ”Every minute, he’s poured into this city. He has changed lives throughout Boston; that’s why so many people are here."

Olajide Ogundipe Jr., of Lower Mills, said it was very surprising Brown brought out Lil Baby and that it was “cool” to see Mayor Wu show support.

“I feel like we did a good job showing up today,” Ogundipe Jr. said.

title: Life sciences lawyer Megan Gates takes over as Pine Street Inn’s new board chair
text:
Megan Gates has been helping Pine Street Inn through volunteering and donations since 2007, and serving on its board since 2012.

Now, her contributions to the homeless services nonprofit will ramp up again, as she starts her term as the organization’s new chair. She took over for former chair Lorn Davis in July, though her first board meeting as chair is scheduled for Sept. 23.

Gates’s day job is as a life sciences lawyer at Covington & Burling, and she also just concluded a term as president of the Boston Bar Foundation. But Gates said she can always make more time for Pine Street Inn, whose namesake shelter is in the South End, where she lives.

Gates said she’s been encouraged by the growing emphasis at Pine Street Inn to develop apartments where previously unhoused people can live, with support services to keep them off the streets and help them rebuild their lives. Among the biggest ones: the 202-unit Lyndia (named after Pine Street Inn president Lyndia Downie) in Jamaica Plain, 111 units in the former YWCA in the Back Bay, and a 99-unit hotel conversion in Dorchester that celebrates its grand opening this fall.

“To witness the evolution toward housing with supportive services is demonstrative of what can happen when we put our minds towards how we can create an environment where people can live and thrive and rebuild their lives,” Gates said.

The Lyndia, which offers 140 units to chronically homeless people, was trumpeted as the largest “permanent supportive housing development” in New England when it opened last year. Several of the city’s biggest corporate players — such as Liberty Mutual, Suffolk Construction, and Mass General Brigham — contributed millions of dollars to make it happen.

“It’s incumbent on the business community to be mindful of how people are able to afford to live in this community, and what we are doing to support that,” Gates said. “Boston is a wonderful community, in that regard. There’s a sense of ‘to whom much has been given, much is expected.’”

title: New CEO of Campus Without Walls connects students and teachers for virtual statewide classes
text:
Arbaje-Thomas was recruited last year to be the chief operating officer, after leading METCO for seven years. Ron Walker, the former state labor secretary, was leading Campus Without Walls on an interim basis and working with her to prepare for the handoff this summer.

“One of the things that I loved, and why I took the job at METCO, was the opportunity for people to learn together from different backgrounds,” she said. “To basically do something even bigger than METCO, I did not even think it was possible.”

The nonprofit’s $1.2 million budget — for its six-person staff, technology, and other expenses — is largely funded through philanthropy, though it did receive a $125,000 earmark in the state budget with help from state Representative Rob Consalvo.

The students at the teachers’ home schools will participate virtually, along with the remote students, to ensure a similar experience. Arbaje-Thomas hopes friendships can develop among them, much like the relationships between METCO students and their suburban counterparts.

About 200 students are lined up. This fall, the nonprofit will offer 15 classes, to study everything from politics to statistics, with most providing college credits through American International College in Springfield. The model is designed to eventually include industry-specific work, to provide job skills training.

“We have great teachers, we have great courses,” Arbaje-Thomas said. “We just can’t get students to all of them. But technology has given us a way for that to happen.”

Two of downtown’s most prominent office buildings just got roughly $100 million makeovers to their lobbies and other areas, and one construction firm was behind both of them.

North Reading-based Columbia recently completed a 113,000-square-foot renovation project for DivcoWest’s One Lincoln tower, and will wrap up work on a similarly sized project at The Chiofaro Co.’s International Place two-tower complex later in September.

For Columbia president Shaun Lover, these projects have been about improving the public areas and adding new amenities to attract employers, and employees, as they weigh postpandemic work options. (For example, at International Place, Columbia built “The Aries Club” meant to be a private members’ club for tenants.)

But they’ve also been about opening these fortresses to the broader community, making them more welcoming. International Place went up nearly four decades ago, hard against what was the elevated Central Artery, while One Lincoln was previously known primarily as State Street’s headquarters. Now, the owners of both properties want to better integrate them into neighborhood.

With so few new buildings going up in Boston currently, these projects represent an important injection of private-sector capital into the economy.

“There’s one tower crane in Boston right now,” Lover said. “[But] there’s this $200 million in investments that put people to work but is also meant to attract tenants and also attract the neighborhood.”

The union push to impose new city standards for unarmed security guards is running up against a powerful opponent: the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce.

The proposal, backed by SEIU Local 32BJ and put forward last month by city councilors Henry Santana and Ruthzee Louijeune, would require employer-funded training for unarmed building guards. (State law already requires something similar for armed guards.)

In an Aug. 11 letter signed by chief executive Jim Rooney, the chamber notes the ordinance “would impact a variety of industries in unpredictable ways” such as office buildings, hospitals, universities, labs, hotels, retailers, bars, and “countless other organizations.”

The chamber basically describes the proposal as a solution in search of a problem. The new rules could also increase hiring costs and impose barriers to recruiting new employees.

32BJ executive vice president Kevin Brown says the union is simply responding to the needs of members. About 800 in Boston, he said, would be affected by the rule.

“Our members said they’re encountering issues like overdoses, people having heart attacks, people who are violent,” Brown says.

Brown said he hopes the council will pass it as soon as sometime in September. Ten of the 13 councilors have signed on, he said, and Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration is on board.

“It probably should have been addressed years ago,” Brown added, “but there’s no time like the present.”

You might say Nth Cycle is finally reaching critical mass, now that it has landed a grant award from the Department of Energy worth up to $100 million.

The Burlington battery recycling startup will use the money to help defray the costs of building a refining facility in South Carolina. The roughly 50-person firm has previously said it also plans to open one in the Netherlands, in addition to an existing plant in Ohio.

The new Southeast facility will annually recycle “black mass” — materials in shredded lithium-ion batteries that can be reused. Nth Cycle’s technology uses electricity to break down these materials, as opposed to using traditional chemicals in a less efficient, more expensive process that produces significantly more pollutants.

The Department of Energy grant represents a rare bit of good news for a local climate-tech startup seeking assistance from the Trump administration. In a press release, chief executive Megan O’Connor praised the administration for recognizing that “keeping recoverable critical minerals in the United States is a matter of national security.”

O’Connor founded the startup with Desiree Plata, an engineering professor at MIT, and Chad Vecitis, Nth Cycle’s chief scientist. It got its start at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, with financial help from the Department of Energy, before relocating to Massachusetts in 2020. In 2021, Nth Cycle received an investment from Clean Energy Ventures of Boston, still one of Nth Cycle’s biggest private investors. The company is now preparing to go public, via a merger with a SPAC firm affiliated with Kensington Capital.

To get such a significant grant from the DOE, Nth Cycle’s original supporter, O’Connor said in an interview, represents “a full circle moment for us.”

title: Massachusetts is going PAC to PAC
text:
A wave of super PACs have emerged this summer, many with a strikingly narrow mission: supporting just one or two state legislative candidates. And their biggest backers? In many cases, it’sother super PACs.

Take the Progressive Cambridge independent expenditure PAC, which was created in July and has already poured more than $181,000 into digital ads, mailers, and mobile billboards to boost state Representative Marjorie Decker as she faces a primary rematch against Evan MacKay, the Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate whom Decker defeated by just 41 votes two years ago.

The PAC has reported just three donors so far: Two service employee unions — SEIU Local 509 and the SEIU state council — kicked in a combined $35,000 while another $85,000 came from a separate super PAC, the Boston Opportunity IE PAC, that had been dormant for years before it made the seven-figure contribution last Tuesday.

The super PAC will undoubtedly have to raise more money to cover tens of thousands of dollars in liabilities it’s racked up.

Meanwhile, on the state Senate side of the ballot, Citizens for an Affordable Massachusetts independent expenditure PAC has spent roughly $43,000 to support state Senator Nick Collins, who is facing two candidates in Tuesday’s primary — most notably Latoya Gayle, a Michelle Wu-backed activist from Dorchester.

That PAC’s second-biggest donor is also another super PAC, this one with ties to former Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh dubbed a “Balanced and Better Boston.” That PAC gave the Collins-backing PAC $12,000.

Gayle is getting some super PAC support, too, from the so-called Boston Leads PAC, a committee created in July that’s also propping up Daniel Lander, another Wu-backed candidate who’s challenging state Senator William Brownsberger.

Boston Leads has spent $53,000 on Gayle and about $31,000 on Lander. And its funding source? Three other super PACs: the Hospitality Workers PAC, and two Wu-aligned super PACs, dubbed “Boston Voice” and “Bold Boston.”

This PAC-to-PAC spending makes the money trail considerably harder to follow — and, by extension, can make it harder to see what interests are actually at play in a legislative race.

Take the group spending for Decker. While Decker can’t coordinate with the super PAC, she has some theories about why two labor unions at least might be going to bat for her.

“I fought to save 170 [Department of Mental Health] case manager jobs. They’re invested, right?” Decker told the Globe at a campaign stop Sunday.

“But,” she added, “we’ve got to find a balance between: What does it look like for advocacy groups to inform, versus other operators out there?”

Outside spending is already adding up across the state this year. Super PACs — which can raise and spend unlimited funds — have already spent more than $1.9 million this year, nearly three times the $659,000 they spent on state-level races in 2024. That’s still well short of 2022, when competitive open races for governor, attorney general, and auditor each generated their own waves of outside spending. (Even the typically little-watched lieutenant governor’s race drew a super PAC then.)

A lot of that action, and money, is still swirling around the top of the ticket this year, too. The Commonwealth Unity PAC, a super PAC backing Republican gubernatorial hopeful Brian Shortsleeve, has spent roughly $809,000 boosting Shortsleeve and battering his rivals. Massachusetts First, a super PAC backing Shortsleeve’s primary opponent, Michael Minogue, has spent considerably less in the primary — less than $160,00.

Governor Maura Healey doesn’t have a super PAC actively spending to support her yet. But a Democratic Governors Association-aligned super PAC that filed paperwork with state regulators in June appears to be waiting in the wings.

WHOLE HOGG: David Hogg wants to oust sitting Democrats. The 8th District — and its incumbent Stephen Lynch — may be his biggest target. by Anjali Huynh, The Boston Globe: David Hogg ruffled feathers among Democrats when he pledged to put millions of dollars toward taking on longtime politicians within his own party in a bid to push younger, liberal candidates into office. His biggest test case may come Tuesday.

The 26-year-old gun control advocate’s organization, Leaders We Deserve, has put half a million dollars toward unseating US Representative Stephen Lynch, the Eighth District’s 71-year-old unapologetically moderate incumbent who’s become one of Hogg’s top House targets this cycle.

PLAYING THE FIELD: Most Democrats Don’t Want to Talk About Transgender Athletes. He’s Leaning In. by Reid J. Epstein, The New York Times: Senator Ed Markey might be the only high-profile Democrat in America eagerly campaigning as a supporter of transgender rights as many other top Democrats have grown cagey on the issue.

MINOGUE’S BLUE PRINT: A Republican candidate for Mass. governor has slathered his campaign in blue. Experts say it might be intentional. by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: Minogue is running for Massachusetts governor in a campaign bathed in blues. The color dominates his lawn signs, campaign website, and, at times, his own clothes. Experts in political branding said the Republican’s embrace of a largely blue color scheme — typically signaling Democratic alignment — sends a message, even if it’s not an intentional one, that could make him more appealing to voters in a state that largely elects Democrats.

LEFT HOOK: Can a progressive overtake two center-left Democrats in N.H.’s 1st Congressional District race? by Steven Porter, The Boston Globe: Democratic congressional candidate Carleigh Beriont said she respects both Stefany Shaheen and Maura Sullivan, the center-left candidates widely viewed as the top two Democratic contenders for New Hampshire’s competitive First Congressional District. But she also views them as “two sides of the exact same coin.”

AND THEN THERE WERE FIVE: Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former congressional staffer running in the Sixth Congressional District, dropped out of the Democratic primary on Saturday and endorsed state Representative Tram Nguyen, lending another last-minute jolt of momentum to the Andover Democrat’s campaign to replace Representative Seth Moulton.

It’s unclear how Lancaster’s exit might sway the outcome of Tuesday’s election, given Lancaster’s name will remain on the ballot. But the Salem Democrat’s departure is the latest in an 11th-hour surge of support for Nguyen, and could add some clarity to a field where Nguyen has positioned herself as the progressive alternative to other two other perceived front-runners, former White House aide Dan Koh and Lynnfield fintech executive John Beccia.

ONE VOTER WHO’S STILL UNDECIDED: Which candidate is the highest profile pol in the Sixth District voting for on Tuesday?

That’s a secret Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll isn’t ready to tell.

“I’m still considering all the choices,” the former Salem mayor said (after a long pause) when we caught her on the campaign trail Sunday. “I haven’t endorsed in that race officially, but I’m looking forward to voting.”

Driscoll isn’t alone in staying out of the race. Nguyen picked up a string of endorsements last week from US Representatives Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan and Attorney General Andrea Campbell. But with just days to go, much of the state’s congressional delegation — Moulton included — still hasn’t taken a side. Neither has Driscoll’s partner in state government, Governor Maura Healey.

The same is true for most of the mayors in the biggest cities across the district, with one notable exception: Peabody Mayor Ted Bettencourt, who endorsed Koh last week.

Senator Elizabeth Warren hasn’t gotten involved in the race herself but her husband, Bruce Mann, donated $1,000 to Nguyen’s campaign last week.

THE DICHOTOMY OF DAN: Just as a union-backed mailer is landing in Sixth District mailboxes touting Dan Koh’s promise not to let AI companies steal workers’ jobs, a super PAC devoted to reining in the influence of the AI industry is taking aim at the Andover Democrat’s support from industry execs.

Guardrails Alliance, an organization formed to counter the influence of pro-AI groups, plans to fly a banner over the North Shore coastline Monday accusing Koh, a former Joe Biden aide, of being “funded by the same AI billionaires” as President Trump. The criticism comes after the Think Big PAC, the Democratic arm of the pro-AI Leading the Future network, spent more than $700,000 on his behalf as of Thursday.

Meanwhile, amid the heaps of political mail flooding Sixth District mailboxes, a similarly neat irony is taking shape.

Mailers from the AFL-CIO that dub him “labor’s endorsed candidate” say Koh will “refuse to allow Big Tech corporations and rapidly evolving technologies like AI” to steal workers’ jobs. They’re landing at the same time as mailers from Think Big, which supports candidates who back a “pro-innovation, pro-AI vision.”

So ... where does the Sixth District hopeful stand? A spokesperson for Koh declined to comment.
