title: Healey, Minogue to meet in November, setting up expensive gubernatorial fight
text:
With the results of the GOP now in hand, the general election will likely be as much about Trump as it will be about Healey’s first term in office.

At her own primary night party at a union hall in Dorchester, Healey was quick to cast blame on Trump for the high cost of living in Massachusetts, telling supporters the president put in place harmful tariffs, cut funding and access to health care, and slashed funding for science, research, and local universities.

“We see the damage Trump is doing every day. He’s raising your costs, he’s terrorizing our communities, he’s taking away your health care and your rights,” Healey said, warning that her Republican opponent “will bring Trump’s agenda to Massachusetts.”

The primary comes as Massachusetts faces challenges on multiple fronts: a housing crunch that is driving many residents to consider leaving the state, for example, and a higher cost of living that is straining household budgets across the economic spectrum.

Healey is running for a second term alongside Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll, a former mayor of Salem who was also unopposed in the primary.

The results on Tuesday are expected to kick into high gear what has already become an expensive gubernatorial election. Minogue has poured more than $15 million of his own money into his gubernatorial bid while Healey had $6.6 million in her campaign account as of the end of July.

At his primary night party in Medford, Minogue did not name Healey in his victory speech, but said “our opponents will choose division” in the race for governor.

“They will choose to dishonestly attack me with political ads, and in fact, they already have begun,” the Hamilton Republican said. “Well, we’re choosing something different. We’re going to go down a different path. Our opponents know what happens when we stand united. They know when we put aside our differences and join together, we will defeat the one-party system.”

The general election battle over the next several months is likely to generate intensified attacks from Democrats on Minogue for his ties to Trump and congressional Republicans.

Unlike in the 2022 election, in which the Republican nominee openly embraced Trump, both Minogue and Shortsleeve had sought to distance themselves from the White House in an apparent bid to make themselves more appealing to unenrolled voters who make up a majority of Massachusetts’ voter rolls.

Trump had not endorsed either candidate in the GOP primary.

Still, Healey and the state Democratic Party have attempted to paint Minogue as “MAGA Mike,” pointing to the hundreds of thousands of dollars he donated to national Republican causes and a super PAC that backed Trump’s successful 2024 bid for the White House.

“In this election, we’re going to send a message that if you support Donald Trump, if you funded him, if you endorse the bad things he’s done to our state, then you cannot be governor of Massachusetts,” Healey said Tuesday night.

Minogue, 59, is a businessman making his first overture into politics after earning a fortune in the medical device industry, where he oversaw the sale of the Danvers-based heart-pump maker Abiomed to Johnson & Johnson in 2022 for $16.6 billion.

He was little known outside the medical field before entering the political fray last year, but has since spent millions of his own dollars to boost his name recognition and catapult himself to the top of the GOP ticket.

He is a “pro-life” Catholic who has said he would “uphold” reproductive rights laws in Massachusetts if elected governor. And he has promised to help deport “illegal immigrants” in the state and reform safety-net benefits for migrants who arrive in the state.

Laureen Goodhue, 64, said she voted for Minogue on Tuesday in Allston because she “aligned with everything that he believed.”

“I feel that he’s more Republican than Shortsleeve,” she said. “Plus, I think he’s pro-life.”

Minogue has also largely pitched himself as a “new kind of governor,” or a political outsider intent on using his business acumen to run the state. He drew heavily on his experience in the military and health care field in his pitch to voters Tuesday night, and labeled himself an “outsider.”

“I am beholden to no special group. I go into this role knowing I will work for you,” he said.

But Minogue faces a steep uphill battle in his campaign to unseat Healey. Polls have shown that Healey led by double digits in a hypothetical head-to-head matchup with Minogue, including in a Suffolk University/Boston Globe survey from June.

Shortsleeve, 54, was also making his first foray into elected politics. But he is best known for leaving venture capital more than a decade ago to serve as acting general manager and chief administrator of the MBTA after a series of major snowstorms in 2015 crushed the transit system.

Shortsleeve conceded the Republican primary to Minogue shortly after 9 p.m. and endorsed his opponent.

“I have been a fighter my entire life, and we fought hard throughout this campaign for the future we believe Massachusetts deserves. Mike Minogue is a fighter, too, and I know he will bring that same fight on behalf of the taxpayers to Beacon Hill,” Shortsleeve said in a statement.

Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor and Shortsleeve’s running mate, locked up the Republican nomination for lieutenant governor after two other candidates were forced out of the race amid a signature fraud controversy earlier this summer.

That means Oliver would pair with Minogue after months of his and Shortsleeve’s campaigns criticizing him as un-electable in a head-to-head matchup with Healey.

Healey, 55, swept into office four years ago as the state’s first woman and first openly LGBTQ elected governor, riding a progressive reputation built over eight years as attorney general when she emerged as one of the state’s most notable Trump antagonists, filing nearly 100 lawsuits against the Republican’s administration during his first term in office.

But since succeeding Baker, Healey has cut a more moderate tone. Healey has regularly touted a $1 billion-a-year tax package she signed in 2023 as one of her signature achievements and has sought to firm up her public safety credentials this year.

She has also leaned into Democratic calls to counter Trump on immigration. In her speech Tuesday, Healey pointed to her past work as attorney general.

“I’m the only one in this race who’s actually prosecuted and put away bad guys, drug traffickers, human traffickers. We can agree that we want violent criminals off the streets and deported. What we can also agree on is that none of what ICE is doing is making us safe,” she said.

title: Senator Ed Markey tops Seth Moulton in bitter Democratic Senate primary, riding progressive chops to nomination
text:
Markey spoke to a jam-packed ballroom at the Omni Parker House in Boston, where supporters and Democratic stalwarts, including Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, packed in to celebrate the incumbent.

Against a backdrop of high school and college-age students, Markey promised the crowd a future chock-full of progressive priorities, from abolishing federal immigration enforcement to passing universal child care to cementing abortion rights in law.

He said the race is “all about the American dream” in Massachusetts and in states where he has backed other successful progressive Democrats this cycle.

“That fight is in our hands here in Massachusetts, in Maine, in Michigan,” he said. “Our progressive movement knows how to fight. We cannot surrender tomorrow.”

About an hour after polls closed, Moulton took the stage at his own election night watch party at a union hall in Dorchester to tell supporters he called Markey to congratulate him on his victory.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy, but it is necessary,” he said. “We started conversations that needed to happen, and I will never stop pushing the Democratic Party and our country to look toward the future.”

With a win in November, Markey would return to Washington for a third full six-year term as the junior senator and extend his time in Washington into a sixth decade.

Markey’s primary victory tells the story of a race in which, despite Moulton’s attempts, age appears to have played little role in many voters’ decisions about whether to back an incumbent who will be 86 by the time his next term would end.

The dynamic complicates the emerging national narrative of Democratic politics in this year’s midterm elections, during which a historic number of incumbent lawmakers have lost primary challenges due to perceptions they had been in office too long, were insufficiently progressive — or both.

Markey ran well to the left of his 47-year old rival, embracing staunch progressive policies — Medicare for All being his most common talking point — as national left-wing figures like Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez embraced him. Markey said shortly before their first debate in July that, should he win, his next term would be his last, saying he needed “to finish this progressive agenda, and then I will step down.”

Moulton repeatedly hammered his argument that Markey’s age was a liability and that new leaders were needed to tackle contemporary problems. Still, many voters said they were skeptical of his liberal bona fides.

This contest did not come close to attracting the national or statewide energy, fund-raising, or media attention that Markey’s battle with Joseph Kennedy III did six years ago. Amid general voter indifference and relative lack of enthusiasm for the candidates, Markey’s ability to rally the progressive faithful was enough to hand him another term this time around in what was expected to be a low-turnout contest.

Much of the race involved both Markey and Moulton vying to prove their progressive credibility to primary voters, as well as their desire to stand out in a race where both candidates often landed on the same side of national issues.

With few genuine policy differences between them, the race was contentious and, sometimes bitter. In their second debate, Moulton unveiled a narrative that Markey was somehow implicated in the Epstein files, a claim that the congressman pushed with little to no evidence and that Markey called “reprehensible” and “character assassination.”

Markey, meanwhile, criticized Moulton as beholden to his financial supporters in the private equity sector. The senator’s supporters went harsher, with Representative Ayanna Pressley in the final weekend calling Moulton’s past comments on trans youth in sports “disqualifying” and saying that Democrats cannot afford “mediocre” representatives.

Moulton had suggested in 2024 that identity politics were to blame for the party’s electoral losses, saying he would not want his two young daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete.”

Moulton has since, and repeatedly this campaign, apologized to the trans community for his comments, saying “he was sorry if my comments hurt you.”

“We don’t accept a younger politician with older politics,” transgender activist Tyler Hack, who founded a political action committee to elect pro-trans candidates to federal office, said at Markey’s election night party. “Throwing trans kids under the bus is . . . a dealbreaker.”

Even as the snipes became sharper, public opinion polls showed a largely consistent race, with Markey often in the lead by double digits. After a Suffolk/Globe poll showed Markey with a double-digit lead last month, Moulton dismissed polling in this election cycle as being “wildly off.”

But the factors that contributed to polling misses elsewhere — like significant consolidation for one candidate or onslaughts of outside spending — weren’t present in Massachusetts. Markey enjoyed far more support from the party establishment and key groups throughout the entire campaign. Moulton also had comparatively few backers in local offices around the state, and zero public supporters among his Massachusetts colleagues in Washington.

While Moulton was the beneficiary of the lion’s share of outside spending in the race, largely through a super PAC funded by his supporters, it was not enough to make the contest closer.

Moulton, a six-term congressman, swept into office 12 years ago by topping a longtime incumbent. But Markey’s ability to cast himself as the ideological choice among a primary electorate that disproportionately leans left paid off.

Doug Rubin, a senior adviser to Moulton’s campaign, told the Globe that “we had a theory of the case that voters were looking for change,” but that “clearly voters in Massachusetts were looking for the future that Markey provided.”

“So credit to them. They ran a very effective campaign,” Rubin said. “The senator has already obviously had a very long and good career, and people really like him.”

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday night in Medford, Deaton, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, indicated he would put up a spirited fight in the general election. Deaton ran for the Senate two years ago, losing to Senator Elizabeth Warren.

“I want people to get past labels and look at who’s the best candidate in each race,” he said. “In the race between me versus Ed Markey, I’m the better candidate, not because of age, not because of how long he’s been in office, because I have real solutions to the problems that people face.”

As Moulton supporters and staff continued to mingle at the Plumbers Local 12 union hall after he conceded the race, several expressed hope he would remain in politics.

“I hope he would” run for office again, said Lei Huang, 59, a Brighton consultant whose teenage daughter volunteered for Moulton. “He has good clarity on what he wants to achieve.”

Melissa Woods, 39, voted for Markey in Allston Tuesday, citing her perspective that he is “just the more seriously progressive candidate.”

Markey’s age, however, was also top of mind for voters, regardless of who they ultimately supported. Betty Ellis, 76, said her decision to vote for Markey was a tough one.

“I really do feel like after 80, you know, age is really a factor,” Ellis, of Cambridge, said. “But I wasn’t thrilled with Moulton, and I thought, ‘Well, I feel like Markey has done a great job.’ I feel like he’s a man of integrity, and if he’s feeling too old, he will step down.”

Norah Burch, 53, said in Allston that she voted for Markey because he’s “doing a great job for however long he’s been doing it.”

“People are like, ‘Oh, he’s so old.’ But I don’t think Moulton’s got what it takes. I don’t care how old he is,” Burch said.

Some older voters were turned off by Moulton’s closing attack on Markey: hammering him for stumbling over details about artificial intelligence programs in their final debate. Moulton’s TV ads highlighting the flub blanketed the airwaves in the closing weeks of the campaign — which Cheryl Hassan, a retired chiropractor from Lynnfield, said she “personally hated.”

“I don’t know either what [AI programs] I use,” Hassan said. “And I’m not stupid.”

Globe correspondent Audrey Tomlin, Kelly Garrity, and Chris Van Buskirk of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: The four races I’m watching Tuesday night
text:
West Roxbury’s Michael Rush is seeking a ninth term in the state Senate, representing Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Westwood, and parts of Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and Hyde Park. (I live in the district.)

A Navy veteran, Rush has served on Beacon Hill since 2003, when he was elected state representative. His first opponent in 16 years is Persis Yu, a Hyde Park attorney, social worker, and first-time candidate challenging him from the left on affordability and State House transparency.

Rush, the Senate Majority Whip, has the backing of the Democratic establishment, including Mayor Michelle Wu. The Dorchester Reporter noted that Rush supported Wu’s tax proposal, while the mayor endorsed challengers to senators who opposed it.

Yu has been a strong fund-raiser. Meanwhile, Globe political reporter Kelly Garrity noted that Rush and other Massachusetts politicians received contributions from Anthropic employees after Rush offered an AI-safety amendment that the company supported and the Senate adopted.

Rush has no apparent campaign website and according to published reports did not debate Yu or show up at a candidate forum with her. He seems to be running on a low-engagement strategy. Voters must decide whether that reflects confidence born of experience or avoidance.

State Senator Patricia Jehlen’s retirement opened a crowded contest over who can best continue her progressive legacy in a district that includes Somerville and Medford, and parts of Cambridge and Winchester.

Four candidates are running: state Representatives Christine Barber and Erika Uyterhoeven, Cambridge Vice Mayor Burhan Azeem, and Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin. (A fifth, Tom Hopcroft, ended his campaign too late to have his name removed from the ballot.)

The contenders have similar progressive priorities. The disagreement centers on how to wield power on Beacon Hill. Barber, endorsed by Jehlen and Governor Maura Healey, argues that legislative experience and coalition-building produce results. Uyterhoeven emphasizes transparency and a willingness to challenge Beacon Hill leadership. Azeem highlights his municipal record, particularly on housing, while McLaughlin calls himself “the working-class” candidate.

Following the money, the Abundant Housing Massachusetts Independent Expenditure PAC reportedly spent $93,000 supporting Azeem, fueling the debate over outside spending. In the end, the race may reveal less about ideology than about which style of progressive leadership voters want.

Six days before the primary, federal prosecutors charged state Representative Francisco Paulino of Methuen with pandemic relief loan fraud and money laundering. They allege that Paulino fraudulently obtained more than $700,000 in pandemic unemployment benefits and business loans before entering the Legislature. Paulino pleaded not guilty.

Paulino, who’s seeking a third term representing parts of Lawrence and Methuen, has refused to drop out, saying that he expects to clear his name. Healey called the allegations “very disturbing.”

His challenger, Lawrence City Councilor Celina Reyes, was already campaigning on greater transparency and accountability on Beacon Hill. A child-care provider and union organizer, Reyes has struggled to fund-raise. The timing of the federal charges complicate the race — by the time Paulino was arraigned, many voters had already cast their ballots. Still, the remaining voters must determine how much unresolved criminal allegations should matter when choosing their representative.

In the 2024 Democratic primary, state Representative Marjorie Decker defeated Evan MacKay by just 41 votes. Two years later, MacKay is back.

Decker, who has represented the Cambridge district since 2013, argues her experience and relationships have delivered results for her constituents. Healey and US Senator Ed Markey have endorsed her. MacKay is a former Harvard labor organizer supported by the Democratic Socialists of America, campaigning again on legislative transparency and challenging Beacon Hill’s concentration of power. They’re both staunch progressives, but their debates have exposed differences over policy approaches.

MacKay entered the rematch with stronger fund-raising than two years ago, while outside groups have spent large sums supporting Decker. The results on Tuesday should settle the question: Did the 2024 razor-thin margin reflect momentary dissatisfaction with Decker or a more durable demand for change?

No Republican or independent candidate is officially running in any of these four contests. Barring a successful write-in campaign, Tuesday’s Democratic primaries will determine who will represent these districts in the State House. That means a relatively small share of the electorate will decide four consequential questions about ideology, political power, and experience.

title: At a Dorchester cemetery, elderly Black women were buried in unmarked graves. Now, there’s an effort to memorialize them.
text:
On Wednesday evening, an art installation was unveiled at the site and the names of the 133 women known to have been buried there were read off during a ceremony. Eventually, the group plans to install permanent memorials with the women’s names.

Nearly 100 people filled the pews of the cemetery’s chapel, as violinist Adrian Anantawan performed as they arrived for the 5 p.m. ceremony.

“We cannot change the circumstances of the burial, but we can change what happens now,” said Diana Lam, president of the Boston Women’s Heritage Trail. “We can speak their names, we can honor their lives, we can tell their stories, and we can ensure the future generations know that these women were here.”

The project began when Joyce Linehan, a former aide to ex-Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh who lives in Dorchester, walked her dog past the burial site and noticed it was marked only by a stone inscribed with the name of the Home for Aged Colored Women. She wondered who was buried there and started asking questions.

Linehan’s friend Karilyn Crockett, also a former city official and a professor at MIT, then launched a multiyear research project that led to the discovery of the buried women’s names and shed light on a mostly forgotten chapter of the city’s history.

“These women were building a city for us and with us at a time [when] they were not given credit or recognition for that at all,” Crockett said.

The women lived in a segregated elder home on Beacon Hill between 1860 and 1944. They were domestic servants and suffrage activists. They were congregants at Twelfth Baptist, then known as the Fugitive Slave Church. Some had been born into Southern slavery and moved north after the Civil War.

They were not welcome at the nearby Home for Aged Women, where the residents were white and mostly Protestant. The homes were only a few blocks apart. Their burial sites were even closer — literally adjacent plots at Cedar Grove. But only one had headstones. The residents of the Home for Aged Colored Women were buried, and then their names — or at least their burial sites — were largely forgotten.

In 2024, Rita Steele, a data analytics professional and avid genealogist, was trying to trace her family tree to its Native American roots. She thought her fourth great-grandmother, Sarah Smith, who died in Boston in 1890, might provide the link.

“So I used one of my successful research strategies (reverse address search) of the address on her death certificate,” Steele said by text message. She assumed the Beacon Hill address was a family home. But instead, “it came back with the name for the Home for Aged Colored Women.”

That discovery led her to a blog post by Linehan about the Dorchester burial site. She got in touch with Linehan and Crockett and has been involved in planning the memorial ever since.

Crockett’s research has proceeded on a parallel track. After learning of the burial site from Linehan, she assigned her MIT graduate students to research the home. The cemetery had handwritten note cards listing the women’s names in its archives. Then they found the home’s records in the archives of the Massachusetts Historical Society.

What emerged was an unusually intimate portrait of the women’s lives. The records showed “who was an avid reader, who was a vegetarian, who didn’t like who,” Linehan said. “There was gossipy stuff in there.”

For Crockett, the research also challenged the assumption that Black Bostonians, especially elderly Black women, must have been isolated, only marginal participants in the life of the city. Eliza Gardner, who received financial assistance from the home, was a prominent public speaker and member of Black political organizations, Crockett said. She was once featured in The Woman’s Era, a newspaper founded in Boston in 1894.

Other women were part of migrations to New England. Some came from Canada, others from the American South.

Annie B. Merrick was born into slavery in North Carolina in 1848, according to Crockett. She moved north and then lived in the Home for Aged Colored Women beginning in 1923. She died at Boston State Hospital in 1941.

Smith, Steele’s ancestor, was born in Newport, R.I., around 1799. Her father had been enslaved and fought in the Revolutionary War. Two of Smith’s brothers were abolitionists who worked with Frederick Douglass. Steele and Crockett are still trying to learn more about Smith herself.

Steele traveled from her home in Maryland to attend the ceremony. “There’s tons of work to be done,” she said. “I hope this is a flicker of light for someone.”

The women, including her ancestor, Smith, are buried in two plots — the one next to the white women’s burial ground and a second one that was used when the first filled up.

The temporary memorial is a “collage” of flowers and women’s portraits formed into a single figure to “reflect both the individuality of each woman and her presence in a greater community,” artist Ekua Holmes said.

The Roxbury-born artist entered the chapel to applause. She drew inspiration from Ellis Wilson’s “Funeral Procession” painting, she said.

The installation will remain there for a year while the nonprofit Boston Women’s Heritage Trail raises money for a permanent memorial that includes all of the women’s names.

Robert MacEachern, who runs the cemetery, estimates the memorial will cost more than $100,000. The past two state budgets earmarked $45,000 combined for the project. A grant from the city of Boston paid for Holmes’s work but is not funding the permanent memorial.

When Steele first learned of Smith’s burial place, she found the circumstances “very disturbing and disappointing.”

“No one knew who they were walking by,” she said. “Like they didn’t mean anything to anyone. . . . But I am so proud that their names are finally being restored.”

Correspondent Madyline Swearing contributed to this story.

title: Financing plan for the T’s Fairmount Line could give the entire system a jolt
text:
The clock is ticking for the MBTA to put the finishing touches on an unusual financing deal within the next few weeks — one that could help determine the entire commuter rail system’s future.

The T is in final negotiations with several private-sector partners to finally redo the Fairmount Line, with battery-powered cars to replace the diesel dinosaurs that rumble through the heart of the city.

They’re working with the familiar faces at commuter rail operator Keolis, and some new ones at the table. This will be the first time the T has relied on a third-party financier — in this case, British infrastructure firm Rock Rail — to buy new commuter rail vehicles on its behalf.

The T board blessed this in June, agreeing to spend $765 million over 15 years to cover the cost of leasing and maintaining seven four-car trainsets that run on electric batteries. The cars will be made by Stadler in Utah, and start showing up for testing in late 2029.

This isn’t only about righting a wrong for Boston’s poorer neighborhoods, by offering trains that arrive at 20-minute intervals. The ramifications go well beyond the Fairmount’s nine-mile corridor through Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park.

General manager Phil Eng sees this as a model that could be replicated as he looks to put the entire commuter rail system on track for electrification, another long-awaited change. What works in Boston’s urban neighborhoods might also work in suburban outposts. The Fairmount purchase is a test run; the deal includes options to procure as many as 96 more new cars, the equivalent of 24 trainsets, for other lines.

Another reason to watch Fairmount: politics. Keolis is in a race to keep its coveted job as the commuter rail operator. By coincidence, bids for the new contract are due later this month. It was once thought delivering an electric train in time for Governor Maura Healey’s reelection campaign in 2026 would give her bragging rights — and maybe help Keolis with its case that it should stick around.

That timing turned out to be wishful thinking. But at least Healey can brag about the financing, right?

Whether this helps the French company’s bid, we may never know. T officials structured the Fairmount financing so a different operator, or even the T itself, can take over the lease.

The more traditional route would be issuing bonds for new trains. But the T says it would have had to cancel or reschedule other critical projects to do so. Plus, Rock Rail takes on some of the risk; lease payments don’t start until these machines are in service.

An upgraded Fairmount has been on the arrivals board for years, thanks to pressure from neighborhood advocates and politicians, along with the Conservation Law Foundation that fought for mitigation to offset Big Dig impacts.

The T did add four stations to Fairmount’s three preexisting ones and its South Station and Readville terminals. And the cost to ride was also cut, to the same price as the subway.

What about subway frequency? A plan from Deval Patrick’s administration to buy self-propelled diesel-powered units was scuttled after Charlie Baker took over, though the T did trim headways in 2020 under Baker.

Finally, we have a plan to go electric — even though it will take four more years to see it in action. T officials decided each car should be wheelchair accessible (in part to adhere to a 2006 legal settlement), not just one per trainset. That drove up costs, and delayed delivery.

In June, board member Mary Skelton Roberts chastised T executives for the delays, and a failure to keep the community apprised. Folks, she said, have been waiting for these trains for ages.

Some still won’t be fully satisfied. City councilor Brian Worrell says the neighborhood might be better served by overhead wires the whole way, instead of batteries, making the line even more like a subway. (The trains will use overhead lines to recharge, but for only a small section.) Worrell has been in the news along with councilor Miniard Culpepper pushing their own transit proposal for the area, an Orange Line extension along Blue Hill Avenue; he says it could augment, not replace, the electrified Fairmount trains.

Kimberly Lyle, head of the Dorchester Bay Economic Development Corp., says she’s just happy to see meaningful progress. Her neighbors deserve a quick commute downtown, and cleaner air, as much as anyone in Boston.

Now, finally, the T is poised to deliver on that promise — and put the wheels in motion for bigger changes down the line.

Republican Mike Minogue is already shattering records for self-funding, pouring $15.8 million into his gubernatorial bid, according to state campaign filings. So who did he surpass? Venture capitalist Chris Gabrieli previously topped the list of self-funders after putting $15.1 million into two unsuccessful gubernatorial and lieutenant governor bids during the 2000s. Former lieutenant governor Kerry Healey was right behind him after spending $11.8 million only to lose the 2006 governor’s race to Deval Patrick. Labor lawyer Shannon Liss-Riordan also bet big on herself, but her $9.3 million wasn’t enough to become attorney general in 2022. Of the top five self-funders, so far only Bain Capital cofounder Mitt Romney – who spent $6.3 million to run for governor in 2002 (equivalent to $11.9 million today) – came away with a win. Kerry Healey, who is now executive chair of the independent Forward Party, said campaign finance reforms are needed. “Whether campaigns are self-funded or funded by others, there is simply too much money spent on politics,” she said.

Welcome to Massport, Taidgh McClory. The real estate consultant was sworn in this week by Governor Maura Healey as the newest member of the Massachusetts Port Authority’s board of directors. Also in attendance at the State House ceremony: board chair Patricia Jacobs, chief executive Rich Davey, and board member Sean O’Brien. McClory takes over for Warren Fields, a Charlie Baker appointee whose seven-year term expired in 2025, but was asked to stay on for another year. Davey says he wanted someone else with real estate experience to take over for Fields, and he reached out to former board member Duane Jackson and Weld-era transportation secretary Richard Taylor for suggestions. Independently, both suggested McClory, who worked at Millennium Partners and CBRE before launching his own firm. He won’t have much time to ease into the unpaid role, with the first board meeting scheduled for next week.

If only lawyer David Lurie were still here to savor this victory. The town of Nahant just won big at the Supreme Judicial Court today, in its years-long fight with Northeastern University over the fate of East Point. The town has a waterfront park there, including an easement over land Northeastern owns. In 2018, the university unveiled plans to expand its marine science campus there, to the chagrin of those in the town. The town then used its eminent domain authority to seize access rights, essentially blocking the expansion. Northeastern sued, saying this was an illegal use of the authority simply to block a project, and a Superior Court judge agreed. But the SJC today overruled that decision: Protecting a park fits as a public purpose for eminent domain. Lurie represented the Nahant Preservation Trust in the case, but died in 2024 before he was able to see it through fruition; former colleague Harley Racer kept the fight going.

Congrats to readers Dr. Jeff Lowenstein and David Ball. Both had more than a feeling for the right answer when we asked the question about where bandleader Tom Scholz worked while putting together rock band Boston’s blockbuster debut album, which came out 50 years ago. The employer was Polaroid, which all but disappeared in bankruptcy more than 20 years ago. It’s been such a long time since we used a Polaroid camera.

Rest in power, Gloria Steinem. The feminist icon and cofounder of Ms. Magazine passed away on Wednesday at age 92. Generations of women have Steinem to thank for her lifelong advocacy for equal rights. There would be no women CEOs, governors, or mayors without her. But her greatest legacy, perhaps, is this: The fight for women’s rights is never done. We can’t let up. She never did.

title: A loss for Mass., a gain for Canada
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

About 350,000 Haitians have sought refuge in the United States since an earthquake devastated their island in 2010, and violent gangs make it so unsafe that the US has banned flights to its capital. Nearly 45,000 Haitians have settled in Massachusetts, and received tens of millions of dollars in federal and state funding for job training and other assistance over the past three years.

But the Trump administration revoked Haitians’ temporary protected status in July and started deporting them.

The damage goes far deeper than the workforce. A Haitian college student in Springfield, Ohio, walked in front of a truck barreling down the highway, an apparent suicide. He had been forced to wear an ankle monitor by immigration authorities and had written an Instagram post a few weeks before about the “shame and humiliation” this caused.

To Canada

Some Haitians who lost their TPS status have fled north to Quebec, a French-speaking province where many have family members and know the language. State officials and local employers say the loss of an estimated 10,000 workers will be devastating for an economy where the skills they have, including caring for elderly and disabled residents, are sorely in need.

One Haitian man I talked to, who went to Canada in July, already had four jobs lined up, including one at a branch of the factory he worked at in Massachusetts. A Haitian woman who had been trained by JVS Boston as a certified nursing assistant, and landed a job at Mass General, also went to Canada. So did her husband, who trained here as a carpenter.

‘Dollars go out the window’

Labor force growth in Massachusetts has come almost exclusively from immigration, the leader of a workforce development program told me, and now that the border is essentially closed, things are going to get “desperate” if new strategies aren’t put in place.

The Guild for Human Services in Concord had to let go of eight Haitian employees with TPS who assisted people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. These workers developed relationships with people, chief executive Amy Sousa said, working nights and weekends for relatively low pay, trained by the nonprofit with more than $240,000 in state funds.

“All those training hours and dollars go out the window,” Sousa said. “We are in desperate need of exemplary employees, and I had to fire eight of them.”

title: ‘Something does not smell right’: As lawsuits plague R.I.’s ‘Conjuring’ house, judge says the cases are a mess
text:
The loan was later purchased from Needham Bank by YouTuber Elton Castee through his Summit & Stone LLC. But the bank alleges that it mistakenly discharged the mortgage after the sale.

A lawsuit filed by Needham Bank brought the saga back into court last week.

Also involved in this lawsuit is Jason Hawes, the Rhode Island-based star of the SyFy television series “Ghost Hunters.” He is listed as an interested party because Nuñez signed an agreement to sell the property to Hawes in December 2025. Hawes filed a warranty deed for the house in June.

But in court on Tuesday, Darigan denied a motion filed by Hawes that sought to compel Summit & Stone to issue a payoff statement so Hawes could pay the remaining mortgage balance. The motion was denied without prejudice, meaning it could be filed again.

Darigan said she is “extremely concerned” and suggested several cases surrounding the property be assigned to a single judge who could better keep tabs on “all of the different tentacles.”

“This case and all the affiliated cases are a mess,” she said.

There are “too many open questions,” Darigan said. Hawes’s ties to the property have not been determined by a court, and it’s still unclear what Summit & Stone “is holding and what is owed,” she said.

“That [is] a fundamental issue that needs to be resolved,” Darigan said. “Is the deed from December a valid deed, and how do we go about consummating the sale completely?”

Hawes’s claims to the property have been challenged before.

Nuñez’s sister, Elizabeth Greenhalgh, of Utah, filed a lawsuit last year alleging Nuñez had been “experiencing serious mental health issues” that impaired her judgment when she signed a warranty deed and power of attorney agreement last year authorizing Julia Demay, a woman described in court documents as her friend, to sell the property to Hawes for $1.3 million. The complaint alleged Hawes was taking advantage of “Nuñez’s lack of legal capacity” for his own personal and financial gain.

Nicole M. Labonte, an attorney for Hawes, said earlier this year that a notary involved in preparing the documents in October 2025 later indicated she had not notarized the documents properly. Nuñez then signed a deed in December with a different notary, Labonte said.

Greenhalgh’s lawsuit was dismissed in April, after a judge found she did not have legal standing. In an affidavit filed in August, Greenhalgh wrote Nuñez has maintained she did not sell the house to Hawes.

Greenhalgh had also petitioned the Suffolk County Probate and Family Court in Massachusetts to appoint her as Nuñez’s guardian and conservator so she could manage her sister’s affairs. On Tuesday, however, a stipulation was filed indicating Greenhalgh and other parties involved — including Nuñez and Demay — had agreed to drop the matter.

“It wasn’t sustainable,” Isaac H. Peres, an attorney representing Demay, said Thursday.

Peres said a medical evaluation for Nuñez was not completed, and a required medical certificate was never filed.

“In the future, if they ever got a certificate, they can come back,” Peres said.

Court filings state Nuñez, who was listed as living in Dorchester, now resides in Utah. Attorneys for Nuñez and Greenhalgh did not return requests for comment.

Summit & Stone also accused Hawes of fraud and exploitation. Labonte, in court in Rhode Island on Tuesday, called those claims “defamatory.”

Summit & Stone filed a petition in January asking a court to place Bale Fire into receivership, a process similar to bankruptcy in state court, citing an outstanding balance on the mortgage of approximately $1.2 million. A judge denied the motion in February.

On Tuesday, Vincent A. Indeglia, an attorney for Summit & Stone, said the company bought the house with the thought that “it was either going to get cash or it was going to get the property, one or the other.”

Darigan said she is “very skeptical about Summit & Stone’s motivations.”

“I don’t buy the arguments that they are concerned about liability to Bale Fire, or to Nuñez, or to anybody else,” Darigan said. “... In a contested property situation, [it] seems to me that people would sit down, particularly a lender, would sit down and have a conversation …. That’s not happening.”

“Fundamental questions about who has what rights and what interests” need to be answered, Darigan concluded at the end of Tuesday’s hour-long hearing.

“Once that’s decided, I think some things can fall into place,” she said. “This case is a problem.”

Material from previous Globe stories was used in this report.

title: Yu who? Meet the progressive who pulled off a Boston-area upset
text:
Her insurgent campaign flew largely under the radar outside of the district stretching from West Roxbury into Boston’s southern suburbs, despite Mayor Michelle Wu coming to the moderate incumbent’s defense in the very district in which she lives.

That was due, in part, to Wu’s other electoral pursuits: The second-term mayor backed two first-time candidates who were trying to take down sitting senators, including one of Rush’s fellow Senate leaders.

“People outside the district didn’t know what was happening,” said Rob Orthman, a Yu backer and co-director of Progressive West Roxbury/Roslindale. “And we were perfectly fine keeping it that way. We did not want to raise attention to this to suddenly start seeing, you know, all the money and support for the incumbent start to flow in.”

Yu was one of a tiny percentage of candidates Tuesday to successfully take out an incumbent by running to their left.

With no Republican on the ballot in November, she effectively clinched the Norfolk and Suffolk seat with her primary victory, taking out not just an eight-term incumbent but also Senate President Karen Spilka’s handpicked majority whip.

So who is this first-time candidate turned (likely) senator-elect — and how did she turn a quiet primary challenge into Tuesday’s biggest down-ballot shocker?

Yu jumped into the race last year, motivated in part by President Trump’s reelection in 2024. In the current political climate, “we need to have steadfast leaders who are protecting our rights, especially on abortion access, especially on LGBTQ+ issues, and especially on immigrant rights,” she said.

But the campaign wasn’t simply a referendum on social issues. Much of her pitch centered on affordability concerns, and, according to Yu, frustration with what voters saw as a Legislature that wasn’t getting enough done. Lawmakers’ resistance to a voter-approved law giving the state auditor the authority to probe the Legislature often came up organically on the trail, Yu said.

“There was a dissatisfaction with the status quo,” the Hyde Park Democrat said. “And people want to know what is actually happening in the Legislature.”

Yu, a Boston Public Schools parent and mother of two, had been active on Boston’s Ward 18 Democratic Committee, but first popped up on Orthman’s radar last spring, he said, as she met with progressive groups around the district to test the waters on a potential state Senate bid.

A consumer protection attorney, “she always likes to say [that] she’s sued the last few presidential administrations on behalf of student loan borrowers, both Democratic and Republican,” Orthman said.

Her campaign was up against some early headwinds. While Rush started off with a cash advantage, Yu outraised him during the campaign, pulling in a little over $156,000 since the start of last September, compared to Rush’s roughly $148,000.

Rush, an Iraq War veteran who first won his seat in 2010, also had some serious institutional support from both Wu and Governor Maura Healey.

The mayor’s support for the more moderate Rush normally would’ve been somewhat surprising. But Rush helped shepherd Wu’s closely watched property tax shift legislation on Beacon Hill, pushing an amendment that the Senate ultimately rejected in January.

That denial prompted Wu to put her political power on the line by backing challengers to Senators Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, and turning those races into something of a proxy war. But her presence was less notable in Rush’s region — and ultimately, didn’t seem to sway voters in her city.

Yu outperformed Rush in Boston, according to unofficial results, earning 57 percent of the vote in the city while Rush carried parts of the district beyond.

“The kind of voter who is highly engaged and supports Michelle is unlikely to be swayed to vote for Rush by her endorsement,” said Matt McCloskey, a Yu volunteer focused on elections data. The district itself changed as well when state lawmakers crafted new maps in 2021, McCloskey said.

“It’s definitely an easier district for a progressive to win now than it would have been in 2020,” he said.

Then there was another notable moment days ahead of the election: When Rush skipped a debate set up by the Dedham and Westwood Democratic town committees, apparently to present a check for state funding in another town in the district.

The move handed Yu and her supporters a ready-made cudgel to hammer Rush heading into the home stretch of the campaign.

Rush has not commented publicly since the loss, and efforts to reach him Thursday were not successful.

Yu, however, said she spoke to Wu briefly Wednesday, and the mayor “was very gracious.”

“It’s a good place-starting conversation, and I definitely look forward to having further ones in the future,” Yu said.

Wu, in a statement, said she offered Yu her “full partnership and support,” and that she looked forward to “working with her as my new state senator to deliver on a shared agenda for the district and the city.”

Notably, Yu isn’t pitching herself as some type of Wu agitator. Case in point: She said that she, too, is supportive of the mayor’s tax shift proposal.

DOWN FOR A COUNT: Back to one of those other Boston-area state Senate races ...

The still too-close-to-call Brownsberger-Daniel Lander contest appears to be headed for a recount.

With just four votes separating the two, per unofficial tallies as of Friday morning, both the Belmont Democrat and the Wu-backed Lander requested a recount, the Globe’s Niki Griswold reports.

It’s a quick turnaround for everyone involved. Brownsberger and Lander had until Thursday afternoon to file their requests. If their petitions advance, local election officials have to complete the recount by 5 p.m. next Friday.

TRUMP BUMP: Trump hails Ed Markey win in Mass.: ‘I couldn’t stand Moulton’ by Sam Brodey, The Boston Globe: Speaking at a White House dinner for Republican candidates Wednesday night, Trump hailed what he called Senator Ed Markey’s 30-point “landslide” win over US Representative Seth Moulton in Tuesday’s primary election.

ABORTION ON THE (2028) BALLOT? Antiabortion activists launch effort to suspend new Mass. abortion law, put repeal before voters by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: Antiabortion activists in Massachusetts filed paperwork with the state launching a bid to suspend and eventually seek the repeal of a law that makes it easier for women to receive an abortion later in pregnancy. That move sets up a potential ballot battle in 2028, and more immediately, kick-starts a scramble to stop the law before it can even take effect.

CHANGING LANES: More parking, fewer bike lanes: City of Boston, T release new Blue Hill Avenue redesign by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: Residents and politicians have for years railed against the city of Boston’s plan to reconfigure Blue Hill Avenue and the impacts that proposed bus and bike lanes could wrought on the busy corridor through the heart of the Black Boston.

Now, city officials and the MBTA say they’ve funneled those concerns into a new design that preserves a controversial center-running bus lane, but significantly expands the portions of the boulevard that would have two traffic lanes on each side, while shrinking the amount of proposed bike lanes.

A LITERAL POWER PLAY: The Globe’s Jon Chesto and Shirley Leung have a look at the unusual financing deal that would grease the wheels for an overhaul of the Fairmount Line — and which in turn could help determine the future of the entire commuter rail system.

The T is working with some familiar faces (commuter rail operator Keolis) and some new ones (British infrastructure firm Rock Rail) in an effort to electrify the line that runs along a nine-mile corridor through Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park, they reported in Thursday’s edition of Power Play.

BREAKING BAD: This Boston firm owes $100,000 because Beacon Hill delayed a Trump tax break. It’s not alone. by Larry Edelman, The Boston Globe: Thousands of Massachusetts businesses — it’s impossible to say exactly how many — may be facing large tax bills as a result of the state’s decision to “decouple” from the R&D deduction provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the GOP’s massive tax and spending bill that President Trump signed in July 2025.

Local companies can still claim the full R&D deduction, which reduces taxable income, for 2025 and again this year. But they cannot do so on state returns, leaving them with higher taxable income — and a bigger Department of Revenue tax bill. A Department of Revenue spokesperson didn’t respond to a request for comment.

HEALTHY DEBATE: One post-primary sign of life on Beacon Hill this week: Lawmakers tasked with hashing out the differences between House and Senate versions of legislation aimed at addressing violence against health care workers kicked off negotiations Thursday, the State House News Service reports. As for the other big healthcare legislation reshaping primary care in Massachusetts that lawmakers punted into conference? Negotiations haven’t gotten rolling yet, following an end-of-formal-session kerfuffle between House leadership and the chamber’s committee chair.

Boston federal judge blasts Trump administration’s changes to international student visas by Michaela Towfighi, The Boston Globe.

Cambridge will pay residents $1,000 to join ‘civic assembly’ on whether to use ShotSpotter by Spencer Buell, The Boston Globe.

What a canceled battery project in Tewksbury says about New England’s aging power grid by Miriam Wasser, WBUR.

SJC says Nahant can take Northeastern University land by Jennifer Smith, CommonWealth Beacon.

New Bedford Police chief recommends termination of 2 officers found to use Flock to track romantic partners by Anastasia E. Lennon, The New Bedford Light.

Former Quincy official’s misconduct dates back to 2014, ex-employees reported by Peter Blandino, The Patriot Ledger.
