title: California made Gavin Newsom famous. Will it drag down his 2028 presidential ambitions?
text:
Vera DeVito, a 78-year-old Democrat who packed into one of Newsom’s eight public events across South Carolina, said she didn’t know much about him or his policies — except that he’s from the Golden State. On that basis alone, she suggested that supporting Newsom could be “risky.”

“It’s going to be hard for him to appeal to the whole country,” she said in the town of Summerville. “Everybody thinks California is different — especially in the South. They’re not crazy about California.”

Newsom’s home state stands in stark contrast with likely primary competitors who hail from battlegrounds like Michigan’s Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania’s Gov. Josh Shapiro. Should they run, which is likely, all could make credible claims that they are in a better position to win over the moderate and independent voters ultimately needed to win the presidency.

Newsom’s team acknowledges that “California derangement syndrome” is real. In the almost half-century since former California Gov. Ronald Reagan first won the presidency, the state has produced a long list of failed White House contenders, including Gov. Pete Wilson, Gov. Jerry Brown, businessman Tom Steyer, and most recently Vice President Kamala Harris.

Despite such daunting history, Newsom is not hiding his interest in the presidency. In an interview, he left open the possibility of announcing his decision before the end of the year.

“It’s the right question. Honestly, I don’t know,” Newsom told The Associated Press. “I think this thing’s happening. I mean, you already feel it, right? There are folks out here — they’re saying they’re already starting to interview state directors. So this thing is going to happen very, very quickly.”

Newsom’s breakneck pace in South Carolina — which included a handful of private engagements in addition to his public events — mirrored or even exceeded that of a presidential campaign.

His visit was billed as part of his “take it back tour” across states in the Deep South where he argues that President Donald Trump and his Republican allies are rolling back civil rights.

He opened the trip on Wednesday with one day in Alabama and finished on Saturday with two stops in North Carolina. But the overwhelming focus was South Carolina, which will host the Democratic Party’s opening presidential primary contest in little more than a year. It was Newsom’s third trip to South Carolina this midterm season.

The voters who crowded into community halls, courthouses and a university lecture hall talked openly about Newsom’s presidential ambitions, even as Democrats try to keep the focus on November’s midterm elections.

“He has strong potential,” said Kirk Bovill, a 65-year-old semi-retired actor and former Los Angeles resident who now lives in Summerville. “The question is how he’s perceived outside of California. People might think he’s too Hollywood.”

“The one thing he does very well: He doesn’t have a problem standing up to Trump,” Bovill continued. “He’s not intimidated.”

Indeed, Newsom’s message this past week was overwhelmingly focused on attacking Trump and rallying Democrats to stand up against him.

“We cannot do business as usual. We need to fight fire with fire,” Newsom told roughly 150 people gathered inside a Lexington, S.C. community center on Friday. “We’ve got to meet this moment and recognize what we’re up against. We’re up against an invasive species in the name of Donald Trump.”

At every stop, Newsom highlighted the hundreds of millions of dollars Trump and his family have made from crypto currency and other private business dealings since the 2024 election; Trump’s decision to dispatch the National Guard to Los Angeles and other major U.S. cities; the federal immigration agents that have descended upon Los Angeles and other cities under Trump’s direction; and Trump’s push to disrupt the midterm elections, including his recent move to limit mail voting.

“Donald Trump is ruthless. He’s ruthless. He’s going to try to steal this election,” Newsom charged. “He is not screwing around. Neither can we.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Republican activists protesting outside of some of Newsom’s stops focused largely on his connection to California.

CJ Westfall, the Republican chairman of Dorchester County, described Newsom as “a far-left extreme Democrat who’s probably the front-runner of this (presidential) race right now.” He was surrounded by protesters who waved signs that read things like, “Wrong Coast” and “Clean Up Your State First.”

“We don’t want Gavin Newsom to California our South Carolina,” Westfall said.

Newsom’s team acknowledges widespread dislike for California, even among some Democrats, but argues that the California governor is gifted and experienced at fighting back against such criticism on the national stage. Newsom is a regular on Fox News, he faced Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in a debate and he was the most prominent national surrogate for former President Joe Biden’s campaign.

Newsom acknowledged that California is both a political liability and “the greatest opportunity” because the California story has only been told on the national stage by “people that have ‘California Derangement Syndrome.’” He said it would play far differently if he’s able to reframe the conversation in 2028.

“In a Democratic primary, in particular — we’ve got the receipts, things that the party is arguing for, we’ve delivered across a spectrum of issues,” he told AP.

Indeed, some of the achievements that Republican critics attack him for are the same issues that might play well among Democratic base voters.

California under Newsom’s leadership has enacted progressive priorities such as expanded healthcare coverage regardless of immigration status, expanded paid sick leave, universal free school meals, a $20 minimum wage for fast food workers, protections for women from other states seeking abortions, aggressive climate change and gun control laws and a death penalty moratorium.

California also remains the nation’s most populous state and the world’s fourth-largest economy, even as critics decry the state’s high taxes that have pushed some businesses and residents alike into other states. The population has been growing since a COVID-era dip, however.

While South Carolina voters may have had mixed views on California, several said they were drawn in by Newsom’s celebrity image. The 58-year-old Democrat certainly looked the part of a made-for-TV president as he charmed voters in his plain white dress shirt with his sleeves rolled up and no tie.

“We don’t get that many famous people here in Aiken. He’s pretty famous,” said 73-year-old Monty Fetterolf, who attended one of Newsom’s Friday events in Aiken, S.C.

DeVito, the 78-year-old Democrat from Summerville, said Newsom still has work to do.

“He’s a little slick — not a lot of meat,” she said after listening to his speech in Dorchester. “But he’s good looking, which helps.”

title: Boston is trying to plant more trees. Residents keep cutting them down.
text:
But at the same time, property owners and residents cleared roughly 120 acres of urban forest from residential land, where officials often have little say over the fate of the trees.

Boston has been working hard in recent years to expand its urban forests, including launching a forestry division and prioritizing plantings in the neighborhoods that need them most. But if the city wants to grow more trees, it has to solve a thorny problem: how to stop residents from cutting them down.

“We’re not going to plant ourselves a robust and vibrant urban forest,” said David Meshoulam, the executive director of Tree Boston, an advocacy nonprofit. “We need to preserve those trees that we have.”

According to Boston’s latest tree assessment, the tree canopy — the branches and leaves that cover the ground when viewed from above — grew modestly by 0.5 percent between 2019 and 2024, covering 28.5 percent of the city when excluding the airport. This marked an improvement from the previous five-year period, when there was no net change in canopy coverage. But the city’s gains on open space and rights-of-way land were largely offset by removals on residential properties, which contain the largest share of tree canopy.

Behind those losses are everyday decisions made by developers and residents: Trees are cut down to make room for housing, meet the stipulations of an insurance company, or create a better view. The problem comes when these collective choices constitute a significant loss of trees.

“There is no regulation, no ordinance, or state protection in place over private trees,” said Diana Fernandez Bibeau, the city’s parks and recreation commissioner, though she noted that Boston’s antiquated zoning laws give the city some room to engage with private landowners about their trees.

Some Massachusetts cities and towns have implemented local laws that regulate the removal of trees on private land, including Somerville and Lexington.

In Cambridge, the City Council passed strict protections for private trees in 2019. The city’s most recent tree report, spanning 2018 to 2024, found that residential properties experienced the most canopy growth, increasing by 4.5 percent.

“That difference is hard to ignore,” said Nasser Brahim, the Mystic River Watershed Association’s director of climate resilience, noting that Boston saw a roughly 1 percent decrease in residential tree canopy around the same time.

Cambridge requires residents to seek a permit to remove a tree that has a diameter of 6 inches or more at roughly chest height. Barring special circumstances, such as if the tree is dead or threatens a nearby home, residents must plant replacement trees or pay into a city fund if they want to cut one down.

David Lefcourt, the city arborist, said the private tree protections required extra staff time but did not necessitate standing up an enforcement division. Cambridge hired an assistant city arborist who is responsible for managing removal permits from private property owners and handling the tree planting side of the program.

Lefcourt said residents help keep an eye out for anyone trying to skirt the law: “It’s pretty tough to get away with,” he said. He tells contractors: “It’s going to be the next-door neighbors, it’s going to be the person walking their dog down the street, saying, ‘Hey, something doesn’t look right in this parcel.’”

An effort to pass a similar measure by Boston’s City Council did not gain traction. In 2023, an ordinance was filed that would have included protections for both public and private trees. The language regarding private trees did not make it into the final policy.

The city said at the time that it was adopting a “phased approach,” allowing it to “lead by example before engaging with the community to extend regulations to trees on private property.”

But Brian Swett, Boston’s chief climate officer, said a private tree ordinance is no longer being explored as a solution in the near term.

Instead, officials said, Boston is looking at other approaches, such as “pedestrian easements” that would allow homeowners to plant trees that the city then takes care of. It is also working with community partners to plant more trees on private land.

“We’ve turned the corner where before 2019, the previous decade, we lost canopy coverage,” Swett said, adding, “We’ve shown the art of the possible in the last five years.”

In the meantime, tensions have flared between landowners seeking to remove trees and some residents who say city regulations on these trees are overdue.

In Hyde Park, several trees were cut down behind an apartment complex in June, including one so large that Becky Shuster, 64, couldn’t get her arms around it.

Shuster, who has lived in a house behind the apartment complex for nearly three decades, said, “I sat there and wept.” She said her deck and home are hotter and sunnier, but she is more concerned about the citywide consequences of trees on private property.

“They destroyed a piece of the tree canopy in Boston, and there’s absolutely no accountability,” she said.

Oleg Uritsky, director of Advanced Property Management, which manages the apartment complex, said the company does not want to remove healthy trees, but the trees that were removed were in bad shape and dropping branches on neighbors’ yards.

Uritsky said new regulations on removing private trees would add bureaucracy, expense, and delays to cases when property owners need to move quickly to protect safety and homes.

A few years ago during a winter storm, a tree fell on Uritsky’s home in Newton, narrowly missing a window by his young son’s crib. He has since sought to have a large branch removed from a second “dangerous” tree in front of his house, but he said a company refused to do it, saying a city inspector “would not be happy.” Newton requires residents to seek a permit to remove trees that have a trunk diameter of 6 inches or more.

“Safety comes first, and to have additional red tape — I don’t think it’s a good idea,” Uritsky said.

While Boston figures out its next steps to protect private trees, advocates said the city’s gains on public land, aided by community partners, are nothing to scoff at.

Life as a city tree is an uphill battle, fought against depleted soils, pollutants like car exhaust and dog urine, and sometimes even vandalism. Planting the tree, by comparison, is the easy part.

Tree Boston plants trees and cares for them for two years before turning them over to the city. On a recent weekday morning in Harambee Park in Dorchester, two watering trucks staffed by a crew from the nonprofit moved from tree to tree, pumping 30 gallons into watering bags. Despite temperatures hovering in the mid-70s, the team was sweating. The park has very little tree cover, even along the pathways that run between playing fields.

Marco Lomax, the tree care coordinator for Tree Boston, knelt by a young London plane tree and gave it a shake to check how well it had rooted in the rocky soil. He pointed to the nearby roadway, where cars spew pollutants that coat trees’ leaves and send toxic runoff into the ground. One time, he said, the nonprofit visited a tree it planted to find a pile of beer bottles and the stakes keeping the tree upright torn out and flung across the grass.

“We’re throwing these trees in the deep end,” he said.

title: ‘Not realistic’: Why many musicians feel they can’t make it in Boston
text:
Since moving, he’s earned six Grammy nominations and released six albums. He’s on a cross-country tour and has 120,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.

Lacossade is one of many Boston musicians who felt they had to leave town to seek fame and fortune. Artists say the music industry in Boston has always been tough — and is only getting tougher.

Since the pandemic, the obstacles for local musicians have multiplied. A slew of performance venues have recently closed, including Thunder Road, ONCE Lounge, and Hennessy’s Bar. At a time of tight budgets, government funding for arts programs has also been slashed.

One of the largest cuts in Mayor Michelle Wu’s $4.9 billion spending plan for the next fiscal year was to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture fund, which supports programs for local musicians and artists such as Beat the Odds, Boston Music Project, and the Roxbury Concert Series.

In January 2023, Allston’s Sound Museum, a studio and rehearsal space, was bought out to be turned into biotech labs, displacing hundreds of musicians. The organizers of this year’s BAMSFest, an annual arts festival, decided to save money by getting rid of music performances. That closed a huge door for rising local artists, as each year around five music acts were selected to perform.

Lacossade started in local Boys and Girls Clubs’ studios and studied audio engineering at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. He’s lived in New York and Atlanta and said his fan bases are stronger in those cities than in Boston. With the cost of living here continuing to soar even as resources and opportunities erode, it’s increasingly difficult to make it in Boston as a creative.

“As much as I would love to live in Boston full time, it’s just not realistic,” he said.

His first Atlanta apartment, which he shared with two roommates, only cost him $550 a month and allowed him to save money while trying to make it in the industry. (That would be much tougher in Boston; the average rent for a three-bedroom apartment is now nearly $5,800 per month.)

City officials say the issue isn’t a shortage of artists, but a dearth of infrastructure — performing venues, affordable housing, and grants — to support them.

“We are producing talent, but it’s seemingly hard to keep them here,” said Kenny Mascary, a member of the Boston Art Commission. “We have a $15 billion sector here in Boston, but it’s invisible.”

He told the Globe that less than 1 percent of the new construction approved by the Boston Planning & Development Agency in the last decade was for creative or cultural uses. Meanwhile, over a quarter of Boston residents say they earn their main income from creative work, according to a 2026 city-conducted report.

Sophia Perez, a recent Berklee College of Music graduate, faces a similar dilemma to Lacossade’s. She likes Boston, but constantly tosses around the idea of moving to New York or even Spain to break into the music industry. She moved here with dreams of becoming an R&B singer-songwriter, and thought she’d get a jump-start from attending a renowned music school.

“I left with my degree not knowing what to do,” she said. “I studied songwriting, and I don’t think there [were] any opportunities for songwriting or singing.”

It’s been over a year since Perez graduated, and she spends most days balancing work at a coffee shop with performing gigs, booked through an agency, playing with a band at weddings and corporate events. Those jobs help pay her bills, but after factoring in costs for her music — studio time, engineers, and musicians — it’s hard to make ends meet.

To record her upcoming album, Perez has been seeking grants and searching for venues where she can perform her music. She also wants to build a community with rising musicians. She feels stuck.

Several local artists say that since there’s little of the pie to go around for them, Boston has developed what some refer to as a “crabs-in-a-barrel” mindset, where there’s less camaraderie and mutual support and more unhealthy competition.

Lisa Bello, Boston’s 2009 Female Vocalist of the Year, is a member of the Recording Academy, the nonprofit responsible for Grammy selections. She has been working as an artist for over two decades, and over that time, as an artist and mentor for rising acts, she has witnessed Boston’s music industry change.

“We complain because the OGs that have been in [the industry] 15-plus years know that there were pockets of time where we were fully supported in the city,” Bello said. She believes that time is over.

She said a main turning point was Live Nation’s increasing domination of some of Boston’s most prominent performing venues over the past 20 years through ownership or other management agreements.

When major entertainment corporations control key spaces like Brighton Music Hall, MGM at Fenway, and Citizens House of Blues, getting booked is harder for smaller local artists who may not generate the revenue an out-of-towner could.

“If you’re a new artist here, you’ve got to go through a gamut to even get on stage,” Bello said.

The closures of performance venues heighten competition in ways that ripple beyond the community of area musicians.

Clay Ferno, the publicist and event producer for the Cambridge rock club Middle East, said he prioritizes local acts for the club’s five venues in Central Square, but space is still tight.

“When venues close down, it hurts us because it increases the demand on the room,” he said. “We don’t have enough rooms to sustain those bands.”

As city leaders and nonprofits take stock of the challenges, they are hopeful that Boston can still be a home for musicians.

Mascary said the city is partnering with the Boston Housing Authority to develop new affordable housing and rehearsal space for artists by the end of 2026. He also wants to restore funding to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture.

The Record Co., a nonprofit that offers low-cost studio and rehearsal spaces in Dorchester and Roxbury, is working against what many artists see as bad vibes in Boston’s industry. When the Sound Museum closed, many of those artists found new homes with The Record Co.

The nonprofit has also received city grants, but after watching such support fluctuate, CEO Bobby Boyd said the organization hopes to be sustainable without government assistance.

A Dorchester native, he thinks Boston can be like New York and Los Angeles as a place to start a successful music career. Boyd said support for local artistry “should be critical infrastructure,” not an afterthought.

“When we exercise our creative genius,” Boyd said, “that’s when we’re at our best.”

title: Marcelo Suárez-Orozco will step down as chancellor of UMass Boston after six-plus years
text:
UMass Boston chancellor Marcelo Suárez-Orozco announced on Tuesday that he plans to step down on Feb. 1 and join the school’s faculty to focus on issues related to climate change and artificial intelligence.

Suárez-Orozco will wrap up a six-and-a-half-year tenure leading the public university on the Dorchester waterfront that serves 15,000-plus students. He stabilized the school’s leadership, oversaw the completion of major campus construction, drew big donations from the business world, and helped elevate the school’s status as a research university. He also raised its profile on the world stage though his work with the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences.

In an interview, he described how he felt it was time to make a change with his 70th birthday approaching this month. His wife, Carola Suárez-Orozco, has also retired, and is working as a senior fellow at Boston College.

As an immigrant to the United States from Argentina at age 17, he related to many of the challenges faced by students at UMass Boston, a school known for the diversity of its student body. (In-state tuition is under $17,000 a year for residents, a fraction of what most schools charge.) He credits them for showing “ganas,” the Spanish word for desire or enthusiasm, to get ahead and make a difference.

“This has been the honor of a lifetime,” said Suárez-Orozco, an anthropologist by training. “We’ve achieved everything we set out to achieve [and] our relationship with the city and with the commonwealth has never been better.”

Suárez-Orozco plans to take a sabbatical before focusing on AI and climate change, and their societal impacts — dual issues that already have been the focus of his efforts at the pontifical academy. He said he doesn’t know yet which UMass Boston department he’ll join.

“I have enough energy to really focus on what I believe are, from a scholarly and a humanistic perspective, the big challenges of our time,” said Suárez-Orozco, who came to UMass Boston as chancellor in the summer of 2020.

At that point, UMass Boston had been without a chancellor for three years, following Keith Motley’s departure.

The school had two interim chancellors before UMass president Marty Meehan recruited Suárez-Orozco for the job.

Suárez-Orozco was working as a dean at University of California Los Angeles at the time, though he was familiar with Boston in part because of time he spent on the faculty at Harvard, where he codirected the Harvard Immigration Project with Carola. His wife was also eager to return to the Boston area.

“I love this city. I think it’s an iconic city,” Suárez-Orozco said. “We have tremendous challenges and tremendous opportunities.”

Early on, Suárez-Orozco worked to build bridges between the school and the city’s business community. Those efforts helped lead to partnerships such as an expanded New Balance sponsorship of a sports management program, Paul English’s launch of an AI program at the school, and millions from Robert and Donna Manning to endow the school’s nursing program. In 2023, the school, with the prodding of dean Venky Venkatachalam, launched what would become BEST Boston, a program that aims to harness students’ brainpower to help small businesses.

Meehan said he wasn’t surprised by Suárez-Orozco’s decision to step down; they had discussed it last year, and Suárez-Orozco talked about wrapping up on June 30 this year. Meehan says he persuaded Suárez-Orozco to consider staying in the role for another six months.

“He’s raised [UMass Boston’s] national and global profile as a top-tier research university,” Meehan said. “While I would have loved to keep him [in that position] longer, he was up front with me and said he wanted to do some other things.”

During his six-plus years, Suárez-Orozco was responsible for raising more than $180 million, Meehan said, a new philanthropic record for a UMass Boston chancellor.

Meehan hopes to name an interim leader later this month. Eventually, he’ll assemble a search committee to vet candidates. He expects that committee will submit three candidates to him, and then he’ll pick a top choice to bring to the board of trustees for approval.

While Meehan said he expects a smooth transition, Suárez-Orozco will leave a lasting legacy.

“He’s credited with turning UMass Boston around in many respects,” Meehan said. “He has brought charisma, leadership, and academic credentials that have made UMass Boston and Massachusetts a better place.”

Jon Chesto can be reached at jon.chesto@globe.com. Follow him @jonchesto.

title: Boston’s housing costs keep climbing. Mayor Wu’s new housing plan aims to bring them down.
text:
A draft of the Wu administration’s new plan, obtained by the Globe, indicates the city hopes to permit 3,000 new housing units annually over her second four-year term. That’s fewer than the 13,000 she set out to build over her first four years in office, but roughly on pace with construction over the last 18 months.

Boston officials stressed the plan is preliminary — drafted by the city’s top housing officials, it has not been finalized by the mayor herself. But a draft was shared with developers and advocates last week, and it outlines how Wu might address one of Boston’s thorniest challenges in her second term.

The new goal of 3,000 units per year is a relatively low bar for a city with more than 675,000 residents that built far more than that just a few years ago. The goal would, though, mark an uptick from the deep lull of the last three years, the slowest period for new development in Boston since the Great Recession.

That modest target is an acknowledgement of the broad market forces that are slowing housing construction across the country, officials said, as well as the lagging growth in the population in Boston itself.

“Our discussions have been framed by: how do we stretch our goals because production is such an important piece of the puzzle?” said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. “But we also don’t want to put out a big round number that we couldn’t achieve in these economic headwinds. We’re trying to thread that needle of something that’s ambitious but possible.”

The high cost of housing is a major issue for Boston, warping the lives of residents across the income spectrum. And the biggest factor keeping prices high and driving them upward, many economists agree, is that there simply aren’t enough homes for everyone who wants to live here.

Rents have declined in cities such as Austin, Texas, that have added a significant number of new units recently. But in Boston, where the rate of building has slowed, rents are still going up.

Wu has, at times, been hesitant to set targets for new construction, citing a commitment to what she describes as a more holistic approach that prioritizes housing for everyone — targeting all the “different stages of life we’re trying to house,” as Bok put it — instead of numerical goals for market-rate building.

This plan follows that same tack.

But developers have frequently complained Wu’s policies — particularly around affordable housing and energy efficiency requirements — have driven up the cost of building and slowed development.

To that end, the draft housing plan includes measures the city hopes may lower costs and boost production, including short-term tax breaks for “high-priority” projects that have been approved but are not financed due to prohibitive construction and borrowing costs.

One challenge is making incentives, such as property tax abatements, meaningful for developers without undermining city finances.

“Tax revenue is what our city runs on, so we have to be really careful about how any abatement is given out,” said Sheila Dillon, the city’s housing chief. “But we are working seriously on using that tool in a targeted way to advance specific, high-quality projects that are truly ready to go if they get that relief. We need housing now, and we need to grow as a city.”

The draft also says City Hall would consider “offering flexibility for how projects meet” Boston’s requirement that 17 percent of units in most new buildings be set aside at affordable rents, plus another 3 percent for Section 8 tenants. Importantly, it stopped short of saying officials would lower the 20 percent target, as some developers have urged. (Wu increased the affordable threshold from 13 percent under her predecessor, Martin J. Walsh.)

Boston would also continue to rework stringent zoning rules to allow for taller and denser housing developments near key transit nodes and in major squares and corridors, the draft plan says, though details were limited. While Boston has moved forward rezoning efforts in some neighborhoods recently, progress has been gradual, and at least one such effort in the Codman Square section of Dorchester was delayed due to pushback from residents.

Wu’s more measured approach to housing development is a shift from Walsh, who preferred to set high long-term goals, at one point saying the city would need to add 69,000 units over a 16-year period, citing population trends.

But growth in Boston has slowed significantly since the COVID-19 pandemic, and when Wu has set housing production goals, they have been more modest.

Her Boston Housing Strategy 2025 said the city would aim to build 13,000 units — 8,300 market rate and 4,700 income-restricted — during her first four years in office.

Those years coincided with rising interest rates and higher materials and construction costs that discouraged construction nationwide; Boston missed its goal by about 1,200 units, permitting 11,804 new homes during that period.

Indeed, 2023 and 2024 were the two slowest years for new housing permits since 2011, with fewer than 2,400 in each. Last year was slightly higher, but still slow, while the first half of 2026 was better yet, with 1,643 units permitted.

That is roughly in line with the goal outlined in the administration’s draft plan, which says that while it’s harder to build now than before, Boston continues to remain ahead of its neighboring communities.

“Boston has far exceeded its share of housing production, while so many others in the region have fallen short,” the plan says.

Much of the strategy focuses on affordable housing, which has been Wu’s top housing priority.

Under her tenure, Boston has built a wave of new subsidized units — funded in part by hundreds of millions of dollars of federal pandemic relief funds. That money is running out, and affordable housing funding generated by new commercial and market-rate housing development is dwindling amid the broader development slowdown.

To offset those losses, the plan says, the city may consider an effort to boost the Community Preservation Act levy it charges property owners. It will also consider tax breaks for affordable housing projects and plans to tweak its Housing Accelerator Fund, a $100 million effort to unlock stalled projects that has not been widely utilized.

The plan also suggests citywide zoning for affordable housing, allowing projects that meet certain affordability requirements in designated locations to build at higher densities. That idea is modeled on a policy Cambridge adopted in 2020 allowing fully-affordable buildings up to 12 and 15 stories tall in key corridors without special approval from a zoning board. And officials said the Boston Housing Authority will continue expanding its affordable housing footprint in the city.

While Boston has policy levers it can pull on its own, many of the Wu administration’s preferred housing solutions — namely, rent control and a small fee on high-dollar real estate transactions to fund affordable housing — hinge on approval from a Legislature that has thus far been skeptical.

Winning over lawmakers and moving forward a broad array of new housing policies, the plan said, is essential to the city’s long-term vitality.

“Boston needs additional market rate housing, but it’s more than this,” said Dillon. “We need a more nuanced, comprehensive plan that also focuses on increased affordability and making sure that all of our populations — including seniors, families with kids, and students — are safely and appropriately housed.“

title: ‘I wear Boston through and through’: WNBA player Taina Mair enjoys an emotional homecoming
text:
When she finally returned to Boston last week, the city made sure she knew how much she meant.

Roxbury Prep, one of the launching pads that lifted Mair from Dorchester to the WNBA, hosted a homecoming last Friday, filling the gym with everyone from starstruck students to proud former coaches.

Mair’s mother, Mercy Pineda, sister Trayana, and brother Talik shared emotional messages. Her mother and sister held back tears. Her brother couldn’t.

“She always said, ‘Ma, I’m going to go out there and I’m going to do what I need to do,’ ” Pineda said. “And that’s what she’s doing. And I’m proud.”

State Representative Chris Worrell presented Mair with an official citation and award. Then City Councilor Brian Worrell declared Sept. 4 “Taina Mair Day” in the city.

Mair was overwhelmed, but also honored to be an example for kids who were sitting where she once sat.

“I don’t even know the word for it, but I’m so grateful,” she said. “This is something that, as a kid, you dream of. When you go away and you do great things, and you come back home and the city shows you nothing but love.

“It’s a top-tier feeling. I’ve never felt like this in my life and I’ve won plenty of championships, I’ve won a lot of things in my life, but this is something different.”

Emma Simmons, principal of Roxbury Prep’s Dorchester campus, coached Mair in middle school and remembered the packed gyms for middle school games. She also remembered Mair working as relentlessly in the classroom as she did on the court — the combination set her apart at an early age and sets an example to this day.

“If you ask, I’d say, 25 percent of our kids right now, what do you want to be when you grow up, they’d say basketball player, football player,” Simmons said. “And she’s one of the only ones that I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re going to get there.’

“I just feel grateful that she’s coming back to Roxbury Prep and she sees us as a home and that my current students can look up to her and see her as a real inspiration.”

From AJ Dybantsa, who took Brockton everywhere he went on his journey to becoming the NBA’s No. 1 pick in June, to Veronica Burton, a star at Newton South who’s now the reigning WNBA Most Improved Player and the engine for the Golden State Valkyries, Mair joins a growing list of players carrying Boston-area basketball onto the sport’s biggest stages.

The closest example Mair had when she was growing up would’ve been Roxbury native Shey Peddy, but Mair was 15 by the time Peddy made her WNBA debut in 2019.

“I feel like I didn’t really have anybody, to be honest,” Mair said. “That’s why me coming back is pivotal for the youth. Just being able to be the person that they can look up to and see they can reach these heights.”

Mair signed a player development contract with the Storm in May that allows her to practice and travel with the team, but limits her to 12 regular-season games. She’s played nine this season, six since late July, putting up her most productive night on Aug. 23 in a loss to the Dallas Wings (6 points in 13 minutes).

With the WNBA season coming to a close at the end of the month, Mair said she already has plans to sharpen her game in the offseason in Poland.

“There’s really levels, and you can see it,” she said. “When you get to the pros, there’s a bigger gap because these girls have been playing for 20-plus years and they know their role, they know what they have to do.

“But I think just coming in, figuring out how to adjust my play style, just being a little more physical, understanding that when you get a shot it needs to be knocked down. You’ve just got to be sharper.”

But on a day dedicated to her, Mair was proud to be an example of what’s possible.

“I wear Boston through and through,” Mair said. “Everywhere I go, I’m like, ‘I’m from Boston.’ You can’t tell me nothing. This is the city where I came from, I grew up here, born and raised.

“So to be able to have that is a special gift for what I’ve done for my city. Just being a role model — or trying to be one — I think having that kind of solidifies me as who I am as a person and who I’m trying to be.”

title: Suspended Boston police officer’s expected guilty plea falls through in illegal nightclub case
text:
The dispute followed a previous plea discussion before retired Superior Court Judge Mary Ames, who had indicated she would sentence McDermott to three years of probation, prosecutors said.

McDermott did not accept the deal at the time while he worked through issues involving his employment and the retirement board, according to his attorney, John Seed.

Seed said in court his client is ready to accept the previous agreement, but Ames retired without imposing the sentence.

Wall said he is not bound by the previous discussions and told the two sides the proposed sentences were too far apart for effective negotiations.

He advised prosecutors and McDermott’s defense that if they want to resolve the case with a plea, they should try to reach a joint sentencing recommendation.

“If you don’t have a joint recommendation, prepare for trial,” Wall said.

A trial date is currently scheduled for Sept. 28. The two sides are due back in court on Monday for a status conference.

“We just came forward to try to resolve the case today, and that didn’t happen,” Seed told reporters outside the courtroom. “We do have a trial date for the end of the month, but we’re still working on that.”

McDermott was indicted in 2024 on charges of witness intimidation, seeking criminal record information under false pretenses, and maintaining a gambling nuisance.

His certification to serve as a police officer remains suspended with the state’s oversight board, the Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission. McDermott also remains suspended without pay from the Boston Police Department, according to Sergeant Detective John Boyle, a department spokesperson.

Prosecutors alleged McDermott and Luigi D’Addieco, a suspended campus police officer for the Boston Public Health Commission, operated the unlicensed nightclub at 360B Centre St., where they offered liquor bottle service, hookahs, and a DJ booth.

The operation caught the attention of law enforcement after a 4:30 a.m. shooting at the club in 2021, according to prosecutors. Evan Velez, of Dorchester, allegedly shot at a bouncer several times during a dispute with the club’s promoter.

Police who responded to the shooting recognized McDermott, who was allegedly armed with a gun and among the last people to leave. McDermott allegedly told officers he did not know what was happening and had merely been attending his brother-in-law’s party.

Prosecutors said security video contradicted McDermott’s account, showing him looking out through the club’s front door and stepping over blood and broken glass before police arrived.

Prosecutors also alleged that McDermott later used a police database without authorization to search for information about the shooting and witnesses.

McDermott and D’Addieco had originally rented the basement to run a heating, ventilation, and air conditioning company, according to court records. Prosecutors alleged that during the pandemic they converted it into a nightclub where patrons could buy full bottles of liquor for more than $100.

McDermott pleaded not guilty to all charges at his October 2024 arraignment and was released on personal recognizance.

He sought dismissal of the witness intimidation charge, arguing there was insufficient evidence. A judge denied the motion on June 25, court records show.

Trial dates for both McDermott and D’Addieco have been postponed multiple times, court records show.

D’Addieco has pleaded not guilty to charges of withholding evidence from a criminal proceeding and maintaining a gambling nuisance. He is due to appear in court Sept. 21 for a pretrial conference, court records show.

title: Alleged Memorial Drive shooter indicted on 43 counts, to be arraigned Thursday
text:
The Aug. 25 indictment moves the high-profile case to Middlesex Superior Court, where Brown will enter a plea Thursday to an array of charges, including six counts of armed assault to murder, a sole count of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery with a firearm, and four counts of attempted assault and battery with a firearm.

The shooting unfolded around lunchtime on May 11, not long after a Massachusetts parole officer called 911 to report that Brown was suicidal and armed with an assault rifle. The officer said Brown had a long criminal record, including a 2020 shootout with Boston police in the South End, and a history of crack cocaine use and mental health problems; he had recently been discharged from a psychiatric hospital.

Middlesex Assistant District Attorney Nicole L. Allain asked the court to hold Brown without bail under the state’s dangerousness law, noting that his criminal history dates back decades. Brown was arrested as a teenager in 1994 in Michigan and charged with armed robbery. His other convictions include drug and gun offenses in Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

At his arraignment, Allain summarized Brown’s alleged actions, including three phone calls with the parole officer during which he repeatedly said he wanted to end his life and talked about crimes he committed but was not prosecuted for.

“These people are going to pay,” she quoted Brown as telling his parole officer not long before the shooting rampage. “I’m not going back to prison.”

In their final conversation, Brown displayed the gun during a FaceTime conversation, standing in a kitchen the officer didn’t recognize, Allain said.

The officer called 911 and requested a well-being check on Brown at his home in Dorchester, but he wasn’t there when police arrived. Police pinged his phone and tracked him to Cambridge.

Less than two hours after the 911 call, Brown allegedly began randomly shooting while walking down Memorial Drive. Motorists ran for cover, some hiding under their cars.

Brown was taken into custody after a state trooper and a Marine veteran returned fire.

Allain said two bullet holes were found in the driver’s side door of the Marine’s car. At least 70 spent shell casings were recovered, she said.

Allain said one victim was shot four times in one leg and the second was shot in the back of the head.

The shooting victims have been identified by family members as Casimir Bangoura, a Cambridge resident who was driving to the car wash, and another man whose first name is Felix, a father of eight. The family declined to provide his last name but said he was an MBTA Ride driver who drove himself to the hospital.

Brown was on parole for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in the South End in 2020, a case that has raised questions about the relatively lenient sentence he received after a judge was persuaded by his intellectual gifts and his commitment to keeping his life on track.

When Brown was released from prison in May 2025 after serving that sentence, he was accepted into the Tufts University Prison Initiative’s yearlong reentry program that combines college coursework with housing, employment, and other services. According to university officials, Brown stopped attending the program in February.

title: Developers want to bring nearly 2,000 units to Southie’s Dot. Ave. ‘as fast as possible’
text:
A development team behind one of New York’s tallest residential skyscrapers intends to build 1,945 homes on a prime South Boston site — property where Southie native Andrew J. Collins long dreamed of building.

New York-based J.T. Magen & Co. and Extell Development in March successfully bid $75 million at a public foreclosure auction — held on St. Patrick’s Day — to buy a collection of industrial property along Dorchester Avenue where it splits from Old Colony Avenue. The site, located midway between the Broadway and Andrew MBTA Red Line stations, is at the heart of a decade-old city plan that called for a corridor of dense, tall development in what is now a low-slung industrial zone.

Now the group has kicked off the city’s formal development-review process, with local partner Thomas O’Brien of The HYM Investment Group this month alerting Boston officials of the plan to build 1.8 million square feet of residential and retail space at 314-420 Dorchester Ave. In terms of space, that’s just a tad larger than the former John Hancock tower in the Back Bay, though the Southie project will be developed as multiple buildings.

Collins, the identical twin brother of state Senator Nick Collins, spent years cobbling together multiple parcels along the Dot. Ave. corridor and pitching a life-science campus there. Despite persuading a number of investors to funnel money toward a project, Andrew Collins never got a development off the ground. Collins has faced a number of lawsuits in state and federal court from investors claiming he owes them around $150 million.

The J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM development is one of the largest new housing projects proposed in Boston in years. The group envisions a collection of four 200-foot residential buildings with about 45,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and is exploring the potential to bring a grocery store to the site.

None of the buildings would rise higher than 200 feet, O’Brien said. At that height, the buildings would be roughly 18 stories. The project would have underground parking, which costs about $350,000 per space to build.

O’Brien, who last year briefly considered challenging Mayor Michelle Wu’s reelection, declined to share an estimated total development cost. However, new high-rise residential construction in Boston these days can cost more than $1 million per unit to build. The development team hopes to have all permits in hand by early next year.

“The idea is to build as fast as possible,” O’Brien said. “Not much housing is being built right now. ... You’d be delivering those units into a market that has not had much new product, and that’s a really important consideration.”

The anemic pace at which Boston is permitting and constructing housing is a top concern for many residents and the regional real estate development community, many of whom have sought to build outside city limits given the expense of developing in Boston. Approving 2,000 units would help the Wu administration’s preliminary goal of adding 3,000 new units annually over her second four-year term, which started in January.

Capping the buildings’ height at 200 feet aligns with the city’s adopted plan for the Dot. Ave. corridor. Still, because the plan’s guidelines were never incorporated in Boston’s zoning code, the J.T. Magen, Extell, and HYM partnership would need additional approval in order to build anywhere near that high.

The first building would likely be situated on a triangular-shaped parcel, currently home to a parking lot and vacant Castle Self Storage facility. The distinctive shape gives Boston-based architecture firm CBT “an opportunity for a really beautiful design,” O’Brien said.

Extell has built in Boston before, but not for decades. In 2006, the firm built the waterfront Intercontinental Hotel and Residences in downtown.

“These are two groups who are very familiar with Boston, and they understand the basic dynamics of what makes our city great,” O’Brien said.

As for the drive-through Dunkin’ located at 75 Old Colony Ave. in the center of the site, the Extell, J.T. Magen and HYM team intends for it to “stay for as long as possible,” O’Brien said.
