title: How does an MBTA Green Line operator make it on $73,000 a year?
text:
“Everybody always says, ‘Hey, the T is a good job. They have good benefits, pension, all that,’ ” he said.

After a training class to learn the ins and outs of operating the light rail, Conveniencia took to the tracks. “It’s muscle memory now,” he said.

Conveniencia bounces between the line’s branches on an often-changing schedule, which is how he likes it. “You’re always seeing something different,” he said, including the cast of characters that boards his trollies. He strives to be the friendly face of an often-unfriendly transit system, taking pride in helping riders navigate diversions, giving tourists directions, and holding the doors for people he sees running to catch the train.

“I know I’m helping everybody get to where they need to go,” he said.

The earnings: Last year, Conveniencia earned about $73,000. Without a college degree or a professional passion, “I didn’t think I would be making this much,” he said. “I’m grateful to be in the position that I’m in.”

And he will soon get a raise. At the end of the month, he said, his roughly $36 hourly wage will grow to about $41, a pay bump built into the MBTA’s union contract. Under the current bargaining agreement, he can expect to make about $49 an hour after he’s been with the T five years.

But those numbers are just on paper. Conveniencia’s biweekly paychecks currently come out to around $1,700 to $1,800, depending on overtime, he said. Deductions for health insurance (about $230), union dues (about $50), and the MBTA retirement fund (about $300) each cut into his take-home pay.

The steady pay, plus the promise of a pension, means Conveniencia is inclined to stay with the MBTA for the long haul. Plus, he knows the job has stability in a topsy-turvy labor market.

When it comes to the T, “I don’t think AI is going to take over,” he said.

The expenses: Conveniencia pays $1,500 a month in rent for an income-restricted studio apartment in Mission Hill, which he found through Metrolist, a city database. It’s a big discount, with the normal rent for such a unit topping $3,000, he said. Utilities, meanwhile, are all on him. He tries to budget at least $300 a month for gas, electricity, Internet, and water.

As for transportation, he sticks to riding the T — his badge gets him free rides — and the occasional Bluebike. Until late last year, he drove a Honda Civic, which cost $800 a month between the car payment and insurance, he said. But in November, he got into an accident, and decided to give it up.

About once a month, Conveniencia goes to Stop & Shop or Price Rite for a big grocery trip, and his last one cost about $200, he said. On workdays, he tends to eat fruit or toast for breakfast, bring leftovers or fruit to work to avoid buying lunch, and turn to simple dinner recipes.

“My meals will pretty much always consist of rice, some type of meat, and beans,” he said.

One more regular expense? “I work in the public, and I just want to make sure I look my best at all times,” he said, so he spends $35 on a weekly barbershop visit.

The debt: While Conveniencia now tries to keep his regular expenses to a minimum, he wasn’t always so prudent.

After getting his first credit card at 19, he began swiping with abandon, recalling dropping “like, $1,000″ on hauls of trendy clothing, or high-end sneakers, his kryptonite. “When I do shop, I kind of go crazy,” he said.

Eventually, he said, he racked up close to $10,000 in credit card debt. “The bulk of it was really just pointless purchases,” he said, plus the ensuing interest and late fees. When his cards maxed out, he turned to the “buy now, pay later” service Klarna, which breaks up purchases into smaller installments. Earlier this year, for instance, he paid for an $860 laptop in four $215 chunks.

“Everything’s at your hands,” he said. “It’s hard to break out of the habit.”

But, finally, he did, once he realized he wanted to buy a house one day, and with the milestone of his 25th birthday approaching.

He made it his mission to free himself of credit card debt by his March birthday, promising himself a trip to the Dominican Republic, where his family is from, if he could do it. Once he no longer had his car to pay for, he began funneling around $1,500 a month to dig himself out of the financial hole, he said.

“I had to cut down on everything,” he said — and he means everything. “I was dating at the time, and basically, I just had to say, ‘I can’t afford to be in a relationship right now,’ ” he said.

In the end, he pulled it off, and booked the Caribbean getaway — on a debit card.

Now that Conveniencia is back in the black, “I feel like a weight’s been lifted off my shoulders,” he said. But the experience left its mark. He limits using credit cards and removed them from his phone’s Apple Pay — while still trying to improve his credit score — and resists Klarna.

“I kind of scared myself,” he said. “I’m still kind of recovering from that.”

The outlook: For Conveniencia, that recovery means unlearning the bad habits that he observed growing up, where “everybody around me maybe drives a really nice car, but might not have enough money to afford the really nice car,” he said.

Don’t get him wrong — he still splurges occasionally, such as on a $220 pair of Nike Jordan shoes or, yes, on a date, where he always expects to spend at least $100. But these days, he tries to follow a simple maxim: “If you don’t have the money to do what you’re trying to do, just don’t do it,” he said.

Beyond that, he’s taking steps to improve his financial literacy, such as reading up on starting a Roth IRA account.

“I was living reactively,” he said. “Now I’m trying to live proactive, so I don’t have to react to my bad decisions.”

The goal: Like so many Boston residents, “my goal is to buy a home,” Conveniencia said. No one in his family owns their home here, he said, and he wants the security of knowing he won’t “get priced out of my city.”

He took one of Boston’s homebuyer classes, which qualifies him for financial assistance programs. “After a year of saving, I want to see how much I’ve saved and see where I can go from there,” he said.

He currently has about $2,500 in his savings account, he said, and he is currently trying to set aside $1,000 a month — money that once went toward paying off debt — with the hope of accumulating at least $12,000 by next September. “Is that possible? I’m not sure,” he said.

It’s something he feels good about working toward. The idea of taking out a mortgage? Not so much.

“I worked so hard this year to get rid of my debt, to now get into a debt of 30 years,” he said. “Granted, at the end of those 30 years, I’ll have something, but I’m like, ‘Man, does it ever end?’ ”

title: Boston and the MBTA redesigned Blue Hill Avenue, again. Opponents warn the changes are ‘not a done deal.’
text:
A vocal movement of opponents warned Thursday: “This is not a done deal.”

Roughly three dozen people called for the elimination of the proposed center-running bus lane in a protest march down Blue Hill Avenue before the meeting. Business owners at the meeting raised concerns that changes to the street, and parking, will spell doom for their storefronts. And dozens of public commenters accused public officials of, once again, not listening to the people of Black Boston, arguing that changes to the avenue will be the harbinger of gentrification.

When Bishop John Borders III asked opponents of the project to stand, half the room rose.

“They have a meeting, but they don’t really listen to us,” said Cynthia Grant Carter, 54. “What’s wrong with what we got?”

The $163 million trove of public money set aside for Blue Hill Avenue would not only go toward adding the bus lane, but also narrowing pedestrian crossings, planting 200 trees, and replacing street lighting — beautification and safety improvements many agree are sorely needed.

The latest proposal preserves roughly 11 of the existing 14 miles of car-travel lanes from Grove Hall through Mattapan Square and increases the total number of parking spots to 717 from 675. It separates some parts of the thoroughfare for car travel during rush hour and parking in off-peak periods.

In the meeting, Wu cited conversations with more than 3,000 people, saying they informed how City Hall and the T created the latest redesign, block by block.

“This is part of a big-picture plan to put dollars where they need to be to ensure we have equity throughout the city and opportunity in every neighborhood,” she said.

In the meeting, just five residents spoke to say they back the plan; two others raised concerns about the pullback of some proposed bike lanes in the latest design.

Carmen Blyden, director of community organizing at Bikes Not Bombs, said she “supports the project” but asked for additional bike parking on the avenue. Tony Baez, a cycling advocate, made the final remarks before public comment was cut off nearly an hour after the meeting’s scheduled 8 p.m. end time.

“I support this project today, just like I did a year ago,” he said. “We are asking drivers to give up 20 seconds, so that bus riders can get 15 minutes.”

But few meeting attendees were otherwise on board.

City councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper called for “real alternatives” to the plan, including a feasibility study on bringing rail back to the corridor. The two councilors have proposed extending the Orange Line subway beneath the street, though Wu’s office has warned it “would take many years ... and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment.”

There’s been long-standing frustration among residents about decades of neglect on the avenue dating to the 1950s, when the streetcar trolley along it was eliminated.

The MBTA previously committed to looking into a rail expansion, and Eng — serving as both the leader of the T and the state’s interim secretary of transportation — said on Thursday that the bus lane “does not preclude future discussions of rail.”

Public officials said Thursday the changes announced last week would immediately make the corridor safer. Blue Hill Avenue is frequently congested and accident-prone, with a crash requiring emergency medical services every three days on average, according to city data.

Justin Rodriguez, a 33-year-old Dorchester resident, said the center-running bus lane would be an “interference” to his commute as a regular bus rider. And frankly, he said he isn’t inclined to trust public officials, even when it comes to repaving sidewalks.

“If the idea didn’t come from people who are here every day, where did it come from?” Rodriguez asked. “These projects happen. We are never asked.”

Muhammed Uddin, owner of American Food Mart on Blue Hill Avenue, said the congestion and parking impacts he believes the center-running bus lane would hurt his business, which opened in 2024.

“It’s going to slow down everything,” Uddin said. “You want the street widely open.”

Dana Dowell, a lifelong Mattapan resident, said she’s “for beautifying our neighborhood and better infrastructure.” But not like this.

“This decision is being forced down our throat,” she said.

Still, some residents hope City Hall backtracks entirely and leaves their neighborhood untouched.

Gwendolyn McLaurin lives around the corner from Blue Hill Avenue and regularly takes the 28 and 31 bus. She believes the city and state should simply back off. No bus lane, no new rail line, no touching the sidewalks.

“There’s already not enough room for everybody. It’s not fair,” she said. “It should stay the way it is.”

Two open houses where public officials plan to share the block-by-block redesign will take place on Monday and Sept. 22 in Dorchester and Mattapan respectively. A final town hall is planned for Sept. 30, which Wu also plans to attend.

Correction: A previous version of this story misidentified Tony Baez’s job. The Globe regrets the error.

title: Man accused of opening fire with assault rifle on Memorial Drive pleads not guilty
text:
There were, according to court documents released Thursday, many close calls on May 11 when Tyler E. Brown IV allegedly opened fire seemingly at random on cars and buildings on Cambridge’s busy Memorial Drive. The mayhem injured two people but, despite the hail of bullets fired in multiple directions, did not kill any of the scores of drivers, pedestrians, or neighbors in harm’s way.

“His actions created chaos, confusion and fear in the motorists, pedestrians, workers, residents and shoppers who were in that area,” Assistant District Attorney Nicole Allain wrote in a court filing released Thursday.

The documents offer the most detailed picture yet of the events leading up to the violence, a portion of the path taken by the high-powered weapon he is accused of using in the attack, and just how close the shooter came to causing more harm than he allegedly did.

Brown, 46, of Dorchester, pleaded not guilty Thursday to 43 counts against him for the shooting, including assault to murder. He appeared in Middlesex Superior Court in a wheelchair and said “hello” and “not guilty,” but nothing else, during a brief hearing.

Brown’s attorney, Carolyn McGowan, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Prosecutors had previously said in court filings that Brown, who had a long rap sheet, had been released from a psychiatric hospital days earlier and was reportedly using crack cocaine.

The outbreak of violence had come with a warning. His parole officer had called 911 to report Brown was suicidal and armed.

Shortly after, investigators said, Brown took an Uber to Kelly Road in Cambridge, before walking to the parking lot of a Dunkin’ Donuts on Memorial Drive.

There, the document says, he approached a man and asked “how he felt about law enforcement and told him that he had ‘served 25 years’ and was ready to ‘take anyone out.’”

Shortly after, the gunman fired bullets at a different car, striking its driver several times. That victim has not been publicly named but has been identified by family members as Casimir Bangoura, a Cambridge resident. He is expected to recover from his injuries.

The other man who was injured was the driver of an MBTA Ride van, who had made a U-turn to flee the shooting when one or more bullets traveled through a rear window, a plastic shield, and a seat before hitting the driver in the back of his head.

The man, previously identified by family as Felix, a father of eight, reportedly drove himself to the hospital and was released that same day.

The bullet fragment, which caused “no serious physical injuries,” was later removed, the document said.

At one moment, the court document said, as the gunman shot into cars stopped at a red light on Memorial Drive, a bullet sailed into the rear lift gate of a USPS truck and through a metal divider, grazing a jacket draped over a driver’s seat before flying through the windshield, only narrowly missing the driver.

At another, the gunman approached a car and smashed its driver-side window with the firearm — but only after the driver had already fled.

Meanwhile, it described how two women inside a school bus van managed to flee as the gunman fired at their vehicle, hitting a side mirror, but missing them. The women, who earlier described their harrowing experience to a reporter, were not injured.

The frenzy ultimately came to an end when a Marine veteran who happened to be driving by pulled a gun from his own car and began firing at the suspect, subduing him.

The unnamed Marine and a state trooper who also traded fire with the gunman were unharmed, even as two bullets penetrated the Marine’s driver-side door.

It was still not clear in court documents how Brown may have come to own the firearm he allegedly used. As a convicted felon, he would not have been allowed to possess it legally.

Records showed the gun, a BCI-Defense Model FF-15, was first bought legally in 2015. Its owner then transferred the gun’s receiver to someone in Maine, who sold it two years later to another person in Maine, who “built an AR pistol from the receiver,” then sold it online in either 2018 or 2019.

The firearm sold again in 2019, either online or at a gun show, prosecutors said. That owner died, and there was no other record of how the gun exchanged hands after.

The charges against Brown include six counts of armed assault to murder, a sole count of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery with a firearm, and four counts of attempted assault and battery with a firearm.

Brown had been held without bail since an earlier arraignment on eight gun-related counts following the May 11 shooting.

Brown had been on parole for a shooting involving four Boston police officers in the South End in 2020, a case that has raised questions about the relatively lenient sentence he received after a judge was persuaded by his intellectual gifts and his commitment to keeping his life on track.

When Brown was released from prison in May 2025 after serving that sentence, he was accepted into Tufts University Prison Initiative, a yearlong reentry program that combines college coursework with housing, employment, and other services. According to university officials, Brown stopped attending the program in February.

He is due back in court for a dangerousness hearing set for Oct. 8.

title: Lighting up the Boston skyline on 9/11
text:
If someone has been sending you this newsletter, it’s time to get your own copy. Sign up at globe.com/powerplay.

Featuring: Gogi Gupta, John Civello, Ben Heller, Bryan Sparkes, Mike Simonelli, Don Chiofaro, Rachel Flor, Danny Lewin, Tom Leighton, Brooks Tingle, Seow Hui Lim, Maggie O’Toole, Edwin Tong, Lui Tuck Yew, Sumbul Siddiqui, Jesse Baerkahn, Mike Minogue, and more.

For one night each year, the Boston skyline takes on a shade of sky blue.

John Civello witnessed it a year ago after leaving work late. The drive across the Longfellow Bridge was one he will never forget. Civello heads up real estate at Akamai Technologies, which had just put up blue lights atop its Cambridge headquarters as a tribute to those who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. He stayed after hours to make sure the installation went OK.

While crossing the Charles, Civello was struck by what he saw in that postcard-perfect view. Tower after tower, lit up with blue. Only then, Civello recalls, did he realize how many others were participating.

This will be the third year Boston hosts our own version of the “Tribute in Light” that takes place in Manhattan each September. There will be more buildings aglow on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the attacks, than there were during Civello’s drive in 2025 — more than 30, in total.

It all began with a pitch from Boston marketer Gogi Gupta two years ago. The founder of Gupta Media emailed business leaders with an idea. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum in New York sends up two beams of blue light every year, an ethereal evocation of the World Trade Center towers, and nearby skyscrapers are lit up in solidarity. Boston, Gupta suggested, should join in.

Gupta was inspired after rereading an excerpt of Garrett Graff’s “The Only Plane in the Sky,” an account of the fateful day. Also, a college classmate from Cornell, Allison Blais, was then the 9/11 Memorial’s chief strategy officer. Mostly, Gupta worried the painful memories were fading as a new generation that only knows 9/11 from history books reached adulthood.

To find real estate contacts, Gupta turned to his leasing brokers at JLL, Ben Heller and Bryan Sparkes, and Mike Simonelli of Structure Tone, the firm that outfitted his Back Bay office.

That first year, it was short notice, less than two days in advance. Many companies need time to hire a contractor; it’s not like flicking on a switch for them. But several prominent tower owners, including BXP and the Chiofaro Co., made it happen.

For Don Chiofaro, there was no question he would light up International Place. He thinks about the firefighters who rushed into the burning World Trade Center, with 70 pounds of equipment on their backs, knowing they might not make it out. That kind of public service doesn’t get appreciated, he says, until it’s needed the most.

This year, the JFK Library illuminates its nine-story atrium overlooking Dorchester Bay. The blue lights went on at dusk on Tuesday, and are being rekindled each night through Friday. Foundation executive director Rachel Flor says it’s an important reminder of the service and sacrifice that we witnessed 25 years ago.

Many of Boston’s tallest office towers will be lit up. Among them: One Financial, South Station, the Pru, One Congress, 100 Federal. At 200 Berkeley St., aka the “Old Hancock Tower,” home to insurer John Hancock, the famous weather beacon at its tip will be lit in blue. CEO Brooks Tingle hopes it can remind people of the resilience, unity, and spirit of service that emerged that day.

For Akamai, it’s personal. Cofounder Danny Lewin, then 31, died in one of the two commandeered planes that took off from Logan. He’s considered the first 9/11 victim, believed to be stabbed after trying to stop the hijackers on American Airlines Flight 11. Lewin remains revered at Akamai; its highest employee award is given out each year in his honor.

Last year, Gupta emailed chief executive Tom Leighton, Lewin’s mentor when they were at MIT, asking Akamai to join. Leighton told Civello: Let’s see if we can make this happen. Civello got to work, and building owner BXP gave its blessing. Contractor Stagedge assembled 90 lights around the roof, echoing the blue shade that would appear on so many buildings across the Charles.

Word is getting out to other cities, too. More than 50 buildings outside of Manhattan — around half of them here — will be lit with blue on Friday night. The next highest concentration? Hartford, where Blais, Gupta’s college friend, now leads The Wadsworth museum.

Every July 4, fireworks light up the night sky in Boston.

Gupta hopes for something similar every Sept. 11, with building crowns alight in blue, sending a simple but powerful message: We remember.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Singapore is the latest country to put down roots in Massachusetts, announcing on Wednesday that it has opened a trade office at the Cambridge Innovation Center in Kendall Square. It’s the fifth US outpost for Enterprise Singapore, the economic development agency that helps Singaporean companies grow globally. The agency also signed an agreement with the Massachusetts Office of International Trade and Investment to encourage collaboration in key sectors including life sciences, climate tech, advanced manufacturing, robotics, and artificial intelligence. Singapore companies already operating here include defense firm MAK Technologies and air cargo handler Worldwide Flight Services. Because Singapore is geographically smaller than Rhode Island, businesses must look abroad to expand. “It’s a survival instinct,” explained Seow Hui Lim, who oversees Enterprise Singapore’s US division. Leaders gathered at a reception at Raffles Boston to celebrate, including Singapore Minister for Law Edwin Tong, Singapore’s Ambassador to the US Lui Tuck Yew, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, Massachusetts economic secretary Eric Paley, and Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce CEO Jim Rooney.

We’ve been as disappointed as most Bostonians to see Faneuil Hall Marketplace struggle with an identity crisis and a backlog of repairs. But here’s some good news: The marketplace’s ground-floor retail occupancy is now 85 percent, up from 76 percent in 2024 when new owner J. Safra Real Estate took over. A spokesman says Safra remains focused on improving the site to reinforce it as “a vibrant and dynamic destination for locals and visitors.” Toward that end, Commodore Builders just wrapped up badly needed paving and masonry fixes, along with other exterior upgrades. And brokerage Graffito SP, led by Jesse Baerkahn, has been busy attracting new tenants such as Azul Mexican Kitchen and gift shop Cognitive Surplus.

First, OpenAI raised a stink about the state Senate’s proposed crackdown on artificial intelligence. Now, the complaints are coming from a giant trade group representing most of the biggest names in tech (Amazon, Google, Meta, et al). That group, NetChoice, published a 1,100-word treatise to Beacon Hill conferees on Tuesday about a measure under consideration for an economic development bill that would require large AI companies to undergo third-party evaluations of possible catastrophic risks every 120 days. NetChoice says this frequent testing, which is supported by AI developer Anthropic, is untenable — particularly with another provision spelling out the state attorney general’s enforcement powers. The group says it’s ready to work with lawmakers as they finalize the bill on guardrails that don’t put these big “AI labs” in legal jeopardy or harm innovation. Not the best timing for Big Tech: A day after NetChoice’s testimony came out, an Anthropic researcher announced to the world that he believes there’s more than a 10 percent chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade.

The rap on Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue is that he has been light on details about his agenda. On Thursday morning, as he attended a rally at Shea Concrete in Amesbury, Minogue unveiled his much anticipated “Blueprint for a Better Future.” What caught our attention: the focus on energy costs, which is a big concern for residents and businesses alike. Minogue wants to cut state mandates from utility bills (which represent as much as a third of the cost of electricity), expand natural gas capacity, and evaluate nuclear energy options. He also would support enacting a gas tax holiday whenever prices at the pump exceed $4 a gallon, which they currently are. How to pay for these policies? One way: Cancel the state’s “net zero” mandate, a sustainability goal that he says costs taxpayers billions of dollars.

Producing more housing is another priority, and Minogue says he would incentivize towns to eliminate energy-efficiency “stretch” codes for buildings and reduce permitting times for single-family homes to 45 days or less. He also would not enforce the MBTA Communities Act, and instead work with municipalities that worry about the strain from new housing on infrastructure and schools.

The upshot: Minogue is staying on the Republican message of cutting taxes and government spending. Appealing to voters on affordability is a textbook political move, but we still don’t have enough details about how the math works out.

In Tuesday’s edition, we chronicled the fight over a new business improvement district in the Back Bay. Some of you have strong opinions about this. One reader, M.R. of Boston, didn’t mince words. “The Back Bay public properties suffer from neglect … [and] to not invest in nightly power washing and needle removal is basic neglect.”

With meteorological summer over, we’ve made a big decision about the future of Power Play: No more Friday sends! We’re sticking to coming out every Tuesday and Thursday.

Turns out our readers prefer that schedule too.

Today’s edition was edited by Greg Huang, Tim Logan, and Aaron Pressman, and produced by Diamond Naga Siu.

Have a question for the team? Email us at powerplay@globe.com.

Delivered Tuesday and Thursday.

title: The Mike Minogue (sort of) helping fund Mike Minogue’s campaign
text:
Michael T. Minogue, that is.

The eponymous donor popped on the Republican candidate’s latest campaign finance report after he donated $75 in mid-August. Sure, that’s not going to buy a whole lotta airtime, but it prompted us to wonder, just who is this other Mike Minogue?

Well, Minogue’s New York namesake is a 25-year veteran of the New York Police Department who retired in 2020. The 56-year-old was born and raised in Brooklyn’s Windsor Terrace neighborhood, a residential enclave near Prospect Park where he lives with his family, including a 16-year-old son named — you guessed it — Michael R. Minogue. (His middle name is Rourke; the gubernatorial candidate’s is Roger).

The retired dad of two stumbled across his Massachusetts doppelnamer late last month, when he met up with a friend for a Mumford & Sons concert at Madison Square Garden.

That friend had just moved to Massachusetts, Minogue said, “and she goes, ‘You’re not going to believe this, but there’s a guy running for governor named Mike Minogue.’ I go, ‘Get the hell out.’”

Naturally, he looked him up.

“I’m sitting at the concert and I find his site,” he said in a phone interview this week. “I go, ‘Holy [expletive]! There is a guy, Michael Minogue.’ And so I got some of his merch.”

In addition to adding the $75 worth of Minogue gear to his cart that doubled as his campaign donation — he bought a “Mike Minogue” hat and a “Minogue for Governor” shirt, and a hoodie is on the way — he said he’s also toying with buying a campaign flag for a property he owns by the water in Breezy Point, Queens. He then promptly started spreading the news.

“I started sending it out to my buddies, like, ‘Hey, look, I’m running for governor’ — you know, as a joke,” he said.

But the joke took off in his close-knit community, and Minogue and his buddies — mostly friends he’s known since kindergarten who still live in the neighborhood — have been lightly following the race since.

“My friends were like, ‘Wow, he just destroyed his opponent over in Massachusetts,’” he said, after Minogue (the candidate) handily beat Brian Shortsleeve in the GOP primary last week.

The merch is already getting a lot of use. The New York Minogue spent Labor Day weekend at his Queens beach property, where the neighborhood celebrates the end of summer with an annual “Mardi Gras” parade (Who cares when the actual holiday is!). He showed up decked out in the full Mike Minogue for Governor ensemble.

One piece in particular is already becoming a wardrobe staple. “This will be my main hat going forward,” he said. “It’s actually a pretty nice hat.”

Massachusetts’s political scene has seen its share of same-named pols and political figures over the years. There’s Charlie Baker, the Democratic operative, and Charlie Baker, the Republican former governor. There are multiple people named Marty Walsh, too — Martin J. Walsh, the former Boston mayor and former US Labor Secretary; his cousin,Martin F. Walsh, a local labor leader; andMarty Walsh of Natick, who once served as an aide to former US Senator Ted Kennedy (and once got an accidental call from Joe Biden looking for Marty Walsh, the mayor).

And state Representative William C. Galvin’s retirement announcement earlier this year caused some confusion. Secretary of State William F. Galvin, who once hinted his current term would be his last, is indeed back on the ballot this fall.

But Minogue, the one from New York, is far less likely to be mistaken for the ultra-wealthy GOP gubernatorial nominee who lives hundreds of miles away.

The New York Minogue, admittedly, is “not the most political individual in the world,” he said, but he is involved with his local Knights of Columbus chapter and, when he does tune into the political realm, leans right.

“People did say to me, you better make sure he’s a Republican before you put his shirt on,” he said.

As for his take on President Trump, the Republican president who Democratic Governor Maura Healey has sought to center in the gubernatorial race here?

“I do agree with a lot of his stuff,” the New York Minogue said. “Maybe not his personality, right? He’s a little aggressive at times. But I do agree with his policies.”

But it wasn’t the Massachusetts Minogue’s policies or past support of Trump that drew the Brooklyn native to the candidate.

No, his reason for his interest in the race was simple: “My name, and his name.”

SAFETY NET: Healey got a fresh boost Thursday in her effort to shore up her public-safety bona fides as she faces a challenge from her right, landing endorsements from four of the state’s major law enforcement unions.

Leaders of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, Massachusetts Coalition of Police, State Police Association of Massachusetts, and State Police Commissioned Officers Association of Massachusetts gathered in Dorchester to encourage voters to cast their ballot for the former attorney general in November. Healey cast herself as the “cheerleader-in-chief for law enforcement.”

Minogue, meanwhile, is drawing a distinction between union leadership and the rank-and-file officers those organizations represent. Minogue has also been endorsed by the Massachusetts Police Association.

“The police, when you talk to them, they’re going to vote for me,” he said at his own campaign event Thursday, per the Globe’s Chris Van Buskirk.

We know for sure he has the backing of at least one (former) police officer: New York’s Mike Minogue. (He just can’t actually vote for his namesake.)

RELATED:Minogue lays out campaign pledges to cut taxes, cancel climate mandates while downplaying legislative approval by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe.

NEW COURSE: The Massachusetts Teachers Association is dropping $500,000 on a new back-to-school ad campaign — but unlike most of the union’s recent ad activity, it’s keeping politics (mostly) out of it.

The latest spots, which will run on digital and streaming platforms through October, feature testimonials from students and parents about the impact educators have had on them. You can check them out here.

It’s a notable palate cleanse from an organization that just shelled out hundreds of thousands of dollars on state legislative elections, and put millions of dollars behind a ballot question two years ago to scrap the MCAS test as a graduation requirement.

BERGER KINGED: Brownsberger emerges victorious in election recount, keeps state Senate seat after Wu-backed challenge by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: State Senator William Brownsberger will keep his seat despite a challenge from first-time candidate Daniel Lander, after an election recount in the hard-fought race Thursday found Brownsberger had claimed 35 more votes than Lander in last week’s primary.

MONEY MOVES: Arizona US Senator Ruben Gallego is tapping Massachusetts’s deep-pocketed Democratic donor base next month. The potential 2028 presidential hopeful will be in Cambridge on Oct. 5 for a fundraiser hosted by Nathalie Rayes, who served as ambassador to Croatia under former President Biden. Tickets for the event range from $1,000 to $7,000, according to a copy of the invite.

PAPER TRAIL: Galvin — the secretary of state, that is — on Thursday referred fraud allegations against repeat US Senate hopeful Shiva Ayyadurai to state prosecutors, saying he received “several complaints” that the independent candidate submitted fraudulent signatures to local officials in an effort to qualify for the November ballot — including the signature of one of the clerks herself. Read more here.

CONVENTIONAL WISDOM: Last time Republicans held a convention in Dallas, unity reigned. This time was very different. by James Pindell, The Boston Globe: The 1984 Republican convention remains the only presidential nomination convention Dallas has ever hosted. And while parts of that previous convention rhyme with this week’s midterm Republican convention, the 1984 version is a helpful frame to examine everything that this week’s version is certainly not.

FACT CHECK: Why you shouldn’t count on Trump’s $5,000 check (which might not cover your higher costs anyway) by Jim Puzzanghera, The Boston Globe: If President Trump’s promise Wednesday night to send Americans big checks sounds familiar, it’s because he’s floated ideas like that before.

NEXT STOP: Boston and the MBTA redesigned Blue Hill Avenue, again. Opponents warn the changes are ‘not a done deal.’ by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: What Boston and MBTA leaders hoped would mark the beginning of the end of the decades-long tussle turned contentious again Thursday, when residents and elected officials packed the first of four planned community meetings this month. Many of them spoke in resistance to the latest plan to reimagine the busy boulevard.

SPRING BREAK: In Springfield, cyberattack has tens of thousands of students, and their parents, waiting and wondering by Danny McDonald, The Boston Globe: At a City Hall news conference on Thursday, Springfield officials said school would resume on Monday after what they called a “sophisticated” group of hackers targeted and breached the district’s systems, causing authorities to nix school for an entire week. “We’re not going to let these SOBs win,” Mayor Domenic J. Sarno told reporters.

9/11 changed their lives. This is what came next. by Chris Serres and Brian MacQuarrie, The Boston Globe.

David Morales will be Providence’s next mayor. His rise will test Rhode Island’s political establishment. by Dan McGowan, The Boston Globe.

Eversource, National Grid in court fight with Hydro-Quebec over Maine power line outage by Jon Chesto, The Boston Globe.

Elizabeth Warren and Daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi Announce Book by Carly Tagen-Dye, People.

Belchertown talk challenges nuclear energy’s role in climate solution by Maddie Fabian, Daily Hampshire Gazette.

GOP secretaries of state, including in New Hampshire, ask Supreme Court to block Trump mail-in ballot rule by Violet Jira, The Washington Post.

Thanks for reading The Scrum.

title: Matthew Rhys makes Emmys history with wins for ‘Widow’s Bay,’ ‘The Beast in Me.’ See the full list.
text:
Hargitay’s opening monologue leaned heavily on jokes about her long-running crime drama, with the host joking that she recognized everyone in the crowd for playing people she’d arrested on the show. The longevity of “SVU” came in for some jokes as well, with Hargitay pretending she didn’t know how to pronounce the word finale since she’d never had one, and honoring network NBC for hitting 100 years, which was how long, she joked, the show has been on.

Burlington native Amy Poehler presented the first award of the night, for supporting actress in a comedy series. The winner was heavy favorite Kate O’Flynn of “Widow’s Bay,” whose perpetually put-upon Patricia spoke to many of the horror comedy’s fans. O’Flynn, who won for her first nomination, honored “all the Patricias out there.” Her co-star, Stephen Root, later took home the award for best supporting actor for his work on the show as well. He made a point of saying “the reason I’m up here is Katie Dippold, Katie Dippold, and Katie Dippold,” a reference to the show’s creator, who also wrote the Boston-set comedy “The Heat.”

The show’s star, Matthew Rhys, made Emmy history as the first actor to win two lead acting categories in the same year, for “Widow’s Bay” and for his role in the limited series “The Beast in Me” earlier in the evening. He thanked Dippold and Hiro Murai, an executive producer and the director of half of the episodes of the series, as well as his agents, the cast and crew, the country of Wales, his sister, and “My parents — they just kicked me onto a stage from a very young age.” Murai would also win an Emmy for his directing on the show.

Dippold also won her own Emmy for her writing on the show. She said that while she’d promised that she’d stay humble if she won, that was no longer the case. Guests would be unable to “step foot in my home without seeing this thing” thanks to a “system of mirrors” to keep the trophy perpetually in their eyeline. She thanked Murai and the “brilliant” Matthew Rhys, joked that his Welsh accent was fake, and said that winning the award was “going to become my entire personality now.”

The series capped off the night with the Emmy for best comedy. “I have to thank my mom for always making Halloween fun,” Dippold said.

Jean Smart won her fifth Emmy for her work as a lead actress in a comedy for “Hacks,” for which she received a standing ovation. She joked that the women, in particular, should be allowed to sit down due to their uncomfortable dresses and shoes, and implied that people were thinking, “She’s not that good. You just stood up because she’s old.”

After a very funny intro from comedian John Mulaney about how men had been “historically unrepresented” on television, Noah Wyle took home the award for the second year in a row for best actor in a drama on “The Pitt.” “I grew up in LA, I’m a Hollywood kid,” he said. “This is the only club I’ve ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me.”

“The Pitt” went on to win the Emmy for best drama, and co-creator R. Scott Gemmill accepted the award on behalf of the show. “We are so blessed to have the most talented and passionate cast and crew,” he said. “We are so blessed to live in this community.” The series is known for its realistic depiction of a hectic city hospital emergency room, and Gemmill encouraged everyone in the room to keep “telling honest stories.”

“People need to know the truth, and we need to continue to tell them that in whatever form we can,” he said.

“Widow’s Bay” won eight Emmys during the earlier ceremonies, with Betty Gilpin taking home the award for outstanding guest actress in a comedy series. Boston Casting’s Angela Peri and Lisa Lobel also earned their first Emmys, with the local casting company winning earlier in the month as part of the “Widow’s Bay” team nominated for outstanding casting for a comedy series.

“Boston Casting is thrilled to bring home the Emmy,” Peri and Lobel said in a statement to the Globe. “We are especially proud of the incredible local actors, who helped create the authentic feeling of a quirky island community off the coast of New England. This Emmy belongs to them, too!”

Julianna Margulies presented her “The Good Wife” co-star Michael J. Fox with the 2026 Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his advocacy and contributions to Parkinson’s disease research. Fox gave a speech about Bob Hope’s status as an inspirational figure for Fox’s own charitable work. Later in the show, Sally Field and Reba McEntire honored the late Dolly Parton, with the latter performing Parton’s “Appalachian Memories.” The inaugural Legacy Award, a newly created honor celebrating the impact of shows from the past, went to “I Love Lucy” during an earlier Emmys ceremony held on Sept. 6.

The “in memoriam” segment led off with Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy, and Dan Levy honoring the late Catherine O’Hara, who had played their mother onscreen, with Culkin becoming noticeably emotional during his speech. New England native Noah Kahan soundtracked the remainder of the segment with a performance of Simon and Garfunkel’s “Bridge Over Troubled Water.”
