title: Police seek person who stole vehicle in Roxbury with child in the back seat
text:
Police are asking for the public’s help in identifying a person suspected of stealing a vehicle in Roxbury that had a child in the back seat.

The individual, who is wanted for kidnapping and larceny, allegedly stole the vehicle around 9:15 p.m. on Saturday in the area of Crawford and Warren streets, officials said.

The vehicle and the child were later found safe about a mile and a half away in Dorchester at Draper and Bentham streets, police said.

Police have released a photo and video of the alleged suspect, the person’s face obscured with a surgical mask and hat. It was taken around 8:34 p.m. on Saturday, roughly 40 minutes before the crime took place.

Police are reviewing the circumstances around the incident and urge anyone with information to contact detectives at (617) 343-4275.

Tips may also be submitted anonymously through the CrimeStoppers Tip Line at 1-800-494-TIPS.

Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism.

title: This is a story about a persistent puddle in Chinatown. But also so much more.
text:
This is a story about a big puddle, yes, but it’s about much more than that: historic marginalization, public health, and city services in a neighborhood that has served as a beachhead for immigrants for more than a century.

But first, the puddle: it’s a collection of rainwater in one of Chinatown’s alleys, near a public parking lot and behind a multilevel brick building whose front faces Edinboro Street. It’s a short walk away from the Chinatown Gate. The body of water remains, with a length of more than 30 paces, three days after the last rain.

It’s been here for years, flooding basements and spawning clouds of mosquitoes in the most urban of landscapes. Locals say it takes weeks of no rain and hot temperatures for the puddle to fully evaporate, only to return after the next storm.

Wen Feng Huang has owned 180 Cafe on Edinboro Street for almost a decade. The backdoor to her business faces the alley. After a rain, whenever a car passes through the puddle, it pushes the water into her basement, flooding it.

What happens after that? She mimes pushing water around with a squeegee. “All the time,” she said through an interpreter.

This year has been particularly bad for the basement flooding. She doesn’t know why, only that it has been a headache.

Like many alleys, the sun doesn’t shine here for a chunk of the day. There are ruts in the pavement.

But this alley happens to have a claim to the most historic passage in Chinatown. It has a name: Ping On Alley, or Alley of Peace and Security. A nearby plaque notes that this is where Boston’s first Chinese immigrants pitched their tents starting in 1875. Until the 1950s, a communal roasting oven, used by residents and restaurants alike, was located here.

Since the 19th century, the plaque informs passersby, “this site has been central to the lives of a growing Chinese community.”

Nowadays, Ping On Alley is more urban eyesore than tourist destination, with cigarette butts and the occasional orange cap of a syringe littering the ground, to say nothing of the ever-present brownish-green pool.

Some restaurant workers ducking in and out of a doorway in the alley shrug when the standing water is broached. On this day, the puddle stretches for five car-lengths, but for some, it’s just a part of the backdrop here; you might as well be asking about the Boston Harbor.

Other residents say its presence speaks to a larger trend of quality-of-life shortcomings in the neighborhood.

“The city needs to pay more attention,” Min Hong Yu, an 80-year-old who has lived in the neighborhood for more than 20 years, said through an interpreter.

But local water and sewer officials say that the alley is a private way, and that their quasi-governmental agency does not own or maintain a drain there. They argue that the private property owners abutting the alley are responsible for the drainage.

Kate DeBeul, a resident of one of the buildings that abuts the alley, thinks that government officials should do more and that citing the fact that Ping On is a private way is a cop-out. After all, she argues, authorities have a responsibility to act if the private property owners are neglectful.

She does not think a similar situation would be tolerated in, say, the Back Bay or the South End. Can you imagine such a thing going unaddressed year after year?

In the meantime, the water in Chinatown stagnates.

Chinatown has weathered neglect and sometimes outright hostility from government authorities for generations. Carved up by highway construction and saddled with a red light district decades ago, Chinatown is currently burdened by bad air quality and targeted by casinos. Temperature-wise, it’s the city’s hottest neighborhood, and also one of its poorest.

Add the Ping On puddle to the list of quality of life issues here.

“This community deserves to have a strong and healthy neighborhood and we’re struggling, to be honest with you,” said City Councilor Ed Flynn, whose district includes Chinatown and who has held hearings on drainage problems in the neighborhood.

The city, he said, should be doing “everything it can” to improve the day-to-day lives of neighborhood residents. That includes making investments to fix improper drainage, he said, because it’s a public health issue.

“Chinatown deserves the same level of respect and basic city services as any other neighborhood,” he said.

Bingxiang Ma, 61, lived for six years in the block on Edinboro Street that faces one side of the alley. The puddle was a constant. Sometimes after a bad basement flood, you could smell a mildewy stench throughout the building, he said.

“The smell was not good, and the mosquitoes of course,” he said through an interpreter.

He now lives across Chinatown. In the alley recently, Ma gestured to faded mud marks on the sides of the buildings of the alley, showing how high the water can get at times.

“It can get up to here,” he said.

City Hall deferred comment to the Boston Water and Sewer Commission. That entity, through a spokesperson, said that the alley is a private way and that the commission “does not own or maintain a drain here.”

“BWSC will work with the abutters/owners to review any upgrades which they may propose to eliminate flooding problems on this private way,” said the spokesperson in a statement.

But that’s not good enough for some frustrated residents who have complained about the flooding and public health problems attached to the puddle for years.

DeBeul, a 33-year-old attorney, said bad drainage has been an issue since she moved into a building that abuts the alley six years ago.

“Nothing has been done,” she said.

Sometimes, during bad rainstorms she can hear water gushing into her building’s basement. Other times, she can smell the musk of muddy rainwater through the drains in her home. She has had to contact an exterminator to help mitigate the mosquitoes in her building, which is situated in what would otherwise could be described as an expanse of concrete, pavement, and brick.

But thanks to Ping On’s urban wetland, she worries about mosquito-borne diseases like West Nile virus, and the health impact of the exterminator spray, which is designed to be used outdoors, she said.

“He was a guy from Dorchester and he thought I was out of my mind saying I have mosquitoes in the third floor of a building,” she said.

Messages left with multiple private property owners who own buildings abutting to the alley were not returned for this story.

“The city refuses to push the abutters to do anything and that’s where I get pissed off,” DeBuel said. “All of your complaints just go ignored, and I think that’s bull(expletive).”

title: Residents will weigh in on proposed game-day parking plan around White Stadium, officials say
text:
The decision about resident parking protections around White Stadium on Boston Legacy FC game days will be put in the hands of the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park, according to city officials.

A survey will ask residents for their opinion on the city’s proposed parking protections in their area, which would go into effect on game days for the National Women’s Soccer League team at White Stadium, city officials said Tuesday evening.

“The neighborhoods decide,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Tuesday evening to around 40 Roxbury residents at the Bruce C. Bolling Municipal Building. “What we do as a city is we put in the policy that we believe best reflects the consensus and decisions and needs of our residents, and then we continue to evaluate.”

The Roxbury meeting was the first of four that will be held with residents and business owners of the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park to share the new transportation plan and request their input on parking restrictions.

For five hours on game days — including two hours before kickoff and one hour after games conclude — the city proposed a “resident parking protection zone” stretching 0.75 miles from the stadium entrance, which residents will vote on.

The survey asks residents whether they approve of the resident parking protection zone, as well as proposed protections for general parking inside Franklin Park, including for golfers and visitors to its zoo.

The results of the survey, which closes Oct. 24, will be shared with neighborhood associations in Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan, which will ultimately vote whether to add the parking restrictions, officials said.

Officials also shared the city’s broader plan to promote public transportation by fans. Boston Legacy FC will fund the operation and enforcement of the plan, according to the city.

There is no spectator parking at White Stadium, officials said.

On game days, the city will provide free shuttles at MBTA stations and at satellite parking lots outside Boston. It will also use a parking lot on Seaver Street as a pickup and drop-off area for game attendees using ride-sharing services like Uber and Lyft.

The city is also upgrading bike and pedestrian pathways around Franklin Park to allow for stadium access.

The renovation of White Stadium drew harsh criticism from opponents concerned that the involvement of Boston Legacy FC, a for-profit sports team, would illegally allow a private company to profit from public parkland and improperly limit the public’s access to the facility.

In August, the city’s $325 million plan to renovate White Stadium was backed by the Supreme Judicial Court when it rejected a lawsuit trying to halt the project, ruling the overhaul does not violate a state law that protects public parkland.

The ruling also ended a yearslong lawsuit to stop the project brought by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, an environmental nonprofit, and a coalition of residents living in the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park.

The renovated stadium will serve as a new hub for Boston Public Schools Athletics and become the home stadium for Boston Legacy FC.

The stadium will still be owned by the city and primarily used by students and Boston residents, officials said at Tuesday’s meeting. The current lease agreement allows Boston Legacy FC to use the stadium for up to 20 home games and 20 practices each year.

Still, Roxbury residents have many concerns about game day operations, ranging from the sale of alcohol to the impact on other community events.

“If someone shows up from out of town and they’re not aware it’s game day, they can have their car towed,” said Louis Elisa, 77, a Seaver Street resident and cofounder of the Franklin Park Coalition, which aims to preserve the historic green space.

“You’re not allowing the people who’ve been in this community, taking care of this park, taking care of this community, to live freely and enjoy themselves,” Elisa said.

Tony Brewer, who lives a few doors down from Elisa, said in an interview that solving the resident parking issue is essential before White Stadium opens.

“We don’t have to fight about it,” Brewer said. “We just need to come up with ways of resolving it in a peaceful manner.”

Lauren Albano can be reached at lauren.albano@globe.com. Follow her on X @LaurenAlbano_.

title: Botox and a brownstone? Boston-area real estate agents are hosting lavish open houses.
text:
“The host feels so good because the guests are saying, ‘Oh my God, this is the best showing we’ve ever been to,’” said Cervasio.

She was hired to turn a realtor’s open house into a curated event. During the COVID pandemic, agents couldn’t host open houses for about two years. That happened at the beginning of a cycle of volatility in the real estate market that continues to shift due to everything from wars and oil prices to elections and housing shortages.

“It’s been an uphill battle, at least on the sales side,” said Sarah Maguire, principal of the Aronson Maguire Group at Compass. “So we started to have to get very creative.”

Throughout Boston, real estate agents are getting savvier when it comes to getting potential buyers and their agents through the doors of open houses. But a free glass of cheap wine and a cheese board doesn’t pull the weight that it used to. As a result, agents are going to tremendous lengths to curate custom events that engage the community, attract unlikely guests, and satisfy builders who want to see a successful return on their investment.

Realizing that free beers and a gift certificate weren’t going to do the trick, Maguire’s team leaned into special events. To highlight a new build in Dorchester, it hired Red Oyster to walk around the open house shucking oysters with pails of empty shells hanging from their matching aprons. The event was a hit.

“They were running around literally shoving oysters down people’s throats with all the accouterments,” said Maguire. “People loved it.”

For another listing that went up between Thanksgiving and Christmas, Maguire needed to drum up interest for three units in a Jamaica Plain development.

“It’s the absolute worst time to sell anything,” said Maguire. “We’re like, what the hell are we going to do? No one’s buying anything. Rates are through the roof.”

Maguire and her team came up with the idea of hosting a holiday market inside the development featuring local makers from Jamaica Plain, West Roxbury, and Roslindale. Vendors sold everything from knitted hats to homemade dog treats throughout the three units. Ultimately, the sale of the units set price records.

“Our sellers need to see that we’re trying to do everything we possibly can to get people through the door,” said Maguire, who has also hosted open houses featuring bouquet-making bars, Botox, a gelato stand, and a tarot card reader.

When the builder of Diana Lannon’s listing told her they wanted the open house for a recently constructed $2.8 million home to be “something like the ones on ‘Million Dollar Listing,’” the popular Bravo real estate show, she knew she had her work cut out for her.

“The reason 100 people show up to an open house on ‘Million Dollar Listing’ is that they’re going to be on TV,” said Lannon, an agent with Gibson Sotheby’s Realty. “I needed to get the most attention on this property.”

But the $2.8 million listing was on the pricier side for Sudbury, and it was in the middle of January, when getting people to leave their homes is tough. Lannon knew she’d have to come up with an unusual idea to reel in attention from people in neighboring suburbs and the city. Knowing a new medspa was opening in town, she came up with the idea for a “Botox and Bubbles” event. She paid for the first few units of Botox and asked interested people — who were invited to the open house on Paperless Post invitations — to sign up ahead of time.

“People from the local area were going to come, but I needed people from the city,” Lannon said. “I needed agents who have higher-end buyers that are selling their $1.5 million or $2 million condo in the city, and want to come to the suburbs, but they want something brand new and luxury.”

There were a few negative reactions. Lannon even received a few “nasty” emails. But on the day of the event, attendees were greeted by champagne and a spread of food from Baker’s Best in Needham. The fireplace glowed, and music played in the background. The medspa was set up in the home office, so guests could get injections in privacy. For a broker open house that typically yields eight agents, around 40 people came through the door, including agents from nearby towns like Wellesley and Lexington.

“They never would have come if I didn’t do that,” she said.

So is investing the time — and significant money — in turning an open house into a custom event worth it?

“It depends on what it is that you’re trying to sell,” said Maguire. “What’s the product? What’s the price point? Where’s the location? Sometimes we have to do these things to appease our sellers. The potential commission that we’re making from it has to be enough for us to cover the cost. These things cost thousands of dollars. The risk has to be worth it.”

title: Larry Edelman says Massachusetts needs another miracle
text:
Shirley Leung: Welcome to “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Shirley Leung. Massachusetts is full of riches. We have the best schools, world-class hospitals, and great quality of life. So why are tens of thousands of people leaving every year and taking their companies with them? Where has our mojo gone?

Larry Edelman, author of The Globe’s incredibly popular newsletter, Trendlines, has been working with colleagues on a new series called “Why Massachusetts Lost Its Mojo and How We Get It Back.”

Welcome, Larry.

Larry Edelman: Hi, Shirley.

Leung: Good to have you back.

Edelman: It’s good to be back.

Leung: So, in the first installment of this series, you quote Hemingway, “Economies fall apart gradually, then all at once.” I’ve never heard that. That was pretty good.

Edelman: I saw that somewhere else and I decided to steal it, but yes.

Leung: And so you’ve been following the Massachusetts economy a really long time. What made you write this series? Was there a specific moment?

Edelman: No, it wasn’t a specific moment. What I did was, for the last couple years — and Trendlines covers the economy — and certain things just kept popping up; The idea that job growth was weak, the outmigration of residents from Massachusetts to other states, all the complaints about the cost of living, the housing prices continuing to rise.

And I kept thinking to myself, “Is something going on here? What is it?” And it just felt like it was ineffable, but that idea that we’ve somehow lost that swagger that Massachusetts used to have before the pandemic, when we were riding high. And I thought, “You know, it’s time to see if we can get to the bottom of that.”

Leung: For me, I wonder if it began with the millionaire’s tax when that passed. That was, what? 2022?

Edelman: Yes. And that’s one of the things. That kind of ramped up, at least from certain business quarters, the complaints about Massachusetts’ cost of living and the taxes. But it’s more than just the millionaire’s tax.

In fact, I heard more complaints about the estate tax, which is the fees that you pay when the estate of somebody who dies goes to their relatives, heirs, [and] so forth. Massachusetts has one of the most onerous estate taxes in the country.

Leung: There’s some disturbing statistics in your series. And I had thought I’d seen them all, you know, also being a business writer.

Massachusetts is last in the country for new business formations. 180,000 people have left the state over the last few years. So what other numbers startled you while researching this series?

Edelman: It was also the degree to which private employment growth, that means employers other than the government, has lagged behind like 41 other states over the last five years.

We’re just really not creating as many jobs as other states are, and that surprised me, that we were so low.

Leung: And why is that? Is that AI? Is [it] that companies are expanding in lower cost states? What’s going on?

Edelman: I don’t think AI. It’s a little too early to attribute any lack of employment growth to AI.

I think it’s more that when companies are looking to expand, they’re doing it elsewhere. And the number of new businesses being formed is very important because that’s where a lot of job growth comes from.

[It’s] people starting a company on their own or with a couple people and hiring, and [then] hiring more. And when you’re not creating a lot of new companies, that’s when you don’t see a lot of job growth.

Leung: And there’s a real ripple effect when we aren’t creating as many jobs. I hear this from real estate developers. This is why they’re not building new towers. There’s no need, you know? There’s no one to fill those new office spaces.

Edelman: That’s right.

Leung: So they’re not building, and then that has an impact on construction, right?

Edelman: It sure does. I don’t think it’s a crisis in terms of tomorrow, we’re gonna have really high unemployment in Massachusetts. What I think it [might be] is a crisis of complacency in that we take things for granted. Massachusetts has been such an economic outperformer for so long that politicians, some business leaders, and other members of the community just assume that it’s going to be like it was.

But, I think the pandemic was a real break in everything that happened after it, especially inflation. The inflation that followed COVID-19 really took Massachusetts, which was always an expensive place to live, and made it just ... I mean, it was straw that broke the camel’s back.

It was that last thing that made it, like, outrageous. I was talking to somebody yesterday whose adult kids earn $400,000 a year. They both have very good jobs, but they’re paying $80,000 or $75,000 in childcare costs.

Leung: Yeah, I believe it.

Edelman: So what used to be very good salaries, people are being squeezed.

Leung: One of the themes in your series is about policy changes and how the policy changes aren’t bold enough. What would move the needle in your mind?

Edelman: Well, I think [the] first thing that has to happen is to make the tax code a little more amenable. I don’t think we need to repeal the millionaire’s tax, but we could do the estate tax. We could bring the estate tax in line with the rest of the country.

I think that there’s a lot of onerous business regulations that could be removed. Other states are doing that. I think that the unemployment system is very expensive in Massachusetts.

Leung: That’s right.

Edelman: And I hear frequent, frequent complaints that it’s really one of those costs that really weigh on businesses when they consider adding employees.

Massachusetts has the most generous benefits in the country. So again, if we could gradually adjust, become more in the norm than we are now, it would be better.

Leung: And is anyone proposing some of those policy changes?

Edelman: Well, getting back to my comment about complacency, a couple years ago, the legislature formed a special commission to review unemployment.

This was after COVID. And remember how the system was swamped and there were billions of dollars going out the door, and then they realized they weren’t following the rules that the [federal government] had set down, and then they tried to claw back all this money. [A] real disaster.

After that, there was a commission put in place to see how they could overhaul unemployment, and they held hearings, and they could not agree on any course of action.

So, that reform effort has just died. Year after year, we just keep going ahead, you know?

Leung: So, we talked earlier about businesses [and] the lack of new businesses forming here in Massachusetts. It’s a real brain drain happening among entrepreneurs. And our colleague, Emma Platoff, wrote a piece about this kid who grew up here. I think he went to school here. Then instead of starting his company here, his biotech company, he did it in California in Silicon Valley. And his parents are still here.

This happens over and over again. People study here, they come up with a great idea, and then they build their billion-dollar idea somewhere else. So, why does this keep happening?

Edelman: I think because there’s a big cultural difference between Boston and Silicon Valley. They just take bigger risks out there, and there’s more venture capital money out there. Boston has a pretty good venture capital community. I don’t mean to run it down at all.

But the amount of money out there is just significantly different, and they are much more willing to place bets on unproven, untested ideas.

Leung: And they can be younger talent, right?

Edelman: Exactly. Here, they’re more conservative when they [are] writing the checks.

Leung: I think entrepreneurs know that you have to have a little gray hair in order to get money here.

Edelman: Yeah. So it’s very hard to compete with Silicon Valley

Leung: But, for a time, we were, though.

Edelman: For a time we were, but the technology changed. And, right now, it’s AI. Everything is AI, right? And we’re just not on the map.

Leung: I mean, and San Francisco is really the epicenter of the world for AI.

Edelman: Which is ironic because MIT has been producing geniuses in AI for decades, you know? And same with other schools around here. And yet, they go to California, if they’re really good.

Leung: Our colleague, Diti Kohli, wrote a piece about higher education and how this feeling of doom in our economy is really tied up in this crisis happening in higher education.

It’s been a bedrock of our state economy, but it’s in trouble. I mean, Trump is pulling back research grants, international students don’t wanna come here. And then there’s this demographic cliff that’s been talked about for the past decade, where you’re gonna have fewer kids going to school.

I mean, is this problem fixable?

Edelman: To a degree. There’s not much you can do about the demographic cliff, right? There’s just going to be fewer high school graduates applying to colleges, so there’s gonna be more competition for those students, right? Colleges are going to have to maybe improve their reputation for being worth going to.

If the world is an AI world, do you really need to go and spend four years getting a liberal arts degree? But at the same time, Washington has made the business model much harder to work because research grants are so important, and they’re coming much slower than they were a year ago.

Some schools are seeing 15 percent, 20 percent decline in their research grants between last year and this year. So that’s another thing. They were very comfortable financially because of the research grants and their endowments. So the business model is gonna have to change for higher education.

Shirley Leung: And do you think it’s gonna be smaller?

I mean, do you think that the kind of the boom times in higher ed, that [it’s] past us?

Edelman: I think we’re past boom time, that’s for sure. And I think we’re past the time where tuition [is] going to be able to go up faster than inflation every year.

I wouldn’t worry so much about Harvard and MIT. There’s always gonna be enough people who want to go there, but the other schools are going to find themselves fighting for students even more than they are today.

Leung: Is there a policy fix beyond the schools themselves? Is there anything that [the] government can do locally?

Edelman: Well, locally, the governor proposed a $400 million infusion of research money, splitting it between public universities and private universities.

Leung: [Which is] stalled on Beacon Hill.

Edelman: Yes. First [they] cut [it] in half, and now [it] still hasn’t gotten anywhere.

So I think they’re, to a certain degree — at least until we have a new administration in Washington that has a different approach to higher ed funding — they’re going to have to learn to get by with fewer revenues coming in from research.

Leung: I mean, how important is higher education to the entire economic ecosystem here?

Edelman: Oh, it’s a central pillar of our economy. Higher ed not only employs a lot of people on campuses, but they also turn out graduates who then go on to work at our companies. In Massachusetts, one of its competitive advantages has always been having a highly-skilled workforce. Then there’s the interaction with the biomedical research world [and] between the medical schools and the biotech companies.

Leung: And the hospitals.

Edelman: And the hospitals. It’s this tightly integrated system that has been previously the envy of other states. If private education weakens, it weakens the whole system.

Leung: Larry, we can’t talk about the Massachusetts economy without talking about housing. And, in many ways our economy’s in trouble because we’re in this housing crisis. We don’t have enough, and enough is not getting built fast enough to keep up with our needs. It’s a huge part of why people are leaving, young people in particular.

And Emma Platoff was out in San Francisco. She wrote about how that city recently cut its affordable housing mandate from 15 percent to 5 percent. Meanwhile, in Boston, it’s 20 percent. Mayor Wu says she won’t change it. So, where do you come down on this debate?

Edelman: I come down on the side of “We have to find a way to build more housing.”

There are plenty of ideas out there. I think reforming the affordable housing requirements is one of them. Coming up with ways to change local zoning laws. That is one of the biggest problems, and The Globe has written about that extensively with the MBTA Communities Act and so forth.

It’s understandable. People don’t want their neighborhoods changing. They like where they live, and they don’t wanna see big apartment buildings built there. But at some point, this is not just politicians. This is like the residents of Massachusetts have to realize that something’s got to change or the young people are just not going to be able to live here and are going to go elsewhere.

The average age of a first-time home buyer is over 40 now. That really says something to me. [When] I bought my first house, I was in my mid-20s.

Leung: Wow. I was in my early 30s.

Edelman: Right. And that would be considered remarkable today. So we’ve got to work on that.

We’ve got to work on zoning, and come up with some way to incentivize builders to go for it and build those homes.

Leung: So it goes way beyond affordable housing.

Edelman: It goes way beyond affordable housing. It’s cultural. It’s the cost of the materials.

When it’s so expensive to build something, you have to price it higher to make your money, so it’s a real bind. And let’s be fair, Massachusetts isn’t the only place where this is going on, but we’re at the top end of that. Let’s see what happens in San Francisco, if it’s a longer term growth in their housing stock.

Leung: In the 1980s, there was a transformation in the Massachusetts economy. We know it as the Massachusetts Miracle, where it was kind of really an inflection point, right? Where industrial was fading, the factories were fading, manufacturing was fading. We were able to pivot, and first into tech, and then into life sciences, really becoming known as a knowledge hub.

Do we need to come up with another pivot?

Edelman: It would help. I think that biotech is struggling a little bit now. It’s getting better. I don’t think it’s going to go away, and we just had these breakthroughs, one in new drugs, one of which from Moderna.

Leung: The cancer vaccine [is] huge.

Edelman: And so, we can still do it. The US economy and the world is going to be reshaped by AI. One of the things that I think Massachusetts would be very well-positioned to capitalize on AI is in applying AI for specific companies.

I’m not talking about building the frontier models that OpenAI and Anthropic are doing. We’re never gonna be in that race. But we can, given our big professional services industry, take those innovations in AI and help companies adapt them and use them and become more efficient. I think that’s one potential place.

Leung: Talk a little bit more about that. In healthcare, people talk about [the uses of AI] in healthcare, right?

Edelman: Yes. One of the places AI has the most potential to be beneficial to humanity is in speeding up the development of new drugs. And it’s already happening in the Mass. biotech community and at the hospitals.

They’re incorporating AI into that. There’s plenty of AI uses in healthcare. But, all these companies out there have to learn what they can do with AI and what they can’t, and how can they improve their operations. We’ve got so many consultants out there and experts in technology who could pivot towards helping companies adapt.

Leung: When you look back to the Massachusetts Miracle, what was it that caused the politicians or businesses — What happened, that got everybody thinking, “Wait a minute, we need something. We need a big pivot. We need to do something here”?

Edelman: It was more luck than anything else. Starting in the early 70s, we had people like Ken Olsen at Digital, and they were working on new computers that were much smaller than the mainframes that were the conventional computers at the time.

Mainframes would take up a whole room. They started making computers that were the size of a big refrigerator. And it wasn’t a government policy. It was that interaction between the higher ed complex and the venture capital complex [that] led to the creation of Digital and Data General and Wang Laboratories’ Prime Computer.

So, it wasn’t a government policy. Michael Dukakis tried to paint the Massachusetts Miracle, which happened partially under his administration, as smart planning. But it was really more luck than anything else.

In contrast, biotech was a conscious decision. And Deval Patrick made a commitment of a billion dollars over 10 years to help fund biotech research in the state, and that paid off hugely, as we all know.

Leung: And that funding continues today. Under Charlie Baker and, now, Maura Healey. We’ve kept it going, but now we’ve got bigger competition, right?

Edelman: I mean, life sciences is well-established. It’s not going anywhere per se, but there’s got to be somewhere else to go for growth.

The growth isn’t going to be there. China’s a real competitor not only in AI, but in biotech. And they’ve been taking researchers, who got their education in the United States, and they’ve brought them back to China. They’ve got more patents going than the US for the first time in the medical world. We need extra areas to add to our growth.

Leung: You got a lot of reader feedback on this series.

Edelman: I sure did, yeah.

Leung: What surprised you the most about the responses?

Edelman: There was a general feeling that we’re shooting ourselves in the foot, that the politicians talk a good game about trying to [make] the business climate more amenable, but they only nibble around the edges.

And that, fairly or not, Maura Healey is taking a lot of the blame now because she’s the one sitting in the corner office at the State House. The reality is that Healey, who’s up for re-election, isn’t running on the economy. She’s running against Trump, and partly because she doesn’t have a lot to run on when it comes to the economy.

A lot of people were frustrated with Beacon Hill, but it’s more than that. They are frustrated with the cost of living. People hate inflation. That’s not something Maura Healey’s responsible for, and there’s nothing she can do about it. But they’re really fed up with the high costs.

They are, I hear it and it makes me so mad every time I do, but they say, “You know, we spent billions of dollars on housing immigrants.” [Or,] “Why didn’t we use that money for our own economy?” I don’t think that’s the right way to look at things, but that feeling is out there. And it’s not just in the MAGA world, you know? There’s an undercurrent of that kind of resentment out there.

[For the] readers, the depth of their love of Massachusetts [as] a place to live is very strong. And you hear from people who say, “Yeah, I changed my residency to Florida, and I go there for six months of the year, but I love coming back to Massachusetts in the summertime. I love going to the Cape. I love going to the Berkshires.” You know what I mean?

That was another thing that I heard was that [the] pull is still there. And people who go to school here like it, but then seem to get forced out by the costs.

Leung: What do you say to readers who just say you’re shilling for the business community?

Edelman: I’d say that’s not my job. I listen to the business community. They have some valid concerns. And they do whine a lot. It’s undeniable, and they’re also disengaged from the greater Boston community more than they should be.

They’ve got to get involved, too. They’ve got to make it clear that if business isn’t working here, then it’s not working for Massachusetts. It’s not working for [the] real people that these jobs pay the salaries [for] that allow people to live in Massachusetts, and it’s a piece of the equation that has to be addressed. I think in progressive Massachusetts, we tend to just dismiss it. It’s like, those are billionaires, millionaires, [and] they’re whining. Let them go somewhere else.

But the economy doesn’t work unless businesses can start here, grow here, and thrive here. That’s what’s getting challenged now, that ability to start businesses and grow them. The established companies — Fidelity’s not gonna be going anywhere, GE Vernova’s not gonna be going anywhere — but to get that generation of new companies coming up, that’s where we really have to work hard.

Leung: So after doing this reporting and this series, are you more pessimistic or more optimistic than when you started?

Edelman: I would say a little more optimistic.

Leung: Really?

Edelman: Yes, I am, because I heard the reaction, and I think that people out there are serious about making some changes. I’m not doom and gloom. I don’t think Massachusetts is circling the drain.

You know, Massachusetts has issues, other places have issues. We’ve just got to get to work on them, and we’ve just gotta take them more seriously.

Leung: So what would you tell a young person who’s deciding whether to stay in Massachusetts or go somewhere else and build their lives somewhere else?

Edelman: I would tell young people that it’s a great place to live. We raised a family here in Dorchester for 30 years and really loved it. But, it requires sacrifices. You have to weigh how much you want to spend on a house, how much you’re gonna be able to afford for childcare, the hassles of traffic, and the T and all that kind of stuff.

Leung: You’re not selling it.

Edelman: But, I did it. I did it, and it was worth it. I think you just [have] to look inside yourself and it’ll be different for everybody else.

If you want a big house with a big yard and not a lot of traffic, then, yeah, go somewhere else. But if you want a city full of smart people with a lot of energy and the ability to get serious things done that are good for the world, Massachusetts is one of the best places in this country to do it.

Leung: Well, Larry, thank you for coming into the studio. Larry Edelman is the author of the Globe’s incredibly popular newsletter, Trendlines. This series is terrific, “Why Massachusetts Lost Its Mojo.”

Maybe we’ll have you back talking about all the solutions that it inspired, right?

Edelman: Yeah, there’ll be more stories. You know, we’ve got more in the pipeline from our reporters. Let’s just say there’s more to come. Thanks, Shirley.

Leung: Thanks, Larry.

Victoria White of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Boston’s tree canopy won’t simply preserve itself
text:
Boston needs a private tree ordinance. There are examples across the country, from Seattle to Washington, D.C., where cities have balanced development with canopy growth.

Boston residents are not new to fighting for tree preservation. Some efforts have resulted in saving trees, such as the mature oak on Hyde Park Avenue in Jamaica Plain, whose cause was championed by its neighbors in September 2023, and the more than 100 trees along Melnea Cass Boulevard that had been slated to be cut down in 2020. Other efforts, like those over Crane Ledge Woods and Morton Street at the Edward Brooke Charter School, are pending.

Despite the heroic advocacy of everyday citizens, countless trees are being felled daily without anyone noticing.

It’s time Boston developed a robust, fair, and forward-thinking private tree ordinance, one that ensures that healthy trees remain rooted and thriving so that the city’s residents can, too.

David Meshoulam

Executive director

Tree Boston

Dorchester

The Boston Globe’s recent story about Boston’s tree canopy raises an important question: If we cannot realistically replant our urban forests at the scale we are losing them, how do we preserve and care for the trees we already have?

I believe part of the answer is in helping residents see trees as the neighbors that they are.

As a longtime Hyde Park resident and an artist working at the intersection of ecology, climate, and community, I think of our relationship with trees as reciprocal. They cool our streets, filter our air, and witness our daily lives. In return, we have a responsibility to care for them.

The City of Boston and advocacy organizations are working to protect our canopy, but stewardship cannot belong only to institutions. It needs to become part of how we relate to the places where we live.

That is where I see a role for my community public art project, Tree Care Hyde Park, which launched this month. The project invites neighbors to do just that — to notice the trees around them and imagine them as collaborators, caretakers, and companions. People may then may be more likely to value trees, advocate for them, and care for them.

Protecting Boston’s urban forest requires more than planting trees. It requires cultivating a culture surrounding them.

Jane D. Marsching

Hyde Park

The writer is a professor at Massachusetts College of Art and Design and director of the sustainability minor.

From the human perspective, tree canopies are cooling and shading systems that, properly deployed and maintained, help make our lives more pleasant and manageable during the summer heat. But ask a forest ecologist and you’ll learn that a robust canopy is far more than that.

Treetop ecosystems support hundreds of different species, some of which go their whole lives without ever touching the ground. Cutting down a big tree is not just killing one living thing — it’s disrupting an entire micro-neighborhood of lives, many of which have unsung roles in maintaining the balance of nature upon which we all depend.

In a time of rapid and traumatic climate change, trees and their inhabitants are both more important and more vulnerable to extreme weather and human destructiveness. Whether it’s an endangered rain forest or a row of trees along a city street, we owe these upright citizens, if you will, a debt of gratitude and respect.

Warren Senders

Medford

title: Boston Teacher’s Union hosts annual back to school fair, promoting lifelong learning
text:
“I used to come here and take books like everyone else because I loved reading,” she said. “So my mom and I decided to come volunteer and hand books to people. Even now, I just walk around and see what books there are and what they have available.”

Sunday’s book fair was one of the most highly attended, according to the union’s president Erik Berg. The event started in 2013, and is organized in coordination with First Book, a nonprofit that aims to deliver quality education to children in low-income communities.

“It’s a fantastic day, and it really sets the tone for getting back to school,” Berg said. “Sometimes we get jaded by the screens that are ubiquitous in our pockets, on our walls, and it’s really heartening and refreshing to remember that [books] still bring out that joy,” he said.

Truc Lai, the family engagement liaison for BPS, said that seeing her students around the room hunting for books was the highlight of the event for her.

“It’s important to be in the community because it shows that I am part of the community and reading is important to me,” she said.

Reading is the foundation of literacy, she explained. Her favorite teacher inspired Lai to get involved with education.

Governor Maura Healey also attended Sunday’s book fair, speaking to attendees at the start of the event.

“There’s nothing more important that we do than invest in kids and invest in their education,” she said to the Globe.

She explained that while speaking with students about what careers they might want to pursue in the future, many wanted to become teachers themselves.

“It means they’ve seen their teacher and they’re inspired by their teacher,” she said.

Outside of the union building, Ashley Santiago, a middle school English Language Arts teacher for Boston Public Schools, was waiting for a ride home with her new stack of books at her feet.

“Seeing the light bulb go off in kids’ heads when they finally figure something out and then [getting] to be excited about that really motivates me,” she said.

Sunday’s fair was the first Santiago had ever attended and she picked out everything from picture books to chapter books to accommodate the different reading levels of her students, she said. Santiago also picked out comic books to show her students that reading can also involve graphics and art.

“I’m also excited for the different ethnicities that are shown through the books,” she said. “I’m just excited to expose that to my kids.”

Across the parking lot, families gathered under white tents with their new reading material, kids playing in the field and dancing to the music that played over a speaker.

One tent offered face painting and glitter tattoos, while another offered hot dogs and chips which could be redeemed with the free ticket used to enter the book fair.

Nicole Ku relaxed at a table near the face-painting line while her children flipped through their new books beside her. When asked if they liked reading, the answer was an astounding yes.

“My favorite book that I got today was Bea’s Bees,” her son smiled.

title: From rats to snowflakes, young Boston area dancers vie for ‘Nutcracker’ roles
text:
For 7-year-old Ava Babbist, Saturday marked her first audition, but she tried not to let her nerves get the better of her.

“I was kind of nervous, and kind of excited,” Babbist said. “It was very hard, but I tried to memorize the positions.”

One of the most popular ballets, “The Nutcracker” can be a difficult production to put together. For José Mateo Ballet Theatre’s director of communications, Madison Sweeney, it is Mateo’s emphasis on diversity that sets his performances apart.

“Really the most unique thing is the fact that we have such a diverse cast,” Sweeney said. “Performing at the Strand Theatre and in a diverse community is really big. For most of the things in José’s Nutcracker, I feel like it’s centered around the magic and how we can create magic in each individual, whether it’s their first time seeing ‘The Nutcracker’ or their 101st time seeing ‘The Nutcracker.’”

Jodie Pemberton, a Cambridge resident and former ballet dancer , brought her daughter Aria to auditions because of Mateo’s reputation in the Cambridge community.

“We came to José Mateo because Aria has always been interested in ballet,” Pemberton said. “I come from a ballet background, and he has a really positive reputation in our city.”

Most parents felt the same. Grant Calderwood brought his 7-year-old daughter, Quitterie, out for similar reasons.

“We chose José Mateo because they have a wide variety of programming and they’re well integrated with the community in Cambridge and in Boston,” he said.

With roles ranging from snowflakes to Mother Ginger’s children, there are plenty of characters for younger dancers — however one role emerged as an unlikely favorite among those auditioning.

“I kind of want to be a rat,” Quitterie said when asked what her dream role would be. “I think a rat just is fun because it makes you laugh a lot. Like when they go out looking for the rats, and they come out and then they hide, and it’s really fun.”

With Mateo’s rendition of “The Nutcracker” sometimes featuring as many as 100 child performers alongside professional dancers, the rehearsal process can be a chaotic one.

“It’s very intense, and it’s very hard work. It takes a village to pull this all together,” Sweeney said.

However, to Sweeney, that hard work is always worth it in the end.

“It’s a huge cast with the skeleton crew, and like it’s all about creating community and working together, and I think that we should get more people coming to the show because it’s a really magical experience.”

José Mateo’s production of “The Nutcracker” will run from Dec. 5-20 at the Strand Theatre in Dorchester.

title: BC High probing alleged use of racist language by students, school says
text:
“The alleged behavior is entirely unacceptable and fundamentally contradicts our mission as a Jesuit, Catholic institution,” the school’s statement said. “Racism in any form will not be tolerated at BC High. We acknowledge the harm caused by these actions and affirm that every individual, both within and beyond our school community, deserves to be treated with dignity and respect.”

It’s not clear if any students were punished, and the statement did not identify the target of the racist speech.

“We will take appropriate disciplinary action in alignment with our school policies, and remain steadfast in upholding a safe, inclusive environment for all,” the school said.

The school also said “student privacy policies prevent us from disclosing the outcome of any disciplinary proceedings.”

In a separate email to the school community Monday, the high school’s president, Grace Cotter, said officials learned of the racist language last week.

“It is with great importance that I write to you today. On Thursday evening, we became aware of TikTok videos alleging the use of racist language by students at Boston College High School,” Cotter said.

She said she recognizes “that these allegations are painful, particularly for our students and alumni of color. To anyone who has experienced racism, I want you to know that we hear you, we take these concerns seriously, and we are committed to ensuring that BC High is a community where everyone feels respected and valued.”

The investigation is ongoing, Cotter said.

“We will not tolerate racist behavior, and we will hold our students accountable for conduct that violates our values,” she said. “My promise to you is that we will address this matter with the seriousness it deserves. We must remain committed to the work of building a school community that reflects our Jesuit mission and our responsibility to be men and women for others.”

title: UMass Boston seniors to teach public health in high schools through a partnership led by Mayor Wu
text:
Wu said Boston’s concentration of universities, hospitals, and research institutions has not, by itself, guaranteed an adequate pipeline into public health careers.

“We have the best academic and healthcare institutions in the world,” Wu said. “We conduct more medical research here than anywhere else in the world, and we’re going to fight for every dollar of NIH [National Institutes of Health] funding and to sustain that, but maintaining that edge and continuing to lead the world in not only healthcare but public health means making sure we are closing the gaps within our community and investing in the next generation of leadership.”

The announcement was held at UMass Boston and was attended by the university provost, chancellors, city council members, teachers, and students. City Councilor John FitzGerald, whose district includes parts of Dorchester, said the arrangement could also help Boston continue to retain workers trained in the city.

“About 80 percent of undergraduates stay in Boston after. That means the training that we do and the education that we’re giving are staying in our city,” he said.

The partnership comes as health departments nationwide confront persistent workforce problems. A survey of nearly 5,000 public health workers conducted in March found growing concerns about burnout and retention. The Public Health Workforce Interests and Needs Survey asked employees what’s changed since 2024, and 35 percent said their feelings of burnout had worsened, including nearly half of workers aged 35 and younger. Among that group, 31 percent said they planned to leave their organization within the next year.

One in four workers also reported that their opportunities for advancement had worsened since 2024.

Boston Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu said, “We’re at a pivotal moment for public health across the country,” pointing to unstable federal funding, difficulty recruiting and retaining workers, and challenges ranging from infectious diseases and substance use to mental health and persistent health disparities.

“Similarly, academic institutions are also facing significant challenges that threaten the pipeline of public health leaders, scientists, educators, and practitioners that our country desperately needs,” Ojikutu said. “This is the time for us to join forces.”

The UMass Boston initiative is the first workforce project to emerge from Boston SPHERE —Strengthening Public Health-Academic Partnerships in Education, Research, and Equity — a broader effort bringing together the Boston Public Health Commission with more than 30 colleges, universities, research centers, and academic medical centers that was announced last Friday.

Participants include Mass General Brigham, Boston Medical Center, Boston Children’s Hospital, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Harvard, MIT’s Broad Institute, Boston University, Northeastern, Tufts, UMass Boston, Fenway Health, the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers, and the Massachusetts Department of Public Health.

Ojikutu said the coalition has three broad goals: developing a more diverse pipeline of public health workers, getting research and new technologies into practical use more quickly, and using that work to reduce racial and other health disparities.

The need for a larger workforce is not unique to Boston. Public health agencies nationally have struggled for years with turnover and staffing shortages. One analysis cited by the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials estimated that state and local health departments would need 80,000 additional workers to provide basic public health services.

UMass Boston launched its Urban Public Health department in 2022. The program has 65 students entering their second, third, and fourth years and expects enrollment to grow to 100 with this fall’s incoming class. Students study epidemiology, environmental health, biostatistics, data science, health systems, and health communication.

Seniors applied for the city program last spring and were selected by the Public Health Commission. During the fall, they will be trained in adolescent health, health education, facilitation, community engagement, and public health practice. In the spring, they will teach high school students under commission supervision.

“Now, we’re currently in the training semester,” said Althea Laci, 23, a UMass Boston senior from Quincy who hopes to work in public health policy. “We are learning how to develop curriculum and navigate conversations that can be sensitive. It’s a lot of practice, practice, practice.”

Massachusetts requires public schools to provide health education, but districts have discretion over the curriculum. Parents can also opt their children out of lessons. The city health commission launched a Health Resource Center Program in 2010 to provide materials to teach students about sexual health, mental health, substance use, and health equity.

Trinity Stinson-Salmon, a 21-year-old senior from Brockton, said she was eager for a chance to work directly with young people while figuring out where she fits within the broad public health field.

The program gives students “a more hands-on avenue” than a traditional classroom experience, she said.

“We get to have in-person experiences, learn from professionals, but also we get to learn more about ourselves and what we can do.”

Students who do not want to teach can pursue other capstone placements in areas such as policy, health communication, and data analysis, said Patricia Janulewicz, chair of UMass Boston’s Urban Public Health Department.

title: Who gets a seat at the toilet? Writer and historian Bryant Simon has answers.
text:
Comfort Kitchen derives its name from the phrase “comfort station,” the term for municipal bathrooms built in the 20th century. Comfort stations provided broad toilet access until the 1940s, when public officials nationwide grew anxious that gay men, the unhoused, and drug users were illicitly loitering in the privacy of said spaces. Then, with the onset of the civil rights movement, some city governments decided to shutter the doors on public restrooms rather than integrate them, Simon explained.

“For Customers Only” details the construction of these municipal facilities, their policing and subsequent closure, our contemporary reliance on the private sector for restroom access in the absence of public facilities, and examines restrooms as a subject of heated social debate.

“Every protest movement of the 20th and 21st century had its moment at the bathroom door,” Simon told the Globe. “The gay rights movement, the civil rights movement, the women’s rights movement, the movement for more adequate housing, and, obviously, the trans rights movement.”

Boston’s own storied history of public bathroom inequity includes a 1973 “pee-in” at Harvard University. When Harvard began allowing women to take entrance exams for admission, administrators made one key oversight — the testing center, Lowell Lecture Hall, had no women’s restroom. As a result, female test takers were forced to rush across the street, costing them exam time, Simon explains in “For Customers Only.”

Prominent Black activist Florynce Kennedy, an early member of the National Organization for Women and founder of the Feminist Party, took to Harvard in support of the test takers, leading a protest outside Lowell Lecture Hall in which demonstrators poured jars of fake urine down the steps.

Harvard’s failure to account for its prospective female students is just one of many instances in “For Customers Only” that illustrate how the fight for restroom access is ultimately a fight for public space. Even after getting past the hurdle of finding a facility, oftentimes, restrooms widely considered to be public — those of cafes, restaurants, and storefronts — are conditionally accessible, Simon explained, citing a 2018 incident at a Philadelphia Starbucks in which two Black men asked to use the restroom, were denied access unless they made a purchase, and were arrested for trespassing.

“Maybe you present in such a way that a store bathroom is open to you,” Simon said. “But for two young Black men, that might require buying something. ... When the private sector controls [a restroom], it might appear public, but it isn’t public to everyone.”

Instances like these beg the question: What makes a restroom truly public?

Simon defines these facilities as “generally maintained by a public entity and open to anyone,” but under that framework, there might be far fewer than we think.

In 2016, The city of Cambridge opened a freestanding, 24-hour toilet kiosk in Harvard Square following the 2012 closure of the public restrooms in Christ Church Cambridge, Simon details in “For Customers Only.” The kiosk, commissioned to match the area’s high-traffic tourism, is a “Portland Loo,” a single-occupancy restroom that officials rolled out in Portland, Ore. in 2008.

There are Portland Loos in Amherst, Greenfield, and Provincetown. In Boston, the city recently released a map of more than 175 locations with access to public restrooms, drinking water, and other essential amenities, including MBTA stations, local fire departments, and coin-operated city toilet stalls.

“We all take our chances when we leave the house,” Simon said. “Ultimately, I think political leaders would benefit from being more aggressive in public bathroom building. ... [We need] progress on this front that affects people in their most intimate and bodily ways.”

Bryant Simon at Comfort Kitchen. Sept. 26, 1-3 p.m. 611 Columbia Road, Dorchester. comfortkitchenbos.com. RSVP on Eventbrite.

title: Amid Hyannis Port brouhaha, Vicki Kennedy speaks out
text:
Featuring: Ted Kennedy, Barry Finegold, Vicki Kennedy, Joe Kennedy III, Patrick Dorton, Adam Hinds, Jim Davis, Bruce Percelay, Dennis Kozlowski, Joe Hale, Jim Smith, Lori Trahan, Ryan Durkin, Enrique Colbert, and more.

Ted Kennedy may have been one of the country’s longest-serving senators, but longevity doesn’t seem to apply to those running his namesake institute.

Since launching in 2009 to honor the late senator’s legacy of bipartisanship, the Edward M. Kennedy Institute for the United States Senate has had a revolving door of leaders: nine presidents and executive directors, plus six board chairs. Forgive me if I’ve missed one, but it’s hard to keep track of all the Kennedy acolytes and interim execs for hire who’ve blown through there.

I’ve been wondering who’s in charge since news broke about a controversial party at the Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port. The institute, among its assets, owns the famous Kennedy home and has been renting it out — including to disgraced former Tyco International boss Dennis Kozlowski for his 80th birthday. That, as you can imagine, didn’t sit well with some of the Kennedys.

Turns out the institute’s last CEO — former state senator and United Nations negotiator Adam Hinds — left at the end of last year, around the same time board chair Bruce Percelay stepped down. For all of you steeped in the nonprofit world, you’re screaming: Who does that?

Hinds, who took the $300,000-a-year post in 2022, had one of the longer tenures, at just over three years. Percelay, a Boston developer and publisher of Nantucket’s N Magazine, was at the helm for about five years.

Since December, Joe Hale, the institute’s chief advancement officer, has filled in as interim CEO. He previously ran the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum.

Then in April, Joe Kennedy III, the former Newton Congressman and Ted Kennedy’s grand nephew who’s served on the board, stepped in as co-chair. He brought in Washington public affairs honcho Patrick Dorton to chair the board with him.

So what does Vicki Kennedy, Ted Kennedy’s widow and the institute’s cofounder, make of all this?

“I don’t see it as revolving, as much as evolving,” Vicki Kennedy told me on Tuesday.

Kennedy explained that the leadership changes reflect how the nonprofit has needed different skill sets at each stage — from concept, to groundbreaking, to broadening its scope.

The institute built its own museum located next to the JFK Library and Museum in Dorchester, on the water at Columbia Point. Visitors can tour a full-scale replica of the US Senate chamber, modeled after the one in DC.

Vicki Kennedy initially served on the institute’s board but gave up her seat in 2021, when she was appointed ambassador to Austria by then-President Joe Biden. She left that post in 2025 and is back in Boston helping raise money and awareness about the institute.

“We have a good leadership team to take it to the next level,” said Kennedy, who does not have a formal managerial role at the institute.

And if you’re wondering what she thought about the Kozlowski party at the Kennedy house, she didn’t want to go there. (Sorry readers, I tried.)

The board is wrapping up a national search for a new CEO and is updating its strategic plan for the next five years, according to the institute’s leadership. The nonprofit said it runs experiential civic education programs and hosted nearly 200,000 students; it plans to unveil new exhibitions and programming this fall.

Despite all the turmoil at the top, the Hinds-Percelay era ushered in a period of relative financial stability. For years, the institute had been losing millions of dollars, especially during the pandemic, when it shut down for about six months. Hinds and Percelay were able to stop the bleeding, and the institute operated in the black in 2022, 2023, and 2024, according to the latest financial filings.

Ted Kennedy was onto something when he wanted to create a place where future generations could learn the value of reaching across the aisle to get big things done. But it remains to be seen if there are enough people who still believe bipartisanship is worth fighting for in a country as deeply divided as ours.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

The numbers are in for lobbying business in the first half of 2026, and the rankings at the top haven’t changed one bit: Boston’s busiest lobbying shop, by far, remains Smith, Costello & Crawford, reporting $4.4 million in lobbying fees in the six-month period. That’s up from $3.7 million in the same time last year. Coming in numbers two and three again: Tremont Strategies ($3.4 million in the first half of 2026) and O’Neill and Partners ($2.7 million).

Smith, Costello & Crawford’s strategy has focused on three sectors that often intersect with government: healthcare, energy, and marijuana. New energy clients, per founding partner Jim Smith, include pump-storage developer Cianbro, battery-storage firm Rhynland Energy, and micro-nuclear generator seller Radiant. On the healthcare side, newcomers include staffing firm Arbor Associates and insurer Altus Dental. Cannabis hasn’t necessarily gone up in smoke, but it’s safe to say that business has mellowed out quite a bit lately.

Whoop executive Ryan Durkin’s effort to get Boston’s big tech companies to make room for promising startups is off to a strong start thanks to Wayfair. The retailer is giving 25,000 square feet at 4 Copley Place to the Massachusetts AI Coalition, which Durkin spearheads. So far, around 90 people from 16 startups have moved in. (Wayfair moves out of Copley Place next year, though a spokesperson says it will continue to support startups after the move.)

General counsel Enrique Colbert says Wayfair, a founder-led company, is proud to support Boston’s startup ecosystem and understands how important access to resources can be for young firms. Durkin posted on LinkedIn: “What we’ve been missing is more of that shared physical gravity, the density that makes a place like San Francisco feel inevitable for founders. Wayfair just did something about it.”

New Balance has a winning way of running down business with the Pentagon. The Boston-based athletic shoe company led by chairman Jim Davis just won a nearly $59 million contract to make the “0430” athletic shoe through 2029 for the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps, via the Defense Logistics Agency. (The other winner was San Antonio Shoemakers, which makes the Mission One sneaker for the military.) New Balance’s shoes will be made at its central Maine factory in Skowhegan. The company’s last military contract concluded in 2018. The new “zero-four-thirty” is named for those early morning wakeup calls that recruits experience in basic training. Better them than us.

As President Donald Trump prepares to talk AI with China’s Xi Jinping in Washington, Congresswoman Lori Trahan was at the State House in Boston today, to promote her federal bill to enact strict safeguards for artificial intelligence. She joined state Senator Barry Finegold, who has his own set of AI rules he’s trying to pass in Massachusetts.

Right now, the odds look better for Finegold’s reforms; they’re up for negotiation in a state House-Senate conference committee dealing with economic development. In D.C., meanwhile, GOP leaders in the House have rebuffed Trahan’s bill so far (at Trump’s behest, she says). That said, Trahan told reporters she’s hopeful about passing something as soon as later this year because public concern over AI has reached a tipping point in recent weeks.

When it comes to big state procurements in Massachusetts, there are two time periods: pre-Applegreen and post-Applegreen. That Irish retailer became known around here last year after its winning bid to redevelop the state’s highway service plazas went south. Global Partners went on a legal and PR campaign when MassDOT picked Applegreen’s bid over Global’s. Eventually, Applegreen backed out.

Governor Maura Healey’s administration knew awarding the service-plaza bid right away to Global could have spurred similar campaigns from other losing bidders. Instead, state officials started a new round of bids, with more guardrails in place.

Now we are post-Applegreen. The gloves are off for losing bidders in other projects who believe they were wronged. Exhibit A: a $2 billion courthouse project in Springfield. Jeb Balise and Dinesh Patel sued the administration, claiming the winning bid from a group led by Virginia real estate firm FD Stonewater benefited from political connections. They haven’t had luck with the legal appeal yet, so they’re ramping up a PR campaign. Our colleague Kelly Garrity notes that Balise has spent $275,000 to encourage voters to urge Healey to scuttle FD Stonewater’s bid. Where will it end? Not everyone can be a winner.

Which American rocker just sued Suno, claiming that the Cambridge AI company was illegally copying his voice for new songs? Send your guess to powerplay@globe.com.

This newsletter was written by Shirley Leung and Jon Chesto, edited by Beth Healy, and produced by Dana Gerber.

title: ‘I’m not your neighbor’: In Southie, a few blocks away is a world apart
text:
West Broadway marks the dividing line between the affluent, where the median family income is more than $250,000, and the underprivileged, where it’s just $60,000. It’s one of the starkest contrasts in Greater Boston, which is among the most income-segregated metropolitan areas in the country and has experienced some of the largest increases in income divergence in recent years, according to new research by the MassINC Policy Center. This polarization has increased more in Massachusetts than in any other state since 2020.

That means fewer neighborhoods with an array of income levels. The rich are clustered with the rich, the poor with the poor.

This separation can limit access to relationships and resources that spur upward mobility, the report states, perpetuating inequities across generations.

Massachusetts also has one of the highest levels of income segregation between school districts, generating a lawsuit in May. This indicates that these sharply divided levels of economic mobility will continue, said Ben Forman, director of the policy center.

“The more the economy produces inequality, the more people sort themselves out,” Forman said.

In West Broadway public housing, home to nearly 1,500 people, some residents play bingo in the West Broadway Task Force building, competing for prizes such as detergent and dish soap. Most tenants stick close to home, said Luz Leon, the task force secretary, who has lived there for more than 20 years. But now that the Family Dollar on West Broadway has closed, Goodwill is one of the only affordable places to shop among a sea of high-end stores.

Leon, 51, is grateful for donations of diapers and Christmas gifts from wealthier residents, whom local nonprofit leaders praise for their generous contributions, but she’s highly aware that they occupy an entirely different space.

“There is a line,” she said. “They can help, but we know our place.”

The seclusion that results from inequality also perpetuates it, said Steven Durlauf, director of the Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility at the University of Chicago. Where children grow up can determine what school they go to, which resources are accessible, how much crime they’re exposed to, and whom their role models are.

It also has a profound impact on how long a person lives. In 2023, the Boston Public Health Commission found a 23-year difference in life expectancy between an area in Roxbury, where the median family income is around $60,000, and one in Back Bay, where it’s more than $250,000.

“There is extremely powerful empirical evidence that neighborhoods matter,” Durlauf said. “They mold people.”

Indeed, low-income people who have contact with well-off residents are more likely to go to college and have higher earnings, recent research shows. And these cross-income interactions also help prosperous people “understand America as a whole,” Durlauf said.

But as the rich keep getting richer, they’re becoming more isolated. The increase in income segregation in Greater Boston over the past four decades has been driven mainly by the rise of high-income households, according to a 2025 Boston Indicators report.

South Boston was solidly working class when public housing was built there in the 1930s and ’40s. But when the waterfront started transforming in the early 2000s, the city allowed luxury developers to pay into an affordable housing fund rather than put those units onsite, and the “white, wealthy waterfront” was born, said Donna Brown, executive director of South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation, who has lived in the neighborhood since 1989.

The gentrification spread, as young college graduates started snapping up apartments near the beach and the T, driving up rents and pricing out working families.

“Everybody benefits from a neighborhood that is safer and nicer,” Brown said.

But it’s unclear how much that’s helped low-income residents.

Sister Margaret Lanen, 86, came to South Boston as part of the Sisters of Notre Dame and has lived in West Broadway housing since 1975. She likes to go walk by the water at Castle Island but stays away from the Seaport, where the unfairness of the economy is on full display.

“There’s so much money available to people who have money,” she said.

Soaring costs make it more challenging for people to work their way out of subsidized housing because they can’t afford to rent nearby, said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. But West Broadway public housing residents are a “force,” she noted, particularly leaders who pushed to create a community garden and build mini soccer pitches open to the neighborhood.

At Fourth Presbyterian Church on Dorchester Street, the congregation is a striking blend of low-income and affluent families. This connection builds empathy and openness, said the Rev. Burns Stanfield, who has been a pastor at the church for 35 years. But he mourns the loss of school-age children as parents increasingly leave for the suburbs.

“Nothing brings out altruism like kids,” he said. “We get better restaurants, we have better coffee, but it seems like less investment in the community as community.”

Income segregation is “extraordinarily hard” to fix without policy solutions, said Durlauf, at the University of Chicago, because parents who can afford to live anywhere want to provide the safest, most-resource-rich environment for their children.

Meier, the South Boston resident, saw this happen as his wife’s Harvard Business School friends left the city for Wellesley after they had children. Meier, who has a PhD in mechanical engineering and is currently a stay-at-home dad, and his wife, the CEO of a small energy company, have no plans to leave.

“It just seems like the American way is to segregate yourself off and set up neighborhoods that are insulated,” he said. “We want our children . . . to understand how the world actually works.”

Sharp income divides aren’t confined to cities. Some affluent suburbs — including Wellesley, Lexington, and Sudbury — contribute greatly to the Boston area’s income segregation. In one census tract in Natick, the median family income is $209,000, according to MassINC data; in an adjacent tract in Framingham, it’s just $49,000.

The high cost of living in Massachusetts, coupled with high rates of income inequity, mean that lower-income households have to grapple with prices shaped by one of the country’s most expensive markets armed with disproportionately low spending power.

“We’re all shopping at the same mall, we’re all shopping at similar grocery stores,” said Rachel Vingsness, executive director of the Natick Service Council, which assists low-income residents. “The cost for everyday living is the same regardless of where you live and what your income and financial situation is.”

Take kids’ sports, she said, where children from well-off families pay to play in club sports year-round and end up dominating school teams that used to be accessible to everyone.

“It’s just getting harder and harder,” she said. “I’m not sure people fully understand what’s happening right in their community or in the community next door to them.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: In its 60th year, Metco is a success, Boston families say — but remains frozen in time
text:
For over 60 years, more than 20,000 predominantly Black and Hispanic children have made similar long journeys to distant schools in wealthier, mostly white suburbs, where they have thrived in higher performing classrooms.

Yet despite indisputable evidence of its academic achievements, Metco remains a Civil Rights-era experiment frozen in time. Its enrollment is roughly what it was when President Jimmy Carter was in office and not a single suburb has been added to the program in nearly a half-century, including some of Boston’s immediate neighbors.

“Metco has shown us that this works, that it is worthy, that it is necessary, that it needs to be expanded,” said Karilyn Crockett, an MIT assistant professor of urban history, public policy, and planning. “There’s more to do.”

Critics such as Crockett question why, after six decades, Massachusetts still relies on a modestly sized, voluntary desegregation effort instead of a bolder, comprehensive solution. The systemic inequities that gave rise to Metco remain in Boston, where classrooms almost entirely serving students of color still lag behind their largely white suburban counterparts.

An expensive housing market reinforces those longstanding racial divisions by limiting where families can afford to live, leaving many city students without access to the same quality of public education available in the suburbs.

Since the first buses rolled out of Roxbury and Dorchester for the suburbs on Sept. 8, 1966, Metco has changed lives by offering Boston students a shot at an education in a wealthy school district.

The benefits are unmistakable. Students have better attendance, are more likely to graduate from high school, are more likely to attend college, and earn more in their careers, researchers have found.

But the sacrifice is real. Generations of Metco students have gotten up earlier, traveled farther, arrived home later, and ultimately had to work harder to obtain the same education as their suburban classmates. They’re outsiders in their own schools and have endured racism, classism, and more from what often is a cultural exchange that runs only in one direction.
