“We see where they live, but they don’t come to see where we live,” said Vanesa Morales of Dorchester, who bought a used Hyundai to drive her Black daughter on nights and weekends for school activities in Wayland. “They don’t really get to know the people in Boston.”

The voluntary state program enrolls 3,200 K-12 students, about 5 percent of the Boston public school enrollment, in 33 suburban communities. But many of Boston’s immediate neighbors don’t participate, forcing some students to travel as far as Sudbury, Marblehead, and Scituate.

Among Boston’s closest neighbors, three — Brookline, Newton, and Needham — participate in Metco. Other nearby wealthier, majority-white suburbs such as Milton, Watertown, and Winchester do not.

Some cities elsewhere do things differently. In Raleigh, N.C., and Louisville, Ky., for example, sprawling school systems encompass both the city and suburbs, broadening the access for students to classrooms beyond where they live.

But Massachusetts assigns students into school systems based largely on municipal borders, and Boston and its suburbs remains racially segregated.

Boston has some strong — and even excellent — schools but quality varies widely. More than 14,000 Boston students attend schools that rank among the state’s lowest-performing.

For most, the higher performing, and largely white, suburban schools remain out of reach unless a family has the money to move.

The stasis is so entrenched that a group of families from Boston and other local cities sued the state in May, demanding education leaders impose more racial integration in public schools. One solution offered in their complaint: expand Metco.

“School segregation deprives all students of the benefits of learning with and from each other in racially and economically diverse schools,” the families said.

Education has always been one of the most powerful engines of upward mobility. It’s why Metco students are willing to travel so far. For the trip to Reading, Daniella packs yarn with her textbooks so she can knit hats and mittens on bus rides that take an hour to get there in the morning and even longer on the way home.

The journey adds to the work, but it has been worth it for Daniella, who has excelled in Reading, according to her mother, Kemeisha Daley.

“It’s a commitment,” Daley said. “If you want it to work, it will work.”

One day last spring, Brodi Morales began his commute before 6 a.m. with a long walk from his Dorchester home to his bus stop. After one ride, he transferred to a second bus for the 15-mile drive to Wellesley High School. His body is so attuned to the long journey that he naps and can wake up just as the driver approaches the school.

“It doesn’t even feel like two hours for me,” Morales said. “I legit sleep on the bus.”

Morales stood outside a largely empty Wellesley High. It was a little after 7:10 a.m., and it took another 20 minutes before the local students began to arrive. Where the yellow bus had left Morales, a fleet of late-model Cadillacs, BMWs, and Mercedes arrived driven by Wellesley parents, a virtual auto show of luxury vehicles dropping off his classmates.

On the chilly morning of Sept. 8, 1966, when buses left Roxbury and Dorchester with 220 youngsters bound for six suburbs, the Globe featured a photo of one under the headline, “History is made in Massachusetts.”

At the time, Paula Jackson was among students from Roxbury headed to Wellesley Senior High School. Now using her married name, Paula Davis, she remembers her mother learning of Metco that summer and becoming intent on enrolling her studious 16-year-old.

Wellesley was welcoming, but breaking down barriers proved hard. Her classmates offered polite smiles but remained distant. Davis was the only Black teen in a roomful of white students.

“My classmates did not know how to relate,” Davis said, “to a person who looked like me.”

But the education in Wellesley was far more rigorous than at Brighton High, set in a building with a new gymnasium, cafeteria, and natural light pouring into classrooms from large windows.

Over time, Davis built friendships. She still has a book of newspaper clippings from back then. In one, a photo shows her smiling with her classmates out on the school lawn. She went on to study business at Aquinas Junior College and worked as a property manager in the Boston area. But she still keeps her high school diploma in like-new condition from when she was awarded it on June 7, 1968.

“It was worth it,” said Davis, now 76. “despite the struggle.”

Metco began after the Boston School Committee resisted desegregating and refused to address inequities facing Black students. Before court-ordered busing nearly tore Boston apart, Metco offered a limited, voluntary solution that sent willing students to suburban schools.

Six decades later, the program formally known as the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity is funded by the state with an annual budget of about $31 million. It is administered by the nonprofit Metco Inc., which also oversees a program that buses about 100 students from Springfield to nearby suburbs.

Boston Metco’s most notable alums include CNN anchor Audie Cornish, Boston’s first acting Black mayor, Kim Janey, and Michael Bivins and Ronnie DeVoe, members of the 1990s bands New Edition and Bel Biv DeVoe. DeVoe, who cohosted a fund-raiser to mark 60 years of “changing lives and creating opportunities,” described himself as a Metco kid from Newton North.

When the nonprofit needed a new leader last fall, Metco named Kandice Sumner, who attended schools in Weston, where she was the high school’s first Black female class president. Sumner’s mother is a Lexington Metco graduate.

“In an ideal world, Metco shouldn’t have to exist, because the things that cause it to exist no longer are a reality,” Sumner said. “This practical world needs Metco.”

Metco is often cast as a gift to Boston students of color, presenting them with access to suburban schools, said Malcolm Cawthorne, a Brookline native who serves as the town’s director of Metco. But the program was also intended to benefit children in the suburbs.

“The root of this,” Cawthorne said, “was to make our districts richer, and make our districts better.”

When suburban and urban students meet halfway, the binds can be transformative. Take the decades-long friendship between Anthony Jones, who is Black and originally from Roxbury, and Jim McCann, a white native of Sudbury.

“My life would definitely be missing something,” McCann said, “had I not met my lifelong best friend through Metco.”

Both men served as the other’s best man at their respective weddings.

The pair met while playing football at Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School, where they graduated in 2004. Their families bonded over dinners while they were in school. Jones sees McCann’s father as a mentor; McCann’s children think of Jones as Uncle AJ.

“This is beyond school friendships, this is family,” Jones said. “The most important thing that happened to me was getting into that Sudbury school.”

But the pressure of making Metco work most often falls to Boston residents whose children are enrolled in the program.

Instead of a cultural exchange, it’s often the job of Boston children and parents to build connections with host communities: planning long commutes and late nights to make time for afterschool sports, to friends hanging out, to meetings between parents and teachers.

“The Metco experience is not for the faint of heart, especially in parenting,” said Christopher Worrell, a state representative from Dorchester who graduated from Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School in 2004. His own children now attend public schools in Newton.

Beyond the commute, racism has been a stubborn part of Metco’s history. Two Boston families filed federal civil rights complaints in recent years alleging discrimination in Melrose and Marblehead. Over the decades, countless other instances of bigotry haven’t resulted in complaints to the federal government.

Abriana Morales, a 2010 graduate of Wayland High School through Metco, described daily prejudice that caused a “mental strain” for families. If a Black boy, for example, played sports, he’d likely be embraced by a suburban school. A Black boy in the chess club? Not so much, she said.

And for Black girls, the pressure is even higher, Morales said. Some get called “loud and ghetto,” she said. If they stand up for themselves, Black girls especially risk being shut down by white peers, she said.

Morales is a teacher at a charter school in Boston, and her brother, Brodi, is the Metco student at Wellesley High whose bus dropped him off last spring a few minutes before the parade of luxury cars.

Brodi’s mother is Vanesa Morales, who bought a used Hyundai when her daughter attended Wayland schools through Metco. Morales enrolled her children in the program because of the topnotch education, she said, but that comes at a cost.

In Wellesley, Brodi said, stereotypes circulate about the Boston neighborhoods where he and other Metco students live. Because of the stigma, Brodi doesn’t always volunteer that he’s enrolled through Metco, and said even some of his teachers don’t know.

Brodi is from a multi-ethnic family: his mother is Hispanic, his sister Black, and he is white.

His mother wants her son to be proud of where he is from.

“I don’t want Brodi to go into Wellesley,” Vanesa Morales said, “and then look down on Boston.”

On a late spring afternoon, Brodi recalled chatting with some Wellesley teens when the topic turned to Dorchester. They didn’t know Brodi lived there, he said, and one of them described it as a dangerous neighborhood.

Brodi didn’t say anything, but the remark stung. He told the story in front of his sister, Abriana Morales, during a recent visit, and she pressed him about that moment in Wellesley.

“That’s your opportunity,” she said, “to be like, ‘I live in Dorchester.’ ”

As they talked in the family’s Dorchester kitchen, a poster on the wall listed “12 things to always remember.” Everyone’s journey is different, read one. Another said: Judgments are not about you.

Brodi considered his sister’s point. His friends wouldn’t care he’s from Dorchester, he argued, so why bring it up?

“It shouldn’t matter,” Brodi said, “where you live.”

title: Pedro Martinez on Game 7 in 2003, no regrets on calling the Yankees his daddy, and a mission to help
text:
“Lawrence has been kind of forgotten a little bit,” said Martinez. “It has gotten kind of old in front of our eyes, but there is so much need. If there’s something I can really identify myself with, it is need. I grew up in those kind of needs. I’m just expressing the cry I had when I was a kid. I get excited every time I see a kid that has an opportunity to become someone.”

Martinez’s new program is designed to bridge resource gaps and enhance classroom learning for young students across Lawrence. His foundation, dedicated to transforming the lives of youth in the United States and the Dominican Republic, was started in 1998 when he joined the Sox after five-plus stellar seasons with the Dodgers and Expos.

“I got a very pleasant surprise when I got to Fenway as soon as I saw the drums and the people with the [Dominican] flag and the atmosphere kind of changing,” Martinez recalled. “Mayor [Thomas] Menino was kind enough to take me in his SUV to give me a tour around Boston, and right away I fell in love with the people … and the Latino community all over the place, and that’s when I landed in Lawrence, Lynn, Dorchester, and all those areas that continue to be linked to me.”

It was in those early Boston days that Martinez’s Fenway mound starts “became the curfew back home in the Dominican every time I pitched.”

A connection was made; an ongoing, lasting relationship because of the Pedro Martinez Foundation.

In 2026, Martinez and teammate/countryman David Ortiz are listed as “special assistants” in the fourth line of the the Red Sox’ official front office directory, just below chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. Martinez occasionally helps young Sox pitchers at spring training, but he was out of the loop when the decision was made to fire manager Alex Cora and six coaches just 27 games into the season.

“I was actually talking to Alex a couple of days before,” Martinez remembered. “When I found out, I wasn’t angry, I just couldn’t understand how everything snowballed to that point.”

Martinez’s beloved former teammate, catcher/captain Jason Varitek, was part of the purge. The Sox claimed Varitek was “reassigned,” but he hasn’t surfaced anywhere in the organization.

Does Martinez think the burned bridge will be repaired?

“I think it’s going to be OK with Jason,” said the three-time Cy Young Award winner. “Jason is a very professional person. He understands that business part, just like Alex Cora.”

What does Martinez think about the local demonization of Rafael Devers?

“This is a very misunderstood kid,” he said. “Devers is very shy. But he is legit. He’s a guy that doesn’t know how to express himself and has a hard time trusting anybody but his father. His father knows the actual truth … Devers is very respectful, a very lovely kid, but now it’s over and the team is on its way to success. … You have to learn to love Boston if you want to survive in Boston. Boston is 24/7 talking about their sports.”

Does Martinez want Payton Tolle or Sonny Gray starting Game 1?

“You don’t go wrong with either one,” he said. “Sonny is a true professional, a true competitor. I love, love Tolle. Just his amazing attitude. I love every single pitch he throws. I love everything about him.

“The Yankees are vulnerable, especially without [Aaron] Judge. I don’t think the Red Sox are intimidated by the Yankees. I think they can beat not only the Yankees but any team in baseball.”

The highlight of Martinez’s baseball career?

“Being part of the 25 that brought the trophy to Boston.”

Ever wish he never said, “The Yankees are my daddies”?

“No. I was being honest. That’s what you guys demand from all of us. The Yankees had my number at that point, and I expressed it. I will tell you in the most honest way, I got my ass kicked.”

Which brings us back to 2003, when Grady Little was fired (almost immediately) after failing to take Martinez out of the game when Pedro was past his pitch limit after seven innings of Game 7 of the ALCS at Yankee Stadium. Martinez had fanned Alfonso Soriano on his final pitch of the seventh, was at 100 pitches, and believed he was done for the night.

“[Red Sox pitching coach] Dave Wallace told me I was done after, so I didn’t put my jacket on,” said Martinez. “I had looked up in the sky and gave thanks to God for the seven innings I pitched. Our bullpen was lights out. All of a sudden Grady was like, ‘I don’t like [Alan] Embree against Nick Johnson in the eighth.’ He said, ‘You give me Nick Johnson and I got the rest of the bullpen for you.’ That’s the true story.”

Back on the mound, leading, 5-2, in the eighth, Martinez retired Johnson on a second-pitch popup to start the inning, then looked to the dugout. Nobody moved.

“Nothing happened,” recalled Martinez. “So I just kept going. I gave up a couple of line drives, and everything just snowballed after that. I thought I made a great pitch on [Jorge] Posada, but Posada blooped it [for a two-run double].”

All in all, it was four straight hits and a tie game before Little finally pulled Martinez after 23 disastrous eighth-inning pitches. Then Aaron Boone (now the Yankees’ manager) happened in the 11th.

Two summers ago, Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin wrote President Joe Biden a letter, imploring America’s tiring leader to end his reelection campaign. As part of his logic, Raskin compared Biden’s career to Martinez’s Game 7 performance, writing that there is “no shame in taking a well-deserved bow … when your arm is tired out.”

Days later, Biden pulled out of the race.

“I don’t know what to tell you about that,” chuckled Martinez. “Grady just told me, ‘Get one more out.’ That was Nick Johnson, right?”

Right.

All these years later, the wounds have healed and Martinez is on a greater mission, taking his message to Lawrence.

“I don’t have enough words to describe how grateful I am to have my opportunity through baseball and make a difference now,” said Martinez. “My message to these kids in Lawrence is that nothing in life is too far away if you have the will, if you have the passion.”

title: Wahlburgers to close Hingham location where chain launched 15 years ago
text:
The original Wahlburgers restaurant in Hingham is closing after nearly 15 years in business, the burger chain announced Tuesday.

The restaurant at the Hingham Shipyard will close Wednesday as its lease comes to an end, the company said in a Facebook post.

Wahlburgers said it is looking for another location in the Boston area.

“As the original Wahlburgers location, Hingham will always hold a special place in our story,” the company’s statement said. “While this location is closing, we’re actively looking for a new home in the Boston area and hope to have more to share soon.”

Wahlburgers is a fast-casual restaurant chain founded by brothers Mark, Donnie, and Paul Wahlberg, who grew up in Dorchester.

The company thanked its customers, employees, and the Hingham community for supporting the restaurant over the years.

“We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who walked through our doors, shared a meal with us and made this restaurant part of their lives,” the statement said.

Besides Hingham, the chain has locations in Boston, Plainville, and Springfield. The restaurant has also expanded to 14 other states, as well as Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, according to the company’s website.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: Business owners along Blue Hill Ave. question if the corridor’s revival is for locals — or to attract wealthy white people
text:
Putting down roots in a neighborhood Warren’s family has lived in for generations, closer to her clients’ and employees’ homes, is about more than being a property owner: It’s about investing in the Black community.

This overhaul, the latest of several attempts to improve traffic and bus travel on Blue Hill Avenue, has the potential to redefine the avenue by spurring more development and attracting new visitors to an area that has long been stigmatized as run-down and unsafe. At the same time, tension is building over who will benefit.

If construction keeps customers away, or the area becomes more expensive, small-business owners of color could be priced out of one of the few affordable commercial areas in the city. And, some local entrepreneurs fear, they could be replaced by wealthier, whiter, enterprises.

A refreshed Blue Hill Avenue would increase property values for people like Warren and her family, who still own the house in Mattapan, but many of the commercial real estate owners who stand to benefit from the multimillion-dollar makeover are far less invested in preserving the authenticity and local flavor of the neighborhood. Some of those owners inherited paid-off properties and live elsewhere, while others scooped up neglected space for a song and are just waiting to cash in. A number of storefronts sit empty.

Even though the latest plan for Blue Hill Avenue would increase parking in some places, disruption during a years-long construction process could keep customers away, putting a strain on the businesses there. And even though the upgrade would likely raise property values, it could also increase taxes for building owners, which could cause them to jack up the rent or sell to the highest bidder. This could have a domino effect: closing down some of the more than 1,100 establishments — some barely hanging on, almost all locally owned — located in the Census tracts along the 3-mile stretch slated for redevelopment, and opening the door to more profitable corporate chains.

Blue Hill Avenue is the most important corridor in the city for Black Bostonians, said Fatima Ali-Salaam, president of the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Council. With the right support and investment, she said, it could become the “Black Wall Street” of Boston.

The city stands to gain from increased tax revenues generated along the refurbished corridor, but it doesn’t conduct economic impact studies before projects. So it’s unclear: Will it generate jobs, or destroy them? Will it increase sales? Drive up prices? Depending on what happens, the diversity and strong local connections that are essential to Blue Hill Avenue’s character could be at risk.

Sami Salameh, who opened Salameh Jewelry in Mattapan Square 30 years ago with his father, a Palestinian tailor, once kept a gold chain and bracelet on layaway for 13 years for a customer who went to prison — and let him purchase it for close to the original price when he got out. A few years ago, Danielle Johnson moved her digital radio station Spark FM from Hyde Park to a second-floor space overlooking Blue Hill Avenue: “Location, location, location,” she said. It makes sense, she said, for a Black media company that broadcasts the community’s concerns about the redevelopment’s proposed center-running bus lane to be based in the middle of the Black community.

But with the rent rising steadily, Johnson is already looking for a new home, and trying to save up to buy a space, preferably before the redevelopment drives prices even higher. “We’re going to be displaced in droves,” she said.

In one of the last affordable areas of the city, largely populated by immigrants and people of color, the overarching worry is not about the bus lane. It’s about being pushed out.

***

From her station on the front porch, Warren’s grandmother, Indianola Walker, watched the neighborhood evolve from white to Black after she and her husband moved into their triple decker off Blue Hill Avenue in 1967.

A federally insured loan program in the late ‘60s aimed at Black home buyers transformed the area, and in just a few years’ time, a majority-Jewish area became a majority-Black one. But by 1974, more than half the people who took advantage of these loans, many of which didn’t require down payments or thorough home inspections, had lost their houses. And the formerly thriving Blue Hill Avenue has never been the same.

Today, parts of the corridor remain run-down, with boarded-up shops and long-vacant storefronts dotting the street alongside numerous corner markets, tire shops, and churches.

For Warren, the ability to bring her educational nonprofit and Sadiddy Lifestyle Beauty Studio to her childhood neighborhood goes beyond her entrepreneurial dreams. The three-building complex on formerly vacant city-owned land, called Blume on the Ave, is being built by an affordable housing developer who also grew up in the area. Condos are being sold at below-market rates, and ground-floor commercial spaces sold at cost, to promote local ownership.

“When we talk about ‘buying back the block’ and we talk about ensuring generational wealth in our communities, that’s what this project is,” said Warren, who has held fund-raisers and applied for loans at three banks to secure funding for her retail space.

Getting loans can be challenging for entrepreneurs of color if they don’t have the right connections or access to capital, said Dariela Villon-Maga, the Blume on the Ave developer, who grew up in Roxbury and lives in Mattapan. Black- and Latino-owned small businesses with low credit risk are less than half as likely to be fully approved for financing as white-owned ones, according to a 2021 survey by the Federal Reserve Banks.

Villon-Maga is one of a number of local professionals, many from immigrant families, who have started investing in their communities before corporate developers start to circle.

Ernst Guerrier, the child of a Haitian cab driver and housekeeper in Mattapan, recently bought his second commercial property in Mattapan Square and hopes to put a restaurant and eight condos on the ground floor. Guerrier’s first job was in the first building he bought, at a fish market still in operation, and he has plans to add 110 units of housing above it. That property also has the square’s only sit-down restaurant, Marabou Cafe, which was just approved for a liquor license.

Guerrier, a 57-year-old real estate lawyer, said his tenants’ leases all include the right to make the first offer if he decides to sell.

“It’s a quiet storm,” he said of local efforts to improve the area. “Within 10 years, I guarantee it, you won’t even recognize Mattapan Square.”

But costs for property owners stand to increase, as building values — and taxes — rise. And that could be an issue for lower-income landlords with run-down buildings in need of repair. Raising the rent or selling the building could force local businesses out — and invite corporate chains in.

Raising prices isn’t a good option either. Of the more than 45,000 residents living in the Census tracts along the avenue, 65 percent are Black and 23 percent are Latino; almost half were born in another country. And nearly 40 percent of households make less than $40,000 a year.

“This is a very economically vulnerable part of the city,” said James Jennings, a professor emeritus at Tufts University who has studied the redevelopment area.

A number of mom-and-pop enterprises along the avenue conduct some business in cash and don’t report it, according to members of the business community. This eases their tax burden but also keeps their total profits off the books, which can make it harder to get loans, and also means they might not qualify for grants like the ones offered during the pandemic. Some of these businesses don’t have lawyers or insurance; some don’t even have leases.

As with houses, commercial buildings in Black communities are often undervalued. Commercial real estate in majority-Black ZIP codes is valued 7 percent lower than comparable properties in areas with fewer Black residents, according to Brookings Institution research. This means building owners are getting less rental income than they could elsewhere and leaves these neighborhoods vulnerable to exploitation by investors who buy properties and use the depreciation as a tax break, opening them up to neglect.

In Roxbury and Dorchester, retail properties are worth $2.8 million each, on average — 43 percent less than in Allston/Brighton and 10 percent less than in the South End, according to the commercial real estate analytics platform CoStar.

The city has awarded grants to more than a dozen businesses on the corridor in recent years, said Mayor Michelle Wu, and a fund is in the works to help mitigate revenue lost during construction. The city, state, and MBTA are “ready to do what’s needed to ensure that our small businesses will be protected,” she said.

“Blue Hill Ave. is a key economic corridor for the city,” she said. “There are so many storefronts and important community hubs along the roadway.”

But promises to refurbish it have been made, and broken, for decades. Many locals feel the revitalization project isn’t for them — it’s for the wealthy white people on their way.

The redevelopment is a “form of trauma,” said Derick Foster-Toney, whose family has run the historic roller skating rink Chez-Vous for more than 50 years and bought the building in the mid-’90s.

The community has been so marginalized, Foster said, it’s hard to believe anyone has its best interests in mind.

“When you’re operating in survival mode for so long,” he said, “who do you really trust to save you?”

***

One of the biggest property owners on Blue Hill Avenue is the Stamatos family, which owns dozens of residential and commercial buildings around Boston and recently purchased the former Kay’s Oasis function hall — just around the corner from the home where Warren’s 94-year-old grandmother lives.

Some of their properties are tidy and well-kept, but others are dilapidated, with chipped paint, crumbling bricks and trash-strewn lots. The first four of 14 buildings on the city’s “problem properties” list are Stamatos-owned — for repeated calls to the police about noise, late-night parties, and poor conditions.

In 2009, on the tail end of the financial crisis, they had purchased more foreclosed housing units than any other buyer in Boston, according to news reports. They have tried to impose huge rent hikes at a newly purchased apartment building in Mattapan, been hit with violations for serving alcohol to underage customers in Roxbury, and been sued by a man who was shot in one of their buildings in Mattapan Square.

A number of Stamatos properties have been cited for code violations involving mice and roach infestations, water leaks, faulty smoke detectors, and unsecured fire escapes. They also owe more than $700,000 in property taxes and fines.

One neighborhood advocate referred to the family as “extractionists” — and despite their neglect and disregard for tenants, they stand to see their investments pay off handsomely as Blue Hill Avenue improves.

Family members and Stamatos Property Management in Jamaica Plain did not respond to requests for comment.

The city can levy fines, withhold permits, and put problematic properties in receivership, but has little oversight over private real estate transactions.

Small business owners have fewer rights than residential tenants do, said Boston College law professor Carlos Teuscher. Commercial building owners know tenants are unlikely to leave once their businesses are established, which gives landlords little incentive to maintain the property. And they can raise the rent as much as they want when a lease is up. Many noncorporate landlords don’t even bother with leases, Teuscher said, leaving tenants unprotected.

“Commercial tenants are assumed to be sophisticated business entities, so there’s very few legal protections,” Teuscher said. “Generally speaking, if it’s not in your lease, tough luck.”

Teuscher surveyed Somerville business owners before the Green Line extension to Union Square in 2022 and found that many landlords had stopped making repairs or offering leases, making it easier to sell or find tenants willing to pay more.

A number of protections can be put in place to help Blue Hill Avenue businesses survive, and thrive, beyond the redevelopment.

The city could institute formal agreements with developers requiring that ground-floor retail space be occupied by local businesses, a share of commercial space be sold at affordable rates, and a percentage of contracts and construction jobs go toward area residents, including apprenticeships that will build new skills, said Jennings, the Tufts urban planning professor. The city can also commit to contracting goods and services from local vendors.

Different types of businesses also have to be accounted for, he said, including the roughly 50 stores along the corridor that accept SNAP payments from low-income residents.

These plans need to be drafted with community input, committed to on paper, and measured and monitored along the way to ensure their success, Jennings said.

“The city has a lot of power, direct and indirect, to say, this is the kind of vision we have for this community, based on community input and community residents, and this is what we need to do,” he said.

Supporting ground-floor retail will be a priority during the zoning process, Wu said, and the city is looking for resources to continue its program to help residents buy commercial space. Community feedback has been part of the process all along, according to the city, which is working with the MBTA to understand businesses’ needs during construction and beyond.

This type of support will go a long way toward winning over the business community, said Denise O’Marde, who owns the smoothie shop Cafe JuiceUp. O’Marde, who bought the building as it was being foreclosed on in 2007, worries that, without assistance, revenue could plummet during construction and she’d be forced to lay off employees, leading to higher unemployment taxes.

Now that there’s a fund dedicated to helping small businesses during the redevelopment, O’Marde said, she supports the redevelopment.

Without help, she said: “We could definitely go under.”

Ursula Vaughn, co-owner of Lawson’s Hair Salon, has already lived through the construction of the Columbus Avenue center bus lane in front of her shop in Egleston Square about five years ago — a process that took away parking and dropped traffic to one lane each way. Now she’s gearing up for a similar disruption at her shop in Mattapan Square, part of a chain started by her father and his brothers in the 1960s.

More than anything, though, Vaughn wants to preserve the cultural and social diversity of Blue Hill Avenue. A number of local business owners said they don’t want to see the corridor turn into the Seaport; they want to maintain its soul, in other words.

A politician who lives in the area told Vaughn: “Mattapan will be a destination.” But attracting visitors shouldn’t be the selling point, she pushed back.

“It’s not a destination,” Vaughn said. “It’s people’s homes and people’s businesses.”

So many Black and brown residents are already leaving the city for less expensive suburbs, she noted. This project, in the heart of Black Boston, could force even more out.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: I spent two weeks waving at strangers
text:
“What’s up?” he asked.

“Oh, nothing, I just …”

I could already feel my cheeks flushing. “Nice place for a walk,” I lamely offered.

“Yeah …” The man put his headphones back on and offered a quick nod as he passed. I looked over my shoulder just in time to see his pace quicken, and I waved again halfheartedly at his retreating back.

Maybe you’ve seen it occasionally at a traffic light when a driver is letting you make a left turn or on a trail in the Middlesex Fells as you step aside to let a runner pass. But in rural corners of New England like the Hilltowns of Western Massachusetts or midcoast Maine, acknowledging passersby with a wave is a cornerstone of daily life.

I first observed the wordless ritual on the island of Vinalhaven. On the island, which is home to one of the Pine Tree State’s largest lobstering fleets, it’s customary for passing drivers to wave at each other. Often this is done by lifting a few fingers from the steering wheel. (Offering a fuller wave is a great way to out yourself as a tourist.) But according to Alison Thibault, an artist who owns a local jewelry store called WindHorse Arts, there’s “a whole language” to the island wave that varies from person to person.

“Some people have such recognizable waves that you know who they are even if they’re driving a car you’ve never seen them in before,” Thibault says. “My own wave changed a few years ago. I now wave with a peace sign, and each time I do it, I’m silently offering peace to that person and to the world around us.”

It’s hard to resist something like this little gesture of goodwill. So back in July, after a family visit to Vinalhaven, during which all of us honed our wave techniques, I decided to conduct an experiment here in Boston. Obviously, I couldn’t wave at every single person I passed while out and about, but I could spend two weeks more systematically offering a wave to strangers at traffic lights and crosswalks and on bike paths.

I started at a bit of a disadvantage. I’m a 6-foot-4 man, and I knew that might make waving unwelcome to certain people — women in particular. So I decided to take some cues from Hannah Truby, a writer and photographer based in Reno who recently wrote an essay for the outdoor magazine Mountain Gazette about how she threads the needle between being gregarious and practicing caution in local woods or on the water. “Gender and perceived safety matter,” Truby says. “Some of my girlfriends don’t greet or wave. Subconsciously, if I’m running alone on a secluded trail, I usually don’t wave to male runners. But if I receive it, I’m down to give it back.” One key element here is that passing trail runners are both in motion. As Truby sees it, being engaged in the same exertive activity can inspire a kind of momentary solidarity. “When you’re having a bad day, and maybe you don’t want to be running, it can feel good to be acknowledged by someone else who’s also toughing it out through a run,” Truby says.

Taking this as a cue, I started by waving on Boston bike trails like the Minuteman Bikeway and the Somerville Community Path. Marinating in sweat, pedaling along under the blazing sun, I raised a few fingers from the handlebar as cyclists approached from the opposite direction, and at least half of them offered something in return: a quick wave, a nod, or a ring of their bell.

Heartened by my success, I decided to try the wave in other venues: on sidewalks and footpaths. I focused on areas with modest crowds, and some pedestrians were more receptive to waving than others. On the Boston Harborwalk near Dorchester Bay, I got smiles and nods. I struck out with passing pedestrians on Commonwealth Avenue in Allston. The best environment turned out to be the path around Jamaica Pond. I was surprised. In my experience, the more crowded a pathway, the less likely people are to acknowledge or greet each other when they pass. Nonetheless, most of the people I waved at chose to pass the greeting back to me. One older gentleman even beat me to it!

Some of us have been acknowledging strangers now and again for some time, offering salutations like “Good morning” and “Hi there” to oncoming walkers as we amble through commercial hubs or public parks. But even for me, happiest when out on foot, regularly choosing to offer a gesture of acknowledgment required a mental gear shift. Matt Jablonski, a climate resilience expert who helped Vinalhaven plan for rising sea levels, described the wave as part of building and maintaining community ties.

During his time on Vinalhaven, which included attending packed town meetings and community gatherings, Jablonski came to appreciate “the cohesion fostered by small, kind gestures, such as waving to anyone and everyone on the island.” After two weeks of waving to the people of Greater Boston, I’m planning to keep the experiment going. For how long, I’m not sure. But at a moment when the world feels like it’s coming apart, I owe it to myself — and the people I pass by — to try.

title: Nurses, advocates rally to keep Carney Hospital, Nashoba Valley Medical Center open
text:
Nurses and advocates from across the state called on Gov. Maura Healey to take executive action to keep Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center open amid bankruptcy proceedings for Steward Health Care.

The two facilities are on track to close by Saturday after Steward Health Care declared bankruptcy earlier this year, a situation that was in part fueled by the company’s decision to sell the land under their hospitals to investors and private equity groups.

Elaine Graves, a nurse at Carney, said she and her colleagues have given their “blood, sweat, and tears” to the community in Dorchester, particularly during Steward’s ownership of the hospital.

Even before the bankruptcy, Graves said, nurses had been “mourning the state of greed” of Steward and the need for action by state officials to protect the hospital and its community.

“Now, we are both angered and saddened by the state’s decision to abandon our hospital and our community and here we are once again to support our community, to plead with the governor and the state to make a different decision and to save our hospital,” she said at a rally on the steps of the State House Wednesday morning.

Healey announced tentative agreements earlier this month to hand over control of four hospitals run by Steward to new owners, including by attempting to seize control of St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton through eminent domain.

But the governor said Carney and Nashoba Valley Medical Center would remain on their paths to closure because no one stepped forward to buy the facilities.

“That’s why those hospitals are set to close because of Steward, because what Steward did in running them to the ground. So it’s an incredibly upsetting reality,” the first-term Democrat previously said.

Advocates have since criticized the governor and her top lieutenants for not attempting to use the eminent domain process to take control of the two facilities in Dorchester and Ayer in the same way state officials are trying to seize St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center.

At the rally, Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune said she is looking for “reasonable solutions” to keep Carney Hospital open and warned that the city’s EMS Department has “no idea what it is going to do now.”

“We are asking for the bare minimum, and we know that it’s possible,” she said. “We didn’t work hard enough, to be frank, to get qualified bidders, and we let Steward do whatever they want.”

A spokesperson for Boston EMS said without Carney Hospital, patients will be transported to other medical facilities in the city, some of which are already experiencing capacity issues.

“This is likely to result in increased transport times for patients traveling farther to the nearest hospital as well as prolonged turnaround times for ambulances. With some of the most highly skilled EMTs and Paramedics, we remain committed to clinical excellence and are prepared to adjust, adding resources, to continue to provide compassionate care and timely delivery of lifesaving care,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Boston EMS transported more than 91,000 patients in 2023 with just over 6,300 taken to Carney, according to the agency. Almost three-quarters of the patients transported to the hospital were between the ages of 23 and 65.

The agency plans to add an additional ambulance that will be staffed 24/7 to increase coverage in Dorchester.

Steward Health Care notified state officials at the end of July that 1,243 employees were set to be laid off when the two hospitals close at the end of August. Members of the state’s Congressional delegation and others have demanded the company pay severance to those workers.

Michelle Travers, a nurse at Nashoba Valley Medical Center, said the bankruptcy proceedings over the past several months have left employees facing an “exhausting and distressing ordeal awaiting decisions that will significantly affect our employees.”

Hospitals like Nashoba Valley Medical Center, she said, are often the first and only point of access to essential medical services for patients in the area.

“The potential closure of Nashoba will have devastating consequences for the health of our community. The closure of Nashoba would force residents in surrounding towns to travel significant distances for emergency care,” she said.

title: Steward Health Care finalizes deals to sell four hospitals in Massachusetts to new owners
text:
Steward Health Care finalized deals to sell four hospitals in Massachusetts to new owners, a move that keeps those facilities from closing after months of concerns that communities could lose access to vital points of care.

The Dallas-based company said Thursday it had entered into “definitive agreements” to sell St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River and Morton Hospital in Tanton to Providence-based Lifespan Health System and both campuses of Holy Family Hospital in Methuen and Haverhill to Lawrence General Hospital.

The company, which has been working through bankruptcy over the past year, said it is also “finalizing an agreement” to sell both Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton and St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton to Boston Medical Center.

Steward Health Care Chief Restructuring Officer John Castellano said the company is “thrilled” to have identified buyers for the four facilities as Steward continues to move through bankruptcy proceedings.

“In Lifespan, Lawrence General Hospital and Boston Medical Center, we have found partners with established track records of treating communities in the northeast United States. Through these transactions, the people of the Commonwealth will continue to receive critically needed care while Steward continues to focus on its ongoing Chapter 11 process,” Castellano said in a statement.

Gov. Maura Healey broadcast the possibility of transferring some hospitals to new operators earlier this month when she announced tentative deals on the four facilities.

“This agreement accomplishes our goal of maintaining and protecting access to care and jobs in Southeastern Massachusetts and the Merrimack Valley, while removing Steward Health Care from Massachusetts once and for all,” Healey said in a statement announcing the deals.

“I welcome Lifespan, its leadership and team to Southeastern Massachusetts and appreciate Lawrence General Hospital for stepping up to preserve care in the Merrimack Valley. All of us will work hard to bring this over the finish line,” she continued.

Healthcare workers are “incredibly relieved” after months of uncertainty that four Steward Health Care hospitals in Massachusetts are in new hands, said Tim Foley, executive vice president of 1199SEIU, a union representing healthcare workers.

“Now, with Steward’s greed and mismanagement in the rear-view mirror at these sites, we can turn our full attention to the essential work of rebuilding our hospitals and caring for our patients,” Foley said in a statement. “We urge Steward to quickly finalize the sale of St. Elizabeth’s and Good Samaritan, so that healthcare workers —and the patients who rely on our care — can stop living in fear, and focus on the future.”

Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer are still scheduled to close by Saturday.

Healey’s administration is attempting to seize St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center through eminent domain, which has drawn resistance from the asset management firm that controls the facility.

“We continue to work as quickly as possible to complete the agreement for another qualified operator to take over Good Samaritan, move forward on our plans to take control of St. Elizabeth’s through eminent domain, and support the communities impacted by the upcoming closures of Nashoba Valley and Carney Hospitals,” Healey said in a statement.

title: Carney Hospital, Nashoba Valley Medical Center set to close Saturday after bankruptcy
text:
It’s likely the end of the line for Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center.

The two medical facilities are set to close Saturday after officials did not find another company to purchase them, a scenario that is set to leave multiple communities without immediate access to health care.

Steward Health Care announced deals to sell six of its hospitals to new owners but Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center were not among them. State officials have previously said no “qualified bidders” stepped forward for the two facilities.

The mood outside Carney Hospital in Dorchester Friday was somber. Employees hugged each other as boxes and supplies were loaded into a moving truck. One person took home a picture of their grandmother, who had worked at the hospital.

Advocates rallied this week to urge Gov. Maura Healey’s administration to take executive action to save the two facilities. The governor has said the state “will ensure that residents continue to have access to high-quality medical care and that all staff” are connected to new jobs.

“We’ve heard the concerns raised by the communities and staff impacted by Steward’s plans to close Carney Hospital and Nashoba Valley Medical Center. We share their frustration – Massachusetts communities should never have been put in this position,” she said in a statement.

Boston Herald photographer Matt Stone contributed reporting.

title: Boston stands to gain 225 new liquor licenses after House, Senate reach deal
text:
Massachusetts House and Senate leadership have reached an agreement on a compromise bill that would add 225 new liquor licenses to the city of Boston over the next three years, many of which would be targeted to minority neighborhoods.

Senate President Pro Tempore William N. Brownsberger, D-Belmont, and House Majority Leader Michael J. Moran, D-Brighton, announced the compromise legislation advanced out of a House and Senate conference committee on Tuesday.

“On behalf of our fellow conferees, we are proud to announce that we have reached an agreement on compromise legislation to expand the number of alcohol licenses in the city of Boston, dramatically expanding equity for restaurant owners in neighborhoods across the city, and increasing economic opportunity in communities of color that have been left out for too long,” Brownsberger and Moran said in a joint statement.

If approved by both branches — which are set to meet next on Thursday — and signed into law by Gov. Maura Healey, the bill would deliver Boston its first major expansion of alcohol-serving establishments since 2014, when 70 liquor licenses were added via a city home rule petition.

A Healey spokesperson said “the governor looks forward to reviewing the bill.”

The legislation had stalled at the end of formal lawmaking about a month ago, after it was approved in different versions by the House and Senate, which favored 205 and 264 liquor licenses, respectively. The city had initially been seeking 250 new non-transferable licenses, through a home petition that was sent to Beacon Hill.

The compromise legislation, which the two lawmakers expect will be sent to the governor’s desk by the end of the week, would add 225 new liquor licenses in Boston over the next three years.

It would target 195 non-transferable licenses to 13 ZIP codes in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, Charlestown, East Boston, and the South End, according to the office of state Sen. Liz Miranda, who sponsored the initial Senate bill and represents parts of Roxbury and Dorchester.

Per conference committee leadership, the licenses would be distributed as five per year, per ZIP code, for three years, in those neighborhoods. Of the five, three would be for all-alcohol sales and two would be for sales of beer and wine.

“This bill is about providing us with gathering spaces in our own communities, but more so, it is about making strides to close the racial wealth gap that has created stark disparities across the city of Boston, particularly in the neighborhoods of Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park,” Miranda said in a statement.

That “lack of opportunity,” Miranda said, “has stripped some of our neighborhoods from having successful restaurants and nightlife, a core tenet of thriving cities. Blue Hill Avenue was once a cultural mecca in our city with successful black-owned restaurants and nightlife, and I believe we can be that again.”

Today, liquor licenses are capped at 1,400 in Boston, per state law, according to Miranda’s office, which said the cost of a license on the so-called secondary market can average $600,000, thereby “excluding neighborhood-based startups and entrepreneurs unaffiliated with chains and conglomerates.”

Miranda’s office said the “legislation will expand economic development in our most underserved neighborhoods who’ve seen a pattern of removal of their liquor licenses to downtown and the Seaport.”

“Of the 1,400-plus liquor licenses in the city of Boston, only 2% were held by Black-owned businesses in a city that is nearly 25% Black and over 50% of color,” her office added. “The secondary market, without needed reform, of sit-down restaurant and bar liquor licenses in the city of Boston has perpetuated the growing racial wealth gap.”

The bill would also tether three new all-alcohol licenses to Oak Square in Brighton, and 15 community licenses for sales of all alcoholic beverages to nonprofits, small theaters and outdoor spaces, according to the statement from Brownsberger and Moran.

Twelve of the 225 new licenses would be unrestricted, or transferable between different neighborhoods, the two lawmakers said.

Mayor Michelle Wu thanked “House and Senate leadership and members, especially members of the Boston delegation, for their partnership to advance this important legislation.”

“Each of these licenses represents new life and economic prosperity for an entrepreneur, a business, a neighborhood, and families throughout our city,” the mayor said in a statement. “We look forward to these 225 opportunities to address disparities in our city and strengthen economic opportunity in our neighborhoods.”

State Sen. Nick Collins, whose district includes South Boston and parts of Dorchester, the South End and Roxbury, previously said greater access to liquor licenses could add roughly 30% additional revenue to a restaurant’s bottom line, while citing Senate conversations with owners, and would increase the meals tax in Boston.

“This is going to bring great economic opportunity and equitable economic development to businesses in our city that deserve it,” Collins said during the July 29 Senate session where that chamber’s initial version of the bill was approved.

The legislation was borne out of a home rule petition introduced by Boston City Councilor Brian Worrell, passed by the Council in April 2023, and signed by Mayor Wu, who joined Worrell and co-sponsor, Ruthzee Louijeune, now the Council president, in lobbying for the legislation on Beacon Hill last October.

Its future appeared uncertain, however, after House and Senate leadership were unable to reach a compromise by the end of formal lawmaking. The House and Senate approved different versions of the bill, in late May and two days before the end of formal sessions, respectively.

title: Quincy Animal Shelter to host adoption event, highlight ‘very sweet’ 10-year-old pup Phil after surgery
text:
Quincy Animal Shelter will host a fund-raiser and adoption in partnership with a newly renovated pizza and gelato shop on Wednesday, the businesses announced.

The adoption event will start at 11:30 a.m. at the newly renovated Boardwalk Pizza and Donato’s Gelato. It will celebrate the businesses opening and “feature several adoptable dogs while shining a spotlight on the shelter’s urgent needs and the work it does to save animals.”

One dog the shelter is highlighting is named Phil, a 10-year-old mutt the shelter rescued last month.

“On Aug. 3, Phil was found in a Quincy Park by good Samaritan,” said Quincy Animal Shelter President Sandra Sines. “He’s a small dog. He weighs about 18, 20 pounds, and he’s a mixed breed, maybe a Shih Tzu or poodle-type dog, white and tan. But when they brought him in, his belly was hanging practically hitting the ground, and there was some kind of growth. Something wasn’t good going on.”

Phil had a “very serious hernia” that had gone untreated for an extended time, Sines said, and required a $4,000 emergency surgery. He went through dental surgery on Friday, she added and will need a follow-up for his hernia.

The shelter reached out to the community but no one came forward for the little dog.

“He’s been through a lot, and he’s still a happy guy,” said Sines. “He’s very sweet.”

Community members are invited to come out to the event and bring their own dogs, the release said. The event will feature a blessing of the dogs by a pastor from St. Gregory’s Parish in Dorchester, and all dogs will receive a “Pup Cup” crafted for their enjoyment, along with complimentary pizza and gelato for the humans.

“Members of the public looking to adopt a new family member are urged to come meet some adorable dogs who are looking for loving homes,” the organizations said.

title: Steward sales in limbo as bankruptcy judges weighs all the options
text:
A U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge has signed off on Steward Health Care selling its six Massachusetts hospitals, saying his decision is the “right answer under the law” and an “easy call.”

Judge Christopher Lopez approved the sale on Wednesday but decided to keep the conditions of the closings in the works so he could have more time to figure out how $17 million in proceeds will be divvied up.

“Are there business reasons? Boy, there are plenty of them to do so,” Lopez said of the justification to approve the sale. “We’ve got multiple declarations showing that the debtors just don’t have the funding, the cash, to continue to fund operations here. There are real people in these hospitals right now.”

The judge added: “There’s no greater business justification than the one that’s been presented here. I heard no one who showed up today say they’re going to put more money and better terms on the table than what’s here.”

Lopez’s approval means three healthcare companies will take over Steward’s hospitals.

St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River and Morton Hospital in Taunton will be sold to Rhode Island-based Lifespan for $175 million, while Lawrence General Hospital will receive Holy Family Hospital facilities in Methuen and Haverhill for $28 million.

The final part of the sale includes Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton and St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton going to Boston Medical Center for as much as $140 million. BMC’s offer is still in the works.

Steward closed its other two Massachusetts facilities, Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, last Saturday.

The approval is being looked at as a “bright new day for healthcare workers and our patients,” said Tim Foley, executive vice president of 199SEIU United Healthcare Workers East.

“With the approved sale of six Steward hospitals today, Massachusetts can finally start to turn the page on Steward’s greed and mismanagement,” Foley said in a statement. “With Steward finally on its way out of Massachusetts, the critical work of transitioning the hospitals to their new owners can begin.”

David Cohen, one of Steward’s lawyers from the firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges, reminded Lopez that the goal is to close the sales no later than Sept. 30, which the judge said he plans to issue the ruling on the conditions well before then.

“I just need time, and I will get there,” Lopez said. “Everybody has been working incredibly hard … I don’t want to start playing around with an order where I haven’t fully appreciated it.”

Lopez approved the sale after hearing arguments Wednesday morning in the Bankruptcy Court Southern District of Texas around an objection that key lenders to the bankrupt Dallas-based healthcare company filed to the proposed plan.

Wednesday’s hearing got into the intricacies of an objection filed by the “first in, last out” or FILO lenders that have pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into Steward as the company headed for bankruptcy.

Steward is trying to sell its “operations, equipment, fixtures, furniture, and operations for zero monetary consideration,” lawyers representing some of the company’s lenders argued in a filing.

“Rather than deliver fair — or any — value to the Debtors, every penny of the sales proceeds will be allocated to the real property for the benefit of the purported landlord’s secured creditor,” the lenders’ lawyers told the court.

The lenders, their lawyers write, “cannot possibly consent to the proposed sales of the Massachusetts Hospitals in their current form, and they do not.”

State House News contributed to this report.

title: BPS has no-show buses, delays as Boston students return to school amid talk of transportation, safety and teacher’s contract
text:
As the majority of BPS students returned to classes Thursday, familiar and new issues came to the forefront for many — from getting students on the bus to renewed talk of keeping students safe following the shooting in Georgia.

BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper and Mayor Michelle Wu started the sunny school day at the Lee K-8 School in Dorchester, greeting students as they hopped off buses and out of cars to return to classes.

With fully-staffed buses and a new bus-tracking app for parents and staff launched, the outlook for BPS transportation this school year was heralded optimistically — but some still reported familiar troubles getting to school.

“This morning, I joined Boston Public Schools teachers and staff at the McKinley South End Academy and the Blackstone School to welcome students for their first day of school,” City Councilor Ed Flynn said Thursday. … “While students were excited and looking forward to the start of school, I spoke with some parents about bus delays and having to drop off their children at school as buses did not pick them up.”

BPS did not report on-time performance data for buses by Thursday evening.

“We know every minute of learning matters,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Wednesday. “And when the buses are late, or when the T is late, it ends up having an impact in many ways, and so that is a top priority to get students to where they need to go on time and safely and reliably.”

Wu said the improvements in bus performance over the last years aren’t an “accident or coincidence,” noting changes to driver’s contracts, driver and bus monitor hiring pushes, and new technology. BPS ended last year on a 90% on-time bus performance, shy of the state-mandated 95% goal.

As of Wednesday night, a spokesperson said, 8,247 BPS parents and guardians had logged into the new Zum app, which was implemented this year to allow families to view student’s bus assignment, track buses and receive alerts. About 22,000 students in BPS take the bus to school, which includes pre-kindergarten and kindergarten students who will not return to school until Monday.

Flynn said one parent “mentioned they drove their child from Hyde Park to a South End School because their bus did not arrive” and another South Boston parent tracked her Murphy School student’s bus on Zum for 45 minutes “only for the app to become unavailable and the bus to never arrive.”

“As we navigate the first week of school, BPS senior leadership and BPS Transportation need to be in better communication with our parents to ensure that our students are picked up on time,” Flynn said.

Following the tragic shooting in which a 14-year-old killed four at Apalachee High School in Georgia on Wednesday, school safety was again a topic as Boston students returned.

Skipper on GBH said these shootings are “too common” nationally and her “thoughts and prayers, as of all BPS’s, are with the families and the victims and all that went through the tragedy yesterday.”

“My hope is that nationally, we start to really take a deeper look at the policies that lead to some of these killings,” Skipper said. “Here in Boston, we’ve worked very hard. We have a new emergency management service department that works with each of our schools, and they submit safety plans. And so we’re feeling really prepared.”

The superintendent also cited the district’s trauma and mental health trained safety specialists and efforts to engage and develop relationships with students. Community members have cited concerns with multiple incidents in which guns were found on BPS campuses in the last school year.

The Boston Teachers Union also faces an expired contract as school returns.

“We know our educators are really concerned about the rising cost of living and deserve to have adjustments so they can support their families, and they’re also concerned about wanting to make sure they’re best serving the young people,” Wu said Wednesday. “So we have to fit all of that within a budget that has a lot of moving pieces for other services.”

Wu said of teachers’ contracts, the city has a history of “having long gaps, and we are determined not to make that happen this year.”

title: Steward Health Care CEO de la Torre could face contempt charge for ignoring subpoena
text:
A day after an attorney wrote that Steward Health Care’s CEO won’t be at a congressional hearing next week despite being subpoenaed, lawmakers said they’re working on a contempt citation against the embattled leader.

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey told reporters Thursday that he and Sen. Bernie Sanders, D-VT, are putting together a bipartisan plan to vote on a contempt citation against Ralph de la Torre, who they say is ultimately responsible for Steward’s failure.

Markey and Sanders, boisterous critics of da la Torre, lead the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, which voted in July to launch a Congressional investigation into what led Steward to file for bankruptcy protections this past May.

That vote also included subpoenaing on-the-record testimony from de la Torre.

But on Wednesday, de la Torre’s attorney Alexander J. Merton wrote a letter to Sanders, highlighting how the CEO is prohibited from speaking on his company’s behalf regarding any “bankruptcy-related issues,” per a federal court order.

An independent subcommittee of Steward’s board of managers established last December has been delegated to speak on the ongoing issues instead of de la Torre, Merton wrote.

The hearing will be held next Thursday no matter what, Markey said. An empty chair will be visible that would have been for de la Torre, continuing a pattern that started in April when de la Torre didn’t offer voluntary testimony at a senate committee field hearing in Boston.

“We will have witnesses that come from the affected communities who will sit in their chairs to testify,” Markey said. “This time not in the Massachusetts State House but in the Capitol of the United States so his story could be told across our country.”

The HELP Committee could vote on a criminal contempt citation against de la Torre which could lead to a trial and jail time or a civil charge that would result in fines until he appears. Both would need Senate approval to go through.

This has been a big week amid the Steward crisis that has rattled Massachusetts’ healthcare system the entire year.

A federal bankruptcy court judge on Wednesday approved the Dallas-based healthcare company’s plan to sell its six Bay State hospitals – St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River, Morton Hospital in Taunton, Holy Family Hospital facilities in Methuen and Haverhill, Good Samaritan Medical Center in Brockton and St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton.

Steward closed its other two Massachusetts facilities, Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, last Saturday.

“Unfortunately, while Dr. de la Torre has continued to fight for Steward hospitals and the patients and communities they serve,” Merton wrote in his letter to Sanders, “members of this Committee continue to cast aspersions on Dr. de la Torre and appear determined to turn the hearing into a pseudo-criminal proceeding in which they use the time, not to gather facts, but to convict Dr. de la Torre in the eyes of public opinion.”

U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren took exception to that comment, especially the “pseudo-criminal proceeding” dubbing.

Speaking to reporters alongside Markey and other leaders, Warren referenced a report earlier this week from the Globe Spotlight Team that found several instances in which de la Torre allegedly dipped into Steward’s bank accounts for his gain.

Some expenditures include the CEO securing a multimillion-dollar apartment and traveling on corporate jets to “far-flung vacation destinations,” the Globe reported.

“It is entirely possible that Mr. de la Torre’s looting of Steward may have involved significant criminal activity, but that is not an excuse for ignoring a subpoena,” Warren said. “Congress has questions to ask, and if Mr. de la Torre believes the answers will put him at risk for going to jail, he can take the Fifth Amendment right out in public for everyone to see.”

Ellen MacInnis, a registered nurse at St. Elizabeth’s and a board member of the Massachusetts Nurses Association, urged the lawmakers to make good on their vows to hold de la Torre accountable.

“While he sailed on his yachts, flew in his jets, vacationed around the world,” MacInnis said, “those of us in the trenches of his depleted and embattled hospitals were forced to care for patients in understaffed units with broken and missing equipment, missing supplies.”

“Nurses brought in their own food to feed diabetic patients at night when the kitchen was closed and we had no options,” she added. “An innocent young mother died because the piece of equipment that could have saved her life had been repossessed by an unpaid vendor.”

title: BPS data show two-thirds of Boston school buses late on first day, city councilor presses for answers: ‘Unacceptable’
text:
A Boston city councilor is pressing for answers from BPS leaders on the many transportation problems that plagued the first week of school, which kicked off last Thursday with just a third of district buses showing up on time to get kids to class.

Councilor Ed Flynn filed a hearing order for the Wednesday Council meeting, that references complaints he says were lodged by “many parents” about “school bus delays and in some instances, no shows for students who were waiting to be picked up,” during the first week of classes at Boston Public Schools.

Flynn wrote in the order that “parents waited with their children for as long as 30 to 45 minutes for school buses, and while some students were eventually picked up, others had to make alternative arrangements to drop off their children when their buses did not come.”

“There should be reliability and predictability in BPS transportation,” Flynn wrote, describing such wait times for students, parents and caregivers as “unacceptable.”

Data released Monday by the Boston Public Schools shed more light on the poor transportation performance seen during the first week of school. Ahead of the school year, the mayor and superintendent had made assurances that a new bus tracker technology app and efforts to solve prior bus driver shortages, via contract changes and hiring pushes, would help to address the district’s long-standing transportation woes.

On Thursday, Sept. 5, 34% of BPS buses were on time for morning drop-off at school, 62% had arrived by the 15-minute mark after the bell rang, and 80% had arrived by the time school had been in session for 30 minutes. The data doesn’t extend past the half hour mark in the information that was provided by BPS.

By comparison, 61% of buses were on time during the first day of school last year, according to Flynn’s hearing order, which points out that the state mandate is to have 95% of buses arrive on time.

In a statement, Superintendent of Schools Mary Skipper attributed the poor on-time performance on the first day of classes to the district working out the kinks of a new bus tracker app, Zum, that rolled out this year, and bus drivers becoming familiar with new school routes. She said the delays were “largely expected.”

“We appreciate our families’ patience as we work through these issues and we understand that many BPS families experienced frustrating transportation delays on the first day of school,” Skipper said in a statement. “We are deeply committed to improving our families’ experiences and our on-time performance.”

“These delays that happen in the first days of school were largely expected due to drivers and bus monitors navigating new routes and greeting new faces for the first time, and the implementation of the new Zum technology that the majority of our bus drivers, families, and school-based staff were using in real-world conditions for the first time,” Skipper added.

The superintendent described the day-over-day improvement seen on Friday, the second day of classes, when two-thirds of buses, or 67%, were on time in the morning, as “significant,” saying that number was comparable to what was seen on the first day of school last year.

The data show on-time performance did improve on Friday, but it also revealed that it worsened again on Monday, to kick off the second week of school, when just 57% of buses were on time to get kids to class in the morning.

Mayor Michelle Wu and Skipper last month announced a new three-year contract that BPS awarded to Zum, a technology platform that has since been implemented districtwide as an app with the aim of providing Boston families with “improved real-time bus tracking and enhanced communication and transparency about their child’s bus,” according to the mayor’s office.

BPS ended last school year with 90% on-time bus performance, shy of the state mandate.

Flynn wrote in his hearing order that while the new Zum app provides real-time information and better predictably, the district should have considered coordinating a “dry run” with drivers, parents and students, so drivers could have familiarized themselves with the routes and issues could have been resolved “ahead of time.”

His order cites instances where the app became unavailable after a parent had been using it to track a school bus for 45 minutes, and had to bring their child to school. On the way back, the same parent’s child was on a school bus for two hours from Dorchester to South Boston before ultimately having to provide the driver with directions to his house, he wrote.

“This is about respect and equal access for all Boston families,” Flynn said in a Monday statement to the Herald.

BPS spokesman Max Baker said, however, that the day-over-day improvement from Thursday to Friday “was encouraging and in line with our experience piloting this new technology during our summer programming.”

The district anticipates continued improvement in on-time performance, as its staff and families become more familiar with using Zum, Baker said. He added that performance improved between days two and three compared to last year, with a 4% and 7% change, respectively.

“Large-scale change always comes with growing pains,” Skipper said, “and we are incredibly grateful to all our bus drivers, operations and school-based staff, and families who are working to help us build an improved transportation system to provide students with safe, reliable, and on-time transportation on a daily basis.”
