title: Boston luxury home sales lead councilors to probe whether City Hall is giving the rich a tax break
text:
Two record-setting home sales in Boston’s most affluent neighborhoods have the Boston City Council looking to probe city assessment practices that may be under-assessing the value of luxury homes and giving a tax break to wealthy owners.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper said he was compelled to put forward a hearing order “to review discrepancies between market value and tax assessed value for residential properties” in city assessing practices after seeing reports about a recent $21 million sale of a Back Bay home that was assessed by the city at $12.5 million.

“Property taxes are one of the most important ways the city funds essential services, and the fairness of that system depends on assessments accurately reflecting market conditions,” Culpepper said last Wednesday at a City Council meeting. “However, recent sales suggested some properties, especially high value homes, are being assessed far below the actual sale price.

“At the same time, some lower-priced homes appear to be assessed at or even above their sale price, raising concerns about whether the current system is applying valuation practices consistently across different segments of the housing market,” Culpepper added. “Ensuring that property assessments are accurate and equitable is essential to maintaining public confidence in our tax system and making sure that the responsibility of funding city services is shared fairly across all homeowners.”

The sale of 59 Commonwealth Ave., an 11,500 square-foot Back Bay home, was recorded on Nov. 24, per the Suffolk Registry of Deeds, and set a record on the luxury market that stood until last month’s $22 million sale of a Beacon Hill home.

The 9,412 square-foot Beacon Hill home at 46 Chestnut St. sold on Feb. 17 for far beyond the city’s assessed value of $5.26 million. The same home had sold for $8.9 million on Sept. 1, 2023, when it was assessed around $3.8 million, city assessing records show.

At a time when the average single-family homeowner was hit this year with a 13% tax hike, Culpepper said the hearing he requested will focus, in part, on reviewing city practices that appear to be under-assessing luxury homes and overassessing homes in less affluent neighborhoods.

“An analysis of residential sales indicates that luxury homes in Boston are assigned a tax assessed value averaging roughly 68% of their sale price, suggesting that some high-value properties may be valued significantly below their actual market value for tax purposes,” Culpepper’s hearing order states.

His order cites unspecified data examining the top 20 luxury property transactions in the City of Boston that show reported under-assessments totaling roughly $35.43 million in 2024 and $43.65 million in 2025, in terms of the city’s assessed value for those luxury homes and the price they sold for on the real estate market.

By contrast, Culpepper cited the sale of a single-family home in Roslindale that sold for roughly $430,000, but was assessed a higher value by the city, of $489,000, or “about 114% of its sale price.”

Assessed value determines how much a homeowner pays in property taxes, meaning that the higher a home’s value, the higher the property taxes.

Such discrepancies are “raising concerns regarding the accuracy and consistency of high-value property assessments and the potential implications for equitable property tax administration in the City of Boston,” Culpepper’s order states.

When asked by the Herald whether he thought the city was intentionally giving a tax break to certain affluent property owners, Culpepper said, “That’s why we’re going to have a hearing to find out exactly how they go about assessing homeowners.”

“I have concerns about whether the current system is applying valuation practices consistently across different segments of the housing market,” Culpepper told the Herald.

Culpepper, who represents District 7, which includes low-income neighborhoods like Roxbury and Dorchester, said he hears constant concerns from his constituents about not being able to afford property taxes.

“So we want to look and see whether they’re being over-taxed because they’re over-assessed, and we won’t know until we really look closer at this and get some data,” Culpepper said.

He said he supported Mayor Michelle Wu’s stalled legislation that would have allowed the city to increase commercial tax rates to lower taxes for homeowners. He called on the state Senate, which has repeatedly killed the bill, to take a vote on it, when asked whether the city should move on to an alternative tax relief option.

A vote was taken by the Senate on the mayor’s bill in January, and it was overwhelmingly defeated. The Senate voted, 33-5, to defeat an amendment filed by state Sen. Michael Rush that closely mirrored the language in Wu’s legislation.

Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, two Boston senators who led the push to kill Wu’s tax bill in late 2024, put forward alternative tax relief measures that were approved by the state Senate, but not the House of Representatives, which passed the mayor’s legislation three times.

Councilor Erin Murphy, who has been pushing for the mayor to move to a “Plan B” for tax relief, said she signed on to co-sponsor Culpepper’s order because the Wu administration failed to provide “good reason” for why certain neighborhoods were seeing assessing discrepancies during a similar Council hearing held last year.

“It didn’t seem equitable,” Murphy said, adding of the abatement process, “The other fear that many residents have is if you file for them to come and check, it could inadvertently negatively impact you in the other way. So sometimes people are afraid for us to check to make sure that they did it right.”

The city was sued in December by a watchdog group that alleges the city has been inflating the assessed value and taxes of commercial properties that file abatements, a practice the group has slammed as retaliatory and unlawful.

Mayor Wu’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Culpepper’s order, which was also co-sponsored by Brian Worrell, and referred to the Council’s Ways and Means Committee for a hearing. All 13 councilors signed on to the order.

title: MBTA: Bus service to increase to higher frequency than pre-pandemic levels
text:
Boston bus service is set to bounce back to an even higher frequency than pre-pandemic levels this spring, the MBTA announced Monday, with subway service to rise as well.

“With bus service now exceeding pre-pandemic levels and more frequent subway trains, riders will see shorter wait times and more dependable trips across the system,” Gov. Maura Healey said. “This is why my administration and the Legislature have prioritized historic investments in the T. We have more work to do, but these improvements show real progress toward building a transportation system that people can count on.”

The T will see service increases across 37 bus routes in and two routes will be upgraded to run every 15 minutes, transit officials said. The agency stated the new updates, in line with the Better Bus Project initiative, starting this spring will bring service frequency over winter 2020 levels.

The T has seen ridership jump since pandemic era lows, reporting its best ridership numbers since 2020 last November. Across the bus system, the agency has piloted several fare-free routes — including of the 23, 28, and 29 routes — which have led to reported increases in ridership.

MBTA General Manager Phil Eng said the T priority is to “increase reliability and deliver more transportation options for our riders.”

The Route 9 and Silver Line 2 buses will become “Frequent Bus Routes,” running every 15 minutes or better on all days, the T stated. Routes including 16, 24, 42, 96, 101, 220 and 455 will see frequency increases.

The MBTA also gave updates on subway service, noting that scheduled weekday Orange Line trips will increase by 8% to “the highest level seen in recent recorded history” as the last pair of CRRC Orange Line cars have been installed.

The Red Line will see increased frequency during weekdays “due to continued track and procedure improvements,” the MBTA said, though service will be impacted by ongoing work in the evening.

“Starting around 8 PM each evening, riders should budget an additional 10 – 15 minutes of travel time if traveling between JFK/UMass and Ashmont and Braintree due to work at Columbia Junction,” the MBTA stated.

The Red Line work is expected to be complete at the end of April.

“With more bus service than before the pandemic and increased subway frequency, we are continuing to make the MBTA a system that people can rely on and want to use,” Eng said.

title: Public speaks out against proposed National Grid rate hikes
text:
LOWELL — More than a dozen people addressed the state Department of Public Utilities during a recent public hearing on a petition by Boston Gas Company, doing business as National Grid, for a $342 million increase that will raise the total delivery service component of a customer’s gas bill.

It’s the company’s first gas rate filing since 2020. The company provides electricity distribution networks, high-voltage electricity transmission networks and gas distribution networks in New England.

While the majority of the speakers at the March 18 hearing asked the DPU to deny the rate request, John Buonopane, the subdistrict director for the United Steelworkers Union 12012, called the rate increase “necessary” to keep the gas utility’s systems “safe and reliable.”

“We support National Grid’s proposal because we care about the safety and reliability of this system. We see what happens firsthand when a gas system is not maintained,” he said, referring to the Merrimack Valley gas explosions of 2018.

In the mid-afternoon of Sept. 13, 2018, 131 fires, three explosions and numerous gas leaks struck the Lawrence, Andover and North Andover communities. One person was killed, about 25 people were injured, dozens of homes were destroyed, gas service to about 8,000 meters was cut off and hundreds of residents were evacuated.

An investigation found that then-Columbia Gas of Massachusetts violated the Natural Gas Pipeline Safety Act, which led to the disaster.

“Our people are the minders of that system,” Buonopane said. “These systems are absolutely necessary.”

National Grid’s filing kicked off an 11-month review process that will culminate with the DPU issuing an order in late November.

If the DPU approves the petition, starting Dec. 1, bills for almost 1 million customers in 144 communities will jump 10% during peak season, and about 20% in the peak off-season.

For residential heating customers in the former Colonial Gas area, which covers Cape Cod and several communities in the Merrimack Valley like Lowell, the average customer bill will go up by about $25 per month, which is a 10.9% increase in the first year.

The monthly bill impacts for commercial and industrial customers range from a decrease of almost 38% to an increase of almost 38%.

The majority of the speakers urged the DPU to either deny or reduce the rate increase, including Mary Wambui, a member of Lowell’s Sustainability Council.

She argued that the rate increase will cause “direct and measurable harm in Lowell.”

“People are limiting their energy use so that they are able to afford groceries,” Wambui said. “Energy poverty is a sign of failure of regulation … The (DPU) should not create another windfall profit for shareholders while we are struggling to pay our bills.”

The price of natural gas delivered to Massachusetts residential customers has risen steadily in the past three decades, according to statistics and analysis by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

The United Kingdom-based company reported record revenues in 2025. In particular, National Grid New England, led by President Lisa Wieland, posted a 23% increase in total underlying operating profit for the six months that ended Sept. 30.

The company has already received significant regulatory approvals from DPU. In June, National Grid New England received approval for around $600 million investment under the Electric Sector Modernization Plan in Massachusetts that supports capital investment in networks and supporting technology, associated operating costs and non-wires alternatives for the next five years.

A company report released in November said National Grid New England’s “Underlying net revenue is expected to be around $400 million higher, driven primarily by rate increases and higher tracker revenue.”

The proposed rate increase concerned Anne Marie Bolduc, of Dracut, who called National Grid a “regulatory monopoly.”

“A rate increase is a privilege in exchange for safe, reliable and professional service,” she said. “National Grid’s recent performance process has not met this standard.”

Bolduc was referencing a billing failure during the winter of 2024-2025, when the company did not issue timely gas bills to approximately 30,000 customers. She called on the DPU to deny the increase.

Lowell resident Sarah Lapp, a member of 350MA of Greater Lowell, a climate justice movement, asked the DPU to consider ways in which National Grid is not investing in infrastructure that could decrease the cost of gas to its customers.

“National Grid walked away from the geothermal pilot proposal they had in the city of Lowell that not only would have potentially provided cheap energy to our residents in an environmental justice and poor community, but also would have set the stage to employ good union jobs for this kind of infrastructure,” Rapp said.

According to previous Sun reporting, the National Grid pilot project was meant to bring geothermal energy to homes in the Acre neighborhood, but was canceled in February 2025, with the energy company citing higher-than-expected costs.

The project was being done in partnership with the city of Lowell and UMass Lowell as one of up to four pilot programs that were approved for Massachusetts. National Grid had hoped to complete at least two projects, in Lowell and Dorchester, but now Dorchester is the only one remaining.

Rapp also asked the DPU to deny the utility’s rate increase.

The DPU will conduct in-person public hearings to receive comments on National Grid’s petition in the following communities through April:

• Thursday, March 26: Dennis-Yarmouth Intermediate Middle School, 286 Station Ave., South Yarmouth.

• Tuesday, March 31: Haverhill High School Auditorium, 137 Monument St., Haverhill.

• Monday, April 6: Breed Middle School Auditorium, 90 O’Callaghan Way, Lynn.

• Thursday, April 9: Acton Town Hall Auditorium, 472 Main St., Acton.

• Wednesday, April 15: Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities, 1 South Station, Third Floor, Boston.

title: U.S. Attorney announces $1M SNAP, Medicaid fraud bust in Massachusetts
text:
Another major public benefits fraud ring has been uncovered in Massachusetts, as U.S. Attorney Leah Foley announced a $1 million scheme busted by the feds involving nine Dominican nationals who used stolen identities to enroll in public assistance programs.

All nine defendants face decades in prison if convicted. It is not clear when the defendants will appear in federal court.

“Nine individuals have been charged in a coordinated federal crackdown on benefit fraud schemes that exploited stolen identities to steal hundreds of thousands of dollars in taxpayer-funded programs – including Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), MassHealth and Social Security benefits. Nearly $9 million in benefit fraud has been uncovered since December 2025,” Foley’s office wrote in a Thursday release.

The feds have charged nine Dominican nationals living in Massachusetts and New Hampshire as part of the U.S. Attorney’s ongoing effort to investigate and prosecute benefits fraud.

Foley’s office says the defendants used stolen identities — typically belonging to U.S. citizens from Puerto Rico — to obtain government-issued IDs. They say this included credentials from the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) and U.S. passports to apply for and receive SNAP, Medicaid and Social Security benefits. The office says that some defendants allegedly stole identities for several years at a time — including one defendant who apparently lived under a stolen identity for over 20 years.

Incredibly, some defendants were arrested multiple times and even convicted under the same false identities, feds say.

“According to the charging documents, the alleged schemes resulted in approximately $943,197 in total losses to public assistance programs – including approximately $149,775 in SNAP benefits, approximately $776,715 in MassHealth benefits and approximately $16,707 in Social Security benefits,” Foley’s office said.

Defendants

The nine individuals arrested include one U.S. Citizen, one Lawful Permanent Resident, and seven illegal immigrants who live in various locations across Massachusetts and New Hampshire. Two of the defendants still can’t be identified by law enforcement. They all face several federal charges related to identity theft and fraud.

— Juan Felipe Chalas, 58, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Salem, N.H., was charged with making a false statement in a passport application, aggravated identity theft and unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits.

— Efrain Rivera, 54, a United States citizen from Puerto Rico, living in New Bedford, Mass., was charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits, misuse of a Social Security number and aggravated identity theft.

— Danis Piron Lara, 51, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Dorchester, Mass. was charged with aggravated identity theft, unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits and making false statements relating to a health care program.

— Erpawi Roque Collado, 53, a Lawful Permanent Resident living in Boston, Mass. who was born in the Dominican Republic, was charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits.

— John Doe aka Wilkin Emilio Pimental Pereyra, 44, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Boston, Mass., was charged with aggravated identity theft, theft of government benefits and unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits.

— John Doe, an individual whose true identity is unknown, who was living in Hyde Park, Mass., was charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits, misuse of a Social Security number and aggravated identity theft.

— Mercedes Soto Capellan, 53, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Lawrence, Mass., was charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits.

— Oscar Gonzalez Melo, 59, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Boston, Mass., was charged with unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits, making false statements related to health care benefits, making false statements related to Social Security benefits and aggravated identity theft.

— Cruz Augusta Pena Arias, 58, a Dominican national unlawfully residing in Salem, Mass., was charged with making a false statement in an application for a United States passport, aggravated identity theft and unlawfully obtaining SNAP benefits.

Following a pattern

The announcement by Foley’s office comes amid a series of SNAP and public benefits fraud busts across the state.

Just this week, one of the defendants in another $1 million SNAP fraud scheme run out of a Leominster restaurant, pleaded guilty in federal court. In December, Foley’s office busted two Haitian nationals in a $7 million SNAP fraud scheme that ran out of a tiny store operating as a front for the criminal operation in Mattapan.

The federal busts come as state Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s office has uncovered tens of millions of dollars in SNAP and Medicaid fraud – including millions of dollars lost to fraud in just the first quarter of FY26 alone, according to a recent auditor’s report.

In February, the Herald reported on a Department of Transitional Assistance (DTA) whistleblower’s claims of “rampant” fraud within the agency.

title: Man killed by Boston Police in carjacking confrontation has history of resisting arrest
text:
The carjacking suspect shot and killed by a Boston police officer earlier this month has a history of resisting arrest — a charge dropped under the policies of previous District Attorney Rachael Rollins.

Stephenson King, 39, of Dorchester, was shot and killed by a Boston police officer a little before 10 p.m. on March 11 in Roxbury.

Police say he did not comply with their demands and gunned his vehicle at officers as he attempted to flee, putting officers at risk and necessitating them to shoot him. The officers were placed on administrative leave as the shooting was investigated by the Suffolk District Attorney’s office.

The next week, prosecutors filed manslaughter charges against Boston Police Officer Nicholas O’Malley for King’s death. O’Malley, 33, pleaded not guilty in Roxbury District Court, where his arraignment was attended by some 50 fellow officers and the head of the police union.

Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association President Larry Calderone told the media outside the courthouse that, to his knowledge, it had been decades since a Boston Police officer was charged for an on-duty death, and that “We shouldn’t be standing here.”

Prosecutor Ian Polumbaum said in court that O’Malley’s interaction with King “didn’t warrant deadly force” as body camera footage showed he was attempting only to flee the scene and showed no indication he was gunning the vehicle at officers. Shooting a fleeing suspect is against Boston Police policy and against the law, he said.

Body camera footage has not been released for public view by request of both the prosecution and the defense — and despite the Boston City Council’s repeated attempts to have it released. For now, the story is told only in competing narratives.

Criminal history

What is public is King’s criminal history, which includes a 2019 case for a similar incident involving officers approaching his vehicle and him not complying with their stated commands. In this incident, he physically resisted his arrest, according to the police report.

On Oct. 21, 2019, a Massachusetts State Police trooper spotted a 2004 Hyundai Elantra registered to King, who at the time had three warrants for his arrest: one for possession with intent to distribute Class D and B drugs, along with firearms charges; another for assault and battery, destruction of property and violation of a protection from abuse order; and one more for threat to commit a crime.

The trooper, who was in the Beachmont area of Revere, called a Revere Police Department detective as he began his pursuit from an unmarked vehicle, according to the police report. That detective and another Revere officer joined in the pursuit in their own vehicles and the three attempted to pull King over, but he didn’t pull over immediately.

The trooper positioned his vehicle in front, blocking King’s forward movement and the Revere officers pulled in behind him, according to the report. King allegedly backed his vehicle at slow speed into the detective vehicle’s bumper. The police told King to stop his vehicle and get out, but King did not comply, the report states, so they moved in to physically extract him.

“King who was still smoking a cigarette was refusing to exit the vehicle and was holding onto the steering (wheel) with the other hand,” the report states. “King who is 6’ tall and weighing more than 200 lbs used his body size to prevent the officers from getting him out of the vehicle.”

The Revere detective pulled at King from the driver’s side, ripping King’s jersey shirt in the process, as the trooper pushed at him from the passenger side, the report states. King was extracted but “still struggling” with the police until they got him to the ground and he gave up, stating “that he was done fighting,” the report states.

Light touch

The incident came at the end of 2019 and was in the early stages of court hearings when the COVID-19 pandemic started changing everything.

Rescheduling orders due to the “State of Emergency surrounding the Covid-19 virus” began in the case in March 2020 and continued until Sept. 15, 2020, when prosecutors dropped the case.

Prosecutor John Blazo, working under the orders of then-DA Rachael Rollins, submitted a “nolle prosequi” — a formal disposition meaning the charges were dropped.

Instead, prosecutors entered into an agreement that King apologize to the arresting officer and complete community service — though even that was negotiable in the era of COVID.

“The defendant wrote and submitted a letter of apology to the officer, but was unable to complete the community service hours due to the COVID-19 pandemic,” the nol. pros. notice, dated Sept. 11, 2020, states. “Specifically, the defendant cares for his 80-year-old grandmother, who due to her age and health, is particularly vulnerable to the virus.

“In lieu of the community service, the defendant has provided a letter documenting the type of care and assistance he provides for his grandmother,” the notice concludes. “Accordingly, the Commonwealth is satisfied that the defendant has complied with the aforementioned conditions and, therefore, continued prosecution of this case would not serve the interests of justice.”

The Rollins tenure

Rollins’ tenure as DA from January 2019 to January 2022 was marked by her controversial “no prosecute” list, which featured 15 crime types ranging from shoplifting and trespassing to drug possession and resisting arrest — like King’s case — that her office would not prosecute.

title: Police Blotter: Shoplifting suspects arrested in Prudential Mall, teen found with large-capacity firearm
text:
A man and woman were arrested after allegedly stealing over $1,700 in merchandise from shops on Newbury Street and in the Prudential Mall, according to Boston Police.

At about 6:40 p.m. Friday, police states they received a report of shoplifters in the Alo store in the Prudential building. The two suspects were reportedly seen “concealing multiple items into a bag and exited the store,” BPD said.

The pair left the store as responding officers were involved with another shoplifting incident, police said.

Later the same day, police received another report of the suspects allegedly stealing from the Alo store on Newbury Street, BPD stated. The male suspect, later identified as Floyd Summerville, 55, of Bronx, New York, exited the store. The female suspect, identified as Tiphaine Jones, 45, remained inside.

Summerville was reportedly stopped on 279 Dartmouth Street and put into handcuffs, at which time officers “recovered stolen merchandise,” police said.

Officers also found a key fob and vehicle parked on Dartmouth Street, recovering more allegedly stolen merchandise inside, Boston Police said. The total merchandise added up to $1,726, according to BPD.

Jones was stopped as she exited the store and arrested, during which she allegedly provided officers with multiple names, police stated. Her identity was determined during the booking process.

Ghost gun seized

title: Pols & Politics: Massachusetts Sen. Liz Miranda’s free tickets raise eyebrows
text:
State Sen. Liz Miranda’s disclosure on social media that she had “dozens” of tickets to a Boston Legacy FC game raised some eyebrows about whether she was gifted the bundle and violated the $50 cap for gifts to state politicians.

“Dear Community — I have dozens of tickets to Boston Legacy v San Diego Wave. Our female soccer team. Friday, April 3 at 7 p.m. Gillette Stadium,” Miranda posted to her Facebook page last Wednesday, inviting people to email her for tickets.

Tickets for Boston Legacy FC home games range from $27 to $244, based on season ticket packages that include 15 home games. Single-match tickets appear to start at a higher price on Ticketmaster, the resale site linked to by the team website.

Politicians in Massachusetts are prohibited from accepting gifts valued at $50 or more given to influence their official actions or because of their official position.

Miranda represents Roxbury, and parts of other neighborhoods like Dorchester and Jamaica Plain that would be impacted by the City of Boston’s $325 million public-private plan to rebuild White Stadium for the Legacy, a new National Women’s Soccer League team playing its inaugural season this year.

Some of Miranda’s constituents are still fighting the city’s stadium plan, including its cost to taxpayers, which grew again in February to $135 million.

A community lawsuit that seeks to stop the project is set to be taken up by the Supreme Judicial Court on Wednesday.

If the court rules in favor of the plaintiffs’ claim that the plan would unconstitutionally privatize public parkland, the city and soccer team would be required to seek two-thirds approval from the state legislature — including Sen. Miranda — to complete the professional stadium rehabilitation project.

A spokesperson for Miranda said Friday that the senator was not given free tickets by the team.

“The senator is not accepting free tickets,” Miranda’s spokesperson said in a statement to the Herald. “Boston Legacy FC is providing tickets directly to constituent community groups, and our office is simply helping share that information so community members are aware of the opportunity.”

— Gayla Cawley

School teacher launches campaign to unseat Auchincloss in primary

A school teacher from Bellingham is launching a Democratic campaign to unseat Congressman Jake Auchincloss (MA-04) in September primary election, running on a platform of lowering costs, investing in public education, and strengthening democratic institutions.

“People are working harder than ever and still falling behind. At the same time, trust in government keeps eroding because too many decisions are shaped by donors and special interests instead of the people those decisions affect,” said Chris Boyd, 31, in a statement announcing his campaign. “That gap between what people are living through and what their government is doing is why I’m running.”

Boyd’s campaign says he is running a grassroots effort centered on three priorities: “lowering the cost of living, defending and reforming America’s democratic institutions, and investing in the next generation.” Specifically, Boyd says he seeks to strengthen collective bargaining rights, reform campaign finance laws, uncap the size of the House of Representatives, increase federal investment in public schools, and bring back New Deal-era programs.

Boyd is also calling for term limits for members of Congress and greater government accountability, also emphasizing what he says is the need for stronger protections for civil liberties.

Boyd has taught in Massachusetts public schools for nearly a decade, primarily in Title I districts.

Deaton calls for suspension of federal and state gas tax

Republican U.S. Senate candidate John Deaton is calling for a six-month suspension of both the state and federal gas taxes as ongoing military action in Iran has caused a recent jump in gas prices across Massachusetts and the rest of the country.

“With gas prices climbing toward four dollars per gallon and higher in many parts of Massachusetts, alongside an overall cost of living that is 48% higher than the national average — driven by housing costs 110% above the national average and utilities 26% higher — families are struggling to afford basic necessities,” Deaton said Friday. “Washington and Beacon Hill must stop burdening taxpayers and deliver immediate relief.”

The federal gas tax is 18.4 cents per gallon on gasoline, while Massachusetts charges 24 cents per gallon – making for an extra 42.4 cents per gallon in taxes for gas in the Bay State.

Shortsleeve, Kennealy commit to WCVB, WBZ debates

Two of the three Republican gubernatorial candidates have accepted invites to join debates hosted by WCVB and WBZ’s Keller @ Large with Jon Keller program.

Brian Shortsleeve and Mike Kennealy have so far accepted the invitations to join the televised debates, with no answer coming in yet from fellow candidate Mike Minogue.

“Debates are a crucial part of the democratic process and I am proud to accept the invitation from WCVB to participate in their televised debate and call on my opponents to do the same,” said Kennealy said as he accepted the WCVB debate.

Shortsleeve also accepted.

“I stand ready, willing and able to answer the tough questions, defend my record and prosecute the case against Maura Healey – any time, any place,” said Shortsleeve, who also bashed Minogue for not committing to any debates thus far.

— Tim Dunn

title: Mass. Parole Board freeing another ’emerging adult’ murderer convicted of brazen daytime shooting
text:
The state’s Parole Board is releasing another “emerging adult” first-degree murderer who killed a hated rival in a brazen broad-daylight shooting in front of a bustling post office.

Patrick Grier was 20 years old in 2008 when he gunned down 16-year-old De’Andre Barboza in Boston.

Grier two years later was convicted of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

But in 2024, Grier became eligible for parole after the state Supreme Judicial Court’s decision in Commonwealth v. Mattis. The court ruled that “emerging adult” offenders who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense could not be sentenced to life without parole.

As a result of the SJC’s decision regarding his first-degree murder conviction, Grier was re-sentenced to life with the possibility of parole after 15 years.

Grier is now 37 years old, and the Massachusetts Parole Board has OK’d his release.

The deadly shooting

Back on Nov. 30, 2008, Grier and his co-defendant — a 16-year-old girl — were at a store in Dorchester, where they saw Barboza.

Grier talked with Barboza, and afterwards Grier appeared quiet and upset.

The next morning, Grier met up with his co-defendant in Dorchester. As the pair were passing a market on Washington Street, they spotted Barboza inside.

Barboza then left the market, and both Grier and Barboza walked toward the Codman Square street corner. When Barboza reached the corner in front of a busy post office, Grier shot him — causing him to fall to the ground.

With Barboza on the ground, Grier continued to fire at him from point-blank range. One shot struck Barboza in the head, while two shots wounded his legs.

Barboza was transported to Boston Medical Center, where he died two days later from the gunshot wound to his head.

Right after the shooting, Grier and his co-defendant fled the scene. Grier threw the gun he used to shoot Barboza at his co-defendant, telling the 16-year-old girl to take it.

She caught the gun, a .22 caliber revolver, and tucked it in her waistband before continuing to flee.

Police officers then apprehended Grier and the 16-year-old girl, and recovered the gun. Samples were taken from their hands, which tested positive for gunshot residue.

Grier and Barboza came from different neighborhoods, and the homicide stemmed from an “ongoing feud,” according to the Suffolk DA prosecutor during the arraignment years ago.

Parole decision

Last year, Grier appeared before the Massachusetts Parole Board for an initial hearing.

“Mr. Grier presented with insight into the causative factors that led to his gang affiliation and offending behavior,” the Parole Board wrote in its ruling. “Mr. Grier began to invest in self-development prior to the Mattis decision, and furthered his rehabilitation by participating in and completing programs related to his need areas.

“Mr. Grier also invested in education – earning his associate’s degree,” the Parole Board added. “In an effort to prepare himself for re-entry, Mr. Grier also developed occupational skills… The Board concludes that Patrick Grier has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society.”

The Massachusetts Parole Board has released dozens of “emerging adult” first-degree convicted murderers who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense.

The Mattis ruling in 2024 made more than 200 convicts eligible for parole hearings.

title: Boston City Council president: Allston-Brighton is ‘enraged’ over mayor’s choice to exclude community center funding
text:
Boston City Council President Liz Breadon said the people she represents in Allston-Brighton are “enraged” over the mayor’s decision to exclude funding for a new community center from the city’s $4.4 billion capital plan.

Breadon said Monday she’s been advocating for the city to fund a new community center to replace Allston-Brighton’s current facility — which is so run down that it can’t even operate on weekends or as a cooling center in hot weather — for six years to no avail.

This year represents a breaking point for the Allston-Brighton community, however, as Breadon said she “was assured that we were moving forward” as a city on building a new Boston Center for Youth and Families facility, given that a number of studies have been conducted and a site has been tentatively agreed upon.

“I was disappointed,” Breadon said after seeing that the project was not included in the five-year capital plan proposed by Mayor Michelle Wu last week. “We had the site, we had these different studies down and the indications where we were moving forward.

“The crazy thing about it is that we are the second largest neighborhood in the city of Boston. We’re approximately the same size as the City of Somerville by population and area, and we have one severely depleted community center that needs to be replaced, and it’s not been given any level of urgency,” Breadon added.

Breadon said the city broke ground last year on two new community centers in the North End and Dorchester, at an anticipated cost of $110 million and $65 million, respectively. She estimates that a new Allston-Brighton community center would cost $70-$80 million.

She said the Allston-Brighton community center is located in the Jackson-Mann Educational Complex in Allston’s Union Square, a campus that housed two schools that have either closed entirely or moved to a new neighborhood.

Breadon said the community favors building a new facility on the same site. She said no further studies are needed. The city’s capital budget allocates $10 million to develop a building program and assess siting options for a new BCYF center, but no funding for new construction, which has angered residents, she said.

“I think people are really disappointed — they’re enraged basically because we have really been scraping together to keep … our youth programs going,” Breadon said. “I’ve been talking about this for six years as a city councilor. Sooner or later, the city has to step up and support our neighborhood.”

The lack of funding for a new Allston-Brighton community center has led Breadon to vote against the city’s capital plan for the past two years — despite being seen as an ally of the mayor. She doesn’t see the $10 million commitment by the city in this year’s capital plan as a “meaningful commitment from this administration to construct a new” facility.

“As with many things in Allston-Brighton, we have lots of studies and not a lot of action,” Breadon said.

She said the center has been operating since the 1970s. Its dilapidated state and lack of funding — just $25,000 was budgeted for programming by the city last year — prevents the facility from offering a full slate of services for residents.

Breadon said the gymnasium and dance studio have failing roofs and floors. The heating, ventilation and air conditioning system doesn’t work, which prevents the center from operating as a cooling center as it should. It is closed on Saturdays, which prevents weekend programming, she added.

“It’s really a very sad situation,” Breadon said. “It’s a very poor reflection on our ability to serve our community here in Allston-Brighton.”

Allstonia reported Wu’s chief of civic engagement Brianna Millor as citing the city’s $48.4 million budget gap and need to prioritize other capital projects like the contentious $325 million White Stadium pro soccer rehab and the $700 million Madison Park high school rebuild as reasons for excluding funding for a new community center.

Breadon said she sees the city’s historic lack of investment in Allston-Brighton as being due to the district’s lack of political connections compared to other neighborhoods, along with a fundamental misunderstanding about its demographics.

“It’s like the neighborhoods that have got the most continue to get more, and those that are left behind are getting less,” Breadon said. “We have been consistently under-invested for decades. I just think that there’s a gross misunderstanding of who we are out here as a community.

“We’re probably one of the most diverse neighborhoods in the city. We don’t have a predominant Hispanic community. We don’t have a predominantly Black community. We just have a lot of different people living out here,” Breadon said. “At this rate, it’ll be a long time before we get the community center we need.”

The Council president plans to hold a “protest rally” with Allston-Brighton elected officials and community members on Tuesday.

Mayor Wu’s office walked back Millor’s reported remarks in a statement on Monday, saying that no project has been “bumped” in favor of another — the current funding authorization simply reflects the different stage that the Jackson Mann project is in.

“The city is working to make Boston the most family-friendly city in the country, and our public assets are especially critical to making our city a home for everyone,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said. “Significant resources to advance the Jackson Mann Community Center project are set aside in this year’s capital budget and will move the project closer towards design even amid the difficult choices required in this economic environment.

“This particular project will not be a simple rebuild, as the former combined school and community center uses must be evaluated in the context of changing school enrollment in the neighborhood and the BPS long-term facilities plan, as well as community desires for housing to potentially be incorporated into the site. We look forward to working closely with residents and elected officials so that the future of this community hub reflects the neighborhood’s evolving needs and priorities.”

As officers got closer to the person who originally split from the group, police said the person fled. Officers then tried to get control of him, and he allegedly pulled out a gun.

“The officer grabbed the slide of the firearm while the suspect maintained a firm grip on the handle and a struggle ensued,” BPD said in a statement. “While grappling with the suspect, the other individual intervened, grabbing the officer in an attempt to pull him away from the armed suspect.”

Eventually, as more officers arrived, they were able to subdue both men and take them into custody. Police said they recovered a Sig Sauer P320 firearm loaded with twenty-one rounds of ammunition from one of the suspects.

title: Police Blotter: MBTA officer attacked, eyes almost gouged
text:

He was arraigned in Boston Municipal Court in Roxbury Monday and held on $100 bail, although Judge David Breen revoked his bail on other pending charges out of Quincy District Court.

While in custody Friday morning, officers responded to his holding cell after he allegedly attacked an officer who was trying to escort him to get fingerprinted, the DA’s office said.

“Jean shouted at the officer that he wanted to go free,” the DA said in a statement, and when the officer said that he was being booked, Jean continued to shout and refused to comply with the officer.

The officer then told Jean to go back into the cell.

“As the officer turned his back to open the cell door, Jean lunged toward the officer, jumped onto his back and bit him on the back of his head,” according to the statement.

Other officers responded and “a violent struggle ensued,” the DA’s office said, in which Jean allegedly began to scratch at and gouge the officer’s eyes. One witnessing officer said Jean also tried to press his thumb into the other officer’s eye sockets.

Jean also allegedly tried to bite a different officer’s hand during the incident, the DA said.

The officer who was initially attacked had severe bruising, burst blood vessels in his eyes, and a cut on his face that required two stitches.

“This was an extraordinary burst of violence that hurt one officer and endangered all the others involved,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I thank the officers for restraining this defendant before he could inflict more injuries and I wish the wounded officer a full and fast recovery.”

title: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu appoints city’s first Black fire commissioner
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu has appointed Rodney Marshall, a 35-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, as the city’s first Black fire commissioner.

Wu announced Thursday that she has appointed Marshall as the fire department’s 45th commissioner. He replaces Paul Burke, who retired this year, and will take over the leadership position later this month after he is sworn into his new role.

“As a distinguished and deeply respected 35-year veteran of the Boston Fire Department, Deputy Chief Rodney Marshall is exceptionally qualified to lead the brave men and women of Boston Fire who put their lives on the line to keep our communities safe,” Wu said in a statement.

“As a lifelong Bostonian, he knows our communities, has demonstrated his leadership on the job and has dedicated his career to serving and protecting our residents,” Wu added.

The mayor also mentioned that she is “deeply grateful for Commissioner Paul Burke’s strong and steady leadership over the past nearly four years, and knows that his legacy in the department and city will continue to have an impact on our neighborhoods.”

Marshall joined the Boston Fire Department in 1991. He is currently the department’s chief of operations for support services.

Upon joining the department, he was assigned to Engine 56, and rose through the ranks to become a fire lieutenant in 1998. That same year, he was awarded the commissioner’s unit citation for saving the lives of multiple residents during a six-alarm fire, the mayor’s office said.

Marshall was later promoted to fire captain in 2005, district fire chief in 2014, and deputy fire chief in 2022. He has been chief of operations since 2022.

His second commissioner’s unit citation came in 2013, for rescuing several people trapped in a bus with severe roof damage, the mayor’s office said.

Marshall, a Dorchester native and Boston College graduate, thanked the mayor “for the privilege of leading the department that has shaped my life and career.”

“As a proud son of Dorchester, I joined the Boston Fire Department because I wanted to give back to the communities where I grew up, and I’m committed to supporting the firefighters and staff who work every day to keep Boston’s neighborhoods safe,” Marshall said in a statement.

Marshall cited his efforts to design and oversee the launch of the fire department’s cadet program, which is aimed at helping city kids become firefighters, as one of his proudest career accomplishments, per the mayor’s office.

Wu’s office did not immediately provide salary information for Marshall’s new position. Burke was paid a base salary of $311,382 as fire commissioner last year, per city payroll records.

The mayor’s decision to appoint a Black fire commissioner came after pressure from city and state elected officials of color.

Boston City Councilor Brian Worrell sent a letter to Wu on Feb. 3 calling for her to “promote from the qualified Black and brown firefighters in leadership that are representative of our city’s diversity.”

“The Boston Fire Department’s 175-year history has not fully reflected the diversity of the communities it is sworn to serve,” Worrell wrote. “Over the past five years, the city has undertaken efforts to make the Boston Fire Department more equitable, through efforts such as the fire cadet program and the hybrid residency model, but leadership representation remains a critical missing piece.

“Our firehouses should reflect the full strength, talent and diversity of Boston, and that reflection must extend to the highest levels of leadership. Appointing Boston’s first Black fire commissioner would send a clear message to current and future firefighters that opportunity is real and leadership is within reach for everyone willing to serve,” Worrell wrote.

Signing onto Worrell’s letter were City Councilors Miniard Culpepper, Ruthzee Louijeune, Julia Mejia, Enrique Pepén, and Henry Santana; state Reps. Russell Holmes, Brandy Fluker Reid, Chynah Tyler, and Christoper Worrell; state Sen. Liz Miranda; and Suffolk Register of Probate Stephanie Everett.

title: Running for a reason: Louis D. Brown Peace Institute goes the extra miles
text:
On Monday, Drudys Ledbetter will be turning the tragic loss of her brother into a cause for good for others experiencing their own grief.

The Sharon resident will set off from Hopkinton and conquer her second straight Boston Marathon, but unlike last year, she says she’s running with her brother, not for.

Ledbetter’s brother, Wolf Ruben Valmond, died at the age 37 in December 2019, when he was shot and killed outside of a bar in Georgia. He had his eyes set on becoming a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent.

Wolf’s death weighs heavy on Ledbetter’s mind.

The Boston native, in her early 40s, is raising $25,000 for the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, a city-based nonprofit that supports families and communities impacted by murder, trauma, grief and loss.

Ledbetter told the Herald that she felt last year that she had tried to run for her brother. That has changed this year, as she feels like she’s running with him.

“In those long runs, you’re by yourself, in your head, and I was very intentional about just moving through whatever grief was left in my body,” Ledbetter said, “and letting it go, and moving into that place of acceptance.”

“I feel when we cross that finish line,” she added, “it’s going to be me and him, going, ‘This is our new normal. This is how we connect. This is how we engage as siblings. This is a beautiful way to bond.’”

Ledbetter, a nurse by training, founded Project Destigmatize Healthcare, a nonprofit that advances research and public education on cannabis and health.

Ledbetter said she remains heavily active in Boston, where she remembers seeing, as a teenager, someone shot and attending funerals for 15-year-olds.

“That’s real in the city of Boston. That trauma is real, Ledbetter said. “Half of the crimes in the city of Boston are not solved. These moms, these families, everyone left behind is carrying this grief forever and ever and ever.”

Last year, while looking to participate in the Boston Marathon, Ledbetter reached out to the Peace Institute to see whether it had any racing bibs since she wanted to run for a “really good reason.”

The institute did not have any bibs.

That changed this year, though, as Ledbetter is captaining a four-member charity team, the institute’s first ever crew of marathon runners.

She said she is getting close to her fundraising goal of $25,000, which she added will make a real difference for the institute.

The institute’s programming is supported through donations, sponsorships and relationships. To further its cause, the institute is constructing a new headquarters, on Westville Street in Dorchester.

“That’s going to be a pillar of peace in the community,” Ledbetter said of the new building. “It’s going to need programming to support the community, the children, the families.”

“We want to make sure that they cannot only build the building,” she added, “but can also support the programming that will come out of that building, as well.”

Ledbetter is an active member of Heartbreak Hill Running Company, attending the club’s weekly Saturday morning long runs in Newton.

“You master the hills,” she said.

title: Boston City Council considering eliminating parking requirements for development
text:
The Boston City Council is considering a measure that would eliminate parking requirements for new residential development.

Councilors Sharon Durkan, Henry Santana and Liz Breadon, the body’s president, put forward an amendment to the city’s zoning code that would eliminate off-street parking minimum requirements tied to residential development in Boston.

The councilors said the amendment is aimed at reducing development costs that are exacerbating the city’s “housing crisis” by stalling production.

“We know that it is harder than ever to build,” Durkan said at last Wednesday’s Council meeting. “Housing production is at historic lows. Costs are rising and people are being priced out of the city. We know we need to do everything we can to increase affordability and expand the housing pipeline.

“This text amendment eliminates costly parking mandates from our zoning code,” Durkan added. “Most of Boston’s housing was built before these rules were made into law. These rules were established in the 1950s out of the false thinking that parking would reduce congestion. Instead, they made it harder to build housing and force developers to build more parking than we actually need.”

Durkan, who represents Beacon Hill and Back Bay, cited a report from the Metropolitan Area Planning Council that found more than a third of all parking in Boston sits empty overnight.

She said her proposed amendment would not ban parking from being built with new residential development, but would allow for flexibility.

“Developers will be able to build parking based on the needs of each project, rather than the outdated rules of the zoning code,” Durkan said.

She said the policy has worked in other Massachusetts cities, like Cambridge and Somerville, which eliminated parking requirements in 2022 and 2024, respectively. Similar reforms have been implemented outside of the Bay State, including Austin, Seattle, Minneapolis, San Francisco, Buffalo and Portland, her amendment states.

Boston eliminated parking minimums for affordable housing projects that include at least 60 percent income-restricted units in 2021, the amendment states.

“For Boston residents, this reform is a common sense, immediate step we can take to lower housing costs, support housing production and build a stronger, more sustainable city,” Durkan said. “The real question is whether we actually have the political leadership to get this done.”

Breadon said there’s been efforts over the last decade to eliminate parking requirements in her district, Allston-Brighton, which has led to “huge projects being approved with little or no parking.”

Developers seeking to build underground parking garages pay between $75,000 to $100,000 per parking space, at roughly one space per housing unit, Breadon said.

“This inevitably is added on to the cost of the housing and makes it more and more difficult for developers to make the numbers work,” Breadon said.

The proposal appears to have divided the Council. Six of the 13 councilors did not sign onto the zoning amendment order, indicating early resistance.

Two councilors who didn’t sign onto the order, Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy, confirmed Friday that they are opposed to the proposed parking changes.

Flynn said developers are not citing parking minimums that he said are disregarded by the Boston Zoning Board of Appeals and Transportation Department “on a routine basis as the reason why we’re not building anything in Boston anymore.”

“It’s that we added increased affordable housing and energy requirements on top of high interest rates, increased construction costs, and tariffs,” Flynn said in a statement to the Herald. “The focus should be on economic development, not parking purity tests.

“District 2 has absorbed as much or more housing as any part of the city,” Flynn said. “With the MBTA needing over $30 billion in repairs and school buses routinely late, working families in Chinatown and South Boston rely on a car to meet their needs. When we don’t include parking in new buildings, those cars invariably wind up on the street and exacerbate our existing parking crisis.”

Murphy, an at-large councilor who lives in Dorchester, said the proposal is not for a “small adjustment to zoning,” but rather, a “sweeping change” that would eliminate parking requirements citywide and create situations where residents won’t have the ability to park their cars at home.

“The language is explicit — no off-street parking shall be required,” Murphy said in a statement to the Herald. “That means housing can be built anywhere in the city with no parking at all. Supporters say the market will decide. But when that decision is wrong, the market does not absorb the impact. Residents do.

“People still own cars,” Murphy said. “They still need to park them. And when there is no off-street parking, that demand spills onto already crowded neighborhood streets. That is not theoretical. That is exactly what residents are already experiencing.”

Murphy said parking is the No. 1 concern cited at community meetings for new development proposals. The proposed amendment, she said, would not work as a “blanket policy” for all Boston neighborhoods.

“What works in Back Bay or the South End does not work the same way in neighborhoods like Mattapan, Lower Mills, Adams Corner, or Orient Heights, where residents rely on their cars as part of daily life,” Murphy said. “Parking in those communities is not optional. It is infrastructure.

“We can build more housing,” Murphy added. “But we should not adopt a citywide policy that removes all parking requirements and leaves our neighborhoods to absorb the consequences.”

title: Editorial: Stop putting Allston-Brighton $$ on the back burner
text:
How did Allston-Brighton become the middle child of Boston neighborhoods?

While City Hall celebrates new community centers in the North End, Grove Hall, an overhaul of the Curley Community Center in South Boston, and upgrades to City Hall plaza itself, Allston-Brighton has been out of the funding loop for years.

Boston City Council President Liz Breadon said Monday she’s been advocating for the city to fund a new community center to replace Allston-Brighton’s current facility — which is so run down that it can’t even operate on weekends or as a cooling center in hot weather — for six years. The City’s response: crickets.

Breadon said her Allston-Brighton constituents are “enraged” over the mayor’s decision to exclude funding for a new community center from the city’s $4.4 billion capital plan.

More than 100 Allston-Brighton residents and elected officials rallied last week in protest, according to the Harvard Crimson. Breadon organized the rally to demand $65 million for a design study and redevelopment of a new community center at the Jackson Mann site.

The project has been stalled since 2019, when the building was deemed suitable for demolition. Since then, the city has conducted multiple studies to assess the site’s financial and programmatic feasibility.

Speaking at the rally, Breadon urged the city to move into the design and construction phase.

“We’ve had a programming study, we’ve had a siting study, we’ve had a land use study and different test fits for different uses of this space,” Breadon said. “It’s time to put up and put our money where our mouth is and build.”

It’s past time to put up, and it begs the question why Allston-Brighton isn’t further up the funding food chain.

The City of Boston Planning Department describes Allston as “a bustling residential and commercial mix.

“Leafy side streets lined with wooden triple-decker houses are home to a diverse community, including longtime residents, students from nearby Boston University and Harvard, recent immigrants, and young professionals.”

Those universities, coupled with corporate offices and biotech sites add up to significant tax revenue for the city. And residents here are every bit as deserving of funding as residents in other neighborhoods. So why the disconnect?

“The crazy thing about it is that we are the second-largest neighborhood in the city of Boston. We’re approximately the same size as the City of Somerville by population and area, and we have one severely depleted community center that needs to be replaced, and it’s not been given any level of urgency,” Breadon said.

Breadon said the city broke ground last year on two new community centers in the North End and Dorchester, at an anticipated cost of $110 million and $65 million, respectively. She estimates a new Allston-Brighton community center would cost $70-$80 million. So we’re not looking at an outlier in terms of expensive projects.

The squeaky wheel gets the grease, especially in local politics. With Breadon representing the neighborhood as well as presiding over the City Council, this is not just an opportunity to wield some clout, but a mandate.

Give Allston-Brighton a better seat at the funding table.

title: Inside the world’s largest art heist when over $500M of paintings were stolen from a Boston museum
text:
By LEAH WILLINGHAM

BOSTON (AP) — For decades, the 1990 theft of 13 artworks from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum — now valued at more than $500 million — has remained unsolved.

It remains the largest art theft in history — far surpassing more recent museum thefts, including a daylight heist at the Louvre that involved far fewer works and was resolved more quickly. In 2013, the FBI said it knew who was responsible for the Boston museum heist but declined to name them, fueling speculation that persists today.

A former FBI agent who led the investigation for more than two decades is now offering the first detailed account of how investigators reached that conclusion — and publicly identifying the men he believes were involved. In a new book, Geoff Kelly traces how the artworks moved through criminal networks, where violence took the lives of key suspects and witnesses, and challenges long-circulating theories by revisiting key details.

The irony at the center is that Gardner’s intention was for the museum to remain frozen in time, stipulating in her will that nothing in the Venetian palazzo-inspired building would be changed after her death. Gardner, who lived in the museum and died there in 1924, intended for the paintings, sculptures and architectural fragments to remain exactly as she had arranged.

The empty gilded frames of the missing paintings still hang in the museum today — silent witnesses to what was taken.

The art heist

Early on March 18, 1990, as Boston wound down from St. Patrick’s Day celebrations, two men dressed as police officers arrived at the museum and convinced a security guard to let them in, violating protocol.

The men handcuffed the guards in the basement and made their way to the museum’s Dutch Room, where they cut Vermeer’s “The Concert” and Rembrandt’s “Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee” from their frames, also taking works by Degas and Manet.

They also took a Napoleonic eagle finial — a decorative metal piece of comparatively little value that investigators later found puzzling — and the museum’s security videotapes.

The museum offered a $5 million reward that they then doubled a decade later for information leading to the recovery of the works.

Boston-area network of criminals

Some tips pointed to the Irish Republican Army and to Boston mob figures, including notorious crime boss Whitey Bulger.

Kelly followed one lead to France, where he watched through binoculars as FBI agents, posing as wealthy intermediaries, lounged on a yacht — drinking champagne and eating strawberries — in an effort to draw out suspected Corsican mob figures.

Closer to home, agents searched houses across New England, relying heavily on informants. A triple murderer known as “Meatball” who was terminally ill secretly recorded conversations with suspected associates in hopes of earning money for his family.

But none of the tips led to the paintings.

Violence complicates matters

In the decades since the robbery, several people believed to have ties to the heist were killed, and another died under suspicious circumstances.

Robert “Bobby” Donati, a Boston mob associate long suspected in the case, was found stabbed to death in 1991, his body left in the trunk of a car after his home had been ransacked.

Years earlier, Donati has visited the Gardner with another known art thief, Myles Connor, to scope it out for a robbery and said that if he ever took the museum’s Napoleonic finial, it would be his “calling card.” Years later, a jeweler told investigators Donati tried to sell a finial from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum but backed off, saying it was “too hot.”

A separate line of evidence centered on George Reissfelder, who investigators believe owned the getaway car.

Kelly tracked down Reissfelder’s brother, a retired military officer who had initially not believed his brother was involved. He broke down after being shown Manet’s “Chez Tortoni,” saying he recognized it as a painting he himself hung above his brother’s bed.

Reissfelder later died under suspicious circumstances. When investigators searched his home, the painting was gone.

Both men had ties to TRC Auto Electric, a Dorchester shop linked to Charles “Chuck” Merlino’s crew.

Investigation with limited resources

Though investigators believed they knew who was responsible, they had a difficult time finding definitive proof.

In its early stages, the FBI assigned a single agent to the case, which Kelly said slowed progress.

“You have to keep in mind when you’re talking about investigations, they come down to dollars and cents,” Kelly said. It was “like pulling teeth” to secure resources. At the time, federal investigators in Boston were heavily focused on violent crime, drug trafficking and organized crime cases.

Kelly said a decision to release surveillance footage despite investigators’ objections became a lasting distraction. With no usable video from the night of the robbery, prosecutors released footage from the night before that showed a museum employee entering the building after his car broke down. Kelly said he objected to the theory that the employee was casing the museum, since that possibility had already been reviewed and dismissed. The footage fueled years of misplaced suspicion, since the man was later determined not to be involved.

Theories about an inside job at the museum

Among the questions that linger is whether it was an inside job.

In photos from that night, a museum guard is seen handcuffed in the basement, his head wrapped in duct tape.

Investigators noted that shortly before the robbery, the guard opened a door against policy — one that faced the area where the thieves were later seen waiting — a move investigators considered highly unusual and suspicious.

“It’s the immutable laws of time and space,” Kelly said. “I think that there was enough information back then that he could have been charged. Would it be enough to convict him? I don’t know.”

By the time investigators examined those questions more closely, Kelly said, the statute of limitations had expired, leaving them with little leverage to compel cooperation.

The museum guard, Rick Abath, denied any involvement in the theft. He died in 2024.

The artworks that disappeared

Kelly personifies the missing artworks and describes them as “perfect fugitives.”

“They don’t go to the doctor. They don’t get stopped for speeding. They don’t leave fingerprints,” he said. “They can just disappear.”

Unlike human fugitives, he said, artworks can also be copied.

Over the years, that has meant chasing down false leads — including paintings spotted in a Reno antique market, hanging in private homes and even one that appeared in an episode of the TV show “Monk.”

Because the works are so recognizable, it’s nearly impossible to sell them publicly.

“Stealing the artwork from the museum, that’s the easy part,” Kelly said. “Profiting from it, that’s the difficult part.”

He imagines the paintings will surface one day — outliving those who carried out the heist.

“I have no doubt they still exist,” he said

title: Boston’s new fire commissioner lives in Canton, despite city’s residency requirement
text:
Boston’s new $318,000 fire commissioner, Rodney Marshall, lives in Canton, but the mayor’s office said he wouldn’t be violating the city’s residency requirement unless he fails to move to the Hub within the next six months.

Marshall made history when he was appointed by Mayor Michelle Wu last month as the city’s first Black fire commissioner, but questions about his residency quickly followed. Those questions intensified as he and the city continued to represent the veteran firefighter as living in Dorchester, despite land records that suggested otherwise.

The Norfolk Registry of Deeds lists Marshall as having owned a four-bedroom home in Canton since 1993.

Still, Marshall represented himself as a Dorchester native and Wu described him as a “lifelong Bostonian” when announcing his appointment. Additionally, he was listed as living at a Dorchester address when his mayoral appointment notice came up for approval by the City Council last Wednesday.

After his Canton residency became public this week, Wu’s office backtracked on the city’s representation of Marshall as a lifelong Boston resident, by admitting that he lives outside of the Hub, but plans to move there in the next six months, to comply with the city’s residency requirement for commissioners.

“The City of Boston’s residency requirement, including the six-month grace period for certain mayoral appointees to establish residency, is set in the municipal code and has been consistently applied across administrations,” a city spokesperson said in a statement to the Herald. “Like his two immediate predecessors before him, incoming Commissioner Marshall will comply with the requirement.”

The Boston Fire Department didn’t address why Marshall has been represented by the city as living in Dorchester, but denied that Marshall described himself as such when speaking with reporters last month after he was announced as commissioner.

“During the media availability following his announcement, the incoming commissioner referred to his strong family and community ties to Grove Hall, where he was born and raised,” a Boston Fire Department spokesperson said in a statement. “He will comply with the residency requirement, just as his two predecessors did.”

Marshall is set to be paid a $318,000 salary as fire commissioner, according to his employment contract. He was sworn into his new role on Friday, and replaces Paul Burke, who retired this year. Burke was paid a $311,382 base salary last year, per city payroll records.

Marshall lives in Canton, but seems to use a Dorchester address for city payroll documents. Land records indicate that address is for a home that was owned by his late father, and is seemingly still in the family, as there was no change of ownership. The address was listed on his appointment notice approved by the Council this week.

His employment contract with the city acknowledges, however, that, “upon appointment, the commissioner shall have six months to reestablish residency within the City of Boston.”

The mayor’s office said the city’s municipal code allows department heads and cabinet positions six months to become residents, but also seemed to contradict land records by stating that Marshall satisfied his 10-year residency requirement before moving out of the city, as allowed for Boston firefighters.

Marshall joined the Boston Fire Department in 1991, two years before he is listed in land records as having purchased a home in Canton.

The mayor’s decision to appoint a Black fire commissioner came after pressure from city and state elected officials of color.

Boston City Councilor Brian Worrell sent a letter to Wu on Feb. 3 calling for her to “promote from the qualified Black and brown firefighters in leadership that are representative of our city’s diversity.”

Marshall was the department’s chief of operations for support services before Wu appointed him as fire commissioner.

He was twice awarded the commissioner’s unit citation — for saving the lives of multiple residents during a six-alarm fire in 1998, and for rescuing several people trapped in a bus with severe roof damage in 2013.

title: Police Blotter: ‘Operation Safe Scooter’ in Roxbury recovers 10 scooters, mopeds
text:
As a result of “Operation Safe Scooter,” Boston Police said they confiscated ten moped/scooters for motor vehicle law violations Monday.

The operation took place around 4 p.m. and was in response to “ongoing public safety concerns regarding the use of these vehicles” on Shirley Street in Roxbury, according to the department.

“The Boston Police Department remains committed to improving traffic safety and will continue to conduct enforcement operations across the city,” the department said in a statement.

The department urged anyone with information about illegal activity related to scooters and mopeds to reach out to BPD.

The operation took place the same day that Governor Maura Healey filed new legislation to regulate e-bike, scooters, and mopeds, known as “micro-mobility devices.”

A statement from Healey’s office said that the law would create a “first-in-the-nation, speed-based framework,” that allows lower speed e-bikes to largely operate like bikes while higher speed bikes, scooters, and mopeds will be limited to riders 16 and older. Drivers of the faster mopeds, e-bikes, and scooters will have to get insurance and register.

The law would also set more restrictions on where high speed devices can operate and give the Registry of Motor Vehicles more control to regulate new technologies without waiting for legislation to pass on Beacon Hill.

“Micro-mobility is already a part of how people get to work, school and around their communities, but right now, the rules are unclear and inconsistent,” Healey said in a statement. “We are seeing too much reckless behavior, more crashes and close calls, and too many people, especially pedestrians and young riders, are at risk.”

Remains of missing Hanson woman found in Plymouth

The Plymouth County District’s Attorney’s Office announced human remains found off Route 3 belong to a Hanson woman who went missing more than six years ago.

A hunter found the remains in a wooded area in Plymouth on March 6, the DA’s office said.

The office contacted the FBI, who was able to match DNA from the remains to Sandra Crispo, a woman who was reported missing by her family after they couldn’t get in touch with her in August of 2019.

Hanson Police, the Mass State Police, and the DA’s office “conducted an extensive and exhaustive investigation into her disappearance,” after Crispo was first reported missing, the DA’s office said.

The investigation remains ongoing and anyone with information was asked to reach out to the Hanson Police Department or the Mass State Police.

Dorchester man sentenced to up to 40 years for abusing foster kids

A judge sentenced a 46-year-old Dorchester man to between 28 and 40 years in prison for abusing two foster children in his care, according the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office.

Taryl Ford, 46, was convicted last month on four counts of aggravated rape, two counts of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14 and one count of disseminating obscene matter to a minor.

Ford’s mother had fostered 34 children over the span of 11 years, while Ford lived in the building and acted as an approved secondary caregiver for the kids, the DA’s office said.

The first victim was abused starting when he was five years old for about a year and the second was abused from age seven to eight. A third child was shown porn by Ford, the DA’s office said.

During the sentencing hearing on Monday, the victim impact statements described how Ford’s crimes profoundly impacted their lives.

One of the victim’s mothers said that Ford “is the monster that lives under the bed but never stays under the bed.”

Because Ford’s mother fostered so many children, prosecutors believe there could be more victims, and the DA’s office encouraged anyone with more information to reach out.

“These courageous victims eloquently described the lasting impacts of this serial abuse on them. And, to their enormous credit, they also expressed their concern for other children who may have been hurt,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said. “We hope anyone else who may have been abused by Taryl Ford will contact authorities. They do not have to bear this pain alone.”
