title: Police Blotter: Man charged in 2023 Caribbean festival shooting sentenced to life
text:
A Dorchester man charged with participating in a harrowing shooting at a festival that left eight people injured was sentenced to life in prison Thursday.

Gerald Vick Jr., 33, was convicted of carrying a firearm without a license (second offense), possession of a large capacity feeding device, and possession of a machine gun, according to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office.

The DA’s Office said that Vick was also charged as a habitual offender because of convictions for two prior crimes, leading a judge to issue a mandatory life sentence. He will have the possibility of parole in 15 years.

Before Vick was supposed to face trial at the end of 2024, the DA said he removed a GPS bracelet and fled the state. He was apprehended six months later in Georgia.

The shooting at the 2023 J’Ouvert parade, a Caribbean festival, took place on Aug. 23 and was observed by officers and caught on surveillance footage, the DA’s Office said.

Officers saw a confrontation between two groups of men, and as they approached, shots rang out. Eight people were injured but no one was killed.

Vick was among the group of men and arrested on the scene that day, according to the DA. Police found a sear switch that was capable of holding 24 rounds; five of the shell casings recovered on the scene were found to have been fired from the gun.

Two other men, Dwayne Francis, 31, and Sebastian Monteiro, 22, were also charged in connection with the shooting. Francis is scheduled to be tried on June 1, while Monteiro was sentenced to four years in prison.

“This was a brazen, unconscionable act of violence made all the worse by being committed in the middle of one of our city’s proudest cultural events, attended by thousands,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I’m grateful for the time and care these jurors took in reviewing all the evidence and testimony before reaching their decision to hold Gerald Vick accountable for his reckless actions.”

MS-13 gang member sentenced for role in 2010 Chelsea murder

A MS-13 gang member was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison by a federal judge for his role in a 2010 Chelsea murder.

Adam Rodriguez, 35, had already pleaded guilty to conspiracy to participate in a racketeering enterprise for his involvement in the killing of Joaquin Aguilar, of Allston.

Rodriguez and other members of the local syndicate of the MS-13 conspired to kill Aguilar because they believe he was a member of a rival gang, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said in a statement.

Aguilar was found stabbed to death under a Chelsea on-ramp. According to the U.S. Attorney, Rodriguez was among the individuals who led the victim to the secluded area, where he was hit over the head and stabbed multiple times.

A secret recording of a gang meeting showed Rodriguez getting disciplined from leaving Massachusetts after the crime without permission, the statement said.

title: Police Blotter: Quincy man injected harmful black-market Botox at Milton spa
text:
A Quincy man admitted in federal court that he was injecting clients of his Milton spa with black-market Botox, which led many of those customers to suffer some serious medical effects.

Rodrigo de Medeiros Siqueira, 33, the proprietor of Rodrigo Beauty at 464 Granite Ave. in Milton, pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to one count of misbranding of a drug after shipment in interstate commerce with the intent to defraud or mislead, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison. U.S. District Court Judge Richard G. Stearns scheduled sentencing for Aug. 12.

The case against Medeiros Siqueira began June 1, 2025, when a physician reported to the Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH) a patient who was suffering from botulism and who reported having received injections of generic Botox at Rodrigo Beauty, according to a law enforcement affidavit filed to support the charge. Botox is a brand name for Botulinum toxin, which is used as a cosmetic treatment for wrinkles.

Then similar reports started rolling in.

Of the six types of botulism — infant botulism, food-borne, wound-associated, adult intestinal toxemia, inhalation, and iatrogenic — botched botox injections can create the last one, according to the affidavit.

This iatrogenic type of poisoning, the affidavit explains, “is caused by botulinum toxin circulating in the blood and producing effects remotely from the injection site … (which) can lead to life-threatening symptoms, including: blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, and/or difficulty swallowing or breathing.”

When confronted by U.S. Food and Drug Administration agents, Medeiros Siqueira said he had obtained the legitimate and FDA-approved Botox brand Daxxify from another spa operated by two licensed nurse practitioners, according to the affidavit. Those nurses told investigators no such thing had occurred. Revance, the maker of Daxxify, also said they had no record of Medeiros Siqueira.

“Manufacturers of other commonly used FDA-approved botulinum toxin products likewise reported that there is no record of Medeiros Siqueira or Rodrigo Beauty ever having purchased their products,” the affidavit states.

Investigators said that it appears that Medeiros Siqueira, who is not certified or licensed to perform Botox injections and is therefore not legally permitted to obtain legitimate Botox products, obtained his wares from less-than-legitimate sources. Investigators say people often purchase alternative products from other countries like China and South Korea both because these are “typically significantly less expensive than FDA-approved” products and because they do not require licensure.

Federal authorities ask that anyone who believes they received an illegal injection from this man or at his spa should fill out the questionnaire at the FDA’s website at https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/criminal-investigations/oci-vw-assistance-rodrigo-beauty.

Illegal immigrant gets to 2+ years for selling ghost guns

An illegal immigrant from El Salvador who was residing in Chelsea was sentenced to more than two years in prison and will be subject to deportation after pleading guilty to selling ghost guns to gang members.

U.S. District Court Chief Judge Denis J. Casper sentenced Melbi Ovidio Ortez, 41, to 27 months in federal prison on the firearms violations. Ortez is subject to deportation after serving his sentence.

Ortez was arrested in June 2025 and in February pleaded guilty to one count of engaging in the business of dealing in firearms without a license and one count of distribution of and possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance.

Prosecutors say that Ortez is an 18th Street Gang associate known to sell guns and drugs to members of the gang. Over a single month last year, from April 3 to May 2, prosecutors say, Ortez sold four pistols, two with defaced serial numbers, making them untraceable ghost guns, and more than 100 rounds of ammunition from behind his house in Chelsea. Those guns were a Glock 9mm, a Sturm and Ruger .22 revolver, a Glock .40, and a Colt .380. He also sold cocaine.

title: Police Blotter: 18-year-old charged in Chelsea stabbing; Mass. Appeals Court affirms Brockton robber’s life sentence
text:
An 18-year-old was arraigned for charges related to the stabbing death of a young man in Chelsea, the Suffolk County DA stated Wednesday.

Jose Joel Umana Janes, 18, was arraigned in Chelsea District Court on Tuesday on a murder charge in connection to the fatal stabbing of 25-year-old Eduardo Rosales López in Chelsea on March 19, the DA said. Janes was ordered held without bail.

“This case pulled together dogged investigative work and available surveillance technology to identify suspects in a terrible burst of violence that ended a young man’s life,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said. “I extend my deepest sympathies to the family and friends of Mr. López.”

On the evening of March 19, López and another man were allegedly walking down Everett Avenue when he had a brief interaction with Janes and four other men, according to court records reported by MassLive. The group allegedly chased López and the other man down the street, before they fled in separate directions and López was caught.

The 25-year-old was then assaulted, fell to the ground and was stabbed several times, and the group fled the scene, with Janes allegedly running in a different direction.

Another one of the alleged attackers, Sergio Josue Castellanos Cerrato, 18, was arrested on the night of the stabbing and previously arraigned on murder charges. He was ordered held without bail.

Investigators tracked Janes through “various sources of surveillance footage,” the DA said, and positively identified him through still images.

“Consistent with Cerrato, Janes is alleged to have chased López and stabbed him with a long, fixed bladed knife after López fell down in the middle of the street,” the DA’s office stated.

Janes will return to court on June 12 for a probable cause hearing.

Appeals Court affirms life sentence

On Tuesday, the state Appeals Court affirmed the convictions of a man found guilty of attacking a Brockton woman in her home in 2013, the Plymouth DA announced.

Brian Vines, 51, was found guilty on charges including armed assault with intent to rob a person 60 years or older, assault and battery on an elder causing serious bodily injury, armed robbery and more in relation to a violent 2013 incident.

The Appeals Court affirmed his convictions Tuesday and denied his motion for a new trial, overruling claims that there were issues with the judge not excusing a juror for cause and the defense counsel was ineffective.

In June 2013, Brockton Police were called to a home on Brookfield Drive for a report of a woman attacked in her home, finding a victim in her 60s “badly beaten and lying in a pool of blood in her kitchen,” the DA said. The victim was beaten and stabbed multiple times, including a slash to her throat.

The woman reported her attacker was Vines, who attended school with her sons, the DA stated. Vines had arrived at her home and asked for her son’s phone number, the victim reportedly told police, before putting her in a chokehold with a gun to her back.

Vines demanded all her money, the woman reportedly said, and then demanded her ATM card and PIN number. He then used a weapon to beat her, stabbed her in her back several times and slit her throat, the DA said.

The defendant was arrested days later after being linked to debit card use, and DNA testing confirmed blood on his clothes, the DA stated.

“I applaud our state Appeals Court for their work on this matter, and I’m grateful to them for keeping Brian Vines in prison, where he belongs,” Plymouth DA Timothy Cruz said. “Vines spent decades preying on vulnerable women and the community is far safer with him incarcerated.”

title: Boston city councilors vow to resign over Mayor Wu’s proposed $724K veterans’ budget cut
text:
A pair of Boston city councilors are vowing to walk away from the job if Mayor Michelle Wu doesn’t fully restore her proposed 14.6% cut to the city’s veterans budget.

The proposal to slash $724,000 from the veterans’ services office has sparked outrage among councilors, former service members, and EMTs who favor a full restoration but argue that it shouldn’t take money away from other departments.

Councilor Ed Flynn, a U.S. Navy veteran who served 24 years, including in Operation Enduring Freedom, called the 14% reduction “significant.” But he said that he’d be “equally outraged” if the mayor looked to cut 25 cents from the budget.

“I would rather resign from my job as a city councilor than vote [for] any budget that hurts veterans,” Flynn said at Thursday’s hearing. “That’s how serious I am about what is taking place today. I am embarrassed … what the city of Boston did, cutting veterans’ services.”

Councilor Erin Murphy, who choked up earlier in the hearing, echoed Flynn’s threat to resign: “I also would rather give up my job than take a vote,” she said, “and maybe I will be outvoted, that makes any cuts, especially where it’s so small.”

The proposed cut to veterans’ services is among the hottest issues this budget season at City Hall, with the City Council backing a resolution for Wu to restore the “devastating” spending reduction.

Wu’s office has defended the mayor’s decision, stating that there won’t be cuts to direct services for veterans and that the reduction reflects broader fiscal constraints facing the city amid a budget crunch.

Robert Santiago, the city’s commissioner of veterans’ services, said Thursday that the proposed cuts won’t affect his office’s ability to carry its current caseload next year.

Areas that would be impacted, Santiago said, include the office’s “Bridge the Gap Mini-Grant Program,” which shares funds with nonprofits that support local veterans through projects covering housing, transportation, health, economic mobility and education.

The planned cuts would also impact the office’s non-personnel expenses, such as city-branded clothing, other promotional items and event supplies and rentals, the mayor’s office has said.

“But any cut like that, it may or may not have an impact,” Santiago said in response to a question from Council President Liz Breadon on whether homeless veterans would be affected.

Wu has proposed a $4.22 million budget for the office next fiscal year, compared to $4.94 million this year, a 14.6%, or $723,753 reduction. Meanwhile, the mayor’s entire city budget request of $4.9 billion would increase current spending by 2.1%.

Murphy said that veterans’ services is one of the smallest funded departments in the city, and any cut would be “unacceptable.”

“This is hard,” Murphy said, fighting through tears. “I am a mom of a soldier who is deployed. … When we have a couple of hundred thousand dollars that’s cut, we can fix that, we can do better, and we should do better.”

Dan Magoon, a Dorchester resident who heads the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes nonprofit, is demanding that the Wu administration “not balance the budget on the backs of our veterans.” He argues that there’s “plenty of waste, fraud and other bloated initiatives that could be cut” elsewhere.

Magoon, who completed three combat deployments between Iraq and Afghanistan from 2003 to 2007, recounted how 16 years ago, he warned the City Council that the city was failing veterans.

“The warning was ignored,” Magoon said. “Unfortunately, three administrations later, the slow erosion of veterans’ services and benefits has become normalized. … It’s not just the budget reduction, it’s the latest step in a systemic betrayal of those who’ve worn the uniform.”

Also catching smoke is a proposal from City Councilor Ben Weber, who chairs the council’s budget process, to slash money from the fire department to restore the mayor’s proposed cut to the veterans budget.

Jason Yutkins, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen Association’s EMS Division, which covers EMTs and paramedics, called Weber’s idea the “wrong approach.”

“It creates a false choice,” he said, “between supporting veterans or supporting public safety in believing that we can only support one over the other. We can, and we should do both.”

title: Editorial: Parole Board left fingerprints on Cambridge shooting
text:
One of the details to emerge after alleged Memorial Drive gunman Tyler Brown was arrested Monday was that the Massachusetts Parole Board released him from MCI-Shirley last year.

Of course it did.

This is the same parole board that’s released a raft of convicted killers onto our streets, disregarding the victims of their crimes, public safety, and the concept of justice in general.

As the Herald reported, Brown had been sent to state prison after he was convicted of shooting at Boston police officers in 2020.

Before springing Brown, the Parole Board said last year “subject has completed Violence Reduction, Criminal Thinking and in Bachelors Program at Tufts University.”

“Subject suffers from MH disorder w/ PTSD, Depression and Anxiety and taking medications on a daily basis,” the board added. “Subject was smoking THC while in community as a tool to increase his appetite. Subject is remorseful about the part he played in the offense.”

Apparently remorse wipes the slate clean. It’s outrageous, but it’s par for the course here.

As Brown allegedly unleashed hell on Memorial Drive Monday afternoon, leaving two people injured, he was shot by a responding State Police trooper and a former Marine who was caught in the Cambridge traffic, according to Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan.

The State Police trooper and former Marine saved lives that day. But the public shouldn’t have to hope for heroes to rush in and rescue them from a hail of bullets. That’s the job of law enforcement, who make arrests, judges who sentence criminals to pay for their crimes, and a parole board that cares about public safety.

Not all these systems are working, and as it stands the public has little recourse when justice goes off the rails.

The Parole Board has immunity in its decision-making and isn’t subject to lawsuits by, for example, someone who was injured after a released convict opened fire while they were driving down the street.

This needs to be re-examined. Lawmakers and activists rail against qualified immunity for police officers, but where is the outrage when people convicted of gun crimes are released from prison and allegedly open fire yet again?

Victims of crime in Massachusetts have an uphill battle for visibility and too often, for achieving justice. The rogues’ gallery of killers released by the Parole Board came with rap sheets often marked by blatant disregard for human life.

Why doesn’t that matter in Massachusetts?

Last week, Gerald Vick Jr., the Dorchester man charged with participating in a harrowing shooting at the 2023 J’Ouvert parade festival that left eight people injured was sentenced to life in prison.

The DA’s Office said he was also charged as a habitual offender because of convictions for two prior crimes, leading a judge to issue a mandatory life sentence. He will have the possibility of parole in 15 years.

If there’s anyone in Massachusetts who believes Vick will still be behind bars in 20 years, they haven’t been paying attention.

title: Police Blotter: Boston stolen scooters and death suspect convicted of rape
text:
Boston cops were really burning rubber on the illegal scooter issue this week.

During yet another targeted enforcement of illegal moped and scooter activity in the city, this time on Kenberma Road in Dorchester, police arrested three teens and recovered nine vehicles, which they say were stolen.

“The investigation was a result of ongoing public safety concerns as well as quality of life issues regarding the use and storage of these vehicles in the Dorchester area,” the Boston Police Department wrote in a statement announcing the arrests.

Police arrested Kevin Afonseca Varela, 18, of Jamaica Plain; Jayden Theodat, 18, of Roslindale; and a 16-year-old juvenile of Dorchester after allegedly finding the trio in a basement scattered with stolen scooters and mopeds at 11 Kenberma Road.

Members of the BPD’s Youth Violence Strike Force — the gang unit — say they saw significant in-and-out moped and scooter activity at that address and moved in. After gaining access to the basement, “officers observed several mopeds in various states of repair as well as an overwhelming odor of gasoline emanating from the mopeds.”

Police say that none of the vehicles were registered and “all of them showed signs of being stolen with exposed wiring and damaged ignitions.”

Man suspected of women’s death convicted of rape

A man who had been set to plead guilty in the 2021 death of one woman was convicted of multiple counts of rape against two different women.

A Boston jury on Friday convicted Rinnyers Pena, 47, of Dorchester, of drugging for sexual intercourse, strangulation, two counts of rape and two counts of photographing an unsuspecting nude person.

Pena is also charged in the death of 38-year-old Alenny Matos, who had been investigated as a missing person beginning on Jan. 27, 2020, until May 9, 2020. On that day, a woman walking her dog in the area of Enneking Parkway within the Stony Brook Reservation in Hyde Park discovered a body in a trash bag, which was then identified as Matos through dental records.

Pena was scheduled to plead guilty to disinterring a body in the Matos case on April 29, but withdrew his plea halfway through the hearing, according to the Suffolk DA’s office. That case will go to trial at a later date.

Police say that Pena had been in contact with Matos by cell phone two days before she was reported missing and a subsequent investigation suggested that he had picked her up from her Dorchester apartment on Jan. 26, 2020, and drove her to his Norton Street residence in Dorchester.

It was Pena’s cell phone that also sealed the case against him regarding the rapes.

While investigating the Matos case, prosecutors say, police found a series of photographs on Pena’s phone. One set depicted a 21-year-old female who appeared “unclothed and unresponsive or incapacitated on Pena’s bed” as well as photos of him doing inappropriate things with her while she was in that state. Another set on a second phone showed something similar with another female victim.

Prosecutors say that Pena confined the first victim in a locked room at a Roxbury rooming house against her will and plied her with opioids to facilitate his sexual abuse of her.

title: Police Blotter: Chelsea man burned children with lighters, heated forks, DA says
text:
A man is being held without bail on charges that he physically abused young children in both Chelsea and Revere, including burning one with a cigarette lighter.

Kener Bautista-Zepeda, 19, is charged with four counts of reckless endangerment of a child, three counts of assault and battery on a child with substantial injury, two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on a child under 14, two counts of strangulation or suffocation, and one count of assault and battery. A Suffolk County grand jury indicted him on the charges earlier this week.

Bautista-Zepeda was arraigned on the charges Friday morning in Suffolk Superior Court. Judge Catherine Ham ordered him held without bail, an order that will be reviewed in a dangerousness hearing scheduled for May 28.

The charges stem from two distinct relationships.

The first involves Bautista-Zepeda’s romantic partner and the child they share in Chelsea. The woman told police on March 12, 2025, that Bautista-Zepeda had physically assaulted her and that as he pushed and punched her, their 2-year-old child began to cry. Bautista-Zepeda then allegedly took a cigarette lighter and used it to burn the child on his upper back, causing a burn mark that prosecutor Allyson Portney described as the size of a nickel.

Then came another instance of alleged child abuse last month in Revere. A mother of a 3-year-old took the child to Boston Medical Center for treatment for wounds including what appeared to be burn marks on the child’s arm caused by a heated fork, according to the Suffolk DA’s office.

Revere Police responded to the hospital and took the woman’s statement. She told them that Bautista-Zepeda had regularly babysat her child. After she noticed the wounds, the mother installed a camera in the child’s bedroom. Prosecutors say the camera recorded damning evidence of Bautista-Zepeda’s assault on the child at around 11 a.m. on April 3.

The recording, as Portnoy described it, depicted the child walking toward Bautista-Zepeda “with his arms outstretched as if to be picked up. Bautista-Zepeda then lifts the child with both hands above his own head and forcefully throws the child down onto the bed.”

As the child cried in pain, Portnoy continued, Bautista-Zepeda punches the child in the abdomen three times and then mounts the child and “places both hands over the child’s mouth and nose, bearing his weight down onto the child through his arms and holding the child down by the neck.

“The child is seen on the video struggling to breathe for approximately nineteen seconds as Bautista-Zepeda held his hands over the child’s mouth and nose,” Portney said.

2 men charged in Boston armed bank robberies

Federal prosecutors have now charged two men with the robberies of two Boston banks last month.

title: Funds for fallen Boston firefighter’s family raise thousands
text:
Members of the community are stepping up to support the family of a Boston firefighter killed in a three-alarm blaze over the weekend.

A GoFundMe started by the Greg Hill Foundation has raised more than $19,000 for the family of Robert “Bobby” “BK” Kilduff Jr as of Monday evening.

The foundation had noted that it would match donations up to $10,000.

According to the fundraiser, Kilduff leaves behind two adult children, a girlfriend, and her kids.

Kilduff died after falling through a third-story window while fighting a fire at home on Treadway Road in Dorchester Saturday night. All five residents of the family made it out of the house alive.

After his death, his colleagues and friends said Kilduff would be remembered both for his dedication to his job and his family.

“He was a jake’s jake,” fellow firefighter Victor Gaybor said. “A hard charger. He was the man. We went to him, and he did what he could for all of us.”

A third-generation firefighter and a Marine, Kilduff saved countless lives, members of the department said.

He was also remembered as a community volunteer, a coach, and a dad.

“More than anything else, BK was passionate about being a father,” the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts, where Kilduff was a part of the staff, wrote in a post on social media. “The PFFM sends all of our love and support to both of his children and will stand with Boston Firefighters Local 718 IAFF to ensure they have whatever they need.”

title: Memorial Day: Boston honors legacy of Puerto Rican veterans
text:
Local leaders capped off Memorial Day weekend with a service at the Puerto Rican Veterans Monument Plaza — the first monument honoring Puerto Rican veterans in the country — to honor a often-overlooked group who’ve sacrificed many throughout the history of the U.S.

“Today’s a very special salute to all our military families, and may God bless always our heroes who gave their lives to preserve our freedom and who served our nation,” said Antonio Molina, president of the Puerto Rican Veterans Monument Square Association. “May God continue to support our freedom, because freedom definitely is not free.”

At the Puerto Rican Veterans Monument in the South End, the mayor and national, state and local representatives gathered with the military community as the morning rain turned to a mild spring afternoon.

Leaders spoke to all those who’d lost their lives in military service Monday, but particularly the Puerto Rican veterans.

U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton noted that since the first Puerto Rican regiment was established in 1899 and since becoming US citizens in 1917 “more than 200,000 Puerto Ricans have worn the uniform of the United States military.”

Mayor Michelle Wu said the group has “part of every conflict in this country and who have stepped up to serve at twice the rate of the population as a whole.” Molina added that Puerto Rico has lost more people per capita in military conflicts than any state in the nation since the Revolutionary War.

“I always think about their incredible service to our nation, giving back, sacrificing, putting themselves in harm’s way, and then I think of their families too, not treated with the same level of respect and dignity across America,” said City Councilor Ed Flynn.

Several elected officials, including Flynn, Moulton, and state Sen. Nick Collins, spoke to their own experience with military service.

“Tragically, while some of those Marines came home to build lives and raise families, others did not,” Moulton said of those he served with. “And today, on Memorial Day, we’re here for them. We’re here to remember the names, the faces, and the unfulfilled futures of the generations of Americans who made the ultimate sacrifice, so that others wouldn’t have to.”

Speakers urged residents to honor Memorial Day by remembering those who’ve lost their lives and committing to acts of service in their memory.

“There is no greater tribute we can offer our fallen Puerto Rican brothers and sisters than to ensure this nation remains a place where every person can live with freedom, dignity, and peace, and we always remember their sacrifice,” said state Rep. John Moran. “May we honor their memory through our actions.”

The mayor heralded Boston’s commitment to the legacy of those who served, saying the names of military members who’ve died are across Boston’s heroes squares and “etched in our hearts.”

The community also took a moment of silence for the firefighter and former Marine Robert “Bobby” Kilduff, who died while going in to rescue people from a house fire in Dorchester late Saturday night, and spoke of his legacy.

“I want to ask everyone to say a prayer for the Kilduff family, for our firefighters, and for our city, because many of those who serve lay everything on the line for our country, and then when they come home, they continue to put their lives on the line,” said Wu. “For all the veterans who are still serving our city, particularly to our first responders, who risk everything 24 hours a day to be there to run towards the danger.”

title: ‘This is a big void’: Robert “BK” Kilduff remembered for his love of family, firefighting
text:
A few weeks ago, Boston Firefighter Robert Kilduff was busy arranging for members of the department to attend the dignified transfer and services of a State Police Trooper killed on the job.

Now, his friends and colleagues are left to figure out how to organize Kilduff’s own send off after he died fighting a fire in Dorchester over the weekend.

“I’ve reached for my phone three or four times to call him,” said Sam Dillon, the president of the Local 718, the Boston Firefighter’s union. “We’re planning his services, we’re trying to take care of his family… We’re gonna get it done, I just don’t know how we’re gonna do it without BK.”

Kilduff, known to his friends as “BK” or sometimes Bobby, was always the person to turn to in moments like this — he had boundless energy, a level head, and a deep well of generosity, several union leaders who called Kilduff their friend told the Herald.

Ed Kelly, the General President of the International Association of Fire Fighters, had a picture on his phone of Kilduff standing next to the widow and baby of young Army Sgt. Shane Duffy, a Taunton native killed in the war in Iraq in 2008. Kilduff, a Marine himself, had helped organize the services.

“This is the epitome of what he did, he just showed up when people needed help,” Kelly said.

“Bobby knew you needed his help before you did,” Rich MacKinnon Jr., president of the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts, added.

Kelly said he’d felt that especially after his son, now 16, was diagnosed with cancer at 4 years old.

Kilduff created a website and a social media campaign to start a prayer chain for Kelly’s son. “I would credit all the prayers that my son got for helping to save his life,” Kelly said.

Kelly had originally worked with Kilduff’s father, Robert Kilduff Sr., who was his vice president at the Local 718 after Kelly was first elected president in the early 2000s. Kilduff Sr. was a father-figure to Kelly, and after he died from a job-related cancer he’d developed after years of firefighting, the younger Kilduff stepped up and became his “right hand.”

And Kilduff did everything, worked late, sometimes slept in his office, always took things off other people’s plates. They joked that they won’t really know the true extent to Kilduff’s responsibilities until the coming weeks and months.

“We’ll know when the rent doesn’t get paid and lights go off,” Jay Colbert, a friend of Kilduff and his family and the VP of IAFF’s District 3, joked.

Somehow, though, between the job, the union, and all the work he did for the community — Kilduff also volunteered for the Gary Sinese Foundation helping the families of fallen first responders and veterans — Colbert said Kilduff still managed to always be there for his family.

“He was the quintessential on-the-scene dad,” Colbert said. “Big Disney guy because his kids liked Disney.”

“I think Bobby liked Disney, too,” Colbert added with a smile and a laugh.

They said that Kilduff’s two children, Mason, 22, a Marine, and Hanna Jane, 24, who is in education, take after him and have shown incredible resilience.

In addition to the more than $60,000 raised by both the Greg Hill Foundation and the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts for them, Kelly said that the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, created in honor of a firefighter who died in 911, has said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

Kelly said they were “completely overwhelmed” and relieved about the stress that they took off their shoulders.

Kilduff is also survived by his longtime girlfriend, who Kelly said, “lost the love of her life,” as well as her daughters who are 12 and 14 years old and Kilduff adored.

The fallen firefighter’s services are scheduled for next week. The wake will be held from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. at Avila Church in West Roxbury on Sunday and the funeral will start at 10 a.m. the next day at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington St. in Boston.

“This is a big void… this is a big, big hit,” Colbert said. “Everybody likes to lionize people that pass away and say all nice things, and a lot of times it’s true, but this is — we cannot overstate what BK meant to us.”

title: Police Blotter: East Boston couple threw wood, sprayed water at victims in alleged racial assault
text:
Noise coming from an East Boston restaurant didn’t sit well with a neighboring husband and wife who allegedly sprayed water and threw pieces of wood at a group of patrons and now face assault charges.

East Boston Judge Debra DelVecchio has ordered Arielle Raso, 37, and her husband, Gregory, 39, to stay away from Tertulia’s Cafe at 26 Porter Street, where an alleged racial assault unfolded Monday night.

Around 8:30 p.m., city police officers returned to Tertulia’s for a reported assault. Less than two hours earlier, BPD had responded to the cafe for a noise complaint from the Rasos, who live next door.

Officers told the couple to contact them again if the noise persisted after 11 p.m. When police returned to the Porter Street restaurant at 8:30, a female alerted them of a verbal altercation between the Rasos and her party.

“The victim said the Rasos complained about the noise and told the victims, who are Hispanic, to ‘get out of this country,’ ” the Suffolk DA’s office said in a release. “They also used racial slurs and threatened to kill the victims.”

The Rasos are accused of breaking off a piece of a shared fence, throwing pieces at the group, and striking a child. The couple also allegedly sprayed the victims with a hose.

“All of the victims reported being hit by water,” the Suffolk DA’s office said. “While interviewing the victims, officers heard Arielle Raso admit she sprayed the group with a hose and heard her say ‘I will kill you, I don’t give a [expletive],’ followed by ‘I’m [expletive] done with all those [multiple racial expletives].’ ”

Arielle Raso, arraigned in East Boston BMC on Tuesday, has been charged with seven counts of assault and battery, seven counts of civil rights violation, seven counts of threatening to commit a crime, and one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on a child under 14.

Gregory Raso has been charged with seven counts of assault and battery, seven counts of civil rights violation, and one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

“The assaults on this group were terrible alone, but the injection of such vile racial rhetoric makes this incident even more appalling,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Our office will not—and our society must not—allow such actions to go unnoticed and unpunished.”

Delvecchio set bail at $750 each, also ordering the Rasos to have no contact with the victims or any restaurant patrons. The Rasos will return to court on July 28 for a pretrial hearing.

Shooting outside a bar near TD Garden

Responding authorities noted they discovered ballistic damage to a parked vehicle and a shattered door at Hotel Indigo, 280 Friend St.

Sullivan’s Tap, at 168 Canal St., posted a video on Instagram showing patrons running for safety after the gunshots. The establishment reported that no one inside was hurt.

The Police Patrolmen’s Association called the incident a “BRAZEN downtown Boston shooting.”

“This is NOT what a safe city looks like,” the union stated on social media on Wednesday. “The numbers don’t lie. Fewer cops means more crime. More crime means LESS SAFETY for EVERYONE.”

No arrests have been made amid the ongoing investigation.

title: Family of fallen Boston firefighter reflects on legacy: ‘My dad was kind of the best’
text:
Robert “BK” Kilduff Jr.’s son and daughter say they were always aware of the dangers of firefighting, but they also knew that their father saved countless lives.

The pain of losing their father is raw, a week after Kilduff died when he fell out of a window while battling a roaring three-alarm blaze in Dorchester last Saturday night.

“It’s unbelievable,” BK’s son, Mason Kilduff, 22, said. “You can never expect it. It’s always on the back of your head, like it’s a ‘what if,’ especially with this job.”

Mason added that his father always set up arrangements for firefighters to mourn fallen first responders, no matter if they died in the line of duty or off the job.

“You never really expect it to happen to you,” BK’s son added, “but we were always aware of the dangers of the job. But I always think about the amount of lives that he saved, himself, … it is unbelievable.”

On Friday, Mason, a Marine; his sister, Hanna Jane Kilduff, 24, studying education; and their father’s longtime girlfriend, Jess Spruell, visited the Boston Fire Rescue 2 station. There, they opened up about their hero’s life and the legacy that he leaves behind.

“He loved his job,” Hanna Jane said. “He loved the people he worked with. He was really proud of the work that he did.”

Just hours before responding to the Dorchester house fire, Kilduff, a 24-year veteran of the force and third-generation firefighter, assisted in a technical rescue, saving a man trapped in an MBTA elevator shaft.

At the scene, Kilduff and his crew stopped flames, shooting through the roof of a three-decker on Treadway Road, from spreading to adjacent houses, saving property and possibly even more lives.

A mayday was called after Kilduff reportedly fell from a third-floor window.

“I always knew that my dad was kind of the best,” Mason told reporters inside the fire station his father worked out of, “whether it was saving lives in a fire, all the volunteering stuff that he did. We were talking about it last night, the lives that he saved that he didn’t know he saved.”

“Being the guy someone could go to,” Mason added of his father, “he didn’t even know that person needed someone to talk to. He was that guy all of the time.”

Though firefighting proved to be one of Kilduff’s main passions, his family said that they will always remember what he did off the job, as a volunteer, as a longtime partner, and as a father.

Outside his job, Kilduff volunteered for the Gary Sinise Foundation, supporting veterans, first responders and the families of fallen heroes across the country.

“He was a hero outside of just being a firefighter,” Hanna Jane said. “I know that people have talked about him as a coach, as a mentor, and obviously as a father. I mean, in every facet of his life, he was always looking to help the people around him. You could be a hero in a lot of ways. He was a hero in all of them.”

Now, the community has rallied to support Kilduff’s family. The Greg Hill Foundation and the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts have raised over $90,000 in separate fundraisers. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation has also said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

Hanna Jane spoke about how she and her father took a trip to Disney World last year. Mason laughed about how he and his father landed on a Duck Boat with Patriots players in the Super Bowl rolling rally parade after the team beat the Seahawks in 2015.

Spruell reflected on how BK, her longtime boyfriend, surprised her family by flying across the country to see her two daughters in Seattle.

“I think making memories was really a priority to him,” Hanna Jane said. “That’s something he always instilled in us: If you have the opportunity to do something, if you’re mulling over a trip that you want to take that you want to do with your family, you should always say yes because you never know how much time you have left with them.”

The fallen firefighter’s wake will be held from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. at Avila Church in West Roxbury on Sunday, and his funeral will start at 10 a.m. on Monday at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington Street in Boston.

“I just want to emphasize how much he loved being a dad,” Spruell said. “He was so strong for them. And I got to see the other side of what he had to do to be the best dad, and I’m just so proud of him. I’m going to miss my best friend.”

title: Wake for fallen Boston firefighter draws hundreds
text:
Hundreds of people lined up outside St. Theresa of Avila to pay their respects to the family of fallen Boston firefighter Robert “Bobby” “BK” Kilduff at his wake Sunday.

Kilduff died while fighting a three-alarm blaze at home in Dorchester May 23. All five residents made it out safely.

As a procession of firefighters and first responders delivered Kilduff and his family to the West Roxbury Church, members of the community stood along the route in the rain, including a little boy in a firefighter’s costume. Afterwards, a line formed down the block, waiting to get inside.

A large America flag hung from Ladder 29 over the scene.

Since his death, the third generation firefighter, union leader, and father has been remembered both for his love of his family and his job.

His kids Hannah Jane, 24, and Mason, 22, said despite all the lives he saved and the effort he put into the community, Kilduff somehow always found time to make memories with them, whether that was a trip to Disney or attending a Pats Superbowl parade and ending up on a duckboat with some of the players.

“I always knew that my dad was kind of the best,” Mason told reporters during a firehouse interview last week.

“I just want to emphasize how much he loved being a dad,” Kilduff’s longtime girlfriend Jess Spruell said. “He was so strong for them. And I got to see the other side of what he had to do to be the best dad, and I’m just so proud of him. I’m going to miss my best friend.”

Fundraisers for Kilduff’s family have raised more than $100,000. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation, created in honor of a firefighter who died in 911, has said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

For Kilduff’s funeral Monday, firefighters from across the country are expected to attended, along side several elected officials including Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.

Kilduff was known for his own work organizing firefighters to make sure they’d attend the services of other first responders. “He just showed up when people needed help,” Ed Kelly, the General President of the International Association of Fire Fighters said of his late friend and colleague.

Kilduff’s funeral services will begin at 10 a.m. at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington St. in Boston.

title: Boston Firefighter Robert ‘BK’ Kilduff Jr. remembered as father, hero at funeral
text:
Fallen Boston firefighter Robert “BK” Kilduff Jr. had warned other firefighters to “get back” right before a portion of a Dorchester home collapsed, and he fell three stories.

Kilduff’s last selfless act mimicked his whole life, fellow Rescue 2 firefighter Lt. Greg Kelly said at his friend and colleague’s funeral service Monday.

“He’s leaving such a hole, I can’t explain it to you,” Kelly said.

Hundreds who filled The Cathedral of the Holy Cross in Boston listened to person after person talk about the ways that Kilduff helped others, while thousands lined Washington Street outside under what started out as a grey sky.

“He spent so much time helping others, he rarely had time for himself,” Vic Gaybor, who also worked alongside Kilduff at Rescue 2, said.

Gaybor said that he and Kilduff referred to themselves as the dynamic duo, even though often they were more like an old married couple, bickering and pulling pranks on each other.

“I’m expecting BK to pop out of a corner and yell, ‘Gotcha’” he said. Oftentimes, the two had such a great time together on the job, that Gaybor said it wouldn’t feel like work.

But when the alarm rang, Kilduff “was the one I wanted on my side,” Gaybor said, explaining his courage was unmatched.

Kilduff was an amazing firefighter, nicknamed “the natural” early in his career, Gaybor said, but he was also dedicated to helping other firefighters and the community.

Gaybor took a long pause standing in front of the mourners, then a big breath before saying, “I wish I could tell you how much I love you.”

As a member of Rescue 2, Kilduff was in one of two specialized units that perform risky, technical rescues city-wide. Several speakers talked about his heroics on the job, including the night of the Dorchester fire that took his life. Along with pushing back his fellow firefighters, Kilduff’s actions helped save the residents of the building, who all made it out alive.

“Because of Bobby Kilduff, five of our neighbors will get to spend more time with the people they love, just like countless other families in our city whose loved ones, sworn and civilian, he saved,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said.

Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall said that the biggest compliment for a firefighter is to be called, “a good jake,” which Kilduff was.

However, “the jake’s jake was an even better man,” Marshall said, adding that Kilduff “preferred to be known as a great dad, a great partner.”

Kilduff’s children Mason, 22, a Marine, and Hanna Jane, 24, an education student, as well as the firefighter’s longtime girlfriend Jess Spruell all spoke at the funeral.

“If you can’t tell from the fact that I look like him but with hair…” Hanna Jane joked as she got up to introduce herself as Kilduff’s daughter.

She described how for her entire life, her dad worked for the Boston Fire Department, which meant she was used to him saving lives and helping others.

In addition to the job, he also worked tirelessly for the union to improve working conditions for other firefighters, and still found time to volunteer for organizations like the Gary Sinise Foundation.

“Nobody was out of the bounds of his compassion,” Hanna Jane said.

But no matter how busy he was, Kilduff was always there for his family.

“He used to say that the only thing he loved more than being a firefighter was being our dad,” she said.

Hanna Jane told the other mourners that she thought because Kilduff knew how precious life was, and how fragile, he always made time for the people that mattered to him. If there was a lesson Kilduff could have imparted, it would have been to, “never postpone joy,” she said.

When Mason spoke next, he joked that speech wouldn’t be as good as his sister’s. Then he started thanking everyone who was in attendance.

“Even the cops, too,” he said, which made the whole church laugh.

Mason said that he and his dad, who was also a Marine, bonded over being Boston guys. The two would call every day, even when Mason was stationed hundreds of miles away, to talk about the city, sports, “what we’d do to fix the Red Sox,” he said.

While Mason was in bootcamp and couldn’t talk on the phone, he said his dad wrote him letters, about 30, which he still has.

Mason described Kilduff as his best friend. “We did everything together,” he said.

“I think if I could be half as good,” Mason said, “we’d be in good shape.”

Standing with them, Spruell said the good in Kilduff was reflected in Hanna Jane and Mason. “You can see his values in them,” she said.

“BK didn’t love half-way,” Spruell said, also next to her two daughters Seren and Brynn, who Kilduff called “his munchkins.”

Spruell remarked how many were at the funeral to honor him, and said that it “reminds us of just how loved he was.”

“If love could have kept someone here forever, BK would have been here a very long time,” she added.

When the services concluded, and the bells rang for Kilduff for the last time, the mourners processed down the aisle of the Cathedral and out to what turned out to be a sunny afternoon.

Kilduff’s coffin, draped with an American flag, was placed back on Engine 42, which had carried him to the services.

The bag pipes played Amazing Grace. Onlookers placed their hands on their hearts and thousands of first responders gave Kilduff a final salute.

People didn’t show up like that because of someone’s titles or accomplishments, Spruell said inside the church, “they show up because of how someone made them feel.”

title: Boston Mayor Wu snubs Senator Collins by endorsing his primary opponent amid ongoing feud
text:
After blowing off his St. Patrick’s Day breakfast, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has snubbed state Sen. Nick Collins again by endorsing his Senate opponent.

Wu backed political newcomer Latoya Gayle Wednesday, in an apparent rebuke of Collins, who she’s sparred with publicly since he blocked her signature tax shift legislation multiple times at the end of 2024, ultimately killing the bill.

“Residents of the 1st Suffolk District deserve a state senator who understands the challenges facing our communities and brings an urgency to find solutions,” Wu said in a statement.

Wu took another swipe at Collins during a Wednesday press conference in Dorchester, where she formally announced her endorsement of Gayle, a senior director of advocacy and family partnerships at Neighborhood Villages.

“We are tired of our own senators blocking solutions that came out of a vote of the City Council and the House of Representatives, town halls, meetings, organizing, unions, state leaders, everyone coming together to say, we need relief, and we need help now,” Wu said, according to the Dorchester Reporter. “We’re tired of feeling like ballot initiatives are the only way to get anything to happen up there.”

Wu has publicly blamed Collins for the failure of her tax shift bill, citing his procedural move to block a vote multiple times before it was ultimately killed by Senate President Karen Spilka due to lack of support.

The bill seeks to provide a tax break to homeowners by increasing commercial tax rates. It was passed by the City Council and House of Representatives three times, but stalled in the Senate.

Wu also snubbed Collins in March, when she chose to skip the annual St. Patrick’s Day Breakfast — and political roast — he hosts in Boston for the first time.

Collins issued a statement through his campaign on Thursday that defended his record, in response to the mayor’s latest endorsement snub.

“Senator Nick Collins has proudly represented the First Suffolk in the Senate for the past eight years,” his campaign spokesperson Vanessa Woo said. “He will continue to do what he does every day — partnering with community leaders to address the challenges residents face, building the local economy, providing working families tax relief, fighting for Boston’s underserved populations, leading state efforts to defend democracy, addressing the mental health and substance abuse crisis, keeping our neighborhoods safe and improving our schools.”

His campaign released an internal polling data memo Wednesday that showed Collins is leading Gayle by a wide margin, 81.7% to 9.5%, three months before the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. A third candidate, Juwan Skeens, is polling at 8.8%.

Collins also boasts a fundraising advantage, with $92,053 cash on hand compared to $15,486 for Gayle, a first-time candidate for elected office from Dorchester. Skeens has about $50 on hand.

Collins, a South Boston Democrat, was first elected to public office in 2010, to the state House of Representatives, and has held his state Senate seat since 2018.

“Senator Collins remains in an incredibly strong position,” his campaign memo stated. “With endorsements from the community, labor and elected leaders coming in the next month, along with the start of a robust media campaign, we only expect his position to grow.”

title: Police Blotter: BPS employee assaulted at Mel King South End Academy
text:

title: Police Blotter: Ex-Tyngsboro daycare worker gets 21+ years in prison for making child porn
text:
A woman who produced pornography of at least three toddlers at a Tyngsboro daycare for the sexual gratification of her trans-woman partner — a former New Hampshire state representative — was sentenced to more than two decades in federal prison.

“Lindsay Groves was every parent’s worst nightmare: a predator hiding in plain sight, in the place they brought their children every morning so that they would be safe and happy while the parents were at work,” federal prosecutors Anne Paruti and Jessica Soto wrote in a sentencing memorandum.

U.S. District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV sentenced Groves, of Hudson, New Hampshire, to 21 years and 10 months in federal prison on Thursday. Groves pleaded guilty last October to three counts of sexual exploitation of children and one count of distribution of child pornography. She will have to register as a sex offender.

Groves immediately filed notice she was appealing the sentence.

Her co-defendant, Stacie Marie Laughton, 41, of Nashua, N.H., a former New Hampshire State Representative, pleaded guilty last November to three counts of sexual exploitation of children and has yet to be sentenced.

Prosecutors had recommended a sentence of 35 years in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release.

Prosecutors wrote that Groves, a teacher at the since-shuttered Creative Minds daycare in Tyngsboro, “took advantage of her access to children to feed the sexual desires of her then-girlfriend,” Laughton.

“In the midst of an ongoing text-based conversation where Groves and Laughton discussed their mutual sexual interest in the children and what they would like to do with the children, the defendant followed through on what they had discussed,” prosecutors wrote.

“She took them into the bathroom, where no one would see what she was doing, and she created graphic imagery of the children’s genitals with her cell phone. She then sent the photographs to Laughton, and the two used the images to fuel their sexually-motivated conversations,” prosecutors continued.

In all, the feds say Groves traded 2,500 text messages with Laughton and that these messages discussed child exploitation at length and included sexually explicit images of children in her care. Prosecutors say she used bathroom breaks and “naptime” routines as opportunities to record the children.

Excerpts from the pair’s text message conversations included in court documents are for the most part extremely explicit, including detailed descriptions of desired activity with the children pictured in the images.

Prosecutors summarized the messages sent over a five week period leading up to their arrest as demonstrating “an active relationship in which they discussed past sexual encounters, explicit descriptions of sex with each other and others, and indicia of their personal relationship. … The messages also included the discussion about and transfer of child pornography featuring Minors 1, 2, and 3, all of whom were at the time three-year-old students at the childcare facility.”

The gravity of the crimes was made apparent not just in the details provided in court documents but by how family members of children at the daycare reacted when the perverted duo appeared in court for their arraignments.

“I want to (expletive) kill that (expletive),” a tearful woman cried from the gallery at the close of the first hearing in federal court in Boston on June 28, 2023.

title: Beach report full of good vibes: Metro coastlines hit new clean water record
text:
The beaches around Boston are making the grade.

Every metropolitan beach from Nahant to Nantasket received water quality scores over 80% for the first time in the since testing began, the conservation group Save the Harbor/Save the Bay announced in their annual Water Quality Report Card.

“The region-wide scores above 80% are a testament to what sustained investment and scientific rigor can achieve,” said the group’s Executive Director, Chris Mancini. “As we mark our 40th anniversary this year, we are as committed as ever to ensuring anyone can confidently get into or out on the water without worrying about bacteria and other pollution.”

The annual Water Quality Report Card assesses water quality at public beaches including Lynn, Nahant, Revere, Winthrop, East Boston, South Boston, Dorchester, Quincy, and Hull using Department of Conservation and Recreation data.

Every beach tested scored above 80% for water quality rating for 2025, the report stated, marking a high level of clean and safe swimming conditions across the region.

The testing measures the number of colony forming units of enterococci bacteria in water samples, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s standard unit used to determine safe swimming conditions.

South Boston’s beaches ranked at the top of the list, with City Point beach receiving a 100% water quality rating for the sixth year in a row. Pleasure Bay dropped slightly to a 97% rating from its typical perfect scores, still maintaining a 100% six-year average, while M Street Beach and Carson Beach rated 94% and 95% respectively.

Among other high scores, Nantasket Beach jumped to a 100% rating in 2025, up from 92% in 2024.

Savin Hill Beach also made a substantial comeback in 2025 with a perfect 100% rating, a sharp incline from 68% the year before, the report showed. The beach showed notable fluctuations in the year’s prior, with an 80% score in 2023 and 94% in 2022.

Nahant Beach saw another jump to 95% after hovering around 80% for the previous four years, the report stated.

Of all the beaches tested, Lynn’s King’s Beach saw the largest rating increase in 2025, from 66% in 2024 — and a record low of 55% in 2023 — to 90% in 2025.

The organization cited a pilot UV treatment program in the beach’s water quality improvement, along with a “dry summer weather and the improvement to the sewage pipes over the years.”

The Massachusetts beaches use a posting a flagging system to alert the public to high bacteria levels, Save the Harbor said, though the “best technology available takes 24 hours to return results, meaning by the time the posting goes up, the information is already out of date.”

The organization recommended residents use the Department of Public Health’s interactive beach water quality dashboard and “not swim 24 hours after a heavy rain fall event,” which is marked by over 0.3 inches of precipitation per hour.

Department of Conservation and Recreation Commissioner Nicole LaChapelle called Massachusetts’s urban beaches “some of the cleanest” in the country, saying it reflects “decades of collaboration and stewardship focused on protecting and improving our public waterfronts.”

“It makes a real difference in how people experience our beaches and waterfronts,” LaChapelle said. “Clean water is essential, and access to it for recreation is a matter of equity. We remain committed to ensuring these coastal spaces stay resilient, accessible, and welcoming for generations to come.”

title: As FIFA Fan Festival opens at Boston City Hall Plaza, officials tell fans to look elsewhere
text:
The FIFA Fan Festival is set to open at Boston City Hall Plaza on Friday, but officials say soccer fans who are looking to get in at the door will have to go elsewhere to watch the World Cup.

The festivities are already sold out on Friday and Saturday, according to officials.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu is encouraging fans to try to grab a spot for the other 14 days of the festival, through June 27. At the same time, she recommends people interested in the excitement to start planning to attend alternative watch parties.

“I also want to be clear that for all of this, throughout the entire time, safety is our number one priority,” Wu said. “We want Fan Fest to be fun and welcoming for everyone, so please just be mindful of increased pedestrian traffic around City Hall, make a plan for how to get here, and register online in advance if you want to attend Fan Fest.”

“Because of capacity, and because of such interest,” the mayor added, “registration doesn’t guarantee entry if the plaza reaches capacity.”

Nearly 150,000 fans have already registered to attend the fan festival, said Mike Loynd, the president and CEO of the Boston Soccer 2026 nonprofit host committee. He noted that capacity is set to 5,000 fans at any one time.

Fans must select the day(s) and match(es) they want to attend the fan festival, and children under 18 must submit a parent/guardian waiver.

“We wanted to give everyone an even chance,” Loynd said, “and we certainly didn’t want to have just a first-come, first-served structure.”

The festival is set to feature live broadcasts of two to three matches a day, musical performances, a curated cultural showcase, and local food vendors. On Saturday and Sunday, Haiti fans and the “Tartan Army” will participate in fan walks around City Hall Plaza, with parking restrictions in effect for all events.

“This is going to be the epic epicenter of Boston soccer football for the next 16 days,” Meet Boston President and CEO Martha Sheridan said. “When you’re standing outside, and you hear the volume on this screen, you know this is going to excite the entire city.”

Elsewhere in the city, the Wu administration is sponsoring community watch parties in Dorchester, East Boston, and at the Parkman Bandstand on Boston Common, among other venues to be announced.

As World Cup ticket costs soar, at least 500 city residents will head to Foxboro to watch games live at Gillette Stadium, rebranded as “Boston Stadium.”

Wu said Thursday that her office has worked with “private sector partners” Boston Soccer 2026 and the state Legislature to secure over 500 “free” tickets for community members, particularly children and their families.

“Soccer belongs to the people,” the mayor said.

title: Police identify eight arrested at Boston City Hall for ‘coordinated disruption’ of Council meeting
text:
Boston Police identified the eight people arrested at Boston City Hall for their “coordinated disruption” of a City Council meeting and said they were charged with trespassing.

Seven were arrested at City Hall. An eighth individual, a 28-year-old woman, was not arrested on scene, but was also charged with trespassing after police took out a criminal complaint at Boston Municipal Court.

The eight people arrested were Jonathan M. Barry, 40, of Roslindale; Nancy Ellen Griffin, 59; Margaret Hughes, 32; Linda A. Jenkins, 77, of Malden; George Lee, Jr., 43, of Dorchester; Vikiana Petit-Homme, 24; Rebecca A. Pierce, 82, of Dorchester; and Ashley Ryder, 28, of Brighton.

Addresses weren’t provided for some of the people, who were arrested after Wednesday’s City Council meeting was interrupted by activists protesting the $4.9 billion city budget for about two hours.

The protest proved to be the only dramatic part of the meeting. The budget was approved nearly unanimously by the Council, 12-1, with about $11.2 million in amendments.

Police detailed efforts to get the situation under control over the course of the lengthy protest, which began at approximately 2:50 p.m., soon after the budget came before the Council for discussion.

At that time, police said, “a group of 15 to 20 individuals who had been seated in the public gallery of the Iannella Chamber rose in unison, unfurled signs bearing political messages, crossed into the restricted area of the chamber, and began loudly chanting and waving signs, bringing the meeting to a halt.”

“City Council President Liz Breadon, who was presiding over the meeting, repeatedly called the chamber to order but was unable to restore decorum due to the level of noise,” police said.

Adult and youth activists chanted, “You failed us,” and “Tell us where the money goes.”

The clash capped a chaotic budget process fueled by community opposition over grant funding and youth job cuts, along with about 400 layoffs at Boston Public Schools.

Police said the decision was made to clear the Council chamber, “due to the rapidly evolving situation, including uncertainty about the chamber’s occupancy level and safe egress.” While bystanders complied, activists remained.

Staff from the city’s Property Management Department, which has the authority to issue trespass notices, advised activists who refused to leave voluntarily that they would be considered trespassing for “actively disrupting a public meeting,” police said.

Police said officers on scene chose to engage in de-escalation, rather than directly interact with the protestors.

Officers enlisted city councilors who volunteered to serve as intermediaries to negotiate with the activists, which led to about half the group leaving voluntarily and being escorted out of City Hall without further incident, police said.

“The remaining eight individuals refused to leave,” police said. “They lay on the floor and linked arms. City Council staff and city officials informed them on multiple occasions that they were required to vacate the premises or face arrest.”

Police said officers allotted another 30 minutes for negotiations, but were told that the remaining protesters “would not leave willingly.”

“Officers then made a formal verbal announcement, in the presence of a PMD representative, informing each individual that PMD had deemed them no longer welcome in City Hall,” police said.

“Officers spoke with each person individually, confirmed they understood the announcement, and offered each a final opportunity to leave,” police added. “Each individual indicated they understood but remained on the floor.”

Police then began making arrests. The Council meeting resumed around 5 p.m.

title: South Boston lemonade stand robbed at gunpoint, police say
text:
Boston Police are investigating two pint-sized hoodlums suspected of putting the squeeze on a children’s lemonade stand in Southie — at gunpoint.

“There is little I can think of more disturbing than the innocence of a children’s lemonade stand being violated by an armed robbery,” Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn, who represents portions of South Boston, said after learning of the crime.

“When something as serious as this happens, we cannot downplay or ignore it. As a City, we have to finally acknowledge we have serious public safety issues in Boston. We desperately need more police officers and to redouble our community policing efforts,” Flynn continued.

Boston Police responded to a report of an armed robbery at 157 W. 9th St. in South Boston at around 4:45 p.m. Wednesday, according to the police report. There, they met up with the child victims who were now with their father.

The children said that two boys had “made several passes by the Lemonade Stand before they approached and asked whether or not they would accept Apple Pay,” according to the report. Before the young lemonade entrepreneurs could respond, however, the child robbers grabbed the stand’s cashbox, which contained about $50 in cash, and one of the suspects flashed a black handgun before the pair ran off.

The children described the suspects, according to the report. One “was described as a dark-skinned black male about 14-years-old wearing a black Nike sheisty, black shirt, unknown color shorts and high white socks, this suspect displayed a black firearm in his waistband.” The second suspect “was described as a light-skinned black male about 11 years-old with a black sheisty and unknown clothing description.”

A “sheisty” is apparently a term for a balaclava, or full-face covering, according to images of the clothing on Nike’s website.

The children told police that the suspects had run off toward W. 9th Street before reaching Dorchester Street. The local police intelligence agency, the Boston Regional Intelligence Center, says its cameras did not face toward the incident.

Police ask that anyone with any information regarding these suspects contact detectives at 617-343-4742 or submit information anonymously through the CrimeStoppers Tip Line by calling 1-800-494-TIPS (8477) or texting the word “TIP” to CRIME (27463).

Hospice care Medicare scam on the rise, feds say

The Federal Bureau of Investigation has issued a warning that scammers are billing victim Medicare accounts for hospice care services — sometimes even for hospices who don’t provide such services.

The FBI says that recent schemes have included “enrolling Medicare recipients in hospice care despite patients having no terminal illness or chronic condition” and even enrolling the patients in hospice care without their knowledge.

“Some scammers use door-to-door solicitation tactics and offer free home services such as house cleaning and meal delivery, which are conditional on using a specific hospice,” the FBI notice states.

The FBI recommends that Medicare enrollees be sure to “never give out Medicare or other insurance information to anyone who is not your doctor,” be wary of “too good to be true offers” or incentives like gift cards, use official resources like Medicare’s Hospice Compare website at Medicare.gov/care-compare/ to look up a provider’s quality rating, and to regularly “review your explanation of benefits statements and Medicare Summary Notices for unknown providers and services.”

People who believe they have been a victim of a fraudulent activity can file a report with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov, and are asked to “include as much information as possible, such as identifying information about the company or health care provider including name, phone number, address, email address, and website.”

title: Boston Fire’s Charitable Association holds annual memorial weeks after on-duty death
text:
The Charitable Association of the Boston Fire Department held its annual Memorial Service at the Firefighter’s Lot at the Forest Hill Cemetery Sunday.

The service has been since the 1890s to commemorate firefighters who have passed away and to ensure they get a proper burial.

title: Boston radio legend Eddie Andelman dies: ‘The godfather of sports radio’
text:
Boston radio legend Eddie Andelman, who “changed and elevated the sports radio game,” has died, his family announced on Monday. He was 89.

Andelman, who was on the local radio airwaves for 42 years, helped launch the sports talk radio format that became the model for today.

“From humble roots in Dorchester, he went onto great success in business and broadcasting,” his sons Dave, Mike and Dan posted on the Phantom Gourmet social media accounts.

“Some call him the godfather of sports radio,” his sons added. “He certainly changed and elevated the sports radio game.”

His children carry on the broadcast tradition as the Phantom Gourmet brothers.

Beginning in 1969, Andelman, along with two other sports enthusiasts, debuted Sports Huddle, providing New England’s rabid sports fans their first opportunity to participate in a live, on-air, interactive sports show.

It quickly became a ratings success on WEEI and then on WHDH, where it ran for 17 years.

“Andelman’s astute observations and good humor attracted fans of all ages to join the discussions,” reads his bio in the Massachusetts Broadcasters Hall of Fame. “The show became a model for similar programs across the country.

“As the audiences grew, the show expanded from a weekly Sunday night feature to a prime time weekday series and was a precursor of the all-sports radio format stations that we know today,” his bio continues.

Over the years, through the Sports Huddle and other venues, Andelman participated in some 13,000 radio broadcasts and over 1,200 television commentaries on channels 5 and 7 as well.

Andelman received numerous awards for his community work, including Jimmy Fund Man of the Year, Joey Fund Man of the Year, and Jewish Big Brother Man of the Year.

His 21 Hot Dog Safaris raised more than $5 million for the Joey Fund-Cystic Fibrosis.

“Eddie worked tirelessly on the Hot Dog Safari for the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation because he loved to give people a great time and he was thankful that his own family was healthy,” his sons wrote.

Andelman and his wife Judi were married for more than five decades.

“Eddie Andelman was loved by his wife of fifty-seven years, worshipped by his sons, and adored by his grandchildren,” his sons wrote.

“There would be no Phantom Gourmet without Eddie Andelman,” they added. “His passion and pride in the work, down-to-earth and sometimes irreverent style, and the reverence for small business owners and hard-working people only enriched our lives and many others as well. We learned all that we do from our dad. He was one of a kind. He helped thousands and entertained millions. Eddie Andelman lived a truly incredible life.”

Those in the sports radio world reminisced about Andelman after news broke of his passing on Monday, sending their condolences to his loved ones.

“Sorry to hear of the passing of Eddie Andelman,” posted Glenn Ordway, who was a longtime sports radio host at WEEI. “He was THE pioneer for Boston sports talk radio who set the bar for all others to live up to. My prayers and condolences to Judy and the entire Andelman family.”

“Legend. Pioneer in sports radio,” posted Mike Mutnansky, formerly of WEEI and now at Barstool Sports. “Truly a 1 of 1 character. And generous to me and many other WEEI interns over the years. Condolences to Eddie’s family and friends.”

title: Boston Police Blotter: Officers break up fight at World Cup watch party
text:
Three men were arrested after a fight broke out during a World Cup watch party at a Downtown bar Monday night.

Boston Police officers responded to Estella Restaurant on Temple Street around 5:44 p.m, according to a police report. The restaurant was in the news earlier this year after it hosted an afterhours party for the New England Patriots, leading the establishment to have its liquor license suspended for a day.

The officers were responding to a radio call for an assist, the report said, and by the time they arrived, they knew that the restaurant was hosting a watch party for the Cape Verde vs. Spain World Cup game.

They also knew that the Transit Police had reported two parties in the bathroom, which the report noted had already led to “multiple arrests.”

When they got to the scene, the officers saw a large crowd inside and outside the restaurant, the report said, with officers seeing two people engaging in a verbal dispute.

They officers tried to de-escalate the argument and separate the individuals.

“After being on the scene for approximately twenty minutes, and as officers were attempting to clear the scene and disperse the crowd, officers observed both parties from the earlier verbal dispute… walk in the same direction on Washington Street and re-engage in a verbal dispute,” the report said.

The suspects, 21-year-olds Kevin Mendes and Geormanie Ortiz, started to fight “in the middle of the street,” according to the report, with other people jumping in to mix.

Officers then say Victor Barbosa, 20, allegedly kick Mendes in the neck multiple times while wearing sneakers.

More officers responded and de-escalated the situation, the report said.

Both Mendes and Ortiz were charged with affray, while Barbosa faces one court of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

Former mailman pleads guilty to failing to deliver mail

Khalea Turner, 29, of Hull, stuffed the mail in a U-Haul storage locker he rented instead of stuffing it in people’s mail boxes, a statement from the office said. The practice went on for about three years between November 2022 and January 2023.
