title: Patriots special teams legend Matthew Slater helps tackle anti-violence campaign
text:
A prominent anti-violence nonprofit in the city is adding a special teammate to help tackle a groundbreaking campaign.

Three-time Super Bowl champion Matthew Slater, who for 16 years was a Patriots’ fan favorite as an elite special teams captain, is helping push a fundraiser for the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute.

Slater will be headlining a fundraiser for the institute next week, while they raise money to construct a building for outreach space — which will be a “place of refuge,” the Pats legend tells the Herald.

The nonprofit is trying to raise a total of $25 million for its “Campaign for Peace,” as the institute looks to build the National Center of Healing, Teaching, and Learning in Dorchester.

“People go through a lot, the human experience brings you a lot, and a lot of it is very hard,” Slater told the Herald this week.

“But to be able to have a space where you can come and try to heal and move forward from that, find common ground with the people you’re in community with, I think we need more spaces like this, and it’s so great to see the work that they’re doing,” he added.

The new center for the Peace Institute — named for founder, president and CEO Chaplain Clementina Chery’s 15-year-old son who was shot and killed in 1993 — will be located at 30 Westville St., across from Up Academy Dorchester.

The Boston-based nonprofit has served the local area since 1994, providing support to families and communities impacted by murder, trauma, grief and loss.

On the L-shaped plot of land, the plan is to build a 19,000-square-foot center with public and private spaces for survivor and reentry support services, counseling, youth programming, training, and arts and movement therapy. The new site will also feature outdoor spaces for gatherings, meditations and community events.

“For the folks in that community to have a place of refuge where they can come and kind of lay their burdens down, I think is huge,” said Slater, who lives in Milton. “It’s so important that we have spaces like that, and they’re harder and harder to come by in the world that we live in, so it’s going to be a beacon of hope.”

Pre-development for the center is well underway, and the institute’s focus this year is on securing the capital needed to begin construction.

“Matthew Slater embodies the values of leadership, service, and community that are central to our mission,” Chery said. “We are honored to welcome him as we bring together supporters committed to building safer, healthier communities.”

The fundraiser “Champions for Peace: An Evening of Life, Legacy, and Action” will be next Thursday, June 25, at Willowbend Country Club in Mashpee.

It will be a “special night of inspiration, connection, and purpose in support of the Institute’s first-of-its-kind National Center of Healing, Teaching, and Learning,” reads a promo for the event.

“Enjoy an elegant evening featuring cocktails, hors d’oeuvres, meaningful conversation, and a powerful program with Matthew Slater, whose leadership on and off the field has inspired countless people,” the promo continues. “Together, we’ll celebrate what’s possible when communities unite around healing, resilience, and action.

“Your participation will help bring to life a groundbreaking Center that will transform a vacant lot in Boston’s Four Corners neighborhood into a national destination for healing, education, and hope,” the fundraiser promo adds. “More than a building, the Center will stand as a beacon of possibility, a place where individuals, families, and communities impacted by violence can find support, connection, and a path forward.”

The fundraiser will be from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m.

General admission tickets cost $100, and VIP access tickets from 6:30 to 7 p.m. to meet Slater and WBZ’s Steve Burton cost $200.

title: Police Blotter: Karen Read case Canton cop Sean Goode gets decertified
text:
Another police officer involved in the Karen Read investigation has had his law enforcement certification suspended.

This time it is Sean Goode, the Canton Police sergeant who recently resigned just ahead of Read’s lawsuit that revealed obscene and racist text messages he shared with ex-State Police Trooper Michael Proctor.

“The Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission hereby suspends the law enforcement certification of the Respondent Sean Goode,” the Commission wrote in its order. “The Commission voted to suspend the Respondent’s certification upon determining that it is in the best interest of the health, safety, or welfare of the public.”

Goode was supervisor of the Canton PD overnight shift when Boston Police Officer John O’Keefe’s body was discovered on the front lawn of another Boston cop’s house on Jan. 29, 2022.

Read’s attorneys expressed a belief during the first of Read’s two trials that Goode, whose testimony was rather limited, was “more of a straight shooter” than other police on the scene in those early hours of the investigation.

That understanding appears shattered after Read successfully obtained text messages shared between Goode and Proctor, the lead investigator of the case that led to Read being charged with O’Keefe’s murder, that painted a picture of two heavily biased and corrupt cops.

Proctor was placed on administrative leave immediately after the first trial ended in mistrial. His time on the stand led to a cross-examination that revealed a slew of wildly offensive text messages he sent to colleagues and even old high school buddies showing clear bias against Read from the start. Proctor was fired after the second trial concluded with Read’s acquittal on all charges save for drunken driving. Proctor at first fought for his job back but ultimately dropped that battle.

The biases of police investigating her laid the foundation for the defense theory of a local conspiracy to frame Read for O’Keefe’s murder and to protect others who were actually responsible.

The lawsuit Read filed earlier this month uncovered much deeper bias than even that revealed by Proctor’s time on the stand. It has also created a mad dash for defense attorneys representing clients investigated by these cops to get all the sordid details to see if the materials could help free their own clients.

“They are not officers who occasionally voiced an offensive remark,” Read’s attorneys wrote of Proctor and Goode in the lawsuit complaint. “They are men whose written and recorded communications — sent to one another and to a circle of like-minded friends over the course of a decade — establish entrenched and unrepentant hatred for women, Black Americans, Asian Americans, Jews, Hispanics, Arabs, and gay people.”

title: Battenfeld: Michelle Wu’s unlikely nemesis — ex-con Dianne Wilkerson — emerges as political force
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu now has an unlikely nemesis – former state Senator and ex-convict Dianne Wilkerson, who has emerged as a political force and no-holds-barred critic of the Wu administration.

Wilkerson, who pleaded guilty to eight felony counts of taking $23,500 in bribes in 2010, has been posting on social media and sending media emails blasting Wu on everything from co-opting Juneteenth for political purposes to the White Stadium project to the city’s redesign plan for Blue Hill Avenue.

Wilkerson, who ran for her old seat in 2022, is trying to mobilize Boston’s Black community in what could be an attempt to put together a powerful voting bloc in a future election. So she is a threat to Wu and has the potential to embarrass her nationally.

Wilkerson says she is “absolutely not” interested in running for political office again but is motivated to speak up for her community in Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan, which she says has been ignored by Wu.

“I am in a place where I can say what I want and need to say without fear of retribution, which has become a hallmark of her mayoralty and quieted so many people,” Wilkerson said in an interview. “I don’t have a contract. I don’t need a contract.”

Wu’s administration has tried to marginalize Wilkerson by pointing out her extortion conviction and questioning whether residents really listen to her. Wilkerson became infamous nationally because of the feds’ picture of her stuffing the bribes into her bra.

But Wilkerson said she will not go away and won’t change her hard-charging style of confronting Wu. And because of Wilkerson’s credibility in the Black community, she represents more of a threat to Wu than Councilor Ed Flynn, who is routinely ignored by Wu.

“It’s not about throwing bombs for me,” she said. “If I don’t feel Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan are getting their due I will say something.”

Wilkerson’s chief complaint is something Wu critics often point to – the mayor’s seeming inability to listen to opposing views and meet with residents like those affected by the White Stadium project in Franklin Park.

“When you called (former Mayor) Marty Walsh he called me back,” she said. “This woman does not do that. If you criticize anything she does you become the enemy. It’s scorched earth.”

Wilkerson, now 71, said she’s been working with Boston mayors since Ray Flynn in the 1980’s and her criticisms are not personal.

“I just deal with facts and that’s what’s driving the Wu cabal so crazy,” she said.

Wilkerson and others most recently appealed to the Trump administration to stop Wu’s plan to turn Blue Hill Avenue into a one-lane street by creating a center lane for buses only. They asked the Trump Department of Transportation to withdraw $80 million in funding for the project.

Wilkerson said she went to the Trump administration to “protect” the Black community – months after Wu said she would protect the city from Trump.

“I am extremely well aware I have an enormous amount of respect from people within this community so it’s driving them nuts,” Wilkerson said. “I don’t have a contract with the city. I don’t want one. They can’t control me in a way they are threatening other people.”

Wilkerson’s latest complaint is about Juneteenth, which Wu and Gov. Maura Healey are turning into a political event in Franklin Park.

“I think it is beyond the height of insult for the mayor and governor to be inviting people to come to Franklin Park to celebrate Juneteenth in the park that you have refused to discuss with the community. What kind of chutzpah does that take?”

title: Woman allegedly struck, killed by carjack suspect in Mattapan
text:
A woman died after being struck by a carjacking suspect in Mattapan Saturday, according to Boston Police.

The suspect, Ibraim Matos, 37, of Hyde Park, faces charges of murder, carjacking, leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death, and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in personal injury, the department said in a statement.

He is expected to be arraigned at Dorchester District Court.

Officers responded to Blue Hill Avenue around 2 p.m. Saturday for a report of a pedestrian hit by a car. When they arrived, the 32-year-old victim was lying on the ground. She was pronounced dead on the scene, police said.

Before hitting the victim, police said the driver allegedly crashed his vehicle up the street, exited his car, then carjacked another vehicle.

In addition to the initial crash near Woodhaven Street and the collision involving the pedestrian near Fairway Street, police said the suspect hit several other vehicles including an MBTA bus.

By the time officer got to the suspect, a large crowd had formed and several community members were restraining Matos, BPD said in a statement.

Video from bystanders at the scene appeared to show people subduing the suspect as he attempted to exited the allegedly stolen vehicle, which had crashed into the bus.

Matos was transported to the hospital and is in police custody.

The department said the victim would be identified after an autopsy was performed and her family was notified.

Boston City Councilor for District 5 Enrique Pepén issued a statement Saturday extending his condolences to the victim’s family.

“Any loss of life under these circumstances is devasting and leaves a lasting impact on our neighborhood,” he wrote.

Pepén also thanked first responders, “who responded so quickly and professionally during a difficult and rapidly evolving situation,” and members of the community, whose actions “reflect the care and concern that so many members of our community have for one another.”

“We are devastated by the senseless act of violence on Blue Hill Avenue that took a woman’s life, left others injured, and has shaken the Mattapan community and our City,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in her own statement. “Our hearts are with the victim’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as everyone impacted by this terrible tragedy.”

title: 16 Boston community center pools open for summer following repair work
text:
With one more pool now open, all but a handful of the city-run community center pools will be operational this summer – after years of maintenance projects had over half closed just a few years ago.

“I know this moment has been a long time coming, so we’re so excited that it’s here,” said Mayor Michelle Wu at the opening of the Hennigan Pool in Jamaica Plain on Monday. “It is really because of years of advocacy, feedback, and community participation in shaping all the different parts of this, that now the Hennigan is back and better than ever.”

This summer, 16 city pools are expected to be open for the summer, according to Boston Centers for Youth and Families: BCYF Condon, BCYF Charlestown, BCYF Clougherty, BCYF Draper, BCYF Flaherty, BCYF Hennigan, BPS Madison Park, BCYF Mason, BCYF Marshall, BCYF Mattahunt, BCYF Mildred, BCYF Perkins, BCYF Paris Street Pool, BCYF Quincy, BPHC South End Fitness Center, and BPS Umana. BCYF Curley Beach will also be open.

Of those, eight have been fixed under the current administration, Wu said, noting “there was a lot of work that we had to dig out from.”

Just three years ago, over half of the city-run public pools were closed for maintenance, sparking widespread frustration during a scorching summer.

Still more work is coming. BCYF pools at Curtis Hall in Jamaica Plain, Mason in Roxbury, and the Mirabella in the North End are still scheduled for upgrades, with Curtis Hall set to close on Friday and Mirabella already shuttered this season.

“We’re going to work as quickly as we can,” Wu said of Curtis Hall. “We need some HVAC upgrades, flooring repair, adding new benches on the pool deck, updated locker rooms, fresh paint, and much more. So, we’re hoping to have it ready in time for next summer, when Jamaica Plate will have two pools online for the first time of a long time.”

BCYF Blackstone in the South End and Holland in Dorchester pools remain listed as currently closed, with no scheduled openings this season.

Public officials heralded widespread work from local advocates and officials in getting pools open for this summer, noting the importance of community cooling sites across neighborhoods as temperatures rise.

The open BCYF pools are free to the public but operate with certain protocol, including requiring registration, only Boston residency, children under eight to be accompanied by an adult, no more than three children under 12 per adult, and more.

The city also invested $114,892 in “Swim Safe” grants this summer season, funding the expansion of free beginner swim lessons for young people across 11 nonprofits. In total, Boston officials estimated over 700 children and teens will receive free swim lessons through the grants.

Chief of Human Services José Massó asked the crowd gathered for the reopening of the Hennigan pool on Monday to raise their hands if they could swim.

“For the folks that did not raise your hand, no worries, do not fret,” Massó said. “This pool is for you, alright. And for the adults in the room, it’s never too late to learn how to swim. It’s a critical skill that I believe everybody should have.”

After a few speeches, Wu, local state Rep. Sam Montaño, City Councilor Ben Weber and a line of excited kids dove into the brand new pool, landing with a giant splash.

“After years of deferred maintenance, this has not been an easy task, but the mayor has stuck with the project,” said Massó. “And each summer we get a little closer to our goal of having all of our pools open.”

title: Boston city councilors pitch MBTA subway alternative to contentious Blue Hill Avenue bus lane redesign
text:
Two city councilors who oppose Boston’s Blue Hill Avenue redesign plan met with MBTA brass to pitch an alternative Orange Line extension through that corridor, but the T says it’s instead studying a connection to the mayor’s Roslindale neighborhood.

A MassDOT spokesperson revealed the DOT and MBTA Orange Line extension study plans Tuesday evening, presenting a stark contrast to what Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell proposed in a meeting earlier in the day with MBTA General Manager and MassDOT Secretary Phillip Eng.

Culpepper and Worrell have proposed extending subway service on the Orange Line from Ruggles station in Roxbury to Mattapan Square via the Blue Line Avenue corridor, an area they described as a “train desert.”

While the councilors described their meeting with Eng as “productive” when speaking with reporters at the state transportation building late Tuesday morning, the T and MassDOT later revealed that the state is already studying the feasibility of an Orange Line extension in Boston, but in a completely different direction.

The direction MassDOT is studying would extend the Orange Line from Forest Hills station in Jamaica Plain to the Roslindale Village commuter rail station. Roslindale — like the extension area proposed by the councilors — lacks a subway connection. It also just so happens to be where Mayor Michelle Wu lives.

“MassDOT, through its Office of Transportation Planning and in collaboration with the MBTA, is conducting a study to determine the feasibility of expanding transit service between the Forest Hills Orange Line station and the Roslindale Village commuter rail station,” MassDOT spokesperson John Goggin said in a statement in response to an inquiry about the councilors’ proposal.

“This study will be funded through Fair Share funding. The study will seek to analyze scenarios for future rapid transit between Forest Hills and Roslindale Village, including potential alignment for Orange Line service or more frequent commuter rail service.

“The study will also evaluate criteria such as ridership, accessibility, social equity, cost, and economic and land use impacts. The study team expects to release a report detailing analyses of each service scenario by fall of 2026,” Goggin added.

When asked whether MassDOT’s plan differed from what the councilors met with Eng about on Tuesday, Worrell told the Herald, “Yes.”

Worrell didn’t respond, however, to further questions nor acknowledge a comment about the study area being where the mayor lives, rather than the corridor Wu is moving forward with a center-running bus lane and redesign plan he opposes.

Mayor Wu’s office indicated that it opposed the councilors’ proposal, and plans to move forward with the city’s $162 million redesign plan for Blue Hill Avenue, despite persistent community opposition.

“The city is always looking to expand public transit access for our residents in partnership with the MBTA,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said in a statement. “However, digging new miles of subway tunnel under city streets would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment.

“Today, Boston has an opportunity to deliver more immediate improvements and beautification of the Blue Hill Ave corridor with nearly $150 million secured in state and federal funds.

“As we continue to work with community members to incorporate feedback into the proposed project design, we are focused on ensuring improvements to speed up commutes, expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor, and boost quality of life for families in our neighborhoods,” Osaghae added.

City officials have stated that federal funding — including the latest $80 million infusion — allocated for the Blue Hill Avenue corridor is contingent upon completion of the transit project the city applied to the feds for, which includes the contentious center-running bus lane.

Culpepper and Worrell contend that’s not necessarily the case. The councilors said they learned from their meeting with Eng that roughly $22 million of the $80 million in federal funding allocated to the city is not tied to the center-running bus lane, and can be used for other purposes, such as beautification and safety.

“What we have seen across the country is that rail has been used for that federal grant, so there’s other cities that have used that same federal grant to extend or install rail, so that is the ask,” Worrell said at the media briefing. “That’s a possible way that we can get funding for this new proposed Orange Line extension.”

The councilors say the city and MBTA can do better than bus service for Boston’s predominantly Black communities of Roxbury, Mattapan and Dorchester — where their proposed Orange Line extension would run through — which “have been promised world-class transit” for “nearly 40 years.”

Staff for the councilors distributed a fact sheet to reporters ahead of their press briefing that stated Culpepper and Worrell, “alongside local advocates, are drawing a line: they’re not anti-transit, they’re pro-justice — and they refuse to accept a process that treats buses as the ceiling for their community’s transit ambitions.”

Culpepper said, however, that they didn’t ask Eng to pause plans for the center-running bus lane, despite their opposition and their plan being pitched as an alternative.

“We didn’t get into that part of the conversation,” Culpepper said when asked if Eng committed to taking the contentious bus lane off the table.

Worrell added, “We were focused on presenting our proposal and the data around why we believe the Orange Line extension is a better fit for this corridor. That was the focus of the meeting today.”

The councilors said the funding breakdown for the city’s Blue Hill Avenue redesign project consists of an $80.3 million Federal Transit Administration Small Starts grant, $38.4 million from the Massachusetts federal match, $18.2 million from the City of Boston, $14.9 million from a federal RAISE grant, and $10.7 million from the MBTA Capital Investment Plan.

title: Boston councilors’ MBTA Orange Line extension plan for Blue Hill Avenue slammed
text:
A plan from two Boston city councilors to extend the MBTA Orange Line below Blue Hill Avenue to replace a contentious center-running bus lane has drawn backlash, with one transit advocate saying it’s not “a serious transit proposal.”

TransitMatters Executive Director Caitlin Allen-Connelly didn’t mince words Wednesday when asked what she thought about a plan Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell pitched Tuesday to MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng.

“I don’t think it’s a serious transit proposal, if they’re proposing something that looks like a concept that they assembled over the weekend with an AI-generated map that’s proposing a multi-billion-dollar rail investment without any discussion of operations or cost or timelines or how it even fits into the existing transit network,” Allen-Connelly told the Herald. “I don’t think it’s a serious transit proposal at all.”

Allen-Connelly said there are “obvious errors” in the map Culpepper and Worrell distributed Tuesday showing their proposed Orange Line subway extension, which the councilors envision as being from the Ruggles station in Roxbury to Mattapan Square via the Blue Hill Avenue corridor.

The bigger problem with the plan, Allen-Connelly said, is that it’s presented as an either-or situation that would take decades and billions of dollars to accomplish, while leaving riders grappling with congestion the center bus lane seeks to resolve — if that lane were to be scrapped for the rail extension, as the councilors prefer.

“It would take decades to plan, fund, design, and build, and the people riding Blue Hill Avenue, the buses there, they need improvements now,” Allen-Connelly said, explaining that roughly 40,000 riders use the corridor daily. “The conversation should be about, what can we do today in the short term to improve speed and reliability, and not about a hypothetical project with no plan for implementation.”

She added that bus and rail improvements “are not competing ideas,” as pitched by the councilors.

“When you do have successful bus priority, it often helps build the case for future rail investments, so higher ridership, faster trips, a stronger corridor performance make it easier to justify a larger capital investment down the road,” Allen-Connelly said. “So, if our goal is eventually bringing higher capacity transit to Blue Hill Avenue, improving bus service is one of the most important steps you can take to set that up for success.

“Transit riders,” she added, “deserve real solutions and not distractions.”

Worrell on Wednesday responded to the criticism, which has also been prominent on social media, by posting “the handmade map of the Orange Line proposal that we asked AI to ‘upgrade’ to its other form.”

“No matter the map, the point remains the same: There is a gaping hole for rail in this section of Boston that aligns with economic, environmental and educational inequalities,” Worrell wrote on social media.

He cited and linked to a 1979 report that he said showed the Orange Line extension to be feasible along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, but said “our community was deemed not worthy of such an investment.

“Meanwhile, investments downtown and in Cambridge and Somerville have moved forward,” said Worrell, who represents Mattapan, Dorchester, and parts of Jamaica Plain and Roslindale.

Worrell and Culpepper contend that the city and MBTA can do better than bus service for Boston’s predominantly Black communities of Roxbury, Mattapan and Dorchester — where their proposed Orange Line extension would run through — which “have been promised world-class transit” for “nearly 40 years.”

They both oppose the city’s $162 million redesign of the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, which is being supported by more than $80 million in federal funding. Mayor Michelle Wu’s office said Tuesday the councilors’ proposal “would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment,” and added that the city is moving forward with the bus lane redesign.

Worrell maintains that the city should change its approach.

“The end goal here is … to provide these communities with equitable transportation,” Worrell said. “The majority of these residents are not ditching their car for a center-running bus lane to nowhere, but they will for a one-seat ride to downtown.”

A MassDOT spokesperson said Tuesday that the DOT and MBTA is already studying the feasibility of an Orange Line extension in Boston, but in a different direction, from the Forest Hills station in Jamaica Plain to the Roslindale Village commuter rail station. The study is funded through Fair Share funding.

Roslindale, like the extension area proposed by the councilors, lacks a subway connection.

title: Police Blotter: FBI seizes 23 drones over Boston Stadium World Cup airspace
text:
Law enforcement seized nearly two dozen drones flying in the restricted airspace over Boston Stadium and World Cup events, the Boston FBI says.

“The FBI is reminding the public to leave your drones at home,” the agency posted to X. “Temporary Flight Restrictions are in effect, and violations may result in enforcement action.

In all, the FBI and its law enforcement partners — which were not named in the statement — have seized 23 drones as of June 11.

The Federal Aviation Administration in May launched “No Drone Zones” for FIFA World Cup 2026 stadiums, fan events and base camps, supported by the Drone Expedited and Targeted Enforcement Response (DETER) program launched a month earlier.

“This program will further deter violations by ensuring swift enforcement action and reinforce the agency’s commitment to protecting the National Airspace System,” FAA Chief Counsel Liam McKenna said when announcing the DETER program in April.

The program prohibited drones “within a 3-nautical-mile radius and up to 3,000 feet above ground level around the stadiums.”

That program is itself part of President Trump’s Executive Order 14305 of June 6, 2025 — the Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty order.

The order targets “unmanned aircraft systems,” or drones, which Trump’s order says “offer the potential to enhance public safety as well as cement America’s leadership in global innovation.” But the order states drones also pose risks: “criminals, terrorists, and hostile foreign actors have intensified their weaponization of these technologies, creating new and serious threats to our homeland.”

$3 billion Russian fraud scheme busted in New England

A “transnational criminal organization” with a base of operations in Russia and elsewhere in Eastern Europe bought up established durable medical equipment companies to run them as shells to fraudulently rip off Medicare to the tune of $3 billion.

That’s according to U.S. Attorney for New Hampshire Erin Creegan, who announced the arrests of two men from the country of Georgia.

“These charges expose the staggering scale of fraud and money laundering that Transnational Criminal Organizations are willing to inflict on our health care system and the people of New Hampshire,” Creegan said Thursday. “This was not a local scheme. It was a transnational operation that stole the identities of New England patients and doctors to defraud our health care system of nearly $3 billion in intended losses and then launder those proceeds internationally to escape detection.”

Kakha Bendeliani, 48, and Goga Danelia, 37, are charged with conspiring to commit money laundering in connection to the scheme.

While the men allegedly used their shell companies to bill Medicare for nearly $3 billion, they ended up netting significantly less — $12.5 million — before their alleged fraud scheme was exposed.

In order to make the scheme work, the organization put up real people as the nominal heads of the once-legitimate businesses while actually orchestrating the scheme from afar, according to the indictment returned on June 17. They then stole the identities of hundreds of thousands of Americans in order to bill Medicare for fake medical expenses.

title: Police Blotter: Girl, 12, killed in Haverhill bus strike
text:
A bus struck a motorized scooter carrying two children in Haverhill, killing one of the children, according to local police.

The crash happened at around 4 p.m. Thursday at the intersection of Portland Street and Fifth Avenue. Both children were transported to area hospitals for treatment.

The 12-year-old girl was pronounced dead. The authorities did not identify her, pending notification of next of kin, but did say she was a student at a Haverhill public school.

Haverhill Mayor Melinda Barrett said her “heart sank” upon hearing the news.

“We as a community are grieving. I have heard from residents who have expressed their sadness, frustration, and fears. I share all those feelings,” Barrett continued.

Suspects arrested in Allston shooting death of boy

Police arrested two people in their 20s in connection with the shooting murder of a 15-year-old boy in Allston last summer.

Boston Police were dispatched just after 8 p.m. on June 12, 2025, to the first block of Gordon Street in Allston for reports of a person shot. They found Phillip Franco, 15, of Brighton, suffering from gunshot wounds on the intersecting Pomeroy Street. He would die five days later at a hospital.

On Friday, police arrested two people in connection to Franco’s death: Armani Collazos, 26, in Brighton, and Miranda Bodden, 22, in Allston.

Collazos faces many charges including murder and assault and battery attempt with a firearm. Bodden faces five counts of accessory after the fact.

Boston man convicted of home invasion murder

A Suffolk Superior Court jury convicted a Boston man for a brutal 2015 Dorchester home invasion that killed one man and left his fiancée with a gunshot wound to the head.

Victor Arrington, 40, of Boston, was first tried for first-degree murder, home invasion, armed assault to murder, unlawful possession of a firearm and two counts of kidnapping in May 2024, but that ended in mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.

But a trial that ended this week — bolstered by location data from Arrington’s phone — led to his conviction. He is expected to be sentenced on June Tuesday. First-degree murder convictions carry a mandatory life prison sentence without possibility of parole.

“This team effort helped secure a just verdict in an extraordinarily harrowing case, notable not only for its shocking violence against completely innocent victims but also for the precedent it set in the use of advanced digital evidence,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said.

Arrington and his two accomplices did not originally intend to murder Richard Long, 37, and maim his fiancée, according to prosecutors.

Arrington and two other men had planned to assault and rob another man who lived on Harvard Street in Dorchester but had entered the wrong home. After assaulting Long and his fiancée and then tying them up with electrical cords, the criminals realized their mistake and opted to kill them to cover their tracks.

The men stabbed Long before shooting him and his fiancée in the head, prosecutors said. They then poured bleach on them and set fire to the kitchen as the couple’s infant child was in the bedroom. The fiancée regained consciousness and alerted a neighbor.

A second man charged in the crime, James Boyd, 33, is scheduled for a change of plea hearing on July 1. A third man was identified but not charged, prosecutors said, because he was murdered in April 2015.

title: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu signs legislation expanding senior property tax exemption eligibility
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu signed an ordinance into law that will increase income eligibility for senior property tax relief each year to keep better pace with inflation, the first such change in 23 years.

The legislation ensures that income and asset limits used to determine eligibility for Boston’s senior property tax exemption will automatically adjust annually based on inflation.

This will prevent seniors from losing eligibility when their Social Security benefits, retirement income and savings increase due to cost of living hikes.

“Moving forward, the city will account for changing economic conditions and automatically adjust the income eligibility every year for the property tax exemption, so people don’t get pushed out of this program,” Wu said Monday at a press conference in Dorchester. “More seniors will be able to qualify for this benefit and keep qualifying year after year.”

Homeowners must be 65 or older as of July 1 to qualify for that fiscal year’s elderly exemption, which provides $1,000 in tax relief.

An additional $1,000 in city tax relief is possible provided that it doesn’t reduce the annual tax bill below the prior year’s bill, and reduce the taxable value of the eligible homeowner’s property below 10% of the assessed value.

Gross income limits, including Social Security benefits, for this fiscal year that ends Tuesday, were $25,980 for single homeowners and $38,970 for married couples.

A homeowner’s whole estate, not including the value of their home, couldn’t be more than $40,000 if single and $55,000 if married for FY26, per the city website.

City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, who introduced the legislation that was passed by the Council last week, said the measure will allow for annual cost-of-living adjustments to income and asset levels, which adds up over time.

Louijeune said numbers crunched by her office indicate that had the city adopted the legislative change back in 2003 — the last time eligibility limits were adjusted in Boston — the income exemption limit for seniors would have been more than $40,000 today, rather than roughly $26,000.

“That’s a big deal,” Louijeune said. “It’s a modest increase, but it’s important because over time, it amounts to a lot of money.”

Prior to Tuesday’s signing, income and asset eligibility limits were fixed under Clause 41C of state law, unless increased by local action, “and may become outdated over time due to inflation and rising costs of living,” Louijeune wrote in the Council order passed last week.

The city opted to act on a provision in state tax law, Clause 41D, that authorizes municipalities to adopt a cost-of-living adjustment mechanism that automatically increases the income and asset eligibility limits annually for the senior tax exemption, based on the percentage increase for the Consumer Price Index for the previous year, as determined by the commissioner of revenue.

Louijeune said Boston joins other cities and towns that have adopted the automatic senior tax exemption adjustment, including Belmont, Braintree, Cambridge, Concord, Milton and Plymouth.

Her Council order was co-sponsored by Councilors Brian Worrell and Ben Weber.

Lillie Bryan, president of the Boston chapter of Mass Senior Action Council, said the annual senior tax exemption eligibility adjustments won’t solve the city’s housing affordability problem, but it will “help seniors who are struggling with property tax bills now, and it will protect seniors who have already qualified from losing the help that they have now.”

Bryan said if there had been annual senior exemption adjustments since 2003, she would have qualified today for property tax relief, along with “many” other seniors present for the signing ceremony.

“Passing 41D means that 20 years from now, other seniors would not have to go through this,” Bryan said.

She joined Wu in taking a swipe at the state Senate for not approving the mayor’s signature tax shift legislation that seeks to provide a tax break to homeowners by shifting more of the city’s tax burden onto commercial property owners.

Wu has endorsed two first-time candidates challenging two Boston senators, Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, whom she blames for killing the tax bill.

“We have to keep pushing as well because the affordability crisis won’t be solved by any single policy,” Wu said. “We need to keep doing everything in our power to back up our state reps, as they’re fighting for these changes up at the State House that the City Council has already pushed through often unanimously.”

By comparison, the senior tax exemption adjustment is a local opt-in measure that doesn’t require approval by the state Legislature. State Reps. Russell Holmes and Brandy Fluker-Reid of Boston were present for the day’s signing ceremony.

title: Boston Police Blotter: BPD Commissioner advises no illegal fireworks, heat safety ahead of July 4th
text:
It’s hot out, the city is on the cusp of the Fourth of July, and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox has some advice and warnings for residents who plan on celebrating.

At the season opening of the Frog Pond spray pool in Boston Common, Cox said officers in stations around the city are there to help people who might be feeling the heat.

In addition to staying hydrated and in cool spaces as much as residents can, Cox said, “Don’t partake in the alcohol,” saying it can make heat-related symptoms worse.

He asked residents to say something if they see something, noting that scooter thefts, street takeovers, and aggravated assaults are up, even though homicides and other crimes are down compared to this time last year.

Cox suggested residents keep GPS devices like AirTags on their scooters to help police find them if they’re stolen. He also asked Bostonians to be on the lookout for troves of improperly stored scooters or large gatherings of people on scooters.

“We’ve also found that a lot of these large gatherings of scooters, they tend to be stolen across the board,” he said.

He also asked that residents call 911 when they see large, afterhours parties.

“The parties are not just a nuisance, they’ve been the center of some of the most extreme violence that we’ve had traditionally in the city,” the commissioner explained.

To discourage some of that behavior, Cox said some parks and streets would be closed this summer.

With America’s 250th birthday on Saturday, he pleaded that people not set off illegal fireworks.

On top of being against the law, “The most important thing people need to understand is that they’re dangerous,” he said. “Every year people lose fingers, toes, and they can lose their life dealing with fireworks… Let the professionals handle it.”

title: Boston trending away from safest major city to crime-ridden Chicago ‘garbage,’ police union leader says
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu has touted Boston as the “safest major city” in America for two years, but the city’s largest police union says the recent spate of violence and attack on cops has it trending more toward Chicago’s lawlessness.

“Safest city in America? Not so much,” the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association posted on social media Tuesday. “The increasing levels of violence and attacks on police should have everyone concerned. And if a triple shooting in Boston’s Theater District doesn’t grab your attention, you may want to check for a pulse.”

The union’s post came on the heels of a Monday night triple shooting, and as videos were going viral of a Boston Police officer who tried to arrest a man Sunday night in Dorchester, but saw his efforts thwarted when a crowd intervened, throwing drinks and objects at the cop before the suspect got away.

BPPA President Larry Calderone told the Herald that the city doesn’t have enough police officers, which is driving the uptick in violence, along with what he described as a ho-hum response from city officials, who aren’t publicly acknowledging the crime spree.

Wu’s office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Calderone put the force at roughly 600 cops short of appropriate staffing levels, which he said equates to “about a third of our workforce.”

He also blasted city councilors for exacerbating the matter by their calls to cut police overtime in the city budget, which he said has led the department to “cut minimum staffing down to the bare bone,” and avoid hiring police on overtime, as was past practice to ensure sufficient cops on the street.

Case in point, Calderone said, was the situation captured on the viral videos. One cop reportedly responded to a street takeover of 100 to 150 people drinking and playing loud music because there weren’t enough police available on duty to send multiple units, he said.

“It’s crazy that we’re jeopardizing public and police officer safety because we’re worried about a buck,” Calderone said. “It’s a recipe for disaster. Somebody’s going to get seriously hurt, and we don’t want to wait that long, and that’s what the members are pissed about.”

Calderone said Boston is still “one of the safest cities” in the country, but he sees it trending in the wrong direction, with weekend shootings becoming more frequent. He sees this summer as a potential tipping point for its safest city reputation.

He pushed back on metrics used by the police and city officials to determine safety. Homicides may be down this year again, Calderone said, but that’s “because the 15 people that have been shot in the last four weeks didn’t die.”

“The department and our elected officials would have you look at Hacky-sack playing cops and FIFA than acknowledge the street takeovers, the violence, the larcenies, the aggravated assaults and the shootings happening every weekend,” Calderone said. “We’re just a few extra shootings away from becoming like Chicago and that’s what we’re worried about.

“If we wait too long and become like Chicago or Baltimore, then we’ve already lost the battle,” Calderone added.

He said violence is up in Boston, but the police department’s manpower is down compared to 18 months ago.

“Those numbers don’t lie, and that’s what makes communities like Chicago and Baltimore,” Calderone said. “That’s what turns once great cities into garbage cities, and we don’t want to see our great city turn into a garbage city that’s ridden with violence.”

When asked about the criticism, BPD spokesperson Mariellen Burns told the Herald the city is “at half the homicides we were at this point last year,” halfway through the year. The Herald reported last month that there were seven homicides, as of mid-June, compared to 16 by that time last year.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox told reporters Wednesday, “We’re at the midway point of the year, and we’re doing pretty well with the city as far as overall crime,” though he said there’s been a “slight uptick in aggravated assaults.”

“We’ve had, certainly, an uptick in street takeovers, things of that nature,” Cox said. “We want to remind the public, if they see something, say something.”

City Councilors Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy made statements this week indicating they agree more with the police union’s take than Wu’s police commissioner.

Both condemned the attack on the city cop and called for increased police staffing, while stating that Boston should no longer be touted by city officials as the “safest major city.”

“It’s a false narrative,” Flynn told the Herald. “Boston residents know it’s not the safest city. When someone is selling drugs in your neighborhood and violent crime is taking place in front of your house, you can’t call Boston the safest city in America.”

Murphy added that city officials “need to stop hiding behind the claim that Boston is the safest city in the country.”

“What does that title mean when residents in too many neighborhoods are witnessing violent crime and telling us they do not feel safe?” Murphy said. “Safety is not a slogan or a ranking. It is whether people feel protected in their neighborhoods, on their streets, or in their homes.”

Calderone said Flynn and Murphy were two of the few councilors to respond to the police union amid their call to action during the latest wave of city violence. Others, he said, were John FitzGerald, Gabriela Coletta Zapata, Henry Santana and Enrique Pepén.

Calderone declined to answer questions about whether his criticism marks a break from the union’s recent support of the mayor, whom the BPPA endorsed in her reelection bid last year and began to engage with on new contract negotiations this week.

Instead, he’s blasting the city councilors who “grandstand against” the police budget while “quietly begging the commissioner for more bodies” in their high-crime neighborhoods, rather than having the “moxie” to publicly “stand up for their constituents.”

“Where is Ruthzee?” Calderone said. “Where is Julia Mejia? Where is Liz Breadon, the Council president? Where are the Worrell brothers? Where is Culpepper? These are their neighborhoods; these are their constituents. … Where’s their courage?”

title: Gaskin: Opposed to White Stadium? Blame Marty Walsh
text:
Some people have wondered why White Stadium became the first and only serious choice for Boston’s new professional women’s soccer stadium.

It was not because Franklin Park has easy traffic access, or because the surrounding neighborhoods have ample parking, or because the environmental and public-land questions were minor, or because the economic impact on Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain had already been independently established.

So why White Stadium?

One possible answer deserves public scrutiny: the tax incentives may have been too valuable to ignore.

Opportunity Zones were created under the 2017 federal tax law signed during the Trump administration to encourage private investment in lower-income communities through capital-gains tax advantages. In 2018, Gov. Charlie Baker nominated Massachusetts’ Opportunity Zone census tracts, based in Boston on recommendations from the Walsh administration, including tracts that covered the Franklin Park area.

The stated local logic was defensive. Boston officials were worried that Opportunity Zones could fuel gentrification by attracting private capital into vulnerable neighborhoods. So rather than nominate every eligible tract, the Walsh administration selected a smaller number, including tracts with significant public ownership or public control. WBUR reported at the time that some Boston Opportunity Zones included land largely off the table for redevelopment, including Franklin Park, cemeteries, open space and public housing.

But that logic had a serious flaw.

If the whole purpose of an Opportunity Zone is to attract private investment, and the most valuable asset inside the zone is public land, then the pressure does not disappear. It shifts. Instead of speculation through ordinary private parcels, the pressure moves toward monetizing, leasing, commercializing or redeveloping public assets.

White Stadium may now be the case study.

At the time, I remember hearing that Franklin Park had been included in an Opportunity Zone and thinking that such a decision should never have been made without a serious community process. Franklin Park is not unused land on a map. It is Boston’s largest park and a shared resource for Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, Jamaica Plain and the entire city. If a federal tax designation could make private investment in or around the park more attractive, residents deserved to know before a stadium deal was moving forward.

There was another cost to that decision.

At the time, John Kingston III, then running for U.S. Senate, was talking about launching a $100 million Opportunity Zone Fund to help redevelop Roxbury and parts of Dorchester. That was exactly the kind of investment Opportunity Zones were supposed to encourage: capital for raw land, abandoned buildings, underused commercial corridors and neighborhood redevelopment.

But when the Opportunity Zone geography was drawn around Franklin Park, public open space and other land largely unavailable for ordinary redevelopment, the incentive for that kind of neighborhood investment was weakened. The tax benefit did not disappear. It was redirected.

The Opportunity Zone program could have been used to help unlock long-neglected parcels in Roxbury and Dorchester, support local ownership, create jobs, build housing and strengthen commercial districts. Instead, Boston placed federal tax incentives around public assets that were supposedly protected from development.

Years later, the most visible private investment opportunity emerging from that geography is not the redevelopment of abandoned buildings in Roxbury. It is a professional sports stadium in Franklin Park.

The public deserves to know whether any part of the White Stadium/Boston Legacy investment has been structured to take advantage of federal Opportunity Zone tax benefits.

Opportunity Zone benefits can be extremely valuable. If an investor makes a qualifying equity investment through a Qualified Opportunity Fund and holds it long enough, the gain on that investment’s appreciation may be excluded from federal capital-gains tax after 10 years.

Consider the growth in women’s soccer franchise values.

Boston reportedly paid a $53 million expansion fee for its NWSL franchise. Current NWSL valuations show the upside: Angel City at about $335 million, Kansas City Current at $315 million, Bay FC at $208 million, and the average NWSL team at about $184 million.

Now do the simple math.

If a qualifying investment tied to Boston women’s soccer rose from the $53 million expansion-fee level to the current NWSL average of $184 million, that would be about $131 million in appreciation. At a 23.8% federal capital-gains rate — 20% capital gains plus the 3.8% net investment income tax — the potential federal tax avoided on that appreciation could be about $31 million.

If the value rose to something closer to Angel City’s $335 million valuation, the appreciation would be about $282 million. The potential federal tax benefit could be roughly $67 million.

Boston says the White Stadium deal includes more than $190 million in private capital investment and tens of millions more for operations and maintenance.

The public has been told this project is about students, women’s sports, community benefits and the revitalization of a neglected stadium. Those may all be part of the story. But they cannot be the whole story if private investors may also be positioned for major tax advantages from a public park and public-school stadium.

Boston can support women’s sports and still demand transparency. Renovating White Stadium and asking hard questions about private financial benefits are not contradictory positions.

The tax benefits would flow to investors. The traffic, parking pressure, disruption and loss of park access would fall on Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain.

That is why disclosure matters.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Battenfeld: Michelle Wu, Boston Police union’s convenient romance may be waning
text:
A year after banding together to claim Boston is the safest major city in the country, Mayor Michelle Wu and the powerful Boston patrolmen’s union appear to be on the outs again.

The on again, off again romance – one primarily of convenience anyway – has hit the skids as the patrolmen’s association now contends the Wu administration is not funding enough police officers and Boston is becoming a dangerous Chicago.

Both need to step up to make the city safer before another long, hot summer escalates tensions and crime.

Back in March 2025, during Wu’s reelection campaign, the BPPA backed Wu, calling her a “friend of law enforcement” and lavishing praise on her for handing them a fat, $82 million contract with 9% salary increases.

“We are the safest major city in America because of your efforts,” Wu said, speaking glowingly of the police just a few years after she was on a “defund the police” kick as a Boston city councilor.

Wu got what she wanted, the endorsement. And the BPPA got what they wanted, a lucrative new contract.

The politically expedient turnaround for Wu, from advocating a 10% cut to the police budget and refusing to accept campaign donations from cops as councilor, to vetoing budget cuts as mayor, appears to be contradictory and confusing.

On the one hand she’s saying the police budget should be cut, but on the other hand she’s defending officers from having their overtime taken away?

And does the BPPA really like her or not? Why didn’t they raise the issue of not having enough police on the beat before endorsing her?

Both the union and Wu are being inconsistent and insincere.

And where was Wu in condemning the most recent attack on a police officer – first reported by the Herald – who was trying to stop a dirt biker in Dorchester and had objects and drinks thrown at him?

The disturbing incident was captured on a viral video for all to see.

Officer Jesse Kennedy responded to a radio call for a loud disturbance at the intersection of Old Road and Ellington Street at around 9:24 p.m., according to a police report from the incident.

Traffic ahead of the intersection was “gridlocked,” the report said, with between 100 and 150 people drinking and playing loud music, “low riders,” mopeds, and dirt bikes blocking the road.

“Throughout this physical struggle multiple members of the group congregating began throwing various items at Officer Kennedy including alcoholic beverages,” the report said.

Cops now appear to be fair game to criminals. Wu should say something to stop it if she really is a friend of the police.

BPPA President Larry Calderone addressed the attack in a Facebook post, calling on the City Council to condemn it.

“USE YOUR VOICE (or speak up) and denounce the violence, denounce the street takeovers, stand up for your police and constituents,” he said. “Unless, of course, you’re okay with Boston feeling more and more like Chicago.”

The BPPA also posted about a shooting in Mattapan, saying, “Boston’s reputation as America’s safest city is under attack. Make no mistake about it. We need more cops.”

Wonder if Wu, who is from Chicago and invented the line about Boston being the safest American city, is listening?

He said violence is up in Boston — with street takeovers, violence, larcenies, aggravated assaults and shootings “happening every weekend” — but the police department’s manpower is down compared to 18 months ago.

“Those numbers don’t lie, and that’s what makes communities like Chicago and Baltimore,” Calderone said. “That’s what turns once-great cities into garbage cities, and we don’t want to see our great city turn into a garbage city that’s ridden with violence.”

Wu’s office said the numbers tell a different story. Data from the Boston Police Department comparing the first six months of 2025 and 2026 show clear progress in reducing serious crime, her office added.

In 2026, shooting victims fell from 58 to 50, a 14% decrease from 2025 and a 22% decrease compared to the last five-year average. Homicides declined from 21 in 2025 to 10 in 2026, reflecting what the mayor’s office called significant progress in preventing the most serious crimes.

Reports of rape decreased from 95 to 68 over the same period, while robberies and attempted robberies remained relatively stable between 2025 and 2026, though Wu’s office didn’t provide figures on that crime statistic.

Domestic aggravated assaults held roughly flat, while non-domestic aggravated assaults rose modestly, which the mayor’s office said underscores the need for continued investment in prevention, intervention and victim support.

The information from the mayor’s office is similar to what Wu’s Police Commissioner Michael Cox told reporters on Wednesday.

“We’re at the midway point of the year, and we’re doing pretty well with the city as far as overall crime,” Cox said, though he mentioned there’s been a “slight uptick in aggravated assaults.”

“We’ve had, certainly, an uptick in street takeovers, things of that nature,” Cox said. “We want to remind the public, if they see something, say something.”

Calderone on Wednesday had pushed back on metrics used by the police and city officials to determine safety. Homicides may be down this year again, he said, but that’s “because the 15 people that have been shot in the last four weeks didn’t die.”

He said Boston is still “one of the safest cities” in the country, but sees it trending in the wrong direction, with weekend shootings becoming more frequent. He sees this summer as a potential tipping point for its safest city reputation.

“We’re just a few extra shootings away from becoming like Chicago and that’s what we’re worried about,” Calderone said. “If we wait too long and become like Chicago or Baltimore, then we’ve already lost the battle.”

title: Police Blotter: Merrimack River too contaminated for July 4th fun, tests show
text:
Portions of the Merrimack River downstream from Haverhill will likely be unsafe to use through the July 4th weekend due to dangerous fecal bacteria levels, though the data shows improvement.

Haverhill found two breaks in its 42-inch sewer pipe following excessive rains in the final days of last month, causing some 8 million gallons of wastewater to spill into the Merrimack River.

Testing of seven river sites downstream of the city showed increasing site contamination until a diversion pipe was installed Wednesday. That day’s sampling still showed six of seven test sites contaminated, but the situation appears to have lessened, with three of seven sites contaminated at Thursday’s testing, the most recent available.

Those sites with dangerous levels of fecal bacteria are Amesbury, Deer Island to the Newburyport Harbormaster’s Pier — this last being seven to eight times the safety limit.

The Merrimack River Watershed Council stressed in a statement that testing takes 24 hours, so no one should assume that the data can show “whether it is safe or unsafe at these locations today.”

“MRWC recommends that people do not engage with the Merrimack River downstream of Ferry Park in West Newbury, including Newburyport Harbor, until further testing can validate that it is safe to do so,” the Council wrote in its statement. “Unsafe conditions will likely extend through the July 4th Weekend. MRWC defers to the state and its testing for determinations at ocean facing beaches.”

Framingham woman is ex-girlfriend from Hell

A Framingham woman is charged with stalking and threatening to kill her ex-boyfriend — and threatening to chop “into little pieces” any cops who would stand in her way.

“If you date another girl, I will kill you,” Emma Hammond allegedly told her ex after grabbing him by the neck outside a Back Bay restaurant last week.

Hammond, 31, was charged in Boston Municipal Court with two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon and one count each of stalking, strangulation or suffocation, assault and battery on a family or household member, assault and battery on a police officer, and resisting arrest.

Judge Paul Treseler set bail at $200 and ordered Hammond to have no contact with the alleged victim.

Hammond and her alleged victim had only dated for about a month before he ended things. He told police that she then bombarded him with phone calls, in-person harassment at his apartment, and frequent appearances at this restaurant. Then Facetime calls from an unknown number threatened his death if he dated anyone else, with displays of guns and machetes.

Boston police responded to the Dartmouth Street restaurant a little before midnight on June 26 for the allegation of her choking him. She was gone when they arrived so they took the man’s statement and left — only to be told she had returned.

When officers arrived to arrest Hammond, she became combative, prosecutors say. She allegedly kicked, flailed her arms, and spit in one officer’s face. When finally handcuffed, she expressed suicidal statements and told officers that she “wish[ed] [she] had a gun to shoot [them],” and that she would “chop [the officers] into little pieces and put [their] bodies in a box because [her] family was part of the Mafia.”

Teen boy charged with shooting teen girl in Boston

A 14-year-old boy faces numerous gun charges, including assault and battery by discharge of a firearm, related to the shooting in May of a 14-year-old girl in Dorchester.

Police responded to Milton Avenue a little after 8 p.m. on May 6 for a report of a person shot. Inside a residence there, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound, according to a Boston Police Department statement. She was transported to a hospital where she has remained in recovery.

At the same home, police allegedly found two teen boys attempting to escape through a rear door. The officers say they found a pistol with an extended magazine in the backpack of one of the boys. Police that day arrested him on firearm and ammunition charges. Following an investigation, the boy was then charged in connection with the girl’s shooting.

Since all parties are juveniles, none was identified in the police statement.

I-495 shutdown identities released

The identities of the two men who died in Tuesday’s shooting in Berlin and the subsequent standoff on Interstate 495 in Lowell have been released.

The victim has been identified as Nicholas Ferreira, 35, of Haverhill, and the suspect as Edward Pyne, 43, of Salem, New Hampshire, according to published reports citing the Worcester County District Attorney’s Office.

title: Celtics’ Jaylen Brown trade leaves Boston fans, community feeling bankrupt: ‘A huge void’
text:
Jaylen Brown came to Boston in 2016 as a raw lottery pick out of California; he leaves a decade later, following a stunning trade to Philadelphia, as an NBA champion and an essential piece of the city’s social fabric.

“What this trade does is show young fans what sports heartbreak is,” Celtics superfan Chris Soldani told the Herald. “There is now a huge void, and a lot of people don’t know how to process this situation.”

Look no further than Randolph for proof. Immediately after learning about the trade, 6-year-old Giovanni “Gio” Jean cried uncontrollably while wearing a No. 7 Celtics jersey autographed by Brown.

His mother, Gigi Durand, captured the moment on video as Gio sobbed, “You are my favorite player in the whole NBA.” Holding up a handmade sign pleading for his idol to “come back one day,” the youngster asked his mother to mail it.

The footage went viral, racking up over 10 million views and drawing a direct response from Brown: “It’s ok lil bro,” he posted, adding a heart emoji. “We will always be friends.”

That instinct to connect directly with the fan base is exactly what drew superfans like Soldani to Brown.

In early May, Brown invited Soldani — known as “Caveman on Causeway” — and several others onto a Twitch livestream he hosted just after the 76ers eliminated Boston. The stream stirred controversy as the longtime Celtic described last year as the favorite of his career despite playing most of it without Jayson Tatum.

Soldani called the bond “one of the most unlikely connections.”

Under the blockbuster deal, Boston sends the 29-year-old 2024 Finals MVP to their bitter Atlantic Division rival for 36-year-old veteran Paul George and four draft picks. Fans say it will take time to overcome losing a superstar who doubled as one of Massachusetts’ most impactful civic anchors.

“With all the impact that Jaylen has on the city, and the youth, and putting money into the city,” Soldani said, “it truly bankrupts the city as a community.”

This spring, Boston Magazine ranked Brown the eighth most influential Bostonian, detailing his work hosting fundraising bowling events and education fairs in Roxbury.

That legacy echoes across local sports talk radio as fans process the gamble taken by front-office architect Brad Stevens — a decision complicated by reports that Brown feels his decade of service ended without the mutual respect he earned.

Gov. Maura Healey noted on social media that it’s “hard to imagine” the Celtics without Brown. She added, “You’ll always have a home in Boston.”

In 2019, Brown founded the 7uice Foundation, a nonprofit providing healthcare, education, and digital literacy resources to underserved youth through its STEM-focused Bridge Program camp.

The work recently drew criticism from the Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance, a state watchdog, after lawmakers approved a $700,000 state earmark for the charity.

“Jaylen Brown is expected to earn roughly $60 million this year,” the Alliance posted. “If he wants to support charitable work through his foundation, that’s commendable. But why are Massachusetts taxpayers being asked to subsidize the private foundation of a multi-millionaire?”

In 2024, Brown also launched the Boston XChange with teammate Jrue Holiday, an incubator aiming to generate $5 billion in wealth for communities of color by providing $100,000 in funding to 10 local businesses annually.

Superfan KJ Green, creator of the “Green Runs Deep” brand, cut straight to the raw reality: “I want to (expletive) die right now.”

Green, who also appeared on the May livestream, praised Brown for making fans feel seen and knowing them by name. “This guy cared about using his platform to build other people up,” Green said. “He helped so many businesses in Boston get to the next level.”

For special education teacher Kaiya Santos, who partnered with Brown in 2023 to redesign a basketball court at Fenelon Street Playground in Dorchester, the loss is personal. “It was clear that the project was not just about beautifying a court,” Santos told the Herald. “It was about the role the space would play in the community. Boston will miss him.”

Mayor Michelle Wu thanked Brown for “shifting the energy” and always “showing up” for the city, even as he became a “Celtics great.”

“We won’t forget the looks on young players’ faces as you pulled up unannounced to tournaments in the park,” Wu posted, “or the hope and determination of entrepreneurs and students reaching for their dreams through the opportunities you made possible. Because of your example, kids in Boston know that faith, consistency, hard work pays off.”

For now, the city seems unwilling to let go: Brown’s larger-than-life posters still hang untouched inside the TD Garden ProShop and throughout the busy North Station concourses.

title: ‘Enough is enough’: City councilors call for ‘public safety summit’ following holiday shootings
text:
Two city councilors are calling for a “Public Safety Summit” following a deadly Fourth of July night in Boston.

“Enough is enough… I am outraged,” City Councilor At-Large Erin Murphy wrote in a statement after news that two people were killed and eleven others were injured in five shooting incidents that began late Saturday night. The shootings occurred in Roxbury and Dorchester.

Murphy wrote it was, “heartbreaking, unacceptable, and a stark reminder that the status quo is not working.”

She called on Mayor Michelle Wu to brief the full council on an updated Summer Public Safety Plan and to convene a citywide “Public Safety Summit” that would include elected officials, neighborhood organizations, violence prevention advocates, first responders, and residents, as well as state and federal partners.

“We cannot continue reacting after tragedy strikes,” Murphy wrote. “Boston residents deserve action, not talking points. They deserve fully staffed police shifts, safer neighborhoods, and leaders willing to put differences aside before more lives are lost.”

In a letter to Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox, District 2 City Councilor Ed Flynn also called for a summit “to address violence and crime in Boston.”

“It’s clear we need a new, comprehensive public safety plan that includes hiring hundreds of police officers every year,” Flynn, whose district includes parts of Downtown, the South End, and South Boston, wrote.

Murphy noted that she, too, has been calling for hiring more officers.

Both councilors had also spoken out last week after another spike in city violence that included an assault on a police officer and a triple shooting.

Murphy, Flynn, and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association had said that staffing issues were in part to blame for a recent uptick.

“I hate to be the person who told them so,” BPPA President Larry Calderone said, “each week, the city is becoming more violent.”

In addition to the shootings, two people we also stabbed during the same time period, while other crimes like larceny, rape, and aggravated assault are seeing an upswing so far this year. Calderone said the department hasn’t been fully staffing shifts or hiring enough new officers to replace retirements.

At a press conference to address the July 4th violence, Cox pushed back on criticism that there aren’t enough officers on the streets.

“Contrary to the word out there, since FIFA, we’ve got many, many officers working, probably far more than any other time period,” Cox said. “We had a lot of people working, that being said there were a lot of parties last night… that kind of volume, we’re probably not used to.”

District 7 Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents parts of Fenway, Roxbury, Dorchester, and the South End, told the Herald in an interview that it was a “terrible night for everyone.”

Culpepper said that, “all hands, all people need to be working on this problem.”

“All of us will work on peace in the city,” he said, adding that he expects to work with Murphy and Flynn. “We want a peaceful summer.”

Culpepper, a pastor who has worked in the community to decrease violence, wants to see a return to a focus on peace, mutual respect, and community policing.

“They can’t arrest their way out of this,” Culpepper said, explaining that he believes seeing clergy and community members out with the police, working together, is better than just seeing more police on the streets. “Strong community policing works best.”

Calderone agreed that he’d like to see Boston Police return to a community policing approach.

He said that community policing means, “the same officer, on the same beat, in the same neighborhood,” explaining that right now, “we don’t have the bodies.”

title: Two killed, 11 others injured in July 4 shootings across Boston
text:
Two people were killed out of the 13 shot in Boston during what Mayor Michelle Wu called a “long and difficult” July 4th night.

Boston Police responded to five separate shootings, with most of the incidents occurring in Roxbury, the department said. The victims have not yet been identified.

Officers were also injured by fireworks during the overnight response, Police Commissioner Michael Cox said at a press conference Sunday to address the violence.

In a video obtained by the Herald, officers are responding to a large and loud crowd, when a firework gets tossed right next to an officer. The firework explodes, someone screams, and people can be seen lying on the ground after the light flashes and the smoke clears.

“Fireworks, firearms, and alcohol — bad combination,” Cox said, “and that’s what you saw around these events.”

He noted that the Fourth of July is always the peak of the year in terms of call volume for Boston and likely all major American cities.

Still, he said, “it was a very high volume.”

“It was a long and difficult night last night,” Wu said. “Our first responders and community safety teams were out throughout the night. This is a busy time of year, and when we see firearms present at large gatherings, that is never, never a recipe for peaceful celebrations.”

Wu said that her thoughts were with those impacted by the violence, especially the families of the victims, and that there has been and will continue to be trauma services available to community members.

She noted that prior to Saturday night, the number of shootings and shooting victims were down in Boston compared to the same time last year.

As of June 28th, Boston Police crime stats showed that 50 people had been shot, five fatally, down 14% from the same period in 2025, and down more than 20% from the five year average.

“We’re still at historic low numbers overall,” she said, “but that is never something we say to suggest that our work is slowing down or finished.”

Wu faced criticism last week after doubling down on rhetoric that Boston was still America’s safest major city, after an uptick in violence that included a triple shooting the weekend before. She held her stance despite calls from some city councilors and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association for more officers on the street to address the increase in crime.

Although she said that numbers were low, Wu said, “We will not be satisfied until there is no violence anywhere in the city of Boston.”

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office is investigating the incidents and asked for anyone with information about the shootings to come forward.

“Last night was obviously a challenging one,” he said. “We need the community’s help and support.”

Officers responded to the first shooting of the night on Fayton Street in Roxbury around 11:54 p.m. The victim’s injuries were life-threatening, and he was transported to the hospital, BPD said, adding that no arrests have been made.

Then, at 12:36 a.m., officers saw someone with a gunshot wound near 500 Blue Hill Ave., ultimately discovering three victims, who were all transported to the hospital.

One victim was pronounced dead at the hospital, and the others have non-life-threatening injuries, according to BPD. A fourth victim from the same incident also admitted themselves to a hospital with a non-life-threatening gunshot wound.

At the same time, another person admitted themself to the hospital for a non-life threatening gunshot wound from a separate incident on Horadan Way.

Just before 2 a.m., officers responded to Draper Street in Dorchester for another person shot with non-life threatening injuries.

The last shooting occurred back in Roxbury around 3:14 a.m. Officers arrived at an address on George Street and found three victims who’d been shot. One person was pronounced dead at the hospital, another was transported with life-threatening injuries, and the third had non-life threatening injuries, police said.

Officials applauded police and EMS for their work. Hayden called it an “extraordinary effort,” and Cox said they’d done a “tremendous job,” despite the challenges.

“There was no question about who was supposed to do what, where, it was just a lot to respond to,” Wu said of night.

She noted the stark difference between the start of the “incredible” day and celebrations for America’s 250th birthday, with the violence that took place later.

“Our first responders do such hard work, they put their all into this,” Wu said. “Everyday they save lives, whether it’s a big holiday weekend or not, they are there for our community.”

title: Boston Police Blotter: Roxbury homicide victim identified
