title: Editorial: What it takes to be ‘the safest city in America’
text:
Boston is the safest city in America — until the shooting starts.

Thirteen people were shot, two fatally, in five separate incidents that occurred throughout the city Saturday night into Sunday morning. Additionally, two people were stabbed and officers were assaulted by fireworks.

In late June, a Boston Police officer tried to arrest a man in Dorchester, but a crowd intervened, throwing drinks and objects at the officer before the suspect got away.

This spike in city violence has officials and residents sounding the alarm for the community.

“Right now, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America. Right now, for people who look like me, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America,” said Steven Wilson Jr. of the Ella J. Baker House.

This is not Boston’s first rodeo — recall the faith-based group Ten Point Coalition, an integral part (with the Boston Police) of the “Boston Miracle” of the 1990s, a period in which violent crime dropped by 79%.

That took coordinated effort, organization, support services and a lot of dedicated people. That success story can, and needs to be, repeated.

City Councilors Erin Murphy, who represents the city at-large, and Ed Flynn, of District 2, filed a resolution calling for a public safety summit.

“After another deadly holiday weekend, we cannot simply issue statements and move on. Boston deserves answers, accountability, and a real plan,” Murphy wrote in a statement.

More police on Boston streets is always top of mind after incidents such as these. But District 7 Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents parts of Roxbury, noted that a plan must include more.

“I do know part of the answer to the question is the community. When we have community policing, it’s when we have peace.”

Culpepper said that he’d like to see a “supplemental budget for peace,” saying, “I pray that we look at more money to fund the groups that do the work every day.”

Culpepper shouldn’t have to pray for needed funds, they should be on the table now.

Violence is a public health crisis, and Boston needs to treat it as such. Remember how we handled COVID? The Boston Foundation established the COVID-19 Response Fund in 2020, to, as it explains on its website, “rapidly deploy flexible resources to organizations in Greater Boston that were providing critical basic needs to communities disproportionately affected by the coronavirus outbreak.”

There’s an outbreak of violence in Boston, and we need a similar fund, or funding in general, to address it. It won’t go away on its own.

Minister Randy Muhammad, the founder of Boston’s chapter of the 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, said that he respected the work of the police, but that their work often comes after violence happens.

“Let’s invest not only in the after,” Muhammad said, “but let’s invest in those that are doing the work to prevent the crisis.”

The situation on Boston streets can get better, or it can get worse. We can be “the safest city in America,” or we can have that boast belied by news of yet another shooting.

The ball’s in City Hall’s court.

title: Boston, US Army announce coastal flooding and sea level rise protection plan
text:
Hundreds of thousands of Bostonians live at risk of worsening coastal flooding, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) states in a draft report set to be released this week outlining massive projects to defend the city’s waterfront over coming decades.

“More than 40% of our residents now live in areas at risk of coastal flooding, including some communities who are more than a mile away from the ocean,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Monday. “Without action, we risk $54 billion in damages to our homes, hospitals, businesses, roads, and other critical infrastructure by the end of the century. And that’s why over the past decade we’ve been working with our local, state, and federal partners to build a climate-ready Boston, and it’s why once again we’re turning to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to help us defend our city.”

The drafted Boston Coastal Storm Risk Management Feasibility Study details over 20 infrastructure projects along 16 miles of the city’s 47-mile coastline to mitigate potentially catastrophic sea level rise and coastal flooding over the coming decades, city and Army officials said Monday.

The study, commissioned to allow Boston to access a 65% federal cost-share for construction of the baseline protection infrastructure, is set to be released in full on Friday. The city and Army are seeking public feedback on the draft, before the release of a final report scheduled for 2028.

The USACE study will “drive one of the biggest investments in our waterfront, more than twice the size of the Boston Harbor cleanup,” Wu said.

Officials outlined the impact of mounting coastal flooding and sea level rise at Langone Park in the North End, built on a sea wall to help the neighborhood withstand flooding.

About one-sixth of Boston is built on filled tidelands and is in “danger of flooding due to sea-level rise and extreme weather,” the city stated. Along with about 284,000 residents in areas at risk of coastal flooding, about 20,000 buildings are at risk of severe flooding, the USACE findings show.

Neighborhoods including Dorchester, Roxbury, the South End, Back Bay, Beacon Hill, East Boston, Charlestown, and Allston are expected to feel impacts, as well as access to hospitals, the MBTA, I-93, the Mass Pike, Logan Airport, and more.

Already 24 severe storms have triggered federal or state disaster declarations in Boston since 1991, and 14 have caused major flooding.

“The reality of this is, after looking at it, doing nothing is not a viable solution,” said Lt. Col. David MacPhail, deputy commander of the USACE New England District. “We have to do something to mitigate this. Without action, the cost of public safety and economic viability from the coastal flooding will be compounded and untenable.”

The study assesses Boston’s “people, the ecosystems of the area, the property, and the critical infrastructure,” MacPhail said, and plans for interventions including seawall improvement, flood walls, berms, levees and surge barriers – a “lattice work of almost puzzle pieces” to build resilience in the 47-mile coastline.

The construction would ultimately close 20 long-term coastal flood pathways, which are inland areas that could flood during extreme weather events. These pathways were identified “by the federal government as key areas of risk that could compromise the safety and economic future of both Boston and the country at large,” city officials said.

At the same time, MacPhail added, there has been effort to “maintain the character and charm” along the Boston Harbor with elements like harbor walks, urban furniture, and other betterments.

All together, the projects are estimated to cost over $10 billion over the next few decades, not including upgrades like green spaces and outdoor recreation expected to be added in, city officials said.

If Boston takes no action, the USACE estimated, the city is projected to lose $54 billion by the end of the century – with about $4 in residents’, businesses’, and the public sector’s avoided disaster losses for every $1 invested.

One study published in the Nature Climate Change journal in June found floods that historically had a 1% chance of striking a coastline in a year are now about 12 times more likely, on average.

Wu said that the city would “have a much better idea” of cost, phasing, funding sources and more following the 2028 final study release.

The Boston Green Ribbon Commission launched a one-year study to identify funding sources for the 35% of the projects non-federal cost share.

City officials urged residents to take part in public comment on the projects from July 24 to Sept. 18, along with an upcoming series of community meetings and webinars.

“If you live or work in Boston or have an interest in Boston, we really do want to hear from you,” said Boston Chief Climate Officer Brian Swett. “Your voice can not only help us protect Boston for generations to come, but also expand your access to green spaces and recreational opportunities right here along the Boston Harbor.”

title: Police Blotter: Four guns recovered in Dorchester arrests
text:
Two men were arrested on gun charges after Boston Police busted a party at a short-term rental in Dorchester.

Around 1 a.m. Monday morning, the owner of a residence on Glenway Street called police to ask them to remove several individuals who he’d rented to using a short-term rental platform, BPD said.

After the owner allowed police inside, the officers encountered a large party, and when they announced their presence, police said that several people tried to leave through an upstairs stairwell.

Officers heard some movement inside one of the residence’s bedrooms and when they opened the door, police said they saw a man, later identified Ryan White Jr., 20, of Randolph, trying to hide what turned out to be a gun under a pillow.

Then, another 20-year-old man, Daktari Rose Deacon, of Hyde Park, left a bathroom that adjoined the bedroom, according to police, who searched the bathroom and found another loaded firearm with an extended magazine.

Police located a third gun and an undisclosed amount of cash inside of a bag in a closet, BPD said.

Randolph was charged with carrying a firearm without a license, carrying a loaded firearm, and possession of ammunition without an FID card. Deacon faces the same charges and an additional count of possession of a large capacity firearm.

Teen arrested for allegedly carrying defaced gun in Harambee Park

During patrols targeted at areas in the city where there’s been a recent spike in gun violence, Boston Police arrested a 14-year-old who they say was carrying around an untraceable firearm in Dorchester.

title: Police blotter: Winthrop man allegedly assaults woman on way to Mass General
text:
A Winthrop man accused of brutally beating up a woman in a spate of alleged domestic assaults, including punching her in the face while on the way to a Boston hospital, is being held without bail.

Anthony Stokes, 39, is scheduled to appear for a dangerousness hearing next week after BMC Central Judge James Coffer ordered him held without bail during his arraignment on Monday.

After allegedly assaulting the victim earlier Saturday night, Stokes is accused of continuing to unleash his violence on the woman as he drove her to Massachusetts General Hospital. He is charged with punching her in the face while en route.

According to the Suffolk County DA’s Office, Stokes instructed the victim to stay in the vehicle and to tell hospital staff and police that a group of women attacked her and that he was “not the perpetrator.”

Boston police responded to Mass General before 8 a.m. Sunday for a domestic violence incident, noticing that the 39-year-old woman had “two swollen eyes, scratch marks on her chest and torso, and bruises on her hands, arms, and chest.”

“Officers learned that a man, later identified as Anthony Stokes, hit her hard in her face while inside his car,” the DA’s office stated in a release on Tuesday. “She was in extreme pain and unable to speak with officers.”

The defendant allegedly later told officers that he and the victim went to an “adult entertainment club,” and that the woman stepped outside to smoke a cigarette at some point before running back inside and accusing him of “letting a group of women physically assault her.”

Stokes allegedly first assaulted the victim earlier Saturday night in the Orient Heights section of East Boston after he consumed alcohol and drove the victim. He then continued driving to Somerset Street in Winthrop, where he “parked the car again, yelled at the victim further and continued to strike her.”

East Boston NeighborHealth instructed the victim to go to Mass General due to the severity of injuries, with staffers offering to call a rideshare. Stokes, though, “insisted on taking her himself and escorted her back to his vehicle.”

Stokes is charged with one count of assault and battery on a family or household member, one count of assault and battery causing serious bodily injury, and one count of intimidating a witness, juror, or court official.

“The facts here point to a serious, sustained assault that left the victim injured and terrorized,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement, “along with being ordered, under extreme duress, to deflect blame from her attacker. Our office will provide this victim with all the support she requires as this case moves forward.”

Guilty plea in Pittsfield drug case

Theodore “Monty” Warren, 42, of Pittsfield, will be sentenced in October after he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to distribute and possession with intent to distribute cocaine and four counts of distribution of and possession with intent to distribute cocaine.

Warren was charged in December 2024 with his co-conspirator Lavante Wiggins, the former dean of Pittsfield High School, according to federal prosecutors.

According to charging documents, Warren participated in a drug trafficking organization that distributed large amounts of cocaine in and around the Pittsfield area. He served as a runner for Wiggins.

Specifically, Warren, under Wiggins’ direction, distributed cocaine to a customer who amassed a debt of more than $34,000 that Wiggins provided on credit. On four separate occasions between September and December 2024, Warren allegedly delivered quantities ranging from 91 grams to 150 grams.

Charges of conspiracy to distribute and possession with intent to distribute cocaine and distribution of cocaine provide for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $2 million.

title: Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia shares ‘heart condition’ after collapse, leading to Council vacancy questions
text:
Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia said Wednesday that she’s wearing a heart monitor for a more serious “heart condition” than the dehydration and exhaustion she initially said caused her to collapse at a meeting two weeks ago.

Mejia attended Wednesday’s City Council meeting and spoke on several issues, but chose to sit down while speaking most of the time, rather than standing up as is typically expected for councilors formally speaking from the Council floor.

She addressed her frailty for the first time more than three hours into her first meeting back since collapsing and being taken by Boston EMS to the hospital during a Council meeting on July 8. Mejia joked that Councilor Ed Flynn was going “to kill” her by repeatedly prompting her to speak as a co-sponsor on his filings.

Mejia, 56, shared that she has a “heart condition” and is wearing a heart monitor, though she didn’t elaborate on the seriousness of her condition.

“It was scary,” Mejia said of her collapse two weeks ago, “and I just want us to learn to take better care of ourselves. If you try to hug me and I push back a little bit, it’s just because I have a little heart monitor.”

The revelation points to a more serious prognosis for the fourth-term councilor who said a day after her health emergency that doctors had initially attributed her collapse to dehydration and exhaustion.

It also leads to questions about whether Mejia, an at-large councilor who was first elected in 2019, will be able to serve out the remainder of her term, which extends through the end of 2027. Mejia shared in 2022 that she had gastric bypass surgery for weight loss in 2018 to handle her diabetes, when denying online chatter accusing her of using drugs.

Also up in the air is the status of another at-large Councilor Henry Santana, who said Tuesday that he has been hospitalized since last week after seeking cardiovascular care, indicating that he too was being treated for a heart condition.

“We have to do a better job,” Mejia said, speaking to both her health and that of her colleague. “We take so many things to heart, literally, and I think it’s really important for us to recognize that, at the end of the day, this is our job and we live to serve, but we can’t die in that service.”

Santana, 30, hasn’t elaborated on his condition. He said he was hospitalized at the Shapiro Cardiovascular Center at Brigham and Women’s Hospital after seeking treatment last Thursday for the “persistent and unresolved health issues” he’s been battling this summer.

Santana, a second-term councilor, was absent from the day’s meeting, and was still hospitalized as of Tuesday, per a statement he released through his office.

The two health scares could create a lane for longtime former Dorchester-centric councilor Frank Baker to finish out one of the at-large terms, following his fifth-place loss in the at-large race last fall.

The city charter dictates that whenever there’s a councilor-at-large vacancy, the fifth-place finisher would be elevated to the Council, if that defeated candidate is “eligible and willing to serve.”

Mayor Michelle Wu worked for months last year to get Santana, her close ally and former employee, reelected to the City Council. That blocked a comeback bid from Baker, a conservative Wu critic supported by former Mayor Marty Walsh.

Wu, who was campaigning for reelection as well, mobilized her campaign to help Santana garner enough signatures to get on the ballot. Santana had been seen as the most vulnerable incumbent councilor, in terms of his potential for losing his seat.

Santana finished fourth in the at-large race, more than 15,000 votes ahead of Baker.

Wu was unsuccessful, however, in keeping Baker from finishing lower in the race, which would have prevented that immediate pathway to the Council for him, should any of the four at-large councilors choose to leave mid-term.

Along with Santana and Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, Wu supported Alexandra Valdez, a City Hall employee who finished sixth in the at-large race.

title: Boston man arrested in deadly July 4 weekend shooting held without bail
text:
Family members of a 24-year-old gunned down during a violent July 4 weekend filled a courtroom Wednesday afternoon for the arraignment of his alleged killer, another 24-year-old accused of doing the shooting.

Catrelle Davis has been charged with murdering Travis Washington in the early morning hours of July 5. Davis allegedly shot the victim while he was standing with a group of people celebrating the holiday on Blue Hill Avenue in Roxbury.

Three other people were shot during the same incident, but none of the others’ injuries were considered life-threatening. Davis has not been charge in connection to those other injuries.

A warrant was issued for Davis and he was arrested Wednesday around 4:35 p.m. in the area of Maple Street and Sonoma Street in Dorchester, according to Boston Police.

Assistant District Attorney Nathan McGregor asked that Davis be held without bail because of the strength of the evidence in the case. The prosecutor said “the entire thing” was caught on video, and “quite clearly” showed the shooting and that Davis was the aggressor.

He asked the court to impound the videos as evidence, which the defense didn’t object to.

Davis was held without bail and will be back in court Sept. 22 for a probable cause hearing.

McGregor also noted that a grand jury investigation into the homicide was ongoing.

People who appeared to be family of Davis were allowed to leave the courtroom first after the hearing, with the large crowd for Washington, wearing pins and t-shirts with his face, filing close behind.

The victim’s family members declined to comment to a reporter after meeting with the prosecutor at Dorchester District Court, following the arraignment.

“Every homicide is a societal tragedy, and the tragedy is magnified when the victim is a young person just getting started in life,” Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I extend my deepest sympathies to Travis Washington’s family and friends, and I thank all of the investigators for their tireless work resulting in Catrelle Davis’s arrest.”

Washington was one of two young men killed over in the early hours after the Fourth of July.

Christopher Washington-Conway, 29, was killed in a triple shooting on George Street, also in Roxbury, according to Boston Police. The department has not announced any arrests in that case.

In total, 13 people were shot in five incidents that occurred that night.

The spike in violence led to calls for a public safety summit as well as more resources for the police department and local anti-violence community groups.

According to the latest crime data, which was published Monday, the total number of victims shot in Boston is up from the same time last year, while shooting fatalities are slightly down.

Between Jan. 1 and July 19, 2025, 12 people were shot and killed in the city, compared to nine so far this year. The department does note that information is preliminary and subject to change.

title: Massachusetts murderer who sexually assaulted, killed 17-year-old girl has been granted parole
text:
A Bay State murderer who sexually assaulted and killed a 17-year-old girl by smashing her head with a rock — pummeling her face beyond recognition — has been granted parole.

Damien Lockhart was 23 years old in 1996 when he murdered 17-year-old Kimberly Bolton in Framingham after she rejected him.

This decision comes as the Parole Board faces criticism for releasing scores of convicted murderers.

On the day of the slaying, Lockhart had suspected that his girlfriend was cheating on him. In a fit of rage, he broke his girlfriend’s television, ripped up her clothes, and smashed a mirror before leaving the house to drink, smoke crack, and try to cheat on her.

Lockhart then met Kimberly and convinced her to go to a secluded spot, where they kissed. When he tried to touch her in a sexual way, she said no.

“One thing was supposed to lead to another and we were going to have sex,” Lockhart told the Massachusetts Parole Board. “When that didn’t happen, my plan changed. Raping her was how I was going to get my needs met.”

Kimberly fought him off, until he hit her in the head with a rock. After she fell to the ground, he heard a groan.

Lockhart said he dragged her to a more secluded spot, and smashed her head seven times with a much larger rock, until she was dead.

Her body was later found by the edge of a railroad dirt access road known as “the Weeds.”

Lockhart had pummeled her face beyond recognition — requiring the use of dental records to confirm her identity.

“It was a particularly brutal thing,” then-Middlesex DA Thomas Reilly told the Herald after the murder in 1996.

A year later, Lockhart pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole.

He also pleaded guilty to attempted rape, and he was sentenced to a concurrent term of 9 to 12 years in prison.

Parole was denied after an initial hearing in 2013, and after review hearings in 2018, 2023 and 2025.

Then earlier this year, Lockhart appeared before the Parole Board for another review hearing.

Two of Lockhart’s family members testified in support of parole, while three members of Kimberly’s family and a Middlesex DA prosecutor testified against parole.

“Mr. Lockhart has followed the Board’s recommendations — since the last hearing he has completed Enhancing Empathy,” the Parole Board wrote in its decision. “The Board considered Dr. DiCataldo’s evaluation in rendering this decision.

“Mr. Lockhart uses a wheelchair due to spinal and hip issues,” the board added. “Mr. Lockhart has family and friend support and a re-entry plan to meet his needs. The Board concludes that Damien Lockhart has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society.”

During past parole hearings, Lockhart apologized to Kimberly’s family. He told the Parole Board that as a teen living in Dorchester, he was an alcoholic and addicted to crack cocaine. He was drinking every day, as well as stealing cars and selling them for parts to support his crack cocaine habit.

He was expelled from school after he showed up drunk and assaulted another student. Lockhart said he never met his father, and his mother was abusive and addicted to drugs.

He told the board that he moved to Framingham to live with an aunt to escape the drugs and violence of his Dorchester neighborhood, but soon found himself smoking crack again. He was expelled from Framingham High School after assaulting a student.

He was previously charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon (scissors) and assault with intent to maim, and he was convicted of arson. The assault with intent to maim stemmed from an incident when he punched his aunt in the nose during a fight.

The arson conviction occurred when he filled a jar full of gasoline, set it on fire, and threw it at a family’s house while they were home. He believed that one of the occupants of the house had previously stabbed a friend of his.

title: Massachusetts Senator Nick Collins undercuts Boston Mayor Michelle Wu on tax relief amid feud
text:
State Sen. Nick Collins fired the latest shot in his ongoing feud with Mayor Michelle Wu by tucking a property tax relief clause into the economic development bill to blunt Boston’s “unnecessary tax increase on homeowners.”

Collins said his property tax relief amendment, which would expand senior tax exemption eligibility and provide rebates to Boston homeowners using city surplus funds, was unanimously approved by the state Senate.

“The purpose of the senior property tax exemption is to support seniors on fixed income who deserve tax relief to ease the burden of the city’s unnecessary tax increase on homeowners,” Collins said from the Senate floor. “In addition, the legislation would authorize the city to issue rebates to homeowners to mitigate unnecessary tax increases levied by the city year after year.”

Collins, a South Boston Democrat, said his amendment to the proposed state economic development bill would expand eligibility of the senior property tax exemption and triple the benefit to $1,500.

It would also provide tax rebates to homeowners using funds from what Collins called the city’s “substantial surplus,” or reserve fund, “to the tune of $1.7 billion that was built up by the taxpayers and that rating agencies suggest the city is stockpiling for small businesses.”

Collins said the amendment would also triple the personal property tax exemption to help businesses “survive the unnecessary tax increases levied on them also by the city, year after year.”

The senator — who has been in the mayor’s crosshairs since his late 2024 move to block her signature tax shift legislation and is facing a primary challenge from a political newcomer backed by Wu — suggested that any opposition from City Hall to the Senate-approved tax relief amendment he proposed would be political.

“These policies, the city is already on record in support of, including passage of the Boston City Council,” Collins said. “For the city to be against it now, they’d have to be for it before they were against it.”

The amendment, co-sponsored by Republican Senate Minority Leader Bruce Tarr, is the latest shot fired in the state Senate’s battle with Wu over how to provide property tax relief to homeowners.

Wu has publicly blamed Collins for the failure of her tax shift bill, citing his procedural move to block a vote multiple times before it was ultimately killed by Senate President Karen Spilka due to lack of support.

The bill sought to provide a tax break to homeowners by increasing commercial tax rates. It was passed by the City Council and House of Representatives three times, but stalled in the Senate.

Wu has endorsed Latoya Gayle, a political newcomer and community activist challenging Collins in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. She has also endorsed her former senior aide Daniel Lander in his bid to knock off William Brownsberger, the President pro tempore of the Senate and the other senator Wu blames for killing her tax bill.

Collins and Brownsberger put forward alternative property tax relief bills that they argue won’t have the same harmful effects on the economy.

Their legislation was approved by the Senate in January but drew opposition from the mayor, who called their bills “costly alternative Senate proposals that require sacrificing needed funding for city services.”

Collins said his new amendment to the Senate version of the state’s economic development bill marks the second time this session that the Senate has moved to approve property tax relief measures.

While Wu has blamed the Senate for this year’s 13% average tax increase for homeowners, due to their failure to approve her legislation, Collins said the city’s “unfair” assessment practices are to blame.

“Finally, the part of the legislation that hits at the heart of why Bostonians continue to see tax increases year after year is due to the city’s unfair assessing practices,” Collins said. “The facts are these: the city is giving wealthy homeowners in Back Bay and Beacon Hill a tax cut by under-assessing their property dramatically.

“At the same time, these unfair assessing practices by the city are hammering the middle class, taxing them to the max or more — communities like Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, South Boston, the South End,” Collins added. “It does not make any sense, and it’s wrong.”

Collins said that, recently, a home in Back Bay valued at $20 million was assessed by the city at $12.5 million. He added that a property on Beacon Hill that sold for $20 million was later assessed by the city at just $5 million.

Meanwhile, in the working class neighborhood of Roslindale, a home that sold last year for $435,000 was assessed later by the city at $485,000, leading to higher property taxes, Collins said.

The senator said the city’s assessment practices have already led to a lawsuit filed by the Pioneer New England Legal Foundation on behalf of commercial property owners who allege the city added assessed value — and therefore, higher taxes — following abatements, and are seeking restitution.

“It is the reason the city’s assessor recently resigned in disgrace,” Collins said, referencing Nicholas Ariniello’s abrupt departure. “This will cost the city. … But while the former assessor skips town, taxpayers will suffer.”

Collins said his amendment seeks to counter “unfair” city assessing practices by giving property owners an additional 75 days to file abatements and “keep their existing assessment intact before their dispute is resolved.”

The senator said, “It’s clear that the city needs assessment reform.”

title: Police Blotter: Man shot to death in Eastie

“A bloody knife was on the floor next to the males,” a department statement said.

The officers separated the men and paramedics were able to offer aid to all three people who police noted were “severely injured.”

After processing the crime and interviewing the individuals involved, detectives determined that one of the men, Kyle Barboza, 42, had attacked the female victim in the hotel room, the statement said.

The victims told police that Barboza had reached out to them earlier in the day and asked if he could stay with them. The couple picked the suspect up and at first “all was normal at the motel,” police said.

But, when the male victim went to the bathroom, Barboza allegedly tried to slit the woman’s throat from behind. When her boyfriend left the bathroom to help her, the suspect then attacked him, too, police said.

“He fought back and was eventually able to force Barboza to the floor and hold him there until police arrived,” the statement said.

The suspect faces two counts each of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury and attempted murder.

The police department said that Barboza is under arrest and still in the hospital, where he’s being monitored by officers.

title: Boston reflects on safety, law enforcement during National Night Out
text:
Boston residents across the city’s neighborhoods came out for the second day of National Night Out events Tuesday, meeting with their local law enforcement and reflecting on safety in the community.

“It’s always nice to see local police officers and people from upper management coming in to kind of introduce themselves, just to meet every meet and greet everyone,” said Chinatown resident John Lam, young daughter performed with a K-Pop dance group during the event Tuesday. “It was good to kind of get everyone in the community out.”

The Boston mayor and public safety leadership made stops in Dorchester, South Boston, Chinatown, the South End, North End and East Boston for National Night Out events with neighborhood residents and local law enforcement on Tuesday, adding to prior stops across the city on Monday.

The annual events aim to enhance “the relationship between neighbors and law enforcement while bringing back a true sense of community” by bringing police and residents together under “positive circumstances,” according to the National Night Out organization.

“You partner with us in so many different ways, whether it’s community meetings, working with our police, our community service officers, our captains, our lieutenants,” said BPD Commissioner Michael Cox during the Chinatown event, which leaders noted is the largest. “Your community leads the way when it comes to partnership and public safety. So we’re here to say thank you to everyone.”

Mayor Michelle Wu responded to recent incidents of violence in Boston, including the shooting of five people in Hyde Park on Monday.

“Any time there’s a family who’s grieving a loss, the whole community is feeling that and will continue to feel that year after year,” said Wu. “And so that’s why it’s so important to not only respond after something might happen, but to do everything we can to prevent situations from ever happening in the first place.”

Wu said he administration has focused on with conversations “between all levels of public safety agencies, community safety partners, and faith leaders, organizations,” adding the collaborations visible at National Night Out are ongoing throughout the year.

“Even though we know that, for instance, the number of homicides is lower this year than it was last year, it’s not about — any time there’s any single incident that causes a sense of worry that is unacceptable,” said Wu. “And we are going to keep at it and continue doubling down until every single part of Boston, every single family knows that they can access all the great opportunities throughout the city.”

Lam said as someone who grew up in Chinatown in the 80s, “it’s definitely gotten a lot better since then.”

“But you know, it’s always good having people look out for each other, and I think that’s the most important thing,” Lam said.

At the event Tuesday, Allyson Murray, a Dorchester resident who attended the event with Boston Senior Home Care in collaboration with other organizations to promote services for older adults, said the giveaways, dim sum and bouncy houses were “a hit” in drawing neighbors out Tuesday

“I think people really like it,” said Murray. “They get it gets a chance to get outdoors, see their neighbors. It’s a beautiful day. So I think it was really well received.”

Murray noted safety issues in her neighborhood Dorchester, adding there’s “some level of angst” everywhere in the city.

Hung Goon, a member of the local neighborhood Chinatown Crime Watch and Boston Chinatown Lions Club, said public safety in the area is “adequate but always could be better.” The crime watch group supports the National Night Out every year, he said, noting the event helps connect residents with law enforcement.

“It’s good to they get to take picture with the the police, fire, and the EMS people, so they’re more used to it,” said Goon. “Chinese people are very conservative. They don’t like to report anything. So hopefully, when they get to meet them, they come out, and hopefully, if they see anything, they say something.”

title: Boston’s summer of violence: Dorchester fatal daylight shooting continues wave
text:
Boston’s summer of violence continued Wednesday with a fatal broad daylight shooting on Blue Hill Avenue in Dorchester, during a week the city has already seen two other deadly bouts of gunfire.

The violence has exacerbated demands from community leaders, city councilors and neighborhood groups that the city’s public safety plan be updated and the violent perpetrators be held accountable.

Entering Sunday, there had been 11 fatal shootings so far this year, down just one compared to the same time period last year, according to preliminary data from the Boston Police Department.

There had also been 17 homicides so far this year, as of the start of the week.

After fatal shootings in Eastie on Sunday, Hyde Park on Monday and Dorchester on Wednesday, this year’s number of shooting deaths matches the five-year average of 14 around this time of the year, BPD numbers show. The Hyde Park death has been ruled a homicide.

Here’s a rundown on the recent summer violence:

Wednesday: Man shot dead at 564 Blue Hill Ave., near the intersection with Seaver Street, abutting Franklin Park Zoo, around 10 a.m.

Monday: One man shot dead, Ky Mani Korey Reynolds, 26, of Dorchester, and four others injured, just after midnight outside of Little Haiti International Cuisine on Hyde Park Avenue.

Sunday: Police called to a shooting on Meridian Street around 1:24 a.m. and found the victim, Joseph Gabriel Lucas Gomez, 21, of East Boston, who was then taken to a hospital where he was pronounced dead.

July 22: A 27-year-old Bedford man, Ashlie Jeremie, is arrested for allegedly killing someone on Boston Common and for attacking another person with a metal pole.

July 18: Police discover an 18-year-old woman, later identified as Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio, suffering from a single gunshot wound in a bedroom of a Mattapan rental home owned by Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley’s husband. The teen was pronounced dead at the scene, and the death has been ruled a homicide.

July 15: A 29-year-old man dies after being shot shortly before noon on York Street in Dorchester. EMS declared the victim dead at the scene.

July 4: Two people were killed out of the 13 shot in Boston during what Mayor Michelle Wu called a “long and difficult” July 4th night. The victims were identified as Travis Deonard Washington, 24, and Christopher Washington-Conway, 29, in separate shootings.

June 22: A 19-year-old was shot to death on Milton Avenue, with the victim identified as Jalen J. Tavares, of Lakeville.

title: Police: Man dead in Blue Hill Avenue shooting
text:
The Boston Police Department is investigating a fatal broad daylight shooting on Blue Hill Avenue in Dorchester.

BPD spokesperson Sgt. Det. John Boyle confirmed with the Herald that the victim, an “adult male,” has died after being shot at 564 Blue Hill Ave., near the intersection with Seaver Street, abutting Franklin Park Zoo, around 10 a.m. on Wednesday.

The confirmation came moments after BPD Superintendent Paul McLaughlin briefed the media at the scene just before noon, reporting that the victim was rushed to the hospital and was in “very critical condition” from “multiple gunshot wounds.”

No suspects were immediately in police custody. McLaughlin said it was too early to determine whether the shooting was gang-related.

“I would say that I do not believe this was a random incident,” McLaughlin said, “so I don’t believe there’s a danger to the rest of the community in the sense that this person is running around and shooting at people.”

“I think this was a situation where the parties are known in one way or another,” he added. “That’s how we’re following up.”

Detectives were canvassing the scene and “looking for video, looking for additional witnesses and evidence.”

“We are following up on information about the shooter, how they got here, how they left,” he said. “Over the next couple of hours, we will have more information on exactly how that happened.”

Police officials were asking the public, “anybody who might have been out here, anyone who has video, driving by,” for assistance.

Anyone with information was strongly urged to contact the Boston Police Homicide Unit at 617-343-4470 or the CrimeStoppers Tip Line at 1-800-494-TIPS or by texting the word “TIP” to CRIME (27463).

The brazen shooting continues Boston’s stretch of summer violence.

Briefing reporters in Dorchester, McLaughlin touched on the Hyde Park shooting that left a 26-year-old man dead and four others injured early Monday morning.

Oliver Derima, 27, of Randolph, was ordered held without bail Tuesday, remaining hidden from courtroom cameras as he was arraigned on murder and other charges stemming from the Hyde Park Avenue shooting death of Ky Mani Korey Reynolds, 26, of Dorchester, just after midnight Monday.

“Clearly, we’ve had a few incidents recently that are very alarming to the public and to us,” McLaughlin said. “That’s why we are committed to taking quick action. … We have a lot of detectives assigned to this, and we are looking to put this case together as quickly as we possibly can.”

The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the department’s largest union, stated in a social media post that this is the latest example why the city needs more officers.

“Broad daylight violence, in addition to being incredibly brazen, is especially concerning for all who live in the city,” the union posted on X. “If bad guys aren’t thinking twice about shooting people at 10:15AM, that’s a problem.”

The union added, “More police presence equals less violence.”

title: Police Blotter: Boston man arrested for Dorchester fatal shooting
text:
Boston Police arrested a 23-year-old man for the Wednesday morning shooting on Blue Hill Avenue in Dorchester.

Billy Thien Huynh was arraigned Thursday in Boston Municipal Court’s Dorchester division in connection with the fatal shooting of a 20-year-old man at 564 Blue Hill Ave. on Wednesday. Boston Police on Thursday identified the victim as Victor Armani Arias Rivera, of South Boston.

“This was a brazen, brutal shooting that took a young man’s life and showed yet again how illegal guns in the hands of people willing to use them are a menace to our city,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a morning release from his office announcing the arrest.

“I grieve for the victim’s family and I thank the Boston police detectives, prosecutors from my office and members of the public for all their efforts leading to such a quick arrest,” Hayden continued.

Huynh faces charges of murder and several firearm-related counts, including carrying without a license. The suspect was ordered held without bail Thursday.

On Wednesday at about 10:14 a.m., police were called to an apartment on Blue Hill Ave. in Dorchester, where they found Rivera suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso, the criminal complaint states. Rivera was pronounced dead an hour later at Boston Medical Center.

According to a witness statement, the complaint says, the suspect arrived at the apartment on a motorcycle, left briefly and then returned with a second man and a young girl in pink on an electric bike. Huynh was allegedly questioning Rivera and a witness about a missing bike, the document states.

Huynh allegedly pulled a gun, the police reported of witness statements, and when Rivera said, “I don’t have your bike,” shot him. The second man with the child reportedly yelled, “Why did you do that,” the complaint states.

“After a short exchange of words, the defendant fired at least two rounds into the top half of his body, ultimately resulting in his death,” said ADA Ashlee Mastrangelo. “The defendant fled the scene on a motorcycle and was later picked up by an Uber in Quincy and turned over to the Boston Police Department.”

The second man allegedly told police Huynh was staying at his house when they received word Huynh’s stolen bike was at Blue Hill Ave. near Seaver St. and went to help him retrieve it. With his daughter present, the witness allegedly told police, “they were not trying to get into any violent altercations.”

After the shooting, the complaint details, the second man left with his daughter and met with his partner. Together, the pair called to tell Huynh he “needed to turn himself in,” ordered him an Uber to take him to BPD headquarters, and met him there, telling officers the defendant “made a bad decision.”

“When the defendant was confronted with that statement, he said, ‘I guess I shot somebody. I was out riding. I guess, I had just snapped, blacked out, and just, now it’s like, I realized what I did and I came in,” Mastrangelo said of a police interview with Huynh.

Following the incident Wednesday, BPD Superintendent Paul McLaughlin said the shooting was one in a string of violent incidents in the city that “are very alarming to the public and to us.” He said they had assigned “a lot of detectives” to the case.

The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the department’s largest union, stated in a social media post that this is the latest example why the city needs more officers.

“Broad daylight violence, in addition to being incredibly brazen, is especially concerning for all who live in the city,” the union posted on X. “If bad guys aren’t thinking twice about shooting people at 10:15AM, that’s a problem.”

Huynh will return to Dorchester District Court on Sept. 4 for a probable cause hearing.

Dorchester shooting suspect arrested

A 32-year-old suspect was charged with murder in connection with the fatal shooting of a man in Dorchester in July, Boston Police reported Thursday.

Hensly Dominique Jeanty, of Dorchester, was arraigned on counts of murder and several firearm charges in Dorchester District Court following his arrest Wednesday.

The charges stem from a July 15 shooting at 15 York St. in Dorchester. At 11:53 a.m. on the date, the criminal complaint states, police responded to the area and found a man shot, identified as Breidy Martinez, 29, of Dorchester.

Martinez was pronounced dead on the scene, according to the court documents.

Police tracked a black Jeep Grand Cherokee from the scene of the shooting to Roxbury on July 15 using video footage and witnesses, finding Jeanty allegedly operating the vehicle, the complaint states. The evidence indicates Jeanty “operated or was an occupant” of the vehicle as it moved from the crime scene to Roxbury, the police reported.

The footage, witnesses and cell phone records allegedly show another person in the car “prior to, during and after” the shooting, the complaint continues. The second individual identified as an occupant or driver was identified as 26-year-old Dradae Montissol.

One occupant of the car was the driver and the other allegedly shot Martinez, police allege.

Montissol also faces identical charges of murder and firearm counts, the criminal complaint states.

title: Boston Police Blotter: Serial shoplifter gets up to three years behind bars
text:

The prison sentence is to be followed by two years of probation, and Croft was ordered to stay away from victims and the locations that he stole from.

According to the DA’s office, Croft targeted Home Depot stores in West Roxbury and the South Bay Mall.

Through a series of thefts from February to June last year, Croft stole $7,000 worth of merchandise in eight incidents that were caught on surveillance footage.

He stole drills, nail kits, wire, circuit breakers, and, in at least one instance, a wheelbarrow — which Croft used to carry other lifted loot from the store, according to the statement.

Croft has more than 80 convictions on his rap sheet, including more than 20 shoplifting charges, the DA said.

“We take great care to provide rehabilitative services to offenders when appropriate, but some individuals require a much different approach. title: Police Blotter: New Hampshire man grabs unemployment checks — while in prison
text:
A New Hampshire man admitted to committing fraud by withholding the fact he was in prison while receiving unemployment checks.

Peter Mancini, 48, will spend up to another five years in New Hampshire prison for this latest criminal offense. He pleaded guilty Wednesday to charges of unemployment fraud and perjury in Grafton Superior Court.

Prosecutors say that Mancini between October 2025 and February 2026 submitted unemployment claims to the state Department of Employment and Security in which he “falsely represented that an offer of employment was rescinded through no fault of his own.” In the last two months of that period “he also represented that he completed work searches and/or was available and able to work, omitting that he was incarcerated.”

For the unemployment fraud, the judge sentenced Mancini to 2 ½ to 5 years in prison, to be served concurrently with a previous, unrelated sentence of witness tampering, which had been suspended until this new crime.

Mancini will also have to pay back the government with a 20% penalty and will owe the N.H. Department of Employment Security $11,785. He’ll be disqualified for unemployment benefits for a year and will be fined $10,000 plus a 24% penalty suspended for 10 years upon good behavior. A 1 ½ to 3 year sentence for perjury is also suspended.

Moped city

The latest crackdown saw 18 mopeds removed in Hyde Park on Thursday for alleged violations of various auto and traffic laws in the areas of Hyde Park Avenue, Cummins Highway, and American Legion Highway.

“The initiative was organized in response to ongoing public safety concerns regarding the use of these vehicles in the Hyde Park neighborhoods,” the Boston Police Department wrote in a statement.

Keyboard warrior

A Cambridge man running a business his investors would come to describe as a scam allegedly retaliated by threats to ruin their own business reputations and even to shoot his investors “in the face.”

Patrick McDonald, 33, of Cambridge, was charged in federal court in Boston Thursday with three counts each of cyberstalking and transmitting a threat in interstate commerce. Each charge, if convicted, carries a penalty of up to 5 years in prison.

McDonald’s alleged campaign of cyber harassment didn’t begin with direct threats to commit violence, however. Instead, “Victim 1” described the 30 to 40 daily emails from McDonald — totaling some 300 to 350 by the Jan. 17, 2025 interview with investigators — as “childish, harassing, and ‘mean’ in nature.”

But by April 27, 2026, Victim 1 said the daily emails had changed, becoming “violent and threatening with threats being made to shoot Victim 1 ‘in the face,’” according to an affidavit filed to support the criminal charges against McDonald. A state court-issued harassment prevention order would expire on May 7.

These communications were in direct response to Victim 1, an investor in McDonald’s business “Waev,” airing concerns about a lack of financial or business transparency about the business and even warning other potential investors off the business he thought could be a scam, according to a law enforcement affidavit supporting the charges.

Victim 1 is described in court documents as a founding partner in a business that invests in blockchain technology and cyber security and had invested $250,000 in Waev. Victims 2 and 3 were also investors who said they also “experienced a flurry of emails from McDonald daily or nearly every day.” The latter two had purchased a house for McDonald to live and work in as part of their investment but then pulled out when they had their own concerns over the business.

“Among other things, McDonald allegedly threatened to shoot victims ‘in the face,’ threatened to kill a victim’s son, sent an email containing a victim’s home address and a threat to tear the victim’s body apart ‘limb by limb,’ and sent images depicting firearms and shootings,” prosecutors summarized.
