title: Boston Police investigating fatal stabbing in Dorchester
text:
A man was stabbed to death in Dorchester early Monday morning, police said.

Boston Police responded to a report of a person stabbed in the area of Wilbert Road and Harvard Street at about 3:20 a.m., and found a man suffering from stab wounds upon arrival.

The man was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said.

The incident is under investigation by the Boston Police Department’s Homicide Unit. No arrests have been made and the victim has not been identified.

Police are urging anyone with information about the stabbing to contact the Homicide Unit at 617-343-4470.

Anonymous tips can also be shared via the CrimeStoppers Tip Line at 1-800-494-TIPS or sent by texting the word “TIP” to CRIME (27463), police said.

The incident comes soon after back-to-back stabbings that occurred last week, between Wednesday night and Thursday morning at, and within steps of, two of the city’s busiest MBTA stations, respectively.

Two people were stabbed near North Station and TD Garden late Thursday morning, in what police believe to be an act of domestic violence, where a man stabbed a woman and then himself. The night before, a man was stabbed to death at South Station after a fight on an escalator.

Police on Monday identified the South Station victim as Latavius Owens, 29, of Memphis, TN.

The escalation in violence this summer has alarmed some city officials and led to calls for more police officers from the city’s largest police union, the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association.

There have been four mass shootings in the past seven weeks across the city, including one this month in Hyde Park that left one person dead and four injured. On July 4th, 13 people were shot, two fatally.

One city councilor, Ed Flynn, has suggested that the National Guard should be deployed to Boston to help police get a handle on crime.

Mayor Michelle Wu, who has stuck to her “safest major city” claim, dismissed Flynn’s call as “irresponsible,” given that she saw him as pushing for a “federal militarization” of Boston streets.

Flynn fired back, by accusing the mayor of downplaying a “public safety crisis.”

After Monday’s stabbing, police directed people “who find themselves in need of emotional support or simply needing to talk to someone about the distressing events in our community,” to the Boston Neighborhood Trauma Team, which provides free, private support 24/7 at 617-431-0125.

title: Jackie Bulger, Whitey’s younger brother, dies. He was 88
text:
John “Jackie” Bulger, the brother of slain mobster James “Whitey” Bulger, died last week in his South Boston home. He was 88.

He is survived by his other brother, William “Billy” Bulger, the onetime head of UMass and past president of the state Senate. He is also survived by his sisters, Carol McCarthy and Sheila McKeon, as well as nieces, nephews, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

Calling hours are Wednesday at the O’Brien Funeral Home, 146 Dorchester St., from 4-7 p.m., with a Prayer Service at 7 p.m. Burial will be private.

Jackie has long been tied to his clan and seldom backed away from a reporter calling for comment. The youngest of the Bulger brothers, Jackie was stripped of his state pension after lying to a grand jury about visiting one of Whitey’s cash-stuffed safe-deposit bank boxes in Florida. Like Whitey, Jackie ended up in custody of the Bureau of Prisons.

But loyalty was a constant in his life, even if he paid for it. The Dorchester Reporter wrote Jackie was the only family member at Whitey’s sentencing hearing and that he was there every day during the trial. The Herald was also there the day Whitey was sent away for life without parole and Jackie walked out to face the cameras.

Whitey was beaten to death at age 89 on October 30, 2018, just 12 hours after arriving at the USP Hazelton prison in West Virginia. Per the Boston Herald, mob hitman Fotios “Freddy” Geas and other inmates attacked him with a padlock in a sock.

Whitey was serving two life sentences, plus five years, for directing or participating in 11 murders during his reign of terror in Boston.

Bulger was the nation’s Most Wanted man while on the run for 16 years until being spotted in 2011 in Santa Monica, Calif., $822,000 in cash hidden in the walls of his apartment where he lived with his lover on the lam.

Jackie and Billy sued the federal Board of Prisons over Whitey’s murder, but ultimately lost. Billy still lives in Southie.

title: Boston Mayor Wu hires new election chief ahead of Sept. 1 primary
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has hired a new leader of the Election Department ahead of the state primary, as the city continues to make changes to try to work itself out of state receivership after a disastrous election two years ago.

Wu on Wednesday announced City Hall veteran Kerry Jordan as the new executive director of the Boston Election Department.

“Kerry is a son of Dorchester, a Boston Public Schools alum, and a dedicated public servant who knows that the right tech tools can help close gaps between the city and our communities,” Wu said at a City Hall press conference. “I can’t think of a better person to lead our city’s elections and elections department.”

Jordan works as chief of staff for the city’s Department of Innovation and Technology and will move into his new position after the primary, on Sept. 8. He was paid $146,264 by the city last year, and it’s unclear whether his new job comes with a pay bump, as Wu’s office could not immediately provide salary details.

The former elections commissioner, seemingly the position Jordan is replacing, was paid $146,416. The job posting listed the city’s salary for the post at $145,000.

Wu said Jordan has worked for the city for 18 years. Jordan added he’s spent the past five years in the Department of Innovation and Technology.

Jordan said he is excited to lead the Election Department, and help ensure that the city meets his “common goal,” which is to hold “fair, secure and accessible elections.”

He replaces Eneida Tavares, the city’s election commissioner since 2019 who bounced to a different city department earlier this year, after overseeing a chaotic 2024 presidential election that led to the city’s Election Department being placed in state receivership for “incompetence,” as Secretary of State William Galvin put it.

City officials said Wednesday that they have made a number of changes aimed at ensuring a smooth primary election on Sept. 1. Galvin’s office said Boston’s performance this election season will determine whether state oversight continues.

“The order that the Secretary issued after the 2024 election stated that the receivership would be in place through the 2026 State Election and would be reassessed after that election,” Galvin spokesperson Debra O’Malley said.

Paul Chong, the city’s registrar and commissioner of public records, would not speculate on whether efforts to improve election effectiveness in Boston would lead to an end to state receivership after the Nov. 3 general election.

“I expect that we’ll have that conversation on the heels of a very successful election,” Chong said. “We’re working closely with our partners in the state government, in Secretary Galvin’s office. We are very confident that we are going to have safe, free, and fair elections.”

Chong said the city has made changes to modernize city elections, such as last year’s expansion of electronic poll books that reduced check-in times for voters, allowed for real-time ballot tracking and the ability to quickly redirect a voter who showed up at the wrong polling site.

Galvin placed the city’s Election Department in receivership in February 2025 for its failure to properly administer the 2024 state and presidential elections, which he said reflected “incompetence” on the part of the city.

Widespread ballot shortages in that fall election left voters waiting in lines for hours to vote. Galvin’s office on Election Day 2024 had to issue a directive to Boston Police to rush ballots to multiple polling locations so residents could vote, as Galvin said city staff wouldn’t answer the phone in the Elections Department.

Chong said the city is “confident we’re going to have plenty” of ballots this time around, for the state primary and general elections, while again citing the electronic poll books and updated procedures that will allow election officials to better track ballot inventory and potential shortages at polling stations.

Wu said the city’s technology changes led to successful elections last year, while emphasizing that “the challenges that we saw in the last presidential” election “were two years ago.”

“Last year was a really important opportunity for us to work hand in hand with the Secretary of State’s office to implement and test out this new technology,” Wu said. “As far as we could tell, the last election cycle in 2025 went very successfully.”

The city will also be under federal oversight this election season. The Department of Justice is sending election monitors to Boston for the Sept. 1 primary.

Chong said the feds will be in town to monitor the Election Department, not voters, who should not be put off from casting their ballots.

“We feel that we are prepared for whoever comes to see what we do and how we do elections in Boston,” Chong said. “I want to emphasize for voters, especially that election monitors are here to observe, if they come, the election department, not voters. And so, I strongly encourage voters to participate in our election this coming September.”

title: Police blotter: 124 forged credit cards, moped sweep and Roslindale home invasion
text:
Boston Police have arrested a 27-year-old man on charges of possessing 124 forged debit cards.

The department says it also seized an “undisclosed amount” of cash inside a vehicle that officers pulled over in Brighton on Tuesday, in the area of Harvard Avenue and Brainerd Road.

Officers pulled the vehicle over after it failed to stop at a red light, and they reportedly recognized the operator, Nicusor Lazar, who was wanted in connection with an ongoing ATM card fraud investigation.

“Officers approached the vehicle and the operator provided an Italian driver’s license and a bank card with the same name,” the BPD said in a release. “As officers were speaking with the operator, they observed a large stack of US currency bundled together in the center console as well as numerous credit/ debit cards in the cup holder.”

Investigators determined that the Italian driver’s license and bank card were fraudulent.

Lazar did not possess a valid license to operate a motor vehicle within the U.S.

Lazar was expected to be arraigned in Brighton District Court on charges of Money Laundering, two counts of Uttering, Identity Fraud, Forgery of an RMV Document, and Furnishing a False ID to Law Enforcement.

Home invasion

A West Roxbury judge has released a Roslindale teenager who allegedly vandalized property and unleashed other violence at her ex-boyfriend’s home.

Boston Municipal Judge Maureen Flaherty released Alyssah Harrison, 19, on personal recognizance and ordered her to stay away from the victims, witnesses and home.

Harrison, charged with home invasion, assault and battery, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and malicious destruction of property, is set to return to court for a pretrial hearing on Oct. 2.

The rampage unfolded on July 22 when Harrison allegedly broke the glass screen of her ex-boyfriend’s front door in Roslindale with an aluminum baseball bat, according to a report that the victim provided to BPD.

The victim alleged that Harrison entered his home, pushed his wife and then punched her in the face, threatening them both with the bat.

“Harrison then ran up the stairs into a bedroom on the second floor and began opening drawers and the closet, as if looking for something,” the Suffolk DA’s office said in a release. “The male victim left the home to contact property security, and the female victim followed Harrison upstairs, where she attempted to physically remove Harrison from the room, resulting in a fight.”

Harrison then allegedly fled the home.

“It’s not hard to imagine the fear these homeowners must have experienced when their peaceful day at home was suddenly turned chaotic and violent due by an armed intruder,” DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Our victim witness advocates are trained in trauma and acquaintance violence scenarios and will provide all the support these victims require as the case moves forward.”

Moped sweep

A targeted enforcement operation in Dorchester and Roxbury seized 31 mopeds, with officers issuing summonses for 12 individuals.

Officers and detectives in Roxbury partnered with members of the BPD’s auto theft unit to crack down on the mopeds that reportedly violated auto laws in the areas of Blue Hill Avenue and Warren Street.

“The initiative was organized in response to ongoing public safety concerns regarding the use of these vehicles in the Dorchester and Roxbury neighborhoods,” the department said in a release.

“The Boston Police Department remains committed to improving traffic safety,” it added, “and will continue to conduct enforcement operations across the city.”

Incident Summary

The BPD responded to 311 incidents in the 24-hour period ending at 10 a.m. Wednesday, according to the department’s incident log. Those included one robbery, three aggravated assaults, one commercial burglary, one residential burglary, one larceny from a vehicle, two auto thefts, and 25 instances of miscellaneous larceny.

title: Gaskin: Boston must innovate homeownership boost
text:
Boston knows how to innovate.

We do it in life sciences, high tech, medicine, biotech, artificial intelligence, climate research, robotics, finance, and higher education.

But when it comes to homeownership, our imagination gets small.

For too many young people and working families, homeownership no longer feels like a life goal. It feels like a fantasy. Not because they lack ambition, but because the math has turned brutal.

Depending on the measure used, the typical Boston home is selling below but approaching $1 million. Redfin recently put Boston’s median sale price at about $852,000. Zillow put Boston’s average home value at about $786,000. Across Greater Boston, the median single-family home price has already crossed the $1 million mark.

So when people say buying a home in Boston costs “around a million dollars,” they are not far off. Once interest rates, closing costs, bidding wars, taxes, repairs, and moving costs are included, the barrier feels even higher.

The result is a city where working people can pay high rent for years but still struggle to buy.

Boston has useful tools. The First-Time Homebuyer Program provides down-payment assistance. ONE+Boston offers discounted fixed-rate mortgages, down-payment and closing-cost help, and no private mortgage insurance for eligible buyers.

If Boston wants to remain a city where working people can build wealth, not just pay rent, we need to lead in innovative home financing the same way.

Around the country, people are experimenting with paths from exclusion to ownership. Boston should study them, adapt them, improve them, and build its own versions.

Napoleon Wallace’s work offers one model. Through Partners in Equity, Wallace and his colleagues help Black, Brown, and women-owned businesses buy the commercial buildings where they operate. The larger insight is that many people can handle monthly payments but cannot overcome the upfront capital barrier. Patient, shared-equity capital can help close that gap.

That same logic applies to Boston homeownership. Many renters already pay $3,000 or $4,000 a month. They are not financially irresponsible. They are cash-constrained, blocked by down payments, closing costs, credit repair, and competition from wealthier buyers. Boston should help them convert some of that burden into equity.

John Wallace’s work in Pittsburgh offers another lesson. Through church-led “withintrification,” the goal is neighborhood improvement without neighborhood removal. Instead of waiting for outside investors to drive up prices, residents, churches, small businesses, and local institutions gain control of land, property, and development from within.

In Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, Hyde Park, East Boston, and Roslindale, the question is not just how to build more housing. It is whether the people who held these neighborhoods together can still own a piece of their future.

Arlo Washington’s work in Little Rock, Arkansas, offers another lesson. Washington, featured in the Oscar-nominated documentary “The Barber of Little Rock,” built People Trust to respond to what he saw as a credit desert. His model grew out of a barber school and expanded into community lending, financial education, and capital access for people traditional banks often overlook.

Boston should ask: where are our credit deserts? A city serious about homeownership needs CDFIs, credit unions, neighborhood lenders, and trusted community institutions at the table.

Bernard Garrett’s story, dramatized in the 2020 film “The Banker,” offers a historical lesson. In the Jim Crow era, Garrett used banking and real estate strategy to get around racist barriers to property ownership. His methods came from a different time, but the lesson remains: access to banking power determines access to ownership.

The Dearfield Fund for Black Wealth offers a contemporary model. It provides down-payment assistance to first-time Black homebuyers. When the homeowner sells or refinances, the fund is repaid and receives a small share of appreciation, allowing the money to help the next family. This is recyclable capital, not charity.

Ben Slayton’s Legacy Home Loans offers another lesson: representation in mortgage lending matters. Who designs the product, explains the terms, understands the borrower, and is committed to closing the racial homeownership gap all matter.

None of these models should be copied blindly. Some need changes to fit Massachusetts law, Boston’s housing market, and consumer protection standards. But that is innovation: study what exists, test what works, reject what harms, and build something better.

Boston should now create a Homeownership Innovation Fund. Bring together the city, CDFIs, credit unions, local banks, hospitals, universities, unions, employers, churches, community development corporations, foundations, and responsible private capital.

The fund should test shared-appreciation down-payment assistance, patient-equity funds, community land trusts, employer-assisted homeownership, church-led development, and neighborhood lending. It should focus on residents close to ownership but blocked by front-end costs — families who can afford monthly payments but cannot assemble $80,000, $100,000, or more just to compete.

Any new model must have guardrails. Boston should not invite predatory rent-to-own schemes or speculative investor products under the banner of innovation. Programs must have plain-language terms, capped investor returns, independent counseling, public reporting, anti-displacement goals, and a clear path to full ownership.

Financing is not a substitute for housing supply. Boston still needs more housing, faster permitting, smarter zoning, more family-sized units, and protection against displacement. But supply alone will not close the ownership gap either. If new housing is built but only high-income buyers can purchase it, Boston will still lose the middle class and widen the racial wealth gap.

If we can lead the world in high tech and life sciences, we can lead the country in creating new paths to homeownership. The question is not whether every Bostonian will own a home. The question is whether Boston will remain a city where ordinary families still have a fair shot.

Right now, too many do not.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: From Boston to big leagues: Coaches reflect on Joshua Baez’s incredible rise
text:
When 23-year-old St. Louis Cardinals outfielder Joshua Baez set an MLB record with three home runs his first three at-bats in the big leagues last Saturday, he officially made his name known among fans of the game.

For many in his native Massachusetts, however, Baez’s explosive start was the next step in a journey they saw since he was dominating the fields around Boston.

Baez began his high school career at Cristo Rey in Dorchester, where he showed up to tryouts his freshman year and impressed immediately.

“We’re a Division 4 school that’s small and really is focused on academics and getting kids up to the college level so they can go to college,” former Cristo Rey head coach Joe Marcucci said. “When he walked onto the field for his first practice as a freshman, I thought to myself, ‘What are you doing here? You need to be at a larger school or a prep school where you can be exposed.’ He hit a ball farther than I’d ever seen at McConnell Park. He hit the highway and the game stopped.”

Baez contributed to a Cristo Rey team that went 11-8 and reached the Div. 4 state tournament. He spent time in the outfield as well as on the mound, which came despite Marcucci noting that Baez preferred to be in the outfield instead of on the bump. Still, the slugger accepted the roles as they came.

“What stood out to me was the joy that he played with and the respect that he had,” Marcucci said. “He respected his coach, he respected his teammates, and even though he was more talented than they were, he was always humble.”

After that first season at Cristo Rey, Baez transferred to Snowden International, a Boston public high school in the Back Bay neighborhood. He was coached there by Christian Ortiz, who is now the head coach at English High, and Ortiz said Baez joined a group that had a similar goal of exceeding on the diamond.

“He approached his development as if he did want to become a professional baseball player, quickly understanding the importance of taking care of his body and mind,” Ortiz said. “At Snowden, he was part of a group where most of his peers were like-minded, whose goals were to also play at the next level, and they fed off one another and pushed one another.

“Joshua was never satisfied with just reliance on raw talent. He was obsessed with the details: refining his mechanics, dialing in his physical conditioning, counting his calories and sharpening his mental game.”

Baez hit .442 with 20 RBIs in that 2019 season for Snowden and helped the team not only win a Boston City League title, but go 16-4 and reach the Div. 4 North semifinals. That translated into excellent summer season where Ortiz fully realized just how high Baez’s ceiling was.

“It wasn’t until the end of his sophomore year, which was the summer season after his Snowden season, when I personally really started to notice that he was transforming into someone unique,” Ortiz said. “He had just turned 16 years old at the end of that school year, he was throwing 88-90 mph, weighed about 200 pounds and was hammering baseballs effortlessly.”

That’s when Baez transferred to NEPSAC power Dexter Southfield, where head coach Dan Donato got the opportunity to aid the young outfielder’s development.

“I’ve been lucky and have had 17 guys make it to the NHL, and a couple of guys make it to the big leagues,” Donato said. “The one thing these guys have in common, and Josh is the best I’ve ever had, is their work ethic. His is off the charts. We would practice for two hours, and he’d still practice for two hours after that.”

Baez was recognized as the Massachusetts Gatorade Player of the Year in the cancelled 2020 season and truly earned the award in his 2021 season at Dexter. Donato said that his intangibles were undeniable during his time with the program.

“He’s 6-foot-three, 235 pounds and ran a 6.31 60-yard dash in high school, the fastest of anyone in the country,” Donato said. “He probably had the most power of anyone coming out that year and threw 98 miles per hour. It takes special tools to get there, and Josh had them.”

That led the way for Baez, who was originally committed to Vanderbilt, to get drafted by the Cardinals at No. 54 overall in the second round in 2021. Baez then spent five-plus seasons in St. Louis’ minor league system and developed into a top prospect. He progressed to Triple-A by this spring, where he showcased his powerful swing by hitting 34 home runs in 103 games to get the promotion he dreamed of this past Saturday.

Baez’s overall production has stalled since that explosive debut — he’s 1-for-22 entering Friday since hitting those trio of home runs at Wrigley Field — but his former coaches have faith he will straighten it out and remain supportive of his future.

“I’ll be honest, I started crying,” Marcucci said of learning of Baez’s debut. “I was so happy for that kid that he had realized his dream.”

title: Senator Nick Collins accuses Boston Mayor Wu of stalling contentious tax hearing until after election
text:
State Sen. Nick Collins accused the City of Boston of stalling a Council hearing on allegations that it is overtaxing middle-class homeowners to shield Mayor Michelle Wu “from scrutiny” before the primary election.

Collins, a South Boston Democrat who has been feuding with Wu for years over his move to block her signature property tax shift legislation, said the mayor is hiding information from his working-class constituents in the First Suffolk District to benefit his primary opponent, Latoya Gayle.

“City Hall inflated property assessments on working-class homeowners in my district, and the public has a right to know why and how,” Collins said Tuesday in a statement to the Herald. “Middle-class families got hammered by the mayor’s assessing officials while the wealthy got a tax break.”

The City Council had initially scheduled a hearing on the tax assessment discrepancies for June 8, but the hearing was later rescheduled for Sept. 3, two days after the Democratic primary between Collins and Wu-backed Gayle.

Collins said the timing appears to be intentional by City Hall. All three councilors who sponsored the hearing order, Miniard Culpepper, Erin Murphy and Brian Worrell, have endorsed Collins in the Senate race. The hearing was scheduled and is being chaired by Councilor Ben Weber, an ally of the mayor.

“A growing $50 million spending deficit and a $150 million White Stadium boondoggle don’t disappear,” Collins said. “The bill lands on the backs of hardworking taxpayers in my district.

“Now the mayor’s assessing officials are hiding information from the Council and the public until after an election to shield the mayor and her proxies from scrutiny,” Collins added. “My constituents deserve better than smoke and mirrors. It’s past time for the mayor and her assessing officials to face the music.”

Wu fired back Saturday through a spokesperson.

“It hurts all of Boston to have a senator who is nowhere to be found when we need action from the state Senate during legislative session, then pops up in an election year to troll the mayor and city workers,” city spokesperson Marcela Dwork said in a statement.

“This isn’t the first time Senator Collins has made false, insulting accusations about hardworking city workers after blocking tax relief that would have saved Boston homeowners more than $150 million in property taxes by now. Instead, corporate real estate interests received a massive tax break, Senator Collins received a flood of campaign donations from them, and now they are also bankrolling his ads in the Boston Herald, on social media, and in the mail. Boston deserves better,” Dwork added.

Wu’s office said the City Council schedules hearings, not the mayor’s office.

Weber, chair of the Ways and Means committee, said the delay was due to turnover in the Assessing Department. Nicholas Ariniello, the city’s longtime assessing commissioner, announced in late May that he was resigning, which became effective on June 30.

A Council notice states that the June 8 hearing was canceled on June 4.

“We tried a few dates in June but they ended up being used for budget-related matters,” Weber told the Herald Friday. “Eventually, the administration asked for more time to allow the new commissioner to settle in and be able to provide answers to our questions, which made sense to me. We tried a few more dates later in the summer but Sept. 3 was the earliest day that worked for everyone.”

The city appointed Hinlan Wong, a senior leader in the assessing department, as interim commissioner in July while it conducts a search for Ariniello’s permanent replacement.

Weber also said the Council had delayed a vote on the city budget on June 3, and canceled the tax hearing to devote more time to debating the mayor’s budget, ahead of a final vote that was held the following week.

“At no point did the preliminary date factor into this,” Weber said, adding of Collins’ assertions, “I guess I would say that he’s just wrong.”

Collins last month had called for an independent investigation into Boston’s tax assessment practices, as it relates to what he called “the city’s unlawful overvaluation of residential property in Boston’s middle-class neighborhoods.”

His First Suffolk District in the Senate encompasses South Boston and portions of Dorchester, Mattapan and Hyde Park.

Culpepper, a councilor sponsoring the hearing, said when introducing the order last March that he was compelled to look into the matter after seeing that luxury homes in Boston’s most affluent neighborhoods were selling for millions of dollars more than what they were assessed, and therefore taxed, at by the city.

“At the same time,” Culpepper said, “some lower-priced homes appear to be assessed at or even above their sale price, raising concerns about whether the current system is applying valuation practices consistently across different segments of the housing market.”

Culpepper added, “Ensuring that property assessments are accurate and equitable is essential to maintaining public confidence in our tax system and making sure that the responsibility of funding city services is shared fairly across all homeowners.”

Homeowners were hit this year on average with a 13% property tax hike.

Weber said there’s research to suggest that tax assessment discrepancies in Boston are legitimate, but pointed to them as being part of a national trend tied to institutional racism.

“My reading is that there is data suggesting that property sales in historically neighborhoods of color are often below the assessed value,” Weber said, “but I think it has more to do with institutional racism into how the properties are listed and the values that maybe people pay for them.”

Weber said those discrepancies aren’t factored into city assessment practices, which results in a situation where properties are sold and listed below the assessed value — leading to property owners paying higher taxes than what their homes are valued at on the real estate market.

“I don’t know what the solution is,” Weber said, “which is why I think it’s worth having a hearing on it and talking about how we can approach that issue.”

title: MBTA announces Orange, Green, Red line closures in September
text:
The MBTA announced a new slate of closures on the Green, Red and Orange lines and Commuter Rail, as well as more station closures and service changes, in September to accommodate a host of ongoing infrastructure projects.

“The MBTA is reminding riders that service outages such as these are a critical and necessary part of maintaining the infrastructure improvements that took place as part of the 2024 Track Improvement Program while also making further system upgrades and modernizing the MBTA’s infrastructure,” MBTA officials stated of the work.

Upcoming planned MBTA closures include: the Orange Line between Forest Hills and Back Bay from Sept. 10 to 14, and the Red Line between JFK/UMass and Ashmont from Sept. 19 to 20.

On the Green Line from Sept. 19 to 20 and Sept. 26 to Oct. 4, all branches will see closures: the B branch between Government Center and Babcock Street, C branch between Government Center and Kenmore, D branch between North Station and Kenmore, and E branch between Heath Street and North Station.

Commuter Rail service will be out on the Framingham/Worcester Line between Framingham and South Station from Sept. 19 to 20; Needham Line between Needham Heights and South Station from 11 p.m. on Sept. 18 to end of service Sept. 20; New Bedford/Fall River, Greenbush, and Kingston lines between South Station and Braintree Sept. 19 to 20.

Orange Line and Red Line closures

The Orange Line closure will accommodate the Ruggles Station Improvements Project to improve subway, Commuter Rail and bus service at “one of the most used stations in the network,” the MBTA said, with concrete repairs at platforms, along stair walls and the Ruggles Street Bridge.

The Red Line closure will likewise allow for bridge work at the Ashmont branch, including repairing columns on the Savin Hill Bridge and installing shielding at the JFK Bridge, T officials said.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will replace both lines along the closure, the MBTA said, reminding riders to “budget ample extra travel time.” Riders in need of accessibility accommodations can also request van service via station personnel or a station call box if they prefer.

T officials also noted Orange Line riders can consider Commuter Rail service as an alternative during the closure.

The Red Line will operate regular and increased frequency weekend service along the Braintree branch during the planned closure.

Green Line station and line closures

The Green Line closure will allow for “critical signal upgrades within the central Green Line tunnel,” T officials said, noting that the over 100 year old line’s signals updates will create safety and reliability improvements.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will run on portions of the B, C and D lines, while E line riders can use the 39 bus with additional buses running to add capacity. Riders can use Orange Line service between Back Bay and North Station, T officials said.

Additionally, on the Green Line Symphony station will remain closed through 2029, Brandon Hall on the C branch will be closed through Oct. 4 and C branch inbound trains will bypass Dean Road from Sept. 14 to Oct. 9.

Blue Line changes

The Blue Line will also see slight changes for one weekend from Sept. 26 to 27, allowing the “Maintenance of Way team” to perform switch work and spot tie replacements at and near the Wonderland stop, the MBTA said.

The trains will operate on a single track between Revere Beach and Wonderland during the weekend, meaning riders will need to board all trains at Wonderland on the outbound platform. Though service will operate between Bowdoin and Wonderland, every other train will terminate at either Wonderland or Orient Heights, the T said.

Commuter Rail closures

On the Framingham/Worcester Line, the closure will allow for Worcester Line track and signal improvements in Wellesley, the MBTA said, enabling potential future upgrades like all-day, 30-minute “Zonal express” bi-directional service to Worcester and local bi-directional service to Framingham.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will replace the service, with four different routes between Framingham and South Station but no stops at Wellesley Farms and Lansdowne. The line will be fare-free during the change.

The Needham Line closure, allowing for parts of the West Roxbury Parkway Bridge Replacement and South Station Signal and Track Improvements projects, will not have shuttle bus replacement. MBTA officials outlined bus service along the 35, 36, 37 and 59 routes and Orange Line service alternatives, reminding riders again to budget for extra time.

The New Bedford/Fall River, Greenbush, and Kingston lines closures will serve the bridge work along the Red Line’s Ashmont branch. Riders were encouraged to use Red Line subway service between South Station and Braintree (via Quincy Center) for Commuter Rail connections beyond Braintree or Quincy Center.

Of the outages, T officials noted the work “cannot be performed during the overnight hours when the MBTA does not operate, and would be extremely inefficient and costly if planned during single weekend outages.”

“Closing a section of the transit system for multiple days is the most efficient way to perform the MBTA’s routine maintenance, revitalization efforts, inspections, and upgrade work, and combines the efforts of multiple contractors and the MBTA workforce around the clock 24/7 to maximize productivity,” the MBTA said. “This work is necessary and continuous to maintain the reliable service riders count on.”

The T also recently announced a $140 million federal FRA investment for the Haverhill Double-Track Project, intended to have a “transformative impact” on Haverhill Commuter Rail Line and region. The project is projected to improve capacity and reliability for the Commuter Rail, Amtrak, and freight service on the line “while supporting the Commonwealth’s goal of advancing regional rail,” T officials said.

title: Finfer: The rent control work must go on
text:
I apologize.

For 32 years I’ve had bad dreams about when rent control ended in 1994 and what’s happened since. So many tens of thousands of people were displaced by rent increases or stayed put and paid more and more of their income for rent.

Rent control was repealed by a 51-49% vote in 1994. I did a lot of work on the 1972 campaign to pass rent control in Boston and to restrengthen the law in 1981 after it had been weakened. I was with the Dorchester Tenants Action Council doing rent control work in the 1970s and with Massachusetts Tenants Organization doing rent control work in the 1980s.

In Boston and now across most of the state, too many tenants pay punishingly high rents.

You might ask what was I doing in 1994 when this was going on? I did do some work against the referendum to repeal it. But I was working on organizing with others a metropolitan-wide interfaith, multi-issue organization that became Greater Boston Interfaith Organization (GBIO) in 1996. GBIO led passage of the Affordable Housing Trust Fund in 2001.

But if I had lifted up my head a bit from organizing that new group which wasn’t facing a deadline, I should have helped on that 1994 campaign a hell of a lot more. I could have organized many others to get out the vote to defeat that referendum. And others could have organized more to join on this. Losing 51-49%. Ugh. I apologize.

This time around, the Homes for All Coalition organized a very, very good campaign that had many tenant, community, and union organizations getting 124,000 voter signatures in the fall 2025 collection period and 25,000 more in the shorter spring 2026 collection period. It had enough to qualify it for the ballot.

Some major landlords agreed to negotiate with the Homes for All Coalition and it looked like a compromise would pass. But the rent control referendum made reference to exempting units used for religious purposes. This was not allowed under the state constitution.

We have to try again in 2029. It’s a long, long time to wait and rents will keep going up. But thanks to all the organizations in the Homes for All Coalition who gathered signatures only to see this be thrown off the ballot, it can be attempted again. The second time around was what finally allowed the Fair Share Amendment (Millionaire’s Tax) to pass.

It’s so very disheartening that tens of thousands of tenants have had to pay exorbitant rents, and that this rent control ballot referendum failed to reach the ballot because of a technicality.

It’s a nightmare. I apologize. But I know we’ll keep fighting.

Lew Finfer was the Director of Dorchester Tenants Action Council for part of the 1970s and of the Massachusetts Tenants Organization during parts of the 1980s. He’s now Director of the Massachusetts Action for Justice.

title: Gaskin: Mayor Wu, do the right thing with White Stadium
text:
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial court has settled whether White Stadium can move forward. It has not settled whether the project will be successful, equitable, environmentally responsible, or meet the needs of Boston Public Schools students. Those questions are now the City’s responsibility. The “right thing” consists of two things: completing the studies necessary to make White Stadium successful and getting all stakeholders on board.

First, do the studies.

I understand why the administration may have hesitated to undertake some of these studies earlier: any negative finding could have become another argument for stopping the project. That is no longer the issue. White Stadium is going forward, so the studies can now identify potential problems early enough to develop solutions.

Start with transportation and parking. The City has proposed plans, but no objective, independent analysis has determined whether they are adequate. We need studies that establish the size and scope of the problems and whether the proposed plans are sufficient.

There should also be an environmental impact study, whether one is legally required or not. You cannot bring as many as 10,000 people into Franklin Park for professional soccer games up to 22 times a year and assume there will be no environmental impact.

An independent economic-impact study is equally important. I have argued that White Stadium should be viewed as an economic-development opportunity for Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain. A professional sports franchise can create jobs, contracts, tourism spending and opportunities for nearby businesses, but Boston will not maximize that opportunity, in a way that is sensitive to community needs without intentional planning connecting the stadium to surrounding neighborhoods and businesses.

We should know how much economic activity White Stadium is expected to generate, where spectators will spend money, what jobs will be created, what those jobs will pay and how nearby businesses can capture some of that spending. The study should also examine property values, commercial rents, housing costs, gentrification and displacement. If public investment makes the neighborhoods around Franklin Park substantially more valuable, homeowners should benefit rather than be pressured to leave because of higher property taxes; renters should not face higher housing costs as the project’s principal economic effect on them; and local businesses should not help create a more attractive district only to be priced out. The analysis should also tell us who captures the value White Stadium creates — workers, neighborhood businesses, homeowners and residents, or primarily outside contractors and property owners.

There also needs to be a serious return-on-investment analysis. Typically, ROI would be part of the business case for building a stadium, but that was not done here. Boston is investing $135 million, and taxpayers should understand what they are receiving; even if the ROI is negative, people need to know because that reveals the true cost of the project.

We also need to settle whether the facility can adequately serve both professional soccer and Boston Public Schools. Critics have questioned whether professional soccer and high school football can effectively share the same field and whether soccer requirements will limit BPS use. What facilities do BPS students need, what will White Stadium provide, where are the conflicts or gaps, and what are the solutions?

The City should also explain how White Stadium fits into Mayor Wu’s broader vision for Roxbury and Dorchester, including the P3 parcel, Madison Park Technical Vocational High School, the proposed Blue Hill Avenue bus project, Franklin Park, Nubian Square, housing and transportation. How do these projects fit together, and what is the City’s larger vision for this part of Boston?

Second, bring in the stakeholders.

The Boston business community should be first to step forward. Where is the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce? A $325 million sports project should be of obvious interest to the region’s business community, as should the travel, tourism and hospitality opportunity. Thousands of people will be coming to professional soccer games, and hotels, restaurants, attractions and other businesses should have a stake in helping Boston maximize that opportunity.

The park and environmental stakeholders should also be at the table. The Emerald Necklace Conservancy, Franklin Park Defenders and others who raised concerns about Franklin Park should still be advocating for the park, helping determine what environmental indicators are monitored and what mitigation occurs if problems emerge. So should neighborhood organizations such as the Garrison Trotter Neighborhood Association and the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, which supports renovating White Stadium for BPS students while advocating for Franklin Park protection, equitable access, transparency and accountability.

If as many as 10,000 spectators are going to arrive at Franklin Park on game days, residents, transportation planners, MBTA officials, parking experts, Boston police and neighborhood businesses should work together before the first game to identify problems and test solutions. BPS parents and students, teachers, coaches, youth organizations, civic institutions, educational and financial institutions, and economic-development organizations should also have a role.

Their involvement should include implementation and monitoring. That monitoring should establish before-and-after measures for things such as noise, air quality, litter and park use so Boston can determine whether conditions improve, worsen or remain unchanged.

The measure of success should not be whether the stadium is completed or professional soccer succeeds. It should be whether Boston can demonstrate that the public investment improved the park, served BPS students, strengthened surrounding neighborhoods and created benefits shared across the city.

White Stadium needs to become an important Boston asset for the citizens of Boston — all citizens, not just some of them.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Boston Police Blotter: Man shot dead in Roxbury
text:
A man was shot dead on Warren Street in Roxbury over the weekend, according to Boston Police.

Officers responded to a radio call for shots fired around 9:23 p.m. Saturday, the department said in a statement. When they arrived at the scene, officers said they found a man suffering from multiple gunshot wounds.

The man was taken to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, police said.

The department has not identified the victim.

BPD’s Homicide Unit is investigating the death and urging anyone with information to reach out at 617-343-4470 or anonymously via the CrimeStoppers Line.

Prior to Saturday’s shooting death, there have been 13 shooting victims killed in Boston since the start of 2026, according to preliminary crime statistics.

More than two dozen arrested during Caribbean Festival

Boston Police reported that they arrested 28 people and issued summons for two more starting Friday night, related to the weekend’s Caribbean Festival.

title: Pols & Politics: Healey’s ratings slump again in latest poll, still favored for reelection
text:
A trend of decreasing favorability ratings for Gov. Maura Healey continues in a poll recently released by the UNH Survey Center and as the September primary election – which will determine Healey’s GOP opponent in November – is just days away.

But despite the unsatisfactory results, Healey was still found to be favored for reelection.

“Half of Massachusetts residents approve of incumbent Democratic Governor Maura Healey’s overall job performance, but majorities disapprove of her handling of housing and the cost of living, the two most important problems cited by Massachusetts residents,” the abstract of the UNH poll, released Thursday, reads. “However, Healey holds wide leads over both Michael Minogue, the frontrunner for the Republican gubernatorial nomination, and Brian Shortsleeve in the November general election.

The poll found 50% of Massachusetts voters surveyed approve of Healey’s performance in her first term, with 48% of respondents disapproving, and 3% left unsure. This breaks down to 75% of Democrats and 43% of Independents approving of her performance, with only 10% of Republicans expressing their approval. Her net approval rating (+2) has increased by five percentage points since June (-3).

The latest polling numbers support a trend for Healey over months of various surveys, with just 39% of respondents in a May MassINC Polling Group survey having a favorable view of her. This came a week after an Emerson College survey found Healey was tied for the highest unfavorability rating amongst voters at 35%. Several other polls found Healey’s approval rating hovering between 35% and 50%.

Healey will face off against the winner of the Republican primary election on Tuesday in a battle between Republican candidates Brian Shortsleeve and Mike Minogue. She does not have a primary opponent.

Commish dinner

A who’s who of former Boston Police Department commissioners dined together in Quincy Thursday night.

Former commissioners Bill Bratton and Willie Gross joined Regan Communications Chairman and CEO George Regan for a dinner at Victory Point in Marina Bay.

The night was complete with a Montilio’s cake and appearance by the “baker extraordinaire” himself, George Montilio. Also joining in was Father Jack Ahern, pastor of St. Gregory Parish in Dorchester, and their longtime friend

The dinner was held in order to honor Bratton and Gross ” for their lifelong dedication to making their communities safer,” a press release states.

Bratton is a native of Dorchester who led not only the Boston police but also the two largest departments in the country, New York and Los Angeles, during an esteemed career.

Gross led the BPD from August 2018 to January 2021.

“Regan and Bratton first met 50 years ago when the former was Mayor Kevin White’s press secretary and the latter was a young, brash, up and coming lieutenant on the BPD,” according to a Regan spokesman.

title: Police Blotter: Fake Massachusetts ‘nurse’ sentenced to 3+ years for pumping clients full of fake Botox
text:
The owner of a Massachusetts spa who falsely advertised herself as a nurse and injected hundreds of clients thousands of times with fake Botox and knock-off fillers will be heading to prison.

U.S. District Court Judge Julia E. Kobick this week sentenced Rebecca Fadanelli, 40, of Stoughton, to three years and 10 months in federal prison. Fadanelli’s crimes netted her more than $1 million in payments from more than 900 afflicted clients of her Skin Beaute Med Spa, with locations in Randolph and South Easton.

“This was not a mistake or a one-time lapse in judgment. Rebecca Fadanelli built a business on deception and repeatedly put profit ahead of the health and safety of the people who trusted her,” U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said following the sentencing.

“Her victims were left with infections, facial paralysis, vision problems, scars and the lasting fear of not knowing what was injected into their bodies,” Foley continued. “As cosmetic injections and med spas continue to grow in popularity, this case underscores a serious and growing public health threat: counterfeit products and unlicensed providers can cause devastating harm.”

Fadanelli, arrested and charged in November 2024, pleaded guilty in April to four counts of importing merchandise contrary to law, two counts of selling or dispensing a counterfeit drug and two counts of selling or dispensing a counterfeit device. In addition to her prison term, she will have to pay $1,001,562 in restitution to her victims and be monitored by authorities for two years following her release.

Federal prosecutors, who asked for 57 months of prison, say Fadenelli administered knock-off Botox, Sculptra and Juvederm from China and Brazil at her business. From March 2021 to June 2024 she performed more than 2,700 botulinum toxin and dermal filler injections and 1,085 filler appointments.

“Many of these procedures resulted in adverse health effects, with multiple clients ending up in the hospital. When clients complained to her about these results, the defendant showed a callous disregard for their health, dismissing their concerns, claiming to be ‘a professional . . . doing everything right,’” prosecutors wrote in their sentencing memo.

“This lack of accountability, much less remorse, has persisted throughout the course of these proceedings. Rather than own up to her crimes, and notwithstanding her guilty plea, the defendant has continually sought to avoid the consequences of her actions, including by continuing to deny the essential facts underlying her offenses of conviction,” prosecutors continued.

The defense asked that Kobick sentence Fadanelli to 10 months in prison, arguing that “Ms. Fadanelli should not be defined by this case.”

They add that Fadanelli, who was born in Brazil and moved to the U.S. in 2004 at 17 years old, had a troubled upbringing and troubled relationships but has worked to improve life for herself and her children. They also say that while Fadanelli admits she was not licensed to perform these injections, she has been trained on the procedure and “her training would be sufficient

to inject cosmetic substances in Brazil.”

The defense sentencing memo shows a medley of educational certificates Fadanelli earned, amassing 168 of them, they claim, while at Wyatt Detention Facility since her arrest in 2024 and that she has a reentry plan and an offer of employment at a steak house in Stoughton. She also plans to seek employment as a Portuguese interpreter.

title: Boston Mayor Wu sticking with center bus lane for Blue Hill Avenue over opposition: ‘Not safe’
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s latest positive spin on the city’s $163 million redesign of Blue Hill Avenue didn’t do much to tamp down the community’s fierce opposition to a center-running bus lane that highlights the project.

Wu held an invite-only virtual press conference last week, which the Herald was not invited to attend and included an updated look at the city’s contentious redesign for Blue Hill Avenue. The major 4-mile street serves as Boston’s central spine, stretching through Roxbury and Dorchester and ending at Mattapan Square.

While Wu released a statement to the rest of the media several days later that said “community input has been critical to shaping a design that responds to the needs of the neighborhoods along Blue Hill Avenue,” critics of the plan say that’s not the case and the project has been rammed through over neighborhood opposition.

“The MBTA and the city has told us that they’ve been involved in meaningful engagement with the community, but from day one, only one option has been presented: the center-running bus lane,” Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents Roxbury, said last Thursday in a video posted to Facebook.

Culpepper said the planned center-running bus lane would create a “dangerous” situation for passengers who have to walk across the street to get on board.

“This is the only option that we have been given,” Culpepper said. “Our community deserves to be at the table, and not on the table when it comes to decisions that affect our daily lives, our livelihoods and our neighborhoods in the long-term. No center-running bus lane down Blue Hill Avenue. It’s just not safe.”

Reggie Stewart, a community organizer and former Roxbury-centric Council staffer, said the mayor’s community engagement process has been about giving residents a chance to help design a project the city has already decided to implement, rather than giving the community a chance to “reject the central policy choice.”

“This entire Blue Hill Avenue ‘community engagement’ process is a masterclass in political gaslighting,” Stewart posted to Facebook last Friday. “The central question has never simply been about where to put parking spaces, trees, loading zones or bus stops.

“The central disagreement is over the center-running busway itself. Yet that decision remains off the table while residents are invited to debate the details around it,” Stewart said.

He added that the Wu administration’s way of rolling out the information in a series of back-to-back meetings in affected communities over the next two weeks, beginning on Thursday, is “racist governance.”

Stewart said the rollout is designed to “distract, disperse, exhaust and overwhelm a coalition that is beginning to coalesce over shared concerns” about projects impacting Black communities: Blue Hill Avenue, White Stadium and Parcel P3.

“This is racist governance,” Stewart said. “And we need to get comfortable applying that word to what the Michelle Wu administration is choosing to do.”

A social media flyer is being distributed ahead of Thursday’s community meeting at Mattapan Town Hall that states a standout is being organized at the location with attendees encouraged to say “Hell no to center bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.”

The flyer states that the project will worsen congestion by removing vehicular traffic lanes to allow for the center-running bus lane, hurt local businesses, make the area dangerous for all road users, and waste public funds.

Wu’s office distributed a press release Saturday that defends the center-running bus lane as a way to improve travel times for the 40,000 daily bus riders who travel on Blue Hill Avenue and ease congestion for all road users.

Her office said the design also includes a two-way, sidewalk-level bike path on the west side of Blue Hill Avenue, separated from traffic, to provide neighborhood cyclist connections to Franklin Park.

The latest updated design revealed last week to the city’s preferred media outlets “incorporates significant changes based on community feedback” from what was originally presented by the city two years ago, per Wu’s office.

Those changes include maintaining at least two general travel lanes in the majority of the corridor, a net increase in parking, including local parking solutions for high-demand areas like Morning Star Baptist Church. It also reflects additional investment in Blue Hill Avenue’s streetscape, with six miles of new sidewalks, 200 new accessible curb ramps, new street lighting, and 200 new street trees.

“This is a true once-in-a-generation opportunity to deliver on improvements that will enhance the quality of life and economic opportunity for our residents, small businesses, and community,” Wu said in a statement.

Roughly $124 million in local, state and federal funds have been secured for the project. Construction is set to begin in 2028.

title: Back to school: 61% of BPS morning buses arrive on-time for first day
text:
The on-time bus performance dropped slightly for Boston schools as over 18,000 students headed back to the first day of classes Tuesday, a slight reduction from last year’s record on-time performance.

“This morning, BPS Transportation achieved a 61% on-time performance (OTP) rate, the second highest first-day rate on record,” a BPS spokesperson stated. … “We will closely monitor the average OTP in the coming days, weeks, and months as we anticipate continued improvement, similar to last year.”

The morning bus on-time performance marks a slight drop from the record 66% reported in 2025, a big jump from the chaotic 34% rate in 2024, and a tie with the 61% the district reported in 2023.

BPS grades 1 through 12 headed back to classes Tuesday morning, while pre-K and kindergarten students will join them Thursday.

On Tuesday morning, 81% of buses arriving within 15 minutes of the bell and 92% arriving within 30 minutes, both metrics falling just slightly short of the 2025 performance, according to district data.

The district reduced the number of uncovered routes to seven of the over 1,300 trips Tuesday morning, compared to nine the previous year.

At Holland Elementary in Dorchester after kids headed into classes early Tuesday morning, BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper said they’d seen “most of the buses arrive on time or early” to the school, adding “this is about continuous improvement for us.”

“Every single first day, we strive to do better,” said Skipper. “We ended last year at 95%, which I think you remember was the benchmark the state had asked us to achieve. And even that, we will continue to strive to increase.”

Overall, morning bus on-time performance averaged 91.4% during the 2025-26 school year, with record performance of 94% or higher reported in November, April, May and June. As part of a deal to avoid state receivership in 2022, which came to an end in 2025, BPS agreed to reach 95% bus on-time performance.

Skipper noted there were 750 buses in operation, and the drivers and bus monitors are “fully staffed.” The district started the year with 609 bus routes, over 730 drivers and 650 bus monitors.

The district reported over 20,000 students taking the bus at the start of last school year, and over 18,000 students riding BPS buses Tuesday.

BPS officials said Tuesday’s “strong start” was a results of reforms and improvements over several years like “stronger contracts, improved staffing, and modernized technology.” The district signed a three-year contract with the Zum app in 2024, which allows parents to track buses, see assignments and receive alerts.

“We also appreciate our students and families for their continued partnership as we work to deliver the best experience for our students,” BPS stated. “BPS will continue working in partnership with Transdev, bus drivers and bus monitors, and our school communities to provide students with safe, reliable transportation to and from school each day.”

Skipper reminded the public to prioritize kids’ safety as buses hit the road again this year, watching to give buses space, anticipating that children may come out in front, and being vigilant at crosswalks.

“Never ever pass a bus or van when it has its sign up,” Skipper said, noting that new safety training helped to bring down accidents last year. … “But often our buses are the recipient of a car hitting them, and so I can’t emphasize enough, when you see a bus and you’re in a car, don’t text. Don’t have a phone near you. Be vigilant and make sure you give safe passage.”

title: Police blotter: Massachusetts restaurateur pleads guilty to paying employees under table
text:
A Massachusetts restaurateur has pleaded guilty to federal charges of paying employees in cash while failing to withhold and pay more than $500,000 in employment taxes.

Marios Michalakis, 44, of Westwood, faces up to five years in prison after he pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston on Tuesday to paying employees in cash “under the table” and failing to pay over $580,000 in taxes owed to the IRS and the state Department of Revenue.

Michalakis ran the scheme at Amelia’s, which he owned and operated in Stoughton, and Sofia Italian Steakhouse, in West Roxbury, from at least January 2016 through December 2022, according to Massachusetts US Attorney Leah Foley’s office.

The restaurateur failed to withhold income taxes, Social Security taxes and Medicare taxes from employee wages.

Michalakis pleaded guilty to six counts of failing to collect, report and pay over federal employment taxes.

His sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 8, when he could face up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000 or twice the gross gain or loss, whichever is greater, together with restitution.

title: Boston Police Blotter: Dead dog, ’emaciated’ animals found in home, DA says
text:
A Boston man faces charges after police responded to a call for a dead dog at his home and found several other neglected animals, according to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office.

Lester James, 39, was arraigned on seven counts of animal cruelty last week, a statement from the office said.

Police initially responded to James’ home on Old Colony Avenue just before noon last Monday after the defendant called 911 to report his pitbull Gwap was dead.

When officers arrived, they said they found Gwap deceased, lying in a cage that had no food or water bowls but was covered in feces and vomit, the statement said.

Six living dogs — two more adult pit bulls, three young pit bulls, and a chihuahua — were also in the home, “emaciated,” according to the DA, who also said the cages and areas where the dogs were kept were covered in feces.

The defendant said he kept the dogs for breeding but wouldn’t tell the police if they’d ever been seen by a veterinarian, the DA’s office said. One of the pit bulls that was changed, Gambit, had recently given birth to the younger dogs, James said to police.

There had been four puppies, but James said his son stepped on one of them and killed it, the DA’s office said, and just two weeks earlier, Gwap, the dead dog, had killed and eaten James’ Yorkshire Terrier.

Boston Animal Care removed all of the living dogs from the home and noted that each animal needed treatment because of their condition.

As of Sunday, Boston Animal Care reported that the dogs were thin, and that several had scratches, bites, and other injuries of varying severity.

“Their overall condition is improving,” the statement from DA’s office said, and they continue to be under the care of City of Boston’s veterinarian and veterinarians at MSPCA-Angell.

“The City of Boston is grateful to our partners at MSPCA-Angell and the dedicated team at Boston Animal Care and Control for their tireless efforts to provide compassionate care, shelter, and support to the animals rescued,” Boston Animal Care said in a statement. “Their partnership and commitment is essential to ensuring our city’s animals receive the care they deserve.”

A judge set bail for James at $5,000 and the defendant was ordered not to possess or care for any animals. He was also ordered to undergo a mental health evaluation.

His next court date is set for Oct. 20.

“When pet owners can’t or won’t properly care for their animals it too often turns into tragedies for the pets and criminal charges for the owners,” Suffolk spokeperson James Borghesani said. “The fact that there are always options available just added to the tragedy.”

title: Police Blotter: Ex-Massachusetts police chief pleads guilty to misusing his office
text:
Former Methuen Police Chief Joseph Solomon, who a city-ordered report said ran his department like “a ‘Don’ of an organized crime family,” has pleaded guilty to 17 state charges related to the misuse of his position of authority.

“Massachusetts communities rely on their police chiefs to make the best decisions for the safety and security of residents. Former Chief Solomon broke that trust by misusing his authority to elevate unqualified officers, putting residents’ wellbeing at risk,” said state Attorney General Andrea Campbell, whose office prosecuted the case.

Solomon was indicted in September 2023 on seven counts of obtaining unwarranted privileges in violation of the civil service laws, six counts of civil service law violations, two counts of perjury by written affidavit, and single counts of uttering a forged document and procurement fraud.

Solomon pleaded guilty to those charges on Friday. He was sentenced to 2.5 years in the House of Correction, with 30 days to serve and the balance suspended for three years. He will lose his city pension, license to carry a firearm, and a private investigator’s license.

Central to the case against Solomon was his promotion of part-time officers — notably Sean Fountain — into full-time officers in a way that circumvented civil service laws. He and Fountain claimed, for instance, that the latter was a graduate of a police academy when he was not.

A report commissioned by the City of Methuen and issued in late May 2023 by the STIRM Group stated “the current investigation does not paint Solomon in a positive light. His leadership style is that of a ‘Don’ of an organized crime family that leads through humiliation, fear, intimidation, and retaliation.”

Even before that, however, the case against Solomon was made in part in the 153-page “Leadership Failures in Methuen Police Contracts” report issued by the state Office of the Inspector General in December 2020.

“I want to acknowledge the hard work and diligence of the prosecution teams from the Attorney General’s Office and the Essex District Attorney’s Office for bringing this case to resolution,” Inspector General Jeffrey Shapiro wrote in a statement following the guilty pleas. “So-called public servants who enrich themselves at the expense of the people they swear an oath to serve must be held to account, no matter how long it takes.”

17 year old packed serious heat

The Boston Police Department says it took a fully loaded revolver off a 17-year-old in Roxbury.

title: Police Blotter: Feds seek more info on ex-Malden school employee accused of exploiting Michigan teens
text:
Federal investigators are seeking more information about a now-former Malden school employee charged with sexually exploiting two minor Michigan girls into submission to him.

Federal investigators arrested Anthony Lamont Fowlkes, 40, at his home in Malden last week on multiple charges related to the sexual exploitation of a child, child pornography, and interstate threats with intent to extort.

“Fowlkes has held positions of trust and HSI wants to identify any other potential victims/survivors,” U.S. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New England wrote on Saturday, adding specifically that he had been employed in the Linden STEAM Academy in Malden.

They ask that anyone who believes their child was affected by Fowlkes to contact the agency at HSI-Fowlkes-Investigation@hsi.dhs.gov.

Fowlkes’ two alleged minor victims were friends who lived in Waterford, Michigan, a northern suburb of Detroit.

A Detroit-based HSI agent, in an affidavit supporting the charges, described Fowlkes as soliciting nude images of the girls and exploiting his possession of these images to force the girls into submission to him as their master. The affidavit asserts that at all times Fowlkes knew the girls were underage.

“Idky (I don’t know why) I had to ask. You know you’re supposed to send them,” Fowlkes allegedly texted the first of the two 16-year-old girls on July 30 when she didn’t send him nudes fast enough in the morning.

This first victim, according to the affidavit, would in the same conversation introduce Fowlkes to a friend.

“She ready to be claimed like I have over you?” Fowlkes asked, and he was assured that the second girl was.

But it wasn’t to be, according to the affidavit. She broke contact with him and blocked him but, through the first girl, Fowlkes threatened to post the nude images she had shared with him online if she didn’t get back in touch. She did, but only to demand that he leave her alone or she would reach out to authorities.

“I DON’T GIVE A (expletive) ABOUT THE COPS. I’M NOT SCARED. GO TO THEM RN (right now), I (expletive)ING DARE YOU,” Fowlkes allegedly texted her.

He allegedly shortly followed up with, “I’m waiting since you want to act so big and (expletive)ing tough. Call them. … Who THE (expletive) do you belong to(?)”

The victims went to their local police departments where their phones were forensically examined, revealing the conversations and leading to the federal investigation, according to the affidavit.

Trinatarios gang member sentenced

The Boston-based feds continue to crack down on the Trinitarios gang active north of Boston, this time with the sentencing to prison of a Lynn member who gunned down two people at a fast food restaurant.

U.S. Senior District Court Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton sentenced 25-year-old Westyn Lantigua, who also goes by “Wes” and “Muddy,” according to prosecutors, to 135 months — which is 11 years and three months — in federal prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release.

Lantigua was first charged along with 21 others in a sweeping February 2025 indictment. U.S. Attorney Leah Foley at the time said that is a great start for “dismantling” the gang’s relentless “bloodshed.”

In Lantigua’s case, he was caught on video waiting for a vehicle he suspected was filled with rival gang members to exit a fast food drive-through in Lynn and then opening fire with a machine gun. Inside the vehicle were not rival gang members but two women, the feds say, who miraculously survived their gunshot wounds.

The Trinitarios organization began in the 1990s by Dominicans in the New York City jail at Rikers Island, according to law enforcement. It is named after three revolutionaries from the Dominican War of Independence against Haiti, which law enforcement says “provides an underlying patriotic veneer to the gang’s activities.”

title: Police Blotter: Underage drinking party turns to teen-on-cop brawl in Roxbury
text:
An underage drinking party on the streets of the Academy Homes development in Roxbury became a brawl with the police that led to the arrests of five people.

It all began with a 911 call from security at the housing complex that about 15 kids were “blocking the roadway, drinking, and smoking.” A pair of Boston police out on patrol heard the call and knew that about five hours earlier the gang squad had arrested an unlawfully armed person in the same development so they headed back into trouble.

The officers arrived in the area of 76 Weaver Way — which like all streets mentioned in this report are part of the same housing development — and found “a large group of individuals congregating near numerous illegally parked vehicles … all appeared to be teenagers, and they were drinking in public, smoking marijuana, and even urinating in public.”

When the cops exited their patrol car, five people hurried from the group and the officers pursued them. The police report goes in-depth on the trials of two police officers trying to keep up with five allegedly high and drunk teens and young adults.

The physicality begins when some of the group start to use their bodies to block the path to Jahmere Antenor, who police say had a gun — a black Polymer 80 Glock with laser attachment and extended magazine without a serial number — in his waistband. An officer “had to physically toss (the interlopers) out of the way,” according to the report.

The two initial cops continue to struggle with the group trying to block the arrest when, finally, backup arrives and the two additional officers “were able to safely tackle Antenor to the ground.” This, the report alleges, riled up the crowd who began “screaming and verbally abusing the officers … in an attempt to intimidate and add confusion to an already hectic scene.”

When officers cuffed another alleged delinquent, Isaiah Morel, 20, for underage drinking, his brother, Samuel Morel, 22, “continued to accost officers” and began pushing them forcibly, according to the police report. He was arrested on charges of interfering with police, disorderly conduct, and assault and battery on a police officer.

Antenor faces multiple firearms charges and resisting arrest. Two others will be summoned for obstruction of justice, according to the report.

AG: Woman let husband die as she ripped off $135K from taxpayers

Massachusetts prosecutors say a Lawrence woman collected $135,000 in state benefits to care for her ailing husband — all while doing nothing and letting him die.

An Essex County grand jury indicted Judit Diaz de Vargas, 49, on involuntary manslaughter, caretaker neglect causing serious bodily injury, caretaker neglect on an elder as well as fraud charges related to Medicaid false claims.

De Vargas pleaded not guilty at Essex Superior Court on Friday, where the judge set her bail at $15,000. She was further ordered not to work in the Personal Care Attendant (PCA) state benefits program or any other MassHealth program, not to work or volunteer with the disabled and elderly community, and other standard requirements including not leaving the commonwealth without permission.

State prosecutors say that not only did de Vargas neglect her husband, leading to his death, but also claimed to be his “ex-daughter-in-law” to bypass MassHealth regulations preventing spouses from serving as personal care attendants that collect funding from the MassHealth program. During her alleged fraud, the taxpayer-funded state program doled out some $135,000 to her based on her submitted timesheets.

But the allegations extend beyond mere neglect, as prosecutors with the state attorney general’s office said that the husband arrived at Lawrence General Hospital extremely emaciated and with more than 10 pressure wounds — at least eight of which were considered severe. He died from sepsis — due to infections to these wounds — four days after arriving at the hospital. Prosecutors say that these wounds would not have progressed this far if he had been provided proper care at home.
