title: Events happening across Mass. to celebrate Juneteenth
text:
A number of events have been happening across Massachusetts this week and they'll continue over the long weekend to celebrate Juneteenth, which commemorates the end of slavery in the U.S.

The holiday officially marks June 19, 1865, when Union troops arrived in Galveston, Texas at the end of the Civil War with an order declaring the state's enslaved people to be free with “absolute equality.” By then, 2 1/2 years had passed since the Emancipation Proclamation declared the freedom of enslaved people in the South.

There was a unity walk Thursday night at Harambee Park in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, marking a meaningful opportunity for neighbors, faith leaders, and public safety officials to come together and walk side-by-side for peace in the city's neighborhoods.

Earlier Thursday in Boston, city and state leaders attended flag raising ceremonies ahead of the Friday holiday.

Gov. Maura Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll attended the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus’ Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at 11 a.m. at the State House.

Mayor Michelle Wu gave remarks at Boston's Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at City Hall Plaza Friday afternoon.

"It just stills gives me goosebumps to know that we are living in a city that takes care of our history, preserves the moments and memorials and spaces, so that we can learn from what's happened and plan for our best possible future," Wu told NBC10 Boston.

Another Juneteenth celebration and flag raising ceremony was held in Beacon Hill, hosted by the Museum of African American History. Joy Street transformed into a community festival featuring live music, spoken word performances, local Black-owned businesses, food vendors, family activities, storytelling, and free admission to the African Meeting House and Abiel Smith School.

On Tuesday, education advocates read aloud a famous Frederick Douglass speech in the shadow of the State House. Delivered 174 years ago, "What to the slave is the Fourth of July" is meant to highlight hypocrisies in the Declaration of Independence because rights in the document, like freedom, did not extend to enslaved people.

While freedom was guaranteed to Americans 250 years ago, for enslaved people, that written guarantee didn't come until almost 100 years later on Juneteenth.

The Center for Law and Education put on the reading with funding from Mass Humanities. On Friday, Mass Humanities will fund about 10 more free public readings from Amherst to Fall River to Salem.

Also Friday in Cambridge, the Black Response hosted its second Juneteenth Festival from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the Cambridge Common in Harvard Square. It will be a fun-filled event with activities for the whole family including bouncy houses, arts and crafts for all ages, school supply giveaways, free ice cream, pizza, fruit salad and empanadas, sensory play spaces, face painting, and lawn games.

The City of Framingham was hosting its third annual Juneteenth flag raising ceremony at noon on the Memorial Building Plaza. There were scheduled to be remarks from the city's diversity, equity and inclusion officer, as well as a presentation on the significance of Juneteenth from a Framingham High student.

“Juneteenth is an opportunity for our community to reflect on our nation’s history, honor those who fought for freedom and justice, and recommit ourselves to building a more inclusive future,” Mayor Charlie Sisitsky said in a statement ahead of the event. “I encourage all residents to join us as we celebrate this important day and the values that unite our community.”

“Juneteenth reminds us that freedom, equity, and opportunity are ideals that require ongoing commitment,” said Jesse Edwards, the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Officer for the City of Framingham. “This event brings our community together to honor the past, recognize progress, and continue the work of creating a more equitable and welcoming Framingham for all.”

Residents were encouraged to attend the event, which was free and open to the public. There is also a community Juneteenth event at Farm Pond on Saturday, June 20, from 1 p.m. to 6 p.m.

Also Saturday in Boston, the public is invited to Franklin Park's Shattuck Picnic Grove for Juneteenth Freedom Day 2026. The event is free and family friendly. It runs from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.

This day has been celebrated even before it was officially recognized as a federal holiday in 2021. Government buildings, banks, schools and some stores are closed in observance.

The history of Juneteenth

This is the fifth year since Juneteenth was designated as a federal holiday by former President Joe Biden, who served as Barack Obama's vice president. But the celebrations, which began in Texas and then spread across the country, have a rich and long history in Black America, with the day often spent gathering for picnics and cookouts.

The holiday — a combination of “June” and “nineteenth” — marks the day when U.S. Maj. Gen. Gordon Granger and his troops arrived in the Texas port city with the declaration of freedom in General Order No. 3.

As the third year of the Civil War neared, President Abraham Lincoln had issued the Emancipation Proclamation declaring the freedom of “all persons held as slaves” in the still rebellious states of the Confederacy. Though, for many, it did not mean immediate freedom but a promise of liberation, to be secured with a Union victory.

About six months after Granger's arrival in Galveston, the 13th Amendment abolishing slavery nationwide was ratified.

Celebrations across the nation this year

Juneteenth’s birthplace is celebrating with a daylong gathering at a Galveston park with music and fireworks, a parade and a worship service in a historic Black church. Nearby Houston lined up of musical artists and a domino tournament at Emancipation Park, established in 1872 by a group of formerly enslaved men.

Hundreds of other cities across the U.S. announced events over the long weekend, including a parade in Atlanta, a bike ride in Los Angeles and a festival on Martha’s Vineyard.

Several cities across the U.S. will host walks named for Opal Lee, the Texas woman who pushed for years to make Juneteenth a federal holiday. Participants will walk 2 1/2 miles to symbolize the 2 1/2 years it took for the Emancipation Proclamation to be enforced in Texas. Lee, known as the “grandmother of Juneteenth,” turns 100 this year.

title: Knox Trail 250 celebration continues in Roxbury
text:
The 250th anniversary of Henry Knox's "Noble Train of Artillery" continued Saturday in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood.

A gathering was held at the First Parish Church of Roxbury where a commemorative program recognized all of the communities along the Knox trail who aided Knox in 1776. There were also outdoor activities beside the Dillaway-Thomas House including a procession of 1776 militia units, horse-drawn sleds, and fife and drum groups.

The Noble Train of Artillery was one of the most extraordinary achievements of the American Revolution.

The next event will be held on March 17 in South Boston, honoring the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day -- Washington's first victory of the Revolution. It will begin with a memorial service in St. Augustine's chapel on Dorchester Street, followed by a short procession up to Dorchester Heights for a commemorative program featuring political and community leaders from around the Commonwealth as well as reenacting units such as the Lexington Minute Men and the 2nd Massachusetts Regiment.

Revolution 250 is a collaborative initiative uniting more than 70 organizations across Massachusetts to plan and promote the Semiquincentennial — the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

title: Man charged with murder in July Dorchester shooting
text:
A man was arrested three weeks after another man was shot to death in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood.

The shooting happened shortly before noon on July 15 on York Street. The victim, 29-year-old Breidy Martinez of Dorchester, was pronounced dead at the scene.

Boston police said that 32-year-old Hensly Dominique Jeanty of Dorchester was arrested around 4 p.m. Wednesday.

He's charged with A straight warrant out of Dorchester District Court charges Jeanty with murder, discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a dwelling, carrying a loaded firearm without a license and carrying a firearm without a license.

At the time of the shooting, police said Martinez was believed to have been riding a motorized scooter found at the scene.

Investigators recovered ballistic evidence in the area of Glenway Street.

Traffic in the area was affected during the investigation.

Anyone with information is asked to call 617-343-4470.

On the day of the shooting, Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said it was too early to say if the shooting was random or targeted, but that there was no reason to believe that the larger community should have any concerns for their safety and welfare.

"As is always the circumstance of a situation like this, we need the help and support of the community. If you know something or have information regarding this matter, please reach out to the Boston Police Department," Hayden said at the time.

The shooting was the second of the day in the city, following a 5 a.m. shooting near Boston Common that left one person injured.

title: Man convicted in 2022 Dorchester shooting that killed teenager to be sentenced
text:
The man convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting of a teenager in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood in 2022 was expected to be sentenced Wednesday, but the case was continued to November.

Zontre Mack, of Canton, opened fire on a group of people on the evening of July 27, 2022, killing 15-year-old Curtis Ashford Jr., the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said.

Curtis' family has said that the recent eighth-grade graduate was on his way to the park to meet up with some friends when the shooting broke out on Ellington Street.

Another man charged in the shooting, Dominick Gavin, has pleaded guilty to a count of accessory after the fact and was sentenced to three to four years in prison.

Mack, who was 18 at the time of the shooting, was identified after investigators found DNA and fingerprints that matched to his in a vehicle that was seen carrying the shooter, prosecutors said.

Mack, now 21, was originally scheduled to be sentenced at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday. The case was continued to Nov. 13.

"Losing someone so young to violence is a blow to the entire city. Every person who cares about the health of our neighborhoods and the safety of our young people—and that should be all of us—should be shocked, saddened and motivated to make things better. But nowhere is Curtis's loss felt more profoundly than by his family and friends, and they will always have our sympathy and our support," Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement.

title: Man convicted of murder in deadly South Shore Plaza shooting
text:
A man was convicted of murder nearly three years after a deadly shooting in a Massachusetts mall.

Dijoun Beasley, a 26-year-old from Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, was fatally shot at South Shore Plaza in Braintree on Jan. 22, 2022.

Julius Hammond-Desir of Maynard, who was 19 at the time, was arrested on a murder charge. The Norfolk County District Attorney's Office said Tuesday that a jury had convicted him of first-degree murder.

Prosecutors say Hammond-Desir is due to be sentenced Thursday in Norfolk Superior Court.

State and local police responded to a call of shots fired with a person down at South Shore Plaza around 3 p.m. on a Saturday. The mall was evacuated and those still inside were ordered to shelter in place until it was safe to come out.

Emergency personnel found Beasley on the ground with at least one apparent gunshot wound. He was taken to a Boston hospital with life-threatening injuries and died several days later.

According to Braintree police, there was an "encounter" between the two men inside a store on the first floor of the mall. Hammond-Desir allegedly approached Beasley, pulled out a firearm and shot him. Police believe Hammond-Desir immediately fled the mall.

Police said at the time that it appeared this was a targeted shooting and not a random event and insisted there was no danger to the community at large.

title: Man sentenced to life in prison for 2019 killing of taxi driver in front of Boston hotel
text:
A man convicted of killing a taxi driver outside a Boston hotel nearly six years ago has been sentenced to life in prison, the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office said Friday.

Phillip Foy, 40, was found guilty Monday of first-degree murder in the June 4, 2019, shooting of Luckinson Oruma, the DA said. The sentence carries a mandatory life sentence, with no chance for parole.

Oruma, a 60-year-old from Dorchester, was a father of five, his boss told NBC10 Boston at the time of the shooting. Several family members attended the sentencing. His son delivered a victim impact statement, describing his father as a “hardworking, devoted, loving dad,” and that “he was doing what he always did, working hard to provide,” when he was killed. He noted that his father put five kids through college while working as a cab driver.

Oruma was parked in front of the Colonnade Hotel on the day of the killing, when Foy got in and asked to be taken to Mansfield. When Oruma declined, Foy got out, opened Oruma's door and attacked him, then shot him multiple times, including while he was lying on the ground, directly underneath Foy, prosecutors said.

Foy then drove the cab down Huntington Avenue and parked, ditched the gun and sat down, without his shoes, in front of a Starbucks. When officers arrived, he grabbed a pedestrian in an attempt to shield himself from them, but was taken into custody, when he claimed the shooting was a case of self-defense.

“The shooting death of Luckinson Oruma was shattering not just for his family and friends, but for anyone who goes to work each day expecting, as they should, to be in a safe environment," Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a media statement after the verdict. "This defendant turned Mr. Oruma’s environment into something tragically different, and I’m very grateful that the jury held him accountable for his devastating actions."

title: Man sentenced to life in prison in deadly South Shore Plaza shooting
text:
A man convicted of murder after a deadly shooting in a Massachusetts mall in 2022 was sentenced Thursday to life in prison.

Dijoun Beasley, a 26-year-old from Boston's Dorchester neighborhood, was fatally shot at South Shore Plaza in Braintree on Jan. 22, 2022.

Julius Hammond-Desir of Maynard, who was 19 at the time, was arrested on a murder charge. The Norfolk County District Attorney's Office said Tuesday that a jury had convicted him of first-degree murder, unlawfully carrying a firearm and unlawfully carrying a loaded firearm.

Prosecutors said Hammond-Desir killed Beasley after encountering him in the Forever 21 store. Surveillance video showed a brief exhange between the two inside the store and the shooting itself. Hammond-Desire was also seen on video fleeing the mall while holding what appeared to be a gun in his waistband.

The mall was evacuated and those still inside were ordered to shelter in place until it was safe to come out.

Beasley was shot in the head and died a day later.

The district attorney's office said Hammond-Desir was sentenced Thursday to a mandatory term of life in prison with the possibility of parole after 25 years on the murder charge. He was sentenced to another 5 years on related firearms charges.

title: Man wanted in 2023 Dorchester shooting that hurt 8 due in court
text:
Nearly two years after violence unfolded near Boston's J'ouvert Parade, the man charged in the case was held without bail, accused of fleeing the state before his original trial was set to start.

It was the first time Gerald Vick has been in a Massachusetts court after allegedly running from authorities the night before he was set to go on trial — and it was a longtime effort by police to capture the man.

The multi-month search began in December of 2024 and ended 13 days ago when 31-year-old Vick, a Dorchester resident, was apprehended by U.S. Marshals in Lithia Springs, Georgia.

Vick appeared in Suffolk Superior Court on Tuesday to answer to a handful of charges, including eight counts of assault and battery with a firearm, unlawful possession of a machine gun, as well as others.

Police said they found him with a pistol, equipped with a Glock switch — a device that makes the gun fire automatically and erratically — as well as a lot of ammo, shortly after shots rang out the morning of Aug. 26, 2023. That was the day of the annual J'ouvert Parade, which is part of the city's Caribbean Carnival Festival.

Investigators believe an argument between two "rival groups" played a role in the incident.

Three other people — Hubman Hunter, Sebastian Monteiro and Dwayne Francis — have also been charged in the shooting.

At Tuesday's appearance, the judge found Vick dangerous, which stands from a previous hearing in the case, and ruled to hold him without bail.

The judge said Vick's past behavior has "shown that he doesn’t have an interest in moving forward with the ordinary administration of justice.”

Vick was originally released on personal recognizance, with the requirements of GPS monitoring and home confinement.

Vick decided to take the case to trial, which was set to begin on Dec. 1, 2024. The night before, police said Vick removed his court-issued GPS ankle monitor and had been on the run ever since.

Eight people were left injured the day of the parade in 2023. Police said at the time that the violence didn't have anything to do with the event itself.

The next court date was set for Aug. 19.

title: Man wanted in 2023 Dorchester shooting that injured 8 arrested in Georgia
text:
A man accused in a shooting that left eight people injured near a Caribbean festival in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood two years ago has been arrested in Georgia.

Violence unfolded on the morning of Aug. 26, 2023, when two groups of people got into an argument on Talbot Avenue while the J'ouvert Parade was happening nearby.

Boston police said Wednesday that 31-year-old Gerald Vick of Dorchester was captured by U.S. Marshals in Lithia Springs, Georgia.

Vick was arrested after the shooting, but police said he has been on the run since removing a court-ordered electronic monitoring bracelet the night before he was set to go on trial. The department asked for the public's help finding him in December.

Charges against Vick include eight counts of assault and battery with a firearm, illegal possession of a firearm, illegal possession of ammunition, carrying a loaded firearm, possession of a machine gun, possession of a large capacity magazine and possession of a firearm in the commission of a felony.

Three other people — Hubman Hunter, Sebastian Monteiro and Dwayne Francis — have also been charged in the shooting.

The Caribbean festival was celebrating its 50th anniversary when the shooting happened. It is not the first time violence has marred the celebrations, but officials said the gunfire didn't have anything to do with the event itself.

title: Work begins on Martin Richard Foundation's Fieldhouse rec center in Dorchester
text:
The groundbreaking for a new state-of-the-art youth recreational facility in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood will get underway on Thursday.

Made possible through a partnership with the Boys & Girls Club of Dorchester and Martin Richard Foundation, the event celebrates the future FieldHouse+, which is set to open in 2026.

The facility, located on Mt. Vernon Street, is designed as an adaptive space for children of all ages and abilities and will feature an indoor turf field, teaching kitchen, community theatre, indoor and outdoor courts, roof garden, indoor running and walking track, a music studio, fitness centers, and more.

The work begins as the Capital Campaign has raised more than 60% of the $70 million fundraising goal toward the project. It is touted as the city's first fully inclusive indoor space for Boston youth.

At age eight, Martin Richard was the youngest person to die in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings. Despite his youth, he was already regarded as a community activist, and his family honors his memory through their work with the Martin Richard Foundation.

title: Boston City Council holding public hearing over Mass. Cass as Wu reveals new plan
text:
A public hearing was held Thursday to address the growing safety issues in Boston's Mass. and Cass area, as city leaders reveal there's a new plan to crackdown on crime in the troubled area.

Residents voiced their concerns as city councilors considered whether to declare the situation at the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, and the impacted neighboring communities, a humanitarian crisis and public health emergency.

The neighborhood has been a hot bed of drugs and mental illness for years.

"This is a public health crisis, this is a public safety crisis, and we need a recovery campus in Boston," said Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune.

The hearing came in response to a resolution that was filed last month by City Councilor Ed Flynn, in which he claimed residents and businesses are having their public safety and quality of life impacted by "piles of trash, including discarded needles, and human feces scattering neighborhoods."

"While the tents are long gone, hundreds of people are sprawled throughout the area every day, engaging in open-air drug dealing, drug use, human trafficking, shoplifting and violent crimes throughout the neighborhoods of South End, Nubian Square, Roxbury, Dorchester, South Boston, Downtown Boston and the Back Bay," the resolution read.

People who live nearby say the issues in the troubled area have only gotten worse since the city cleared out the tent encampments and crime is spreading into residential areas of the South End and Roxbury.

The Wu administration says declaring a public health emergency will do nothing, as it won't unlock funds or resources. It acknowledges quality of life issues like fights and alcohol have gotten worse, but say major crime in the area has gone down.

The administration says it is increasing patrols with newly graduated police officers, adding a bike patrol and increasing needle pickup hours.

"We want to make sure that you understand that we understand that this is a humanitarian crisis, and we feel the urgency," said Boston Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu. "But a public health emergency is not the way to go. It's not going to do anything in this case."

Residents say they're tired of meetings and want something done.

"I am disgusted with the way the city has taken care of this problem," said Boston resident Linda Zablocki. "Really, nothing has happened. All we've done is cleaned a little bit of Mass. and Cass, and it has all dispersed to the neighborhood, so the quality of life has gone downhill faster than a ski slope."

A memo about the city's response plan released this week says open substance use in any part of Boston is illegal and unacceptable.

"As we have built up a coordinated citywide response to shut down encampments, decrease overdose mortality, and continue to strengthen the continuum of care, our focus is now on ending outdoor substance use in Boston and the criminal activity that supports it," the memo said.

The nearly 100 new Boston police officers who graduated from the academy last week will be a boost that helps the department combat crime and drug use. The memo also notes that the city directed organizations who distribute tents and meals outdoors to start giving that assistance through "authorized indoor programs.."

Meanwhile, Josh Kraft, who is running for mayor, released a strongly-worded statement about Wu's proposal:

"This is yet again another example of Mayor Wu responding to an emergency only when it becomes politically expedient. After years of ignoring this human catastrophe, she flip flops during an election year, taking a hard-line reaction to the problems at Mass and Cass," Kraft said in the statement. "Her plan, if we can even call it that, is just a cheap political fix that does nothing to address the underlying causes behind this problem, which is why, as mayor, I will have a recovery first approach that combines proactive police enforcement and collaboration with nonprofits, other municipalities, and the state government, with which this administration has refused to engage."

title: Mike Minogue coasts past Brian Shortsleeve, will face Gov. Healey
text:
Promising to "fix" Massachusetts, Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue will spend the next nine weeks trying to convince voters that he can serve them better than Gov. Maura Healey has for almost four years.

The 59-year-old former CEO of Danvers-based medical device company Abiomed, Minogue on Tuesday night defeated businessman and former MBTA head Brian Shortsleeve in the Republican primary for the corner office, per the Associated Press. The AP called the race for Minogue at 8:44 p.m. As of 9:10 p.m., the AP said about 7% of votes had been counted, with 73.6% in favor of Minogue.

"The good news is it's going to be a little bit of an earlier night. The better news is we won," Minogue said during his election night party, vowing to bring an outsider's approach to shake up state government.

"Because of you, this is more than a campaign, this is a movement," Minogue told his supporters. "And because of your courage and your willingness to say, 'it's time to do something different, it is time to put people before politics.' Because of that, we are going to make history in 63 days."

The Republican ticket is now poised to feature Minogue with Shawn Oliver, who ran unopposed but also in tandem with Shortsleeve.

"This primary is over. Now it’s time to come together," Shortsleeve said Tuesday night, endorsing Minogue.

Republican candidate for treasurer Elizabeth Dionne and GOP contender for U.S. Senate John Deaton also attended the election night party. Both Dionne and Deaton ran unopposed in their primaries, coasting to their nominations.

The contentious race between Shortsleeve and Minogue featured both infighting revolving around the soul of the state's Republican Party and cohesion among candidates about issues including state's cost of living, economic competitiveness, immigration, job growth and government accountability.

Spending heavily from his own pockets, Minogue held few media events and also refused to debate Shortsleeve during the primary cycle, electing only to say that he would win the primary and debate Healey in the leadup to the general.

Minogue describes himself as pro-life Catholic who would "uphold" current abortion laws; believes the state should lean on natural gas — not "disruptive" and "expensive" offshore wind; and says he would "repeal or cancel all unfunded mandates," among various other proposals.

When signature fraud woes derailed and disrupted the campaigns of two other statewide Republican candidates, Minogue condemned Oliver for filing complaints about fraudulent signatures submitted on behalf of GOP candidates. Standing by Oliver, Shortsleeve in June called the party "incompetent and ineffective" and said "the hypocrisy being demonstrated by Minogue and his MassGOP minions will do lasting damage to the Republican Party's attempts to improve election security and generate more confidence in election outcomes."

Now Minogue and Oliver are ticket mates.

"Together we will unify the party," Oliver said Tuesday night as he congratulated Minogue on his win.

Republicans face an uphill battle to win the corner office and if he is elected Minogue would face Democratic super-majorities in the Legislature. Minogue and Healey are mindful that voters here have a history of electing Republican governors, from William Weld to Paul Cellucci, Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker.

Complaints over fraudulent nomination signatures sunk Minogue-backed lieutenant governor hopeful Anne Brensley and Anne Manning-Martin. Brensley ultimately opted to run as a write-in for secretary of state and Manning-Martin chose the same avenue to continue her campaign for lieutenant governor.

Minogue has funneled $15.8 million into his campaign since last October, and has repeatedly said he has the resources to win the primary and general elections. Shortsleeve had significantly less cash on hand than Minogue during their primary contest. At the end of July, Shortsleeve had roughly $526,800 cash on hand compared to Minogue's $8.1 million.

A graduate of West Point and Operation Desert Storm veteran, Minogue grew up as the youngest of four in New Jersey. After returning home from his military service, he spent 11 years working for GE HealthCare before leading Abiomed, which Johnson & Johnson reportedly bought for $16.6 billion in cash. Minogue's government experience is limited to the time he spent on the Governor's Advisory Council on Veteran's Services under former Gov. Charlie Baker, according to his LinkedIn. He also founded MedTechVets, a nonprofit helping military veterans find careers in the medical device industry. Minogue and his wife, Renee, created the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation in 2015 to support faith-based education, healthcare innovation, children and veterans. His religious, military and healthcare backgrounds underpin his profile.

"From leading soldiers in combat to pioneering the field of heart recovery, Mike Minogue has spent his life serving others. A man of faith, husband, and father of five, he’s committed to serve Massachusetts with integrity and heart," his website says.

Minogue has run on the slogan "AAOK," which stands for Accountability, Affordability, Opportunity and Keeping communities safe.

While Minogue has been a prolific donor and supporter of President Donald Trump and other national Republicans, he said in July that he has a different outlook on tariffs than Trump, specifically opposing tariffs on medical device companies. Minogue also said he doesn't support cuts to the National Institutes of Health, that he thinks "everyone that's entitled to Medicaid needs to get it," and that he doesn't agree with Trump's assessment that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing a "great job."

After Healey signed a bill loosening abortion restrictions in August, Minogue's campaign said he'd "rather see the people of Massachusetts voice their opinion and decide this - not the politicians." Shortsleeve has called himself a "pro-choice Republican," and his campaign said he would have also signed the abortion law.

Minogue has also said that he would uphold the state's "common sense" laws regarding LGBTQ+ protections.

A Trump-aligned candidate in a state where Trump is unpopular, especially among Democrats, Minogue will look to entice the block of unenrolled voters who collectively outnumber registered Democrats. Both Minogue and Healey will compete over which candidate is better suited to address the high costs of energy, housing and healthcare.

Maura Healey calls for Minogue to agree to debate

The general election had already begun by the time Healey took the stage at her election night party in Dorchester, shortly after the AP called the race for Minogue. She was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and officially won the nomination shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m.

She jabbed at her new opponent, drawing a connection between the Republican candidate and President Donald Trump, as well as Minogue's documented personal anti-abortion stance. Healey will likely try to draw attention to Trump and abortion on the campaign trail over the next few months, as the state has consistently voted against Trump in presidential elections and even many independent voters support pro-abortion policies.

"Mike Minogue? He’s given more than a million dollars to Trump. He held a fundraiser for JD Vance at his waterfront mansion. By the way, that means Mike Minogue saw what Donald Trump did in his first term and said - sign me up, I want more of that!" Healey said in her prepared speech.

According to the written speech, Healey also planned to point out Minogue's financial support for conservative media organization PragerU, which she called on Thursday "a right-wing propaganda machine that promotes racist and anti-gay views, denies climate change, and spreads extremism and misinformation."

She continued, "Mike Minogue supports Donald Trump’s agenda that is raising your costs and killing Massachusetts jobs. He’s pro-ICE and anti-choice. Look, Donald Trump is gonna be president for two more years. Who your governor is right now matters more than ever."

Healey cast the general election in the terms of "whose side you're on" which she described, "Mike Minogue stands with Donald Trump, I'll always stand with you."

Wednesday morning the Healey-Driscoll campaign called on Minogue and Oliver, their Republican opponents, to accept debate invitations to provide voters with a clear picture of the race this fall.

Healey has agreed to participate in two statewide live, televised debates in the general election. The first debate is scheduled to be aired live on Oct. 8, followed by a second debate later in October.

“This fall, voters deserve to see the clear choice in this election on the debate stage,” Healey-Driscoll Campaign Manager Katie Prisco-Buxbaum said in a statement. “While Governor Healey works every day to lower costs and stand up to Donald Trump, Mike Minogue is dodging debates and questions about his extreme views and his support for Donald Trump’s pro-tariff, pro-ICE, and anti-choice agenda.”

Brian Shortsleeve

Shortsleeve, a former Marine and Harvard College graduate, just barely made the September ballot in April at the state GOP convention, where he raked in 15.5% of delegate votes to Minogue's 70.38%. The threshold to survive was 15%.

Just before 9 p.m., Shortsleeve, his wife and their three sons gathered on stage to again address supporters.

"While we came up short tonight, I believe that our message was heard, and I am proud of the campaign we ran," Shortsleeve said, drawing a round of applause from supporters who held up Shortsleeve campaign posters.

Shortsleeve also quickly endorsed his opponent, saying he would do everything he could to get Minogue elected.

"However, you supported me, I'm asking you: Join me in supporting Mike Minogue," Shortsleeve said. "Let's unify this party. Let's bring Independents and Democrats into this movement, and most importantly, let's defeat Maura Healey."

Without explaining how he would do it, Minogue has said he intends to initiate the voter-approved legislative audit on his first day in office. Shortsleeve said he would veto the Legislature's budget appropriation until lawmakers comply with the audit law.

Shortsleeve promised to "audit every state agency for waste, fraud, abuse and inefficiency"; to "conduct independent performance audits to evaluate whether programs are producing measurable results"; and implement a front-end identity and eligibility verification for SNAP recipients.

The party's two gubernatorial candidates were also largely aligned on immigration. When Healey signed the long-awaited PROTECT Act, an attempt to protect immigrants in Massachusetts from ICE, Shortsleeve said that Healey "prioritizes politics over public safety."

Minogue's platform outlines that Massachusetts will not be a "sanctuary state" and that "illegal immigrants will not have free Right to Shelter." Minogue's website also says that "girls need fair and safe sports."

title: The Mass. housing market is so competitive people are buying burned-out homes
text:
Even homes destroyed by fire can attract strong interest from buyers across the Boston area, highlighting just how competitive—and unconventional—the Massachusetts housing market has become.

In Dorchester, a burned and condemned multi-family property recently went under agreement in just two days, according to the listing agent.

“It’s not your typical buyer,” said Anthony Bruno of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty. “You’re dealing with contractors, developers—people who know what it takes to bring something like this back.”

Why fire-damaged homes are still selling

Despite significant damage, these properties are drawing investors eager to take on major renovation projects. Bruno says the current buyer is looking to keep the existing structure and rebuild, possibly adding additional units depending on zoning.

“There’s only so much land,” he said. “Opportunities like this attract developers who are ready to move quickly.”

In a tight housing market like Boston’s—where inventory remains limited—these types of properties can offer rare opportunities for expansion or redevelopment.

A Melrose homeowner’s different path

In Melrose, one fire-ravaged property tells a different story about what happens after disaster strikes.

Paul Schille has owned his property since 1982. The original house, built in the mid-1800s, was destroyed in a fire that displaced his family and forced a series of difficult decisions.

“It was very, very stressful,” Schille said. “We were looking for homes almost every night.”

At one point, the property was listed for $650,000, drawing attention for what appeared to be a burned-out home selling at a high price. But Schille says the real value was in the land.

“This happens to be a quarter acre—and that’s big for Melrose,” he explained.

Developers expressed interest, with some considering multi-unit construction, but zoning challenges and timing issues slowed the process. Ultimately, the deal didn’t come together.

Starting over after losing everything

After months of uncertainty—and ongoing battles with insurance—Schille made a major decision.

“I said, this is way too stressful… I’m going to build the house myself,” he said.

With no prior construction experience, Schille stepped in as his own general contractor, overseeing the demolition of the damaged home and starting from scratch.

“When it happened, I had to really get in gear,” he said.

The rebuilding process took 19 months and required more money than his insurance coverage provided. Schille says he put everything he received from insurance back into the home, ultimately spending about $775,000 on the rebuild.

Now worth nearly $1.8 million

Today, the property has been completely transformed into a new two-family home—now valued at around $1.8 million.

“I couldn’t be happier with the way the house turned out,” Schille said.

He credits the Melrose community for helping his family through the crisis.

“The community was outstanding,” he said. “We had so many offers for help.”

Lessons for homeowners

Schille says the experience taught him important lessons—especially about insurance.

“You should talk to your insurance agent almost every year,” he said. “Make sure it’s insured at the proper value—because prices go up quickly.”

He also recommends homeowners consider working with a public adjuster when navigating insurance claims after a disaster.

A sign of the times in Boston real estate

From Dorchester to Melrose, these cases underscore a broader trend: even severely damaged homes can attract serious interest in Greater Boston’s competitive housing market.

For developers, agents say the appeal is clear—limited land, strong demand, and the potential to build equity. For homeowners like Schille, the journey is far more personal—one of loss, resilience, and rebuilding from the ground up.

“I love the place,” he said. “I love the community.”

title: Yeast, mold in marijuana products prompts warning from Mass. cannabis board
text:
Several marijuana products sold across Massachusetts were recently found to have mold and yeast in them above acceptable limits, the Cannabis Control Commission said in a health advisory Monday.

The strains — Slap N Tickle, Tiger’s Eye, Carbon Fiber, Frosted Jungle, Highland OG and Silver Kush — were sold as recently as last month, according to the announcement. They passed initial testing before the contaminants were found through additional compliance testing.

No illnesses connected with the issues have been reported, the commission said. Anyone with the affected marijuana was urged to destroy or return it and contact the retailer, and anyone who uses the product and undergoes adverse health effects was urged to seek medical attention and reach out to the store they got it from.

There were two sets of potentially contaminated products, according to the Cannabis Control Commission:
