title: Massachusetts' 2026 primaries are in the books. Here are the results
text:
The November midterm election matchups are set in Massachusetts after Tuesday's primaries.

There were no major upsets. Sen. Ed Markey and Congressman Stephen Lynch both fended off younger challengers, while Mike Minogue coasted past Brian Shortsleeve in the race for governor.

See more on the election results in Massachusetts below.

Who won the primaries in Massachusetts?

See Massachusetts' primary election results here

Congressional incumbents

Congressional incumbents in Massachusetts who faced primary opponents Tuesday mostly fared well, though two were still sweating out the results as the day closed.

In and around Boston, U.S. Rep. Stephen Lynch was holding off challenger Patrick Roath in the Eighth District. Results from the Associated Press showed Lynch with 57% to Roath's 43% as of 10:35 p.m., when about 43% of the vote had been tallied. Roath campaigned on the idea of generational change, while Lynch leaned on the idea that there's still room for what he called a "moderate Democrat" brand of politics in Washington, D.C. Republican Robert Burke of Dedham will fill out the opposite side of the ballot in the general election.

In the western part of the state's First District, longtime U.S. Rep. Richard Neal of Springfield looked to be eking out a primary win over South Hadley's Jeromie Whalen. Neal dispatched challengers in 2018 and 2020 (when he ground out a 59% to 41% victory over then-Holyoke Mayor Alex Morse), but had not been challenged since. With 61% of the vote in as of 10:30 p.m., the AP had Neal leading Whalen 54% to 46%, a tighter margin than the 2020 result.

No Republican ran for the seat this year, leaving Neal poised to return for a 20th term if he survives the primary.

Late Tuesday night, Our Revolution Executive Director Joseph Geevarghese said the yet-uncalled Neal-Whalen race was "far closer than virtually anyone expected" and called it evidence that "Whalen showed what is possible, and this should be Neal's last term in Congress."

"The final numbers will come in, but the message is already clear: the ground is shifting — not just in Western Massachusetts, but across the country. Voters are increasingly ready for a new generation of leaders willing to take on corporate power and fight unapologetically for working people," he said.

Meanwhile, Rep. Tram Nguyen of Andover was on track to finish behind former Marty Walsh aide Dan Koh in the crowded Democratic primary for the Sixth District. The AP called the race for Koh just before 10:30 p.m., when about 62% of ballots had been counted and Koh was leading Nguyen with 42.4% support to her 29.4%. Essex Republican Micah Jones, who is running with the endorsement of former Gov. Charlie Baker, awaits in the Nov. 3 general election.

In the Fourth District that snakes from Boston's immediate western suburbs along the I-95 corridor towards Fall River and the South Coast, U.S. Rep. Jake Auchincloss outlasted challenger Jason Poulos of Sherborn. Brookline Republican Thomas Stalcup awaits Auchincloss in the general. The AP said about 37% of the vote had been counted as of 9:50 p.m., with Auchincloss taking 72% of it.

U.S. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark of Revere, the highest ranking woman in the U.S. House, was the victor of a three-way Democratic primary in the Fifth District that also included Tarik Samman of Cambridge and Jonathan Paz of Waltham. No Republican sought the seat this year, setting Clark up to return to her leadership post in D.C. The AP called Clark's primary around 9:30 p.m. when about 10% of the vote was in, with Clark carrying about 75% of it.

U.S. Rep. Bill Keating of Bourne, a former county prosecutor and state senator, is set up to face Republican candidate R. Tyler MacAllister of Mattapoisett in the general election after outpolling primary challenger Craig Swallow of New Bedford on Tuesday. Keating has represented the Ninth District for eight terms. When the AP called the race for Keating at 9:50 p.m., about 7% of votes had been counted and 77% were for Keating.

U.S. Rep. Lori Trahan of Westford is lined up to compete with Republican Gary Grossi of Acton in the general after neither had a primary contest. U.S. Reps. James McGovern of Worcester and Ayanna Pressley of Boston faced no opponent in Tuesday's primary and also have no Republican opponent in November.

Legislative incumbents

Many legislative incumbents facing primary challenges appeared to have survived Tuesday's elections, but several of the night's most closely watched contests remained unresolved as ballots continued to be counted, leaving open questions about the strength of the anti-incumbent and progressive currents that animated campaign season.

The races will not determine control of Beacon Hill. Democrats currently hold 166 of the Legislature's 197 filled seats, compared with 30 Republicans and one independent, and will mathematically retain overwhelming majorities heading into 2027. Instead, the contests offered a series of tests of individual incumbents, and in several open seats, the ideological and political direction of districts that are virtually certain to remain Democratic.

In the Senate, four Democratic incumbents were facing primary challengers, including two members of the chamber's leadership ranks. Two of those contests remained too close to call around 10:30 p.m. Tuesday. The incumbents held substantial leads in the others.

In the Suffolk and Middlesex District, Senate President Pro Tempore William Brownsberger led Democratic challenger Daniel Lander, 55.7% to 44.4% according to the Associated Press, with 59% of the vote counted as of roughly 10:30 p.m. The race has carried broader significance because Lander, a former senior policy adviser to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, framed his challenge around generational change to the status quo and the divide between Brownsberger's suburban Belmont base and Lander's Boston home in Fenway.

The contest has also been a proxy for tensions between Wu and Senate leadership.

A second leadership test was even tighter. In the Norfolk and Suffolk District, longtime Sen. Michael Rush held 53.8% to civil rights attorney and consumer advocate Persis Yu's 46.2%, with 52% of ballots counted. The AP had not declared a projected winner.

Rush had not faced a primary or general election opponent since 2012, making Tuesday's contest an unusual test after more than a decade without an electoral challenge.

Sen. Nick Collins was also leading in the First Suffolk District, where he held 59.4% to Latoya Gayle's 38%, with 20% of votes counted. Gayle, who is aligned with Wu's political orbit, has made the race another closely watched contest involving an incumbent and a challenger associated with the mayor's supporters. Collins had not been declared the winner as of the latest count.

In the Norfolk, Plymouth and Bristol District, Sen. William Driscoll led Tony King and Michael Zullas with 65.1% of the vote, compared with 27% for Zullas and 7.9% for King, with 22% counted according to the AP. The race remained uncalled.

The most consequential Senate races for the future of open seats were also still developing.

In the Second Middlesex District, Rep. Erika Uyterhoeven led fellow Rep. Christine Barber, 38.5% to 30.9%, with 81% counted. Cambridge City Councilor Burhan Azeem had 14.7% and Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin had 13.8%. No winner had been called.

The four-way contest is taking place for the seat being vacated by longtime Sen. Pat Jehlen and has attracted candidates from the district's progressive political base. Uyterhoeven has pushed for greater openness in the Legislature's processes.

In the Fifth Middlesex District, Rep. Kate Lipper-Garabedian held a considerable lead as of 10:30 p.m., claiming 73.5% of the vote with 56% counted in the Democratic primary for the seat being vacated by Sen. Jason Lewis. Malden City Councilors Carey McDonald and Ryan O'Malley were also competing.

The House picture was similarly mixed, with several incumbents declaring victory or being called winners while other races remained unsettled.

Rep. Lisa Field declared victory in the Third Bristol District after facing Taunton Police Chief Edward Walsh in the Democratic primary. Field won a special election to the seat last year by just 15 votes after a recount and is now preparing for another November contest against Republican Larry Quintal. Walsh entered the primary after legislation concerning his mandatory retirement age stalled on Beacon Hill.

The AP called Rep. Andrew "Dru" Tarr's victory in the Fifth Essex District at 10:21 p.m. Tarr, who won the seat in a spring special election following the death of Rep. Ann-Margaret Ferrante, was leading Democrat Sarah Wilkinson. Tarr could face Republican Christina Delisio in November.

Rep. John Lawn was also declared the winner by the AP at 10:20 p.m., defeating Newton City Councilor Alison Leary, 63.6% to 36.4%, with 99% counted. Lawn is the chairman of the Health Care Financing Committee and a longtime ally of Speaker Ron Mariano.

Rep. Angelo Puppolo Jr. declared victory in the 12th Hampden District over younger progressive challenger Michael Lachenmeyer. With 49% counted, Puppolo had 68.9% to Lachenmeyer's 31.1%. Lachenmeyer had sought to make housing and affordability central issues and portrayed the longtime Springfield-area lawmaker as part of an entrenched establishment. Puppolo's campaign said it won every precinct, except for one.

Rep. Mike Connolly also declared victory in the 26th Middlesex District. With 21% counted, Connolly held 81.6% to Neil Miller's 18.4%. The Cambridge representative is himself considered a member of the Legislature's progressive wing, making the race less a traditional moderate-versus-progressive contest than a debate over transparency, accountability and generational change.

Another closely watched Cambridge contest remained unresolved. In the 25th Middlesex District, challenger Evan MacKay led Rep. Marjorie Decker, 53% to 47%, with only 8% of votes counted, according to the AP. MacKay nearly defeated Decker in the 2024 Democratic primary, losing by just 41 votes after a recount. House leadership has rallied behind Decker this year.

An open House seat in Cambridge also changed hands, after Barber gave it up to run for Senate. The AP called the 34th Middlesex District race for Somerville City Councilor Will Mbah at 10:09 p.m., with 54.1% and 99% counted.

In the 27th Middlesex seat Uyterhoeven left open, the AP called victory for Ben Ewen-Campen.

In western Massachusetts, the open First Franklin District remained too close to call. With 37% counted, former Rep. Natalie Blais aide Corinne Coryat led former Greenfield City Council President Lora Wondolowski, 54.2% to 45.8%. Independent Amy Lavalle has already secured a place on the November ballot.

In the 19th Suffolk District, Rep. Jeffrey Turco led paramedic LeeAllen Meyer, 60.1% to 39.9%, with 62% counted. The contest had pitted one of the House's more moderate Democrats against a challenger campaigning on a progressive agenda and abortion access.

At least two other House primaries had no publicly available vote totals at the time: the Democratic and Republican contests for the open 9th Bristol District, where Democrats Edward Pacheco and Stephen Medeiros were competing and Republicans Chester Tam and Henry Bousquet were also seeking their party's nomination. The district is the only one in Massachusetts where both parties had contested primaries, setting up a November race in one of the Republicans' better potential pickup opportunities.

The Republican primary in the Second Plymouth District, where first-term Rep. John Gaskey faced Carver Select Board member Mark Townsend, also had no publicly available vote totals.

The night's results thus far largely reinforced the broader picture that had defined the campaign: Massachusetts remains a state where most legislative incumbents face little or no electoral competition, and Tuesday's contests were unlikely to alter the basic partisan balance on Beacon Hill.

But the races that remained unsettled will offer a more nuanced measure of voter sentiment.

Governor's race

Promising to "fix" Massachusetts, Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue will spend the next nine weeks trying to convince voters that he can serve them better than Gov. Maura Healey has for almost four years.

The 59-year-old former CEO of Danvers-based medical device company Abiomed, Minogue on Tuesday night defeated businessman and former MBTA head Brian Shortsleeve in the Republican primary for the corner office, per the Associated Press. The AP called the race for Minogue at 8:44 p.m. As of 9:10 p.m., the AP said about 7% of votes had been counted, with 73.6% in favor of Minogue.

"The good news is it's going to be a little bit of an earlier night. The better news is we won," Minogue said during his election night party, vowing to bring an outsider's approach to shake up state government.

"Because of you, this is more than a campaign, this is a movement," Minogue told his supporters. "And because of your courage and your willingness to say, 'it's time to do something different, it is time to put people before politics.' Because of that, we are going to make history in 63 days."

The Republican ticket is now poised to feature Minogue with Shawn Oliver, who ran unopposed but also in tandem with Shortsleeve.

"This primary is over. Now it’s time to come together," Shortsleeve said Tuesday night, endorsing Minogue.

Republican candidate for treasurer Elizabeth Dionne and GOP contender for U.S. Senate John Deaton also attended the election night party. Both Dionne and Deaton ran unopposed in their primaries, coasting to their nominations.

The contentious race between Shortsleeve and Minogue featured both infighting revolving around the soul of the state's Republican Party and cohesion among candidates about issues including state's cost of living, economic competitiveness, immigration, job growth and government accountability.

Spending heavily from his own pockets, Minogue held few media events and also refused to debate Shortsleeve during the primary cycle, electing only to say that he would win the primary and debate Healey in the leadup to the general.

Minogue describes himself as pro-life Catholic who would "uphold" current abortion laws; believes the state should lean on natural gas — not "disruptive" and "expensive" offshore wind; and says he would "repeal or cancel all unfunded mandates," among various other proposals.

When signature fraud woes derailed and disrupted the campaigns of two other statewide Republican candidates, Minogue condemned Oliver for filing complaints about fraudulent signatures submitted on behalf of GOP candidates. Standing by Oliver, Shortsleeve in June called the party "incompetent and ineffective" and said "the hypocrisy being demonstrated by Minogue and his MassGOP minions will do lasting damage to the Republican Party's attempts to improve election security and generate more confidence in election outcomes."

Now Minogue and Oliver are ticket mates.

"Together we will unify the party," Oliver said Tuesday night as he congratulated Minogue on his win.

Republicans face an uphill battle to win the corner office and if he is elected Minogue would face Democratic super-majorities in the Legislature. Minogue and Healey are mindful that voters here have a history of electing Republican governors, from William Weld to Paul Cellucci, Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker.

Complaints over fraudulent nomination signatures sunk Minogue-backed lieutenant governor hopeful Anne Brensley and Anne Manning-Martin. Brensley ultimately opted to run as a write-in for secretary of state and Manning-Martin chose the same avenue to continue her campaign for lieutenant governor.

Minogue has funneled $15.8 million into his campaign since last October, and has repeatedly said he has the resources to win the primary and general elections. Shortsleeve had significantly less cash on hand than Minogue during their primary contest. At the end of July, Shortsleeve had roughly $526,800 cash on hand compared to Minogue's $8.1 million.

A graduate of West Point and Operation Desert Storm veteran, Minogue grew up as the youngest of four in New Jersey. After returning home from his military service, he spent 11 years working for GE HealthCare before leading Abiomed, which Johnson & Johnson reportedly bought for $16.6 billion in cash. Minogue's government experience is limited to the time he spent on the Governor's Advisory Council on Veteran's Services under former Gov. Charlie Baker, according to his LinkedIn. He also founded MedTechVets, a nonprofit helping military veterans find careers in the medical device industry. Minogue and his wife, Renee, created the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation in 2015 to support faith-based education, healthcare innovation, children and veterans. His religious, military and healthcare backgrounds underpin his profile.

"From leading soldiers in combat to pioneering the field of heart recovery, Mike Minogue has spent his life serving others. A man of faith, husband, and father of five, he’s committed to serve Massachusetts with integrity and heart," his website says.

Minogue has run on the slogan "AAOK," which stands for Accountability, Affordability, Opportunity and Keeping communities safe.

While Minogue has been a prolific donor and supporter of President Donald Trump and other national Republicans, he said in July that he has a different outlook on tariffs than Trump, specifically opposing tariffs on medical device companies. Minogue also said he doesn't support cuts to the National Institutes of Health, that he thinks "everyone that's entitled to Medicaid needs to get it," and that he doesn't agree with Trump's assessment that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing a "great job."

After Healey signed a bill loosening abortion restrictions in August, Minogue's campaign said he'd "rather see the people of Massachusetts voice their opinion and decide this - not the politicians." Shortsleeve has called himself a "pro-choice Republican," and his campaign said he would have also signed the abortion law.

Minogue has also said that he would uphold the state's "common sense" laws regarding LGBTQ+ protections.

A Trump-aligned candidate in a state where Trump is unpopular, especially among Democrats, Minogue will look to entice the block of unenrolled voters who collectively outnumber registered Democrats. Both Minogue and Healey will compete over which candidate is better suited to address the high costs of energy, housing and healthcare.

The general election had already begun by the time Healey took the stage at her election night party in Dorchester, shortly after the AP called the race for Minogue. She was unopposed in the Democratic primary, and officially won the nomination shortly after polls closed at 8 p.m.

She jabbed at her new opponent, drawing a connection between the Republican candidate and President Donald Trump, as well as Minogue's documented personal anti-abortion stance. Healey will likely try to draw attention to Trump and abortion on the campaign trail over the next few months, as the state has consistently voted against Trump in presidential elections and even many independent voters support pro-abortion policies.

"Mike Minogue? He’s given more than a million dollars to Trump. He held a fundraiser for JD Vance at his waterfront mansion. By the way, that means Mike Minogue saw what Donald Trump did in his first term and said - sign me up, I want more of that!" Healey said in her prepared speech.

According to the written speech, Healey also planned to point out Minogue's financial support for conservative media organization PragerU, which she called on Thursday "a right-wing propaganda machine that promotes racist and anti-gay views, denies climate change, and spreads extremism and misinformation."

She continued, "Mike Minogue supports Donald Trump’s agenda that is raising your costs and killing Massachusetts jobs. He’s pro-ICE and anti-choice. Look, Donald Trump is gonna be president for two more years. Who your governor is right now matters more than ever."

Healey cast the general election in the terms of "whose side you're on" which she described, "Mike Minogue stands with Donald Trump, I'll always stand with you."

Shortsleeve, a former Marine and Harvard College graduate, just barely made the September ballot in April at the state GOP convention, where he raked in 15.5% of delegate votes to Minogue's 70.38%. The threshold to survive was 15%.

Just before 9 p.m., Shortsleeve, his wife and their three sons gathered on stage to again address supporters.

"While we came up short tonight, I believe that our message was heard, and I am proud of the campaign we ran," Shortsleeve said, drawing a round of applause from supporters who held up Shortsleeve campaign posters.

Shortsleeve also quickly endorsed his opponent, saying he would do everything he could to get Minogue elected.

"However, you supported me, I'm asking you: Join me in supporting Mike Minogue," Shortsleeve said. "Let's unify this party. Let's bring Independents and Democrats into this movement, and most importantly, let's defeat Maura Healey."

Without explaining how he would do it, Minogue has said he intends to initiate the voter-approved legislative audit on his first day in office. Shortsleeve said he would veto the Legislature's budget appropriation until lawmakers comply with the audit law.

Shortsleeve promised to "audit every state agency for waste, fraud, abuse and inefficiency"; to "conduct independent performance audits to evaluate whether programs are producing measurable results"; and implement a front-end identity and eligibility verification for SNAP recipients.

The party's two gubernatorial candidates were also largely aligned on immigration. When Healey signed the long-awaited PROTECT Act, an attempt to protect immigrants in Massachusetts from ICE, Shortsleeve said that Healey "prioritizes politics over public safety."

Minogue's platform outlines that Massachusetts will not be a "sanctuary state" and that "illegal immigrants will not have free Right to Shelter." Minogue's website also says that "girls need fair and safe sports."

Sen. Ed. Markey prevails over Rep. Seth Moulton

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey secured the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts’ Senate primary Tuesday, once again fending off a push for generational change as he seeks a third term.

Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who had attempted to argue that it was time to do away with the “status quo” in his pursuit to oust the octogenarian.

Yet Markey successfully pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters. Perhaps no other issue defined the race more than transgender rights, and Markey repeatedly hit Moulton for previously saying he would not want his daughters to play against transgender athletes.

“Massachusetts needs a senator who stands up and fights back, a senator who never forgets who they are fighting for,” Markey said during his victory speech. “That has been the mission of my life, and it always will be.”

In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, where Democratic winners are expected to prevail in the general election in November. Markey will face Republican John Deaton, who who lost to Sen. Elizabeth Warren by about 20 points in 2024 and was unopposed in his primary Tuesday.

Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s, prompting Moulton to make his “status quo” arguments on the campaign trail and to question Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.

“Generational change isn’t about compromising, to do the small things better,” Markey said Tuesday. “It’s about fighting to do the big things best.”

In a concession speech, Moulton said he would now support Markey.

“Challenging the establishment and calling for a new generation of leadership isn’t easy. But it is necessary,” Moulton told supporters. “We started conversations that needed to happen.”

“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight, but I am confident others will be inspired to buck the system when they’re told to wait their turn,” he added.

The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on the ballot. Similar dynamics played out in several congressional races, but ultimately, the older incumbents won Tuesday. In the 8th Congressional District, longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch defeated Patrick Roath. And in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, Rep. Richard Neal defeated public school teacher Jeromie Whalen to advance to the general election.

During the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.

Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.

Moulton later apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.

“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”

Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.

Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.

Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation’s most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.

Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.

“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. “He’s doing a good job. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”

Longtime Democratic House incumbents also defeated younger challengers

Lynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He won Tuesday’s primary against Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.

Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.

In the 1st District Democratic primary in western Massachusetts, Neal, 77, bested Whalen, 39.

Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.

Whalen was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

District Attorney races

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden secured renomination in a race against two challengers, including his predecessor, Rachael Rollins.

Democrat Djuna Perkins claimed victory in a tight primary race for Norfolk County District Attorney. With 98% of the vote in, Perkins was leading with 28.95%, followed closely by Adam Deitch at 26.28%.

"We did it! Yesterday, we finished first in a field of 7 candidates running to be the Democratic nominee for Norfolk County District Attorney. I am so grateful for the countless volunteers, tens of thousands of voters who supported us, my dedicated campaign team and endorsers, and my family who supported me every step of the way in this 23-month long campaign," she wrote in a statement.

Perkins ran a campaign based on calls for reform in the office in the wake of the Karen Read and Sandra Birchmore trials.

"This campaign has never been about me. It has always been about restoring justice and integrity to a broken criminal justice system here in Norfolk County; ensuring that no one is treated differently under the law due to political connections, money or privilege; protecting victims of crime; prosecuting those who prey upon or harm others; and keeping every resident of Norfolk County safe," the statement continued.

Deitch conceded on Wednesday, saying he'd called Perkins to congratulate her.

"A new administration will take office in a few months, and our job does not end with this election — it continues. We must keep fighting for a justice system defined by fairness, trust, and accountability and where, at its core, everyone is treated the same," he said in a statement.

There are no Republican challengers. Independent Joe Pagliarulo advanced straight to the ballot.

title: Inside NBC10 Boston's investigation into a ‘tenant from hell'
text:
The NBC10 Boston Investigators have been uncovering so-called professional tenants for years now, and now we're getting a behind-the-scenes look at the reporting process on perhaps the most shocking story yet.

Ryan Kath joins JC Monahan on this week's Just Curious with JC to discuss a story that is drawing attention from thousands -- the story of an elderly Boston resident trapped inside her own home with the "tenant from hell".

An elderly homeowner reached out to the NBC10 Investigators about her ordeal with a tenant living on the first floor of her property in Dorchester. Despite not paying rent, it took more than a year and numerous housing court appearances to get an eviction.

Since airing in April, the story has struck a nerve with tens of thousands of people, highlighting the broad scope of the issue.

title: Woman gave fake Botox injections at her Mass. beauty spas for years, feds say
text:
A woman posing as a nurse has given thousands of injections of counterfeit Botox and fillers at her Massachusetts beauty spas, federal prosecutors said Friday.

Rebecca Fadanelli, 38, was arrested Friday on suspicion of importing fake Botox and the fillers Sculptra and Juvederm from Brazil and China, the U.S. Attorney's Office for Massachusetts said. The Stoughton woman continued offering counterfeit beauty treatments through Skin Beaute Med Spa up through this week, according to the criminal complaint filed in court, despite her offices in Randolph and South Easton having been searched.

Fadanelli was due in federal court in Worcester Friday afternoon to face charges of importing and and selling counterfeit drugs and devices, which bring the possibility of decades in prison and hundreds of thousands of dollars in fines for a conviction, prosecutors said. It wasn't immediately clear if she had an attorney who could speak to the charges.

"For years, Ms. Fadanelli allegedly put unsuspecting patients at risk by representing herself to be a nurse and then administering thousands of illegal, counterfeit injections," acting U.S. Attorney Joshua Levy said in a statement, saying she "ignored safety regulations against bringing unapproved, counterfeit drugs and devices into our country and endangered the health of hundreds of her clients."

His office asked anyone who believes they may have gotten a counterfeit treatment at Skin Beaute Med Spa or through Fadanelli since 2021 to reach out — see the link below.

Fadanelli an aesthetician who isn't licensed or certified to give prescription drugs, collected more than half a million dollars from Botox appointments and more than $400,000 from filler appointments between March 2021 and March 2024, prosecutors said.

Federal customs investigators had already been looking into whether Fadanelli, who also goes by Rebecca Daley and Rebecca Hawthorne, when a client filed a complaint to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration saying she had "bumps" in her lips and forehead tingling after receiving a filler treatment from Fadanelli in Randolph and never received a copy of the prescription for the substance that Fadanelli had injected despite asking for it, according to the court documents.

Over the next few years, investigators seized packages with apparently counterfeit injectable prescription drugs labeled Botox, Sculptra and Juvederm, and found her entering the country at Boston's Logan International Airport with prescription drugs and vials of liquid, the documents said. A search turned up no record of Fadanelli buying the real prescription drugs through the companies that make them.

When agents searched the Skin Beaute Med Spa businesses in late June, Fadanelli allegedly told them a certified nurse is the only person who administers the drugs, but a former employee told investigators that Fadanelli administered the drugs, saying she was a nurse.

The former employee also said that she'd been told the Botox cost $50 through a China-based ecommerce platform, according to the criminal complain, which noted that authentic Botox costs more than 10 times as much. The employee also claimed that when her packages started to be intercepted, Fadanelli began shipping them to different addresses, including to an acquaintance in Boston's Dorchester neighborhood.

A confidential source had an April consultation with Fadanelli in which she quoted $450 for a Botox treatment, according to the complaint. That same source called and made an appointment for a treatment with Fadanelli last week.

title: Bankruptcy judge approves sale of 6 Steward hospitals in Mass.
text:
A U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge approved the sale of six Steward Health Care hospitals in Massachusetts Wednesday, though he left some of the exact details of the deals to be resolved before the end of the month.

Judge Christopher Lopez made the decision after hearing arguments Wednesday morning, including around an objection that key lenders to the bankrupt company filed to the proposed sales. The judge said he would approve the sales, though he wanted Steward and the lenders to iron out differences around how a certain $17 million in proceeds is divvied up.

"This sale needs to happen, and it will happen," Lopez said from the bench in Houston, Texas. He added, "What I am saying is you're going to be authorized to sell it, but I'm going to withhold $17 million bucks, which is the short funding shortfall."

The judge said his decision to hold aside some of the sale proceeds to still be allocated "should not hold up these sales" and that he would have a ruling well before the targeted transaction close date of Sept. 30.

Approved was Steward's plan to sell St. Anne's Hospital in Fall River and Morton Hospital in Taunton to Lifespan for $175 million; the Holy Family Hospital facilities in Methuen and Haverhill to Lawrence General Hospital for $28 million, and Good Samaritan Medical Center and St. Elizabeth's Medical Center to Boston Medical Center for as much as $140 million. Steward closed its other two hospitals here, Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, on Saturday.

More Steward Health Care news

Wednesday's hearing got into the meat of an objection filed by the "first in, last out" or FILO lenders that have pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into Steward as the company headed for bankruptcy. Those lenders said they "cannot possibly consent to the proposed sales of the Massachusetts Hospitals in their current form, and they do not." It was their arguments that swayed Lopez to require a resolution of the $17 million issue.

"The Debtors’ sale process has resulted in bids for the Massachusetts Hospitals for an aggregate purchase price of $343 million, subject to certain adjustments ... However, this figure is misleading as the entirety of the Purchase Price will be allocated towards the real property and therefore flow to benefit the purported landlord (MPT and Macquarie) and more specifically will flow to the purported landlord’s secured lender," the FILO lenders wrote in the objection.

title: Runner heartened by support after finishing Boston Marathon with fractured pelvis
text:
When Siobhan Salani reached Boylston Street near the end of the Boston Marathon, she was limping and far behind most of the field.

But she was not alone.

Friends and family lined up behind her, with strangers cheering her on, as she pushed through the final stretch. The moment, captured on video by NBC10 Boston's Brianna Borghi, quickly struck a nerve online.

"I looked behind me. I was like, 'Wow, all my people are behind me, there are strangers here, there's people yelling my name,'" Salani said.

Borghi posted the video to TikTok, where it has since drawn more than 2.5 million views and thousands of supportive comments.

"I think it goes along with the whole Boston Strong movement," she said. "It's the kindness that comes not only from the people who know and love you, but the kindness that comes from strangers is incredible."

Salani later shared that she completed the race while dealing with a fractured pelvis, walking the final 13 miles.

"I was going to run it whether I was walking or crawling," she said.

Salani, a first-grade teacher at Saint John Paul II Catholic Academy Lower Mills in Dorchester, ran the marathon with the Corey C. Griffin Foundation and raised more than $15,000.

CCGF supports high-impact educational, health care and mentorship programs for youth from under-resourced communities in Massachusetts. Salani said her students have directly benefited from the foundation's work.

"There are big events that I really love that Corey Griffin does with my students. They put on a field day for our kids at the end of the year, so all the volunteers come and they just give them the best day ever and they have jumpy houses and games and snacks and it’s just so much fun," she said. "At Christmas time, they bring all the kids from our school to the Cathedral in Boston, and they give them a big Christmas gift and they call it Corey's Christmas."

Knowing firsthand the impact that CCGF has on so many children made her journey along the marathon route even more personal.

"I think my students were my biggest motivation the whole time," she added.

Now, she is looking forward to bringing her marathon medal back to her students and says all of them will get to try it on.

She did not finish with an official time, but Salani said the experience became about much more than the clock.

"I believe everything happens for a reason," she said. "Even if I had finished like an hour earlier, or if things had gone to plan, if I wasn't dealing with my back injury and just everything else, none of that would have been able to happen. My family and friends would have never been able to be at the finish line and right behind me."

She truly believes everything happens for a reason.

"It didn't go as expected, but I think it went better than I really could have imagined," she said.

title: 4 injured in shooting, stabbing incident in Mattapan late Monday
text:
Four people were injured in what police described as a domestic violence incident that led to a shooting and stabbing late Monday night in the Mattapan neighborhood of Boston, according to police.

Boston Emergency Medical Services said that its crews responded to a reported shooting on Regis Road in Mattapan at 11:14 p.m. Four people were taken to area hospitals, they said.

Boston police confirmed Tuesday morning that four victims sustained serious injuries in what they described as "a shooting and stabbing incident." They said a 47-year-old woman, a 16-year-old girl and a 4-year-old boy all suffered gunshot wounds, and an 18-year-old girl suffered a stab wound.

Officials said while the injuries were serious, the four victims are expected to survive.

They said 46-year-old Calvin Stokes, of Mattapan, was arrested around 3 a.m. following a traffic stop in Roslindale in connection with the incident, which appears to have stemmed from a domestic violence situation.

Court documents described a struggle, with a knife grabbed from the kitchen. The victims had various shots to their arms and legs, and Stokes' significant other had multiple gunshot wounds to her torso.

If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline by calling 1-800-799-SAFE (7233), visiting www.thehotline.org or texting LOVEIS to 22522.

Stokes was arraigned Tuesday in Dorchester District Court on charges of being an armed career criminal, four counts of assault with intent to murder, assault and battery with a knife, unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of a firearm subsequent office, unlawful possession of ammunition and discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a dwelling. He has pleaded not guilty.

A neighbor who declined to go on camera told NBC10 Boston they've seen the family and described the incident as a"family issue" that started several days ago.

“They’re usually hanging outside or like Easter they were taking pictures.”

Stokes is being held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing set for early next week.

title: The soccer show will go on in Boston as World Cup licenses are approved by FIFA
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said FIFA has granted the city's licenses for the Boston Fan Fest and various other neighborhood watch parties planned during this summer's World Cup, which will allow games to be shown there.

"We got our licenses," she said during an appearance on GBH News' "Boston Public Radio" on Wednesday. She said this includes the FIFA Fan Festival Boston activation planned for City Hall Plaza, as well as six different watch parties planned in various neighborhoods.

Her office announced later that the free watch parties will be held in Dorchester and East Boston and on the Boston Common, with further locations to be announced — see the full schedule below.

Wu was asked by host Jim Braude why the Fan Festival only runs from June 12-27, even though the World Cup runs through July 9.

"We will still have watch parties in different places, and we had some private funding and other resources to support neighborhood block parties," she said. "But the security screening protocols and infrastructure is really intense to be able to host Fan Fest and accommodate large crowds... it does require shutting down access to a big part of City Hall Plaza for 24 hours even when the Fan Fest isn't running, so there was a little bit of a tradeoff there. Did I wish we could have had a much longer Fan Fest and private resources and committee funding to do so? Yes. We had talked through that. This is what we were able to do."

Ultimately, she said that was a decision made by the Boston Host Committee, Boston26.

Wu was also asked about the high cost of attending World Cup matches in Boston, including why a city like Philadelphia can offer cheaper train fares to their games and how New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani was able to make 1,000 tickets available for $50 apiece as part of a lottery.

"I think you know where I stand. I am always for trying to remove every barrier to public transit," she said. "I know there are costs to offset, and the T is really ramping up capacity in a heroic way compared to what they are used to, their standard levels of service. I always believe we should make it as easy as possible for people to ride transit."

Wu said ticket prices to the games are also set at this point, and she is not able to offer cheaper tickets like Mamdani.

More Massachusetts World Cup news

Part of the reason other cities were able to do this is that they were able to secure sponsorships to offset the costs or because they have sports hosting commissions as part of their permanent structure that bid for, host and have an entire fundraisign and resource generating infrastructure built up over time.

"Some of these cities are places we should learn from," Wu said.

Asked if she is happy with the Boston26 organizing committee, the mayor offered a tepid endorsement.

"I think there are many people who have stepped up to take on really complicated work. Every major event is unique," Wu said. "In this case, FIFA is its own unique entity to work with. Just getting licenses... you really have to be on their timeline, adn their requirements for security, it's a lot to manage. I think Boston and Greater Boston and the Massachsuetts region, we know how to host big events. We will find a way no matter what the situation is. There's been a lot of turnover there, a lot of fits and starts. It's a lesson for me. As we look to host big events, we hae to have the underlying infrastructure. We have to really learn from this and be prepared and build permanent structures to handle this."

That said, the mayor said she is expecting the World Cup to be a tremendous experience in Boston and across Massachusetts.

"I think we will have a great World Cup," Wu said. "This is an incredible, generational opportunity for us... We will be busy all summer long. We're really good also as a region of recognizing our shortcomings. We hold ourselves to high standards. We're going to work as hard as we possibly can until we kick off, and afterward I think it's also important to recognize what we did well and get back to pushing ourselves to be better next time."
